entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Visual library 🌳 The tree 🫧 Gas exchange 🩺 Assess 🚨 When it fails ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Respiratory · Assessing Lungs I · Fundamentals

The upside-down tree — and the one place gas exchange actually happens NG-004 RESPIRATORY ADHD-friendly visual edition The respiratory system looks like an upside-down tree : the trachea is the trunk, branching into the right & left bronchus , then smaller bronchi , then tiny bronchioles , ending at the alveolar sacs — this is where all the action happens. Right lung = 3 lobes . Left lung = 2 lobes . 🌳 Upside-down tree Trachea → bronchus → bronchi → bronchioles → alveolar sacs . 3️⃣ Right = 3 · Left = 2 The heart t
STEP 1 · THE ROAD MAP Air takes exactly one road in and one road out. Learn the road and every respiratory topic gets easier.

entries.h: 🫁 The airway tree & the lobes — one picture, everything labeled
entries.t: EXAM TIP The RIGHT mainstem bronchus is shorter, wider and more vertical than the left — which is why aspirated food, fluid and a too-deep endotracheal tube all end up in the right lung. 🧠 “Trunk → two big branches → little branches → twigs → grapes.” Trachea → bronchus → bronchi → bronchioles → alveolar sacs. And R ight is R ight there — short, wide, straight down.

entries.h: 🔢 Lobes: 3 on the right, 2 on the left
entries.t: Right lung — 3 lobes: upper, middle, lower. Divided by the horizontal and oblique fissures. Left lung — 2 lobes: upper, lower. One oblique fissure. The left upper lobe has a tongue-shaped tip called the lingula — the “missing middle lobe” in disguise. 🧠 “The heart stole the left lung's middle lobe.” The cardiac notch is the dent where the heart sits — 2 lobes on the left, forever.

Visceral pleura — hugs the lung itself Parietal pleura — lines the inside of the chest wall Pleural space — a thin film of fluid between them; it lets the two surfaces glide instead of grinding Air in that space = pneumothorax . Fluid in that space = pleural effusion . Inflamed, dry surfaces rubbing = a pleural friction rub . 🧠 “Visceral = viscera (organ). Parietal = the wall (like a parapet).”

entries.h: 🌬️ Follow one breath, start to finish
entries.t: 👃 Nose / mouth — warmed, humidified, filtered ▼ 🗣️ Pharynx → larynx (epiglottis closes over it when you swallow) ▼ 🌳 Trachea — the trunk, held open by C-shaped cartilage rings ▼ 🔀 Carina → right & left bronchus ▼ 🌿 Bronchi (smaller branches) → bronchioles (tiny branches) ▼ 🫧 ALVEOLAR SACS — where all the action happens Conducting zone vs respiratory zone: everything from the nose down to the terminal bronchioles is a pipe — it moves air but exchanges nothing (this is the anatomic dead space ). Only the alveoli exch
STEP 2 · THE ACTUAL POINT The alveolar sac is where gas exchange occurs — exchanging CO₂ for oxygen, in the little capillary beds wrapped around each alveolus.

entries.h: 🔬 Inside an alveolus — the respiratory membrane, cut open
entries.t: Blood in, blood out. Deoxygenated blood arrives from the pulmonary artery, drops off CO₂ , picks up O₂ , and leaves through the pulmonary vein. The whole trade happens across a membrane thinner than a sheet of tissue paper. 🧠 “Blood in, blood out — grapes trade with the vine.” The alveolus hands over O₂ and takes back CO₂. Anything that sits between them (fluid, pus, scar) blocks the trade.

entries.h: ➡️ Why gases move at all — diffusion
entries.t: Answer first: gases move from high concentration to low concentration . No pump required. Alveolar air is high in O₂ → O₂ moves into the blood Returning blood is high in CO₂ → CO₂ moves into the alveolus and gets exhaled Speed depends on surface area , membrane thickness , and the pressure gradient 🧠 “Gases roll downhill.” Every respiratory disease either flattens the hill (low FiO₂, low gradient), thickens the wall (edema, pneumonia, fibrosis) or shrinks the field (atelectasis, emphysema).

V = ventilation (air getting in). Q = perfusion (blood getting there). Gas exchange needs both, in the same place, at the same time. Shunt — blood arrives, air doesn't (pneumonia, atelectasis, pulmonary edema) Dead space — air arrives, blood doesn't (pulmonary embolism) 🧠 “Shunt = wasted blood. Dead space = wasted air.” Both end in hypoxemia, for opposite reasons. 🩺
STEP 3 · WHERE & HOW TO LISTEN Listen in between the ribs — the IN-tercostal space, the space IN between the ribs.

Anterior = front, on the chest. Posterior = back, and it mostly assesses the LOWER lobes — because most of the lung mass sits behind you. 🧠 “IN-tercostal = IN between.” Ribs block sound; the spaces don't. And always go side to side , never straight down one lung — you are comparing, not touring.

1 Position the client upright — high Fowler's. Sitting up lets the bases expand. 2 Use the diaphragm — the big flat part of the stethoscope — pressed firmly. 3 Place it in the intercostal spaces , the part in between the ribs. 4 Have the client breathe through the mouth, slowly and deeply . Listen to a full inspiration AND expiration at each spot. 5 Compare side to side , apex → base, front and back. ❌ Never listen through a gown or clothing — it manufactures fake crackles. 🧠 “Sit up · big side · between the ribs ·

Q: What are normal breath sounds? Vesicular breath sounds — soft & low-pitched breezy sounds heard over most of the peripheral lung fields . Sound Where it's NORMAL Vesicular — soft, low-pitched, breezy Most of the peripheral lung fields ⭐ Bronchovesicular — medium pitch, equal in and out Around the upper sternum and between the scapulae Bronchial / tracheal — loud, high-pitched, hollow Directly over the trachea TRAP Hearing a bronchial sound out in the periphery is abnormal — dense, consolidated tissue (like pneum

entries.h: 📊 Breath sounds at a glance — normal vs adventitious
entries.t: 🧠 “Crackles = wet · Wheeze = tight · Rhonchi = gunk · Stridor = STOP.” Stridor is the only one on this list that means get help right now . 🚨
STEP 4 · IT'S CRITICAL TO KNOW Three things happen to alveoli: they fill up, they collapse, or they get infected. All three block gas exchange.

entries.h: 🫧 One alveolus, four states — normal vs. the three things that go wrong
entries.t: It's critical to know: it is typical for clients in heart failure (with heavy fluid in the body) to have fluid in the lungs — pulmonary edema. The wet lungs block oxygen from getting in. Or, if these little alveoli collapse — like in atelectasis — then gas exchange can't happen, and infection settles in, resulting in pneumonia . 🧠 “Wet, flat, or infected — pick your poison, same result.” All three widen the distance between air and blood. That is the entire pathophysiology of hypoxemia in one sentence.

entries.h: 🚨 The cascade the source warns about
entries.t: 💓 Heart failure — heavy fluid in the body ▼ 💧 Fluid in the lungs = pulmonary edema ▼ 🎈 Alveoli collapse = atelectasis ▼ 🦠 Infection settles in = pneumonia 🧠 “Wet → flat → infected.” That's the order the source teaches it, and it's the order it happens in a real post-op or heart-failure client.

entries.h: ✅ Prevent the collapse — the nursing wins
entries.t: Incentive spirometry — the single best post-op tool; teach slow, deep inhalation and hold Turn, cough & deep breathe · early ambulation Reposition every 2 hours · sit upright — high Fowler's for anyone short of breath Adequate pain control — a client splinting from pain will not breathe deeply Hydration to keep secretions thin (unless fluid-restricted) 🧠 “Deep breaths pop the balloons back open.” Atelectasis is the one respiratory complication nurses genuinely prevent.

entries.h: 🚨 Red flags at the bedside — escalate, don't chart and wait
entries.t: 🔇 Absent sounds over a lung field 😮‍💨 Stridor upper airway obstruction 💙 Central cyanosis lips, tongue 🧠 New restlessness earliest hypoxia sign 🫁 Accessory muscles retractions · tripoding 🩸 Pink frothy sputum flash pulmonary edema 👉 Full detail on hypoxia and the oxygen devices is on NG-006 — Hypoxia & O₂ Devices . 🧠 Restlessness before cyanosis. The brain complains long before the lips turn blue. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🌳 Trachea → bronchus → bronchi → bronchioles → alveolar sacs Upside-down tree. 3️⃣ / 2️⃣ Lobes Right 3 , left 2 — the heart takes the space. 🫧 Alveolus = gas exchange CO₂ out, O₂ in, in the capillary beds. 🩺 Vesicular = normal Soft, low-pitched, breezy, peripheral fields.

Q1: Say the airway road in order. Show answer Trachea (windpipe, the trunk) → right & left bronchus → bronchi (smaller branches) → bronchioles (tiny branches) → alveolar sacs, where all the action happens. Q2: How many lobes in each lung, and why the difference? Show answer Right lung 3 lobes, left lung 2 lobes. The heart sits in the cardiac notch on the left, so there's no room for a third lobe. Q3: Where exactly does gas exchange happen? Show answer In the alveolar sac — specifically across the respiratory membra

entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Visual library 🧨 Hypoxia 🔎 Signs 😷 Devices 🛡️ Safety ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Respiratory · Oxygenation & Airway I · Fundamentals of Nursing

Low oxygen — how to spot it, and what to put on the face NG-006 RESPIRATORY ADHD-friendly visual edition Hypox emia = low oxygen levels in the blood . Hypox ia = low oxygen supply in the body tissues . Hypoxemia dominoes into hypoxia — low oxygen in the blood means low oxygen delivery to the tissues. Then you pick the device that fixes it. 🩸 emia = blood · ia = tissue Hypox emia is the lab. Hypox ia is the patient. 🧠 Restlessness is FIRST Brain first: restless → agitated → confused . Cyanosis is LATE. 📈 Early vital
STEP 1 · TWO WORDS, ONE DOMINO Get the two words straight first — half the exam questions are just testing the vocabulary.

entries.h: 🩸 The domino — blood first, tissue second
entries.t: 🧠 “-EMIA is in the blood (an- emia , hyperglyc- emia ). -IA is the whole person.” The blood number falls first; the tissues suffer second.

entries.h: 🧯 Why the oxygen is low — 4 reasons
entries.t: Not enough air in — hypoventilation, opioid oversedation, airway obstruction Membrane too thick — pulmonary edema, pneumonia, fibrosis Blood bypassing air — shunt from atelectasis or consolidation Air bypassing blood — dead space, as in a pulmonary embolism Also: low hemoglobin (anemia) means fewer carriers, and poor perfusion (shock) means the loaded blood never arrives. 🧠 “Can't get air in · can't cross over · wrong place · no truck.” Four failure points on the same delivery route.

entries.h: 🚩 Who is at risk right now on your unit
entries.t: 🛌 Post-op anesthesia + pain + flat 💊 Opioids sedation → ↓RR 🫁 COPD/asthma chronic disease 💓 Heart failure pulmonary edema 🦠 Pneumonia consolidation 🧓 Immobility atelectasis 🧠 The post-op client on opioids lying flat is the classic exam setup. Sit them up and assess before anything else. 🔎
STEP 2 · EARLY vs LATE The brain complains first. If you wait for blue lips you waited too long.

entries.h: 🧠 Head-to-toe — early signs (act) vs late signs (emergency)
entries.t: ATI QUESTION “Which of the following are early indications that the client is developing hypoxemia? Select all that apply.” ✅ Restlessness · Confusion · Hypertension · Tachypnea. ❌ Bradycardia — that is a LATE finding. 🧠 “Everything goes UP before it goes DOWN.” Rate up, pressure up, agitation up. When the numbers finally fall, the client is crashing.

Answer first: the earliest sign of hypoxia is a change in mental status — restlessness. The brain is the most oxygen-hungry organ in the body, so it complains first. ❌ Never medicate new restlessness or agitation as “anxiety” before you have checked oxygenation. 🧠 “A restless patient is a hypoxic patient until proven otherwise.” Sedating them is the classic wrong answer.

entries.h: 🚨 Paradoxical breathing — what it looks like
entries.t: Normally the abdomen rises on inspiration. In paradoxical breathing the chest and abdomen move in opposite directions — the abdomen sinks in as the chest rises. It signals diaphragmatic fatigue or flail chest and is a sign of impending respiratory failure . 🧠 “See-saw belly = call for help.” This is not a “watch and see” finding. 😷
STEP 3 · WHAT GOES ON THE FACE Low flow first, then the masks, then the precision device. Learn the picture and the numbers follow.

entries.h: 👃 Low-flow & simple: nasal cannula · simple face mask · Venturi
entries.t: 🧠 V · V — Venturi Mask = Very Accurate O₂. The color-coded barrel mixes a fixed amount of room air with the oxygen, so the FiO₂ stays exactly where you set it.

entries.h: 🎈 Reservoir devices & the special cases: partial rebreather · non-rebreather · face tent
entries.t: 🧠 “Partial has holes. Non-rebreather has flaps.” The flutter valves are the whole difference — they stop room air (and exhaled air) from diluting the oxygen, which is why the NRB gets the highest percentage.

entries.h: 🚨 Don't let the EXAMS trick you — the non-rebreather rules
entries.t: Answer first: if the reservoir bag is fully deflated on inspiration → INCREASE the oxygen flow rate. The bag must stay at least partly inflated so the client always has a full breath of oxygen waiting. ❌ Do NOT open the flutter valves ❌ Do NOT tighten the face mask straps first ✅ Turn the flow up first, then reassess the bag with each breath ✅ Used for medical emergencies and for carbon monoxide poisoning — CO binds hemoglobin far more tightly than O₂, so you flood the system with the highest FiO₂ available TRAP In

entries.h: 📏 FiO₂ comparison — line them all up
entries.t: 🌡️ Face tent is not on the scale because its delivered FiO₂ is variable and imprecise — it is chosen for humidity and comfort (facial trauma, burns), not for a specific percentage. 🧠 Order of climbing: cannula → simple mask → partial rebreather → non-rebreather. Venturi steps out of the ladder — it is for precision , not for maximum.

entries.h: 📋 All of it in one table
entries.t: Device Flow FiO₂ Use it when / watch for Nasal cannula 1–6 L/min ~24–44% Short-term low oxygenation after surgery . Long-term use dries the nasal mucous membranes → humidify. Client can eat & talk. Simple face mask 6–10 L/min 40–60% The step between cannula and the rebreathers. Never run it below the minimum flow — exhaled CO₂ gets rebreathed. Partial rebreather 6–11 L/min ~60–75% Looks very similar to the NRB. Key difference = the flutter valves (the partial rebreather's ports are open). Non-rebreather 10–15 L/min
STEP 4 · OXYGEN IS A DRUG It needs an order, it has a dose, it has side effects, and it can start a fire.

🚭 NO smoking post the sign, in the room & on the door 🕯️ No open flame candles, lighters, matches 🧴 No petroleum products use water-soluble lubricant 🔌 Check electricals no frayed cords, no static-prone blankets 🧯 Know the extinguisher and the shut-off valve 🛢️ Secure cylinders upright, chained, away from heat ❌ Oxygen does not burn — it makes everything else burn faster and hotter. That is why a single spark matters. 🧠 “Oxygen is the accelerant, not the flame.”

Oxygen requires an order — flow rate, device, and target saturation (unless it's an emergency, where you act and then obtain the order) Titrate to the prescribed target SpO₂ , then reassess Humidify for higher flows and long-term use — dry gas cracks the mucosa and causes nosebleeds Skin checks : behind the ears, over the cheekbones, the bridge of the nose, and the nares — pad the pressure points Oral & nasal care — masks dry everything out Reassess after every change: LOC, RR, work of breathing, SpO₂, color 🧠 “Ord

Clients with chronic CO₂ retention are usually given controlled, low-flow oxygen titrated to a lower target saturation prescribed by the provider, and the Venturi mask is preferred because the FiO₂ does not drift. ❌ Never withhold oxygen from a client who is acutely hypoxic. Treat the hypoxia, then titrate down and monitor for rising drowsiness or a falling respiratory rate. 🧠 “Low and precise, not none.” The wrong answer is refusing to oxygenate a blue patient.

entries.h: 🪜 Priority action when you find a hypoxic client
entries.t: 1 Stay with the client and position upright — high Fowler's, or tripod if that is what they are already doing. Gravity is free oxygen. ▼ 2 Assess airway & breathing — patency, rate, effort, breath sounds, SpO₂, color, level of consciousness. ▼ 3 Apply / increase oxygen per the order or protocol; step up to a higher-delivery device if the target is not met. ▼ 4 Call for help — rapid response or provider — and prepare for an ABG, chest X-ray and further treatment. ▼ 5 Treat the cause — suction secretions, reverse ove

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🩸 Hypoxemia = blood PaO₂ less than 80 mmHg (typical adult reference range — verify against your lab). Hypoxia = tissues. 🧠 Restless first Then agitated, then confused. Cyanosis is LATE. V = Very Accurate Venturi = the most precise device · unstable COPD. 🎈 Deflated bag → ↑ flow NRB 10–15 L/min · 60–100% · emergencies & CO poisoning.

Q1: Define hypoxemia and hypoxia, and state the link. Show answer Hypoxemia = low oxygen levels in the blood. Hypoxia = low oxygen supply in the body tissues. Hypoxemia dominoes into hypoxia, because low oxygen in the blood means low oxygen delivery to the tissues. Q2: Which findings are EARLY indications of hypoxemia? Show answer Restlessness, agitation/irritability, confusion, tachypnea (RR over 20), tachycardia (HR over 100), and hypertension (systolic over 140). Bradycardia, hypotension and cyanosis are LATE. entries.h: Herbal Supplements · NG-230 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Visual library 🌿 Know them ⚠️ Interactions 🗣️ Always ask ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Pharmacology · Complementary & Alternative Agents

Not "just vitamins" — they interact like drugs because many act like drugs NG-230 PHARM ADHD-friendly visual edition Herbal & dietary supplements are NOT regulated by the FDA the same way prescription drugs are — no proof of efficacy is required before sale. Patients often don't think of them as "medications" and don't report them unless specifically asked. Yet several of the most common ones cause serious, well-tested bleeding and serotonin interactions. 🗣️ ALWAYS ask "Not FDA-regulated like drugs" + patients don'
STEP 1 · WHAT EACH ONE IS FOR A quick field guide — what it's used for, matched to what it's tested on.

Herb Used for Nursing watch-point Saw Palmetto (SP) Swollen prostate — BPH (Benign Prostatic Hypertrophy) Mild GI upset; may add to effect of other hormone/BPH therapies Black Cohosh Menopause — hot flashes Possible hepatotoxicity reports; avoid with liver disease Hawthorn extract Heart / mild HF support Drug-drug interaction PRIORITY — can potentiate cardiac glycosides & antihypertensives Glucosamine Joint / arthritic pain ⚠️ Watch for hypoglycemia when combined with anti-diabetic medications Evening Primrose Oil

These raise bleeding risk, especially combined with anticoagulants/antiplatelets (warfarin, DOACs, aspirin, clopidogrel): 🌳 Ginkgo Biloba 🧄 Garlic 🫚 Ginger 🧴 Vitamin E 🐟 Omega-3 🌱 Ginseng 🧠 "The G's (mostly) bleed." Ginkgo, Garlic, Ginger, ginseng — plus Vitamin E and omega-3 — round out the bleed-risk crew.

Supplements are regulated as food-category products , not drugs — manufacturers don't have to prove safety or efficacy before selling them. Potency and purity can vary between brands and even between bottles. 🧠 "Not tested like a drug ≠ not acting like a drug." Just because it's sold OTC in the supplement aisle doesn't mean it's inert. ⚠️
STEP 2 · THE HIGH-YIELD DANGERS St. John's Wort is the single most heavily tested herb — it both weakens drugs and can trigger serotonin syndrome.

EXAM TIP St. John's Wort speeds up the liver's CYP450 enzymes , which clears many drugs faster than normal — so blood levels drop and the drug becomes less effective . 🧠 "St. John's Wort works against your other drugs." It doesn't just fail to help — it actively lowers the level of many drugs it's combined with, including birth control and warfarin. Reduced INR on a client taking both = St. John's Wort is the classic culprit.

entries.h: 🚨 St. John's Wort + antidepressants — serotonin syndrome
entries.t: St. John's Wort has serotonergic activity of its own. Combined with SSRIs, MAOIs, or TCAs , serotonin can build to dangerous levels. Never mix St. John's Wort with SSRIs, MAOIs, or TCAs — screen for it every time an antidepressant is on the med list. 🧠 "Sunshine herb, serotonin storm." St. John's Wort feels harmless because it's "natural" — but stacked serotonin from any source (herb + antidepressant) can kill.

Because so many supplements affect bleeding, sedation, or drug metabolism, the general teaching point is: stop most herbal supplements 2–3 weeks before a scheduled surgery , and always disclose supplement use during pre-op screening. Hawthorn is specifically flagged as a priority drug-drug interaction to review before any procedure. 🧠 "2 to 3, before they cut on me." Two to three weeks is the standard teaching window for stopping most herbal supplements pre-op. 🗣️
STEP 3 · THE NURSING PRIORITY If you don't ask, they usually won't tell you — this is the single highest-yield nursing action on this whole page.

1 🗣️ Ask specifically — "any vitamins, herbs, or supplements?" Don't assume they'll volunteer it 2 🩸 Screen for bleed-risk herbs if the patient is on any anticoagulant/antiplatelet 3 ☀️ Screen for St. John's Wort if the patient is on an antidepressant, OCP, or warfarin-type drug 4 🔪 Ask about supplements at every pre-op assessment — plan to stop 2–3 weeks out 5 🍬 Watch glucose if glucosamine + anti-diabetic medications are both on the list 🧠 "Ask like it's a drug — because it acts like one." This is the single test

Client is on… Ask about… Warfarin / DOAC / aspirin Ginkgo, garlic, ginger, vitamin E, omega-3, ginseng SSRI / MAOI / TCA St. John's Wort — serotonin syndrome risk Oral contraceptives St. John's Wort — reduced efficacy Anti-diabetic medication Glucosamine — hypoglycemia risk Cardiac / antihypertensive meds Hawthorn — priority drug-drug interaction

"BLEED & BLOCK": BLEED — ginkgo, garlic, ginger, vitamin E, omega-3, ginseng BLOCK — St. John's Wort blocks other drugs from working by speeding their clearance 🧠 One family raises bleeding risk, the other lowers everything else's effectiveness — know which is which. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🗣️ Not FDA-regulated patients don't report it — always ask 🩸 Ginkgo/garlic/ginger/vit E ↑ bleeding with anticoagulants ☀️ St. John's Wort induces CYP450 → ↓ OCP & warfarin efficacy; + serotonin syndrome risk 🔪 Stop 2–3 weeks pre-op disclose at every pre-op screen

Q1: A client on warfarin also takes ginkgo biloba and garlic supplements. What's the concern? Show answer Increased bleeding risk — ginkgo, garlic, ginger, vitamin E, omega-3, and ginseng all add to anticoagulant/antiplatelet bleeding risk. Q2: How does St. John's Wort reduce the effectiveness of oral contraceptives and warfarin? Show answer It induces liver CYP450 enzymes, which metabolizes those drugs faster — blood levels drop and efficacy is reduced (e.g., breakthrough bleeding on OCPs, falling INR on warfarin)
