Alpha & beta receptors — the drugs that squeeze NG-053 Cardio · Pharmacology ADHD-friendly visual edition Vaso-PRESS-ors PRESS on the blood vessels , increasing blood pressure in order to squeeze oxygen-rich blood back to the CORE of the body and perfuse the vital organs — sort of like squeezing a toothpaste bottle. They do it by activating alpha & beta receptors inside the heart and blood vessels. Indications: raise the BP · shock · cardiac arrest (ACLS). 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🐍 Alpha 1 = AN
STEP 1 · THE RECEPTORS Four receptors explain every one of these drugs. Learn the receptors and you never have to memorize a drug list again.

entries.h: 🗺️ The receptor map — where each receptor lives and what it does
entries.t: 🧠 “1 heart, 2 lungs, Alpha the Anaconda, Dopamine does the kidneys.” Beta 1 = you have 1 heart. Beta 2 = you have 2 lungs. Alpha 1 wraps the vessels like a snake. Say it four times and it's yours.

entries.h: ⭐ Where each drug LANDS — the receptor matrix
entries.t: Relative strengths only — the exact effect of dopamine and epinephrine shifts with the infusion rate. No doses are given here on purpose; always titrate to the ordered MAP goal per protocol. 🧠 Read the matrix as a shape. Norepinephrine = mostly squeeze. Dobutamine = mostly force. Epinephrine = everything . Phenylephrine = squeeze only. Vasopressin = a different door entirely.

entries.h: 🔤 Agonist vs antagonist — the whole vocabulary
entries.t: AGonists ADD ➕ ANTagonists are ANTI ➖ Alpha agonist — more constriction → BP UP (vasopressors) Alpha-1 antagonist — less constriction → BP DOWN (the “-osin” drugs; phentolamine) Beta agonist — faster, stronger heart; open lungs (vasopressors, albuterol) Beta antagonist — slower, weaker heart (beta blockers, the “-olol” drugs) + Chronotropic = more beats/min (chronos = time) + Inotropic = more forceful beats → cardiac output UP – Chronotropic = fewer beats – Inotropic = less force SOURCE FIX The source lists clonidi

VasoPRESSors PRESS on the vessels. Squeezing narrows the container, so the same volume generates a higher pressure — and blood is pushed inward toward the CORE , where the vital organs are. The trade-off: the core wins and the periphery loses . Fingers, toes, gut and skin are the tissue you sacrifice to keep the brain, heart and kidneys perfused. That is why you assess extremities every shift on a pressor. 🧠 Squeeze the toothpaste tube. Same paste, narrower tube, more pressure at the opening. And if the tube is emp
STEP 2 · MATCH IT Pick the drug that fixes the broken part. Every choice on this page reconciles with the hypovolemic, cardiogenic and septic shock pages.

entries.h: 💧 Rule zero: fluids come before pressors
entries.t: Why: blood pressure is a number ; perfusion is flow . Vasoconstricting an under-filled circulation raises the number while cutting flow to the gut, kidneys and extremities — you can normalize a MAP and still let the patient die of tissue ischemia. The exception: cardiogenic shock , where the tank is already overfull — fluid boluses cause flash pulmonary edema. There you support the pump instead. 🧠 “Fill before you squeeze.” One sentence that answers a whole category of exam questions — and the one thing every shock

entries.h: ⭐ The reconciliation table — pressor by shock type
entries.t: Shock What's broken First-line drug Why that one Septic 🦠 PIPES — vasodilation + capillary leak, SVR ↓↓ Norepinephrine after 30 mL/kg crystalloid Strong alpha-1 squeeze restores the missing SVR, with modest beta-1 support and fewer tachyarrhythmias than dopamine . Add vasopressin (V1) to spare the dose; epinephrine is an alternative add-on. Hypovolemic 🩸 TANK — volume is gone No pressor as primary therapy Volume & blood products Nothing to squeeze. A pressor is only a short bridge while blood is being obtained — it

entries.h: 💊 The main vasopressors — one line each
entries.t: Norepinephrine — alpha-1 +++, beta-1 ++. First-line in septic shock. Epinephrine — alpha-1 +++, beta-1 +++, beta-2 ++. Anaphylaxis & cardiac arrest. Vasopressin — V1 receptors, not adrenergic. Second agent in septic shock. Dopamine — dose-dependent : dopaminergic → beta-1 → alpha-1 as the rate rises. Named on the source card for cardiogenic shock. More tachycardia and arrhythmias. Dobutamine — beta-1 +++. An INOTROPE, not really a pressor — it can lower blood pressure through mild beta-2 dilation. Phenylephrine — p

entries.h: 🫀 Inotrope vs vasopressor — not the same job
entries.t: INOTROPE VASOPRESSOR Makes the pump squeeze harder (beta-1) Makes the pipes squeeze tighter (alpha-1) Raises cardiac output Raises SVR / MAP May lower BP May lower cardiac output (more afterload to push against) Dobutamine , digoxin, milrinone Norepinephrine , phenylephrine, vasopressin Dopamine & epinephrine do BOTH — which is why their effects shift with the rate 🧠 Pump vs pipes, again. A failing pump needs an inotrope. Failing pipes need a pressor. Naming the broken part picks the drug every single time. 🪜
STEP 3 · WHEN PRESSORS ENTER Same four stages as every shock page — mapped to the moment a vasopressor becomes the right answer.

entries.h: 🪜 The 4 stages of shock — identical on every shock page
entries.t: Stage What's happening What you see I · INITIAL Cardiac output falls just enough that cells switch to anaerobic metabolism → lactic acid builds, blood glucose rises. Nothing. Signs & symptoms are ABSENT in this stage — only a rising lactate gives it away. II · COMPENSATORY The sympathetic nervous system and renin–angiotensin–aldosterone rescue the pressure: catecholamines, vasoconstriction, ADH and aldosterone hold on to salt and water. Tachycardia · tachypnea · restless & anxious · cold clammy skin · narrowing pul

entries.h: 📈 Stage progression — where the vasopressor belongs
entries.t: 🧠 The pressor belongs at stage III, not stage II. If the stem says the patient is still hypotensive after adequate fluid , that phrase is the green light. Without it, the answer is fluid. 👀
STEP 4 · KEEP THEM SAFE These are high-alert drugs. The nursing care is as tested as the pharmacology.

entries.h: 🚨 Extravasation — the emergency with an antidote
entries.t: Why phentolamine? The damage is caused by alpha-1 vasoconstriction strangling the local tissue. Phentolamine is an alpha-adrenergic antagonist — it blocks the very receptor the vasopressor is over-stimulating , so blood flow returns before the tissue dies. Prevention beats rescue: give vasopressors through a central line whenever possible, on a dedicated lumen and an infusion pump, and assess the site frequently. 🧠 “Phentolamine un-does the anaconda.” Alpha-1 agonist squeezed the tissue shut; the alpha-1 blocker le

🎯 Titrate to the ordered MAP — usually ≥65 mmHg . Continuous BP, ideally an arterial line . 📟 Continuous ECG — dysrhythmias and tachycardia are the main dose-limiting effects 🚽 Hourly urine output — the real proof organs are being perfused 🫱 Assess extremities every shift and with every rate change — color, temperature, pulses, cap refill. Digital ischemia is a real complication. 🩸 Glucose — epinephrine raises blood sugar 💉 Always on an infusion pump , dedicated line, and check compatibility 📉 Wean gradually — neve

Receptor Adverse effect Alpha-1 🐍 Peripheral / digital ischemia , gut and renal hypoperfusion, extravasation necrosis, reflex bradycardia , rising afterload the failing heart must fight Beta-1 1️⃣ Tachycardia >100/min and dysrhythmias NCLEX TIP , increased myocardial oxygen demand — dangerous in an ischemic heart, chest pain Beta-2 2️⃣ Vasodilation that can drop the diastolic BP , tremor, hypokalemia (K⁺ driven into cells), hyperglycemia 🧠 Every pressor buys pressure with oxygen. You are asking a starving heart to

entries.h: 📚 Teach & connect — how this page fits the others
entries.t: 🩸 Hypovolemic volume, not pressors 🫀 Cardiogenic dobutamine ± norepi 🦠 Septic norepinephrine 1st 🐝 Anaphylactic epinephrine IM 🦴 Neurogenic fluids + tone + atropine ⚡ Arrest epinephrine (ACLS) One rule ties them together: name the broken part first — pump, tank, or pipes — then pick the drug that fixes that part. A pressor fixes pipes . An inotrope fixes the pump . Fluid and blood fix the tank . Nothing else needs to be memorized. 🧠 Say the chain out loud: “Tank empty → fill it. Pump broken → strengthen it. Pipes w

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🐍 α1 squeeze · 1️⃣ β1 heart 2️⃣ β2 lungs · 🫘 dopaminergic = renal vessels 💧 Fill before you squeeze Pressors go in at stage III — hypotension despite adequate fluid 💊 Septic = norepinephrine Add vasopressin (V1). Cardiogenic = dobutamine. Anaphylaxis = epinephrine IM. 🚨 Extravasation = phentolamine Stop · leave the catheter & aspirate · notify · elevate · infiltrate the antidote

Q1: What does each receptor do — alpha-1, beta-1, beta-2, dopaminergic? Show answer Alpha-1: constricts blood vessels (SVR ↑, BP ↑) — "the anaconda." Beta-1: 1 heart — positive chronotropic (rate) and inotropic (force), so cardiac output rises. Beta-2: 2 lungs — dilates bronchi and also skeletal-muscle vessels. Dopaminergic: dilates renal and mesenteric vessels at low dopamine rates. Q2: Why fluids before pressors? Show answer Blood pressure is a number; perfusion is flow. Vasoconstricting an under-filled circulati

Inflammation of the pericardium — the sac around the heart NG-066 CARDIO ADHD-friendly visual edition Inflammation OUTside the heart muscle — the two-layer sac (pericardium) that wraps the heart gets irritated, roughens, and rubs. Less cardiac output = less oxygen OUT to the body. Left untreated, fluid can build in that sac and squeeze the heart — that next stage is Cardiac Tamponade, NG-178 . 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🧨 Inflammation OUTside the heart The sac around the heart is irritated, not th
STEP 1 · THE IRRITATED SAC One structure explains the whole disease — the pericardium is a two-layer bag with a thin film of fluid between the layers so the heart can slide and beat without friction.

entries.h: 🫀 Normal → inflamed → fluid-filled: the same sac, three stages
entries.t: EXAM TIP Pericarditis, effusion, and tamponade are one continuum — the same pericardial sac getting worse. Know where a client sits on this line and you know what to do next. 🧠 "A wet balloon inside a paper bag." The heart is the balloon, the pericardium is the bag. A little lubricant is fine — irritate the bag (pericarditis) and it rubs; fill the bag with water (effusion) and it strangles the balloon (tamponade). Same bag, three chapters of the same story.

🦠 Infection — viral is the most common cause ❤️‍🔥 Post-MI — acute MI, or weeks later as Dressler syndrome (autoimmune reaction after cardiac injury) 🧬 Autoimmune disorders — lupus , scleroderma , rheumatoid arthritis (RA) 🧪 Uremia — high BUN from renal failure 🔪 Cardiac surgery, chest trauma, radiation, malignancy 🧠 "I AM U" — I nfection · A utoimmune (lupus/scleroderma/RA) · M I (post-MI or Dressler) · U remia. Whatever irritates the sac gets remembered as "I am you" — the pericardium reacting to insult.

entries.h: 🔤 Say the word — it tells you the disease
entries.t: Peri = around 🔄 Card = heart ❤️ -itis = inflammation 🔥 Peri · card · itis = inflammation of the sac AROUND the heart — not the heart muscle (that's myocarditis) and not the inner lining/valves (that's endocarditis, NG-229 ). 🧠 Peri = "perimeter." The perimeter fence around the property (the heart) is what's on fire — the house itself is still standing. 🔎
STEP 2 · SPOT IT A grating sound plus a pain pattern that flips with position — and an ECG that looks nothing like a heart attack's.

entries.h: 👂 Pericardial friction rub — grating, scratchy, "leather on leather"
entries.t: Caused by the two roughened, inflamed pericardial layers rubbing against each other with every heartbeat. Best heard with the diaphragm of the stethoscope, at the left sternal border, with the client leaning forward and holding their breath. 🧠 "Squeaky new leather boots." The rub sounds like two pieces of dry leather grinding together — that's exactly what two inflamed pericardial layers with no smooth fluid between them are doing.

entries.h: 📍 Pain pattern — worse SUPINE, better sitting up & leaning forward
entries.t: This is the single biggest way pericarditis pain differs from cardiac/MI pain. Lying flat lets the inflamed layers press together over a larger area; leaning forward pulls the heart away from the anterior pericardium and eases the rub. Pain is often sharp, stabbing, pleuritic — it also worsens with deep inspiration, coughing, and swallowing. Feature 🔥 Pericarditis pain ❤️ Cardiac / MI pain Quality Sharp, stabbing, pleuritic Crushing, pressure, squeezing Position Worse supine, better sitting forward No position make

Pericarditis causes diffuse, concave-up ST elevation across most leads, plus PR segment depression — because the inflammation coats the whole outer heart, not one blocked artery. 🧠 "Blanket vs. bullet." Pericarditis throws a blanket of ST elevation over the whole ECG; an MI fires one bullet into one territory of leads.

🧫 WBC elevated — over 10,000 📈 C-reactive protein (CRP) — elevated 📈 ESR (erythrocyte sedimentation rate) — elevated ❤️ Troponin — may be mildly elevated if the myocardium is also irritated (myopericarditis); markedly elevated troponin points more toward MI 🧠 Inflammatory labs, not cardiac-damage labs. WBC/CRP/ESR say "something is inflamed" — they don't localize to a blocked artery the way a big troponin spike does. 🩺
STEP 3 · CALM THE SAC Treat the inflammation, watch for fluid, drain if it builds — and never miss the jump to tamponade.

Class Drug from the source Why NSAIDs 💊 Indomethacin First-line — reduces inflammation & pain Corticosteroids 💉 Prednisone Used when NSAIDs fail or cause is autoimmune 🧠 "NSAID first, steroid second." Start with indomethacin; save prednisone for when NSAIDs aren't enough — steroids can make some causes (like post-MI pericarditis) worse if used too early.

entries.h: 🚨 Pericardiocentesis — the needle in the heart sac
entries.t: A needle drains fluid or blood that has collected in the pericardial sac. Not routine for simple pericarditis — reserved for a large effusion or tamponade. 🖥️ Continuous cardiac monitoring during & after 💉 Catheter often left attached to a drainage system 📋 Assess drainage type & speed — sudden drop in drainage with rising pressure = re-accumulation 🧠 See the full drainage picture on NG-178 Cardiac Tamponade — this is where pericarditis becomes an emergency.

1 🪑 Sit up, lean forward — the tripod position eases pain & the rub 2 🛏️ Avoid lying flat when pain is active 3 🧊 Rest, treat fever, monitor pain trend 🧠 "Lean in to ease it." Every teaching point here is just: don't lie flat, do lean forward.

As pericarditis worsens, fluid can accumulate in the pericardial sac (pericardial effusion) and eventually compress the heart. New muffled/distant heart sounds, JVD, or a falling BP = report immediately. 🔥 Pericarditis — inflamed layers ▼ 💧 Pericardial effusion — fluid accumulates ▼ 🚨 Cardiac tamponade — Beck's triad, pulsus paradoxus → NG-178 🧠 "Rub goes quiet = get worried." If a friction rub you've been hearing suddenly disappears, don't assume it's better — it may mean fluid has built up enough to separate the

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🧨 Pericardium irritated = less output, still a real drop in oxygen delivery 🛏️ Flat = fire, forward = fine Opposite of MI, which no position relieves 👂 Grating friction rub diaphragm, left sternal border, leaning forward 🚨 Fluid builds → tamponade Beck's triad next — see NG-178

Q1: When is pericarditis pain worst, and when is it best? Show answer Worst lying flat (supine); best sitting up and leaning forward. Also worse with deep breathing, coughing, and swallowing. Q2: How does that pain pattern help you rule OUT an MI? Show answer MI pain is not positional — no position change relieves crushing/pressure cardiac pain. If leaning forward helps, think pericarditis, not MI. Q3: What does a pericardial friction rub sound like, and how do you best hear it? Show answer Grating, scratchy, "leat

HTN — the silent killer, staged, sourced & matched to the right drug class NG-068 Cardio ADHD-friendly visual edition Persistently elevated arterial blood pressure — usually silent until it has already damaged an organ. Two big questions drive this whole topic: where is it coming from (primary vs secondary), and which lever fixes it — lifestyle first, then the right drug class for the right patient. This page is the overview that ties your ACE inhibitor, ARB, beta blocker, CCB, clonidine, diuretic & nitrate pages t
STEP 1 · PRIMARY vs SECONDARY Same number on the cuff, two very different reasons it got there.

entries.h: ⭐ The core equation — everything else is commentary on this
entries.t: BP = CO × SVR ( C ardiac O utput × S ystemic V ascular R esistance) Anything that raises how much blood the heart pumps out, or how tightly the vessels squeeze around it, raises the pressure. Every risk factor, every cause, and every drug class on this page works by pushing one of those two numbers up or down. 🧠 “Pump harder or squeeze tighter — either one raises the number.” Diuretics and vasodilators attack the equation from opposite sides but land on the same number.

entries.h: 🧭 Primary vs secondary — where the ~90/10 split comes from
entries.t: 🧠 “ROPE” for secondary causes — R enal disease · O SA · P heochromocytoma / aldosteronism · E ndocrine & Estrogen (OCPs, pregnancy). Pull the rope (fix the cause) and the BP often comes down on its own.

entries.h: ⚠️ Modifiable risk factors — the ones she can change
entries.t: 🧂 High-sodium diet ⚖️ Obesity 🛋️ Physical inactivity 🚬 Smoking 🍺 Excess alcohol 😖 Chronic stress, poor sleep 🧠 These six are exactly the six targets of the lifestyle modification card in the CARE section below.

entries.h: 🧬 Non-modifiable risk factors — the ones she can't
entries.t: 📅 Age — risk rises as vessels stiffen 🧬 Family history / genetics 🌍 Race — Black adults have earlier onset, higher rates & often more severe disease 🚻 Sex — higher risk in men at younger ages; women's risk rises after menopause 🧠 Can't change these — so the modifiable list works harder to compensate. 🔎
STEP 2 · STAGING & TARGET ORGANS Numbers on a chart — until they've been high long enough to hit an organ.

entries.h: 📏 BP categories — a labeled bar scale
entries.t: Only one value has to fall in a category to qualify for it — whichever number (systolic or diastolic) is worse determines the stage. 🧠 “130 starts the staging, 180 is a crisis.” Anchor those two numbers and interpolate the rest — but always double-check the exact table your instructor is using.

Urgency: severely elevated BP without acute symptoms of organ damage. Usually managed with oral meds and close follow-up. Emergency: severely elevated BP with acute target-organ damage — chest pain, dyspnea, vision changes, confusion, worsening renal function. This is an ICU-level, IV-drip situation . 🧠 Symptoms are what turn "urgency" into "emergency." Same terrifying number, totaly different level of response.

Most people feel nothing until damage has already started. When symptoms do show up — severe headache, visual changes, nosebleed, dizziness — the pressure is often already very high. This is exactly why routine screening matters more than waiting for symptoms. 🧠 A disease with no early warning system needs a nurse with a cuff instead.

entries.h: 🗺️ Target organ damage — the body map
entries.t: 🧠 "HEBK" — H eart · E yes · B rain · K idneys. Say it like "he broke" — that's exactly what unchecked HTN quietly does. 🩺
STEP 3 · LIFESTYLE + THE RIGHT DRUG Lifestyle changes come first and stay first — drugs get layered on top, matched to who the patient is.

DASH = Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension: fruits, vegetables, whole grains, low-fat dairy, lean protein; low in saturated fat, sodium & added sugar. Sodium restriction guidance commonly cited by the AHA is roughly <2,300 mg/day , with greater BP benefit closer to 1,500 mg/day — confirm the exact figure your course uses. Weight loss and exercise (regular moderate aerobic activity most days of the week) both independently lower BP; alcohol should be kept to a moderate amount or avoided. 🧠 "DASH away the salt, w

entries.h: 🎯 Which drug class for which patient — the overview
entries.t: This is the map, not the manual — full mechanism, side effects & teaching for each class live on their own pages. Patient picture Preferred class See the full page No compelling indication — first-line for most adults Thiazide diuretic, ACE inhibitor, ARB, or CCB Diuretics · ACE Inhibitors · ARBs · CCB Diabetes or CKD with proteinuria ACE inhibitor or ARB — kidney-protective ACE Inhibitors · ARBs Black adult, no CKD CCB or thiazide diuretic often preferred first CCB · Diuretics Heart failure with reduced EF ACE inh

entries.h: ⚠️ One NCLEX trap that lives on this page
entries.t: Never let clonidine stop abruptly — rebound hypertensive crisis. It's the single most-tested safety point that touches this overview; full teaching is on the Clonidine page. 🧠 Clonidine doesn't get to just stop — it gets tapered .

Every one of these drug classes attacks BP = CO × SVR from a different angle: diuretics shrink volume, ACEi/ARB relax vessels & protect kidneys, beta blockers slow & soften the heart, CCBs relax vessels or slow the heart depending on type, clonidine turns down sympathetic outflow centrally, and nitrates dilate veins to drop preload. 🧠 Learn the equation once here, then every drug page is just "which side of CO × SVR does this one push?" ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🤫 Silent killer No symptoms until organ damage — screen regularly. 📏 Normal <120/<80 Stage 1 starts around 130/80, crisis >180/>120 — but confirm your course's exact table. 🧬 90% primary, 10% secondary Secondary has a fixable ROPE: Renal, OSA, Pheo/aldosteronism, Endocrine/Estrogen. 🎯 Match the patient DASH + sodium + weight + exercise + alcohol first, then the drug class that fits this patient.

Q1: What's the core equation behind every blood pressure number? Show answer BP = Cardiac Output × Systemic Vascular Resistance. Every risk factor and every drug class pushes one of those two numbers. Q2: A patient has HTN caused by pheochromocytoma. Primary or secondary — and what's different about the plan? Show answer Secondary — there's one identifiable cause. Treating the pheochromocytoma can improve or resolve the BP, unlike primary HTN which is managed, not cured. entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🧨 Cause 🔎 Clues 📈 EKG & Labs 🗺️ Which artery 🩺 Care ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Cardio · Pathophysiology Course

Myocardial Infarction — the heart muscle DIES NG-071 Cardio · ACS ADHD-friendly visual edition Myocardial Infarction (MI) = the heart muscle DIES — “necrosis” — from lack of oxygen. This happens when there's a blockage of the coronary arteries , the “O₂ tubes” feeding the heart. The blockage is almost always a ruptured atherosclerotic plaque + clot — stage 4 of NG-145 . Time = muscle. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 💥 Plaque SNAP → clot Atherosclerosis stage 4. The clot — not the narrowing — is what in
STEP 1 · THE BLOCKED O₂ TUBE The coronary arteries feed the heart itself. Block one, and the muscle downstream starves, then dies.

entries.h: 💔 Ischemia → Injury → Infarct: three zones, one blockage
entries.t: PATHO TIP Necrosis begins within about 20–40 minutes of total occlusion and spreads outward from the inner layer (subendocardium) toward the outer layer over the next several hours. That is why every minute of door-to-balloon time is muscle. 🧠 “Ring of fire.” Dead center 🔴, burning ring 🟠, smoky edge 🟡. The EKG shows you which ring you're looking at: Q = dead · ST = injury · T = ischemia.

Letter Risk factor The accurate detail S S tress · S moking · S timulants Caffeine, amphetamines, cocaine — cocaine causes coronary spasm plus clotting (see NG-098) O O besity BMI 25–29.9 = overweight · ≥30 = obesity. Central/abdominal fat carries the most risk. D D iabetes & hypertension Older texts: HTN >140/90 . 2017 ACC/AHA: HTN starts at ≥130/80 ; ≥140/90 is stage 2. D D iet High cholesterol, animal & trans fats → feeds the plaque (NG-145 & NG-242) A A ge & sex Risk climbs for men ≥45 , women ≥55 . Men earlier

C — CAD “coronary artery disease” plaque is building ▼ A — ACS “acute coronary syndrome” the umbrella term ▼ 🙂 Stable angina — “Safer” — relieved by rest & nitro 😰 Unstable angina — “Unsafe” — UNrelieved , at rest, troponin negative ▼ M — MI — heart muscle dies , troponin positive ACS = unstable angina + NSTEMI + STEMI. The one thing that separates unstable angina from NSTEMI is the troponin . 🧠 “CAM” films the whole movie: C AD builds the set → A CS is opening night → M I is the tragedy. Stable = safer , unstable

entries.h: 💔 The MI that isn't a plaque
entries.t: Most MIs are type 1 — plaque rupture + thrombus. But the muscle can also die when supply and demand split apart : 🌀 Coronary spasm — Prinzmetal/variant angina, cocaine (NG-098) 📉 Severe hypotension / shock — no pressure, no coronary flow 🫀 Sustained tachydysrhythmia — demand outruns supply 🩸 Severe anemia or hypoxia — the blood arrives, but empty-handed 💉 Coronary embolus or dissection 🧠 Supply vs demand — the heart's checkbook. An MI happens when the heart spends more O₂ than the coronary account can deliver, no m
STEP 2 · SPOT IT Classic crushing chest pain is one presentation — and the one that kills quietly is the one that doesn't look like that.

PAIN: substernal chest pain radiating to the jaw, neck, left arm, mid-back/shoulder , or felt as heartburn (epigastric) . KEY WORDS = PRIORITY “Sudden” · “Crushing” · “Radiating” — if the stem says any of these, treat it as cardiac until proven otherwise. 🫁 SOB — “dyspnea,” “labored breathing” 🤢 Nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain 💦 Diaphoresis — sweating, often cold and drenching 🥶 Pale, cool, “dusky” skin 😰 Anxiety — classic “impending sense of doom” 😵 Dizziness, syncope, palpitations 🧠 Angina takes a break; an MI d

entries.h: ⭐ ATYPICAL presentations — women, diabetics & older adults
entries.t: NCLEX TIP A woman or diabetic with unexplained fatigue, nausea and dyspnea gets an EKG — not an antacid. Delay in recognition is a documented reason women have worse MI outcomes. 🧠 “Women whisper, men shout.” The classic elephant-on-the-chest is the loud version. In women, diabetics and older adults, the MI whispers : tired, nauseated, short of breath, jaw aches. Believe the whisper.

entries.h: 🆚 STEMI vs NSTEMI vs Unstable angina
entries.t: STEMI NSTEMI Unstable angina Artery 100% occluded — complete, sustained Partly / intermittently occluded Partly occluded, no muscle death yet Depth of damage Transmural — full thickness of the wall Subendocardial — inner layer only None (ischemia only) EKG ST ELEVATION in ≥2 contiguous leads (new LBBB is treated as an equivalent); Q waves may develop ST depression and/or T-wave inversion — or a normal EKG ST depression / T inversion / normal Troponin ✅ POSITIVE ✅ POSITIVE ❌ NEGATIVE — this is the whole difference T
STEP 3 · READ THE PROOF EKG first — within 10 minutes of arrival for any chest pain. Then serial troponins. The EKG tells you how fast ; the troponin tells you whether .

entries.h: 📈 The four tracings you must recognize on sight
entries.t: 🧠 “Elevation = elimination. Depression = deprivation.” ST up means the artery is eliminated (fully shut) — go to the cath lab. ST down / T flipped means the muscle is only deprived — treat, then stratify.

Q waves usually appear hours to days after the infarct and are often permanent — the EKG's tattoo of an old MI. 🧠 Q = “Quit.” That muscle quit for good. ST elevation is happening now ; a pathologic Q already happened .

1 12-lead EKG within 10 min of arrival — for any chest pain or MI symptoms 2 Serial troponins — a baseline plus repeat draws per the assay/protocol 3 Continuous cardiac monitoring + IV access + O₂ if hypoxic 4 Echo (wall motion, EF) · CXR · cath for the definitive picture 🧠 “Strip before you stick.” EKG comes before labs — a STEMI on the strip sends her to the cath lab before a single troponin has resulted.

entries.h: 🧪 Cardiac markers — troponin vs CK-MB vs myoglobin
entries.t: Marker Rises Peaks Back to normal Why you'd use it Troponin I / T ⭐ 3–4 h (high-sensitivity assays: 1–3 h) 12–24 h 10–14 days The diagnostic marker. Most cardiac-specific. Serial draws show the rise and fall . CK-MB 4–6 h 12–24 h 48–72 h Because it clears fast, a second rise flags RE-infarction while troponin is still elevated. Myoglobin 1–3 h — earliest 6–9 h ~24 h Fast but not specific — rises with any muscle injury. Mostly historical now. hs-CRP Inflammation, not injury Risk stratification only — not an MI diagn
STEP 4 · LOCALIZE IT The leads with ST elevation tell you which artery is blocked — and which artery tells you which complication to watch for.

entries.h: 🫀 The coronary tree — who feeds what
entries.t: Artery Wall it feeds Leads with changes Watch for LAD left anterior descending ANTERIOR wall + SEPTUM + much of the left ventricle V1 V2 septal · V3 V4 anterior The “widow-maker.” Biggest infarcts → heart failure, cardiogenic shock , ↓EF, bundle branch blocks LCx left circumflex LATERAL wall of the left ventricle (± posterior) I aVL V5 V6 Often quieter on the 12-lead — posterior involvement can hide as ST depression in V1–V2 RCA right coronary INFERIOR wall, right ventricle , and in most people the SA & AV nodes II

Answer first: Be very cautious with nitroglycerin in an inferior (RCA) MI — up to about half of inferior MIs involve the right ventricle . The infarcted RV can't pump forward — it survives on preload Nitro drops preload → BP can crash suddenly and severely Clues: inferior ST elevation + hypotension + clear lungs + JVD Confirm with right-sided leads (V4R) Treatment leans on IV fluids to fill the RV 🧠 “Inferior = fill her, not chill her.” A right ventricle in trouble wants volume , not vasodilation. Hypotension + cle

⚡ Minutes–hours: dysrhythmias — V-fib is the leading cause of early death after MI. This is why she's on a monitor. 🫁 Hours–days: heart failure & cardiogenic shock — crackles, ↓BP, ↓urine, cool skin (NG-196) 🔊 Days: papillary muscle rupture → sudden new murmur + flash pulmonary edema 💥 Days: ventricular free-wall or septal rupture → sudden collapse, tamponade 🩹 Days–weeks: pericarditis — sharp pain, better sitting forward , friction rub (Dressler syndrome later) 🎈 Weeks: ventricular aneurysm & mural thrombus → embo
STEP 5 · DURING & AFTER During the pain: MONA (with modern asterisks). After: stabilize the clot, rest the heart, and send her home able to protect it.

entries.h: 🚨 DURING — any chest pain: MONA , updated
entries.t: M Morphine — for pain unrelieved by nitro . Qualified now: use judiciously. O Oxygen — only if SpO₂ <90% or she's in distress. Not routine anymore. N Nitroglycerin — SL 0.4 mg q 5 min , max 3 doses . A Aspirin — CHEWED , non-enteric-coated, 162–325 mg . Give it FIRST. Why morphine got an asterisk: it still relieves pain, anxiety and preload — but registry data linked morphine to worse outcomes in NSTE-ACS , and it slows absorption of oral antiplatelets (clopidogrel/ticagrelor), delaying their effect. It also masks

💊 SL 0.4 mg q 5 min × 3 max . Pain still there after 3? = MI (injury) — activate EMS/the MI protocol. 📉 Nitro drip: hold/stop if SBP <90 or a drop of >30 mmHg from her baseline 💥 NEVER with a PDE-5 inhibitor — sildenafil and the other “-afil” drugs — the combination can cause fatal hypotension (avoid within 24 h ; ~ 48 h for tadalafil) ⚠️ Caution in RV/inferior MI — preload dependent (see above) 🤕 Headache is expected — it means it's working & potent 🪑 Change positions slowly — orthostatic hypotension/syncope 🌡️ St

🛑 Heparin PREVENTS clot growth — it does NOT dissolve an existing clot 💥 Only fibrinolytics ("-ase": alteplase, tenecteplase) actually dissolve clot 🧪 Monitor aPTT for IV unfractionated heparin. A commonly taught therapeutic range is 46–70 seconds , but every lab publishes its own — the real target is about 1.5–2.5 × the control value 💉 Antidote: protamine sulfate 🩸 Monitor platelets — a falling platelet count on heparin suggests HIT 📋 Low-molecular-weight heparin (enoxaparin) doesn't need routine aPTT monitoring S

entries.h: 💊 AFTER the MI — the take-home drug set
entries.t: Class Job Nursing watch A — Antiplatelets aspirin + clopidogrel Stop new platelet plugs — especially critical after a stent Bleeding, bruising, black stools. Many protocols hold if platelets fall to about 50,000/mm³ or less (normal 150–400 K ) — follow the order. Antiplatelets are followed by platelet count, not INR or aPTT. C — Cholesterol lowering “-statin” Lower LDL and stabilize the plaque cap (NG-145 / NG-242) Muscle pain/tenderness without injury → report ; liver enzymes; no grapefruit ; take in the evening B

D Diet — low sodium & fluid restriction as ordered (a commonly taught target is 2 g sodium / 2 L fluid per day). Report new, rapid weight gain — that's water, and water means heart failure. Daily weights: same time, same scale, same clothes. R Reduce stress, alcohol, caffeine and cholesterol (animal fats) E Exercise — build toward about 30 min × 5 days/week , through cardiac rehab . Stop and rest for chest pain, and take nitro as prescribed. S Smoking cessation — the single highest-yield change she can make S Sex —

🧪 Potassium 3.5–5.0 mEq/L — ACE inhibitors and ARBs push it up 🥗 Teach: avoid salt substitutes (they're potassium chloride) and don't load up on high-potassium foods without checking 📈 High K⁺ = peaked T waves , widening QRS, ST changes → cardiac monitor first 💪 Watch for muscle cramps, spasms, weakness 📉 Low K⁺ (from diuretics) is just as arrhythmogenic — flattened T, U waves 🧠 “Peaked T = potassium's peak.” Tall pointy T waves after starting a “-pril” or “-sartan” = check the K⁺ and get her on the monitor.

entries.h: ✅ Nursing priorities in the first hour
entries.t: 1️⃣ Assess — pain (OPQRST), vitals, SpO₂, lung sounds, skin 2️⃣ 12-lead EKG within 10 min + continuous monitoring 3️⃣ Aspirin chewed , IV access ×2, labs including troponin 4️⃣ Nitro per protocol with BP before/after every dose 5️⃣ Semi-Fowler's , calm environment, keep her at rest — reduce O₂ demand 6️⃣ Prepare for reperfusion — cath lab consent, NPO, check bleeding contraindications if fibrinolytics 7️⃣ Stay with her — anxiety itself raises catecholamines and O₂ demand 🧠 Everything in that list does one of two th

SAY IT OUT LOUD 📈 ST ↑ = STEMI Full thickness · fully blocked · reperfuse now . ST ↓ / T flip + troponin = NSTEMI. 🧪 Troponin 3–4 h → 10–14 d CK-MB clears in 48–72 h → catches re-infarction . 💊 A-N-O-M Aspirin chewed · nitro ×3 · O₂ only if SpO₂ <90% · morphine only if still hurting. 🗺️ II·III·aVF = RCA Inferior MI → bradycardia, blocks, RV infarct → careful with nitro .

Q1: What's the one lab that separates NSTEMI from unstable angina? Show answer Troponin. Positive = NSTEMI (muscle died). Negative = unstable angina (ischemia only). Both can show ST depression or T-wave inversion. Q2: A client with chest pain has ST elevation in II, III and aVF. Which artery, and what's your nitro concern? Show answer RCA — inferior wall MI. Up to half involve the right ventricle, which is preload dependent, so nitroglycerin can cause severe hypotension. Look for hypotension + clear lungs + JVD, g

entries.h: ACE Inhibitors · NG-091 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 💊 What it does ⚠️ Watch for 🗣️ Teach ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Cardio · Antihypertensive Drug Classes

Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme Inhibitors — the "-PRIL" drugs NG-091 CARDIO ADHD-friendly visual edition Block ACE , the enzyme that converts Angiotensin I → Angiotensin II — upstream in the RAAS pathway. Less angiotensin II means less vasoconstriction and less aldosterone , so blood pressure drops. Because ACE also breaks down bradykinin , blocking it lets bradykinin build up — that's the signature dry cough & angiedema that ARBs do NOT cause. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🔗 Paired with NG-137 ARBs —
STEP 1 · THE MECHANISM One pathway explains the whole drug class — block the enzyme, and everything downstream of it shrinks.

entries.h: 🧬 The RAAS pathway — where ACE inhibitors block it
entries.t: EXAM TIP ACE inhibitors block Angiotensin I → Angiotensin II , the conversion step. This is the SAME shared diagram used on the ARB page — compare where each class blocks the cascade. 🧠 "PRIL blocks the Pril-conversion, not the reception." ACE inhibitors act upstream , at the enzyme — angiotensin II is never made. ARBs act downstream , at the receptor — angiotensin II is made but can't bind. Same ending pathway, different blockade point.

entries.h: 🔤 Say the suffix — it tells you the class
entries.t: -PRIL = ACE inhibitor 🫀 Lisinopril (Prinivil, Zestril) Enalapril (Vasotec) — also comes IV as enalaprilat Captopril (Capoten) — shortest half-life, dosed 2–3×/day Ramipril (Altace) 🧠 "PRIL" sounds like "drill" — it drills into the ACE enzyme upstream, before angiotensin II ever exists.

Hypertension — first-line in many guidelines Heart failure — reduces afterload & remodeling Post-MI — cardioprotective Diabetic nephropathy — protects the kidney by lowering intraglomerular pressure 🧠 "Pril protects the kidney AND the heart." One drug, two organs it's guarding — that's why it's a diabetic/CKD favorite even at normal BP.

entries.h: 💊 Common generics, trade names & typical adult dosing
entries.t: Generic Trade Typical range Route Lisinopril Prinivil, Zestril 10–40 mg once daily PO Enalapril Vasotec 5–40 mg /day (1–2 doses) PO / IV (enalaprilat) Captopril Capoten dosed 2–3×/day , empty stomach PO Ramipril Altace 2.5–20 mg /day PO Ranges are typical adult maintenance doses — always titrate to the prescriber's order and the client's response; practice varies by indication. 🧠 Captopril = "Capture it on an empty stomach." It's the odd one out — shortest acting, dosed multiple times a day, food cuts its absorptio
STEP 2 · THE DANGER LIST The cough is annoying, the angiedema is an airway emergency, and the potassium creeps up quietly.

Angiedema can happen with the first dose or years into therapy . It is bradykinin-driven , not allergic in the usual IgE sense — antihistamines and epinephrine may not fully reverse it. Higher risk in Black patients and those with a prior history of angiedema on any ACE inhibitor. 🧠 "No PRIL, ever again." A client with ACE-inhibitor angiedema does not get re-challenged with any -pril — switch classes (often to an ARB, though ARBs carry a small residual risk too).

Biggest drop after the very first dose . Give it at bedtime the first time, and teach the client to rise slowly — sit on the edge of the bed before standing. 🧠 "First pril, first fall risk." Same first-dose orthostatic teaching applies to ARBs — it's a RAAS-wide effect.

Aldosterone normally makes the kidney excrete K⁺ . Block aldosterone → K⁺ stays in → hyperkalemia . Watch peaked T waves on ECG. Avoid stacking with K⁺-sparing diuretics, K⁺ supplements, and salt substitutes (often potassium chloride). 🧠 "Pril keeps potassium." Teach clients to check the ingredient label on salt substitutes before assuming "salt-free" is safe.

🤰 Pregnancy 2nd/3rd trimester — fetal renal injury/death 🫁 Angiedema hx with any ACE inhibitor 🩸 Bilateral renal artery stenosis 🍌 Hyperkalemia pre-existing 💧 Volume depletion severe dehydration 🧠 "No PRIL in pregnancy — ever." Confirm pregnancy status before starting, and stop immediately if pregnancy is discovered. 🗣️
STEP 3 · WHAT THE CLIENT NEEDS TO HEAR Get up slowly, skip the salt substitute, report the cough — and never double up on labs.

1 🧎 Rise slowly — sit, then stand, especially the first few doses 2 🧂 Avoid salt substitutes — many contain potassium chloride 3 🧪 Routine labs — potassium & renal function (BUN/creatinine) 4 🤧 Report a dry, hacking cough — may need to switch to an ARB 5 🚨 Report facial/lip swelling or trouble breathing immediately 🧠 "SALT-K-COUGH" — Slowly rise · Avoid salt subs · Labs (K⁺/renal) · Tell them about the cough.

NSAIDs — blunt the antihypertensive effect, raise renal injury risk Potassium-sparing diuretics / K⁺ supplements — additive hyperkalemia Lithium — decreased clearance → possible lithium toxicity Diuretics (loop/thiazide) — additive hypotension, especially the first dose 🧠 "Pril + NSAID = pressure won't fall, kidneys might." NSAIDs fight the BP-lowering effect and stress the kidney at the same time.

entries.h: 🆚 ACE inhibitor vs ARB — tell them apart
entries.t: Feature ACE Inhibitor (-PRIL) ARB (-SARTAN) Blocks The enzyme (Angiotensin I → II) — upstream The AT1 receptor — downstream Bradykinin Builds up (ACE breaks it down normally) Unaffected Dry cough YES — classic side effect No Angiedema Yes (bradykinin-driven) Rare, lower risk Hyperkalemia Yes Yes — same mechanism First-dose hypotension Yes Yes Pregnancy Contraindicated 2nd/3rd trimester Contraindicated 2nd/3rd trimester When to choose First-line unless contraindicated Client can't tolerate the ACE-inhibitor cough 🧠

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🫀 -PRIL blocks ACE, upstream — angiotensin II never forms 🤧 Cough & angiedema bradykinin buildup — unique to ACE inhibitors, not ARBs 🧎 First dose give at bedtime, rise slowly 🍌 Hyperkalemia skip salt substitutes, monitor K⁺

Q1: Where in the RAAS pathway do ACE inhibitors act? Show answer Upstream, at the ACE enzyme — they block the conversion of Angiotensin I to Angiotensin II. Q2: Why do ACE inhibitors cause a dry cough but ARBs don't? Show answer ACE also breaks down bradykinin. Blocking ACE lets bradykinin build up, causing cough and angiedema. ARBs act at the receptor and never touch bradykinin. Q3: A client on lisinopril reports lip and tongue swelling. What's the priority? Show answer Angiedema — an airway emergency. Stop the dr

The AV-node “reset button” for SVT NG-094 Cardiac Drugs ADHD-friendly visual edition Adenosine is the 1st-line drug for supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) . It briefly blocks conduction through the AV node , interrupting the reentry circuit that's causing the fast rhythm. It works so well it can stop the heart for a few seconds — which is the plan, not a complication. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🚦 Blocks the AV node briefly interrupts the SVT reentry circuit. 💨 Flush IV fast, push fast half-life is
STEP 1 · INTERRUPT THE CIRCUIT SVT is an electrical loop running through the AV node — adenosine breaks the loop for a moment.

entries.h: 🚦 Mechanism: transiently blocks the AV node
entries.t: SVT is often caused by a re-entry circuit that keeps racing back through the AV node . Adenosine slows/briefly blocks conduction through the AV node , which interrupts the loop and lets the heart's normal pacemaker (the SA node) take back over in normal sinus rhythm . 🧠 “aDENosine hits the DEN.” The AV node is the “den” where the reentry signal keeps circling — adenosine plugs the den for a moment and the loop can't continue.
1st-line drug for supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) — a common test question is simply: “Which drug does the nurse anticipate the provider will order?” Answer: adenosine .

1 🫃 Vagal maneuver first — bearing down like a bowel movement (Valsalva) 2 💉 Adenosine — IV push, fast 3 ⚡ Synchronized cardioversion if the rhythm doesn't convert or the patient is unstable 🧠 Try the body first, then the drug, then the shock. 👀
STEP 2 · EXPECTED VS. DANGEROUS Most of what happens after this drug is supposed to happen — knowing which is which is the whole skill.

entries.h: 〰️ A few seconds of asystole on the monitor — EXPECTED, not an emergency
entries.t: Because adenosine briefly blocks the AV node, a short pause — even a few seconds of asystole — on the monitor is the drug working as intended . Don't call a code for it; stay calm, keep watching, sinus rhythm typically follows. 🧠 “The flat line is the point.” That pause IS the therapy interrupting the SVT loop.

Before pushing the dose, tell the patient they may briefly feel: 😰 A sense of impending doom 💢 Chest pressure/tightness 🔥 Flushing 😮‍💨 Shortness of breath These pass within seconds because the drug's half-life is so short.

Avoid in patients with 2nd- or 3rd-degree AV block or sick sinus syndrome (unless they have a functioning pacemaker) — the AV node is already struggling to conduct, and adenosine would block it further. 🧠 Don't block a door that's already stuck shut. 🧑‍🏫
STEP 3 · HOW IT'S ACTUALLY GIVEN Technique matters here more than almost any other IV push drug.

entries.h: 💨 Flush IV fast, push fast — and why
entries.t: Adenosine is metabolized almost instantly, so it's given as a rapid IV push over 1–2 seconds through a proximal IV site , immediately followed by a fast saline flush to chase the dose into central circulation before it's gone. 🧠 “Push it like it's disappearing — because it is.” A slow push means the drug breaks down in the tubing before it ever reaches the AV node.

entries.h: 🗣️ What to tell the patient before you push it
entries.t: "You may feel a sense of doom, chest pressure, or flushing for a few seconds — that's the medicine working, and it passes quickly. You might also notice the monitor pause briefly — that's expected too."

Supraventricular tachycardia — heart rate >150 bpm Try a vagal maneuver before reaching for the drug If adenosine doesn't convert it, synchronized cardioversion is next 🧠 “SUPER tachy” = SVT. Super fast, narrow-complex, and it's the AV node driving the loop. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🚦 Blocks the AV node breaks the SVT reentry loop 💨 Push fast, flush fast half-life is only seconds 😱 Doom, pressure, flushing brief — warn the patient first 〰️ Brief asystole = expected not a code — stay calm

Q1: How does adenosine break SVT? Show answer It transiently blocks conduction through the AV node, interrupting the reentry circuit driving the tachycardia so the SA node can resume normal sinus rhythm. Q2: Why must adenosine be given as a fast IV push with an immediate flush? Show answer Its half-life is only seconds — a slow push lets it break down before reaching the heart, so it's pushed rapidly through a proximal site and chased with a fast saline flush. Prinzmetal / vasospastic angina — the artery clenches NG-098 Cardio · Angina ADHD-friendly visual edition Every other angina is a plumbing problem. This one is a muscle cramp. The coronary artery goes into SPASM — the smooth muscle in the wall clamps down and shuts off flow — even in an artery with little or no plaque . It strikes at REST , classically at night or in the early morning , and it opens right back up with nitrates and calcium channel blockers. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🌀 SPASM, not p
STEP 1 · A CRAMP IN THE ARTERY Same cross-section you learned on NG-145 — but this time the lumen closes because the wall squeezes , not because a plaque grew.

entries.h: 🌀 Spasm closes the artery — then lets go
entries.t: 🧠 “A charley horse in the coronary.” A leg cramp doesn't mean your leg is clogged — the muscle just seized. Variant angina is that cramp, in an artery wall. Stretch it out (nitrate, calcium channel blocker) and flow returns instantly.

😖 Trigger — cold, stress, smoking, cocaine ▼ 🧬 Endothelial dysfunction — the lining fails to release enough nitric oxide , its natural relaxer ▼ 💪 Hyperreactive smooth muscle — calcium floods in and the wall contracts hard ▼ 🌀 Focal spasm → flow stops → transmural ischemia → chest pain + ST elevation ▼ 😮‍💨 Spasm releases → flow returns → EKG normalizes 🧠 Nitric oxide is the artery's chill pill. Nitrates literally donate what the endothelium isn't making. Calcium channel blockers take away the calcium the muscle nee

🥶 COLD cold air, cold water 😖 STRESS emotional surge 🚬 SMOKING the biggest one 💊 COCAINE & stimulants 🌬️ Hyperventilation 🍺 Alcohol in some clients 🌙 Circadian midnight–early a.m. 💉 Vasoconstrictors triptans, ergots Smoking is the standout risk factor — variant angina often shows up in a younger client who smokes and who may have few traditional cholesterol risk factors. 🧠 “CSSC” — Cold, Stress, Smoke, Cocaine. Picture standing outside in the cold at 3 a.m., stressed, smoking. That's the exact scene the exam will d

entries.h: 🚨 Cocaine chest pain — the trap inside the trap
entries.t: Answer first: Do NOT give a beta blocker for cocaine-induced chest pain. Cocaine stimulates both alpha and beta receptors. Blocking beta leaves alpha unopposed → worse vasoconstriction & spasm , higher BP What is used instead: benzodiazepines (calm the sympathetic surge), nitrates , calcium channel blockers , aspirin Cocaine can cause a true MI in a young person with clean arteries — it causes spasm and raises platelet aggregation and raises O₂ demand all at once Ask about recent use in every young adult with chest
STEP 2 · TELL THEM APART This table is the whole exam question. Three anginas, three different stories — and only one of them is a spasm.

🙂 STABLE angina “safer” 😰 UNSTABLE angina “unsafe” 🌀 VARIANT / Prinzmetal vasospastic Cause Fixed plaque — stable, thick-capped, narrows the lumen ~70%+ Plaque rupture + partial clot — the cap tore but the artery isn't fully shut SPASM of the smooth muscle — plaque may be minimal or absent What brings it on Exertion or emotion — a predictable amount of activity, every time Less and less exertion — now happens at rest , new, worsening, longer At REST — not related to exertion. Cold, stress, smoking, cocaine, hyperve

entries.h: ⏰ When each one hurts — a 24-hour view
entries.t: 🧠 The single best assessment question in this whole topic: “What were you doing when the pain started?” Climbing stairs → stable. Sitting still, and it's new/worse → unstable. Sound asleep at 3 a.m. → variant. 🔎
STEP 3 · CATCH IT IN THE ACT The hard part is that everything is normal between attacks — you have to catch the EKG during the pain.

entries.h: 📈 The EKG signature: ST elevation that comes and goes
entries.t: NCLEX TIP ST elevation that resolves completely and a negative troponin = think spasm . A true STEMI's ST elevation does not simply melt away, and its troponin rises. But you never assume — every ST elevation is treated as a STEMI until the picture proves otherwise. 🧠 “The STEMI that ran away.” Elevation during the pain, flat line after the nitro, troponin negative — the artery cramped, then let go.

📈 12-lead EKG DURING an episode — the money shot. Transient ST elevation in the affected artery's leads. 📼 Ambulatory/Holter monitoring — catches nighttime episodes she sleeps through 🧪 Serial troponins — negative in a pure spasm; positive means muscle actually died 🩻 Coronary angiography — often shows little or no significant fixed obstruction , which is the diagnostic surprise 💉 Provocative testing (e.g., ergonovine or acetylcholine during cath) can reproduce spasm in specialized settings 🏃 Exercise stress testin

Answer first: variant angina is usually benign with treatment — but a prolonged spasm can still cause real damage. 💔 MI if the spasm lasts long enough to infarct ⚡ Ventricular dysrhythmias during the ischemic window — including V-tach/V-fib 🫥 Syncope during an attack (often from a dysrhythmia or heart block) 💀 Sudden cardiac death — rare, but the reason it gets treated aggressively 🔁 Spasm can also occur on top of existing plaque — the two are not mutually exclusive 🧠 Any chest pain gets the EKG and the workup. "It
STEP 4 · UNCLENCH IT Two drug classes make the artery relax, one drug class can make it worse, and one habit undoes everything.

entries.h: 💊 What works — and why it works

entries.t: amlodipine, diltiazem, verapamil, nifedipine Block the calcium the smooth muscle needs to contract → the artery can't clamp . This is the prevention drug — scheduled, daily, often dosed to cover the nighttime hours. Watch: hypotension, headache, flushing, peripheral edema; diltiazem & verapamil also slow HR — hold parameters per order. Verapamil → constipation.

SL nitroglycerin for an attack; long-acting isosorbide for prevention Donate nitric oxide → immediate vasodilation. Relief is fast , which is itself a diagnostic clue. Watch: headache (expected), orthostatic hypotension — sit down first. Never with PDE-5 “-afil” drugs.

Blocking beta-2 leaves alpha vasoconstriction unopposed → the spasm can get worse . Same logic as cocaine chest pain. EXAM TIP "Which order does the nurse question?" — a nonselective beta blocker (e.g. propranolol) prescribed for vasospastic angina. Also on board: aspirin is used cautiously here (high doses can inhibit protective prostacyclin), a statin if there's any coexisting atherosclerosis, and treating any coexisting CAD as usual. Stents and bypass do NOT fix spasm — you cannot stent a muscle cramp; the arter

1 🚭 STOP SMOKING. Non-negotiable and the highest-yield intervention — nicotine is a direct vasoconstrictor and smoking is the leading modifiable trigger. 2 🥶 Avoid cold exposure. Dress warm, scarf over the mouth in cold air, warm the car before going out, avoid cold-water plunges. 3 🚫 No cocaine or stimulants. Ask without judgment; this changes the emergency treatment. 4 😌 Stress reduction. Sleep, relaxation practice, treat anxiety — sympathetic surges are triggers. 5 💊 Take the CCB even when she feels fine — it's

1️⃣ Stop activity, sit or lie her down , stay with her 2️⃣ 12-lead EKG NOW — while the pain is happening. This is the diagnosis. 3️⃣ Vitals + continuous monitoring — watch for dysrhythmias 4️⃣ Nitroglycerin per protocol , checking BP before and after each dose 5️⃣ O₂ only if hypoxic (same rule as NG-071) 6️⃣ Serial troponins to rule out infarction 7️⃣ Document the time, trigger, duration and what relieved it — the pattern is the diagnosis 🧠 Get the strip while it hurts. Twenty minutes later that EKG is normal, and

❌ Nonselective beta blocker for vasospastic angina — can worsen spasm ❌ Beta blocker for cocaine chest pain — unopposed alpha ❌ Nitrates within 24 h of a PDE-5 “-afil” drug — profound hypotension ❌ Triptans & ergotamines (migraine drugs) — vasoconstrictors, avoid ❌ Stents don't prevent spasm — the muscle can still cramp ✅ Exercise stress test normal ≠ no disease in this client 🧠 Everything on this list either squeezes an artery that's already squeezing, or drops a BP that's about to drop. That's the whole rule. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🌀 Spasm, not plaque Artery clamps and lets go. Cath can look nearly clean. 🛏️ Rest · night · early a.m. Wakes her from sleep. Exertion is NOT the trigger. 📈 Transient ST elevation Resolves fully · troponin negative 💊 CCB + nitrates Prevent + relieve. Avoid nonselective beta blockers.

Central Alpha-2 Agonist — quiets the brain's "raise BP" signal NG-110 CARDIO ADHD-friendly visual edition Clonidine is a CENTRAL alpha-2 AGONIST — it stimulates alpha-2 receptors in the brainstem, which turns DOWN sympathetic outflow to the whole body. It does not act on the blood vessels directly the way peripheral antihypertensives do. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🚫 Common mix-up to correct: Clonidine is NOT an alpha-BLOCKER/antagonist. It is an alpha-2 AGONIST — it turns the "lower blood pressure
STEP 1 · THE MECHANISM The action happens in the brainstem first — everything else in the body is just following orders.

entries.h: 🧠 Central vs peripheral — where the "off switch" is
entries.t: EXAM TIP Clonidine stimulates alpha-2 receptors in the vasomotor center of the brainstem (medulla) . This is the OPPOSITE location from drugs that act directly on peripheral blood vessels. 🧠 "Clonidine calms the COMMAND CENTER, not the roads." It turns down the brain's signal to constrict — it never touches the blood vessels directly. That's the "central" in central-acting.

Central alpha-2 agonist — antihypertensive Brand: Catapres (oral), Catapres-TTS (patch), Kapvay (ER, used for ADHD) Also used for opioid/alcohol/nicotine withdrawal symptom control, and severe pain (epidural, specialty use) 🧠 "AGO-nist AGO-es and does something." Agonist = activates the receptor. Antagonist = blocks it. Clonidine activates alpha-2 — it's an AGO-nist, not an alpha-blocker.

Hypertension — often an add-on when other classes aren't enough Withdrawal symptom management — blunts the sympathetic surge of opioid/alcohol/nicotine withdrawal ADHD — extended-release form (Kapvay) 🧠 Clonidine shows up far outside cardiology because it turns down the whole sympathetic "fight or flight" system, not just blood pressure.
🧠 "Patch = once a WEEK, not once a day." Mixing up patch frequency with oral dosing is a common med-error trap on exams. ⚠️
STEP 2 · THE DANGER LIST The same abrupt-stop rebound crisis as beta blockers — plus sedation because this drug lives in the brain.

entries.h: 🚨 Never stop abruptly — rebound hypertensive crisis
entries.t: 💊 Clonidine taken daily — sympathetic outflow chronically suppressed ▼ 🛑 Abrupt discontinuation — brainstem suppression suddenly lifts ▼ 🚨 Sympathetic surge → rebound HYPERTENSIVE CRISIS, tachycardia, agitation Same warning as beta blockers, but the mechanism differs : with clonidine, the brainstem's own suppression is removed centrally; with a beta blocker, peripheral receptors that adapted to blockade become suddenly unopposed. Both endings look similar — a catecholamine surge and a BP spike — but the starting po

Because clonidine acts in the brain , expect drowsiness, sedation, dry mouth, and dizziness — more prominent than with peripherally-acting antihypertensives. Caution with other CNS depressants (opioids, benzodiazepines, alcohol) — additive sedation. 🧠 "It's IN the brain, so it acts LIKE a brain drug." Sedation and dry mouth are the giveaway that this isn't just a vessel drug.

Expect bradycardia and hypotension as therapeutic (and sometimes excessive) effects. Monitor HR and BP, especially when initiating or combining with a beta blocker. 🧠 Combining clonidine + beta blocker stacks bradycardia risk — and complicates which drug to taper first if both are discontinued.

🛑 Never stop abruptly rebound crisis 😴 Sedation caution with other CNS depressants 🫀 Bradycardia monitor HR 🩹 Patch adherence skin irritation, must replace on schedule 🧠 If a patch falls off or a dose is missed, contact the provider rather than doubling up — the abrupt-withdrawal risk is the same as any missed dose of this class. 🗣️
STEP 3 · WHAT THE CLIENT NEEDS TO HEAR Never miss a dose or pull the patch early — and know this drug works in the brain, not the vessels.

1 ❌ Never stop abruptly — taper only under provider guidance 2 🩹 Patch: change weekly , rotate sites, keep an extra on hand 3 😴 Expect drowsiness/dry mouth — caution with driving, alcohol, sedatives 4 🧎 Rise slowly — hypotension/dizziness possible 5 🩺 Monitor HR/BP regularly, especially with other rate-lowering drugs 🧠 "Never skip, never yank the patch." Both a missed oral dose run and an early patch removal can trigger the same rebound crisis.

Beta blockers — additive bradycardia; sequencing matters if stopping both CNS depressants (opioids, benzodiazepines, alcohol) — additive sedation Tricyclic antidepressants — may reduce clonidine's antihypertensive effect 🧠 Always double-check what else lowers HR or sedates the client — clonidine adds to both.

entries.h: 🆚 Clonidine vs Beta Blockers — same warning, different wiring
entries.t: Feature Clonidine Beta Blockers Site of action Central — brainstem alpha-2 receptors Peripheral — beta receptors on heart/lungs/vessels Type of action AGONIST (stimulates alpha-2) Antagonist (blocks beta) Result ↓ sympathetic outflow from the brain Blocks sympathetic signal already reaching the receptor Abrupt stop Never — rebound hypertensive crisis Never — rebound hypertension/tachycardia Extra route option Transdermal patch, weekly Ophthalmic (timolol) for glaucoma 🧠 "Same ending, different beginning." Both drug

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🧠 Central α2 AGONIST not an antagonist — stimulates the brainstem to turn sympathetic tone down 📉 ↓ Sympathetic outflow ↓HR, ↓BP, ↓renin — all downstream of the brain signal 🩹 Patch = weekly rotate sites, don't remove early ❌ Never stop abruptly rebound hypertensive crisis — same rule as beta blockers

Q1: Is clonidine an alpha agonist or an alpha antagonist? Show answer Agonist — it stimulates central alpha-2 receptors in the brainstem, which lowers sympathetic outflow. It does not block a receptor. Q2: How is clonidine's mechanism different from a peripherally-acting antihypertensive? Show answer Clonidine acts centrally in the brainstem to turn down the sympathetic signal at its source; peripheral drugs act directly on the blood vessels or heart where the signal arrives. TOF — four defects, one blue baby · the CYANOTIC classic NG-118 CARDIO · PEDS ADHD-friendly visual edition Tetra = 4. Four defects that all push the same direction: blood is blocked on the way to the lungs, so it takes the hole instead and goes RIGHT → LEFT , straight out to the body without ever picking up oxygen. That is cyanosis . When it happens all at once it is a “TET SPELL” — and the first thing you do is knees to chest . 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 4️⃣ P·R·O·V P ulmonary stenosis · R V hype
STEP 0 · SAME PICTURE AS EVERY PAGE Same drawing as the ASD/VSD/PDA page and the stenosis page. Learn the normal, then add the four changes.

entries.h: 🫀 The normal heart — the drawing all four pages share
entries.t: right heart · O₂-poor left heart · O₂-rich L → R shunt R → L shunt obstruction (bow-tie) 🧠 “Blue in on the left of the page, red out on the right.” Right heart (blue) is drawn on your left, left heart (red) on your right — an anatomic view, facing the patient.

entries.h: 🔁 BASE NORMAL CIRCULATION — identical on every page in this set
entries.t: Say this out loud before every defect: Body ➡ SVC + IVC ➡ RIGHT ATRIUM ▼ tricuspid valve ➡ RIGHT VENTRICLE ▼ pulmonic valve ➡ PULMONARY ARTERY ➡ LUNGS (pick up O₂) ▼ pulmonary veins ➡ LEFT ATRIUM ▼ mitral valve ➡ LEFT VENTRICLE ▼ aortic valve ➡ AORTA ➡ body The LEFT side is a high-pressure pump; the RIGHT side is a low-pressure pump. That one fact predicts every shunt on every page: if there is a hole, blood takes the easy road and goes LEFT → RIGHT — back into the lungs — until something blocks the right side or r

entries.h: 🧭 How to read every diagram in this series
entries.t: Blue chambers = right heart, O₂-poor blood. Red chambers = left heart, O₂-rich blood. Topaz arrow = a LEFT → RIGHT shunt (acyanotic). Amethyst arrow = a RIGHT → LEFT shunt (cyanotic) — the TOF arrow . Citrine bow-tie ▶◀ = an obstruction — TOF has one, at the pulmonary valve. Lavender = heart muscle. A thick lavender wall = hypertrophy. 🧠 Read the drawing right. It is an anatomic view, so the patient's RIGHT heart is on YOUR LEFT . That is why a “ left-to-right ” shunt arrow points ← to your left on every diagram in

entries.h: ⭐ Why TOF turns a baby blue — one sentence
entries.t: Answer first: the pulmonary valve is narrowed , so the right ventricle cannot push blood forward into the lungs. Pressure in the right ventricle climbs until it is higher than the left . Now the hole (the VSD) runs backwards : blue blood crosses RIGHT → LEFT and is picked up by the overriding aorta , which sits directly over the hole. Blue blood is pumped out to the body. Less blood reaches the lungs → decreased pulmonary blood flow → hypoxemia and cyanosis . 🧠 “Blocked in front, hole in the middle, aorta on top.”
STEP 1 · TETRA = 4 · P·R·O·V All four drawn on the same base heart, in one picture — because they only make sense together.

entries.h: 💜 All FOUR components on one drawing — P · R · O · V
entries.t: 🧠 “PROVe it's Tetralogy.” P ulmonary stenosis · R ight ventricular hypertrophy · O verriding aorta · V SD. Say PROV out loud four times — it is worth an easy point.

What: the outflow from the right ventricle to the lungs is narrowed (the citrine bow-tie ▶◀). Why it matters: this is the engine of the whole disease . The tighter the stenosis, the higher the RV pressure, the bigger the right-to-left shunt, the bluer the child. Sound: a systolic ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border — the murmur is from the stenosis , not from the VSD. 🧠 Pinch the straw, the drink backs up. Pinch the pulmonary artery and the right ventricle backs up into the hole.

What: the RV muscle thickens (the fat lavender wall) because it is pushing against a narrowed valve every single beat. Why it matters: hypertrophy is a result , not a cause — and it is what makes RV pressure exceed LV pressure, which is what reverses the shunt. X-ray classic: a “boot-shaped heart” — the uplifted apex of a thick right ventricle. 🧠 “Lift weights, grow muscle.” The RV lifts against a closed door all day, so it bulks up. A boot -shaped heart kicks the door.

What: the aorta is shifted over the septum , so its opening sits directly on top of the hole — it collects blood from BOTH ventricles. That is why the funnel in the drawing is blue on the left and red on the right . Why it matters: it is the delivery route . Without it, blue blood would just cross into the LV; with it, blue blood is aimed straight at the body. 🧠 “The aorta sits on the hole like a chimney on a crack.” Whatever comes up the crack goes straight out the chimney.

What: a hole between the ventricles — the same hole you learned on the ASD/VSD/PDA page. Why it matters: in an isolated VSD the shunt runs LEFT → RIGHT and the baby stays pink. In Tetralogy the pulmonary stenosis flips the pressures, so the very same hole now runs RIGHT → LEFT and the baby turns blue. EXAM TIP The hole did not change — the pressure did. That single idea is the difference between the acyanotic group and the cyanotic group. 🧠 “Same hole, opposite direction.” Direction is decided by pressure , never b

entries.h: 💜 The rest of the cyanotic & mixed family — know the one-liners
entries.t: Defect One-line definition Treatment Tetralogy of Fallot 4 defects: P·R·O·V — right-to-left shunt, decreased pulmonary blood flow Surgical repair (VSD patch + relieve the outflow obstruction) Tricuspid atresia Closure of the tricuspid valve — no door from RA to RV — so an ASD (and usually a VSD/PDA) is what keeps the child alive Surgical repair , in staged operations Transposition of the great arteries (TGA) Reversal of the 2 main arteries leaving the heart — the pulmonary artery and the aorta are swapped, creating
STEP 2 · MOST TESTED A hypercyanotic episode. Answer first: knees to chest. Then oxygen, then calm, then call.

entries.h: 🚨 During an episode — the IMMEDIATE action is the POSITION
entries.t: 1 🦵 POSITION FIRST — knee-to-chest (infant) or squatting (older child). It is the fastest, cheapest intervention and it works in seconds. 2 💨 Give oxygen — blow-by or mask, whatever the child will tolerate without fighting. 3 🤫 Calm and comfort — a quiet, dim room. Crying makes the spell worse, so soothing IS treatment. 4 📞 Notify the provider · anticipate IV fluids and morphine as ordered, and continuous monitoring. Never leave the child, and never force a struggling child into a mask — agitation deepens the spell

entries.h: 🔎 What a spell looks like & what sets one off
entries.t: During the spell: 💙 Sudden deep cyanosis — much bluer than the child's baseline. 😤 Deep, rapid breathing (hyperpnea). 😡 Irritability & inconsolable crying , then limpness / lethargy . 🔇 The murmur gets QUIETER — less blood is crossing the narrowed pulmonary valve. NCLEX TRAP 😵 Severe spells: syncope, seizure , and they can be fatal. Classic triggers: 🌅 Waking up in the morning — the most classic time of all. 😭 Crying , a tantrum, pain, or a procedure. 🍼 Feeding and straining with a bowel movement . 🛁 A warm bath an

entries.h: ✅ PREVENTION — the 5 source tips, and why each one works
entries.t: 1 😴 DO NOT interrupt sleep , and give a calm, quiet environment upon waking — waking is the peak spell time. 2 🍼 Offer a pacifier during crying — sucking soothes and stops the crying that triggers spells. 3 🥄 Small & frequent feedings — a big feed is too much work for a hypoxic infant. 4 🤱 Swaddle or hold the infant during procedures — containment lowers distress. 5 💧 Prevent dehydration and treat fever/constipation — dehydration thickens already-thick blood and invites spells and clots. 🧠 “Let them sleep, let them

entries.h: 🩸 The three chronic hypoxia signs — cyanosis, clubbing, polycythemia
entries.t: Answer first: polycythemia in a cyanotic child is a CLOT problem, not a “good compensation.” Thick blood plus dehydration is how these children stroke. So the nursing priorities are: keep fluids up, treat fever early, avoid long NPO windows without IV fluids, and report a hemoglobin over 22 g/dL . 🧠 “Blue → thick → sticky → stroke.” Four words, the whole chain. Break it with water .

entries.h: 🚨 The 5 heart-failure signs to REPORT — HF = HEAVY FLUID
entries.t: ⚖️ Weight GAIN water gain 👀 Puffiness around the eyes periorbital edema 🥶 Pale, cool extremities 🧷 Reduced number of wet diapers less urine out 🍼 Decreased feeding tires out fast 🧠 “HF = HEAVY FLUID.” Heavy on the scale · heavy eyes · heavy breathing · light diaper . Five signs, one phrase. 🩺
STEP 3 · FIX IT, THEN TEACH IT Treatment is surgical. Everything else is keeping the child calm, hydrated and out of a spell until then.

Complete repair — usually in the first year of life : the surgeon patches the VSD and relieves the right ventricular outflow obstruction (the pulmonary stenosis). Once the VSD is closed and the outflow is open, the shunt has nowhere to go and the child pinks up. Palliative shunt — if the infant is too small or too unstable for full repair, a systemic-to-pulmonary shunt (the modified Blalock–Taussig shunt) is placed to send more blood to the lungs until repair is possible. Before surgery, nursing keeps the child out

entries.h: 🚨 DISCHARGE TEACHING — what parents must call about
entries.t: Report immediately: 💙 A spell — any sudden deepening of cyanosis, especially with limpness or fainting. ⚖️ The 5 heart-failure signs — weight gain, puffy eyes, pale cool skin, fewer wet diapers, decreased feeding. 🩸 Hemoglobin over 22 g/dL at a clinic draw. 🌡️ Fever , vomiting, diarrhea — anything that dehydrates. 🧠 Neuro changes : extreme irritability, seizure, weakness on one side (stroke from thick blood). Teach the position at home: 🦵 Every caregiver must be able to demonstrate the knee-to-chest position before

Never treat a quieter murmur as improvement in a bluer child — it means less blood is crossing the stenosis. Never let a TOF child go long without fluids — dehydration triggers spells and clots. Never expect a normal O₂ sat. Baseline in TOF is 65–85% ; treat the child, not the number. ❌ Don't reach for oxygen before positioning — knees to chest is step one. ❌ Don't force a screaming child into a mask; agitation deepens the spell. 🧠 “Position, then oxygen.” If both are options on the exam, the position wins.

entries.h: 🧪 Labs & monitoring you will actually see
entries.t: 🧪 Hemoglobin & hematocrit — both high from polycythemia. Report Hgb > 22 g/dL . 📉 Iron studies — a “normal” Hgb in a cyanotic child can actually mean relative anemia , which makes hypoxia worse. Iron deficiency is a real spell risk. 💨 Continuous pulse oximetry with the child's documented baseline at the bedside. 🫁 ABG during a spell: low PaO₂, and metabolic acidosis if it is prolonged. 📷 Chest x-ray : the classic boot-shaped heart . Echocardiogram confirms all four defects. 🧠 “High H&H is not good news here.” It is

SAY IT OUT LOUD 4️⃣ PROV P ulmonary stenosis · R VH · O verriding aorta · V SD 💜 RIGHT → LEFT CYANOTIC · decreased pulmonary blood flow · sat 65–85% 🦵 KNEES TO CHEST The first action in a tet spell. Older child squats. 🩸 Hgb > 22 g/dL → report Polycythemia = clot risk. Hydrate. Treatment = surgical repair .

entries.h: ⭐ One last time — where Tetralogy sits
entries.t: Group Shunt direction Pulmonary blood flow Blue? Defects 💛 ACYANOTIC LEFT → RIGHT ↑ INCREASED — too much blood to the lungs No (pink at first) ASD · VSD · PDA · AVSD 🧡 OBSTRUCTIVE none — the road is narrowed normal or ↓ , depending on where the narrowing is Usually no Pulmonic stenosis · Aortic stenosis · Coarctation of the aorta 💜 CYANOTIC RIGHT → LEFT ↓ DECREASED — blood skips the lungs YES Tetralogy of Fallot · Tricuspid atresia 🩵 MIXED both ways — red and blue blood mix varies Yes Transposition of the great art

Q1: Name the four defects of Tetralogy of Fallot. Show answer PROV — Pulmonary stenosis, Right ventricular hypertrophy, Overriding aorta, VSD. Tetra = 4. Q2: A 6-month-old with TOF suddenly turns deeply blue and is breathing hard after waking. What is your FIRST action? Show answer Place the infant in the knee-to-chest position immediately. Then give oxygen, keep the child calm and quiet, and notify the provider. An older child would be told to squat. Q3: Why does knee-to-chest / squatting work? Show answer Folding
