entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🔥 Risk factors ⚙️ Mechanism 💥 Complications ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Cardio · Pathophysiology Course PVD set ← 1 · Patho & Signs 2 · Causes & Complications 3 · Treatments →

Peripheral Vascular Disease II · why it happens and what goes wrong NG-127 CARDIO ADHD-friendly visual edition Think of anything that SCARS the lining of a blood vessel. Every arterial risk factor on this page does exactly one thing — it injures the endothelium. Fat, calcium and clot then settle into those tiny tears and become plaque . Veins fail a different way: pressure and stasis blow out the valves. Different insult, different complication list. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🩹 One idea: SCARRING
STEP 1 · WHAT SCARS THE VESSEL Split them the way the exam splits them: what the client can change, and what they can't.

entries.h: 🔥 MODIFIABLE — anything that scars the lining of the blood vessels
entries.t: Risk factor How it damages the vessel The number 🚬 Smoking Chemicals directly scar the lining ; nicotine also causes vasoconstriction, so a narrowed vessel gets squeezed narrower. The #1 modifiable risk factor for PAD. Quitting is the single highest-yield teaching point. 🍬 Diabetes (uncontrolled) High sugar turns the blood to mud / syrup — thick, sticky blood scrapes and scars the vessel wall. Also causes neuropathy, so injuries go unfelt. A1C ≥6.5% diagnoses DM; a common general adult target is <7% . Fasting gluco

entries.h: 🧬 NON-MODIFIABLE — the three you can't teach away
entries.t: 🎂 AGE vessels stiffen with time ⚧️ GENDER 🧬 GENETICS family history These still matter on the exam — they tell you who to screen . They just aren't where the teaching plan goes. 🧠 “The three G's you can't fix: Getting older, Gender, Genes.” If a question asks which risk factor the nurse should focus teaching on , the answer is never one of these three — pick smoking, diet, activity or glucose control.

entries.h: 🧪 The lipid panel, on one bar scale
entries.t: 🧠 LDL = “Lousy, Lodges in the wall.” HDL = “Healthy, Hauls it away.” So for LDL you want the number LOW ; for HDL you want it HIGH . Triglycerides flip high over 150 .

entries.h: ⚖️ Same leg, two different risk lists — arterial vs venous
entries.t: The exam loves to hand you a risk history and ask which kind of vascular disease to expect. They do not share a cause.
🚬 Smoking (strongest) 🍬 Diabetes 🧈 High LDL / low HDL 💥 Hypertension 🎂 Age, male sex, family history 💔 Known CAD, prior MI or stroke ⬇️ Still DANGLE the leg

🧍 Prolonged standing or sitting (nurses, teachers, cashiers) 🤰 Pregnancy · 💊 estrogen ⚖️ Obesity 🩸 Previous DVT — scarred valves 🎂 Age · family history of varicose veins 🏋️ Heavy lifting, chronic straining ⬆️ Still ELEVATE the leg 🧠 “Arteries get CLOGGED, veins get CLOGGED-UP-TRAFFIC.” Arterial risk is anything that builds plaque . Venous risk is anything that makes blood sit still or push back down — standing, pregnancy, obesity, an old clot. ⚙️
STEP 2 · THE MECHANISM From a scratch in the lining to a hard, narrow, rupture-ready artery — and the parallel story in the veins.

entries.h: 🧱 ATHEROSCLEROSIS in five frames — hardening & narrowing that limits O₂ perfusion
entries.t: 🧠 “Scratch → Snack → Scab → Stone → Snap.” Risk factors scratch the lining, lipids & macrophages snack in the tear, the body throws a fibrous scab (cap) over it, calcium turns it to stone , and one day the cap snaps and a clot forms. Five words, whole disease.

🧠 “CAIF” — Carotid, Aorta (abdominal), Iliac, Femoral. Say it like “safe” with a C. Top to bottom: neck → belly → hip → thigh . The pain lands one level below the block, so hip pain = iliac, calf pain = femoral.

entries.h: 🌊 The venous mechanism: pressure, not plaque
entries.t: Notice what is not in this chain: no plaque, no lipids, no ischemia. That's why statins and antiplatelets don't fix a venous leg — compression and elevation do. 🧠 “Pool → Pressure → Puddle → Pigment → Punch-through.” Five P's for the venous side, so you don't mix them up with the arterial 6 P's of emergency . 💥
STEP 3 · WHAT IT COSTS Plaque doesn't just narrow — it can burst, leading to a blood clot that can kill the client. And a starving foot eventually dies.

entries.h: 🚨 The rupture tree — one burst plaque, four ways to die or lose a limb
entries.t: 🧠 “Legs today, heart tomorrow.” If a question gives you a PAD client and asks what else to assess, the answer lives in the chest or the neck — not the leg you're looking at.

1 Non-healing wound — a tiny toe injury that will not close, because healing needs oxygen the artery can't deliver. 2 Arterial ulcer — round, punched-out, on a toe, heel, or lateral ankle. Very painful. 3 Infection / osteomyelitis — antibiotics can't reach tissue that blood can't reach. 4 GANGRENE — black, dry, mummified toes. Tissue is dead. 5 AMPUTATION — the reason foot inspection and smoking cessation are the two biggest teaching points in this whole topic. Diabetes doubles this pathway: ischemia stops healing,

entries.h: 🫙 Venous endgame: varicose veins → stasis ulcer → clot
entries.t: 🪱 Varicose veins — dilated, twisted, rope-like superficial veins. Cosmetic first, painful and heavy later. 🟤 Venous stasis dermatitis — itchy, weepy, brown, scaly skin at the ankle. Scratching becomes the wound. 🧱 Lipodermatosclerosis — the calf hardens and tapers, giving the classic “inverted champagne bottle” leg. 🕳️ Venous stasis ulcer — the medial-malleolus ulcer from page 1. Slow, weepy, recurrent, notoriously hard to heal. 🦠 Cellulitis — broken, boggy skin is an open door for infection. 🩸 DVT — stagnant blood

entries.h: ⭐ Complication cheat-sheet — which side did the damage?
entries.t: Finding on the exam question 🩸 Arterial 🫙 Venous Ulcer that will not heal Toe / heel / lateral ankle, dry, punched out Medial ankle, weepy, irregular Black, dry, mummified tissue Gangrene — yes, this is the arterial ending Not typical Brown discoloration around the ankle No Hemosiderin staining — yes Sudden cold pulseless painful limb Acute arterial occlusion — 6 P's, emergency No Sudden unilateral warm swollen calf No DVT — emergency because of PE Life-threatening downstream event MI · stroke · limb loss Pulmonary

entries.h: ➡️ You know the damage — now the fixes

entries.t: ABI & Doppler, antiplatelets, statins, angioplasty/stent, bypass, endarterectomy — plus the C-words to avoid . ⬇️ DANGLE / hang the legs down

Compression stockings, limit standing, elevation, calf pumping, vein ablation/ligation — plus anticoagulation if a clot forms. ⬆️ ELEVATE above the heart PVD set ← 1 · Patho & Signs 2 · Causes & Complications 3 · Treatments → ＋ DVT → ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🩹 SCARS S moking · C holesterol · A high BP · R esting (sedentary) · S ugar. All scar the lining. 🧱 Plaque recipe Lipids + calcium + clot under a fibrous cap . Hardening & narrowing = less O₂ perfusion. 📍 CAIF sites C arotid · A bdominal aorta · I liac · F emoral. Pain lands below the block. 💥 Rupture = clot = limb ischemia · MI · stroke . Venous clot instead goes to the lungs (PE) .

Q1: In one sentence, what do ALL the modifiable arterial risk factors have in common? Show answer They all scar/injure the lining (endothelium) of the blood vessel — and plaque settles into those tears. Q2: What three things make up an atheroma? Show answer Lipids, calcium and possible clots — sitting in large arteries under a fibrous connective-tissue cap. Q3: Arteriosclerosis vs atherosclerosis? Show answer Arteriosclerosis = hardening/stiffening of the artery wall (general term). Atherosclerosis = fatty plaque i

entries.h: Septic Shock · NG-129 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🧨 Cause 🔎 Clues 🪜 4 Stages 🩺 Care ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Cardio · Pathophysiology Course

The PIPES blow wide open — infection everywhere NG-129 Cardio · Shock ADHD-friendly visual edition Septic shock results from a widespread bloodborne infection that overwhelms the body — typically bacterial, from something ordinary like pneumonia , a UTI or a kidney infection that got worse. A systemic cytokine release inside the bloodstream causes extreme vasodilation and fluid leakage from the capillaries . The blood is still there — it's just in all the wrong places. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🚿
STEP 1 · INFECTION GOES SYSTEMIC An ordinary infection escapes into the bloodstream, the immune system overreacts, and the overreaction — not the germ — is what causes the shock.

entries.h: 🦠 From a UTI to a code: infection → sepsis → septic shock
entries.t: 🧠 “Sepsis is the body's friendly fire.” The bacteria start it, but the cytokine storm — the immune response — is what dilates the vessels and drops the pressure. That's why antibiotics alone don't fix the shock.

🦠 Bacteria & endotoxin reach the bloodstream ▼ 🌊 Systemic cytokine release (TNF-α, interleukins) → nitric oxide ▼ 🚿 Extreme vasodilation — SVR falls through the floor ▼ 💧 Capillary leak — plasma escapes into the tissues (relative hypovolemia) ▼ 🧩 Microclots block capillaries — maldistribution of what blood is left ▼ 💀 Cells starve despite a "normal" blood volume → lactate ↑ → MODS Septic shock is a distribution problem, not a volume problem — which is why fluids alone can't fix it and why a vasopressor is eventuall
STEP 2 · WARM THEN COLD Septic shock is the only shock that changes what the skin feels like as it gets worse. Know both faces.

entries.h: ⭐ WARM phase vs COLD phase — the single most tested distinction
entries.t: Why the switch happens — say this out loud: early, cytokines dilate every vessel ( SVR ↓↓ ) and the heart answers with a high cardiac output , so warm blood is being flung out to the skin → warm, flushed, dry, bounding, wide pulse pressure . Later, the capillary leak has drained the intravascular volume, sepsis-induced myocardial depression weakens the heart, and endogenous catecholamines plus acidosis plus the vasopressors you started clamp the periphery → output falls, skin goes cold, clammy and mottled, pulse pr

entries.h: 🚨 Signs & symptoms from the source — expanded
entries.t: 📉 Severely low blood pressure. The source says <80 systolic — that is profound, late hypotension. The clinical triggers are earlier: SBP <90 , a drop of ≥40 from the patient's baseline, or MAP <65 . 🥶 Cold, clammy skin, pale & cool extremities — late/cold phase 🫱 Delayed capillary refill >3 sec , mottling 🧠 Confusion & disorientation — mental status change NCLEX TIP 🧪 High WBC . Source: >10,000 (above the normal adult range of 5,000–10,000/mm³ ). Formal sepsis criteria use >12,000 OR <4,000 , or >10% bands. 🌡️ Temp

qSOFA — 2 of 3 at the bedside, no lab needed: 🌬️ RR ≥22 🧠 Altered mentation 📉 SBP ≤100 Labs that matter: 🧪 Lactate — >2 mmol/L is part of the septic-shock definition; ≥4 triggers aggressive fluids. Recheck it to prove you're winning. 🧫 Blood cultures ×2 from separate sites — always BEFORE the first antibiotic 🩸 CBC with differential , procalcitonin, CRP 🫘 BUN/creatinine (AKI), LFTs & bilirubin , platelets (fall in DIC), PT/INR & fibrinogen 🫧 ABG — metabolic acidosis; ScvO₂ for oxygen extraction 🧠 “qSOFA = 22, confu

entries.h: 📊 Where septic shock sits among the shocks
entries.t: Type Preload (CVP/PAWP) CO SVR Skin Hypovolemic ↓↓ ↓ ↑ Cold, clammy, pale Cardiogenic ↑↑ ↓↓ ↑ Cold, clammy, mottled Septic — warm / early ⬅️ ↓ ↑ ↓↓ WARM, flushed, dry Septic — cold / late ⬅️ ↓ ↓ ↑ Cold, clammy, mottled Neurogenic ↓ ↓ ↓↓ WARM, dry, pink + BRADYcardia Anaphylactic ↓ ↓ ↓↓ WARM, flushed + hives / swelling Septic shock is the only type that occupies two rows — it is the only shock whose fingerprint changes over time. 🧠 Warm + fever + confusion + wide pulse pressure = septic, early. Same patient six hour
STEP 3 · STAGE IT Same four stages as every shock — here they are with the septic patient's own findings, including where warm becomes cold.

entries.h: 🪜 The 4 stages of shock — identical on every shock page
entries.t: Stage What's happening What you see I · INITIAL Cardiac output falls just enough that cells switch to anaerobic metabolism → lactic acid builds, blood glucose rises. Nothing. Signs & symptoms are ABSENT in this stage — only a rising lactate gives it away. II · COMPENSATORY The sympathetic nervous system and renin–angiotensin–aldosterone rescue the pressure: catecholamines, vasoconstriction, ADH and aldosterone hold on to salt and water. Tachycardia · tachypnea · restless & anxious · cold clammy skin · narrowing pul

entries.h: 📈 Stage progression — septic findings on each stage
entries.t: 🧠 Watch the pulse pressure, not just the BP. WIDE in the warm phase (dilated pipes drop the diastolic), NARROW in the cold phase (clamped pipes raise it back). The pulse pressure flips before the patient does. 🩺
STEP 4 · THE FIRST HOUR Emergency treatment: supplemental oxygen, intravenous fluids, antibiotics — and the drugs that put tone back in the pipes.

entries.h: ⏱️ The 1-hour sepsis bundle — five things, in this order
entries.t: Cultures come before antibiotics — but antibiotics are never delayed for cultures. Draw them fast, then hang the drug. Every hour of delay costs survival. 🧠 “Lactate, Cultures, Antibiotics, Fluids, Pressors.” L-C-A-F-P — “Let's Cure A Failing Patient.” That is the whole first hour.

entries.h: 💊 Why norepinephrine, and why only after fluids
entries.t: Question Answer Why fluids first? Capillary leak has genuinely emptied the intravascular space. Squeezing an empty circuit raises the number on the monitor while cutting off the gut, kidneys and fingers. Give 30 mL/kg of isotonic crystalloid (0.9% NS or LR) first. Why norepinephrine first-line? The core defect is lost vessel tone (SVR ↓↓) . Norepinephrine is a powerful alpha-1 vasoconstrictor with modest beta-1 support — it fixes exactly what is broken and causes fewer tachyarrhythmias than dopamine . What's added

entries.h: ✅ Everything else that has to happen
entries.t: 🫁 Supplemental oxygen ; intubate and use lung-protective ventilation if ARDS develops 🔪 SOURCE CONTROL — drain the abscess, remove the infected line, debride the wound. Antibiotics cannot fix a collection nobody drained. 🧫 De-escalate antibiotics once cultures and sensitivities return 🩸 Glucose control — sepsis and stress raise blood glucose; follow the unit protocol 🛡️ Prophylaxis — VTE and stress-ulcer prevention 🌡️ Temperature support — warm the hypothermic patient, treat fever for comfort 🧼 Prevention is nursin

entries.h: 📈 Is it working? & what can still go wrong
entries.t: Signs you're winning: 🎯 MAP ≥65 holding with less pressor 🧪 Lactate clearing on the recheck 🚽 Urine ≥30 mL/hr ( ≈0.5 mL/kg/hr ) 🧠 Mental status improving ; skin warming with a rising BP Complications to watch for: 🫁 ARDS — refractory hypoxemia, bilateral infiltrates 🩸 DIC — clotting and bleeding at once; falling platelets, oozing IV sites 🫘 AKI — rising creatinine, anuria 💀 MODS — the endpoint of refractory shock 🧠 Careful: warm skin can mean improving (perfusion restored, BP up) or the early warm phase . Read it t

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🚿 SVR ↓↓ is the problem Cytokines → vasodilation + capillary leak. Same blood, bigger pool. 🔥→🥶 Warm then cold Warm/flushed/wide pulse pressure early · cold/mottled/narrow late ⏱️ L-C-A-F-P Lactate · Cultures · Antibiotics · Fluids 30 mL/kg · Pressors 💊 Norepinephrine first Then vasopressin. Extravasation antidote = phentolamine .

Q1: Why is early septic shock WARM and late septic shock COLD? Show answer Early: cytokines cause massive vasodilation (SVR ↓↓) and the heart compensates with a HIGH cardiac output, flinging warm blood to the skin — warm, flushed, dry, bounding pulses, wide pulse pressure. Late: capillary leak has drained the intravascular volume, sepsis-induced myocardial depression drops the output, and catecholamines plus acidosis clamp the periphery — cold, clammy, mottled, narrow pulse pressure. Warm turning cold means it is g
🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 💊 What it does ⚠️ Watch for 🗣️ Teach ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Cardio · Antihypertensive Drug Classes

Angiotensin Receptor Blockers — the "-SARTAN" drugs NG-137 CARDIO ADHD-friendly visual edition Block angiotensin II from binding the AT1 receptor — downstream in the RAAS pathway. Same end result as an ACE inhibitor (less vasoconstriction, less aldosterone, lower BP), but angiotensin II is still made — it just can't act. Because bradykinin is untouched, ARBs are the go-to substitute when a client can't tolerate the ACE-inhibitor cough . 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🔗 Paired with NG-091 ACE Inhibitor
STEP 1 · THE MECHANISM Same cascade as ACE inhibitors — the block just happens one step later.

entries.h: 🧬 The RAAS pathway — where ARBs block it
entries.t: EXAM TIP ARBs block angiotensin II at the AT1 receptor — angiotensin II is still made, it just can't bind and do its job. This is the SAME shared diagram used on the ACE Inhibitor page — compare where each class blocks the cascade. 🧠 "TAN blocks the target, not the tap." Angiotensin II still flows (the "tap" isn't shut, unlike with -pril), but it can't dock at the receptor — so it can't do its job.

entries.h: 🔤 Say the suffix — it tells you the class
entries.t: -SARTAN = ARB 🫀 Losartan (Cozaar) — 50 mg once daily PO Valsartan (Diovan) — 80–160 mg once daily PO Irbesartan (Avapro) — 150 mg once daily PO 🧠 "SAR-TAN, easy to ID-tify." Every ARB generic name ends in -sartan — no exceptions, unlike some other drug families.

Hypertension Heart failure — alternative when ACE inhibitor not tolerated Diabetic nephropathy — same renal protection as ACE inhibitors Often first-choice in Black patients on monotherapy in some guideline pathways, and when an ACE-inhibitor cough has already occurred 🧠 "Same job, no cough." Wherever you'd reach for an ACE inhibitor, an ARB is the backup plan when the cough won't quit.

entries.h: 💊 Common generics, trade names & typical adult dosing
entries.t: Generic Trade Typical dose Route Losartan Cozaar 50 mg once daily PO Valsartan Diovan 80 mg or 160 mg once daily PO Irbesartan Avapro 150 mg once daily PO Doses shown are typical starting/maintenance figures — titrate to the prescriber's order and the client's response. 🧠 All once-daily. Unlike captopril's multiple-times-a-day dosing, the ARB family is built for once-a-day adherence. ⚠️
STEP 2 · THE DANGER LIST No cough — but the same hypotension, potassium, and pregnancy risks carry straight over from the ACE inhibitors.

Biggest drop after the very first dose , same as ACE inhibitors. Give the first dose at bedtime , teach rise slowly , and use fall precautions especially in older adults. 🧠 "Both PRIL and TAN drop you fast." This is a RAAS-wide effect — identical teaching for both drug classes.

Blocking the AT1 receptor blocks aldosterone release just as effectively as blocking ACE — kidney keeps K⁺ instead of excreting it. Same monitoring: avoid salt substitutes , watch peaked T waves, check labs. 🧠 "Downstream doesn't mean different destination." ARBs block a later step, but the K⁺-sparing effect on the adrenal gland is the same as an ACE inhibitor's.

🤰 Pregnancy 2nd/3rd trimester — same fetal renal risk as ACE inhibitors 🩸 Bilateral renal artery stenosis 🍌 Hyperkalemia pre-existing 💧 Volume depletion severe dehydration 🚫 Don't combine ARB + ACE inhibitor together — no added benefit, added risk 🧠 "Never PRIL + TAN at the same time." Dual RAAS blockade raises hyperkalemia and acute kidney injury risk without improving outcomes — pick one class, not both. 🗣️
STEP 3 · WHAT THE CLIENT NEEDS TO HEAR Same rise-slowly and potassium teaching as ACE inhibitors — but no cough conversation needed.

1 🧎 Rise slowly — sit, then stand, especially the first few doses 2 🧂 Avoid salt substitutes — many contain potassium chloride 3 🧪 Routine labs — potassium & renal function 4 🚻 Confirm no pregnancy before starting; stop immediately if pregnant 5 ✅ Reassure: unlike an ACE inhibitor, this class is not expected to cause a dry cough 🧠 "Same slow rise, no dry surprise." Everything you teach for an ACE inhibitor applies here — minus the cough conversation.

NSAIDs — reduced antihypertensive effect Potassium-sparing diuretics — elevated K⁺ (hyperkalemia) Lithium — possible lithium toxicity Loop diuretics — decreased diuretic effect Hypoglycemics (insulin) — increased hypoglycemia risk 🧠 Interactions mirror the ACE inhibitor list almost line for line — because the downstream physiology they're both shutting off is the same.

entries.h: 🆚 ACE inhibitor vs ARB — tell them apart
entries.t: Feature ACE Inhibitor (-PRIL) ARB (-SARTAN) Blocks The enzyme (Angiotensin I → II) — upstream The AT1 receptor — downstream Bradykinin Builds up (ACE breaks it down normally) Unaffected Dry cough Yes — classic side effect NO — this is why it's the substitute Angiedema Yes (bradykinin-driven) Rare, lower risk Hyperkalemia Yes Yes — same mechanism First-dose hypotension Yes Yes Pregnancy Contraindicated 2nd/3rd trimester Contraindicated 2nd/3rd trimester When to choose First-line unless contraindicated Client can't t

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🫀 -SARTAN blocks the AT1 receptor, downstream — angiotensin II still forms 🚫 No bradykinin buildup no cough, minimal angiedema — the substitute for ACE intolerance 🧎 First dose give at bedtime, rise slowly — same as ACE inhibitors 🍌 Hyperkalemia same K⁺ risk, same salt-substitute teaching

Q1: Where do ARBs act in the RAAS pathway, compared to ACE inhibitors? Show answer ARBs act downstream, at the AT1 receptor, blocking angiotensin II from binding. ACE inhibitors act upstream, at the enzyme, preventing angiotensin II from being made at all. Q2: A client switches from lisinopril to losartan because of a cough. Why does this fix it? Show answer ARBs don't affect ACE, so bradykinin is broken down normally and doesn't build up — no bradykinin buildup means no cough. Q3: Should a client ever be on an ACE

The mechanism page — MI, angina & statins all start here NG-145 Cardio · Vessels ADHD-friendly visual edition Hardening & narrowing of the blood vessels, limiting blood flow (O₂ perfusion). Risk factors scar & stretch the artery lining → tiny tears → lipids, calcium & macrophages settle into the tears and build atheromas (plaque) → the artery goes hard and narrow. Then the plaque bursts, a clot forms, and it can kill the client. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🩹 Scratch → Snack → Scar → SNAP The whole
STEP 1 · WHY THE WALL TEARS Plaque never lands on a healthy wall. Something has to scratch the lining first — that is the entire story.

entries.h: 🔤 Say the word — it tells you the disease
entries.t: Athero- = gruel / porridge 🥣 — the soft fatty mush in the core of the plaque -Sclerosis = hardening 🧱 — what the wall becomes Atheroma = the plaque itself: lipids + calcium + macrophages ± clot PATHO TIP Arterio sclerosis = any hardening/stiffening of arteries (includes plain aging & calcium). Athero sclerosis = the fatty-plaque version. All atherosclerosis is arteriosclerosis; not all arteriosclerosis is atherosclerosis. 🧠 “Oatmeal in the pipes.” Picture cold oatmeal (athero = porridge) glued to the inside of a pi

entries.h: 🔬 How a scratch becomes a plaque — the foam-cell cascade
entries.t: Fatty streaks can start in childhood and adolescence . By the time she has symptoms, the wall has been building for decades — which is exactly why prevention is the nursing answer. 🧠 “Injured wall orders take-out.” The torn lining lets LDL in, LDL goes rancid , macrophages arrive to “clean up,” get stuffed (foam cells), and die right there. The garbage crew becomes the garbage.

entries.h: ⚠️ Modifiable risks — what scratches the wall
entries.t: 🚬 Smoking — direct endothelial toxin, also ↓HDL. The single biggest one she can change. 🩸 Hypertension — shear force sandblasts the lining 🍟 High LDL / low HDL , diet high in animal fats & trans fats 🍬 Diabetes / insulin resistance — sugar is chemically corrosive to endothelium ⚖️ Obesity BMI ≥30 & central (abdominal) fat 🛋️ Sedentary lifestyle · 😖 chronic stress · ☕ stimulants 🧠 “SODA” — S moke · O besity · D iabetes/ D iet · A rterial pressure. Every one of them is a hand holding sandpaper against the artery lini

entries.h: 🔒 Non-modifiable risks — what she can't change
entries.t: 🎂 Age — risk climbs for men ≥45 and women ≥55 🚻 Sex — men earlier; women's risk catches up after menopause 👪 Family history of premature CAD — a first-degree male relative <55 or female <65 🧬 Genetics — e.g. familial hypercholesterolemia = very high LDL from childhood 🌍 Health inequities — higher CVD burden in Black adults is driven largely by access, stress & social determinants, not by race itself 🧠 Non-modifiable = the deck she was dealt. Modifiable = how she plays it. Exam questions about teaching always live i

entries.h: ⭐ Source-check: two numbers people repeat wrong
entries.t: Often written as… The accurate version “Obesity = BMI over 25” 25.0–29.9 = overweight ; ≥30 = obesity . Both raise risk — just don't call 26 obese on a test. “HTN = over 140/90” Under the 2017 ACC/AHA thresholds, hypertension starts at ≥130/80 ; ≥140/90 is stage 2 . Older texts still teach 140/90 — know both. 🧠 If two sources disagree on a cut-off, the direction of the answer never changes : higher BMI, higher BP, higher LDL = more plaque. Pick the answer that lowers the number. 🧱
STEP 2 · WATCH IT CLOSE One artery, four snapshots. Learn this picture once — MI, angina and the statins page all point back to it.

entries.h: 🧱 Scratch → Snack → Scar → SNAP — the artery cross-section, stage by stage
entries.t: 1 · Scratch Endothelial injury from BP, smoke, sugar, LDL. Nothing visible yet. 2 · Snack LDL in → oxidized → macrophages eat → foam cells → fatty streak. 3 · Scar Smooth muscle + collagen build a fibrous cap ; calcium hardens it. Lumen narrows. 4 · SNAP Cap ruptures, blood hits the lipid core, platelets + fibrin = thrombus . Tissue dies. 🧠 “Scratch, Snack, Scar, SNAP.” Say it as a rhythm. Four S's, four panels, four exam answers: risk factors → cholesterol → stable angina → MI . Every other cardio page in this set

entries.h: 📈 How much narrowing before she feels it?
entries.t: EXAM TIP A plaque can sit at <50% for years with a totaly normal history and normal EKG. “No symptoms” never means “no disease.” 🧠 “70 to complain, 90 to be in pain at rest.” Around 70% she gets chest pain only when she asks the heart to work ; near 90% the pain shows up sitting still.

The scary one is not the biggest plaque. Many fatal events come from a plaque that was only moderately narrowing — but had a thin, inflamed cap . 🧠 “Thin cap = thin ice.” Thick crust holds your weight; thin crust drops you into the water. Statins are so powerful partly because they thicken and calm the cap , not just lower a number.

entries.h: 💥 What the clot does next — 3 endings
entries.t: 🧱 Plaque cap ruptures ▼ 🩸 Platelets + fibrin build a thrombus on the spot ▼ 🫀 Stays put → occludes that artery = MI (NG-071) 🧠 Breaks off → travels = embolus → ischemic stroke 🦶 Downstream → acute limb ischemia (6 P's) or mesenteric ischemia 🧠 Thrombus stays, embolus escapes. “Throm-STAYS, em-BOLTS.” Same clot, different address — and the address decides whether it's a heart attack, a stroke, or a cold blue foot. 🔎
STEP 3 · WHERE IT SHOWS UP Atherosclerosis has no symptoms of its own — it borrows the symptoms of whatever organ it starves.

entries.h: 🗺️ Main sites — same plaque, different disease name
entries.t: Site What she complains of Carotid 🧠 Carotid bruit , TIA, amaurosis fugax, ischemic stroke Coronary 🫀 Angina, MI, sudden cardiac death, ischemic cardiomyopathy Abdominal aorta 🎈 AAA — pulsatile abdominal mass, back pain. Never palpate deeply if AAA is suspected. Iliac / femoral 🦵 Intermittent claudication , cool shiny hairless legs, weak pulses, PAD (NG-045) Renal 🫘 Hypertension that won't respond to meds, rising creatinine Mesenteric 🍽️ Abdominal pain after eating ("intestinal angina"), weight loss, food fear 🧠 “C

Total cholesterol — goal <200 mg/dL LDL "Lousy" — goal <100 mg/dL (lower targets if she already has CAD/diabetes) HDL "Happy" — goal >40 mg/dL (higher is better; women's protective level runs higher) Triglycerides — goal <150 mg/dL hs-CRP — inflammation marker; supports risk staging, not a diagnosis A1c <5.7% normal — diabetes accelerates every stage on this page 🧠 L = Lousy (want it LOW) · H = Happy (want it HIGH). If the letter and the arrow both start with the same feeling, you got it right. Full drug detail on

Lipid panel — fasting is traditional; many labs now accept non-fasting for screening Carotid duplex ultrasound — non-invasive, measures % stenosis ABI (ankle-brachial index) — screens leg arteries; ≤0.90 supports PAD Coronary artery calcium score (CT) — quantifies calcified plaque burden CT angiography / cardiac catheterization — cath is the gold standard and can stent in the same visit Stress test — unmasks flow limits that rest EKG hides 🧠 Ultrasound looks, calcium score counts, cath fixes. Escalate in that order
STEP 4 · STOP THE BUILD You cannot un-build a plaque overnight — but you can stop the scratching, shrink the core and thicken the cap.

A Antiplatelet & Antilipid — aspirin/clopidogrel where indicated; a statin is the backbone (NG-242) B Blood pressure & Beta blockers — less shear force on the wall, less O₂ demand C Cholesterol diet & Cigarette cessation — smoking cessation is the highest-yield single change D Diabetes control & Diet — A1c to goal, DASH/Mediterranean pattern, less saturated & trans fat E Exercise & Education — aim for about 30 min × 5 days/week as tolerated 🧠 “ABCDE” = the alphabet of arteries. If a question asks for the priority t

🥓 LIMIT saturated fat 🍩 AVOID trans fat 🧂 LIMIT sodium 🐟 MORE fatty fish 🥣 MORE soluble fiber (oats, beans) 🥬 MORE veg & fruit 🌰 MORE nuts, olive oil 🍬 LESS refined sugar Why fiber? Soluble fiber binds bile in the gut → the liver pulls LDL out of the blood to make more bile. Same trick the bile acid sequestrants use. 🧠 “Oats mop the pipes.” Oatmeal = the porridge that fights the porridge (athero). Cute enough to stick.

🫀 Chest pain/pressure not relieved by rest → call 911, do not drive yourself 🧠 BE-FAST : Balance, Eyes, Face droop, Arm weakness, Speech, Time — stroke is atherosclerosis of the neck 🦵 6 P's : Pain, Pallor, Pulselessness, Paresthesia, Paralysis, Poikilothermia = acute limb ischemia 🎈 Tearing back/abdominal pain + pulsatile mass → possible AAA rupture, emergency 🧠 Same disease, three phone calls: chest = 911, face droop = 911, cold blue leg = 911. Plaque doesn't care which artery it lives in — the urgency is identic

Procedure What it does Nursing watch PCI / angioplasty + stent Balloon squashes the plaque, stent props the artery open Site bleeding/hematoma, distal pulses, kidney function after contrast, dual antiplatelet therapy adherence CABG Bypass graft routes blood around the blocked segment Sternal precautions, chest tubes, dysrhythmias, graft patency Carotid endarterectomy Plaque is physically peeled out of the carotid Neuro checks, neck swelling/hematoma → airway , BP control Peripheral bypass / atherectomy Restores flo

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🩹 Scratch → Snack → Scar → SNAP Injury · fatty streak · fibrous plaque · rupture + thrombus 🧱 Atheroma = lipids + calcium + macrophages in LARGE arteries 💥 Rupture > narrowing The clot on a thin-capped plaque is what kills 🚭 Priority teaching Stop smoking · statin · BP · A1c · move 30 min × 5/wk

Q1: Define atherosclerosis in one line. Show answer Hardening & narrowing of the blood vessels, limiting blood flow (O₂ perfusion) — caused by atheromas (plaque) of lipids, calcium and macrophages in large arteries. Q2: What are the four stages? Show answer Scratch (endothelial injury) → Snack (LDL + foam cells = fatty streak) → Scar (fibrous cap + calcium) → SNAP (rupture + thrombus). Q3: Which is more dangerous — a 90% stable plaque or a 50% plaque with a thin inflamed cap? Show answer The thin-capped one. It's t

The four LEFT-to-RIGHT shunts — the ACYANOTIC group NG-151 CARDIO · PEDS ADHD-friendly visual edition Four holes in four places, one story : the strong left side pushes blood back into the right side → too much blood to the lungs → a murmur , a baby who sweats while feeding , can't gain weight , and slides into heart failure & pulmonary hypertension . The baby stays pink — that is why this group is called ACYANOTIC . 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → ➡️ LEFT → RIGHT Strong left side pushes into the weak
STEP 0 · LEARN THIS ONCE Every page in this set draws on this exact same picture. Learn the normal first — a defect is only a change to one line of it.

entries.h: 🫀 The normal heart — the drawing all four pages share
entries.t: right heart · O₂-poor left heart · O₂-rich L → R shunt R → L shunt obstruction (bow-tie) 🧠 “Blue in on the left of the page, red out on the right.” Right heart (blue) is drawn on your left, left heart (red) on your right — because it is an anatomic view, facing the patient.

entries.h: 🔁 BASE NORMAL CIRCULATION — identical on every page in this set
entries.t: Say this out loud before every defect: Body ➡ SVC + IVC ➡ RIGHT ATRIUM ▼ tricuspid valve ➡ RIGHT VENTRICLE ▼ pulmonic valve ➡ PULMONARY ARTERY ➡ LUNGS (pick up O₂) ▼ pulmonary veins ➡ LEFT ATRIUM ▼ mitral valve ➡ LEFT VENTRICLE ▼ aortic valve ➡ AORTA ➡ body The LEFT side is a high-pressure pump; the RIGHT side is a low-pressure pump. That one fact predicts every shunt on every page: if there is a hole, blood takes the easy road and goes LEFT → RIGHT — back into the lungs — until something blocks the right side or r

entries.h: ⭐ THE classification you are tested on — put every defect in one of these boxes
entries.t: Group Shunt direction Pulmonary blood flow Blue? Defects 💛 ACYANOTIC LEFT → RIGHT ↑ INCREASED — too much blood to the lungs No (pink at first) ASD · VSD · PDA · AVSD 🧡 OBSTRUCTIVE none — the road is narrowed normal or ↓ , depending on where the narrowing is Usually no Pulmonic stenosis · Aortic stenosis · Coarctation of the aorta 💜 CYANOTIC RIGHT → LEFT ↓ DECREASED — blood skips the lungs YES Tetralogy of Fallot · Tricuspid atresia 🩵 MIXED both ways — red and blue blood mix varies Yes Transposition of the great art

entries.h: 🧭 How to read every diagram in this series
entries.t: Blue chambers = right heart, O₂-poor blood. Red chambers = left heart, O₂-rich blood. Topaz arrow = a LEFT → RIGHT shunt (acyanotic). Amethyst arrow = a RIGHT → LEFT shunt (cyanotic). Citrine bow-tie ▶◀ = an obstruction , a narrowed road. 🧠 Read the drawing right. It is an anatomic view, so the patient's RIGHT heart is on YOUR LEFT . That is why a “ left-to-right ” shunt arrow points ← to your left on every diagram in this series. Same picture, four pages.

Answer first: the problem is not oxygen — it is VOLUME . Extra blood is dumped back into the lungs with every beat. The lungs get wet, the heart works harder, and every calorie the baby eats gets burned just breathing. So the signs are work-of-breathing and growth signs, not blue signs: tachypnea, sweating with feeds, feeds > 30 min , poor weight gain, frequent respiratory infections. 🧠 “Pink but pooped.” The color is fine; the work is not. 🕳️
STEP 1 · SAME PICTURE, FOUR EDITS Same base heart, four times. Only one thing changes each time — where the hole is.

entries.h: 1️⃣ ASD — A trial S eptal D efect · hole between the ATRIA · ACYANOTIC, left→right
entries.t: What it is: a hole between the atria — the upper chambers. Classic sign: a systolic ejection murmur high at the left upper sternal border with a fixed, widely split S2 — the split does not change with breathing. That fixed split is the ASD giveaway. Course: many small ASDs close on their own . Larger ones are closed with a catheter-delivered occluder device or surgical repair . NCLEX TIP A murmur alone in an ASD child is expected — it is the sound of the shunt. It is not the thing you report first. Report the failu

entries.h: 2️⃣ VSD — V entricular S eptal D efect · hole between the VENTRICLES · the most common defect
entries.t: What it is: a hole between the ventricles — a septal opening in the lower chambers. Classic sign: a loud, harsh, holosystolic (whole-systole) murmur at the LEFT STERNAL BORDER — classically the lower left sternal border. Often a palpable thrill . Feeding clue from the source: grunting during feeding — the baby is working to breathe while eating. NCLEX TRAP Loud does not mean big. A small VSD makes the loudest murmur, because a tiny hole makes more turbulence. A huge VSD can be almost silent. Never rank a defect by

entries.h: 3️⃣ PDA — P atent D uctus A rteriosus · the fetal duct that never closed
entries.t: What it is: an opening that connects the AORTA to the PULMONARY ARTERY . In the fetus this duct is supposed to be open — it lets blood skip the airless lungs. It should close in the first days of life. Patent = still open. Classic sign: a loud, continuous, MACHINE-LIKE murmur — heard in systole and diastole, best at the left upper chest / under the left collarbone. Also: bounding pulses and a wide pulse pressure — the aorta is bleeding pressure off into the pulmonary artery all through diastole, so the diastolic BP

entries.h: 4️⃣ AVSD — A trio v entricular S eptal D efect · both holes + one common valve
entries.t: What it is: BOTH ASD & VSD — 2 holes: the Atria & the Ventricles — plus the tricuspid and mitral valves failing to separate, leaving one common AV valve . The middle of the heart simply did not form. Strong association: Down syndrome (trisomy 21) . If the stem says “infant with Down syndrome, murmur, poor feeding, sweating” — think AVSD. Why it is the sickest of the four: two shunts + a leaky common valve = the biggest volume load. These infants go into heart failure early , often by 6–8 weeks of life, and need sur

entries.h: ⭐ Tell the four apart by SOUND — the murmur map
entries.t: 🧠 “ A ll P eds V alves M urmur” — top to bottom on the chest: A SD high · P DA under the collarbone · V SD low sternal border · M itral/apex last. 🔎
STEP 2 · THE 4 NCLEX SIGNS The source gives four. Learn them in this order — they are how a shunt baby actually shows up.

entries.h: ⭐ The 4 signs of a left-to-right shunt — 1 sweat · 2 murmur · 3 no weight · 4 heart failure
entries.t: 1 💦 Diaphoresis DURING FEEDINGS — the baby sweats, most on the forehead and scalp. Feeding is a marathon for a failing heart. 2 🎵 Heart murmur — the sound of blood crossing the hole. 3 ⚖️ Poor weight gain — calories in, calories burned breathing. Growth stalls on the chart. 4 🚨 Increased risk: HEART FAILURE & PULMONARY HYPERTENSION — the endpoint if nobody fixes the hole. 🧠 “SMall Weight, big Heart” — S·M·W·H: S weating with feeds · M urmur · W eight won't climb · H eart failure. Four letters, four NCLEX tips.

entries.h: 💦 What “sweating with feeds” actually looks like
entries.t: Why: feeding is the hardest physical work an infant does. A heart already pumping extra volume cannot keep up, so the baby sweats, grunts, breathes fast, and quits early . 🧠 “A sweaty feed is a failing heart.” Healthy babies don't sweat through a bottle.

entries.h: ⚖️ Poor weight gain — the growth chart tells on the heart
entries.t: Answer first: weigh the infant daily, same scale, same time, same amount of clothing . A weight that will not climb — or a sudden jump — is the most sensitive peds cardiac number you have. Two different meanings: a flat weight = not enough calories / too much work. A sudden gain = fluid , i.e. heart failure. 🧠 “Slow gain = starving heart · Fast gain = drowning heart.”

entries.h: 🚨 The 5 heart-failure signs to REPORT — HF = Heavy Fluid
entries.t: ⚖️ Weight GAIN water gain 👀 Puffy eyes periorbital edema 🥶 Pale, cool extremities 🧷 Fewer wet diapers 🍼 Decreased feeding Earliest signs of heart failure in an infant are TACHYCARDIA and TACHYPNEA at rest — before the puffiness, before the weight. Why puffy eyes and not ankles? Infants lie flat. Fluid pools where gravity puts it, and in a baby that is the face and eyes , not the legs. Never wait for ankle edema in an infant. 🧠 “HF = HEAVY FLUID.” Heavy on the scale · heavy eyes · heavy breathing · light diaper. Fiv

entries.h: 📈 The ending nobody wants: too much lung blood → pulmonary HTN → the shunt REVERSES
entries.t: Answer first: once the shunt reverses, it is irreversible and the child is no longer a surgical candidate for a simple repair. This is exactly why holes get closed early instead of “watched forever.” 🧠 “Ice-man-er” — Eisenmenger. The lungs turn to stone, the pressure flips, and the pink baby goes blue . It is the one way an acyanotic defect becomes cyanotic . 🩺
STEP 3 · CLOSE IT, FEED IT, PROTECT IT Three jobs: close the hole, get calories in, and keep the heart from failing while you wait.

entries.h: 🩹 Treatment by defect — straight from the source, expanded
entries.t: Defect Hallmark Treatment Group ASD Systolic murmur + fixed split S2 Closes naturally (many small ones) · device closure in the cath lab · surgical repair Acyanotic · L→R VSD Systolic murmur at the left sternal border , loud & harsh; grunting with feeds Closes naturally (small) · surgical patch repair (large) Acyanotic · L→R PDA Loud MACHINE-LIKE continuous murmur , bounding pulses, wide pulse pressure Indomethacin or ibuprofen (NSAID) · surgical ligation / coil closure Acyanotic · L→R AVSD Early heart failure; str

entries.h: 💊 The one drug pair you must not swap — close the duct vs KEEP the duct open
entries.t: 🔒 CLOSE the duct 🔓 KEEP the duct OPEN Indomethacin · ibuprofen — NSAIDs Prostaglandin E1 (alprostadil) — a continuous IV infusion How: NSAIDs block prostaglandin , and prostaglandin is what holds the duct open. Take the prostaglandin away → the duct closes. How: gives back the prostaglandin, so the duct stays patent. When: a PDA that is dumping too much blood into the lungs — usually a premature infant. When: a duct-dependent defect, where the duct is the only path keeping the baby alive (critical coarctation, seve

entries.h: ✅ Feeding the shunt baby — calories are the treatment
entries.t: 🍼 Small, frequent feedings — big feeds exhaust them. ⏱️ Cap the feed at about 30 minutes . Longer than that costs more calories than it delivers — gavage/NG feed the rest rather than letting the baby work. 🥛 Higher-calorie formula / fortified breast milk as ordered — more calories in less volume. 😴 Cluster care and let them sleep — rest is a cardiac intervention. ⚖️ Daily weight , same scale, same time. 🧷 Count wet diapers — falling output is an early failure sign. 🧠 “Small, frequent, fortified, finished in 30.” Fo

entries.h: 💊 Holding the line until surgery: HF medications
entries.t: 💧 Diuretic — furosemide : pulls the extra lung water off. Watch potassium , daily weights, strict I&O. 💪 Digoxin : makes each beat stronger and slower. 🩸 ACE inhibitor (e.g. captopril, enalapril) : lowers afterload so the left ventricle has less resistance to push against — that shrinks the left-to-right shunt. Digoxin in peds — the parts that get tested: ❤️ Count the APICAL pulse for a full minute before every dose. 🛑 Hold and call: commonly taught parameters are apical rate < 90–110 in an infant and < 70 in an ol

🦷 Infective endocarditis prophylaxis — antibiotics ( amoxicillin is first-line) before dental and certain procedures for children with prosthetic material or valves , unrepaired cyanotic defects , or a repair with prosthetic material within the first 6 months . Good daily oral care matters more than the pill. 💉 Keep immunizations current , including influenza ; RSV prophylaxis (palivizumab) is given to infants with hemodynamically significant heart disease. 🤧 Avoid crowds & sick contacts — a shunt baby tolerates RS

SAY IT OUT LOUD ➡️ L → R = pink ASD · VSD · PDA · AVSD are all ACYANOTIC with ↑ pulmonary blood flow . 🦆 Machine-like = PDA Continuous “washing machine” murmur + bounding pulses. Duct = DUCK. 🔊 Loud harsh LSB = VSD Fixed split S2 high on the left = ASD. Down syndrome + early HF = AVSD. 💦 Sweat · murmur · no weight · HF The 4 NCLEX signs of a left-to-right shunt.

Defects 💛 ACYANOTIC LEFT → RIGHT ↑ INCREASED — too much blood to the lungs No (pink at first) ASD · VSD · PDA · AVSD 🧡 OBSTRUCTIVE none — the road is narrowed normal or ↓ , depending on where the narrowing is Usually no Pulmonic stenosis · Aortic stenosis · Coarctation of the aorta 💜 CYANOTIC RIGHT → LEFT ↓ DECREASED — blood skips the lungs YES Tetralogy of Fallot · Tricuspid atresia 🩵 MIXED both ways — red and blue blood mix varies Yes Transposition of the great art

Q1: Which way does blood shunt in ASD, VSD, PDA and AVSD, and why? Show answer LEFT → RIGHT. The left side is the high-pressure pump, so blood takes the easy road back into the low-pressure right side and returns to the lungs. Result: increased pulmonary blood flow, acyanotic. Q2: A newborn has a loud, continuous machine-like murmur and bounding pulses. Which defect, and which drug closes it? Show answer PDA — patent ductus arteriosus, the opening connecting the aorta to the pulmonary artery. Indomethacin (or ibupr

entries.h: Inotropic, Chronotropic, Dromotropic · NG-152 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 📖 Define ↕️ Directions 📋 The Table ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Cardio · Cardiac Pharmacology

Three suffixes that decode every cardiac drug question you'll ever see NG-152 Cardio ADHD-friendly visual edition Every cardiac drug — digoxin, beta blockers, CCBs, epinephrine, atropine, adenosine — can be fully described by what it does to three things: how hard the heart squeezes, how fast it beats, and how quickly the signal crosses the AV node. Learn these three words and the direction arrows, and every other cardiac drug page starts making sense together . 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 💪 INO =
STEP 1 · THE THREE WORDS Same root pattern every time: what it means, then which direction is "positive."

Ino- refers to muscle fiber/strength. Inotropic effects change how hard the ventricle squeezes with each beat — this is contractility , which drives stroke volume . 🧠 "Ino = the squeeze." Positive inotropes are the drugs you reach for when the heart isn't squeezing hard enough (cardiogenic shock, acute HF).

Chrono- = time (chronology). Chronotropic effects change how many times per minute the heart beats — driven mainly by the SA node . 🧠 "Chrono = the clock." Positive chronotropes speed the clock (atropine, epinephrine); negative chronotropes slow it (beta blockers, digoxin).

entries.h: 🛣️ Dromotropic — conduction speed through the AV node
entries.t: Dromo- = running/racetrack (like a hippodrome ). Dromotropic effects change how fast the electrical signal travels through the AV node on its way from the atria to the ventricles — the AV node is the "gatekeeper" between them. 🧠 "Dromo = the road." Think hippodrome — a racetrack. Negative dromotropes put up a toll booth at the AV node; positive dromotropes open the highway.

entries.h: 🔤 Word roots — why the syllables mean what they mean
entries.t: Ino- — Greek is / inos , "fiber, muscle" → force of the squeeze Chrono- — Greek chronos , "time" → rate , the clock Dromo- — Greek dromos , "running, racetrack" → speed through the AV node -tropic — "turning toward, affecting" 🧠 "Force, Clock, Track." Three roots, three totaly separate jobs — never let one drug's effect on one blur into your answer for another. ↕️
STEP 2 · POSITIVE vs NEGATIVE Same three words, opposite arrows — and why a nurse actually cares which way each one points.

entries.h: ↕️ Positive vs negative, side by side
entries.t: Property POSITIVE (↑) NEGATIVE (↓) Clinical relevance Inotropic force ↑ contractility → ↑ stroke volume & CO ↓ contractility → ↓ stroke volume & CO Positive inotropes support a failing pump (cardiogenic shock, acute HF); negative inotropes reduce myocardial oxygen demand Chronotropic rate ↑ heart rate ↓ heart rate Positive chronotropes treat symptomatic bradycardia; negative chronotropes treat tachyarrhythmias & reduce cardiac workload Dromotropic AV node speed ↑ conduction speed ↓ conduction speed Negative dromotr

entries.h: 🚨 The digoxin hold parameter comes from this page
entries.t: Digoxin is negative chronotropic — it slows the heart on purpose. That's exactly why you check an apical pulse for a full minute before giving it, and hold the dose and notify the provider if the apical pulse is below 60 bpm in an adult. 🧠 Slow drug + slow heart = don't stack them. The chronotropic direction of the drug is the nursing safety check.

Digoxin + a beta blocker, or digoxin + a non-dihydropyridine CCB (verapamil/diltiazem), both push chronotropic and dromotropic effects further negative — additive risk of severe bradycardia or heart block. 🧠 If two drugs both live on the "negative" side of the same dial, expect the effect to add up — not cancel out. 📋
STEP 3 · EVERY DRUG, ONE GLANCE This is the page. Every arrow below is the reason a cardiac drug is prescribed — or the reason it's dangerous in combination.

entries.h: ⭐ Core six — the drugs you'll see constantly
entries.t: Drug Inotropic Chronotropic Dromotropic Why / when Digoxin cardiac glycoside ↑ Positive ↓ Negative ↓ Negative Boosts contractility for HF while slowing rate/AV conduction for rate control in AFib — the classic "mixed" drug Beta blockers e.g. metoprolol, atenolol ↓ Negative ↓ Negative ↓ Negative Block beta-1 → all three go down together; reduces myocardial oxygen demand and rate-controls arrhythmias Calcium channel blockers non-dihydropyridine — verapamil, diltiazem ↓ Negative ↓ Negative ↓ Negative Same "all three d

entries.h: ➕ Bonus drugs from the original source graphic
entries.t: Drug Inotropic Chronotropic Dromotropic Why / when Dobutamine ↑↑ Positive ↑ Positive (mild) ↑ Positive (mild) Beta-1 selective — main job is boosting contractility in cardiogenic shock/acute HF, rate effect is a side effect to watch Dopamine ↕ dose-dependent ↕ dose-dependent ↕ dose-dependent Low dose = mostly renal/mesenteric vasodilation; higher doses recruit beta-1 (↑ force & rate) then alpha-1 (vasoconstriction) Amiodarone — to mild ↓ ↓ Negative ↓ Negative Class III antiarrhythmic; slows rate & conduction with c

Not all CCBs behave the same on this table. Non-dihydropyridines (verapamil, diltiazem) act directly on the heart — negative triad, just like a beta blocker. Dihydropyridines (amlodipine, nifedipine) mainly relax peripheral vessels and have little direct cardiac effect. 🧠 Full mechanism and teaching for both types live on the Calcium Channel Blockers page — this table is only the ino/chrono/dromo summary.

entries.h: 🎯 The one anchor to memorize first
entries.t: 🧠 "Stronger, but slower and steadier." One arrow up (force), two arrows down (rate & conduction) — that's digoxin's whole personality in one picture. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 💪 Ino = force ⏱️ Chrono = rate · 🛣️ Dromo = AV node speed. ➕ / ➖ Positive = more/faster. Negative = less/slower. Same word, opposite arrow. 📋 Beta blockers & non-DHP CCBs All three arrows down together — the "matched negative" pattern. 📋 Digoxin & atropine The two drugs where the arrows don't all point the same way.

Q1: What does "dromotropic" mean, and where does the effect happen? Show answer The speed of electrical conduction through the AV node — the gatekeeper between the atria and ventricles. Q2: A patient is on digoxin. What are its three effects? Show answer Positive inotropic (↑ contractility), negative chronotropic (↓ heart rate), negative dromotropic (↓ AV conduction) — the one drug where the arrows split. Q3: Why is adenosine effective at terminating SVT? Show answer It is profoundly negative dromotropic — it trans

entries.h: PVD — Treatments · NG-161 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🔬 Diagnose 💊 Treat 🎓 Teach ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Cardio · Pathophysiology & Pharmacology PVD set ← 1 · Patho & Signs ← 2 · Causes & Complications 3 · Treatments

Peripheral Vascular Disease III · what you actually do about it NG-161 CARDIO · PHARM ADHD-friendly visual edition Every treatment on this page is chosen by answering one question first: arterial or venous? Arterial legs get antiplatelets, statins, walking programs and DANGLING . Venous legs get compression, less standing and ELEVATION . Give the venous treatment to an arterial leg and you can cost the client the limb. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 📏 ABI ≤ 0.90 = PAD Ankle-brachial index. Normal 1.00
STEP 1 · PROVE WHICH ONE Before you treat, confirm the side. One cheap bedside number does most of the work.

entries.h: 📏 ABI — the ankle-brachial index , the single test for PAD
entries.t: ≤0.90 confirms PAD. ≤0.40 = severe — expect rest pain, ulcers, tissue loss. >1.40 is NOT “extra healthy.” It means the vessel is calcified and won't compress — common in long-standing diabetes and renal disease. The result is unreliable ; the provider orders a toe-brachial index or imaging instead. 🧠 “One is fine, under nine is a sign, over one-four is a lie.” ABI 1.0 = healthy · <0.90 = PAD · >1.40 = falsely high from stiff, calcified vessels.

entries.h: 🔊 Doppler & duplex ultrasound — listen to the flow
entries.t: Handheld Doppler — when you cannot palpate a pulse, you listen for it. Chart “Doppler-only,” never “absent,” until you've tried the Doppler. Duplex ultrasound — ultrasound + color flow. Shows where the narrowing is, how fast blood moves through it, and on the venous side shows valve reflux and clot . Venous duplex is the go-to test for suspected DVT. SEE NG-223 🧠 “Duplex = double duty.” One probe answers both questions: is the artery narrowed, and is the vein clotted or leaking backward?

Segmental limb pressures — cuffs up the leg localize the level of the block (thigh, calf, ankle). Exercise / treadmill ABI — a resting ABI can look normal; walking unmasks the drop. CT angiography / MR angiography — maps the vessels before a procedure. Contrast angiography — the invasive gold-standard map. Nursing: assess allergy (iodine/shellfish history) and kidney function (BUN/creatinine) before, hydrate after, monitor the puncture site, and check distal pulses frequently afterward. 🧠 Any test with the word “an
STEP 2 · OPEN THE PIPE Two drug jobs on the arterial side: stop platelets from clumping, and stop plaque from building. Then the mechanical fixes.

entries.h: 💊 “AC” = Anti-Clogging of Arteries — A for ASA, C for Clopidogrel
entries.t: Drug group What it does Nursing watch-outs 🅰️ ANTIPLATELET (anti-clumping) A SA · aspirin C lopidogrel Keeps platelets from clumping together on rough plaque. This is not a blood thinner in the anticoagulant sense — it stops the first step of clot formation. ⚠️ BLEEDING. Teach: soft toothbrush, electric razor, no NSAID stacking, report black tarry stools, bleeding gums, unusual bruising, blood in urine. Take aspirin with food for GI upset; report ringing in the ears (tinnitus). Held before some procedures — on prov

entries.h: 💊 The other lipid drugs you'll see beside a statin
entries.t: Ezetimibe — blocks cholesterol absorption in the small intestine. Often added when a statin alone isn't enough. Fibrates (gemfibrozil, fenofibrate) — mainly lower triglycerides . Combined with a statin they raise muscle-injury risk. Niacin — raises HDL; causes flushing . Flushing is uncomfortable, not dangerous. Bile acid sequestrants (cholestyramine, colesevelam) — bind bile in the gut. Cause constipation , and can block absorption of other drugs, so they are separated in time from other medications. 🧠 “Statin sto

entries.h: 💊 Drugs aimed at the symptom, not the plaque
entries.t: Cilostazol — improves walking distance in intermittent claudication (vasodilation + antiplatelet effect). ❌ Contraindicated in heart failure. Takes weeks to show benefit — teach the client not to quit early. Pentoxifylline — makes red cells more flexible so blood flows through narrow vessels more easily. Antihypertensives / glucose control — treat the risk factors that keep the plaque growing. Venous side: there is no “statin for veins.” If a clot forms, the drugs are anticoagulants — heparin, warfarin, DOACs. SEE

entries.h: 🛠️ INTERVENTIONS — mechanical ways to reopen or reroute
entries.t: 🩸 ARTERIAL procedures 🫙 VENOUS procedures Angioplasty ± stent — balloon opens, mesh holds. Atherectomy — shaves the plaque out. Bypass graft (e.g. femoral-popliteal) — reroutes blood around the block. Endarterectomy — surgeon strips plaque out of the vessel, classically the carotid . Amputation — last resort for gangrene. Sclerotherapy — injected agent scars a varicose vein closed. Endovenous ablation — laser/radiofrequency seals the vein. Vein ligation & stripping — the vein is tied off and removed. Debridement +
STEP 3 · THE PART THEY TEST If you only memorize one thing from all three pages, memorize the direction of the legs.

Straight from the source: “PVD with varicose veins — wear compression socks & limit standing to aid with blood return to the heart.” Compression + elevation + movement are the entire venous plan. 🧠 “Veins Vacuum UP ⬆️ · Arteries carry blood AWAY, so let them HANG ⬇️.” V for V acuum and the V shape points up . A for A way and the leg goes down . Say it before you answer any position question.

entries.h: 🅲 AVOID the C's — everything that CONSTRICTS or CHILLS the vessel
entries.t: 🦵 C — Cross legs kinks the flow 👖 C — Constrictive clothing tight socks, garters, belts 🚬 C — Cigarettes scars + vasoconstricts ☕ C — Caffeine vasoconstricts 🥶 C — Cold temperatures vasoconstricts 💅 T — Toenails trimmed ONLY by the provider / podiatrist Every C does the same thing: it makes an already-narrow vessel narrower. The T is different — it prevents a wound that a poorly perfused foot cannot heal. 🚭 Smoking cessation is the single most important teaching point in arterial disease. Nothing else on the list c

entries.h: 🚶 The walking program — pain is the dose, not the danger
entries.t: A supervised walking program is first-line therapy for stable claudication. Walking repeatedly to the point of moderate pain stimulates collateral vessels — the body's own bypass. Done regularly over weeks, pain-free walking distance increases. Stop and report instead of pushing through if pain becomes rest pain , or the foot turns cold, numb or pale — that's ischemia, not exercise. 🧠 “Walk to the pain, not through the pain.” Claudication pain during a program is expected and therapeutic. Rest pain is never therape

entries.h: 🧦 Compression stockings — right leg, right way, right time
entries.t: Confirm arterial supply first — compression on an arterial leg can cause tissue death. ABI is what tells you it's safe. Correctly sized and measured — a stocking that rolls down becomes a tourniquet. Inspect skin and pulses each time they come off. 🧠 “Stockings before standing.” Put them on before the legs fill up — once the leg is swollen, the stocking is both harder to apply and less effective.

entries.h: 👣 Foot care teaching — the checklist that saves the limb
entries.t: 🔍 Inspect both feet daily , including between the toes and the soles (a mirror helps). Report any new redness, blister, crack or sore the same day . 🧼 Wash with mild soap and lukewarm water — test the water with a thermometer or the elbow , never with the foot. Pat dry, especially between the toes. 🧴 Lotion on the tops and bottoms — not between the toes (moisture there breeds fungus and breakdown). 💅 Toenails trimmed straight across by the provider or podiatrist. Never let the client cut their own corns or calluses

entries.h: 📚 The PVD set, in one line each
entries.t: PVD set ← 1 · Patho & Signs ← 2 · Causes & Complications 3 · Treatments ＋ DVT → Page 1 — Patho & Signs: arteries can't get blood IN (cool, pale, pulseless, toe ulcers, claudication) · veins can't get blood OUT (warm, brown, swollen, medial ankle ulcers, aching). Page 2 — Causes & Complications: risk factors scar the lining → plaque → rupture → limb ischemia, MI, stroke · venous pooling → stasis ulcer, DVT, PE. Page 3 — Treatments (here): ABI proves which side · antiplatelet + statin + walking + revascularization fo

SAY IT OUT LOUD 📏 ABI Ankle ÷ arm systolic. 1.00–1.40 normal · ≤0.90 = PAD · ≤0.40 severe · >1.40 calcified & unreliable . 💊 A · C · statin A SA + C lopidogrel = anti-clumping (bleeding risk) · statin = liver toxic, NO grapefruit, muscle pain + dark urine → report . 🅲 5 C's + T C ross · C onstrict · C igarettes · C affeine · C old · T oenails by the provider only. ↕️ Direction VEINS = ELEVATE ⬆️ (Vacuum) · ARTERIES = HANG ⬇️ (Away). Compression = venous only.

Q1: The ankle systolic is 90 and the highest arm systolic is 120. What is the ABI and what does it mean? Show answer 90 ÷ 120 = 0.75 → PAD in the mild-to-moderate range (0.41–0.90). Expect intermittent claudication. Q2: A client with long-standing diabetes has an ABI of 1.6. Is their circulation excellent? Show answer No. Above 1.40 means the vessels are calcified and won't compress, so the reading is falsely high and unreliable. Expect the provider to order a toe-brachial index or imaging. Q3: A client on lovastat

entries.h: Beta Blockers · NG-176 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 💊 What it does ⚠️ Watch for 🗣️ Teach ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Cardio · Antihypertensive Drug Classes

The "-OLOL" drugs — cardioselective vs nonselective NG-176 CARDIO ADHD-friendly visual edition Block beta receptors to slow the heart down and take load off it. Beta-1 lives mostly in the heart ; beta-2 lives mostly in the lungs and blood vessels . Cardioselective drugs hit mostly beta-1; nonselective drugs hit both — which is exactly why nonselective agents are dangerous in asthma/COPD. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🫀 -OLOL = beta blocker Metoprolol, atenolol, propranolol — slows HR, drops BP, reduc
STEP 1 · THE MECHANISM One receptor map explains the whole class — where a drug lands decides what it's safe for.

EXAM TIP Cardioselective beta blockers act mainly on beta-1 receptors in the heart. Nonselective beta blockers hit both beta-1 and beta-2 — including beta-2 receptors in the bronchioles and blood vessels. 🧠 "Cardio-SELECT-ive SELECTS just the heart." Nonselective has no "select" in the name — it hits everything with a beta receptor, heart AND lungs.

entries.h: 🔤 Say the suffix — it tells you the class
entries.t: -OLOL = beta blocker 🫀 Metoprolol (Lopressor) — cardioselective Atenolol — cardioselective Propranolol (Inderal, Inderal LA, Innopran XL) — nonselective Sotalol (Betapace, Betapace AF) — nonselective, also an antiarrhythmic Timolol — nonselective; ophthalmic form treats glaucoma 🧠 "A/M come home to the heart" — A tenolol / M etoprolol are the classic cardioselective pair.

Hypertension Cardiac arrhythmias — slows conduction Heart failure (select agents, carefully titrated) Angina — reduces myocardial O₂ demand Glaucoma — timolol eye drops reduce intraocular pressure MI prevention / post-MI 🧠 4 B's from lecture: B radycardia · B P decrease · B ronchial constriction (nonselective) · B lood sugar masking.

Generic Trade Dose Route Propranolol (nonselective) Inderal, Inderal LA, Innopran XL 80–320 mg/day in 2–4 divided doses PO, IV, PO-ER Metoprolol (cardioselective) Lopressor 25–100 mg/day as a single dose PO, IV, PO-ER Sotalol Betapace, Betapace AF 80 mg twice daily PO Timolol ophthalmic 1 drop of 0.25% in each affected eye, twice daily ~ 12 hr apart Ophthalmic 🧠 Metoprolol = give on an empty stomach per label guidance — build that into medication teaching. ⚠️
STEP 2 · THE DANGER LIST Slow heart, low BP, tight airways, and a hidden blood sugar problem — check before you give, not after.

entries.h: 🩺 Hold parameters — check HR & BP before every dose
entries.t: Always follow the specific prescriber parameters on the order — hold thresholds vary by client and indication. Take HR and BP immediately before giving the dose. 🧠 "No pulse check, no pill." A beta blocker is one of the few meds where skipping the vital-sign check before administration is a med error risk in itself.

Blocking beta-2 receptors in the bronchioles removes bronchodilation and can trigger bronchospasm in a client with a history of asthma or COPD. Never give a nonselective beta blocker (like propranolol) to a client with an asthma history — use a cardioselective agent instead, and even then, use caution. 🧠 "2 for the airway, 1 for the heart." Beta-2 open airways; blocking beta-2 closes them. Cardioselective drugs try to spare that receptor — nonselective ones don't.

Normally, low blood sugar triggers a sympathetic response — tachycardia, tremor, sweating. Beta blockers blunt tachycardia and tremor , hiding two of the earliest warning signs. Diaphoresis (sweating) may be the only clue left. 🧠 "Beta blocks the alarm bell, not the fire." The hypoglycemia is still happening — the client just can't feel the usual warning signs. Teach diabetics to check blood glucose rather than rely on symptoms.

💊 Beta blocker taken daily — receptors adapt, upregulate ▼ 🛑 Abrupt discontinuation — receptors suddenly unopposed ▼ 🚨 Rebound hypertension, tachycardia, angina, MI risk Always taper the dose down over days to weeks under provider guidance — never stop cold turkey, even if the client "feels fine." 🧠 "Wean, don't wham." Same rebound-crisis warning applies to clonidine — both drugs quiet the sympathetic system, and stopping suddenly lets it come roaring back.

Cold hands/feet, dizziness, lightheadedness Confusion, depression, unusual fatigue Rash, fever, sore throat, unusual bleeding/bruising Slow pulse or difficulty breathing/wheezing 🧠 Teach the client to notify their provider for any of these — several overlap with the hold-parameter red flags. 🗣️
STEP 3 · WHAT THE CLIENT NEEDS TO HEAR Check your own pulse, never quit cold turkey, and know your diabetes symptoms may hide.

1 🩺 Check pulse before each dose — hold and call if below parameters 2 ❌ Never stop abruptly — taper only under provider guidance 3 🍬 Diabetics: check glucose, don't rely on tremor/tachycardia 4 🫁 Asthma/COPD history? Flag it before starting a nonselective agent 5 🧎 Rise slowly — orthostatic hypotension can occur 🧠 "PULSE-TAPER-SUGAR-BREATHE." Four words, four teaching points, in the order they matter most.

Antidepressants — bradycardia, increased beta-blocker effect NSAIDs — decreased beta-blocker effect Diuretics — increased hypotension Clonidine — paradoxical hypertensive effects if combined/stopped incorrectly Cimetidine, lidocaine — increased beta-blocker toxicity 🧠 Clonidine + beta blocker is a special case — if both are being stopped, the beta blocker is typically tapered off first to avoid unopposed alpha stimulation and a hypertensive spike.

entries.h: 🆚 Cardioselective vs Nonselective — tell them apart
entries.t: Feature Cardioselective Nonselective Receptors blocked Mainly β1 (heart) β1 AND β2 (heart + lungs/vessels) Examples Metoprolol, atenolol Propranolol, sotalol, timolol Asthma/COPD Preferred, still use caution Avoid — bronchoconstriction risk Diabetic hypoglycemia masking Less pronounced More pronounced Abrupt stop Never — rebound risk Never — rebound risk 🧠 "Select the heart, spare the lungs — until you go nonselective." The suffix -olol tells you the family; the selectivity tells you who's safe to give it to. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🫀 -OLOL blocks beta receptors — cardioselective (β1) vs nonselective (β1 + β2) 🫁 Nonselective + asthma = bronchospasm risk — avoid 🩺 Check HR/BP first hold below parameters, commonly HR <60 ❌ Never stop abruptly rebound HTN & tachycardia — taper only

Q1: Why is a nonselective beta blocker risky in a client with asthma? Show answer It blocks beta-2 receptors in the bronchioles too, removing bronchodilation and risking bronchospasm. Cardioselective agents mainly spare beta-2. Q2: What should the nurse do before giving a scheduled beta blocker? Show answer Check apical HR and BP; hold the dose and notify the provider if they're below the ordered parameters (commonly HR under 60 bpm). Q3: Why should a beta blocker never be stopped abruptly? Show answer The body has

entries.h: Cardiac Tamponade · NG-178 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🧨 Cause 🔎 Clues 🩺 Care ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Cardio · Pathophysiology Course Pericardial pair ← 1 · Pericarditis 2 · Cardiac Tamponade

Fluid crushes the heart — a true medical emergency NG-178 CARDIO ADHD-friendly visual edition Fluid or blood fills the pericardial sac and compresses the heart so it can't fill or pump . Blood pressure crashes fast — this can kill the client . Most often the end stage of untreated Pericarditis, NG-066 , or from acute trauma. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 💧 Fluid crushes the heart Compression on the heart = a critical client — think "C-C" for Cardiac tamponade / Compression / Critical. 🎯 Beck's triad
STEP 1 · THE SQUEEZE Same sac as pericarditis — now it's full, and the heart is the one paying the price.

entries.h: 🫀 Normal → inflamed → fluid-filled: the same sac, three stages
entries.t: EXAM TIP Tamponade is what happens when the pericardial sac fills with fluid or blood faster than it can stretch — the rigid outer layer has little give, so pressure inside rises and squeezes the heart chambers shut . 🧠 "C-C-C" for tamponade: C ardiac tamponade = C ompression on the heart = C ritical client! Three C's, one emergency.

⚡ Acute 🐢 Chronic Trauma — stabbing, gunshot, MVA Pericarditis that progresses to effusion (NG-066) MI with free wall rupture Malignancy, uremia, radiation Aortic dissection Autoimmune disease (lupus) Post cardiac surgery/procedure Chronic renal failure 🧠 "Sudden vs. slow fill." Acute causes fill the sac fast — a small volume can already be deadly because the pericardium has no time to stretch. Chronic causes fill slowly, so the sac stretches and can hold much more before symptoms appear.

The pericardium is fibrous and doesn't stretch quickly. As fluid rises, pressure inside the sac rises too — first the right atrium and ventricle collapse (low pressure chambers), then venous return falls , stroke volume falls , and cardiac output falls . 🧠 "Least resistance wins." The right side of the heart is the weakest, lowest-pressure chamber — it's the first to collapse under rising pericardial pressure. 🔎
STEP 2 · SPOT IT One triad, one pulse sign, one ugly ECG — memorize all three and you'll catch this before the crash.

entries.h: 🎯 Beck's triad — JVD + muffled heart sounds + hypotension
entries.t: B ig jugular veins ( JVD ) · E xtreme low BP (hypotension) · C an't hear heart sounds (muffled) — all three together = Beck's triad . 🧠 "BEC" spells it. B ig neck veins · E xtreme hypotension · C an't hear the heart. Three letters, three findings, one emergency.

entries.h: 🌬️ Pulsus paradoxus — systolic BP drop > 10 mmHg on inspiration
entries.t: Normally, systolic BP dips only slightly with inspiration. In tamponade, the rigid fluid-filled sac makes the ventricles compete for the same tiny space — inspiration pulls extra blood into the right heart, pushing the septum into the left ventricle and dropping left-sided stroke volume & systolic BP by more than 10 mmHg (example: 120/80 → 110/80 ). 🧠 "Paradox = backwards." You'd expect breathing to barely touch BP — in tamponade, a deep breath in visibly drops the pulse. Measure it with a manual BP cuff: note the

Fluid around the heart dampens the electrical signal reaching the skin — QRS complexes look short (low voltage) and can alternate in height beat-to-beat (electrical alternans) as the heart swings inside the fluid-filled sac. 🧠 "Muffled on paper too." If the sac muffles the heart SOUNDS, it also muffles the heart's ELECTRICAL signal — low voltage QRS is the ECG's version of Beck's triad. 🩺
STEP 3 · RELIEVE THE PRESSURE This is an emergency — the fluid has to come out, and the client needs continuous monitoring while it does.

A needle/catheter is advanced into the pericardial sac to drain the compressing fluid or blood, immediately relieving pressure on the heart. 1 🖥️ Cardiac monitor — continuous ECG throughout 2 💉 Catheter attached to a drainage system 3 📋 Assess drainage — type & speed of fluid removed 🧠 "Drain it, watch it, trend it." After the needle comes out, keep watching — if drainage suddenly slows while pressure symptoms return, the sac may be re-accumulating.

📞 Notify the provider immediately — this is an emergency 🩺 Continuous VS & cardiac monitoring, frequent BP 💧 IV access, prepare for fluids to temporarily support preload 🛏️ Position of comfort, often upright/leaning forward 😮‍💨 Reassess for worsening JVD, muffled sounds, falling BP 🧠 Beck's triad worsening = call now. Don't wait for all three to be dramatic — any one trending the wrong way is your cue to escalate.

Tamponade Tension pneumothorax Muffled heart sounds Absent breath sounds one side JVD + hypotension JVD + hypotension (both!) Trachea midline Tracheal deviation away from affected side 🧠 "Trachea tells them apart." Both cause JVD and a crashing BP — a deviated trachea points to pneumothorax, a midline trachea with muffled heart sounds points to tamponade.

Most chronic tamponade traces back to untreated pericarditis → pericardial effusion → tamponade . Review the full continuum, the friction rub, and the positional pain pattern that gives the earliest warning on NG-066 Pericarditis . 🧠 Catch it as a rub on NG-066, and you never have to treat it as tamponade on this page. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 💧 Fluid crushes the heart Compression = critical client, can kill fast 🎯 Beck's triad JVD + muffled heart sounds + hypotension 🌬️ Pulsus paradoxus Systolic BP falls >10 mmHg on inspiration 🚑 Pericardiocentesis Monitor, catheter, assess drainage

Q1: What three findings make up Beck's triad? Show answer JVD (big jugular veins), muffled/distant heart sounds, and hypotension (extreme low BP). Q2: What is pulsus paradoxus and how much of a drop counts? Show answer A systolic BP drop of more than 10 mmHg during inspiration (e.g., 120/80 falling to 110/80). Q3: What procedure relieves cardiac tamponade, and what three things does the nurse do around it? Show answer Pericardiocentesis — continuous cardiac monitor, catheter attached to a drainage system, and asses

Pulmonic stenosis · Aortic stenosis · Coarctation of the aorta — the OBSTRUCTIVE group NG-183 CARDIO · PEDS ADHD-friendly visual edition Nothing is leaking here — something is BLOCKED . A valve or a stretch of the aorta is too narrow , so the chamber behind it has to squeeze harder and gets thick (hypertrophy) . Most of these babies stay pink . The one unmissable fingerprint of coarctation is a blood pressure gap between the arms and the legs — high & bounding above, low & weak below . 📄 Simple Nursing original — o
STEP 0 · SAME PICTURE AS EVERY PAGE Same drawing as the ASD/VSD/PDA and Tetralogy pages. Nothing about the chambers changes here — the ROAD narrows, not the wall between them.

entries.h: 🫀 The normal heart — the drawing all four pages share
entries.t: right heart · O₂-poor left heart · O₂-rich L → R shunt R → L shunt obstruction (bow-tie) 🧠 “Blue in on the left of the page, red out on the right.” Right heart (blue) is drawn on your left, left heart (red) on your right — because it is an anatomic view, facing the patient.
