Defects 💛 ACYANOTIC LEFT → RIGHT ↑ INCREASED — too much blood to the lungs No (pink at first) ASD · VSD · PDA · AVSD 🧡 OBSTRUCTIVE ← YOU ARE HERE none — the road is narrowed normal or ↓ , depending on where the narrowing is Usually no Pulmonic stenosis · Aortic stenosis · Coarctation of the aorta 💜 CYANOTIC RIGHT → LEFT ↓ DECREASED — blood skips the lungs YES Tetralogy of Fallot · Tricuspid atresia 🩵 MIXED both ways — red and blue blood mix varies Yes Transposition o

entries.h: 🧭 How to read every diagram in this series
entries.t: Blue chambers = right heart, O₂-poor blood. Red chambers = left heart, O₂-rich blood. Citrine bow-tie ▶◀ = an obstruction — the star of this page, three times. Thick pale outline around a chamber = hypertrophy — that chamber is working against the block. 🧠 Read the drawing right. It is an anatomic view, so the patient's RIGHT heart is on YOUR LEFT . Same picture, four pages.

entries.h: ⭐ Why an obstructive lesion causes trouble — one sentence
entries.t: Answer first: pressure backs up behind the narrowing , and the chamber that has to push through it gets thick and eventually tired . Pulmonic stenosis backs pressure up into the right ventricle . Aortic stenosis backs pressure up into the left ventricle . Coarctation backs pressure up into everything proximal to the pinch — the left ventricle, and the vessels feeding the head and arms. 🧠 “Behind the dam, the water rises.” Whatever sits before the narrowing takes the pressure hit. 🚧
STEP 1 · SAME PICTURE, ONE PINCH EACH Same base heart, three times. Only one thing changes each time — WHERE the road narrows.

entries.h: 1️⃣ PULMONIC STENOSIS — narrowed pulmonary valve · OBSTRUCTIVE, right-sided
entries.t: What it is: the pulmonic valve (RV → pulmonary artery) is narrowed . The right ventricle must generate much higher pressure to push blood into the lungs. Classic sign: a systolic ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border , often with a palpable thrill . Mild cases can be asymptomatic and found on a routine exam. NCLEX TIP Severity, not color, drives urgency. Mild/moderate pulmonic stenosis stays pink and may just be watched. Critical pulmonic stenosis in a newborn can be duct-dependent for pulmonary blood fl

entries.h: 2️⃣ AORTIC STENOSIS — narrowed aortic valve · OBSTRUCTIVE, left-sided, the higher-stakes one
entries.t: What it is: the aortic valve (LV → aorta) is narrowed . The left ventricle — already the strongest chamber — must work even harder to push blood out to the whole body. Classic sign: a harsh systolic ejection murmur at the right upper sternal border / aortic area , radiating to the neck/carotids. May have a weak, thready pulse and narrow pulse pressure in severe cases. NCLEX TRAP Because the LV is a systemic pump, severe aortic stenosis in a newborn is an emergency — it can present as duct-dependent systemic circula

entries.h: 3️⃣ COARCTATION OF THE AORTA — a pinch in the aorta itself · OBSTRUCTIVE — makes its own BP pattern
entries.t: What it is: the aorta itself is narrowed , classically near where the ductus arteriosus attaches — just past the arch, after the vessels to the head and arms have already branched off. Classic signs: higher BP and bounding pulses in the arms , lower BP and weak or absent pulses in the legs . Cool lower extremities. Older children may report leg cramps/fatigue with exercise, headaches, or epistaxis; infants may present in shock when the PDA closes. NCLEX TIP Check BOTH arms, not just one. If the narrowing sits at or
STEP 2 · MOST TESTED One diagram, one idea: compare the arms to the legs. It is the single fastest way to catch coarctation at the bedside.

entries.h: 🚨 The hallmark assessment — BP and pulses in all four limbs
entries.t: 🧠 “High up top, low down below.” Bounding radial pulses + high arm BP, paired with weak or absent femoral pulses + low leg BP, is coarctation until proven otherwise.

Answer first: palpate a radial pulse (wrist) and a femoral pulse (groin) at the same time . Normally they arrive together. In coarctation, the femoral pulse arrives noticeably later and weaker than the radial pulse — blood is taking a slower, harder route around/through the narrowed segment to reach the legs. 🧠 “The femoral pulse is running late.” A delayed, weak femoral pulse next to a strong, on-time radial pulse is a classic bedside finding — no equipment needed.

entries.h: 🔎 Pulmonic vs Aortic vs Coarctation — tell them apart
entries.t: Pulmonic stenosis Aortic stenosis Coarctation Blocked chamber Right ventricle Left ventricle Aorta itself Murmur location Left upper sternal border Right upper sternal border, radiates to neck May be absent or heard back/interscapular Key exam clue Murmur ± thrill Weak pulses, narrow pulse pressure if severe Arm BP > leg BP , radial-femoral delay Critical newborn risk Duct-dependent pulmonary flow Duct-dependent systemic flow — shock risk Shock as PDA closes 🧠 “P is for pulmonary (right), A is for aorta (left), C i

entries.h: ⚠️ Why a “pink” diagnosis can still be an emergency
entries.t: Obstructive lesions are usually acyanotic — but severe or critical narrowing in a newborn can be duct-dependent : the baby only survives because the PDA is still open, letting blood bypass the block. As the ductus closes naturally in the first days of life , a critical obstruction can suddenly cause shock, poor perfusion, and cardiovascular collapse — this is why every newborn gets pulses and perfusion checked before discharge. 🧠 “No cyanosis ≠ no emergency.” Watch perfusion and pulses, not just skin color, in a ne
STEP 3 · FIX THE ROAD Two roads to relieve the block: catheter-based or surgical. Nursing priorities are the same for all three defects.

Defect Catheter-based option Surgical option Pulmonic stenosis Balloon valvuloplasty — usually first-line Valve repair/replacement if balloon fails or valve is dysplastic Aortic stenosis Balloon valvuloplasty Valve repair/replacement for severe or recurrent disease Coarctation Balloon angioplasty ± stent Surgical resection of the narrowed segment, especially in infants SEE NG-201 for full pre- and post-catheterization care (pulse checks, straight-leg positioning, site care) and post-surgical / chest tube care that

1 🩸 4-limb BP and pulses on admission and with every set of vitals — your baseline for catching coarctation and for comparing after repair. 2 👀 Watch for signs of heart failure — tachypnea, diaphoresis with feeds, poor weight gain — especially with moderate-severe stenosis. 3 🚨 Report poor perfusion in a newborn — weak/absent pulses, mottling, cool extremities, irritability or lethargy can mean the duct is closing on a critical lesion. 4 💊 Anticipate prostaglandin E1 orders for a duct-dependent critical lesion — ke

Echocardiogram — confirms the diagnosis and severity (gradient across the valve/narrowing). 4-extremity BP documented as its own vital sign set when coarctation is suspected. Pulse oximetry pre- and post-ductal (right hand vs a foot) can also help detect duct-dependent lesions. 🧠 “Pre vs post-ductal sats” — right hand = pre-ductal, either foot = post-ductal. A gap between them points to a duct-dependent problem.

Keep all follow-up cardiology visits — narrowing can recur (recoarctation) as the child grows. Endocarditis prophylaxis may be needed for certain dental/surgical procedures — ask the cardiologist which category applies. Report headaches, nosebleeds, leg cramps with exercise, or a new BP gap between visits. 🧠 “Fixed once doesn't mean fixed forever.” A repaired coarctation still needs a cardiologist for life. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🚧 Blocked, not leaking Pulmonic, aortic, coarctation — all OBSTRUCTIVE . The chamber behind the block hypertrophies. 🦵🤚 Arms high, legs low Coarctation's fingerprint: high BP + bounding pulses (arms) vs low BP + weak/absent pulses (legs). ⏱️ Radial-femoral delay Femoral pulse arrives late and weak compared to the radial pulse in coarctation. 🚨 Critical = duct-dependent Watch perfusion, not just color — a closing PDA can unmask a severe block fast in a newborn.

entries.h: Hypovolemic Shock · NG-184 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🧨 Cause 🔎 Clues 🪜 4 Stages 🩺 Care ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Cardio · Pathophysiology Course

The TANK is empty — hemorrhagic & non-hemorrhagic NG-184 Cardio · Shock ADHD-friendly visual edition Volume is gone. Blood loss from trauma, a gunshot wound, surgery — or fluid loss from burns , vomiting, diarrhea, or DKA. Less volume in → less preload → less cardiac output → tissue starves. The fix is not a drug. The fix is volume, and stopping the leak. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🪣 Empty tank Preload ↓↓ · CO ↓ · SVR ↑ · skin COLD, clammy, pale . 💓 Fast & narrow Tachycardia + narrowing pulse pres
STEP 1 · WHERE IT WENT Volume either left the body, or left the bloodstream and stayed inside the body. Both empty the tank.

entries.h: 🪣 The tank, and the two ways it empties
entries.t: A swollen, edematous patient can still be in hypovolemic shock. The edema is the missing volume — it's just in the wrong compartment. 🧠 “Out of the body, or out of the vessel.” Bleeding puts the volume on the floor. Burns and third spacing put it in the tissue. Either way the pump has nothing to pump.

🚗 Trauma — MVC, crush, long-bone or pelvic fracture 🔫 Gunshot / stab wound 🔪 Surgery — intra-op and post-op bleeding 🫃 GI bleed — varices, ulcer (watch for melena, hematemesis) 💥 Ruptured AAA or ruptured ectopic pregnancy 🤱 Postpartum hemorrhage — boggy uterus Hidden bleeds you can't see: chest, abdomen, retroperitoneum, pelvis, thigh. A femur fracture can hide over a liter. 🧠 “Blood on the floor + four more.” The four hidden places blood goes: chest, abdomen, pelvis/retroperitoneum, long-bone thigh . Don't rule ou

Burned capillaries leak plasma into tissue for the first 24–48 hours . The patient swells while the circulation empties. Parkland (consensus) formula: 4 mL × kg × %TBSA of lactated Ringer's in the first 24 hours — half in the first 8 hours from the TIME OF THE BURN , the rest over the next 16. Titrate to urine output , the real endpoint: ≈ 0.5 mL/kg/hr in adults (higher in children and electrical burns). 🧠 “4 · kg · TBSA — half in 8.” The clock starts when the burn happened, not when the patient arrived. If they go
STEP 2 · SPOT IT EARLY Cold, fast, dry, and not making urine — with a blood pressure that lies to you until it's late.

entries.h: ⭐ How much blood is gone? The 4 classes of hemorrhage
entries.t: Class Loss HR BP Urine Mental status I <15% (<750 mL) <100 Normal >30 mL/hr Slightly anxious II 15–30% (750–1500 mL) 100–120 Normal — but pulse pressure NARROWS 20–30 mL/hr Mildly anxious III 30–40% (1500–2000 mL) 120–140 FALLS 5–15 mL/hr Confused IV >40% (>2000 mL) >140 Profoundly low Negligible Lethargic → unresponsive Adult circulating volume is roughly 5 L ( ≈70 mL/kg ). The blood pressure does not fall until Class III — about 1.5 liters gone. 🧠 “Tennis, football, both.” Class II ≈ 15–30 %, Class III ≈ 30–40 %,

💓 Tachycardia — first, and often the only early change 🤏 Narrowing pulse pressure (diastolic rises as vessels clamp) 🥶 Cold, clammy, pale/mottled skin ; cap refill >3 sec 🫱 Weak, thready peripheral pulses 🫁 Tachypnea , then air hunger 😰 Restless, anxious → confused → lethargic 👅 Thirst , dry mucous membranes, poor skin turgor 🚽 Urine <30 mL/hr , dark and concentrated 🫗 Flat neck veins , low CVP 🧍 Orthostatic hypotension — SBP drop ≥20 mmHg or DBP drop ≥10 mmHg on standing 🧠 “FLAT and FAST.” Flat neck veins, flat CV

entries.h: 🧪 Labs — and the trap inside them
entries.t: 🩸 Hgb & Hct — may be NORMAL in the first hours of acute hemorrhage 🧪 Lactate >2 mmol/L = tissue starving; >4 = severe 🫧 ABG — metabolic acidosis, base deficit 🫘 BUN:creatinine >20:1 = prerenal (dehydration) pattern 💧 Urine specific gravity >1.030 (normal 1.005–1.030 ) , urine sodium low 🧂 Serum osmolality & sodium ↑ in pure water/fluid loss 🧠 “You can bleed to death with a normal H&H.” Treat the patient's vital signs and skin, not the hemoglobin. The number catches up hours later.

entries.h: 📊 Where hypovolemic sits among the shocks
entries.t: Type Preload (CVP/PAWP) CO SVR Skin Hypovolemic ⬅️ ↓↓ ↓ ↑ Cold, clammy, pale Cardiogenic ↑↑ ↓↓ ↑ Cold, clammy, mottled Septic — warm / early ↓ ↑ ↓↓ WARM, flushed, dry Septic — cold / late ↓ ↓ ↑ Cold, clammy, mottled Neurogenic ↓ ↓ ↓↓ WARM, dry, pink + BRADYcardia Anaphylactic ↓ ↓ ↓↓ WARM, flushed + hives / swelling 🧠 Hypovolemic and cardiogenic look identical at the skin — both cold, clammy, thready. The neck veins separate them: flat = empty tank, distended = broken pump. 🪜
STEP 3 · STAGE IT Same four stages as every shock — here they are with the bleeding patient's own findings written in.

entries.h: 🪜 The 4 stages of shock — identical on every shock page
entries.t: Stage What's happening What you see I · INITIAL Cardiac output falls just enough that cells switch to anaerobic metabolism → lactic acid builds, blood glucose rises. Nothing. Signs & symptoms are ABSENT in this stage — only a rising lactate gives it away. II · COMPENSATORY The sympathetic nervous system and renin–angiotensin–aldosterone rescue the pressure: catecholamines, vasoconstriction, ADH and aldosterone hold on to salt and water. Tachycardia · tachypnea · restless & anxious · cold clammy skin · narrowing pul

entries.h: 📈 Stage progression — hypovolemic findings on each stage
entries.t: 🧠 “15 · 30 · 40.” Under 15 % nothing shows. At 30 % the heart is racing but the cuff still lies. Past 30 % the pressure finally drops — and you are already behind. 🩺
STEP 4 · PLUG IT & FILL IT Two jobs, in this order: stop the loss, then replace the loss. Everything else is support.

1 Stop the loss — direct pressure, tourniquet, uterine massage, endoscopy, OR. You cannot out-transfuse an open artery. ▼ 2 Oxygen — high-flow; the remaining red cells must carry more ▼ 3 Two large-bore IVs ≥18 gauge (or an intraosseous line) — short and fat beats long and thin ▼ 4 Warmed isotonic crystalloid — 0.9% NS or lactated Ringer's ▼ 5 Blood products for hemorrhage — PRBCs; massive transfusion protocol gives PRBC : FFP : platelets ≈ 1:1:1 ▼ 6 Position & warm — supine, legs elevated ~20–30°, blankets and flu

entries.h: 💧 Which fluid — and why not the others
entries.t: Use Why 0.9% Normal Saline ✅ Isotonic — stays in the vessel. Large volumes can cause hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis . Lactated Ringer's ✅ Isotonic, more physiologic. Contains potassium and lactate — caution in renal failure and liver failure . PRBCs / whole blood ✅ The only fluid that also carries oxygen . Required for real hemorrhage. D5W, 0.45% NS ❌ Hypotonic — leaves the vessel and swells cells. Never a resuscitation fluid. 🧠 “Isotonic stays.” If the tank is empty you need fluid that stays in the pipes . Anyt

🌡️ Warm every fluid and blood unit — cold blood causes hypothermia and arrhythmia 🧊 The lethal triad: hypothermia + acidosis + coagulopathy — each one worsens the other two 🧪 Massive transfusion watch: low calcium (citrate binds it), high potassium , low platelets, dilutional coagulopathy 💉 Tranexamic acid (TXA) in trauma is given within 3 hours of injury 👀 Stay with the patient for the first 15 minutes of a blood transfusion — reactions happen early 🧠 “Cold, sour, leaky.” Hypothermia (cold) + acidosis (sour) + coa

🚽 Urine ≥ 30 mL/hr the best bedside endpoint 🎯 MAP ≥ 65 perfusion restored 💓 HR falling less SNS drive needed 🫱 Warm, dry skin cap refill < 3 sec 🧠 Alert & oriented brain is perfused 🧪 Lactate clearing recheck it Over-resuscitation is real: new crackles, JVD, rising CVP, dropping SpO₂ and frothy sputum mean you've pushed past the target into fluid volume overload . Slow the rate and tell the provider. 🧠 The urine bag is the cheapest hemodynamic monitor in the room. Kidneys are the first organ sacrificed and the fir

Never give hypotonic fluid to resuscitate Never lead with a vasopressor before volume Never use full Trendelenburg — legs up ~20–30° only Never wait on a hemoglobin to decide someone is bleeding Never infuse cold blood fast without a warmer 🧠 Each “never” here is a classic distractor. If an option delays volume or delays stopping the bleed, it's wrong. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🪣 Empty tank Preload ↓↓ · CO ↓ · SVR ↑ · cold, clammy, pale · flat neck veins 🤏 Narrow pulse pressure The earliest BP change — long before the systolic drops 🩸 30% before BP falls Class III (1500 mL) is when the systolic finally moves 🪜 I · C · P · R Initial → Compensatory → Progressive → Refractory

Q1: Trauma patient, BP 116/92, HR 118, RR 26, cool clammy skin, urine 20 mL/hr. What stage and what class? Show answer Compensatory (stage II), roughly Class II hemorrhage (15–30 %, 750–1500 mL). Note the narrowed pulse pressure — the diastolic climbed because the vessels are clamped down. Act now; do not wait for the systolic to fall. entries.h: Calcium Channel Blockers · NG-195 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics ⚡ What it does 🔀 Two families 👀 Watch for 🧑‍🏫 Teach ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Cardiovascular Pharmacology · Antianginal & Antihypertensive Agents

CCBs — one drug class, two very different jobs NG-195 Cardiac Drugs ADHD-friendly visual edition CCBs stop calcium from crossing into cardiac & vascular smooth muscle cells. Less calcium in the cell = the vessel relaxes and widens . But there are two families that split off from there — one only touches vessels, the other also touches the heart itself — and mixing that up is the #1 way this topic gets missed. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🚧 Ca++ can't get in Blocked calcium channel → smooth muscle re
STEP 1 · BLOCK THE DOOR Calcium is what lets muscle fibers contract — take the calcium away and the muscle relaxes.

entries.h: 🚪 Mechanism: block the calcium channel, relax the muscle
entries.t: Systemic & coronary artery smooth muscle — and the heart's own conduction cells — depend on Ca++ moving across the cell membrane to contract or fire an impulse. CCBs inhibit that calcium movement , so there's less calcium available for the muscle fiber or the nerve impulse. 🧠 “No calcium, no clench.” Whatever calcium touches — a vessel wall or the AV node — a CCB makes it let go.

💢 Hypertension — vessels dilate, resistance drops 💔 Angina pectoris — less O2 demand on the heart ⚡ Vasospastic (Prinzmetal's) angina — CCBs relax the coronary artery spasm itself 💓 Rate control in atrial fibrillation — non-DHPs only (see next section) 🧠 Prinzmetal's angina is caused by a coronary spasm , not a clot — so a drug that relaxes smooth muscle (CCB) is the answer, not an anticoagulant.

🫀 Sick sinus syndrome ⛔ 2nd or 3rd degree AV block 📉 Ventricular dysfunction — reduced ejection fraction / HF 🚨 Cardiogenic shock These matter most for the non-dihydropyridines — verapamil & diltiazem also slow the heart, so giving them to an already-slow or already-failing heart can push it over the edge. 🔀
STEP 2 · SPLIT THE CLASS Same mechanism, two different targets — this split is the single most-tested idea on this drug class.

🌸 Dihydropyridines (“-dipine”) 🫀 Non-dihydropyridines Example Amlodipine (Norvasc) Diltiazem (Cardizem) · Verapamil (Calan) Main target Peripheral & coronary blood vessels — vasodilation Blood vessels + the heart itself — vasodilation, ↓contractility, ↓conduction Effect on HR Little direct effect — can trigger reflex tachycardia as BP drops Slows HR — negative chronotropic Effect on AV node Minimal Slows AV conduction — negative dromotropic Used for Hypertension Rate control in atrial fibrillation / SVT Classic sid

entries.h: ❌ Never combine a non-dihydropyridine with a beta blocker
entries.t: Both verapamil/diltiazem and beta blockers slow the SA node, slow the AV node, and reduce contractility. Given together, those effects add up — the classic result is severe bradycardia or complete heart block . 🫀 Non-DHP CCB slows AV node + 💊 Beta blocker also slows AV node ▼ 🚨 Additive bradycardia / heart block 🧠 Two brakes on the same pedal. One drug that slows the heart is fine — two stacked on the same node is how you stall it out. 👀
STEP 3 · SIDE EFFECTS & INTERACTIONS Vasodilation causes most of these — and a few interactions raise CCB levels dangerously.

🧠 CNS: dizziness, fatigue 🫀 CV: peripheral edema, angina, bradycardia, hypotension, palpitations 🍽️ GI: gingival hyperplasia, nausea 🩸 Derm: flushing 🧠 “GEE-B-D” — Gums swell, Edema, Extra beats (palpitations), Bradycardia, Down goes BP. Vasodilation + a slower heart explains almost the whole list.
Arterioles dilate more than veins do, so pressure pushes fluid into the tissue around the ankles. This is a drug effect , not heart failure — but still assess for true HF signs to be sure.

Drug What happens Cimetidine ↑ CCB effect Theophylline ↑ theophylline toxicity Digoxin ↑ digoxin toxicity risk Rifampin ↓ CCB effect Grapefruit juice 🍇 Avoid large amounts — can raise CCB blood levels 🧠 Grapefruit is not a “safe fruit” on this drug. It blocks the enzyme that breaks the CCB down, so more drug stays in the blood.

💉 Monitor BP & pulse frequently ⚖️ Monitor I&O and daily weight 🫁 Assess for HF: peripheral edema, crackles, dyspnea, weight gain, JVD 💔 Angina: location, duration, intensity, triggers ✋ Have the client check their own pulse & report sudden changes 🧑‍🏫
STEP 4 · WHAT SHE NEEDS TO HEAR Simple, repeatable rules the patient can actually follow at home.
✋ Check your own pulse — report a sudden change 🧍 Rise slowly — dizziness/orthostatic drop is possible 🦷 Keep dental visits current — gingival hyperplasia can develop

Large amounts of grapefruit juice raise CCB blood levels. Not a strict full ban in every case, but she should ask her prescriber before making it a daily habit. 🧠 “Grapefruit turns the dose up.” One glass on its own isn't the danger — a daily habit is.

entries.h: ❌ Never stop a CCB abruptly without talking to the prescriber
entries.t: Abrupt discontinuation, especially of a non-DHP used for rate control, can rebound the heart rate/rhythm it was controlling. Taper under supervision. 🧠 Same rule as beta blockers — anything that's been braking the heart needs to be released slowly, not slammed off. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🚧 Block Ca++ = smooth muscle relaxes = vessel dilates 🌸 -dipine = vessels only = HTN = reflex tachycardia/edema risk 🫀 Diltiazem/verapamil = vessels + heart = afib rate control ❌ Non-DHP + beta blocker = additive bradycardia/heart block

Q1: What do calcium channel blockers actually block, and what does that cause? Show answer They block calcium from crossing into cardiac/vascular smooth muscle cells — less calcium means the muscle relaxes, so vessels dilate and cardiac workload drops. Q2: Amlodipine causes ankle swelling and a slightly faster heart rate. Which family is it, and why? entries.h: Cardiogenic Shock · NG-196 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🧨 Cause 🔎 Clues 🪜 4 Stages 🩺 Care ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Cardio · Pathophysiology Course

The PUMP is broken — CARDIOgenic = CARDIAC fails NG-196 Cardio · Shock ADHD-friendly visual edition The heart fails to pump blood out of the heart and to the body — like in a heart attack where heart muscle DIES , or a heart failure exacerbation . The tank is full. The pipes are fine. The motor quit. That is why this is the only shock with a HIGH preload — and the only one you must not flood with fluid. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🫀 CARDIOgenic = CARDIAC fails Preload ↑↑ · CO ↓↓ · SVR ↑ · skin cold
STEP 1 · THE MOTOR QUIT Something destroyed, stunned or disorganized the muscle — and the same volume that used to move forward now backs up.

entries.h: 🫀 Forward failure and backward failure — from one dead wall
entries.t: One failing ventricle produces both problems at once — that is why the cardiogenic patient is hypotensive AND fluid-overloaded at the same time, a combination no other shock produces. 🧠 “Cold in front, wet behind.” In front of the pump: nothing gets delivered (cold skin, low BP, no urine). Behind the pump: everything piles up (JVD, crackles, S3).

💔 Myocardial infarction — the #1 cause. Heart tissue dies and stops contracting (classically a large anterior/LV infarct) 🫀 Heart failure exacerbation — already-weak muscle decompensates ⚡ Lethal dysrhythmias — VT, rapid AF, complete heart block: no organized squeeze, no output 🎈 Acute valve failure — papillary muscle rupture → sudden mitral regurgitation 🕳️ Ventricular septal rupture post-MI 🦠 Myocarditis or cardiomyopathy 💊 Overdose of beta-blockers or calcium channel blockers 🧠 “MI, muscle, rhythm, valve.” Four

💔 Heart muscle dies or fails ▼ 📉 Stroke volume ↓ → cardiac output ↓ ▼ 🩸 BP falls → coronary arteries get less blood too ▼ 💔 More muscle becomes ischemic ▼ 🌀 Output falls further — the loop feeds itself Meanwhile the SNS raises HR and SVR to defend the BP — which raises myocardial oxygen demand on a heart that already can't get oxygen. Compensation makes it worse. 🧠 “The heart steals from itself.” Coronary arteries fill during diastole from aortic pressure. When BP falls, the pump's own supply line is the first thin
STEP 2 · READ THE TREND One set of vitals means nothing. Four sets in a row, each worse than the last — that's cardiogenic shock announcing itself.

entries.h: ⭐ The exhibit question: just look at the blood pressure
entries.t: Classic stem — a client with an MI confirmed by elevated troponin . Which complication should the nurse report? Open the exhibit and the blood pressure goes lower and lower while the pulse and respirations climb. 🧠 “Down, down, down.” If the exhibit gives you a column of blood pressures and each is lower than the one above it after an MI, the answer is cardiogenic shock — nothing else in that stem produces a steady downhill BP.

📉 Sustained hypotension — often SBP < 90 , MAP < 65 💓 Tachycardia > 100/min and dysrhythmias NCLEX TIP 🥶 Cold, clammy, mottled skin ; cap refill > 3 sec ; weak thready pulse 🎈 JVD — distended neck veins 🫁 Crackles , dyspnea, orthopnea, frothy pink-tinged sputum 🔊 S3 gallop — the sound of a volume-overloaded ventricle 😖 Chest pain , anxiety, sense of impending doom 🧠 Confusion, restlessness → lethargy 🚽 Urine < 30 mL/hr 🧠 “Cold hands, wet lungs, fat neck.” Three findings you can get in ten seconds at the bedside — a

🧪 Troponin — elevated confirms myocardial injury 📈 12-lead ECG — ST elevation, new LBBB, dysrhythmia 🫀 Echocardiogram — ejection fraction, wall motion, valve rupture (normal EF 55–70% ) 🩻 Chest X-ray — pulmonary edema, enlarged heart 🧫 BNP — elevated with volume overload/HF 🧪 Lactate ↑ , metabolic acidosis on ABG 📟 Hemodynamics: PAWP > 18 mmHg , cardiac index < 2.2 L/min/m² , SVR ↑ 🧠 High wedge + low index = cardiogenic. "Wedge" (PAWP) is a window onto the left atrium — high wedge means the left ventricle isn't emp

entries.h: 🧊💧 The COLD & WET quadrant — where cardiogenic shock lives
entries.t: 🧠 “Cold & Wet = Cardiogenic.” Both C-words. Cold skin (no forward flow) plus wet lungs (backward congestion) is the fingerprint that separates this from every other shock.

entries.h: 📊 Where cardiogenic sits among the shocks
entries.t: Type Preload (CVP/PAWP) CO SVR Skin Hypovolemic ↓↓ ↓ ↑ Cold, clammy, pale Cardiogenic ⬅️ ↑↑ ↓↓ ↑ Cold, clammy, mottled Septic — warm / early ↓ ↑ ↓↓ WARM, flushed, dry Septic — cold / late ↓ ↓ ↑ Cold, clammy, mottled Neurogenic ↓ ↓ ↓↓ WARM, dry, pink + BRADYcardia Anaphylactic ↓ ↓ ↓↓ WARM, flushed + hives / swelling Cardiogenic is the only row with an UP arrow in the preload column. 🧠 Same cold skin, opposite neck. Hypovolemic = flat neck veins. Cardiogenic = distended. That single finding tells you whether to give
STEP 3 · STAGE IT Same four stages as every shock — here they are with the failing-pump patient's own findings written in.

Signs & symptoms are ABSENT in this stage — only a rising lactate gives it away. II · COMPENSATORY The sympathetic nervous system and renin–angiotensin–aldosterone rescue the pressure: catecholamines, vasoconstriction, ADH and aldosterone hold on to salt and water. Tachycardia · tachypnea · restless & anxious · cold clammy skin · narrowing pul

entries.h: 📈 Stage progression — cardiogenic findings on each stage
entries.t: 🧠 In cardiogenic shock, stage II is a set of vitals — not one. The compensatory stage looks like “BP 128/82, HR 96” . It only reveals itself when you line it up next to the last set. 🩺
STEP 4 · HELP THE PUMP Make the heart squeeze better, make its job easier, and open the blocked artery — without drowning it in fluid.

Positive INOtropic = more forceful contraction → more blood comes OUT of the heart → cardiac output rises. That is exactly what a failing pump needs. Drug What it does Watch for Dopamine 💊 (vasopressor) Dose-dependent: low = dopaminergic (renal vessels), moderate = beta-1 inotropy & chronotropy, high = alpha-1 vasoconstriction. Tachycardia >100/min and dysrhythmias NCLEX TIP ; extravasation risk Dobutamine 💊 Nearly pure beta-1 — raises contractility and cardiac output with little vasoconstriction. The inotrope of c

entries.h: 💊 Digoxin safety — the part that gets tested
entries.t: 🫀 Take the apical pulse for a full minute before every dose — hold if under 60 and notify the provider 🧪 Typical therapeutic serum level 0.5–2.0 ng/mL (many HF protocols target the lower end) 🍌 Hypokalemia makes digoxin toxic at a normal level — watch K⁺ with any diuretic 🤢 Toxicity: anorexia, nausea/vomiting, visual changes — yellow-green halos , confusion, bradycardia, dysrhythmias 💉 Antidote: digoxin immune Fab 🧠 “Low K, high dig.” Potassium and digoxin compete for the same pump site — drop the potassium and the

entries.h: 🚨 Fluids: the exception to every other shock
entries.t: In hypovolemic and septic shock you fill the tank first . In cardiogenic shock the tank is already overfull — the pump just can't move it. ❌ No large fluid boluses in LV cardiogenic shock — they cause flash pulmonary edema ✅ Careful diuresis (e.g. IV furosemide) to unload the congested lungs, guided by BP ✅ Nitrates reduce preload and afterload — only if the blood pressure tolerates it ⚠️ Exception to the exception: a RIGHT ventricular infarct (with an inferior MI) presents with hypotension, JVD and CLEAR lungs — t

The real cure for MI-related cardiogenic shock is opening the artery — emergency cardiac catheterization with PCI (or CABG). Everything else is a bridge to that. 🎈 IABP — intra-aortic balloon pump, as drawn above 🔩 Impella / VAD — pumps that take over ventricular work 🫁 ECMO — bypasses heart and lungs entirely in the sickest patients 🩺 Treat the rhythm — cardiovert/defibrillate, pace a bradycardia 🫀 Reduce oxygen demand — rest, pain control, anxiety control, correct hypoxia and anemia 🧠 “IN with diastole, OUT with

entries.h: 🐝 Also on this source card: ANAPHYLACTIC shock
entries.t: A severe allergic reaction — bee sting, peanut, shellfish, latex, penicillin, contrast dye. Mast cells dump histamine, vessels dilate everywhere, capillaries leak, and the airway swells shut. It is a distributive (pipe) shock, not a pump problem. 🚨 What you see ✅ What you do Hives/urticaria · flushing · angiedema of lips & tongue · stridor · wheezing · throat tightness · hypotension · tachycardia · GI cramping/vomiting · sense of impending doom 1. Show answer Cardiogenic shock. Alert the primary health care provider immediately — the steadily falling blood pressure with rising pulse and respirations after an MI is the classic exhibit pattern. Three different diseases of the heart muscle itself — dilated, hypertrophic, restrictive NG-197 CARDIO ADHD-friendly visual edition Cardiomyopathy is disease of the heart muscle itself, and it comes in three shapes: Dilated (a stretched, floppy muscle), Hypertrophic (a huge, thickened muscle that can block outflow), and Restrictive (a rock-hard, stiff muscle that can't relax). All three end the same way — LESS cardiac output, LESS oxygen-rich blood out to the body. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🎈 Dil
STEP 1 · THREE SHAPES, ONE PROBLEM Same end result — less cardiac output — but the muscle gets there three completely different ways. The shape tells you everything else.

entries.h: 🫀 Heart-shape comparison: how each chamber geometry differs from normal
entries.t: EXAM TIP All three cardiomyopathies drop cardiac output — but they get a very different-shaped heart to do it. 🧠 "Distended, Trophy, Rock-hard." D ilated = D istended thin balloon. H ypertrophic = H uge trophy-like muscle in the septum. R estrictive = R ock-hard, can't RE-fill. Say the shape, get the disease.

Fibrosis (stiff, hard scarring) of the myocardium & endocardium plus dilated chambers — a stretched, floppy muscle that struggles to squeeze oxygen-rich blood out. Common causes: ischemic heart disease, viral myocarditis, chronic alcohol use, peripartum, idiopathic. 🧠 A worn-out rubber band stretched too many times — it still moves, but the snap (squeeze) is gone.

The muscle — especially the septum — grows huge and thick, which can obstruct the aortic valve/outflow tract , blocking oxygenated blood from reaching the body. Obstructive Non-obstructive Blocks the aortic valve outflow Does not block outflow 🧠 Mostly genetic (autosomal dominant) — the #1 reason to screen family members of a young sudden cardiac death victim.

The heart muscle becomes stiff and can't RE -fill during diastole — REstrictive . Emboli (blood clots) are common because blood stagnates in a chamber that won't relax and empty well. Common causes: amyloidosis, sarcoidosis, hemochromatosis, endomyocardial fibrosis. 🧠 A rock doesn't stretch to catch water — a stiff ventricle doesn't stretch to catch returning blood. 🔎
STEP 2 · SPOT IT A murmur that breaks the normal rules, a lab that grades how bad the failure is, and the sign that makes hypertrophic the deadliest of the three.

entries.h: 🚨 Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy — sudden cardiac death in young athletes
entries.t: Typically asymptomatic — no s/s — until heavy exercise , when the thickened septum obstructs outflow during high demand and the client can die suddenly . This is why HCM is the classic cause of sudden collapse in young, seemingly healthy athletes. 🧠 "Fine until the finish line." A perfectly healthy-looking teen athlete who collapses during a game is the textbook HCM story — screen family history before it happens, not after.

entries.h: 🔊 The murmur that breaks the rules — louder with Valsalva/standing
entries.t: Most murmurs get quieter when preload drops (Valsalva strain, standing) because there's less blood to make noise. HCM is the opposite: less blood in the ventricle lets the thick septum obstruct the outflow tract more , so the murmur gets LOUDER . Squatting or lying down (more preload) makes it softer . 🧠 "HCM plays by opposite rules." If a murmur gets LOUDER with Valsalva or standing, and softer with squatting/lying flat — that's hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, not a normal flow murmur.

entries.h: 🧪 BNP — grades how bad the failure is
entries.t: B-type (brain) natriuretic peptide is released when ventricles stretch/strain — the higher it climbs, the worse the heart failure. 🧠 Bigger number = bigger stretch. BNP is the heart shouting how hard it's straining to keep up.

😮‍💨 Low oxygen, fatigue, dizziness, syncope 😵 Restlessness, agitation, altered LOC (poor perfusion) 🫁 Left-sided failure → lung fluid (crackles) 💧 Right-sided failure → edema, ascites, JVD 🔊 New murmur (often S3 ), cardiomegaly 🧠 Same heart-failure playbook you already know — cardiomyopathy is just the muscle problem causing it.

📷 Chest X-ray & MRI — chamber size & wall thickness 🫀 Echocardiogram — measures ejection fraction (EF) : 55–70% normal, ≤40% = heart failure range 🩻 Angiography — highlights coronary arteries, rules out ischemic heart disease as the cause 🧠 EF tells you the pump strength; angiography tells you why. Rule out a blocked artery before calling it a primary cardiomyopathy. 🩺
STEP 3 · PROTECT THE PUMP Pharmacology flips for hypertrophic — know the "NO DDD" rule cold, and check three numbers before every digoxin dose.

✅ Give — reduce contractility, slow HR, let it fill ❌ NO DDD — worsens the obstruction B eta blockers D ilators C alcium channel blockers D igoxin D iuretics 🧠 "BC, no DDD." Beta blockers & Calcium channel blockers slow the heart and give it more time to fill around the obstruction. Dilators, Digoxin, and Diuretics all shrink ventricular volume or boost contractility — both make the outflow obstruction worse .

entries.h: 🚨 Digoxin — hold if any of these three
entries.t: 1 💓 Apical pulse below 60 bpm 2 🧪 Potassium (K+) below 3.5 — raises risk of dig toxicity 3 🧪 Digoxin level over 2.0 — toxic Toxicity signs: vision changes (halos, yellow-green tint), nausea/vomiting, fatigue, dizziness. 🧠 "Pulse, Potassium, Peak level" — the 3 P's to check before you push dig. Any one abnormal = hold and notify.

NO strenuous activity — especially HCM, can worsen aortic outflow blockage ⚖️ Daily weights, strict I&O for fluid status 🧂 Sodium/fluid restriction as ordered for HF symptoms 🚨 Teach family of HCM clients: screening & sudden death risk with exertion 🧠 "Rest the trophy." A hypertrophied heart already fights its own outflow tract — heavy exertion is the thing most likely to push it over the edge.

Type Muscle Chamber Classic risk Dilated Stretched, floppy Enlarged, thin-walled Progressive heart failure, S3 Hypertrophic Thick septum Small, obstructed outflow Sudden death in young athletes , louder murmur w/ Valsalva Restrictive Rock-hard, stiff Normal/small, can't fill Emboli, diastolic failure 🧠 One table, three whole diseases — if you can fill in every cell from memory, you know NG-197 cold. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🎈 Dilated Distended, floppy, weak squeeze — S3, cardiomegaly 🏆 Hypertrophic Sudden death in young athletes; murmur LOUDER with Valsalva/standing 🧱 Restrictive Rock-hard, can't refill, emboli common 🚫 NO DDD in HCM No Dilators, Digoxin, Diuretics — check pulse/K+/level before any dose

Cardiac catheterization, post-op care, and the 3-chamber chest drainage system NG-201 CARDIO · PEDS ADHD-friendly visual edition Whichever defect a child has — hole, block, or blue baby — surgery or a cardiac catheter procedure is usually the definitive fix. This page is the after : what you assess before, what you watch for after, and how to manage the chest tube that comes home from the OR with almost every open-heart repair. Know your 3 chambers cold — it is one of the most-tested skills in peds cardiac nursing.
STEP 0 · SAME PICTURE AS EVERY PAGE Same drawing as the rest of the set. Every defect on every page — hole, block, or blue baby — can end up here: the OR or the cath lab.

entries.h: 🫀 The normal heart — the drawing all four pages share
entries.t: right heart · O₂-poor left heart · O₂-rich L → R shunt R → L shunt obstruction (bow-tie) 🧠 “Blue in on the left of the page, red out on the right.” Right heart (blue) is drawn on your left, left heart (red) on your right — an anatomic view, facing the patient.

entries.h: ⭐ Every group on this page's set, and how each gets fixed
entries.t: Group Shunt / flow Fixed by 💛 ACYANOTIC LEFT → RIGHT, ↑ pulmonary flow Device closure (cath) or surgical patch 🧡 OBSTRUCTIVE narrowed road Balloon valvuloplasty/angioplasty (cath) or surgical repair 💜 CYANOTIC RIGHT → LEFT, ↓ pulmonary flow Surgical repair — usually open-heart 🩵 MIXED both ways Staged surgical repair 🧠 “Cath first when you can, cut when you must.” Many holes and blocks close with a catheter device or balloon. Cyanotic and mixed defects — and blocks that fail catheter repair — need open-heart surger

entries.h: 🔁 Two routes to the same goal — cath lab vs OR
entries.t: Cardiac catheterization Open-heart surgery Access Femoral vein/artery — no chest incision Sternotomy (chest incision) Used for ASD/VSD/PDA device closure, balloon valvuloplasty, balloon angioplasty ± stent for coarctation Complex repairs — Tetralogy, transposition, large VSDs, coarctation resection Chest tube? Usually none Yes — placed during surgery to drain the chest Recovery focus Access-site & pulse checks Incision, pain, respiratory effort, chest tube 🧠 “No cut, no tube.” A chest tube almost always means the c
STEP 1 · SET THE BASELINE Whatever you assess before the procedure is what you compare everything to afterward.

entries.h: 🚨 Ask about an iodine / contrast allergy
entries.t: Cardiac catheterization uses iodinated contrast dye . An iodine or shellfish allergy history must be flagged before the procedure — the team may premedicate or choose an alternate approach. 🧠 “Dye day, ask about iodine.” Any procedure with contrast = ask the allergy question.

Children are typically kept NPO around 4–6 hours before a cath or surgery requiring sedation; infants often get a shorter NPO window because they tolerate fasting less well and are at higher risk for hypoglycemia. Exact hours vary by facility protocol and anesthesia team — always confirm the order. 🧠 “Littler belly, shorter wait.” Infants generally get shorter NPO times than older children.

Weight in kilograms — needed later to judge chest tube drainage rates. Baseline vital signs and O₂ saturation. Mark and document baseline pulses in both extremities — you will compare post-procedure pulses to this. 🧠 “Can't know what changed if you never charted normal.”

Age-appropriate teaching, honest and simple explanations, comfort items from home, and — when the unit allows it — a parent present for induction can meaningfully reduce a child's fear and distress. 🧠 “Prep the parent, calm the child.” An anxious caregiver makes a harder induction.

entries.h: 🩺 What a cardiac catheterization actually does
entries.t: A thin catheter is threaded through the femoral vessels up to the heart. It can be diagnostic (pressures, oxygen saturations, angiography to map the anatomy) or interventional — closing a hole with a device, opening a narrowed valve with a balloon, or placing a stent in a narrowed vessel. 🧠 “Same door, two jobs.” The femoral approach can look, or it can fix — sometimes both in one trip. 🔎
STEP 2 · MOST TESTED Answer first: after a cath, the #1 priority is the pulse below the site. After surgery, it is airway/breathing and the incision.

entries.h: 🚨 PRIORITY #1 after cardiac catheterization — pulses distal to the site
entries.t: Check the pulse below (distal to) the femoral access site frequently in the first hours — often per protocol every 15 minutes initially, then tapering. Expected/normal: a weak but present pulse right after the procedure, warm foot, brisk capillary refill. REPORT NOW A cool, cold, pale, or pulseless extremity distal to the site — this can mean arterial occlusion or thrombosis and needs the provider immediately. Keep the leg straight for roughly 4–8 hours post-cath (per facility protocol) to protect the access site f

Assess for bleeding or an expanding hematoma at the site. No baths / no submerging the site until it's healed — infection risk. Watch for signs of infection at the puncture site. 🧠 “Dry, flat, warm below.” Dry site, flat (no swelling), and a warm limb below = a good site check.

Cool, cold, pale, or pulseless extremity distal to the site. Bleeding, swelling, or a new/expanding hematoma at the site. Fever, warmth, or purulent drainage at any surgical/access site. Significant skin breakdown (for example, severe diaper rash) from prolonged bedrest/immobility in an infant — keep skin clean, dry, and pressure-relieved. 🧠 “Cold, hot, wet, sore — say something.”

Elevate the head of the bed after surgery — this reduces the work of breathing. Manage pain proactively so the child can breathe deeply, cough, and reposition — undertreated pain slows respiratory recovery. Restrict heavy lifting/strenuous activity for roughly 3–4 weeks after sternotomy while the bone and incision heal — follow the surgeon's specific activity order. Teach families to report fever, a warm/red incision, or foul-smelling purulent drainage — signs of surgical site infection. 🧠 “Sit up, ease up, watch t
STEP 3 · THE HIGH-YIELD SKILL Chest tubes drain excess blood, fluid, and air after cardiac surgery so the lungs can fully re-expand and blood doesn't collect around the heart.

entries.h: 🫧 The 3 chambers, in order — patient → collection → water seal → suction control → wall
entries.t: 🧠 “Catch it, seal it, control it.” ① Catch the drainage (collection) → ② Seal the chest so air can't come back in (water seal) → ③ Control how much suction reaches the chest (suction control).

entries.h: ① Collection chamber — what it does
entries.t: The nearest chamber to the patient. All drainage flows in here first and collects in graduated (marked) columns so you can measure the amount over time. Every time you round: note the amount, color, and consistency of drainage, and mark the level with the time so trends are visible at a glance. 🧠 “The measuring cup.” This chamber is purely for collecting and measuring — nothing else happens here.

entries.h: ② Water seal chamber — what it does
entries.t: A tube sits submerged a couple of centimeters under sterile water. This creates a one-way valve : air and fluid can bubble out of the chest, but water blocks air from being sucked back in . Watch the water level here for tidaling (normal) and bubbling (can be normal or abnormal — see the cards below). 🧠 “The one-way door.” Air can leave through it; nothing gets back in through it.

entries.h: ③ Suction control chamber — what it does
entries.t: Connected to wall suction . It regulates how much negative pressure actually reaches the chest — turning the wall suction dial up does not increase chest suction; the water level (or a dry-suction dial) sets that. Gentle, continuous bubbling in this chamber is expected and normal — it just means suction is working. 🧠 “The pressure regulator.” This chamber decides how hard the system pulls — the wall dial doesn't.

Expected Alarming — report Color Sanguineous → serosanguineous, getting lighter over time Sudden return to bright red, frank blood Rate Steadily decreasing hour to hour A sudden increase, or output cited in some protocols as roughly >3 mL/kg/hr sustained (thresholds vary — follow facility policy ) Dressing Dry to lightly stained Saturated dressing / visibly pooling blood Patient Stable vitals ↑HR, ↓BP, muffled heart sounds — think tamponade SOURCE NOTE Some course materials also cite roughly >5–10 mL/kg in the firs

entries.h: 〰️ TIDALING — what it means, and how to tell why it stopped
entries.t: Answer first: tidaling is the water level in the water-seal tube rising and falling with breathing — it rises with inspiration and falls with expiration in a spontaneously breathing patient (this reverses on positive-pressure ventilation). Tidaling means the tube is patent and there is still air space to fill — it is normal. Tidaling stops because… ✅ Lung has re-expanded ❌ Tube is kinked / clamped / obstructed Breath sounds Improved, equal, clear Decreased or absent on that side Respiratory effort Comfortable, easy

entries.h: 🚨 Continuous bubbling in the WATER SEAL chamber = an AIR LEAK
entries.t: Intermittent bubbling in the water seal chamber — for example, with a cough or forceful exhale — can be a normal transient finding as trapped air escapes. Continuous, vigorous bubbling in the water seal chamber is abnormal — it means air is continuously entering the system, either from the patient's pleural space (an air leak in the lung) or from a loose connection or crack somewhere in the tubing/system. FIRST STEP Check every connection along the tubing for a loose fitting before assuming the leak is coming from

entries.h: ✅ Routine chest tube care — do this every shift
entries.t: ⬇️ Keep the unit below chest level always 📏 Keep it upright never on its side 🌀 Keep tubing free of kinks/loops check every round 🩹 Keep dressing occlusive reinforce, don't remove 🧰 Bedside kit: sterile gauze, tape, sterile water, clamp ready before you need it 🚶 Encourage deep breathing helps re-expansion POLICY VARIES Routine stripping/milking of chest tube tubing and routine clamping are generally avoided outside of specific ordered situations — both practices vary by facility policy, so follow your unit's proto
STEP 4 · ACT FAST Both are rare, both are tested, and they are NOT the same problem — know which one you're looking at before you act.

entries.h: 🚨 Emergency 1 — the chest tube comes OUT of the patient
entries.t: 1 🩹 Cover the insertion site immediately with sterile occlusive gauze, taped on 3 sides only. The open 4th side acts like a one-way flutter valve — air can escape but is less likely to be pulled back in. 2 🧍 Stay with the patient and assess breathing/color continuously. 3 📞 Call for help immediately — this needs provider evaluation and likely a new tube. 🧠 “3 sides, not 4.” Taping all 4 sides can trap air inside the chest and cause a tension pneumothorax — always leave one side open.

entries.h: 🚨 Emergency 2 — the tubing DISCONNECTS from the drainage unit
entries.t: Here the tube is still in the patient — only the connection to the collection unit came apart. Two approaches are taught; follow your instructor/facility's specific policy : Submerge in sterile water Clamp near the chest What you do Put the open tubing end ~2 cm under sterile water Briefly clamp the tubing close to the chest wall Why Recreates the one-way water-seal effect right away Temporarily stops air from moving through the open tube Watch for Get a new sterile system connected as soon as possible Unclamp the

Tube pulled OUT of patient Tubing disconnects from unit Where's the break? At the chest wall / insertion site Somewhere along the tubing, away from the chest Immediate action Sterile gauze, taped on 3 sides Submerge end in sterile water or clamp, per policy Shared steps Stay with the patient · assess airway/breathing/color · call for help right away ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🩸 Pulses first, after a cath Weak = expected. Cool/pale/pulseless = call. Straight leg, no baths on the site. 🫧 Catch → Seal → Control Collection measures it, water seal keeps air from re-entering, suction control sets the pressure. 〰️ Tidaling stops = check WHY Good breath sounds + no kink = lung re-expanded. Bad breath sounds + a visible kink = fix the tube, then call. 🚨 Continuous bubbling ≠ suction chamber Water seal chamber bubbling continuously = air leak . Suction chamber gentle bubbling = no

Tube OUT of patient Tubing disconnects from unit Do this first Sterile gauze taped on 3 sides Submerge in sterile water or clamp — per your policy Then Stay with the patient · call for help immediately 🧠 “3 sides for a hole, water or a clamp for a break.” BASE → BEFORE → AFTER → CHEST TUBES → EMERGENCIES NG-201 · Congenital heart defects · NUR 235 peds · ADHD-friendly visual edition

Lanoxin — the classic narrow therapeutic index drug NG-208 Cardiac Drugs ADHD-friendly visual edition Digoxin makes the heart squeeze harder and beat slower — great for heart failure and atrial fibrillation, terrible if the dose creeps even a little too high. Narrow therapeutic index means the safe dose and the toxic dose are close together — this is the drug that punishes skipped assessments. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 💪 Squeeze harder, beat slower +inotropic (↑contractility), −chronotropic (↓HR)
STEP 1 · SQUEEZE + SLOW Two effects, three big words — memorize the words and the drug makes sense.

entries.h: 💓 Mechanism: positive inotrope, negative chronotrope & dromotrope
entries.t: Digoxin increases cardiac output through positive inotropic activity — an increase in the force of contraction. It also slows conduction velocity through the AV node (negative dromotropic effect) and decreases heart rate (negative chronotropic effect). 🧠 “INO up, CHRONO & DROMO down.” Ino = force (up). Chrono = rate (down). Dromo = conduction speed through the AV node (down). One drug, opposite directions on purpose.
📉 Heart failure — stronger contraction improves cardiac output 💓 Atrial fibrillation — slows AV conduction to control ventricular rate
Digitalis toxicity, known hypersensitivity Ventricular fibrillation / ventricular tachycardia Cardiac tamponade, restrictive cardiomyopathy AV block 👀
STEP 2 · TOXICITY — NARROW MARGIN The therapeutic dose and the toxic dose sit close together — this is why every dose gets checked.

Levels drawn immediately before the next dose (trough), or 6–8 hours after the last dose regardless of route. Above roughly 2 ng/mL is considered toxic and is reported to the provider. below 0.8 sub-therapeutic 0.8 – 2 ng/mL THERAPEUTIC above 2 TOXIC

👁️ Visual disturbances — blurring, yellow-green halos ("Van Gogh vision") 🍽️ GI: nausea, anorexia 💓 Arrhythmias 🧠 Confusion — especially in older adults 😴 Weakness, drowsiness, headache 🧠 “Yellow halo = too much Lanoxin.” If a patient describes lights with a yellow-green ring, think digoxin toxicity first.

Potassium and digoxin compete for the same binding site on the pump. When K+ is low, there's less competition — more digoxin binds , increasing the chance of toxicity even at a "normal" dose. 🧠 Thiazide & loop diuretics cause hypokalemia — giving them alongside digoxin is a classic setup for toxicity. Watch potassium closely.
Thyroid hormone — decreases digoxin's effect Thiazide/loop diuretics — increase hypokalemia risk → increased digoxin toxicity risk
For serious toxicity, digoxin immune Fab binds free digoxin so it can no longer act on the heart — used for life-threatening arrhythmias or a significantly elevated level. 🧑‍🏫
STEP 3 · THE RULE THAT PREVENTS THE ER VISIT One physical assessment, done correctly, catches most problems before they become toxicity.

entries.h: ✋ Apical pulse for a FULL minute before every dose
entries.t: Count the apical pulse (not radial) for a full 60 seconds before administering. If the rate is <60 bpm in an adult, hold the dose and notify the provider — don't give it and hope. 🧠 “Apical, full minute, under 60 — don't give it.” Radial pulses can miss irregular or weak beats; the apex catches the true rate the drug is acting on.

✋ Check your own pulse before each dose; report a rate under 60 or a big change ⚖️ Weigh daily — sudden gain can signal worsening HF 👁️ Report visual changes, nausea, confusion right away 💊 Never double up a missed dose

In children, the dose is withheld and the provider notified if the apical pulse is below 70 bpm ; in infants, below 90 bpm . Kids run faster baseline heart rates, so the hold threshold is higher than the adult 60 bpm rule. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 💪 +Inotrope, −chrono/dromotrope stronger squeeze, slower/less-conducted beat 🧪 0.8–2 ng/mL therapeutic range — above is toxic ✋ Apical × 1 min, hold if <60 notify the provider, don't give 🟡 Yellow-green halos classic toxicity sign · antidote = DigiFab

Q1: Name digoxin's three cardiac effects in one sentence. Show answer Positive inotrope (↑force of contraction), negative chronotrope (↓heart rate), negative dromotrope (↓AV node conduction). Q2: A patient's digoxin level comes back at 2.6 ng/mL. What does that mean? Show answer That's above the therapeutic range of 0.8–2 ng/mL — it's a toxic level and should be reported to the provider. Q3: Why does hypokalemia increase the risk of digoxin toxicity? Show answer Potassium and digoxin compete for the same binding si
🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics ⚡ What it does 👀 Watch for 🧑‍🏫 Teach ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Cardiovascular Pharmacology · Antianginal Agents

Nitroglycerin & the nitrate family NG-216 Cardiac Drugs ADHD-friendly visual edition Nitrates release nitric oxide , which relaxes the smooth muscle layer of blood vessels — widening the artery/arteriole and letting more blood (and O2) flow through . That's the whole drug in one sentence. Everything else is protocol, tolerance, and one absolute interaction that can kill. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🩸 NO = vessels open Nitric oxide relaxes smooth muscle → vessels widen → less O2 demand on the heart.
STEP 1 · OPEN THE PIPES One gas molecule explains the entire drug class.

entries.h: 🩸 Mechanism: nitric oxide relaxes the vessel wall
entries.t: Nitrates relax the smooth muscle layer of blood vessels , increasing the lumen of the artery or arteriole and increasing the amount of blood flowing through. Veins dilate more than arteries — so the biggest effect is less blood returning to the heart (↓preload) , which means less work and less O2 demand for the heart muscle. 🧠 “NO means GO.” Nitric oxide (NO) = the vessel opens up and blood GOes through. The whole point is to make the heart's job easier, not to fix a clot.

🚨 Relieve pain of an acute anginal attack 🛡️ Prevent angina attacks — prophylaxis 💔 Treat chronic stable angina pectoris 🧠 Three jobs, one mechanism: rescue (SL, acute), prevention (long-acting forms), maintenance (chronic stable angina).
👅 Sublingual tablet or spray — rescue, fast onset 🩹 Transdermal patch / ointment — steady, long-acting 💊 Oral extended-release — scheduled prevention 💉 IV — acute, closely monitored settings 👀
STEP 2 · SIDE EFFECTS & THE ONE ABSOLUTE NO Most side effects are just vasodilation happening where you don't want it — one interaction is never optional.
🧠 CNS: headache (can be severe/persistent), dizziness, weakness, restlessness 🩸 CV: hypotension, flushing (surface capillaries dilating) 🌸 Derm: rash

entries.h: 🤕 Headache is EXPECTED — not a reason to stop
entries.t: The same vasodilation that relieves chest pain also dilates cerebral vessels. Headache is a common, benign side effect — it usually eases with continued use and can be treated with a mild analgesic. 🧠 “No headache, no nitrate.” Ironically, a mild headache is often a sign the drug is working — don't let the patient stop it on their own for this alone.

Sildenafil, tadalafil, and vardenafil (drugs for erectile dysfunction / pulmonary hypertension) both cause vasodilation through the same nitric-oxide pathway. Combined with a nitrate, the two vasodilating effects stack — the result can be severe, life-threatening hypotension and cardiovascular collapse . Always ask about ED medication use before giving a nitrate, and never give a nitrate to a patient who has recently taken one. 🧠 “Two vasodilators, one blood pressure to crash.” Always ask before you give — this is
Vasodilation drops BP — teach the patient to sit or lie down before taking a nitrate and to rise slowly afterward to avoid fainting.

Known hypersensitivity to the drug Severe anemia Closed-angle glaucoma Head trauma / cerebral hemorrhage — vasodilation can worsen intracranial pressure Constrictive pericarditis Allergy to adhesive (transdermal forms)

entries.h: 🌙 Tolerance — why a nitrate-free interval matters
entries.t: With continuous exposure (long-acting oral, ointment, or patch forms), blood vessels stop responding to the nitrate — the drug simply quits working as well. Scheduling a daily nitrate-free interval (commonly overnight) lets the vessels "reset" so the next dose works again. 🧠 “No break, no bang.” Skip the nitrate-free window and the drug quietly stops protecting against angina, even though the patch is still on. 🧑‍🏫
STEP 3 · THE CHEST PAIN PROTOCOL One protocol she should be able to say in her sleep.

entries.h: 🚨 Sublingual nitro for chest pain — the protocol
entries.t: 1 🛑 Stop what you're doing, sit or lie down 2 👅 Take 1 sublingual tablet or spray at the onset of chest pain 3 ⏱️ Wait 5 minutes 4 ☎️ Pain still there? Call EMS immediately — don't drive yourself, don't wait for more doses 5 🔁 May repeat every 5 minutes, up to 3 doses total while waiting for EMS to arrive Call EMS as soon as pain persists after the first dose — don't wait to "use up" all 3 doses before getting help. 🧠 “1, 5, CALL.” One tablet, five minutes, then call — everything after that is happening on the way
Remind the patient a headache is an expected side effect , not a reason to discontinue therapy on their own — a mild analgesic can help, and it often improves with continued use.

Don't rub ointment forms in with bare fingers — it absorbs through skin and can cause a severe headache Sit or lie down before taking a dose — fall risk from a sudden BP drop Avoid alcohol unless cleared by the prescriber — compounds the hypotension

💓 Heart rate well above the patient's normal baseline ⚖️ Rapid weight gain 🦵 New/unusual swelling of the extremities, face, or abdomen 😮‍💨 Dyspnea, angina, severe indigestion, or fainting 📓 Keep a log of anginal attacks — date, time, drug, dose used — bring it to every visit ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🩸 Nitric oxide = vasodilation = ↓preload = ↓O2 demand 💊 1 tab, wait 5, then call EMS if pain isn't relieved 🤕 Headache is expected not a reason to stop the drug ❌ Never with PDE5 inhibitors severe hypotension risk

Q1: How do nitrates relieve angina? Show answer They release nitric oxide, relaxing vascular smooth muscle — vessels dilate (mostly veins), which drops preload and lowers the heart's oxygen demand. Q2: A patient takes sublingual nitro for chest pain and it's still there 5 minutes later. Next step? Show answer Call EMS immediately — do not wait to take all three doses before getting help. Q3: A patient wants to stop their nitrate patch because of a daily headache. What do you teach? Show answer Headache is an expect

Deep Vein Thrombosis — a CLOT in a deep vein · plus Raynaud's & Buerger's NG-223 CARDIO ADHD-friendly visual edition A clot in a deep vein is not dangerous where it sits — it is dangerous where it GOES. Blood from a leg vein travels to the right heart and straight into the lungs. That is why the calf you find swollen today is a pulmonary embolism tomorrow, and why you never massage or vigorously palpate a calf you suspect of clotting . Related PVD 1 · Patho & Signs PVD 2 · Causes & Complications PVD 3 · Treatments
STEP 1 · VIRCHOW'S TRIAD Three conditions make blood clot where it shouldn't. Every risk factor you'll ever be asked about slots into one of them.

entries.h: 🌀 VIRCHOW'S TRIAD — the three-legged stool every DVT stands on
entries.t: 🧠 “SHIP” — Stasis · Hypercoagulability · Injury to the Pipe. Picture the classic exam client: a ship passenger on a long flight (stasis), dehydrated with a cocktail (hypercoagulable), just out of knee surgery (vessel injury). All three legs of the triad in one sentence — that client clots.

entries.h: ⚠️ Risk factors, sorted by which leg of the triad
entries.t: Triad leg Who's at risk 🧍 STASIS Post-op & immobile clients · bed rest · casts and splints · paralysis/stroke · long car rides and flights · prolonged sitting · heart failure · obesity · pregnancy (the uterus compresses pelvic veins) 🩹 INJURY Orthopedic surgery — especially hip and knee replacement · major trauma and fractures · central lines and IV catheters · smoking 🧬 HYPERCOAG Cancer (and chemotherapy) · dehydration · pregnancy and postpartum · estrogen therapy / oral contraceptives , especially in a smoker ove

entries.h: 🫙 Deep vs superficial — why only one of them scares you
entries.t: Superficial thrombophlebitis — clot in a surface vein. You can see and feel a red, tender, cord-like vein just under the skin. Uncomfortable, usually treated with warm compresses, elevation and anti-inflammatories. DVT — deep vein thrombosis — clot in a deep vein (calf, popliteal, femoral, iliac). You cannot see it. It sits in a high-volume vein with a straight path to the lungs. That path is the whole point: leg vein → inferior vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → PE . 🧠 “Superficial you
STEP 2 · SPOT IT Four letters for the leg. One line for the lungs. And one thing your hands must never do.

entries.h: 🐄 COWS — the DVT sign set, and the S that changes everything
entries.t: C CALF PAIN & CRAMPING — aching, tightness or a “charley horse” that doesn't ease. Often worse with walking or dorsiflexion , and tender along the vein. O ONE-SIDED SWELLING (unilateral) — this is the money sign. Measure calf circumference at the same marked point on both legs and compare. Two swollen legs points at the heart; one swollen leg points at a vein. W WARM & RED — blood pooling behind the clot makes the skin warm, red/erythematous and shiny-tight . May come with a low-grade fever. S SOB & CHEST PAIN = PE

entries.h: 🚫 NEVER massage or vigorously palpate a calf you suspect has a clot
entries.t: Why: the thrombus is only loosely attached. Pressure, kneading or forceful dorsiflexion can dislodge it into the circulation , and a venous clot goes straight to the lungs . Homans' sign (calf pain on forced dorsiflexion) is no longer used — it is unreliable, it misses most DVTs, and the maneuver itself risks dislodging the clot. Inspect and measure instead. Do NOT apply SCDs to a leg with a known acute DVT unless the provider specifically orders it. SCDs are a prevention device. Gentle inspection, gentle circumfer

entries.h: 🔬 Confirming it — what actually diagnoses a DVT
entries.t: Venous duplex ultrasound — the first-line, non-invasive test . Shows the clot and whether the vein compresses. D-dimer — a fibrin breakdown product. A normal D-dimer helps rule OUT a clot; an elevated one does not rule it IN (it rises with surgery, trauma, infection, pregnancy, cancer). Wells score — a clinical probability tool that decides whether the client goes straight to ultrasound. For suspected PE: CT pulmonary angiography is the standard confirming study. ABG may show hypoxemia with a low CO₂ from blowing o

entries.h: 🚨 PE — what it looks like when the clot arrives
entries.t: 😮‍💨 SUDDEN shortness of breath — the hallmark. Abrupt, not gradual. 💥 Sharp, pleuritic chest pain — worse on deep breath. 💓 Tachycardia and tachypnea ; low SpO₂ despite effort. 😰 Anxiety, restlessness, a sense of impending doom — take this seriously, it is a real early sign of hypoxia. 🩸 Cough, sometimes with blood-streaked sputum (hemoptysis) . 📉 Hypotension, cyanosis, syncope = massive PE, obstructive shock. 🧠 “Sudden + Short of breath + Sharp chest pain + Scared = PE.” Four S's. In a post-op client with a swolle

entries.h: 🚨 PE ESCALATION — priority actions in order
entries.t: 1 STAY with the client and sit them UP — high Fowler's. It maximizes lung expansion immediately and costs nothing. ▼ 2 Apply OXYGEN and put on continuous pulse oximetry. Hypoxia is what's killing them right now. ▼ 3 CALL — provider / rapid response. Use the call light or a colleague so you never leave the client alone. ▼ 4 Vital signs, cardiac monitor, IV access. Establish or confirm a patent IV — the treatment is going to be intravenous. ▼ 5 Anticipate: IV heparin, CT pulmonary angiography , ABG, D-dimer, ECG, and
STEP 3 · STOP THE NEXT ONE Anticoagulants don't dissolve the clot — they stop it from growing while the body breaks it down. Prevention is where nursing wins.

entries.h: 💊 Anticoagulant comparison — which lab watches which drug
entries.t: Drug Route & speed Monitoring Nursing key points Heparin unfractionated IV drip or SC. Immediate onset — this is the one you start in an emergency. aPTT (some facilities use anti-Xa). Therapeutic ≈ 1.5–2.5× the control value. Also follow PLATELETS. Antidote protamine sulfate . Watch for HIT — heparin-induced thrombocytopenia: platelets fall (classically >50% drop) and the client paradoxically clots . Stop the heparin and notify. Never rub SC injection sites. LMWH enoxaparin, dalteparin SC, weight-based, more predic

entries.h: 🩸 Bleeding precautions — the same teaching for every anticoagulant
entries.t: 🪥 Soft toothbrush, electric razor , no flossing with force. 🚽 Report black tarry stools, pink/red urine, coffee-ground emesis, bleeding gums, nosebleeds, unusual bruising , or a headache/confusion after a fall. 💊 No NSAIDs or aspirin unless the provider ordered them; check every OTC and herbal product. 🪪 Wear medical-alert identification and tell every dentist and surgeon. 🩹 Hold pressure longer after venipunctures and injections; avoid IM injections when possible. 🤕 Fall precautions — a head strike on an anticoagu

🚶 Early ambulation after surgery — the single most effective prevention. 🦵 SCDs / intermittent pneumatic compression and graduated compression (TED) stockings for immobile clients. Check skin under them; make sure they aren't rolled or bunched. 💉 Prophylactic anticoagulation — low-dose SC heparin or LMWH for at-risk hospitalized and post-op clients. 💧 Hydration — dehydrated blood is thick blood. 🦶 Ankle pumps, calf exercises and position changes for anyone on bed rest. ❌ No pillows under the knees, no leg crossing,

🦶 C — Calf exercise & isometrics 💧 H — Hydration thin the blood 🚶 A — Ambulation keep moving 🪑 N — No long sitting car · airplane · bed rest 🧦 T — TED & SCDs after the clot is resolved Two nuances the exam cares about: Elevate the affected leg to promote venous return and reduce swelling — the same rule as every venous problem. SEE NG-161 About activity during the acute clot: older teaching was strict bed rest to keep the clot from moving. Current practice for most stable clients is early ambulation once therapeuti

entries.h: 🕸️ When drugs aren't enough: the IVC filter
entries.t: What it is: a small mesh basket placed in the inferior vena cava to catch clots traveling from the legs before they reach the lungs. Who gets one: clients who cannot take anticoagulants (active bleeding, recent neurosurgery) or who keep throwing clots despite therapeutic anticoagulation. What it does NOT do: it does not dissolve clots and it does not prevent new ones from forming — it is a net, not a treatment. 🧠 “A pool skimmer, not a filter for the water.” It catches what floats by; it doesn't clean the pool. Ant

entries.h: 🎨 Also on this card: Raynaud's vs Buerger's
entries.t: 🤍 RAYNAUD'S · “R = Ring finger” 🖤 BUERGER'S · “B = Black fingers & toes” Spasm of small arteries in the fingers (and toes), triggered by COLD and STRESS . Buerger's disease (thromboangiitis obliterans) — inflammation and clotting of small and medium arteries and veins in the hands and feet . Classic color sequence: WHITE (spasm, no blood) → BLUE (deoxygenated) → RED (blood rushes back). Numbness, tingling, throbbing. Tissue actually dies: intense pain, claudication of the arch of the foot, cold sensitivity, ulcers,

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🐄 COWS C alf pain · O ne-sided swelling · W arm & red · S OB + chest pain = PE, call now . 🌀 Triad Stasis · vessel Injury · Hypercoagulability. Post-op ortho client in bed = all three. 🚫 Hands off No massage, no vigorous palpation, no Homans'. Look, measure, report. 🧪 WEPT W arfarin → PT/ INR 2.0–3.0 → vitamin K · H eparin → a PTT 1.5–2.5× → protamine · DOAC → no routine lab.

Q1: Name Virchow's triad. Show answer Venous stasis, endothelial/vessel wall injury, and hypercoagulability. Q2: A post-op client has a warm, red, swollen LEFT calf that is 3 cm larger than the right. What must you NOT do? Show answer Do not massage or vigorously palpate the calf, and do not perform a Homans' maneuver — you could dislodge the clot and cause a PE. Notify the provider; anticipate a venous duplex ultrasound. Q3: Which lab monitors heparin, and what is its antidote? Show answer aPTT (therapeutic roughl
