Infective & noninfective inflammation of the heart's INNER lining & valves NG-229 CARDIO ADHD-friendly visual edition Inflammation INside the heart — bacteria (or, less often, sterile clot/inflammation with no bacteria) seed the endocardium and valves, growing a vegetation that keeps valves from closing fully. Less cardiac output = less oxygen OUT to the body, plus pieces of that vegetation can break off and embolize to the brain, lungs, and fingertips. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🦠 Bugs on the val
STEP 1 · BUGS FIND A DOOR A valve gets damaged or exposed, bacteria land on it, and a vegetation grows — the whole disease follows from that one event.

entries.h: 🫀 A heart valve with vegetation growth
entries.t: EXAM TIP Infective endocarditis = bacteria seed a valve (often one already scarred or abnormal), forming a sticky vegetation of fibrin, platelets, and bacteria. The leaflets can't close fully → regurgitation → the vegetation keeps growing and keeps shedding infected emboli. 🧠 "Mold on the valve." Picture the vegetation exactly like fuzzy mold growing on a screen door — the door (valve) can't shut all the way anymore, and little bits of mold keep breaking off and traveling.

💉 Dirty needles — IV drug use 🦷 Dental visits without antibiotic prophylaxis in an at-risk client 🔪 Heart surgery — valve replacement & CABG 🤒 Untreated strep throat 🧠 "Four doors bacteria walk through." Needles, teeth, surgery, and an ignored strep infection — every route is a break in a barrier that lets bacteria reach the bloodstream and then the valve.

🦠 Infective 🧊 Noninfective Bacteria present — "mold on the valve" No bacteria — sterile inflammation/clot only Needs antibiotics Treat the underlying cause (e.g., lupus, cancer) 🧠 Say the word: Endo (inside) + card (heart) + itis (inflammation) = inflammation INSIDE the heart — the lining & valves, not the sac around it (that's pericarditis, NG-066 ) and not just the muscle (myocarditis). 🔎
STEP 2 · SPOT IT One mnemonic for the systemic picture, four unmistakable fingertip-and-eye findings, and the culture rule that changes the whole plan.

C — C lots in the heart & brain — risk for stroke/CVA; monitor for agitation, change in level of consciousness L — L ung fluid — crackles O — O verheated — fever T — T oo little oxygen — low cardiac output Plus: clubbing fingers , new or changing heart murmur , fatigue, and the four classic peripheral findings below. 🧠 A CLOT is exactly what's forming — on the valve, and sometimes flying to the brain. The mnemonic is the pathophysiology.

entries.h: 🖐️ The four classic exam findings — each one is visually distinct

entries.t: OUCH — painful/tender raised nodules on finger/toe pads. Immune complex deposition.
Painless flat macules on palms/soles — from septic microemboli.
Thin red-brown lines under the nail bed — tiny clots (microemboli).

Retinal hemorrhages with a pale white center — seen on fundoscopic exam. 🧠 "Osler = Ouch, Janeway = No way (no pain)." Both are red/purple skin lesions from the same immune/embolic process — the ONE thing that tells them apart on an exam is pain. Splinters live under the nail; Roth spots live in the eye.

Draw blood cultures from multiple sites before the first dose of antibiotics. Giving antibiotics first can sterilize the blood and make it impossible to identify the organism — which is exactly what guides therapy. 🩸 Multiple sets, different venipuncture sites, before treatment starts 🫀 Echocardiogram — visualizes the vegetation directly 🧫 Elevated WBC, inflammatory markers 🧠 "Culture first, cure second." If a question shows antibiotics being hung before cultures are drawn, that's the error to catch.

Pieces of the vegetation can break off and travel to the brain. New agitation or a change in level of consciousness in an endocarditis client is a stroke until ruled out. 🧠 The C in CLOT is not abstract — it's a real embolus that can lodge in the brain within minutes. 🩺
STEP 3 · CLEAR THE INFECTION, PROTECT THE VALVE Antibiotics do the heavy lifting; teaching and prophylaxis keep it from happening again.

💉 IV antibiotics — organism-specific, typically a prolonged course; started only after cultures are drawn 🔪 Valve repair or replacement for severe damage, large/embolizing vegetations, or heart failure from valve destruction 🧠 "Bugs out, then rebuild." Kill the infection first — surgery on an actively infected valve is reserved for those who need it urgently (large vegetations, heart failure, uncontrolled infection).

🪥 Brush 2x /day with a soft toothbrush NO flossing — can introduce bacteria into the bloodstream 🦷 Routine dental care is still important — just done with antibiotic prophylaxis, not skipped 🧠 "Brush soft, skip the string." Any break in the gum line is a door bacteria can walk through straight to a damaged valve.

entries.h: 🦷 Dental & procedure prophylaxis for at-risk clients
entries.t: Clients with a history of endocarditis , a prosthetic heart valve , certain congenital heart disease , or a cardiac transplant with valve regurgitation need prophylactic antibiotics before dental work or other procedures that can cause bacteremia. 📣 Tell every provider — dentist, surgeon, even routine procedures — about the history of endocarditis 🪪 Consider a medical alert card/bracelet 🧠 "Announce it before they touch you." The single biggest prevention failure is the client not mentioning their history — make th

1 🩸 Cultures before antibiotics — never reverse the order 2 🧠 Monitor — new agitation or altered LOC = possible embolic stroke 3 📣 Let all providers know of history of endocarditis 4 🦷 Dental visits/surgery in an at-risk client require prophylaxis 5 💊 Antibiotic adherence — the full prolonged course, every dose 🧠 "CLOT" gets you the signs; this ladder gets you the actions. Say both out loud and you have the whole page. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🦠 Vegetation on the valve Fibrin + platelets + bacteria stop the leaflets from closing 🩸 Cultures BEFORE antibiotics Never sterilize the sample before you identify the bug 🖐️ Osler = ouch, Janeway = no way Splinters under nails, Roth spots in the eye 🦷 Prophylax the at-risk valve Prosthetic valve or prior endocarditis + dental work = antibiotics first

Q1: What must happen before the first dose of antibiotics is given? Show answer Blood cultures — multiple sets from different sites — must be drawn first, or the organism may never be identified. Q2: How do you tell Osler nodes apart from Janeway lesions? Show answer Osler nodes are painful/tender nodules on the finger or toe pads. Janeway lesions are painless flat macules on the palms or soles. Q3: What does the CLOT mnemonic stand for? Show answer Clots in the heart & brain (stroke risk) · Lung fluid (crackles) ·

entries.h: Cholesterol Lowering Agents · NG-242 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 💊 The 6 classes 🧪 The numbers ⚠️ Watch for 🗣️ Teach ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Cardio · Pharmacology

Statins · Ezetimibe · Sequestrants · Fibrates · Niacin · PCSK9 NG-242 Cardio · Pharm ADHD-friendly visual edition Indication: high cholesterol — hypercholesterolemia · hyperlipidemia · dyslipidemia (different names for the same thing). Every drug on this page is aiming at one target: the plaque from NG-145. Lower the LDL, calm the artery wall, and thicken the fibrous cap so it doesn't rupture . Statins are the backbone. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 💊 “-statin” Blocks the liver enzyme that MAKES chol
STEP 1 · SIX DIFFERENT ATTACKS Each class hits cholesterol at a different address: the liver factory, the gut doorway, the bloodstream, or the liver's recycling receptors.

🧠 “Factory, Door, Highway.” Statins & PCSK9 shut down the factory (liver). Ezetimibe & sequestrants guard the door (gut). Fibrates & niacin clean up the highway (blood). Every drug on this page has one of those three addresses.

atorvastatin · simvastatin · lovastatin · rosuvastatin · pravastatin MOA: it prevents cholesterol production in the liver — technically by blocking the enzyme the liver needs to make cholesterol: HMG-CoA reductase . Less cholesterol made inside → the liver puts out more LDL receptors → it pulls LDL out of the blood . ⬇️ Biggest LDL drop of any oral class — the reason it's first-line 🛡️ Also stabilizes the plaque cap and lowers inflammation — benefit beyond the number (NG-145) 🫀 Started for essentially every post-MI

💊 “-statin” (lovastatin, simvastatin…) 🍄 NYSTATIN Cholesterol-lowering — blocks HMG-CoA reductase in the liver ANTIFUNGAL — treats yeast infections (oral thrush, candidiasis, diaper rash) Oral tablet, usually once daily Often a swish-and-swallow or swish-and-spit suspension, or a topical powder/cream Watch: muscle pain, liver enzymes Watch: it must contact the fungus — hold it in the mouth, don't eat/drink right after EXAM TIP NYstatin = NO cholesterol. It's for YEAST. 🧠 “NY = New York yeast — a bagel.” NY statin b

entries.h: 🗂️ The other five classes, cleanly separated

entries.t: ezetimibe MOA: blocks cholesterol absorption at the small-intestine brush border — dietary and biliary cholesterol never gets in. Use: usually added on to a statin when LDL isn't at goal, or used alone if she can't tolerate statins. Modest LDL lowering on its own. Watch: generally well tolerated — GI upset/diarrhea; rare myalgia (more likely when combined with a statin); can raise liver enzymes when combined.

entries.h: 💊 BILE ACID SEQUESTRANTS — the bile sponge
entries.t: cholestyramine · colestipol · colesevelam MOA: bind bile acids in the gut so they're excreted in stool . The liver must then use up cholesterol to make new bile → blood LDL falls. Same trick as the soluble fiber in oatmeal. Big advantage: not absorbed systemically — it works entirely inside the gut. Watch: CONSTIPATION (the classic), bloating, gas. May RAISE triglycerides — a poor choice if TGs are already high. HUGE NURSING POINT It binds other drugs and the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, K . Give other medications

gemfibrozil · fenofibrate MOA: speed the breakdown and clearance of triglyceride-rich particles (they activate the pathway that boosts lipoprotein lipase). Best at: lowering TRIGLYCERIDES — the go-to for very high TGs, including preventing pancreatitis . Modest HDL rise, little LDL effect. Watch: GALLSTONES (cholelithiasis), GI upset, ↑ liver enzymes, and myopathy — the risk climbs sharply when combined with a statin (gemfibrozil is the worst offender). Use with caution in kidney disease.

entries.h: 💊 NIACIN (nicotinic acid, vitamin B₃) — the HDL raiser
entries.t: niacin · extended-release niacin MOA: reduces the liver's release of VLDL → ↓LDL and ↓triglycerides , and it raises HDL more than any other agent . Watch — the one everybody tests: FLUSHING — hot, red, itchy face and neck. It's prostaglandin-mediated and harmless but miserable. 💊 Take aspirin about 30 minutes before the dose (if the provider approves) to blunt flushing 🍺 Avoid alcohol and hot drinks around the dose — they intensify flushing ⏳ Extended-release forms flush less; flushing fades over weeks of consisten

entries.h: 💉 PCSK9 INHIBITORS — the injectable heavy hitters
entries.t: alirocumab · evolocumab MOA: monoclonal antibodies that block PCSK9 , the protein that destroys LDL receptors. Block it → the liver keeps far more LDL receptors → it vacuums LDL out of the blood. Very large LDL reductions. Use: familial hypercholesterolemia , or established atherosclerotic disease when a maximally tolerated statin (± ezetimibe) isn't enough, or true statin intolerance. Route: SUBCUTANEOUS injection every 2–4 weeks — not a pill. Teach self-injection, site rotation, refrigerate and let the pen reach

Class LDL Triglycerides HDL Signature adverse effect Statins ⬇️⬇️⬇️ biggest ⬇️ ⬆️ slight Myopathy / rhabdo , ↑ liver enzymes Ezetimibe ⬇️ modest ↔️ / slight ⬇️ ↔️ Well tolerated; GI upset Bile acid sequestrants ⬇️⬇️ ⬆️ can raise ↔️ / slight ⬆️ Constipation + binds other drugs Fibrates ↔️ / slight ⬇️ ⬇️⬇️⬇️ biggest ⬆️ Gallstones , myopathy with statins Niacin ⬇️ ⬇️⬇️ ⬆️⬆️ biggest FLUSHING , ↑ glucose, ↑ uric acid PCSK9 inhibitors ⬇️⬇️⬇️ huge ↔️ slight ⬆️ Injection-site reaction, SubQ route 🧠 Match the drug to the ab
STEP 2 · KNOW THE NUMBERS COLD Four numbers. Three you want low , one you want high . These are standard adult reference targets.

entries.h: 🧪 Target vs bad — the bar scale
entries.t: EXAM TIP Clients with known heart disease or diabetes are usually pushed to a lower LDL than 100 — the <100 figure is the general adult target, not a ceiling for high-risk clients. Practice varies; follow the provider's stated goal. 🧠 Count down by 50s: 200 → 150 → 100 → and HDL is the odd one at 40 going UP. Total 200 , trigs 150 , LDL 100 , HDL 40+ . L DL = L ousy = L ow. H DL = H appy = H igh.

Lipid panel — baseline, then to check response (often re-checked weeks to months after a change) ALT & AST — baseline liver function before starting a statin; re-check if she has symptoms CK (creatine kinase) — drawn when she reports muscle pain, to look for myopathy/rhabdo Creatinine / BUN — kidney function, especially with rhabdo risk or fibrates A1c / glucose — statins and niacin can nudge glucose up Uric acid — niacin can precipitate gout 🧠 “Muscle pain → CK. Yellow eyes → ALT/AST.” The complaint tells you whic

entries.h: 🍽️ Diet still does half the work
entries.t: 🥣 Soluble fiber (oats, beans, barley, psyllium) — binds bile, same mechanism as sequestrants 🐟 Fatty fish & omega-3s — help triglycerides 🥑 Swap saturated & trans fats for unsaturated (olive oil, nuts, avocado) 🍬 Cut refined sugar & alcohol — the biggest drivers of high triglycerides 🏃 Exercise — the most reliable way to raise HDL 🚭 Smoking cessation — smoking lowers HDL directly 🧠 “Sugar makes triglycerides; fat makes LDL; movement makes HDL.” Three sentences, three numbers, three behaviors. ⚠️
STEP 3 · THE STATIN ADVERSE EFFECTS ATI, HESI and Kaplan all ask the exact same question about statins — and the answer is always the muscles.

entries.h: 💪 Muscle pain without injury = REPORT IT
entries.t: Answer first: new muscle aches, cramps, spasms, tenderness or weakness that she cannot explain by exercise or injury → notify the HCP . This is the single most tested statin fact. 🧠 “Sore muscles → dark pee → sick kidneys.” Three beats, in that order. Rhabdo isn't “muscle pain,” it's muscle dissolving — and the kidney is downstream of the mess.

🧪 Baseline liver enzymes (ALT/AST) before starting; re-check if she develops symptoms 💩 Report clay-colored stools — the classic source cue 💛 Jaundice (yellow skin/sclera), dark urine , RUQ pain , unusual fatigue, loss of appetite, nausea 🍺 Limit alcohol — adds liver insult ⚠️ Use caution/avoid in active liver disease Serious statin liver injury is uncommon , but the teaching point is constant: symptoms get reported, not waited out. 🧠 “Clay stool, dark pool, feeling cruel.” Pale stools + dark urine + fatigue = live

entries.h: 🍊 Grapefruit — and the St. John's wort correction
entries.t: Answer first: No grapefruit or grapefruit juice with simvastatin, lovastatin or atorvastatin. Why: grapefruit inhibits the CYP3A4 enzyme that clears these statins → the drug builds up → higher myopathy/rhabdo risk Not all statins: pravastatin and rosuvastatin aren't metabolized by CYP3A4, so grapefruit is far less of an issue with them — but teach the rule as written on her bottle SOURCE CHECK St. John's wort is also on the avoid list — but for the opposite reason : it induces CYP3A4 and can make the statin less ef

entries.h: ⚠️ The rest of the statin cautions
entries.t: Caution What to do about it Pregnancy & breastfeeding Standard nursing teaching is to avoid statins in pregnancy and to use reliable contraception; a client planning pregnancy should talk to her provider before stopping or continuing. Cholesterol is needed for fetal development. New-onset diabetes / ↑ A1c A small, real effect. It does not outweigh the cardiovascular benefit — monitor glucose, don't stop the statin on your own. Alcohol & liver disease Limit alcohol; caution in active hepatic disease. Kidney disease
STEP 4 · WHAT SHE TAKES HOME Timing, expectations, and the three exam questions that are really the same question.

entries.h: 🌙 Why statins are taken at night
entries.t: 🌙 The liver makes most of its cholesterol overnight — HMG-CoA reductase activity peaks in the night/early morning hours 💊 So the short-acting statins — simvastatin, lovastatin, fluvastatin — are taken in the evening (dinner or bedtime) so the drug level peaks when the enzyme is busiest 🍽️ Lovastatin is specifically taken with the evening meal — food improves its absorption ☀️ Long-acting statins — atorvastatin and rosuvastatin — can be taken at any time of day , because their effect lasts a full 24 hours ⏰ The best

Q1: How does a statin lower cholesterol? Show answer It prevents cholesterol production in the liver by blocking the enzyme the liver needs — HMG-CoA reductase. Less made inside → more LDL receptors → LDL pulled out of the blood. Q2: The client on lovastatin reports new leg aches with no injury. Action? Show answer Notify the HCP. Muscle pain/tenderness/cramps without injury can signal myopathy and possible rhabdomyolysis — expect a CK level, and ask about dark, cola-colored urine and weakness. Q3: Why no grapefrui
One clogs vessels, the other cannot form a clot. Both are inherited, and both have one intervention that matters most.

Every sickle cell trigger takes away oxygen or water, so the treatment list is simply the trigger list read backwards. Swipe it sideways if it is cut off, or tap to open it full size. Abnormal hemoglobin S makes red cells stiffen into a crescent shape when stressed. The rigid cells jam in small vessels, causing pain and tissue infarction. Everything that triggers a crisis reduces oxygen or water. So treatment is simply the reverse. Trigger Treatment Hypoxia — altitude, infection, exertion Oxygen Dehydration Aggress

Autosomal recessive. Two genes = disease; one gene = trait , usually symptom-free Symptoms do not appear before about 6 months , because fetal hemoglobin protects Infection is the leading cause of death in young children — the spleen is damaged early, so penicillin prophylaxis and full vaccination are essential Acute chest syndrome — chest pain, fever, hypoxia, new infiltrate. A leading cause of death; a medical emergency Splenic sequestration — sudden splenic enlargement, rapid drop in hemoglobin, shock

A missing clotting factor — factor VIII in hemophilia A, factor IX in B. X-linked recessive , so it affects boys, carried by mothers. Lab Result aPTT Prolonged PT Normal Platelet count Normal — the platelets are fine, the factor is missing Bleeding time Normal

The hallmark. Warm, swollen, painful joint with reduced movement. Repeated bleeds destroy the joint permanently. Treatment: RICE + factor R est — immobilize; do not move it I ce C ompression E levate above the level of the heart Give the missing factor — this is the definitive treatment No aspirin, no NSAIDs. Acetaminophen is the safe analgesic. No IM injections, no rectal temperatures, no contact sports.

Swimming and cycling with a helmet are encouraged; contact sports are not Soft toothbrush ; electric razor when older Medical alert identification Dental work needs factor cover Teach parents to recognize a joint bleed early — a tingling or warmth before visible swelling

Immune thrombocytopenic purpura — platelets destroyed after a viral illness. Low platelets , petechiae and bruising, often in an otherwise well child. Usually self-limiting. Hemophilia = normal platelets, missing factor. ITP = low platelets.

Sickle crisis = oxygen, hydration, analgesia, warmth. Never cold, never aspirin Sickle symptoms start after 6 months Hemophilia has NORMAL platelets — only the factor is missing Joint bleed → immobilize, ice, elevate, give factor Acetaminophen only — no aspirin or NSAIDs in either condition Sources. Written from CDC , HealthyChildren.org (AAP) , MedlinePlus and OpenStax A&P 2e (CC BY 4.0).
Sort them by which way blood shunts. Left-to-right floods the lungs; right-to-left makes a blue baby.

There is only one sorting rule and it is a picture: which way is the blood going through the hole. Everything else follows from that. Swipe it sideways if it is cut off, or tap to open it full size. Ask which way the blood is going through the hole. Left to right = too much lung blood = heart failure. Right to left = deoxygenated blood to the body = cyanosis. Group Blood goes Result Examples Acyanotic Left → right Pulmonary overload, heart failure , poor feeding, sweating, poor growth ASD, VSD, PDA , coarctation, p

A narrowing of the aorta. The classic finding is a blood pressure difference : High blood pressure and bounding pulses in the ARMS Low blood pressure and weak or absent pulses in the LEGS Cool lower extremities; leg pain on exertion in older children Always compare upper and lower limb pulses and pressures in a child with hypertension. Coarctation is a fixable cause that is missed by only checking an arm.
P ulmonary stenosis R ight ventricular hypertrophy O verriding aorta V SD

Sudden deep cyanosis, usually triggered by crying, feeding or straining — anything that drops systemic resistance and sends more blood right-to-left. Put the infant in the KNEE-CHEST position immediately. Older children squat instinctively - it does the same thing. Why it works: flexing the hips raises systemic vascular resistance, which pushes blood back through the pulmonary artery to be oxygenated. Then: calm the child, oxygen, morphine if ordered, IV fluids .

It looks like feeding trouble, not like adult heart failure. Sweating with feeds ; tiring after a few minutes Poor weight gain — often the earliest sign Tachypnoea and tachycardia at rest Hepatomegaly — the pediatric equivalent of peripheral edema Periorbital edema rather than ankle swelling Ankle edema is an adult sign. In a baby, look at the liver and the weight chart.

entries.h: 🍽️ Feeding a baby in heart failure
entries.t: Small, frequent feeds ; limit each to about 30 minutes — longer burns more calories than it delivers Higher-calorie formula Feed at the first hunger cue , before crying exhausts them Cluster care to allow long rests Daily weights — the best measure of both nutrition and fluid

Count the apical pulse for a full minute before every dose Hold and report: <90–110 in an infant, <70 in a child Early toxicity in a child is usually vomiting and bradycardia — not the visual changes adults get Watch potassium — low potassium worsens digoxin toxicity Never repeat a dose that was vomited, and never mix digoxin into a bottle of formula - if the feed is not finished, the dose is unknown.

Fever for 5 or more days plus red eyes, strawberry tongue , cracked lips, rash, and swollen red hands and feet that later peel. It inflames coronary arteries and causes aneurysms , so treatment is IVIG plus aspirin — the one situation where a child is deliberately given aspirin. After IVIG, live vaccines must be delayed about 11 months - the antibodies block the immune response.

Left-to-right = failure. Right-to-left = blue. Tet spell → knee-chest immediately Coarctation: arms high, legs low — compare both Infant heart failure = sweating with feeds, poor weight gain, hepatomegaly Apical pulse for a full minute before digoxin Kawasaki is the exception where aspirin is given Sources. Written from CDC , NHLBI , HealthyChildren.org (AAP) , MedlinePlus and OpenStax A&P 2e (CC BY 4.0).

Synchronized or not · what each device is for · living with one NG-405 Cardiovascular ADHD-friendly visual edition The whole topic turns on one distinction: cardioversion is synchronized, defibrillation is not . Synchronized means the shock waits for the R wave. If there is no R wave to wait for, you cannot synchronize. Cardioversion SYNCHRONIZED · low energy · a pulse is present Defibrillation NOT synchronized · high energy · V-fib or pulseless V-tach Pacemaker Too slow — it makes the heart beat ICD Too fast and l

Synchronized means the shock waits for the R wave. Put the two strips side by side and there is nothing left to memorize. Swipe it sideways if it is cut off, or tap to open it full size. Four things, four jobs Pacemaker — for rhythms that are too slow . Symptomatic bradycardia, complete heart block, sick sinus syndrome. It fires an impulse when the heart does not. ICD — for rhythms that are too fast and lethal . It watches, and if it sees ventricular tachycardia or fibrillation it shocks. Many are combined with a p

Doing it safely Confirm the rhythm and check for a pulse before choosing the mode. Turn the sync button ON for cardioversion, OFF for defibrillation. Check it every single time — some machines reset to off after each shock. “All clear” — look at the bed, look at yourself, look around, then shock. Nobody touching anything. Remove oxygen from the immediate area; remove nitroglycerin patches. Pads go at least 2.5 cm from a pacemaker or ICD , or use anterior-posterior placement. Resume compressions immediately after a

Living with a device — the teaching Carry the device card at all times and wear medical identification. Take your own pulse daily and report a rate below the set rate. No MRI unless the device is certified MRI-conditional. Tell every provider, including the dentist. Airport security: show the card, ask for a hand search, do not linger in the archway. Mobile phone on the opposite ear , and not carried in a breast pocket over the device. Microwaves, hair dryers and electric blankets are fine. Keep away from strong ma

Cardioversion SYNCHRONIZED · low energy · a pulse is present Defibrillation NOT synchronized · high energy · V-fib or pulseless V-tach Pacemaker Too slow — it makes the heart beat ICD Too fast and lethal — it shocks the heart back What is the difference between cardioversion and defibrillation? Show answer Cardioversion is synchronized to the R wave and used when there is a pulse. Defibrillation is unsynchronized, for V-fib and pulseless V-tach. Why can V-fib not be cardioverted? Show answer There is no organized R

When the body's temperature vital sign drops too far NG-041 Nursing Core ADHD-friendly visual edition Hypothermia is a core body temperature below 95°F (35°C) — well under the typical adult range from NG-079 Vital Signs . The body becomes like a popsicle : organs slow down, can't compensate for heat loss, and the cold, irritated heart muscle can throw a deadly arrhythmia. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🧊 <95°F (35°C) the definition — cross-ref NG-079's ~98.6°F typical baseline. 🚨 Cold heart = irritabl
STEP 1 · WHY THE BODY SHUTS DOWN One number defines it, one mechanism explains everything else that happens after.

entries.h: 🌡️ The definition — and why the heart is the danger
entries.t: Hypothermia = core temp below 95°F (35°C) . Below that line, organs — including the myocardium (heart muscle) — cool down and become unable to compensate for ongoing heat loss. Stage cutoffs vary slightly by source/protocol — treat as typical teaching bands, not one hard rule. 🧠 "Popsicle physiology." Everything about hypothermia's cause is one idea: the body is freezing and can't keep up.

entries.h: 🚨 Why the heart is the emergency
entries.t: The nearly-frozen myocardium becomes irritated , which can trigger deadly arrhythmias — especially Ventricular Fibrillation (V-Fib) . 🧠 NCLEX priority: attach cardiac monitor 1st , anticipate defibrillation 2nd .

👴 Older adults reduced thermoregulation 👶 Infants large SA:mass ratio 🏚️ Homeless / outdoor exposure 🍺 Intoxicated vasodilation + impaired judgment 🩸 Trauma / burns 🦋 Hypothyroid 🧠 "Old, young, drunk, hurt." Four groups that can't compensate for cold as well as a healthy adult. 🔎
STEP 2 · SPOT IT Heart and lungs both tell on a cooling body — and the findings get quieter, not louder, as it worsens.

💓 Pulses : weak and thready — from the cold heart muscle 🫁 Wheezing may be heard — indicates bronchospasm 🫁 Crackles at the lung bases — indicates pulmonary edema from fluid buildup SEE ALSO NG-082 Assessment Locations — where to listen for these lung/heart findings. 🧠 "Quiet, not loud." As hypothermia worsens, vital signs typically slow and weaken — don't expect a loud, obvious presentation.

Stage Approx. temp Typical presentation Mild 90–95°F (32–35°C) Shivering, tachycardia, tachypnea, mild confusion Moderate 82–90°F (28–32°C) Shivering stops, decreased LOC, bradycardia, bradypnea, arrhythmia risk rises Severe <82°F (<28°C) Unresponsive, high risk of V-Fib/asystole; pulses may be very hard to detect These bands are commonly taught but vary by textbook/protocol — verify against your program's source. 🧠 "Not dead until warm and dead." A profoundly hypothermic client can look clinically dead but may sti
Do not move a hypothermic client roughly or abruptly — jostling a cold, irritable heart can precipitate V-Fib. 🧠 "Gentle hands, cold heart."

Rewarming the extremities before the core can push cold, acidotic peripheral blood back toward the heart, dropping core temperature further and worsening arrhythmia risk. 🧠 "Trunk first, limbs later." 🩺
STEP 3 · REWARM SAFELY Airway and circulation first, then rewarm from the inside out — three tiers depending on severity.

1 🫁 Airway — anticipate mechanical ventilation if severe 2 🫀 Circulation — attach cardiac monitor, anticipate defibrillation 🧠 1st = monitor, 2nd = defib-ready. A cold, irritable heart needs continuous monitoring before anything else once airway is secured.
For mild hypothermia: Remove wet/cold clothing Cover with warm blankets — head & trunk Warm, dry environment

For moderate–severe hypothermia: Warmed IV fluids via 2 large-bore IVs Warm, humidified oxygen More invasive core-warming measures for severe cases, per facility protocol 🧠 "2 big lines, warm inside." Two large-bore IVs of warmed fluid is the classic active internal intervention.

entries.h: 🌡️ Passive vs active rewarming — side by side
entries.t: 🧠 "Blankets for mild, lines for the sick." Passive external rewarming is enough for mild cases; moderate-to-severe cases need active internal warming plus continuous cardiac monitoring.

NG-079 Vital Signs — the ~98.6°F typical baseline this condition drops well below. NG-082 Assessment Locations — where to auscultate the wheezing/crackles and palpate the weak, thready pulses described above. NG-190 Head-to-Toe Assessment — temperature's place inside the full systematic exam. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🧊 <95°F (35°C) the definition of hypothermia 🚨 V-Fib risk cold, irritated myocardium — monitor 1st, defib-ready 2nd 🫁 Wheezing + basilar crackles bronchospasm + pulmonary edema 🌡️ Trunk before limbs avoid afterdrop when rewarming

Q2: What is the priority arrhythmia risk in hypothermia, and what are the first two nursing actions? Show answer Ventricular fibrillation (V-Fib) from the cold, irritated myocardium — attach the cardiac monitor first, anticipate defibrillation second. Therapeutic Patient Positions & Their Indications NG-072 Nursing Core ADHD-friendly visual edition Every position is a tool, not a default. The nurse picks a position to ensure comfort and safety while preventing complications related to the client's condition, treatment, or procedure. Pick the wrong one and you can drop a blood pressure, aspirate a patient, or blow a fresh surgical line. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → ⬇️ Trendelenburg Head down, feet up — for shock / hypotension & central line work.
STEP 1 · THE PURPOSE Positioning is never random — every position serves comfort, safety, a procedure, or a physiologic goal.

To ensure client comfort and safety while preventing complications related to the client's condition, treatment, or procedure. 🫁 Respiratory support — upright positions ease breathing & maximize lung expansion. ❤️ Hemodynamic support — head-down positions increase venous return in shock. 🩹 Post-procedure protection — the right position protects a fresh surgical site or line. 🛡️ Skin integrity — repositioning at least every 2 hours prevents pressure injury. 🚽 Access for a procedure — enemas, pelvic exams, and childb

entries.h: 🦴 Body alignment matters in every position
entries.t: Whatever position you choose, keep the spine neutral, support joints in slight flexion , and use pillows/wedges to prevent foot drop , shoulder subluxation, and skin shear. 🧠 Alignment first, position second. A "correct" position with a dangling foot or twisted neck is still a bad position.

Bedbound clients: reposition at least every 2 hours . Chair-bound: shift weight every 15 minutes , full reposition every 1 hour . 🧠 "2 in bed, 1 in the chair." Bed = every 2 hours; chair = every 1 hour (with small shifts every 15 min). 🧍
STEP 2 · KNOW EACH ONE Seven named positions — picture each one, memorize the one-line indication.
Indication: Abdominal, facial & extremity surgeries; the default "at rest" position. 🧠 Supine = spine. You're flat on your spine, face up.

Indication: Drainage of the mouth after oral/neck surgery; allows full extension of hip & knee joints. 🧠 Prone = face-down on the ground. Good for drainage — gravity pulls secretions out of the mouth.
Indication: GI issues, rectal surgery, and pressure-injury prevention (alternate sides). 🧠 Right lateral = right side down. Name the side that's touching the mattress.
Indication: Administering enemas, perineal exams, and comfort in pregnancy. 🧠 Sims' = "S" for enema. Upper knee climbs toward the chest, upper arm flexes at the elbow.

Indication: Cardiac issues, shortness of breath (SOB), or NG tube feeding — gravity keeps the diaphragm free & secretions out of the airway. 🧠 Low → high: Semi-Fowler's 30–40° → Fowler's 45–60° → High-Fowler's 90° . Higher angle = more respiratory/cardiac relief.

Indication: Hypotension/shock (increases venous return), GYN & abdominal hernia surgery, central line placement/removal, and treatment of venous air embolism (traps air away from the pulmonary outflow tract). 🧠 Trendelenburg = treat the pressure that's TOO LOW. Feet up sends blood back to the heart and brain.

Indication: Promotes perfusion during surgery in obese patients; helps prevent aspiration. 🧠 Reverse = the opposite problem. Same tilted-bed idea as Trendelenburg, flipped — head high instead of head low.
Indication: Gynecological procedures & childbirth — most commonly seen in OB. 🧠 Lithotomy = "L" for labor and delivery. Stirrups + legs up = the classic OB/GYN table position.

Position Correct use Common wrong-answer trap Trendelenburg Hypotension/shock, GYN & hernia surgery, central line access NOT for a patient with increased ICP or respiratory distress — head-down worsens both Semi/High-Fowler's SOB, cardiac patients, tube feeding NOT flat — never feed or run a tube feeding with HOB flat Sims' Enemas, perineal exams, pregnancy comfort Confused with plain lateral — Sims' specifically flexes the upper leg and arm Prone Oral secretion drainage, full hip/knee extension Avoid in late pregn
STEP 3 · SAFE POSITIONING Assess before you move, support what you place, and reassess after.

Assess hemodynamic stability (a hypotensive patient can drop further with rapid position changes — reposition slowly). Assess lines, drains, and dressings before and after the move. Assess skin at every position change for redness/breakdown. Check for orders/contraindications (spinal precautions, recent surgery, ICP). 🧠 CHECK before you ACT. Robo's study map: Step → Check → Act — assess first, every time.

🛏️ Pillows/wedges under joints to maintain neutral alignment. 🦶 Footboards or high-top sneakers to prevent foot drop . 🌀 Trochanter rolls to prevent hip external rotation (supine). 🎈 Pressure-redistribution mattress for high pressure-injury risk. 🧠 Support the gaps. Anywhere there's an empty space between the body and the bed, put a pillow there.

entries.h: 🚨 The one you must never forget
entries.t: Never leave a patient flat during or right after a tube feeding or oral meal — keep HOB elevated 30–45° for at least 30–60 minutes after to prevent aspiration. 🧠 "Flat feeds fail." Flat + feeding tube = aspiration pneumonia risk.

Positioning covers bed mobility — how a client lies. Once they're moving out of bed, body mechanics, gait belts, and assistive devices take over. See the companion page for safe transfers, ambulation, and fall prevention. ➡️ See NG-167 — Ambulation (Body Mechanics & Mobility) for logrolling, transfers, and the wide-base-of-support principles that protect both nurse and patient during a position change. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD ⬇️ Trendelenburg Shock, GYN/hernia surgery, central lines ⬆️ Fowler's SOB, cardiac, NG feeding — never flat while feeding 🤰 Sims' Enemas, perineal exam, pregnancy comfort 🦵 Lithotomy OB/GYN procedures — stirrups, hips flexed

Q1: A hypotensive post-op patient needs a BP boost fast — which position? Show answer Trendelenburg — head down, feet up increases venous return to the heart. Q2: A patient with SOB and a new NG tube feeding — which position and why? Show answer Semi- or high-Fowler's (30–90°) — eases breathing and prevents aspiration during the feed. Q3: What's the difference between lateral and Sims' position? Show answer Lateral is simple side-lying; Sims' is semi-prone with the upper leg flexed toward the chest and upper arm fl

entries.h: PPE & Infection Control · NG-073 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🧤 Standard 🚧 Transmission 🥽 Don/Doff ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Nursing Core · Fundamentals of Nursing Course

Standard Precautions · Transmission-Based Precautions · Donning & Doffing NG-073 Nursing Core ADHD-friendly visual edition Every barrier you put on — gloves, gown, mask, goggles — exists to stop germs moving between a contaminated surface and a clean one. Standard precautions apply to every patient, every time ; transmission-based precautions stack an extra barrier on top when you know (or suspect) contact, droplet, or airborne spread. The doffing order — not donning — is the single highest-yield NCLEX point in thi
STEP 1 · THE FLOOR EVERYONE STANDS ON The baseline layer of protection used on every patient, every encounter — regardless of diagnosis or infection status.

entries.h: 🦠 Why this whole topic exists: nosocomial infection
entries.t: Sterile & aseptic technique exist to drastically reduce (and ideally eliminate) the chance of bacteria entering a wound, catheter site, or sterile body cavity — cutting the risk of a nosocomial infection , also called a healthcare-associated infection (HAI) : "nosocomial" literally means "hospital-acquired." 🧠 "Standard is the floor, transmission is the extra wall." You never drop standard precautions to add contact/droplet/airborne — you always add the new layer on top of gloves + hand hygiene + everything standar

Touching blood , body fluids, secretions, excretions Touching contaminated items or surfaces Touching mucous membranes Touching non-intact skin 🧠 "If it's wet and it's not yours, glove up." Any body substance that isn't sweat = standard-precaution glove indication.

Use during procedures & patient-care activities when contact of your clothing or exposed skin with blood, body fluids, secretions, or excretions is anticipated — think splash, spray, or heavy contact, not just a quick vitals check. 🧠 Gown = protects your clothes ; gloves = protect your hands . Different barrier, different job.

Wear a surgical mask within 3 feet (<3 ft) of a patient when respiratory secretions or splash to the face are anticipated — this is a standard-precaution mask, distinct from the N95 respirator reserved for airborne precautions (Step 2). 🧠 "3 feet, surgical. Airborne, N95." Distance-based splash protection is a different tool from a fit-tested airborne respirator — don't mix them up on the exam. 🚧
STEP 2 · ADD THE RIGHT WALL Three categories, three barriers, three sets of diseases — contact, droplet, and airborne each protect against a different way germs travel.

entries.h: 🚧 Contact vs. Droplet vs. Airborne — side by side
entries.t: Type Extra barrier How it spreads Example diseases 🤲 Contact Gown + gloves for touching patient/environment Direct or indirect touch — skin, equipment, surfaces MRSA, VRE, C. diff, wounds, scabies 💧 Droplet Surgical mask, < 3 ft or entering room Large respiratory droplets — cough, sneeze, talking Flu, strep, pertussis, mumps, rubella 🌬️ Airborne N95 respirator + negative-pressure room Tiny particles that float & travel on air currents Measles, TB, Varicella (chickenpox/shingles) 🧠 Barrier scales with particle size.

S carlet fever, Strep pharyngitis P ertussis (whooping cough), Parvovirus B19 (5th disease) I nfluenza (also contact) D iphtheria (pharyngeal) E piglottitis (H. influenzae type b) R ubella (German measles) M umps, Meningitis (meningococcal), Mycoplasma pneumonia A de N ovirus (also contact) 🧠 "SPIDERMAN swings 3 feet, then stops." Droplets are heavy — they can't hang in the air like Spider-Man's web across a whole room. Mask up within 3 feet, no negative pressure room needed.

M easles T uberculosis (TB) V aricella — chickenpox and disseminated herpes zoster/shingles (airborne + contact) 🧠 MTV plays on air. All three float on air currents across a whole room — door stays closed, negative-pressure room, fit-tested N95 .

M ultidrug-resistant organisms — MRSA, VRE R espiratory infections — RSV, parainfluenza S kin infections — impetigo, lice, scabies, herpes simplex W ounds with excessive drainage / staph E nteric — C. diff , norovirus, rotavirus (soap & water only — sanitizer does NOT kill C. diff spores) E ye infections — conjunctivitis 🧠 "MRS WEE has an accident" — she picked up a resistant bug, has a runny nose, a rash, a weepy wound, and can't make it to the bathroom. Everything on this list is something your hands or gown can

entries.h: 🧻 Special case: C. diff needs soap & water, not sanitizer
entries.t: EXAM TRAP Alcohol-based hand sanitizer does not kill Clostridioides difficile spores. For diarrheal illnesses of unknown origin or confirmed C. diff , norovirus , or rotavirus — wash with soap and water every time. Also remember Hepatitis A is spread through stool, so diapered or incontinent patients need the same enteric-contact awareness. 🧠 "Spores laugh at sanitizer." Friction + running water physically washes spores away; alcohol gel just isn't strong enough to destroy them. 🥽
STEP 3 · THE ORDER THAT'S TESTED Putting PPE ON is forgiving. Taking it OFF is not — the doffing order is the single highest-yield fact in this topic.

1 🥼 Gown — tie in back 2 😷 Mask or respirator — mold to nose, check seal 3 🥽 Goggles or face shield 4 🧤 Gloves — pull cuffs over gown sleeves 🧠 "Gown-Mask-Goggles-Gloves = GMGG, biggest to hands." You build the barrier from your core outward — gloves go on last so the cuff seals over the gown sleeve.

entries.h: 🥽 Doffing (taking OFF) — most contaminated FIRST, hand hygiene LAST
entries.t: 🧤 Gloves first — they touched the patient directly and are the most contaminated item on your body 🥽 Goggles / face shield next — grab by the strap/ear pieces only, never the front 🥼 Gown next — unfasten at the neck, pull down and away rolling it inside-out, contaminated side stays inward 😷 Mask / respirator last of the PPE — touch only the ties/loops, never the front panel 🧼 Hand hygiene — the true final step of every doffing sequence 🧠 "Doffing runs backward from donning — remove the dirtiest thing first." Donnin

entries.h: 🚨 NCLEX trap: why gloves come off first
entries.t: Gloves are the single most contaminated surface on your body after patient contact — leaving them on while you touch your goggles, gown ties, or mask would transfer pathogens straight to those "cleaner" surfaces. Removing them first protects everything you touch next. 🧠 If an NCLEX question asks "what do you remove first?" and gloves are an option — gloves win, every time.

Peel gloves off touching only the outside-to-outside , then tuck the second glove inside the first Discard PPE in the designated receptacle before leaving the room Perform hand hygiene immediately after the last item comes off 🧠 "Glove in a glove." The classic peel-and-tuck keeps the contaminated outer surface balled up inside, away from your bare skin. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🧤 Standard precautions = every patient, every time — gloves, gown, mask as indicated 🚧 Contact / Droplet / Airborne = gown+gloves / mask <3ft / N95 + negative pressure 🧠 SPIDERMAN · MTV · MRS WEE = droplet · airborne · contact disease mnemonics 🥽 Doffing: gloves first, wash last = the #1 tested fact in this topic

Q1: What is the very first item removed when doffing PPE? Show answer Gloves — they're the most contaminated item and removing them first prevents transferring pathogens to your goggles, gown, or mask. Q2: A patient has active TB. What PPE and room setup are required? Show answer Airborne precautions — a fit-tested N95 respirator and a negative-pressure isolation room with the door closed (MTV: Measles, TB, Varicella). Q3: A patient has C. diff diarrhea. Is alcohol-based hand sanitizer enough? Show answer No — sani

entries.h: Sterile Technique · NG-074 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🧾 Before 🧤 During 📋 After ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Nursing Core · Fundamentals of Nursing Course

Surgical Asepsis · Sterile Field Setup · Sterile Gloving NG-074 Nursing Core ADHD-friendly visual edition Sterile technique is performed to drastically reduce — and ideally eliminate — the chance of bacteria entering a wound, catheter site, or sterile body cavity , cutting the risk of a nosocomial (hospital-acquired) infection . Four rules protect the entire field: the 1-inch border is contaminated , anything below waist level is contaminated , reaching over the field contaminates it, and wet = contaminated. Steril
STEP 1 · PURPOSE, SUPPLIES, ASSESS Know why you're doing this, gather everything within reach, and screen the patient before you ever open a kit.

entries.h: 🎯 Purpose & when sterile technique is used
entries.t: Surgical procedures, catheter insertion/changes, chest tube care, cervical checks, and any time you're working on a body part that wouldn't normally contact bacteria — a sterile body cavity, a fresh wound bed, the bloodstream. Surgical asepsis ("sterile technique") aims to eliminate organisms entirely — a much higher bar than the "reduce" goal of medical/clean asepsis (see the Asepsis & Handwashing page). 🧠 "If it doesn't normally meet germs, it gets sterile technique." Skin meets germs all day — a fine needle aspi

Sterile kit (pre-packaged, unexpired) Running water and soap Sterile gloves — sometimes packaged inside the kit A clean, dry surface for setup Clean paper towels 🧠 Check the expiration date before you even open the outer wrapper — an expired kit is treated as non-sterile.

Confirm the need for the procedure Assess the site for existing infection Screen for latex, iodine, or adhesive allergies Assess pain level — give analgesia 30–45 min before the procedure for comfort 🧠 "LIA before you begin" — L atex, I odine, A dhesive. Ask about all three before you open a single package.

Risk for infection Risk for impaired tissue integrity Risk for pain Risk for hypersensitivity reaction — think latex/iodine/adhesive 🧠 Same four risks apply to nearly every sterile procedure — infection, tissue damage, pain, and allergy — build your care plan around these before you even touch the kit. 🧤
STEP 2 · FIELD SETUP & STERILE GLOVING Four rules govern the entire field. Break one, and the whole field — or your glove — is contaminated.

entries.h: 📏 The four rules of a sterile field
entries.t: 📏 The outer 1-inch border of any sterile drape or package is always contaminated — nothing sterile may cross it ⬇️ Anything held below waist level , or out of your direct line of sight, is contaminated 🙅 Never reach over a sterile field — go around it instead 💧 Wet = contaminated — moisture wicks bacteria through a barrier by capillary action ("strike-through") 🧠 "Border, Below, oveR, dRip" — the four rules all start with the idea of a boundary: the 1-inch edge, the waistline, reaching, and moisture all create an i

entries.h: 🧾 Setting up the sterile field — step by step
entries.t: 1 🧼 Check the expiration date on the package and perform hand hygiene 2 📦 Open the kit using the special flap so the first flap opens away from you 3 🤏 Pinch the remaining flaps on their outside corners only and pull them back gently 4 🚫 Do not touch the inside — everything inside is sterile except the 1-inch border 5 🗑️ Throw the outer wrapper away 6 🧤 Get sterile gloves ready on a clean, dry surface next to the field 🧠 "Flap away, pinch the corners, hands stay out." The whole setup is really one rule repeated: yo

1 🧼 Wash hands the same thorough way as before; dry with a clean paper towel 2 📦 Open the glove wrapper so the gloves lie in front of you — do not touch them yet 3 ✋ With your dominant hand, grab the other glove by the folded wrist cuff only 4 🧤 Slide that glove on, leaving the cuff folded — don't let the outside touch your skin 5 🤲 Slide the fingers of your gloved hand under the cuff of the second glove to lift it — glove that hand keeping fingers flat, thumb away from skin 6 🔄 Reach under both cuffs and unroll th

entries.h: 🚨 Break in technique — what to do
entries.t: If a gloved hand touches anything outside the sterile field — a rail, your own skin, an unsterile surface — remove the gloves, wash hands again, and redo the entire gloving sequence with a brand-new pair. Once gloved, touch only your sterile supplies. 🧠 There is no "just this once." Any break in sterile technique means starting the gloving sequence completely over — there's no partial fix. 📋
STEP 3 · DOCUMENT & TEACH The procedure isn't done when the field comes down — document it and prep the patient to protect the site themselves.

Date and time of the procedure Type of procedure performed Fluid/exudate from the site — color, amount, odor Follow hospital policy for dating, timing & initialing dressings, specimens, or catheter sites Document the client's tolerance of the procedure 🧠 "CTFO" — C olor, amount ( T otal), odor, F luid type — describe drainage the same four ways every time.

Practice good personal hygiene Ask for analgesia before pain becomes unbearable — don't wait it out Know the signs & symptoms of infection and when to notify the HCP 🧠 Teach the same infection red flags every time: increasing redness, warmth, swelling, pain, purulent drainage, or fever — call the HCP if any appear.

🌡️ Fever >100.3°F 🔴 Increasing redness around the site 🥵 Warmth & swelling 🤕 Increasing pain not resolving 🧪 Purulent drainage foul odor 🧠 Any one of these after a sterile procedure is enough to notify the HCP — don't wait for all of them to appear together. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 📏 1-inch border = always contaminated, even on a sterile drape ⬇️ Below waist / out of sight = contaminated 💧 Wet = contaminated strike-through wicks bacteria through the barrier 🔄 Any break = start over new gloves, rewash, redo the whole sequence

Q1: How much of a sterile drape's border is considered contaminated? Show answer The outer 1 inch — everything inside that border is sterile, the border itself is not. Q2: A nurse's sterile glove brushes the bed rail. What now? Show answer Remove the gloves, wash hands again, and redo the entire sterile gloving sequence with a new pair — there's no partial fix for a break in technique. Q3: Why is a wet sterile drape considered contaminated? Show answer Moisture allows bacteria to wick through the barrier by capilla

entries.h: Vital Signs · NG-079 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🌡️ The 5 Vitals 🔎 Spot the Pattern 🩺 Priority Actions ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Nursing Core · Fundamentals of Nursing

Temp · Pulse · Respirations · BP · SpO2 — and Pain, the "extra" vital sign NG-079 Nursing Core ADHD-friendly visual edition Vital signs are the baseline data every assessment starts with — one number, one set of locations, one reason it moves. This page is the foundation card for the whole Nursing Core batch: NG-082 Assessment Locations zooms into exactly where you find these, and NG-190 Head-to-Toe puts them inside the full physical exam. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🖐️ 5 vitals, 1 baseline Temp ·
STEP 1 · KNOW THE BASELINE One number, one set of locations, one reason it moves — learn all three together and the rest of nursing school gets easier.

entries.h: 🫀 Where these vitals live on the body
entries.t: Pulses can be palpated at seven classic sites; the apical pulse and lung sounds are auscultated , not palpated. Full landmark detail lives on NG-082 Assessment Locations — this is the quick map. SEE ALSO NG-082 Assessment Locations — exact landmark technique for every point above, plus heart, lung & bowel auscultation.

Vital Sign Typical adult reference range Common sites What moves it How we classify it 💓 Pulse 60–100 bpm Radial, carotid, brachial, femoral, popliteal, dorsalis pedis, posterior tibial, apical Exercise, cardiac output changes, fluid volume shifts Absent, weak, normal, increased, bounding 🩸 BP < 120 /< 80 mmHg Brachial (standard), radial, popliteal, posterior tibial Acid–base balance, activity, fluid volume shifts Normal, hypotensive, hypertensive (staged) 🫁 Respirations 12–20 breaths/min Anterior & posterior chest

~98.6°F / 37°C is the commonly-cited average — real "normal" is a range , roughly 97.8–99.1°F , and it shifts with time of day, age, and site measured. Febrile = has a fever Afebrile = no fever Sites, most → least invasive-accurate: rectal ≈ temporal > oral > axillary 🧠 Cross-ref: hypothermia is core temp <95°F (35°C) — full pathophysiology on NG-041 Hypothermia.

60–100 bpm at rest. Always note rate, rhythm, AND quality — three data points, one vital sign. 0 = absent 1+ = weak / thready 2+ = normal 3+ = increased / full 4+ = bounding 🧠 Irregular rhythm? Count the apical pulse for a full 60 seconds — never a 15-second count ×4.

12–20 breaths/min, counted for a full minute without the client knowing (they'll change their pattern if they notice you counting). Eupnea = normal, unlabored Tachypnea = fast, > 20 Bradypnea = slow, < 12 Apnea = absent breathing 🧠 "Count the chest, not the story." Keep your fingers on the pulse site while you covertly watch the chest rise — the client relaxes their breathing when they think you're still counting pulse.

Systole = max contraction of the left ventricle (top number). Diastole = pressure of the resting ventricles (bottom number). 🧠 "Systole = Squeeze." Both start with S — the squeeze makes the top number.

95–100% is the typical adult reference range. Below that, hypoxia is commonly taught in tiers: 🧠 "85 = call for backup." Under 85% is severe hypoxia — that's an emergency escalation, not a "recheck in an hour."

Pain is assessed at every vitals check using a 0–10 numeric scale (or a validated behavioral/faces scale for nonverbal clients). It's subjective — the client's report is the data Ask location, quality, timing, aggravating/relieving factors Reassess after every intervention 🧠 "Pain is what the patient says it is." Never substitute your own judgment of how much pain "looks right." 🔎
STEP 2 · READ THE CLUES Individual numbers matter less than the pattern they make together — a fast pulse plus a rigid belly tells a very different story than a fast pulse alone.
🧠 "HF = Heavy Fluid." Crackles at the lung bases = think fluid overload / heart failure. SEE ALSO NG-082 Assessment Locations — exact anterior/posterior auscultation sequence & ladder pattern.

Value Resp. acidosis Resp. alkalosis pH ↓ low ↑ high pCO2 ↑ high ↓ low HCO3 normal (acute) normal (acute) Respiratory problems move pH and pCO2 in opposite directions; verify the full ROME/Tic-Tac-Toe method your program teaches.
🔥 Fever (febrile) — above the client's typical baseline 🧊 Hypothermia — core temp <95°F (35°C) SEE ALSO NG-041 Hypothermia — full stages, rewarming priorities, at-risk populations.

Category Typical range (mmHg) Hypotension < 90/60 Normal < 120/80 Elevated 120–129 /< 80 Hypertension (staged) ≥ 130/80 , higher stage ≥ 140/90 Category cutoffs are updated periodically by clinical guidelines — verify the current version your program/facility uses.

A pulse can be the "right number" and still be abnormal — rate is only 1 of 3 things you must chart : rate, rhythm, quality. 🧠 "Number's fine, pattern's not." A rate of 88 with a thready, irregular, weak quality is NOT a normal finding — always chart all three. 🩺
STEP 3 · ACT ON IT Vital signs exist to trigger an action — know what each red-flag pattern means you do next.

entries.h: 🚨 Airway → Breathing → Circulation — the universal priority order
entries.t: 1 🫁 Airway — is it open/patent? Position, suction, anticipate advanced airway if needed 2 💨 Breathing — rate, effort, SpO2, adventitious sounds 3 🫀 Circulation — pulse, BP, cap refill, cardiac monitor if unstable 🧠 ABC never changes. Whatever the diagnosis, the priority framework for an unstable vital sign pattern is always Airway → Breathing → Circulation.
SpO2 <85% — severe hypoxia New irregular pulse — get a full apical minute + notify Temp <95°F — hypothermia protocol Rigid, board-like abdomen + fever + tachycardia — think peritonitis

A single normal-range vital sign doesn't rule out deterioration — always compare to the client's own trend , not just the textbook range. 🧠 "Trend beats snapshot." A BP of 110/70 is reassuring for most people — but it's a red flag if their baseline is 160/95.

entries.h: 🗺️ Where this page fits in the batch
entries.t: NG-082 Assessment Locations — precise pulse points, lung/heart/bowel auscultation landmarks. NG-190 Head-to-Toe Assessment — the full systematic exam sequence, using this page's normal ranges as its baseline. NG-041 Hypothermia — deep dive on the temperature vital sign gone dangerously low. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🌡️ 98.6°F / 37°C typical average temp — real range ~97.8–99.1°F 💓 60–100 bpm rate + rhythm + quality, every time 🫁 12–20/min count a full minute, don't let them notice 🌬️ 95–100% SpO2 <85% = severe hypoxia, escalate now

Q1: A client's pulse is irregular. How should the nurse count it? Show answer Count the apical pulse for a full 60 seconds — never estimate an irregular rhythm from a partial count. Q2: SpO2 reads 83%. What tier of hypoxia is this and what's the priority? Show answer Severe hypoxia (typically taught as Q3: What three things must be charted for a pulse, not just the number? Show answer Rate, rhythm, and quality (e.g., 0 absent to 4+ bounding). Q4: Why is pain called the "5th (or 6th) vital sign"? Show answer Because

entries.h: Assessment Locations · NG-082 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 💓 Pulses 🫁 Lung Auscultation 🫀 Heart & Abdomen ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Nursing Core · Fundamentals of Nursing

Exactly where to put your fingers and your stethoscope NG-082 Nursing Core ADHD-friendly visual edition Every vital sign from NG-079 has a physical spot on the body where you actually collect it. This page is the landmark map — pulse points, lung auscultation ladder, heart's five listening points, and the abdomen's four quadrants. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 💓 7 pulse points Radial, brachial, carotid, femoral, popliteal, dorsalis pedis, posterior tibial. ⚠️ Never both carotids at once Bilateral pre
STEP 1 · FIND THE BEAT Same seven sites you saw on NG-079 — here's the exact anatomy and the one you never press on both sides at once.
🧠 "CBR-FPD-T" top to bottom: Carotid, Brachial, Radial, Femoral, Popliteal, Dorsalis pedis, Tibialis (posterior). Walk down the body and you hit every site in order.
Never palpate both carotid pulses at the same time — bilateral compression can slow the heart rate (vagal response) or reduce blood flow to the brain. 🧠 "One side of the neck at a time — always."

entries.h: ✅ Circulation checks — distal to the pulse
entries.t: Capillary refill : press nail bed, should return <3 sec Skin turgor : pinch skin, should return <3 sec Temperature should be equal bilaterally in all extremities SEE ALSO NG-190 Head-to-Toe — where these fit in the full exam sequence. 🫁
STEP 2 · WALK THE LADDER A systematic zig-zag down the chest, comparing side to side at every stop — never straight down one side then the other.

Start top-right, above the clavicle — listen for a full inhale + exhale Move to the opposite side , same spot — compare quality, depth, extra sounds Move down one interspace at a time, comparing side-to-side every stop Continue through the 6th ICS at the midaxillary line (armpit) — this covers the lower lobes Flip to posterior: client leans forward, hands in lap to separate the scapulae for a clean listen 🧠 "HF = Heavy Fluid." The lung bases are the best place to catch crackles from fluid overload / heart failure.

Use the ulnar and palmar surfaces of your hands against the chest wall while the client says "ninety-nine" — vibration should feel equal bilaterally. 🧠 Increased fremitus = consolidation (e.g., pneumonia). Decreased = air/fluid blocking transmission (e.g., pneumothorax, effusion).
Correct client language for shortness of breath: "It's hard for me to breathe and I feel short winded all the time." Dys-PNEA = Difficult breathing — a PRIORITY symptom.

Ensure the airway is open Monitor O2 saturation Place client in High Fowler's Evaluate effectiveness of respiratory effort after intervening 🧠 Most important objective data confirming hypoxia: ABGs (arterial blood gases) — not just the SpO2 number.

Bluish discoloration from hypoxia is checked at: Nailbeds — peripheral cyanosis Conjunctiva — central/mucosal cyanosis, more reliable in darker skin tones Earlobes 🧠 Also watch for: clubbing of the fingernail beds (chronic hypoxia), vertigo /dizziness, and increased pulse rate as signs of longer-term hypoxia. 🫀
STEP 3 · THE OTHER TWO STOPS Five points for the heart, four quadrants for the belly — and one order you can't mix up.

entries.h: 🫀 Heart auscultation — 5 points, "All Pigs Eat Too Much"
entries.t: 🧠 "All Pigs Eat Too Much" — A ortic, P ulmonic, E rb's point, T ricuspid, M itral, top to bottom down the left sternal border, ending at the apex (mitral/apical — the same spot you count the apical pulse from NG-079).
Listen for sounds in all four quadrants . If absent, listen for a full 5 minutes before charting "absent." 🧠 Chart as active, hyperactive, or hypoactive — never just "present."

entries.h: 🚨 The order you can't mix up: IAPP
entries.t: 1️⃣ Inspect ▼ 2️⃣ Auscultate ▼ 3️⃣ Percuss ▼ 4️⃣ Palpate The abdomen is the ONE exception to the usual inspect→palpate→percuss→auscultate order — palpating or percussing first can artificially stimulate bowel sounds and give a false reading. 🧠 "Look, Listen, THEN Touch" for the belly — auscultate before you ever press on it.

Belly should be flat , non-pulsating , and even/symmetric . Ask about pain with palpation — a rigid, board-like abdomen with fever and tachycardia is peritonitis until proven otherwise and is a priority to report. SEE ALSO NG-190 Head-to-Toe Assessment — where heart, lung, and abdominal auscultation fit into the full systematic exam sequence. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 💓 7 pulse points never both carotids at once 🫁 6th ICS midaxillary lowest stop on the ladder = lower lobes 🫀 APE To Man Aortic → Pulmonic → Erb's → Tricuspid → Mitral 🩻 Auscultate before palpate only true for the abdomen

Q1: Why should you never palpate both carotid pulses at once? Show answer Bilateral pressure can slow the heart rate via a vagal response or reduce cerebral blood flow. Q2: Where is the best place to auscultate for fluid overload in the lungs? Show answer The posterior lung bases — listen for crackles ("HF = Heavy Fluid"). Q3: What's the correct order of abdominal assessment, and why is it different from other systems? Show answer Inspect, Auscultate, Percuss, Palpate — auscultate before touching so you don't artif

entries.h: Diet Types · NG-084 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🥣 Diet Progression 🩺 Therapeutic Diets 🍽️ Nursing Care ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Nursing Core · Fundamentals of Nursing

Diet Progression & Special Therapeutic Diets NG-084 Nursing Core ADHD-friendly visual edition Diets are ordered along a texture ladder — NPO to regular — and layered with disease-specific restrictions like renal, cardiac, or diabetic diets. Know both axes: how solid the food is, and what it's restricting. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🚫 NPO Nothing by mouth — not even ice chips. Pre-op cutoff often midnight. 🥤 Clear → Full → Soft → Regular The texture progression after NPO, step by step. 🧂 Cardiac di
STEP 1 · TEXTURE LADDER Post-op and GI-recovery diets advance one texture step at a time — never skip a rung.
🧠 "See it, sip it, sneak it in, chew it." Clear (see through it) → Full (sip it, dairy added) → Pureed/mechanical soft (blend/chop it) → Soft/Regular (chew it).

No food or water, not even ice chips. Classic use: before surgery, often ordered as NPO after midnight . 🧠 "N-P-Zero." NPO status means zero intake — ice chips still count as intake and are not automatically allowed.
Any liquid you can see through : clear juice (apple, not orange), gelatin/Jell-O, broth, water, clear sports drinks, black coffee/tea. 🧠 If you can read a newspaper through it, it's clear.
Everything in clear liquid plus liquid dairy (milk, custard, ice cream) and all other juices (with pulp okay). 🧠 "Full = clear + dairy." One-word difference from clear liquid: dairy is now allowed.

Pureed: clear + full liquid, plus pureed meats, eggs, and fruits — anything that can go in a blender. Mechanical soft: clear + full liquid, plus chopped, diced, or ground food. 🧠 Pureed = blender. Mechanical soft = knife. Same base diet, different processing tool.
Easy-to-digest foods that are low in fiber — a bridge between mechanical soft and a full regular diet. 🧠 Soft = gentle on a healing gut, not just gentle to chew. 🩺
STEP 2 · MATCH THE DIET TO THE DISEASE These restrict or emphasize specific nutrients based on a diagnosis — layered on top of, not instead of, the texture diet.

No added salt, less than 2 g of sodium/day . Often paired with a low-cholesterol diet (less than 300 mg cholesterol/day) for cardiovascular disease. Used for heart failure, hypertension, and coronary artery disease — excess sodium pulls in fluid, raising blood pressure and cardiac workload. 🧠 "Salt holds water, water raises pressure." Every gram of sodium the patient skips is a little less fluid the heart has to move.

Typically restricts sodium, potassium, phosphorus, and sometimes protein and fluid , depending on the stage of kidney disease and dialysis status. Exact restrictions vary by lab values and nephrology orders — always individualized. ➡️ See the Renal batch pages (electrolyte imbalances, AKI/CKD) for the lab values and pathophysiology behind each restriction. 🧠 Renal diet = the kidneys can't clear it, so the plate has to. Failing kidneys can't excrete potassium/phosphorus/fluid — diet does the filtering job the kidney

A balance of protein and carbohydrates , no added sugar (soda, refined pasta, white bread). Modern practice favors a consistent-carbohydrate approach — same amount of carbs at each meal/snack, timed with insulin — over a strict "diabetic diet" of banned foods. 🧠 Consistency > restriction. The goal isn't zero carbs, it's predictable carbs the insulin dose can match.

Minimizes undigested material reaching the colon — used for IBD flares, diverticulitis, bowel rest, or before/after bowel surgery . Restricts raw fruits/veggies, whole grains, nuts, and seeds. 🧠 Low-residue = "give the gut a break." Less bulk moving through an inflamed or healing bowel.

Ordered after a swallow evaluation (often with speech-language pathology); texture is modified for both food and liquids to reduce aspiration risk. Food levels (general concept): pureed → mechanically altered/ground → soft & bite-sized → regular, with each step requiring less oral processing. Liquid thickness levels (general concept): thin → nectar-thick → honey-thick → pudding-thick, from least to most viscous. Exact level names and numbering vary by facility and by the framework used (e.g., IDDSI) — always follow
STEP 3 · INTAKE, MONITORING & TEACHING Diet orders only work if intake is actually monitored and the patient understands why.

Weigh at the same time every day , same scale, same clothing — usually first thing in the morning after the first void. All liquid intake/output measured in mL . 1 oz = 30 mL — the conversion you'll use constantly. 🧠 Same time, same scale, same clothes. Any variable you change makes the trend meaningless.

Restriction: heart failure and other conditions where fluid backs up into the lungs/body — educate the patient on why , don't just enforce it silently. Encouragement: some clients need more than the recommended intake — offer favorite (diet-appropriate) drinks and keep the pitcher full and fresh. 🧠 Same intervention, opposite direction — always check the order before assuming "more fluids is always better."

Age: decreased metabolism, decreased thirst mechanism, increased fiber need in older adults. Financial constraints — fixed income, cost of protein. Religion — restricts certain foods (pork, seafood) or requires fasting periods. Appetite — illness, eating disorders, or bad past experiences with "hospital food." Environment — hospital smells/sights are not always conducive to eating. Disease & medications — a newly diagnosed diabetic may dislike the options offered; some meds suppress appetite. 🧠 Nutrition isn't just

Explain the reason for every diet restriction — adherence improves when the patient understands the "why," e.g., low-sodium prevents fluid overload in heart failure. Confirm understanding of any fluid restriction and how to track it at home. For dysphagia diets, reinforce that thickened liquids and modified textures are a safety measure, not a punishment. Coordinate with dietitian/speech-language pathology for complex or combined therapeutic diets. 🧠 "Bland but explained." A low-sodium tray tastes worse — patients

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🚫 NPO Nothing at all — not even ice chips 🥤 Clear vs Full Full liquid = clear liquid + dairy 🧂 Cardiac diet Low sodium, < 2g/day 🩸 Renal diet Restricts Na, K, phosphorus ± protein/fluid

Q1: What's the difference between clear liquid and full liquid diets? Show answer Clear liquid is anything you can see through (broth, clear juice, gelatin, water). Full liquid is clear liquid plus liquid dairy and all other juices. Q2: A heart failure patient is on a low-sodium diet — how much sodium per day, and why? Show answer Less than 2 g/day. Sodium holds fluid, and in heart failure the heart can't pump that extra fluid forward, so it backs up into the lungs/body. Q3: What nutrients does a renal diet typical

Detailed: Pathophysiology, Assessment & Multimodal Treatment NG-086 Nursing Core ADHD-friendly visual edition Pain is whatever the patient says it is — the 5th vital sign, and the single most reported symptom in healthcare. Assess it, believe it, and treat it with the smallest effective combination of pharmacologic and nonpharmacologic tools. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🎯 Pain = subjective Believe the patient's number, not your own guess. 🪜 WHO ladder Non-opioid → weak opioid → strong opioid, addin
STEP 1 · HOW PAIN WORKS Nociception is the whole pathway from tissue injury to the brain's perception of pain.

Nociceptors are pain receptors on nerve endings that respond selectively to painful stimuli. Nociception is the transmission of that pain signal. Chemical substances at the injury site (prostaglandins, bradykinin, substance P) increase pain sensitivity; others (endorphins, enkephalins) decrease it. 🧠 "TTPM" — T ransduction, T ransmission, P erception, M odulation. Pain isn't a single event, it's a relay race.

entries.h: ⭐ COX-1 vs. COX-2 — why it matters for NSAIDs
entries.t: COX-1 COX-2 "Housekeeping" enzyme — protects gut lining, supports platelet function Induced by inflammation — drives pain, fever, swelling Blocking it → GI ulcers/bleeding risk Blocking it → reduces pain/fever/inflammation 🧠 COX-1 protects, COX-2 provokes. Non-selective NSAIDs block both — that's why they can cause GI upset while also relieving pain. See NG-256 NSAIDs for drug-level detail.

Endorphins and enkephalins are the body's own opioids — they inhibit substance P (a neurotransmitter that amplifies pain signals), naturally decreasing pain sensation. 🧠 "Endorphins are the body's built-in morphine." Exercise, laughter, and touch can boost this system — part of why nonpharmacologic care genuinely reduces pain, not just distracts from it.

entries.h: 📈 Acute vs. chronic pain — different bodies, different exam answers
entries.t: Acute pain Chronic pain Sudden onset, specific to an injury; lasts seconds up to 6 months Persistent, often malignant or non-malignant, lasts longer than 6 months ↑ cardiac output, impaired insulin response, immune suppression, ↑ cortisol, ↑ fluid retention Immune suppression, depression, disability, fatigue, anger, inability to perform ADLs Visible physiologic signs (↑ HR, ↑ RR, diaphoresis, grimacing) Often NO visible signs — normal vitals do not rule out chronic pain 🧠 NCLEX trap: A calm patient with normal vita
STEP 2 · ASK BEFORE YOU TREAT A structured history plus the right scale for the right patient — assessment always comes before the medication.

Letter What it means P Provocation/Palliation — aggravating & alleviating factors: what makes it worse? What makes it better? Q Quality — dull, sharp, stabbing, burning? R Region/Radiation — where is the pain? Does it radiate? S Severity — rate on a 0–10 scale T Timing — when did it start? What was happening at onset? Duration? 🧠 "Please Quit Radiating, Send Timely help." Many programs also teach OLDCART (Onset, Location, Duration, Characteristics, Aggravating/Alleviating, Radiation, Treatment) — same core question

0 None 1-3 Mild 4-6 Mod 7-9 Severe 10 Worst Gold standard when the patient can self-report — always use the patient's own number over a nurse's visual guess. 🧠 Pain is whatever the patient says it is, at the intensity they say it is.

Wong-Baker FACES scale — young children or anyone who can't use numbers; picks a face from smiling to crying. FLACC scale — infants, nonverbal, or cognitively impaired patients. Scores F ace, L egs, A ctivity, C ry, C onsolability, 0–2 each (0–10 total). CPOT / behavioral pain scales — sedated or intubated ICU patients; observe facial expression, body movement, muscle tension, ventilator compliance. 🧠 "Can't talk? Watch, don't guess." Nonverbal patients still feel pain — behavior is the vital sign when words aren't

entries.h: ⭐ Factors that influence how pain is expressed
entries.t: Past experience with pain shapes current perception and coping. Anxiety and depression both decrease the pain threshold — psych distress makes pain feel worse. Age and gender influence reporting and treatment bias. Culture — different cultures teach different "appropriate" pain responses; stoicism does not mean absence of pain. 🧠 Never assume — ask. A stoic patient from a culture that discourages outward pain expression can still be in severe pain; the number they give you is still the truth. 💊
STEP 3 · MULTIMODAL & STEPPED The WHO pain ladder steps therapy up with severity — and nonpharmacologic care belongs at every step, not just the mild ones.

entries.h: 🪜 WHO analgesic ladder — match the drug class to the severity
entries.t: 1 Mild pain (1–3): non-opioids — acetaminophen and/or NSAIDs (± adjuvant) 2 Moderate pain (4–6): weak/mild opioids (e.g., tramadol, codeine combinations) ± non-opioid 3 Severe pain (7–10): strong opioids (e.g., morphine, hydromorphone, fentanyl, oxycodone) ± non-opioid Multimodal analgesia = combining drug classes with different mechanisms (e.g., an NSAID + an opioid + a nonpharmacologic measure) to get better relief at lower opioid doses — fewer side effects, less respiratory depression risk. 🧠 The ladder adds, it

entries.h: 💊 Pharmacologic categories — see the dedicated pages for drug detail
entries.t: Non-opioids: NSAIDs (ketorolac, ibuprofen) for mild pain; acetaminophen can be given with NSAIDs and carries a hepatotoxicity risk at high/chronic doses. Opioids: tramadol, codeine (Tylenol #3), meperidine, oxycodone, fentanyl, morphine, hydromorphone. Adjuvants/routes: topical agents, local anesthesia, intraspinal (epidural/intrathecal) analgesia. Delivery methods: routine around-the-clock dosing for constant pain; PRN for breakthrough pain; PCA (patient-controlled analgesia) pump for self-titrated IV opioid dosin

entries.h: ✅ Nonpharmacologic interventions — real tools, not "just distraction"
entries.t: Cutaneous stimulation: TENS unit, massage Thermal therapy: heat and cold application Cognitive-behavioral: distraction, relaxation, guided imagery, hypnosis Music therapy Complementary: acupuncture 🧠 Nonpharm ≠ optional extra. These work through real physiologic pathways (e.g., gate-control theory, endorphin release) and should be layered in at every rung of the ladder, not reserved for "mild" pain only.

entries.h: 🚨 Opioid safety priorities — assess before AND after every dose
entries.t: Priority Why Respiratory rate Hold and notify provider if RR < 12/min — respiratory depression is the #1 life-threatening opioid adverse effect. Sedation level Increasing sedation precedes respiratory depression — a rising sedation score is an earlier warning sign than the RR itself. Bowel function Opioid-induced constipation is nearly universal — prophylactic bowel regimen, not PRN. Naloxone Opioid antagonist reversal agent — know where it is and keep it available for any patient on IV/high-dose opioids. 🧠 "Sedati

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🎯 Pain = subjective Trust the patient's number over your own guess 🪜 WHO ladder Mild → weak opioid → strong opioid, always adding non-opioid + nonpharm 🧒 FLACC / FACES Use behavior scales for nonverbal or pediatric patients 🚨 RR < 12 Hold the opioid dose, notify the provider, have naloxone ready

Q1: What does PQRST stand for in a pain assessment? Show answer Provocation/Palliation, Quality, Region/Radiation, Severity, Timing. Q2: A calm patient with normal vital signs rates their chronic pain 8/10 — what should the nurse do? Show answer Believe the reported number and treat accordingly — chronic pain often shows no visible physiologic signs, unlike acute pain. Q3: Which scale is used for a nonverbal, cognitively impaired patient? Show answer The FLACC scale (Face, Legs, Activity, Cry, Consolability) or ano
