entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 📖 Terms 🔎 Spot it ⚖️ Conflicts 🎯 NCLEX ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Nursing Core · Legal & Ethics Series

The 6 ethical principles every legal/ethics NCLEX question is built on NG-133 NURSING CORE Series: Legal & Ethics 1 of 5 ADHD-friendly visual edition Every ethics/legal NCLEX question — informed consent, restraints, refusing treatment, AMA discharge, advance directives — is secretly testing one of six words : autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence, justice, fidelity, and veracity . Learn these six cold first — the rest of this series (Tort Law, Informed Consent, Advance Directives, AMA & Mandatory Reporting) is just
STEP 1 · KNOW THE WORDS Six pillars hold up every ethical decision a nurse makes — memorize the word, the one-line gloss, and one real example each.

entries.h: 🏛️ The six pillars of nursing ethics
entries.t: 🧠 "A Big Nurse Just Feels Very (caring)." A(utonomy) — B(eneficence) — N(onmaleficence) — J(ustice) — F(idelity) — V(eracity). Say the sentence, tap one pillar per word.

The client's right to make their own healthcare decisions , as long as they are a competent adult who has been informed of the risks. Example: Respecting a competent client's right to refuse a treatment — even a Jehovah's Witness refusing a life-saving blood transfusion, or a client signing out AMA. 🧠 NCLEX trap: the nurse's job is to educate on the risks, not to override the choice. Ignoring a competent refusal = a violation of autonomy (and can become battery — see Tort Law, page 2 of this series).

Doing and promoting good for the client — actively acting in their best interest, not just avoiding harm. Example: Calling a client's family to tell them their loved one is "critically ill and we are caring for their needs" so the family isn't left in the dark. 🧠 Beneficence = doing the good thing. Nonmaleficence (next card) is its quieter twin — not doing the bad thing.

= "first, do no harm" To avoid causing harm to the client, intentionally or through carelessness. Example: Double-checking a drug dosage with another nurse before giving a high-alert medication. 🧠 "Mal" = bad (think "malicious"). Non-mal-eficence = actively steering away from the bad outcome.

Treating clients fairly and equally — resources, time, and care distributed equitably regardless of race, gender, religion, culture, insurance status, or ability to pay. Example: Providing the same standard of care to every client on the unit, not just the ones who tip better or complain loudest. 🧠 Justice ≠ identical. True justice is equitable — the client who needs more gets more; the point is no one is shorted because of who they are .

Staying loyal to the client and following through on your responsibilities and promises — even the small ones. Example: Client reports 8/10 pain ; the nurse states she will return with pain medication — and does . 🧠 Fidelity = "I do what I said I'd do." Every broken small promise ("I'll be right back") chips away at trust — and is a fidelity violation, even if nothing bad happens medically.

To tell the truth — full, accurate information, even when it's uncomfortable. Example: A medication error occurs with NO adverse effect on the client — the nurse still reports it , and still tells the client/family it happened. 🧠 Veracity is tested by the "no harm done" trap. If the stem says "no harm resulted," students often think "so don't bother reporting." Wrong — veracity says report it anyway.

Not always grouped with the classic 6, but shows up constantly on ethics questions: to protect the client's rights, health, and safety — speaking up on their behalf. Example: Reporting a critical change in the client's condition to the HCP right away. Example: Relaying a client's wish (e.g., about code status or a treatment refusal) to the care team when they cannot speak for themselves. 🧠 Advocacy is the action arm of autonomy + beneficence combined — you protect the client's right to choose (autonomy) and their w
STEP 2 · MATCH THE SCENARIO NCLEX never says the word "autonomy" out loud — it gives you the scenario and makes you name the principle.

Scenario Principle tested Client reports 8/10 pain; nurse promises to return with pain meds — and does Fidelity 🤝 Nurse calls family: "he is critically ill and we are caring for his needs" Beneficence 💙 Nurse double-checks a drug dosage with a coworker before giving it Nonmaleficence 🚫 A medication error happens with zero adverse effect — nurse reports it anyway Veracity 🗣️ Nurse provides the same quality of care regardless of race, gender, religion, or culture Justice ⚖️ Nurse respects a competent client's decisio
🧠 Every fidelity question has this exact shape: promise made → promise kept. If the nurse promises and does NOT follow through, that's a fidelity violation — same principle, opposite direction. ⚖️
STEP 3 · PRIORITIZE The hardest ethics questions pit two good principles against each other — you have to know which one wins, and why.

entries.h: 🪢 The classic tug-of-war: Autonomy vs. Beneficence
entries.t: If the client is competent, informed, and adult , their right to choose (even to refuse) outranks what the nurse or family thinks is "best." The nurse's job shifts to educate, document, and support — not override. 🧠 "Competent wins." The single fastest way to answer an autonomy-vs-beneficence question: ask "is this client competent?" If yes — autonomy wins almost every time.

entries.h: 🚧 When autonomy does NOT automatically win
entries.t: 🧒 Client is a minor without emancipated status 🧠 Client lacks decision-making capacity — unconscious, severely impaired, actively intoxicated 🚨 True emergency , life/limb at risk, no surrogate reachable ⚠️ Client is a danger to self or others (may trigger a legal hold — varies by state ) 📋 Mandatory reporting laws override confidentiality/autonomy (abuse, certain communicable diseases) 🧠 These five exceptions come back in full on page 4 (Advance Directives) and page 5 (AMA & Mandatory Reporting) of this series.

entries.h: 🔀 Nonmaleficence vs. Beneficence — the subtle one
entries.t: Nonmaleficence (avoid harm) is usually the floor ; beneficence (do good) is the ceiling . A nurse must always clear the floor, and should reach for the ceiling when possible — but never sacrifice "do no harm" chasing "do more good." Example: Restraining an agitated client "for their own good" (beneficence reasoning) without meeting the legal criteria can cross into harm — false imprisonment (see Tort Law, next page). 🧠 "First, do no harm" outranks "do more good." If an intervention risks harm, that's a nonmaleficen
STEP 4 · DON'T GET FOOLED These six words are the connective tissue for the rest of this legal & ethics series — here's where they trip students up.

If a competent client refuses treatment and the nurse personally disagrees with the choice, the correct action is still to respect autonomy — document the refusal, ensure the client is informed, and notify the HCP. Overriding it can become battery . 🧠 The nurse's opinion is not a legal override. Feelings ≠ authority.

entries.h: ⭐ Trap: "no harm was done, so why report it?"
entries.t: A med error with zero adverse effect must still be reported — that's veracity , not overkill. Reporting also protects the next client and feeds facility safety data. 🧠 "No harm" changes the outcome, not the obligation to be honest.

entries.h: ✅ Foundation: the ANA Code of Ethics
entries.t: The American Nurses Association (ANA) establishes the ethical standards for the entire nursing profession — every one of these six terms traces back to that Code. 🧠 If a question asks "who sets nursing's ethical standards," the answer is the ANA — not a hospital's individual policy. 🔗 Where this goes next: Autonomy violated by force = NG-172 · Tort Law (battery, false imprisonment). Autonomy exercised through a signature = NG-192 · Informed Consent . Autonomy exercised in advance = NG-212 · Advance Directives . Aut

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🅰️ Autonomy Competent client's choice — nurse educates, doesn't override 💙🚫 Beneficence / Nonmaleficence Do good / avoid harm — nonmaleficence is the floor ⚖️ Justice Equitable care, regardless of who the client is 🤝🗣️ Fidelity / Veracity Keep the promise · tell the truth, even with no harm done

Q1: A client with 8/10 pain is told by the nurse "I'll be back with your medication," and the nurse returns as promised. Which principle? Show answer Fidelity — following through on a promise/responsibility. Q2: A medication error occurs but causes zero harm. Should the nurse report it? Show answer Yes — veracity requires honesty regardless of outcome. Q3: A competent adult refuses a blood transfusion the nurse believes is life-saving. What wins? Show answer Autonomy — for a competent, informed adult, their choice

entries.h: Ambulation (Body Mechanics & Mobility) · NG-167 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🦴 Mechanics 🚶 Assessment & Devices 🩺 Safety & Falls ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Nursing Core · Fundamentals of Nursing

Body Mechanics, Mobility & Fall Prevention NG-167 Nursing Core ADHD-friendly visual edition Coordinated effort to maintain balance, posture, and body alignment while lifting, moving, and ambulating clients — protecting both the patient and the nurse's own spine. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🦴 Wide base, bent knees Feet apart, knees flexed, load close to the body — never the back. 🎗️ Gait belt = default Use it for any client with fall risk or weakness before ambulating. 🦯 Cane on the STRONG side Adva
STEP 1 · PROTECT THE SPINE Purpose: the safe, coordinated practice of maintaining balance, posture, and alignment while lifting, moving, and ambulating clients.

entries.h: 🏋️ The five rules of safe lifting
entries.t: 🦶 Wide base of support — feet shoulder-width apart. 🦵 Bend at the knees , not the waist — squat, don't stoop. 🎒 Keep the load close to the body's center of gravity. 💪 Use arms/legs to lift — never twist or lift with the back . 🫃 Tighten abdominal & gluteal muscles before the move to brace the core. 🧠 "Squat, don't stoop." If your back is rounding forward, you're doing it wrong — drop your hips, not your spine.

Arrange for help before moving a client — never solo a heavy or unpredictable transfer. Encourage the client to assist when able. Avoid twisting — keep back, neck, pelvis, and feet aligned and facing the same direction. Position yourself close to the client or object. 🧠 Close and squared-up. The nearer you are, and the more your whole body faces the load, the less shear on your spine.

Uncoordinated lifts — no count-of-three teamwork Manual lifting without equipment Lifting while tired Repetitive lifting, transferring, repositioning Prolonged standing 🧠 The team lift. The person bearing the brunt of the load calls the count of three — everyone moves together, not one person straining alone.

entries.h: 🔁 Moving a client in bed — slide, don't drag
entries.t: Slide the client toward you using a pull/draw sheet instead of dragging skin across linen — dragging causes shear and friction injury to fragile skin. 🧠 Sheet, not skin. The pull sheet takes the friction so the patient's skin doesn't have to. 🚶
STEP 2 · GAIT, ROM & TOOLS Know what normal gait and range of motion look like — then match the right assistive device to the client.

entries.h: 🩺 Mobility assessment — what to ask & observe
entries.t: Daily activity & endurance: "What does your day look like? What makes you tired?" Exercise goals and mobility problems: pain, SOB, or discomfort with movement? Physical/mental alterations and external factors affecting ambulation. Range of motion (ROM): the full movement potential of a joint — flexion & extension. Active ROM Passive ROM Patient moves the limb themselves, no assistance Therapist/equipment moves the joint — no effort from the patient 🧠 Active = "I move it," Passive = "you move it."

Normal Abnormal Head erect, spine straight, arms swing in alternation with legs; one leg in stance while the other swings Ataxia, Parkinsonian gait, scissor gait, steppage gait, spastic hemiparesis Straight line ear–shoulder–hip in alignment Abnormal spinal curvature (scoliosis), can't maintain alignment independently Full ROM, no joint deformity Limited ROM, swelling, heat, tenderness, crepitation, deformity Voluntary, controlled, coordinated movement Tremors, tics, chorea, dystonia, fasciculations 🧠 Watch the who

Age & developmental level Attitudes & family values Neuromuscular / joint disorders Trauma to the musculoskeletal system Mental health & medications (sedation, weakness) Lifestyle, stress, environment 🧠 Mobility isn't just "can they walk" — it's biology, environment, and psychology all together.

entries.h: 🦯 Assistive devices — match the tool to the deficit
entries.t: Device Best for / key point Cane 🦯 Mild weakness/balance issues on one side. Held on the strong side; advance with the weak leg. Walker 🚶 Greater instability; needs more support & upper-body strength. All 4 legs contact the floor before stepping — never "walk" it by only advancing 2 legs at a time unless it's a rolling walker with wheels . Crutches 🩼 Non-weight-bearing or partial weight-bearing on one leg. Weight goes through the hands/palms , never the axillae — axillary pressure risks nerve damage (crutch palsy)
STEP 3 · PREVENT THE #1 INJURY Falls are the leading cause of hospital-acquired injury — assess risk before every transfer.

entries.h: 🚨 Fall risk assessment — before you move anyone
entries.t: History of falls, gait/balance problems, or use of an assistive device Medications: sedatives, opioids, antihypertensives, diuretics (orthostatic hypotension risk) Cognitive status: confusion, dementia, impulsivity Sensory deficits: vision, hearing, peripheral neuropathy Environment: clutter, poor lighting, wet floors, improper footwear, tubing/lines underfoot 🧠 Assess before you ambulate, not after they fall. Most inpatient fall-risk tools (e.g., Morse Fall Scale) score history, mental status, gait, and IV/meds —

Gait belt on any client identified as fall risk Bed in lowest position , brakes locked, call light within reach Non-skid footwear before every ambulation Clear the path — cords, tubing, clutter out of the way Orthostatic check: sit → dangle → stand, pausing at each step 🧠 "Sit, dangle, stand" — never rush a first mobilization. Orthostatic hypotension causes a huge share of first-time-up-out-of-bed falls.

entries.h: ⚠️ Signs of activity intolerance — stop and reassess
entries.t: Significantly increased pulse, respirations, or BP; SOB/dyspnea; weakness; pallor; confusion; vertigo; pain. 🧠 If any of these appear during ambulation, stop, sit the patient down, and reassess vitals before continuing.

Ambulation starts with safe bed mobility . Before a client stands, they need to be positioned and moved correctly in bed — logrolling, using a pull sheet, and choosing the right position to sit up from. ➡️ See NG-072 — Positioning for the named bed positions (Fowler's, lateral, Sims', etc.) that set up a safe transfer to standing. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🦴 Bend knees, not waist Wide base, load close, use legs to lift 🦯 Cane = strong side Advance cane + weak leg together 🩼 Crutches = weight on hands Never the armpits — nerve damage risk 🚨 Sit, dangle, stand Check orthostatics before first ambulation

Q1: What are the core body mechanics rules for lifting a client? Show answer Wide base of support, bend at the knees not the waist, keep the load close to the body, use arms/legs not the back, and tighten the abdomen/glutes before moving. Q2: Where should crutch weight be borne, and why? Show answer On the hands/palms — weight on the axillae can cause nerve compression ("crutch palsy"). Q3: Which side does a cane go on, and how does the patient step? Show answer The strong side. The cane and the weak leg advance to

entries.h: Med Math Memory Tricks · NG-171 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🧮 Formulas ✍️ Work it out 🔁 Convert & traps ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Nursing Core · Fundamentals of Nursing

Memory Tricks for Dosage Calculation NG-171 Nursing Core ADHD-friendly visual edition Three formulas run almost every med-math question you'll ever see : D/H×Q for tablets & liquids, mL/hr for pumps, and gtt/min for gravity tubing. Learn the formula, learn where the numbers plug in, and always convert your units first. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🎯 D/H × Q Desired ÷ Have × Quantity = amount to give. 💧 gtt/min (mL × drop factor) ÷ min — gravity/manual tubing. 🖥️ mL/hr mL ÷ hr — what you program into
STEP 1 · KNOW THE THREE Almost every dosage-calc question on the NCLEX is one of these three formulas wearing a different costume.

entries.h: 💊 The master formula: D/H × Q — "Desired over Have, times Quantity"
entries.t: USE FOR tablets, capsules, and oral/IM liquids — anything where the drug comes in a fixed strength and you need to figure out how many units to give. 🧠 "What you WANT, over what you'VE GOT, times what it comes IN." D = the order, H = the label/vial, Q = tablet or mL that dose is packaged as. Multiply last, always.

Formula mL/hr = Volume (mL) ÷ Time (hr) USE FOR anything running on an electronic infusion pump — you program the rate directly in mL per hour. 🧠 "Pump = per hour." If it has a screen and buttons, it wants mL/hr .

Formula gtt/min = (mL/hr × drop factor) ÷ 60 USE FOR manual/gravity tubing with no pump — you count drops falling in the drip chamber per minute. 🧠 "No pump = count the drops." Drop factor (gtt/mL) is printed right on the IV tubing package.

entries.h: ⚖️ Weight-based dosing — same D/H×Q, plus one extra step
entries.t: Many pediatric doses, and adult doses ordered as "per kilogram," use mg/kg or mcg/kg/min . You must find the total dose before you can use D/H×Q. Step 1 Weight (kg) × ordered dose (mg/kg) = total dose Step 2 If divided doses: total dose ÷ number of doses/day = dose per administration Step 3 Now plug that number into D/H × Q like any other order. 🧠 "Weight first, formula second." A weight-based order is never the final number to give — it's the D you still have to run through D/H×Q.

entries.h: 📐 Body Surface Area (BSA) — the formula behind chemo & some pediatric dosing
entries.t: Some high-alert doses (chemotherapy, certain pediatric meds) are ordered per m² of body surface area instead of per kilogram, because BSA correlates better with organ function and drug clearance. Mosteller formula BSA (m²) = √[ height (cm) × weight (kg) ÷ 3600 ] Then Total dose = BSA (m²) × ordered dose (mg/m²) 🧠 BSA math is high-stakes — verify with a second RN. These are exactly the calculations where facilities require an independent double-check before the drug leaves the Pyxis. ✍️
STEP 2 · PLUG IN NUMBERS The same five formulas, now with numbers plugged in step by step. All example numbers below are made up for practicing the math only — not real drug orders.

EXAMPLE PROBLEM · not a real order Ordered (D) 500 mg Have (H) 250 mg per tablet Quantity (Q) 1 tablet Plug in 500 ÷ 250 × 1 = 2 tablets 🧠 If D and H are already the same unit, the math is just a simple ratio.

EXAMPLE PROBLEM · not a real order Ordered (D) 750 mg Have (H) 250 mg per 5 mL Quantity (Q) 5 mL Plug in 750 ÷ 250 × 5 = 15 mL 🧠 Q is whatever volume H is measured in — here H is "per 5 mL," so Q = 5 mL, not 1.

EXAMPLE PROBLEM · not a real order Step 1 154 lb ÷ 2.2 = 70 kg Step 2 70 kg × 5 mg/kg/day = 350 mg/day Step 3 350 mg ÷ 2 doses = 175 mg/dose q12h 🧠 Weight goes to kg before anything else touches it. Skipping the lb→kg conversion is the single most common weight-based math error.

entries.h: 🖥️💧 Worked example — pump (mL/hr) vs. gravity tubing (gtt/min)
entries.t: EXAMPLE PROBLEM · not a real order Ordered 1000 mL over 8 hr, drop factor 15 gtt/mL Pump 1000 ÷ 8 = 125 mL/hr Gravity Step 1 1000 ÷ 8 = 125 mL/hr Gravity Step 2 (125 × 15) ÷ 60 = 31.25 Pump: 125 mL/hr · Gravity: round to 31 gtt/min 🧠 Same order, two different final answers depending on the equipment. Round gtt/min to a whole drop — you cannot count a quarter of a drop falling in the chamber.

entries.h: ⚡ Shortcut: skip step 2 for common drop factors
entries.t: Because 60 minutes is always the denominator, common drop factors simplify to one quick division of mL/hr: Drop factor Tubing type Shortcut from mL/hr 10 gtt/mL Macrodrip gtt/min = mL/hr ÷ 6 15 gtt/mL Macrodrip gtt/min = mL/hr ÷ 4 20 gtt/mL Macrodrip gtt/min = mL/hr ÷ 3 60 gtt/mL Microdrip gtt/min = mL/hr (1:1) 🧠 Microdrip = 60, and 60 makes gtt/min and mL/hr the SAME NUMBER. Microdrip tubing (60 gtt/mL) is used for peds, critical care, and any fluid needing very precise, small-volume control — the exact drop facto
STEP 3 · SAME UNITS FIRST Every formula above only works if D and H are already in the same unit — convert before you calculate, not after.

entries.h: 🪜 The metric staircase — mcg ⇄ mg ⇄ g, and mL ⇄ L
entries.t: Same rule for volume: 1 L = 1000 mL . And for weight: 1 kg = 2.2 lb — lb → kg, divide by 2.2; kg → lb, multiply by 2.2. 🧠 "Small word, small step; big jump, big multiply." Kilo → milli → micro is always ×1000 each step down. Confusing mcg and mg is a 1000-fold overdose — always double-check the abbreviation before you calculate.

A misread or miswritten unit — mcg mistaken for mg — is a 1000× dosing error . High-alert IV drips are especially at risk because they're often dosed in mcg/kg/min . 🧠 "Micro is minuscule." mcg is always the smallest, most cautious unit in the room — if a number in mcg looks small, that's normal, not a mistake.

Calculating a weight-based dose using pounds instead of kilograms gives an answer that's roughly 2.2× too high . Always convert weight to kg before multiplying by mg/kg. 🧠 Weight-based order? Kilos or it doesn't count. If the chart shows lb, convert first — every single time.

entries.h: ⚠️ NCLEX trap: pump formula vs. gravity formula
entries.t: Using gtt/min math when the fluid is actually running through an electronic pump (or vice versa) gives a nonsense rate. Pump screens want mL/hr; gravity tubing needs a drop count. 🧠 "Buttons = mL/hr. No buttons = count drops." Look at the equipment before you pick the formula.

Using 15 gtt/mL math on 60 gtt/mL microdrip tubing (or the reverse) throws the whole answer off. The drop factor is printed on the tubing package — never assume it. 🧠 Read the box before you do the math. Different tubing, different formula — every time.

entries.h: 🚨 High-alert meds: math isn't the only safety check
entries.t: Insulin, heparin, IV opioids, chemotherapy, and other high-alert drugs typically require an independent double-check by a second RN before administration — regardless of how confident you are in your own calculation. Correct math does not replace a required double-check. 🧠 "High alert, second set of eyes." Facility policy, not your certainty, decides when a double-check is required — always verify the policy for the specific drug. ⚡
SAY IT OUT LOUD 🎯 D/H × Q Desired ÷ Have × Quantity = amount to give 💧 gtt/min (mL/hr × drop factor) ÷ 60 🖥️ mL/hr Volume (mL) ÷ Time (hr) 🔁 Convert first kg/g/mg/mcg ×1000 down, ÷1000 up · lb÷2.2=kg

Q1: What's the master oral/IM dosage formula? Show answer D/H × Q — Desired dose ÷ Have (dose on hand) × Quantity (the form that dose comes in). Q2: An electronic pump is infusing fluid — which formula do you use, mL/hr or gtt/min? Show answer mL/hr = Volume (mL) ÷ Time (hr). gtt/min is only for gravity/manual tubing with no pump. Q3: Before calculating a weight-based dose given in pounds, what must you do first? Show answer Convert pounds to kilograms (lb ÷ 2.2 = kg) before multiplying by the mg/kg order — skippin

entries.h: Tort Law · NG-172 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🧾 Basics ⚖️ Negligence 🚨 Intentional 🎯 NCLEX ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Nursing Core · Legal & Ethics Series

Negligence, malpractice, and the intentional torts that show up on every NCLEX legal question NG-172 NURSING CORE Series: Legal & Ethics 2 of 5 ADHD-friendly visual edition A tort is a wrongful act or violation of someone's rights that creates legal liability. Nursing torts split into two families: unintentional (negligence, malpractice — you didn't mean to cause harm, but you did) and intentional (assault, battery, false imprisonment, defamation — willful acts that violate a client's rights). The burden of proof a
STEP 1 · DEFINE THE TERM One umbrella word — tort — covers everything from an honest mistake to a deliberate violation.

entries.h: ⚖️ Tort = a wrongful act that creates legal liability
entries.t: 🧠 "Innocent until proven, and it's not your job to prove it." Whoever brings the claim (the accuser) has to prove the nurse was liable — the nurse doesn't have to prove innocence.

Civil Criminal Crime against an individual Crime against the state Most nursing torts land here More serious — can involve licensure loss, jail 🧠 Most malpractice suits are civil — but abuse, patient abandonment with harm, or falsifying records can escalate to criminal .

Used to determine the standard of care in every negligence/malpractice case: "What would a reasonable, prudent nurse — with similar training and experience, in a similar setting — have done in this same situation?" 🧠 It's not "what would a perfect nurse do" — it's what a reasonably careful peer would do. This test comes back on the Informed Consent page too. ⚖️
STEP 2 · UNINTENTIONAL TORTS Same family, different license — malpractice is negligence committed by a licensed professional.

entries.h: 🪜 The 4 elements of negligence — ALL FOUR must be present
entries.t: Example: A nurse doesn't wash hands before inserting a Foley catheter ( breach — a duty existed) and the client develops a catheter-associated UTI ( causation + damages ). All four elements present = negligence. 🧠 "DBCD — Don't Break the Client's Duty." Duty → Breach → Causation → Damages. Miss any one link and there's no negligence claim, no matter how careless the nurse was.

The failure to provide adequate care that another reasonable, prudent nurse would provide in a similar situation. Example: A nurse identifies an absent peripheral pulse in a client's casted extremity in the early morning — but doesn't report it to the HCP until the early afternoon. The delay is the breach. 🧠 Withholding informed consent can itself be negligence — if a provider doesn't obtain proper consent, that provider can be found negligent.

entries.h: 🩺 Malpractice — negligence with a license attached
entries.t: Illegal, improper, or negligent actions by a licensed professional — practice that falls below the accepted standard of care. Example: An RN fails to check the dosage printed on a medication vial, and the client is harmed as a result. 🧠 Malpractice = negligence + a license. Every malpractice case is negligence, but not every negligence case is malpractice — malpractice specifically requires the person to be a licensed professional acting within their scope.

Desertion of a client by anyone who has already assumed responsibility for their care — for example, leaving an assignment or ending a nurse-client relationship without properly transferring care or giving adequate notice. 🧠 Once a nurse accepts an assignment (duty exists), walking away without a proper hand-off is abandonment — even if the intent was reasonable (e.g., leaving because the assignment felt unsafe). Always notify the charge nurse/supervisor first. 🚨
STEP 3 · WILLFUL ACTS These are deliberate — no accident excuse. Assault and battery are the two NCLEX loves most.

entries.h: 🆚 Assault (the threat) vs. Battery (the act) — A comes before B
entries.t: 🧠 "A & B, in order — Assault before Battery." The threat (A) doesn't require contact; the act (B) does. Both can happen in one scenario: threatening an NG tube (assault) then inserting it anyway over refusal (battery).

Using physical restraints, seclusion, or a chemical restraint to keep someone against their will — without a valid order/indication. Example: Using restraints on a competent client just to prevent them from leaving the facility. Chemically restraining a competent client able to make their own decisions is both false imprisonment and assault/battery. 🧠 A restraint used for the wrong reason (convenience, punishment, "they might leave AMA") is false imprisonment — see page 5 for the correct AMA process.

entries.h: 📚 Defamation of character — Libel vs. Slander
entries.t: Making false, rude, or insulting remarks that harm a client's (or coworker's) reputation. Libel Slander Written Spoken 🧠 "LIBEL lives in the LIBRARY" — both start with L, and a library holds written words. Example: break-room gossip about a coworker's alleged affair with a client = slander (spoken).

Violating a client's confidentiality rights — including HIPAA violations. Example: Discussing a client's diagnosis where others can overhear, or accessing a chart with no professional reason to. 🧠 Confidentiality violations sit at the intersection of tort law and HIPAA — same act, two different legal exposures. 🎯
STEP 4 · DON'T GET FOOLED The exam loves to mix these terms up on purpose — here's how to keep them straight.

entries.h: 🔀 Side-by-side: the pairs students swap by mistake
entries.t: Term Definition Key distinguisher Negligence Failure to provide the care a reasonable, prudent peer would Anyone with a duty of care Malpractice Negligence committed by a licensed professional , below standard of care Requires a license Assault Threat of harm No contact required Battery Unconsented harmful/offensive contact Contact did occur False imprisonment Restricting freedom without valid cause Restraints/seclusion misused Libel Defamation Written Slander Defamation Spoken

entries.h: 🚨 Highest-yield fact: treatment without consent = battery
entries.t: This single fact links Tort Law directly to the next page in this series. Any invasive procedure, medication, or treatment given without valid consent — even if medically appropriate — is legally battery. 🧠 See NG-192 · Informed Consent for exactly how consent is obtained, witnessed, and withdrawn.

In any tort claim, the accuser must prove all required elements. A nurse is not required to prove they did nothing wrong — the plaintiff must prove the nurse did. 🧠 This is why thorough, honest documentation matters so much — it's the nurse's best defense if an accusation is ever made. 🔗 Series link: These terms are built on the six ethical principles from NG-133 · Ethical Key Terms (battery = a violation of autonomy; false imprisonment = a violation of autonomy done under a false banner of beneficence). Restraint

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🧾 Burden of proof On the accuser, not the nurse 🪜 4 elements Duty → Breach → Causation → Damages 🆚 Assault → Battery Threat, then act — in that order 🔒 No consent = Battery, every time

Q1: A nurse skips hand hygiene before a Foley insertion and the client develops a UTI. Which 2 elements of negligence does this satisfy at minimum? Show answer Breach (skipped standard technique) and causation/damages (the UTI resulted) — plus duty, since a nurse-client relationship existed. All four elements are present. Q2: A nurse says "I'll restrain you if you get up again" but never actually restrains the client. What tort is this? Show answer Assault — the threat of harm, without any actual contact. Q3: A com

entries.h: Delegation · 5 Rights · NG-180 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics ✋ 5 Rights 🧩 Who does what 🛡️ Stay safe ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Nursing Core · Fundamentals of Nursing

The 5 Rights of Delegation NG-180 Nursing Core ADHD-friendly visual edition Delegation transfers the task, never the responsibility. The RN is still accountable for choosing to delegate correctly and for supervising the outcome — which is exactly why assessment, evaluation, teaching, and any task requiring nursing judgment can never be delegated to a UAP. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → ✋ 5 Rights Task · Circumstance · Person · Direction/Communication · Supervision. ✅ UAP CAN Stable vitals, ADLs, ambul
STEP 1 · BEFORE YOU DELEGATE Every one of these five has to be true before a task leaves the RN's hands.
🧠 "TCP-DS" — T ask · C ircumstance · P erson · D irection · S upervision. If any one of the five is missing, don't delegate the task.

Right Task — the task is stable, routine, standardized, and does not require nursing judgment. Right Circumstance — the client's condition is stable and predictable for this task, right here, right now. Do not delegate a task for an unstable client — even a normally-delegable task like vital signs becomes RN-only if the client is unstable. 🧠 Stable task + stable client = safe to hand off. Either one being unstable cancels the delegation.

Only delegate tasks allowed by state Nurse Practice Act and workplace/facility policy , to someone whose knowledge, skill, and experience matches the task. Assess the assistant's competency to perform the task safely before delegating. "Right Person" applies at every level — RN → LPN/LVN, and RN/LPN → UAP/CNA. 🧠 Scope of practice isn't optional. "I thought they could do it" is not a defense — verify competency first.

Give a clear, concise description of the task, the goal, the expected time frame, and exactly when to report back . 🧠 "Task + Time frame + Tell me." Every delegated order needs all three, or the AP doesn't know when something is wrong.

Follow up, and evaluate the outcome of the delegated task. Always reassess tasks you have delegated — supervision doesn't end when you walk away. 🧠 Delegate, don't disappear. The RN checks the work and the outcome, every time. 🧩
STEP 2 · SCOPE OF PRACTICE Delegation flows downhill from RN → LPN/LVN → UAP/CNA — and the higher-judgment tasks stop at the top.
🧠 "Judgment doesn't roll downhill." The higher the level of clinical judgment a task requires, the closer it stays to the RN.

entries.h: ✅ CAN delegate to UAP/CNA — stable, routine, predictable tasks
entries.t: 🩺 Vital signs stable client 🚶 Ambulation stable client 🛁 ADLs bathing, grooming, feeding, toileting 🔄 Position changes turning, repositioning 📋 Record I & O recording only ⚖️ Weighing routine daily weight 🧠 "SAP" = Stable, no Assessment, Predictable. If a task is routine and doesn't require interpreting data, it's usually delegable to a UAP.

entries.h: ❌ CANNOT delegate to UAP/CNA — RN judgment tasks
entries.t: 🧠 Assessment initial or ongoing 📊 Evaluation interpreting labs, vitals trends, pain 🗣️ Teaching any patient education 💉 IV push meds RN only 🩸 Blood products transfusions 🧪 Central line drugs chemo, TPN 🧠 "ATE-B" never leaves the RN — A ssess · T each · E valuate · B lood/high-risk meds. Say it like "eat a B" — the RN always eats that whole plate alone.

✅ LPN/LVN CAN ❌ LPN/LVN CANNOT Reinforce/secondary teaching (not initial teaching) Initial, first, or primary assessment Follow-up assessment (not initial/primary) First/initial patient teaching Administer PO, SQ, IM medications IV push medications Maintain IVs; calculate & monitor IV flow rates Titrate (change) an IV drip rate Administer IVPB (piggyback) medications Independent evaluation of outcomes Monitor an ongoing blood transfusion Initiate/administer a blood transfusion CAUTION IV push scope for LPN/LVN vari
STEP 3 · SUPERVISE & PROTECT You can delegate a task — you cannot delegate the responsibility for the outcome.

entries.h: 🚨 Keywords that mean "do NOT delegate — RN territory"
entries.t: 🆕 New admission ⚡ Sudden change in status 🥇 First time doing anything 🏥 Post-op / returning from a procedure 📉 Unstable vitals, labs, blood sugar 🧾 Discharge teaching 🧠 "New, First, Sudden, Unstable" = RN. Any client who is new to the unit, newly changed, or newly unstable needs the RN's own eyes first.

entries.h: 🚦 Stable vs. unstable — the same task, two different answers
entries.t: 🧠 Vital signs on Monday ≠ vital signs on the day of a code. A task being "usually delegable" never overrides an unstable client in front of you right now.
🧠 Delegation is a loop, not a handoff. The RN's job doesn't stop until the outcome has been evaluated and reassessed.

The RN (or LPN/LVN) may be legally liable if negligent in supervising the UAP/CNA — even though the UAP performed the task itself. Delegating the task transfers the action , not the accountability. Failing to check competency, give clear direction, or follow up = negligent supervision. 🧠 "You picked them, you own the pick." If the delegation decision itself was unsafe, the licensed nurse who made it is accountable.

entries.h: 📝 ATI-style scenario: delegating vital signs to an AP
entries.t: An RN delegates routine vital signs to an assistive personnel (AP). Which actions should the nurse plan to take? Confirm the client is stable and the task is appropriate to delegate right now. Confirm the AP has the skill/competency to perform vital signs correctly. Communicate the specific time frame for when the AP should report results back to the RN. Tell the AP what values require an immediate report (e.g., outside expected parameters). Follow up — review the results and reassess the client as needed. 🧠 Vitals

SAY IT OUT LOUD ✋ TCP-DS Task · Circumstance · Person · Direction · Supervision ✅ UAP stable vitals, ADLs, ambulation, positioning, I&O ❌ RN only assessment, evaluation, teaching, IV push, unstable client ⚖️ Still liable negligent supervision = RN/LPN accountability

Q1: Name all 5 Rights of Delegation. Show answer Right Task, Right Circumstance, Right Person, Right Direction/Communication, Right Supervision/Evaluation. Q2: A newly admitted client needs vital signs — can this be delegated to a UAP? Show answer No — a new admission requires the RN's initial assessment; "new admission" is a keyword that keeps the task with the RN. Q3: Can an LPN/LVN reinforce diabetic teaching a patient already received from the RN? Show answer Yes — LPN/LVN can provide secondary/reinforcing teac

entries.h: Head to Toe Assessment · NG-190 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🧾 Before You Begin 🚶 Head to Toe 🚩 Normal vs Red Flag ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Nursing Core · Fundamentals of Nursing

The full systematic exam, top to bottom, in order NG-190 Nursing Core ADHD-friendly visual edition This is the master reference page for the batch — the sequence that ties everything together. It leans on NG-079 Vital Signs for normal ranges and NG-082 Assessment Locations for exact pulse/auscultation landmarks, so you're not re-learning them here — just placing them in the walk-through. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🧾 Consent → privacy → hands Always before you touch the client. 🚶 Head → neck → ches
STEP 1 · PREP Six things happen before your hands ever touch the client — every single time.

1 👋 Introduce yourself 2 🚪 Provide privacy 3 🧼 Wash hands 4 📝 Obtain consent 5 ⚠️ Assess for allergies 6 🧠 Obtain a psychosocial assessment 🧠 "I Prep With A Plan" — Introduce, Privacy, Wash hands, Allergies, Psychosocial, (consent tucked in with intro). Do this before the first vital sign.

Vital Typical adult reference range BP < 120 /< 80 mmHg (typical normal; staged hypertension begins ≥ 130/80 ) Pulse 60–100 bpm RR 12–20 breaths/min Temp ~ 98.6°F / 37°C SpO2 > 95% FULL DETAIL NG-079 Vital Signs — hedged reference ranges, classification tiers, and why "normal" varies by source. 🚶
STEP 2 · THE WALK-THROUGH Same direction every time — head/neck, chest, abdomen, extremities/circulation. Consistency is what lets you spot when something's off.
🧠 "HEN-CAB-E" — Head, Eyes/ENT, Neck, Chest, Abdomen, Breast, Extremities. Same order, every client, every time — that consistency is what makes a change stand out.

Hair — clean, well-kept? Cranial nerves assessed (if in program scope) Eyes — PERRLA , sclera white, conjunctiva pink/moist, no debris/drainage Nares — check patency, occlude one nostril at a time Mouth — oral mucosa pink & moist, no caries/redness/lesions; tongue midline Jaw/neck — palpate for swollen or painful lymph nodes 🧠 PERRLA = Pupils Equal, Round, Reactive to Light & Accommodation.

Heart : 5-point auscultation (Aortic → Pulmonic → Erb's → Tricuspid → Mitral) Lungs : RR should be even & unlabored ; auscultate anterior + posterior ladder Breast (if in scope) : check for lumps, drainage, nipple size/color changes FULL DETAIL NG-082 Assessment Locations — the exact 5 heart points and lung auscultation ladder.

Shape : flat, non-pulsating, even Bowel sounds : active in all 4 quadrants; if absent, listen 5 min before charting "absent" Order : Inspect → Auscultate → Percuss → Palpate Ask about pain on palpation FULL DETAIL NG-082 Assessment Locations — the four-quadrant map.

Peripheral pulses : radial, brachial, femoral, popliteal, dorsalis pedis, posterior tibialis (never palpate both carotids at once) Capillary refill : <3 sec Skin turgor : returns <3 sec ; skin warm, dry, intact Temperature equal in all extremities ROM in all joints + DTRs (if in program scope) FULL DETAIL NG-082 Assessment Locations — every pulse landmark, illustrated. 📌 Program note: not every nursing program teaches DTRs, cranial nerve exams, or breast exams as part of the routine head-to-toe — check your school'
STEP 3 · KNOW THE DIFFERENCE Same eight stops — here's what "normal" looks like next to what should make you stop and reassess.

System Normal finding Red flag Eyes PERRLA, sclera white Unequal/nonreactive pupils Neck No swollen/painful nodes Tender, enlarged lymph nodes Lungs Even, unlabored RR 12–20 Crackles, wheezes, rhonchi, labored breathing Heart Regular rate & rhythm at all 5 points New murmur, irregular rhythm Abdomen Flat, non-pulsating, active bowel sounds x4 Rigid/board-like, absent sounds x5min, pulsating mass Pulses 2+ bilateral, equal Absent, markedly unequal, thready/weak Skin Warm, dry, intact; cap refill & turgor <3s Cool/cl

entries.h: 🚨 Priority combo: rigid belly + fever + tachycardia
entries.t: Board-like abdomen, fever >100.3°F, rebound tenderness, restlessness, tachycardia/tachypnea = suspected peritonitis — report to the HCP as a priority.
Jumping around the body (e.g., checking a pulse, then eyes, then coming back to the chest) increases the chance of missing a finding . Stick to head-to-toe order every time.

entries.h: 🩻 IAPP — the one order that flips for the abdomen
entries.t: Touching the belly before listening can stir up bowel sounds and give a false reading — so auscultation jumps ahead of percussion and palpation for this one system only.

NG-079 Vital Signs — the normal reference ranges used throughout this exam. NG-082 Assessment Locations — the exact landmarks for every pulse, heart point, lung stop, and bowel quadrant referenced above. NG-041 Hypothermia — what happens when the temperature stop on this exam is dangerously abnormal. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🧾 6 prep steps intro, privacy, hands, consent, allergies, psychosocial 🚶 Head → toe, always never skip around the body 🩻 Abdomen = IAPP auscultate before you touch 🩺 Vitals + Locations this page is the index — see NG-079 & NG-082 for detail

Q2: What is the correct order for abdominal assessment, and why does it differ from other systems? Show answer Inspect, Auscultate, Percuss, Palpate — palpating first can artificially stimulate bowel sounds and give a false reading. entries.h: Informed Consent · NG-192 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics ✅ Elements 👥 Who consents 🩺 Nurse's role 🎯 NCLEX ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Nursing Core · Legal & Ethics Series

Voluntary · Informed · Competent — and the one distinction NCLEX tests every single time NG-192 NURSING CORE Series: Legal & Ethics 3 of 5 ADHD-friendly visual edition Informed consent is required before any invasive procedure or surgery. It's the paperwork proof of autonomy (page 1) — and skipping it is legally battery (page 2). The single most-tested fact on this whole topic: the provider obtains consent — the nurse witnesses the signature and confirms the client actually understands. 📄 Simple Nursing original —
STEP 1 · WHAT MAKES IT VALID Miss any one of these three and the "signed" consent isn't legally valid.
🧠 "VIC gives consent." V(oluntary) — I(nformed) — C(ompetent). No VIC, no valid signature.

Given freely, without coercion, pressure, or undue influence — from staff, family, or anyone else. 🧠 A client who signs only because a family member is standing over them insisting has not given truly voluntary consent.

The provider must disclose: the diagnosis , the nature and purpose of the treatment, the risks and benefits , and the alternatives — including the alternative of no treatment at all . 🧠 If any of these pieces is missing, the consent is not truly "informed" — even with a signature on the form.

The client must be a legal adult (or emancipated minor), alert and oriented , and not impaired by sedating medications, illicit substances, or acute intoxication at the time of signing. 🧠 Pre-op sedation is the classic trap: once meds are given, that client can no longer legally sign — consent must be obtained before sedation. 👥
STEP 2 · IDENTIFY THE RIGHT SIGNER When the client can't sign for themselves, the law has a specific order of who steps in.

entries.h: ❌ Who generally cannot consent for themselves
entries.t: 🧒 Minors — unless legally emancipated (state-dependent) 😵 Clients who are unconscious or have severely impaired cognition 💉 Clients who are sedated or acutely intoxicated ⚖️ Clients under a court-appointed guardianship for decision-making 🧠 In these cases, consent shifts to a legal guardian, healthcare proxy/durable power of attorney for healthcare, or — in a true emergency — the emergency-treatment doctrine.

entries.h: 🚨 Involuntary psychiatric admission ≠ loss of consent rights
entries.t: Clients admitted involuntarily still have the right to informed consent for their general medical treatment. An involuntary hold addresses safety — it does not strip away every other legal right. 🧠 Classic ATI trap: students assume "involuntary" means "no rights." Wrong — see page 5 (AMA & Mandatory Reporting) for the full right-to-refuse discussion.

entries.h: 🌳 Decision tree: client can't sign — now what?
entries.t: 🧠 Telephone consent for an emergent surgery must be witnessed by 2 authorized individuals (commonly two staff on separate extensions/lines) — a single witness is not enough. 🩺
STEP 3 · THE #1 NCLEX DISTINCTION The provider explains and obtains; the nurse verifies and witnesses. Confusing these two is the most common wrong answer.

entries.h: 🚫 The provider obtains consent — the nurse is NOT the one explaining risks/benefits
entries.t: 🧠 "Provider persuades, nurse notices." If a question asks who should explain surgical risks, the answer is almost never "the nurse" — it's the surgeon/provider performing the procedure.

entries.h: 🔄 Client can withdraw consent at any time
entries.t: Consent isn't a one-way door. If the client expresses doubt, asks a new question, or says they've changed their mind — even minutes before the procedure — the nurse must stop, notify the provider, and hold the procedure . 🧠 A signed form does not lock a client in. "I don't want this anymore" always overrides a signature.

An ethics committee is a healthcare team that provides guidance during an ethical dilemma — it gives recommendations , and does NOT impose a decision on the care team or family. The ANA (American Nurses Association) sets the ethical standards for the whole nursing profession — first covered on page 1 of this series. 🧠 If a stem asks "who makes the final call in an ethical dilemma," it's never the ethics committee — they advise, the care team/family/client still decide. 🎯
STEP 4 · DON'T GET FOOLED Real exam-style stems, straight from the source material.

"A nurse applies restraints without a prescription on a client who threatens to leave AMA. Select all that apply — which are intentional torts?" Correct: Battery, False imprisonment. Not correct: Malpractice and Negligence are unintentional torts, and HIPAA is a federal privacy law, not itself an intentional tort category. 🧠 Sort by the word first — "intentional" rules out negligence and malpractice immediately.

"Two nurses overhear a coworker say she believes a married HCP is in a relationship with a client." This is slander — a spoken, harmful (and unverified) statement about someone's reputation. 🧠 Say it out loud = slander. Write it down = libel.

"Client needs emergency surgery but cannot sign the operative consent form due to sedation. Priority action?" Obtain telephone consent from a family member , witnessed by 2 authorized individuals . 🧠 "Cannot sign" ≠ "skip consent." The team pivots to the next legally valid pathway — it doesn't disappear. 🔗 Series link: Skipping this whole process is NG-172 · Tort Law 's definition of battery. The right being protected here is NG-133 · Ethical Key Terms 's autonomy. Advance consent for future incapacity is covered n

SAY IT OUT LOUD ✅ VIC Voluntary · Informed · Competent = valid consent ✍️ Provider obtains Nurse witnesses signature, checks understanding ☎️ 2 witnesses For telephone/emergency consent 🔄 Withdraw anytime A signature never locks a client in

Q1: Who is legally responsible for explaining the risks and benefits of a surgical procedure? Show answer The provider/HCP performing the procedure — not the nurse. The nurse witnesses the signature and verifies understanding. Q2: What are the 3 requirements for valid consent? Show answer Voluntary, Informed, and Competent (capacity). Q3: A client who was involuntarily admitted for psychiatric treatment needs an appendectomy. Do they still have the right to informed consent? Show answer Yes — involuntary admission

entries.h: Advance Directives · NG-212 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 📜 What they are 🚦 Code status 🩺 Nurse's role 🎯 NCLEX ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Nursing Core · Legal & Ethics Series

Living wills, durable power of attorney for healthcare, code status, and the PSDA NG-212 NURSING CORE Series: Legal & Ethics 4 of 5 ADHD-friendly visual edition Advance directives are legal documents that spell out a client's wishes for medical care before they become unable to speak for themselves — think a client with a GCS < 7 or aphasia from an intracerebral hemorrhage. This is autonomy (page 1) exercised in advance, so it survives even after the client can no longer voice a choice. 📄 Simple Nursing original —
STEP 1 · TWO MAIN TYPES One document says what you want; the other says who decides for you.

entries.h: 📜 From client wishes to the chart
entries.t: 🧠 Documentation goes TWO places: the client's medical record, AND copies handed out to family, friends, and everyone named as a healthcare proxy. A living will locked in a safety-deposit box does neither.

A document, separate from a final will , that describes the kind of treatment wanted if the client becomes incapacitated or unable to communicate — e.g., whether they want life-sustaining measures like a ventilator or tube feeding. 🧠 It's about what — the treatments themselves.

entries.h: 🖋️ Durable Power of Attorney for Healthcare (DPOA-HC)
entries.t: Assigns another person — a health care proxy / surrogate — to make medical decisions for the client if they become incapacitated. NCLEX TIP There are many types of general Power of Attorney — always clarify it's specifically the healthcare POA that's needed. 🧠 It's about who — the decision-maker, not the decisions themselves.

✅ Commonly does NOT need to be notarized — can typically be completed right in the healthcare setting ✅ Commonly requires 2 witnesses ❌ Witnesses cannot be the nurses or HCPs directly involved in that client's care ❌ Witnesses cannot be individuals named as the healthcare proxy Exact witness count and notarization requirements are set by state law and vary — always verify the specific state's requirements rather than assuming one universal rule. 🧠 The witness has to be neutral — not treating, not benefiting from th

entries.h: 🚨 Portable orders: POLST / MOLST & DNR bracelet
entries.t: POLST (Physician's Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment) — actual medical orders, signed by a provider, that summarize the client's wishes and travel with them across care settings (home, EMS, hospital). Terminology varies by state — some regions use MOLST or another name. A DNR bracelet is a portable, visible way to communicate code status outside the hospital record. 🧠 A living will is a wish ; a POLST is a standing medical order — that's why POLST can be acted on immediately by EMS. 🚦
STEP 2 · KNOW THE LADDER From everything to nothing — know exactly what each order does and does not include.
🧠 DNR/DNI/AND are NOT "do not treat." Comfort measures, oxygen by nasal cannula, IV fluids, and symptom-relief medications can still be given — those are not considered resuscitative efforts.

Default is full treatment / full code . The law requires the facility to give written information outlining the client's rights and options for stating their wishes. 🧠 Silence defaults to "do everything," not "do nothing."

A federal law that protects and ensures client rights in determining end-of-life care. It requires facilities to ask every admitted client whether they already have an advance directive. 🧠 The PSDA is a process requirement (ask on admission), not a guarantee every client will have one. 🩺
STEP 3 · FACILITATE, DON'T STALL CARE When code status is unclear, the nurse verifies without abandoning the client.

entries.h: 🌳 Client's condition is worsening — code status unclear. What now?
entries.t: 🧠 Two things happen in parallel, not in sequence. The nurse does NOT stop caring for the client while the chart is searched — assessment and verification happen at the same time.

The nurse's role is to open the door for advance care planning discussions, provide facility information, answer process questions, and notify the provider or ethics resources as needed — not to pressure a client toward a specific choice. 🧠 This mirrors the informed consent rule from page 3: the nurse supports the process, the client (or their legal decision-maker) makes the actual choice.

entries.h: 🗺️ Where the ethics of dying live on this site
entries.t: 🔗 The euthanasia, DNR ethics, grief, and end-of-life communication angle is covered in depth on the Mental Health batch's NG-065 · Death & Dying and NG-222 · Death, Dying, Grief & Loss pages — this page focuses on the legal document itself. 🎯
STEP 4 · DON'T GET FOOLED These exact questions have appeared on Kaplan, HESI, and Saunders-style review material.

entries.h: 🚨 "My living will is secured in a safety-deposit box"
entries.t: This is the most concerning statement a client can make — an advance directive that no one can access in an emergency is functionally useless. The correct nursing response is to encourage a copy in the chart and with family/proxies. 🧠 A perfect document with zero accessibility = zero protection.

entries.h: ⭐ Newly diagnosed with mild Alzheimer's — priority teaching
entries.t: Encourage the client to complete an advance directive BEFORE cognitive abilities decline further — this is one of the most frequently missed NCLEX questions on this topic. 🧠 Capacity to complete an AD requires being competent at the time of signing — waiting until symptoms progress may mean it's too late.

entries.h: ✅ Timing matters — plan early, not in crisis
entries.t: Advance care planning conversations are ideally started at a calm, non-emergent time — not in the middle of an acute decline, when stress and impaired capacity make truly informed decisions harder. 🧠 If the exam gives you a chance to teach proactively, that's usually the better answer than waiting. 🔗 Series link: Advance directives are the future-tense version of NG-192 · Informed Consent , and both protect the NG-133 · Ethical Key Terms principle of autonomy. When no AD exists and a client wants to leave AMA inste

SAY IT OUT LOUD 📝 Living Will The "what" — treatments wanted/not wanted 🖋️ DPOA-HC The "who" — names a healthcare proxy 👥 2 witnesses Not the treating nurse, not the proxy ❓ No AD found = default to full treatment

Q1: What's the difference between a Living Will and a Durable Power of Attorney for Healthcare? Show answer A Living Will states WHAT treatments are wanted/not wanted; a DPOA-HC names WHO will make decisions if the client becomes incapacitated. Q2: Can the treating nurse witness a client's advance directive? Show answer No — witnesses cannot be nurses/HCPs directly involved in that client's care, or anyone named as the healthcare proxy. entries.h: Asepsis & Handwashing · NG-214 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🧼 Asepsis 🖐️ Technique ⏰ When ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Nursing Core · Fundamentals of Nursing Course

Medical vs. Surgical Asepsis · Handwashing Technique · Hand Hygiene Moments NG-214 Nursing Core ADHD-friendly visual edition Asepsis is the absence of disease-causing organisms. Handwashing is the single best way to prevent the spread of germs — full stop. Everything else in infection control (gloves, gowns, sterile fields) is layered on top of this one habit. Two flavors exist: medical asepsis "clean technique" reduces organisms; surgical asepsis "sterile technique" eliminates them. Clean / low-organism zone Conta
STEP 1 · TWO LEVELS OF "CLEAN" Same goal — keep organisms away from the patient — but two very different bars for how clean is clean enough.

🧼 Medical / clean 🧫 Surgical / sterile Reduces number of organisms Eliminates organisms Gloves + hand hygiene as your PPE Sterile field, sterile gloves, sterile drape Meds, feeding, vitals, most dressings Surgery, catheters, chest tubes, cervical checks 🧠 "Medical trims the lawn, surgical salts the earth." Clean technique cuts the germ count down; sterile technique aims for none at all.

😷 Cover coughs into your shoulder or elbow , not your hands — otherwise wash immediately after 💅 No acrylic or gel nails — bacteria hide underneath where handwashing can't reach 💍 Keep jewelry minimal — any surface that can harbor bacteria will grow it 🚫 Never place anything on the floor — the floor is always contaminated 🛏️ Never shake linens when changing a bed — this launches organisms into the air ➡️ Move from clean areas to dirty areas , never the reverse 💦 Avoid splashing when emptying body fluids — pour clos
STEP 2 · SOAP + WATER + FRICTION The single most effective infection-control action a nurse performs, done correctly, every time.

Good hand hygiene requires soap, water, and friction — the physical rubbing is what actually lifts organisms off the skin, not just the soap itself. 🧠 "0:15 to 2:00 — sing it twice." The classic teaching trick: humming "Happy Birthday" twice through covers about 20 seconds, comfortably inside the required range.

Hands are visibly soiled After caring for a patient with C. diff , norovirus, or rotavirus Before eating, after using the restroom 🧠 "Soap beats spores." Alcohol sanitizer cannot destroy C. diff spores — only mechanical washing with soap, water, and friction removes them.

entries.h: 🧴 When alcohol-based hand sanitizer is okay
entries.t: Use alcohol-based hand sanitizer only when hands are not visibly soiled , and only as an occasional substitute between actual soap-and-water washes — not as a full replacement for it. 🧠 "Sanitizer is a bridge, not a destination." It fills the gaps between real washes; it never fully replaces them.

💅 Acrylic / gel nails bacteria hide beneath 💍 Excess jewelry rings, bracelets 🧴 Sanitizer only when hands are soiled 🛏️ Shaking linens launches organisms airborne 🪑 Items on the floor always contaminated 🧠 Every item on this list creates a hiding spot or a launch pad for organisms — undoing the work good handwashing just did. ⏰
STEP 3 · THE KEY MOMENTS Hand hygiene isn't random — it's tied to specific moments around every patient contact.

Wash before seeing a client, after seeing a client, before putting on gloves, and when changing gloves — those four moments form the backbone of every patient encounter. The WHO "5 Moments for Hand Hygiene" is the standard framework taught worldwide: 1) before touching a patient, 2) before a clean/aseptic task, 3) after body fluid exposure risk, 4) after touching a patient, 5) after touching a patient's surroundings. 🧠 "Before you, before clean, after risk, after you, after their space." Four of the five moments br

Gloves are not a substitute for hand hygiene. Wash before putting gloves on and after taking them off — and every time you change gloves between tasks or patients. 🧠 "Gloves protect the glove, not skip the wash." A puncture, a tiny tear, or contamination on removal all still reach bare skin without hand hygiene bookending the glove.

entries.h: 🚨 NCLEX trap: "just changed gloves" ≠ clean hands
entries.t: Changing gloves without hand hygiene in between is a classic exam distractor — the correct sequence is always remove gloves → wash/sanitize hands → don new gloves , never glove-to-glove. 🧠 If an answer choice skips the hand hygiene step between glove changes, it's wrong — no exceptions. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🧼 Medical = reduce Surgical = eliminate — different goal, different bar ⏱️ 15 sec – 2 min soap + water + friction is what actually removes organisms 🧴 Sanitizer only if hands aren't soiled never for C. diff, norovirus, rotavirus ⏰ WHO's 5 Moments before patient · before clean task · after fluid risk · after patient · after surroundings

Q1: What's the difference between medical and surgical asepsis? Show answer Medical (clean) asepsis reduces the number of organisms; surgical (sterile) asepsis aims to eliminate them entirely. Q2: How long should a proper handwash last? Show answer At least 15 seconds, up to 2 minutes for heavily soiled or high-risk hands — soap, water, and friction together are what remove organisms. Q3: A nurse's hands aren't visibly soiled between two clean tasks on the same patient. Is alcohol-based sanitizer acceptable? Show a

entries.h: AMA & Mandatory Reporting · NG-220 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🚪 Leaving AMA 🔒 Who can't leave 🚨 Mandatory reporting 🎯 NCLEX ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Nursing Core · Legal & Ethics Series

The right to refuse and leave — and the legal duty to speak up for someone who can't NG-220 NURSING CORE Series: Legal & Ethics 5 of 5 ADHD-friendly visual edition Two forces, same series: a competent client's autonomy lets them leave against medical advice — and the nurse's duty to protect the vulnerable requires mandatory reporting when someone can't protect themselves. This is the final page — the exact edge cases where the six ethical principles from page 1 collide in real practice. 📄 Simple Nursing original —
STEP 1 · THE RIGHT TO REFUSE A competent client can walk out — the nurse's job is to inform, document, and never obstruct.

entries.h: ✅ Right to refuse — even if involuntarily admitted
entries.t: Clients have the right to refuse medications or other therapies if they are competent to do so — even if they were involuntarily admitted (except in true emergency situations where there is imminent danger). Example: a client who is Alert & Oriented x4 and a Jehovah's Witness refusing blood products — even if their partner (who is not a Jehovah's Witness) wants them to receive it. The nurse follows the competent client's wishes, not the family's. 🧠 This is autonomy in its purest form — the family's opinion does not

🧠 "INDS-SR" won't roll off the tongue, so picture it as a checklist you read left to right: inform → notify → no security → discuss → sign → remove lines. Step 3 is the single most-tested step — calling security to physically stop a competent client can itself become false imprisonment.

entries.h: ⭐ Assessing the risk before they walk out
entries.t: Was the client properly educated on why staying matters? Are they competent to make this decision right now? Do they have a legal hold in place? 🧠 Three quick questions, asked in order, decide the whole scenario.

entries.h: 🔄 If the client refuses to sign the AMA form
entries.t: The nurse still documents the refusal to sign — a client cannot be forced to sign anything, but the discharge (and the fact that risks were explained) is still documented in the chart. 🧠 Refusing to sign the AMA form does not equal being forced to stay. 🔒
STEP 2 · CAPACITY CHECK The right to leave only applies to someone who can actually understand the choice they're making.

🍺 Acutely intoxicated — e.g., drinking heavily for 12 hours and unable to walk safely 🗣️ Actively psychotic with command hallucinations to harm self or others (e.g., voices telling them to hurt someone) 👑 Severe impairment of reality testing that removes capacity to understand the decision (e.g., a client who believes they are a historical figure) ⚖️ Client is under an active legal/involuntary hold for danger to self or others (specific hold names/timeframes vary by state) 🧠 The common thread isn't the diagnosis —

entries.h: 🏥 Voluntary psychiatric admission, wants to leave
entries.t: A client admitted voluntarily for an anxiety disorder demands release. Initial nursing action: notify the client's primary HCP — the client generally retains the right to leave unless they meet criteria for an emergency hold. 🧠 Voluntary admission ≠ locked in. The HCP evaluates whether a hold is legally justified; the nurse doesn't unilaterally block the door.

"You don't have to take the medication if you don't want to" is the most therapeutic nursing response to a competent client's refusal. 🧠 Respecting the refusal — not arguing, bargaining, or threatening — is the correct action. 🚨
STEP 3 · PROTECT THE VULNERABLE When someone can't advocate for themselves, the law requires the nurse to.
🧠 "PICS" — Protect · Interview (separately) · Collect (evidence) · Safety plan. Do them in that order — safety always comes before evidence-gathering.

entries.h: ⚠️ Report only after a full assessment
entries.t: Suspected abuse is reported only after a detailed assessment and full history — not on a hunch alone. Once that threshold of reasonable suspicion is met, reporting is mandatory , not optional. 🧠 "Report only after assessment" ≠ "wait and see." A completed assessment that raises suspicion still legally obligates the report.

🧒 Suspected child abuse or neglect 👴 Suspected elder or dependent-adult abuse/neglect 🦠 Certain communicable diseases to public health authorities 🔫 Gunshot or stab wounds , in jurisdictions that require it 🧠 Exact reportable conditions and timeframes are set by state law and facility policy — always verify locally rather than assuming one national rule.

entries.h: 🗺️ Related page in the Mental Health batch
entries.t: 🔗 Full signs/symptoms of physical, emotional, sexual abuse and neglect across the lifespan are covered on the Mental Health batch's NG-139 · Abuse & Neglect page — this page focuses on the nurse's legal reporting duty. 🎯
STEP 4 · DON'T GET FOOLED This closes out the whole 5-page series — every trap here reaches back to an earlier page.

Calling security to physically prevent a competent client from leaving is never the correct AMA response — it risks false imprisonment (see page 2, Tort Law). 🧠 The nurse's tools here are words and documentation, not force.

entries.h: ⭐ Trap: family overrides a competent client
entries.t: A family member's wishes do not override a competent client's own informed refusal — this is autonomy (page 1) at its strongest test. 🧠 If the stem pits family against a competent client, the client's voice wins.

entries.h: ✅ The full-circle idea of this series
entries.t: Ethical principles (page 1) → become legal exposure when violated (page 2, Tort Law) → get formalized through signed process (page 3, Informed Consent) → extend into the future (page 4, Advance Directives) → and hit their real-world limits here, where competence, refusal, and duty to protect all meet. 🧠 Every legal/ethics question on this exam is really just asking: "is this client competent, and whose right is being protected?" 🔗 Series link: Start over from NG-133 · Ethical Key Terms , or review NG-172 · Tort Law

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🚪 Competent = can leave Even if involuntarily admitted, except true emergencies 🚫 Never call security Risk of false imprisonment 🛡️ PICS Protect → Interview separately → Collect → Safety plan 📋 Full assessment first Then reporting is mandatory, not optional

Q1: A competent client wants to leave AMA and staff are worried. What should the nurse NOT do? Show answer Call security to physically stop them — this risks false imprisonment. Instead: inform of risks, notify the provider, discuss risks, get the AMA form signed (or document refusal), and remove lines/tubes. Q2: An intoxicated client who cannot walk wants to leave. Can they sign out AMA? Show answer No — acute intoxication that impairs capacity means they cannot legally/safely be allowed to sign out AMA at that ti
Protecting a patient who cannot protect themselves, and caring well when cure is no longer the goal.

entries.h: 🚨 Neutropenia — the number that changes everything
entries.t: Below 500 she cannot make pus, redness or swelling - so a single temperature is the only sign left, and it is an emergency. Swipe it sideways if it is cut off, or tap to open it full size. ANC < 500 Severe neutropenia. Below this the patient cannot mount a normal inflammatory response, so the usual signs of infection — pus, redness, swelling — may be absent entirely . A single temperature of 38C / 100.4F in a neutropenic patient is a medical emergency. Cultures and IV antibiotics within the hour. Absolute neutrophi

Hand hygiene — the single most effective measure, by a wide margin Private room; positive-pressure room if available No fresh flowers, no potted plants, no standing water — all harbor organisms Dedicated equipment; meticulous line and catheter care Screen staff and visitors for any infection Daily oral care with a soft brush; inspect for mucositis

No rectal temperatures, suppositories or enemas - they break mucosa and seed bacteria No urinary catheter unless genuinely necessary No live vaccines for the patient or household contacts No intramuscular injections if platelets are also low

Avoid crowds and anyone unwell No raw fruit or vegetables , no undercooked meat or eggs, no unpasteurized dairy No gardening, no cleaning litter trays or cages Take temperature daily and know the number to call Report fever, chills, sore throat, cough, burning on urination, or any new pain

Palliative care Hospice When Any time , from diagnosis Prognosis usually 6 months or less Alongside treatment? Yes — curative treatment continues Curative treatment has stopped Goal Comfort, dignity, quality of life Palliative care is not giving up, and it does not require stopping treatment. That misconception is the point of many questions.

entries.h: 🚨 Pain at the end of life
entries.t: There is no maximum opioid dose when titrating to comfort. Doses that would be unsafe in other contexts are appropriate here. Fear of respiratory depression is not a reason to under-treat a dying patient's pain. Relieving suffering is the goal of care. Give analgesia around the clock , not only on request — steady levels control pain far better than chasing it.

The best response almost always stays, listens and reflects rather than reassuring, redirecting or explaining. Do Do not “Tell me more about that.” “Everything will be fine.” Sit down. Allow silence. Change the subject “This sounds frightening.” “Don’t think like that.” Ask what matters most to them Speak only to the family

Fever + ANC < 500 = emergency No rectal anything in neutropenia Hand hygiene beats every other precaution Palliative can start at diagnosis ; hospice comes later No opioid ceiling at end of life Sources. Written from MedlinePlus , NINDS , CDC and OpenStax A&P 2e (CC BY 4.0).
The two axes that answer most pediatric questions: what stage they are in, and what they fear.

entries.h: ⭐ Erikson, play and what they need
entries.t: Stage Age Erikson Play Fears most Infant 0–18 mo Trust vs mistrust Solitary Separation from carer Toddler 18 mo–3 y Autonomy vs shame Parallel — beside, not with Separation ; loss of routine Preschool 3–6 y Initiative vs guilt Associative Bodily harm / mutilation School age 6–12 y Industry vs inferiority Cooperative , team games Loss of control; not measuring up Adolescent 12–18 y Identity vs role confusion Peer group Being different ; body image Match the intervention to the fear and most questions answer themselv

entries.h: 🧠 The two responses that keep reappearing
entries.t: Toddler having a tantrum → ignore the behavior, keep them safe. Attention reinforces it. Toddler resisting care → offer two acceptable choices , never an open question. “Pink cup or blue cup?” not “Will you take your medicine?”

Age Motor Social / language 2 months Lifts head when prone Social smile 4 months Rolls front to back Laughs, coos 6 months Sits with support ; rolls both ways Babbles; stranger anxiety begins 9 months Sits alone, crawls, pincer grasp “Mama/dada” nonspecific 12 months Walks ; birth weight TRIPLES 1–3 words; waves bye 15 months Walks well 3–5 words 2 years Runs, kicks a ball 2-word phrases ; ~50% intelligible 3 years Tricycle 3-word sentences ; ~75% intelligible 4 years Hops, dresses self ~100% intelligible 5 years S

Words per phrase roughly equals age in years at 2 and 3 Intelligibility: 2 y = 50%, 3 y = 75%, 4 y = 100% Weight doubles at 6 months, triples at 12 Posterior fontanelle closes by 2–3 months ; anterior by 12–18 months A sunken fontanelle means dehydration. A bulging fontanelle means raised intracranial pressure.

Unintentional injury is the leading cause of death in children past infancy — and the type changes predictably with what they can newly do. Age Main risk Teach Infant Suffocation, falls, choking Back to sleep , empty crib, rear-facing car seat Toddler Drowning, poisoning, falls, burns Locked cupboards, stair gates, never alone near water, pot handles turned in Preschool Road traffic, burns, drowning Supervision, road safety, swimming lessons School age Bicycles, sport, pedestrian Helmets , booster seat until the be

No honey before 12 months — infant botulism No cow’s milk before 12 months Choking foods to avoid under 4: nuts, whole grapes, hot dogs, popcorn, hard candy Rear-facing car seat in the back until at least 2 years Solids from about 6 months , iron-fortified cereal first, one new food every 4–7 days
FLACC — non-verbal, under 3 FACES — about 3 and older Numeric 0–10 — about 8 and older Children under-report pain to avoid injections. Behavior and physiology count as evidence.

Toddler = parallel play, limited choices, autonomy Preschooler thinks illness is a punishment — say it is not Adolescent = confidentiality Weight doubles at 6 months, triples at 12 Sunken = dehydrated. Bulging = raised ICP. Ignore the tantrum; keep them safe 📌
