SSRI · SNRI · TCA · MAOI · atypicals — four rules that apply to all of them NG-010 MENTAL HEALTH · Pharmacology ADHD-friendly visual edition There are five antidepressant classes and dozens of drug names — but four rules cover almost every antidepressant question you will ever see . Learn these four and you can answer a question about a drug you have never heard of. This is the umbrella page : each class has its own deep-dive page linked at the bottom. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 1️⃣ Suicide risk g
STEP 1 · LEARN THESE, ANSWER ANYTHING Start with the synapse — every rule below is a consequence of what happens in this one gap.

entries.h: 🔬 The synaptic cleft — what every antidepressant is doing down there
entries.t: EXAM TIP Nearly all antidepressants raise the amount of neurotransmitter sitting in the gap between two neurons. SSRIs and SNRIs block the reuptake pump ; TCAs block the same pumps plus several other receptors; MAOIs destroy the enzyme that breaks the transmitter down . Different doors, same result: more transmitter in the cleft. And that is also why combining two of them is so dangerous. One mechanism, three outcomes: too little transmitter (depression), enough (treatment), far too much (serotonin syndrome). 🧠 "Fi

entries.h: 1️⃣ Increased risk of suicide — the first few weeks are the danger window
entries.t: Antidepressants can increase suicidal thoughts in the first few weeks of treatment . The classic explanation: energy and motivation return before the mood does — so a client who was too depressed to act now has enough drive to act, while still feeling hopeless. 📞 Notify the provider of ANY suicidal thought — this is not a "monitor and re-assess" item. ❓ Clarify any new prescription — check it against everything else the client takes before the first dose. 👀 Ask directly. "Are you having thoughts of hurting or killi

entries.h: 2️⃣ Slow onset & slow taper — NEVER stop abruptly
entries.t: ⏳ Full therapeutic effect takes about 4–6 weeks — some improvement earlier, but do not judge the drug a failure at 2 weeks. 🗣️ Teach: "Keep taking it even when you feel better" — feeling better is the drug working, not a reason to stop. 📉 Taper on a schedule set by the provider. The client should never run out and never self-discontinue. ⚠️ Discontinuation symptoms are not addiction — antidepressants are not addictive; the brain simply needs time to re-adapt. 🧠 "Slow on, slow off." Four words, two rules. Weeks to s
STEP 2 · SEROTONIN SYNDROME This is the single most tested antidepressant fact in the entire curriculum.

❌ SSRI + St. John's wort — the herb is serotonergic. Ask about supplements every time. ❌ MAOI + ANY antidepressant — TCA, SSRI, SNRI. This is the classic lethal pairing. ❌ MAOI or SSRI + other serotonergic drugs: triptans, tramadol, linezolid, buspirone, lithium, dextromethorphan . ⏳ Switching between an SSRI and an MAOI requires a washout period — typically about 2 weeks in either direction, and longer (about 5 weeks) after fluoxetine because of its long half-life. Stopping one drug "the day before" starting an MA

entries.h: 4️⃣ ALL psych drugs cause weight changes — and antidepressants decrease BP
entries.t: 🧠 "Every psych drug moves the scale and drops the pressure." Two vitals to check at every visit: weight and orthostatic BP . 🗣️
STEP 3 · THE MOST-MISSED QUESTIONS Three question types from the source — work through the reasoning, not the memorizing.

entries.h: 🎯 Missed question #1 — "Which medications have the most potential risk for injury ?" (SATA)
entries.t: READ THE STEM "Risk for injury" in a psych stem almost always means which drugs are SEDATING → falls . Option Pick it? Why 1. Amitriptyline ✅ YES TCA — strongly sedating + anticholinergic + orthostatic hypotension. Triple fall risk. 2. Diphenhydramine ✅ YES Sedating antihistamine, anticholinergic — a classic fall/confusion drug in older adults. 3. Colace (docusate) ❌ no A stool softener. No sedation, no CNS effect. 4. Alprazolam ✅ YES Benzodiazepine — CNS depressant, sedation, impaired balance. 5. Buspirone ❌ no No

entries.h: 🎯 Missed question #2 — "Which drug combinations should the nurse question?" (SATA)
entries.t: Combination Question it? Why Sertraline + selegiline ✅ YES SSRI + MAOI — the forbidden pairing. Serotonin syndrome. Alprazolam + citalopram ❌ no A benzo with an SSRI is commonly prescribed together; monitor for additive sedation, but it is not a "question the order" combination. Buspirone + phenelzine ✅ YES Buspirone is serotonergic; phenelzine is an MAOI . Serotonin syndrome + hypertensive risk. Lithium + ketorolac ✅ YES NSAIDs reduce lithium excretion → rising level → lithium toxicity . St. John's wort + buspiron

entries.h: 🎯 Missed question #3 — "Which of these should concern the nurse?"
entries.t: Statement / situation Concern? Reasoning 1. Amitriptyline prescribed to treat fibromyalgia pain ❌ no A recognized off-label use of TCAs for chronic pain — not a red flag by itself. 2. Headache while on phenelzine 🚨 YES An MAOI + a new severe headache is the classic first sign of a hypertensive crisis from tyramine. Check the BP now. 3. Taking St. John's wort with sertraline 🚨 YES Two serotonergic agents → serotonin syndrome . Rule 3. 4. Discontinuing escitalopram the day before starting isocarboxazid 🚨 YES An SSRI

entries.t: 1 "It takes 4 to 6 weeks to feel the full benefit. And expect some change in weight; we'll track it." 6 " No alcohol — it

Q1: Name the 4 rules. Show answer 1) Increased risk of suicide, especially in the first few weeks. 2) Slow onset and slow taper — never stop abruptly. 3) Never mix — SSRI + St. John's wort, or MAOI + any antidepressant. 4) All psych drugs cause weight changes and decrease BP (slow position changes). Q2: List the 5 signs of serotonin syndrome. Show answer Agitation, hyperthermia, clonus/hyperreflexia, diaphoresis, tremor. Often also hypertension, tachycardia and muscle rigidity. Q3: A client says "I've taken it 12 d

Alpha · Beta · Central — the adrenergic-blocking map, and the PERIPHERALLY ACTING half of it NG-013 PHARM · Cardio ADHD-friendly visual edition ABC is how the antihypertensive adrenergic blockers get sorted: A lpha, B eta, C entral. The whole family turns down the sympathetic "fight-or-flight" signal — the only question on the exam is WHERE the drug turns it down . Peripherally acting = out at the nerve ending / receptor in the body, inhibiting norepinephrine in the PNS → treats HTN + BPH . Centrally acting = up in
STEP 1 · WHERE IT ACTS One sympathetic signal, two places to cut it: in the brain before it's sent, or in the body where it lands.

entries.h: 🗺️ The ABC map — Alpha, Beta, Central
entries.t: EXAM TIP Every drug in this family is an adrenergic blocking drug (an antiadrenergic ). They all end the same way — vasodilation and a lower blood pressure . They differ only in which point of the sympathetic pathway they interrupt . Left panel: the drug never lets the order leave the brainstem. Right panel: the order is sent, but the doorbell is taped over. 🧠 "C is for Cranium." C entral drugs work in the C ranium (clonidine, methyldopa — both start with a soft C sound). A lpha blockers work A way from the brain —

entries.h: 💊 The four prototype drugs — memorize this grid
entries.t: Generic Trade Central / Peripheral Typical starting dose Route Clonidine Catapres CENTRAL 🧠 0.1 mg (100 mcg) BID PO, transdermal patch Methyldopa — CENTRAL 🧠 250–500 mg 2–3×/day PO Doxazosin Cardura, Cardura XL PERIPHERAL 🎯 1 mg once daily PO Prazosin Minipress PERIPHERAL 🎯 1 mg 2–3× daily PO Notice both peripheral drugs start at 1 mg and both end in -osin . Notice both central drugs are the odd, old-fashioned names. 🧠 "-OSIN means OUTSIDE." Doxaz osin , praz osin , tamsul osin — the -osin ending marks the peripher

entries.h: ⭐ Why do we give it? — the indications
entries.t: 🩸 Hypertension (HTN) — both halves of the family 🚽 BPH (benign prostatic hyperplasia) — peripheral only ; relaxes prostate/bladder-neck smooth muscle so urine flows 💓 Certain cardiac arrhythmias EXAM TIP If a male client is on an -osin drug, ask which problem you're treating — the same tablet can be prescribed for the blood pressure OR the urine stream . 🧠 "Peripheral = Pressure + Pee." Two P's for the peripheral half. Central only gets the first P.

entries.h: 🎯 Alpha-1 blockade in the prostate — the BPH half
entries.t: Same alpha-1 receptor, different organ: block it in the vessel and pressure drops; block it in the prostate and the stream opens. 🧠 "Relax the gate, let the water out." The prostate wraps the urethra like a fist. Alpha-1 blockade opens the fist. ⚠️
STEP 2 · ADVERSE EFFECTS Turn the sympathetic system down and everything it normally keeps "up" sags — pressure, pulse, gut motility, saliva, tears, erections.

entries.h: 🚨 Adverse effects — organized by body system
entries.t: 🧠 "Everything DRIES, everything SLOWS, everything SAGS." Dries = eyes & mouth. Slows = heart rate, AV conduction, bowel. Sags = blood pressure and erections. Then add the two lab words the source calls out: sodium retention and hyperkalemia .

entries.h: 🪑 First-dose / orthostatic hypotension — the fall risk
entries.t: Give the first dose at bedtime and stay with the client on the first ambulation. Sit 1 min , stand 1 min , then walk. 🧠 "First dose, floor dose." The very first tablet is the one that puts them on the floor.

Add this… …and you get Adrenergics (sympathomimetics) Risk of hypertension — they push the exact system we're blocking Levodopa Hypotension + decreased levodopa effect Anesthetic agents Increased anesthetic effect — flag before surgery Beta blockers Hypertension (rebound risk, especially if clonidine is stopped while the beta blocker continues) Lithium Lithium toxicity 🧪 Haloperidol Psychotic behavior reported 🧠 "A-L-A-B-L-H" → A drenergics · L evodopa · A nesthetics · B eta blockers · L ithium · H aloperidol. Say

entries.h: 🚫 Contraindications — they split by central vs peripheral
entries.t: 🧠 CENTRALLY acting — do NOT give with 🎯 PERIPHERALLY acting — do NOT give with Active hepatic (liver) disease — methyldopa is hepatotoxic MAOI antidepressant therapy — dangerous BP swings Ulcerative colitis Peptic ulcer disease — the older peripheral agents increase GI secretion & motility Plus the universal ones: known hypersensitivity, and caution in any client already on another sympatholytic or with an existing cardiac conduction problem. 🧠 "Central hits the LIVER, peripheral hits the GUT." C = liver + MAOI. P
STEP 3 · NURSING MANAGEMENT Everything here is straight nursing-management scoring: measure it, weigh it, taper it, and never trim the patch.

entries.h: ✅ The monitoring ladder — in the order you'd actually do it
entries.t: 1 BP & pulse BEFORE the first dose — then frequently during initial dose adjustment and every increase, then periodically throughout therapy. ▼ 2 Intake & output ratios + DAILY WEIGHT — these drugs cause sodium retention . 1 kg = 1 L of fluid. ▼ 3 Assess for edema daily — especially at the beginning of therapy. Check dependent areas: ankles, sacrum in a bedbound client. ▼ 4 Titrate SLOWLY in clients with cardiac conditions or on other sympatholytic drugs — and report significant changes . 🧠 "BIER" — B P & pulse · I

✂️ Do NOT cut or trim the unit — cutting destroys the rate-controlling membrane and dumps the dose. 🚿 May stay on during bathing or swimming. 🔄 Rotate sites; apply to clean, dry, hairless intact skin. 🧠 "Trim it = dump it." A trimmed patch is a broken dam.

💊 Client on clonidine for months ▼ 🚫 Runs out / "I felt fine so I stopped" ▼ 📈 Sympathetic system rebounds, unopposed ▼ 🚨 REBOUND HYPERTENSION — severe BP spike, headache, agitation, tachycardia Never stop an adrenergic blocker abruptly. Taper on a schedule; teach the client to refill before the last tablet. 🧠 "The brake pedal you can't just lift." These drugs hold the sympathetic brake down. Lift your foot suddenly and the car lurches forward — that lurch is rebound HTN.

entries.h: 🆚 Don't mix up the three "peripheral" mechanisms
entries.t: Mechanism Example drugs What actually happens Presynaptic NE-release blocker reserpine, guanethidine-class NE is never released from the nerve ending (see NG-260) Postsynaptic α1 blocker doxazosin, prazosin , tamsulosin NE releases normally but can't bind — this page (depth in NG-141) Central α2 agonist clonidine, methyldopa Brainstem sends less sympathetic outflow in the first place All three are antiadrenergic . All three drop BP. Only the middle one also treats BPH. 🧠 Supply · Door · Order. Presynaptic cuts the

Q1: What does "peripherally acting" mean in one sentence? Show answer It inhibits norepinephrine in the peripheral nervous system — at the nerve ending or at the alpha-1 receptor on the target tissue — so the vessel (and the prostate) relaxes. Indications: HTN and BPH. Q2: Which half of the family is contraindicated in active hepatic disease and with MAOI therapy? Show answer The CENTRALLY acting half (clonidine, methyldopa). The peripherally acting agents are the ones flagged for ulcerative colitis and peptic ulce

Antacids — aluminum · magnesium · calcium · sodium bicarbonate NG-014 GI · Pharmacology ADHD-friendly visual edition Antacids are the only acid drug that does not touch the acid factory . PPIs and H2 blockers stop acid from being made ; an antacid simply combines chemically with the hydrochloric acid already sitting in the stomach and raises the pH . That gives them the fastest onset and the shortest duration in the whole family — and it is also why almost every antacid problem on the exam is about the metal cation
STEP 1 · CHEMISTRY IN THE STOMACH A base meets an acid in the lumen. That's it — no receptor, no pump, no enzyme.

entries.h: 🔬 The stomach wall in cross-section — where the acid comes from and where the antacid works
entries.t: EXAM TIP Acid is made by parietal cells deep in the gastric glands and pumped into the lumen. A protective mucus–bicarbonate layer normally keeps it off the epithelium. When that layer fails, acid burns the wall — that is an ulcer . The antacid never enters the cell; it works out in the lumen, neutralizing acid that has already been secreted. Parietal cells (gold) sit at the base of the gastric glands. The mucus–bicarbonate layer (teal) is the only thing between pH 1–2 acid and living tissue. 🧠 "Antacid = ANT-acid

entries.h: ⚡ Where antacids sit in the acid-drug family — fastest on, first off
entries.t: Approximate teaching timeline — exact figures vary by product and whether the stomach is empty. 🧠 "Antacid = the fire extinguisher. PPI = the sprinkler system." One puts out the flames right now; the other keeps the building from catching fire at all.

entries.h: ⭐ Why are they used? — the indications
entries.t: 🔥 Heartburn, acid indigestion, sour stomach 🚪 GERD — gastresophageal reflux disease 🕳️ Peptic ulcer — symptomatic relief 🫘 Aluminum carbonate: treats hyperphosphatemia in chronic renal failure — it binds phosphate in the gut so it is never absorbed EXAM TIP An aluminum antacid ordered for a dialysis client is a phosphate binder, not a heartburn drug — and it must be given with meals for that purpose. 🧠 "Aluminum = ALso a phosphate binder." Same tablet, completely different reason.

STEP 2 · THE CATION DECIDES EVERYTHING Learn the metal, not the brand. Every adverse effect on this page comes from the cation riding along with the base.

Same class, opposite bowel problems — which is exactly why combination products (aluminum + magnesium, e.g. magaldrate) exist: the two cancel each other out. 🧠 "A & C = Cork it. Mg = Must go." A luminium & C alcium C onstipate. M agnesium M akes you run. Combination antacids pair them on purpose to keep the bowels even.

STEP 3 · THE 1–2 HOUR RULE The biggest antacid error in practice is not an overdose — it is giving another pill at the same time.

entries.h: ⏱️ No oral drug within 1 to 2 hours of an antacid
entries.t: An antacid does two things to other drugs: it binds them in the gut so they never get absorbed, and it raises gastric pH so pH-dependent drugs dissolve differently. Both mean the other drug stops working . entries.h: Allopurinol & Colchicine · NG-015 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 💊 What each does ⚠️ Watch for 🗣️ Teach & test traps ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Pharmacology · Gout · Two-Drug Head-to-Head

One prevents the attack. One treats the attack. Neither one is a painkiller. NG-015 PHARM · Musculoskeletal ADHD-friendly visual edition Gout is uric acid build-up that crystallizes inside a joint and sets off ferocious inflammation. Two drugs get confused on every single exam : allo P urinol = P revents future attacks by lowering uric acid, and a C olchicine = a C ute attacks . Neither is given to reduce pain — that job belongs to an NSAID like naproxen or ibuprofen. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🛡️
STEP 1 · TWO DIFFERENT JOBS Start with the joint — once you can see the crystals, both drugs make obvious sense.

entries.h: 🦶 Inside the joint — normal vs. gouty, side by side
entries.t: EXAM TIP Uric acid is the waste product of purine breakdown. When blood levels stay high, it drops out of solution as needle-shaped monosodium urate crystals in the cool peripheral joints — classically the first metatarsophalangeal joint (the great toe) . The crystals themselves aren't the pain; the neutrophils that swarm them are. Left: cartilage smooth, fluid clear, capsule thin. Right: crystals in the fluid, neutrophils piling in, capsule swollen, cartilage eroding, and a chalky tophus after years. 🧠 "Crystals a

entries.h: 🧪 Allopurinol — turn the uric acid tap DOWN
entries.t: Allopurinol is a xanthine oxidase inhibitor . Xanthine oxidase is the enzyme that converts hypoxanthine → xanthine → uric acid . Block it and less uric acid is ever made — so blood levels fall, crystals dissolve back into solution, and future attacks stop happening. 🧠 "ALLO = A Low Level." Allopurinol's whole purpose is a low uric acid level — and that lab value is how you evaluate whether it worked.

entries.h: 🔥 Colchicine — stop the neutrophils from ever reaching the joint
entries.t: Colchicine is not an analgesic and not a urate-lowering drug . It interferes with the microtubules that a neutrophil needs in order to crawl, so the white cells can't migrate into the joint and can't set off the inflammatory cascade. Give it at the very first sign of a flare — the earlier it starts, the better it works. Colchicine does not remove the crystals. It removes the response to them — which is why the attack settles but the uric acid level does not change. 🧠 "Colchicine cancels the CALL-OUT." The crystals
STEP 2 · THE TOXICITY THAT LIMITS EACH DRUG Each drug has one signature warning. Allopurinol's is on the skin. Colchicine's is in the gut.

entries.h: 🚨 Allopurinol + a rash = STOP the drug and report it
entries.t: A rash on allopurinol is never "just a rash." It can be the first sign of a severe, potentially fatal hypersensitivity skin reaction (Stevens–Johnson syndrome / toxic epidermal necrolysis). Any new rash → hold the dose and notify the provider immediately. 🧠 "Rash ALL Over — ALLopurinol = Deadly." The word ALL is hiding in the drug name and in "all over." One rash, one action: stop and report.

entries.h: 🚨 Colchicine: GI toxicity is the dose-limiting effect
entries.t: The dose you can give is limited by the gut, not by the joint. Nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramping and — above all — diarrhea are the early toxicity signal. 💊 Colchicine started for the flare ▼ 🤢 Nausea · vomiting · abdominal pain ▼ 💩 DIARRHEA = hold the dose & notify the provider ▼ 🚨 Ignored → dehydration, electrolyte loss; with prolonged/high dosing: bone-marrow suppression & myopathy 🧪 Monitor CBC with longer courses — watch for anemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia. 💪 Report new muscle pain or weakness (myopath

entries.h: 🧪 How you evaluate each drug — completely different endpoints
entries.t: 🧠 "Lab for the preventer, joint for the treater." Allopurinol is judged by a number . Colchicine is judged by the joint . 🗣️
STEP 3 · THE QUESTIONS THEY ACTUALLY ASK Almost every gout item is a variation of "which drug, which moment?"

entries.h: 📊 The three-drug decision table — the whole topic in one grid
entries.t: 🛡️ ALLOPURINOL 🔥 COLCHICINE 💊 NSAID (naproxen, ibuprofen) When Between attacks — daily, long-term During the acute attack, started early During the acute attack Job Lowers uric acid production (xanthine oxidase inhibitor) Blocks neutrophil migration → shuts inflammation down PAIN relief + anti-inflammatory Pain relief? NO NO — it is not an analgesic YES — this is the pain drug Acute attack? Do NOT start it during a flare — a new start can prolong/worsen it. Already taking it? Keep taking it. Yes — this is its momen

5-ASA drugs — mesalamine · balsalazide · olsalazine · sulfasalazine NG-016 GI · Pharmacology ADHD-friendly visual edition Aminosalicylates are the first-line anti-inflammatory class for inflammatory bowel disease . What makes them different from every other IBD drug: they exert a TOPICAL anti-inflammatory effect in the bowel — the drug has to physically land on the inflamed lining to work. The exact mechanism of action is unknown. Because the effect is topical, the entire pharmacology of this class is really a deli
STEP 1 · TOPICAL ANTI-INFLAMMATORY Look at the bowel wall first. Once you see which layer is inflamed, the whole class makes sense.

entries.h: 🔬 Bowel wall in cutaway — inflamed vs. healed on aminosalicylate
entries.t: EXAM TIP In ulcerative colitis the inflammation is confined to the mucosa and submucosa and it is continuous from the rectum upward. That superficial, continuous pattern is exactly why a drug that sits on the surface can work — a topical anti-inflammatory can reach mucosal disease, but it cannot reach through a full-thickness inflammatory tract. Gold dots = neutrophils packing the crypts (crypt abscesses), the histologic hallmark of active disease. Green = the 5-ASA drug sitting on the mucosal surface, exactly wher

entries.h: 🗺️ Delivery is the whole game — where each formulation releases
entries.t: 🧠 "Low disease, low route." Rectum only → suppository. Rectum + sigmoid → enema. Whole colon or small bowel → oral, in the coating that opens at the right pH/time.

entries.h: 💊 The four drugs — dose & specific use

This is the differentiator the exam wants. A 5-ASA works on the lining . A corticosteroid or biologic works through the bloodstream , dampening immunity everywhere. 🎯 Aminosalicylate (this page) 💉 Systemic IBD drugs Acts topically in the bowel — must contact the mucosa Act body-wide through the circulation Adverse effects are mostly GI + headache/dizziness Adverse effects are infection, glucose, bone, growth Used for mild–moderate disease and to hold remission Used to rescue a severe flare or when 5-ASA fails No ro
STEP 2 · ADVERSE EFFECTS, CONTRAS & TRAPS The adverse effects mimic the disease — which is exactly what makes them tricky.

🤕 Abdominal pain 🤢 Nausea 💩 Diarrhea 🤯 Headache 💫 Dizziness fall risk 🌡️ Fever report it 🥱 Weakness EXAM TIP Abdominal pain, nausea and diarrhea are also the symptoms of the disease. That is why the source insists you question the patient about the type and intensity of symptoms BEFORE the first dose — without a baseline you cannot tell a drug reaction from a flare. 🧠 "You can't judge the change if you never measured the start." Baseline symptom assessment is the whole reason this is a nursing-management question,

❌ Known hypersensitivity ❌ Hypersensitivity to sulfonamides and sulfites — ask about a sulfa allergy before every dose, especially with sulfasalazine ❌ Intestinal obstruction — a drug that must travel to the colon cannot be given into a blocked bowel ❌ Children younger than 2 years Caution: aminosalicylates are pregnancy category B — except olsalazine, which is category C — and all are used with caution during pregnancy and lactation (safety has not been established). 🧠 "SOB-2" — S ulfa/sulfite allergy · O bstructi

entries.h: ⭐ NCLEX TIP — the obstipation trap: loose stool that is actually constipation
entries.t: A client with hypoactive bowel sounds and severe obstipation can leak liquid stool around a hard fecal mass — and it presents as loose stool . If you read that as diarrhea and treat it as a flare, you are treating the exact opposite of the real problem. That patient needs completely different drug therapy. 🧠 "Quiet gut, liquid stool = a plug, not a flare." Listen before you believe the stool. Hypoactive bowel sounds flip the entire care plan.

STEP 3 · NURSING MANAGEMENT This is a nursing-process class: baseline, assess, report, replace fluids.

1 Review the chart for the course of treatment and find the reason the drug was prescribed — active flare or maintenance changes everything you teach. ▼ 2 Question the patient about the type and intensity of symptoms — pain, discomfort, diarrhea or constipation — to create the baseline for evaluating effectiveness. ▼ 3 Assess for relief of symptoms and monitor vital signs . ▼ 4 Monitor fluid intake & output — chronic diarrhea is a fluid and electrolyte problem before it is anything else. ▼ 5 🚨 REPORT: abdominal dis

entries.h: 🚨 Why "abdominal distention" is on the report list
entries.t: Worsening distention with fever and pain in a colitis client can signal severe colonic dilation — a surgical emergency, not a drug side effect. Never dismiss a newly distended, tender abdomen as "just the IBD." 🧠 "Big belly + hot + hurting = phone, not chart."

entries.h: 💧 Chronic diarrhea — what to actually offer
entries.t: If diarrhea is chronic, encourage increased fluid intake . The source names the exact options: 🍵 Weak tea 💧 Water 🍲 Bouillon salty broth 🧃 Pedialyte electrolytes 🥤 Gatorade electrolytes 📋 Monitor fluid intake & output — the number, not the impression. ⚖️ Daily weight is the fastest fluid-loss detector. 🧪 Ongoing diarrhea also risks hypokalemia — watch for muscle weakness and cramps. 🧠 "Water alone won't fix a salt problem." Broth and electrolyte drinks replace what water can't.

As an infusion it appears to produce an antispasmodic effect on GI smooth muscle and to protect against the development of stomach ulcers . entries.h: Angina · Stable vs Unstable · NG-017 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🧨 Why it hurts 🟢 Stable 🔴 Unstable 🔎 Tell apart 💊 Nitro ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Cardio · Pathophysiology Course 🫀 CHEST-PAIN SET NG-017 Stable vs Unstable NG-098 Variant (Prinzmetal) NG-071 Myocardial Infarction NG-145 Atherosclerosis

Stable vs. Unstable — the same pipe, two different stories NG-017 CARDIO ADHD-friendly visual edition Angina is the heart muscle shouting that it isn't getting enough oxygen . Stable angina is chest pain induced by physical activity — stairs, yard work, sex, anything that causes exertion — and it stops when the activity stops . Unstable angina is pain at REST — a warning sign for an MI , because the coronary arteries are more severely narrowed. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → ⚖️ Supply < Demand Angina
STEP 1 · SUPPLY vs DEMAND The heart muscle feeds itself through the coronary arteries. Narrow those pipes and the muscle starts complaining.

entries.h: 🫀 The coronary artery tree — the heart's own blood supply
entries.t: EXAM TIP The coronaries branch off the aorta just above the aortic valve and wrap around the outside of the heart. They fill during DIASTOLE — when the heart relaxes. That is why a very fast heart rate makes angina worse: less relaxing time = less coronary filling. 🧠 “LAD = the widow-maker's highway.” L AD → L eft front. C ircumflex → C urves around the side. R CA → R ight + the R hythm nodes.

entries.h: ⚖️ The one equation behind every kind of angina
entries.t: Answer first: angina happens the moment oxygen DEMAND outruns oxygen SUPPLY . Everything you do for a client with angina either lowers demand or raises supply . 🧠 “The muscle is yelling: HEY, I don't have enough oxygen!” That shout is the pain. Ischemia is reversible — infarction is not.

entries.h: 🧱 Cross-section of the artery — how a plaque narrows the pipe
entries.t: Angina starts with atherosclerosis . Look at the wall layers: endothelium → intima → media (smooth muscle) → adventitia . Plaque builds inside the intima and pushes into the lumen. 🧠 “Stable plaque = a speed bump. Ruptured plaque = a road-block being built while you drive.” That is exactly why unstable angina is unpredictable. 🟢
SIDE A · PREDICTABLE Classic exertional angina — it shows up when you work, and it leaves when you stop.

entries.h: 🚶 Patho & causes — chest pain induced by physical activity
entries.t: Stable angina is chest pain induced by any physical activity — walking up stairs, working in the yard, or even sex. Anything that causes exertion! There is less oxygen delivered to the heart muscles during the physical exertion , so the muscle produces pain — the heart saying “HEY, I don't have enough oxygen!” Naturally, the pain stops when the physical activity stops . 🪜 Stairs 🌿 Yard work 🛏️ Sex 🥶 Cold air 🍔 Heavy meal 😤 Stress 🧠 S · S · S — S table Angina · S afer Angina · S tops with rest. Three S's, one idea.

entries.h: 📈 The exertion curve — stable pain has a shape you can draw
entries.t: 🧠 If you can predict what brings the pain on and predict what makes it stop, it's stable. Lose the prediction, lose the stability. 🔴
SIDE B · EMERGENCY Pain at rest. This is acute coronary syndrome until proven otherwise.

entries.h: 🚨 Pain at rest! — a warning sign for MI
entries.t: Pain at rest! This is a warning sign for an MI (heart attack) . It is the more severe angina because it means more severe narrowing of the coronary arteries , resulting in less oxygen to the heart muscles . At rest , or with minimal effort New onset angina in someone who never had it More frequent, more intense, or lasting longer than the client's usual pattern Not relieved by rest or by the usual nitroglycerin 🧠 U · U · U — U nstable Angina · U nsafe Angina · U nrelieved pain at rest.

entries.h: 🔬 Partial vs. total occlusion — where angina ends and MI begins
entries.t: Same artery, two amounts of clot. Partial occlusion starves the muscle ( ischemia — reversible). Total occlusion kills it ( infarction — permanent). HIGH YIELD Unstable angina and NSTEMI look identical at the bedside. The difference is the troponin : unstable angina = troponin stays normal; NSTEMI = troponin rises. Both are treated as acute coronary syndrome. 🧠 “Trop tells the truth.” Pain can lie, the ECG can be subtle — the troponin tells you whether muscle actually died.

entries.h: 🚨 Do this NOW for unstable / rest pain
entries.t: 1 Stop activity, sit or lie down , stay with the client. 2 Call for help / activate EMS — this is a suspected ACS. 3 12-lead ECG and cardiac troponins. 4 Oxygen if hypoxemic , IV access, continuous cardiac monitoring, vital signs. 5 Aspirin (chewed) and nitroglycerin as prescribed — after checking blood pressure and PDE-5 inhibitor use. 🧠 “Rest pain gets a rhythm strip.” Any chest pain at rest earns an ECG — do not talk yourself out of it.

entries.h: ♀️ Atypical presentations — the ones that get missed
entries.t: Not everyone clutches their chest. Women, older adults, and people with diabetes more often present with: Fatigue that is new and unexplained Shortness of breath without chest pain Nausea / indigestion-type discomfort Jaw, neck, back or epigastric discomfort Dizziness or a sense of doom ❌ Never rule out cardiac pain just because it is not “crushing substernal chest pain.” 🧠 Diabetic neuropathy can silence the pain — a “silent MI” still infarcts. Trust the vitals and the ECG, not just the complaint. 🔎
SIDE A vs SIDE B One table. If you own this table you own the question.

12-lead ECG — first, and fast Cardiac troponin — serial draws; the marker that separates angina from MI Stress test (exercise or pharmacologic) — for stable angina, never during unstable pain Coronary angiography / cardiac cath — sees the actual narrowing, can stent it Lipid panel, A1c, BP — the risk factors driving the plaque 🧠 Stress test = stress the STABLE. Stressing an unstable client on purpose is the wrong answer every single time.

entries.h: 🎯 Modifiable risk factors — the real long game
entries.t: Smoking — cessation is the single highest-yield change Hypertension and hyperlipidemia control Diabetes / glucose control Obesity , sedentary lifestyle, poor diet Stress management & sleep Non-modifiable: age, male sex, family history, ethnicity. See NG-145 Atherosclerosis . 🧠 The plaque took decades to build — the teaching is about slowing it down , not erasing it. 💊
TREATMENT · TEACH THIS COLD The drug the exam loves. Read every line — most of these are pure test points.

entries.h: 💥 How it works — NitrO = O₂ to the heart
entries.t: Nitroglycerin is a vasodilator . It relaxes the smooth muscle in blood vessels, which dilates the veins (less blood returning to the heart = less preload = less work ) and dilates the coronary arteries (more oxygen delivered). Net effect: oxygen demand drops and oxygen supply rises — the pain stops. 🧠 “Nitr-O gives O₂.” The O in the middle of the drug name is the oxygen it sends to the heart.

❌ NO “-afil” drugs with nitroglycerin. Sildena fil , tadala fil , vardena fil + nitrates = profound, potentially FATAL hypotension . Both drug classes are vasodilators. Stacked together the blood pressure can bottom out and the client can arrest. Always ask about erectile-dysfunction and pulmonary-hypertension medications before giving nitroglycerin — including the ones bought without a prescription. Practice varies on the exact interval, but the standard teaching is that nitrates must be withheld for at least 24 h

entries.h: 💊 Sublingual nitroglycerin — how the client takes it
entries.t: Answer first: 0.4 mg SL tablet (or metered spray), 1 dose , then repeat every 5 minutes up to 3 doses total . Call 911 if the pain is unimproved or worsening 5 minutes after the FIRST dose — do not wait for all three. 🧠 “Sit, slip it under, wait five, call.” Sit down first — nitro drops blood pressure and standing up mid-dose is how people fall.

✅ YES Original dark container · a purse is OK · cool, dark, dry ❌ NO LIGHT Light degrades it — keep it in the amber bottle ❌ NO HEAT Not the car, not a hot pocket ❌ NOT a pill box Not a plastic bag, not loose in a pocket 🗓️ Replace the supply every 6 months (or per the manufacturer's expiration) — old tablets lose potency. 🧠 “Dark bottle, cool purse, new every 6 months.” A tablet that doesn't tingle or doesn't work may simply be dead.

entries.h: 🩹 Transdermal patch — the other half of the question
entries.t: 1 patch daily — scheduled, NOT PRN One patch at a time — never two Rotate the site daily · clean, dry, hairless area on the upper body (chest, upper arm, subclavian area) ❌ Not on hairy, scarred, burned, callused or broken skin Showering is fine · wash hands after applying Nurses wear gloves — absorbing it causes a major headache A nitrate-free interval (commonly 10–12 hours, usually overnight) is prescribed to prevent tolerance TEST TIP Patch fell off more than an hour ago and chest pain starts? Take the SL nitro

entries.h: 🎯 The goal, in the client's own words
entries.t: NO chest pain during daily activities — “I can comb my hair, get dressed, put on make-up, and make my bed without chest pain.” That is what a successful plan looks like, and it is how the exam words the evaluation question. 💇 Comb hair 👕 Get dressed 💄 Make-up 🛏️ Make the bed 🚿 Shower 🍳 Cook a meal Other prescribed therapies you'll see alongside nitrates: aspirin/antiplatelets , beta blockers ( NG-176 ), calcium channel blockers ( NG-195 ), statins ( NG-242 ), and revascularization with PCI/stent or CABG . 🧠 “Activi

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🟢 Stable · Safer · Stops with rest Exertional, predictable, brief. 🔴 Unstable · Unsafe · Unrelieved Pain at rest = warning sign for MI. 💊 0.4 mg SL · q5min · max 3 Call 911 if pain persists 5 min after dose 1. ☠️ Nitro + “-afil” Sildenafil & friends = fatal hypotension. Always ask.

Q1: What triggers stable angina, and what relieves it? Show answer Physical exertion — stairs, yard work, sex, anything that causes exertion. It stops when the physical activity stops (and responds to nitroglycerin). Q2: What is the single defining feature of unstable angina? Show answer Pain at REST. It means more severe narrowing of the coronary arteries and it is a warning sign for an MI. Q3: A client takes one SL nitroglycerin tablet and 5 minutes later the pain is the same. entries.h: Anorexia Nervosa · NG-018 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🧨 What it is 📊 Who & why 🔎 Findings 🩺 Care 🚨 Refeeding ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Mental Health · Psychiatric Care 🍽️ EATING DISORDERS SET NG-018 Anorexia Nervosa NG-106 Bulimia Nervosa NG-221 CBT NG-271 Therapeutic Communication

A serious, treatable illness — and a medical emergency when the body starts to fail NG-018 Mental Health ADHD-friendly visual edition Anorexia nervosa is an eating disorder in which the client is preoccupied with weight and with what they eat , driven by a distorted body image and an unrealistic fear of being overweight . The behaviors lead to restriction and malnutrition . It carries the highest mortality rate of any mental health disorder — from medical complications and from suicide — so the nursing priorities a
STEP 1 · THE DISORDER Two things define it: what the client believes about their body, and what the body does when it is starved.

entries.h: 🪞 Distorted body image — the core feature
entries.t: ATI Anorexia nervosa: the client has an unrealistic fear of obesity . KAPLAN Clients see themselves as overweight even when they are not. This is a perceptual disturbance, not vanity and not a choice — arguing with the perception does not change it. 🧠 “The mirror lies, and the client believes it.” Your job is not to win the argument about the mirror — it is to keep the body safe while therapy works on the belief.

entries.h: 📖 The clinical picture, in plain words
entries.t: Preoccupation with weight and with what is eaten Intense fear of gaining weight, even as nutritional status worsens Distorted body image — self-evaluation is dominated by body shape and weight Persistent restriction of nutritional intake leading to malnutrition Often accompanied by excessive, driven exercise ❌ Never describe the client as “just being dramatic” or “doing it for attention” — in the chart or out loud. 🧠 Fear · Perception · Restriction. Three words that separate anorexia nervosa from every other diagno

entries.h: 🔄 How is this different from bulimia?
entries.t: 🪞 ANOREXIA 🔄 BULIMIA Restriction is the main behavior Binge then compensatory behavior Body weight is significantly low for the person Weight is often normal or near-normal Behavior feels consistent with the client's goal (ego-syntonic) — insight is often limited Behavior often causes shame and is hidden Danger: starvation physiology + refeeding Danger: electrolyte loss from compensatory behavior 👉 Full page: NG-106 — Bulimia Nervosa . 🧠 “Anorexia restricts. Bulimia cycles.” Both end at the same monitor — the cardi
STEP 2 · RISK FACTORS No single cause — biology, psychology and environment all contribute.

entries.h: 🚨 The number the exam wants: highest mortality of any mental disorder
entries.t: KAPLAN Which statements are true regarding anorexia nervosa? ✅ Clients see themselves as overweight. ✅ Adolescent females are the most affected group. ✅ Anorexia nervosa has the highest mortality rate of all mental disorders — from medical complications and from suicide. Because suicide is a leading cause of death in this disorder, suicide risk assessment is part of routine care — not something you do only if the client seems sad. 🧠 “Deadliest diagnosis on the psych unit.” If a question asks which mental health dis

Adolescent females are the most affected group — but it occurs across all genders, ages, body sizes and backgrounds Often begins in adolescence or young adulthood Higher risk in environments that emphasize appearance or leanness (certain sports, dance, modeling) ❌ Never rule the diagnosis out because the client is male, older, or does not “look like” they have an eating disorder. 🧠 The stereotype is a trap. Assess the behavior and the physiology , not the appearance.

Biological/genetic — family history of eating disorders, anxiety or mood disorders Psychological — perfectionism, rigidity, low self-esteem, a strong need for control Social/cultural — appearance pressure, weight-related teasing, social media comparison Trauma or major life transition as a trigger Frequently coexists with depression ( NG-112 ), anxiety ( NG-236 ) and obsessive-compulsive traits ( NG-075 ). 🧠 “Control is the theme.” When everything else feels unmanageable, intake becomes the one controllable variabl
STEP 3 · WHAT THE BODY SHOWS Starvation → malnutrition. The body turns the thermostat down and every system slows.
🧠 “Everything slows and everything shrinks.” Slow heart, slow gut, slow hormones, slow temperature. Lanugo is the body's last attempt to stay warm — remember it as “the blanket the body grows.”

Body fat is the body's insulation. When the fat layer under the skin thins, the body loses heat quickly, so it grows a coat of fine, soft, downy hair — lanugo — to trap warmth against the skin. 🧠 “No blanket of fat → grow a blanket of hair.” Lanugo, cold intolerance and low body temperature are all the same finding wearing three different names.

entries.h: 💓 The cardiac picture — why the potassium matters
entries.t: Answer first: starvation causes bradycardia and hypotension , and hypokalemia (potassium below 3.5 mEq/L) causes cardiac dysrhythmias. Put those together and you have the most dangerous combination on this page. HESI An adolescent client with anorexia nervosa — which physical findings support the diagnosis? ✅ Lanugo · ✅ Irregular heart rate · ✅ A pulse rate in the 40s · ✅ A serum potassium well below the reference range . 🧠 “Slow pulse + low K⁺ = monitor.” Those two findings together are what turn a psychiatric adm

Potassium — hypokalemia < 3.5 mEq/L → dysrhythmias ⭐ (typical adult reference range is 3.5–5.0 mEq/L — verify against your lab) Phosphorus & magnesium — critical before and during nutritional restoration Sodium and overall fluid balance CBC — anemia, leukopenia; albumin/prealbumin — protein status Glucose — hypoglycemia; renal & liver function ECG — rate, rhythm, QT interval 🧠 “K, Phos, Mag.” Those three letters are the whole refeeding-safety story — memorize them as a set.

Care is typically outpatient , but admission is indicated when the client is medically unstable : Unstable vital signs — bradycardia, hypotension, hypothermia Cardiac dysrhythmia or ECG changes Significant electrolyte disturbance Severe dehydration or rapid clinical deterioration Severe malnutrition requiring supervised nutritional restoration Suicidal ideation or inability to be safe in the community 🧠 “Unstable body → inpatient bed.” The decision is medical, not motivational. 🩺
STEP 4 · WHAT THE NURSE DOES Medical stability first, structure second, insight third — in that order.

HESI What is the focus for the acute phase of treatment? Restoring nutritional status and medical stability — the body has to be safe before therapy can do its work. 1 Medical stability — vital signs including orthostatics and temperature, cardiac monitoring when indicated, electrolytes, hydration. ▼ 2 Supervised nutrition per the prescribed plan — stay with the client during each meal and for 1 hour after ; one-on-one supervision during feedings . ▼ 3 Objective monitoring — strict record of intake and output , mor

entries.h: ⚖️ Why weights are done that way
entries.t: Morning, before any oral intake — removes the effect of food and fluid Same scale, same time, similar clothing, after voiding Consistency is what makes the trend meaningful Many programs discuss whether to share the number with the client — follow the treatment plan , because the number itself can be distressing 🧠 “Same scale, same time, empty bladder, before breakfast.” Change one variable and the trend becomes meaningless.

Cognitive behavioral therapy — help the client examine dysfunctional thoughts and beliefs (see NG-221 ) Family-based treatment — first-line for many adolescents Nutritional counseling with a registered dietitian Group and individual therapy ; treat coexisting depression/anxiety Medication may be prescribed for coexisting conditions — it is an adjunct, not the treatment for the eating disorder itself 🧠 “Feed the body, then challenge the thought.” A starved brain cannot do therapy well — that is why nutrition comes f

Encourage and reinforce “progress toward a healthy weight” and toward the client's own goals. Keep the tone matter-of-fact, warm and non-judgmental , and keep limits consistent between staff so the plan never becomes a negotiation. ✅ “I'll sit with you during your meal.” States the expectation calmly and offers presence — no bargaining, no bribery. ❌ “You look so much better already!” Comments on appearance land as comments about weight. Keep feedback on effort and progress , not on the body. ✅ “It sounds like eati

Suicide risk — ask directly, document, follow unit protocol Orthostatic vital signs , apical pulse for a full minute Fall risk — weakness, dizziness, syncope Skin integrity over bony prominences Bathroom supervision per the plan of care 🧠 Ask about suicide out loud. Asking never plants the idea — not asking is what costs lives in the deadliest psychiatric diagnosis.

This is an illness , not a choice or a phase Do not police, comment on, or bargain over food at home — follow the team's plan Avoid weight and appearance talk altogether, including about yourselves Recovery is not linear — relapse is common and is not failure Know the warning signs that need urgent review: fainting, chest pain, palpitations, confusion 🧠 “Be the parent, not the food police.” The team owns the meal plan; the family owns the relationship. 🚨
STEP 5 · THE HIDDEN EMERGENCY The most dangerous moment is not the starving — it is the first days of feeding again.

entries.h: 🔬 The mechanism — why the labs crash when nutrition restarts
entries.t: Answer first: when nutrition resumes after prolonged malnutrition, insulin surges and drives phosphate, potassium and magnesium out of the bloodstream and into the cells , along with fluid. The serum levels fall fast — and that can cause cardiac failure, respiratory failure, dysrhythmias, seizures and delirium. 🧠 “Feed too fast, the labs fall through the floor.” Remember the trio as “Phos, K, Mag — the refeeding three.” Phosphorus is the headline.

Start nutritional restoration slowly and advance gradually, exactly as prescribed Check electrolytes before starting and frequently during the first days — especially phosphorus , potassium and magnesium Replace electrolytes as prescribed before and during advancement Thiamine and other vitamins are commonly prescribed before nutrition is advanced Cardiac monitoring and close attention to fluid balance — daily weights and strict I&O Watch for edema, shortness of breath, confusion, weakness, palpitations — report im

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🪞 Distorted body image Unrealistic fear of obesity — a perceptual disturbance, not a preference. 🚨 Highest mortality Of all mental health disorders. Assess suicide risk routinely. 💓 Low HR · low BP · low temp + hypokalemia (K⁺ < 3.5 ) = dysrhythmia risk. 🍽️ Supervise + record Stay through the meal and 1 hr after · strict intake · morning weights · no exercise.

Q1: What is the core psychological feature of anorexia nervosa? Show answer A distorted body image with an unrealistic fear of obesity — clients see themselves as overweight. It is a perceptual disturbance, so arguing with it does not help. Q2: Which mental health disorder has the highest mortality rate, and why? Show answer Anorexia nervosa — from medical complications of starvation and from suicide. That is why suicide risk assessment is part of routine care. Q3: Name the classic physical findings. entries.h: Antidysrhythmics I — Vaughan-Williams Classes · NG-019 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🗺️ The 4 classes ⚡ How they work 🎯 Rhythm → drug 🚨 Watch for Nursing Field Notes / Cardio · Series: Antidysrhythmics 1 of 4 Antidysrhythmics series 1 · The 4 classes 2 · ABCDs — atrial → 3 → 4 →

The Vaughan-Williams map · four classes, four channels, one heartbeat NG-019 CARDIO ADHD-friendly visual edition An antidysrhythmic never adds a beat — it changes ion traffic inside cardiac cells so the electrical signal starts, travels and resets differently. Vaughan-Williams sorts them by which door they slam shut : sodium , beta , potassium , calcium . Learn the door and you already know the ECG change, the side effect, and the rhythm it treats. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🔤 Some Block Potassium
STEP 1 · THE MAP Don't memorize 30 drugs. Memorize four doors — then hang the drugs on the door they close.

entries.h: 🧠 Meet your study buddy — she only knows one sentence, and it's the whole classification
entries.t: 🧠 “Some Block Potassium Channels.” Say it four times out loud. S odium → B eta → P otassium → C alcium, in order I · II · III · IV . If you can say the sentence you can rebuild the entire Vaughan-Williams table from scratch.

Answer first: they slow how fast the impulse fires and travels → the QRS gets wider . Ia — quinidine, procainamide, disopyramide · moderate block, also blocks K⁺ → QT ⬆ Ib — lidocaine, mexiletine · weak block, shortens the action potential · ventricles only Ic — flecainide, propafenone · strongest block · QRS ⬆⬆ , no QT change 🧠 “Double Quarter Pounder, Lettuce More, Fries Please.” Ia = D isopyramide · Q uinidine · P rocainamide · Ib = L idocaine · M exiletine · Ic = F lecainide · P ropafenone.

entries.h: 2️⃣ Class II — beta blockers SEE NG-176
entries.t: Answer first: they take the epinephrine foot off the pedal at the SA and AV node → slower rate, slower AV conduction, PR ⬆ . Names end in -olol / -lol — metoprolol, atenolol, propranolol, esmolol The workhorse for rate control in A-fib & A-flutter and for SVT Only antidysrhythmic class with proven mortality benefit after MI and in heart failure Full drug page: NG-176 · Beta blockers 🧠 “-LOL lowers the two L's” — L ow heart rate, L ow blood pressure. Nothing funny about it.

Answer first: they block the K⁺ exit doors, so the cell takes longer to reset → refractory period ⬆ and QT gets long . Amiodarone — the "everything" drug; blocks Na⁺, K⁺, Ca²⁺ and beta receptors Sotalol — Class III plus a beta blocker (that's why it slows the rate too) Dofetilide, ibutilide, dronedarone — started with the client on a monitor 🧠 “AmIODarone, sotALOL, dofetILIDE, ibutILIDE.” Class III names have that long, drawn-out sound — just like the long QT they cause.

entries.h: 4️⃣ Class IV — calcium channel blockers SEE NG-195
entries.t: Answer first: the SA and AV nodes run on calcium , not sodium — block Ca²⁺ and you slow the top of the heart. Only the non-dihydropyridines count here: diltiazem and verapamil The -dipine drugs (amlodipine, nifedipine) work on vessels , not rhythm Uses: rate control in A-fib / A-flutter , and SVT Full drug page: NG-195 · Calcium channel blockers 🧠 “Diltiazem & Verapamil = the heart's CCBs. -dipine = the vessels' CCBs.” If the question is about a rhythm , it is never amlodipine.

entries.h: 📋 The one table to photograph before the exam
entries.t: Class Door it blocks Phase ECG fingerprint Signature drugs Ia Na⁺ (moderate) + K⁺ 0 & 3 QRS ⬆ and QT ⬆ quinidine · procainamide · disopyramide Ib Na⁺ (weak) 0 little change · shortens AP lidocaine · mexiletine Ic Na⁺ (strong) 0 QRS ⬆⬆ flecainide · propafenone II β₁ receptors 4 HR ⬇ · PR ⬆ metoprolol · atenolol · esmolol · propranolol III K⁺ 3 QT ⬆ amiodarone · sotalol · dofetilide · ibutilide IV Ca²⁺ (L-type) 2 & nodal HR ⬇ · PR ⬆ diltiazem · verapamil “Other” doesn't fit the 4 — varies adenosine · digoxin · magnes
STEP 2 · THE ACTION POTENTIAL One curve explains every class. Find the phase, and you have found the drug.

entries.h: 📈 The cardiac action potential — with every class parked on its phase
entries.t: 🧠 Read the curve left to right and count off the classes: “Up · notch · plateau · down · drift.” The up is sodium (I), the plateau is calcium (IV), the down is potassium (III), the drift is the pacemaker that beta blockers (II) flatten.

entries.h: 🫀 Two kinds of heart tissue — and each class only likes one
entries.t: 🧠 “Nodes run on calcium, muscle runs on sodium.” That single fact is why verapamil slows a rate but never converts VT, and why lidocaine converts VT but does nothing for A-fib.

entries.h: 🔬 Class I split three ways — same door, different grip
entries.t: EXAM TIP Dashed gray line = the normal action potential. The colored line is what the drug does to it. 🧠 “A-lengthens, B-shortens, C-stays the same.” Ia = A dds length (QT ⬆) · Ib = B rief (shortens) · Ic = C onstant length but the C omplex (QRS) is huge. 🎯
STEP 3 · WHO GETS WHAT The exam rarely asks "what class is amiodarone." It asks "the client is in this rhythm — what do you expect the provider to order?"

Rhythm Usual first move Class Symptomatic bradycardia HR <60 Atropine — then pacing / dopamine / epinephrine if it fails “Other” Stable SVT Vagal maneuvers → adenosine → beta blocker or diltiazem “Other” → II / IV A-fib / A-flutter — rate control Beta blocker or diltiazem / verapamil (digoxin as an add-on) II / IV A-fib / A-flutter — rhythm control Amiodarone , sotalol, dofetilide, flecainide, propafenone III / Ic Stable ventricular tachycardia Amiodarone , procainamide or sotalol · lidocaine as an alternative III

🐢 RATE control 🎵 RHYTHM control Leave A-fib in place — just slow the ventricles Try to force it back to normal sinus Class II beta blockers · Class IV diltiazem/verapamil · digoxin Class III amiodarone/sotalol/dofetilide · Class Ic flecainide/propafenone Safer, easier, usually first More proarrhythmic — needs monitoring & anticoagulation planning 🧠 “Rate = the node. Rhythm = the muscle.” Slowing the ventricular response is a node job (II, IV). Changing the actual rhythm is a muscle job (I, III).

entries.h: 🔗 The four "doesn't-fit-a-class" drugs already have their own pages
entries.t: Adenosine — the 6-second reset button for SVT → NG-094 Digoxin — slows AV conduction and strengthens the squeeze → NG-208 Beta blockers in full detail → NG-176 Calcium channel blockers in full detail → NG-195 The ABCD bedside shortcut — Atropine, Adenosine, Beta blockers, Calcium channel blockers, Digoxin — is the whole of part 2 of this series . 🧠 Vaughan-Williams is the classroom map. ABCD is the bedside map. You need both, and they overlap on purpose.

entries.h: 🧪 The labs that decide whether any of this works
entries.t: K⁺ 3.5–5.0 mEq/L Low K⁺ = every antidysrhythmic misbehaves & digoxin turns toxic. Mg²⁺ 1.3–2.1 mEq/L Low Mg²⁺ is the setup for torsades — replace it before blaming the drug. QTc >500 ms High torsades risk. Prolonged is >450 (men) / >470 (women). Digoxin 0.5–2.0 ng/mL Narrow window — always check with the apical pulse. Standard adult reference ranges — always confirm against your own facility's lab sheet, they vary slightly. 🧠 “Potassium and magnesium are the two batteries.” Put a rhythm drug into a client with a de
STEP 4 · THE DANGER LIST The one sentence that shows up on every antidysrhythmic exam: the treatment can become the disease.

entries.h: 🚨 Proarrhythmia — and the QT interval that predicts it
entries.t: Who prolongs the QT? Class Ia and Class III — plus a long list of non-cardiac drugs (many antipsychotics, methadone, ondansetron, some antibiotics and antifungals). Stacking two of them is the classic hidden trap. What you do about it: baseline & follow-up 12-lead ECG with a QTc , keep K⁺ and Mg²⁺ replete , and hold the drug and call the provider if the QTc exceeds 500 ms or grows more than about 60 ms from baseline. 🧠 “Long QT = a long fuse.” The longer the reset takes, the more time a stray beat has to land in th

entries.h: 💊 Amiodarone — the most effective and the most toxic
entries.t: Answer first: it works on almost every rhythm, and it damages almost every organ. Long half-life measured in weeks , so side effects linger after you stop it. 🫁 Pulmonary fibrosis — new dry cough, dyspnea → baseline & periodic chest X-ray + PFTs 🦋 Thyroid — it is iodine-rich; causes hypo or hyper → check TSH 🫀 Liver — monitor LFTs 👁️ Corneal microdeposits — halos, blurred vision → yearly eye exam 🌞 Photosensitivity & a blue-gray skin discoloration — sunscreen, cover up 💓 Bradycardia, hypotension, QT ⬆ — continuous

Ia · procainamide — a lupus-like syndrome (joint pain, rash, fever, positive ANA). Also blood dyscrasias → CBC. Ib · lidocaine — toxicity is neuro first : perioral tingling, metallic taste, tinnitus, confusion, twitching → seizures . Never use the lidocaine with epinephrine for IV cardiac use. Ic · flecainide — contraindicated with structural heart disease or prior MI ; it raised mortality in that group. II · beta blockers — bradycardia, bronchospasm in asthma/COPD, masks hypoglycemia (the tachycardia warning disap

entries.h: ✅ The nursing priority ladder — works for every drug in this chapter
entries.t: 1 Apical pulse for a full minute + BP before every dose. Common hold parameters: HR <60 or SBP <90 — but always follow the provider's written parameters. ▼ 2 Continuous ECG for anything IV. Look at PR, QRS width and QTc, not just the rate. ▼ 3 Replace the batteries. Check and correct K⁺ and Mg²⁺ — and renal function, since most of these drugs are cleared renally or hepatically. ▼ 4 Assess the client, not the monitor. Level of consciousness, chest pain, dizziness, skin color, urine output. Treat the client, not the

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🔤 Some Block Potassium Channels I sodium · II beta · III potassium · IV calcium 📐 Read it off the ECG Wide QRS = Class I · long QT = Class III (or Ia) · long PR = Class II or IV 🚨 Long QT = torsades QTc >500 ms → hold & call. Treat torsades with IV magnesium . ⚡ Unstable = electricity Cardiovert (with a pulse) or defibrillate (pulseless) before any drug.

Q1: Name the four Vaughan-Williams classes and their channel — in order. Show answer “Some Block Potassium Channels.” I = sodium channel blockers · II = beta blockers · III = potassium channel blockers · IV = calcium channel blockers. Q2: A client on quinidine has a QTc of 520 ms. What do you do? Show answer Hold the dose and notify the provider — QTc over 500 ms is high torsades risk. Check and replace K⁺ and Mg²⁺, keep the client on continuous ECG, and review every other QT-prolonging drug on the MAR. Q3: Why is

Anti-Nausea & Vomiting — one reflex, four receptors, four drug classes NG-020 PHARM · GI ADHD-friendly visual edition Vomiting is a reflex run by the vomiting center in the medulla . Four different pathways can pull its trigger, and each pathway uses a different receptor . That is the whole logic of this drug class: match the antiemetic to the receptor that is being stimulated . Chemo → serotonin. Motion → histamine & acetylcholine. Drugs & toxins in the blood → dopamine. Pick the wrong receptor and the drug does n
STEP 1 · THE FOUR INPUTS Learn this one picture and you never have to memorize a drug list again — you derive it.

entries.h: 🧠 The vomiting center, the CTZ, and the four roads that reach them
entries.t: EXAM TIP The vomiting center sits in the medulla and is the final common pathway — it actually fires the reflex. The chemoreceptor trigger zone (CTZ) sits next to it in the area postrema on the floor of the fourth ventricle , in a spot with essentially no blood–brain barrier — so it can "taste" drugs, toxins and metabolic waste circulating in the blood and tell the vomiting center about them. Gold dashed arrows = the four stimulus roads. The CTZ (teal) senses the blood; the vomiting center (red) pulls the trigger.

entries.h: 🔒 Four receptors, four blockers — the membrane close-up
entries.t: 🧠 "Four locks, four keys." 5-HT₃ = -setron · D₂ = -pramide / -perazine · H₁ = -zine (meclizine, dimenhydrinate) · muscarinic = scopolamine . Match the lock to the cause.

entries.t: Class Receptor Prototype drugs Best for Signature adverse effect Serotonin antagonists -setron 5-HT₃ Ondansetron (Zofran) , granisetron, palonosetron Chemotherapy -induced N/V · post-op N/V · gastroenteritis 🚨 QT prolongation → Torsades de Pointes · headache · constipation Dopamine antagonists D₂ (± 5-HT₃ at high dose) Metoclopramide (Reglan) , prochlorperazine, promethazine CTZ-driven N/V · gastroparesis · post-op 🚨 EPS — dystonia, akathisia, tardive dyskinesia · sedation · hypotension Antihistamines H₁ Meclizine,
STEP 2 · THE TWO THAT GET TESTED Ondansetron's danger is on the monitor. Metoclopramide's danger is on the face.

entries.h: 🚨 HESI EXIT priority side effect: ondansetron → Torsades de Pointes
entries.t: Ondansetron prolongs the QT interval . A long QT can degenerate into Torsades de Pointes — a polymorphic ventricular tachycardia that presents as syncope and can deteriorate into ventricular fibrillation. 🧪 Check potassium and magnesium before and during therapy — hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia lengthen the QT further, and a vomiting patient is already losing both. 📈 Know the baseline QTc ; use caution with congenital long QT and with other QT-prolonging drugs (many antipsychotics, some antibiotics, antiarrhythmics

entries.h: 🚨 Metoclopramide → EPS: lip smacking · puffing of the cheeks · blinking of the eyes
entries.t: Metoclopramide blocks dopamine — and dopamine blockade anywhere produces extrapyramidal symptoms . The three key words from the source are the classic features of tardive dyskinesia , which may be irreversible . Question the prescription and REPORT TO THE HCP IMMEDIATELY. 🚫 HESI: metoclopramide is contraindicated with a bleeding duodenal ulcer — and with GI obstruction or perforation, because it increases GI motility and would worsen the bleed or rupture. 🕰️ EPS risk climbs with higher doses, longer duration and ol

entries.h: 😴 Antihistamines & scopolamine — sedation and dry everything
entries.t: 🩹 Scopolamine patch: apply behind the ear on clean, dry, hairless skin; wash hands before and after — drug on the fingers rubbed into an eye causes a dilated pupil and blurred vision . ⏱️ Apply several hours before the trip; it is prophylaxis, not rescue. 🛏️ Sedation is expected with H1 antiemetics — fall precautions, no driving, no alcohol. 👵 In older adults , anticholinergics cause confusion, urinary retention and constipation — a common cause of new delirium. 💉 Promethazine IV carries a serious risk of severe ti

entries.h: 🚨 The vomiting itself is a nursing emergency
entries.t: 💧 Dehydration — poor turgor, dry mucous membranes, low urine output, tachycardia, hypotension. Monitor I&O and daily weight. 🧪 Hypokalemia and hypochloremia from lost gastric contents → muscle weakness, dysrhythmias. ⚖️ Metabolic alkalosis — you are literally vomiting acid out of the body. 🫁 Aspiration risk — position side-lying or upright , especially if the client is sedated or has a decreased LOC. 🩸 Hematemesis or coffee-ground emesis, or vomiting after a head injury → escalate immediately. 🧠 "Every vomit costs
STEP 3 · THE QUESTIONS THEY ASK Two exam scenarios show up again and again — one is a priority-action item, one is a report item.

entries.h: ⭐ HESI: child vomits DURING a chemotherapy infusion — priority action?
entries.t: 1 STOP the chemotherapy infusion. 🛑 ▼ 2 Flush the line. 💧 ▼ 3 Administer ondansetron. 💊 WHY THIS ORDER You always remove the cause before you treat the symptom . Giving the antiemetic first while the offending drug keeps infusing is treating around the problem. ATI: ondansetron is used to decrease nausea and vomiting caused by chemotherapy . 🧠 "Stop · Flush · Zofran." Three beats. If an option says "administer the antiemetic" but another says "stop the infusion" — stopping wins.

⏰ Give it BEFORE the trigger — before chemo, before the car ride, before ambulating post-op. Antiemetics prevent far better than they rescue. 🥤 Small sips of clear fluids; advance slowly. Cold, dry, bland foods; avoid strong smells and greasy food. 🪑 Sit upright after eating; rise slowly (many of these drugs drop the BP). 🚗 No driving and no alcohol on any sedating antiemetic. 🦷 Dry mouth: sugar-free gum, ice chips, frequent oral care. 📞 Report: uncontrolled vomiting, signs of dehydration, abnormal movements of the

entries.h: 🆚 Antiemetic vs. emetic — opposite drugs, opposite goals
entries.t: 🤢 ANTIEMETIC (this page) 🤮 EMETIC Blocks the reflex — stops vomiting Provokes the reflex — induces vomiting Chemo, post-op, motion, pregnancy, gastroenteritis Historically for certain ingestions — largely abandoned in modern poisoning care Risk: sedation, EPS, QT prolongation Risk: aspiration, esophageal injury, delaying real treatment Metoclopramide also appears as a GI stimulant / prokinetic — it speeds gastric emptying. Same drug, second indication, same EPS warning. 🧠 If a question offers both an emetic and an

🤮 NG-035 Emetics — the opposite drug class ⚡ NG-117 GI Stimulants — metoclopramide as a prokinetic 🧠 NG-235 Antipsychotics — EPS & tardive dyskinesia in depth 💩 NG-142 Anti-diarrheals — the other end of the GI upset ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🧠 Vomiting center + CTZ Medulla fires the reflex · CTZ tastes the blood (no BBB) 🚨 Ondansetron 5-HT3 · chemo & post-op · QT → Torsades · check K⁺ & Mg²⁺ 👄 Metoclopramide D2 · EPS : lip smacking, puffed cheeks, blinking → report · avoid in bleeding ulcer 🎢 Motion sickness H1 (meclizine, dimenhydrinate) + scopolamine patch · sedation & dry mouth

Q1: What is the priority side effect of ondansetron? Show answer QT prolongation leading to Torsades de Pointes. Check baseline QTc and correct hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia — both of which the vomiting itself causes. Q2: A child vomits during a chemo infusion. Priority nursing action? Show answer Stop the chemotherapy, flush the line, then administer ondansetron. Q3: A client on metoclopramide has lip smacking, puffing of the cheeks and blinking. What now? Show answer These are extrapyramidal symptoms / tardive d

entries.h: Antidysrhythmics II · NG-057 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🗺️ ABCD map ⬆️ Atropine ⬇️ Adenosine 🅱️ Beta blockers Nursing Field Notes / Cardiac Pharmacology · Series: Antidysrhythmics 2 of 4 Antidysrhythmics series ← 1 · The 4 classes 2 · ABCDs — atrial 3 · C & D → 4 · LAP →

The ABCD s — atrial rhythm drugs · A tropine · A denosine · B eta blockers NG-057 CARDIO PHARM ADHD-friendly visual edition Page 1 sorted the drugs by channel . This page sorts them by where in the heart they land . ABCD drugs work at the TOP of the heart — the SA node and the AV node — so they fix atrial and nodal rhythms. Two of them are opposites: atropine speeds a slow heart UP , adenosine slams a fast heart DOWN . Learn them as a pair and you can never mix them up. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive →
STEP 1 · WHERE THEY LAND One picture decides everything: is the problem at the top of the heart or the bottom?

entries.h: 🤖 Meet Sparky , your rhythm robot — she only says one thing
entries.t: 🧠 Start at the TOP and walk the alphabet down. A-B-C-D live upstairs at the SA and AV node = atrial and nodal rhythms. L-A-P lives downstairs in the ventricles (page 4) — like something sitting in your lap .

entries.h: 🫀 The heart, cut open — and the two neighborhoods these drugs work in
entries.t: 🧠 “Upstairs is a traffic problem. Downstairs is a house fire.” Upstairs rhythms mostly change the rate — you have time to give a drug. Downstairs rhythms kill the pump — you reach for electricity first.

entries.h: ⭐ Count the rate the way the NCLEX counts it
entries.t: Answer first: count the R waves in a 6-second strip and multiply by 10 . That is the whole trick. 🧠 “Count 8, add a zero.” 8 × 10 = 80 . On a bradycardia strip you will only find 4–5 R waves — that is your 40–50 .

entries.h: 🧪 The one question that sorts every rhythm on this page
entries.t: Answer first: before you pick a drug, ask too slow, or too fast? Too slow ( <60 ) with symptoms → atropine , then pacing Too fast & narrow & regular ( 150–250 ) → vagal, then adenosine Too fast & irregular (A-fib / A-flutter) → rate control : beta blocker, or a CCB (page 3) Fast + unstable (low BP, altered, chest pain) → synchronized cardioversion , not a drug Unstable means the rhythm has stopped perfusing: SBP < 90 , altered mental status, chest pain, shortness of breath, cold clammy skin. Electricity beats pharm

entries.h: 📊 The three drugs on one line
entries.t: Drug Given for What it does to the rate The #1 thing to watch Atropine anticholinergic Symptomatic bradycardia Rate goes UP ⬆ Tachycardia, urinary retention, dry mouth, confusion in older adults Adenosine AV nodal blocker SVT (stable, narrow, regular) Rate slams DOWN ⬇ — brief pause Short asystole, flushing, chest tightness, "doom" feeling — expected Beta blockers -olol HTN · SVT · sinus tach · rate control in A-fib / A-flutter Rate eases DOWN ⬇ and stays there Bradycardia + hypotension, bronchospasm, masked hypogl
STEP 2 · SPEED IT UP Puts the heart rate really HIGH — like sitting on top of a PINE tree . atro PINE .

entries.h: ⚡ How it works — it cuts the brake cable, it does not press the gas
entries.t: 🧠 “Atropine doesn't push the gas — it cuts the brake cable.” That is why every atropine side effect is just “the parasympathetic system switched off” somewhere else in the body.

entries.h: 🚨 Give it for SYMPTOMATIC bradycardia — not just a low number
entries.t: Answer first: a rate under 60 is only a problem when the client shows signs of poor perfusion . 🧠 Mental status changes — confusion, agitation, "just not acting right", dizziness 💙 Pale, dusky, cyanotic or cool clammy skin 📉 Hypotension — the classic stem reads 88/65 😮‍💨 Chest pain, dyspnea, syncope or near-syncope A sleeping marathon runner with a heart rate of 48 and a clear head does not get atropine. An athlete's resting bradycardia is normal for them. 🧠 “Treat the client, not the number.” The word symptomatic

entries.h: ✅ How it's given — and the goal
entries.t: IV push , on a continuous ECG monitor . Standard adult ACLS dosing is 1 mg IV every 3–5 minutes to a maximum of 3 mg — always confirm your facility's protocol. Goal: get back to normal sinus rhythm , 60–100 , evenly spaced, with a P wave before every QRS — and the symptoms gone . If atropine fails: transcutaneous pacing , and/or a dopamine or epinephrine infusion. Have the pacer pads on the client before you need them. Push it fast. A slow atropine push can paradoxically worsen bradycardia. Give it as a rapid bolus

entries.h: ⭐ TOP MISSED TEST QUESTION — “which strip shows the medication worked?”
entries.t: A client has a heart rate of 38 , a BP of 88/65 , and reports confusion and dizziness. Atropine is given. Which ECG strip shows the medication was effective? ▼ after atropine ▼ The correct answer is the strip with 8 R waves in 6 seconds (rate 80), evenly spaced, P before every QRS . Not the fastest strip, not the most "active-looking" strip — the normal one. ❌ A strip at 140 is not success — that's overshoot into tachycardia. ❌ A chaotic strip with no P waves is not success — that's a new dysrhythmia. ✅ Success = r

entries.h: ⚠️ Side effects — everything dries up, slows down, or blurs
entries.t: Answer first: block the parasympathetic system everywhere and you get the classic anticholinergic picture. 👁️ Can't SEE blurred vision, dilated pupils, photophobia 🚽 Can't PEE urinary retention 👄 Can't SPIT dry mouth 💩 Can't POOP constipation, ↓ bowel sounds 🥵 Can't SWEAT hot, flushed, dry skin — overheating risk 🧠 Confusion especially in older adults Use caution in: narrow-angle glaucoma , BPH / urinary retention, and myasthenia gravis . 🧠 “Blind as a bat, dry as a bone, red as a beet, mad as a hatter, hot as a ha

Answer first: atropine works at the AV node . If the block is below the node, there is nothing for it to unblock. Mobitz II second-degree block and third-degree (complete) heart block with a wide QRS — atropine is unlikely to help and pacing is the answer. Hypoxia-driven bradycardia — fix the airway and oxygen first. A bradycardic hypoxic client needs oxygen , not a rate drug. Bradycardia in a child is almost always hypoxia until proven otherwise — oxygenate and ventilate before you reach for any drug. 🧠 “Wide and
STEP 3 · SLAM IT DOWN DE creases the heart rate — like sending the fox DE N-wards, D ownstairs. Full drug page: NG-094 .

entries.h: 🚨 Know how this rhythm looks — Super Fast = SVT
entries.t: Reading it: narrow QRS (the signal came from above the ventricles) · regular · 150–250 bpm · you cannot find a P wave because it is buried in the previous T wave. Causes: stimulants (caffeine, energy drinks, decongestants, cocaine), strenuous exercise, hypoxia , fever, anxiety, underlying heart disease. Feels like: sudden pounding palpitations that start and stop abruptly, chest flutter, lightheadedness, anxiety. 🧠 “SVT = Super Very Turbo.” S uper F ast = S upraventricular. Narrow and fast and regular — one look an

entries.h: ✅ The order of operations for stable SVT
entries.t: 1 Is the client STABLE? Check BP, level of consciousness, chest pain, skin. Unstable → synchronized cardioversion, immediately. ▼ 2 Vagal maneuvers first. Have the client bear down like they're having a bowel movement (Valsalva), or apply ice-cold stimulation to the face. Free, fast, and it works often enough to try. ▼ 3 Adenosine — rapid IV push with an immediate flush. Standard adult dosing is 6 mg rapid IV push, then 12 mg if it does not convert — always confirm your facility's protocol. ▼ 4 Still in SVT → a bet

entries.h: ⭐ THE two key points — this is what gets tested
entries.t: 🧠 “FAST in, FLUSH after, ARM up.” 1–2 second push · 20 mL saline chaser · elevate. Skip any one of the three and the drug never reaches the AV node.

entries.h: 🚨 Warn the client FIRST — the heart is supposed to stop for a moment
entries.t: Answer first: a brief pause / asystole on the monitor after the push is expected, not an emergency . It is the AV node rebooting. 😳 Flushing — a hot, red wave over the face and chest 🫁 Chest tightness or pressure, shortness of breath 😨 A "feeling of impending doom" — clients describe it as terrifying ⏱️ It all passes in seconds because the half-life is that short What you say beforehand: "This medicine works in about ten seconds. You may feel flushed, a heavy squeeze in your chest, and like something is very wrong.
STEP 4 · THE BRAKES Names end in -olol . Full drug page: NG-176 · they are Vaughan-Williams Class II (see NG-019 ).

entries.h: 🎯 Two receptors, two very different consequences
entries.t: 🧠 “β₁ = ONE heart · β₂ = TWO lungs.” Cardioselective drugs ( metoprolol, atenolol, esmolol — the ones starting A – M ) mostly spare β₂; propranolol hits both. Selectivity is lost at higher doses, so asthma is still a caution.

entries.h: 🚨 The 4 B's — memorize these as the side-effect list
entries.t: B — Bradycardia (HR below 60 ) and low BP B — Bronchospasm — avoid in asthma and COPD B — Blood glucose masking — the drug hides the tachycardia, tremor and palpitations of hypoglycemia. Diaphoresis is the warning sign that survives. B — Bad for clients in decompensated / end-stage heart failure (it is negative inotropic; it is started only when the client is compensated and stable) Plus: orthostatic hypotension — dizziness on standing. Teach slow position changes : lie → sit → dangle the legs → stand. 🧠 “-LOL lowe

entries.h: ⭐ COMMON QUESTION — “what drug caused this rhythm?”
entries.t: 5 R waves in 6 seconds × 10 = a rate of 50. Regular, P before every QRS, narrow — this is sinus bradycardia , not a block and not a new dysrhythmia. Answer: a beta blocker (the classic stem names propranolol ). Digoxin and calcium channel blockers can do the same thing — see page 3 . 🧠 Slow + regular + P waves present + a drug on the MAR ending in -olol = you found your culprit.

entries.h: ✅ Before you give it, and what you teach
entries.t: Before EVERY dose: Apical pulse for a full 60 seconds + blood pressure Common hold parameters: HR < 60 or SBP < 90 — always follow the provider's written parameters Hold and notify the provider rather than skipping silently Listen to lung sounds if the client has any airway history What the client must hear: Never stop a beta blocker abruptly — rebound tachycardia, hypertension, angina and even MI Take your own pulse daily and record it; report a rate under 60 Change position slowly — sit on the edge of the bed bef

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🌲 atroPINE = up a PINE Symptomatic bradycardia. Goal = NSR 60–100 , evenly spaced, P before every QRS. 🦊 adenosine → the DEN SVT. 1–2 second IV push + 20 mL flush + elevate. A pause is expected. 💊 -LOL = the 4 B's B radycardia · B ronchospasm · B lood sugar masking · B ad in heart failure. 🔢 6-second × 10 8 R waves = 80 . 5 R waves = 50 . 4 R waves = 40 .

Q1: What does the ABCD mnemonic tell you about where these drugs work? Show answer They work at the TOP of the heart — the SA node and AV node — so they treat atrial and nodal rhythms: sinus brady, sinus tach, SVT, A-fib and A-flutter. LAP drugs (page 4) work at the bottom, in the ventricles. Q2: A client has a heart rate of 46 and is asleep, alert when woken, BP 118/72. Does she get atropine? Show answer No. Atropine is for symptomatic bradycardia — hypotension, altered mental status, chest pain, dyspnea, pale/dus
