entries.h: Quick Overview — Abdominal Assessment · NG-046 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🗺️ Map 👂 Technique 🔗 Apply it ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / GI · Master Reference & Assessment Course

Quick Overview — the master quadrant map for the whole GI batch NG-046 GI · Assessment ADHD-friendly visual edition This page is your reference map — the 4 abdominal quadrants , the one rule that's backwards from every other assessment (auscultate BEFORE palpate), and where the pain shows up for the diseases in this batch. Learn this page once, apply it to every GI diagnosis you study. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🗺️ 4 quadrants RUQ · LUQ · RLQ · LLQ — split at the umbilicus. 👂 Listen BEFORE you tou
STEP 1 · THE 4 QUADRANTS Draw a cross through the umbilicus — everything the exam asks about lives in one of these four boxes.

entries.h: 🧭 The abdomen, divided into 4 quadrants (RUQ / LUQ / RLQ / LLQ)
entries.t: 🟦 RUQ = liver/gallbladder 🟩 LUQ = stomach/spleen/pancreas 🩷 RLQ = appendix 🟨 LLQ = sigmoid colon 🧠 “RUQ, LUQ on top — RLQ, LLQ down below.” Right is always the patient's right, not yours — stand at the bedside and mirror it in your head.
R/L = patient's Right / Left U = Upper (above umbilicus) L = Lower (below umbilicus) Q = Quadrant 🧠 Always the patient's right/left , never the observer's — a classic first-semester trap.

🫃 Contour: flat, rounded, scaphoid (sunken), or distended ⚖️ Symmetry: should be symmetric side to side 🩹 Skin: no lesions, striae are common/benign, no bulging at umbilicus (hernia) 💓 No visible pulsations (except faint epigastric aortic pulsation is normal in thin clients) 🧠 Look before you touch — a visibly distended, rigid, or asymmetric abdomen changes your whole plan before you even auscultate. 👂
STEP 2 · THE ORDER IS BACKWARDS Every other body system: inspect → palpate → percuss → auscultate. The abdomen breaks that rule on purpose.

1 👀 Inspect — contour, symmetry, skin, pulsations 2 👂 Auscultate — bowel sounds in all 4 quadrants 3 🥁 Percuss — tympany (gas) vs dullness (fluid/organ) 4 🤲 Palpate — light first, then deep, tender areas LAST Why? Percussion and palpation can stimulate or falsely change bowel motility/sounds — so you must listen first to get an accurate baseline. 🧠 “Look, Listen, Tap, Touch.” Every other system is Inspect-Palpate-Percuss-Auscultate — the abdomen swaps the last two to the front: I-A-P-P .

entries.h: 👂 Bowel sounds — how to actually listen
entries.t: 📈 Hyperactive ("borborygmi") — early obstruction, gastroenteritis, diarrhea 📉 Hypoactive — post-op ileus, peritonitis, opioids 🚫 Absent — must listen 5 full minutes per quadrant before documenting "absent"; late obstruction, paralytic ileus, peritonitis = emergency 🧠 “Silence is not nothing — silence is an emergency.” Never chart "absent bowel sounds" after a quick listen.

entries.h: 🤲 Palpation — light, then deep, painful area LAST
entries.t: ✅ Start away from the painful area ✅ Light palpation first (~1 cm), then deep (~5–8 cm) 🚨 Guarding, rigidity, rebound tenderness = peritoneal signs → stop, this is an emergency finding 🧠 If a stem describes a rigid, board-like abdomen with rebound tenderness, fever, and rising pain — think peritonitis , report to the HCP immediately, don't keep palpating. 🔗
STEP 3 · WHERE EACH DISEASE LIVES Same 4-box map, now with the special signs and diagnoses from this batch pinned onto it.

entries.h: 📍 Special signs by location — the batch cheat-sheet
entries.t: 🧠 One map, four diseases. Every time you learn a new GI diagnosis this batch, come back and pin it on this same quadrant map — the location IS the clue. Quadrant / point Special sign Condition RUQ Murphy's sign — pain & inspiratory pause on deep RUQ palpation Cholecystitis (gallbladder) LUQ / Epigastric Pain boring straight through to the back Pancreatitis RLQ McBurney's point — 1/3 way from iliac crest to umbilicus; + Rovsing's sign Appendicitis LLQ Constant, localized aching pain, fever, ↑WBC Diverticulitis Periu

🪵 Rigid, board-like abdomen 🤲 Rebound tenderness 🌡️ Fever > 100.3°F 📈 Increasing, worsening pain 💓 Tachycardia / tachypnea + restlessness 🧠 This exact red-flag cluster = peritonitis — you'll see it repeat across GERD, pancreatitis, appendicitis, and diverticulitis pages. Learn it once here.

Chart: contour → symmetry → bowel sounds (present/hyper/hypo/absent, which quadrants) → tenderness/guarding location → masses/pulsations. 🧠 “Look, Listen, Tap, Touch — then write it down in that order.” Matching your documentation order to your exam order keeps you from skipping steps. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🗺️ 4 quadrants RUQ · LUQ · RLQ · LLQ around the umbilicus 👂 Auscultate before palpate the one backwards order in nursing assessment ⏱️ 1 min/quadrant, 5 min to call "absent" don't rush bowel sounds 📍 Location = diagnosis RLQ appendix · RUQ gallbladder · LUQ pancreas · LLQ sigmoid

Q1: What is the correct order of abdominal assessment, and why does it differ from other systems? Show answer Inspect → Auscultate → Percuss → Palpate. Auscultation comes before palpation because percussion/palpation can alter bowel motility and change the sounds you hear. Q2: How long should you listen before charting "absent" bowel sounds? Show answer A full 5 minutes per quadrant — don't document "absent" after a quick listen. Q3: A client has pain and an inspiratory pause when you press deep under the right cos
🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics ⚙️ Action ⚠️ Watch For 🎓 Teach ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / GI Pharmacology · Motility Drugs

Antiflatulents — Simethicone & Activated Charcoal NG-099 GI · Pharmacology ADHD-friendly visual edition Antiflatulents don't stop gas from forming — they change how it leaves. Simethicone is a mechanical, defoaming agent that merges tiny gas bubbles into bigger ones so they're easier to belch or pass. It is not absorbed systemically and has essentially no adverse reactions, making it one of the safest drugs in the entire GI class. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 💨 Mechanical, not chemical Defoams gas b
STEP 1 · POP THE BUBBLES Two very different mechanisms share a shelf: one defoams gas, the other adsorbs it (and other things).

entries.h: ⚙️ Mechanism: reduce flatus via natural expulsion
entries.t: Antiflatulents work by reducing flatus in the GI tract via expulsion — belching or passing gas. Simethicone is a defoaming agent that disperses and prevents the formation of gas pockets: it merges many tiny trapped bubbles into fewer, larger bubbles that the gut can move and expel normally. 🧠 "Simethicone pops the foam." Think of shaking a soda bottle — lots of tiny bubbles = pressure and pain. Simethicone is the swirl that turns foam into a few big bubbles that escape easily.

Field Charcoal Simethicone Trade Charcocaps, Flatulex Gas-X, Mylicon, Maalox, Mylanta Use Intestinal gas, diarrhea; poisoning antidote Postop distention, dyspepsia, IBS, peptic ulcer Dose 520 mg PO after meals 40–125 mg QID after meals & at bedtime 🧠 Charcoal = "chars" toxins; Simethicone = "pops" bubbles. Different mechanisms, same shelf.

Postop gas distention & air swallowing Dyspepsia Peptic ulcer Irritable bowel syndrome Diverticulosis Charcoal only: prevents pruritus with kidney dialysis; poisoning antidote ⚠️ caution use 🧠 "PIP-D + D" — P ostop distention, I BS, P eptic ulcer, D yspepsia, D iverticulosis. ⚠️
STEP 2 · KNOW THE RISKS This is the safest class you'll study all semester — but "safe" is still an exam trap.

No adverse reactions have been reported for simethicone. The only listed contraindication is known hypersensitivity . That makes this class an outlier compared to almost every other GI drug you'll study — most others have a whole list of things to watch for. 🧠 Exam trap: "no adverse reactions have been reported" does NOT mean zero contraindications — hypersensitivity still applies, and it's still a drug that needs monitoring for effectiveness.

Can decrease the effectiveness of other drugs — its adsorbent/defoaming action can interfere with absorption Space administration apart from other oral medications when possible Pregnancy category C — use cautiously 🧠 "Charcoal binds more than gas." Activated charcoal is well known for adsorbing other drugs onto its surface — that's exactly why it's also used as a poisoning antidote.

entries.h: 🧠 NCLEX trap: it does NOT prevent gas
entries.t: Explain to the patient that this medication does not prevent the formation of gas — it only helps expel gas that has already formed. Diet and exercise are what actually prevent it. 🧠 "Pops it, doesn't stop it." Simethicone treats the gas that's already there. 🎓
STEP 3 · TIMING & TECHNIQUE Administration timing is the whole nursing management picture for this drug class.

1 🔎 Assess before & periodically during therapy — abdominal pain, distention, bowel sounds, frequency of belching/flatus 2 ⏰ Give after meals and at bedtime for best results 3 🧴 Shake liquid preparations well before giving 4 🍬 Chew tablets thoroughly for faster, more complete results 5 💧 Drops: mix with 30 mL cool water, infant formula, or other liquid as directed — shake well 6 📞 Notify HCP if symptoms are persistent 🧠 "After you eat, before you sleep." That's the whole administration schedule in one line.

Beyond gas relief, charcoal can be used to prevent pruritus associated with kidney dialysis , and as an antidote in poisoning — a very different job from simethicone's mechanical defoaming. 🧠 "Charcoal wears two hats" — GI comfort drug on one shelf, poison antidote in the ED on the other.
⏰ After meals + bedtime 🧴 Shake liquids well first 🍬 Chew tabs fully 🚶 Diet + exercise actual prevention 📞 Report persistent symptoms ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 💨 Defoaming agent merges gas bubbles, doesn't chemically neutralize acid ✅ Essentially no adverse effects the safest GI drug class you'll study ⏰ After meals + bedtime the whole dosing schedule ⚠️ Doesn't prevent gas diet/exercise are prevention; this treats what's already there

Q1: Name one key clue that simethicone is mechanical, not chemical. Show answer It's a defoaming agent that disperses gas pockets and merges bubbles — it is not absorbed and doesn't neutralize acid. Q2: Name one priority nursing assessment before and during therapy. Show answer Assess abdominal pain, distention, and bowel sounds; track frequency of belching and passage of flatus. Q3: Name one teaching point patients often get wrong. Show answer This medication does not prevent gas formation — it only helps expel ga

entries.h: Crohn's & UC — Treatments & Complications · NG-111 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🚨 Complications 💊 Pharmacology 🩺 Care ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / GI · Pathophysiology Course

Treatments & Complications — the companion to NG-030 (Patho, Signs, Causes) NG-111 GI ADHD-friendly visual edition Both are Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD) . This page picks up where NG-030 left off: what goes wrong when it's not controlled , the drugs that control it , and the nursing care that keeps a flare from becoming an emergency. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🕳️ Crohn's tunnels Fistulas, strictures, abscesses — transmural damage. 🎈 UC balloons Toxic megacolon → rupture → peritonitis. 🔪 Surger
STEP 1 · WHAT GOES WRONG Crohn's digs tunnels through the wall. UC balloons the colon out. Both roads can end in peritonitis.

entries.h: ⚖️ Crohn's vs UC — the complication & cure table
entries.t: 👑 Crohn's 🩸 UC Location 📍 Mouth to anus , skip lesions, mainly small intestine Colon & rectum only , continuous Depth 🔬 Transmural — through every layer Mucosal — surface layer only Signature complication Fistulas, strictures, abscesses, obstruction Toxic megacolon , severe bleeding Cancer risk Increased, but lower than UC Higher colon cancer risk with long-standing disease Surgical cure? 🔪 NOT curative — disease can recur anywhere in the GI tract Colectomy IS curative — removing the colon removes the disease 🧠 "Yo

Deep, transmural inflammation burrows all the way through the bowel wall, creating: 🕳️ Fistulas — abnormal tunnels connecting bowel to bladder, vagina, skin, or other bowel loops 🪢 Strictures — scarred, narrowed segments → obstruction 🫙 Abscesses — pockets of infection 🧠 Deep = damage that lasts. Transmural inflammation means Crohn's leaves permanent structural changes — strictures and fistulas don't heal shut on their own.

entries.h: 🎈 UC: the colon balloons — toxic megacolon
entries.t: Toxic megacolon — severe inflammation paralyzes colon motility, the colon distends massively , and the wall can rupture , spilling bowel contents and causing peritonitis — a deadly infection of the peritoneal cavity. 🧠 Toxic megacolon = UC's emergency. Fistulas/strictures are Crohn's signature; toxic megacolon → rupture → peritonitis is UC's.

entries.h: 🚨 Peritonitis red flags — Report to HCP
entries.t: 🌡️ Fever over 100.3°F 🤲 Rebound tenderness 🪵 Rigid abdomen "board-like" 📈 Increasing pain & tenderness 😰 Restless 💓 Fast HR & RR tachycardia/tachypnea 🧠 Same 6 red flags, every abdominal-emergency page in this course (appendicitis, diverticulitis, IBD) — memorize this list once, apply it everywhere. 💊
STEP 2 · CLIMB THE LADDER Treatment steps up in intensity as disease gets harder to control — cheapest/safest drugs first.

1 🧴 Aminosalicylates (5-ASA): Sulfasalazine — "STOPS the body attacking itself" — first-line, especially for UC 2 🔥 Corticosteroids: Prednisone — "soothes the swelling" — induces remission fast, not for long-term use 3 🧬 Immunomodulators: azathioprine, 6-mercaptopurine — maintain remission 4 🎯 Biologics (anti-TNF): infliximab, adalimumab — for moderate–severe disease; screen for TB/infection first 5 🔪 Surgery — for complications or disease that won't respond 🧠 "Soothe, then Stop, then Suppress, then Surgery." Stero

Drug Memory clue Loperamide (Imodium) "LOW bowel movements" Dicyclomine "Dry Cycle" — antispasmodic, dries up cramping/spasm 🧠 Caution: antidiarrheals can be risky during a severe flare — slowing the bowel can contribute to toxic megacolon. Give as prescribed and monitor closely.

Most clients get a colostomy or ileostomy after a bowel resection , where the diseased segment of bowel is removed. 🧠 Surgery in Crohn's treats the complication in front of you (a stricture, fistula, abscess) — it does not remove the disease. 🩺
STEP 3 · SUPPORT THE WHOLE PERSON Fluid & electrolytes, nutrition, and psychosocial support — the day-to-day nursing that keeps a flare from becoming an emergency.

📋 Strict I&O monitoring — closely, every shift 💧 Encourage fluids — roughly 2 L /day, more with diarrhea to prevent dehydration 🧪 Hypokalemia — K⁺ 3.5 mEq/L or less — from ongoing diarrhea, monitor for weakness & dysrhythmias 💊 Daily multivitamin containing calcium — malabsorption + steroid use raise osteoporosis risk Low K⁺ 3.5 mEq/L Normal 5.0 High K⁺ 🧠 Diarrhea drains potassium. Any IBD client with active diarrhea is a hypokalemia risk until proven otherwise — check the K⁺.

🥩 High protein & high calorie — healing & malabsorption needs 🥣 Low fiber during flares — rest the irritated bowel 🍽️ Small, frequent meals 📓 Keep a food journal to spot personal triggers ❌ Avoid alcohol; reduce caffeine (coffee, tea) — both irritate the gut 🧠 "High protein, low fiber, small & often." Feed the healing, rest the lining.

💊 Give analgesics as prescribed for pain 🧠 Encourage clients to discuss feelings — chronic disease, body image with an ostomy 😌 Stress reduction — stress is a known flare trigger (see NG-030) 🧠 IBD is chronic and relapsing — psychosocial support is not optional extra care, it's core to preventing the next flare.

entries.h: 📝 NCLEX SATA practice — client with UC, select all interventions
entries.t: Which of the following belong in the plan of care? (Select all that apply.) ✅ Discuss plans to decrease stress ✅ Encourage fluids, roughly 2 L/day, more with diarrhea ✅ Monitor for K⁺ 3.5 mEq/L or less (hypokalemia) ✅ Administer analgesics for pain ✅ Avoid alcohol; reduce caffeine 🧠 SATA questions on IBD almost always bundle: stress reduction + fluids + K⁺ monitoring + analgesics + avoid alcohol/caffeine — learn this cluster as one unit. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🕳️ Crohn's Fistulas, strictures, abscesses — surgery NOT curative. 🎈 UC Toxic megacolon → rupture. Colectomy IS curative. 💊 5-ASA → steroid → biologic → surgery the treatment ladder. 🚨 Fever + rigid + rebound = peritonitis, report to HCP.

Q1: Which disease is cured by a colectomy, and why? Show answer Ulcerative colitis — disease is confined to the colon, so removing the colon removes the disease. Crohn's can recur anywhere in the GI tract, so surgery is not curative. Q2: Name Crohn's signature complications versus UC's signature complication. Show answer Crohn's: fistulas, strictures, abscesses (transmural damage). UC: toxic megacolon (can rupture → peritonitis). Q3: What's the first-line drug class for IBD, and its memory clue? Show answer Aminosa

entries.h: GI Stimulants · NG-117 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics ⚙️ Action ⚠️ Watch For 🎓 Teach ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / GI Pharmacology · Motility Drugs

Prokinetic Agents — Metoclopramide (Reglan) NG-117 GI · Pharmacology ADHD-friendly visual edition Prokinetics speed the stomach up. Metoclopramide increases upper GI motility without increasing acid secretion — food (and the nausea) moves out faster. The trade-off: it crosses into the brain and blocks dopamine there too, which can trigger EPS and, with long-term use, irreversible tardive dyskinesia . 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🚀 Prokinetic, not an acid drug Speeds gastric emptying — it does not lo
STEP 1 · SPEED IT UP One receptor explains the whole drug — block dopamine in the gut and brain, and everything else follows.

entries.h: ⚙️ Mechanism: sensitizes the gut to acetylcholine
entries.t: Increases motility of the upper GI tract without increasing secretions. By sensitizing GI smooth muscle to the effects of acetylcholine, it increases the tone and amplitude of gastric contractions — resulting in faster emptying of gastric contents into the small intestine. It also blocks dopamine receptors in the brain's vomiting center, giving it an antiemetic effect on top of the prokinetic one. 🧠 "Re-GLAN-ce forward." Pro kinetic = PRO (forward) + KINETIC (movement) — Reglan pushes gastric contents forward into

Field Detail Generic Metoclopramide Trade Reglan Use GERD, diabetic gastroparesis, prevention of chemo- and postop-related N/V Dose 10–15 mg PO; 10–20 mg IM/IV 🧠 "REGLAN = Re-GLANd the gut." One drug card, one job: get the stomach moving again.

GERD — speeds emptying so less sits around to reflux Diabetic gastroparesis — delayed emptying from autonomic neuropathy Chemo-induced N/V — blocks CTZ dopamine receptors Immediate postoperative period — postop ileus / N&V 🧠 "GDC-P" — G ERD, D iabetic gastroparesis, C hemo N/V, P ostop. Four reasons, one prokinetic. ⚠️
STEP 2 · KNOW THE RISKS Block dopamine in two places — one calms the vomiting center, the other can move on its own for the rest of the patient's life.

entries.h: 🚨 EPS → Tardive Dyskinesia — the never-forget adverse effect
entries.t: Higher doses or prolonged administration can produce CNS symptoms: restlessness, drowsiness, dizziness , and extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS) — tremor, involuntary limb movements, muscle rigidity, facial grimacing, and depression. Tardive dyskinesia — nonreversible, involuntary muscle spasms typically linked to conventional antipsychotics — is known to occur with long-term use (12 weeks or more) of metoclopramide. Report EPS immediately — do not wait to see if it resolves , because catching it early is what prevents p

Hypersensitivity to the drug GI obstruction, gastric perforation, or hemorrhage — never push a prokinetic against a blocked or torn gut Pheochromocytoma Parkinson's disease or a seizure disorder if also taking other drugs that cause EPS 🧠 "Don't push against a wall." If the gut is obstructed or perforated, forcing motility just adds pressure to a broken pipe.
🧠 One blockade, two outcomes. Wanted dopamine block = no vomiting. Unwanted dopamine block = EPS.

With… Effect Cholinergic blockers / opioids ↓ effectiveness of metoclopramide Cimetidine ↓ absorption of cimetidine Digoxin ↓ absorption of digoxin MAOIs ↑ risk of hypertensive episode Levodopa ↓ effectiveness of both drugs 🧠 Reglan vs. Levodopa: a tug-of-war over dopamine. Reglan blocks the dopamine receptor; levodopa is trying to feed it dopamine. They cancel each other out.

Diabetes and cardiovascular disease Pregnancy and lactation — excreted in breast milk 🧠 NCLEX trap: rapid IV infusion can cause sudden restlessness/anxiety (akathisia) that gets mistaken for the patient's baseline anxiety — it's actually an EPS symptom. 🎓
STEP 3 · SAFE ADMINISTRATION Timing, rate, and what to tell them before they leave with a script.

1 🍽️ Give on an empty stomach 2 💧 IV: monitor infusion rate frequently — too rapid an infusion may induce cardiac arrhythmias 3 🥛 Chew tablets thoroughly , follow with a full glass of water or milk 4 📋 Track bowel movements — can cause constipation OR diarrhea 5 🚱 Watch for dehydration — poor skin turgor, dry mucous membranes, decreased/absent urine output, concentrated urine, restlessness, irritability, ↑RR, confusion 🧠 "Empty in, slow in." Empty stomach for absorption, slow IV rate for the heart.

Magnesium-containing antacids can produce a laxative effect and cause diarrhea. Aluminum- or calcium-containing antacids can cause constipation . Do not use maximum OTC antacid dose > 2 weeks without provider supervision — overuse can cause the stomach to secrete excess acid. 🧠 "Mag = go, Al/Ca = whoa." Magnesium moves things; aluminum/calcium slow things down.
🍽️ Empty stomach before dosing 🥛 Chew + fluids full glass 📋 Track BMs const. or diarrhea 🚨 Report EPS don't wait 💧 Watch fluids dehydration signs ⛔ No GI obstruction never rule ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🚀 Prokinetic = speeds gastric emptying, not an acid drug 🧠 Dopamine blocker = EPS risk, same family as antipsychotics 🍽️ Empty stomach = how you give it 🚨 12+ weeks = tardive dyskinesia risk, report EPS now

Q1: Name one key clue that metoclopramide is a prokinetic, not an acid reducer? Show answer It increases motility of the upper GI tract and increases the tone/amplitude of gastric contractions — it does not lower stomach acid. Q2: Name one priority nursing action with IV metoclopramide. Show answer Monitor the infusion rate frequently — too rapid an infusion may induce cardiac arrhythmias. Q3: Name one teaching point about EPS. Show answer Report any tremor, facial grimacing, rigidity, or involuntary movement immed

entries.h: Histamine H2 Antagonists · NG-119 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🚫 What it does ⚠️ Watch for 🗣️ Teach ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / GI · Pharmacology Course · Acid-Reducer Family 2 of 4

Histamine H2 Blockers — Acid Reducers NG-119 GI · Pharmacology ADHD-friendly visual edition H2 blockers reversibly block histamine at the H2 receptor on the parietal cell — less potent than a PPI but faster to kick in and generally a safer long-term profile . Pairs with PPIs (NG-140) , the master cheat-sheet on Acid Prevention (NG-233) , and Mucosal Protectants (NG-254) . 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🚫 Reversible receptor block Sits on the H2 receptor — doesn't destroy the pump. 🔤 “-tidine” = H2 blo
STEP 1 · BLOCK THE RECEPTOR One receptor, one competitive blocker — histamine can't dock, so the pump never gets the "turn on" signal.

entries.h: 🔑 Mechanism — histamine can't find its lock
entries.t: EXAM TIP H2 antagonists reduce gastric acid secretion by inhibiting the action of histamine at H2 receptor cells on the parietal cell. Unlike a PPI, this is a reversible , competitive block — one receptor, not the whole downstream pump. 🧠 “Parking spot, not a wrecking ball.” An H2 blocker just occupies the parking spot (the H2 receptor) so histamine can't pull in — it doesn't destroy the pump itself, which is why the effect wears off faster and is weaker than a PPI.

Generic Trade Used for Typical adult dose* cimetidine Tagamet Gastric/duodenal ulcers, GERD, hypersecretory conditions, GI bleeding, heartburn 800–1600 mg/day PO; 300 mg q6h IM/IV famotidine Pepcid Same indications as cimetidine 20–40 mg PO or IV if unable to take PO ranitidine Zantac (historical) Same indications as cimetidine 150–600 mg/day PO; 50 mg q6–8h IM/IV, max 400 mg/day *Verify against current facility policy and prescriber order. Note: ranitidine (Zantac) products were withdrawn from the U.S. market in 2
🔥 Heartburn, acid indigestion, sour stomach — frequently OTC 🚪 GERD 🦠 Gastric or duodenal ulcer 🌋 Gastric hypersecretory conditions (excess HCl secretion)

entries.h: ⚡ H2 blocker vs. PPI — onset & strength
entries.t: H2 blocker PPI Mechanism Reversible receptor block Irreversible pump block Potency Lower Higher Onset Faster Slower to peak 🧠 Full comparison lives on NG-233 Acid Prevention — this is the quick preview. ⚠️
STEP 2 · SAFETY Cimetidine is the interaction-prone troublemaker of this family — know it by name.

💫 Dizziness, somnolence 🤕 Headache 🌀 Confusion, hallucinations — especially older adults 💩 Diarrhea 🚻 Reversible impotence (cimetidine specifically — antiandrogenic effect) 🧠 “Confused Grandpa on Tagamet.” Cimetidine in an older adult = watch for confusion/CNS changes before anything else.

🚫 Hypersensitivity 🩺 Renal or hepatic impairment — use cautiously 👴 Severely ill, older, or debilitated patients 🍬 Cimetidine — use cautiously in patients with diabetes 🤰 Pregnancy category B — cimetidine, famotidine, ranitidine; category C — nizatidine

entries.h: 🔀 Drug interactions — cimetidine is the big one
entries.t: Interacts with What happens Antacids, metoclopramide Decreased absorption of the H2 antagonist Carmustine Decreased white blood cell count Opioid analgesics Increased risk of respiratory depression Oral anticoagulants Increased risk of bleeding Digoxin May decrease serum digoxin levels Extra caution with cimetidine: it is a potent inhibitor of hepatic CYP450 enzymes, so it can raise blood levels of many other drugs cleared through the liver — one more reason famotidine is preferred when a choice is available. 🧠 “Ci
STEP 3 · PATIENT & NURSING TEACHING Same spacing rules as every acid drug — plus know that OTC availability changes the teaching conversation.

Lower-dose H2 blockers (e.g., famotidine 10–20 mg ) are sold over the counter for occasional heartburn. Teach patients that OTC use is for short-term, occasional symptoms — persistent or worsening heartburn needs a provider evaluation, not just a bigger OTC dose.
Because an antacid can interfere with absorption of other oral drugs, give any other oral medication — including an H2 blocker — 1–2 hours apart from an antacid dose.

1 ⏱️ IV push/infusion: monitor rate closely — too rapid an infusion may induce cardiac arrhythmias 2 📋 Track bowel movements — may cause constipation or diarrhea 3 💧 Watch for dehydration — poor skin turgor, dry mucous membranes, decreased urine output, restlessness, confusion 4 🥛 Chew tablets thoroughly , then drink a full glass of water or milk 5 👴 Older adults: reassess mental status after starting — cimetidine especially

entries.h: 🔗 See it in context — the acid-reducer family
entries.t: H2 blockers sit in the middle of the potency ladder: stronger and longer-lasting than an antacid, weaker than a PPI, and — unlike sucralfate — they actually reduce acid rather than just coating the ulcer. ⛽ NG-140 PPIs — irreversible, most potent 📊 NG-233 Acid Prevention — master comparison table 🛡️ NG-254 Mucosal Protectant — barrier, not a suppressor ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🚫 Reversible block H2 receptor, not the whole pump 🔤 -tidine Cimetidine, famotidine, ranitidine ⚡ Faster, weaker than a PPI — middle of the potency ladder 🧠 Cimetidine = confusion in elderly + CYP450 interactions

Q1: How does an H2 blocker reduce acid, and how is that different from a PPI? Show answer It reversibly blocks histamine at the H2 receptor on the parietal cell so the pump never gets the "turn on" signal — a PPI instead irreversibly disables the pump itself, which is why PPIs are stronger. Q2: What suffix identifies this drug class? Show answer -tidine — cimetidine, famotidine, ranitidine. Q3: Which H2 blocker carries the most drug-interaction risk, and why? Show answer Cimetidine — it's a potent CYP450 inhibitor

entries.h: Proton Pump Inhibitors · NG-140 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics ⛽ What it does ⚠️ Watch for 🗣️ Teach ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / GI · Pharmacology Course · Acid-Reducer Family 1 of 4

Acid Reducers — the strongest acid blockers in the class NG-140 GI · Pharmacology ADHD-friendly visual edition PPIs irreversibly shut off the final step of acid production — the proton pump itself — making them the most potent acid suppressors nursing students will see. Compare with H2 blockers (NG-119) , the master cheat-sheet on Acid Prevention (NG-233) , and Mucosal Protectants (NG-254) . 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → ⛽ Irreversible pump block Strongest acid suppression of any class — the pump has
STEP 1 · CAP THE PUMP One enzyme system explains the whole drug class — cap the pump, and acid production stops at the source.

entries.h: 🌋 Mechanism — a cap on the volcano
entries.t: EXAM TIP PPIs suppress gastric acid secretion by irreversibly inhibiting the H⁺/K⁺-ATPase (proton pump) enzyme system of the gastric parietal cells — the final common step in acid production, no matter what triggered it (histamine, gastrin, or acetylcholine). 🧠 “Cap the volcano.” It doesn't matter which trigger lit the fuse — histamine, gastrin, or acetylcholine — a PPI caps the one shared pump at the very end of the line. That's why PPIs out-suppress every other acid drug class.

Generic Trade Used for Typical adult dose* esomeprazole Nexium Erosive esophagitis, GERD, H. pylori eradication, NSAID-associated gastric ulcers 20–40 mg/day PO omeprazole Prilosec Same as above + hypersecretory conditions, heartburn, ↓ risk of upper GI bleed 20–60 mg/day PO pantoprazole Protonix GERD, erosive esophagitis, hypersecretory conditions 40 mg/day PO/IV hypersecretion: 80 mg IV q12h lansoprazole Prevacid Same as esomeprazole + cystic fibrosis-related malabsorption 15–30 mg/day PO *Verify against current

🚪 GERD & erosive esophagitis 🦠 Gastric & duodenal ulcers tied to H. pylori infection 🌋 Pathologic hypersecretory conditions (e.g., Zollinger-Ellison syndrome) 🩸 Prevention of GI bleeding in high-risk patients on antiplatelet drugs 🏥 Stress-ulcer prophylaxis in hospitalized/surgical patients

⛽ PPI (omeprazole or lansoprazole) 💊 Anti-infective #1 — amoxicillin 💊 Anti-infective #2 — clarithromycin 🧠 “1 pump + 2 antibiotics = triple play.” The PPI isn't treating the infection — it's dropping the acid so the antibiotics can do their job and the ulcer can heal. ⚠️
STEP 2 · SAFETY Common effects are mild — the ones that matter are the ones that build up over months of use.
🤕 Headache 🤢 Nausea 💩 Diarrhea 🌀 Abdominal pain 🧠 Mild & common — not the exam trap. The trap is the long-term list next door.

entries.h: 🚨 Long-term use = the exam trap quartet
entries.t: 🧠 “Bone, Bug, B12, Bounce.” Long-term PPI use can fracture a Bone , invite a Bug (C. diff), starve out B12 , and cause acid to Bounce back hard if stopped cold-turkey.

🚫 Hypersensitivity to the drug class 👴 Older adults, hepatic impairment — use cautiously 🤰 Omeprazole = pregnancy category C ; lansoprazole, rabeprazole, pantoprazole = category B (contraindicated in pregnancy/lactation per source material — verify current labeling)

Interacts with What happens Sucralfate Decreased absorption of the PPI Ketoconazole, ampicillin Decreased absorption of the anti-infective Oral anticoagulants Increased risk of bleeding Digoxin Increased absorption of digoxin Benzodiazepines, phenytoin Risk for toxic antiseizure/sedative drug levels Clarithromycin (with omeprazole) Increased plasma levels of both drugs Bisphosphonates Increased fracture risk 🗣️
STEP 3 · PATIENT & NURSING TEACHING Timing makes the drug work — safety monitoring makes the drug work safely long-term.
🧠 Right place, right time. The pump has to be actively pumping for the PPI to bind it — take it too late (after eating) and fewer pumps are caught.

Do not crush or chew enteric-coated tablets or delayed-release capsules — the coating protects the drug from stomach acid until it reaches the small intestine. If the patient cannot swallow, some capsules may be opened and the granules sprinkled on food — verify with pharmacy first.

1 ⏱️ IV infusions: monitor rate closely — too rapid an infusion may induce cardiac arrhythmias 2 📋 Track bowel movements — PPIs can cause constipation or diarrhea 3 💧 Watch for dehydration — poor skin turgor, dry mucous membranes, decreased urine output, restlessness, confusion 4 🕐 Space from antacids — give other oral drugs 1–2 hr apart from an antacid dose 5 🦴 Long-term therapy: discuss bone density screening & do not taper/stop abruptly without provider guidance

entries.h: 🔗 See it in context — the acid-reducer family
entries.t: PPIs are the most potent class but the slowest to fully kick in (days for maximum effect). For the full side-by-side, see the master comparison on Acid Prevention . 💊 NG-119 H2 Antagonists — reversible, faster onset, less potent 📊 NG-233 Acid Prevention — master comparison table 🛡️ NG-254 Mucosal Protectant — barrier, not a suppressor 🧠 Potency order: PPI > H2 blocker > antacid for acid suppression — but antacid wins for speed of relief, and mucosal protectant doesn't reduce acid at all. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD ⛽ Irreversible pump block Most potent acid suppression of any class 🔤 -prazole Omeprazole, esomeprazole, pantoprazole, lansoprazole ⏱️ 30–60 min before meals Empty stomach — swallow whole 🦴🦠🩸🔁 Fracture · C. diff · B12 deficiency · rebound hyperacidity

Q1: Why are PPIs the strongest acid-reducer class? Show answer They irreversibly block the H⁺/K⁺-ATPase proton pump — the final shared step in acid production, no matter which trigger (histamine, gastrin, acetylcholine) started it. Q2: When should a PPI be given relative to meals? Show answer 30–60 minutes before a meal, on an empty stomach, swallowed whole. Q3: Name the four long-term risks of PPI therapy. Show answer Fracture risk (hip/wrist/spine), C. diff infection, vitamin B12 deficiency/anemia, and rebound hy

Loperamide · Diphenoxylate/Atropine · Difenoxin/Atropine · Bismuth Subsalicylate NG-142 GI · Pharmacology ADHD-friendly visual edition These drugs slow the gut down — the mirror opposite of laxatives. The single highest-yield rule in this whole page : never give an antidiarrheal when diarrhea is infectious or bloody — slowing transit traps the pathogen or toxin inside and can trigger a life-threatening complication. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🐌 Slows motility Mirror opposite of laxatives — same or
STEP 1 · SLOW THE GUT Two families, one goal — slow peristalsis so more water and electrolytes get reabsorbed before the stool leaves.

Difenoxin (Motofen) and diphenoxylate (Lomotil) are chemically related to opioid drugs — they decrease intestinal peristalsis by acting on opioid receptors, and each is paired with a small dose of atropine to discourage abuse. Loperamide (Imodium) also acts on opioid receptors in the gut wall to slow motility, but it does not meaningfully cross into the CNS — so it carries far less sedation and abuse potential than diphenoxylate or difenoxin. 🧠 "Lopera-MIND stays local." Loperamide acts on opioid receptors right in

Generic (Trade) Use / Dose Loperamide (Imodium) Acute diarrhea, chronic diarrhea with IBS · 4 mg initial, then 2 mg after each loose stool — max 16 mg/day Diphenoxylate/atropine (Lomotil, Lonox) Acute diarrhea · 5 mg PO QID Difenoxin/atropine (Motofen) Acute diarrhea · 2 tabs initial, then 1 tab per loose stool — max 8 tabs/day Bismuth subsalicylate (Pepto-Bismol, Bismatrol) N/V, diarrhea, cramps, H. pylori adjunct · 2 tabs or 30 mL PO q30min–1h, up to 8 doses/24h Tincture of opium (Paregoric) Severe diarrhea · 0.6

Loperamide — acute diarrhea AND chronic diarrhea associated with IBS Difenoxin & diphenoxylate — acute diarrhea Bismuth — also nausea, vomiting, cramps, and adjunct in H. pylori duodenal ulcer therapy 🧠 Only loperamide is labeled for chronic use — it's the one your provider reaches for when a patient has IBS-related diarrhea long-term. 🚨
STEP 2 · KNOW THE RISKS Slowing the gut is helpful when diarrhea is just diarrhea — and dangerous when the diarrhea is trying to flush something out.

entries.h: 🚨 NEVER give for infectious or bloody diarrhea
entries.t: Antidiarrheals are contraindicated when diarrhea is associated with organisms that can harm the intestinal mucosa — E. coli , Salmonella , and Shigella spp. — as well as with pseudomembranous colitis , abdominal pain of unknown origin , and obstructive jaundice . Also contraindicated in children younger than 2 years old . 🧠 "STOP." S almonella/Shigella/ E. coli · T oxin needs to leave · O bstructive jaundice or unknown-origin pain · P seudomembranous colitis — any one of these means STOP, don't give the antidiarrhe

Anorexia, nausea, vomiting, and constipation (rebound) Abdominal discomfort, pain, and distention Dizziness, drowsiness, headache Sedation and euphoria — opioid-related, watch for misuse potential with diphenoxylate/difenoxin 🧠 Sedation + euphoria is the tell that these are opioid-related drugs, even though they're sold over the counter.

With… Effect Antihistamines, opioids, sedatives, hypnotics ↑ CNS depression Antihistamines, antidepressants ↑ cholinergic-blocking effects (atropine component) MAOIs ↑ risk of hypertensive crisis 🧠 Two drug families stacked = two sets of side effects: opioid sedation AND anticholinergic drying.
Severe hepatic impairment Most agents are Pregnancy Category C Loperamide is Category B but not recommended in pregnancy/lactation 🎓
STEP 3 · MONITOR & REHYDRATE The drug slows the gut — the nurse's job is to watch fluid balance and know when to escalate.

1 📋 Review the chart — confirm the reason the drug was ordered 2 🗣️ Ask about type & intensity of symptoms — establish a baseline to judge effectiveness 3 🩺 Monitor vital signs and assess for relief of symptoms 4 🚨 Report abdominal distention, fever, or abdominal pain 5 💧 If chronic diarrhea: encourage fluids — weak tea, water, bouillon, or electrolyte drinks (Pedialyte, Gatorade) 6 📊 Monitor I&O 🧠 "Chart it before you medicate it." Baseline symptoms + I&O let you actually prove the drug worked.

entries.h: 🧪 When to stop and call the provider
entries.t: If diarrhea persists for more than 2 days while using an OTC antidiarrheal, the patient should discontinue use and seek treatment from the primary health care provider. 🧠 "2 days, then it's not self-care anymore."
📋 Baseline symptoms first 💧 Fluids weak tea, electrolytes 🚨 Report fever, distention, pain ⛔ Never if bloody/infectious ⏱️ >2 days stop, call provider ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🐌 Slows peristalsis opposite mechanism from laxatives 🚨 Never for infectious/bloody E. coli , Salmonella, Shigella, C. diff colitis 💧 Chart I&O watch fluid & electrolyte balance ⏱️ >2 days stop OTC use, call the provider

Q1: Name one key clue that loperamide is different from diphenoxylate/difenoxin. Show answer Loperamide acts on opioid receptors locally in the bowel wall with minimal CNS penetration, so it carries far less sedation/abuse potential than diphenoxylate or difenoxin. Q2: Name one priority — when should you withhold an antidiarrheal? Show answer When diarrhea is caused by organisms that harm the mucosa (E. coli, Salmonella, Shigella), pseudomembranous colitis, abdominal pain of unknown origin, or obstructive jaundice

Dicyclomine (Bentyl) — Anticholinergic for IBS Cramping NG-144 GI · Pharmacology ADHD-friendly visual edition Dicyclomine is an anticholinergic — it blocks acetylcholine's muscarinic receptors on GI smooth muscle, so the muscle relaxes and secretions dry up . That's exactly what a cramping, loose-stool IBS gut needs — and exactly why it causes the classic anticholinergic tetrad: can't see, can't pee, can't spit, can't 💩 . 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🌀 Anticholinergic Relaxes smooth muscle + dries s
STEP 1 · RELAX THE SPASM One receptor, blocked everywhere — the gut relaxes, and so does everything else that runs on acetylcholine.

entries.h: ⚙️ Mechanism: blocks acetylcholine at the smooth muscle
entries.t: Dicyclomine is an antispasmodic / anticholinergic . It antagonizes muscarinic acetylcholine receptors on GI smooth muscle, producing relaxation of smooth muscle and drying of secretions . Less acetylcholine signal reaching the gut wall means fewer, weaker spasms — and a calmer, less crampy bowel. 🧠 "Dicyclo-CALM." The name is a mouthful, but the job is simple: calm the smooth muscle down.

Field Detail Generic Dicyclomine Trade Bentyl Class Antispasmodic / Anticholinergic Indication IBS with many loose stools per day (cramping, diarrhea-predominant) Typical dose 20 mg PO QID (some regimens start at 10 mg QID; max ~160 mg/day divided QID — verify facility protocol) 🧠 "Bentyl bends the bowel back to calm."

entries.h: 🔗 Ties back to the IBS page
entries.t: IBS can present as diarrhea-predominant (IBS-D) , constipation-predominant (IBS-C) , or mixed. Dicyclomine targets the cramping/spasm component that comes with IBS-D — it does not treat the underlying disorder, only the smooth-muscle symptom. See the Irritable Bowel Syndrome page for the full symptom picture, Rome criteria clues, and diet triggers. 🧠 IBS = the disease. Dicyclomine = one tool for one symptom (the cramp), not a cure. ⚠️
STEP 2 · THE ANTICHOLINERGIC TETRAD Every anticholinergic side effect is the same story: acetylcholine gets blocked somewhere the patient still needed it.

entries.h: 🚫 "Can't see, can't pee, can't spit, can't 💩"
entries.t: Blocking acetylcholine doesn't stay in the gut — it hits every muscarinic receptor in the body: blurred vision (can't see), urinary retention (can't pee), dry mouth (can't spit), and constipation (can't poop). 🧠 "Dry as a bone, red as a beet, blind as a bat, mad as a hatter." The classic anticholinergic toxidrome rhyme — this drug is a mild, therapeutic version of that same picture.

Paralytic ileus & bowel obstruction — never relax a gut that's already not moving Narrow-angle glaucoma — cataracts are OK , this is specifically narrow-angle glaucoma Urinary retention > 400 mL — full bladder, don't add a drug that can't let it empty Myasthenia gravis — anticholinergics worsen muscle weakness Severe ulcerative colitis — risk of toxic megacolon if motility is over-suppressed 🧠 "NO pee, NO see, NO spit, NO 💩" — turn each "NO" into a contraindication: NO (full bladder) pee, NO (narrow-angle glaucoma)

entries.h: 🌡️ Caution: heat, elderly, and stacking anticholinergics
entries.t: 🧠 "No sweat, big problem." Anticholinergics block sweating too — the patient can't cool down in the heat. 🎓
STEP 3 · SAFE ADMINISTRATION Time the dose, protect the bladder, and keep the patient out of the heat.

1 ⏰ Give 30–60 minutes before meals — relax the gut before it has to work 2 🚱 Have the patient void before dosing when possible; monitor I&O for urinary retention 3 👂 Assess bowel sounds before and during therapy 4 🌡️ Avoid hot environments & strenuous exercise — decreased sweating raises heat-stroke risk 5 🚶 Rise slowly — orthostatic changes; avoid driving until effects on vision/alertness are known 6 🍷 Avoid alcohol and other CNS depressants — additive drowsiness 🧠 "Before the meal, before the mistake." Give it b

Older adults are more sensitive to anticholinergic burden — watch for confusion, sedation, and fall risk . Avoid stacking dicyclomine with other anticholinergic drugs (antihistamines, some antidepressants, some bladder drugs) whenever possible. 🧠 Confusion in an older adult on an anticholinergic is a medication problem until proven otherwise.
⏰ Before meals 30–60 min 🚱 Void first watch I&O 🌡️ Avoid heat can't sweat ⛔ Never if obstructed 👁️ Never narrow-angle glaucoma ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🌀 Anticholinergic relaxes smooth muscle, dries secretions 🚫 Tetrad can't see, can't pee, can't spit, can't 💩 ⏰ Before meals 30–60 min ahead of eating 🚨 Never obstruction/ileus or narrow-angle glaucoma

Q1: Name one key clue that dicyclomine is anticholinergic. Show answer It relaxes GI smooth muscle and dries secretions by blocking acetylcholine's muscarinic receptors. Q2: Name one priority assessment before giving a dose. Show answer Assess for urinary retention (have the patient void first if possible) and assess bowel sounds/history of obstruction or ileus. Q3: Name one teaching point about environment. Show answer Avoid hot environments and strenuous exercise — decreased sweating raises the risk of heat strok

Acute & Chronic — the pancreas digests itself NG-159 GI ADHD-friendly visual edition Autodigestion — digestive enzymes activate inside the pancreas instead of the duodenum, so the pancreas digests itself . Epigastric/LUQ pain that radiates to the back , sky-high lipase , and a gut that must be put to complete rest (NPO) while IV fluids and pain control lead the way. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🍺 #1 cause = alcohol Gallstones are #2. Together they cause most cases. 🔪 LUQ/epigastric → back Pain worse
STEP 1 · AUTODIGESTION One organ, two jobs — when the digestive job turns on itself, the endocrine job (glucose control) gets dragged down with it.

entries.h: 🥞 The pancreas has two completely different jobs
entries.t: Exocrine = digestive enzymes into the duodenum. Endocrine = hormones into the blood. Pancreatitis is an exocrine disease that drags the endocrine side down with it. 🧠 “The chef poisons the kitchen.” Enzymes are supposed to cook (digest) food in the duodenum — in pancreatitis they turn on early, inside the pancreas itself .

1️⃣ Trigger injures pancreatic cells (alcohol toxin, gallstone blocking duct, ERCP trauma) ▼ 2️⃣ Digestive enzymes activate prematurely, inside the pancreas instead of the duodenum ▼ 3️⃣ Enzymes digest pancreatic tissue itself = autodigestion → inflammation, edema, possible hemorrhage/necrosis 🧠 Pancre ATE itis — the pancreas literally starts to eat itself.

entries.h: 🍺 Top causes — I GET SMASHED (short list she needs)
entries.t: 🍷 Alcohol abuse — most common cause overall 🪨 Gallbladder disease / gallstones — a stone blocks the shared duct 🩺 ERCP — Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangio­Pancreatography , a known post-procedure trigger 🫁 Cystic fibrosis — thick mucus plugs pancreatic ducts 🧪 Also: hypertriglyceridemia, hypercalcemia, some drugs, trauma 🧠 “Booze & Stones.” If an NCLEX stem doesn't name a drug or CF, the answer is almost always alcohol or a gallstone .

entries.h: ⭐ Acute vs Chronic — same organ, different timeline
entries.t: Acute Chronic Sudden onset, reversible if caught early Irreversible fibrosis & scarring over years Usually gallstones or alcohol binge Usually long-term alcohol abuse Enzymes markedly elevated Enzymes may be normal — gland is “burned out” Goal: rest the pancreas, treat the trigger Goal: enzyme replacement (see NG-217) + manage diabetes 🧠 Acute = attack. Chronic = aftermath. Chronic disease is why students learn pancrelipase — the scarred gland can't make its own enzymes anymore. 🔎
STEP 2 · SPOT IT Pain location, two hemorrhagic skin signs, and the one lab that beats the others.

entries.h: 🔪 Pain — epigastric / LUQ radiating straight to the back
entries.t: Sudden, severe, boring pain — worse lying flat or after a fatty meal/alcohol; classically eased by sitting up & leaning forward (fetal/knee-chest position takes pressure off the retroperitoneal pancreas). 🧠 “LUQ, then out the back door.” If a stem says epigastric pain boring through to the back, think pancreas first.

entries.h: 🚨 Cullen's sign vs Grey Turner's sign — hemorrhagic pancreatitis
entries.t: Blue-gray bruising = retroperitoneal bleeding tracking through tissue planes → hemorrhagic/necrotizing pancreatitis , a severe complication. 🧠 “Cullen circles the belly button, Turner takes the flanks.” Both = internal bleeding, not a bruise from trauma.
Lipase is more specific to the pancreas & stays elevated longer — trust lipase over amylase. 🧠 “LIPase LINGERS.” Both rhyme with staying power — lipase is the one you can still catch days later.

entries.h: 🧪 The rest of the lab panel
entries.t: 📈 Elevated glucose — “hyperglycemia,” damaged islet cells 📈 Elevated WBC — over 10,000/mm³ , inflammation 📈 Elevated bilirubin — jaundice if biliary cause 📉 Hypocalcemia — calcium binds to fat that's been “saponified” by leaked lipase 📈 Elevated PT/aPTT — coagulation disrupted in severe disease 💧 Ascites may develop from third-spacing/peritoneal irritation 🧠 “Calcium goes where the fat goes.” Watch for Chvostek's/Trousseau's signs of hypocalcemia in severe pancreatitis.

entries.h: 🚨 Priority assessment after ERCP — SATA style
entries.t: COMMON NCLEX QUESTION Post-ERCP epigastric pain = assess this client FIRST — think pancreatitis until ruled out. Findings consistent with acute pancreatitis (select all that apply): gray-blue flank discoloration , abdominal guarding & tenderness , LUQ pain radiating to the back , elevated amylase/lipase, hyperglycemia, elevated WBC. 🧠 If the stem mentions a recent ERCP + new epigastric pain, your nursing brain should say “pancreatitis” before anything else. 🩺
STEP 3 · REST THE PANCREAS Stop feeding the fire, replace fluid, control pain safely, and watch for the complications that kill.

1 💧 IV fluids — aggressive resuscitation, third-spacing is huge 2 💊 IV pain control — hydromorphone (Dilaudid) preferred 3 🚫 NPO — complete bowel rest stops enzyme stimulation 4 🩹 NG tube to suction if vomiting/distention 5 🩸 Monitor glucose — treat hyperglycemia with insulin NCLEX TIP Fluids + pain control together are the top priority intervention for acute pancreatitis — not just one alone. 🧠 “NPO, IV, and PAIN-O.” Nothing by mouth, fluids running, pain treated — in that order of urgency.

Older NCLEX-style teaching says avoid morphine — thought to spasm the sphincter of Oddi and worsen pain. Hydromorphone (Dilaudid) is the classic preferred choice. 🧠 Practice varies by facility — for exam purposes, remember hydromorphone yes, morphine caution .

Class Drug Proton pump inhibitor Pantoprazole — cuts acid, reduces pancreatic stimulation H2 blocker Famotidine Opioid analgesic Hydromorphone (Dilaudid) Insulin Sliding scale for stress hyperglycemia 🧠 Antacids/PPIs/H2 blockers aren't random — less stomach acid hitting the duodenum means less signal for the pancreas to secrete enzymes.

Acute phase: NPO → clear liquids → advance to low-fat, low-sugar diet as tolerated. Fat is the biggest enzyme trigger. 🍟 NO Fried Chicken high fat 🥔 NO Chips high fat 🥛 NO Whole Milk+Cookies fat + sugar 🍗 Grilled Chicken lean protein — OK 🥔 Baked Potato OK 🧀 Reduced-Fat Cheese + whole wheat crackers — OK In chronic pancreatitis , the gland can no longer make its own enzymes → lifelong pancreatic enzyme replacement (pancrelipase) with every meal and snack — see NG-217 for full drug teaching. 🧠 “Low fat keeps it flat

🫧 Pseudocyst fluid-filled sac ☠️ Necrosis tissue death → sepsis 🫁 ARDS Acute Resp. Distress Synd. 🪵 Peritonitis board-like abdomen 🩸 Hypotension shock, fluid loss 🍬 Diabetes chronic disease outcome REPORT TO HCP Fever >100.3°F , rebound tenderness, rigid/board-like abdomen , increasing pain, restlessness, tachycardia/tachypnea. 🧠 Same red-flag cluster you'll see across every GI page this batch — memorize it once, apply it everywhere: fever + rigid belly + rising pain + restless + fast HR/RR = call the provider now.

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🍺 Alcohol + gallstones = the two big causes 🔪 LUQ pain → back worse flat, better leaning forward 🧪 Lipase > amylase more specific, stays up longer 🚫 NPO + fluids + pain rest the pancreas first

Q1: Which lab value is more specific for pancreatitis and stays elevated longer? Show answer Lipase — amylase rises fast but falls within days; lipase lingers. Q2: What do bluish bruises around the umbilicus vs at the flanks indicate, and what are they called? Show answer Retroperitoneal hemorrhage from hemorrhagic/necrotizing pancreatitis — Cullen's sign (umbilicus) and Grey Turner's sign (flanks). Q3: What is the priority nursing intervention combo for acute pancreatitis? Show answer IV fluids and pain control, p

Gallbladder Inflammation — Biliary Colic vs. Acute Attack NG-179 GI ADHD-friendly visual edition Inflammation of the gallbladder — typically caused by gallstones (cholelithiasis) that block the cystic duct, so bile backs up and inflames the gallbladder wall. Classic picture: RUQ pain that radiates to the right shoulder , worse after a fatty meal, plus a positive Murphy's sign . 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 📍 RUQ → right shoulder The signature pain pattern of gallbladder disease. 🚨 Fever + chills + t
STEP 1 · THE BLOCKED DUCT One blocked duct explains the whole disease — bile with nowhere to go inflames the gallbladder wall.

entries.h: 🫘 Gallstones block the cystic duct → bile backs up → inflammation
entries.t: DEFINITION Inflammation of the gallbladder , typically caused by gallstones (cholelithiasis) that block the ducts leading out of the gallbladder, causing a backup of bile. 🧠 "Stone in the road = bile with nowhere to go." The gallstone plugs the cystic duct — bile can't drain, pressure builds, the wall inflames.

🥓 High-fat diet ⚖️ Obesity 🎂 Age over 40 ♀️ Female sex & history of pregnancy (estrogen raises cholesterol saturation in bile) 🧠 "Fat, Forty, Female, Fertile" — the classic 4 F's for gallstone risk. Not every client fits the mnemonic, but it's a fast recall trigger.
RUQ 🫘 gallbladder pain LUQ RLQ LLQ Pain classically radiates to the right shoulder / scapula — referred pain from the phrenic nerve. 🔎
STEP 2 · COLIC VS. ACUTE ATTACK Biliary colic is the stone moving; acute cholecystitis is the gallbladder actually inflamed and infected.

Feature 🌗 Biliary colic 🔥 Acute cholecystitis Cause Stone temporarily blocks the duct, then passes/repositions Stone stays lodged — persistent obstruction & inflammation, often with infection Pain pattern Comes and goes, often after a fatty meal, resolves within a few hours Constant, severe RUQ pain that doesn't resolve on its own Fever Usually absent Present — fever with chills Murphy's sign Usually negative Positive — pain + sudden inspiratory arrest on RUQ palpation 🧠 "Colic comes and goes; cholecystitis stays a

📍 RUQ pain "radiates to the right shoulder" 🌡️ Fever with chills 💓 Tachycardia 🖐️ Positive Murphy's sign 🥓 Pain worse after a high-fat meal — fat triggers cholecystokinin release, gallbladder contracts against the blockage

entries.h: 🚨 RED FLAG — call the provider now
entries.t: These suggest complication (perforation, empyema, ascending cholangitis): 🌡️ High fever, rigors 💛 Jaundice bile duct involvement 💓 Marked tachycardia 🪵 Rigid abdomen peritonitis 🧠 Fever + jaundice + RUQ pain together = think Charcot's triad (ascending cholangitis) — an emergency, not routine colic.

Examiner presses on the RUQ and asks the client to take a deep breath. Pain + sudden stop of inspiration = positive sign — the inflamed gallbladder drops onto the examiner's fingers on inhalation. 🧠 "Murphy's law — you get caught mid-breath." A positive sign literally stops the breath. 🩺
STEP 3 · REST THE GALLBLADDER, THEN REMOVE IT NPO during the attack, low fat always, and surgery is the definitive fix.

1 NPO status — nothing by mouth; eating triggers more pain & complications 2 IV fluids, pain control, antiemetics as ordered 3 Antibiotics if infection suspected 4 Monitor for surgical vs. non-surgical management 🧠 NPO first, always. Any fat or food makes the gallbladder contract against a blocked duct — that's exactly what you don't want.

💥 Lithotripsy — shock waves break up stones; used when stones are small enough 🔪 Cholecystectomy — surgical removal of the gallbladder, done when stones are too large or disease is recurrent/severe 🧠 Lithotripsy shatters; cholecystectomy removes. If the stone's too big to shatter, the whole organ comes out.

🚶 Assist with early ambulation — prevents pneumonia 🫁 Deep breathe & cough — priority teaching for an open cholecystectomy (bigger incision, higher pneumonia risk) 🚿 No baths — shower only , protects the incision 🔴 Report redness/swelling at incision sites to the surgeon 🧠 KAPLAN QUESTION Priority action for a client scheduled for an open cholecystectomy ? Demonstrate ways to deep breathe and cough. A bigger incision near the diaphragm = higher risk of shallow breathing & pneumonia post-op.

HESI QUESTION Following a laparoscopic cholecystectomy , which instructions would the nurse include? Select all that apply. ✅ May take a shower ✅ Wait about 1 week after surgery before returning to work (varies with procedure & provider order) ✅ Lose weight if overweight ✅ Avoid fatty, fried foods HESI QUESTION A nurse caring for a patient who recently had the gallbladder removed knows the patient will have difficulty digesting large amounts of which nutrient? Fats — bile helps emulsify fat, and without a gallbladd

SAY IT OUT LOUD 📍 RUQ → right shoulder Classic pain radiation pattern 🖐️ Positive Murphy's sign Pain + inspiratory arrest 🥓 Fatty food = trigger Low-fat diet, NPO during acute attack 🫁 Deep breathe & cough Priority teaching after open cholecystectomy

Q1: Where does gallbladder pain classically radiate? Show answer RUQ pain radiating to the right shoulder/scapula. Q2: What's the difference between biliary colic and acute cholecystitis? Show answer Biliary colic is intermittent pain as a stone temporarily blocks/moves, usually without fever. Acute cholecystitis is constant pain with fever, chills, and a positive Murphy's sign — the duct stays blocked and the gallbladder becomes inflamed/infected. Bulk-Forming · Osmotic/Saline · Stimulant · Stool Softener · Lubricant NG-185 GI · Pharmacology ADHD-friendly visual edition Five different mechanisms, one shared goal: relieve constipation. This is the mirror image of the Anti-diarrheal page — instead of slowing motility and drying secretions, laxatives pull water in, irritate the bowel wall, or add bulk to speed things up. Pick the class by how fast you need it to work. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🪑 5 classes, 5 mechanisms Pick by onset time and
STEP 1 · PICK THE MECHANISM Same destination, five different roads — bulk it, wet it, irritate it, soften it, or lubricate it.

entries.h: 📊 The 5 laxative classes, side by side
entries.t: Class Mechanism Example Typical onset Bulk-forming Absorbs water, adds bulk → stimulates peristalsis mechanically Psyllium (Metamucil) 12–72 hr Osmotic (hyperosmolar) Dehydrates local tissue → irritation, ↑ peristalsis Lactulose (oral) / Glycerin (rectal) Oral 24–48 hr ; rectal 15–60 min Saline Pulls water into intestine osmotically → ↑ pressure, ↑ peristalsis Magnesium hydroxide (MOM) 30 min – 6 hr Stimulant / irritant Direct action on intestinal wall → ↑ peristalsis Bisacodyl, Senna, Cascara sagrada Oral 6–12 hr

Stimulant, emollient, saline — evacuate the colon before rectal/bowel exams or surgery Stool softeners / mineral oil — prevent straining (post anorectal surgery, post-MI) Psyllium / polycarbophil — IBS and diverticular disease Hyperosmotic (lactulose) — reduces blood ammonia in hepatic encephalopathy 🧠 "Don't strain that heart or that stoma." Stool softeners are the classic answer for the post-MI or post-rectal-surgery patient.

🚽 Laxatives 🚫💧 Antidiarrheals Pull water INTO the gut Promote water reabsorption ↑ peristalsis ↓ peristalsis Treats constipation Treats diarrhea 🧠 Same gut, opposite dial. If you can explain one page, you can explain the other by just flipping every arrow. ⚠️
STEP 2 · KNOW THE RISKS "Natural" and "OTC" doesn't mean risk-free — electrolytes, obstruction, and dependence are all real.

Constipation (paradoxically), diarrhea with water/electrolyte loss , abdominal pain or discomfort, nausea, vomiting, perianal irritation, fainting, bloating, flatulence, cramps, and weakness. Prolonged use can cause serious electrolyte imbalances and the "laxative habit" — dependence on a laxative to have a bowel movement. 🧠 "Bulk without water is a brick, not a broom." Always pair bulk-forming laxatives with a full glass of water or more.

Known hypersensitivity Persistent abdominal pain Nausea or vomiting of unknown cause Signs of acute appendicitis 🧠 "Don't clear an appendix that's about to burst." Never give a laxative for an undiagnosed acute abdomen — it can worsen a surgical emergency.

Mineral oil impairs absorption of fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, K Laxatives may reduce absorption of other drugs present in the GI tract Surfactants (like docusate) given with mineral oil can increase mineral oil absorption Milk, antacids, H2 antagonists, and PPIs should not be given 1–2 hours before bisacodyl tablets — the enteric coating can dissolve early, causing gastric irritation/dyspepsia and a weaker laxative effect 🧠 "ADEK gets locked out" with chronic mineral oil use — the fat-soluble vitamins ride out wi

Magnesium products — use cautiously in any degree of renal impairment (risk of accumulation) Tartrazine (yellow dye) in some products may cause allergic reactions, including bronchial asthma, in susceptible patients Cascara sagrada or senna can cause pink-red, red-violet, red-brown, yellow-brown, or black urine — expected, harmless discoloration 🧠 Weird urine color after senna? Expected, not an emergency. Reassure, don't panic. 🎓
STEP 3 · PREVENT DEPENDENCE The best long-term laxative is fiber, fluid, and movement — drugs are the backup plan.

1 ⛔ Avoid long-term use unless recommended by the HCP — risk of "laxative habit" / dependence 2 ⚖️ Not for weight loss — read and follow label directions 3 🚫 Do not use with abdominal pain, nausea, or vomiting present 4 📞 Notify the HCP if constipation isn't relieved, or if rectal bleeding/other symptoms occur 5 💧 Prevent the need: plenty of fluids, exercise, high-fiber/roughage diet — the real long-term fix 🧠 "Fiber, fluid, feet." The three F's prevent constipation without a single pill.

Take with a full glass of water or more , every time. Without enough fluid, the swelling mass can obstruct the esophagus, stomach, small intestine, or colon — especially in a patient with known intestinal stenosis. 🧠 "Water is not optional here — it's the drug."
💧 Full glass water bulk-forming ⏱️ Short-term only avoid habit ⛔ Never abd. pain, N/V 🥗 Fiber + fluids real prevention 📞 Report bleeding, no relief ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🪑 5 classes bulk, osmotic/saline, stimulant, softener, lubricant 🚨 Never with abdominal pain, N/V, or suspected appendicitis 💧 Fluid = safety especially with bulk-forming agents ⚠️ Short-term only long-term use → dependence + electrolyte loss

Q1: Name one key clue that tells bulk-forming apart from stimulant laxatives. Show answer Bulk-forming absorbs water and adds mechanical bulk (onset 12–72 hr); stimulant laxatives directly irritate the intestinal wall to trigger peristalsis (onset 6–12 hr oral, much faster rectally). Q2: Name one priority — when should a laxative be withheld? Show answer Persistent abdominal pain, nausea/vomiting of unknown cause, or signs of acute appendicitis — never mask a possible surgical abdomen. Q3: Name one teaching point a

entries.h: Uric Acid Inhibitors · NG-188 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics ⚙️ What it does 👀 Watch for 🗣️ Teach ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Pharmacology · Musculoskeletal & Gout

Antigout drugs — Allopurinol, Febuxostat, Colchicine, Probenecid NG-188 Pharmacology ADHD-friendly visual edition Gout = urate crystals crystallizing in a joint — usually the big toe. Xanthine oxidase inhibitors (allopurinol, febuxostat) lower uric acid production for long-term prevention; colchicine calms the acute inflammatory attack; probenecid pushes uric acid out through the kidneys. Know which drug treats the flare vs which one prevents the next one. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🦴 Podagra Clas
STEP 1 · CRYSTALS & ENZYMES Three different strategies aimed at the same molecule: uric acid.

entries.h: 🦴 Gout pathophysiology — crystals in the joint
entries.t: 🧠 “Podagra = toe on fire.” Gout out of nowhere, overnight, in the big toe — that's the textbook presentation.
🧠 Allopurinol & Febuxostat = production plants shutting down. Fewer crystals form because less uric acid is made in the first place.

Probenecid increases renal excretion of uric acid — it doesn't lower production, it helps the kidneys clear it faster. 🧠 “Pro-BEN-ecid pushes it out the BEN(d) in the pipes” — think plumbing, not production.

Generic Trade Use Dose Allopurinol Zyloprim Chronic gout management, prophylaxis 100–800 mg/day PO Febuxostat Uloric Newer XO inhibitor, same goal as allopurinol — Colchicine — Acute attack relief + prophylaxis (2nd line) Prophylaxis 0.5–0.6 mg/day; Acute: 0.5–1.2 mg PO or 2 mg IV, then 0.5–1.2 mg PO q1–2h or 0.5 mg IV q6h until relief or toxicity Probenecid — Uricosuric — increases renal excretion — 🧠 Two lanes to remember: Allopurinol/Febuxostat = prevent the next attack . Colchicine = treat the attack happening
STEP 2 · REACTIONS & INTERACTIONS One rash you can't ignore, one drug that's dangerous enough to be second-line, and interactions worth memorizing.

entries.h: 🚨 Allopurinol rash → can progress to Stevens-Johnson syndrome
entries.t: 🧠 “Rash = red flag, not just red skin.” Of every adverse effect on this page, this is the one that changes your next action immediately.

🤕 Headache 🚽 Urinary frequency 🩹 Skin rash — allopurinol (see above) 🤢 Colchicine: severe nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, bone marrow depression — why it's 2nd line 🧠 Colchicine is powerful but toxic — used for acute attacks/2nd line specifically because of its narrow safety margin.

❌ Colchicine — serious GI, renal, hepatic, or cardiac disease; blood dyscrasias ❌ Probenecid — blood dyscrasias, uric acid kidney stones, children <2 years ❌ Febuxostat — do not give with azathioprine, mercaptopurine, or theophylline 🧠 Azathioprine & mercaptopurine are also broken down by xanthine oxidase — blocking that enzyme lets these drugs build up to toxic levels .

With… Effect Ampicillin + allopurinol ↑ risk of rash Theophylline + allopurinol ↑ theophylline toxicity Aluminum-based antacids + allopurinol ↓ allopurinol effectiveness Penicillins/cephalosporins/sulfonamides + probenecid ↑ serum level of the anti-infective Barbiturates/benzodiazepines + probenecid ↑ serum level of the sedative NSAIDs + probenecid ↑ serum level of the NSAID Salicylates (aspirin) + probenecid ↓ probenecid effectiveness — avoid 🧠 Probenecid interactions all share one theme: it blocks renal excretion
STEP 3 · WHAT THE CLIENT NEEDS TO HEAR Hydration, timing, and when to call — the same three buckets every time.

entries.h: 💧 Hydration & food — the core teaching points
entries.t: 🧠 “Flush it, don't crush it.” Water dilutes the urine so uric acid doesn't crystallize into kidney stones while levels are dropping.

😴 May cause drowsiness — avoid driving/hazardous tasks if it occurs 🚫 Avoid alcohol & other CNS depressants 📅 Colchicine is short-term only — 2–3 weeks max 📞 Notify provider if pain isn't relieved within a few days 📞 Notify provider immediately if a skin rash occurs 🧠 “2–3 and done.” Colchicine's short-term rule is a favorite NCLEX distractor — students assume all gout meds are long-term, but colchicine isn't for chronic daily use.

Allopurinol/febuxostat are for prevention , not for stopping a flare already in progress — starting them mid-attack can actually prolong it. Colchicine is the go-to for the acute attack itself. 🧠 “Don't start the fire extinguisher mid-fire.” If a stem describes an active, painful gout attack and asks which drug to add — think colchicine, not allopurinol. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🦴 Gout = urate crystals classic site: big toe (podagra) 🚨 New rash = stop & call allopurinol can progress to Stevens-Johnson 💧 10 glasses/day during acute attack, take with food ⚔️ Prevent vs treat allopurinol prevents · colchicine treats the flare

Q1: How do allopurinol and febuxostat lower uric acid levels? Show answer They inhibit xanthine oxidase, the enzyme that produces uric acid, reducing serum uric acid and urate crystal deposits in joints. Q2: What adverse skin finding on allopurinol requires immediate provider notification? Show answer Any new skin rash — it can progress to exfoliative dermatitis or Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Q3: Why is colchicine reserved as second-line therapy despite being effective? Show answer It can cause severe nausea, vomitin
