entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics ⚙️ What it does 👀 Watch for 🗣️ Teach ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / GI Pharmacology · Enzyme Replacement

Pancreatic Enzyme Replacement Therapy (PERT) NG-217 GI Pharmacology ADHD-friendly visual edition Replaces the digestive enzymes a damaged pancreas can no longer make — lipase, protease, amylase — so a client with chronic pancreatitis (see NG-159) or cystic fibrosis can actually digest fat, protein, and carbs. The whole drug lives or dies on one rule : take it WITH every meal & snack . 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → ⏱️ WITH food, every time Not before, not after — or the drug does nothing. 💊 Swallow wh
STEP 1 · REPLACE THE ENZYMES Same three enzymes the healthy pancreas makes — given from a capsule instead.

entries.h: 🥞 Indication — when the pancreas can't do its own job
entries.t: Given for pancreatic exocrine insufficiency : chronic pancreatitis , cystic fibrosis , or after pancreatectomy/pancreatic cancer — situations where the gland is too damaged or missing to secrete its own digestive enzymes. 🧠 All three enzyme names end in -ASE — that's your clue it's an enzyme: lip ase , prote ase , amyl ase .

Exogenous lipase, protease, and amylase (from pork pancreas) mix with food in the small intestine and break down fat, protein, and carbohydrate — the same job the client's own damaged pancreas can no longer do. 🧠 “Borrowed enzymes, borrowed digestion.” The drug doesn't fix the pancreas — it substitutes for it, meal by meal, forever.

Chronic pancreatitis scars & fibroses the gland until it can't secrete enough of its own enzymes → malabsorption of fat/protein/carbs → weight loss & steatorrhea . Pancrelipase is the lifelong fix. 🧠 Also used in cystic fibrosis — thick mucus plugs the pancreatic duct the same way it plugs the lungs, so enzymes never reach the gut. 👀
STEP 2 · OUTCOMES & REACTIONS One expected outcome to confirm it's working, and the reactions that mean stop and reassess.

entries.h: ✅ Expected therapeutic outcome — reduction in fatty stools
entries.t: 🧠 HESI/Kaplan trap: “Reduction in fatty stools is an expected outcome” is TRUE — that's the goal, not an adverse effect.

🤢 GI upset — nausea, abdominal cramping 🩸 Hyperuricemia at very high doses 🫁 Fibrosing colonopathy — rare, linked to very high doses in children with CF 🐷 Allergic reaction — it's pork-derived; caution with pork allergy 🧠 “Pig, pork, pancrelipase.” Three P's — remember the pork origin when screening allergies.

🧂 Antacids can alter the pH needed for enteric coating to release properly 🩸 May decrease absorption of oral iron supplements 🧠 Give with a cold beverage , not a hot one — heat can break down the enzymes before they even reach the gut. 🗣️
STEP 3 · MAKE IT WORK EVERY TIME Timing and swallowing technique are the whole test question here.

entries.h: ⏱️ Timing — WITH the meal, not before, not after
entries.t: 🧠 “No food, no dose — with food, right now.” The single most-tested fact on this drug is the timing rule.

entries.h: 💊 Capsule handling — swallow whole, do not crush or chew
entries.t: Enteric-coated beads protect the enzymes from stomach acid until they reach the intestine. Crushing/chewing destroys the coating and lets active enzymes irritate/digest the oral mucosa. 🧠 If the client can't swallow capsules: open & sprinkle beads on a small amount of soft, acidic food (like applesauce) and swallow immediately without chewing — never mix into the whole meal or a hot/alkaline food.

💊 Take with every meal & snack , not before/after 🥤 Swallow whole with a cold beverage 🚫 Never crush or chew enteric-coated capsules/beads 🧼 Wipe mouth after taking to prevent mucosal irritation 💩 Report if fatty, floating, foul stools continue — dose may need adjusting 💧 Maintain good hydration 🧠 “ENZYME” — E very meal/snack · N ever crush · Z ero skipped doses · Y ou swallow whole · M ix beads only in soft acidic food if needed · E xpect less fatty stool. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD ⏱️ WITH food, every time Not before, not after. 💊 Swallow whole never crush/chew enteric-coated beads 💩 Less fatty stool = drug is working 🥞 Ties to chronic pancreatitis & CF gland can't make its own enzymes

Q1: When should pancrelipase be taken relative to meals? Show answer With every meal and snack — not before, not after — or it won't mix with food to digest it. Q2: What expected outcome tells you the drug is working? Show answer A reduction in fatty, floating, foul-smelling stools (steatorrhea) and improved weight gain. Q3: A client can't swallow the capsule whole — what's the safe alternative? Show answer Open the capsule and sprinkle the beads on a small amount of soft, acidic food (e.g. applesauce), then swallo

entries.h: Acid Prevention — Master Comparison · NG-233 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🧴 The family 📊 Compare 🗣️ Teach ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / GI · Pharmacology Course · Acid-Reducer Family 3 of 4 — THE CHEAT SHEET

Antacids · H2 Blockers · PPIs — the master comparison page NG-233 GI · Pharmacology ADHD-friendly visual edition This page is the tie-breaker for the whole acid family: three drug classes, three speeds, three strengths. Deep-dive the individual classes on PPIs (NG-140) , H2 Antagonists (NG-119) , and Mucosal Protectant (NG-254) — come back here whenever they blur together. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🧴 Antacid = fastest, shortest Neutralizes acid immediately but wears off quickly. 🚫 H2 blocker = mi
STEP 1 · MEET EVERY PLAYER Four ways to fight acid — neutralize it, block its release two different ways, or coat the wound so it can't reach it.

🧠 “Neutralize, Block-A, Block-B, Coat.” Antacid neutralizes acid already made · H2 blocker & PPI both reduce production (different mechanisms) · mucosal protectant coats the ulcer and never touches acid levels at all.
Sodium bicarbonate (Alka-Seltzer) Calcium carbonate (Tums, Rolaids) Aluminum hydroxide Magnesium hydroxide (Milk of Magnesia) Immediately neutralizes acid — but ONLY temporary, not long-lasting.

🪨 Aluminum constipation 🦴 Calcium constipation 💧 Magnesium diarrhea 🎈 Sodium fluid retention — avoid in HF 🧠 “Al & Ca CLOG, Mg goes.” Al uminum and Ca lcium clog you up (constipation) — M a g nesium is mellow and moves things along (diarrhea). S odium swells — never for a heart-failure patient.

entries.h: 💊 H2 Blockers & PPIs — the two "reduce production" classes, side by side
entries.t: H2 Blockers PPIs Suffix -tidine — ranitidine, famotidine -prazole — omeprazole, esomeprazole, pantoprazole MOA Reversibly blocks H2 receptors on the stomach's parietal cells Inhibits the proton pump in the parietal cells Indications GERD & ulcer (duodenal/gastric) prevention Stress-ulcer prevention, GERD, heartburn 🧠 Full drug-by-drug breakdown, dosing, and adverse effects for each class live on their own pages — NG-119 and NG-140 . 📊
STEP 2 · THE MASTER TABLE When two of these blur together on an exam, this is the table that untangles them.

Antacid H2 Blocker PPI Mucosal Protectant Example Calcium carbonate Famotidine Omeprazole Sucralfate Mechanism Neutralizes existing acid Reversibly blocks histamine at H2 receptor Irreversibly blocks the proton pump Coats the ulcer — does NOT neutralize acid Onset Minutes — fastest ~30–60 min Slower — days for full effect Needs an acidic environment to activate Duration Shortest — wears off fast Moderate Longest — 24+ hr per dose Local, until next dose Relative potency Lowest Middle Highest N/A — different job enti
🧠 The two bars are mirror images: the class with the shortest onset has the lowest potency, and the class that takes longest to kick in gives the strongest suppression. 🗣️
STEP 3 · HESI-STYLE TRAPS Every acid drug shares the same spacing rule — the traps are in the details that are different.

entries.h: 🚨 HESI-style trap: sodium bicarbonate + heart failure
entries.t: NOT for heart failure patients — sodium bicarbonate antacid adds a sodium load that promotes fluid retention. Sodium = swells.

Antacids can interfere with the absorption of other oral drugs. Separate any other medication by 1 hour before or after an antacid — this rule repeats across every acid-drug page in this family. 🧠 “Anti-Acid = Anti-Mixing.” The whole point of the name doubles as the safety rule: don't mix it with other meds too closely in time.

entries.h: 🎓 One card per class — PPI teaching highlights
entries.t: ⏱️ 30 min before meals timing 🍽️ No overeating prevents reflux 🦴 Porous bones get bone density tests 🦠 C. diff risk possible GI infection 🚭 No stress / smoking worsens acid 💊 No NSAIDs + ASA = GI bleed risk PPIs are also used for stress-ulcer prophylaxis in hospitalized/surgical patients — one of the most common inpatient reasons you'll see one ordered.

entries.h: 🔗 Go deeper — one page per class
entries.t: ⛽ NG-140 PPIs — full mechanism, dosing & long-term risks 🚫 NG-119 H2 Antagonists — full mechanism, dosing & interactions 🛡️ NG-254 Mucosal Protectant — sucralfate & misoprostol ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🧴 Antacid Fastest onset, lowest potency, wears off fast 🚫 H2 blocker Middle ground — reversible, moderate ⛽ PPI Slowest onset, highest potency, lasts longest 🕐 1–2 hr rule Always space acid drugs from other oral meds

Q1: Rank the three acid-suppressing classes from fastest onset to slowest. Show answer Antacid (minutes) → H2 blocker (~30–60 min) → PPI (slowest, days for full effect). Q2: Rank them from lowest potency to highest. Show answer Antacid (lowest) → H2 blocker (moderate) → PPI (highest). Q3: Which antacid ingredient is contraindicated in heart failure, and why? Show answer Sodium bicarbonate — the sodium load promotes fluid retention. Q4: What's the one rule that applies to every drug in this family? Show answer Space

entries.h: Mucosal Protectant · NG-254 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🛡️ What it does ⚠️ Watch for 🗣️ Teach ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / GI · Pharmacology Course · Acid-Reducer Family 4 of 4

Sucralfate & Misoprostol — barrier drugs, not acid reducers NG-254 GI · Pharmacology ADHD-friendly visual edition This class doesn't touch acid levels at all — it builds a physical shield over the wound instead. Compare with the acid-suppressing trio: PPIs (NG-140) , H2 Antagonists (NG-119) , and the master cheat-sheet on Acid Prevention (NG-233) . 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🛡️ Sucralfate = paste, not a pill for acid Forms a physical barrier over the ulcer — needs an acidic stomach to work. ⏱️ Emp
STEP 1 · BUILD A SHIELD Two drugs, two completely different jobs — one coats the wound, the other rebuilds the mucus that protects it.

entries.h: 🩹 Sucralfate — a bandage that needs acid to stick
entries.t: EXAM TIP Sucralfate (Carafate) is given to treat and prevent stomach and duodenal ulcers . It forms a thick, sticky paste that physically coats the ulcer crater , shielding it from stomach acid and enzymes — it does not neutralize or reduce acid . 🧠 “No acid, no armor.” Sucralfate is the opposite of every other drug on this page — it actually needs stomach acid around to turn into its sticky, protective form. Raise the pH too early (antacid, H2 blocker, PPI) and it never activates.

A synthetic prostaglandin that increases the protective mucous layer inside the stomach. NSAIDs work by blocking prostaglandins — which is exactly why chronic NSAID use erodes the stomach lining. Misoprostol replaces that missing prostaglandin. 🧠 “Miso replaces what NSAIDs erase.” Given specifically to prevent NSAID-induced gastric ulcers in high-risk, long-term NSAID users.

Sucralfate — treat & prevent gastric and duodenal ulcers Misoprostol — prevent NSAID-associated gastric ulcers 🧠 Neither drug is a first-line therapy on its own for most patients — they're used alongside acid reducers or specifically for NSAID-risk prevention. ⚠️
STEP 2 · SAFETY Sucralfate's biggest risk is a missed dose window. Misoprostol's biggest risk is a missed pregnancy test.
💩 Constipation — most common (aluminum-containing salt) 🩺 Caution in renal impairment — aluminum can accumulate with reduced kidney clearance

entries.h: 🚨 Misoprostol — major adverse effect: MISCARRIAGE RISK
entries.t: Reliable birth control is required for anyone of childbearing potential taking misoprostol. 🧠 “Miso starts labor — that's the danger.” The exact reason misoprostol is used in obstetrics for cervical ripening/labor induction is the exact reason it's dangerous in an unintended pregnancy — same drug, same mechanism.

Drug Do not combine with Why Sucralfate Antacids, other oral meds too close in time Antacids raise pH and block sucralfate's activation; also physically interferes with binding/absorption of other drugs Misoprostol Antacids Antacids decrease misoprostol absorption 🗣️
STEP 3 · TIMING IS THE WHOLE LESSON Get the clock right and this drug class works exactly as designed.

entries.h: ⏱️ Sucralfate timing — the whole teaching point
entries.t: 🧠 “Taken LATE, SucralfATE.” Give it on an empty stomach — roughly 1 hour before meals and at bedtime — and keep a 2-hour buffer from antacids or other meds so nothing raises the pH too soon.
💧 Give with a full glass of water 📋 Monitor bowel pattern — watch for constipation 🩺 Use cautiously with renal impairment 🕐 Do not give within 2 hr of an antacid or another acid-changing drug

🚨 Confirm negative pregnancy test before starting in a person who could become pregnant 💊 Ensure reliable contraception is in place throughout therapy 🕐 Space away from antacids 🗣️ Teach the patient exactly why — cervical ripening & uterine contractions

entries.h: 🔗 See it in context — the acid-reducer family
entries.t: Mucosal protectants are the odd one out on the potency ladder — they don't reduce acid at all, so they don't compete for "strongest" or "fastest." They're a completely separate strategy: physically shielding the wound while the acid-reducing drugs do the acid-lowering work. ⛽ NG-140 PPIs — irreversible, most potent 🚫 NG-119 H2 Antagonists — reversible, faster onset 📊 NG-233 Acid Prevention — master comparison table ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🛡️ Sucralfate Coats the ulcer — needs acid to activate, doesn't lower acid ⏱️ 1 hr before meals + bedtime, empty stomach, 2-hr gap from other meds 🌸 Misoprostol Replaces prostaglandin — prevents NSAID ulcers 🚨 Pregnancy danger Cervical ripening + contractions = miscarriage risk

Q1: Why must sucralfate be given on an empty stomach, separate from antacids? Show answer Sucralfate needs an acidic environment to activate and form its protective paste. An antacid (or H2 blocker/PPI given too close in time) raises stomach pH and can prevent it from binding to the ulcer. Q2: How does misoprostol protect the stomach? Show answer It's a synthetic prostaglandin that replaces the protective mucous-stimulating prostaglandins that NSAIDs block — used to prevent NSAID-associated gastric ulcers. Q3: What

entries.h: GI Key Terms · NG-293 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 📖 Words 🩸 Bleed & Acid 🧪 Labs ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / GI · Pathophysiology Course

The vocabulary every other GI page assumes you already know NG-293 GI ADHD-friendly visual edition Every GI diagnosis is a vocabulary test first. Learn these words once , here — dysphagia, reflux, PUD, hematemesis, melena, H. pylori — and the next three pages (Hiatal Hernia, Peptic Ulcer Disease, Gastritis) read like plain English instead of a foreign language. 📖 Learn it once These words repeat on every GI page — Hiatal Hernia, PUD & Gastritis all assume you already know them. 🩸 Up vs down Hemat emesis & melena =
PART 1 · SYMPTOM WORDS Trace the GI tract start to finish — each stop has its own vocabulary word waiting to trip you up on an exam.

EXAM TIP Match the word to the organ — most GI vocabulary questions are really anatomy questions in disguise. 🧠 “Top to bottom, name the trouble.” Esophagus = achalasia/dysphagia · Stomach & duodenum = PUD/gastritis · Small intestine = malabsorption · Colon = volvulus/megacolon · Rectum = where lower bleeding shows itself.

entries.h: 😮 Anorexia vs Cachexia — not the same word
entries.t: Anorexia lack or loss of appetite for food — the desire to eat is gone. Cachexia severe weakness & wasting of the body from chronic illness — the body is consuming itself , not just skipping meals. 🧠 “Anorexia = Appetite gone. Cachexia = Can't keep weight on.” Anorexia is about wanting food; cachexia is about the body's metabolism eating the patient alive.

Dysphagia difficulty swallowing . Achalasia the lower esophageal muscles fail to relax , so food can't pass into the stomach. Volvulus twisting of the intestine → bowel obstruction. Megacolon abnormal dilation of the colon with abdominal distention. 🧠 “V for tWisted, Mega for stretched.” Volvulus = pretzel-twisted bowel. Megacolon = balloon-stretched bowel. Both end in obstruction, opposite mechanism.

Malabsorption inability to absorb nutrients from certain foods. Lactose intolerance malabsorption of dairy — missing the enzyme lactase. Celiac disease malabsorption of gluten — an autoimmune reaction that damages the villi of the small intestine. 🧠 Lactose = milk. Gluten = wheat/barley/rye. Both show up as bloating, gas & diarrhea after the trigger food — the fix is avoidance, not a pill. 🩸
PART 2 · BLEED & ACID WORDS The ligament of Treitz is the dividing line — everything above it bleeds one way, everything below it bleeds another.

entries.h: 🩸 Hematemesis · Melena · Hematochezia — where is the bleed?
entries.t: 🧠 “Melena is Molasses from way up High. Hematochezia is Hot red, close to the exit.” Both start with hemat-/hemato- = blood; the ending tells you the form it takes on the way out.

Reflux stomach contents flowing backward into the esophagus. GERD G astro e sophageal R eflux D isease — chronic reflux. Dyspepsia "heartburn" — burning epigastric pain, not actually the heart. Epigastric pain pain in the upper-mid abdomen, over the stomach. 🧠 Dyspepsia sits behind the sternum, not inside it. That's why heartburn feels cardiac but is actually the esophagus.

PUD Peptic Ulcer Disease — acid erodes through the mucosa, an open sore/hole in the stomach or duodenum. Gastritis inflammation of the stomach lining — no hole yet, just irritated. H. pylori spiral bacteria that burrows into gastric mucus and drives both chronic gastritis and PUD. 🧠 Gastritis = irritated. PUD = a hole punched through. Same acid-vs-mucus fight, different depth of damage — see the Gastritis & PUD pages for the full picture.

entries.h: 🚨 Perforation → Peritonitis — one word you must recognize fast
entries.t: Perforation the ulcer erodes all the way through the stomach/duodenal wall. Peritonitis the leaked contents inflame/infect the peritoneal cavity — surgical emergency . 🌡️ Fever over 100.3°F · 🤲 rebound tenderness · 🪵 "rigid" or "board-like" abdomen · 📈 increasing pain · 😰 restless · 💓 tachycardia/tachypnea 🧠 "BOARD" — B oard-like rigid abdomen · O ver 100.3°F · A gitated & restless · R ebound tenderness + R ising pain · D ashing HR & RR. This exact word set reappears on the PUD page — memorize it once, here. 🧪
PART 3 · LABS THAT TALK Three organs, three panels — liver, pancreas, and the bacteria that connects to the next two pages.

🧠 "A-B-C, the liver's ID." A lbumin · B ilirubin · C lotting factors — the three things a sick liver stops making correctly. ALT/AST are the "leak" enzymes that spill out when liver cells are injured.
🧠 "AmyLASE = carbohydrateS, LiPASE = fat." Not protein — that's broken down by pancreatic proteases (trypsin). Both spike hard in pancreatitis.

Test What it tells you Urea breath test Non-invasive; detects active infection via labeled CO₂ Stool antigen test Non-invasive; can confirm eradication after treatment Biopsy during EGD Direct visualization + tissue sample; most definitive Serology (IgG) Can stay positive for life — not reliable to confirm cure 🧠 NCLEX trap: a positive IgG antibody test does NOT mean the infection is still active — antibodies persist. Use breath or stool antigen testing to confirm the bug is actually gone. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 📖 Anorexia ≠ Cachexia appetite loss vs. body wasting from illness 🩸 Melena = high & black Hematochezia = low & red 🧪 A-B-C Albumin · Bilirubin · Clotting factors = liver 🦠 H. pylori = root cause behind PUD AND Gastritis

Q1: What's the difference between hematemesis, melena, and hematochezia? Show answer Hematemesis = vomiting blood. Melena = black, tarry stool from an upper GI bleed. Hematochezia = bright red blood in/from stool, usually a lower source. Q2: A patient's IgG H. pylori antibody test is positive one year after treatment. Is the infection still active? Show answer Not necessarily — IgG antibodies can stay positive for life. Use a urea breath test or stool antigen test to confirm eradication. Q3: Which liver labs make u

entries.h: Hiatal Hernia · NG-294 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🧨 Cause 🔎 Clues 🩺 Care ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / GI · Pathophysiology Course

The stomach pushes up through the diaphragm NG-294 GI ADHD-friendly visual edition Part of the stomach herniates through the diaphragm and ends up sitting in — or beside — the esophagus. It's one of the most common causes of chronic reflux (see the GERD page, NG-036) because it drags the LES out of its normal high-pressure zone. See NG-293 Key Terms for dysphagia, reflux & epigastric pain. ⬆️ Stomach through the hole The hiatus = the diaphragm's opening for the esophagus. Herniate through it = hiatal hernia. 🔥 GERD
STEP 1 · THE WEAK HOLE The diaphragm has a normal opening for the esophagus — when it stretches wide, the stomach follows.

entries.h: 🫁 Two types — same weak spot, different behavior
entries.t: EXAM TIP Sliding = most common (95%) . Paraesophageal is rarer but is the one that can strangulate. 🧠 "Sliding SLIDES together, PARA rolls up PAST it." In sliding, the GEJ and stomach move together like a drawer sliding up. In paraesophageal, the GEJ stays anchored and the fundus rolls up alongside — that's the dangerous one.

entries.h: 🔤 Say the word — it tells you the disease
entries.t: Hiatus = the diaphragm's normal opening for the esophagus 🕳️ Hernia = protrusion of an organ through a weak spot ⬆️ Hiatal hernia = part of the stomach pushes through the diaphragm's esophageal opening , ending up in — or beside — the chest. 🧠 Same word family as an inguinal hernia — an organ escaping through a weak spot — just a different hole.

entries.h: ⚠️ Risk factors — what widens the hole
entries.t: 🏋️ Straining / lifting heavy objects 💪 Weightlifting exercises 📈 Increased abdominal pressure (coughing, pregnancy, ascites) ⚖️ Obesity 🧠 "Push down there, pop up here." Anything that raises pressure below the diaphragm forces the stomach up through it — the exact opposite direction of normal digestion. 🔎
STEP 2 · SPOT IT Reflux, swallowing trouble, and chest symptoms that mimic cardiac disease — plus the one complication that can't wait.

entries.h: 🔥 Signs & symptoms — same reflux pattern as GERD
entries.t: 😖 Dysphagia — difficulty swallowing (see NG-293) 🔥 Gastric reflux — heartburn / epigastric pain 💔 Chest pain & SOB — can mimic a cardiac event Because a sliding hernia drags the LES out of the diaphragm's high-pressure zone, it reproduces the exact same reflux pattern taught on the GERD page — worse when lying flat, better sitting up. 🧠 "Chest pain + SOB — rule out the heart first." A hiatal hernia can look exactly like angina. Cardiac causes get ruled out before anyone blames the diaphragm.

Barium swallow — outlines the herniated stomach on X-ray EGD — direct visualization, same scope used for GERD/PUD Chest X-ray — sometimes an incidental finding 🧠 EGD = "Every Gut Door" — Esophagus → Gastro → Duodenum, the same three-door scope from the GERD page.

🌀 Fundus rolls & twists (like a volvulus , NG-293) ▼ 🩸 Blood supply cut off ▼ ☠️ Necrosis / perforation — EMERGENCY 🧠 Sudden severe chest pain + can't vomit + can't pass a nasogastric tube = strangulated hiatal hernia until proven otherwise. This is a surgical emergency, not a diet fix.

entries.h: 📋 Sliding vs. Paraesophageal — tell them apart
entries.t: Type I · Sliding Type II · Paraesophageal ~95% of hiatal hernias Less common, more dangerous GE junction slides up with the stomach GE junction stays put; fundus rolls up beside it Main problem: reflux (GERD-like) Main problem: strangulation risk Usually managed medically (same as GERD) Often repaired surgically even without symptoms 🧠 NCLEX trap: not every hiatal hernia needs surgery — sliding hernias are usually managed like GERD. Paraesophageal hernias are the ones providers worry about even before symptoms show
STEP 3 · TAKE THE PRESSURE OFF Every intervention does one of two things: lowers abdominal pressure, or keeps acid from climbing — the same two levers as GERD.

1 🏋️ Avoid lifting / straining 2 👖 NO tight clothing — "girdle," tight waistbands 3 🍽️ Small, frequent, low-fat meals 4 🛏️ Sit up / elevate HOB after eating & at night 🧠 "Sound familiar?" This is the exact same "SEE-3" logic from GERD: sit up, elevate, eat small, wait before lying down — because it's the exact same LES/pressure problem underneath.

🚬 NO Tobacco ☕ NO Caffeine 🍫 Chocolate 🌿 Peppermint 🍺 Alcohol 🥓 High-fat foods go low fat Low fat diet = BEST — every item on this list can weaken the LES or raise abdominal pressure. 🧠 Same "midnight snack tray" mnemonic as GERD (NG-036) — every single item loosens the same door.

Nissen fundoplication — wraps the fundus of the stomach around the lower esophagus and sutures it, tightening the LES and reducing the hernia back below the diaphragm. Reserved for: paraesophageal hernias (often even if asymptomatic, due to strangulation risk), or sliding hernias with severe reflux unresponsive to medical management. 🧠 Fundoplication = Fold the Fundus 🎀 — same surgery referenced on the GERD page, because a hiatal hernia and GERD are treated with the same fix once medication fails. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD ⬆️ Sliding = 95% GEJ + stomach slide up together = GERD-like reflux 🌀 Paraesophageal = danger fundus rolls up beside esophagus = strangulation risk 🏋️ Avoid straining lifting, tight clothing, obesity all raise abdominal pressure 🎀 Fundoplication fixes the hernia AND tightens the LES

Q1: What's the difference between a sliding and a paraesophageal hiatal hernia? Show answer Sliding (Type I, ~95%): the GE junction slides up with the stomach — causes GERD-like reflux. Paraesophageal (Type II): the GE junction stays put while the fundus rolls up beside it — risk of strangulation. Q2: Why does a hiatal hernia cause the same symptoms as GERD? Show answer It drags the LES out of the diaphragm's normal high-pressure zone, so acid climbs the same way it does in GERD — worse lying flat, better sitting u

entries.h: Peptic Ulcer Disease · NG-295 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🧨 Cause 🔎 Clues 🩺 Care ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / GI · Pathophysiology Course

PUD — when acid finally wins and eats a hole through the wall NG-295 GI ADHD-friendly visual edition Gastric acid erodes the GI lining and creates an open sore — a hole — in the stomach or duodenum (rarely the esophagus). Same acid-vs-mucus fight as Gastritis (NG-296), just deeper — see NG-293 Key Terms for dyspepsia, hematemesis & melena. 🕳️ Mucus loses the fight PUD = acid eats all the way through the protective mucus + wall. 🍽️ Gastric hurts WITH food Duodenal hurts 2–3 hrs AFTER food & at night — opposite timin
STEP 1 · MUCUS LOSES Normally the stomach protects itself from its own acid — PUD is what happens when that protection fails.

entries.h: 🧫 The mucosa fight — protection vs. attack
entries.t: EXAM TIP Every risk factor either strips the mucus/bicarbonate layer or increases the acid attacking it . 🧠 "No mucus, no protection." This exact crater picture is the same mental model used on the Gastritis page — Gastritis is the mucosa getting irritated, PUD is the acid finishing the job and punching all the way through.

🦠 1. H. pylori bacteria — burrows into the mucus layer 💊 2. NSAIDs — naproxen · indomethacin · ibuprofen — block protective prostaglandins 😰 3. Stress — prolongs the ulcer, delays healing 🧠 "Bug, drug, and a bad mood." H. pylori (bug), NSAIDs (drug), stress (mood) — the three-way cause of nearly every PUD case tested.

Occur within hours of a traumatic event — linked to low blood flow/perfusion to the GI tract, called mucosal ischemia . 🔥 Curling's ulcer — after severe burns 🧠 Cushing's ulcer — after head injury / increased ICP 🧠 "Curling = Cooked skin, Cushing = Cranium." Curling's follows burns; Cushing's follows a brain injury. Both are ICU emergencies — patients often get prophylactic acid reducers for exactly this reason. 🔎
STEP 2 · TIME THE PAIN Gastric and duodenal ulcers hurt on opposite schedules — that timing is the highest-yield fact on this whole page.

entries.h: 🍽️ Gastric vs. Duodenal — opposite pain timing
entries.t: Gastric ulcer (stomach) Duodenal ulcer (duodenum) Pain increases WITH food — 30–60 min after meals Pain decreases WITH food , returns 2–3 hrs later — worse at night Weight LOSS — patients avoid eating Weight GAIN — patients eat to relieve pain More likely to vomit blood — hematemesis More likely melena — dark tarry stool 🧠 "Gastric = Grief with food, Duodenal = Delight then Delayed pain." If eating makes it worse, blame the stomach. If eating helps but the pain sneaks back a couple hours later (especially at night)
🤮 Hematemesis — vomiting blood 💩 Melena — black, tarry stool 📉 Dropping H&H, tachycardia, hypotension 🧠 Report black tarry stools to the HCP — every time, no exceptions.

🌡️ Fever over 100.3°F 🤲 Rebound tenderness 🪵 "Rigid" / "board-like" abdomen 📈 Increasing pain · 😰 restless · 💓 tachycardia/tachypnea 🧠 "BOARD" — same word set from NG-293/GERD. A board belly = report to the HCP now.

Chronic scarring/swelling near the pylorus blocks emptying → early satiety, bloating, nonbilious vomiting of undigested food. 🧠 Think of it as the ulcer's scar tissue becoming a speed bump the stomach can no longer empty over.

Test Client education EGD — Esophagogastroduodenoscopy NPO 8 hrs before · no smoking beforehand Upper GI series with barium contrast During: abdominal cramping expected. After: chalky white stool — increase fluids to flush the contrast; may need a mild laxative. 🧠 EGD = "Every Gut Door" — Esophagus → Gastro → Duodenum, same scope taught on the GERD page. 🩺
STEP 3 · KILL THE BUG, CALM THE ACID Treat the cause (H. pylori), reduce the acid, protect the mucosa — and teach what to never take again.

Standard therapy combines 2 antibiotics + a PPI (triple therapy) or adds bismuth (quadruple therapy): 💊 Amoxicillin 💊 Clarithromycin 💊 Tetracycline 💊 Metronidazole 🩷 Bismuth (Pepto-Bismol) 🧠 NCLEX trap: a PPI alone will calm symptoms but will NOT cure PUD if H. pylori is present — the antibiotics are what actually eradicate the cause.

Class Example Name clue Antacids 🧴 — "ANT-acid" = against acid H2 blockers 🚫 Ranitidine -tidine PPIs ⛽ Omeprazole -prazole 🧠 Same "TIDY the acid, PRAZOLE the pump" mnemonic from GERD (NG-036) — this ladder repeats across every acid-related GI page.

💊 Sucralfate — coats & sticks to the ulcer crater; give on an empty stomach , separate from antacids by ~30 min 💊 Misoprostol — prostaglandin analog; protects mucosa + reduces acid ⚠️ Misoprostol is contraindicated in pregnancy — it can induce uterine contractions/abortion 🧠 "Sucralfate = a bandage. Misoprostol = a baby's biggest NO." Always confirm pregnancy status before starting misoprostol.

💊 NSAIDs naproxen, ibuprofen, indomethacin ☕ Caffeine coffee, soda, tea 🍺 Alcohol 🚬 Cigarettes tobacco 🌶️ Spicy foods 🥓 Fatty / fried foods 🍋 Acidic foods 😰 Unmanaged stress prolongs the ulcer 🧠 "NCAAS" — N SAIDs · C affeine · A lcohol · A cidic/spicy/fried foods · S tress. Cut all five and the mucosa finally gets a chance to heal.

entries.h: 🎯 Common NCLEX question — Select All That Apply
entries.t: "The nurse is educating the client on peptic ulcer prevention. Which statements show correct understanding?" ✅ "I will not drink beer at the party this weekend." ✅ "I will avoid using naproxen." ✅ "I should avoid drinking excess coffee or soda." ✅ "I will start smoking cessation." ❌ "I will avoid spicy foods, but fried chicken is okay." — fried food is also a trigger; this statement is INCORRECT. 🧠 Watch for the half-right answer choice — it avoids one trigger but keeps another. SATA questions punish partial unders

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🕳️ PUD = acid erodes ALL THE WAY through the mucosa 🍽️ Gastric hurts WITH food Duodenal hurts 2-3 hrs later & at night 🦠 H. pylori needs antibiotics — a PPI alone won't cure it 🪵 Board-like belly = perforation/peritonitis → report to HCP

Q1: A patient's pain worsens 30-60 minutes after eating and they've lost weight. Gastric or duodenal ulcer? Show answer Gastric ulcer — pain increases with food, patients often lose weight from avoiding meals. Q2: Why won't a PPI alone cure PUD caused by H. pylori? Show answer A PPI only reduces acid — it doesn't kill the bacteria. Eradication requires antibiotics (e.g., amoxicillin + clarithromycin) combined with a PPI, or a bismuth-based quadruple regimen. Q3: Which drug used for PUD is contraindicated in pregnan

The timing trick: duodenal ulcer hurts about two hours after eating and food helps; gastric ulcer hurts within thirty minutes and food makes it worse. — swipe it sideways if it is cut off, or tap to open it full size. 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🧨 Cause 🔎 Clues 🩺 Care ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / GI · Pathophysiology Course

Inflammation of the stomach lining — PUD's earlier, shallower cousin NG-296 GI ADHD-friendly visual edition Gastritis = inflammation of the gastric mucosa — the same protective-mucus-vs-acid fight taught on the PUD page (NG-295), just shallower: irritated, not yet a hole. See NG-293 Key Terms for hematemesis, epigastric pain & H. pylori. 🔥 Acute = short & irritated Alcohol, aspirin/NSAIDs, spicy food — inflames but doesn't punch through. ⏳ Chronic = H. pylori Long-term inflammation → mucosal atrophy over years. 🎗️
STEP 1 · IRRITATED, NOT PUNCTURED Same mucosa-vs-acid fight as PUD — the difference is depth. Gastritis stops at "irritated"; PUD goes all the way through.

entries.h: 🧫 The mucosa fight — irritated surface vs. eroded crater
entries.t: EXAM TIP Gastritis is diffuse inflammation of the surface ; PUD is a discrete hole. Same attackers, different depth. 🧠 "Gastritis is a burn, PUD is a hole." Both live on the same mucosa-vs-acid diagram used on the PUD page — gastritis is the surface losing the fight, PUD is the surface being punched all the way through.

entries.h: 🔤 Say the word — it tells you the disease
entries.t: Gastro = stomach 🫙 -itis = inflammation 🔥 Gastritis = inflammation of the stomach lining . Two flavors: acute (short-term) and chronic (long-term). 🧠 Every "-itis" word in medicine means the same thing: inflammation of whatever comes before it.

🍺 Alcohol & spicy food 💊 Aspirin 💊 NSAIDs — naproxen · indomethacin · ibuprofen Patho: inflammation of the gastric mucosa — reversible once the trigger is removed. 🧠 "AAA-NSAID" — Alcohol, Aspirin, and NSAIDs are the acute triad. Same drug list as PUD's NSAID warning.

Type A · Autoimmune Type B · H. pylori Antibodies destroy parietal cells in the fundus/body H. pylori infection, usually the antrum — most common type Loses intrinsic factor → B12 malabsorption → pernicious anemia Strongly linked to PUD & gastric cancer 🧠 "A for Antibody/Anemia, B for Bug." Type A is autoimmune and causes B12-deficiency anemia; Type B is the bacterial one and is far more common. 🔎
STEP 2 · SPOT IT Acute gastritis announces itself; chronic gastritis often stays quiet until complications show up.

🤮 Hematemesis — vomiting blood 🔥 Epigastric pain ("heartburn") & cramps 😐 Chronic gastritis can be vague or asymptomatic — bloating, early satiety, dull dyspepsia 😵 Type A (autoimmune) may show B12-deficiency signs : fatigue, glossitis (smooth red tongue), paresthesias 🧠 "Loud when acute, quiet when chronic." Acute gastritis often hurts right away; chronic gastritis can hide for years until a complication forces the diagnosis.

⏳ Chronic inflammation, untreated ▼ 🕳️ Mucosal atrophy ▼ 🎗️ ↑ Risk: Peptic Ulcer Disease & Gastric Cancer 🧠 Type A chronic gastritis also raises pernicious anemia risk — always check a CBC and B12 level if it's suspected.

EGD with biopsy — confirms inflammation/atrophy, rules out cancer H. pylori testing — breath, stool antigen, or biopsy (see NG-293) CBC + B12 level — screens for anemia in chronic/autoimmune gastritis 🧠 EGD = "Every Gut Door" — same three-door scope used across GERD, Hiatal Hernia, and PUD.

entries.h: 📋 Acute vs. Chronic — tell them apart
entries.t: Acute Gastritis Chronic Gastritis Short-term inflammation Long-term inflammation → atrophy Causes: alcohol, spicy food, aspirin, NSAIDs Cause: H. pylori infection (Type B) or autoimmune (Type A) Usually reversible once trigger removed Can progress to PUD, gastric cancer, or pernicious anemia (Type A) Presents loudly: hematemesis, epigastric pain Often silent or vague until complications appear 🧠 NCLEX trap: "gastritis" alone isn't enough of an answer — know whether the stem is describing acute (reversible, trigger-
STEP 3 · REMOVE THE TRIGGER, HEAL THE LINING Stop what's causing the irritation, calm the acid, and treat H. pylori if it's the driver — same toolkit as PUD.

Class Example When used Antacids 🧴 — Quick symptom relief H2 blockers 🚫 Ranitidine -tidine Reduce acid production PPIs ⛽ Omeprazole -prazole Strongest acid suppression; part of H. pylori therapy Antibiotics 💊 Amoxicillin, Clarithromycin, Metronidazole, Tetracycline + Bismuth Eradicate H. pylori (Type B chronic gastritis) Vitamin B12 💉 Cyanocobalamin injections Type A autoimmune gastritis with pernicious anemia 🧠 Same acid-reducer ladder as GERD and PUD — the only new addition here is B12 replacement for autoimmune

🍺 Alcohol 💊 NSAIDs/aspirin 🌶️ Spicy food 🚬 Smoking ☕ Caffeine Small, bland meals during a flare while the mucosa heals. 🧠 Acute gastritis is often self-limited — remove the trigger and the mucosa heals on its own within days.

🩸 Watch for hematemesis / melena — sign of bleeding, notify HCP 🧪 Trend H&H if bleeding is suspected 😵 Screen chronic/Type A patients for B12 deficiency 🔬 Chronic gastritis needs periodic surveillance EGD given cancer risk 🧠 "Gastritis today, PUD or cancer tomorrow if ignored." That's why chronic gastritis gets monitored long-term, not just treated once. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🔥 Acute = short-term, reversible — alcohol, aspirin, NSAIDs ⏳ Chronic = long-term atrophy — H. pylori (Type B) or autoimmune (Type A) 😵 Type A autoimmune → ↓ intrinsic factor → B12 deficiency 🎗️ Chronic → risk ↑ risk for PUD AND gastric cancer

Q1: What's the pathophysiologic difference between gastritis and PUD? Show answer Gastritis is diffuse inflammation of the surface mucosa. PUD is acid eroding all the way through the wall, creating an open sore/hole. Q2: Name the two types of chronic gastritis and their key difference. Show answer Type A (autoimmune) — destroys parietal cells, causes B12 deficiency/pernicious anemia. Type B (H. pylori) — the more common type, strongly linked to PUD and gastric cancer. Q3: Why can't oral vitamin B12 fix a Type A gas

entries.h: Dumping Syndrome · NG-297 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🧨 Cause 🔎 Clues 🩺 Care ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / GI · Pathophysiology Course

Rapid Gastric Emptying After Stomach Surgery NG-297 GI ADHD-friendly visual edition The stomach empties too fast — undigested, hyperosmolar food "dumps" straight into the small intestine after eating, dragging fluid out of the bloodstream with it. Seen after bariatric / gastric surgery (gastric bypass, sleeve or partial gastrectomy). Comes in two timed flavors : early (fluid shift) and late (reactive hypoglycemia) — the exam wants you to tell them apart by the clock. 🌪️ Stomach empties too fast Hyperosmolar chyme d
STEP 1 · WHY IT DUMPS A surgically altered stomach can't hold food back — it floods the small intestine all at once.

entries.h: 🫙 A shortcut stomach empties in one big splash
entries.t: MECHANISM After bariatric/gastric surgery the pyloric sphincter is bypassed, removed, or resized — there's no "gate" left to slow food down. A hyperosmolar bolus of food dumps straight into the duodenum/jejunum instead of trickling in over hours. 🧠 “No gate, big splash.” Whatever slows the stomach down is gone after surgery — food doesn't trickle, it dumps .

entries.h: 🔪 Who gets it — post-op key terms
entries.t: 🍽️ Gastrojejunostomy — Billroth II surgery ✂️ Partial gastrectomy 👙 Sleeve gastrectomy 🩺 Any bariatric surgery (gastric bypass) — often for morbidly obese clients 🧠 If the stem says “status-post gastric surgery” + symptoms after eating → think dumping syndrome first.

entries.h: 💧 The osmotic pull, in one line
entries.t: Hyperosmolar chyme in the small bowel pulls water from the plasma into the intestinal lumen by osmosis. Result: intravascular volume drops fast → the classic early triad of hypotension, tachycardia, and bowel distension . 🧠 “Sugar pulls water.” Wherever concentrated solute goes, water follows — straight out of the vessels and into the gut. 🔎
STEP 2 · SPOT IT — WATCH THE CLOCK Same diagnosis, two completely different timers and two completely different mechanisms.

entries.h: ⏱️ Early vs. Late Dumping — the classic NCLEX pairing
entries.t: 🍽️ Meal eaten 15–30 min 🌪️ EARLY dumping 30–90 min 🙂 quiet window 1–3 hr 🍬 LATE dumping 🌪️ EARLY (15–30 min) 🍬 LATE (1–3 hr) Mechanism Hyperosmolar chyme pulls fluid from plasma → intestinal lumen → hypovolemia Reactive hypoglycemia — rapid carb load spikes glucose → insulin overshoots → glucose crashes Key signs ↓BP , ↑HR , diaphoresis, dizziness, flushing, cramping abd pain, N/V, urge to lie down, borborygmi (loud bowel sounds) Shakiness, sweating, confusion, palpitations, hunger, weakness — the classic hypoglyce

📉 Hypotension & tachycardia 💦 Sweating, dizziness 😣 Severe cramping abdominal pain 🤢 Nausea & vomiting ⏱️ All ~30 minutes AFTER eating 🧠 “DUMPing = DUMPing of blood pressure.” The name of the syndrome is the name of the vital sign that crashes.

entries.h: 🧪 Common exam question — walk through it
entries.t: Client recovering from a partial gastrectomy: vomiting, severe abdominal pain, BP 105/62 , HR 122 , T 100.5°F . Best nursing action? ❌ Administer a bolus of IV fluid (not first — not an independent action without an order) ❌ Assess blood glucose for hypoglycemia (that's the late-dumping workup, and still not the first move) ✅ Immediately notify the HCP/surgeon (correct — new post-op instability needs the provider now) ❌ Insert nasogastric tube (not indicated by this picture) 🧠 New tachycardia + hypotension + pain a

Any post-gastric-surgery client is also a fresh abdominal-incision client — know this emergency cold. 1 🧍 Stay with the client & call for help 2 🛏️ Position: low Fowler's, knees bent 3 🩹 Cover the wound with sterile gauze soaked in saline 4 📞 Report to HCP/surgeon 🧠 Never push organs back in, and never leave the wound uncovered. Do not let the client cough forcefully until it's addressed. 🩺
STEP 3 · SLOW THE DUMP Diet is the main treatment — slow the food down and take gravity out of the equation.

1 🥩 High protein, fiber & fat — low carbohydrate (simple sugars are the trigger) 2 🍽️ Small, frequent meals 3 🛏️ Lie down after eating — left side-lying , slows gastric emptying further 4 🚱 No fluids with meals — separate liquids by 30 min before/after food 🧠 “Slow, Small, Side, Separate.” Slow carbs · Small meals · Side-lying after · Separate fluids by 30 min.

🍬 Simple sugars candy, juice 🥤 Fluids w/ meals 🍞 Refined carbs white bread 🍦 Very hot/cold foods can worsen sx 🧠 If it's sweet and fast , it's off the menu — sugar is exactly what triggers both the fluid shift and the insulin overshoot.

🚫 NPO until bowel sounds return 🦵 Apply SCDs (sequential compression devices) 🚶 Early ambulation 💨 Incentive spirometer every hour while awake 🤲 Splint the incision when coughing 🧠 Same post-op bundle you'd use anywhere: move the lungs, move the legs, move the gut — carefully.

Persistent/severe dumping syndrome may need medication or, rarely, revision surgery. 💉 Octreotide (somatostatin analog) — slows gastric emptying & intestinal transit; used for refractory cases 🥄 Pectin / guar gum fiber supplements can slow carbohydrate absorption 🔪 Surgical revision — last resort if conservative measures fail 🧠 Diet changes come first — always. Medication is for the clients diet couldn't fix. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🌪️ Fast stomach empty = hyperosmolar dump after gastric surgery ⏱️ 30 min = EARLY, fluid shift, ↓BP/↑HR ⏱️ 1–3 hr = LATE, reactive hypoglycemia 🍽️ Small, low-carb meals + lie down after + no fluids with food

Q1: What causes early dumping symptoms? Show answer Hyperosmolar chyme dumps into the small intestine and osmotically pulls fluid out of the bloodstream — causing hypotension, tachycardia, cramping, N/V about 15–30 min after eating. Q2: What causes late dumping symptoms, and when? Show answer Reactive hypoglycemia — a fast carb load spikes glucose, insulin overshoots, glucose crashes — roughly 1–3 hours after eating. Q3: Name the 4 diet teaching points. Show answer High protein/fiber/fat + low carb; small frequent

entries.h: TPN & Enteral Feeding · NG-298 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 💉 TPN 🧃 Enteral ⚠️ Refeeding ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / GI · Med-Surg Pathophysiology

Two Ways to Feed a Client Who Can't Eat NG-298 GI ADHD-friendly visual edition TPN = complete nutrition through a vein , bypassing the gut entirely. Enteral feeding = nutrition through a tube into a working GI tract . Pick TPN when the gut doesn't work; pick enteral when it does — "if the gut works, use it." Both share the same deadly complication if you refeed too fast: refeeding syndrome . 💉 TPN = IV, no gut Hyperosmolar — central line only, never peripheral. 🧃 Enteral = tube, gut intact NGT/PEG/G-tube — HOB up 3
SIDE A · FEEDING THE BLOOD, NOT THE GUT Total Parenteral Nutrition — a bag of complete nutrition that skips digestion entirely.

entries.h: 🩸 What it is & why it needs a central line
entries.t: TPN delivers the client's entire nutrition — dextrose, amino acids, lipids, electrolytes, vitamins — straight into the bloodstream , bypassing normal digestion in the GI tract. Because the solution is very hyperosmolar (thick) , it must run through a large, high-flow central vein so it dilutes quickly instead of damaging a small peripheral vein. 🧠 “TPN is too thick for a thin vein.” Central line only — PICC, subclavian CVC, or internal jugular line, tip ending near the superior vena cava.

🔥 Severe pancreatitis (bowel rest, NPO) 🩹 Crohn's disease flare (NPO to rest the gut) 🔥 Severe burns / major trauma — hypercatabolic states 🧬 Prolonged bowel obstruction, short bowel syndrome 🎗️ Chronic malabsorption, some oncology clients 🧠 Reach for TPN when the gut is injured, obstructed, or needs total rest .

Never give IV push or piggyback meds through the TPN line ⏳ Start and stop slowly — taper, don't abruptly stop 🔁 Change bag & tubing every 24 hours ⚖️ Daily weights, strict I&O 🧪 Monitor glucose regularly (often q4–6h) 🧠 “One line, one job.” The TPN lumen carries TPN only — nothing else shares that line.

entries.h: 🚨 TPN complications — know the direction of each swing
entries.t: Complication Signs Priority action 🍭 Hyperglycemia Glucose >180 mg/dL , polyuria, polydipsia, N/V, headache, abd pain Monitor glucose, sliding-scale insulin per order 🩸 Hypoglycemia (abrupt stop) Shaky, sweaty, confused — because the pancreas is still pumping insulin for a sugar load that suddenly stopped Hang D10W (10% dextrose in water) immediately if a new bag isn't ready 🦠 Infection (CLABSI) Fever, chills, redness at insertion site Sterile dressing technique, monitor site, blood cultures if febrile 🔥 Stress ulc
SIDE B · FEEDING THE GUT DIRECTLY Tube feeding — used whenever the GI tract still works but the client can't eat by mouth.

entries.h: 🧃 What it is — tube into a working gut
entries.t: Enteral feeding delivers formula directly into the stomach or small intestine through a tube — the GI tract must be intact and functioning . Common access: NGT (nasogastric, short-term), PEG (percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy), G-tube or J-tube (jejunostomy, long-term/surgical). 🧠 "Gut works → use it." Enteral is always preferred over TPN when the GI tract can absorb nutrients — it's cheaper, safer, and preserves gut mucosa.

🛏️ HOB 30–45° during feeds and 30–60 min after 🔁 Continuous feeding preferred over bolus — especially on mechanical ventilation No bolus feeding via NG tube in a mechanically ventilated client 💧 Check gastric residual volume per protocol 🧠 "A-A" — A spiration & A irway obstruction are the two big enteral dangers. Elevate the head, keep it that way.

📍 Tube displacement/dislodgement 🎈 Abdominal distention 🧱 Clogged tube — flush with water before & after meds/feeds 🫁 Aspiration pneumonia 🧠 Key point: If a PEG tube dislodges and is less than 7 days old , the tract isn't mature — notify the HCP who inserted it before attempting to replace it.

entries.h: 🔀 TPN vs. Enteral — tell them apart fast
entries.t: 💉 TPN 🧃 Enteral Route IV — central line (PICC, subclavian, internal jugular) Tube — NGT, PEG, G-tube, J-tube Requires a working gut? No — bypasses the GI tract entirely Yes — GI tract must be intact/functioning Main risk Infection (CLABSI), hyper/hypoglycemia Aspiration, tube displacement/clogging Monitoring Glucose, daily weight, site/dressing, electrolytes Tube placement, HOB position, residuals, bowel sounds Shared danger Refeeding syndrome — if either is started too fast in a malnourished client 🧠 "If the gut w
STEP 3 · THE SHARED KILLER COMPLICATION Too much nutrition, too fast, in a starved body — the electrolytes crash exactly when the heart needs them most.

entries.h: 🚨 Mechanism — where the electrolytes actually go
entries.t: In starvation, the body shifts to fat/protein metabolism and total-body electrolyte stores quietly deplete even while serum levels look normal. Reintroducing carbohydrates too quickly spikes insulin — insulin drives glucose, potassium , magnesium , and phosphate all into the cells , and serum levels of these three crash. 🧠 "Feed fast, crash hard." The very electrolytes the heart depends on get dragged out of the blood the moment nutrition restarts too quickly.

🍽️ Anorexia nervosa, chronic alcoholism 🚫 Anyone NPO for a prolonged period before feeding starts ⏱️ Onset: 24–48 hours after starting enteral OR parenteral nutrition 🧠 Severely malnourished + fed aggressively = the classic refeeding setup.

entries.h: 🧪 The 3 electrolytes to trend (adult reference ranges)
entries.t: Electrolyte Normal range 🟣 Phosphate (PO₄) 3.0–4.5 mg/dL 🟢 Potassium (K⁺) 3.5–5.0 mEq/L 🔵 Magnesium (Mg²⁺) 1.3–2.1 mEq/L 🧠 "PKM" — P hosphate, K alemia, M agnesium — the refeeding trio, all trending down together.

🍽️ Aggressive refeeding in a malnourished client ▼ 📉 Hypophosphatemia + hypokalemia + hypomagnesemia ▼ 💔 Torsades de Pointes → V-fib → cardiac arrest Low magnesium is a classic trigger of Torsades de Pointes (alongside post-MI and hypoxia). Treatment: IV magnesium sulfate. 🧠 Prevention beats treatment: start nutrition low and slow, advance gradually over days, correct/replace electrolytes before and during feeding, and give thiamine supplementation for at-risk clients. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 💉 TPN = central line, bypasses gut entirely 🧃 Enteral = tube feeding, gut must work, HOB up 🚫 Never stop TPN abruptly = hang D10W if bag delayed ⚠️ Refeeding syndrome = ↓K⁺ ↓Mg²⁺ ↓PO₄ → Torsades — feed slow

Q1: Why must TPN run through a central line and not a peripheral IV? Show answer TPN is hyperosmolar/very thick — a peripheral vein can't handle it. A central line (PICC, subclavian, internal jugular) ends near the SVC, where high blood flow dilutes it immediately. Q2: TPN bag runs empty and a new one isn't ready. What do you hang? Show answer 10% dextrose in water (D10W) — to prevent rebound hypoglycemia from abruptly stopping the insulin-stimulating TPN solution. Q3: What's the #1 aspiration precaution for entera

entries.h: Irritable Bowel Syndrome · NG-299 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🧨 Cause 🔎 Clues 🩺 Care ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / GI · Pathophysiology Course

IBS — A Functional Gut Disorder NG-299 GI ADHD-friendly visual edition IBS is a functional disorder of the large intestine — cramping, bloating, pain, and altered bowel habits (diarrhea, constipation, or both) with no structural damage and no inflammation on scope or biopsy. Keep in mind: IBS is NOT IBD (Crohn's/ulcerative colitis) and it is NOT celiac disease — same symptoms, completely different pathology. 🌀 Functional, not structural The colon looks normal on scope — it's how it behaves , not how it looks. 🚩 Red
STEP 1 · WHY THE GUT MISBEHAVES Nothing is structurally wrong — the gut-brain signaling and motility are just miswired.

entries.h: 🌀 A functional disorder — the colon "acts up" without being damaged
entries.t: IBS involves visceral hypersensitivity (the gut feels normal stretch as pain) and altered motility (too fast → diarrhea, too slow → constipation), driven by dysregulated brain–gut axis signaling. There is no inflammation, no ulceration, no villous atrophy — a colonoscopy and biopsy in true IBS come back essentially normal. 🧠 "Miswired, not damaged." IBS is a signaling problem, not a structural disease — that's the whole reason biopsies look normal.

😖 Stress / anxiety 🍽️ Certain foods (gas-producing, high-FODMAP) 🦠 Post-infectious (after a GI infection) 🩸 Hormonal changes 🧠 Triggers flare IBS — they don't cause tissue damage the way IBD's triggers do.
IBS-D — diarrhea-predominant IBS-C — constipation-predominant IBS-M — mixed (both) 🧠 Same disease, three different bowel habits — treatment (fiber vs. antidiarrheal) depends on which one. 🔎
STEP 2 · SPOT IT — AND SPOT WHAT IT ISN'T Symptoms overlap with IBD and celiac disease on paper — the exam wants you to know the tell.

😣 Crampy abdominal pain, relieved by defecation 🎈 Bloating, excess gas 🔄 Alternating diarrhea & constipation (or one predominant pattern) 💧 Mucus in the stool ⏱️ Chronic/recurrent — ≥3 months , symptom-based diagnosis (Rome IV criteria) 🧠 Pain that gets better after a bowel movement is a hallmark of IBS.

entries.h: 🚩 Red flags that mean it is NOT just IBS
entries.t: Blood in the stool Unintentional weight loss Fever Nighttime symptoms that wake the client from sleep Symptom onset after age 50 🧠 IBS is a diagnosis of exclusion — red flags mean rule out IBD, celiac disease, or colorectal cancer first.

🌀 IBS Functional No inflammation 🩹 IBD (Crohn's/UC) Structural inflammation 🌾 Celiac Autoimmune Villous atrophy 🧠 Look, don't just listen. Same complaints on history — but only IBD and celiac show up on scope/biopsy. IBS never does.

entries.h: 🧪 Common exam question — spot the correct diet picks
entries.t: Which meal choices demonstrate correct understanding of an IBS diet? Beans · Cornbread · Fruit salad · Steak · Tomato basil soup · Yogurt with granola ❌ Beans (legume — classic gas-producer) ❌ Cornbread (refined, low fiber, doesn't help symptom control) ✅ Fruit salad (low-gas fiber source) ✅ Steak (protein, not a gas producer) ✅ Tomato basil soup (well-tolerated, non-gas-forming) ❌ Yogurt with granola (dairy + high-fiber granola can both trigger gas/bloating) 🧠 Correct answers = 3, 4, 5. The pattern: skip legumes,
STEP 3 · MANAGE THE TRIGGERS There's no cure — management is diet, stress control, and symptom-targeted medication.

📓 Keep a symptom/diet/stress journal to identify personal triggers 🏃 Exercise 3× per week 💧 Increase fiber & fluid intake — gradually , to avoid worsening gas/bloating 🧘 Stress management techniques 🧠 Journal first. You can't limit a trigger you haven't identified yet.
🫘 Legumes beans 🥚 Eggs 🥛 Dairy yogurt, milk 🍎 Some fruits gas-producing ☕ Caffeine 🍷 Alcohol 🧠 "LEDA" — L egumes, E ggs, D airy, A lcohol/caffeine — the reduce-and-limit list.

Symptom pattern Drug class / example Why 💢 Cramping / spasm (any subtype) Antispasmodics — e.g., dicyclomine Relaxes smooth muscle, reduces cramping 💩 IBS-D Antidiarrheals — e.g., loperamide Slows transit, firms stool 🚽 IBS-C Fiber supplements (psyllium), osmotic laxatives Adds bulk/water to soften & regulate stool 🦠 Either Probiotics May help rebalance gut flora & reduce bloating 🧠 Treat the bowel pattern , not just the diagnosis — IBS-D and IBS-C get opposite medications. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🌀 Functional = no inflammation, no structural damage 🚩 Blood, fever, weight loss = NOT IBS — work it up 📓 Journal + fiber + exercise = core management 🚫 IBS ≠ IBD ≠ Celiac = three different pathologies, same complaints

Q1: What makes IBS "functional" rather than structural? Show answer No inflammation, ulceration, or villous atrophy is found on colonoscopy/biopsy — the problem is altered motility and visceral hypersensitivity, not tissue damage. Q2: Name 3 red-flag symptoms that mean it's probably NOT just IBS. Show answer Blood in stool, unintentional weight loss, fever, nighttime symptoms, or onset after age 50 — any of these should prompt work-up for IBD, celiac, or colorectal cancer. Q3: How is IBS different from celiac disea

entries.h: Celiac Disease · NG-300 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🧨 Cause 🔎 Clues 🩺 Care ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / GI · Pathophysiology Course

Autoimmune Reaction to Gluten NG-300 GI ADHD-friendly visual edition An autoimmune reaction to gluten (the protein in wheat, rye & barley) causes the immune system to attack the lining of the small intestine , flattening the villi that absorb nutrients. Less absorptive surface = malabsorption of fats, nutrients, and fat-soluble vitamins. This is autoimmune , not functional (IBS) and not the same as inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) — three different diseases that all show up with GI complaints. 🌾 Gluten = the trigge
STEP 1 · GLUTEN TRIGGERS AN IMMUNE ATTACK One protein sets off an autoimmune reaction that flattens the gut's absorptive surface.

entries.h: 🏔️ Normal villi vs. celiac villous atrophy
entries.t: MECHANISM Ingested gluten triggers an autoimmune response that damages the small intestine's mucosa. The finger-like villi that normally increase absorptive surface area flatten out (villous atrophy) — nutrients, especially fats, pass through unabsorbed. 🧠 "Flat villi, empty tank." No finger-like projections left = no efficient absorption = malnutrition even while eating a normal amount of food.

entries.h: 🌾 The gluten grains — what to avoid
entries.t: 🌾 Wheat — bread, pasta, spaghetti, breaded meats 🍞 Rye 🍺 Barley — including most beer 🧠 "WRB" — W heat, R ye, B arley. Hidden in dinner rolls, breaded meat, spaghetti, and beer.

🧬 Genetic link — HLA-DQ2 / DQ8 , tends to run in families 🦋 Often coexists with Type 1 diabetes and autoimmune thyroid disease 🧒 Can present in childhood or adulthood 🧠 One autoimmune disease raises suspicion for another — celiac travels with T1DM and thyroid disease. 🔎
STEP 2 · SPOT MALABSORPTION Everything downstream traces back to one thing: fat and nutrients aren't getting absorbed.

🌾 Gluten ingested ▼ 🛡️ Autoimmune attack on small intestine mucosa ▼ 🏔️ Villous atrophy — absorptive surface lost ▼ 💩 Steatorrhea, weight loss, vitamin/mineral deficiency 🧠 Every symptom below is just this cascade wearing a different hat.

💩 Steatorrhea — fatty, foul-smelling, floating stools (fat malabsorption) 🌀 Diarrhea, abdominal pain, bloating ⚖️ Weight loss, fatigue (iron-deficiency anemia) 🧒 In children: stunted growth , delayed puberty 🦴 Osteoporosis/osteopenia (Ca²⁺ & vitamin D malabsorption) 🔴 Dermatitis herpetiformis — itchy, blistering rash 🧠 "Steatorrhea = the fat you didn't absorb, floating in the toilet."

Fat malabsorption takes vitamins A, D, E, K down with it. A night vision D bone health E antioxidant K clotting 🧠 "ADEK" — the fat-soluble vitamins go wherever fat goes. No fat absorption, no A/D/E/K absorption.

🧪 Serology first — tissue transglutaminase IgA (tTG-IgA), endomysial antibody (EMA) 🔬 Confirm with small bowel biopsy — shows villous atrophy Do NOT start a gluten-free diet before testing — it causes a false-negative result 🧠 Test first, treat second. Going gluten-free early erases the very evidence the test is looking for. 🩺
STEP 3 · LIFELONG GLUTEN-FREE The only treatment is diet — there is no medication that lets a celiac client eat gluten safely.

🍗 Plain meats — fish, beef, chicken, turkey 🌾 Grains: rice, corn, potatoes, soy, quinoa 🥜 Nuts, beans, legumes 🍎 Fruits & vegetables 🧠 "RCPSQ" — Rice, Corn, Potatoes, Soy, Quinoa — the go-to safe starches.
🍞 Dinner rolls 🍗 Breaded meat 🍝 Spaghetti 🍺 Beer rye & barley 🧠 Read every label — sauces, soups, and processed foods can hide wheat as a thickener.

entries.h: 🌀 Tell them apart — the 3-way mix-up (same as IBS/IBD)
entries.t: 🌾 Celiac Autoimmune Villous atrophy 🌀 IBS Functional No inflammation 🩹 IBD (Crohn's/UC) Structural inflammation Celiac = immune system attacking gluten-exposed mucosa. IBS = motility/sensitivity problem, nothing structurally wrong. IBD = chronic structural inflammation/ulceration independent of gluten. 🧠 Gluten-free helps celiac only — it will not fix IBS or IBD, even though all three can cause diarrhea and abdominal pain.

Gluten-free is not just wheat-free — rye and barley are excluded too Oats are naturally gluten-free but are frequently cross-contaminated during processing — advise caution unless labeled "certified gluten-free" The diet is lifelong , not just during symptomatic flares Monitor for fat-soluble vitamin deficiency (A, D, E, K) and iron-deficiency anemia even after diagnosis 🧠 "Lifelong, not just flare-long." Stopping the diet once symptoms improve lets the villi flatten right back out. ⚡
SAY IT OUT LOUD 🌾 Gluten = wheat, rye, barley autoimmune trigger 🏔️ Villous atrophy = malabsorption, steatorrhea 🅰️🅳🅴🅺 fat-soluble vitamins lost 🥗 Lifelong gluten-free test before treating

Q1: What causes celiac disease's intestinal damage? Show answer An autoimmune reaction to gluten (wheat, rye, barley) that attacks the small intestine mucosa, causing villous atrophy — flattened villi and a smaller absorptive surface. Q2: Why does celiac disease cause fatty, foul-smelling stools? Show answer Steatorrhea — with fewer villi to absorb fat, undigested fat passes into the stool. Q3: Which vitamins are at risk, and why? Show answer Fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K — they require fat absorption to be t
🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🧨 Cause 🔎 Clues 🩺 Care ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / GI · Pathophysiology Course

When the Gut Goes Quiet NG-301 GI ADHD-friendly visual edition Inability to pass stool — fancy words for: infrequent bowel movements or difficult passage of stools that persists for several weeks or longer . Defined as fewer than 3 stools/week plus hard, lumpy stools and straining. 🚽 <3/week = the rule Fewer than 3 stools/week + hard/lumpy + straining. 🧂 Fiber NEEDS fluid Fiber without fluid makes constipation worse , not better. 🪜 3-step ladder Laxatives → Fluid & fiber → Change habits. 🚨 Ache ≠ surgical belly Rig
STEP 1 · WHY THE GUT SLOWS Slow transit = more time for the colon to pull water back out of the stool.

entries.h: 🐌 Mechanism: slow transit = a drier, harder stool
entries.t: EXAM TIP The colon's job is to reabsorb water from stool as it passes through. The slower the transit, the longer water has to be pulled out — so a sluggish colon makes a harder, drier stool that is painful and difficult to pass. 🧠 "Slow gut, dry rock." The longer stool sits, the more water the colon steals back — a sluggish colon always ends in a harder stool.

😖 Stress 🥦 Low fluid & fiber intake — not enough fruits, veggies, whole grains 🛌 Immobility — bedrest, post-op, low activity 💊 Medications — opioids , iron, anticholinergics, calcium-channel blockers, aluminum/calcium antacids 🦋 Hypothyroidism — slows everything, including the gut 🧪 Hypokalemia — low K⁺ slows smooth muscle motility 🤰 Pregnancy , aging, ignoring the urge to go 🧠 "SLIM-HH" — S tress · L ow fiber/fluid · I mmobility · M edications (opioids!) · H ypothyroid · H ypokalemia.

entries.h: 🧂 The trap: fiber WITHOUT fluid backfires
entries.t: Fiber inflates with fluid to scrub the GI tract and bulk the stool. Too much fiber without high fluid intake can actually cause constipation — a dry fiber mass is harder to move, not easier. The fix is never fiber alone — it's fiber + fluid , together, every time. 🧠 Fiber is a sponge, not a broom. A dry sponge just sits there — it needs water to expand and do its job. 🔎
STEP 2 · READ THE STOOL The Bristol scale turns "what does the stool look like" into a number you can chart.

Use this scale to describe & chart stool consistency objectively — type 1–2 signals constipation , type 3–4 is the goal (normal), type 5–7 signals diarrhea. 1 Hard lumps “nuts” 2 Lumpy log 3 Cracked log 4 Smooth log ideal 5 Soft blobs 6 Mushy 7 Watery diarrhea 🧠 1–2 = plugged, 3–4 = perfect, 5–7 = flooded. Chart the number, not just "constipated" or "loose."
🚽 Passing fewer than 3 stools/week 🪨 Lumpy or hard stools — Bristol type 1–2 😣 Straining to have a bowel movement 🎈 Abdominal bloating, distension 🙁 Sensation of incomplete evacuation

A hard mass of stool becomes stuck ( fecal impaction ). Liquid stool from higher up leaks around the blockage and looks like diarrhea — this is fecal incontinence (encopresis) , an easy trap to mistake for the opposite problem. 🧠 "Leaky around the rock." "Diarrhea" in a chronically constipated client = check for impaction before you chart it as loose stool.

entries.h: 🚨 Tell it apart from an acute surgical abdomen
entries.t: Simple constipation pain is diffuse, crampy , and eases after a bowel movement. A different pattern means STOP — this is not simple constipation. 💩 Simple constipation 🚨 Acute surgical abdomen Pain Diffuse, crampy, comes & goes Localized — e.g. RLQ, worsening, constant Palpation Soft abdomen Rigid / board-like + rebound tenderness Vitals Normal Fever, tachycardia, tachypnea Action Fiber, fluid, laxative per protocol Report to HCP immediately — see Appendicitis (NG-302) 🧠 Never treat a rigid, feverish, rebound-tende
STEP 3 · REBUILD THE HABIT Three steps, always in this order — meds get the backlog moving, then fiber/fluid, then a rebuilt habit.

1 💊 Laxatives & stool softeners — get things moving now 2 🥦 Fluid & fiber — the long-term fix 3 🕐 Change habits — schedule regular toilet visits after meals (gastrocolic reflex), keep a bowel diary, use a reward system for effort 🧠 NCLEX TRAP: reward the effort — sitting on schedule, trying — NOT the bowel movement itself . Rewarding only successful BMs teaches shame, not habit.

Class Example / clue Bulk-forming 🌾 Psyllium (Metamucil) — needs fluid! Osmotic 💧 PEG (MiraLAX), lactulose, milk of magnesia Stimulant ⚡ Senna, bisacodyl — short-term only Stool softener 🧴 Docusate sodium — prevention, not rescue 🧠 Softeners prevent, stimulants rescue. Give docusate before straining starts; save senna/bisacodyl for when it already has.

💧 Fluids 1.5–2 L/day (unless restricted) 🥦 Fiber 25–30 g/day — increase gradually 🚶 Ambulation / regular exercise ⏱️ Respond to the urge — don't hold it 🌀 Abdominal massage, warm fluids in the AM 🧠 "Move it, wet it, feed it." Ambulation + fluid + fiber, every single day.

🚫 Chronic stimulant laxatives risk of dependence 🩸 Ignore blood in stool report — r/o cancer 🪵 Rigid, feverish belly = NOT simple constipation ⚖️ Unexplained weight loss refer for workup 🧠 New-onset constipation with weight loss or blood, especially in an older adult, is a red flag — not routine constipation teaching. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🚽 <3/week + hard stool + straining = constipation. 🧂 Fiber needs fluid or it makes things worse. 🪜 Laxative → fiber/fluid → habit always in that order. 🚨 Rigid + rebound + fever = surgical abdomen, not constipation.

Q1: How many stools/week defines constipation? Show answer Fewer than 3/week, plus hard/lumpy stools and straining. Q2: A client increases fiber but not fluid — what happens? Show answer Constipation can get worse — fiber needs fluid to expand and move through the GI tract. Q3: What's step 3 of the 3-step treatment ladder? Show answer Change habits — scheduled toileting after meals, bowel diary, and a reward system for effort (not for each BM). Q4: What does "diarrhea" in a chronically constipated client make you s

The Classic RLQ Surgical Abdomen NG-302 GI ADHD-friendly visual edition Inflammation of the appendix , located in the RLQ (Right Lower Quadrant) of the abdomen. Untreated, it can perforate → peritonitis — a medical emergency . 🎯 Pain migrates Starts at umbilicus → moves to RLQ / McBurney's point. 🙅 3 NEVERs NO heat · NO laxatives · NO enemas. 💉 NPO + IV fluids first Pain meds ONLY after the surgeon has seen the client. 🚨 Sudden pain relief = 🚩 Can mean the appendix just ruptured — not that it's "better." 🧨
STEP 1 · A BLOCKED TUBE One obstruction explains the entire cascade — from swelling to rupture.

entries.h: 🧭 Where it lives & the obstruction → perforation cascade
entries.t: 🧠 "Blocked pipe, backed-up pressure, blown gasket." Fecalith blocks → pressure builds → tissue dies → the appendix bursts.

Most often a fecalith (hardened stool) obstructs the appendiceal lumen. Can also be lymphoid tissue swelling, a foreign body, or a tumor. 🧠 Appendicitis = "the left-behind organ that gets clogged." No real digestive job — but it can still get plugged and become dangerous.

🚫 The appendix has no room to swell — a rigid tube 🩸 Swelling → cuts off its own blood supply → ischemia 💥 Ischemic tissue ruptures → gut contents spill into the sterile peritoneal cavity 🧠 A ruptured appendix is a race against the clock — this is why "watch and wait" is never the plan. 🔎
STEP 2 · READ THE PAIN PATTERN Where the pain starts, where it ends up, and what happens when you press and let go.

entries.h: 🎯 The classic pain migration — this IS the exam question
entries.t: COMMON EXAM QUESTION What's the typical pain presentation? Pain starts around the umbilicus, then moves to the right lower quadrant — described as "pain between the right hip area and belly button." 🔵 Vague, dull pain around the umbilicus (belly button) ▼ hours later 🔴 Sharp, localized pain at McBurney's point (RLQ) 🧠 Wrong-answer traps on this question: pain starting in the LUQ, radiating to the shoulder, or "diffuse all over" are distractors — the correct pattern is umbilicus → RLQ .

🌡️ Low-grade fever 📍 RLQ pain with rebound tenderness 🤢 Nausea, vomiting, anorexia 🪵 Rigid, "board-like" abdomen 💓 Tachycardia, tachypnea 🧠 "Rebound tenderness" = pain that spikes when you release the pressure, not when you press it — this is the hallmark peritoneal sign.
🧪 CBC — leukocytosis (↑ WBC) 📷 CT scan — confirms diagnosis 📡 Ultrasound — preferred in children & pregnancy ⚠️ Minimize repeated palpation — raises perforation risk

entries.h: 🚨 Complication: perforation = peritonitis — a medical emergency
entries.t: 🌡️ Fever — over 100.3°F 🤲 Rebound tenderness 🪵 "Rigid" or "board-like" abdomen 📈 Increasing pain, tenderness 😰 Restless 💓 Fast HR & RR (tachycardia / tachypnea) 🧠 Sudden, total pain relief after hours of steady RLQ pain is NOT a good sign — it can mean the appendix just ruptured and the pressure released. Report it immediately, don't chart it as "improved." 🩺
STEP 3 · PROTECT THE SURGICAL PICTURE Before surgery: don't mask it, don't move it, don't feed it. After surgery: get them up and breathing.

1 🚫 NPO — nothing by mouth, surgery is likely 2 💧 IV normal saline or LR (Lactated Ringer's) 3 💊 Pain meds: IV morphine/hydromorphone — ONLY after the surgeon has assessed the client 🧠 Why wait on pain meds? Masking the pain and exam findings too early can hide the very signs (rebound tenderness, location, rigidity) the surgeon needs to make the call.

🔥 NO heat pad or blanket 💊 NO laxatives 💦 NO enemas All three can increase pressure or blood flow to an inflamed appendix and trigger rupture. 🧠 Constipation care (fiber, fluid, laxatives — see NG-301) is the opposite of what an inflamed appendix needs.

Definitive treatment — surgical removal of the appendix, done urgently once diagnosis is confirmed to prevent rupture. 🧠 Appendectomy = PRIORITY once diagnosed — this is not a "schedule it for next week" surgery.

🚶 Early ambulation 🌬️ Deep breathe & cough + incentive spirometer 🛁 Shower ONLY no tub baths 🏋️ Avoid heavy lifting 👀 Report redness/swelling/drainage at incision site Prevent pneumonia: assist with early ambulation, deep breathing/coughing, incentive spirometer. Prevent infection: shower-only bathing, monitor incision. 🧠 "Walk, breathe, watch the wound." The three post-op jobs that prevent the two big complications — pneumonia and wound infection. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🎯 Umbilicus → RLQ the classic pain migration. 🙅 NO heat, laxatives, enemas all can trigger rupture. 💉 NPO + IV fluids first pain meds only after surgeon sees them. 🚨 Sudden relief = 🚩 rupture not improvement — report immediately.

Q1: Describe the classic pain pattern of appendicitis. Show answer Pain starts around the umbilicus, then migrates to the right lower quadrant (McBurney's point). Q2: Name the 3 never-do interventions before an appendicitis diagnosis is confirmed. Show answer No heat pad/blanket, no laxatives, no enemas — all can increase pressure or blood flow and trigger rupture. Q3: When can the client receive pain medication? Show answer Only after the surgeon has assessed the client — masking pain too early can hide key exam f
