entries.h: Diverticulitis & Diverticulosis · NG-303 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🧨 Cause 🔎 Clues 🩺 Care ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / GI · Pathophysiology Course

Diverticulosis vs Diverticulitis — Pouches vs Pouches on Fire NG-303 GI ADHD-friendly visual edition Diverticulosis = little pouches ("stress bubbles") on the colon wall — usually silent. Diverticulitis = those pouches become inflamed & infected — pain, fever, and a possible medical emergency . 🫘 -OSIS = pouches, quiet -ITIS = pouches inflamed & infected. 📍 LLQ pain "Left-sided appendicitis" — sigmoid colon. 🍿 Flip the diet Flare = low fiber/NPO. Quiet = HIGH fiber. 🚫 NO barium enema/colonoscopy during an acute fla
STEP 1 · POUCHES FORM, THEN CATCH FIRE Low fiber → chronic constipation → high pressure → pouches. Then something plugs a pouch and it gets infected.

entries.h: 🫘 Two stages of the same disease
entries.t: 🧠 "-OSIS is quiet, -ITIS is on fire." Same word root as every other -osis/-itis pair — osis = condition present, itis = inflammation happening now.

🥦 Low fiber diet → chronic constipation 📈 Increased pressure within the bowel from straining 🌰 Popcorn, seeds, nuts — classically taught to lodge in a pouch and trigger inflammation 👴 Aging — colon wall weakens over time ⚖️ Obesity, low activity, smoking 🧠 Note: newer evidence questions whether seeds/nuts/popcorn truly trigger flares, but this pairing is still classically tested — know it for the exam.

entries.h: 📍 Where it hurts — and why it's called "left-sided appendicitis"
entries.t: Diverticula form most often in the sigmoid colon (descending colon), which sits in the Left Lower Quadrant (LLQ) — a mirror image of appendicitis' RLQ location. 🧠 RLQ = appendicitis. LLQ = diverticulitis. Same pain pattern, mirrored side. 🔎
STEP 2 · SPOT THE FLARE Fever + LLQ pain + rising WBC = an active flare, not the quiet pouches.

entries.h: ⚖️ Diverticulosis vs Diverticulitis — the exam table
entries.t: 🫘 Diverticulosis 🔥 Diverticulitis What Pouches present, no inflammation Pouches inflamed & infected Symptoms Usually asymptomatic , found incidentally Fever & chills , LLQ pain Labs Normal ↓ H/H · ↑ WBC Diet High fiber — keeps bowels clean NPO → clear liquids → low fiber during flare Danger Low — manage with diet Can perforate → peritonitis — emergency 🧠 Flip the diet with the diagnosis: quiescent = load up on fiber; flaring = starve the inflamed pouch (NPO/low residue).
🌡️ Fever & chills 📍 Pain LLQ (descending & sigmoid colon) 🤢 Nausea, change in bowel habits
Decrease H/H (Hemoglobin & Hematocrit) — from bleeding/inflammation. Increase WBC — infection is present. 🧠 ↓H/H + ↑WBC — bleeding down, fighting cells up. Chart both.

entries.h: 🚨 Complication: perforation → peritonitis — Report to HCP
entries.t: 🪵 Rigid, "board-like" abdomen 📈 Worsening abdominal pain, distension 🌡️ High fever, tachycardia NCLEX TIP Report to HCP immediately — this is a medical emergency. 🧠 Same peritonitis picture as appendicitis (NG-302) — different organ, identical red flags. 🩺
STEP 3 · MATCH THE DIET TO THE PHASE The single most tested idea on this topic: the diet flips depending on whether the bowel is inflamed right now.

entries.h: 🍽️ Diet progression during an acute flare
entries.t: 🚫 NPO nothing by mouth 🥤 Clear liquids jello, broth, juices 🥣 Low fiber diet let the bowel rest 🥦 High fiber again once resolved HIGHLY TESTED Diverticulitis flare-up: NPO → clear liquid diet → low fiber → eventually back to high fiber. Diverticulosis (quiescent): high fiber diet = clean bowels & avoids constipation — the opposite instruction. 🧠 "Starve the flare, feed the quiet." Low fiber only exists to rest an inflamed bowel — it is never the long-term diet.
💉 IV normal saline 💊 Pain meds — morphine, hydromorphone 🚫 NPO — bowel rest 🌡️ Monitor for fever, rising pain, rigidity
💦 NO barium enema ↑ abdominal pressure 🔬 NO colonoscopy perforation risk Both procedures push pressure or air into an already-inflamed, possibly weakened bowel wall.

🥦 High fiber diet — cleans the bowel, prevents constipation 💧 Adequate fluids to go with that fiber 🚶 Regular exercise, avoid straining 🌰 Avoid: popcorn, seeds, nuts (classic teaching) 🧠 "POPCORN" — the classic 3: P opcorn · seeds/n O ts · avoid — P revent straining, C onstipation control, O bserve for flare, R egular exercise, N utrition = high fiber. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🫘 -OSIS = quiet pouches 🔥 -ITIS = inflamed & infected. 📍 LLQ pain = "left-sided appendicitis," sigmoid colon. 🍽️ Flip the diet Flare = NPO→low fiber. Quiet = high fiber. 🚫 No enema/colonoscopy during an acute flare.

Q1: What's the difference between diverticulosis and diverticulitis? Show answer Diverticulosis = pouches present, no inflammation, usually asymptomatic. Diverticulitis = those pouches are inflamed and infected — fever, LLQ pain, ↑WBC. Q2: What diet do you give during an acute diverticulitis flare? Show answer NPO → clear liquids → low fiber, progressing back to high fiber once the flare resolves. Q3: What diet is recommended for diverticulosis (no active flare)? Show answer High fiber diet — keeps bowels clean and

entries.h: GI Bleed · NG-304 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🧨 Cause 🔎 Clues 🩺 Care ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / GI · Pathophysiology Course

Gastrointestinal Hemorrhage — Upper vs. Lower NG-304 GI ADHD-friendly visual edition Bleeding anywhere inside the GI tract — the whole job is figuring out WHERE . Split the tube at the ligament of Treitz : bleed above it is an upper GI bleed , bleed below it is a lower GI bleed . Enough blood loss fast enough → hypovolemic (hemorrhagic) shock . 🩸 Coffee grounds & tar = UP Hematemesis / melena = upper GI bleed. 🍷 Bright red = DOWN Hematochezia = lower GI bleed. 🧪 Hgb < 7 = transfuse "Hemoglobin less than 7 = heaven"
STEP 1 · FIND THE TUBE, PICK A SIDE One landmark splits the whole GI tract into "upper" and "lower" — everything else follows from that split.

entries.h: 🗺️ The ligament of Treitz is the dividing line
entries.t: DEFINITION A GI bleed is bleeding anywhere inside the GI tract , classified as upper or lower — one of the biggest jobs is figuring out the exact location because it changes every intervention that follows (NGT? scope type? drug?). 🧠 "Treitz splits the tube." Above the ligament of Treitz = upper (mouth-side). Below it = lower (anus-side). Everything about a GI bleed — the symptom, the scope, the NGT rule — depends on which side.

🔥 Gastritis 🚪 GERD / esophagitis 🕳️ Peptic ulcer disease — most common cause 🩸 Esophageal varices — from portal hypertension / cirrhosis, can rupture & exsanguinate fast 🤮 Mallory-Weiss tear — forceful vomiting/retching 🧠 "GGPV" — G astritis · G ERD · P eptic ulcer · V arices. The V is the scary one — varices bleed the fastest and hardest.

🩹 Hemorrhoids — most common lower cause 🎗️ Colorectal cancer 🕳️ Diverticulosis 🔥 Ulcerative colitis 🌸 Angiodysplasia (older adults) 🧠 "HeCDU" — He morrhoids · C ancer · D iverticulosis · U lcerative colitis.

entries.h: 🚨 RED FLAG — call the provider now (hemorrhagic shock)
entries.t: Any GI bleed can outrun the body's ability to compensate. These signs mean the client is decompensating — report immediately: 📉 Hypotension falling BP 💓 Tachycardia HR > 100 🥶 Cool, clammy diaphoretic 😶 Pale skin 😵 Dizzy, fatigue 🧪 Hgb < 7 transfusion trigger 🧠 "Cool, pale, fast, low" — cool clammy skin + pale + fast HR + low BP is the classic hemorrhagic shock picture. Don't wait for BP to crash — tachycardia is the FIRST compensatory clue. 🔎
STEP 2 · READ THE BLOOD What color, and which end — that's the whole exam question.

entries.h: 🔬 Upper vs. lower GI bleed — side by side
entries.t: Feature ⬆️ Upper GI bleed ⬇️ Lower GI bleed Vomit Hematemesis — vomiting blood; classic "coffee-ground emesis" (blood partially digested by acid) Not typical Stool Melena — black, tarry, foul-smelling stool (digested blood) Hematochezia — bright red blood per rectum (fresh, undigested) BUN:Cr ratio Often elevated — digested blood protein is absorbed and broken down to urea Usually normal Scope used EGD (esophagogastroduodenoscopy) Colonoscopy 🧠 "Coffee grounds and tar are OLD — bright red is FRESH." The higher up t

entries.h: 🖼️ Coffee-ground emesis vs. bright red stool

entries.t: 🩸 Blood volume drops ▼ 💓 Compensatory tachycardia ▼ 📉 Hypotension — decompensating ▼ 🥶 Cool, clammy, pale, dizzy, confused 🧠 Tachycardia shows up before BP drops — it's the body compensating. Don't wait for hypotension to call it a bleed.

Low CBC labs = low H/H (hemoglobin & hematocrit). critical low normal Adult reference (varies by lab): Hgb M 14–18 / F 12–16 g/dL . Hgb < 7 g/dL = transfusion trigger. 🧠 "Hemoglobin less than 7 = heaven" — rhymes on purpose. Below 7 , send blood.

entries.h: 🧫 Diagnostics — Guaiac Fecal Occult Blood Test (gFOBT)
entries.t: 1 🧤 Gather supplies, wash hands, don non-sterile gloves 2 📦 Open card, apply stool sample to both boxes on the slide 3 🧴 Open the back, apply 2 drops developing solution, wait 30–60 sec 4 📝 Document results — blue = positive for occult blood Definitive location & source is found by EGD (upper) or colonoscopy (lower) — the scope both diagnoses and treats. 🩺
STEP 3 · STOP THE BLEED, REPLACE THE VOLUME Stabilize first, scope second, feed last.

1 Lower the head of the bed — improves perfusion to vital organs 2 IV normal saline — 2 large-bore IVs, stabilizes blood pressure 3 Oxygen 4 Blood transfusion — when Hgb < 7 , type & crossmatch PRBCs 🧠 "LOB" — L ower HOB · O xygen & IV fluids · B lood if Hgb < 7 . Also: keep the client NPO in case of emergency endoscopy.

entries.h: ❌ NGT lavage — upper GI only, one huge exception
entries.t: Nasogastric lavage (NGT) can be used to assess/clear an upper GI bleed. NEVER insert an NGT if esophageal varices are known or suspected — the tube can rupture the fragile varix and cause catastrophic bleeding. 🧠 "Varices + tube = trouble." If the chart says cirrhosis or varices, the NGT answer on the exam is always "no."

entries.h: 💊 Drugs that stop a variceal bleed
entries.t: 💧 Octreotide — reduces splanchnic blood flow & portal pressure 💊 IV PPI (e.g., pantoprazole) — reduces acid, protects a healing ulcer 🩸 Blood products — PRBCs, FFP, platelets as ordered 🧠 Octreotide = "shrink the plumbing." It squeezes down splanchnic vessels so varices bleed less.

entries.h: 🔪 Surgery / procedures — find it & fix it
entries.t: 🔭 Endoscopy (EGD) — upper GI: cauterize, clip, or band a bleeding varix/ulcer 🔭 Colonoscopy — lower GI: locate & treat the source 🩹 Angiography / embolization if bleeding can't be localized or controlled by scope 🧠 "Scope up = upper, scope down = lower." EGD goes in the mouth; colonoscopy goes in the rectum.

Client stays NPO before the procedure, then advances slowly once bleeding is controlled and gag reflex has returned: 🍎 Apple juice clear liquid 🍲 Broth soup clear liquid 🍵 Unsweetened tea clear liquid Advance diet as tolerated — clear liquids → full liquids → soft → regular, watching for return of nausea, pain, or bleeding. ⚡
SAY IT OUT LOUD 🩸 Coffee grounds / melena = upper GI bleed 🍷 Hematochezia = lower GI bleed, bright red 🧪 Hgb < 7 = transfuse (heaven) ❌ Varices = never NGT lavage

Q1: Client has coffee-ground emesis and black tarry stools. Upper or lower GI bleed? Show answer Upper — hematemesis/coffee-ground emesis and melena are both upper GI bleed clues. Q2: What lab value triggers a blood transfusion? Show answer Hemoglobin less than 7 g/dL — "Hgb less than 7 = heaven." Q3: Client with known esophageal varices needs gastric lavage. What do you do? Show answer Do NOT insert an NGT — it can rupture the varix. Notify the provider instead. Q4: HR 128, BP 84/52, skin cool and clammy. What's h

entries.h: Small Bowel Obstruction · NG-305 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🧨 Cause 🔎 Clues 🩺 Care ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / GI · Pathophysiology Course

SBO — Mechanical vs. Non-Mechanical (Paralytic Ileus) NG-305 GI ADHD-friendly visual edition A blockage in the small intestine — food, fluid & gas back up behind the block. Two flavors: mechanical (a physical block — adhesions, hernia, tumor, volvulus) and non-mechanical ( paralytic ileus — the bowel just stops moving). Untreated → bowel perforation & peritonitis . 🌀 The classic triad Colicky pain + distension + vomiting. 🚨 Fever + tachycardia + rigid belly = bowel perforation, notify HCP. 🎧 Bowel sounds tell locat
STEP 1 · WHAT'S BLOCKING THE TUBE Split obstruction into two categories: something physically in the way, or the bowel simply stopped moving.

DEFINITION A small bowel obstruction is a blockage in the small intestine that stops the normal flow of contents. 🧠 "Mechanical = something's IN the way. Paralytic = nothing works, PERIOD." One is a roadblock; the other is a stalled engine.

🩹 Adhesions (scar tissue) — from prior surgery, most common cause 🕳️ Hernias 🌀 Volvulus — twisting of the bowel 📥 Intussusception — bowel telescopes into itself 🎗️ Tumor (cancer) 🧠 "AHVIT" — A dhesions · H ernias · V olvulus · I ntussusception · T umor. Adhesions from a past surgery are the #1 answer.

entries.h: ⚠️ Non-mechanical (paralytic ileus) — think "why isn't it moving?"
entries.t: 🔪 Recent abdominal surgery (bowel handling) 💊 Opioids & anticholinergics slow motility 🧂 Electrolyte imbalance — hypokalemia is classic 🦠 Peritonitis / sepsis 🧠 A quiet, non-tender, evenly distended belly after surgery = suspect ileus, not a mechanical block.

entries.h: 🚨 RED FLAG — call the provider now (bowel perforation)
entries.t: An unrelieved obstruction stretches the bowel wall until it perforates → contents spill into the peritoneum → peritonitis is a medical emergency . 🌡️ Fever sudden 💓 Tachycardia 💨 Tachypnea 🪵 Rigid, board-like abdomen 🎈 Worsening distension 🧠 COMMON EXAM QUESTION Client with an SBO suddenly develops tachycardia, tachypnea, and a high fever. Most likely problem? Bowel perforation — notify the HCP immediately. (Not PE, pneumonia, or atelectasis — those don't fit a sudden fever + rigid abdomen picture in this context.)
STEP 2 · THE CLASSIC TRIAD Colicky pain, a swelling belly, and vomiting that won't quit — plus bowel sounds that tell you exactly where the block is.

⚡ Colicky pain intermittent, cramping 🎈 Abdominal distension 🤮 Frequent nausea & vomiting 🧠 "Colic, Cramp, Can't-keep-it-down." Three C-sounding clues = triad of SBO: C olicky pain, belly bloats like a b C alloon (distension), and C an't stop vomiting.
🧠 Loud before, quiet after. The gut is straining to push past the block (hyperactive above); nothing gets through to the segment below (hypoactive/absent).

🌀 Obstruction — pain, distension, vomiting ▼ 🎈 Worsening distension, dehydration, electrolyte loss ▼ 🚨 Peritonitis — medical emergency 🧠 If it's not relieved, the bowel wall stretches until it tears. Every unmanaged SBO is a countdown to perforation.

"Client with a small bowel obstruction suddenly develops tachycardia and tachypnea with a high fever . What is most likely the problem?" 1. Pulmonary embolism — ❌ no chest/leg clue given 2. Bowel perforation, notify HCP — ✅ correct answer 3. Pneumonia — ❌ no respiratory clue given 4. Atelectasis — ❌ doesn't cause fever/tachycardia like this 🧠 New fever + tachycardia + tachypnea in the context of a known obstruction = perforation until proven otherwise. 🩺
STEP 3 · REST THE GUT, RELIEVE THE PRESSURE Stop feeding it, decompress it, and don't slow it down further with opioids.

1 NPO — nothing by mouth, rest the bowel 2 NGT insertion — nasogastric tube for decompression + IV fluids 3 Semi-Fowler's position 4 Pain control — non-opioid preferred 🧠 "NNSP" — N PO · N GT · S emi-Fowler's · P ain control (non-opioid). Rest it, drain it, sit it up, treat pain smartly.

Opioids further slow GI motility — the last thing a stalled bowel needs. 💊 Morphine 💊 Hydrocodone 💊 Hydromorphone 🧠 Opioids = "constipation in a syringe." They slow the very motility the bowel is already failing at.

Clients who fail to improve need a bowel resection to remove the diseased/dead segment, and may need a temporary ostomy until the bowel heals. 🧠 NGT + NPO buys time — surgery is the fallback if the obstruction won't resolve or perforation occurs.

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🌀 Triad Colicky pain + distension + vomiting 🚧 Mechanical = physical block (adhesions #1 cause) 😴 Paralytic ileus = bowel just stops moving ❌ No opioids NPO + NGT + semi-Fowler's + non-opioid pain control

Q1: What's the classic triad of small bowel obstruction? Show answer Colicky abdominal pain, abdominal distension, and frequent nausea/vomiting. Q2: Client's bowel sounds are hyperactive in the upper abdomen and absent lower down. What does that tell you? Show answer The obstruction is between the two — hyperactive sounds occur above the block, hypoactive/absent sounds occur below it. Q3: What's the most common cause of mechanical SBO? Show answer Adhesions (scar tissue) from prior abdominal surgery. Q4: Why avoid

entries.h: Colon & Esophageal Cancer · NG-306 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🧨 Risk Factors 🔎 Clues 🩺 Screening & Care ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / GI · Pathophysiology Course

Risk Factors, Screening & Early Clues NG-306 GI ADHD-friendly visual edition Colorectal cancer = cancer of the colon (large intestine) & rectum, the "exit door" of the GI tract. Esophageal cancer = cancer of the "food tube" carrying food from mouth to stomach. Both share the same three modifiable risk factors — Obesity, Alcohol, Tobacco — and both are caught early with screening , not waiting for symptoms. 🔤 "OAT" risk factors Obesity · Alcohol · Tobacco — shared by both cancers. 🔥 GERD → Barrett's → cancer Chronic
STEP 1 · WHO'S AT RISK Two different organs, the same three lifestyle risks, plus organ-specific ones.

O — Obesity (BMI over 30 ) A — Alcohol T — Tobacco (cigarettes, cigars, chewing tobacco) 🧠 "Eat your OATs — or don't." Obesity, Alcohol, Tobacco raise the risk of BOTH colorectal and esophageal cancer — and they're the same three things you teach the client to change.

🕳️ Diverticulosis 🔥 Ulcerative colitis (long-term, chronic inflammation) 🧬 Family history of colorectal cancer 🧠 Long-standing colon inflammation (UC, Crohn's) + family history = earlier & more frequent screening than average risk. Most colorectal cancer follows this polyp → cancer sequence over years — which is exactly why screening catches it early.

🔥 Chronic GERD / acid reflux — the #1 organ-specific risk 📈 Untreated reflux → esophagitis → Barrett's esophagus → cancer 🧠 Barrett's = the "burnt" esophagus. It's a precancerous change (normal cells replaced by intestinal-type cells) — the reason GERD is treated seriously, not just as heartburn. 🔎
STEP 2 · SPOT IT EARLY Early cancer is often silent — these are the clues that finally show up, plus the exact exam scenario.

A — Abdominal pain B — Bleeding : blood in stools, low hemoglobin C — Change in bowel habits Unexplained weight loss is also a major red-flag clue for both cancers. 🧠 "ABC — and don't forget the C" (weight loss). Any client with new bowel habit changes + unexplained weight loss + falling H&H needs a colonoscopy, not reassurance.

🍽️ Dysphagia — progressive difficulty swallowing (solids → liquids) ⚖️ Unexplained weight loss 😖 Chest/retrosternal pain 🍽️ Odynophagia — painful swallowing 🧠 Esophageal cancer symptoms often start subtle and progress — "food gets stuck" is the classic early complaint.

Client with a family history of colorectal cancer , unexplained weight loss , change in bowel habits , and Hgb of 9 (down from 14 just 12 months earlier) — which diagnostic test is expected? Correct answer: Colonoscopy 🧠 A dropping H&H over months + bowel habit change + family history = colon cancer workup, and the test is always the scope.

entries.h: 🚨 Post-colonoscopy complication — perforation is an emergency
entries.t: 🌡️ Fever 💓 Tachycardia 💨 Tachypnea 🪵 Rigid, board-like abdomen = distension A perforated bowel spills contents into the peritoneum → peritonitis, a medical emergency. 🧠 Any procedure that goes through bowel wall (colonoscopy, EGD) carries the same perforation red flags — memorize this cluster once, apply it everywhere. 🩺
STEP 3 · CATCH IT EARLY, MODIFY THE RISK Screening intervals, bowel prep, and the same three lifestyle changes that lower risk for both cancers.

Risk category Screening plan Average risk Start age 45 , repeat every 10 years if normal Family history of colorectal cancer Start earlier & screen more often — provider individualizes timing Ulcerative colitis / Crohn's (long-standing) More frequent surveillance colonoscopy per GI provider 🧠 "45 and alive, every decade you thrive" — average-risk screening starts at 45 , repeats every 10 years if results are normal.

🥤 Clear liquid diet + laxative bowel prep — e.g., polyethylene glycol (brand: GoLYTELY ) 🌙 NPO after midnight 🧠 A clean colon = a scope that actually sees the polyp. Bowel prep compliance is the #1 reason a screening exam fails.

entries.h: 🔭 What the scope is used for
entries.t: Passed up through the rectum to inspect the colon for tumors, polyps , and to evaluate other GI conditions like ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease . 🧠 It's both a screening tool AND a treatment tool — polyps can be removed (polypectomy) during the same procedure.

O Obesity → lose weight — BMI goal < 30 A Alcohol → stop T Tobacco → smoking cessation High-fiber diet (e.g., cabbage, whole grains) also supports colon health and regular bowel elimination. 🧠 Same "OAT" letters from risk factors become the teaching plan — reduce the exact same three things that raised the risk. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🔤 OAT Obesity · Alcohol · Tobacco — shared risk, shared teaching 🔥 GERD → Barrett's → cancer The esophageal cancer pathway 🔭 Age 45 , every 10 years Average-risk colonoscopy screening 📉 ABC Abdominal pain · Bleeding · Change in bowel habits

Q1: What three lifestyle risk factors raise the risk of BOTH colorectal and esophageal cancer? Show answer Obesity, Alcohol, Tobacco — "OAT." Q2: What untreated condition can progress to esophageal cancer, and what's the precancerous step in between? Show answer Chronic untreated GERD → esophagitis → Barrett's esophagus (precancerous) → esophageal cancer. Q3: When does average-risk colorectal cancer screening start, and how often does it repeat? Show answer Age 45, repeated every 10 years if colonoscopy results are

entries.h: 🍽️ Pediatric GI — Pyloric Stenosis, Intussusception & Hirschsprung
entries.t: Three conditions defined by how the baby vomits and what the stool looks like.

Three completely different pictures of a gut. Once you can see the blockage in each, the vomit and the stool stop needing to be memorized. Swipe it sideways if it is cut off, or tap to open it full size. Pyloric stenosis Intussusception Hirschsprung Age 3–6 weeks 6 months–3 years Newborn Vomit Projectile , non-bilious Bile-stained Bile-stained Stool Constipated, small Currant-jelly — blood and mucus Ribbon-like ; no meconium in 48 h Abdomen Olive-shaped mass RUQ; visible peristaltic waves Sausage-shaped mass ; chil

The pyloric muscle thickens and blocks the stomach outlet. Metabolic alkalosis with hypokalemia and hypochloremia — from losing gastric acid Dehydration, weight loss, fewer wet diapers Treated surgically (pyloromyotomy); feeds resume within hours The acid-base picture is the exam point: vomiting stomach contents means losing hydrogen and chloride, so the blood turns alkalotic.

One segment of bowel telescopes into the next , cutting off its blood supply. Sudden severe intermittent pain — the child draws the knees to the chest and screams, then is calm between episodes Currant-jelly stool — blood and mucus Palpable sausage-shaped mass A normal brown stool before surgery may mean the bowel has reduced itself. Report it immediately - the operation may be canceled. Treated by air or contrast enema , which often reduces it; surgery if that fails or the bowel is necrotic.

A segment of colon has no ganglion cells , so it cannot relax and propel stool. No meconium within 48 hours — the classic newborn clue Ribbon-like, foul stools; distension; poor feeding Diagnosed by rectal biopsy; treated surgically Watch for enterocolitis - explosive diarrhea, fever and a rapidly worsening child. It is the life-threatening complication.

entries.h: 🩺 Dehydration — the thread through all of them
entries.t: Weight change is the most accurate measure of fluid loss in a child. Children have proportionally more body water and lose it faster than adults. Sign Mild Moderate Severe Weight loss 3–5% 6–9% ≥10% Capillary refill <2 s 2–3 s >3 s Mucous membranes Slightly dry Dry Parched, no tears Urine Slightly reduced Reduced, dark Minimal or none Behavior Normal, thirsty Irritable Lethargic , sunken fontanelle In an infant, the earliest reliable signs are fewer wet diapers and no tears when crying. Ask about both, every time.

Projectile vomiting + still hungry + olive mass = pyloric stenosis , with metabolic alkalosis Currant-jelly stool = intussusception ; a normal stool before surgery must be reported No meconium in 48 hours = Hirschsprung Daily weight is the best measure of dehydration ORS, not water or juice Sources. Written from CDC , HealthyChildren.org (AAP) , MedlinePlus and OpenStax A&P 2e (CC BY 4.0).

entries.h: 👶 Cleft Lip & Palate, PKU & Newborn Screening
entries.t: Feeding a baby who cannot make suction, and the two screened conditions where early treatment prevents permanent damage.

She cannot make suction. That single mechanical fact explains the bottle, the upright hold and the constant burping. Swipe it sideways if it is cut off, or tap to open it full size. The lip and palate fuse early in pregnancy. When fusion is incomplete the baby cannot generate suction, so feeding is the immediate problem and speech is the long-term one. Cleft lip Cleft palate Repaired at 2–3 months (often quoted 10 weeks) 9–18 months , before speech develops Main problem Appearance, some feeding Feeding, speech, rec

Special wide-based or squeezable bottle with a long soft nipple Hold upright — near-sitting — to reduce nasal regurgitation and aspiration Burp frequently — they swallow a lot of air Aim to finish a feed in about 20–30 minutes ; longer burns more calories than it delivers Breastfeeding is often possible with an isolated cleft lip The first priority is always weight gain , because surgery requires adequate growth.

Nothing hard or pointed in the mouth - no straws, no spoons into the mouth, no pacifiers, no suctioning of the suture line. Elbow restraints to stop hands reaching the face — removed regularly for range of movement and cuddles Position: after lip repair, on the back or side , never prone on the suture line. After palate repair, prone or side-lying is often allowed to drain secretions — follow the surgeon Prevent crying — it stresses the suture line. Anticipate needs, cuddle, medicate for pain Clean the suture line

The heel-prick screen looks for conditions where early treatment prevents permanent damage and late treatment cannot undo it. Taken after the baby has had 24–48 hours of feeding — some tests need protein intake to be accurate.

The enzyme that breaks down phenylalanine is missing, so it builds up and damages the developing brain. Untreated → irreversible intellectual disability , seizures, a musty body odor, fair hair and skin Treated → normal development . The entire difference is diet Lifelong low-phenylalanine diet: restrict high-protein foods — meat, fish, eggs, dairy, nuts, beans — with a special formula providing the rest. Aspartame contains phenylalanine. Diet drinks and sugar-free products must be avoided - that is why they carry

Also screened, also silent at birth, also causes irreversible intellectual disability if missed. Late signs: prolonged jaundice, poor feeding, constipation, large tongue, hoarse cry, sluggishness, cool mottled skin. Lifelong levothyroxine started early prevents all of it. Crush the tablet and give in a small amount of formula or water — never in a full bottle, because an unfinished feed means an unknown dose .

Sickle cell disease, cystic fibrosis, galactosemia, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, and various metabolic disorders — the exact list varies by state or country. A positive screen is not a diagnosis — it triggers confirmatory testing. Say that clearly to parents, who are usually frightened by the call.

Cleft lip repaired ~2–3 months; palate ~9–18 months Nothing pointed in the mouth after repair; elbow restraints Prevent crying — it stresses the suture line PKU = low-phenylalanine diet for life ; no aspartame Screen needs 24–48 hours of feeding first Congenital hypothyroidism: start levothyroxine early , never in a full bottle Sources. Written from CDC Diabetes , NIDDK , HealthyChildren.org (AAP) and MedlinePlus .

Rigid abdomen · rebound tenderness · a surgical emergency NG-397 Gastrointestinal ADHD-friendly visual edition The peritoneum is inflamed, almost always because something perforated and spilled into it. The abdomen becomes board-like and silent , and she will not let you press on it. This is a surgical problem, not a medical one. Liters of fluid leave the circulation and sit in her abdomen doing nothing. That is why the blood pressure falls while the abdomen gets bigger. Swipe it sideways if it is cut off, or tap to open it full size. What spills, and what happens next A hollow organ perforates — a ruptured appendix, a perforated ulcer, diverticulitis, bowel obstruction, trauma. Gastric contents, stool or bile enter the sterile peritoneal cavity. Bacteria multiply fast. The peritoneum inflames and weeps fluid — liters of it — out of the cir

How she presents Severe, constant abdominal pain , worse with any movement — even the bed being bumped. Rigid, board-like abdomen. Involuntary guarding — she cannot relax it. Rebound tenderness — it hurts more when you release than when you press. Absent bowel sounds , distension, nausea and vomiting. She lies still with her knees drawn up . Anyone rolling around is probably colicky, not peritonitic. Fever, tachycardia, shallow rapid breathing — deep breaths hurt. Later: hypotension, oliguria, altered mental status

What you do Nothing by mouth. Immediately. NG tube to suction — decompresses the gut and stops more spilling. Large-bore IV, aggressive fluids. She has lost liters into her abdomen. Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics after cultures. Semi-Fowler’s — it localizes the contamination to the lower abdomen and eases breathing. Analgesia, oxygen, urinary catheter to track output. Prepare for surgery. The source has to be closed. What you monitor Urine output — the first thing to fall when she is volume depleted. Under 30 mL/hr

The further along the bowel the stoma sits, the thicker the output and the lower the fluid loss. That sentence answers most of the questions. Swipe it sideways if it is cut off, or tap to open it full size. Three ostomies, three outputs Ileostomy — from the small bowel. Output is liquid to semi-liquid, continuous, and enzyme-rich . Highest risk of dehydration, electrolyte loss and skin breakdown. Expect 500 to 1300 mL a day. Colostomy — from the large bowel. The further along, the more water has been reabsorbed: as

Assessing it Color: pink to beefy red is healthy. Pale, dusky, purple, black — report. Moisture: moist and shiny is healthy. Dry and dull is not. Height: should protrude slightly. A retracted stoma leaks under the wafer; a prolapsed one telescopes out and needs review. Surrounding skin: intact, no redness or erosion. Excoriation means the appliance is leaking or the opening is cut too large. Output: amount, consistency and color, matched to the type. What to report Any color other than pink or red No output for 4 t

Appliance technique Empty the pouch when it is one-third to one-half full. A heavy pouch pulls the wafer off. Change the wafer every 3 to 7 days , or immediately if it leaks. Change it in the morning before eating , when output is lowest. Measure the stoma and cut the opening 1/8 inch (2 to 3 mm) larger . Too big exposes skin to effluent; too small strangles the stoma. entries.h: Lab tests by condition · ABSN Study Hub
entries.t: 🏠 ABSN Study Hub 🧠 Super Mega Quiz 🩺 Bedside tests ABSN Study Hub

Start from the disease, not the test. Every condition below lists the test that confirms it, the ones that back it up, and the ones you keep watching — and what an abnormal result actually means. CONFIRMS is the test that makes the diagnosis — the one an exam question is usually asking for. SUPPORTS points that way without settling it. MONITOR is what you keep checking once treatment starts. Search a condition, a test, or a value 📕 All 🫀 Heart & vessels 🫁 Lungs & breathing 🚰 Kidney & urinary 🧪 Endocrine 🩸 Blood & i

Tests for Myocardial infarction (MI) Test What the result tells you Troponin I or T confirms The one that confirms it. Rises 3–4 h after the injury, peaks 12–24 h, and stays up 10–14 days. Most specific to cardiac muscle — a raised troponin with chest pain is an MI until proven otherwise. 12-lead ECG confirms Done within 10 minutes of the door. ST elevation = STEMI and the cath lab is activated; ST depression or T inversion = NSTEMI. CK-MB supports Rises 4–6 h, back to normal in 48–72 h. Because it clears fast it i

Tests for Heart failure Test What the result tells you BNP / NT-proBNP confirms The lab that separates cardiac from pulmonary shortness of breath. Under 100 makes heart failure unlikely; over 400 makes it likely. Released by stretched ventricles. Echocardiogram confirms Confirms it and gives the ejection fraction — under 40% is reduced (systolic), preserved EF points to diastolic failure. Chest X-ray supports Big heart, pulmonary congestion, pleural effusions. BMP and creatinine monitor Watched constantly on diuret

Tests for Infective endocarditis Test What the result tells you Blood cultures confirms Three sets from three different sites, drawn before the first antibiotic. This is the confirming test and the order matters more than the speed. Transesophageal echo confirms Shows the vegetations on the valve. ESR and CRP monitor Raised, and they track whether the treatment is working. Read the full page on Infective endocarditis →

Tests for Pericarditis Test What the result tells you ECG confirms Diffuse ST elevation in nearly every lead with PR depression — the pattern that separates it from an MI, where elevation is regional. Echocardiogram confirms Looks for the effusion and for tamponade. ESR, CRP, WBC supports Raised with the inflammation. Troponin supports Can be mildly up if the muscle underneath is irritated — not as high as an MI. Read the full page on Pericarditis →

Tests for Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) Test What the result tells you Venous duplex ultrasound confirms The confirming test — non-invasive, and it sees the clot. D-dimer supports Very sensitive, not at all specific. A negative D-dimer is the useful result: it rules a clot out. A positive one only means go and look. PT/INR and aPTT monitor Baseline before anticoagulation starts, then the number you titrate to. Platelet count monitor Checked on heparin — a falling platelet count is heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. Rea

Tests for Pulmonary embolism Test What the result tells you CT pulmonary angiogram confirms The confirming test. Check BUN and creatinine first — it is an iodine contrast study. D-dimer supports Same rule as DVT: a negative result is the one that helps. ABG supports Low PaO₂ with a low PaCO₂ — respiratory alkalosis, because she is blowing off CO₂ trying to breathe. V/Q scan supports Used instead of CT when contrast is contraindicated — pregnancy, kidney injury, iodine allergy. Read the full page on Pulmonary emboli

Tests for Hypertension Test What the result tells you No lab confirms it confirms The diagnosis is made from repeated blood pressures, not bloodwork. The labs are looking for what it has damaged and whether something is causing it. BMP — potassium and creatinine supports A rising creatinine means the kidneys are being damaged; a low potassium can point to hyperaldosteronism as the cause. Urinalysis supports Protein in the urine is early kidney damage. Lipid panel and TSH supports Cardiovascular risk, and thyroid di

Tests for Atherosclerosis and hyperlipidemia Test What the result tells you Lipid panel confirms Fast 9–12 hours first. LDL is the one to drive down, HDL is the one you want high, and triglycerides are the one that moves most with diet. Read the full page on Atherosclerosis and hyperlipidemia →

Tests for Shock (any cause) Test What the result tells you Serum lactate confirms The number that says the tissues are not getting oxygen. Over 2 is abnormal, over 4 is severe. It is also how you tell whether resuscitation is working. ABG supports Metabolic acidosis with a low bicarbonate as the lactate builds. Blood cultures confirms Two sets before antibiotics if it might be septic. CBC, BMP, coagulation monitor Source, kidney injury, and whether it has tipped into DIC. Read the full page on Shock (any cause) →

Tests for Pneumonia Test What the result tells you Chest X-ray confirms The confirming test — infiltrate or consolidation in a lobe. Sputum culture and sensitivity confirms Collected before the first antibiotic, first thing in the morning, a deep cough and not saliva. CBC supports White count up with a left shift. In an older adult it can be normal even with a real pneumonia — confusion may be the only sign. Blood cultures supports If she is admitted or septic. Pulse oximetry and ABG monitor How much it is costing

Tests for Asthma Test What the result tells you Spirometry with reversibility confirms The confirming test: FEV₁ improves by 12% or more after a bronchodilator. Peak expiratory flow monitor Her own personal best is the yardstick. Green 80–100%, yellow 50–79%, red under 50% and that is an emergency. ABG monitor Early attack shows respiratory alkalosis. A CO₂ that is normalizing in a struggling asthmatic is not reassuring — it means she is tiring, and it is the sign that comes before respiratory arrest. Read the full

Tests for COPD Test What the result tells you Spirometry confirms FEV₁/FVC under 0.70 after a bronchodilator confirms it — obstruction that does not fully reverse. ABG supports Chronic compensated respiratory acidosis: CO₂ high, bicarbonate high to match, pH near normal. That is her baseline, not an emergency. CBC supports Hematocrit high — the marrow making more red cells to carry the oxygen she cannot get. Read the full page on COPD →

Tests for Tuberculosis Test What the result tells you Sputum for acid-fast bacilli confirms Three early-morning specimens. This is what confirms active disease. Mantoux (TST) supports A screen, not a diagnosis. Read at 48–72 hours, and measure induration, not redness. A positive test says exposed — the chest X-ray and sputum say active. IGRA blood test supports A blood alternative to the skin test, and it is not confounded by a previous BCG vaccination. Chest X-ray supports Upper lobe infiltrates and cavitation. Re

Tests for ARDS Test What the result tells you ABG confirms Hypoxaemia that will not correct however much oxygen you give — that refractoriness is the hallmark. PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio of 300 or less. Chest X-ray confirms Bilateral white-out infiltrates. Echocardiogram / BNP supports Done to prove it is not cardiac pulmonary edema. Read the full page on ARDS →

Tests for Acute respiratory failure Test What the result tells you ABG confirms This is the diagnosis. PaO₂ under 60 is hypoxaemic failure; PaCO₂ over 50 with a pH under 7.35 is hypercapnic failure. Read the full page on Acute respiratory failure →

Tests for Cystic fibrosis Test What the result tells you Sweat chloride test confirms The confirming test — over 60 mmol/L on two occasions. Newborn screen (IRT) supports Immunoreactive trypsinogen picks it up before symptoms. Genetic testing supports CFTR mutations. Read the full page on Cystic fibrosis →

Tests for Acute kidney injury Test What the result tells you Serum creatinine confirms The confirming number: a rise of 0.3 mg/dL in 48 hours, or one and a half times baseline. BUN:creatinine ratio supports Over 20:1 says the problem is before the kidney — dehydration, blood loss, low output. Around 10:1 with a high creatinine says the kidney itself. Urine output confirms Under 0.5 mL/kg/hr for 6 hours. Often the first thing to change. Potassium monitor The one that kills. It cannot be excreted, and it climbs. Urin

Tests for Chronic kidney disease Test What the result tells you GFR confirms What stages it. Under 15 is end-stage and dialysis territory. Creatinine and BUN confirms Both climb and stay up. Phosphate high, calcium low supports The kidney stops activating vitamin D, so calcium falls, phosphate rises, and PTH goes up trying to fix it. Hemoglobin monitor Anemia, because the kidney is no longer making erythropoietin. Potassium and bicarbonate monitor Potassium high, bicarbonate low — metabolic acidosis. Read the full

Tests for UTI and pyelonephritis Test What the result tells you Urine culture and sensitivity confirms The confirming test, and the one that picks the antibiotic. Collect it before starting treatment. Urinalysis supports Nitrites and leukocyte esterase positive, WBCs and bacteria on microscopy. CBC supports White count up — more so with pyelonephritis, which also brings flank pain and fever. Blood cultures supports If she is febrile and systemically unwell. Read the full page on UTI and pyelonephritis →

Tests for Glomerulonephritis Test What the result tells you Urinalysis confirms Red cell casts are the finding that names it — plus protein and tea- or cola-colored urine. ASO titre supports Raised after a streptococcal throat or skin infection, which is the usual trigger in a child. Complement C3 supports Low while it is active, back up as it resolves. BUN, creatinine, GFR monitor How much function has been lost. Read the full page on Glomerulonephritis →

Tests for Nephrotic syndrome Test What the result tells you 24-hour urine protein confirms Over 3.5 g in 24 hours is the confirming number. Serum albumin confirms Low — it is all going out in the urine, and that is why she edematous. Serum cholesterol supports High. The liver makes more lipoprotein as the albumin drops. Urinalysis supports Frothy urine, heavy protein, and — unlike glomerulonephritis — not much blood. Read the full page on Nephrotic syndrome →

Tests for Kidney stones Test What the result tells you Non-contrast CT of the abdomen confirms The confirming test, and no contrast means no renal risk. Urinalysis supports Blood in the urine in almost every case. Strain every urine and send the stone confirms What the stone is made of decides the diet and the drug afterwards. Serum calcium and uric acid supports Looking for the reason she made it. Read the full page on Kidney stones →

Tests for BPH Test What the result tells you PSA supports Raised in BPH and in prostate cancer, so it is a prompt to look further, not an answer. Post-void residual confirms How much she cannot empty. Urinalysis and creatinine monitor Infection from stasis, and back-pressure on the kidneys. Read the full page on BPH →

Tests for Diabetes mellitus Test What the result tells you Hemoglobin A1C confirms 6.5% or more confirms it. It is the three-month average, so it cannot be fooled by one good morning. Target under 7% for most people once treated. Fasting plasma glucose confirms 126 mg/dL or more on two separate occasions. Fast 8 hours. Oral glucose tolerance test confirms 2-hour value of 200 or more. Random glucose confirms 200 or more with the classic symptoms — thirst, urinating constantly, losing weight. Read the full page on Di

Tests for DKA Test What the result tells you Serum glucose confirms Over 250, but usually not enormous — it is the acid that is the emergency, not the sugar. ABG confirms pH under 7.30 with bicarbonate under 18 — metabolic acidosis. Kussmaul breathing is her blowing off CO₂ to compensate. Ketones confirms Positive in serum and urine. This is the difference from HHS. Anion gap monitor Over 12, and closing it is how you know the treatment is working. Potassium monitor Serum potassium can look high while total body po

Tests for HHS Test What the result tells you Serum glucose confirms Over 600, often far higher than DKA. Serum osmolality confirms Over 320 — this is what causes the altered mental status. Ketones and pH confirms Minimal ketones and a normal pH. That absence is what separates it from DKA. Read the full page on HHS →

Tests for Hypothyroidism Test What the result tells you TSH confirms The screening test and the one that moves first. High TSH with a low free T4 is primary hypothyroidism — the gland has failed and the pituitary is shouting at it. Free T4 confirms Low. Lipid panel supports Cholesterol runs high while she is undertreated. Read the full page on Hypothyroidism →

Tests for Hyperthyroidism and Graves Test What the result tells you TSH confirms Low — suppressed, because there is already too much hormone. Free T4 and T3 confirms High. Thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin supports Positive in Graves disease specifically. Radioactive iodine uptake supports High and diffuse in Graves. Read the full page on Hyperthyroidism and Graves →

Tests for Cushing’s syndrome Test What the result tells you Low-dose dexamethasone suppression test confirms The confirming test — in Cushing’s the cortisol does not suppress the way it should. 24-hour urine free cortisol confirms High. Late-night salivary cortisol confirms High — the normal night-time dip is gone. Glucose high, potassium low, sodium high supports What too much cortisol does to the chemistry. Read the full page on Cushing’s syndrome →

Tests for Addison’s disease Test What the result tells you ACTH stimulation test confirms The confirming test — give ACTH, and the cortisol fails to rise. Serum cortisol confirms Low, especially the morning sample. Sodium low, potassium high, glucose low supports The mirror image of Cushing’s, and the combination worth memorising. Read the full page on Addison’s disease →

Tests for SIADH Test What the result tells you Serum sodium confirms Low — dilutional. Under 120 brings seizures. Serum osmolality low, urine osmolality high confirms Dilute blood and concentrated urine. She is holding on to water she does not need. Urine sodium supports High. Read the full page on SIADH →

Tests for Diabetes insipidus Test What the result tells you Serum sodium and osmolality confirms Both high — she is pouring water out and the blood is concentrating. Urine specific gravity confirms Under 1.005. Enormous volumes of urine that look like water. Water deprivation test confirms Withhold fluid and the urine still will not concentrate. Read the full page on Diabetes insipidus →

Tests for Parathyroid disorders Test What the result tells you Serum calcium and PTH together confirms Hyper: calcium high, phosphate low, PTH high. Hypo: calcium low, phosphate high, PTH low. Chvostek and Trousseau signs supports Bedside tests for the low-calcium end — facial twitch, and carpal spasm under a blood-pressure cuff. Read the full page on Parathyroid disorders →

Tests for Anemia Test What the result tells you CBC with MCV confirms The MCV sorts it: small cells point to iron deficiency, large cells to B12 or folate, normal size to blood loss or chronic disease. Ferritin, iron, TIBC confirms Ferritin low is the earliest sign of iron deficiency — it falls before the hemoglobin does. Reticulocyte count supports Whether the marrow is responding. Low means it cannot; high means it is trying. B12 and folate supports For the large-cell picture. Read the full page on Anemia →

Tests for Sickle cell disease Test What the result tells you Hemoglobin electrophoresis confirms The confirming test — it shows hemoglobin S. Newborn screening confirms How it is usually found now, before any crisis. CBC and reticulocytes monitor Chronic anemia with a high reticulocyte count from the constant turnover. Read the full page on Sickle cell disease →

Tests for Hemophilia Test What the result tells you aPTT confirms Prolonged. PT and platelet count are normal , and that combination is the clue. Factor VIII or IX assay confirms Names it: VIII is hemophilia A, IX is B. Read the full page on Hemophilia →

Tests for DIC Test What the result tells you Platelets low, PT and aPTT prolonged confirms Clotting factors are being consumed faster than they are made. D-dimer very high, fibrinogen low confirms Clotting and bleeding at the same time — that paradox is the diagnosis. Read the full page on DIC →

Tests for Leukemia Test What the result tells you Bone marrow biopsy confirms The confirming test. CBC with differential and peripheral smear confirms Blast cells; white count may be very high or very low. Absolute neutrophil count monitor Under 500 is severe neutropenia — a fever there is an emergency, and it may be the only sign of infection she can mount. Read the full page on Leukemia →

Tests for HIV Test What the result tells you 4th-generation antigen/antibody immunoassay confirms The screening test — it picks up p24 antigen early, before antibodies appear. Antibody differentiation assay confirms Confirms a positive screen. CD4 count monitor Under 200 is AIDS by definition, and the point at which prophylaxis starts. Viral load monitor Whether the treatment is working. Undetectable is the goal. Read the full page on HIV →

Tests for Anticoagulant monitoring Test What the result tells you Warfarin → PT/INR monitor Target 2–3 for most, 2.5–3.5 for a mechanical valve. Over 4 is a bleeding alarm. Antidote is vitamin K. Heparin → aPTT monitor 1.5–2.5 times the control. Antidote is protamine sulfate. Platelet count on heparin monitor A falling count is heparin-induced thrombocytopenia — stop the heparin. Read the full page on Anticoagulant monitoring →

Tests for Pancreatitis Test What the result tells you Serum lipase confirms The confirming test — more specific to the pancreas than amylase and it stays raised longer, so it still catches a late presentation. Serum amylase supports Rises too, but it also rises in other abdominal problems. Serum calcium monitor Falls — and a falling calcium is a bad sign, not an incidental one. Glucose and WBC supports Both up. Read the full page on Pancreatitis →

Tests for Cholecystitis Test What the result tells you Abdominal ultrasound confirms The confirming test — stones, a thick wall, fluid around the gallbladder. Bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase supports Raised if a stone is obstructing the duct. WBC supports Up with the inflammation. Read the full page on Cholecystitis →

Tests for Hepatitis Test What the result tells you Hepatitis serology panel confirms Names which one: anti-HAV IgM for acute A, HBsAg for B, anti-HCV for C. ALT and AST confirms Markedly raised — hundreds to thousands. ALT is the more liver-specific of the two. Bilirubin supports Up, and it is what makes her jaundiced and itchy. PT/INR monitor Prolonged only in severe disease — the liver has stopped making clotting factors, and that is the worrying one. Read the full page on Hepatitis →

Tests for Cirrhosis Test What the result tells you Serum albumin confirms Low — the liver is not making it, and that is why she has ascites and edema. PT/INR confirms Prolonged. Clotting factors come from the liver too. Serum ammonia monitor High, and it tracks with the confusion of hepatic encephalopathy. Bilirubin and platelets supports Bilirubin up, platelets down from portal hypertension and a big spleen. Read the full page on Cirrhosis →

Tests for GI bleed Test What the result tells you Upper endoscopy or colonoscopy confirms Finds and treats the source — the confirming test. Hemoglobin and hematocrit monitor Serially. The first draw can look normal because she has lost whole blood and not yet diluted. BUN supports Rises in an upper GI bleed — blood in the gut is protein, and it gets absorbed. Type and crossmatch confirms Sent early, before it is needed. Read the full page on GI bleed →

Tests for Peptic ulcer and H. pylori Test What the result tells you Urea breath test or stool antigen confirms Confirms H. pylori, and confirms cure afterwards. Stop PPIs beforehand or you will get a false negative. Endoscopy with biopsy confirms Sees the ulcer and rules out cancer. Read the full page on Peptic ulcer and H. pylori →

Tests for Celiac disease Test What the result tells you Tissue transglutaminase IgA confirms The screening test — and she must still be eating gluten when it is drawn, or it will be falsely negative. Small bowel biopsy confirms Confirms it. Read the full page on Celiac disease →

Tests for Appendicitis Test What the result tells you CT of the abdomen confirms The confirming test. No blood test diagnoses appendicitis. WBC supports Up with a left shift — supportive, never sufficient. Read the full page on Appendicitis →

Tests for Crohn’s and ulcerative colitis Test What the result tells you Colonoscopy with biopsy confirms Confirms it and tells the two apart — skip lesions through the whole wall in Crohn’s, continuous shallow disease from the rectum up in UC. ESR, CRP, faecal calprotectin monitor How active it is right now. CBC and albumin monitor Anemia from blood loss, low albumin from malabsorption. Read the full page on Crohn’s and ulcerative colitis →

Tests for Meningitis Test What the result tells you Lumbar puncture confirms The confirming test. Bacterial: cloudy, high protein, low glucose , neutrophils. Viral: clear, normal glucose, lymphocytes. That glucose is the fastest way to tell them apart. CT head before the LP confirms Done first if there are signs of raised pressure — herniation is the risk. Blood cultures confirms Before antibiotics. Read the full page on Meningitis →

Tests for Stroke Test What the result tells you Non-contrast CT head confirms First, and fast. It is not there to show the stroke — it is there to rule out a bleed before anyone gives a thrombolytic. Blood glucose confirms Checked immediately. Hypoglycaemia imitates a stroke exactly, and it is fixable in a minute. PT/INR, aPTT, platelets confirms Whether thrombolysis is safe. Read the full page on Stroke →

Tests for Seizures Test What the result tells you EEG confirms Shows the abnormal electrical activity. Glucose and sodium confirms Both are reversible causes, and both get checked first. Anticonvulsant drug levels monitor Phenytoin 10–20 mcg/mL. Most breakthrough seizures are a level that has drifted, not a new problem. Read the full page on Seizures →

Tests for Myasthenia gravis Test What the result tells you Acetylcholine receptor antibodies confirms Positive in most cases — the confirming blood test. Tensilon (edrophonium) test confirms Strength improves briefly. It also tells a myasthenic crisis (improves) from a cholinergic crisis (gets worse). EMG with repetitive stimulation supports The response fades with repetition — which is the disease in one picture. Read the full page on Myasthenia gravis →

Tests for Guillain-Barré syndrome Test What the result tells you Lumbar puncture confirms High protein with a normal cell count. That mismatch has a name — albuminocytologic dissociation — and it is the classic finding. Vital capacity at the bedside monitor The number that actually matters day to day. A falling vital capacity means the paralysis is climbing towards the diaphragm. Read the full page on Guillain-Barré syndrome →

Tests for Multiple sclerosis Test What the result tells you MRI with gadolinium confirms Plaques scattered in space and time — the confirming test. Lumbar puncture supports Oligoclonal bands in the CSF. Read the full page on Multiple sclerosis →

Tests for Osteoporosis Test What the result tells you DEXA scan confirms The confirming test. A T-score of −2.5 or lower is osteoporosis; −1 to −2.5 is osteopenia. Calcium and vitamin D supports Checked before starting treatment. Read the full page on Osteoporosis →

Tests for Rheumatoid arthritis Test What the result tells you Anti-CCP antibody confirms More specific than rheumatoid factor, and it appears earlier. Rheumatoid factor supports Positive in most, but also positive in plenty of people without RA. ESR and CRP monitor How active the disease is now. Read the full page on Rheumatoid arthritis →

Tests for Gout Test What the result tells you Joint aspiration confirms Needle-shaped urate crystals in the fluid — the confirming test. Serum uric acid supports Usually high, but it can be normal during an acute attack, so a normal level does not rule it out. Read the full page on Gout →

Tests for Rhabdomyolysis Test What the result tells you Creatine kinase confirms Enormously raised — this is the confirming test. Urine myoglobin confirms Tea-colored urine that tests positive for blood with no red cells on microscopy. Potassium and creatinine monitor Potassium pours out of the broken muscle, and the myoglobin injures the kidney. Read the full page on Rhabdomyolysis →

Tests for Osteomyelitis Test What the result tells you Bone biopsy and culture confirms The confirming test, and what chooses the antibiotic. MRI confirms Earliest imaging to show it. ESR, CRP, blood cultures supports Raised; cultures may name the organism. Read the full page on Osteomyelitis →

Tests for Compartment syndrome Test What the result tells you Compartment pressure measurement confirms Over 30 mmHg. This is a clinical emergency — pain out of proportion, and pain on passive stretch, come before any number. Creatine kinase monitor Rising if muscle is already dying. Read the full page on Compartment syndrome →

Tests for Preeclampsia and HELLP Test What the result tells you Blood pressure and urine protein confirms 140/90 or higher after 20 weeks with proteinuria. That pair is the diagnosis. Platelets, liver enzymes, hemolysis confirms HELLP: hemolysis, e levated l iver enzymes, l ow p latelets under 100,000. The name is the lab panel. Creatinine and uric acid monitor Both rise as it worsens. Magnesium level monitor Once magnesium sulfate is running: 4–7 mEq/L is therapeutic. Lost reflexes come first, then respiratory dep

Tests for Gestational diabetes Test What the result tells you 1-hour 50 g glucose challenge supports The screen at 24–28 weeks. No fasting needed. 3-hour 100 g OGTT confirms The confirming test — two abnormal values make the diagnosis. Read the full page on Gestational diabetes →

Tests for Rh incompatibility Test What the result tells you Blood type and Rh confirms On every pregnant patient at the first visit. Indirect Coombs on the mother confirms Whether she has already made antibodies. Direct Coombs on the newborn confirms Whether the baby’s cells are coated. Read the full page on Rh incompatibility →

Tests for Preterm labour Test What the result tells you Fetal fibronectin supports Most useful when it is negative — that makes delivery in the next two weeks very unlikely. Cervical length on ultrasound supports Short cervix raises the risk. Group B strep culture confirms 35–37 weeks, or on admission in preterm labour. Read the full page on Preterm labour →

Tests for Placenta previa and abruption Test What the result tells you Transabdominal ultrasound confirms Confirms previa — and until it has, no vaginal examination . CBC and coagulation studies monitor Abruption can consume clotting factors and tip into DIC. Kleihauer-Betke supports How much fetal blood has crossed into the mother. Read the full page on Placenta previa and abruption →

Tests for Glaucoma Test What the result tells you Tonometry confirms The confirming test. Dr. Halecka gives normal as 12–20, with anything over 22 suspicious — use her numbers on the exam. The textbook says 10–21. Visual field testing confirms Peripheral vision goes first in open-angle, and she will not notice until a lot is gone. Ophthalmoscopy supports Cupping of the optic disc. Gonioscopy confirms Looks at the drainage angle — open or closed. Read the full page on Glaucoma →

Tests for Macular degeneration Test What the result tells you Amsler grid confirms The one to match with macular degeneration. Straight lines look wavy, and the center goes missing. Optical coherence tomography confirms Images the layers of the macula. Fluorescein angiography supports Shows the leaking vessels of the wet type. Read the full page on Macular degeneration →

Tests for Cataract Test What the result tells you Slit-lamp examination confirms Done by the ophthalmologist at around 40× magnification. No blood test and no drop diagnoses or treats a cataract — surgery is the only fix. Visual acuity supports How much it is costing her. Night driving and glare go first. Read the full page on Cataract →

Tests for Retinal detachment Test What the result tells you Ophthalmoscopy confirms Sees the detached retina — the confirming test. Ocular ultrasound supports Used when blood or a cataract blocks the view. An eye ultrasound generally means trauma or a tumor is being considered. Read the full page on Retinal detachment →

Tests for Otitis media Test What the result tells you Otoscopy confirms A red, bulging, immobile tympanic membrane — the confirming finding. Tympanometry supports Measures whether the drum moves; flat tracing means fluid behind it. Read the full page on Otitis media →

Tests for Major burns Test What the result tells you Urine output monitor The number that steers fluid resuscitation — 30–50 mL/hr in an adult, and it matters more than the formula. Hematocrit supports High early from haemoconcentration as plasma leaks out of the vessels. Potassium monitor High in the first 24–48 hours as cells rupture, then low once fluid shifts back. Carboxyhaemoglobin and ABG confirms If there is any chance of smoke inhalation. Pulse oximetry reads falsely normal in carbon monoxide poisoning. Al

Tests for Cellulitis Test What the result tells you Clinical diagnosis confirms Looked at, and the border marked with a pen so you can see whether it is spreading. CBC and blood cultures supports If she is febrile or systemically unwell. Read the full page on Cellulitis →

Tests for Sepsis Test What the result tells you Serum lactate confirms Drawn within the first hour, and repeated. Over 2 is abnormal, over 4 is severe. Blood cultures confirms Two sets from two sites, before the first antibiotic. After the antibiotic they may grow nothing. CBC supports White count high or low — a low count is the more ominous of the two. Procalcitonin supports Points towards a bacterial cause. Read the full page on Sepsis →

Tests for C. difficile Test What the result tells you Stool PCR or toxin assay confirms Confirms it. Only test a stool that is actually loose — testing formed stool finds carriers, not disease. WBC supports Can be strikingly high. Read the full page on C. difficile → Nothing matches that. Try a shorter word — potassium rather than serum potassium level .
