Specific Phobia · Agoraphobia · Social Anxiety NG-077 MENTAL HEALTH ADHD-friendly visual edition A phobia is an excessive, irrational fear of a specific object or situation, out of proportion to the actual danger, that drives avoidance . The client usually has insight — they know the fear "doesn't make sense" — but can't switch it off. First-line treatment is systematic desensitization : exposure, in small steps, paired with relaxation. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 😨 Fear + Avoidance Excessive, irra
STEP 1 · THE FEAR MAP One definition drives the whole topic — an out-of-proportion fear that the amygdala refuses to downgrade.

entries.h: 😨 Three fear disorders, easy to blur together
entries.t: Disorder What's feared Example Specific phobia One object or situation Spiders, heights, needles, flying Social anxiety disorder Being watched, judged, or embarrassed in front of others Public speaking, eating in front of coworkers Agoraphobia Being trapped — unable to escape or get help if panic strikes Open spaces, crowds, riding trains/buses, being outside alone 🧠 Agoraphobia is not "fear of open spaces" alone — it's fear of not being able to escape . It's the disorder most often paired with panic attacks.

entries.h: 🧬 Mechanism: a conditioned alarm that won't reset
entries.t: A learned/conditioned fear response (classical conditioning) — sometimes after one bad experience, sometimes with no clear trigger — paired with an amygdala that overreacts to the stimulus and a prefrontal cortex that struggles to override it with logic. 🧠 “The alarm is real, the danger isn't.” The amygdala fires exactly like it would for a real threat — that's why reassurance alone doesn't fix it.
🕷️ Arachnophobia spiders 🐾 Zoophobia animals 🚪 Claustrophobia closed-in spaces 🏙️ Agoraphobia trapped / no escape

entries.h: 🎯 Specific phobia vs. Agoraphobia — same fear machinery, different target
entries.t: 🧠 Both are fear-driven avoidance — but agoraphobia's target is escape access , not one object. That's why it clusters with panic disorder. 🔎
STEP 2 · SPOT IT Anticipatory dread before exposure, a full sympathetic surge during it, and one exact phrase to say back.

entries.h: 🚨 Exposure to the phobic stimulus = sympathetic surge
entries.t: 🧠 Same autonomic surge seen in panic attacks, PTSD flashbacks, and blocked OCD rituals — the anxiety-spectrum disorders all share one alarm system.

entries.h: 🗣️ Therapeutic communication — say this exact type of line
entries.t: Client: "I am so terrified of heights that the thought of going up my stairs makes me feel like I am going to hyperventilate. I know it sounds ridiculous." Best nurse response: "You feel like your fear does not make sense, but it is very real to you." 🧠 Assess first, reflect the feeling — don't argue the logic. Never say "that's silly" or try to talk the client out of the fear with facts.

Increased comfort while exposed to the phobia Verbalizing feelings & insight about the anxiety (self-observation) Self-distraction — focusing on something other than the phobia 🧠 Improvement = staying in the situation longer, not avoiding it faster. "I planned to skip the party" is avoidance, not coping.

entries.h: ⭐ Phobias can be a piece of a bigger picture
entries.t: Phobic symptoms can be a manifestation of PTSD — a trauma survivor may develop a specific, situational fear tied to reminders of the event. Screen broadly; don't assume every phobia stands alone. 🩺
STEP 3 · EXPOSE GRADUALLY Build a ladder of fear, climb it slowly, and pair every rung with relaxation.

The client and therapist build a fear hierarchy — least feared to most feared — then move up one rung at a time , pairing each exposure with a relaxation technique, until anxiety at that step is tolerable before advancing. 🧠 “Desensitize = de-SIZE the fear, one small step at a time.” The opposite approach — flooding (rapid, full-intensity exposure) — is more distressing and is not the typical first-line choice.

Benzodiazepines — short-term / situational use for acute exposure anxiety, not a long-term fix SSRIs — first-line long-term medication for social anxiety disorder Beta-blockers (e.g., propranolol) — sometimes used off-label before a specific feared performance event to blunt physical symptoms (tremor, racing heart) 🧠 Medication supports exposure therapy — it does not replace it. Desensitization is the durable fix.

entries.h: 🚨 Never do this with a phobic client
entries.t: Never argue the client out of the fear with logic or facts Never force full, unprepared exposure without a hierarchy Never dismiss the fear as silly or exaggerated ✅ Do validate: the fear doesn't have to make sense to be real to them

Daily stress-reduction practice (breathing exercises, scheduled relaxation, regular exercise) builds resilience between exposure sessions and lowers the baseline anxiety the client brings into each new hierarchy step. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 😨 Fear + Avoidance excessive, irrational, drives avoidance 🚪 Agoraphobia fear of being trapped / no escape — pairs with panic disorder 🪜 Systematic desensitization gradual hierarchy + relaxation = first-line 🗣️ Validate the feeling don't argue the logic

Q1: A client says "I am terrified of being outside alone." Which phobia? Show answer Agoraphobia — fear of being in places/situations where escape or help might not be available, including being outside alone, crowds, or public transit. Q2: What is the best nursing response to "I know my fear of heights sounds ridiculous"? Show answer "You feel like your fear does not make sense, but it is very real to you." Validate the feeling, don't argue the logic. Q3: Which intervention is a client who avoids flying most likel

entries.h: PTSD & Acute Stress Disorder · NG-078 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🌩️ Cause 🔎 Clues 🩺 Care ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Mental Health · Anxiety-Spectrum Disorders

& Acute Stress Disorder (ASD) NG-078 MENTAL HEALTH ADHD-friendly visual edition Both ASD and PTSD are anxiety-spectrum responses that can develop after exposure to a traumatic event. One clock separates them: symptoms in the first month = ASD; symptoms past one month = PTSD. Four symptom clusters describe the whole clinical picture, and the nurse's first job — every time — is a safety check before anything else. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🕐 One-month line ASD = first month after trauma. PTSD = sym
STEP 1 · THE TIMELINE Same trauma-response biology — the only thing that changes the diagnosis is the calendar.

entries.h: 🕐 ASD → PTSD: one timeline, one cutoff
entries.t: 🧠 “Under a month = ASD. Over a month = PTSD.” Same symptom clusters both sides of the line — only the duration changes the label.

Directly experiencing a threat to life, serious injury, or sexual violence Witnessing the event happen to someone else Learning it happened to a close family member or friend Repeated professional exposure to trauma details (e.g., first responders) 🧠 Keep assessment clinical and non-graphic — you do not need event detail to identify the diagnosis or plan safe care.
Prior trauma history Lack of social support after the event Co-occurring substance use Severity/duration of the traumatic exposure 🔎
STEP 2 · FOUR CLUSTERS Four symptom clusters cover the whole clinical picture — plus the physiology behind a flashback.

entries.h: 🧩 The 4 symptom clusters — memorize this grid
entries.t: 🧠 “I AM H” — I ntrusion · A voidance · M ood/cognition (negative) · H yperarousal. All four must be present for the PTSD diagnosis, not just one.

entries.h: 🚨 A trauma reminder can trigger a full sympathetic surge
entries.t: 🧠 A war veteran hearing a car backfire and feeling like they're back in combat is hyperarousal + intrusion firing together — reassure them of present safety first.

Client: "The war was years ago, but I still remember my friends who were killed. I don't know why I lived and they died." Nurse's priority response: "Are you having any thoughts of harming yourself?" 🧠 Survivor's guilt is a red flag for self-harm risk. Always screen for safety before exploring the feeling further.

Self-harm: thoughts or plans Substance use (drugs & alcohol) — common coping attempt Relationships with family & friends — isolation is a warning sign For sexual assault survivors: assess for guilt/shame; reinforce they could not have anticipated it and did not deserve it 🩺
STEP 3 · PACE & PROCESS Let the client set the pace, normalize the reaction, and lean on trauma-focused therapy before medication.

1 Safety screen first — self-harm/suicidal ideation, every encounter 2 Encourage the client to talk at their own pace — never force detail before they're ready 3 Explain that difficult symptoms after trauma are normal — normalize, don't pathologize the reaction 4 Assess substance use and relationships — common coping/withdrawal patterns 5 Connect to trauma-focused therapy — CBT, EMDR, or group therapy as tolerated 🧠 “Pace, Place, Process.” Let them set the pace, keep them safe in place, then help them process — in

Trauma-focused CBT — helps the client reframe distorted trauma-related beliefs (guilt, danger, self-blame) and gradually process memories. EMDR (Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing) — the client recalls the trauma in brief segments while following bilateral stimulation (e.g., guided eye movements); thought to help the brain reprocess the memory so it feels less distressing. Prolonged exposure therapy — structured, repeated recounting of the memory in a safe setting to reduce its emotional charge over time

Drug class Note SSRIs — sertraline, paroxetine FDA-approved, first-line pharmacologic option TCAs — amitriptyline, imipramine Older alternative, more side effects Prazosin Off-label, targets trauma-related nightmares specifically 🧠 Avoid long-term benzodiazepines in PTSD — dependence risk, and evidence doesn't support them as an effective core treatment; they don't treat the underlying avoidance/re-experiencing symptoms.

entries.h: 🚨 Never do this with a trauma client
entries.t: Never push the client to describe trauma details before they're ready Never minimize the reaction ("it was years ago, just move on") Never assume every trauma survivor's symptoms look the same ✅ Do reinforce: the feelings are a normal response to an abnormal event ✅ For assault survivors: reinforce they could not have anticipated it and did not deserve it ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🕐 1 month ASD before it, PTSD after it 🧩 4 clusters Intrusion · Avoidance · Mood/cognition · Hyperarousal 🚨 Safety first always screen for self-harm before anything else 💊 Trauma-focused CBT / EMDR + SSRIs; avoid long-term benzos

Q1: What separates Acute Stress Disorder from PTSD? Show answer Duration. ASD occurs within the first month after trauma; if symptoms persist beyond one month, it's PTSD. Q2: Name the 4 PTSD symptom clusters. Show answer Intrusion/re-experiencing, avoidance, negative alterations in mood/cognition, and hyperarousal/reactivity. Q3: A veteran expresses survivor's guilt about friends killed in combat. What's the nurse's priority response? Show answer Ask directly: "Are you having any thoughts of harming yourself?" Safe

entries.h: Sleep & Circadian Rhythm · NG-089 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🧨 Cause 🔎 Clues 🩺 Care ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Mental Health · Fundamentals: Rest & Sleep I

The Body Clock, Sleep Architecture & Circadian Disorders NG-089 Mental Health ADHD-friendly visual edition One master clock, the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), uses light hitting the retina to time everything — melatonin release, body temperature, cortisol, and when you feel sleepy. Chronic sleep loss raises risk for HTN, obesity, depression, diabetes & stroke . This is the biology page — see Sleep Hygiene (NG-135) for the practical nursing-teaching companion. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🧠 SCN = ma
STEP 1 · THE BODY CLOCK Light in, melatonin out — one feedback loop drives the entire 24-hour rhythm.

PATHWAY Light hits photoreceptors in the retina → signal travels the retinohypothalamic tract → reaches the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) in the hypothalamus, the brain's master circadian clock → SCN tells the pineal gland to hold back or release melatonin . 🧠 "No light, all right (to sleep)." Any bright light late at night — including phone/screen light — tricks the SCN into thinking it's still day and delays melatonin release.
Core body temperature dips to its lowest point in the early morning hours, then climbs through the day and peaks in the evening — the two rhythms run in sync to time sleep onset and wake.

Even a few days of poor sleep raises risk for: ❤️ Hypertension ⚖️ Obesity 😔 Depression & decreased cognitive function 🩸 Diabetes 🧠 Stroke 🧠 "HODDS." HTN · Obesity · Depression · Diabetes · Stroke — the five-condition list chronic sleep debt drags up. 🔎
STEP 2 · ARCHITECTURE & DISORDERS A normal night cycles through stages every 90 minutes — a misaligned clock or a broken cycle both look different from the outside.

entries.h: 🔁 Stages of sleep — repeats about every 90 minutes
entries.t: Stage What's happening Stage 1 Wakefulness → sleep, non-REM. Lasts a few minutes; loss of awareness but easily aroused. Stage 2 Light sleep, non-REM. 10-20 minutes; vitals & metabolism start to decrease. Stage 3 Deep / slow-wave / delta sleep, non-REM. Vitals decrease further; difficult to awaken; physical/cognitive restoration . REM Rapid eye movement; vivid dreaming; begins ~ 90 min after falling asleep and recurs every ~ 90 min; psychological rest . 🧠 "1-2-3-REM, then repeat." Deeper each stage, then REM breaks

entries.h: ✈️ Circadian rhythm disorders — the clock and the schedule disagree

entries.t: Rotating or night-shift work forces sleep against the SCN's light-set schedule → insomnia during intended sleep + excessive sleepiness on shift, with real accident/error risk.

Crossing time zones faster than the SCN can re-entrain (roughly 1 day per time zone) → fatigue, GI upset, trouble sleeping/waking on the new local clock. Eastward travel is typically harder to adjust to than westward.

The internal clock runs later than the desired schedule — can't fall asleep until very late (e.g., 2-6am ), then struggles to wake for school/work. Common in adolescents/young adults. 🧠 Management lever = light & melatonin timing. Bright light exposure at the right time of day (and avoiding it at the wrong time), plus timed melatonin, helps re-entrain the SCN in all three — the specific timing differs by disorder and is individualized by a sleep specialist.
Difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep, awakening too early, or not feeling rested on waking. Chronic insomnia: occurs 3 + nights/week for more than 3 months.

Obstructive (OSA): soft tissue in the mouth/throat relaxes and blocks the airway Central: the CNS fails to signal the body to breathe — no airway blockage, the drive to breathe itself pauses Both show cycles of breathing stops/starts, with pauses lasting more than 10 seconds .

😴 Sudden "sleep attacks" — falls asleep without warning 💪 Cataplexy — sudden muscle weakness triggered by strong emotion 👁️ Hypnagogic hallucinations — vivid hallucinations at sleep onset 🧠 Linked to a lack of REM regulation — REM-like features intrude into wakefulness 🧠 Huge safety risk — driving, walking, standing. The highest-priority assessment question is about safety during high-risk activities: "Do you have difficulty staying awake while driving?" 🩺
STEP 3 · ASSESS & SUPPORT Ask about safety first, then hand off to the practical teaching page for what to actually change.

Disorder Priority nursing question / focus Narcolepsy Safety during driving/high-risk activity — "Do you have difficulty staying awake when you are driving?" Insomnia Sleep pattern history, safety, and contributing factors (stress, environment, meds, substances) before jumping to a sleep aid Sleep apnea Witnessed breathing pauses, snoring, daytime sleepiness — screen for OSA vs. central pattern Circadian disorders Work schedule, travel history, and usual bed/wake times — mismatch between the clock and the required
Disturbed sleep pattern related to anxiety or alteration in client routine — common framing when the SCN's schedule is disrupted by stress, travel, or shift changes.

entries.h: 🔗 Where the "what to do about it" lives
entries.t: This page explains why the clock runs the way it does and what disrupts it. The actionable teaching — light exposure timing, caffeine/alcohol cutoffs, bedroom environment, hospital-unit strategies — is the companion page. 🔗 See NG-135 — Sleep Hygiene for the practical nurse-teaching checklist built directly on this page's biology. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🧠 SCN Master clock in the hypothalamus, set by light through the eyes 🌑 Melatonin Pineal gland releases it in the dark → sleepy 🔁 90-min cycle Stage 1 → 2 → 3 (delta) → REM, repeating all night ✈️ 3 disorders Shift work · Jet lag · Delayed sleep phase — clock vs. schedule mismatch

Q1: What structure is the body's master circadian clock, and what sets it? Show answer The suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) in the hypothalamus — set primarily by light entering the eyes via the retinohypothalamic tract. Q2: What gland releases melatonin, and when? Show answer The pineal gland — release increases as light fades in the evening and is suppressed by light exposure. Q3: How often does the sleep-stage cycle repeat, and which stage brings vivid dreaming? Show answer About every 90 minutes; REM sleep brings

entries.h: ADD & ADHD · NG-093 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🧨 Cause 🔎 Clues 🩺 Care ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Mental Health · Psychiatric Care Course

Attention Deficit (Hyperactivity) Disorder NG-093 Mental Health ADHD-friendly visual edition Low dopamine & norepinephrine in the brain's reward/focus circuits means the brain can't rank what deserves attention — so it either drifts (inattentive), revs (hyperactive-impulsive), or both (combined type). Treatment lives on a separate page — see ADHD Meds (NG-234) . 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🧪 2 low chemicals Dopamine & norepinephrine — the "reward vs. risk" & impulse-control messengers. 🎭 3 presenta
STEP 1 · THE BRAIN CHEMISTRY One circuit explains the whole picture — the brain's "is this worth my attention" filter runs low on fuel.

entries.h: 🧠 The prefrontal circuit runs low on dopamine & norepinephrine
entries.t: EXAM TIP Low dopamine & norepinephrine in the prefrontal cortex — the neurotransmitters that help the brain weigh reward vs. risk and control impulsivity & mood . Clients with ADHD are therefore more likely to also carry anxiety and substance use risk — the brain chases whatever raises dopamine fastest. 🧠 "Low fuel, low filter." Dopamine is the brain's reward fuel — without enough, the brain can't decide what's worth focusing on, so it grabs whatever is loudest (impulsivity) or nothing at all (inattention).

🧬 Genetic / family history — highly heritable 🤕 History of head trauma — TBI (traumatic brain injury) 🚬 Prenatal exposure — nicotine, alcohol, or substance use in pregnancy 👶 Low birth weight / prematurity 🧠 "Hit head, hooked on risk." A documented head injury is the classic ATI risk-factor trap — kids with a serious TBI are more likely to develop ADHD later.

entries.h: 🔤 Say the terms — ADD vs. ADHD
entries.t: ADD = Attention Deficit Disorder — inattentive symptoms without the motor hyperactivity ADHD = Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder — the umbrella term used in current diagnostic criteria (DSM-5-TR), covering all three presentations below "ADD" is older/lay terminology — on exams, ADHD is the umbrella and the presentation (inattentive / hyperactive-impulsive / combined) is the specifier. 🔎
STEP 2 · SPOT THE PRESENTATION Three faces of the same low-dopamine circuit — know which symptoms build which type.

entries.h: 🎭 Three DSM presentations — same disorder, different symptom mix

entries.t: Reduced ability to focus, easily distracted, poor follow-through, disorganized, loses items, forgetful in daily activities.
Restless "always on the go," excessive talking, blurts answers, interrupts, difficulty waiting turn.

Meets criteria for both — the most commonly diagnosed presentation, especially in school-age children. 🧠 DSM checklist = "6-6-12-2." 6 or more symptoms · lasting more than 6 months · onset before age 12 · present in 2 + settings (home and school). One setting only ≠ ADHD — it might just be that classroom.

🏃 Hyperactivity — "restless," can't stay seated 🧠 Inattention — "reduced ability to focus" 🗣️ Impulsiveness — "excessive talking," blurts, interrupts 😔 Low self-esteem & impaired social skills — from repeated correction/rejection 🧠 "HII-L" — H yperactive · I nattentive · I mpulsive · L ow self-esteem. Say it like "hee-ill" — the disorder hurts before it heals.

entries.h: 🚨 Priority nursing diagnosis: Risk for injury
entries.t: Impulsivity + hyperactivity outrun judgment — a child may run into traffic, climb, or act before thinking. On a HESI/ATI question, "risk for injury" is the nursing diagnosis to pick when ADHD is the stem. 🧠 Aggressive/agitated child? Distract & redirect — e.g., ask them to blow up a balloon. Gives the excess energy somewhere safe to go instead of escalating. 🩺
STEP 3 · STRUCTURE, SAFETY, COMMUNICATION Non-drug care is structure and predictability; medication management lives on its own page — see NG-234 .

1 👁️ Get eye contact BEFORE speaking — confirms attention is captured first 2 💬 Use simple, short language — one instruction at a time 3 🔁 Have the child repeat back what was said — confirms it was received 4 🌟 Offer praise upon task completion — reinforces the behavior you want repeated 🧠 "Eye-Say-Say-Yay." Eye contact → Say it simply → child Says it back → Yay (praise). Kaplan's favorite right answer is a hug/praise after the task is completed — not before, and not as a bribe up front.

entries.h: 📋 Structure & scheduling — the #1 classroom/home teaching point
entries.t: 📅 Provide a written or typed daily schedule — predictability lowers anxiety and impulsive behavior ⏱️ Allow regular breaks 👁️ Combine verbal instructions with visual cues 📏 Establish consistent rules — same expectations every day 📉 Do not overload with homework — decrease amount assigned 🧠 On an ATI-style stem — "9-year-old on bedrest with ADD, which action should the nurse prioritize?" — the answer is give a written/typed daily schedule , not medication or restraint.

Stimulants (methylphenidate, amphetamine salts) and non-stimulants (atomoxetine, guanfacine/clonidine ER) treat the same low-dopamine/norepinephrine circuit covered above. Full mechanism, monitoring, and teaching are on the ADHD Meds page (NG-234) — this page is diagnosis & non-drug care only, so the two pages together are the complete topic. 🔗 See NG-234 — ADHD Meds for: stimulant mechanism, growth/cardiac monitoring, controlled-substance status, drug holidays, and non-stimulant options. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🧪 Low dopamine + norepinephrine = poor reward/risk filter + poor impulse control 🎭 3 types Inattentive · Hyperactive-Impulsive · Combined 📅 Best intervention Written/typed daily schedule — structure & consistency 🚨 Priority Dx Risk for injury — impulsivity outruns judgment

Q1: What two neurotransmitters are low in ADHD, and what do they normally do? Show answer Dopamine & norepinephrine — they help the brain weigh reward vs. risk and control impulsivity/mood. Q2: A child has a serious head injury history. What's the connection to ADHD? Show answer TBI (traumatic brain injury) is a documented risk factor — increases the likelihood of developing ADHD later. Q3: What's the priority nursing diagnosis for a hospitalized child with ADHD? Show answer Risk for injury — impulsivity and hypera

entries.h: Alcohol Abuse · NG-096 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🍺 Cause 🔎 Withdrawal 🩺 Safety ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Mental Health · Communication & Therapy Foundations

CNS depression, the withdrawal clock, and the two emergencies that follow it NG-096 MENTAL HEALTH ADHD-friendly visual edition Alcohol is a CNS depressant — chronic use quiets the brain, and the brain compensates by revving up its own excitability. Stop the alcohol suddenly, and that compensation is unopposed — vitals spike, seizures can happen, and delirium tremens (DTs) can kill. Two other life-or-death traps live on this page: Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome and the thiamine-before-glucose rule. 📄 Simple Nursing ori
STEP 1 · WHAT ALCOHOL DOES One mechanism explains both intoxication and withdrawal — alcohol depresses the CNS, and the brain fights back by upregulating itself.

entries.h: 😴 Alcohol = CNS depressant — vitals go low & slow
entries.t: EXAM TIP Alcohol is a toxin that causes central nervous system depression — vital signs run low and slow, and coordination & balance suffer (ataxia, slurred speech). 🧠 "Low and slow means alcohol's in tow." Any time vitals trend down together with slurred speech and poor balance, think acute intoxication.

Escape from problems Cover up depression & anxiety 🧠 Alcohol use disorder is often a symptom of an underlying mood problem — that's why counseling's primary goal is identifying triggers, not just stopping the drink.

Alcohol metabolism in the liver disrupts normal glucose production. Monitor blood glucose levels at night — hypoglycemia can happen hours after the last drink, especially in malnourished or diabetic clients. 🧠 Alcohol intoxication can look like a diabetic emergency — always check a glucose on an intoxicated or withdrawing client; don't assume it's "just the alcohol." 🔎
STEP 2 · THE CLOCK THAT CAN KILL Withdrawal severity rises on a predictable timeline — DTs are the single most dangerous point on it.

entries.h: ⏱️ Alcohol withdrawal timeline — know every stage
entries.t: 🧠 "24 shakes, 48 seizes, 72 crazes." ~24 hr = anxious & shaky · ~48 hr = seizure risk · 48–72 hr = DTs, the peak danger window.

entries.h: 🌡️ DTs vital sign pattern — read the numbers
entries.t: 🧠 If a chart shows fever + tachycardia + hypertension + tachypnea in a client with a recent drinking history, think withdrawal — not just "anxiety."

Hyperreflexia — hand tremors Diaphoresis (sweating) Hallucinations Tachycardia — HR over 100 bpm Hypertension Fever Confusion & restlessness 🧠 "SHAKE-HHF" — S weating · H and tremors/hyperreflexia · A gitation/confusion · K razy visions (hallucinations) · E levated HR · H ypertension · F ever. DTs is a medical emergency.

The CIWA-Ar (Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol, revised) is a structured bedside scoring tool — tremor, sweating, anxiety, agitation, hallucinations, orientation, headache, nausea are each scored, and the total drives symptom-triggered treatment decisions. Higher score = more severe withdrawal = closer monitoring. 🧠 Score drives care, not the calendar. CIWA-Ar lets the team treat the client's actual symptom burden instead of a fixed timer. For the specific medication class and taper approach used
STEP 3 · PROTECT THE BRAIN Seizure precautions come first; then protect against a second, quieter emergency — Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome.

Any client in alcohol withdrawal (or sudden benzodiazepine/barbiturate withdrawal — cross-tolerant, same mechanism) needs seizure precautions in place immediately : padded rails, bed in low position, suction & oxygen at bedside, quiet low-stimulation environment. 🧠 Sudden withdrawal from alcohol, benzodiazepines, or barbiturates can all cause seizures — they share the same GABA mechanism, so nursing precautions look the same across all three.

entries.h: 🧠 Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome — the "why thiamine first" rule
entries.t: Chronic alcohol use causes poor nutrition and impairs thiamine (vitamin B1) absorption. Thiamine is required as a cofactor to metabolize glucose. If glucose is given before thiamine is replaced, the sudden glucose load consumes the little thiamine the client has left — precipitating or worsening Wernicke's encephalopathy. 🧠 "Thiamine before the sweet stuff." Any malnourished or chronic-alcohol-use client who needs IV glucose (D50, dextrose fluids) should get thiamine first — this is a classic standalone NCLEX point

After detox, the primary goal of recovery is total abstinence — meaning NO alcohol, forever. Moderation is not the treatment goal for alcohol use disorder. 🧠 Abstinence, not moderation — a very common wrong-answer trap is "cut back to a couple drinks a week."

The primary goal of counseling is to help the client identify factors that trigger alcohol use — not to lecture about consequences or "cover up" the underlying depression/anxiety that drives the drinking. 🧠 "Triggers, not tricks." Effective intervention = develop motivation & self-help skills, and pinpoint the trigger, every time.

📎 The specific drug class used to prevent seizures/DTs (benzodiazepines, dosed by CIWA-Ar symptom score) and the general safety comparison with opioid withdrawal are covered in detail on the Pharmacology batch's Withdrawal Meds (NG-277) page — refer there for drug names, taper approach, and monitoring parameters rather than duplicating them here. Use Therapeutic Communication (NG-271) techniques when counseling: open-ended questions to explore triggers, reflecting instead of lecturing, and never giving false reassu

SAY IT OUT LOUD 😴 Intoxication = low & slow Withdrawal = high & fast — opposite directions. ⏱️ 24-48-72 Anxious → seizures → DTs, the killer window. 🧠 Thiamine before glucose Prevents Wernicke-Korsakoff — high-yield standalone fact. 🚫 Total abstinence Recovery goal is zero alcohol, not moderation.

Q1: A client reports drinking a pint of vodka daily and is 48–72 hours post-last-drink. What is the priority concern? Show answer Delirium tremens — the most dangerous window (48–72 hours), with confusion, hallucinations, tachycardia, hypertension, and fever. Q2: Why must thiamine be given before IV glucose in a chronic alcohol use client? Show answer Glucose metabolism requires thiamine as a cofactor — giving glucose first in a thiamine-deficient client can precipitate or worsen Wernicke encephalopathy. Q3: What i

entries.h: Atypical Antidepressants · NG-101 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 💊 What it does ⚠️ Watch for 🗣️ Teach ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Mental Health · Psychiatric Care

Trazodone · Bupropion (Wellbutrin) · Mirtazapine — the ones that don't fit the SSRI/SNRI/MAOI mold NG-101 MENTAL HEALTH ADHD-friendly visual edition "Atypical" just means none of these three work through the standard SSRI/SNRI/MAOI mechanism — each has its own quirky target, and each earns its spot on the exam through one signature side effect : trazodone's priapism, bupropion's seizure risk, mirtazapine's weight gain. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 😴 Trazodone = sleep Sedating → used off-label as a s
STEP 1 · MECHANISM Three drugs, three different targets — none of them are classic serotonin reuptake blockers.

entries.h: 🧠 Three different mechanisms, one drug class label
entries.t: 🧠 “SARI sleeps, NDRI energizes, NaSSA feeds.” Match the mechanism to the side-effect profile and you'll never mix these three up.

Indication: depression; very commonly used off-label as a sleep aid at lower doses because of its sedating effect. Mnemonic: TraZZZadone / TRANCE-adone — sleepy and sedated. 🧠 If the question describes a depressed client with severe insomnia getting a low-dose bedtime medication that isn't a benzodiazepine — think trazodone .

Indication: depression and as an aid to stop smoking (marketed as Zyban for that indication, same drug). Comes in SR (sustained-release) and XL (extended-release) formulations. 🧠 “Bupropion helps you quit and stay energized.” It's the antidepressant of choice when a client also wants to stop smoking or is worried about sexual side effects/weight gain.

Indication: depression, especially useful when the client also has significant insomnia and poor appetite/weight loss — the side effects become the therapeutic benefit. 🧠 “Mirtaz-appetite.” Picture a fork and a pillow — this drug makes people eat and sleep, which is exactly what an underweight, sleepless depressed client needs. ⚠️
STEP 2 · SIDE EFFECTS Each drug has one signature danger sign the exam loves to test.

entries.h: 🚨 Trazodone — priapism is a medical emergency
entries.t: 😴 Sedation, drowsiness 📉 Orthostatic hypotension — dizziness with position changes 🚨 Priapism — rare but serious: an erection that persists for hours unrelated to sexual activity Priapism is a urologic emergency — untreated, it risks permanent tissue damage. Teach the client to go to the emergency department immediately if this occurs. 🧠 Rare ≠ ignorable. Priapism is the one trazodone side effect tested over and over precisely because students forget to mention it's an emergency.

Avoid bupropion in clients with: 🌀 A seizure disorder or history of seizures 🍽️ A current or past eating disorder (anorexia or bulimia nervosa) — electrolyte shifts from purging further lower the seizure threshold 🧠 “Bu-PRO-pion, PRO the seizures? No — PRO-tect against giving it in seizure/eating-disorder history.” Seizure risk is the #1 safety flag for this drug.

😴➡️😳 Insomnia (opposite of trazodone/mirtazapine) 🤕 Headache ⚖️ Weight loss — unlike most antidepressants 💚 No significant sexual side effects — a real advantage over SSRIs (see NG-205) 🧠 If the question says a client switched antidepressants because of sexual dysfunction, bupropion is a classic answer choice.

😴 Significant sedation — dose at bedtime ⚖️ Weight gain and increased appetite (the flip side of bupropion) 😵 Dizziness, dry mouth Low sexual side-effect profile, similar advantage to bupropion, but the mechanism and target population differ. 🧠 Bupropion and mirtazapine are opposites on sleep and weight — insomnia/weight loss vs. sedation/weight gain — pick based on what the client needs more of.

entries.h: 🧍 Side-effect body map — three drugs, three signature effects
entries.t: 🧠 One glance, one drug: droopy face + warning = trazodone , alert face + down arrow = bupropion , droopy face + up arrow = mirtazapine . 🗣️
STEP 3 · PATIENT EDUCATION Formulation rules, timing, and what to do if a warning sign shows up.

entries.h: 🚫 Bupropion SR/XL — never crush, chew, or cut
entries.t: 🚫 Never crush 🚫 Never chew 🚫 Never cut 🚫 Never double up on a missed dose Crushing/chewing an XL (extended-release) or SR (sustained-release) tablet dumps the full dose at once — this spikes blood levels and raises seizure risk sharply. 🧠 Extended-release + seizure-risk drug = never crush, ever. The whole point of the SR/XL coating is to prevent exactly the kind of dose spike that could trigger a seizure.

💊 Take at night — sedation is expected and useful for sleep Avoid alcohol and other sedatives (benzodiazepines, antihistamines) — additive CNS depression 🧍 Teach slow position changes to reduce orthostatic hypotension/fall risk 🚨 Go to the ED for any erection lasting more than a few hours

Can be started while the client is still smoking, with a target quit date set during treatment Take earlier in the day — insomnia is common if dosed at night Report new or worsening seizures, tremor, or agitation immediately

Take at bedtime — sedation is the point, not a problem to fight Expect increased appetite and possible weight gain — monitor weight over time Avoid driving/operating machinery until the sedating effect is known 🧠 Mirtazapine and trazodone both sedate, but only mirtazapine reliably drives appetite up — that's the differentiator.

entries.h: 🌳 Decision path — from patient picture to drug
🎯 Pick the right drug for the patient
entries.t: Patient picture Best-fit drug Why Depressed + severe insomnia, no other complaints Trazodone Sedating; low-dose off-label sleep aid Depressed + wants to quit smoking, worried about sexual side effects Bupropion Dual indication; no sexual side effects; energizing Depressed + poor appetite, underweight, can't sleep Mirtazapine Sedating + appetite-stimulating Seizure disorder or active eating disorder Avoid bupropion Lowers seizure threshold 🔗 For SSRI, SNRI, and MAOI mechanisms, interactions (serotonin syndrome, tyra

SAY IT OUT LOUD 😴 Trazodone sedating, sleep aid, watch for priapism ⚡ Bupropion seizure risk — avoid in seizure/eating disorder hx, never crush SR/XL 🍽️ Mirtazapine sedation + weight gain, good for poor sleep & appetite 💚 No sexual side effects bupropion (and mostly mirtazapine) — unlike SSRIs

Q1: A client on trazodone reports an erection lasting several hours with no sexual activity. What should the nurse instruct? Show answer Go to the emergency department immediately — priapism is a urologic emergency. Q2: Which client would be a poor candidate for bupropion? Show answer A client with a seizure disorder or an active/past eating disorder (anorexia or bulimia) — bupropion lowers the seizure threshold. Q3: A client is prescribed bupropion XL. Which teaching point is essential? Show answer Never crush, ch

entries.h: Bulimia Nervosa · NG-106 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🧨 Cause 🔎 Clues 🩺 Care ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Mental Health · Psychiatric Care Course

A serious, treatable eating disorder — the electrolytes are the emergency NG-106 Mental Health ADHD-friendly visual edition Bulimia nervosa is defined by recurrent episodes of binge eating followed by compensatory behaviors to prevent weight gain — self-induced vomiting, laxative or diuretic misuse, fasting, or excessive exercise. Clients often maintain a normal or near-normal body weight , which can hide the diagnosis. The #1 nursing priority is fluid & electrolyte monitoring — especially hypokalemia , because it
STEP 1 · THE CYCLE One repeating cycle explains the whole disorder — and it's driven by a distorted body image, not appetite.

EXAM TIP Bulimia nervosa involves 2 linked phases : 1) recurrent episodes of binge eating — consuming a large amount of food with a sense of loss of control — 2) followed by compensatory behavior to prevent weight gain, such as self-induced vomiting, misuse of laxatives/diuretics, fasting, or excessive exercise. Underneath it all sits a distorted body image and an obsessive drive to control weight. 🧠 "Binge, then bounce back the weight." The compensatory step is what defines bulimia — it's the attempt to "undo" the

Distorted body image — perception doesn't match reality Obsessive desire to control or lose weight Often coexists with anxiety, depression, or low self-esteem 🧠 The behaviors are about control , not hunger — treat the underlying emotional driver, not just the eating pattern.

entries.h: ⚖️ Bulimia vs. Anorexia — don't confuse them
entries.t: Bulimia Nervosa Anorexia Nervosa Body weight Usually normal or near-normal Significantly low for age/height Pattern Binge eating + compensatory behavior Severe, sustained food restriction Insight Often feels shame/guilt, more likely to recognize the behavior is a problem Frequently denies the severity of low weight 🧠 "Bulimia hides in a normal-looking body." Don't rule out bulimia just because weight looks unremarkable — this is the exact trap the exam sets. 🔎
STEP 2 · SPOT IT The body keeps the score — dental, glandular, and electrolyte clues, plus the environmental evidence.
🧠 "Teeth, cheeks, knuckles, skin." These four findings appear even when the scale gives no clue at all.

Repeated vomiting and laxative/diuretic misuse drain potassium, chloride, and hydrogen ions , producing hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis . 🧠 "K+ below normal = call it a cardiac problem." Hypokalemia is the single most dangerous complication of bulimia — it can trigger a fatal dysrhythmia.

Hidden or discarded food wrappers Laxative or diuretic boxes found discarded Frequent bathroom trips right after meals Weight fluctuations without an obvious dietary explanation 🧠 The evidence is usually environmental, not verbal — clients rarely disclose these behaviors on their own.

Bulimia is a medical and psychiatric condition, not a choice or a moral failing. Approach assessment and conversation with the same clinical neutrality used for any other disease — avoid commenting on weight, food choices, or appearance, and focus questions on feelings, stress, and control . 🧠 Sample short-term goal (ATI): "Verbalizing the desire to increase control over stressful situations" — reframes the goal around coping, not weight. 🩺
STEP 3 · STABILIZE & TREAT Electrolytes first, structure second, therapy for the long haul — and watch for refeeding syndrome if nutrition rehab begins.

🧪 Hypokalemia (K⁺ < 3.5 mEq/L ) → cardiac dysrhythmia risk — obtain baseline ECG, trend labs 🧪 Watch chloride and acid-base status — vomiting causes metabolic alkalosis 💧 Assess for dehydration from vomiting, laxative, or diuretic misuse 🧠 "Electrolytes before everything." A bulimic client can look medically stable and still be in cardiac danger from their potassium level alone.

entries.h: ⚠️ Refeeding syndrome — risk during nutritional rehabilitation
entries.t: If treatment includes structured nutritional rehabilitation after a period of chaotic or restricted intake, the reintroduction of food can trigger refeeding syndrome : an insulin surge drives potassium, phosphate, and magnesium into cells, causing a dangerous drop in serum levels. See NG-298 (TPN & Enteral Feeding) for the full refeeding syndrome electrolyte workup — same mechanism applies here whenever malnourished clients begin structured nutrition rehabilitation. 🧠 "Feeding too fast can crash the labs." Start nu

1 👀 1-on-1 supervision during meals 2 ⏱️ Supervise 1–2 hours after each meal to prevent compensatory behavior 3 📓 Food diary during hospitalization to track intake and patterns 4 🍽️ Regular, structured meals — helps break the binge/compensate cycle 🧠 "Watch the meal, then watch the hour after." The compensatory behavior almost always happens right after eating.

Drug Role Fluoxetine (SSRI) FDA-approved pharmacologic option for bulimia nervosa Bupropion (Wellbutrin) Avoided — associated with increased seizure risk in bulimia nervosa 🧠 "Fluoxetine yes, Bupropion no." If bupropion shows up as an answer choice for bulimia, it's the trap, not the treatment.

Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) is the first-line, evidence-based psychotherapy for bulimia nervosa Explore stress, control, and coping — the eating pattern is a symptom, not the root problem Approach with a calm, non-judgmental, therapeutic tone — shame worsens the cycle Coordinate with dietitian, therapist, and medical team for a whole-person plan 🧠 "Treat the person, not the plate." Sustainable recovery comes from addressing the emotional drivers alongside the physical stabilization. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🔄 Binge → compensate The defining two-part cycle 🚨 Hypokalemia Most dangerous complication — cardiac dysrhythmia risk 🦷 Teeth, cheeks, knuckles Dental erosion, parotid swelling, Russell's sign 🍽️ Supervise meals 1-on-1 during + 1–2 hr after, plus food diary

Q1: What electrolyte imbalance is the priority to monitor in bulimia nervosa, and why? Show answer Hypokalemia (K⁺ below 3.5 mEq/L) — it can cause life-threatening cardiac dysrhythmias. Q2: A client with bulimia nervosa has a normal body weight. Does that rule out the diagnosis? Show answer No — clients with bulimia often maintain a normal or near-normal body weight, unlike anorexia nervosa. Don't rule it out based on appearance. entries.h: Depression: Nursing Care · NG-112 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🧨 Cause 🔎 Clues 🩺 Care ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Mental Health · Psychiatric Care

Suicide risk assessment · therapeutic communication · milieu safety NG-112 MENTAL HEALTH ADHD-friendly visual edition Once you know a client is depressed, the nursing job shifts to one priority : is this client safe? That means asking about suicide directly , recognizing the paradox where a sudden lift in mood can mean rising danger, and building a safe, structured, low-demand environment while therapy and medication take weeks to work. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🚨 Ask directly “Do you have though
STEP 1 · WHAT KIND, AND WHY Depression isn't one thing — the type changes the teaching. The mechanism is the same low-neurotransmitter picture underneath all of them.

entries.h: 🗓️ Four faces of depression — same low mood, different timeline
entries.t: 🧠 “The Big 4” — M DD hits hard & leaves, D ysthymia stays low forever, S AD comes back every winter, P eripartum shows up around baby. Same low mood, four different clocks.

Depression is linked to low levels of serotonin, norepinephrine & dopamine in the brain — everything runs low and slow : mood, energy, sleep, appetite, concentration. 🔗 Full neurotransmitter diagram & the 9-symptom "SIG E CAPS" breakdown live on NG-031 Depression: Signs & Symptoms — this page assumes that baseline and focuses on what the nurse does about it . 🧠 Low & slow = the whole disease in three words.

👪 Family history of depression or suicide 🔁 Prior suicide attempt — the single strongest predictor 🍺 Substance use disorder 🏥 Chronic or terminal illness, chronic pain 😔 Recent loss — job, relationship, bereavement 🧍 Social isolation, lack of support system 🧠 A prior attempt is the single biggest red flag in the whole chart — always screen history before you screen today's mood. 🔎
STEP 2 · SPOT THE RISK Symptoms tell you the client is depressed. Risk clues tell you whether they are about to act on it — a completely different question.

S leep changes I nterest lost (anhedonia) G uilt / worthlessness E nergy loss (anergia) C oncentration poor A ppetite/weight change P sychomotor slowing or agitation S uicidal ideation + depressed mood most of the day, most days. Diagnostic threshold and full detail on NG-031 .

entries.h: 🚨 A PRIORITY: suicide risk — the warning signs that override everything else
entries.t: 🎁 Giving away cherished/valued possessions 💬 Statements: “I can't go on,” “I do not want to live,” “I won't be a problem much longer,” “This will all be over soon” 📈📉 A sudden, abrupt change in energy — in either direction 🗒️ Making final arrangements, settling affairs, saying goodbye 🧠 “Gifts + goodbyes = red flags.” A depressed client who suddenly starts giving things away or sounds like they're wrapping things up is telling you something — take it literally, not figuratively.

entries.h: ⚠️ The classic NCLEX trap — calmer or more energetic can mean MORE danger, not less
entries.t: Early in treatment, physical energy and psychomotor drive can return before the depressed, hopeless mood lifts. The client now has both the intent (still hopeless) and the energy (newly restored) to act on a plan — this is one of the highest-yield NCLEX points in psych. A client who suddenly seems calm, smiling, and "cured" after being severely depressed needs closer observation, not less. 🧠 “Energy comes back before hope does.” Never chart a sudden mood lift as reassuring without reassessing suicidal ideation firs

entries.h: 🗣️ Ask it directly — the exact assessment questions
entries.t: “Have you had any thoughts of hurting yourself?” “Do you have a plan to end your life?” “Do you have access to the means to carry out that plan?” “Do you want to die?” Asking directly does not plant the idea and does not increase risk — it is the single most important, evidence-based nursing action. Vague or indirect questions get vague, unreliable answers. 🧠 “Plan + means + intent” = the three things every suicide risk assessment must uncover. The more specific and immediate the plan and access, the higher the ris
STEP 3 · KEEP THEM SAFE Least restrictive environment that is still safe — then presence, structure, and time while treatment works.

1 Continuous 1:1 observation — active plan, means, and intent = highest risk, arm's-length supervision at all times 2 Room close to the nurses' station , not an isolated private room 3 Remove harmful objects from the room and environment per unit protocol (means restriction) 4 Supervise during meals and personal care 5 Reassess every shift — thoughts can escalate or de-escalate quickly 🧠 Risk level sets the observation level. The more specific the plan and the more available the means, the further right on this sta

✅ Use simple, direct language — depressed clients have low concentration/energy for complex conversation ✅ Sit with the client , even in silence — your presence is an intervention ✅ “I'd like to hear about how you are feeling now” — open, non-judgmental ✅ Reflect and validate feelings without minimizing them Never use empty reassurance — “everything will be fine,” “you have so much to live for” — it shuts the conversation down and feels dismissive. 🧠 Presence > advice. The best therapeutic response is almost always

Offer a structured program of activities the client can choose to join Invite and encourage group participation — do not command it Assist with ADLs — offer to help the client get dressed, sit with them, walk with them Look for improvement clues : talking about future plans, goals, family, holidays — a genuine sign of progress vs. the false calm of a fixed plan 🧠 A client who says “I talked with my family about ways we can celebrate the holidays together” is showing real improvement — future-oriented language is re

Depression commonly causes appetite and weight change (usually loss) — poor intake is a real medical risk, not just a symptom to note. Small, frequent, high-calorie / high-protein meals and snacks Stay with the client during meals Weekly weighing — the most reliable way to evaluate whether nutrition interventions are working 🧠 Trend the weight, not the tray. A client can pick at food and still be losing ground — the weekly weight is the objective outcome measure.
🧠 Exact time frames vary by client and reference — the concept, not the calendar, is what's tested: stabilize → protect against relapse → protect long-term . ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🎁 Giving things away + goodbye statements = act on it, don't dismiss it ⚠️ Sudden calm/energy = reassess risk, not reassurance 👁️ Highest risk = continuous 1:1 observation 🗣️ Ask directly “Do you have a plan?” never increases risk

Q1: A client with major depression and suicidal ideation is suddenly calmer and more energetic. What should the nurse consider? Show answer This can mean INCREASED suicide risk — the client may now have the energy to act on a plan. Increase the level of observation/precautions and reassess immediately, don't assume improvement. Q2: A client says he has no reason to continue living. What should the nurse ask first? Show answer Ask directly and specifically: "Do you have any plans to end your life right now?" — asses

entries.h: Panic Attack · NG-126 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics ⚡ Cause 🔎 Clues 🩺 Care ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Mental Health · Anxiety-Spectrum Disorders

Discrete Episode of Intense Fear + Autonomic Surge NG-126 MENTAL HEALTH ADHD-friendly visual edition A panic attack is a sudden surge of intense fear or discomfort that peaks within about 10 minutes , dominated by physical symptoms so convincing the client often believes they're dying. It can occur on its own (panic disorder) or inside OCD, phobias, or PTSD. Classic ER teaching point: rule out a cardiac event first — panic attacks can mimic an MI closely enough that you don't get to assume. 📄 Simple Nursing origina
STEP 1 · THE SURGE One nervous-system event explains the entire attack — a sympathetic surge with no "off" switch for several terrifying minutes.

entries.h: ⚡ The full sympathetic ("fight or flight") surge
entries.t: 🧠 Same surge as OCD/phobia/PTSD, maximum volume. This diagram is the physiology behind every anxiety-spectrum "clue" in this batch — panic attack is just the surge without a specific external trigger required.

Panic attack = the discrete episode itself — can occur inside OCD, a phobia, PTSD, or generalized anxiety, or entirely out of the blue. Panic disorder = recurrent, unexpected panic attacks plus persistent worry about having another one — often leading to avoidance behavior (agoraphobia). 🧠 One attack ≠ a disorder. It's the pattern + fear of the next one that upgrades it to panic disorder.

Can be spontaneous/unexpected (no identifiable cause) or situational — inside a phobia exposure, an OCD ritual interruption, or a PTSD trauma reminder. All share the same underlying nervous-system surge. 🔎
STEP 2 · RULE OUT THE HEART The symptoms overlap with a heart attack closely enough that the ER workup comes before the psych label.

entries.h: ❤️ Panic attack vs. myocardial infarction — the classic mimic
entries.t: 🧠 “Rule the heart out before you rule the mind in.” A client having surgery with chest pain, choking, and hot flashes still gets worked up for cardiac causes first — the diagnosis of panic disorder comes after that workup is clear.
Fear of death — "impending doom" Feelings of detachment / derealization Chest pain & heart palpitations Trembling & numbness Hyperventilation Sweating & hot flashes Nausea & choking sensation

A client becomes increasingly anxious, sweats profusely, breathes rapidly, and states "I feel like I'm having a panic attack." Best actions (select all that apply pattern): stay by the client's side, escort to a quiet place, use a comforting tone. 🧠 If an option involves leaving the client to get something (even a good idea, like medication) before staying with them first, it's usually a distractor — presence comes first. 🩺
STEP 3 · STAY & GROUND Presence and grounding stop the acute attack; SSRIs and CBT prevent the next one.

1 REMAIN with the client — the #1 priority, do not leave them alone 2 Move to a quiet, low-stimulation room 3 Speak calmly , using simple, short, clear sentences 4 Coach slow, paced breathing — counted inhale/exhale to break hyperventilation 5 Once it resolves , assess triggers and connect to a longer-term coping plan 🧠 “Stay, Space, Speak, Slow (breathing).” All four before you ever reach for a medication.
🧠 Pair with slow, paced breathing (in for 4 counts, hold 4 , out 4 ) to break the hyperventilation cycle.

Drug class Role Benzodiazepines Short-term / PRN for an acute attack — rapid onset SSRIs / SNRIs First-line long-term prevention for panic disorder Beta-blockers ("-lol", e.g. atenolol) Blunt physical symptoms (racing heart, tremor) 🧠 Benzos calm the attack ; SSRIs prevent the next one. CBT is the durable, non-drug foundation either way.

entries.h: 🚨 Never do this during a panic attack
entries.t: Never leave the client alone during the episode Never assume "it's just anxiety" without ruling out a cardiac cause when symptoms are new or ambiguous Never crowd the client's space or raise your voice ✅ Do stay, keep it quiet, keep your voice calm, and coach the breathing ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD ⏱️ Peaks <10 min sudden onset, self-resolving 🧍 REMAIN with client #1 priority, never leave them alone ❤️ Rule out MI first ECG + troponin before "it's anxiety" 🖐️ 5-4-3-2-1 grounding + slow paced breathing

Show answer Rule out a cardiac cause (ECG, troponin) before attributing the symptoms to panic — panic attacks are a diagnosis of exclusion in this setting. Q2: What is the nurse's #1 priority action during an active panic attack? Show answer Remain with the client — stay by their side, don't leave them alone. Therapeutic Communication — Part 2 of a 4-page Schizophrenia series NG-128 Mental Health Series 2 of 4 · communication techniques This page assumes you already know the vocabulary from NG-049 (hallucinations, delusions, disorganized speech). Here we cover how to talk to a client experiencing psychosis — what to say, what never to say, reality orientation vs. validation, and the therapeutic milieu. Drug therapy is on NG-165 & NG-235 . 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🚫 Never argue You cannot logic someon
STEP 1 · THE RULES BEHIND EVERY RESPONSE Every "correct" NCLEX answer for psychosis traces back to these four rules.

1 Never argue with or challenge a delusion. A fixed false belief cannot be reasoned away — trying only proves to the client that you're "against" them too. 2 Never pretend to see or hear a hallucination. Lying breaks trust the moment the client realizes it — and they usually do. 3 Do not directly reinforce the false belief either — you also don't say "yes, I believe the FBI is watching you." 4 Respond to the feeling under the content. Fear, isolation, and distress are real even when their cause is not. 🧠 "Honest +

entries.h: ⚖️ Reality orientation vs. validation therapy — know the debate
entries.t: Reality orientation — gently, calmly stating the objective facts ("I don't see anyone else in the room") without arguing. Validation therapy — focuses on the emotion and meaning behind the experience rather than correcting facts; used more often in dementia-related psychosis where reorientation can increase agitation. 🧠 For schizophrenia , standard exam practice favors brief, gentle reality orientation paired with feeling-focused validation — not pure validation therapy alone. Know both terms; questions may test th

"What are the voices saying?" "What do you see?" "Describe what you are seeing right now." "How does it feel to think you are being watched?" "What activities did you enjoy in the past?" (assesses anhedonia/avolition from NG-049) 🧠 Open-ended assessment questions gather data without confirming or denying the content — the safest way to explore a hallucination or delusion. 💬
STEP 2 · SCRIPTED RESPONSES Real NCLEX/HESI/Kaplan-style stems — memorize the shape of the correct answer, not just the words.

Client: "There are strange people in the corner of my room laughing at me and saying horrible things." ✅ therapeutic "I don't hear any voices, but I know this is frightening for you." ❌ avoid "There's no one there, you're imagining it." (dismissive, argues the point) ❌ avoid "Oh yes, I can see them too." (dishonest, reinforces the hallucination) 🧠 Formula: "I don't [see/hear] X, but I [know/understand] it feels real/frightening to you." Same sentence shape works for every hallucination question.

Client: "Do you see those cameras in the ceiling? I'm being watched all the time." ✅ therapeutic "Those are sprinklers, not cameras. It might be frightening to think that others want to hurt you." (brief factual correction once, then pivot to feeling) ❌ avoid Long explanations/arguing about why the belief is false — repeated debate reinforces the delusion's importance instead of reducing it. Client refusing food: "The voices say the food is poisoned." ✅ therapeutic "I understand the voices are very real to you, but

"You see yourself as the savior" — accusatory, shuts down trust Arguing facts repeatedly — cannot out-logic a fixed delusion Ignoring the client and walking away — client with schizophrenia leaving the room when a nurse asks about their day is not the nurse's cue to just "let them go quietly" — approach again later, offer a shorter/simpler interaction, don't abandon the therapeutic relationship Whispering or laughing near the client — easily misread as part of a persecutory delusion 🧠 "I see you as my client" is a

entries.h: ✅ Building blocks of every good response
entries.t: State the facts calmly, once — "I see you are frightened, let's go to your room and talk about this." Acknowledge the client's feelings explicitly, every time. Focus on reality and reinforce it verbally, without arguing. Keep sentences short and concrete — disorganized speech + concrete thinking (NG-049) means idioms and long explanations may not land. 🧠 "FACTS-FEELINGS-REALITY" — every correct answer stacks these three in some order. 🏥
STEP 3 · THE ENVIRONMENT AS TREATMENT Communication isn't just words — the unit environment itself is a therapeutic tool.
🧠 Decrease environmental stimuli — dim lighting, fewer people, less noise — reduces the raw sensory input that psychosis has to sort through, which can lower agitation and hallucination intensity.

entries.h: 🧊 Catatonic presentation — a special communication case
entries.t: Catatonia with catalepsy can include immobility, bizarre posturing, muscle rigidity, mutism, severe negativism, and staring. 🧠 Priority: ensure physical safety (fall/injury prevention, nutrition/hydration, skin integrity) while continuing to speak to the client normally — hearing may be intact even without a visible response.

entries.h: ✅ Nutrition & fluid monitoring belongs in the plan too
entries.t: Disorganized behavior, paranoia about food, or catatonia can all reduce oral intake. Fluid and nutritional intake is a standard plan-of-care item — not just a "medical" concern, it's a communication + safety issue (offering sealed food, eating with the client, structured mealtimes). 🧠 Don't let "communication" tunnel-vision you away from basic physiologic needs on a care-plan question. 🩺
STEP 4 · WHAT OUTRANKS COMMUNICATION Good communication supports safety — it never replaces a safety assessment.

If voices are instructing the client to harm self or others, this is a priority safety issue , not just a communication moment — assess plan/means/intent and escalate per unit protocol immediately. 🧠 Carrying NG-049 forward: suicide risk is HIGH in schizophrenia at every phase — command hallucinations raise that risk further and change your very next action.

NG-235 — Antipsychotics (drug reference) Typical vs. atypical, mechanism, EPS, NMS, agranulocytosis. 🧠 If a question is testing what to say , you're on the right page. If i

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🚫 Never argue Delusions can't be reasoned away 🙅 Never pretend Don't claim to see/hear what isn't there ❤️ Validate feelings "I don't hear voices, but I know this is scary for you" 🏥 Milieu matters Safety, structure, low stimulation, consistent staff

Q1: A client says "I understand that the voices are very real to you, but I do not hear them" — is this therapeutic? Show answer Yes — it is honest (the nurse denies hearing the voices) while validating the client's experience as real to them. Q2: What should the nurse NEVER do when a client reports a hallucination? Show answer Never pretend to see or hear it (dishonest) and never argue that it isn't real (ineffective, damages trust). The Teaching Checklist — What To Actually Tell The Patient NG-135 Mental Health ADHD-friendly visual edition The practical companion to the biology. Every habit below exists to protect the light-melatonin-SCN loop taught on Sleep Circadian Rhythm (NG-089) — this page is the actionable half: what to do at home, and what to do at the bedside in the hospital. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → ☀️ Bright & active by day Sun in the morning sets the clock; save the dim, quiet room for night. ☕ Cut caffeine/nico
STEP 1 · THE 60-SECOND RECAP Every recommendation on this page is protecting the same light-melatonin loop — full mechanism on NG-089.

entries.h: 🔁 Light & timing set the clock — habits either help or fight it
entries.t: The SCN uses light exposure to time melatonin release and body temperature. Bright light + activity by day, dim light + quiet by night is the whole strategy — every bullet below is one specific way to deliver that pattern consistently. 🔗 See NG-089 — Sleep Circadian Rhythm for the full SCN/melatonin/light mechanism behind every item here. ✅
STEP 2 · WHAT TO TEACH A short, consistent list beats a long one nobody remembers — group it by when it happens in the day.

entries.h: ✅ Routine sleep schedule — the foundation habit
entries.t: 1 🛏️ Go to bed & wake up at the same time every day — including weekends 2 ☀️ Open blinds/curtains in the morning — bright light resets the clock 3 🏃 Be sunny, bright & active during the day — schedule activities/interventions in daylight hours 4 🌡️ Quiet, cool, dark room at night — lower the temperature, dim the lights 🧠 "Bright by day, dim by night." Consistency in timing matters as much as any single behavior — an irregular schedule fights the SCN even if every other habit is perfect.

entries.h: ❌ Avoid in the hours before bed
entries.t: 🍷 NO nightcap alcohol ≠ sleep aid ☕ NO caffeine coffee, tea, soda, chocolate 🚬 NO nicotine cigarettes, chew 🏋️ Strenuous exercise avoid late afternoon 🌶️ Spicy food before bed 🍔 Large meal/snack right before bed 🍞 Going to bed hungry either extreme disrupts sleep 📱 Non-sleep activities in bed TV, phone, work, reading Caffeine & nicotine — avoid 4-6 hours before bed ; alcohol is never a routine sleep aid despite the common "glass of wine at night." 🧠 "Bed is for sleep only." If reading helps you wind down, do it in
⏱️ Limit naps to 20 minutes, up to 2 times per day 🚫 No naps in the late afternoon/evening — eats into nighttime sleep drive 🏥
STEP 3 · NURSING PROCESS The same habits, translated into a unit — plus one safety rule that overrides all of them.

entries.h: 🚨 Hospital safety rules — the two you cannot compromise
entries.t: 🔔 NEVER turn off/disable essential equipment alarms at night to let a patient sleep — cardiac monitor, ventilator, and other patient-safety alarms stay on; that is a safety risk, not a comfort measure 💊 NEVER increase a client's sedation dose at night just to promote sleep — sedation is not the same as restorative sleep and adds respiratory/fall risk 🧠 Comfort measures are never a substitute for safety. If a stem offers "silence the alarms" or "increase the sedative" as ways to help a hospitalized client sleep, bot

entries.h: ✅ What actually helps in the hospital
entries.t: ☀️ Open blinds/curtains in the morning for sunlight 📅 Schedule interventions & activities during the day when possible 🌙 Dim the lights at night 🤫 Cluster care — group tasks to limit waking the client overnight 📋 Determine the client's usual bedtime and plan the routine around it 😷 CPAP for known sleep apnea, if ordered 🌿 OTC options — melatonin or chamomile for rest, when appropriate 💊 Prescription sleep medication — a last resort, not the first intervention

A Assess sleep pattern history, disorders, and life changes affecting sleep (e.g., anxiety, routine disruption) D Disturbed sleep pattern r/t anxiety or alteration in client routine P Client will sleep 8 hours nightly, lights out at 10:00 pm , in a quiet cool dark room away from the nurses' station at 68°F I Implement the daily-habit & hospital-safety interventions above E Evaluate — did the client sleep 8 hours, lights out at 10 pm as planned? 🧠 "ADPIE ends where it starts." The evaluation question is always a dir

Every intervention above is protecting the light → SCN → melatonin pathway. If a question asks why morning light or a dark bedroom matters, the mechanism — not just the checklist — is what's being tested. 🔗 See NG-089 — Sleep Circadian Rhythm for the SCN/melatonin mechanism, sleep-stage architecture, and circadian disorders (shift work, jet lag, delayed sleep phase) this checklist is built on. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD ☀️ Bright/active by day Dim/quiet/cool by night — same schedule daily ☕ 4-6 hour cutoff Caffeine & nicotine before bed; alcohol is never a sleep aid 🛏️ Bed = sleep only No screens/work/reading in bed — 20-min naps max, 2x/day 🚨 Hospital rule Never silence safety alarms or increase sedation just to promote sleep

Q2: What is the single most important morning habit for circadian health? Show answer Opening the blinds/curtains for bright light exposure at a consistent wake time — it resets the SCN each day. Q3: What are the two hospital "never" actions for helping a client sleep? Show answer Never turn off/disable essential equipment alarms, and never increase seda

Recognition · Mandatory Reporting · Safety Planning NG-139 Mental Health ADHD-friendly visual edition Nurses are mandated reporters . This page covers recognition of physical, emotional, sexual, financial abuse and neglect across child, elder, and intimate-partner contexts, plus the objective documentation and safety-planning steps that follow — clinical and factual, not graphic . 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🧩 5 forms Physical · emotional · sexual · financial · neglect. 🚪 IPV priority action Separa
STEP 1 · NAME THE TYPE Abuse is not only physical — and it happens across every age group in different patterns.
🧠 "PESFN" — say it like "pieces-fin": P hysical · E motional · S exual · F inancial · N eglect. Every abuse question is really asking "which piece is missing?"

A form of abuse that happens when the caregiver fails to provide for the needs of the elderly client — either emotionally, physically, or socially . 🧠 Neglect is a failure to act , not a direct act — that's what separates it from active physical/emotional abuse in documentation.

entries.h: 💔 Intimate partner violence (IPV) — key word definition
entries.t: Intimate partner violence is domestic violence or abusive behavior inflicted by one partner against the other — physically, emotionally, verbally, sexually, or financially. Abusive partner traits: extreme jealousy & possessiveness Abuse gets more intense during pregnancy 🧠 Pregnancy is a documented high-risk window for IPV escalation — screen every pregnant client privately, every visit. 🔎
STEP 2 · SPOT THE PATTERN Signs cluster differently by population — know the elder-neglect picture and the IPV screening questions cold.

entries.h: 👵 Elder neglect — what the nurse observes
entries.t: 🧠 Assessment case: a 79-year-old weighs 93 lbs, wears old dirty clothes, and is admitted with pneumonia. The comment that suggests significant abuse risk : "Our family is poor, so my daughter gets my monthly retirement and Social Security checks." → financial exploitation as part of neglect .

entries.h: 🩹 Caregiver Role Strain (CRS) — a risk factor to assess, not blame
entries.t: Assess stressors & unmet needs of the caregiver Ask about the nature & requirements of providing daily care 🧠 Neglect isn't always malicious — an overwhelmed, unsupported caregiver is a known risk factor . Assessing CRS is prevention, not accusation.

PRIORITY Have the partner leave the room to speak with and examine the client in private . "Is anyone hurting you?" "When you and your spouse disagree, what happens?" "Has your spouse ever threatened you verbally or with violence?" 🧠 Bruises in various stages of healing on assessment = ask these three direct, private questions — never in front of the suspected abuser.

entries.h: ⚠️ Why victims stay — and when danger peaks
entries.t: Financial dependence Fear of harm (to self, children, pets) Child custody concerns Religious or cultural beliefs Abuse is expected to worsen when the victim moves toward independence from the abuser — leaving is statistically the most dangerous point in an abusive relationship. 🧠 Never judge "why don't they just leave." The nurse's job is safety planning for whenever the client is ready — not pressuring them to leave on the nurse's timeline. 🛡️
STEP 3 · REPORT, DOCUMENT, PLAN SAFETY Reporting is mandatory; documentation and safety planning are the nurse's core interventions.

entries.h: 📣 Mandatory reporting — a nurse's legal duty
entries.t: 1 🚨 Ensure immediate safety — treat injuries, separate client from suspected abuser for the interview 2 📞 Report per state law & facility policy — nurses are mandated reporters for suspected child abuse/neglect and elder abuse in every U.S. state; reporting is not optional and does not require the client's/family's consent 3 📝 Document objectively — direct quotes, measured/described findings, no personal conclusions 4 🧷 Preserve evidence if applicable per facility protocol 5 🏠 Safety-plan & connect to resources bef

Assure the victim they are not alone Preserve physical evidence , if applicable Convey concern & respect — nonjudgmental attitude Affirm the client did not deserve or cause the abuse Help identify triggers and destructive patterns; learn alternative responses (psychotherapy/talk therapy) Develop a safety plan — local shelter contact information 🧠 Priority action before discharge home: provide contact information for the local shelter.

Use the client's own words in direct quotes Describe findings objectively (size, location, color) — avoid concluding "abuse" in the chart; describe, don't diagnose intent Use a body map/diagram where available Note who was present during the exam and interview Avoid leading questions; ask open-ended questions in private 🧠 Objective ≠ vague. "3 cm bruise, left forearm, purple-yellow" is objective. "Client was clearly beaten" is not — that's a conclusion, not a finding.

A client experiencing IPV states: "I should try to identify issues that increased my partner's stress level." This statement needs correction — it reflects internalized responsibility for the abuser's behavior. Effective teaching redirects the client toward recognizing that the abuse is not their responsibility to prevent or manage , and toward safety planning instead. 🧠 A common NCLEX trap: a statement that sounds like insight ("I'll manage their stress") can actually indicate the client still blames themselves —

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🧩 5 forms Physical · emotional · sexual · financial · neglect 🚪 IPV Interview privately, away from the partner 📣 Mandated reporter Suspicion is enough — report per policy/law 🏠 Before discharge Give local shelter contact info
