Show answer Elder neglect with financial exploitation — a caregiver failing to meet physical/financial needs. Q2: A client has bruises in various stages of healing. What must the nurse ask? Show answer "Is anyone hurting you?" / "What happens when you and your spouse disagree?" / "Has your spouse ever threatened you verbally or with violence?" — asked in private. Q3: When is IPV danger

entries.h: Depression: Procedures (ECT/TMS) · NG-149 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🧲 ECT vs TMS 📋 Before ⚡ During 🛌 After ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Mental Health · Psychiatric Care

ECT · TMS · Vagus Nerve Stimulation — non-drug options for treatment-resistant depression NG-149 MENTAL HEALTH ADHD-friendly visual edition When medication and therapy alone haven't worked, or a client needs a fast, safe response (severe suicidality, catatonia, psychotic depression, pregnancy), the next step is a brain-stimulation procedure . ECT is the most tested — think of it as a controlled, monitored "reset" that induces a brief, therapeutic seizure. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → ⚡ ECT = brief s

SIDE BY SIDE Two procedures for the same client. Almost every exam item turns on one of the four rows highlighted in red. ⚡ ECT Asleep. A seizure is induced on purpose under anesthesia. Memory loss expected. 🧲 TMS Awake. Magnetic pulses, no seizure intended — but a seizure is its rare serious adverse effect. 🚨 The trap “TMS causes no seizure” describes the mechanism . Asked for an adverse effect , the answer is seizure .

Feature ⚡ ECT 🧲 TMS What it does Electrical stimulus induces a brief generalized seizure Repeated magnetic pulses to a mood-regulation area (left prefrontal cortex) Anesthesia Yes — general anesthesia + muscle relaxant None. Client is awake and alert Seizure Induced — that is the treatment Not induced, but a rare, serious adverse effect Adverse effects Confusion + short-term memory loss (expected, temporary) · headache · muscle aches · nausea Scalp discomfort at the site · headache · lightheadedness · facial twitch

Both statements are true at once, and exams are built on the gap between them: ECT — a seizure is deliberately induced . It is the therapy. Roughly 30–60 seconds, under anesthesia with a muscle relaxant so the body stays still. TMS — no seizure is intended . Magnetic pulses only, client awake. But a seizure is TMS's rare and most serious adverse effect — which is why metal in the head and a seizure history matter so much. 🧠 Read the stem twice. “How does it work?” → TMS induces no seizure. “What adverse effect do y

entries.h: 🧲 Why metal is the TMS dealbreaker
entries.t: TMS is a magnet . A strong, rapidly changing magnetic field will heat or move ferromagnetic metal, so anything metal in or near the head rules it out: Aneurysm clips and coils Cochlear implants Deep-brain stimulators and other implanted electrodes Bullet fragments or shrapnel Dental fillings and braces are generally fine — they sit far enough from the coil. 🧠 Magnet = metal question. If an implant appears in a TMS stem, it is almost always the answer.

entries.h: ✅ What you teach, side by side
entries.t: Before ECT: nothing to eat or drink for 6–8 hours, you will be asleep, you will be confused for a while afterward and that is expected, and you may not drive for the whole course. Before TMS: you stay awake, it takes 20–40 minutes, you will hear loud clicking so you will wear earplugs, your scalp may feel sore where the coil sits, and you can drive yourself home . 🧠 The single teaching difference clients ask about first: ECT costs you the day. TMS costs you the hour.

ECT seizes on purpose. TMS pulses — and seizes by accident. ECT = A nesthesia · S eizure · M emory loss TMS = A wake · M agnet · M etal is the contraindication 🧠 If the stem mentions NPO, consent, or a crash cart it is ECT. If it mentions an office visit, earplugs, or driving home it is TMS. 📋
STEP 1 · PREP & SCREEN Same prep as any procedure under brief general anesthesia — plus a few psych-specific holds.

entries.h: 🚨 Screen the whole history — report to the HCP
entries.t: ECT briefly raises intracranial pressure and stresses the cardiovascular system during the seizure, so the biggest contraindication-style concerns are: 🧠 Cerebral neoplasm / space-occupying brain lesion — raised ICP risk ❤️ Recent myocardial infarction — cardiac stress risk 👁️ Recent stroke, retinal issues, or other high anesthesia risk — verify per facility screening 🧠 Same red flags as any general anesthesia case — a fresh MI or a brain lesion means the heart or the skull can't safely tolerate the stress of a sei

✅ Signed informed consent ✅ NPO 6–8 hours before the procedure ✅ Have the client void immediately before ✅ Remove dentures and contact lenses ✅ Baseline vital signs 🧠 Read this list and you're really reading a pre-op checklist — ECT is done under brief general anesthesia, so treat it like surgery prep.

Do not give anticonvulsant medications — e.g. valproic acid , carbamazepine — before ECT. These drugs work by raising the seizure threshold , which fights the entire point of the treatment: ECT needs a seizure to be therapeutic. 🧠 Anticonvulsant = anti-seizure = anti-ECT. If the goal is to trigger a seizure, don't give the drug whose job is to prevent one.

A client with depression often has poor nutritional intake going into the procedure — assess and correct this beforehand where possible: offer high-calorie fluids/snacks earlier in the day, and let the client help select menu items when eating is allowed. 🧠 Depression's appetite loss doesn't pause for procedure day — keep nutrition on the plan right up to the NPO window. ⚡
STEP 2 · THE PROCEDURE A brief, monitored, medically induced seizure — not the uncontrolled event people picture.

ECT induces electrical activity across the scalp to trigger a generalized seizure — think of it as jump-starting the brain's chemistry. Because the client is under general anesthesia with a muscle relaxant, there is no violent outward convulsing. Each seizure is brief — generally 15–60 seconds (exact duration varies by reference/response) Given 2–3×/week for a course totaling roughly 6–12 treatments 🧠 “Jump-start, not lightning strike.” The client is asleep, paralyzed by the muscle relaxant, and monitored the entir

entries.h: 🧰 Equipment that must be at bedside
entries.t: ❤️ Cardiac monitor 🛒 Crash cart 🫁 Oxygen 🧹 Suction 🧠 “C-C-O-S” — Cardiac monitor · Crash cart · Oxygen · Suction. If it's on a code cart, it needs to be in the ECT room.

ECT is performed by a team including anesthesia provider + psychiatrist , typically in a monitored procedural setting (often same-day/outpatient once stable). The nurse's role during the procedure is continuous monitoring and immediate post-ictal recovery care. 🧠 Same team structure as any brief anesthesia procedure — anesthesia manages sedation, psychiatry manages the treatment itself.
STEP 3 · RECOVER & TEACH Expect brief confusion and short-term memory loss — reassure, reorient, and protect until it clears.

entries.h: 🧠 Expected side effect: temporary confusion & short-term memory loss
entries.t: The most important nursing action when a client wakes up confused with memory gaps is to remind the client that the memory loss is temporary — reorient to person/place/time, stay calm and simple, and reassess after the full course. 🧠 Expected ≠ ignored. Confusion/memory loss is a known, temporary effect — but the nurse still reorients every time and documents severity.

entries.h: 🚗 Teaching: no driving during the course
entries.t: No driving for the duration of the ECT treatment course — confusion/memory effects make it unsafe Arrange transportation to and from every session Avoid major decisions or signing important documents until memory clears 🧠 If confusion is expected after the treatment, driving is off the table for the whole course — not just treatment day.

Recovery-room style monitoring: vitals, airway, LOC until fully awake Reorient frequently — person, place, time Reassess mood & suicidal ideation once alert — ECT does not remove the need for ongoing safety checks Offer food/fluids once fully awake and gag reflex intact 🧠 Waking up from ECT is a lot like waking up from any anesthesia — airway, orientation, and safety come first, memory reassurance comes right after.

entries.h: 🧲 Non-drug alternatives: TMS & Vagus Nerve Stimulation
entries.t: Feature ⚡ ECT 🧲 TMS (transcranial magnetic stimulation) Anesthesia Yes — general anesthesia + muscle relaxant No anesthesia needed Mechanism Electrical stimulus induces a generalized seizure Repeated magnetic pulses stimulate a targeted mood-regulation area of the brain — no seizure induced (though a seizure is its rare adverse effect — see ECT vs TMS ) Memory effects Temporary short-term memory loss/confusion is expected Minimal to no memory effects Setting Monitored procedural/OR-style setting Outpatient office v

SAY IT OUT LOUD 📋 Before Consent + NPO 6–8h + hold anticonvulsants + remove dentures/contacts 🧰 Equipment Cardiac monitor · crash cart · oxygen · suction, every time 🧠 After Confusion & short-term memory loss — remind: it's temporary 🚗 Teach No driving for the whole treatment course

Q1: A client with severe depression and poor nutritional intake is scheduled for ECT. Which orders would the nurse expect (select all that apply)? Show answer NPO 6–8 hours before the procedure, signed informed consent, remove dentures/contacts, screen for recent MI or cerebral neoplasm and report to the HCP, hold anticonvulsant medications (e.g. valproic acid, carbamazepine). Q2: A client has temporary confusion and memory loss after ECT. What is the most important nursing action? Show answer Remind the client tha

entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🎯 Approach 🚧 Barriers 💉 LAIs 🩺 Priorities ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Mental Health · Psychiatric Care Course

Pharmacology — Treatment Approach & Adherence — Part 3 of a 4-page series NG-165 Mental Health Series 3 of 4 · schizophrenia-specific drug approach 📍 SCOPE OF THIS PAGE: schizophrenia treatment strategy — why adherence fails, insight/anosognosia, and long-acting injectables. For the full antipsychotic drug reference (typical vs. atypical, mechanism, EPS, NMS, agranulocytosis) go to NG-235 . Medication only works if it's taken. This page is about why clients with schizophrenia stop taking antipsychotics and what the
STEP 1 · THE STRATEGY Medication controls symptoms — it does not cure schizophrenia. The plan is lifelong management, not a short course.

entries.h: 🎯 The 3-part non-drug foundation every regimen sits on
entries.t: 1 🏠 Safe, structured environment that promotes trust (see the milieu on NG-128) 2 🔉 Decrease environmental stimuli — lowers agitation and the intensity of positive symptoms 3 🚨 Always monitor for suicide risk — carried forward from NG-049, true across every phase of care 🧠 Drugs treat the brain chemistry ; the milieu and monitoring treat the whole person . Medication is the top of the pyramid, not the whole pyramid.

entries.h: 💊 What antipsychotics are FOR in schizophrenia
entries.t: Primarily reduce positive symptoms (hallucinations, delusions, disorganized thinking) by blocking excess dopamine in the mesolimbic pathway (mechanism detail on NG-049 & NG-235). Negative and cognitive symptoms respond far less — they need psychosocial rehab, social skills training, and sustained therapeutic engagement alongside medication. 🧠 A client whose hallucinations stopped but who is still flat, avolitional, and isolated is not "treatment failure" — it means the drug did its job on the pathway it can reach.

entries.h: 🚫 Delusions & hallucinations — the caution rules again
entries.t: Never label the voices as "not real" or argue with the delusion Always present reality gently, without debate 🧠 Full scripted responses and the reasoning behind them live on NG-128 — this page only flags that the rule applies during medication teaching conversations too. 🚧
STEP 2 · WHY CLIENTS STOP TAKING MEDS Nonadherence is the single biggest driver of relapse back into the active phase (NG-049) — and it's rarely about "not caring."

Because the same disease process that causes positive/negative/cognitive symptoms (NG-049) can also impair the brain's ability to recognize it has an illness, many clients genuinely believe nothing is wrong — this drives medication refusal more than any other single factor. 🧠 An-osos-GNOSIA = "no knowledge" (a- without, gnosis- knowledge). Approach with patience and repetition, not confrontation — arguing with impaired insight works about as well as arguing with a delusion.

Distressing side effects — EPS, sedation, weight gain (full list on NG-235) make clients stop on their own Cognitive symptoms — trouble remembering to take a daily pill Cost & access — some agents and required lab monitoring are expensive Stigma — fear of being seen taking psychiatric medication Substance use — co-occurring use disorders interfere with routines 🧠 A good adherence assessment asks about all five , not just "did you take your pills."

entries.h: 📉 The relapse cascade — why adherence is the priority intervention
entries.t: 💊 Medication stopped ▼ 🧠 Dopamine dysregulation returns unchecked ▼ 🔁 Relapse into the ACTIVE phase (NG-049) 🧠 Every barrier above is really a fork in this cascade — the earlier you intervene, the more relapses you prevent. 💉
STEP 3 · SOLVING THE DAILY-PILL PROBLEM When a client understands the plan but the barrier is remembering or wanting to take a pill every day, the fix is architectural, not motivational.

entries.h: 💉 What a long-acting injectable (LAI) antipsychotic actually solves
entries.t: 🧠 LAIs don't fix anosognosia — the client still has to agree to come in for the injection. What they fix is forgetting and daily ambivalence . They are one tool among several, not a cure for lack of insight.

entries.h: ✅ Who is a good LAI candidate
entries.t: Client tolerates the oral form of that same drug well (a trial oral dose usually precedes the first injection) History of relapse specifically tied to missed oral doses Prefers less frequent dosing / values not having a daily pill routine 🧠 Injectables still carry the same warnings and adverse effect profile as the oral version of that drug — check NG-235 for the specific agent's side-effect and EPS profile.

Keep every scheduled injection appointment — missing the window lets drug levels fall Report injection-site reactions (pain, induration, redness) Continue attending follow-up and monitoring appointments — an LAI does not remove the need for ongoing psychiatric care 🧠 "Set it and forget it" ≠ "never follow up." The injection schedule is set, but monitoring is not optional. 🩺
STEP 4 · THE TWO EMERGENCIES YOU MUST CATCH Full mechanism and drug-by-drug detail for both of these lives on NG-235 — this is the "don't miss it" summary.

Key signs: fever/hyperpyrexia , muscle rigidity , altered mental status , and autonomic instability (diaphoresis, unstable BP, tachycardia). Priority action: 1. Hold the antipsychotic 2. Assess the client 3. Notify the HCP immediately. 🧠 Full pathophysiology and the complete drug list live on NG-235 — remember it here as "the emergency that can happen on any antipsychotic, at any point in treatment."

Clozapine requires mandatory, regular monitoring of the complete blood count (CBC) and absolute neutrophil count (ANC) due to agranulocytosis risk. 🧠 Priority to monitor = ANC/CBC. Report sore throat, fever, or flu-like symptoms immediately — full mechanism and reporting thresholds are on NG-235.

entries.h: 🗺️ Where the rest of this topic lives — the 4-page series
entries.t: NG-049 — Signs & Symptoms Definitions used here: positive/negative/cognitive symptoms, phases of illness. NG-128 — Communication Full say/don't say scripts for delusions & hallucinations, the milieu. NG-165 — You are here Pharmacology: treatment approach, adherence barriers, anosognosia, LAIs. NG-235 — Antipsychotics (drug reference) Typical vs. atypical, mechanism, EPS, NMS detail, agranulocytosis, QT prolongation. 🧠 If the question is "why won't the client take their meds" or "what's an LAI," you're on the right

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🧠 Anosognosia ≠ denial Neurological, not a choice — the #1 barrier to adherence 🚨 NMS Fever + rigidity + altered mental status + autonomic instability → hold, assess, notify HCP 💉 LAIs Remove the daily-pill decision, not a cure for lack of insight 🧪 Clozapine Mandatory ANC/CBC monitoring — agranulocytosis risk

Q1: A client insists nothing is wrong with them despite an active schizophrenia diagnosis. Is this denial or anosognosia — and does it matter? Show answer Likely anosognosia — a neurological inability to recognize the illness, not a conscious choice. It matters because arguing or confronting doesn't work; patience and repeated gentle reality-based conversation does. Q2: What problem does a long-acting injectable antipsychotic solve — and what does it NOT solve? Show answer It removes the daily pill-taking decision/

Cognitive Behavioral Therapy — first-line talk therapy NG-221 MENTAL HEALTH ADHD-friendly visual edition CBT is talk therapy that reframes thinking to change how a client feels and behaves. It's first-line treatment for anxiety, phobias, PTSD, OCD, depression, and eating disorders — this page's cognitive triangle and distortion list is the toolkit those disease-specific pages point back to. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🔺 Thoughts → Feelings → Behaviors Change the thought, and the feeling & behavior
STEP 1 · THE MECHANISM One triangle explains why CBT works — thoughts drive feelings, feelings drive behavior, and behavior reinforces the original thought.

entries.h: 🔺 Thoughts ↔ Feelings ↔ Behaviors — a closed loop
entries.t: EXAM TIP CBT works by interrupting the loop at the thought — because thoughts are the easiest of the three to catch and challenge in the moment. 🧠 "Catch it, check it, change it." CBT teaches clients to catch the automatic thought, check it against evidence, and change it — which breaks the loop before the feeling and behavior follow.

A common type of psychotherapy (talk therapy) that helps clients reframe thought processes to slowly cope with stress & anxiety. PTSD & OCD Eating disorders — anorexia & bulimia Depressive disorders Phobias & panic disorder 🧠 CBT = the default first answer. When an NCLEX question asks "what non-drug therapy," CBT is very often the correct first-line choice.

This mechanism is assumed knowledge on the Phobias , PTSD & Acute Stress Disorder , and Depression pages in this batch — they will say "treat with CBT" without re-explaining it. 🧠 Know this triangle cold — it's the shared foundation under several other disease pages. 🌀
STEP 2 · NAME THE BROKEN THOUGHT These are the specific "thought errors" CBT targets — spotting the pattern is half the treatment.

Distortion Example Catastrophizing ⚡ "If I fail this quiz, I'll fail nursing school and never get a job." All-or-nothing / black-and-white thinking ⚪⚫ "If I'm not perfect at this, I'm a total failure." Overgeneralization 🔁 "I got one bad grade — I'm always going to be bad at this." Mind reading 🔮 "My coworker didn't say hi — she must hate me." Emotional reasoning 💭 "I feel anxious about the flight, so it must actually be dangerous." Personalization 🎯 "My patient's blood sugar dropped — that's totaly my fault." Labe

Examining negative automatic thoughts and consciously restating them in a more balanced, positive way. Nurse teaches reframing to counteract depression. Effective teaching indicator: client says "I have many friends who love me and care for me." 🧠 Reframe = same facts, new lens. The event doesn't change — the interpretation does.

Gradual, ranked exposure to a feared object or situation, paired with relaxation, until anxiety fades. Client: "I only travel by train — I'm terrified of flying." → Best intervention: systematic desensitization . 🧠 Desensitization = a fear ladder , climbed one safe rung at a time, never jumping to the top. 🛠️
STEP 3 · WHAT SESSIONS LOOK LIKE Five building blocks, used together across a course of treatment.

1 Learn about the disorder — psychoeducation on symptoms & triggers 2 Exposure — systematic desensitization to feared situations/events (behavioral strategy) 3 Self-observation & monitoring — track thoughts, moods, triggers 4 Relaxation techniques — deep breathing, guided imagery, biofeedback 5 New coping skills & cognitive restructuring — reframe distorted thoughts 🧠 "LEARN, EXPOSE, OBSERVE, RELAX, REFRAME." Say it as a checklist for any CBT-based question — most answer choices map onto one of these five.

A mind-body intervention: the client concentrates on mental images to reduce stress and anxiety and improve concentration. Advantages: relaxation, inner peace, improved concentration. Focuses on descriptive mental pictures. 🧠 Guided imagery = a mental vacation the client controls.

Like guided imagery, but with machines/monitors that give real-time feedback (heart rate, muscle tension) to help the client learn to control the stress response — teaching the body to respond differently to stress. 🧠 Biofeedback = guided imagery + a screen. The device turns an invisible stress response into something the client can actually watch and change.

entries.h: 👥 Milieu & group therapy — supporting structures around CBT
entries.t: Therapeutic milieu: a safe, structured social & physical environment — the goal of every psych/behavioral health unit. Group therapy goal: reduce isolation in a structured, controlled environment; primary focus is personal feelings that affect behavior. Silent member → encourage interaction, or divide into pairs. Aggressive/interrupting member → "You seem very upset" — let the group handle it first. For personality disorders specifically, milieu's primary goal is managing the effect of the behavior on the entire gr

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🔺 Thought → Feeling → Behavior Interrupt the thought to change the loop. 🌀 Name the distortion Catastrophizing, all-or-nothing, mind reading, personalization, labeling. 🪜 Fear = desensitize gradually Systematic desensitization, ranked exposure. 🛠️ 5 strategies Learn, expose, observe, relax, reframe.

Q1: What are the three points of the cognitive triangle? Show answer Thoughts, feelings, and behaviors — each influences the other two, forming a loop. Q2: A client says "I made one mistake at work, so I'm a complete failure." Which cognitive distortion is this? Show answer All-or-nothing (black-and-white) thinking, with elements of labeling. Q3: A client is terrified of flying and only travels by train. Best CBT-based intervention? Show answer Systematic desensitization — gradual, ranked exposure paired with relax

entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 📦 Loss types 🌀 Complicated grief ⚖️ End-of-life ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Mental Health · Psychiatric Care Course

Types of Loss · Complicated Grief · End-of-Life Decisions NG-222 Mental Health ADHD-friendly visual edition Not every loss looks the same, and not every grief resolves normally. This page maps what kind of loss a client is facing, when grief has become unhealthy , and the spectrum of end-of-life decisions nurses must understand and document objectively — factually, without personal judgment. For the full DABDA / Bowlby grief-stage content and defense mechanisms, see NG-065 (Death & Dying) — not repeated here. 📄 Sim
STEP 1 · NAME WHAT WAS LOST "Loss" isn't only death — sorting the source and the verifiability of a loss shapes how the nurse responds.
🧠 "SEEL" — S elf-aspect · E xternal object · E nvironment · L oved one. Ask "what category did this client just lose?" before choosing an intervention.

entries.h: 🔎 Actual, Perceived & Anticipatory loss — is it verifiable, and has it happened yet?
entries.t: Type Definition Example Actual loss Can be recognized / verified by others Death, divorce Perceived loss Experienced by the person but cannot be verified by others Loss of freedom when becoming a stay-at-home parent; loss of a valued personal item; loss of financial independence Anticipatory loss Grief experienced before the loss has actually occurred A family member is actively dying but has not yet passed 🧠 Perceived loss is real grief even though no one else can see it. A classic NCLEX trap is to under-validate

entries.h: ⏳ Bonus pair: Situational vs. Maturational loss
entries.t: Situational loss — unexpected, caused by an external event (e.g., a new cancer diagnosis in a family member) Maturational loss — expected with normal life transitions (e.g., graduating high school and leaving friends behind) 🧠 Situational = sudden/unplanned. Maturational = scheduled by life stage. Both are still legitimate grief, even though maturational loss is "supposed to happen."

Kübler-Ross's 5 stages (DABDA), Bowlby's 4 stages, defense mechanisms (displacement, projection, identification, sublimation, etc.), and adult/pediatric grief-support interventions are covered in full depth on the paired page. → Open NG-065: Death & Dying (grief stages + defense mechanisms) 🌀
STEP 2 · WHEN GRIEF STOPS BEING HEALTHY Normal grief softens with time. Watch for grief that gets stuck, gets buried, or gets dangerous.

entries.h: 📉 Normal grief tapers — unhealthy grief subtypes don't
entries.t: 🧠 Complicated grief needs a duration AND a functional criterion: lasts more than 6 months and leaves the person unable to perform daily activities. Sadness alone at 7 months is not automatically "complicated."

Subtype What it looks like Unresolved Extended in length & severity — same stages, but grieved far longer than expected Inhibited Normal stages of grieving are suppressed rather than experienced Exaggerated Uses dangerous activities (e.g., substance use, self-harm) to lessen the pain of grieving Complicated Lasts >6 months and causes inability to perform daily activities 🧠 "UIEC" — U nresolved lasts too long · I nhibited is bottled up · E xaggerated turns dangerous · C omplicated disables daily life.

Fails to grieve at all Refuses to participate in normal cultural/memorial activities Recurrently symptomatic on the anniversary of the loss or on holidays Persistent guilt Continued searching for the lost person Small, unrelated events trigger grief symptoms Unable to discuss the loss without crying/becoming tearful, even long after Relationships with friends and family deteriorate 🧠 Not one sign alone — it's the pattern plus duration that flags complicated grief for referral (e.g., grief counseling, psychiatric ev

STEP 3 · KNOW THE VOCABULARY, STAY OBJECTIVE This is ethics/policy content — legality varies by state and country. The nurse's job is to know the definitions, follow facility policy, and document objectively without personal judgment.

entries.h: ⚖️ The end-of-life decision spectrum — from direct action to non-intervention
entries.t: 🧠 Direction matters, not just outcome. Active euthanasia and assisted death cause death directly; passive euthanasia and DNR allow death by not intervening or by stopping extraordinary measures. Legality of the first two varies widely by jurisdiction — always defer to current law and facility policy, not personal opinion.

Active euthanasia — actions that bring about the client's death directly, with or without the client's consent Physician-assisted death (assisted suicide) — giving the client the means to end their life if they request it; the client, not the clinician, performs the final act Passive euthanasia — withholding life-sustaining therapy or withdrawing extraordinary means of life support (e.g., removing a feeding tube or ventilator, allowing the client to die without intervention) DNR / no-code status — an order specifyi

entries.h: 🩺 The nurse's role — stay factual, stay neutral
entries.t: Know your facility's policy and your state's law before discussing any of these terms with a client/family Clarify code status and advance directives on admission; confirm the client (or their designated surrogate) actively participated in the decision Provide factual information within your scope; refer ethics/legal/spiritual-care questions to the appropriate resource Document objectively — what was said and done, not personal opinion Support the client's and family's decision without imposing personal values (non

Grief-stage recognition (DABDA, Bowlby), defense mechanisms, and adult/pediatric grief-support interventions are covered in depth on the paired page — use it alongside this one rather than duplicating that content here. → Open NG-065: Death & Dying ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 📦 4 sources of loss Self · object · environment · loved one 🔎 Actual / perceived / anticipatory Verifiable · felt-only · before it happens 🌀 Complicated grief >6 months + can't function daily ⚖️ DNR ≠ do not treat Comfort/symptom care continues; only resuscitation is withheld

Show answer Anticipatory loss — grief experienced before the loss has actually occurred. Q2: A client says becoming a stay-at-home parent cost them their independence, but no one else seems to notice or validate it. What type of loss is this? Show answer Perceived loss — experienced by the person but cannot be verified by others. Q3: A client's grief has lasted 9 months and they can no longer

Phases of Crisis · De-escalation · Restraints & Seclusion NG-228 Mental Health ADHD-friendly visual edition A crisis moves through predictable phases — recognizing which phase a client is in tells you whether to talk, redirect, or physically intervene. The core rule: always use the least restrictive intervention that keeps everyone safe , and escalate toward restraints/seclusion only when verbal and environmental measures fail. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🌡️ 4 phases Trigger → Escalation → Crisis →
STEP 1 · WHERE ARE THEY IN THE CRISIS A crisis is not a single event — it's a rising and falling curve, and each phase calls for a different response.

🧠 "TECP" — T rigger · E scalation · C risis · P ost-crisis. A client saying "I feel like I can barely get out of bed in the morning" a day after an outburst = phase 4, post-crisis disorganization & depression, not a new problem.

A client becomes agitated and threatens to punch another client. Priority action: Eliminate the trigger using nursing measures and interventions 🧠 Stopping the trigger stops the climb up the curve — act at phase 1–2, before the crisis peak, whenever possible.

entries.h: 🔎 Determine the true source of anger
entries.t: A client is yelling and screaming at staff. Action to take: Determine the true source of the client's anger 🧠 The visible target (a staff member, a roommate) is often not the real trigger — assess before assuming. 🗣️
STEP 2 · CALM COMMUNICATION & SAFE APPROACH Words and environment first — most crises never need to reach restraints.

1 💬 Explain all activities of care clearly & calmly 2 🎯 Eliminate the trigger 3 🔇 Low-stimulation environment — NOT near the nurses' station 4 🔎 Determine the source of the anger 5 🤲 Acknowledge the client's emotions 🧠 Sample scripting: "I'm Lily and I'm here to help" (identify yourself, calm tone) → "I see you are upset" (acknowledge the emotion, don't argue with it).

entries.h: 🪑 First action when a client throws a chair
entries.t: A client becomes angry and throws a chair in the dayroom. First intervention: Acknowledge the client's emotions 🧠 Validate before you redirect — arguing or issuing commands first tends to escalate further.

A client with a history of poor impulse control bursts into a verbal tirade in the dayroom. Priority action: Remove other clients from the day room 🧠 Milieu safety first — protect bystanders before continuing to work with the escalated client.

entries.h: 🛡️ Personal safety when approaching an angry client
entries.t: 🧠 4 safety rules: have other staff as backup · stand far enough away to avoid injury · identify yourself & remain calm · give simple directions in a calming voice. Never let yourself be positioned between the client and the exit. 🔒
STEP 3 · LEAST RESTRICTIVE → MOST RESTRICTIVE Medication and seclusion come before restraints — and restraints carry strict legal timelines once used.

🗣️ Verbal de-escalation & environmental changes ▼ 💊 PRN medication (anxiolytic/antipsychotic) ▼ 🚪 Seclusion (alone in a safe room) ▼ ⛓️ Physical restraints — last resort 🧠 Always try the least restrictive option that keeps the client and others safe before moving to the next step. Restraints/seclusion require a provider's order — they are never a first response or a punishment.

Class Example drug (brand) Anxiolytic — benzodiazepine "-pam" / "-lam" Lorazepam (Ativan) Typical antipsychotic Haloperidol (Haldol) Atypical antipsychotic Ziprasidone (Geodon) For a client displaying violent behavior, the provider may prescribe lorazepam, haloperidol, and/or ziprasidone — select-all-that-apply pattern. 🧠 "-pam/-lam" = benzo family (lorazepam, diazepam) — fast-acting anxiolytic for acute agitation, distinct from the antipsychotics used for the same scenario.

1 📄 Get a provider's order for restraints — renewed every 4 hours for adults 2 🩺 Client must be assessed by the HCP within 1 hour of the order 3 📝 Document every 15 minutes 4 🤲 Monitor & meet physical needs continuously 🧠 Within the first hour after restraints + seclusion are applied , the nurse must: meet the client's physical needs, obtain a prescription for the restraints, and objectively document the client's behavior.

When intervening with a violent client, the nurse should: identify themselves to the client and remain calm. When a client threatens to harm a staff member, the appropriate intervention is: address the patient with simple directions and a calming voice. 🧠 Never argue, raise your voice to match theirs, or make sudden movements — calm, simple, predictable communication is itself a de-escalation tool. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🌡️ 4 phases Trigger → Escalation → Crisis → Post-crisis 🎯 First move Eliminate the trigger 🪜 Least restrictive first Verbal → meds → seclusion → restraints ⏱️ Restraints HCP assess in 1 hr · document q15min · renew q4h adult

Q1: A client says, "I feel like I can barely get out of bed in the morning" the day after an outburst. Which crisis phase? Show answer Post-crisis disorganization & depression (phase 4). Q2: A client threatens to punch another client. What is the nurse's priority action? Show answer Eliminate the trigger using nursing measures and interventions. Q3: How often must a restrained adult client be reassessed by the HCP, and how often must the nurse document? Show answer HCP assessment within 1 hour of the order, renewed

Stimulants & Non-Stimulants for ADHD NG-234 Mental Health ADHD-friendly visual edition Two families, one goal — boost dopamine & norepinephrine signaling in the prefrontal circuit described on the ADD & ADHD page (NG-093) . Stimulants work fast and are first-line; non-stimulants are the option when stimulants aren't tolerated, are contraindicated, or carry abuse risk. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 💊 First-line = stimulants Methylphenidate & amphetamine salts — Schedule II controlled substances. ❤️ Sc
STEP 1 · MECHANISM Both drug families raise dopamine & norepinephrine in the synapse — they just get there differently.

entries.h: ⚡ Stimulants — flood the synapse with dopamine & norepinephrine
entries.t: MOA Methylphenidate and amphetamine salts block reuptake and increase release of dopamine & norepinephrine at the synapse — the opposite problem from the low-dopamine circuit on the ADHD page, corrected chemically. Drug Brand Class Methylphenidate Ritalin Stimulant Amphetamine mixture salts Adderall Stimulant Dextroamphetamine Dexedrine Stimulant Indications: ADHD in children & adolescents — and narcolepsy (same wakefulness-driving mechanism treats both). 🧠 "Stim = same fix, better click." Stimulants don't sedate a

entries.h: 🧭 Non-stimulants — a different route to the same circuit
entries.t: Atomoxetine (Strattera) — selective norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (blocks NE reuptake specifically, not dopamine directly) Guanfacine ER (Intuniv) & Clonidine ER (Kapvay) — central alpha-2 agonists that improve prefrontal signaling and calm hyperactivity/impulsivity 🧠 Non-stimulants take longer to reach full effect (days–weeks) but carry no abuse potential and are not controlled substances — the trade-off for a slower onset.

History of substance use disorder in the child/family Cardiac contraindication to stimulants Significant anxiety — stimulants can worsen anxiety; alpha-2 agonists can help both Prefer to avoid controlled-substance prescribing/storage issues ⚠️
STEP 2 · PRIORITY MONITORING Screen the heart before the first dose, then track growth and vitals at every visit after.

entries.h: 🚨 Cardiac screening — BEFORE starting a stimulant
entries.t: 🧠 "Heart first, pill second." The exam trap is jumping straight to prescribing — the priority assessment is always the cardiac screen before therapy starts.
Appetite suppression from stimulants can slow growth velocity. Monitor and report height/weight trends with the HCP at each visit — a crossing percentile line is the flag, not a single low number.

entries.h: ⚠️ Expected side effects to teach families
entries.t: 🍽️ Loss of appetite & weight loss 😴 Loss of sleep / insomnia 🌀 Restlessness 💓 Increased HR & BP 🧠 "WAR" — W eight/appetite loss · A ppetite down · R estlessness + racing heart. Stimulant side effects mirror the drug's own name.

Methylphenidate and amphetamine salts are Schedule II controlled substances — high abuse/diversion potential, no automatic refills, prescriptions typically limited to a set supply and cannot be called in. Drug holiday: a planned, HCP-directed medication-free period (e.g., weekends, school breaks, summer) sometimes used to let appetite/growth catch up and to reassess whether continued therapy is still needed. Practice varies by provider and patient — always an HCP decision, never a parent-initiated stop. 🧠 Never abr
STEP 3 · PATIENT & FAMILY EDUCATION Timing prevents the worst side effect, and knowing the non-stimulant alternatives prevents an exam trap.
🧠 A late dose = a wired brain at bedtime. Schedule the last daily dose early enough that stimulant effects wear off well before bedtime.

entries.h: ✅ What to teach at every visit
entries.t: 📈 Track appetite & weight — report a declining growth curve 💤 Report new or worsening insomnia ❤️ Report chest pain, palpitations, or fainting immediately 📚 Watch for improvement in school performance — expected therapeutic response 🔒 Store securely — Schedule II, diversion risk in the household

entries.h: 🧭 Stimulant vs. non-stimulant — tell them apart
entries.t: Feature Stimulants Non-Stimulants Examples Methylphenidate, amphetamine salts, dextroamphetamine Atomoxetine, guanfacine ER, clonidine ER Onset Fast — hours Slow — days to weeks for full effect Controlled substance Yes — Schedule II No Key risks Appetite/growth suppression, insomnia, ↑HR/BP Sedation, hypotension; alpha-2 agonists → rebound HTN if stopped abruptly 🧠 "Stim = Schedule II, Non-stim = no schedule." If a stem mentions abuse potential, refill restrictions, or diversion risk, the drug is a stimulant. If it

entries.h: 🔗 Clonidine & guanfacine — same drug class, more than one job
entries.t: Clonidine and guanfacine are central alpha-2 agonists . In ADHD, extended-release forms calm the hyperactive-impulsive circuit. But clonidine specifically shows up on other pages of this course too — same mechanism, different indication each time : 🔗 See the Cardiovascular batch (NG-110) for clonidine's use in hypertension management, and the Pharmacology batch (NG-243) for its broader alpha-2 agonist profile — including use in opioid/alcohol withdrawal symptom control. Same drug, three different course units. 🧠 "C

SAY IT OUT LOUD 💊 First-line Stimulants — methylphenidate & amphetamine salts, Schedule II ❤️ Screen first Cardiac history + baseline VS before the first dose 📏 Track Height/weight trend every visit — growth suppression risk 🧭 Alternative Atomoxetine, guanfacine/clonidine ER — non-stimulant, no abuse risk

Q1: What must be assessed before starting a stimulant for ADHD? Show answer Cardiac history — personal and family history of sudden cardiac death/arrhythmia, plus baseline BP, HR, and ECG if indicated. Q2: What two growth parameters need ongoing monitoring on a stimulant? Show answer Height and weight trends — report to the HCP if percentiles start declining. Q3: When should the last daily dose be given, and why? Show answer Early in the day, not in the evening — late dosing causes insomnia. Q4: Name a non-stimulan

Typical vs. Atypical Drug Reference — Part 4 of a 4-page Schizophrenia series NG-235 Mental Health / Pharmacology Series 4 of 4 · the drug reference 📍 SCOPE OF THIS PAGE: the broad antipsychotic drug reference — first-generation (typical) vs. second-generation (atypical), mechanism, and every major side effect including EPS, NMS, and agranulocytosis. For schizophrenia-specific adherence issues and LAIs, see NG-165. Antipsychotics are used far beyond schizophrenia — bipolar mania, Tourette's, agitation, and more. Th
STEP 1 · MECHANISM & THE TWO GENERATIONS Every antipsychotic blocks dopamine — the generations differ in how selectively, which sets up their whole side-effect profile.

🧠 Every antipsychotic in this class blocks D2 dopamine receptors somewhere in the brain — the difference between drugs is how selective that blockade is, which is the whole story behind typical vs. atypical.

Blocks D2 receptors broadly across dopamine pathways, including the ones that control movement (nigrostriatal pathway) — this is exactly why EPS is common and prominent with this class. Prototype: Haloperidol (Haldol) Indications: schizophrenia; Tourette's syndrome (to control motor tics/movements); severe agitation. 🧠 "Typical = Tics." Strong D2 blockade in the movement pathway is a package deal with typicals — expect EPS.

Also blocks serotonin (5-HT2A) receptors in addition to D2 — this extra serotonin blockade is thought to indirectly restore some dopamine release in the movement pathway, lowering EPS risk compared to typicals. Prototypes: Clozapine, Risperidone Indications: schizophrenia and schizoaffective disorder, especially clients not responding to other antipsychotics (clozapine specifically reserved for treatment-resistant cases). 🧠 "Atypical = Ate-ypical calories." Trade less EPS for more metabolic side effects — weight ga
STEP 2 · MOVEMENT SIDE EFFECTS EPS = movement disorders from D2 blockade in the nigrostriatal pathway. Four distinct presentations — know them by name and by timeline.

EPS type What it looks like Nursing priority Acute dystonia Sudden spasm of neck/face/tongue muscles; can involve the airway Report immediately — often treated with an anticholinergic/antihistamine per order Akathisia Subjective inner restlessness, can't sit still, pacing Often mistaken for anxiety or worsening psychosis — ask directly, don't assume Pseudoparkinsonism Tremor, rigidity, shuffling gait, masked face Fall-risk precautions; mimics Parkinson's disease but is drug-induced and often reversible Tardive dysk
STEP 3 · WHAT YOU CANNOT MISS Two reactions turn a routine antipsychotic order into an emergency — recognize them fast.

entries.h: 🚨 Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) — can occur with ANY antipsychotic
entries.t: Life-threatening reaction characterized by: 🌡️ High fever & diaphoresis (hyperpyrexia) 🧠 Change in mental status 💪 Muscle rigidity 🫨 Tremors Priority actions: 1 HOLD the antipsychotic 2 Assess the patient (vitals, mental status, labs) 3 Notify the HCP immediately 🧠 NCLEX trap: "I should not be concerned about fever and muscle stiffness" is a statement that needs further teaching — fever + rigidity on an antipsychotic is never a "wait and see."

Priority to monitor: CBC and absolute neutrophil count (ANC) — required regularly (e.g., weekly during initial treatment per protocol) for as long as clozapine is prescribed. Report to provider immediately: Sore throat Fever Flu-like symptoms These are early infection signs from a dangerously low neutrophil count — high risk for serious, potentially fatal infection. 🧠 "CloZAPine ZAPs WBCs." No lab work, no clozapine refill — this is one of the strictest monitoring requirements in psychiatric pharmacology. 📋
STEP 4 · NAME, SIDE EFFECTS, TEACHING Four commonly tested antipsychotics, side by side.

Drug Generation Normal side effects Killer / must-report side effects Notes Haloperidol (Haldol) 1st gen (typical) Sedation, anticholinergic effects, EPS (all 4 types) NMS Schizophrenia; Tourette's for motor tics Clozapine 2nd gen (atypical) Weight gain, drooling, sedation — no need to report these Agranulocytosis (report sore throat/fever/flu-like sx); NMS Reserved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia; requires ANC/CBC monitoring Risperidone 2nd gen (atypical) Weight gain, sedation, orthostatic hypotension NMS; u
🧠 Get a baseline ECG before starting, and avoid stacking with other QT-prolonging drugs.

NG-165 — Pharmacology (schizophrenia-specific) Adherence barriers, anosognosia, long-acting injectables. NG-235 — You are here The drug reference: typical vs. atypical, EPS, NMS, agranulocytosis, QT. 🧠 This page is the reference card — come back here anytime a question names a specific drug or side effect. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🔷 Typical vs 🔶 Atypical Typical = more EPS. Atypical = more metabolic side effects. ⚠️ 4 EPS types Dystonia (fast), akathisia, pseudoparkinsonism, tardive dyskinesia (slow, may be permanent) 🚨 NMS Fever + rigidity + altered mental status + tremor → HOLD, assess, notify HCP 🧪 Clozapine Agranulocytosis — ANC/CBC monitoring, report sore throat/fever

Q1: What's the core mechanistic difference between typical and atypical antipsychotics? Show answer Typicals block D2 receptors broadly and strongly (more EPS); atypicals add serotonin (5-HT2A) blockade, which lowers EPS risk but raises metabolic side effect risk. Q2: A client on a new antipsychotic is pacing constantly and reports feeling like they "can't sit still." What is this, and what should the nurse NOT assume it is? Show answer Akathisia (an EPS) — the nurse should not simply assume it's anxiety or worseni

Benzodiazepines & Buspirone — Two Opposite Strategies for Anxiety NG-236 MENTAL HEALTH ADHD-friendly visual edition This page is the pharmacology companion to every anxiety-spectrum page in this batch. Two very different drugs both treat anxiety: benzodiazepines work in minutes by boosting GABA, but carry real dependence risk and are meant for short-term use only . Buspirone works on serotonin instead, takes weeks to kick in, and carries essentially no abuse potential — the trade-off is right there in the numbers.
STEP 1 · HOW IT WORKS Two receptor systems, two speeds — GABA calms fast, serotonin calms slow.

entries.h: 🧬 GABA vs. serotonin — the whole page in one diagram
entries.t: 🧠 “Benzos open a door, buspirone retrains the doorman.” One is immediate mechanical relief; the other is a slow receptor-level adjustment — that's why the onset times are worlds apart.

Alpra zolam , Mida zolam — " -lam " Tema zepam , Clona zepam , Dia zepam — " -pam " MOA: increases GABA (the brain's major inhibitory neurotransmitter) effect at the GABA-A receptor → widens the chloride channel → CNS-wide slowing. Indications: anxiety, seizures, muscle spasm, alcohol/sedative withdrawal, procedural sedation. 🧠 “Low and slow vitals” — expect BP, HR, and RR to trend down with a working dose. Too far down = toxicity.

MOA: partial agonist at serotonin 5-HT1A receptors (with some dopamine activity) — a completely different pathway from benzos or barbiturates. Key point: non-habit-forming, no abuse potential — and it does not potentiate CNS depression from alcohol the way benzos do. Patient teaching: "drive the BUSpirone" — okay to drive/operate machinery, unlike a benzo. 🧠 NOT used for acute attacks — onset is 2–4 weeks, so it has no role in stopping a panic attack in progress.

Phenobarbital — increases GABA effect similarly to benzos, but by prolonging how long the chloride channel stays open rather than how wide. Lasts longer in the body ("takes longer to kick in, takes longer to get out"), which means a higher risk of toxicity — hypotension, respiratory depression. Largely replaced by benzodiazepines for anxiety because of this narrower safety margin, though still used for seizure control. 🧠 “PHENO-barbital, stuck behind bars a long time” — sedation lasts long, and so does the risk. ⚠️
STEP 2 · SAFETY Onset speed and dependence risk are mirror images of each other — chart it out side by side.
🧠 If the question says "acute panic attack, right now" — the answer is a benzodiazepine , never buspirone.

Feature Benzodiazepines Buspirone Mechanism ↑ GABA at GABA-A receptor Partial agonist at serotonin 5-HT1A Onset Minutes 2–4 weeks Use in acute attack Yes — first choice No — too slow Dependence / abuse potential High — short-term use only None Sedation Significant Minimal Alcohol interaction Dangerous — additive CNS/respiratory depression No significant potentiation Driving / machinery Avoid OK — "drive the BUSpirone" Antidote Flumazenil None needed

entries.h: ⚠️ Benzo dependence & withdrawal — the trade-off for speed
entries.t: Physical dependence can develop with regular use, even at therapeutic doses. Never stop a benzodiazepine abruptly — withdrawal can include rebound anxiety, tremor, autonomic instability, and seizures . Always taper. 🧠 Don't confuse the two uses of benzos: here they're the drug being taken for anxiety (short-term only, dependence is the risk). Separately, benzodiazepines are also the drugs used to manage other withdrawal syndromes (like alcohol withdrawal, on a taper protocol) — a supervised, monitored, very differe

Benzos: sedation, respiratory depression, hypotension, fall risk (especially older adults) Additive risk: combining with alcohol or opioids compounds CNS/respiratory depression Barbiturates: same risks, amplified by the longer half-life ✅
STEP 3 · PATIENT EDUCATION Antidotes, interactions, and the exact points that show up on the exam.

Toxicity Antidote Benzodiazepine overdose Flumazenil Opioid overdose Naloxone (brand: Narcan) Buspirone No specific antidote needed — minimal CNS-depressant overdose risk 🧠 “Flu-mazenil flushes the benzo. Nal-oxone knocks out the opioid.” Keep the two straight — a classic mix-and-match NCLEX question.

Take at bedtime if prescribed that way; don't skip doses Stop drinking alcohol — dangerous additive sedation Do not operate dangerous machinery or drive Avoid muscle relaxants and other CNS depressants Avoid valerian root, ginkgo, and ginseng — can add to sedation or affect anxiety/bleeding risk Report any history of reaction to another benzodiazepine (e.g., midazolam) — cross-sensitivity within the class Never stop abruptly — taper under supervision

OK to drive — "drive the BUSpirone" Explain the delayed onset ( 2–4 weeks) up front, or clients stop taking it thinking it "isn't working" Not for an acute panic attack — it will not help in the moment No physical dependence, no withdrawal taper required 🧠 If a question describes a client wanting relief "right now," buspirone is the wrong answer every time.

Never combine a benzodiazepine + opioid + alcohol — the classic respiratory-depression triad Never discontinue a benzodiazepine abruptly after regular use — seizure risk Never expect buspirone to abort an active panic attack 🚨 Phenobarbital toxicity picture: hypotension + increasing sedation — report immediately ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🧪 Benzos = ↑GABA fast, effective, short-term only 🐢 Buspirone = 2–4 wks non-habit-forming, no abuse potential 🆘 Flumazenil / Naloxone benzo antidote / opioid antidote 🚫 Never stop benzo cold taper — withdrawal seizures possible

Q1: Why can't buspirone be used to stop an acute panic attack? Show answer Its onset is delayed 2–4 weeks — it works on serotonin 5-HT1A receptors through gradual adaptation, not the immediate GABA boost a benzodiazepine provides. Q2: What's the antidote for a benzodiazepine overdose? For an opioid overdose? Show answer Flumazenil for benzodiazepines; naloxone (Narcan) for opioids. Q3: Why should a client never stop a benzodiazepine abruptly? Show answer Physical dependence can develop even at therapeutic doses; ab

The classic mood stabilizer — narrow therapeutic index, big teaching load NG-250 MENTAL HEALTH ADHD-friendly visual edition Lithium is the oldest, most classic mood stabilizer for bipolar disorder — and it has one of the narrowest therapeutic windows of any drug you'll give. The dose that treats mania and the dose that poisons the client are close together, so almost everything taught about lithium is really teaching about staying in that window . 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🔋 Lithium = bipolar Lon
STEP 1 · WHY WE GIVE IT A long-term mood stabilizer — not a fast fix, and not forgiving of a narrow miss.

🧠 Never memorize just one number. Ranges are cited slightly differently across references — know the concept (narrow window, routine level checks) and confirm the exact cutoffs against your current course/facility reference.

Bipolar disorder — primarily to control/prevent manic episodes and stabilize mood over the long term Schizoaffective disorder Given for long-term (maintenance) treatment — it is not a fast-acting rescue medication for acute agitation. 🧠 Lithium Battery — “B” for Bipolar. A battery is a long-lasting power source, and lithium is a long-term mood stabilizer — both about the long haul, not a quick charge.

The exact mechanism isn't fully settled, but lithium is thought to stabilize neuronal cell membranes and alter sodium transport/second-messenger signaling in neurons, dampening the mania cycle over time. Because lithium is handled by the kidneys largely like sodium, everything about its safety profile traces back to fluid and sodium balance — that connection is the highest-yield idea on this whole page. 🧠 Lithium rides the same train as sodium. Whatever changes sodium and fluid balance changes the lithium level too
STEP 2 · TOXICITY SIGNS Early toxicity is mild and easy to miss — late toxicity is a medical emergency.

entries.h: 📈 Early → late toxicity — a progression, not a single moment
entries.t: 🧠 “GI + tremor + ringing ears = catch it early.” Any client on lithium with new nausea, a fine tremor, or tinnitus needs a level checked before symptoms progress to confusion and seizures.

entries.h: 🫘 Kidney signs the source flags directly
entries.t: 🧪 Rising creatinine above the client's baseline — a general marker of reduced kidney function; know your lab's normal range and trend the client's own baseline 🚽 Low urine output — roughly <30 mL/hr is a widely-used nursing threshold for concerning oliguria and should be reported 🧠 Kidneys clear lithium — hurt kidneys mean lithium has nowhere to go but up. That's why renal signs and lithium toxicity travel together.

Ringing in the ears is a distinctive, easy-to-remember early sign that shows up disproportionately often on exams for lithium specifically — flag it whenever it appears alongside a mood-stabilizer client. 🧠 If a psych-unit client on a mood stabilizer suddenly complains their ears are ringing, think lithium level before anything else. 🩺
STEP 3 · MONITOR & TEACH Almost every teaching point here exists to protect the narrow therapeutic window.

entries.h: 🧂 The single highest-yield teaching point — sodium & fluid intake
entries.t: Do NOT restrict sodium or water intake while on lithium — a low-sodium diet raises the lithium level toward toxic Maintain consistent, adequate daily sodium and fluid intake — don't swing between diets Replace fluids aggressively during vomiting, diarrhea, heavy sweating, or fever ("stomach flu" is a real high-risk toxicity trigger) — report excessive urination too, since both dehydration and unusual polyuria disturb the balance Serum sodium <135 mEq/L (hyponatremia) raises toxicity risk and needs prompt attention

Avoid NSAIDs — ibuprofen, naproxen — in clients on lithium. NSAIDs decrease renal blood flow , which reduces lithium clearance and pushes levels up toward toxic. A client who says "I take ibuprofen for headaches" while on lithium needs further teaching. 🧠 Less blood to the kidney = less lithium leaving the body. Same underlying logic as the sodium teaching — anything that stresses the kidney raises the level.

🫘 Renal function — baseline and periodic (BUN/creatinine) — lithium is renally cleared 🦋 Thyroid function (TSH) — baseline and periodic — lithium can cause hypothyroidism/goiter over time 🩸 Lithium level — routine trough levels, drawn per protocol (commonly ~12 hours after the last dose) to guide dosing ❤️ Baseline ECG may be considered in some clients, per facility protocol 🧠 “Kidney, thyroid, level” — the routine lithium labs. All three get checked before starting and then on an ongoing schedule for the life of t

entries.h: ✅ Continue vs. hold — reading a level correctly
entries.t: If the lithium level comes back within the client's therapeutic range and the client has no toxicity symptoms , the correct answer is usually to continue the current dose — a therapeutic level is a normal, expected finding, not a reason to hold or adjust the medication. ✅ Level in range, no symptoms → continue current dose ⚠️ Level high or symptomatic → hold the dose, notify the HCP, reassess hydration/sodium/renal status 🧠 A common test trap is treating a normal, in-range level as if it were a problem. Read the le

Lithium carries known reproductive/teratogenic risk , particularly with first-trimester exposure — this is generally taught as a reason for close specialist involvement and risk-benefit discussion, not a page to memorize an exact defect statistic from. Any client of childbearing age on lithium should be counseled about pregnancy planning and contraception. 🧠 Pair this with the reproductive-risk contrast already flagged for anticonvulsant mood stabilizers: different mechanisms, but the same nursing habit — always sc

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🔋 Long-term bipolar drug narrow therapeutic window — that's the whole story 🧂 Don't restrict salt/water low sodium/dehydration → toxic lithium levels 🚫 No NSAIDs ↓ renal blood flow → ↑ lithium level 🧪 Renal + thyroid + level baseline, then routine, for the life of therapy

Q1: A client on lithium develops a stomach virus with vomiting and diarrhea. What's the nursing priority? Show answer Aggressively replace fluids/sodium and monitor closely for toxicity — vomiting/diarrhea causes dehydration and sodium loss, which raise the lithium level toward toxic. Hold the dose and notify the HCP if toxicity signs appear. Q2: A client on lithium reports taking ibuprofen regularly for headaches. What's the concern? Show answer NSAIDs decrease renal blood flow and reduce lithium clearance, increa

Real symptoms, no medical cause — and the imposter that isn't a mental illness at all NG-270 MENTAL HEALTH ADHD-friendly visual edition These disorders are constantly confused with each other and with a condition that isn't even a psychiatric diagnosis. The physical symptoms are real — the client is not faking, and there is NO medical cause on testing. The one exception on this whole page is malingering , which IS intentional and IS for a clear external reward. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🩻 SSD = u
STEP 1 · DEFINITIONS Same theme across all four: the mind is producing (or fixating on) physical illness — the difference is what drives it and whether it's conscious.

EXAM TIP Unexplained physical symptoms — abdominal pain, weakness, chest pain, shortness of breath — with NO medical cause. All diagnostic tests come back negative. Symptoms are real; the client is not making them up or faking it. Clients obsessively focus time & energy on the symptoms, often seeing many different doctors to get a diagnosis that doesn't exist. The pain is typically driven by stress. 🧠 SSD = the body speaking stress. Not fabricated, not for a reward — just a real symptom with a psychological driver.

Preoccupation with having or getting a serious illness, despite few or no actual physical symptoms and reassuring test results. The fear itself is the disorder — not the symptom. 🧠 SSD = symptom-focused. Illness anxiety = fear-focused — one has the body complaint front and center, the other is mostly worry about a disease that isn't there.

Neurological-type symptoms (paralysis, blindness, seizures, numbness) that have no medical explanation — the classic teaching example is a symptom appearing after a major psychological stressor. 🧠 Conversion = stress "converted" into a neuro symptom — not fabricated, and often triggered by an identifiable stressful event.

Intentionally produces or fakes symptoms/injuries — but the motivation is internal: to assume the "sick role" and receive care/attention, not for money, time off, or any other outside reward. 🧠 Factitious = fakes it on purpose, for the attention of being sick itself — the "gain" is psychological, not material. 🔎
STEP 2 · THE MASTER COMPARISON Two axes decide everything here: is the symptom production conscious, and is there an external reward?

entries.h: 🧭 Conscious vs. unconscious, internal vs. external gain
entries.t: 🧠 "Fake it for feelings vs. fake it for a favor." Factitious disorder fakes illness for the emotional payoff of being cared for. Malingering fakes illness for a concrete outside reward — and that distinction is exactly why malingering isn't classified as a mental illness.

Disorder Core feature Intentional? Gain Somatic Symptom Disorder Real, unexplained physical symptoms; obsessive focus on them No None Illness Anxiety Disorder Preoccupied with fear of having/getting a serious illness No None Conversion Disorder Neuro symptom (paralysis, blindness) tied to a stressor No None Factitious Disorder Deliberately fakes/produces symptoms or injury Yes Internal — the "sick role" Malingering (not a mental illness) Deliberately fakes symptoms for a specific known reason Yes External — money,
STEP 3 · WHAT NOT TO DO MATTERS MOST The nursing approach across SSD, illness anxiety, and conversion disorder is almost entirely about what to avoid.

entries.h: 🚫 Don't let the exam trick you — the 3 big NEVERs
entries.t: 💊 NEVER reinforce negative test results → asking for more pain meds 🗣️ NEVER debunk don't say "your symptoms aren't real" 🔬 NEVER over-test don't advocate for more diagnostics or a new diet plan — it's psychological 🧠 "Don't feed it, don't fight it, don't chase it." Don't feed the sick role, don't fight the client's reality, don't chase more tests that won't find anything.

Gently limit the time spent discussing physical symptoms in conversation — redirect toward coping and function instead of the symptom itself. 🧠 Redirect, don't dismiss. Acknowledge the symptom once, then pivot to coping strategies.
Deep-breathing Meditation Exercise 🧠 Since the physical symptoms are stress-driven, stress-reduction is the actual treatment lever — not more imaging.

Help the client connect symptom flares to specific life stressors — building the mind-body insight is the long-term goal, alongside CBT-based reframing (see NG-221). 🧠 Insight is the win condition. The goal isn't "no more symptoms" overnight — it's the client starting to see the stress connection.

📎 Use Therapeutic Communication (NG-271) techniques here: state facts without debating the client's reality, use open-ended questions to explore stressors, and never give false reassurance ("it's all in your head" is never acceptable). CBT (NG-221) cognitive restructuring is a common adjunct treatment for the anxiety driving these disorders. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🩻 SSD = real symptom, no cause Not faked, stress-driven. 🎭 Factitious = fakes for sick role Intentional, internal/psychological gain. 🎯 Malingering ≠ mental illness Intentional, external gain (money, avoiding work). 🚫 Never debunk or over-test Limit focus on symptoms; teach coping instead.

Q1: A client has chronic unexplained abdominal pain with all negative workups and is not faking it. What disorder fits? Show answer Somatic Symptom Disorder — real symptoms, no medical cause, not intentional. Q2: How is factitious disorder different from malingering? Show answer Both are intentional faking, but factitious disorder is for internal/psychological gain (the sick role); malingering is for a clear external gain (money, avoiding work or legal trouble) and is NOT classified as a mental illness. The techniques that carry every mental health page in this batch NG-271 MENTAL HEALTH ADHD-friendly visual edition This is the reference page. Every other Mental Health topic — schizophrenia communication, crisis management, grief & loss, panic attacks — assumes you already know these techniques. Learn them here , once, cold. Therapeutic = client-centered, open, exploring. Non-therapeutic = nurse-centered, closing, judging. One word test: does it hand the floor back to the client, or take it away? 📄 Simple Nursing
STEP 1 · WHAT TO SAY Every therapeutic technique does one of three jobs: opens the door, hands back the feeling, or confirms you heard right.

EXAM TIP Therapeutic communication is client-centered — the nurse's opinions, advice, and personal stories stay out of it. The nurse's only jobs are to open , reflect , and clarify . 🧠 "Ask, don't answer." If the nurse's sentence gives information the client didn't ask for (advice, an opinion, a personal story), it broke the loop.

Require an in-depth response — not a yes/no answer. "How do you cope with anxiety?" "What event in your life has been the most stressful?" "Tell me more about what led to your hospitalization." "What are you feeling right now?" 🧠 "What/How, not Do/Did." Closed questions start with a verb ("Did you..."); open questions start with what, how, tell me .

entries.h: 🪞 Reflecting — return focus to the client
entries.t: Bounce the client's own feeling or question back to them, so they keep exploring it instead of the nurse answering for them. Client: "Do you think I should leave him?" → Nurse: "What do you think you should do?" 🧠 Reflecting = a mirror. The client's own feeling comes right back at them.

Repeat the patient's own words (or close to it) to confirm understanding — not just parroting. "Am I correct in restating that you are feeling less anxious today?" "In looking back at what you said, you stated you are feeling better." 🧠 Restating = echo with a purpose. It checks accuracy before the conversation moves on.

Broad opening: a wide-open invitation with no agenda — "Tell me what's on your mind today." Offering self: the nurse's presence, without demanding a response — "I'll stay with you for a while." 🧠 "You seem to be in pain; I'll stay with you for a while" is both offering self and stating an observation in one line — a classic exam answer.

Sitting with a client without filling every gap gives them room to think, cry, or organize their thoughts. Silence is therapeutic, not awkward. 🧠 Never leave the room to "give them privacy" to grieve — that's abandonment, not silence. Stay, and be quiet.

entries.h: 📌 Stating facts / voicing doubt — reality check
entries.t: Presents objective reality without arguing, used to gently challenge misconceptions or delusions without direct confrontation. "I don't hear any voices, but I know this is frightening for you." 🧠 State facts, don't debate. The nurse reports their own reality — never says "that's not real" or argues the delusion away.

entries.h: 🧩 The combo answer — often the "most correct" NCLEX choice
entries.t: The highest-scoring answer often states an observation AND asks an open-ended follow-up in the same sentence. "This experience has been overwhelming for you. What are you feeling right now?" "The sudden death of your husband is hard to accept. Tell me about how you are feeling?" "You seem very distressed over learning you have asthma." "You're feeling angry that your family continues to hope for you to be cured?" 🧠 "Name it, then ask it." Name the feeling you observe → invite them to say more. When two answer choic
STEP 2 · WHAT NOT TO SAY These blocks show up as wrong-answer distractors on almost every psych question — know them as well as the right answers.

entries.h: ⚖️ Side by side — the master comparison

entries.t: Open-ended question "What are you feeling right now?" Reflecting "What do you think you should do?" Restating "You stated you're feeling better today." Silence / offering self Sitting quietly with the client, present & available. Stating facts "I don't hear voices, but I know this feels real to you." Broad opening "Tell me what's on your mind."

Closed / yes-no question "Are you feeling better?" Giving advice / opinion "I think you should leave him." False reassurance "Everything is going to be alright." Leaving the room "I'll give you privacy to grieve." Asking "Why?" "Why do you feel angry when...?" Personal experience "I lost my grandfather too, so I understand." 🧠 "THERAPEUTIC hands the mic to the client. NON-THERAPEUTIC grabs it back." Every non-therapeutic block on the left column below does the same thing: it centers the nurse , not the client.

entries.h: 🚫 Never: give advice or personal opinions
entries.t: "I'm sure you'll do the correct thing" or "I think you should..." — the nurse's job is to help the client find their own answer, not hand over one. 🧠 Advice = the nurse's problem to solve, not the client's — it removes the client's autonomy.

"It will be ok" / "Don't worry" — minimizes the client's real fear and shuts the conversation down instead of opening it. 🧠 "Ok" is a closed door. False reassurance sounds kind but ends the exploration.

"Why do you feel angry?" / "Why did you leave your child alone?" — "why" sounds accusatory and makes the client defensive, even when the nurse means well. 🧠 Swap "Why" for "What" or "How" — "What led you to feel angry when...?" gets the same information without the blame tone.

Stepping out "to give privacy" during a crying or grieving moment is abandonment, not kindness. Stay and offer silent presence instead. 🧠 Presence > privacy. On the top-missed NCLEX grief question, "leave the room" is almost always the wrong choice.

Changing the subject, dismissing, or rushing past an emotional statement tells the client their feelings don't matter. 🧠 Name it, don't skip it. If the client says something heavy, the nurse's next line should acknowledge it — not move on.

Arguing with a delusion ("that's not real") or defending yourself/the facility puts the nurse on the opposite side of the client instead of alongside them. 🧠 State your own reality — don't attack theirs. Compare: "I don't hear any voices" (ok) vs. "You're wrong, there are no voices" (not ok). 🩺
STEP 3 · REAL SCENARIOS These techniques come back on every other Mental Health page in this batch — schizophrenia, crisis management, grief & loss. Practice choosing the therapeutic line here first.

Scenario: An elderly client is losing their spouse to pancreatic cancer. Which response is most therapeutic? Response Verdict "I know this is a difficult time for you. Tell me how you have been coping with this loss." ✅ Best — states observation + open question "What are your feelings & thoughts about attending a support group?" ✅ Therapeutic — open, explores "It takes time to deal with a lost spouse, but it will be ok." ❌ False reassurance "I recently lost my grandfather to cancer, so I understand." ❌ Personal exp

Silent member: encourage interaction, or pair them off in smaller groups. Aggressive/interrupting member: "You seem very upset" — allow the group to handle it before the nurse intervenes directly. 🧠 Group therapy goal = reduce isolation in a structured, controlled environment — not to "fix" any one member.

A safe, structured social & physical environment — the goal of every behavioral health unit. Clients are oriented to their environment, rights, and responsibilities and encouraged to interact within the community. 🧠 Milieu = the unit itself is the treatment. Structure + community + safety, all day, not just during scheduled therapy.

entries.h: 🔗 Cross-referenced by nearly every page in this batch
entries.t: 📎 Use these exact techniques when reading: Schizophrenia — Communication , Crisis Management , Death, Dying, Grief & Loss , and Abuse & Neglect . This page is the master reference — those pages will assume you already know open-ended questions, reflecting, restating, silence, and the non-therapeutic blocks above. When another page says "use therapeutic communication," it means: ask open-ended , reflect their words , stay present in silence , and never advise, falsely reassure, ask "why," or leave the room. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD ❓ Open, not closed "What/How/Tell me" — never a yes/no question. 🚫 Never "Why?" Sounds accusatory — swap for "what." 🪞 Reflect & restate Hand the feeling back; confirm you heard right. 🤝 Stay, don't leave Silence + presence beats "I'll give you privacy."

Q1: A client says "I can't believe my wife died yesterday. I keep expecting to see her." Best response? Show answer "It must be hard to accept that she has passed away" — states the observation, invites more without arguing or reassuring falsely. Q2: Why is asking "Why did you...?" avoided in therapeutic communication? Show answer It sounds accusatory and puts the client on the defensive — swap "why" for "what" or "how." Q3: A grieving client cries during conversation. What should the nurse do? Show answer Stay and

Ask directly · a plan is the risk · safety comes before everything NG-399 Mental Health ADHD-friendly visual edition Asking someone directly whether they are thinking of killing themselves does not plant the idea . It is the single most important assessment question in psychiatric nursing, and it has to be asked in plain words. Ask it directly “Are you thinking of killing yourself?” What raises risk most A specific plan, the means, and a time The dangerous lift Sudden calm after depression — she has decided Priorit

The sudden calm after a long low is not recovery. She has decided, and the energy to act has come back with it. Swipe it sideways if it is cut off, or tap to open it full size. How you assess it Work through these in order. Each step raises the risk level. Ideation — “Are you thinking about killing yourself?” Plain words. Not “hurting yourself”, which means something different. Plan — “Have you thought about how?” A specific method is a large jump in risk. Means — “Do you have access to that?” A gun at home, saved

What she might say or do “Everyone would be better off without me.” “I won’t be a problem much longer.” Giving away possessions, making a will, saying goodbye Sudden withdrawal, or sudden calm Increased alcohol or drug use Hoarding medication, buying a weapon Reckless behavior, a sense that nothing matters Take every statement literally. Do not reinterpret it as attention-seeking. How to respond in the moment Stay with her. Do not leave to go and find someone. Use her words back. “You said you would not be a proble

What you actually do Ensure immediate safety. One-to-one observation for high risk — that means constant, arm’s-length, including in the bathroom . Remove the means. Belts, shoelaces, cords, razors, glass, plastic bags, medication. Search belongings per policy. Notify the provider and document the exact words she used. Build a safety plan with her, not for her. Restrict access at home: lock or remove firearms and medication, involve family. Treat the underlying illness and the substance use. Environment and observa

Ask it directly “Are you thinking of killing yourself?” What raises risk most A specific plan, the means, and a time The dangerous lift Sudden calm after depression — she has decided Priority Safety first. Never leave a high-risk patient alone. Does asking about suicide put the idea in someone’s head? Show answer No. Asking directly is the correct action and it does not increase risk. Which single factor best predicts a future attempt? Show answer A previous attempt. A severely depressed patient suddenly seems peac
