One order. Every strip. Every time. — rate ▸ rhythm ▸ P ▸ PR ▸ QRS NG-011 CARDIAC · RHYTHM ADHD-friendly visual edition Students try to read strips by recognizing pictures , and then panic when the picture is slightly off. This page teaches the other way: a five-question procedure you run in the same order on every strip, so the rhythm names itself at the end. This page is the method. Its sister page NG-090 — the 9 ECG strips is the rhythm album; come here to learn how to measure , go there to learn what each rhyth

entries.h: THE PAPER, THE WAVES, THE ORDER
entries.t: STEP 0 · SET-UP Before you can measure anything, you have to know what one box is worth and what each bump is.

The ECG is not the heartbeat — it is the electricity that triggers the beat. Every wave on the strip is one structure in the conduction system doing its job. 🧠 P = the little atria, QRS = the big ventricles, T = the recharge. The atria are small, so their wave is small. The ventricles are huge, so their wave is huge.

ECG paper runs under the stylus at a standard 25 mm/second . That is the whole trick: distance across the page IS time. 🧠 “Small four, big twenty.” Small box 0.04 s , large box 0.20 s . Five large boxes = one second.

entries.h: 🧭 The loop — run it in this order, always
entries.t: 🧠 “Really Rushed People Pick Quick.” R ate · R hythm · P waves · P R interval · Q RS. Say it on the way into the room.

entries.h: 🧪 What every wave, segment and interval means
entries.t: MARK WHAT IT IS NORMAL (adult) P wave Atria depolarizing <0.12 s wide, <2.5 mm tall, upright in II PR interval Start of P → start of QRS: atria + the AV delay 0.12–0.20 s (3–5 small boxes) QRS complex Ventricles depolarizing <0.12 s (under 3 small boxes) ST segment Ventricles fully depolarized, plateau flat on the baseline T wave Ventricles repolarizing (recharging) upright, rounded, same direction as QRS QT interval Total ventricular depolarize + recharge ≈0.36–0.44 s; rate-dependent R-R interval Beat to beat — th

entries.h: 🚨 STEP 0 — look at the patient, not the monitor
entries.t: Before you interpret anything, answer three things: Is there a pulse? A perfect-looking rhythm with no pulse is PEA — a cardiac arrest . Is the patient symptomatic? Chest pain, syncope, hypotension, altered mental status, shortness of breath. Symptoms drive urgency far more than the rhythm name. Is it real, or is it artifact? Shivering, brushing teeth, a loose lead or a disconnected electrode all mimic dangerous rhythms. Never treat a monitor tracing without laying hands on the patient. 🧠 “Feel before you fix.” Pul

entries.h: ✅ Artifact vs a real rhythm — how to tell fast
entries.t: Artifact usually has real QRS complexes marching through it — look for the underlying beats inside the noise. Artifact often stops when you touch the leads or ask the patient to hold still. The patient looks fine : talking, pink, good color, normal blood pressure. Real V-tach or V-fib has no pulse or a very sick patient to go with it. 🧠 “The toothbrush rhythm.” Chaotic strip + a chatty patient brushing their teeth = artifact.

entries.h: 📍 Why lead II is the monitoring lead
entries.t: Lead II runs from the right arm to the left leg — almost exactly along the normal direction of atrial depolarization. That makes the P wave biggest and clearly upright in lead II. Since three of your five steps depend on seeing the P wave, this is the lead you monitor in. If the P waves are hard to see, change the lead before you decide they are absent . 🧠 “Two to see the P.” Lead II is where P waves live.

entries.h: ⭐ The three questions this method answers
entries.t: ⏱️ How fast? Step 1 — the rate. 📍 Where did the beat start? Steps 3 and 5 — P waves say atria/SA, QRS width says above or below the ventricles. 🚦 Did it get through? Steps 2 and 4 — regularity and PR interval tell you whether every signal made it to the ventricle. GO DEEPER Once you have those three answers, the rhythm name is almost automatic — look it up on NG-090 · The 9 ECG strips . 1️⃣
HOW FAST? Normal 60–100 /min. Two counting methods; you must know which one is legal on which strip.

Most printed strips are exactly 6 seconds long and have 3-second markers along the top edge. Count the QRS complexes between the two outer markers and add a zero . 🧠 “Count the beats, add a zero.” 8 beats → 80. 5 beats → 50. 13 beats → 130.

Land on an R wave that sits on a heavy line, then count the heavy lines to the next R wave saying 300 · 150 · 100 · 75 · 60 · 50 . Where does the sequence come from? There are 300 large boxes in a minute, so 300 ÷ (large boxes between R waves) = the rate. Two boxes → 150. Three → 100. It is just division you memorized. 🧠 “Three Hundred Silly Hens Sat Silently.” 300-150-100-75-60-50. Sing it once and it sticks.

entries.h: ⭐ Which method, when — the rule that gets tested
entries.t: METHOD USE IT WHEN NEVER USE IT WHEN 6-second × 10 Any strip. Regular or irregular. — (always allowed) 300-150-100 Rhythm is regular and you want a fast answer Rhythm is irregular — the answer changes with every pair you pick 1500 ÷ small boxes Regular, and you need a precise number Irregular rhythms If the rhythm is irregular, the 6-second method is the only correct one. 🧠 Irregular = only the 6-second ruler. Uneven gaps make box-counting meaningless.

entries.h: 🧮 Method C — the 1500 rule (the precise one)
entries.t: 1500 ÷ number of SMALL boxes between two R waves = rate Why 1500? There are 1500 small boxes in one minute ( 25 mm/s × 60 s = 1500 mm ). 20 small boxes → 1500 ÷ 20 = 75 15 small boxes → 1500 ÷ 15 = 100 25 small boxes → 1500 ÷ 25 = 60 🧠 1500 small · 300 large · 30 large in a 6-second strip. Three numbers, one ruler.

entries.h: 📈 Count the ATRIAL rate too when they disagree
entries.t: The rate you report is normally the ventricular rate — count QRS complexes, because that is what produces a pulse and a blood pressure. But if there are more P waves than QRS complexes, count both : count P waves for the atrial rate and QRS complexes for the ventricular rate. Atrial ~300 , ventricular ~150 → 2:1 atrial flutter. Atrial ~80 , ventricular ~35 → think complete heart block. 🧠 QRS makes the pulse. P waves that never reach a ventricle move no blood.

entries.h: 🚨 Rate red flags at the bedside
entries.t: Below 60 with symptoms — dizziness, hypotension, chest pain, confusion. Symptomatic bradycardia needs action; asymptomatic athletes do not. Above 150 — filling time drops so far that cardiac output falls even though the heart is racing. Sudden change in rate is more alarming than a rate that has been stable for hours. Any rate with no pulse = arrest. Start CPR. 🧠 “Too slow to perfuse, too fast to fill.” Both ends of the scale drop cardiac output.

Under 60 “…bradycardia” 60–100 “normal…” / “sinus…” Over 100 “…tachycardia” The rate supplies half the rhythm's name. Step 3 and Step 5 supply the other half (where the beat came from). 🧠 Name = SPEED + ORIGIN. “Sinus” + “bradycardia”. “Atrial” + “fibrillation”. “Ventricular” + “tachycardia”. 2️⃣
EVEN GAPS? Measure R to R. Regular means every gap is the same — not “roughly the same”.
🧠 “Marching band or drunk walk.” Regular = boots hitting the ground in time. Irregularly irregular = someone staggering — no pattern you can predict.

entries.h: ✅ How to actually march it out
entries.t: 1 Lay a plain paper edge along the top of the strip. 2 Pencil a tick on two neighboring R waves. 3 Slide the paper so the second tick sits on the third R wave. 4 Does the first tick land on the second R? Keep sliding along the whole strip. 5 Ticks keep hitting R waves = regular. Ticks drift = irregular. Calipers do the same job faster; the paper trick works when you have no calipers, which is most of the time on a med-surg floor. 🧠 Two ticks and march. Same technique for P-P as for R-R.

PATTERN WHAT YOU SEE CLASSIC CAUSE Regular All R-R gaps identical Sinus rhythms, SVT, V-tach, flutter with fixed conduction Regularly irregular An irregularity that repeats in a pattern Wenckebach; a bigeminal pattern of extra beats Irregularly irregular No pattern at all, ever Atrial fibrillation — the classic answer Regular with an interruption Regular, then one odd beat or one pause A single premature beat (PAC/PVC) or a dropped beat 🧠 “Irregularly irregular” is nearly always A-fib on an exam. Say the phrase, pi

Two rulers, two answers: P-P regular but R-R irregular → the atria are steady; some signals are not getting through. Think AV block . Both regular and equal → normal conduction, one signal one beat. P-P not measurable at all → there are no organized P waves. Think A-fib or flutter . 🧠 Atria have their own ruler. When R-R is a mess, always go back and check P-P.

An irregular rhythm is not just a naming problem: Pulse deficit — some beats are too weak to reach the wrist. Apical and radial pulses differ. Count apical for a full minute. Loss of atrial kick — in A-fib the atria quiver instead of contracting, costing roughly a fifth to a third of cardiac output. Clot risk — blood pooling in a quivering atrium forms clots, which is why A-fib is an anticoagulation conversation. 🧠 Quiver → pool → clot → stroke. That chain is the whole reason A-fib is scary.

Write it the way the chart wants it: “R-R regular” , “R-R irregularly irregular” , or “regular with one premature beat” . Avoid “kind of regular”. If the gaps are not equal, it is irregular , and that changes which rate method you are allowed to use in Step 1. 🧠 Step 2 feeds back into Step 1. If you find irregular, go back and re-count with the 6-second method. 3️⃣
WHO STARTED IT? Three questions: is a P there, do they all look alike, and does each one own a QRS?
🧠 “Every P needs a partner.” A lonely P (no QRS after it) means the signal was blocked. A lonely QRS (no P before it) means the beat did not start in the SA node.

entries.h: ✅ The three P questions, in order
entries.t: 1 PRESENT? Is there a P wave at all? No P → the SA node is not driving. 2 UNIFORM? Do all the Ps look the same? Different shapes = beats starting in different places. 3 1 : 1? One P before every QRS, one QRS after every P? Extra Ps = something is being blocked. 🧠 “P·U·1” — Present, Uniform, One-to-one. Three ticks and Step 3 is done.

entries.h: 🧪 What a normal P wave looks like
entries.t: Upright in lead II (the impulse is traveling toward the positive electrode). Rounded and smooth — not notched, peaked or biphasic. Under 0.12 s wide (under 3 small boxes) and under 2.5 mm tall. All identical to each other across the strip. One per QRS , at the same distance in front of each QRS. A P wave that satisfies all five means the beat is sinus in origin — this is what earns the word “sinus” in a rhythm name. 🧠 Upright + uniform + 1:1 = the SA node is in charge.

entries.h: ⚠️ Inverted, buried or missing P waves
entries.t: If the beat starts in the AV junction instead of the SA node, the atria depolarize backwards . That gives you one of three pictures: Inverted P before the QRS — the atria fired just before the ventricles. No visible P — the P is hidden inside the QRS because both fired together. Inverted P after the QRS — the atria fired late. All three = a junctional beat or rhythm. The QRS stays narrow , because the signal still uses the normal ventricular highway below the AV node. 🧠 Junctional = backwards P, normal QRS. The pac

entries.h: 🚨 “No P waves” — what it narrows down to
entries.t: BASELINE INSTEAD OF P RHYTHM R-R Fine wavy, chaotic quiver Atrial fibrillation Irregularly irregular Repeating sawtooth F waves Atrial flutter Often regular Flat, P hidden in QRS Junctional rhythm Regular Nothing at all, wide bizarre QRS Ventricular rhythm / V-tach Usually regular P waves present but too fast to see clearly SVT (P buried in the T wave) Very regular, very fast SEE THE STRIPS Each of these is drawn full size on NG-090 · The 9 ECG strips .

entries.h: ❌ The trap: calling a P wave absent when it is only hidden
entries.t: Before you write “no P waves”, do two things: Change the lead. P waves can be tiny in one lead and obvious in another. Lead II is your friend. Look inside the T wave. At fast rates the P wave sits on top of the previous T, giving it a strange notch or extra peak. That notch is the P wave. Never diagnose A-fib on a single noisy lead without checking regularity as well. 🧠 “Camel-hump T” = a P wave hiding. Fast and regular with a lumpy T is SVT, not A-fib. 4️⃣
DID IT GET THROUGH? Start of P to start of QRS. Normal 0.12–0.20 s — three to five small boxes.

entries.h: 📐 Measuring it — and what the number means
entries.t: Measure from the very first upstroke of the P wave to the very first deflection of the QRS — not from the top of the P and not to the R peak. Some quick-reference sheets round the range to 0.10–0.20 s ; the standard adult teaching range is 0.12–0.20 s , so use 3–5 small boxes . 🧠 “Three to five, alive.” Under 3 boxes = the signal skipped the delay. Over 5 boxes = the AV node is dragging its feet.

entries.h: 🪜 The block ladder — what a bad PR looks like
entries.t: 🧠 “If the R is far from P, then you have a first-degree. Longer, longer, longer, drop — then you have a Wenckebach. If some Ps just don't get through, then you have a Mobitz II. If Ps and Qs don't agree, then you have a third-degree.”

1 Count the small boxes from the start of P to the start of QRS. 3–5 is normal. 2 Is it the SAME on every beat? Constant vs lengthening is the whole difference between type I and type II. 3 Is every P followed by a QRS? A P with nothing after it is a dropped beat. 🧠 Length · consistency · completeness. Three checks, one interval.

entries.h: 📊 Sorting the AV blocks side by side
entries.t: BLOCK PR DROPPED QRS? WORRY LEVEL 1st degree >0.20 s, constant No Usually benign; watch and document 2nd degree type I (Wenckebach / Mobitz I) Progressively longer Yes, cyclically Often stable; watch, treat if symptomatic 2nd degree type II (Mobitz II) Constant Yes, suddenly Unstable — can progress to complete block 3rd degree (complete) No relationship at all P and QRS independent Emergency — needs pacing Type I lengthens then drops. Type II drops without warning. 🧠 “Type I is polite — it warns you. Type II just l

entries.h: 🚨 The blocks that need a pacemaker conversation
entries.t: Mobitz II and complete (3rd degree) heart block are the two that classically progress and classically need pacing — transcutaneous pacing at the bedside, then a transvenous or permanent pacemaker. Have the transcutaneous pacer pads and the crash cart available; keep the patient on continuous monitoring and on bed rest until a decision is made. Atropine is the standard first drug for symptomatic bradycardia by protocol, but it works at the AV node and is often ineffective in high-grade/infranodal block — do not let

entries.h: ⚠️ A short PR is a finding too
entries.t: A PR under 0.12 s means the signal reached the ventricle faster than the AV node should allow — it took a shortcut, or the beat did not start in the SA node. Junctional beats — starts below the atria, so there is less distance to travel. Pre-excitation (an accessory pathway) — the signal bypasses the AV delay entirely. 🧠 Short PR = the signal cheated. Long PR = the signal queued. 5️⃣
FROM ABOVE OR BELOW? Under 0.12 s (under 3 small boxes) is narrow. Narrow and wide are two different worlds.

entries.h: ↔️ Narrow vs wide — and why the width tells you the origin
entries.t: A narrow QRS means the signal used the His–Purkinje express lanes , so both ventricles fired almost simultaneously — fast, so the complex is thin. A wide QRS means the signal spread muscle cell to muscle cell , which is slow — so the complex smears out. 🧠 “Narrow = normal road. Wide = off-road.” Skinny QRS = the beat came from above the ventricles.

entries.h: ⭐ The single most useful line on the page
entries.t: NARROW <0.12 s Beat started above the ventricles — sinus, atrial or junctional. “Supraventricular.” WIDE ≥0.12 s Beat started in the ventricle, or a bundle branch is blocked, or a pacemaker is firing. Combine it with rate and you have a working diagnosis before you name anything: wide + fast + regular is treated as ventricular tachycardia until proven otherwise. 🧠 “Wide and fast — assume the worst.” Treat wide-complex tachycardia as V-tach.

entries.h: 📊 Four reasons a QRS is wide
entries.t: CAUSE CLUE ON THE STRIP Ventricular origin (PVC, V-tach, idioventricular) No related P wave; T wave points the opposite way to the QRS Bundle branch block Normal P with a normal PR, but the QRS is wide — often notched, “rabbit ears” Paced beat A sharp vertical pacer spike right before the wide QRS Severe hyperkalemia / some drug toxicity Progressive widening, peaked T waves, flattening P waves LINK Potassium ranges and the hyperkalemia picture live on NG-088 · Potassium, sodium & chloride (potassium 3.5–5.0 mEq/L )

Measure from the start of the QRS to the end of the T wave . Typical adult ≈0.36–0.44 s , but it shortens as the rate rises, so it is always read against the rate. Quick bedside sanity check: at a normal rate, the QT should be less than half the R-R interval . Long QT → risk of torsades de pointes . Causes include low potassium, low magnesium, low calcium and QT-prolonging drugs. Check the QT whenever a patient is on a rhythm drug, an antipsychotic or certain antibiotics. 🧠 “Low K, low Mag, long QT, torsades.” Magn

entries.h: 🚨 The two strips that end the assessment early
entries.t: Wide, fast, no pulse → pulseless V-tach. Shock. Start CPR. Chaotic with no identifiable complexes → V-fib. Shock. Start CPR. Flat line → asystole. Do NOT shock. CPR and epinephrine, and check leads in more than one lead first. Never work through five interpretation steps on a pulseless patient — start compressions. 🧠 Shock the V's — V-tach (pulseless) and V-fib. Asystole and PEA are never shocked.

Your five answers assemble into a sentence: [rate word] + [origin word] + [regularity/qualifier] Rate 45, regular, upright Ps 1:1, PR 0.16, QRS 0.08 → sinus bradycardia . Rate 130, irregularly irregular, no Ps, QRS 0.08 → atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response . Rate 180, regular, no Ps, QRS 0.16 → ventricular tachycardia . 🧠 Measure first, name last. The name is the output, never the starting point. 🧪

entries.h: WORKED STRIPS — RUN ALL FIVE STEPS
entries.t: PRACTICE Cover the answer boxes, work the strip yourself, then check. Do this three times and the order sticks.

entries.h: 🟩 PRACTICE STRIP 1 — run the five steps before you read the boxes
🟦 PRACTICE STRIP 2 — the rate changed, nothing else did
🟧 PRACTICE STRIP 3 — two boxes fail at once
🟪 PRACTICE STRIP 4 — everything looks fine until Step 4
🟥 PRACTICE STRIP 5 — stop at Step 0 and check a pulse
🎓 Quick-fire self test — cover the answers
entries.t: Q. A strip is irregularly irregular. Which rate method are you allowed to use? ▸ Only the 6-second strip × 10 . Box-counting methods need equal R-R intervals. Q. How many small boxes is a normal PR interval? ▸ 3 to 5 small boxes = 0.12–0.20 s . Q. The PR gets longer, longer, longest, then a QRS is missing. Name it. ▸ Second-degree AV block type I (Wenckebach / Mobitz I). Q. QRS is 0.14 s. What does that tell you about where the beat started? ▸ It is wide : either a ventricular focus, a bundle branch block, or a pac

entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🏷️ Types ⚡ SNS 🥤 Levels ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Mental Health · Psychiatric Care

NG-021 MENTAL HEALTH ADHD-friendly visual edition The mind goes into a state of panic — so the body goes into fight or flight. The SNS (sympathetic nervous system) switches on, shunting blood away from the extremities toward the core for the vital organs & increasing the vital signs . 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → ⚡ SNS Sssspeeds up vitals HR ⬆ BP ⬆ RR ⬆ sugar ⬆ & pupils dilate! 🥤 S · M · L · XL Mild → Moderate → Severe → Panic attacks! 😱 "Impending doom" = SEVERE Can NOT respond to directions. 👋 Mom
STEP 1 · NAME IT Seven classifications — same anxious engine, different trigger.

🌫️ GAD G eneral A nxiety D isorder 🙈 SAD S ocial A nxiety D isorder 💥 Panic disorder 👋 Separation Anxiety NCLEX EXAMS 🕷️ Phobias 🔁 OCD O bsessive C ompulsive D isorder 💭 PTSD P ost- t raumatic S tress D isorder 🧠 "Generally Sad, Panicky & Separated — Phobic, Obsessed, Traumatized." One sad sentence = G AD · S AD · P anic · S eparation · P hobias · O CD · PT SD.

📝 HESI Question — Client states… "every time I need to leave the house for work … Mom becomes extremely anxious and cries that something terrible is going to happen to me." … supports which psychiatric diagnosis? ✅ Separation anxiety disorder

The anxiety is glued to the goodbye — distress fires when the person leaves, not at the workplace or the crowd. 🧠 "Terrible things happen when you LEAVE" = separation anxiety. The trigger is the door , not the destination. ⚡
STEP 2 · FEEL IT Pathophysiology — panic in the mind flips the fight-or-flight switch in the body.

entries.h: 🏃 Fight or flight — what the SNS does to the body
entries.t: During severe anxiety the mind goes into a state of panic & so the body goes into fight or flight mode, turning on the SNS — sympathetic nervous system . 🧠 MEMORY TRICK — "SNS — Sssspeeds Up the Vital Signs!" Increasing the HR, BP, RR, sugar levels, & dilating the pupils!

entries.h: 🧪 ATI Question — physiological signs of anxiety
entries.t: Which of the following are physiological signs of anxiety? Select all that apply — all five! ✅ Increased pulse rate 📈 ✅ Hyperglycemia 🍬 ✅ Dilated pupils 👁️ ✅ Dilated bronchioles 🫁 ✅ Peripheral vasoconstriction 🥶

The SNS tells the body to shunt blood flow away from the extremities & toward the core of the body for the vital organs — and to increase the vital signs . 🧠 "Core gets the blood, hands get the cold." Everything that helps you run goes UP — everything at the edges gets clamped DOWN. 🥤
STEP 3 · GRADE IT Grade anxiety like a drink order — the exam question is almost always "which level is this?"
🧠 Order it like a soda: S mall = Mild · M edium = Moderate · L arge = Severe · EXTRA Large = Panic Attacks! Same first letters — Small-Mild is the only mismatch to memorize.

entries.h: 📊 Mild vs Moderate vs Severe — what you'll see
entries.t: Level 👀 What you see 🧠 Perception 😤 Mild Restless , irritability intact 😟 Moderate Increased RR & HR · pacing back & forth Slightly reduced perception 😱 Severe Increased RR & HR "hyperventilation" · pacing back & forth · feeling of "Impending Doom" Perception is GREATLY reduced: can NOT respond to directions 🧠 The 3 D's of SEVERE: Doom, Death-talk, Deaf to directions. If perception is gone and they can't follow you — it's severe.

entries.h: 🚨 Exam alert — every one of these clients is SEVERE
entries.t: 📝 ATI: "The client is pacing the hallway and tells the nurse he has a feeling of impending doom." → Severe 📝 HESI Q1: patient tells the nurse, "I feel like I am going to die." → Severe 📝 HESI Q2: male patient is running & keeps repeating, "They are coming!" — neither follows staff directions nor responds to verbal efforts to calm him → Severe Can't follow directions = severe — every time. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🥤 S / M / L / XL Mild · Moderate · Severe · Panic attacks! 🩸 Blood → CORE Away from extremities, toward vital organs. 😱 "I'm going to die" + deaf to directions = SEVERE anxiety. ⚡ SNS Sssspeeds up HR · BP · RR · sugar ⬆ + pupils dilate.

NG-022 CARDIO ADHD-friendly visual edition Given to speed up a slow heart rate with symptomatic bradycardia . Key word: Symptomatic — the symptoms, not just the slow number, are what call for the drug. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 💊 AtroPINE = speed up The drug for a slow heart rate with symptomatic bradycardia. 🧠 A·I·C symptoms Mental status changes: Agitation · Irritability · Confusion. ✅ Working = NSR Normal Sinus rhythm and reversal of the symptoms. ⚡ Drug fails → pace 1st Atropine · 2nd Externa
STEP 1 · WHY GIVE IT Spot the slow heart that is actually in trouble — the key word buys the drug.

Atropine is given to speed up a slow heart rate with symptomatic bradycardia . 🔑 Key word: Symptomatic — the exam clue is the word, not just the number. 🧠 Drug name trick: Atro-PINE 🌲 — picture a PINE tree: tall & upright . Atropine stands a slumping heart rate back up.

entries.h: 🚩 Signs: symptomatic bradycardia — mental status changes
entries.t: 1. Agitation 😤 2. Irritability 😠 3. Confusion 😵‍💫 🧠 A slow pump makes a grumpy brain — A·I·C : A gitated · I rritable · C onfused. 💡
STEP 2 · HOW IT WORKS One drug, one flick: brake off, gas on.

entries.h: 💡 MOA — like flicking a light switch
entries.t: Atropine acts to increase the heart rate by blocking the action of the vagus nerve to block the PNS (parasympathetic nervous system) — REST & DIGEST — and turns ON the SNS (fight & flight) in the heart, like flicking a light switch. 🧠 Block the brake → the gas takes over. Vagus on vacation 🏖️ = heart rate climbs. 🐇
STEP 3 · DID IT WORK? Effectiveness lives on the strip AND in the patient — you need both.

entries.h: 📈 Key points — atropine is effective when we see normal sinus rhythm and reversal of the symptoms
entries.t: They will show you normal sinus rhythm like this & no more hypoxic symptoms, like confusion, agitation, hypotension or syncope.

entries.h: ✅ Reversal of the symptoms — what disappears
entries.t: No more hypoxic symptoms : 😵‍💫 Confusion 😤 Agitation 📉 Hypotension 😵 Syncope 🧠 When atropine works, the symptoms CASH out: C onfusion · A gitation · S yncope · H ypotension — all gone.

entries.h: ⚡ Side note — if drugs do not work
entries.t: If drugs do not work to fix the problem, then we have to put the patient on external pacing . Correct sequence: 1 💊 Atropine — 1st: try the drug 2 ⚡ External pacing — 2nd: when the drug fails 🧠 No pace from the pill? Pace with the pads. Drug first, pacer second.

Atropine for a client with a heart rate of 38 , bp of 88/65 , reports confusion and dizziness. Which ECG strip would show medication effectiveness? ✅ CORRECT: the Normal Sinus rhythm strip — rate lands in 60–100 . 🧮 Count it: R peak × 10 → 8 × 10 = 80 ✅ 🧠 Don't pick the strip that just looks “nicer” — count the R peaks, × 10 , and check it sits in 60–100 . ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 💊 AtroPINE speeds up symptomatic bradycardia 🧠 A·I·C Agitation · Irritability · Confusion = symptomatic ✅ NSR + symptoms reversed = the drug worked (60–100) ⚡ 1st drug · 2nd pads Atropine → external pacing

Q1: What key word makes bradycardia an atropine problem? Show answer SYMPTOMATIC — symptomatic bradycardia. Q2: Name the 3 mental status changes of symptomatic bradycardia. Show answer Agitation, Irritability, Confusion (A·I·C). Q3: HR 38, BP 88/65, confusion & dizziness — which ECG strip shows the med worked? Show answer Normal Sinus rhythm, 60–100 — R peak × 10: 8 × 10 = 80. Q4: Atropine doesn't fix it — what's next, and in what order? Show answer External pacing. Sequence: 1st Atropine, 2nd External pacing. SLOW

entries.h: Bipolar Disorder · NG-023 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🧨 Cause 🌊 Cycles 🔎 Clues 🩺 Care ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Mental Health · “Psychiatric Care”

NG-023 MENTAL HEALTH ADHD-friendly visual edition A mood disorder with cycling periods of lows with Depression followed by highs with Acute Mania. Two extremes, one client — the swing itself is the disease. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🎭 Lows ↔ Highs Depression cycles with Acute Mania around a mood baseline. 🧬 Genetics = 10x Family member with bipolar → 10x more likely to have it. 💊 SSRIs → mania SSRIs (antidepressants) can trigger a manic episode. 🔁 4 in 12 months Four+ mood episodes in a 12-month
STEP 1 · WHAT & WHY Pathophysiology: one mood, two runaway directions — and what pushes the wave into motion.

entries.h: 🌊 The mood wave — one client, two extremes

entries.t: The cause is unknown , but genetics plays a big part: having a family member with bipolar makes clients 10x more likely to have it. 🧠 One relative = 10x. Bipolar runs in the family line — a single affected family member multiplies the risk tenfold.

SSRIs (antidepressants) can trigger a manic episode. The drug that lifts the low can overshoot the baseline and fire the client into a high. 🧠 Slingshot rule: pull a low mood up with an SSRI and it can slingshot straight past baseline into mania . 🌊
STEP 2 · READ THE WAVE Types of bipolar disorders — each type is just a different wave pattern.

entries.h: 📈 Four swing patterns — one glance each
🔢 The numbers trick — types by digits
entries.t: Bipolar 1 — 1 episode of mania that lasts over 1 week or need for hospitalization Bipolar 2 — 2 episodes of milder high hypomania , which can last longer Cyclothymia — milder lows & milder highs cycling over a period of 2 years Rapid Cycling — 4 episodes of depression & mania within a 12 month period 🧠 Count the waves: 1 BIG week · 2 mild highs · 2 mellow years · 4 -in- 12 fast. The number in the name sizes the wave.

HESI Q “Four or more mood episodes in a 12-month period, the patient is said to be…” → Rapid cycling ATI Q “Five acute manic episodes in one year” → Rapid cycling 4 is the floor — 5 in a year still counts. 🔎
STEP 3 · SPOT THE PHASE Name the phase first — everything the client says, wears, and does is a clue.

entries.h: ⚖️ Depression vs Acute Mania — the seesaw
entries.t: 🌧️ DEPRESSION 🔥 ACUTE MANIA Mood 🎭 Declined mood , low mood Elevated mood — euphoric, “More energy + Maniac” Energy 🔋 Low energy & motivation High energy , hyperactivity Danger 🚨 High risk for suicide Even aggression with violence 🧠 MEMORY TRICK (source): D epression = D eclined mood · M ania = M ore energy + M aniac.

entries.h: 🔥 Acute mania — the M·A·N·I·A acrostic (source mnemonic)
entries.t: M More energy & Mood Swings — euphoric energy, impulsive, grandiosity hallucinations & delusions of grandeur A Agitation — ✅ set limits & structured environment N Non-stop talking & Flight of ideas — colorful bizarre clothing choices 🌈 I Insomnia — “Cannot sleep for days” 🌙 A Attention span POOR — easily distracted = ✅ reduce stimuli

entries.h: 🎯 Exam radar — what they pick for “manic phase”
entries.t: HESI Q Select all that apply: The client is quickly angered 😠 Flight of ideas Going rapidly from one activity to another Colorful & outlandish clothing 🌈 ATI Q Symptoms with manic behavior: More talkative than usual 🗣️ Easily distracted Intense need for activity

KAPLAN Q Acute manic phase — client says: “I just bought myself a home computer and a large screen TV for the family.” Most accurate interpretation? Mood disturbance and judgment that is poor at this time ✅ Expect hyperactivity & irritable 🧠 Big buys = broken brakes. Impulsive spending is grandiosity + poor judgment — not generosity. 🩺
STEP 4 · KEEP THEM SAFE Safety first in both directions — the low can end a life, the high can burn one out.
During depression: clients have low mood, low energy, & motivation & high risk for suicide . The phase with no energy is the phase that can turn deadly — stay vigilant.

SAUNDERS Q Assessment finding that requires immediate intervention ? Nonstop physical activity and poor nutritional intake ✅ — burning fuel the body never takes in Constant delusions 🧠 Engine redlined, tank empty. Nonstop motion + no food = the mania emergency.

entries.h: ✅ Make the environment do the work
entries.t: 😠 Agitation → Set limits & a structured environment 🧱 🎈 Easily distracted (attention span POOR) → Reduce stimuli 🔇 🧠 The 3 S’s of mania care: S et limits · S tructure · S lash the stimuli. ⚡
SAY IT OUT LOUD 🎭 Depression ↔ Acute Mania cycling lows & highs around baseline 🔁 4 episodes / 12 months = Rapid cycling 🚨 Depression phase = high risk for suicide 💊 SSRIs can trigger a manic episode

Q1: A client’s parent has bipolar disorder. How much more likely is the client to have it? Show answer 10x more likely — genetics plays a big part (the cause itself is unknown). Q2: Four or more mood episodes in a 12-month period — what is this called? Show answer Rapid cycling (HESI & ATI favorite — 5 manic episodes in a year counts too). Q3: In acute mania, the client announces: “I just bought a home computer and a large screen TV.” Best interpretation? Show answer Mood disturbance and judgment that is poor at th

entries.h: Bladder Antispasmodics · NG-024 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🛡️ Block ⚠️ Beware 🧑‍🏫 Teach ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Renal + Fluid · Urinary Drugs

NG-024 RENAL + FLUID ADHD-friendly visual edition Cholinergic blocking drugs that inhibit bladder contractions and delay the urge to void — they counteract smooth muscle spasm of the urinary tract by relaxing the detrusor and other muscles through action at the parasympathetic nerve receptors. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🚫 The 4 Can'ts “Can't see, can't pee, can't spit, can't sh**” — classic anticholinergic effects. 🔥 No sweat = heat stroke Decreased sweating → heat prostration in hot climates. 🩹 N
STEP 1 · HOW & WHO Block the “squeeze now!” signal — a calm detrusor holds urine and waits.

entries.h: 🗺️ The mechanism: jam the signal, calm the bladder
entries.t: 🧠 “Anti-SPASM = Anti-ACh.” Block the parasympathetic “pee now” signal → the detrusor chills out → the urge can wait.

Used to relieve symptoms of: Dysuria — painful or difficult urination Urinary urgency & frequency Nocturia — excessive urination during the night Suprapubic pain Urge incontinence 🧠 “URISPAS makes URInary Symptoms PASS” — but only the symptoms . Other drugs treat the cause .

entries.h: 🧠⚡ Neurogenic bladder — the other big use
entries.t: Other antispasmodics treat bladder instability — urgency, frequency, leakage, incontinence, and painful or difficult urination — caused by a neurogenic bladder . Neurogenic bladder = impaired bladder function caused by a nervous system abnormality — typically an injury to the spinal cord. 🧠 Broken wiring 🧠→🫙 = twitchy tank. Spinal cord injury scrambles the signals; the blocker mutes the false alarms. ⚠️
STEP 2 · WATCH FOR Anticholinergic drugs dry you out and heat you up — know the “can'ts” cold.

entries.h: 🚨 Adverse reactions — “Can't see, can't pee, can't spit, can't sh**”
entries.t: 👁️ Can't see 🚽 Can't pee 💧 Can't spit 💩 Can't sh** Dim vision decreased production of tears Urinary hesitancy Dry mouth decreased sweating Constipation or diarrhea GI disturbances 😴 Drowsiness · nausea & vomiting · nervousness · vertigo · headache · rash 👵 Mental confusion — particularly in older adults ⚠️ 🟤 Urine may take on a dark brown color 🧠 Everything DRIES and SLOWS : eyes, mouth, sweat, gut, bladder outflow — a blocked “rest & digest” system can't make fluids or move things along.

🥵 High temperatures / hot climate ▼ 🚱 Decreased sweating (the body's AC is off) ▼ 🌡️ Heat prostration — fever & heat stroke Take precautions in hot climates or high temperatures — teach this before summer, not after. 🧠 No sweat → overheat. Blocked ACh = no sweat glands on duty.

entries.h: 🔄 Interactions — who gets stronger, who gets weaker
entries.t: Mixed with… Effect Meperidine, flurazepam, phenothiazines ⬆ antispasmodic effect Tricyclic antidepressants ⬆ antispasmodic effect Antibiotics / antifungals ⬇ anti-infective effectiveness Haloperidol (Haldol) ⬇ antipsychotic effectiveness 🧠 “My Friends Party Together” = M eperidine · F lurazepam · P henothiazines · T CAs — the party crowd pumps the blocker UP ; germ-fighters & Haldol get shut DOWN . 🧑‍🏫
STEP 3 · MANAGE & EDUCATE The exam lives in the patient teaching — patch rules, ghost shells, and dosing.

entries.h: 💊 The drug lineup — know your doses
entries.t: Generic Trade Use Dose Oxybutynin Ditropan Overactive bladder, neurogenic bladder 5 mg orally BID or TID Solifenacin Vesicare Overactive bladder 5 mg/day orally Trospium Sanctura Overactive bladder 20 mg orally TID 🧠 “O.S.T. — the Overactive-bladder Stop Team.” Doses climb 5 → 5 → 20 ; only O xybutynin also covers the neurogenic bladder.
Take three to four times daily as prescribed 🕒 Treats symptoms only — other drugs are given to treat the cause 🧠 Urispas = band-aid, not cure. Symptoms pass; the cause still needs its own drug.

Take with or without food 🍽️ The outer coating may not disintegrate and sometimes may be observed in the stool — not a cause for concern 👻 🧠 “Ghost shell in the bowl.” The XL shell passes empty — the medicine already got out.

entries.h: 🩹 Transdermal patch — the ritual, in order
entries.t: 1 🗑️ Remove the old patch first 2 🧼 Pick a clean, dry area — hip, abdomen, or buttocks 3 🩹 Apply the new patch to that site 4 🔁 Rotate sites with every new application — every 7 days 🗓️ 🧠 “Weekly parking rules: new week, new spot.” H-A-B lot only — H ip · A bdomen · B uttocks. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🚫 The 4 Can'ts Can't see · pee · spit · sh** — anticholinergic effects. 🔥 No sweat = heat stroke Heat prostration risk in hot climates — take precautions. 🩹 Rotate patch q7 days Hip · abdomen · buttocks, clean & dry, remove old first. 💊 Shell in stool = fine Ditropan XL coating may appear in stool — no concern.

Q1: How do bladder antispasmodics work? Show answer They're cholinergic blockers — they relax the detrusor via the parasympathetic nerve receptors, inhibiting bladder contractions and delaying the urge to void. Q2: Your client on oxybutynin is moving to Arizona in July. What must you teach? Show answer Heat prostration risk — decreased sweating can cause fever and heat stroke in high temperatures; take precautions. Q3: A client sees the Ditropan XL tablet in their stool. Priority response? Show answer Reassure — it

entries.h: BLS & CPR · NG-025 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 💔 Stop 🙌 Start ⚡ Shock ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Nursing Core

NG-025 NURSING CORE ADHD-friendly visual edition Done for clients who go into cardiac arrest — meaning the heart has stopped pumping! Immediate CPR with chest compressions provides IMMEDIATE oxygen & perfusion to the brain & vital organs to prevent damage & even DEATH. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🙌 Alone? PUSH first Start compressions BEFORE calling for help. ⏱️ 100–120 /min Depth at least 2–2.4 in (5–6 cm) . 🫁 30:2 manual Intubated = breath every 6 sec , no interruption. ⚡ Defib: NO sync button NO
STEP 1 · WHY THE HEART STOPS Cardiac arrest has many triggers — commonly described as the Hs & Ts.

Caused by a variety of factors : 💨 Hypoxia — no oxygen on board 🫁 Respiratory failure — the lungs quit first, the heart follows ☠️ Toxins 🩸 Blood clots ⚡ Electrolyte imbalances — Na⁺ · Cl⁻ the heart's wiring salts ➕ & others 🧠 AIR · POISON · PLUMBING · WIRING — no air (hypoxia, respiratory failure), poison (toxins), blocked plumbing (blood clots), bad wiring (electrolytes). All roads end in CARDIAC ARREST .

entries.h: 🚨 Why compressions can't wait — #1 Immediate CPR with high quality compressions
entries.t: 💔 CARDIAC ARREST — heart stops pumping → no blood is moving ▼ 🙌 Chest compressions = you become the pump ▼ 🧠 IMMEDIATE oxygen / perfusion to the brain & vital organs ▼ ✅ Prevents damage & even DEATH! 🙌
STEP 2 · PUMP & BREATHE The adult BLS sequence — the order IS the exam question.

1 🙌 Chest compressions IMMEDIATELY. If NO caregivers are around to help , start compressions BEFORE calling for help — you are the only caregiver! NCLEX TIP “Most students get this wrong on exams.” ▼ 2 🎯 Hands in center of chest — lower half of sternum ▼ 3 💪 High quality compressions: rate 100–120/min , depth at least 2–2.4 in (5–6 cm) NCLEX TIP ▼ 4 🫁 Breaths: manual = 30 compressions & 2 rescue breaths · intubated = every 6 sec without interruption ▼ 5 🖐️ Every 2 min : pause compressions to assess pulse — 10 secon

entries.h: 🎯 Where to push — center of chest, lower half of sternum
🔑 KEY Numbers — say them in your sleep
entries.t: ⏱️ Rate 100–120 per minute ⬇️ Depth 2–2.4 in at least · (5–6 cm) 🫁 Manual breaths 30 : 2 compressions : rescue breaths 🫁 Intubated q 6 sec without interruption 🖐️ Pulse check 2 min pause · 10 seconds 🧠 During CPR, compressions are paused every 2 mins to assess pulse — a 10-second peek, then hands right back on.

Manual 😮‍💨 Intubated 🧵 30 compressions & 2 rescue breaths Every 6 seconds without interruption O₂ 00:06 🧠 “Tube = 6.” A tube in the throat means a breath every 6 ticks of the clock — and the pushing never stops .
🙌 Compress 2 min ▼ 🖐️ Pause — assess pulse · 10 seconds ▼ 🙌 Compress 2 min … repeat Push, peek, push — the clock never runs long without hands on the chest. ⚡
STEP 3 · AED & DEFIB Pads on, everyone clear, shock — then hands straight back on the chest.

entries.h: 🔌 AED pads — where they go (8 years & older)
⚡ How to SHOCK an adult — in order
entries.t: 1 🔌 Defibrillator pads are placed 2 📣 Call out & look to make sure everyone is clear 3 🙌 Continue chest compressions immediately after the shock 🧠 “Pads · People clear · Push again.” P-P-P — the shock is a comma, not a period: hands go right back on the chest.
❌ NO IV sedation needed. ❌ NO synchronized button. That is for cardioversion — an arrested heart has no rhythm to sync to, and an unconscious client needs no sedating. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🙌 Only caregiver? Compressions BEFORE calling for help. ⏱️ 100–120 · 2–2.4 in Rate per minute · depth (5–6 cm). 🫁 30:2 · tube q6s Pulse check every 2 min — 10 sec . ⚡ Shock → push again Compressions immediately after the shock.

Q1: You're the ONLY caregiver and your client goes into cardiac arrest. First action? Show answer Start high-quality chest compressions immediately — BEFORE calling for help. (Most students get this wrong!) Q2: Compression rate and depth for an adult? Show answer 100–120/min, at least 2–2.4 inches (5–6 cm) deep — hands on the lower half of the sternum. Q3: The client is intubated. How do you deliver breaths? Show answer Every 6 seconds, without interrupting compressions. (Manual = 30 compressions : 2 rescue breaths
🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🔥 Cause 🔎 Clues 🚿 Care ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Skin + Wound · Pathophysiology Course

NG-026 SKIN + WOUND ADHD-friendly visual edition Burn injuries = direct tissue damage from exposure to sun, chemicals, thermal (boiling liquids), or electricity — the deeper the damage goes, the higher the degree. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🚿 The 3 C's Cool water · Cover · Clothing removal. 🧊 NO ice, NO creams No antibiotic ointment to open skin either. 💧 Moist + blisters = 2nd° “Red, moist, shiny fluid filled vesicles.” 🤍 Waxy white / charred = 3rd° Dry, leathery, non-blanchable. 🔥
STEP 1 · WHAT & WHY Four ways to cook skin — and the six floors the damage can reach.

entries.h: 🔥 Four causes of direct tissue damage
entries.t: ☀️ Sun the slow roast 🧪 Chemicals the splash that keeps burning ♨️ Thermal boiling liquids — the classic scald ⚡ Electricity the current cooker 🧠 “Some Cooks Touch Electricity” = S un · C hemicals · T hermal · E lectricity — the 4 burn makers.
1️⃣ Epidermis — the top coat 2️⃣ Dermis — the working middle 3️⃣ Subcutaneous tissue — “that fatty bubble looking tissue” Under the skin we find fascia, muscle & bone .

Degree = depth. Each degree of burn reaches one floor deeper into the stack — that's how you'll read the diagram below. 🧠 “Every Day Someone Finds My Burns” = E pidermis · D ermis · S ubcutaneous · F ascia · M uscle · B one — top to bottom. 🔎
STEP 2 · READ THE DEPTH Look at the burn, name the floor it reached — dry & red, wet & blistered, or waxy & dead.

entries.h: 🕳️ Burn depth map — how far down did it go?
🌡️ Degree vs degree — the look test
entries.t: Degree Thickness What you see 👀 1st° ☀️ Superficial Dry with blanchable redness 2nd° 💧 Partial thickness “Red, moist , shiny fluid filled vesicles” · painful blisters 3rd° 🤍 Full-thickness Dry waxy white, leathery, or charred black · non-blanchable 4th° 🦴 Full-thickness Deepest — down where fascia, muscle & bone live 🧠 “1 is red, 2 is wet, 3 is dry & dead.” And the blanch test: if it blanches, blood still branches — 3rd° won't blanch. 🚿
STEP 3 · PREHOSPITAL · MINOR BURNS Three C's, in order — and two traps the exam loves.

C 🚿 Cool water — briefly soak the area. ❌ NO ice, creams, or antibiotic ointment to open skin C 🩹 Cover the area — “Clean dry cloth” C 💍 Clothing & jewelry removal — only if NOT adhered to the skin 🧠 Cool it, Cover it, Clear it off — 3 C's, in that order. Cool the burn, never the whole patient.
❌ NO ice on the burn ❌ NO creams ❌ NO antibiotic ointment to open skin 💊🚫 ❌ Don't pull off anything stuck to the burn Cool water only — soothe it, don't smother it.

entries.h: ⭐ Stuck to the skin? Step away NCLEX TIP
entries.t: HCP removes anything sticking to the skin. You remove clothing & jewelry that is not adhered — if it's melted in or stuck on, it stays until the HCP takes it off. 🧠 “If it's stuck, it stays — the HCP peels, not you.” ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🚿 Cool · Cover · Clothing The 3 C's of prehospital burn care. 🧊 NO ice · creams · ointment Cool water only on the burn. 💧 Wet + painful blisters = 2nd° partial thickness. ⭐ Stuck to skin = HCP's job Only remove what's NOT adhered.

Q1: A burn is “red, moist, shiny” with fluid-filled vesicles and painful blisters. What degree? Show answer Second-degree (partial thickness). Q2: First C of prehospital burn care — and what do you NEVER apply? Show answer Cool water, briefly soak the area — NO ice, creams, or antibiotic ointment to open skin. Q3: The client's shirt is stuck to the burn. Do you remove it? Show answer NO — only remove clothing/jewelry that is not adhered. The HCP removes anything sticking to the skin. NG-027 SKIN + WOUND ADHD-friendly visual edition Burn injuries = direct tissue damage from exposure to sun ☀️, chemicals 🧪, thermal (boiling liquids) 🍲, or electricity ⚡ — how DEEP the damage goes decides the degree. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🧯 The 3 C's C ool water · C over · C lothing removal. 🧊 Cool water — NEVER ice No creams, no antibiotic ointment to open skin. 🛢️ Tar burn? Immediate action = cooling the injury with water. 💧 Big burn: Airway → IV fluids Full thickness 20%: after a patent ai
STEP 1 · WHAT BURNED IT Four ways to cook skin — then know the layers the heat digs through.

entries.h: 🔥 Types & causes — direct tissue damage from exposure to:
entries.t: ☀️ Sun 🧪 Chemicals 🍲 Thermal boiling liquids ⚡ Electricity 🧠 “SCorched by The Elements” — S un · C hemicals · T hermal · E lectricity.
Epidermis — the surface Dermis — the middle Subcutaneous tissue — “that fatty bubble looking tissue” Under the skin we find fascia, muscle, & bone — the deeper the burn digs, the higher the degree. 🔎
STEP 2 · READ THE DEPTH Degree = depth. Match what you SEE on the surface to how far down the damage goes.

entries.h: 🗺️ The depth map: degree by skin layer NCLEX TIP
🧾 What you see, degree by degree
entries.t: Degree Looks like 1° superficial Dry with blanchable redness 2° partial thickness “Red, moist, shiny fluid filled vesicles” — painful blisters 3° full-thickness Dry waxy white, leathery, or charred black — non-blanchable 4° full-thickness Deepest of all — past the skin itself

✅ 1° blanches — press it, it whitens, color returns. Surface only. ❌ 3° does NOT blanch — waxy, leathery, charred tissue can't respond. 🧠 “If it blanches, skin still dances.” Blanchable = superficial. Non-blanchable + leathery = full-thickness trouble. 🩺
STEP 3 · COOL · COVER · CLOTHES Minor burn prehospital care = the 3 C's — and the exam loves what you DON'T put on a burn.

entries.h: ✅ Prehospital care for minor burns — the 3 C's
entries.t: C 💧 Cool water — briefly soak the area. NO ice, creams, antibiotic ointment to open skin C 🩹 Cover the area — “clean dry cloth” C 👕 Clothing & jewelry removal — only if not adhered 🧠 C · C · C = Cool it, Cover it, Cut the Clothes. Water is the only thing that touches a fresh burn.

❌ NO ice on the burn ❌ NO creams or antibiotic ointment to open skin ❌ Never rip off adhered clothing — HCP removes anything sticking to the skin Cool water only — soak briefly, then cover with a clean dry cloth.

entries.h: 💧 Kaplan question: the big-burn priority NCLEX TIP
entries.t: Client with full thickness burns covering 20% of the body . Priority of care after ensuring a patent airway : ➡️ IV fluids 🧠 A before F: secure the A irway, then pour the F luids.

🛢️ Tar burn — the nurse instructs firefighters: the immediate action ? ➡️ Cooling the injury with water 🧪 Chemical burn — the first consideration in immediate care? ➡️ REMOVING ALL clothing — including gloves, shoes, and any undergarments 🧠 Tar = water first 💧 · Chemicals = strip everything 👕. Cool the sticky, shed the soaked. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🧯 Cool · Cover · Clothes off The 3 C's of minor burn care. 🫧 Blisters = 2° partial “Red, moist, shiny fluid filled vesicles.” 🖤 Waxy · leathery · charred = 3° full-thickness, non-blanchable. 💧 Airway ✔ → IV fluids The big-burn priority order.

Q1: Firefighter with a tar burn. Immediate action? Show answer Cooling the injury with water. Q2: Chemical burn at a factory. First consideration in immediate care? Show answer Removing ALL clothing — including gloves, shoes, and any undergarments. Q3: Full thickness burns over 20% of the body — priority after a patent airway? Show answer IV fluids. Q4: Minor burn — what NEVER goes on it? Show answer No ice, no creams, no antibiotic ointment to open skin — cool water only, then cover with a clean dry cloth. CAUSE →

entries.h: Cardiovascular Key Terms · NG-028 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🫀 Pump 📈 Push 🧪 Proof ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Cardio · Pathophysiology Course

NG-028 CARDIO ADHD-friendly visual edition The heart acts like a pump , pumping oxygen-rich blood OUT to the body — mainly possible with the help of the “big momma” LEFT ventricle! Acting like a slingshot, it shoots blood out through the aorta & arteries to perfuse (oxygenate) the vital organs. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🏹 A-A · 🌀 V-V Arteries push blood A way · Veins V acuum it back. 🌊 CO = SV × HR Normal cardiac output 4–8 L/min . 📉 EF ≤ 40% = BAD! Indicates heart failure (normal 55–70% ). 🚨 Tro
STEP 1 · THE PLUMBING One pump, three loops — every circulation term lives on this map.

entries.h: 🗺️ The circulation term map — 3 loops, 1 big momma
entries.t: 🧠 Pulmonary Picks up O2 · Systemic Ships it out · Coronary feeds the Crew (the heart muscle itself).

The heart pumps oxygen-rich blood OUT to the body — mainly thanks to the LEFT ventricle . Acting like a slingshot 🏹, the LEFT ventricle shoots oxygen-rich blood out through the aorta & arteries to perfuse (oxygenate) the vital organs.

entries.h: 🔄 Cardiac basics — arteries vs veins MEMORY TRICK
entries.t: Arteries push oxygen-rich blood away from the heart to perfuse the tissues. Veins vacuum DE-oxygenated blood back to the RIGHT side of the heart. 🧠 A-A: A rteries push O2-rich blood A way · V-V: V eins V acuum DE-oxygenated blood back.
The movement of oxygen-rich blood from the heart to the rest of the body through the arteries — and back to the heart via the veins.
The movement of blood between the heart & lungs . Deoxygenated blood travels through the RIGHT side into the lungs to absorb O2 and release CO2 — then back to the LEFT side to be pumped to the body.
Supplies oxygen-rich blood to the myocardium (heart muscle) via the coronary arteries . The pump has to feed itself first! 📈
STEP 2 · THE NUMBERS How hard, how much, how often — the hemodynamic vocabulary.

entries.h: 🧮 The one formula to rule them all KEY NUMBERS
entries.t: 🧠 Cardiac OUTput = O2 blood OUT to the body. How much OUT per minute? Squeeze-size × squeeze-count.
The number of times the heart beats in a minute. Normal: 60–100 bpm
The amount of blood pumped by the left ventricle of the heart in 1 heart contraction .
The amount of blood the heart pumps in 1 minute . Normal: 4–8 L/minute
The filling & stretching of the ventricles’ myocardium (heart muscle) right before contraction (pump) . 🧠 PREload = PREfill. The balloon stretch BEFORE the squeeze.

The amount of resistance the heart has to overcome to eject blood out of the ventricles & into systemic circulation (the blood vessels). Also known as systemic vascular resistance (SVR) . 🧠 AFTERload = the fight AFTER the fill — shoving the door (SVR) open to get blood out.
The percentage of blood leaving the heart each time it contracts (in 1 pump). 🧠 “Life begins at 55” — EF under 55 is slipping, and 40 or less = the heart is failing . 🧪
STEP 3 · THE LABS When the muscle is damaged, it leaks evidence into the blood.

entries.h: 🚨 Cardiac enzymes & the ROMI panel PATHO TEST TIP
entries.t: Cardiac enzymes are released into the circulation when the heart muscle is damaged from lack of oxygen (ischemia) , indicating myocardial necrosis (tissue death) during a myocardial infarction (MI) — heart attack. ROMI panel = the cardiac enzymes taken after a heart attack (MI): Troponin · Myoglobin · CK-MB

Proteins found in both skeletal and cardiac muscle fibers that regulate muscular contraction . #1 indicator = Myocardial Infarction (MI) — heart attack. Troponin > 0.5 🧠 “Top test” = T-T: T roponin over 0.5 · T rauma to heart muscles.
Any damage to muscle tissue — including myocardial necrosis. Not picky about which muscle got hurt.
Muscle enzyme on the ROMI panel — the cardiac-specific form is CK-MB , drawn after a heart attack (MI).

entries.h: 💙 Natriuretic peptides — ANP & BNP TEST TIP
entries.t: ANP — A trial N atriuretic P eptides BNP — B rain or B -Type N atriuretic P eptides BNP is very helpful in diagnosing the severity of CHF — Congestive Heart Failure. 🧠 B-B: B NP = B ulging ventricles. The more the ventricles bulge, the higher the BNP.

entries.h: 📶 BNP staircase — CHF severity KEY NUMBERS
entries.t: 🧠 BNP climbs by threes: 3-6-9. 3 00 Mild → 6 00 Moderate → 9 00 SEVERE. Under 100? You're fine. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🏹 Arteries Away 🌀 Veins Vacuum back to the RIGHT side. 🌊 CO = SV × HR 4–8 L/min · HR 60–100 bpm. 📉 EF 55–70% normal ≤ 40% = BAD → heart failure. 🚨 Troponin > 0.5 = MI BNP 3-6-9 = mild → moderate → SEVERE CHF.

Q1: What is the cardiac output formula, and what is a normal CO? Show answer CO = SV × HR — normal is 4–8 L/minute. Q2: A client's ejection fraction is 38%. What does that indicate? Show answer 40% or LESS is BAD — it indicates heart failure (normal EF is 55–70%). Q3: What is the #1 lab indicator of a myocardial infarction, and at what level? Show answer Troponin greater than 0.5 — “Top test: Troponin over 0.5, Trauma to heart muscles.” Q4: BNP comes back at 650. How severe is the CHF? Show answer 600+ = Moderate C

NG-029 GI ADHD-friendly visual edition Liver cirrhosis — THINK liver “Scarrrosis.” Normal healthy tissues get replaced with SCAR tissue , making the liver hard like a rock! 🪨 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🪨 Scarrrosis Scar tissue replaces healthy tissue — liver hard like a rock. 🏭 4 jobs: G·A·D·ABC Glycogen · Ammonia detox · Drugs · makes Albumin, Bile, Coag factors. 💛 Bilirubin ↑ = jaundice Yellow skin & eyes — the sclera goes yellow. 🩸 #1 concern = BLEEDING No coagulation factors → blood can’t clot
STEP 1 · WHY IT SCARS Years of inflammation turn a soft working liver into a rock.

entries.h: 🪨 Watch a liver turn to rock — chronic hepatitis, year after year
entries.t: 🧠 Cirrhosis? THINK “Scarrrosis.” Say it with the growl — scarrr tissue is the whole disease.

entries.h: 🧨 Causes — anything that causes inflammation & scarring to the liver
entries.t: 🍺 Alcohol abuse 🔥 Chronic Hepatitis — hepatitis = inflammation 🫁 Cystic fibrosis — serious mucus clogs the entire body & the liver 🧠 Scars come from an A·C·H e: A lcohol · C ystic fibrosis · H epatitis (chronic) — a liver that ACHes for years turns to rock.
Since normal healthy tissues get replaced with SCAR tissue , the liver becomes hard like a rock . A rock can’t do the liver’s jobs — so every job below starts to fail. 🏭
STEP 2 · WHAT THE LIVER DOES 4 major roles & responsibilities — know the jobs, and the failures explain themselves.
🧠 A healthy liver is G.L.A.D. — G lycogen stored · L ets go of ammonia (detox) · A BCs produced · D rugs metabolized. A cirrhotic liver is NOT glad.

entries.h: 🚌 B — Bile: “the Bile Bus” (Memory Trick from the source)
entries.t: Bile is the Bile Bus — it helps scoop up excess Cholesterol & Bilirubin and take them from the body to the toilet via the bowels. 🧠 Bile Bus passengers: Cholesterol & Bilirubin. No bus service = passengers pile up in the blood (see CRASH 💥).

entries.h: 💧 A — Albumin: the body’s transport truck
entries.t: 🚚 Transports drugs in the body 💦 Also attracts water 🦴 Binds with Calcium ( Ca ) 🧠 A — Albumin · A — Attracts water, drugs & binds with calcium (source mnemonic — double-A it!)

entries.h: 🩸 C — Coagulation factors: the clotting crew
entries.t: The liver produces coagulation factors — the crew that makes blood clot. A rock-hard liver can’t make the crew… and that sets up the #1 danger waiting in CRASH 💥. 💥
STEP 3 · WHEN THE LIVER FAILS Each lost job becomes a finding you can see — or a danger you must catch.

entries.h: 💛 The jaundice cascade — when the Bile Bus stops running
entries.t: 🪨 Liver fails → no more Bile Bus service ▼ 📈 Higher cholesterol & HIGH bilirubin — the passengers pile up in the blood ▼ 💛 Bilirubin causes jaundice in the body ▼ 👀 Yellowing of the skin & the eyes — specifically the white part of the eye, called the sclera 🧠 Bus breaks down → Bili backs up → Body turns banana-yellow. Look at the sclera first.

In liver disease, the blood can’t clot fast enough & leads to a HUGE risk of bleeding . Our #1 concern is the BLEEDING! 🧠 Hard as a rock → blood won’t clot. Scarred liver = no coagulation factors = bleeder.
Which complication is a patient with cirrhosis at risk for? Show answer ● Bleeding 🩸 — the liver can’t make coagulation factors. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🪨 Scarrrosis Scar tissue → liver hard like a rock. 🚌 Bile Bus riders Cholesterol & Bilirubin → out via the bowels. 💛 Jaundice = bilirubin ↑ Yellow skin & sclera (white of the eye). 🩸 #1 concern: BLEEDING Blood can’t clot fast enough.

Q1: In cirrhosis, what replaces the normal healthy liver tissue — and what does it do to the liver? Show answer SCAR tissue — it makes the liver hard like a rock (“Scarrrosis”). Q2: Name the 3 causes from this card. Show answer Alcohol abuse · Chronic hepatitis (inflammation) · Cystic fibrosis (mucus clogs the body & liver) — the liver’s A·C·He. Q3: What does the liver PRODUCE? (A·B·C) Show answer A – Albumin · B – Bile · C – Coagulation factors. Q4: HESI-style — which complication is the cirrhosis patient at risk

NG-030 GI ADHD-friendly visual edition IBD — Inflammatory Bowel Disease — is the umbrella over Crohn's disease and Ulcerative Colitis (UC) . Both are autoimmune diseases ( the body is attacking itself ), so signs & symptoms come & go . 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 👑 Crohn's = "Crown's" Mouth → anus, skip lesions, NO blood . 🩸 UC = colon bleeds 15–20 bloody liquid stools per day. 🧈 Fatty stools = Crohn's Steatorrhea + 5 loose stools/day (mucus/pus). 🔥 Flares = the 3 S's Stress · Smoking · Sepsis (inf
STEP 1 · WHAT'S INFLAMED & WHERE Two diseases, one umbrella — the exam lives in the differences. Look at the pattern.

entries.h: 🗺️ Side by side: patchy tunnels vs one long bleeding sore

entries.t: Inflammation granulomas ( bumps & lumps ) from mouth to anus , but mainly in the small intestines , that do not bleed . This deep inflammation can lead to fistulas — open tunnels of the GI tract that can contaminate the body . 🕳️ Inflamed tissue: fistulas, fissures, & abscesses 🫘 Granulomas (bumps & lumps) 🗺️ Skip lesions TEST TIP 🧠 Memory trick: Crohn's = "Crown's disease" 👑 — the crown starts at the head ( mouth ) and the disease can run all the way down to the anus .

Inflammation & ulcers in the colon — "big long open sores that bleed" — leading to decreased hemoglobin . 🚽 15–20 bloody liquid stools per day 🧪 Anemia 📉 Decreased H/H (Hemoglobin & Hematocrit) 🧠 UC = "U C blood." Ulcerative Colitis is the one where yo U C (see) blood — Crohn's doesn't bleed. 🚽
STEP 2 · READ THE STOOL The stool count, the fat, and the blood tell you which disease you're looking at.

entries.h: ⚖️ Crohn's vs UC — the exam table
entries.t: 👑 Crohn's 🩸 UC Where 📍 Mouth → anus , mainly small intestines Colon Pattern 🗺️ Skip lesions TEST TIP — patchy, deep Continuous — one long stretch of sores from the rectum up Tissue 🔬 Granulomas (bumps & lumps) · fistulas, fissures & abscesses Ulcers — "big long open sores that bleed" Stools 🚽 5 loose stools/day ( mucus/pus ) + Steatorrhea 🧈 (fatty stools) 15–20 bloody liquid stools per day Blood 🩸 ❌ NO blood — main difference from UC ✅ Bleeds → anemia , ↓ H/H 🧠 Crohn's counts to 5 and stays fatty; UC unloads 15–20
Rebound tenderness — pain that spikes when you press down and let go — is a Report to HCP finding. Don't sit on it.

entries.h: 🧪 Labs — why UC drains the blood count
entries.t: Big long open sores bleed → decreased hemoglobin → Anemia with ↓ H/H ( Hemoglobin & Hematocrit ). 👑 Crohn's does not bleed — so no anemia clue there. 🔥
STEP 3 · WHY IT FLARES Autoimmune = the body attacks itself — so symptoms come & go with the 3 S's.

Both conditions are autoimmune diseases ( the body is attacking itself ), so naturally signs & symptoms come & go during times of stress, smoking & sepsis (infection). S 😖 Stress NCLEX TIP S 🚬 Smoking S 🦠 Sepsis (infection) 🧠 Three S's strike the match: S tress · S moking · S epsis — and the bowel catches fire 🔥 (flare!).
IBD = Inflammatory Bowel Disease — the family name that covers both. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 👑 Skip lesions + granulomas = Crohn's — deep, patchy, NO blood. 🩸 15–20 bloody stools/day = UC → anemia, ↓ H/H. 🚨 Rebound tenderness = Report to HCP. 🔥 3 S's flare IBD Stress · Smoking · Sepsis (infection).

Q1: Client reports 15–20 bloody liquid stools per day. Crohn's or UC? Show answer UC — colon ulcers (big long open sores) bleed → decreased hemoglobin, anemia, ↓ H/H. Q2: "Skip lesions" and granulomas show up in the question stem. Which disease? Show answer Crohn's ("Crown's") — patchy deep inflammation, mouth to anus, mainly small intestines, NO blood. Q3: Your IBD client develops rebound tenderness. What do you do? Show answer Report to HCP — rebound tenderness is a red-flag finding. Q4: Name the 3 S triggers tha

NG-031 MENTAL HEALTH ADHD-friendly visual edition Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) , also called clinical depression , is when a client experiences a severe depressed mood , loss of enjoyment in life , low energy & a few other critical signs and symptoms. Everything is low & slow — it is thought to be from low levels of neurotransmitters within the brain. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → ⬇️ Low & slow Low Serotonin · Dopamine · Norepinephrine . 🔢 5 of 9 = MDD Diagnosis needs 5 or more symptoms. 🚫🎉 Anhedo
STEP 1 · WHY IT HAPPENS Three neurotransmitters run low — and the whole client runs low with them.

entries.h: 🧠 Pathophysiology: the three tanks are low
entries.t: 🧠 “Sad Dogs Nap” = S erotonin · D opamine · N orepinephrine — all three down , so the client is low & slow .

Stressful life event ATI Substance abuse disorders Chronic illness Genetics: Family history Female 🧠 “SAD GF” — S tress · A ddiction (substance abuse) · D isease (chronic illness) · G enetics · F emale. ATI QUESTION …a risk factor for depression? ✅ Stressful life events

KAPLAN QUESTION Client has recently become unemployed and reports feeling depressed. The nurse understands which statement to be true? ✅ Unemployment is a significant potential stressor 🧠 Lost job, lost house, lost person → stressor . If the stem hands you a life event , that is the risk factor. 🔎
STEP 2 · COUNT TO FIVE Nine symptoms exist — you only have to count five of them to land on MDD.

entries.h: 🔢 Diagnosis: how many symptoms? HESI · ATI
entries.t: HESI ATI Diagnosis: 5 or more symptoms out of the 9 .

1 😞 Depressed mood (hopeless, empty) 2 🚫🎉 Anhedonia (loss of joy / interest in life) 3 ⚖️ Weight loss (anorexia) or Wt. Gain 4 🐢 Psychomotor retardation NCLEX TIP Slower speech, response time, & Decreased movement 5 🛏️ Insomnia or hypersomnia (sleeping too much) 6 🔋 Fatigue (Anergia) 7 😔 Feelings of worthlessness or Guilt 8 🌫️ Difficulty concentration 9 🚨 Suicidal thoughts (Recurrent) assess it directly, every time — this is the finding you report 🧠 “SIG E CAPS” + depressed mood covers all 9 → S leep (5) · I nteres

entries.h: 🗣️ Anhedonia — hear it in the quote HESI
entries.t: Q1: “Life just doesn’t have any joy in it anymore. Things I once did for pleasure aren’t fun.” ✅ Answer: Anhedonia 🧠 An-hedonia = “no hedonism.” No pleasure, no fun, no interest — the joy switch is off.

entries.h: 🛏️ The sleep complaint they test HESI
entries.t: Q2: Which complaint regarding sleep would the nurse expect from a patient diagnosed with major depression? ✅ “I wake up about 4 am and cannot go back to sleep. I feel tired all the time” 🧠 4 a.m. and wide awake 🌑 — early-morning waking + tired all day is the depression sleep answer (insomnia or hypersomnia both count).
🗣️ Slower speech ▼ ⏱️ Slower response time ▼ 🚶 Decreased movement 🧠 Low neurotransmitters → low & slow client. Speech slow, answers slow, body slow — that is psychomotor retardation. 🧒
STEP 3 · WHO TO SCREEN Kids and teens don’t look sad — they look angry, tired, and suddenly different.

Adolescents 10 – 19 years 😠 Angry, aggressive outbursts & vandalism / skipping class 😴 Napping during day ⚖️ Weight loss or gain — “suddenly” “rapidly” 🙍 Low self-esteem (withdrawal) 🧠 Teens ACT OUT, adults shut DOWN. On peds items, anger + skipping class + a sudden change is depression until screened otherwise.

👤 ADULT (the 9) 🧒 ADOLESCENT 10–19 Mood 🙂↔️🙁 Depressed mood — hopeless, empty Irritability · angry, aggressive outbursts Behavior 🎭 Psychomotor retardation — slow speech & movement Vandalism / skipping class · withdrawal, low self-esteem Energy 🔋 Fatigue (Anergia) Anergia · napping during day Interest 🚫🎉 Anhedonia — lost joy in life Anhedonia — quits the team / the hobby Appetite ⚖️ Weight loss (anorexia) or gain Appetite changes — weight change “suddenly” “rapidly” 🧠 The 4 A’s of the teen 🅰️ — A nger (irritability

entries.h: 📝 ATI QUESTION Assessing an adolescent who has depression — which findings should the nurse expect? (Select all that apply)
entries.t: ✅ Irritability ✅ Anergia ✅ Anhedonia ✅ Appetite changes

entries.h: ⭐ TOP Missed NCLEX QUESTION — which pediatric clients should the nurse screen for depression? (Select all that apply)
entries.t: ✅ 😴 10 year old taking frequent naps during class time ✅ 🚫🎉 16 year old quit the chess team despite being the team captain ✅ 😠 14 year old sent home from school due to angry outbursts & skipping class ✅ ⚖️ 17 year old suddenly lost 15 lbs (6.8 kg) in 4 weeks → 48.2 kg 🧠 Nap · Quit · Rage · Drop. Four teens, four disguises, one screen: depression . ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD ⬇️ Serotonin · Dopamine · Norepinephrine = low & slow 🔢 5 or more of 9 = MDD diagnosis 🐢 Slow speech + slow movement = psychomotor retardation 🚨 Recurrent suicidal thoughts = symptom 9 — assess & report it

Q1: Client says “Life just doesn’t have any joy in it anymore. Things I once did for pleasure aren’t fun.” Name the symptom. Show answer Anhedonia — loss of joy / interest in life. Q2: How many symptoms are needed to diagnose MDD? Show answer 5 or more of the 9 symptoms. Q3: Which sleep complaint would the nurse expect in major depression? Show answer “I wake up about 4 am and cannot go back to sleep. I feel tired all the time.” Q4: Four findings to expect when assessing an adolescent with depression? Show answer I

NG-032 RENAL + FLUID ADHD-friendly visual edition Diuretics work by altering the reabsorption or excretion of electrolytes and alter fluid volume. Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors are sulfonamides without bacteriostatic action — they inhibit the CAH enzyme , which results in excretion of Na⁺ K⁺ HCO₃⁻ and H₂O . 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🚫 Sulfa allergy = don't give Allergy to sulfonamides → this drug should not be given. 🍌 Think HYPOkalemia May cause hypokalemia — monitor serum K⁺ & electrolytes. ☀️
STEP 1 · HOW & WHY One enzyme gets switched off — and four things wash out the door with the urine.

entries.h: 🫘 The map: where the block happens

entries.t: Diuretics work by altering the reabsorption or excretion of electrolytes and alter fluid volume . Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors: sulfonamides without bacteriostatic action — they inhibit the CAH enzyme , which results in excretion of Na⁺ K⁺ HCO₃⁻ and H₂O . 🧠 “Salt, Sparks, Soda & Sea” — the 4 things that wash out: Na⁺ salt · K⁺ sparks (the electrical one) · HCO₃⁻ soda (baking soda IS bicarb) · H₂O sea.

Hypertension 🫀 — and used with antihypertensives To reduce edema 🦵 Glaucoma 👁️ Seizures ⚡ Renal disease 🫘 🧠 “High Eyes, Wet Legs, Sparky Brain, Sick Kidney” — H ypertension · E dema · G laucoma (eyes) · S eizures · R enal disease. Say it as a little rhyme and the 5 reasons stick.

entries.h: 💊 The two drugs — generic, trade, safe dose, route
entries.t: Generic Trade Safe dose Route Acetazolamide Diamox 250–1000 mg/day in 1–4 divided doses PO Methazolamide Neptazane 50–100 mg 2–3 times daily PO 🧠 Both end in “-ZOLAMIDE” — and -zolamide = sulfa cousin . Hear that ending, ask about a sulfa allergy before you hand it over. 💊🚫 ⚠️
STEP 2 · ADVERSE & DANGER Who must never get it, what it does head-to-toe, and what it fights with.

Hypersensitivity Electrolyte imbalances Severe kidney or liver dysfunction Anuria 🚱 (no urine being made) Mannitol: active intracranial bleeding — except during craniotomy (source lists this line under Mannitol)

entries.h: ⭐ Simple Nursing Brain bits NCLEX TIP
entries.t: If a client has an allergy to sulfonamides this drug should not be given. ❌ Sulfa allergy on the chart → 🛑 hold the dose and notify the provider. 🧠 “No SULFA, no -zolamide.” Assess for allergy to sulfonamides before the first dose — this is the assessment question they love to ask.

🧠 NEURO Dizziness, headache, encephalopathy, lightheadedness, weakness, fatigue 👂 EENT Hearing loss, tinnitus 🫀 CV Orthostatic hypotension (stand up slowly!) 🚽 GU Electrolyte imbalances, glycosuria 🤢 GI Anorexia, nausea, vomiting 🧴 DERM Rash, photosensitivity (sunburns fast) 🍬 ENDO Hyperglycemia, hyperuricemia 💧 F & E Dehydration, hypocalcemia, hypochloremia, hypokalemia , hypomagnesemia, hyponatremia, metabolic alkalosis 🦴 MS Arthralgia, muscle cramps, myalgia 🧠 Two “HYPERs” hide in a sea of “HYPOs”: the sugar and
🧪 Source also lists metabolic alkalosis under Fluid & Electrolytes — worth double-checking against your pharm text before an exam.

Give it with… …and this happens Primidone ⚡ Decreased effectiveness of primidone Barbiturates & aspirin 💊 Decrease diuretic effectiveness Tricyclic antidepressants 🧠 Can lead to toxicity 🚨 🧠 “P-B-A-T” — P rimidone loses its punch · B arbiturates & A spirin blunt the diuretic · T CAs turn toxic . Two get weaker, one gets dangerous. 🧑‍🏫
STEP 3 · MANAGE & EDUCATE Nursing management — what you monitor, and what the client goes home knowing.

M Morning dosing ☀️ — Take early in the morning so the extra trips to the bathroom don't wreck the night O Output & intake 🚽 — Monitor intake and output ratios R Record weight daily ⚖️ — “Weigh yourself daily,” and monitor daily weight N Never stop the drugs abruptly 🛑 — unless you speak with the DR I Intake of fluids stays up 💧 — Do not reduce fluid intake N No alcohol, no OTCs 🚫🍷 — avoid alcohol and non-prescription drugs G GI upset? 🥛 — take the med with food or milk 🧠 “Take it in the MORNING” is both the rule a

🫀 Monitor BP and pulse frequently 🚫 Assess for allergy to sulfonamides NCLEX TIP ⚖️ Monitor intake and output ratios and daily weight 🧪 These drugs may cause hypokalemia — monitor serum potassium levels and electrolytes 🧠 “Cuff, Scale, Chart, K⁺” — blood pressure cuff · daily scale · I&O chart · serum K⁺ . Four checks, every shift. ✅

💪 Muscle cramps · weakness · general weakness 😵‍💫 Dizziness · restlessness 💩 Diarrhea · GI distress 🥤 Excessive thirst 💓 Rapid pulse · increased heart rate or pulse 🧠 Most of that list is one story: the potassium and the fluid left the building. Cramps + weakness + thirst + a racing pulse = call. 📞 ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🚫 Sulfa allergy = this drug should not be given 🧂 Salt · Sparks · Soda · Sea = Na⁺ · K⁺ · HCO₃⁻ · H₂O all excreted 🌅 M-O-R-N-I-N-G = the whole teaching plan in one word 🍌 Hypokalemia watch = monitor serum K⁺ + electrolytes

Q1: The chart says “allergy: sulfonamides.” Acetazolamide is due. What do you do? Show answer Do NOT give it — if a client has an allergy to sulfonamides this drug should not be given. Hold and notify the provider. Q2: Which electrolyte problem does this class famously cause, and what do you monitor? Show answer Hypokalemia — monitor serum potassium levels and electrolytes (plus I&O and daily weight). Q3: When should the client take it, and what should they NOT do with fluids? Show answer Take early in the morning

entries.h: Drug Abuse · NG-033 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🗝️ Words 👀 Watch 💊 Treat ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Pharmacology · Mental Health “Psychiatric Care”

NG-033 PHARMACOLOGY ADHD-friendly visual edition Alcohol & Drug Abuse on the NCLEX is three things: the 6 key definitions they test you on, the signs & symptoms that give away which substance is on board, and the nursing interventions & medications that follow. Learn the words, then read the body. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🦷 Meth = teeth · 👃 Coke = nose Meth = dental problems . Cocaine = nasal damage . 💤 Opioids = 4 S’s S mall pupils · S low breathing · S lurred speech · S leepy. 🌊 Withdrawal fli
STEP 1 · 6 KEY DEFINITIONS Half of these questions are vocabulary in a costume — name the word and the answer appears.
decreased response to a drug / alcohol 2
symptoms that develop after abruptly stopping drugs / alcohol 3
the body’s physical addiction to a drug / alcohol 4

the recurrence of drug / alcohol use after remission 🧠 “More · Must · Miss · Meet again.” Tolerance = you need more . Dependence = your body must have it. Withdrawal = your body screams when it misses it. Relapse = you meet again after remission.

5. Denial & projection 6. Enabling & codependence These are what the family says — the exam hands you a quote and asks you to name the behavior: “It is my fault that my spouse drinks so much” “I will take care of the children so that my spouse can drink” “I have lied to my spouse’s boss about why he missed work” 🧠 Enabling = “I’ll cover for you.” Lying to the boss, covering the kids, cleaning up the mess — every one of those sentences keeps the drinking possible .

HESI Patient with chronic pain… a regular dose of analgesic medication is ineffective in reducing the patient’s pain? ➡️ The patient is showing signs of tolerance ATI …client who abuses alcohol & illicit drugs… spouse tells the nurse: “have lied to his boss, his children, and his friends and I just don’t think I can do this anymore.” Which best describes this behavior? ➡️ Enabling Both answers are just definition #1 and definition #6 wearing a story. 🎭 🧠 Same dose, less effect = tolerance . Same mess, someone else
STEP 2 · SPOT THE SUBSTANCE Uppers push the vitals UP. Opioids pull everything DOWN. Withdrawal flips the opioid picture over.

entries.h: 🎚️ The dial: uppers push UP, opioids pull DOWN
entries.t: ⚡ Stimulants — cocaine & methamphetamines act on the brain , so heart rate and blood pressure climb toward HIGH . 💤 Opioids — respiratory rate, pupils and level of consciousness all slide toward LOW (RR norm 12 – 20) . The NORMAL band in the middle is what you are comparing every vital sign against. 🧠 “Uppers UP, opioids OUT.” Cocaine & meth drive HR & BP toward HIGH ; opioids drag breathing & consciousness toward LOW .

Cocaine & Meth. or Methamphetamines are both stimulants that act on the brain to increase the heart rate & blood pressure . Body clue 🔍 Substance Dental problems 🦷 Methamphetamines Nasal damage 👃 Cocaine HESI Q1: …significant dental problems . The nurse expects that this patient abuses which substance? ➡️ Methamphetamines NCLEX TIP HESI Q2: The nurse finds that a patient who is a drug addict has nasal damage . Which substance does the nurse suspect? ➡️ Cocaine NCLEX TIP 🧠 M eth wrecks the M olars · C ocaine wrecks

Decreased respiratory rate (norm: 12 – 20) Narrowed “constricted” pupils Sedation & coma Slurred incoherent speech KAPLAN A client uses heroin several times a day. Which signs and symptoms does the nurse expect? Select all that apply. ➡️ Constricted pupils · Depressed respirations · Drowsiness or sedation · Slurred incoherent speech 🧠 The 4 S’s of opioids on board: S mall pupils · S low breathing · S lurred speech · S leepy (sedation → coma).

entries.h: 🚨 The vital sign that wins the question
entries.t: HESI Which vital sign would be most concerning to the nurse? ➡️ Respirations 10 breaths/min Normal is 12 – 20 — a decreased respiratory rate is the opioid finding that outranks everything else on the flow sheet. 🧠 Opioids don’t kill by pain — they kill by pauses. Breathing is always the vital sign to grab first.

💤 Opioids ON board 🌊 Opioid WITHDRAWAL Pupils 👁️ Narrowed “constricted” Dilated pupils Sleep 😴 Sedation & coma Insomnia Skin & nose 💧 — Runny nose · Diaphoresis (sweating) 🧠 “RIDD” — the body trying to get rid of the drug: R unny nose · I nsomnia · D iaphoresis · D ilated pupils. 💊
STEP 3 · SAFETY FIRST, THEN MEDS Safety and sleep come before everything else — then the three medication names.

1 🛏️ Providing safety and sleep NCLEX TIP the first-line intervention in substance abuse disorders HESI 2 🕯️ Provide a calm atmosphere for the agitated client who fights against the nurse 3 🫀 Monitor respiratory and cardiac status stimulants drive HR & BP up — opioids drive respirations down KAPLAN The client is agitated and fights against the nurse… positive for cocaine … priority intervention? ➡️ Provide a calm atmosphere and monitor respiratory and cardiac status 🧠 “Safe · Sleep · Serene · Scan.” Safe ty and sle

Drug What it does Naltrexone Prevents relapse by reducing cravings Clonidine Lowers BP Methadone Low dose opioid (wean off addiction) HESI …teaching a patient with a new prescription for naltrexone ? ➡️ “It helps prevent relapse by reducing your drug cravings” 🧠 N altrexone = N o cravings · C lonidine = C alms the pressure down · M ethadone = a M easured dose to wean off.

entries.h: 🧾 Which meds treat opioid withdrawal ? ATI
entries.t: Treatment for opioid dependence… which medications are used for treatment of opiate withdrawal ? Select all that apply. ✅ Clonidine ✅ Methadone — low dose opioid Methadone is a low dose opioid used to wean off addiction ; Clonidine lowers BP . Naltrexone was not on that withdrawal list — its job is preventing relapse by reducing cravings . 🧠 C + M carry you through the Coming-off. N keeps you from going back.

entries.h: 🔁 Where each drug sits on the timeline
entries.t: 🌊 WITHDRAWAL — runny nose · sweats · insomnia · dilated pupils ▼ 💊 Clonidine (lowers BP) + Methadone (low dose opioid to wean off) ▼ 🛡️ Naltrexone — prevents relapse by reducing cravings 🧠 Relapse is definition #4 — the recurrence of drug/alcohol use after remission . Naltrexone is the drug aimed straight at it. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🚨 Respirations 10 /min = the most concerning vital sign (norm 12–20) ⚡ Stimulants ⬆ HR & BP Cocaine + Meth act on the brain 👁️ Pinpoint vs Dilated Pinpoint = on board · Dilated = withdrawal 💊 C + M vs N Clonidine + Methadone = withdrawal · Naltrexone = no cravings
