NG-034 RENAL + FLUID ADHD-friendly visual edition An imbalance is just an electrolyte's job going wrong. Potassium pumps, sodium swells, magnesium mellows, calcium contracts — so every sign you assess is that job turned up or turned down . 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🔀 K & Na follow the number High K = high signs. Low K = low & slow. 🔁 Mg & Ca run BACKWARDS Low Mg / low Ca = excited . High = sedated. 🚨 Peak · Twist · Shallow · Seize The four findings that kill. 🪞 Phosphate = calcium flipped Read th
STEP 1 · THE MASTER RULE Twelve imbalances, one question: is the body EXCITED or SEDATED ?

entries.h: ⚡😴 The excitability checkerboard — low value vs HIGH value
entries.t: ↔ swipe the chart sideways to read it all 🧠 “K and Na are honest — Mag and Calcium are liars.” High potassium really does make everything high; high magnesium makes everything low.

entries.h: 🗣️ The naming rule + the jobs TEST TIP
entries.t: HYPER = “HIGH” (over the range) · Hypo = “low” (below the range). P — Potassium K+ Pumps the heart · P riority ⭐ S — Sodium Na+ Swells the body with FLUID (BP · blood volume · pH) M — Magnesium Mg+ Mellows the muscles C — Calcium Ca Contracts the muscles — keeps the 3 Bs strong: 🦴 B one · 🩸 B lood (clotting) · 🫀 B eats (heart) 🧂 Chloride Cl− is related to sodium — same three jobs. ⚖️ Phosphate has an inverse relationship with Calcium : Ca HIGH = Phosphate Low · Ca Low = Phosphate HIGH. 🧠 The job predicts the sympto

entries.h: 💦 Engine 1 — the LOWs: fluid out, electrolytes out
entries.t: Fluid loss = electrolyte loss. “Where fluids flow, Electrolytes Goooo!” 🍑 The 4 Ds + A (low K+): D iarrhea · D iuretics · D iet · D KA · A ldosterone 😅 Low Na+: sweating · excess water intake (running in the extreme heat) TEST TIP · SIADH (excess ADH) · vomiting & diarrhea · diuretics & diuresis · diet low in salt · low aldosterone 🤮 Low Cl−: vomiting → alkalosis 🌾 Low Mg+: Crohn's disease · celiac disease 🧠 Memory Trick for AL (dosterone): A – A dds Sodium · L – L oses Potassium. So LOW aldosterone does the revers

entries.h: 🧱 Engine 2 — the HIGHs: can't clear them, or making too many
entries.t: 🫘 Renal failure TEST TIP (chronic kidney disease) → HYPERkalemia · HYPERmagnesemia · HYPERphosphatemia — and HYPOcalcemia (phosphate's mirror) 🧪 Low aldosterone → HYPERkalemia 🦴 Hyperparathyroidism — High PTH = High Calcium → HYPERcalcemia + HYPOphosphatemia. Also cancer , immobility , genetics 🏜️ Low ADH — DI: Diabetes Insipidus (Think D ry I nside) , rapid respirations, watery diarrhea, loss of thirst → HYPERnatremia 🍷 Alcoholism · malnourishment → magnesium trouble 🧠 “Kidneys quit, the highs sit.” K+, Mg+ and Ph
STEP 2 · READ THE BODY Four systems tell the whole story — heart, nerves & muscles, gut, lungs & brain. Find the system, then ask: excited or sedated?

entries.h: 🫀 The heart — the strip names the electrolyte
entries.t: ↔ swipe the chart sideways to read it all 🫀 What the heart shows Which imbalance Peaked T waves & ST elevation severe: V Fib & Cardiac Arrest · hypotension & bradycardia ⬆️ HYPERkalemia (over 5.0 ) Flat T waves, ST depression & U wave low & slow pump ⬇️ HYPOkalemia Torsades de Pointes & V Fib TOP TESTED ⬇️ HYPOmagnesemia (below 1.3 ) Heart block · hypotension · bradycardia ⬆️ HYPERmagnesemia (over 2.1 ) Weak B eats — cardiac dysrhythmias ⬇️ HYPOcalcemia (below 9.0 ) 🧠 Peak = potassium HIGH. Twist = magnesium LOW. O

entries.h: 💪 Nerves & muscles — the reflex tells you the direction
entries.t: ⬆️ HYPERkalemia: increased DTR · paralysis & paresthesia (tingling) · muscle weakness (general feeling of heaviness) ⬇️ HYPOkalemia: decreased DTR · muscle cramping & flaccid paralysis (paralyzed limbs) ⬇️ HYPOcalcemia: T – T rousseau's Sign (“twerking arm” when BP cuff on) + T etany · C – C hvostek's Sign (cheek smile when stroking face) ⬆️ HYPERcalcemia: severe muscle weakness & lethargy · bone pain 💧 Sodium: low = fatigue & muscle cramps · HIGH = increased muscle tone 🧠 T rousseau = T werking arm · C hvostek = C

💨 Fast: diarrhea + hyper active bowel sounds 🧊 Frozen: constipation + hypo active bowel sounds ⬆️ HYPERkalemia (HIGH pumps) ⬇️ HYPOmagnesemia ⬇️ HYPOcalcemia ⬇️ HYPOkalemia — paralytic ileus (paralyzed intestine) PRIORITY risk for SBO ⬆️ HYPERmagnesemia ⬆️ HYPERcalcemia 🎈 HIGH sodium — body big & bloated: edema · flushed “red & rosey” skin · increased muscle tone · swollen dry tongue 👅 · nausea & vomiting. HIGH chloride copies it. 🧠 Excited gut runs 💩 · sedated gut stops 🧊. A frozen gut in a low-K+ client is the on

entries.h: 🫁🧠 Lungs & brain — where it turns deadly
entries.t: 🚨 Shallow Respirations! MOST DEADLY → ⬇️ HYPOkalemia (the breathing muscles are muscles too) 😴 Depressed respirations → ⬆️ HYPERmagnesemia (too mellow) 🚨 Respiratory arrest → ⬇️ HYPOnatremia 🧠 Headache = cerebral edema · mental status changes · seizures & coma → ⬇️ HYPOnatremia 🌡️ Fever → ⬇️ HYPOchloremia (the only difference from low sodium) 🧠 Low salt drowns the brain 🌊 · low potassium drops the breath 🫁. Two different “low & slow,” two different killers.

entries.h: 👯 The look-alikes — twins that share a picture
entries.t: The twins Same picture The tell 🔍 ⬇️ HYPOkalemia ⬆️ HYPERmagnesemia Low & slow everywhere — depressed & shallow respirations, hypoactive bowel sounds, decreased DTR The strip: flat T + U wave = low K+ · heart block = high Mg+ ⬆️ HYPERkalemia ⬇️ HYPOmagnesemia Excited everywhere — increased DTR, diarrhea, hyperactive bowel sounds The strip: peaked T = high K+ · Torsades = low Mg+ ⬇️ HYPOcalcemia ⬆️ HYPERphosphatemia Trousseau's & Tetany · Chvostek's · weak B 's (bones, blood, beats) None — “Think Low Calcium signs.”
STEP 3 · WHAT KILLS FIRST Sort every finding by how fast it kills — that is exactly how the exam sorts them too.

entries.h: 📏 The whole board — where the number sits, what waits at each end
entries.t: ↔ swipe the chart sideways to read it all Note: the source card prints HYPOkalemia as “below 3.0”; the normal range it gives is 3.5 – 5.0 , so anything under 3.5 is already low.

entries.h: 🚨 The killers — in order of how fast they end the shift
entries.t: 1 🫁 Shallow Respirations — ⬇️ HYPOkalemia MOST DEADLY potassium runs muscles, and breathing is muscle work 2 🌀 Torsades de Pointes & V Fib — ⬇️ HYPOmagnesemia TOP TESTED 3 ⛰️ Peaked T waves → V Fib & Cardiac Arrest — ⬆️ HYPERkalemia K+ = P riority because K+ P umps the heart 4 🧠 Seizures & Coma · Respiratory Arrest — ⬇️ HYPOnatremia (cerebral edema) 5 🧱 Heart block · hypotension · bradycardia — ⬆️ HYPERmagnesemia 6 🚽 Paralytic ileus (paralyzed intestine) — ⬇️ HYPOkalemia · PRIORITY risk for SBO 🧠 “Peak · Twist · Sh

P = P otassium · P umps the heart · PRIORITY . Its window is tiny — 3.5 – 5.0 — and both ends land on the rhythm strip. That is why it leads every electrolyte list you will ever see. ⚖️ Second in line: magnesium , because low Mg+ is the one that produces Torsades de Pointes . 🧠 Heart first, breath second, brain third. If two electrolytes are abnormal, answer the one on the monitor.

entries.h: 🎯 The most-tested short list TEST TIP
entries.t: “ The MOST deadly conditions are typically the MOST tested conditions, since the main goal of nursing school is to create safe nurses. ” 🌀 Torsades de Pointes = LOW magnesium TOP TESTED 🫘 Renal failure / CKD TEST TIP → HYPOcalcemia and HYPERphosphatemia 💦 Excess water intake (running in the extreme heat) TEST TIP → HYPOnatremia 🗣️ HYPER = “HIGH” · Hypo = “low” — read the word before you read the number 🧠 “Kidneys quit, the highs sit.” K+ ⬆ · Mg+ ⬆ · Phosphate ⬆ — and calcium ⬇ , every time. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🔀 K & Na are honest The value and the body go the same way. 🔁 Mg & Ca are liars Low = excited · HIGH = sedated. 🚨 Peak · Twist · Shallow · Seize High K · low Mg · low K · low Na. 🧱 Kidneys quit, the highs sit K⬆ Mg⬆ Phos⬆ — and calcium ⬇.

Q1: The monitor shows a flat T wave with a U wave, and the client's breathing is shallow. Name the imbalance — and why it's the priority. Show answer HYPOkalemia. Shallow respirations are its MOST DEADLY sign — low potassium takes the breathing muscles with it. Q2: Two clients. One is hyperreflexic with diarrhea; the other is hyporeflexic with depressed respirations. Same electrolyte — which, and which direction each? Show answer Magnesium. Low Mg+ = mellow lost → excited (hyperreflexia, diarrhea, Torsades). High M

NG-035 GI ADHD-friendly visual edition Drugs that make a person vomit on purpose. The one to know is ipecac syrup — used to empty the stomach rapidly when someone has ingested poison or for drug overdose . The exam lives in the contraindications . 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 💧 15 mL + 1–2 glasses water Ipecac syrup dose after suspected poisoning. ☎️ Call poison control FIRST Before using ipecac syrup, call the hotline for advice. 🚫 Caustic · corrosive · petroleum Kerosene & friends — high risk of p
STEP 1 · THE DRUG & THE DOSE One drug, one job: bring the poison back up — fast, and only when it is safe to.

entries.h: 🤮 Ipecac syrup — the only name on the card
entries.t: Generic / Trade: n/a Use: Induction of vomiting post poison ingestion or drug overdose Indication: used to empty the stomach rapidly when someone has ingested poison or for drug overdose. Ipecac syrup is available both as a nonprescription product and as an FDA-approved prescription product. 🧠 “E-metic = Empty.” Emetics e mpty the stomach; anti-emetics stop the emptying. Same root, opposite jobs.
🧠 “15 · water · 20 · once.” Say it like a phone number. Four numbers, whole dose card.

entries.h: ☎️ Before the bottle is opened HIGH YIELD
entries.t: Before using ipecac syrup to treat poisoning, call a poison control hotline for advice. Only use under the supervision of a licensed healthcare provider. The phone call comes before the syrup — every single time. 🧠 “Dial before you spill.” Poison control 📞 → provider supervision 🩺 → then the 15 mL .

Retained exactly as written on the source card: “They neutralize or reduce the acidity of stomach and duodenal contents by combining with HCl and increasing the pH of the stomach acid. They may increase the sphincter tone of the lower esophagus. Examples of antacids include aluminum (Amphojel), magaldrate (Riopan), and magnesium (Milk of Magnesia).” ⚠️ Read this as an antacid fact, not an emetic fact. The paragraph names antacids and describes neutralizing acid — the opposite of inducing vomiting. Learn it with the
STEP 2 · WHEN NOT TO GIVE Every gate must be clear. One red gate = no ipecac, no exceptions.

entries.h: 🚦 The gate ladder — clear all six

entries.t: 💧 Dehydration ▼ 🧪 Electrolyte imbalance ▼ 📈 Tachycardia ▼ 🤢 Nausea, vomiting — the effect and the side effect 🧠 “Fluid out = D.E.T. bill.” D ehydration → E lectrolyte imbalance → T achycardia. Vomiting always sends a bill.
Activated charcoal decreases the effects of ipecac. The charcoal binds in the gut — the syrup loses its punch. 🧠 “Charcoal kills the encore.” Black powder in = no big performance out.

entries.h: 🛑 Do not use — the full contraindication list
entries.t: 🚫 Do not give if… Why / detail Patient is fully conscious (as written on the source card) Source wording retained — see the note below. Not under a licensed provider's supervision Only use under the supervision of a licensed healthcare provider . Turpentine, corrosives, alkalies (lye for soap), strong acids, petroleum distillates, kerosene, cleaning fluid, paint thinner, furniture polish Caustic or corrosive agents such as kerosene bring a high risk of pulmonary aspiration . Comatose, altered mental status, or at r
STEP 3 · NURSING MANAGEMENT What you must know — and who you must call — before anything goes down the hatch.

entries.h: 🩺 Before giving the emetic you must know…
entries.t: 1 🧪 The chemical ingested what exactly went in — this decides caustic vs not 2 ⏰ The time ingested how long it has already been in the stomach 3 👀 What symptoms occur before being brought in seizures or altered mental status here = stop 4 ☎️ The primary healthcare provider should also call the poison control center to obtain information on proper treatment HIGH YIELD 🧠 The 3 W's + 1 call: W hat chemical · W hen ingested · W hat symptoms — then the provider calls poison control . No W's, no ipecac.

Call the poison control hotline for advice before using ipecac syrup. Give only under the supervision of a licensed healthcare provider . Give 15 mL syrup, then 1–2 glasses of water . May repeat once in 20 minutes if vomiting does not occur. Watch for dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, tachycardia .

Never with caustics, corrosives, petroleum distillates — turpentine, lye, strong acids, kerosene, cleaning fluid, paint thinner, furniture polish. Never if comatose, altered mental status, or aspiration risk . Never during seizures — or if the substance can cause seizures or AMS. Never in pregnancy or lactation, or with Crohn's disease . Never when vomiting would worsen the condition — bradycardia, severe hypertension, hemorrhagic diathesis . ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🤮 Emetic = Empty Empty the stomach fast after poison or overdose. 😴 Not alert = no ipecac Comatose · AMS · aspiration risk · seizures. 🧠 3 W's before you give What chemical · When ingested · What symptoms. 💧 D.E.T. bill Dehydration · Electrolytes · Tachycardia.

Q1: What is the ipecac syrup dose, and what follows it? Show answer 15 mL ipecac syrup followed by 1–2 glasses of water — may be repeated ONCE in 20 minutes if vomiting does not occur. Q2: A child drank kerosene. Give ipecac? Show answer NO — caustic/corrosive agents such as kerosene bring a high risk of pulmonary aspiration. Same for turpentine, lye, strong acids, petroleum distillates, cleaning fluid, paint thinner, furniture polish. Q3: Three things you must know BEFORE giving the emetic? Show answer The chemica

Gastresophageal Reflux Disease NG-036 GI ADHD-friendly visual edition Fancy words for heartburn or acid reflux where stomach acids burn the esophagus , leading to pain, inflammation, & even CANCER called Barrett's esophagus — if the chronic acid reflux is not treated. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🚪 It's all about the LES Anything that weakens or damages the Lower Esophageal Sphincter → reflux. 🛏️ Worse pain = lying down Dyspepsia “heartBURN” that fires up when flat. ⏱️ 3 hours + HOB up No eating 3 h
STEP 1 · THE LOOSE DOOR One muscle explains the whole disease — when the door won't stay shut, acid climbs.

entries.h: 🚪 The LES is a door between the stomach & the esophagus
entries.t: EXAM TIP Anything that can weaken or damage the LES — the L ower E sophageal S phincter, the muscle that closes the opening between the stomach & esophagus. 🧠 “Loose lid = burning kid.” The LES is the lid on a jar of acid — tighten the lid (meds, small meals, gravity) and the burn stops. Everything in this whole topic is either loosening the lid or tightening it .

entries.h: 🔤 Say the word — it tells you the disease
entries.t: Gastro = Stomach 🫙 Esophageal = Esophagus 🚪 Reflux = flowing back ⬆️ Gastro · Esophageal · Reflux · Disease = stomach contents flowing back into the esophagus. 🧠 Dyspepsia = “heartBURN” — the burn isn't the heart at all, it's the esophagus sitting right behind it.

entries.h: ⚠️ Risk factors — what loosens the lid
entries.t: 😖 Stress ⚖️ Obese — BMI over 30 (BMI >30 ) 🫁 Hiatal hernia — at the diaphragm 🧠 “SOH” — S tress · O bese · H iatal hernia. Say it like a sigh — “sohhh…” — the sound of a lid going slack. 🔎
STEP 2 · SPOT IT A burn that gets worse when they lie flat — plus the scope that looks, and the emergency that follows it.
🧠 “Flat = fire, upright = alright.” If the question puts the client flat after a meal , the answer is heartburn getting worse.

🔥 Chronic acid reflux, not treated ▼ 😣 Pain & inflammation of the esophagus ▼ 🎗️ CANCER — Barrett's esophagus 🧠 Barrett's = the “burnt” esophagus. Barrett and burn-it rhyme — years of burn-it turns into cancer.

Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy = EGD — E sophago g astro d uodenoscopy. E = E sophagus 🚪 G = G astro (stomach) 🫙 D = D uodenal (duodenum) 🌀 🧠 EGD = “Every Gut Door.” The camera passes three doors in a row : E sophagus → G astro → D uodenum.

entries.h: 🚨 Complication of procedures: Peritonitis PRIORITY — Report to HCP!
entries.t: 🌡️ Fever — over 100.3°F 🤲 Rebound tenderness 🪵 “Rigid” or “board-like abdomen” 📈 Increasing pain, tenderness 😰 Restless 💓 Fast HR & RR (tachycardia / tachypnea) 🧠 “BOARD” — B oard-like rigid abdomen · O ver 100.3°F · A gitated & restless · R ebound tenderness + R ising pain · D ashing HR & RR. A board belly after a scope = call the provider. 🩺
STEP 3 · CALM THE ACID Three levers: drop the acid 💊, drop the trigger foods ❌, and use gravity ⬇️ — surgery only tightens what's left.

Class Drug from the source Name clue Antacids 🧴 — “ANT-acid” = against acid Histamine receptor blockers 🚫 Ranitidine -tidine PPIs: Proton pump inhibitors ⛽ Omeprazole -prazole 🧠 “TIDY the acid, PRAZOLE the pump.” Rani tidine = his t amine receptor blocker · Ome prazole = P roton P ump I nhibitor. Three tiers, one job: reduce acid.

entries.h: ❌ AVOID Eating — and the big three NOs
entries.t: ☕ NO Caffeine coffee 🚬 NO Cigarettes tobacco 🍺 NO Alcohol 🍟 Fried Foods fries, fried chicken 🥓 Fatty Foods go low fat 🍋 Citrus acidic 🥛 Dairy milk, cheese 🍫 Chocolate 🌿 Peppermint / Spearmint low fat diet = BEST Why this exact list? Every item on it can weaken or damage the LES — no lid, no protection. 🚪 🧠 Picture the worst midnight snack in nursing school : a chocolate-dipped peppermint patty, fried in fat , washed down with citrus juice, milk , coffee and booze — with a cigarette after. Every single item on that

1 🍽️ Eat small meals 2 🪑 Sit up after meals 3 ⏱️ AVOID eating before lying down — 3 hours after meals 4 🛏️ Elevate HOB at night 🧠 “SEE-3” — S it up after meals · E levate HOB · E at small meals · 3 hours before lying down. You have to SEE-3 to sleep.

entries.h: 🔪 Surgery: two ways to tighten the same sphincter
entries.t: ⚡ Stretta procedure 🎀 Fundoplication Delivers radiofrequency energy waves through electrodes Wrap the upper curve of the stomach — called the fundus — around the esophagus & sew it shut 🎯 Tighten the LES 🎯 Helping to tighten this esophageal sphincter 🧠 Stretta = Zap it tight ⚡ · Fundoplication = Fold the Fundus 🎀. Both answers to the same question: how do we tighten the LES? ⚡
SAY IT OUT LOUD 🚪 Weak LES = acid climbs = GERD 🛏️ Lying down = worst heartburn pain 🍟 Low fat diet = BEST · no caffeine, cigarettes, alcohol 🪵 Board-like belly = peritonitis → report to HCP

Q1: When is GERD pain the worst? Show answer Lying down — flat = fire. Sit up after meals and elevate the HOB at night. Q2: One muscle explains GERD — which one, and why? Show answer The LES (Lower Esophageal Sphincter) — the muscle that closes the opening between the stomach & esophagus. Anything that weakens or damages it causes reflux. Q3: How long after a meal before the client may lie down? Show answer 3 hours — plus small meals, sit up after eating, elevate HOB at night. Q4: After an EGD the client has a feve

NG-037 CARDIO ADHD-friendly visual edition Congenital Heart Defects II. Every defect sorts into one of three buckets by which way the blood moves : RIGHT to left = hypoxia (blue baby), LEFT to right = CHF (heavy fluid), or a valve that is simply stenosed (obstructive). Pick the direction and the whole picture follows. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🚨 Starts with T = TROUBLE TOF · TGA · Truncus · Tricuspid atresia = RIGHT to left = hypoxia. 💧 HF = Heavy Fluid ASD · VSD · PDA · AVSD = LEFT to right = CH
STEP 1 · RIGHT → LEFT · HYPOXIA Blood skips the lungs and goes out unoxygenated — the MOST deadly & MOST tested group.

entries.h: 🔀 One question sorts every defect: which way does the blood shunt?
entries.t: Orientation: the RIGHT heart is drawn on your left — like you're facing the patient. So forget left/right on the page and watch the colors : 🔵 blue crossing into red = right→left · 🔴 red crossing into blue = left→right. TOF · TGA · Truncus · Tricuspid atresia ASD · VSD · PDA · AVSD 🧠 “Right to left = the baby turns BLUE. Left to right = the lungs get WET.” One arrow decides the whole story.

entries.h: ⭐ Memory Trick — if it starts with T, then it's trouble NCLEX TIP
entries.t: T - Trouble! — the RIGHT to left blood-flow defects: T — T etralogy of Fallot (TOF) ⭐ T — T ransposition of the Great Vessels (TGA) ⭐ T — T runcus Arteriosus T — T ricuspid Atresia ⭐ TOF & TGA are the 2 MOST tested. The whole group is the MOST deadly — low oxygen is always a priority on the NCLEX. 🧠 Four T's, one problem: they all take blood AWAY from the lungs and push it from the right → LEFT side of the heart → blue babies .

1 · Pulmonary valve — pinched, so less blood reaches the lungs 2 · Right ventricle 3 · Ventricular septal defect — the hole blue blood crosses through 4 · Aorta — sits over the hole, so it carries blue blood out 🧠 “TROUBLE!” — TOF is the poster child of the T's. 4 defects, 1 heart: P ulmonary valve · R ight ventricle · V SD · A orta = “Poor Ricky's Very Anxious” heart.

The great vessels have traded places : the aorta leaves the RIGHT ventricle and the pulmonary artery leaves the LEFT ventricle. Blue blood is launched straight back OUT to the body. 🧠 TGA = “The Great swAp.” The vessels are on the wrong ventricles — plumbing crossed at birth.

One single trunk leaves the heart where two separate vessels belong — so lung blood and body blood come out of the same pipe . Another T that steals oxygen. 🧠 TRUNK = one tree, two branches. If there's only one trunk, nothing gets a clean, separate supply.

The tricuspid valve has no opening , so blood can't take the normal road from RA → RV. It detours across to the LEFT side instead — right to left again. 🧠 A-tresia = Absent opening. The door between RA and RV is bricked shut , so the blood takes the shortcut to the left.

entries.h: 🚨 Signs & symptoms — the blue baby NCLEX TIP
entries.t: 🫐 Cyanosis blue skin 🍼 Poor feeding & weight gain 🖐️ Clubbing fingers 💨 Dyspnea & Tachypnea 🩸 Polycythemia too many red blood cells 🧊 Blood clot risk! Hypoxia (low O₂) comes from RIGHT to left blood flow — there is decreased blood flow to the lungs , so it results in oxygen problems. 🧠 “Blue Babies Can't Do Push-ups” — B lue skin (cyanosis) · B ad feeding & weight gain · C lubbing · D yspnea/tachypnea · P olycythemia.

🫁 Hypoxia (low O₂) ▼ 😱 Body says “OHHH SNAP! I better make more oxygen carriers.” ▼ 🔴 A lot of red blood cells are created to compensate = polycythemia ▼ 🚗 Instead of perfusing the body, the extra RBCs cause a traffic jam — thick, viscous blood ▼ 🧠 Clogs the tiny vessels in the brain → deadly blood clot → delayed stroke! 🧠 More carriers ≠ more oxygen. The fix for a traffic jam isn't more cars — it's water to keep the lanes moving.

entries.h: 🧪 Report Hemoglobin OVER 22 g/dL NCLEX TIP
entries.t: Report Hemoglobin level OVER 22 g/dL — this is PRIORITY & must be reported to the health care provider! 🩸 Why so high? Polycythemia — the hypoxic body builds extra oxygen carriers, so the Hgb climbs and the blood turns thick & viscous . ⚠️ Blood clot risk! 🧠 “Over 22 = the blood is GLUE.” Glue clots — so you report it.

1 💧 Hydration — the priority intervention for the right→left (hypoxia) defects 2 🧪 Report Hemoglobin over 22 g/dL to the health care provider 🧠 Thick blood needs THIN fluid. Polycythemia = a traffic jam of red cells → hydrate to keep the tiny brain vessels open. 💧
STEP 2 · LEFT → RIGHT · CHF Blood loops back through the lungs instead of going out — the heart gets overloaded and fails.

entries.h: 💧 CHF (Congestive Heart Failure) — LEFT to right flow
entries.t: These four defects push blood from the LEFT side back to the RIGHT : ASD · VSD · PDA · AVSD . 🧠 Memory Trick — HF = Heart Failure. HF = Heavy Fluid. Left to right, the lungs and the pump get heavy with fluid. 🧠 Every left→right defect hides a “D” — AS D · VS D · P D A · AVS D = a D oor left open. Open door → blood D etours back to the lungs.
A hole in the septum between the two atria — red blood leaks back into the right side and takes another lap through the lungs.
A hole in the septum between the two ventricles — the strong left pump squeezes blood straight into the right pump. (This same hole is defect #3 of TOF.)

Patent = still open. A duct still connects the aorta to the pulmonary artery , so body-bound blood is siphoned back toward the lungs . 🧠 P = Patent = the Pipe never closed. A shortcut between the two big vessels.
One large central hole where the atrial and ventricular septa meet — an ASD and a VSD in the same spot. The biggest left→right leak of the four.

entries.h: 💦 Signs & symptoms — the heavy, wet baby NCLEX TIP
entries.t: Diaphoresis & Grunting — during feedings 🍼 Dyspnea 💨 Tachypnea & Tachycardia 📈 Poor weight gain ⚖️ 🧠 Feeding is a baby's workout. Sweating & grunting through a bottle is the infant version of getting winded on the stairs.

entries.h: 👀 What you'll SEE & count NCLEX TIP
entries.t: 1 🤍 Pale, cool extremities 2 👁️ Puffiness around the eyes (periorbital edema) 3 🧷 Reduction in number of wet diapers 🧠 P-P-D: Pale · Puffy · Dry diapers. And remember: Weight Gain = Water Gain ⚖️💧 — the scale is a fluid monitor, not a growth chart. 🚧
STEP 3 · OBSTRUCTIVE No shunt at all — the door out is just too narrow.

Stenosis = a narrowed valve. Two to know: Pulmonary Stenosis & Aortic Stenosis . Nothing crosses the septum here — the blood simply can't get out fast enough through a squeezed doorway. 🧠 “Stenosis = Squeezed.” 🫁 P ulmonary squeezes the road to the lungs · 🧍 A ortic squeezes the road to all the body.
The pulmonary valve is narrowed — the RIGHT ventricle has to force blood through a squeezed doorway on its way to the lungs .
The aortic valve is narrowed — the LEFT ventricle has to force blood through a squeezed doorway on its way out to the body .

🔵 RIGHT → LEFT 💧 LEFT → RIGHT 🚧 OBSTRUCTIVE Defects The 4 T's TOF · TGA · Truncus · Tricuspid atresia The 4 D's ASD · VSD · PDA · AVSD Stenosis Pulmonary · Aortic Big problem Hypoxia (low O₂) MOST deadly & MOST tested CHF HF = Heavy Fluid Narrowed valve squeezed exit Looks like Cyanosis · clubbing · polycythemia · clot risk Sweating & grunting with feeds · puffy eyes · dry diapers — Remember “If it starts with T — it's trouble” Weight Gain = Water Gain Stenosis = Squeezed ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🚨 T = Trouble TOF · TGA · Truncus · Tricuspid atresia = right→left = hypoxia. 💧 HF = Heavy Fluid ASD · VSD · PDA · AVSD = left→right = CHF. 🧪 Hgb > 22 = report Polycythemia → thick blood → delayed stroke. 💦 Hydrate the blue baby Priority intervention for right→left defects.

Q1: Name the 4 defects that start with T — and why are they trouble? Show answer Tetralogy of Fallot, Transposition of the Great Vessels, Truncus arteriosus, Tricuspid atresia — RIGHT to left blood flow takes blood away from the lungs → hypoxia (blue babies). MOST deadly & MOST tested; TOF & TGA top the list. Q2: A cyanotic infant's hemoglobin is 23.4 g/dL. What do you do, and why? Show answer Report it — OVER 22 g/dL is PRIORITY and must go to the health care provider. Polycythemia makes thick, viscous blood → tra

entries.h: Heart Failure · NG-038 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🧨 Cause 🔎 Clues 🩺 Care ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / CARDIO · Pathophysiology Course

NG-038 CARDIO ADHD-friendly visual edition The heart fails to maintain adequate cardiac output (oxygenated blood pumped OUT to the body) due to impaired pumping ability. Blood that can't go forward has to go somewhere — it backs up. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 💔 HF = Heavy Fluid Fails to pump forward → fluid backs up. Weight Gain = Water Gain. 💧 L = LUNG fluid LEFT-sided HF: crackles, pink frothy sputum, orthopnea. 🧍 R = ROCKS BODY RIGHT-sided HF: peripheral edema, JVD, big belly. 💊 Furosemide = “B
STEP 1 · WHY THE PUMP FAILS A weak pump makes two problems at once: too little blood forward, too much fluid backward.

entries.h: 💔 The patho in one straight line
entries.t: 🫀 Weak heart = weak pump — impaired pumping ability ▼ HF = Heart Failure — failure to pump blood forward → ↓ cardiac output to the body ▼ 🚧 Blood dams up behind the pump ▼ HF = Heavy Fluid — backs up in lungs / body ▼ ⚖️ Weight Gain = Water Gain 🧠 Two HFs, one heart. H eart F ailure = nothing goes forward . H eavy F luid = everything goes backward . Scale up 3 lb overnight? That's water, not cake.

entries.h: 🫀 “Weak heart = weak pump” — what damages the muscle
entries.t: After a heart attack (MI — myocardial infarction) dead muscle doesn't squeeze Ischemic heart disease — low oxygen to heart muscles ( CAD, ACS ) HTN (high BP) the pump wears out pushing against a wall of pressure

entries.h: 🫁 What pushes the RIGHT side to fail
entries.t: Pulmonary HTN Stiff “fibrotic” lungs Left-sided HF can cause Right HF HIGH YIELD The left side floods the lungs → the flooded lungs choke the right side → now both sides fail.

1 Hypertension (high BP) is the #1 risk factor 2 Atrial fibrillation & other dysrhythmias 3 Mitral valve regurgitation 4 Cardiomyopathy 🧠 “A salty HAM-C sandwich wrecks the pump.” H ypertension (#1) · A -fib & dysrhythmias · M itral regurgitation · C ardiomyopathy. 🔎
STEP 2 · WHICH SIDE? Ask one question: where did the fluid land? Lungs = left. Body = right.

entries.h: 💧 Left vs Right — follow the backup
entries.t: 🧠 “LEFT = Lungs. RIGHT = the Rest of you.” The left heart sits next to the lungs, so left failure floods the lungs . The right heart collects from the body, so right failure floods the body .

entries.h: ⚖️ Signs & symptoms — left vs right side by side
entries.t: 💧 LEFT-sided HF 🧍 RIGHT-sided HF Memory trick 🧠 L = LUNG fluid R = ROCKS BODY with fluid Fluid lands in 💧 Pulmonary Edema — the lungs The body & the periphery Breathing 🎧 Crackles in lungs — “Rales that don't clear with a cough” Pink Frothy “blood tinged” sputum Orthopnea — difficulty breathing when lying flat — Body & belly 🎈 — Peripheral Edema · JVD (big neck veins) Abdominal Growth : Ascites (fluid in abdomen), Hepatomegaly (big liver), Splenomegaly (big spleen) Scale ⚖️ — Weight Gain = Water Gain Causes 🧨 HTN (

entries.h: 🚨 KEY WORDS — the exam is warning you
entries.t: “New, sudden, worsening, rapid symptoms” New productive cough with pink frothy sputum + worsening crackles = fluid is filling the lungs right now . #1 Action is Furosemide = “Body Dried” KEY WORDS 💊 In the classic exam stem the correct first action was “Give bumetanide IV Push — YES” — not assess, not notify. 🧠 Loud words = loop diuretic. If the stem says new / sudden / worsening / rapid — you dry the body , you don't just watch it.

entries.h: 🫁 Pulmonary edema crisis — how it sounds
entries.t: 💧 Fluid backs into the lungs ▼ 🎧 Crackles — “Rales that don't clear with a cough” ▼ 🩸 Pink Frothy “blood tinged” sputum ▼ 🛏️ Orthopnea — can't breathe lying flat

🧪 Labs: BNP (brain type natriuretic peptides) B = Broken ventricles Over 900+ = SEVERE HEART FAILURE 📈 Echocardiogram → Ejection Fraction “blood pumped out of heart” 40% or LESS = BAD 40–55% 55–70% = NORMAL 55 to 70 is heaven · 40 or less is a mess. 🩺 Hemodynamic Monitoring “Swanz Ganz” (Pulmonary Artery catheter) normal 2 – 8 mmHg Over 8 = is NOT GREAT! 🧠 B = Broken ventricles (BNP) · “55 to 70 is heaven, 40 or less is a mess” (EF) · “Over 8 and you're late” (PA pressure). 🩺
STEP 3 · ACT IN ORDER Pulmonary edema crisis (lung fluid) — the order is the exam question.

H 🛏️ HOB 45 degree or higher Semi-Fowler's, High-Fowler's, orthopneic position O 💨 Oxygen P 💊 Push Furosemide + Morphine , Positive inotropes drain the fluid, calm the work of breathing, help the squeeze E 🧂 End sodium & fluids — Sodium Swells the body NO drinking fluids + STOP IV fluids 🧠 Give the drowning patient H.O.P.E. — H OB up · O xygen · P ush furosemide / morphine / positive inotropes · E nd sodium & fluids. And Furosemide = “Body Dried”

🧂 Sodium Swells the body — every gram of salt drags water back in. ❌ NO drinking fluids ❌ STOP IV fluids You are trying to dry this patient out — do not pour more in. ⚖️ Daily weights tell you if it's working: Weight Gain = Water Gain.

entries.h: 🍟 Food: which item should the HF patient avoid?
entries.t: ❌ Chips — NO SODIUM! ❌ Grilled chicken & fries — NO! ❌ Canned beans — NO! ✅ Fruits ✅ Veggies ✅ Bread 🧠 “Canned, Crunchy, or Fried → tell it goodbye.” Salt hides in the bag, the box and the can — not in the produce aisle.

✅ Walking ✅ Increase fiber ✅ Stool softeners ❌ Drink extra water — NO! Normally you'd push fluids for constipation — but this heart is already drowning, and fluids are restricted. 🧠 Move it and fiber it — don't flood it.

Q1. A client with chronic heart failure took cold medicine for her flu. She presents with a new productive cough with pink frothy sputum and worsening crackles . What action should the nurse take first ? Show answer ✅ Give bumetanide IV push — YES. (Not: assess lung sounds · notify the HCP · clock out for lunch.) “New, sudden, worsening, rapid symptoms” → dry the body out. Q2. Which food item should the heart failure patient avoid ? Select all that apply. Show answer ❌ Chips (NO SODIUM!) · ❌ Grilled chicken & fries

SAY IT OUT LOUD 📈 EF 55–70% = normal 40% or LESS = BAD (heart failure) 🧪 BNP over 900+ = SEVERE heart failure · B = Broken ventricles 🆘 H.O.P.E. HOB 45°+ · Oxygen · Push furosemide · End sodium & fluids 🧂 Sodium Swells the body No chips, no canned beans, no fries. Weight Gain = Water Gain.

Q1: Crackles that don't clear with a cough + pink frothy sputum — which side failed? Show answer LEFT — L = LUNG fluid. Q2: JVD, ascites, peripheral edema and 4 lb weight gain — which side? Show answer RIGHT — R = ROCKS BODY with fluid. Weight Gain = Water Gain. Q3: Ejection fraction is 32%. What does that mean? Show answer 40% or LESS = BAD → heart failure. Normal is 55–70%. Q4: What is the #1 risk factor for heart failure, and the #1 action in a fluid crisis? Show answer Risk factor: Hypertension (high BP). Actio

entries.h: Heart Failure · Pharmacology & Care · NG-039 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🚨 Crisis 💊 Meds 🧪 Numbers 🏠 Teach ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / CARDIO · Pharmacology

NG-039 CARDIO ADHD-friendly visual edition HF = HEART FAILURE (failure to PUMP forward) → HF = HEAVY FLUID in the lungs & body. So every drug and every rule on this page does one of two jobs: take fluid OFF, or make the pump's job easier. 🔁 Patho, signs & causes live on NG-038 — this page is the treatment, pharmacology, monitoring & patient teaching half (with a 10-second refresher below). 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 💧 Furosemide is #1 “Body Dried” — drain the fluid in a pulmonary edema crisis. 🧪 B
STEP 1 · RESCUE THE LUNGS Pulmonary edema is the emergency — the lungs are drowning while you read the chart.

entries.h: 🔁 10-second refresher — LEFT vs RIGHT (full detail on NG-038)
entries.t: ⬅️ L — LEFT-sided HF = LUNG fluid ➡️ R — RIGHT-sided HF = ROCKS the BODY with fluid Signs 🔎 “Pulmonary Edema” · Crackles “rales” that don't clear with cough (NOT rhonchii or wheeze) · Frothy pink “blood tinged” sputum · Orthopnea — dyspnea while lying flat Peripheral Edema (pitting) · Weight Gain = Water Gain · JVD (big neck veins) · Abdominal Growth: Ascites · Hepatomegaly (big liver) · Splenomegaly (big spleen) Causes 🧨 weak heart = weak pump — MI (heart attack) · Ischemic Heart Disease (CAD, ACS) Left sided HF c
“new · sudden · worsening · rapid” = Pulmonary Edema CRISIS (Lung Fluid!) NCLEX TIP Those four words in a stem are the whole question — stop reading for a diagnosis and start draining fluid.

Furosemide = “Body Dried” Drain the fluid. It is the first drug in the crisis, before anything else gets added. 🧠 “Wet lungs? Body Dried.” — if the stem says new/sudden/worsening + crackles or pink frothy sputum, the answer is the loop diuretic , not the inhaler.

entries.h: 🆘 Priority interventions — HOPE for pulmonary edema
entries.t: H HOB 45 degrees + 🛏️ semi-Fowler's, high-Fowler's, orthopneic position — gravity pulls fluid off the lungs O Oxygen 💨 P Push Furosemide + Morphine , Positive inotropes 💊 E End sodium & fluids 🧂 (Sodium Swells) NO drinking fluids + STOP IV fluids 🧠 HOPE — sit them up , give them air , push the fluid out, and stop pouring more in. In that order. 💊
STEP 2 · A B C D D D Six drug classes, four jobs: less fluid in, less pressure out, slower rate, stronger squeeze.

entries.h: 🗺️ The map: where each class hits the failing pump
entries.t: 🧠 “A B C — D D D” = A CE/ A RBs · B eta blockers · C alcium channel blockers · D iuretics · D ilators · D igoxin. The A B C lower the pressure, the D D D deal with the fluid and the squeeze.

A – ACTS on BP only (not HR) A–ACE “-pril” — Lisinopril “chill pril” · 1st choice A–ARBs “-sartan” — Losartan “relax man” · 2nd choice Watch the four A-C-E cautions: A–Avoid Pregnancy A–Angiedema (Airway Risk) 🚨 *only ACE C–Cough *only ACE E–Elevated K+ (normal 3.5–5.0) 🧠 A-A-C-E — A void pregnancy · A ngiedema · C ough · E levated K+. Cough is annoying → switch to the “-sartan” ; angiedema is an airway emergency .

Ateno LOL — “LOL = LOW” Blocks both BP & HR (AVOID Low HR & BP) ⚠️ Caution — HOLD IF: B–Bradycardia (< 60) & BP low (90/60) B–Breathing problems “wheezing” (Asthma, COPD) B–Bad for Heart Failure patients — only hold if the patient is in an acute exacerbation of CHF B–Blood sugar masking “hides S/S” (Diabetics) 🧠 4 B's to hold a “-lol”: Brady · Breathing · Bad-CHF-flare · Blood sugar. Say it as “LOL = LOW” — low HR, low BP, and a low blood sugar you can't feel coming.

Calms BP & HR (AVOID Low HR & BP) Nifedipine “-dipine” — “declined BP & HR” Amlodipine — “chill heart” What each letter actually drops: Class BP HR A — ACE / ARB ⬇️ down untouched B — Beta blocker ⬇️ down ⬇️ down C — CCB ⬇️ down ⬇️ down 🧠 “-dipine = dipped” — the numbers dip . Same hold-your-horses thinking as the beta blocker: check HR and BP before you give it .

Nitroglycerin · Isosorbide Nitroglycerin = “Nitro = Pillow for heart” ⛔ Caution: NO Viagra “-afil” — Sildenafil = DEATH! 🛑 Nitro drip — STOP for either of these: NCLEX TIP Side effect 😕 Adverse effect 🚨 HA (headache) — expected, treat it Low BP — SLOW position changes 🧠 “Nitro + -afil = no tomorrow.” 💀 And remember the split: headache = side effect, low BP = adverse effect.

💦 K+ WASTING 🛡️ K+ SPARING Drugs 💊 Furosemide & Hydrochlorothiazide Spironolactone — “Spares potassium” Caution ⚠️ Low K+ — potassium leaves with the water Potassium climbs — normal 3.5–5.0 Teach 🍌 EAT melons, banana & green leafy AVOID salt substitutes, melons & green leafy 🧠 “Waste it → eat it. Spare it → skip it.” Furosemide wastes K+ so you eat the bananas & greens; spironolactone spares K+ so you skip them (and the salt substitute — it's potassium in disguise).

entries.h: ⭐ D — Digoxin (Inotropic) — “Digs for a DEEP contraction” TEST TIP
entries.t: Increased contractility — the pump squeezes harder, so more blood actually leaves the heart. 🩺 Before you give it Apical Pulse × 1 full minute — stethoscope, not the wrist, not 15 seconds ☠️ Toxicity — over 2.0 Vision changes · N/V 🧪 Potassium 3.5 or less = higher risk for toxicity (and K+ wasting diuretics put it there) 🧠 “Dig hits the EYES and the BELLY.” 👀🤢 Vision changes + nausea/vomiting = check the level. And low K+ → high dig risk — the two D's talk to each other. 🧪
STEP 3 · DIAGNOSTICS & MONITORING Four numbers tell you how bad it is and whether your care is working.

🧠 “CVP over 8 = the tank is over-full.” Pair it with the rest of your diagnostics: 🧪 BNP (Broken Ventricles) · 📈 Echo (EF & LVH) · 💓 ECG (dysrhythmias — atrial fibrillation) · ⚖️ daily weights & I's and O's . 🏠
STEP 4 · DR. BEDS Nursing care & discharge teaching — six letters that cover the whole shift and the whole home.

D Diet: Low SCC 🍽️ — Sodium, Calories, Cholesterol Low Sodium & Fluid — 2 L + 2 g or LESS / day R Risk for Falls! ⚠️ — Change positions slowly! B Blood Pressure & BNP 🧪 — should NOT be increasing E Elevate HOB & Legs 🛏️ (with pillows) — high Fowler's D Daily Weights and I's and O's ⚖️ Over 3 lbs/day or 5 lbs in 7 days = Worsening! S Stairs 🪜 — No sex until able to climb 2 flights of stairs without dyspnea Stockings 🧦 (TED hose) — decreases blood pooling, remove daily 🧠 DR. BEDS writes your care plan: D iet · R isk

S Sodium 🧂 — Sodium Swells C Calories 🍟 C Cholesterol 🧈 Low Sodium & Fluid: 2 L fluid + 2 g sodium or LESS per day. NO OTC meds — Cough or Flu, Antacids or NSAIDS NO Canned or packaged foods — chips, sauces, meats, cheeses, wine 🧠 “Two & two, nothing from a can.” 2 L fluid, 2 g sodium — and if it came in a can, bag, jar or bottle , it's already salted for you.

🚫 NEVER massage calves (CHF patients) 🚫 NO Viagra “-afil” with nitrates — Sildenafil = DEATH! 🚫 In a crisis: NO drinking fluids + STOP IV fluids ✅ Change positions slowly — low BP + diuretics = fall risk ✅ Remove TED hose daily 🧠 “3 in a day, 5 in a week.” ⚖️ A gain of 3 lbs in a day or 5 lbs in 7 days means the fluid is winning — Weight Gain = Water Gain. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🆘 HOPE HOB 45°+ · Oxygen · Push furosemide + morphine + positive inotropes · End sodium & fluids 💊 A B C — D D D ACE/ARB · Beta blocker · CCB — Diuretics · Dilators · Digoxin 👀🤢 Dig over 2.0 Vision changes + N/V · apical pulse × 1 min · K+ ≤3.5 raises risk 🚫 Never massage calves …and never nitro with an “-afil.”

Q1: A chronic HF client has a new, sudden worsening cough with pink frothy sputum. What is the #1 action? Show answer Furosemide — “Body Dried.” Those key words = pulmonary edema CRISIS. Then the rest of HOPE: HOB 45°+, oxygen, morphine/positive inotropes, end sodium & fluids (stop IV fluids too). Q2: What do you check before giving digoxin, and what says “toxic”? Show answer Apical pulse × 1 full minute. Toxicity is a level over 2.0 — vision changes and N/V. Potassium 3.5 or less = higher risk for toxicity. Q3: A

NG-040 GI ADHD-friendly visual edition An inflammatory condition of the liver , commonly caused by a viral infection . Hepat = liver, -itis = inflammation. There are 5 types , but the most tested are B & C . 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🔤 Vowels from the bowels A & E = fecal-oral (food & water). 🩸 B · C · D = body fluids Blood, sex, IV drugs, tattoos, razors. 💛 ↑ Bilirubin = the yellow trio Jaundice · dark urine · clay-colored stools. 🛏️ Biopsy → RIGHT side Lay on the right side to prevent bleeding.
STEP 1 · HOW IT GETS IN Two doors into the liver: what you swallow, and what gets into your blood.

entries.h: 🚪 The two doors — transmission routes of A · B · C · D · E

entries.t: A – A nus to mouth BC – B lood C ultures & S ex E – E . Coli water (contaminated water) 🧠 New hook: “Vowels come from the bowels.” The vowels A and E are the two you eat and drink — everything else rides in on blood .
BCD = blood & body fluids 💉 IV drug use , 🖋️ tattoos, 📌 body piercings 🪒 Sharing razors ❤️ Unprotected sex 🧠 B·C·D = Blood · Coitus · Drugs. Anything that swaps fluids — needles, ink, blades, sex.

entries.h: 📊 All 5 types side by side HIGH YIELD
entries.t: Type Transmission · 🧠 hook 💊 Treatment A 🍽️ Fecal-oral (contaminated food) 🧠 “ A nus to mouth” Typically resolves on its own with bed rest B 🩸⭐ Blood & body fluids 🧠 “ B lood C ultures & Sex” Typically resolves on its own with bed rest C 🩸⭐ Blood & body fluids 🧠 “ B lood C ultures & Sex” Treated with antiviral medications D 🔗 Co-infection with Hep B 🧠 D = D uo — it needs B — E 💧 Fecal-oral (contaminated drinking water) 🧠 “ E . Coli water” — 🧠 “D is a leech.” Hep D can only show up as a co-infection with Hep B — no

entries.h: 🍷 Not every hepatitis is a virus
entries.t: Most cases are viral — but non-viral causes are: 🍷 Alcohol 🛡️ Autoimmune disease — where the body attacks itself

Modes of transmission for hepatitis C ? Select all that apply. 1. Blood · 2. Contaminated water · 3. Fecal oral · 4. Semen · 5. Vaginal secretions Show answer ✅ 1 Blood · 4 Semen · 5 Vaginal secretions — C = blood & body fluids. ❌ Water & fecal-oral belong to the vowels A and E . 🔎
STEP 2 · WHAT YOU SEE A sick liver leaks enzymes, backs up bilirubin, and stops making the proteins that hold you together.
🤕 Headache 🌡️ Fever 😴 Fatigue (malaise) 🤢 N/V — nausea & vomiting 🧠 “Hepatitis Feels like a Flu First.” Headache · Fever · Fatigue · N/V come before the yellow shows up.

Elevated bilirubin shows up on the outside: 💛 Jaundice 🧉 Dark colored urine 🧱 Clay color stools “Pale stools” 🌀 Itching “pruritus” 🧠 “Dark pee, pale poo, yellow you.” Bilirubin can't get out through the stool , so it comes out through the skin and urine .

entries.h: 🧪 Lab → sign: what each broken liver job looks like
entries.t: 🧠 “A · B · C — then A.” A LT/AST ⬆ · B ilirubin ⬆ · C lotting times PT/aPTT ⬆ · A lbumin ⬇ — three go up, albumin is the only one that drops. 🧠 Bruise = Blood won't clot. Swell = no Albumin. Two signs, two labs, done. 🎯 Saunders: The nurse is teaching the client with viral hepatitis … this disease is characterized by which specific assessment findings? SATA NCLEX TIP Show answer ✅ Jaundice · Clay-colored stools · Elevated bilirubin levels · Dark or tea-colored urine
After procedure → lay on the RIGHT SIDE to prevent bleeding. Your own body weight becomes the pressure dressing over the biopsied liver. 🧠 “Biopsy? Be RIGHT.” Right side down — lie on the liver.

entries.h: 🚨 Complications — where this can end up
entries.t: 💥 Acute liver failure 🪨 Cirrhosis 🎗️ Liver cancer 🫗 Gallbladder issues 🧠 “Failure, Scar, Cancer, Gall.” The liver's four bad endings — the reason the teaching in CARE actually matters. 🩺
STEP 3 · TREAT & TEACH Most of this exam content is patient teaching — rest, feed, protect, and stop poisoning the liver.

entries.h: ✅ Education — the 5 things you teach every hepatitis client
entries.t: 1 🍽️ Small frequent meals to prevent nausea Low protein (all liver disease) · Low fat foods (until nausea subsides) 2 😴 Frequent rest periods 3 ❤️ Protected sex! 4 🚫 AVOID drinking alcohol / Acetaminophen (Tylenol) NCLEX TIP 5 🪒 AVOID sharing shaving razors, toothbrushes 🧠 The 5 S's: S mall meals · S leep (rest) · S afe sex · S kip alcohol & Tylenol · S top sharing razors & toothbrushes.

entries.h: 💊 Treatments — it depends on the letter
entries.t: A & B — typically resolves on its own with bed rest 🛏️ C — treated with antiviral medications 💊 🧠 “A & B go to Bed — C gets the Cure.” C = the one with the antiviral.
NEVER drink alcohol 🍷 — a second hit on an already inflamed liver. NEVER take acetaminophen (Tylenol) 💊 NCLEX TIP NEVER share razors or toothbrushes 🪒🪥 — tiny amounts of blood carry B, C & D.

🍽️ Saunders — acute-phase diet The nurse should incorporate which dietary plan to ensure optimal nutrition … during the acute phase of hepatitis? SATA Show answer ✅ Consume multiple small meals throughout the day ✅ Allow the client to select foods that are most appealing ✅ Eliminate fatty foods from the meal trays until nausea subsides 🌀 The itch A client is admitted with hepatitis and complains of constant itching . What interventions would the nurse recommend? SATA 1. Apply a moisturizer · 2. Avoid the sun · 3. A

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🔤 A & E from the bowels Fecal-oral: food (A) & water (E). 🩸 B · C · D = blood & fluids D only comes as a co-infection with B. 🧪 ⬆ALT/AST ⬆Bili ⬆PT/aPTT ⬇Albumin Bruising = clotting; edema = albumin. 🖐️ The 5 S's Small meals · Sleep · Safe sex · Skip alcohol/Tylenol · Stop sharing.

Q1: Which hepatitis types come from contaminated food and water? Show answer A and E — fecal-oral. “Vowels from the bowels.” Q2: Hep D shows up on the lab report. What else must be there? Show answer Hepatitis B — D is a co-infection with Hep B. Q3: Which position after a liver biopsy, and why? Show answer Lay on the RIGHT side — to prevent bleeding. Q4: Two things the client must absolutely avoid? Show answer Alcohol and acetaminophen (Tylenol) — plus no sharing razors or toothbrushes. 📌

entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 💧 Where water moves 🕳️ How it is lost 🎈 Third spacing 🛡️ Compensation ⚡ Recall Nursing Field Notes / Renal & Fluid · Pathophysiology 💧 FLUID BALANCE SET I · NG-054 Compartments & controls II · NG-055 Losses & shifts III · NG-059 Measure & monitor

WHY the water leaves, and WHERE it goes when it does NG-055 RENAL + FLUID · PATHO ADHD-friendly visual edition What this page covers, and what it doesn't. NG-054 (Fluid Balance I) gave you the three compartments and the hormones that run them. This page is the mechanism page : the four pressures that decide which compartment water sits in, every route water leaves the body, the three big “drains” (DI, DKA, diuretics), third spacing, and how the body compensates while it happens. NG-059 (Fluid Balance III) is next:
STEP 1 · MECHANISM Water never moves “because”. It moves because something pushed it or something pulled it.

entries.h: 🗺️ The three rooms, drawn to scale
entries.t: Total body water is roughly 60% of adult body weight — less in older adults and in people with more body fat, more in infants. 🧠 “Two thirds in, one third out.” Two thirds of your water is INSIDE cells. Only about 1/12 of it is in the bloodstream — which is why small losses hit the BP hard.

entries.h: ⚖️ The tug-of-war — the four Starling forces
entries.t: At the arterial end, pressure wins and fluid filters out to feed the tissue. At the venous end, albumin wins and most of it is pulled back. Whatever is left over is collected by the lymphatics . Break any part of that and you get edema. 🧠 “Push out, pull back, mop up.” Hydrostatic pushes · oncotic pulls · lymph mops.

entries.h: ⭐ Hydrostatic vs oncotic in one line each
entries.t: Hydrostatic pressure The push of fluid against a wall. In a capillary it is basically the blood pressure. High hydrostatic pressure = fluid squeezed OUT into the tissue. Oncotic (colloid) pressure The pull of large proteins — mainly albumin — that cannot leave the vessel. It drags water back in behind it. Heart failure and venous obstruction raise hydrostatic pressure. Liver failure, nephrotic syndrome and malnutrition drop albumin. Both end in edema, for opposite reasons. 🧠 “Hydro = hose. Onco = sponge.” A hose sp

entries.h: 🚪 Four ways things cross a membrane
entries.t: PROCESS WHAT MOVES DRIVEN BY Osmosis WATER only Concentration of particles — water goes to the saltier side Diffusion Solutes High concentration → low concentration Filtration Water + solutes together Hydrostatic PRESSURE (higher → lower) Active transport Solutes, uphill ATP — e.g. the sodium–potassium pump Only osmosis moves water on its own. That is why sodium controls where water sits: water chases sodium. 🧠 “Where sodium goes, water follows.” Sodium is the ECF's water magnet.

entries.h: 🧫 Tonicity — what a solution DOES to a cell
entries.t: DRUG PAGE For which IV bag is which, see NG-213 and NG-120 · IV solutions . 🧠 “HypO = O for swOllen. HypER = shrivEled.” Hypotonic swells the cell; hypertonic shrivels it.

entries.h: 🅰️ Albumin is the whole story of oncotic pressure
entries.t: Typical adult albumin is 3.5–5.0 g/dL (varies by lab). It is made in the liver , and it is too big to slip out of a healthy capillary — so it stays in the plasma and holds water there like a magnet. Liver failure → cannot make it. Nephrotic syndrome → loses it into the urine. Severe burns → leaks it out of damaged capillaries. Malnutrition → no protein to build it from. All four end with the same picture: edema everywhere and an empty circulation at the same time. 🧠 “No albumin, no magnet, no water in the pipes.”

entries.h: 🧪 Osmolality — the one number for “thick or thin?”
entries.t: Serum osmolality measures how crowded the blood is with particles. Typical adult reference is about 275–295 mOsm/kg , and it varies by lab. HIGH osmolality Blood is concentrated → the patient is dry , or the sodium/glucose is high. LOW osmolality Blood is dilute → too much water, or the sodium is low. Sodium is the biggest single driver, which is why a quick mental estimate of osmolality is roughly double the sodium plus a small contribution from glucose and urea. 🧠 “Osmolality follows sodium.” Sodium up → osmolali
STEP 2 · CAUSE Four big buckets: out of the gut, out of the kidney, out of the skin, out of the vessels.

entries.h: 🗺️ The map of losses — sensible and insensible
entries.t: 🧠 “Sensible = you can measure it. Insensible = you can't.” Sweat you can see is sensible; the water vapor leaving your lungs and skin all day is not.

entries.h: ⭐ THE TOP 4 CAUSES — the four boxes to memorize
entries.t: 🤮 VOMITING & DIARRHEA the most common of all 🚽 THE 3 D's DI · DKA · Diuretics 🔥 SEVERE BURNS no skin = no barrier 🌡️ HOT & SWEATING fever, heat stroke, thyroid crisis Every one of these is isotonic loss to start with — whole fluid goes out, water and electrolytes together — so the sodium can look completely normal in a patient who is badly dry. 🧠 “Gut · kidney · skin · heat.” Four boxes. If you can list them you have the exam question.

entries.h: 🚽 THE 3 D's — where each one drains the tank
entries.t: 🧠 DI = “Dry Inside.” DKA = “D for Dry.” Diuretics end in “-ide” = the body is dr-ied.

Not diabetes mellitus. There is no sugar problem here at all — the problem is no ADH (or kidneys that cannot respond to it). The collecting duct cannot pull water back → liters of very dilute urine . Urine specific gravity is LOW (dilute); serum sodium and osmolality climb. The patient is desperately thirsty and cannot keep up. 🧠 “DI = Dilute In the toilet, Dry Inside.” Opposite of SIADH, which holds water in.

Blood glucose climbs so high that sugar spills into the filtrate. Sugar is an osmotic particle , so it drags water out with it into the urine. Classic story: polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia — peeing, drinking, eating. Kussmaul respirations (deep and fast) blow off acid — and add to the insensible water loss. Often triggered by an infection , which adds fever and more losses on top. The patient loses water, sodium and potassium at the same time, so the potassium picture is a trap: total body potassium is low even w

These are the losses we cause on purpose — and the ones we most often overshoot. Loop diuretics (e.g. furosemide) act on the loop of Henle. Strongest effect; potassium is wasted. Thiazides (e.g. hydrochlorothiazide) act on the distal tubule. Gentler; potassium also wasted. Potassium-sparing agents lose water without losing potassium — the risk flips to hyper kalemia. Never give a scheduled diuretic without checking the potassium, the blood pressure and yesterday's weight. DRUG PAGES Loop · Thiazide · K-sparing · Os

entries.h: 🤮 The gut losses — and what goes with the water
entries.t: ROUTE ALSO LOSES ACID–BASE RESULT Vomiting / NG suction Hydrogen ions (acid), chloride, potassium Metabolic ALKALOSIS Diarrhea Bicarbonate (base), potassium Metabolic ACIDOSIS Fistula / drains / ostomy Depends on the site; often large volumes Variable — measure it Both ends lose potassium. Any patient with prolonged vomiting or diarrhea is a hypokalemia risk. 🧠 “Vomit up = pH up. Diarrhea down = pH down.” The direction the fluid leaves matches the pH.

entries.h: 🔥 Burns — the fastest fluid loss in nursing
entries.t: Burnt skin is no longer a barrier, and the injured capillaries leak plasma and albumin , not just water. Losses are largest in the first 24–48 hours , then the fluid starts to shift back. Fluid resuscitation is calculated by formula against body weight and % body surface area burnt — follow the ordered protocol; do not estimate. Urine output is the main bedside measure of whether resuscitation is working. 🧠 “No skin, no lid.” Water evaporates straight off a burn, hour after hour.

entries.h: ➕ The losses the source sheets forget
entries.t: Hemorrhage — losing whole blood, so hemoglobin and hematocrit fall instead of rising. NPO / no access to water — a confused, sedated, aphasic or restrained patient cannot ask for a drink. Fever & tachypnoea — every degree of fever and every fast breath adds insensible loss. Bowel prep and contrast studies — a scheduled, predictable, preventable deficit. Wound drains, chest tubes, paracentesis — measured, but easy to leave off the total. Hyperventilation and mouth-breathing on high-flow oxygen dries mucous membranes

entries.h: 🧭 Not all dry is the same — the tonicity of the loss
entries.t: 🧠 Isotonic = the pipes empty, the cells are fine. Hypertonic = the cells shrink. Hypotonic = the cells swell. Only the last two put the BRAIN at risk. 🎈

entries.h: THIRD SPACING — THE FLUID YOU CAN'T FIND
entries.t: STEP 3 · THE TRAP The fluid is still in the body. It is just in a compartment that does nothing useful.
🧠 “Heavy but empty.” The scale goes UP while the blood pressure goes DOWN. That combination is the signature of third spacing.

The first space is intracellular . The second is intravascular . Anywhere else the fluid collects is a third space: Peritoneal cavity → ascites (liver failure, cancer, heart failure) Pleural space → pleural effusion Interstitium → generalized edema / anasarca Bowel lumen → ileus and obstruction (liters can sit in a paralyzed gut) Injured tissue → burns, crush injury, big surgical fields, pancreatitis 🧠 “First cell, second vessel, third nowhere useful.”

Third-spaced fluid does not circulate . So the patient can be: Fluid-overloaded on the outside — swollen, heavy, tight skin, a big belly. Fluid-depleted on the inside — tachycardic, hypotensive, oliguric, poorly perfused. Give a diuretic to “treat the swelling” and you pull the little volume they have left out of the pipes. Never assume visible swelling means the circulation is full. 🧠 “Swollen ≠ full.” Check the pulse, the BP and the urine output before you judge volume.

entries.h: ⏳ It happens in two phases — and the second one is the trap
entries.t: 1 LOSS phase. Fluid shifts out of the vessels into the third space. The patient looks dry inside: fast pulse, low BP, low urine output — while gaining weight. 2 MOBILIZATION phase. Days later the fluid shifts back into the circulation. Now the risk flips to fluid OVERLOAD — crackles, bounding pulses, rising BP, big diuresis. The IV fluids that were exactly right in phase 1 can drown the patient in phase 2. Watch daily weights and lung sounds across both phases. 🧠 “Out, then back.” Fluid that left the pipes always t

entries.h: 🧪 What the labs do in third spacing
entries.t: Hematocrit rises — plasma left the vessel but the red cells didn't, so the blood is concentrated. BUN rises out of proportion to creatinine — a classic pre-renal pattern. Albumin is often low — and low albumin is frequently what caused the shift in the first place. Sodium is unreliable — it depends on what was lost with the water. 🧠 “Concentrated blood, empty patient.” High Hct + low BP = the fluid is somewhere else.

Daily weight , same scale, same time, same clothing — the single best measure. Abdominal girth daily, marked at the same spot, if ascites is present. Strict I&O , including drains and ostomy output. Vital signs and urine output trends — these tell you about the circulation, not the swelling. Skin care — edematous skin tears and breaks down fast. NEXT PAGE Exactly how to do each of these, with the numbers: NG-059 · Fluid Balance III . 🧠 Weight is water. 1 kg = 1 L . The scale never lies about fluid. 🛡️
STEP 4 · COMPENSATION Compensation is why a dry patient can look fine — and why they crash without warning.

entries.h: 🛡️ Four compensations, in order of speed
entries.t: 🧠 “Beat · Hold · Salt · Sip.” Heart beats faster → ADH holds water → aldosterone holds salt → thirst says sip.

entries.h: ⭐ The order the vital signs change
entries.t: 1 Heart rate rises. Earliest and most sensitive. A resting pulse that climbed 20 beats overnight is a fluid problem until proven otherwise. ▼ 2 Urine output falls. The kidney holds on. Watch for output under 30 mL/hr . ▼ 3 Orthostatic changes appear. Dizzy on standing, BP drops when upright, pulse jumps. ▼ 4 Resting blood pressure falls. LAST. By the time the BP is low, a lot of volume is already gone. 🧠 “The pulse warns; the pressure confirms.” Waiting for a low BP is waiting too long.

Infants and small children — huge surface area for their size, high water turnover, small reserves. They dry out in hours, not days. Older adults — less total body water, blunted thirst, reduced ability to concentrate urine, often on diuretics. Anyone on a beta-blocker — the heart cannot speed up , so your earliest warning sign is missing. Confused, sedated, aphasic or restrained patients — cannot report thirst. Patients with kidney disease — cannot fine-tune water and sodium at all. 🧠 “Very young, very old, beta-b

entries.h: 📉 Why compensation makes the labs confusing
entries.t: Holding on to water and salt changes the numbers you are using to assess the patient : ADH holds water → urine gets small, dark, concentrated (specific gravity climbs). Aldosterone holds sodium → serum sodium can look normal despite a real deficit. Reduced kidney flow → BUN rises faster than creatinine , a pre-renal pattern. Plasma volume shrinks → hematocrit rises , which looks like a healthy blood count but is not. 🧠 “Dry blood reads HIGH.” Concentrated plasma exaggerates every value in it.

Once the compensations run out, perfusion collapses: Hypotension that no longer responds to position changes. Weak, thready, very fast pulse ; cool, pale, clammy, mottled skin. Urine output under 30 mL/hr , then none. Altered mental status — restlessness first, then confusion and lethargy. Rapid shallow breathing as the body tries to compensate for acidosis. Never treat new restlessness in a fluid-depleted patient as anxiety — treat it as poor cerebral perfusion until proven otherwise. GO DEEPER NG-050 · Shock 🧠 Re

Something makes fluid leave (gut · kidney · skin · vessel) ▼ Plasma volume falls — the pipes are underfilled ▼ Starling forces shift · fluid may third space instead of returning ▼ Compensation switches on: HR ↑, ADH, aldosterone, thirst ▼ Compensation fails → hypotension → hypovolemic shock 🧠 Read this cascade once a day for three days and you will never have to memorize a symptom list again — you will be able to predict them. ⚖️ Two forces Hydrostatic pushes out · albumin pulls in · lymph mops up. Break any one →

entries.h: Fluid Balance III · NG-059 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics ⚖️ The scale 📋 I&O 🚽 The urine 🧪 The labs 🖐️ Hands-on 🚨 When to act Nursing Field Notes / Renal & Fluid · Assessment & Monitoring 💧 FLUID BALANCE SET I · NG-054 Compartments & controls II · NG-055 Losses & shifts III · NG-059 Measure & monitor

Measure it, monitor it, and know the number that means CALL NG-059 RENAL + FLUID · ASSESSMENT ADHD-friendly visual edition What this page covers, and what it doesn't. NG-054 is the compartments and the hormones. NG-055 is why fluid is lost and where it shifts. This page is the toolkit — the seven measurements you actually take at the bedside, what each number means, and the exact threshold that turns a finding into a phone call. For the head-to-toe symptom picture of each disorder go to NG-207 · FVO vs FVD , NG-169
STEP 1 Daily weight beats every other measure, because it catches the fluid the I&O sheet never sees.

entries.h: ⭐ Weight IS water — the one conversion you need
entries.t: 🧠 “A liter is a kilo is 2.2 pounds.” Say it once. It converts every fluid question you will ever get.

entries.h: ✅ How to weigh so the number means something
entries.t: 1 Same scale every time — scales disagree with each other by more than the change you are looking for. 2 Same time of day , ideally early morning. 3 After voiding , before breakfast. 4 Same clothing — no shoes, no heavy blankets, no equipment on the bed scale. 5 Document immediately and compare with yesterday, not with admission. 🧠 “Same scale, same time, same clothes, empty bladder.” Four sames.

CHANGE MEANS ABOUT ACTION Under 1 lb in a day <0.5 L Normal variation — document 2–3 lb in ONE day ≈1–1.5 L Report it 5 lb in ONE week ≈2.3 L Report it 2 lb/day for 3 days ≈3 L accumulating Escalate — this is a trend A gain is retained fluid until proven otherwise. A loss is lost fluid until proven otherwise. Real tissue does not change that fast. 🧠 “Two-to-three in a day, five in a week.” Those two numbers get you the exam point.

entries.h: ⚠️ When the scale and the I&O disagree
entries.t: They disagree constantly, and the scale usually wins . Reasons: Insensible losses are never charted — lungs, skin, sweat, fever. Missed intake — the ice chips, the sips with medications, the family's soda. Missed output — the incontinence pad, the emesis in the sink, the soaked dressing. Third spacing — the fluid stays in the body, so the weight goes up even with a negative balance. 🧠 “The sheet can lie. The scale can't.” Fluid has mass, whichever compartment it is hiding in.

entries.h: 🧮 Worked example — do this once and it sticks
entries.t: Yesterday 70.0 kg . This morning 72.2 kg . Intake and output charted as roughly even. Blood pressure has drifted from 128/76 to 104/62 , pulse from 78 to 106 , urine output 22 mL/hr . Gain = 2.2 kg ≈ 2.2 L ≈ 4.8 lb. Definitely reportable. But the BP is down and the pulse is up — the circulation is under filled. Weight up + circulation down = third spacing , not simple overload. Never reach for a diuretic on the weight gain alone — you would pull volume out of an already-empty vascular space. Report the full picture
STEP 2 The I&O sheet is only as good as the least careful person who touched it this shift.
🧠 “Liquid at room temperature counts.” Jelly, ice cream and popsicles are fluids. Ice chips count as roughly half their volume.

POSITIVE balance In > Out. Fluid is accumulating. Expect the weight to rise. NEGATIVE balance Out > In. Fluid is being lost. Expect the weight to fall. Then check whether the weight actually did what you predicted . If it did not, something is missing from the sheet — or fluid is third spacing. 🧠 Predict, then check. The mismatch is the finding, not the error.

entries.h: ⚠️ The five most commonly missed entries
entries.t: IV medication volumes — every piggyback bag and every flush. Tube-feed flushes — small, frequent, and they add up to hundreds of milliliters a day. Incontinence — weigh the pad if your unit does that (1 g ≈ 1 mL). Bowel prep and diarrhea — huge volumes, rarely measured. Irrigation — only the amount that does not return counts as intake. 🧠 “Flushes are fluids.” The one nobody charts.

Total at the end of every shift , not at the end of the day — a running total catches problems earlier. Report the 24-hour balance alongside the weight change, so they can be compared. A patient on strict I&O needs every container measured, not eyeballed. Use a graduate. Communicate the running total at handover — the next nurse cannot recreate it. 🧠 “Total at the end of every shift.” Eight hours of drift is easier to fix than 24.

entries.h: 🧾 A normal adult day, for comparison
entries.t: IN ≈ mL OUT ≈ mL Drinks 1200–1500 Urine 1500 Water in food 700–1000 Skin (insensible + sweat) 500–600 Metabolic water 200–300 Lungs (vapor) 300–400 Faeces 100–200 TOTAL ≈2500 TOTAL ≈2500 Figures are typical adult approximations and vary with body size, diet, activity and climate. 🧠 “2500 in, 2500 out.” Roughly half the output is urine you can actually measure. 🚽

entries.h: WHAT THE URINE IS TELLING YOU
entries.t: STEP 3 Volume answers “are the kidneys being perfused?”. Concentration answers “is the body holding on?”.

entries.h: 🚽 Output — the numbers that trigger a call
entries.t: 🧠 “Thirty an hour, half a mil a kilo.” Two ways of saying the same threshold — and the per-kilogram one is the safer answer on an exam.
🧠 “Low when Liquidy, High when Dry.” Dilute urine = too much water. Concentrated urine = not enough.

The weight of the urine compared with the weight of plain water. Water is 1.000 ; typical urine runs 1.005–1.030 . Above 1.030 — very concentrated. The kidney is conserving water hard. Think deficit. Below 1.005 — very dilute. Too much water on board, or the kidney has lost the ability to concentrate . Stuck around 1.010 regardless of hydration — “fixed” specific gravity, a red flag for kidney disease. GO DEEPER NG-269 · Urinalysis 🧠 Water is 1.000, so anything above it is “stuff dissolved in it”.

entries.h: ⚠️ When specific gravity lies to you
entries.t: FALSELY HIGH FALSELY LOW / UNRELIABLE Glucose in the urine Chronic kidney disease (cannot concentrate) Protein in the urine Diabetes insipidus IV contrast dye Recent diuretic dose Some IV colloid solutions Very high fluid intake just before the sample Never diagnose fluid status from a single specific gravity. 🧠 Anything dissolved makes it heavier. Sugar and protein fake dehydration.

Low urine output has three possible causes and you check them in this order: 1 Mechanical. Is the catheter kinked, clamped, obstructed or lying under the patient? Is the patient in retention? Bladder scan. 2 Pre-renal. Is there enough volume and pressure reaching the kidney? Check BP, pulse, weight, recent losses. 3 Renal / post-renal. Is the kidney itself injured, or is there obstruction above the bladder? Check creatinine, BUN, nephrotoxic drugs. GO DEEPER NG-047 · Acute vs chronic renal failure 🧠 “Tube, tank, ti

entries.h: 🎨 Color is a screening tool, not a diagnosis
entries.t: Very pale / clear — dilute. Overload, diuresis, or DI. Dark amber — concentrated. Deficit, unless something is coloring it. Cloudy with odor — think infection, not fluid status. Tea/cola colored — think blood, myoglobin or bile. Escalate. B vitamins turn urine bright yellow; some drugs and beetroot turn it orange or red. Ask before you panic. 🧠 “Color screens, gravity measures, volume decides.” 🧪

entries.h: THE LAB PANEL — DILUTE OR CONCENTRATED?
entries.t: STEP 4 One rule runs this whole section: the values move with the WATER, not with the substance.
🧠 “LOW when Liquidy · HIGH when Dry.” Say it out loud once for each row of the table.

entries.h: 🧪 BUN and the BUN : creatinine ratio
entries.t: BUN (typical 10–20 mg/dL ) rises when the kidney is under-perfused, because slow-moving filtrate lets more urea be reabsorbed. Creatinine (typical 0.6–1.2 mg/dL ) is much steadier. BUN up, creatinine normal , ratio above roughly 20:1 → pre-renal : dehydration, low output, GI bleed, high protein load. Both up together , ratio near 10:1 → intrinsic kidney damage. Ranges vary by laboratory — always read the range printed on the report. 🧠 “BUN runs ahead when the tank is low.” A lonely high BUN is usually a fluid probl

entries.h: 🩸 Hematocrit — the exception you will be tested on
entries.t: Hematocrit is the percentage of blood that is red cells . It rises when the plasma shrinks even though no new red cells were made. Dehydration Plasma down, cells the same → Hct HIGH (hemoconcentration). Overload Plasma up, cells the same → Hct LOW (hemodilution). But in HEMORRHAGE the patient loses plasma AND cells — so Hct and hemoglobin FALL. That is why a normal Hct early in a bleed is falsely reassuring. 🧠 “Dry blood looks rich. Bleeding blood looks poor.”

entries.h: 🧂 Sodium — the trickiest one on the panel
entries.t: Sodium (typical 135–145 mEq/L ) is a concentration , not an amount. It tells you the ratio of sodium to water, so it can be abnormal from either side. Low sodium can mean too little sodium or too much water. High sodium can mean too much sodium or too little water — and water loss is far more common. Normal sodium does not rule out a large isotonic fluid deficit. Both directions put the brain at risk, because brain cells swell or shrink with the shift. LINK NG-088 · Potassium, sodium & chloride 🧠 “Sodium is a ratio

A single lab value is a photograph. Fluid status is a film. Pull up the last three of every value and look at the direction. Line the labs up against the weights and the I&O for the same days. If Hct, BUN, osmolality and specific gravity are all rising together , the patient is drying out — no single value needed to be dramatic. 🧠 Three numbers moving the same way is a trend. Trends are what you hand over and escalate.

Basic metabolic panel — sodium, potassium, chloride, bicarbonate, BUN, creatinine, glucose. Serum osmolality — the direct measure of concentration. Urine specific gravity and urine osmolality — what the kidney is doing about it. Hematocrit and hemoglobin — concentration, plus a bleeding check. Albumin — the oncotic pull; low albumin explains a lot of edema. LINK NG-227 · Vitamins & electrolytes · NG-134 · Mag, calcium, phosphate 🧠 Magnesium 1.3–2.1 mEq/L · calcium 9.0–10.5 mg/dL · albumin 3.5–5.0 g/dL . Ranges vary
STEP 5 Everything in this section is free, takes under a minute, and gets tested in clinical.
🧠 “Full veins, full tank. Flat veins, flat tank.” Just remember to position the bed the same way every single time, or you are comparing two different tests.
🧠 “Twenty over ten.” Systolic down 20, or diastolic down 10 — that is a positive test.
🧠 “Sternum, not the hand.” The back of an older adult's hand always tents.

entries.h: 🫁 Lung sounds — the measurement that catches overload first
entries.t: Listen to the bases first and posteriorly — fluid settles with gravity. New fine crackles that do not clear with coughing are the earliest lung sign of overload. Add respiratory rate, work of breathing and oxygen saturation to the picture. Pink frothy sputum with severe breathlessness is pulmonary edema — an emergency. Never leave a patient flat when they are developing crackles — sit them up. 🧠 “Crackles at the bases = the tide is coming in.”

entries.h: 🧠 Mental status — an early sign in BOTH directions
entries.t: OVERLOAD Sodium falls as blood is diluted → brain cells swell → headache, confusion, seizures. DEFICIT Poor cerebral perfusion, sodium rises → restlessness, then confusion and lethargy. Compare with the previous shift , not with your idea of normal. Family saying “that's not like her” is assessment data. 🧠 Restless comes before unresponsive. New agitation is a perfusion problem until proven otherwise.

Press firmly over a bony prominence for several seconds; the depth and duration of the pit is the grade, commonly recorded as 1+ to 4+ . Dependent edema collects wherever gravity takes it — ankles when up, sacrum when in bed. Check the sacrum on every bedbound patient. Periorbital puffiness is often the earliest visible site, especially in the morning. Edema is a late sign — several liters are usually retained before pitting appears. FULL GRADING SCALE NG-169 · Fluid overload has the 0+ to 4+ chart in detail. 🧠 “Gr
STEP 6 Measuring is only useful if you know which number picks up the phone.

entries.h: 🎛️ The dashboard — six tiles, every shift
entries.t: 🧠 Photograph this one. It is the whole page compressed into six boxes.

entries.h: 🚨 Escalate NOW for any of these
entries.t: Urine output under 30 mL/hr for two consecutive hours, with a patent catheter. New crackles, new breathlessness, or a falling oxygen saturation. Systolic BP falling with a rising pulse — compensation is running out. New confusion, restlessness or a drop in level of consciousness. Weight change of 2–3 lb in a day or 5 lb in a week . Sodium outside 135–145 mEq/L with any neurological change. 🧠 Breathing · pressure · pee · brain. Four things that make you call.

entries.h: 📞 How to hand it over — SBAR in fluid language
entries.t: S Situation. “Mrs L in 412 has gained 2.2 kg overnight and her urine output is 22 mL/hr.” B Background. “Day 3 post-op, on IV fluids at 125 mL/hr, history of heart failure.” A Assessment. “BP down from 128/76 to 104/62, pulse up from 78 to 106, new crackles at both bases.” R Recommendation. “I think she is third spacing. Can you review the fluid order and would you like labs?” 🧠 Give the trend, not the snapshot. “Up from” and “down from” are the words that get action.

entries.h: ⭐ The one-line summary of all three pages
entries.t: NG-054 — WHERE the water lives and what controls it ▼ NG-055 — WHY it leaves and where it shifts to ▼ NG-059 — HOW you measure it and when you call Then apply it to a patient using NG-207 · FVO vs FVD . 🧠 Three pages, three verbs: WHERE · WHY · HOW.

Q. A patient gains 2 kg overnight. About how much fluid is that? ▸ About 2 liters . 1 kg = 1 L = 2.2 lb . Q. Minimum acceptable adult urine output? ▸ 30 mL/hr , or 0.5 mL/kg/hr . Q. Urine specific gravity is 1.032. Fluid overload or deficit? ▸ Deficit — the urine is concentrated, so the body is conserving water. (Rule out glucose, protein and contrast first.) Q. Which lab moves the OPPOSITE way to the others in hemorrhage? ▸ Hematocrit and hemoglobin FALL , because red cells are lost along with the plasma. Q. BP dr

The complications — and every single one starts with back-pressure NG-109 GI · HEPATIC ADHD-friendly visual edition What this page covers, and what it doesn't. NG-029 (Cirrhosis I) covered the pathophysiology, the causes and the liver's four jobs. This page is the complications page : portal hypertension, ascites, esophageal varices and the bleeding emergency, hepatic encephalopathy, coagulopathy, jaundice and SBP — what you SEE and what the LABS show.
