entries.h: PORTAL HYPERTENSION — THE ROOT OF EVERYTHING
entries.t: STEP 1 · CAUSE One blocked organ, four escape routes, and every escape route is a complication.

entries.h: 🪨 What the scar actually does to the blood flow
entries.t: Cirrhosis replaces soft, spongy liver tissue with fibrous scar and regenerative nodules . Scar tissue cannot be squeezed through, so the pressure in the portal vein climbs. 🧠 “The liver turns to rock.” Nothing flows through rock — so the river floods backwards.

entries.h: 🗺️ Where the blocked blood escapes to
entries.t: 🧠 “Water finds a way.” Esophagus, umbilicus, rectum, spleen — the four escape routes, the four classic signs.

The portal vein normally runs at a low pressure. In cirrhosis the pressure rises; a portal pressure gradient above roughly 10 mmHg is the level at which the classic complications start to appear, and higher pressures carry a higher bleeding risk. Blood that cannot get through the liver is forced into small collateral veins that were never built to carry that volume — so they stretch, thin out, and eventually tear. 🧠 “Dam the river, flood the side streets.” Collaterals are the flooded side streets.

entries.h: 👀 What you can see at the bedside
entries.t: Distended, tense abdomen with a fluid wave and shifting dullness (ascites). Caput medusae — dilated veins radiating from the navel. Splenomegaly — you may see it on imaging and the platelet count reflects it. Hemorrhoids that are new or worsening. Weight gain and increasing abdominal girth without eating more. 🧠 Measure girth at the SAME marked spot every day, or the number means nothing.

Blood dams back into the spleen and it enlarges. An enlarged spleen sequesters and destroys platelets , so the platelet count falls. Now stack that on top of a liver that cannot make clotting factors: fewer platelets AND fewer clotting factors at the same time. That is why a cirrhotic patient bruises from a blood-pressure cuff. LINK NG-153 · WBC & coagulation panel 🧠 “Big spleen eats platelets.” Two bleeding problems for the price of one.

entries.h: ⚠️ Splenomegaly also means a fragile spleen
entries.t: An enlarged spleen sits below the left ribs and is easier to injure. Avoid vigorous abdominal palpation over the left upper quadrant. Teach the patient to avoid contact sports and heavy lifting. Sudden severe left upper quadrant pain with hypotension is an emergency. 🧠 “Handle the left upper quadrant gently.” 🎈

entries.h: ASCITES — THE BELLY FULL OF FLUID
entries.t: STEP 2 · CLUES Three mechanisms at once. Patients say they look pregnant; the exam calls it third spacing.

entries.h: 💧 Why the fluid collects — and where
entries.t: 🧠 A-A: Ascites = Abdominal fluid. And remember the pair that follows it: no NG tube, no straining.

📏 Abdominal girth daily, tape at a spot marked on the skin, measured at the same point in the breathing cycle. ⚖️ Daily weight — same scale, same time, after voiding. 1 kg = 1 L . 🥁 Percussion — dull over fluid, tympanic over the floating bowel; dullness shifts when the patient rolls. 🌊 Fluid wave — a tap on one flank transmits a wave to the other hand. LINK NG-059 · Fluid balance III has the full measuring toolkit. 🧠 Girth and weight, every single day. Trends beat single measurements.

entries.h: 🫁 Why a big belly becomes a breathing problem
entries.t: Liters of fluid push the diaphragm up and stop the lungs expanding. Shortness of breath, especially lying flat; the patient will not want to lie down. Rapid, shallow breathing; falling oxygen saturation. Position: semi-Fowler's or high Fowler's to let the diaphragm drop. Never lie a patient with tense ascites flat for comfort — it makes the breathing worse. 🧠 “Big belly, sit them up.” Positioning is a real intervention here, not a comfort measure.

Ascitic fluid is a warm pool of protein sitting in the abdomen. It can become infected without any obvious source — no perforation, no surgery, nothing. Fever , sometimes low-grade or absent in a very sick liver patient. Abdominal pain or tenderness , rebound tenderness. New or worsening confusion — often the first thing the nurse notices. Worsening ascites that suddenly stops responding to treatment. Diagnosis is by sampling the ascitic fluid; treatment is antibiotics per culture and protocol. 🧠 New confusion + fe

entries.h: ✅ Nursing priorities for the ascitic abdomen
entries.t: Position semi- to high Fowler's for breathing. Daily weight, girth and strict I&O. Low-sodium diet , and a fluid restriction if one is ordered. Skin care — stretched, edematous abdominal skin breaks down and weeps. Support the abdomen when the patient moves; teach them to splint when coughing. Monitor for SBP — temperature, abdominal tenderness, mental status. NEXT PAGE Paracentesis, albumin and diuretics are on NG-148 · Cirrhosis III . 🧠 Sit up · weigh · measure · watch the skin · watch the temperature. 🚨
STEP 3 · THE KILLER This is the complication that kills people quickly, and the one every exam asks about.

entries.h: 💣 What varices are, and why they rupture
entries.t: 🧠 “A ticking time bomb of blood.” Thin-walled veins with the pressure of a whole blocked circulation behind them, sitting on top of the airway.

entries.h: 🚨 FIRST ACTION when the patient vomits blood
entries.t: A AIRWAY. Turn the patient side-lying so blood drains out of the mouth instead of into the lungs. Suction at the bedside, oxygen on. ▼ B BREATHING. Oxygen, monitor saturation, watch for aspiration. ▼ C CIRCULATION. Vital signs, large-bore IV access, blood work and type and cross, prepare for volume and blood products. ▼ D Call for help and prepare for urgent endoscopy. Keep the patient NPO. Some questions ask “what is the FIRST action?” and the safest answer is the one that protects the airway ; others ask “what wo

A new nasogastric tube in a patient with known or suspected varices — a tube passed blindly down the esophagus can tear a varix open. Question the order and speak to the provider. Anything that causes straining — enemas that require bearing down, hard suppositories, and any instruction to push. Also question aspirin and NSAIDs unless specifically ordered, and any invasive oral or esophageal device. 🧠 “No tube down the pipe.” If the exam gives you an NG tube order in a varices patient, that is the answer.

Bearing down (the Valsalva maneuver ) raises intra-abdominal and intrathoracic pressure. That pressure is transmitted straight to the already-stretched varices. Teach: do not strain with bowel movements, do not hold your breath when moving up the bed. Stool softeners as ordered so that stools stay soft. Also avoid heavy lifting and forceful coughing where possible. 🧠 “Don't push.” The exam wording is usually “avoid straining when having a bowel movement.”

entries.h: 👀 Recognizing a bleed before it is obvious
entries.t: SIGN WHAT IT MEANS Hematemesis — bright red vomit Active, brisk upper GI bleeding Coffee-ground emesis Blood that has been sitting in the stomach Melaena — black tarry stool Digested blood from an upper GI source Rising pulse, falling BP Losing volume — often before any visible blood New confusion Poor perfusion, and a protein load feeding ammonia production Falling hematocrit Losing red cells as well as plasma GO DEEPER NG-304 · GI bleed 🧠 Black tarry stool is old blood; bright red vomit is new blood. Both are eme

Non-selective beta blockers as prescribed, to lower portal pressure. Check heart rate and blood pressure against the hold parameters before every dose. Endoscopic banding of known varices, done electively. No alcohol, no NSAIDs, no straining, no blind NG tubes. Teach the patient and family what hematemesis and melaena look like, and to call emergency services. 🧠 Prevention beats resuscitation. The beta blocker is doing quiet work every day. 🧠
STEP 4 · THE BRAIN Cloudy brain from ammonia. The nurse usually spots it before the lab does.

entries.h: 🧪 Where the ammonia comes from and where it ends up
entries.t: 🧠 Protein → ammonia → liver → urea → urine. Break the liver step and the ammonia goes to the brain instead.

entries.h: 🖐️ Asterixis — how to test for it
entries.t: 🧠 “The liver flap.” Arms out, hands back, watch. It looks like a bird flapping its wings.

1 Ask the orientation questions. Name, date of birth, date, place. Ask them the same way every shift. 2 Extend the arms and watch the hands. Asterixis is the classic motor sign. 3 Compare with the previous shift's documentation and with recent ammonia levels — the direction of travel matters more than one number. That trio is the answer to the classic select-all-that-apply question about detecting hepatic encephalopathy. 🧠 “Ask · Extend · Compare.” Three assessments, one diagnosis.

1 Subtle. Disturbed sleep pattern (awake at night, sleepy by day), mild forgetfulness, slight personality change. Families notice this first. ▼ 2 Obvious. Lethargy, disorientation, asterixis , inappropriate or bizarre behavior. ▼ 3 Marked. Very drowsy but rousable, confused, incoherent speech, cannot follow commands. ▼ 4 Coma. Unresponsive. Airway and aspiration risk. 🧠 Sleep pattern first, coma last. Day–night reversal is a real early sign, not just “bad sleep”.

GI bleeding — a huge protein load dumped into the gut. This is the big one. Constipation — ammonia sits in the bowel longer and is reabsorbed. Infection , including SBP. Dehydration and electrolyte disturbance , often from over-diuresis. Sedatives and opioids , which the failing liver cannot clear. A large protein meal in a patient who is already borderline. Never give a sedative to “settle” a confused cirrhotic patient without a provider's assessment. 🧠 Bleed · block · bug · dry · drug. Five triggers to check when

Fall precautions — bed low, call bell in reach, frequent rounding. Aspiration precautions — assess swallowing before anything by mouth; keep them sitting up. Reorient calmly and keep the environment consistent; involve family who know their baseline. Skin and pressure care — a lethargic patient does not reposition themselves. Document the mental status in the same words each time so the next nurse can compare. TREATMENT Lactulose and non-absorbed antibiotics are covered on NG-148 and NG-122 · Lactulose . 🧠 Confused
STEP 5 · LABS Which ones go up, which go down, and — more usefully — why.

entries.h: 📊 Every value, and the reason behind it
entries.t: 🧠 “The liver's ABC goes DOWN: Albumin, Bile handling, Coagulation. Everything the liver was supposed to REMOVE goes UP.”

The liver makes most clotting factors and needs vitamin K to activate several of them. It also sits upstream of a spleen that is now destroying platelets. PT · PTT · INR All PROLONGED — it takes longer to clot. Platelets LOW — trapped and destroyed in a big spleen. Result: bruising from a blood-pressure cuff, bleeding gums, prolonged oozing from any puncture, and a GI bleed that will not stop on its own. LINK NG-153 · Coagulation panel 🧠 “High PT, low platelets, easy bleeder.”

entries.h: 🅰️ Low albumin drives half the picture
entries.t: Typical adult albumin is 3.5–5.0 g/dL . In cirrhosis it falls, and that single value explains several findings at once: Ascites and peripheral edema — nothing left to hold water in the vessels. Low total calcium — much of the calcium in blood is carried bound to albumin, so the total falls with it (typical calcium 9.0–10.5 mg/dL ). Drugs behave unpredictably — many are albumin-bound, so more free drug circulates. 🧠 Low albumin = low calcium reading + water in the wrong place.

entries.h: 🦴 Low calcium — the two classic signs
entries.t: TROUSSEAU'S SIGN Inflate a blood-pressure cuff above systolic for a few minutes → the hand and wrist go into carpal spasm. CHVOSTEK'S SIGN Tap over the facial nerve just in front of the ear → the facial muscles twitch. Also watch for numbness and tingling around the mouth and in the fingers, muscle cramps, and hyperactive reflexes. 🧠 “TrousseauS = Spasm of the hand. ChvosteK = Cheek.”

entries.h: 🧪 Enzymes vs function — a distinction that gets tested
entries.t: TELLS YOU TESTS Liver cells are being DAMAGED ALT, AST (leaked out of injured cells) Liver FUNCTION is failing Albumin, PT/INR, bilirubin, ammonia Enzymes can even be near normal in end-stage cirrhosis — there are too few working liver cells left to leak anything. A normal ALT does not mean a healthy liver. 🧠 Enzymes = damage. Albumin, INR and bilirubin = function. Function is what matters.

entries.h: 🎓 Select all that apply — the classic version
entries.t: Which values are expected to be ELEVATED in worsening liver failure? ✅ Ammonia — the liver cannot convert it to urea. ✅ Bilirubin — it cannot be cleared into the bile. ✅ Prothrombin time (PT) / INR — fewer clotting factors, so it takes longer. ❌ Albumin — goes DOWN; the liver cannot make it. ❌ Calcium — goes DOWN, largely because albumin does. 🧠 The trick in this question is that albumin and calcium travel together , and they travel in the OPPOSITE direction to everything else. 💛

entries.h: JAUNDICE, ITCHING AND THE REST OF THE BODY
entries.t: STEP 6 · HEAD TO TOE The visible signs that make an exam question recognizable in one sentence.
🧠 “The Bile Bus has stopped running.” The pigment cannot get to the toilet, so it goes into the skin instead.

SYSTEM WHAT YOU FIND 👁️ Eyes / skin Yellow sclera and skin, spider angiomas, palmar erythema, easy bruising, scratch marks 🧠 Neuro Confusion, day–night reversal, asterixis, lethargy → coma 🫁 Respiratory Shortness of breath from a raised diaphragm; rapid shallow breathing 🍽️ GI Anorexia, nausea, distended abdomen, hemorrhoids, melaena, hematemesis 🚽 Renal Dark tea-colored urine, low output if the circulation is depleted 🦵 Peripheral Peripheral edema, muscle wasting despite a big belly 🩸 Hematological Low platelets,

entries.h: 🎓 The select-all you will actually see
entries.t: Worsening liver failure — which findings should the nurse expect? ✅ Enlarged abdomen from ascites ✅ Bruise marks on the skin ✅ Fatigue and possible confusion ✅ Sclera that appears yellow ✅ Reports of itchy skin All five are correct — and each maps to one failed liver job: fluid handling, clotting, ammonia clearance, bilirubin clearance, bile salt clearance. 🧠 Every symptom = one job the liver stopped doing. Learn the jobs, predict the symptoms.

Any hematemesis or melaena — treat as a bleed until proven otherwise. New or deepening confusion , new asterixis, day–night reversal. Fever or abdominal tenderness in a patient with ascites — think SBP. Sudden increase in girth or weight , or breathlessness lying down. Falling blood pressure with a rising pulse. Reduced urine output — hepatorenal involvement is a serious development. 🧠 Bleed · Brain · Belly · BP. Four B's that get the phone picked up. 🩸 One cause, four escapes Portal hypertension → varices · caput

What the nurse actually DOES — procedures, drugs, diet, safety, teaching NG-148 GI · HEPATIC · NURSING CARE ADHD-friendly visual edition What this page covers, and what it doesn't. NG-029 is the pathophysiology. NG-109 is the complications and the labs. This page is the care page : paracentesis and liver biopsy step by step, the drug map, the diet and fluid rules, bleeding and itching precautions, and exactly what you teach before discharge. Nothing here cures cirrhosis — every intervention on this page treats a co
STEP 1 · DIAGNOSTICS Two procedures, two positions, and both of them are exam questions about what the nurse does FIRST.
🧠 “Bladder, Baseline, Belly, Bolt upright.” Empty bladder → baseline vitals → weight and girth → high Fowler's.

entries.h: 🩻 Liver biopsy — and the position that gets tested
entries.t: 🧠 “bIopsy → RIGHT side.” The liver is on the right, so you lie on the right and let your own body weight hold the pressure.

entries.h: ✅ Paracentesis — the FIRST action, and why
entries.t: “Which action should the nurse take first?” Have the patient empty their bladder. The needle goes into the lower abdomen, and a full bladder sits right in that path. Puncturing it is exactly the complication the step prevents. Then, in order: baseline vital signs → weight and abdominal girth (mark the spot) → position upright → consent and sterile set-up. 🧠 Bladder before needle. Every time, no exceptions.

entries.h: 🚨 After a paracentesis — what you are watching for
entries.t: Hypotension and tachycardia — taking liters off fast shifts volume out of the circulation. Leakage at the puncture site — apply a dry sterile dressing and monitor it. Signs of infection or bowel injury — fever, worsening abdominal pain, rigid abdomen. Re-measure weight and girth and compare with the pre-procedure figures. Record the fluid — amount, color and clarity. Cloudy fluid suggests infection. IV albumin is often ordered after a large-volume tap to keep the circulation from collapsing. 🧠 Take fluid off → pres

entries.h: 🧪 The other tests you will see ordered
entries.t: TEST WHAT IT ANSWERS Liver function panel ALT, AST, bilirubin, albumin — damage and function Coagulation panel PT, PTT, INR, platelets — can this patient clot? Serum ammonia Supports hepatic encephalopathy; trend it Abdominal ultrasound Liver texture and size, ascites, portal flow, spleen size Upper endoscopy Looks directly at varices — and can band them Ascitic fluid analysis Cell count and culture — is this SBP? 🧠 Coagulation studies come BEFORE any invasive procedure in a liver patient.

Check PT, PTT, INR and platelets — and report abnormal results before the procedure starts. Confirm consent and a valid time-out. Establish IV access and know where the blood products are. Take baseline vital signs — you cannot detect a change without them. Anticipate that bleeding will be the complication , not infection. 🧠 Every hole you make in this patient is a hole that keeps bleeding. 💊
STEP 2 · PHARMACOLOGY Match the drug to the complication it treats, and the monitoring writes itself.
🧠 Never memorize a cirrhosis drug on its own — memorize it attached to the complication it exists to fix.

entries.h: 💩 Lactulose — the most tested drug on this page
entries.t: DRUG PAGE NG-122 · Lactulose & sodium polystyrene sulfonate 🧠 “Lose the ammonia · Loose bowels · Lose potassium.” Three L's, one drug.

entries.h: 🅰️ IV albumin — the one students get wrong
entries.t: 🧠 Albumin RAISES the blood pressure. Bounding pulses and a rising BP mean it is working — not that something has gone wrong. Keep listening to the lungs anyway.

An aldosterone antagonist (spironolactone) is the usual first choice, because aldosterone excess is one of the three drivers of ascites. A loop diuretic is often added. Aldosterone antagonist Potassium-SPARING → watch for HYPER kalemia. Loop diuretic Potassium-WASTING → watch for HYPO kalemia. Together they can partly balance each other, but the potassium still has to be checked. Potassium reference 3.5–5.0 mEq/L . Monitor daily weight, girth, I&O, blood pressure and electrolytes. Diuresing too fast can trigger enc

entries.h: ❌ Drugs to be very careful with
entries.t: Sedatives, benzodiazepines and opioids — the failing liver cannot clear them, so they accumulate and can precipitate encephalopathy. Acetaminophen / acetaminophen — hepatotoxic; only under provider direction, and never with alcohol. NSAIDs and aspirin — bleeding risk on top of an existing coagulopathy, and they worsen kidney function and fluid retention. Any hepatically metabolized drug may need a dose adjustment. Doses are individualized — follow the order. Never give an over-the-counter analgesic to a cirrhotic p

The liver needs vitamin K to activate several clotting factors, so it may be given to try to improve the PT/INR. It does not work if there are no liver cells left to use it. Fresh frozen plasma replaces clotting factors when bleeding or before a procedure. Platelets are given for severe thrombocytopenia with bleeding. Packed red cells for significant blood loss. All blood products follow your facility's transfusion policy, with the required checks and monitoring. 🧠 Vitamin K is the ingredient; the liver is the kitc
STEP 3 · NUTRITION Low sodium, controlled fluid, adequate calories, and absolutely no alcohol.
🧠 “Low sodium, Low swelling.” Salt holds water; water becomes ascites.

No salt shaker at the table and none added in cooking. Read labels — the sodium is mostly hidden in processed food, not in the shaker. Worst offenders: canned soup, deli meat, bacon, cheese, tinned vegetables, sauces, takeaway, salted snacks . Use herbs, lemon, garlic and pepper for flavor instead. Check with the provider before using a salt substitute — many are potassium chloride, which matters if the patient is on a potassium-sparing diuretic. 🧠 “The salt is in the box, not the shaker.” Labels beat willpower.

entries.h: 🥚 Protein — say “ask the provider”, not “restrict it”
entries.t: Protein is broken down into ammonia, so older teaching restricted it in everyone with cirrhosis. Current practice is more nuanced: These patients are usually malnourished and losing muscle , and muscle actually helps clear ammonia. So protein is generally kept adequate , and restricted only in specific situations. In active hepatic encephalopathy , a dietary consult to limit protein is a classic exam answer — and remains part of the picture on many exams. Safest position for the nurse: follow the ordered diet and g

entries.h: 💧 Fluid restriction — how to make it bearable
entries.t: Spread the allowance across the day and save some for the evening. Use small cups — the same volume feels like more. Ice chips count as roughly half their volume; frozen fruit pieces last longer. Frequent mouth care and sugar-free hard candy or gum for dry mouth. Avoid salty food — it makes the thirst much worse. Include everything liquid: soup, jelly, ice cream, IV medications. 🧠 Thirst is driven by SALT. Cutting sodium is what makes a fluid restriction tolerable.

Oral care BEFORE meals — this is the classic exam answer for improving intake. Small, frequent meals — a full ascitic abdomen makes large meals impossible. A bedtime snack helps, because a cirrhotic liver has poor glycogen stores overnight. Supplements and vitamins as ordered — thiamine and folate are commonly needed, especially with alcohol-related disease. Weigh regularly , but remember that ascites hides real weight loss. 🧠 Big belly, wasting muscles. The scale can look stable while the patient is starving.

Complete abstinence, permanently, whatever the original cause of the cirrhosis was. There is no safe amount for a liver that is already scarred. Offer referral to a support program rather than a lecture. Watch for alcohol withdrawal in a newly admitted patient — it can start within hours and is dangerous in someone who is already confused. Check mouthwashes, cough syrups and tonics for alcohol content. 🧠 Scar tissue never comes back. Stopping alcohol protects the liver cells that are left. 🩸
STEP 4 · PROTECT This patient cannot clot, cannot stop scratching, and may not be thinking clearly.

entries.h: 🩸 Bleeding precautions — the do / do-not board
entries.t: 🧠 “Soft brush, electric razor, no tube, no push.” Four things, and they cover most of the questions on this topic.
🧠 “Cool · cream · cover · clip.” Cool cloth, moisturiser, gloves and sleeves, short nails.

Vital signs first : a rising pulse and falling blood pressure often come before visible blood. Check stools for melaena and test as ordered; note any bright red rectal bleeding. Check emesis for coffee-ground appearance. Falling hematocrit and hemoglobin. New confusion — because the blood in the gut is a large protein load that raises ammonia. Never dismiss new confusion in a cirrhotic patient as “just their baseline”. GO DEEPER NG-304 · GI bleed 🧠 A GI bleed here causes TWO emergencies: shock, and encephalopathy.

Fall precautions — bed low and locked, call bell in reach, non-slip footwear, frequent rounding. A confused patient who falls now has a bleeding risk plus a head injury risk . Reorient calmly , keep the room consistent and involve family who know the baseline. Aspiration precautions if the patient is lethargic — sit them up, assess swallowing. Document mental status in the same words each shift so changes are obvious. 🧠 Confusion + no clotting = every fall is a bleed.

Reposition regularly ; edematous, jaundiced skin over a distended abdomen breaks down fast. Semi- to high Fowler's for breathing when there is ascites. Elevate edematous legs when sitting; avoid tight clothing and tight stockings unless ordered. Inspect pressure areas, the sacrum and any weeping skin at every turn. Handle gently — bruising is easy and skin tears easily. 🧠 Sit up to breathe; turn often to protect the skin.

Q. Cirrhosis with suspected gastresophageal varices — which order would the nurse question? ▸ New nasogastric tube insertion. A blindly passed tube can rupture a varix. Q. Portal hypertension, ascites and varices — which teaching is correct? ▸ Avoid straining when having a bowel movement. Valsalva raises the pressure in the varices. Q. Highest priority for a patient with RUPTURED varices? ▸ Protecting the airway. Blood is pouring in above the airway. Q. The patient is vomiting and the nurse notes hematemesis. Which
STEP 5 · TEACH Cirrhosis is managed at home. What the patient can recognize is what keeps them alive.

entries.h: 📞 Call the provider for any of these
entries.t: Vomiting blood or vomit that looks like coffee grounds — call emergency services. Black, tarry or bloody stools. New confusion, unusual sleepiness, day–night reversal, or a hand tremor/flap — often reported by family before the patient notices. Rapid weight gain — more than 2–3 lb in a day or 5 lb in a week — or a belly that suddenly grows. Fever, or new abdominal pain and tenderness. Shortness of breath , or breathlessness lying flat. Bruising or bleeding that will not stop. 🧠 Blood · Brain · Belly · Breathing. Te

⚖️ Weigh every morning — same scale, same time, after the toilet, before breakfast. Write it down. 🧂 Stick to the sodium limit and read every label. 💧 Keep to the fluid allowance if one has been ordered, spread across the day. 💊 Take the medicines exactly as prescribed — including the lactulose, even when the stools are inconvenient. 🚫 No alcohol , and no over-the-counter medicines without checking first. 🧠 The bathroom scale is the home monitor. A written weight chart is the single most useful thing a patient can

A patient with even mild encephalopathy may not recognize their own confusion. The family is your early warning system. Show them how to test for asterixis — arms out, hands back. Teach them the orientation questions to ask. Explain that sleeping all day and being awake all night is a warning sign, not just a habit. Show them what melaena looks like. Make sure someone else knows the medication list . 🧠 “Not like himself” is assessment data. Take it seriously every time.

COMPLICATION WHAT PREVENTS IT AT HOME Ascites returning Low sodium, fluid limit, diuretics as prescribed, daily weight Variceal bleed Beta blocker as prescribed, no straining, no alcohol, no NSAIDs Encephalopathy Lactulose to 2–3 soft stools a day, avoid constipation, treat infections early Infection / SBP Report fever or belly pain immediately; keep vaccinations up to date as advised Bleeding injury Soft brush, electric razor, no contact sports, careful with knives and tools Skin breakdown Moisturise, short nails,

If you can tell that story out loud, you know cirrhosis. 🔬 Two positions Paracentesis = high Fowler's , bladder empty FIRST. Post-biopsy = RIGHT side . 💊 Lactulose 2–3 soft stools/d

ACE Inhibitors · Beta Blockers · Calcium Channel Blockers · Alpha-1 Blockers · Alpha+Beta Blockers · Central Alpha-2 Agonists NG-157 PHARM · CARDIOVASCULAR Series: NCLEX Drug Review 3 of 8 ADHD-friendly visual edition The whole antihypertensive installment fits on one equation: BP = cardiac output × systemic vascular resistance . Every drug on this page lowers blood pressure by attacking one side of that multiplication — or both. Learn which side each class pulls on and the side effects stop being random : pull on
STEP 1 · WHAT'S IN THIS SET Cora's 3-part study map for every drug on this page: CLASS → ACTION → WATCH . Six classes, all of them pressure-lowering.

💊 ACE Inhibitors "-pril" 🫀 Beta Blockers "-olol" 🧱 Calcium Channel Blockers 🚪 Alpha-1 Blockers "-zosin" 🔀 Alpha + Beta Blockers "-lol" 🧠 Central Alpha-2 Agonists 🧠 Suffix triage first. "-pril" → ACE. "-olol" → beta. "-dipine" → calcium (vessel type). "-zosin" → alpha-1. If it ends in "-lol" but is carvedilol or labetalol , it is the dual alpha+beta blocker.

entries.h: ⚖️ The one equation this whole page hangs on
entries.t: acts on the pump acts on the pipes acts on both 🧠 Pump or pipes? Ask it for every antihypertensive you meet. Pump drugs give you bradycardia, fatigue and heart block. Pipe drugs give you dizziness, flushing, headache and ankle edema.

entries.h: 📇 Brand ↔ generic — the pairs NCLEX actually asks
entries.t: Class Brand Generic ACE inhibitors "-pril" Altace ramipril Capoten captopril Prinivil, Zestril lisinopril Vasotec enalapril Beta blockers "-olol" Inderal propranolol non-selective Lopressor metoprolol tartrate immediate release Toprol-XL metoprolol succinate extended release Tenormin atenolol beta-1 selective Calcium channel blockers Cardizem diltiazem non-DHP Verelan, Isoptin, Calan verapamil non-DHP Norvasc amlodipine DHP Procardia nifedipine DHP Alpha-1 blockers "-zosin" Minipress prazosin Hytrin terazosin Alpha

entries.h: 🚨 The suffix trap that costs points
entries.t: Alpha-1 blockers end in "-zosin" — pra zosin , tera zosin , doxa zosin . They are not the same as Zosyn , which is an antibiotic (piperacillin–tazobactam) and has nothing to do with blood pressure. 🧠 "Zosin lowers, Zosyn kills." One relaxes vessels; one kills bacteria.

entries.h: ⭐ Two "-lol" drugs that are not plain beta blockers
entries.t: Carvedilol and labetalol block alpha-1 and beta receptors. They lower BP two ways at once, so orthostatic hypotension is more prominent than with a pure beta blocker. 🧠 "CarLa does both." Car vedilol + La betalol = alpha AND beta.

Some review sheets file clonidine (Catapres) under "alpha-2 antagonists." Clonidine is a central alpha-2 agonist — it stimulates the presynaptic autoreceptor, which turns sympathetic outflow down . The mechanism the sheet describes (less norepinephrine released, less sympathetic activity) is the agonist mechanism. 🧠 Agonist that acts like a brake. Stimulating an inhibitory autoreceptor reduces output — that is why an agonist lowers BP here.

entries.h: 🔎 One-line identity card for all six
entries.t: 💊 ACE inhibitors · ramipril, captopril, lisinopril, enalapril Does Blocks angiotensin I → angiotensin II ⇒ vasodilation, ↓ aldosterone Watch Dry cough, angiedema, ↑ K⁺, ↑ creatinine, first-dose hypotension 🫀 Beta blockers · propranolol, metoprolol, atenolol Does Blocks beta-1 ⇒ ↓ HR, ↓ contractility, ↓ AV conduction, ↓ renin Watch Bradycardia, fatigue, masked hypoglycemia, bronchospasm (non-selective), rebound if stopped 🧱 Calcium channel blockers · diltiazem, verapamil, amlodipine, nifedipine Does Blocks Ca²⁺ entr
STEP 2 · MECHANISM Six classes, four physical addresses: the RAAS cascade, the adrenergic synapse, the calcium channel, and the heart's own wiring.

entries.h: 🔗 Address 1 — the RAAS cascade, and where "-pril" cuts it
entries.t: 🧠 "PRIL puts the cough on the pillow." The cough is dry, nagging, non-productive and does not respond to cough syrup — the fix is switching to an ARB (see installment 4).

entries.h: 🔌 Address 2 — the adrenergic synapse: alpha-1, alpha-2, beta-1, beta-2
entries.t: 🧠 "1 heart, 2 lungs." Beta- 1 = one heart. Beta- 2 = two lungs. Alpha- 1 = arteries squeeze. Alpha- 2 = the auto-brake on the nerve itself.

Action: block conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II (a potent vasoconstrictor) ⇒ vasodilation and ↓ peripheral vascular resistance without directly increasing cardiac output, rate or contractility. Aldosterone falls too, so sodium and water are retained less. 🧪 Check the potassium. Less aldosterone = potassium held in = ↑ K⁺ . 📈 Monitor BUN and creatinine — renal function can fall, especially with volume depletion. ⭐ Also protective in heart failure and diabetic kidney disease, not just hypertension. ⚠️ Ang

Action: prevent sympathetic stimulation of the heart ⇒ ↓ heart rate, ↓ force of contraction, ↓ myocardial irritability, depressed SA-node automaticity, slower AV and intraventricular conduction — and suppressed renin release from the kidney. 💓 Net effect: ↓ myocardial oxygen demand — which is why they help angina and post-MI. 🫁 Non-selective agents (propranolol) also hit beta-2 ⇒ may cause bronchoconstriction. 🩺 Take an apical pulse for a full minute before giving. 🧠 "Beta blockers take the ABCDEs down": ↓ A utomat

entries.h: 🧱 Address 3 — the calcium channel, and the two CCB personalities
entries.t: 🧠 "DIP into the vessels; VERy DILigent about the heart." "- dip ine" = vessel-selective. Ver apamil and dil tiazem also work on the heart's rate and conduction.

Action: block alpha-1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle ⇒ arteries and veins dilate ⇒ ↓ peripheral vascular resistance ⇒ ↓ BP. The same receptors sit in the bladder neck and prostate, which is why this class also treats BPH urinary symptoms. ⚠️ First-dose phenomenon. The very first dose (and every dose increase) can drop BP hard enough to cause syncope. Standard teaching: give the first dose at bedtime , and get up slowly afterwards.

Action: stimulates alpha-2 receptors in the brainstem ⇒ less norepinephrine released ⇒ ↓ sympathetic outflow ⇒ ↓ HR, ↓ SVR, ↓ BP. It works "upstream," in the brain, rather than at the vessel itself. ⚠️ Rebound hypertension is severe. Stopping clonidine abruptly can cause a rapid, dangerous BP surge with tachycardia, sweating and agitation. It must be tapered . Transdermal patches are applied to a clean, dry, hairless site and rotated.

entries.h: ⚡ Address 4 — the heart's wiring, and what a beta blocker does to it
entries.t: 🧠 Bradycardia is not a side effect — it is the mechanism. The nursing job is deciding how much slowing is acceptable, using the prescriber's hold parameters. 🚨
STEP 3 · ASSESS Almost every adverse effect on this page is the drug's own mechanism, taken one step too far.

entries.h: 🧍 Body map — where the side effects show up

entries.t: Swelling of the lips, tongue, periorbital tissue, face or larynx in a patient on any "-pril." Airway comes first. ❌ Hold the drug and notify the prescriber immediately. 🫁 Assess airway, voice change, stridor, difficulty swallowing. ⏱️ It is not dose-related and can appear after long uneventful use. ⚠️ Once a patient has ACE-inhibitor angiedema, that class is generally avoided for life.

The early warning signs of low blood sugar — tachycardia, tremor, palpitations — are sympathetic signs. Block beta receptors and the patient loses them. 💦 Diaphoresis usually still happens (cholinergic), so sweating becomes the key clue. 🧪 Teach diabetic patients to check glucose more often, not to rely on how they feel. 🧠 "Beta blockers steal the alarm bell but leave the sweat."

Beta blockers and clonidine must never be discontinued abruptly. The receptors have up-regulated; removing the block unmasks a surge of sympathetic activity. 🫀 Beta blocker withdrawal → rebound tachycardia, hypertension, angina, risk of MI or dysrhythmia. 🧠 Clonidine withdrawal → severe rebound hypertension, agitation, sweating, headache. 📉 Both must be tapered over days to weeks per prescriber direction.

entries.h: ⚠️ The dangerous combination on this page
entries.t: Verapamil or diltiazem + a beta blocker. Both slow the SA node and the AV node. Stacked together they can cause profound bradycardia, heart block or hypotension. ⚠️ If you see a non-dihydropyridine CCB and a beta blocker ordered together, that is a legitimate reason to call the prescriber and to monitor rate and rhythm closely.

Grapefruit inhibits intestinal CYP3A4, so more drug reaches the bloodstream. With CCBs that means exaggerated hypotension, flushing and headache. 🧠 "Grapefruit makes the dose bigger without changing the pill." Teach avoidance rather than timing tricks.

entries.h: ✅ Before you give it — the pre-dose check
entries.t: 🩺 Apical pulse for one full minute before any beta blocker, verapamil, diltiazem or digoxin-type drug. 🩸 Blood pressure — including a standing reading if orthostatic symptoms are a concern. 🧪 Potassium and creatinine before and during ACE-inhibitor therapy. 📋 Compare to the prescriber's written hold parameters ; if none exist, ask for them. ⚠️ Commonly written parameters are "hold and notify if apical HR is below 60/min or systolic BP is below about 90–100 mmHg ," but the exact numbers are prescriber- and facility-

entries.h: 🫁 Why a non-selective beta blocker is risky in asthma
entries.t: 🧠 Selectivity is dose-dependent. "Cardioselective" agents like metoprolol and atenolol lose their beta-1 selectivity as the dose climbs — asthma caution never fully disappears. 📋

entries.h: TEACH — WHAT THE PATIENT MUST HEAR
entries.t: STEP 4 · EDUCATE Antihypertensives are taken by people who feel fine. Adherence teaching is the intervention.

entries.h: ✅ Orthostatic hypotension — the universal teaching point
entries.t: 🛏️ Dangle at the side of the bed before standing; rise in stages. 🚿 Warn about hot showers, hot tubs, alcohol and standing still — all worsen it. 💧 Report dizziness, lightheadedness or near-fainting rather than "pushing through." 🧍 Fall precautions for older adults, especially at night. 🧠 "Sit, dangle, stand, wait." Four beats before walking away from the bed.

entries.h: 📈 Self-monitoring is part of the prescription
entries.t: 🩸 Home BP and pulse log — pulse matters as much as pressure on this page. ⚖️ Daily weight at the same time, same scale, same clothing; report a sudden gain. 📞 Report a resting pulse under about 60/min , new swelling, or fainting. 💊 Bring the log to every visit — dose changes are made from trends, not single readings.

Most "salt substitutes" are potassium chloride . On an ACE inhibitor, potassium is already being retained. ⚠️ Teach patients to avoid potassium-based salt substitutes and to check with the prescriber before any potassium supplement — including combination products and some sports drinks.

💊 Captopril is classically taught to be taken on an empty stomach — about an hour before meals — because food reduces its absorption. 🍲 Carvedilol is taken with food to slow absorption and reduce orthostatic hypotension. 🛏️ First "-zosin" dose at bedtime. ⏰ Extended-release products (Toprol-XL, Verelan, Procardia XL) are taken whole, once daily.

ACE inhibitors are contraindicated in pregnancy — they cause fetal injury. Any patient of childbearing potential needs that conversation and a plan. Labetalol is one of the agents commonly used to treat hypertension in pregnancy. 🧠 "PRILs are not for pregnancy." Both start with P.

entries.h: 💊 NSAIDs quietly undo this whole page
entries.t: NSAIDs promote sodium and water retention and blunt the antihypertensive effect of ACE inhibitors, beta blockers and diuretics — and add kidney risk on top of an ACE inhibitor. 🧠 Ask about over-the-counter drugs. Patients rarely list ibuprofen as "a medication."

entries.h: 📊 Pick-the-drug table — the distinguishing feature for each class
entries.t: If the question mentions… Think Because New dry, nagging, non-productive cough ACE inhibitor Bradykinin accumulation Rising serum potassium ACE inhibitor Aldosterone suppressed Swollen lips/tongue after a first dose or after months ACE inhibitor (angiedema) Airway emergency Apical pulse 52, patient fatigued Beta blocker or non-DHP CCB Negative chronotropic effect Asthma history + wheezing after a new BP pill Non-selective beta blocker Beta-2 blockade in the airway Diabetic who "no longer feels" lows Beta blocker Ad

SAY IT OUT LOUD 💊 "-pril" Cough · ↑K⁺ · angiedema · not in pregnancy 🫀 "-olol" Apical pulse first · never stop abruptly · masks lows 🧱 CCB "-dipine" = vessels & edema · verapamil/diltiazem = heart & constipation 🚪 "-zosin" · 🧠 clonidine First dose at bedtime · taper clonidine or BP rebounds

Q1: A patient on lisinopril develops a persistent dry cough. What is the cause and the usual fix? Show answer Bradykinin accumulation from ACE inhibition. It does not respond to cough medicine; the prescriber usually switches the patient to an ARB. Q2: Which lab must be monitored on an ACE inhibitor, and which way does it move? Show answer Potassium — it goes UP, because aldosterone is suppressed. Creatinine and BUN are watched too. Q3: What assessment is done immediately before giving metoprolol? Show answer Apica

entries.h: 🧠 The four mnemonics to walk into the exam with
entries.t: "PRIL puts the cough on the pillow" — ACE inhibitor cough, plus ↑K⁺. "1 heart, 2 lungs" — beta-1 cardiac, beta-2 pulmonary. "DIP into the vessels; VERy DILigent about the heart" — CCB families. "CarLa does both" — carvedilol and labetalol block alpha and beta. 🧠 Say each one out loud twice, then close the page and rebuild the six-class list from the suffixes alone. Nitrates · ARBs "-sartan" · Cardiac Glycosides (digoxin) · Oral Antidiabetics: Sulfonylureas, Biguanides, Glitazones & Gliptins NG-186 PHARM · CARDIAC + ENDOCRINE Series: NCLEX Drug Review 4 of 8 ADHD-friendly visual edition Two halves, one page. The cardiac half is about oxygen supply and demand — nitrates open the pipes, ARBs stop angiotensin II at the receptor, and digoxin makes the pump squeeze harder while beating slower. The diabetes half is four oral classes that lower glucose in four completely different pl
STEP 1 · WHAT'S IN THIS SET Cora's 3-part study map for every drug on this page: CLASS → ACTION → WATCH .

💥 Nitrates 🔒 ARBs "-sartan" 🫀 Cardiac Glycosides 🍬 Sulfonylureas 🥛 Biguanides metformin 💧 Glitazones 🔁 Gliptins DPP-4 inhibitors 🧠 Suffix triage: "-sartan" → ARB. "-gliptin" → DPP-4. "-glitazone" → insulin sensitizer. "-ide" endings (glyburide, glipizide, glimepiride) → sulfonylurea. Nitrates and digoxin have no suffix — memorize them by name.

entries.h: 📇 Brand ↔ generic — the pairs NCLEX actually asks
entries.t: Class Brand Generic Nitrates Nitro-Bid, Tridil, Transderm-Nitro, Nitrostat nitroglycerin Imdur isosorbide mono nitrate Isordil, Sorbitrate isosorbide di nitrate ARBs "-sartan" Atacand candesartan Cozaar losartan Diovan valsartan Cardiac glycoside Lanoxin digoxin Sulfonylureas Amaryl glimepiride DiaBeta, Glynase, Micronase glyburide Glucotrol, Glucotrol XL glipizide Biguanide Glucophage metformin Glitazones Actos pioglitazone Avandia rosiglitazone Gliptin (DPP-4) Januvia sitagliptin ⚠️ Mono- vs di-. Isosorbide mono

entries.h: 🫀 Where the cardiac half acts — one map
entries.t: 🧠 Angina is an arithmetic problem. Supply (coronary flow) must cover demand (rate × wall tension × contractility). Nitrates lower demand and raise supply at the same time. ⚙️
STEP 2 · MECHANISM Four mechanisms to hold: a dilated vein, a blocked receptor, a poisoned sodium pump, and four different glucose levers.

Action: relax vascular smooth muscle. Venous dilation predominates at lower doses ⇒ ↓ preload ; arterial dilation adds ⇒ ↓ afterload . Both drop myocardial oxygen demand. Coronary arteries dilate, improving supply. 🎯 Used to treat and prevent angina , and to lower blood pressure. 🤕 Headache is the classic expected effect — it usually eases with continued therapy. 📉 Check BP before each dose; hypotension and reflex tachycardia are the limiting effects. 🧠 "Nitro = less work for the heart." Less blood coming back, les

Never give a nitrate to a patient who has taken a PDE-5 inhibitor. That is sildenafil (Viagra), tadalafil (Cialis) or vardenafil (Levitra) — the "-afil" drugs. Both dilate vessels through the same nitric-oxide pathway. Stacked, they can cause profound, refractory hypotension. ⚠️ Always ask before giving nitroglycerin for chest pain — including in the emergency setting and including for female patients, since PDE-5 drugs have other uses such as pulmonary hypertension.

Continuous nitrate exposure produces tolerance : the drug stops working. The standard fix is a daily nitrate-free window. 🔄 Rotate patch sites; remove the old patch before applying a new one. ⏱️ Common regimen: wear the patch about 12–14 hours , then leave it off for a 10–12 hour patch-free interval — usually overnight. 🧤 Wear gloves and avoid touching ointment or patch adhesive; wipe the old site. 🧠 "Patch off at night, receptors reset by morning."

entries.h: 🔒 ARBs vs ACE inhibitors — same pathway, two different cut points
entries.t: 🧠 "ACE cuts the supply line; the SARTAN locks the door." Same destination, different tactic — which is exactly why the cough disappears on an ARB but the potassium problem does not.

entries.h: 🫀 Digoxin — inside the heart muscle cell
entries.t: 🧠 "Dig makes it STRONGER and SLOWER." Positive inotrope, negative chronotrope, negative dromotrope — three words, one drug.

entries.h: 🎯 Narrow therapeutic index — the digoxin window
entries.t: ⚠️ A digoxin level in the "therapeutic" band does not rule out toxicity if the potassium is low. Treat the patient and the potassium, not just the number.

entries.h: 🍬 The diabetes half — four classes, four addresses
entries.t: 🧠 "Squeeze, Silence, Sensitize, Signal." Sulfonylureas squeeze insulin out · metformin silences the liver · glitazones sensitize muscle and fat · gliptins boost the gut's signal .

entries.h: 🔬 Inside the beta cell — why a sulfonylurea causes hypoglycemia and a gliptin usually doesn't
entries.t: 🧠 Forced vs amplified. A sulfonylurea pushes insulin out no matter what the glucose is doing. A gliptin only turns up a signal the meal already started.

entries.h: 💉 IV nitroglycerin — the details that get tested
entries.t: 🎛️ Always on an infusion pump , titrated to blood pressure and pain, with continuous monitoring. 🧪 Nitroglycerin adsorbs onto standard PVC tubing , so the manufacturer's supplied or specially designated tubing is used — check the product and facility protocol. 📉 Take a blood pressure before starting and with every titration; hypotension is the dose-limiting effect. 🧠 Tridil is the IV one. Nitrostat is the sublingual tablet, Nitro-Bid the ointment, Transderm-Nitro the patch.

Rescue: sublingual nitroglycerin — fast on, short-lived, taken at the moment of chest pain. Maintenance: isosorbide mononitrate (Imdur) or dinitrate (Isordil) — taken on a schedule to prevent angina, never to treat an attack in progress. ⚠️ A patient who reaches for Imdur during chest pain has been taught wrong. Rescue therapy is the sublingual tablet or spray.

entries.h: 🔒 Why ACE + ARB together is generally avoided
entries.t: Both suppress the same pathway. Combining them adds little benefit and stacks the same risks — hyperkalemia, hypotension and renal injury . 🧠 One brake on the RAAS at a time. If you see both on the same MAR, it is worth a clarification call.

entries.h: ✅ Where digoxin actually earns its place
entries.t: 🫀 Heart failure — improves contractility and cardiac output, and can reduce symptoms. 💓 Atrial fibrillation / flutter — slows the ventricular rate by slowing AV conduction. 🧪 Because it is renally cleared and has a narrow window, it needs level checks, potassium checks and pulse checks in a way most cardiac drugs do not. 🧠 Digoxin does not fix the underlying disease — it changes how the heart behaves while the disease is treated. 🚨
STEP 3 · ASSESS Digoxin toxicity and hypoglycemia are the two emergencies hiding on this page.
🧠 "A-B-C-D of dig toxicity": A norexia first · B radycardia · C onfusion & C olour vision (yellow-green) · D ysrhythmias.

💓 Apical pulse for one full minute. Hold and notify if it is below 60/min in an adult (or outside whatever parameters are written). 🧪 Check the most recent K⁺ , magnesium and renal function. 🍽️ Ask about appetite, nausea and vision changes — these come before the rhythm changes. ⚠️ Pediatric hold parameters are different and higher — always use the age-appropriate order.

Rare, but serious. Suspect it with malaise, myalgia, unusual somnolence, abdominal distress, hyperventilation and unexplained hypotension in a patient on metformin. 🧪 Risk rises with renal impairment, dehydration, hypoxia, sepsis, heart failure and heavy alcohol use. 💉 Iodinated contrast studies: metformin is commonly withheld around the procedure and restarted only after renal function is rechecked. Follow the facility protocol — the exact timing varies. 🧠 "Metformin hates dye and dehydration."

Pioglitazone and rosiglitazone reduce insulin resistance, but they cause renal sodium and fluid retention — which means edema, weight gain, and the risk of precipitating or worsening heart failure . ⚖️ Daily weights; report a rapid gain. 🫁 Report new or worsening dyspnea, orthopnea or ankle swelling. 🧪 Liver enzymes are monitored with this class. ⚠️ Not appropriate for patients with symptomatic heart failure. This is the "-glitazone" question NCLEX loves.

The sulfonylureas are the class on this page that most reliably causes it. Metformin, glitazones and gliptins rarely cause it alone, but can when combined with insulin or a sulfonylurea. 😰 Shaky, sweaty, tachycardic, hungry, irritable, confused; late — seizure, unresponsiveness. 🍬 Conscious and able to swallow: give a fast-acting carbohydrate, recheck in about 15 minutes, repeat if still low, then follow with a longer-acting snack or meal. 💉 Unresponsive: nothing by mouth — glucagon or IV dextrose per protocol. 🧠 O

Cases of acute pancreatitis have been reported with DPP-4 inhibitors. Teach patients to report severe, persistent abdominal pain that may radiate to the back , with or without vomiting — and to stop the drug and seek care. 🧠 "Januvia + knife-in-the-back pain = stop and call."

Class Hypoglycemia alone? Signature adverse effect Key monitoring Sulfonylureas glimepiride, glyburide, glipizide Yes — highest here Hypoglycemia, weight gain Glucose; take with the first meal of the day Biguanide metformin Not usually GI upset (most common); lactic acidosis (rare) Renal function; hold around iodinated contrast per policy Glitazones pioglitazone, rosiglitazone Not usually Edema, weight gain, heart-failure risk Daily weight, edema, dyspnea, liver enzymes Gliptins sitagliptin Not usually Reports of p

entries.h: TEACH — WHAT THE PATIENT MUST HEAR
entries.t: STEP 4 · EDUCATE Sublingual nitroglycerin technique and hypoglycemia self-rescue are the two things that save lives at home.

entries.h: ✅ Sublingual nitroglycerin — the technique to teach
entries.t: 🪑 Sit or lie down first. The drug drops blood pressure; standing invites a fall. 👅 Place one tablet under the tongue and let it dissolve — do not chew or swallow it. 📞 If chest pain is unimproved or worsening about 5 minutes after the first dose, call emergency services , then continue as directed — commonly up to a total of three doses, five minutes apart. 🫙 Store in the original dark container , tightly closed, away from heat, light and moisture. Do not decant into a pill organizer. 📅 Note the expiry and replacem

Throbbing headache and flushing are common and reflect vasodilation. Patients often stop the drug because of it — so teach it in advance. 💊 It usually lessens with continued use. 🗣️ Tell patients to report it rather than skip doses, so the prescriber can adjust. 🌀 Dizziness on standing is expected; sit up slowly.

entries.h: 🔒 ARB teaching — almost ACE, with one difference
entries.t: 🧪 Potassium still rises — avoid potassium-based salt substitutes. 🤰 Contraindicated in pregnancy , like ACE inhibitors. 🗣️ Report swelling of the face, lips or tongue — angiedema is far less common, but not impossible. 🫖 The cough is what is missing : an ARB is the usual switch when an ACE inhibitor causes one.

💓 Teach the patient (or caregiver) to take their own radial pulse for a full minute before each dose and to hold and call if it is below the number the prescriber set. 🍽️ Report loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting or diarrhea — these usually come first. 👁️ Report blurred or yellow-green vision, halos around lights . 🍌 Ask before starting or stopping a diuretic, potassium supplement or antacid. ⏰ Take it at the same time each day; do not double up on a missed dose without instruction. 📋 Carry an up-to-date medication

🍽️ Metformin with food reduces the GI upset; extended-release tablets are swallowed whole. 🌅 Sulfonylureas with the first meal of the day — and never skip that meal after taking one. 🍬 Everyone on a sulfonylurea carries a fast-acting carbohydrate. 🍷 Alcohol lowers glucose and can cause a flushing reaction with some sulfonylureas. 🤒 Sick-day rules: illness, vomiting or poor intake change everything — patients need a written plan.

If the question mentions… Think Because Chest pain + a "-afil" drug taken today Hold the nitrate Severe additive hypotension Patch worn continuously, drug "stopped working" Nitrate tolerance Needs a daily nitrate-free interval Persistent dry cough on an antihypertensive Switch to an ARB Bradykinin is not affected by "-sartan" Loss of appetite + halos around lights Digoxin toxicity GI first, then visual Digoxin + furosemide, patient weak and nauseated Check potassium Hypokalemia potentiates digoxin Scheduled for a C

🧪 Check glucose more often — illness usually pushes it up , even when eating less. 💧 Keep fluids going; dehydration is what turns metformin from safe into risky. 📞 Call for persistent vomiting, inability to keep fluids down, or glucose readings outside the range the prescriber set. ❌ Do not simply stop the medication without instruction — but do report that you are ill. 🧠 "Sick days need a written plan, not a guess."

entries.h: 🧾 The two "always ask" questions on this page
entries.t: 💊 Before nitroglycerin: "Have you taken anything for erectile dysfunction or pulmonary hypertension in the last few days?" 🩻 Before contrast imaging: "Are you taking metformin, and what did the ordering team say about holding it?" ⚠️ Both questions are asked before the drug or the scan, not after. They are the highest-yield safety checks in this installment. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 💥 Nitrates Sit down · SL · call for help · never with "-afil" · patch-free interval 🔒 "-sartan" Receptor block · no cough · still ↑K⁺ · not in pregnancy 🫀 Digoxin Apical pulse 1 min · anorexia first · halos · low K⁺ = toxic 🍬 Orals Sulfonylurea = hypoglycemia · metformin = GI & contrast · glitazone = edema · gliptin = pancreatitis

Q1: A man with chest pain says he took tadalafil last night. What do you do about the nitroglycerin order? Show answer Do not give it. Nitrates and PDE-5 inhibitors together can cause profound, hard-to-treat hypotension. Notify the prescriber and report the timing of the dose. Q2: Why is a transdermal nitrate patch removed for part of every day? Show answer To prevent tolerance. A common regimen is wearing it about 12 to 14 hours, then a 10 to 12 hour patch-free interval, usually overnight. Q3: What is the mechanis

entries.h: 🧠 The mnemonics to walk in with
entries.t: "Nitro + afil = no fill" — never combine nitrates with PDE-5 inhibitors. "ACE cuts the supply line; the SARTAN locks the door." "Dig makes it stronger and slower" — and A-B-C-D for its toxicity. "Squeeze, Silence, Sensitize, Signal" — sulfonylurea, metformin, glitazone, gliptin. 🧠 Close the page and rebuild the seven classes from the four mnemonics alone before you move on to installment 5. Set 2 — the harder gases: normal pH, partial compensation, and the mixed disorders NG-193 RESPIRATORY · ACID-BASE ABG Series 4 of 4 ADHD-friendly visual edition Set 1 gave you gases where the pH told you the answer. This set does not. Here the pH is often normal — and a normal pH does not mean a normal patient. It usually means the body has already fixed the problem, and your job is to work out which system caused it and which one did the fixing. When the pH is inside the range, the tie-breaker is 7.40. Above it, b

entries.h: THE METHOD — FIVE STEPS, EVERY TIME
entries.t: STEP 1 · TOOL Same five steps for every gas on this page. Do them in order and never skip step 4.

entries.h: 📏 The reference values you are comparing against
entries.t: pH 7.35–7.45 7.40 = midpoint PaCO₂ 35–45 mmHg · the LUNG value HCO₃⁻ 22–26 mEq/L · the KIDNEY value PaO₂ 80–100 mmHg · oxygenation only ⚠️ These are typical adult reference ranges and they vary between laboratories , with altitude, and with age. Always classify against the range printed on the report you are holding. 🧠 CO₂ is an acid; HCO₃⁻ is a base. High CO₂ pushes pH down. High HCO₃⁻ pushes pH up. Everything on this page follows from those two sentences.

Look at the pH. Below 7.35 = acidemia. Above 7.45 = alkalemia. Inside the range = normal — but keep reading . Look at the PaCO₂ — the respiratory arm. Above 45 = acid. Below 35 = base. Inside = normal. Look at the HCO₃⁻ — the metabolic arm. Below 22 = acid. Above 26 = base. Inside = normal. Match. Which arm points the same way the pH does? That arm is the primary problem . If the pH is normal, compare it to 7.40 to decide which side it leans. If both arms point the same way as each other, it is a mixed disorder. Na

entries.h: 📉 The pH ruler — with the compensation zones marked
entries.t: 🧠 Gas 1 and Gas 8 sit on the exact same pH (7.37) but have opposite primary problems. The pH alone can never finish the job.

entries.h: 🌳 The decision tree — trace it with your finger
🪢 Why "who's winning the tug of war?" actually works
entries.t: 🧠 Compensation never overshoots. The body pulls the pH back toward 7.40 but does not drag it past. That is precisely why the side of 7.40 identifies the culprit.

entries.h: 🧭 ROME, drawn — and the right way round
entries.t: ⚠️ Check you have ROME the right way round. Respiratory = O pposite (pH and CO₂ disagree). Metabolic = E qual (pH and HCO₃⁻ agree). Getting these swapped flips every answer on the page.

entries.h: ✅ Write it down in this order, every single time
entries.t: 1️⃣ pH: low / normal / high — and if normal, above or below 7.40 . 2️⃣ CO₂: acid / normal / base . 3️⃣ HCO₃⁻: acid / normal / base . 4️⃣ Primary: the arm that agrees with the pH direction. 5️⃣ Compensation: none / partial / full. 6️⃣ Then — separately — the PaO₂ . 🧠 Six lines on scrap paper beats trying to hold it all in your head under exam pressure.

entries.h: ❌ The four mistakes that cost the most marks
entries.t: ❌ Stopping at "pH is normal, so this gas is normal." ❌ Forgetting to compare a normal pH to 7.40 . ❌ Calling a mixed disorder "partially compensated." ❌ Never looking at the PaO₂ . ⚠️ Three of those four appear somewhere in the eleven gases below. They are deliberate. 🧮
STEP 2 · PRACTICE Cover the verdict, work the five steps yourself, then uncover. Every answer here was derived from the numbers, not copied.

entries.t: pH 7.37 normal — acid side PaCO₂ 52 HIGH = acid HCO₃⁻ 32 HIGH = base PaO₂ 78 borderline low pH 7.37 sits inside 7.35–7.45 ⇒ no acidemia or alkalemia is being reported. Keep going. PaCO₂ 52 is above 45 ⇒ the respiratory arm is acidic . HCO₃⁻ 32 is above 26 ⇒ the metabolic arm is alkalotic . Both arms are abnormal and pointing opposite ways, so one is the problem and the other is the fix. The pH is 7.37 , which is below 7.40 ⇒ acid is winning ⇒ the acid value (PaCO₂) is the primary. ROME check: respiratory opposite —

entries.t: pH 7.43 normal — base side PaCO₂ 43 normal (top end) HCO₃⁻ 33 HIGH = base PaO₂ 92 normal pH 7.43 is inside the range ⇒ no acidemia or alkalemia reported. PaCO₂ 43 is inside 35–45 ⇒ the respiratory arm is normal . HCO₃⁻ 33 is above 26 ⇒ the metabolic arm is alkalotic . Only one arm is abnormal, so it must be the primary. The pH is 7.43 , above 7.40 ⇒ base is winning, which matches the raised bicarbonate. ROME check: metabolic equal — HCO₃⁻ up, pH up. ✓ ⇒ metabolic alkalosis . The pH is inside the normal range ⇒ by t

entries.h: 🔍 A note on the numbers, so nothing surprises you later
entries.t: On a real analyzer the three values are mathematically linked — pH, PaCO₂ and HCO₃⁻ always hang together, because the bicarbonate is calculated from the other two. Teaching sheets often round each number independently, so a practice trio can be a little "off" from a physiologically exact gas. That does not change anything you do. The classification method is what is being tested , and it gives the same answer either way. Gases 3 to 11 below have been checked to hang together properly. 🧠 If a real gas ever looks int

pH 7.26 LOW = acidemia PaCO₂ 62 HIGH = acid HCO₃⁻ 27 slightly HIGH = base PaO₂ 52 LOW = hypoxemia pH 7.26 is below 7.35 ⇒ acidemia . The pH itself already names the direction. PaCO₂ 62 is well above 45 ⇒ respiratory arm is acidic — it points the same way as the pH. HCO₃⁻ 27 is just above 26 ⇒ metabolic arm is mildly alkalotic — the opposite way. The arm that matches the pH is the respiratory one ⇒ respiratory acidosis . ROME: CO₂ up, pH down — opposite. ✓ The mildly raised bicarbonate is the kidneys trying to help.

entries.h: 🧪 Gas 4 acute anxiety / panic, rapid deep breathing
entries.t: pH 7.53 HIGH = alkalemia PaCO₂ 30 LOW = base HCO₃⁻ 24 normal PaO₂ 101 normal / high-normal pH 7.53 is above 7.45 ⇒ alkalemia . PaCO₂ 30 is below 35 ⇒ respiratory arm is basic (CO₂ has been blown off). HCO₃⁻ 24 is inside 22–26 ⇒ metabolic arm is normal . Only the respiratory arm is abnormal and it points the same way as the pH ⇒ respiratory alkalosis . ROME: CO₂ down, pH up — opposite. ✓ The metabolic arm has not moved at all ⇒ uncompensated . This makes sense: renal compensation takes hours to days , and this probl

pH 7.22 LOW = acidemia PaCO₂ 20 LOW = base HCO₃⁻ 8 VERY LOW = acid PaO₂ 100 normal pH 7.22 is below 7.35 ⇒ acidemia , and a marked one. PaCO₂ 20 is below 35 ⇒ respiratory arm is basic — the opposite direction to the pH, so it is not the cause. HCO₃⁻ 8 is far below 22 ⇒ metabolic arm is strongly acidic — same direction as the pH. The metabolic arm matches ⇒ metabolic acidosis . ROME: metabolic equal — HCO₃⁻ down, pH down. ✓ The very low CO₂ is the lungs compensating by hyperventilating (this is what Kussmaul respira

entries.t: pH 7.47 HIGH = alkalemia PaCO₂ 48 HIGH = acid HCO₃⁻ 34 HIGH = base PaO₂ 86 normal pH 7.47 is above 7.45 ⇒ alkalemia . PaCO₂ 48 is above 45 ⇒ respiratory arm is acidic — the opposite direction to the pH. HCO₃⁻ 34 is above 26 ⇒ metabolic arm is basic — the same direction as the pH. ROME: metabolic equal — HCO₃⁻ up, pH up. ✓ The raised CO₂ is the lungs hypoventilating on purpose to hold acid in. The other arm has clearly moved b

entries.h: 🧪 Gas 7 long-standing hyperventilation (e.g. chronic hypoxic drive)
entries.t: pH 7.42 normal — base side PaCO₂ 30 LOW = base HCO₃⁻ 19 LOW = acid PaO₂ 96 normal pH 7.42 is inside the range ⇒ no acidemia or alkalemia reported. This is where students stop too early. PaCO₂ 30 is below 35 ⇒ respiratory arm is basic . HCO₃⁻ 19 is below 22 ⇒ metabolic arm is acidic . Both arms abnormal, opposite directions. Tie-break on 7.40 : the pH is 7.42 , above it ⇒ base is winning ⇒ the base value (the low CO₂) is primary ⇒ respiratory alkalosis . ROME: CO₂ down, pH drifting up — opposite. ✓ pH is back inside

pH 7.37 normal — acid side PaCO₂ 32 LOW = base HCO₃⁻ 18 LOW = acid PaO₂ 92 normal pH 7.37 is inside the range — the same pH as Gas 1 , and the answer will be completely different. PaCO₂ 32 is below 35 ⇒ respiratory arm is basic . HCO₃⁻ 18 is below 22 ⇒ metabolic arm is acidic . Both abnormal, opposite ways. Tie-break: pH 7.37 is below 7.40 ⇒ acid is winning ⇒ the acid value is primary. Here the acid value is the bicarbonate , not the CO₂ ⇒ metabolic acidosis . ROME: metabolic equal — HCO₃⁻ down, pH down. ✓ The low
STEP 3 · LEVEL UP When both arms point the same way, nobody is compensating — and that is its own diagnosis.

pH 7.04 VERY LOW = acidemia PaCO₂ 58 HIGH = acid HCO₃⁻ 15 LOW = acid PaO₂ 42 SEVERELY LOW pH 7.04 ⇒ profound acidemia . PaCO₂ 58 is high ⇒ respiratory arm is acidic . HCO₃⁻ 15 is low ⇒ metabolic arm is acidic too. Both arms point the same way as the pH. There is no "other arm" left to be the compensator — both systems are contributing ⇒ this is a mixed (combined) acidosis . Ventilation has failed and tissue hypoperfusion is generating lactic acid. Compensation is absent by definition : a mixed disorder has no compe

pH 7.55 HIGH = alkalemia PaCO₂ 33 LOW = base HCO₃⁻ 28 HIGH = base PaO₂ 97 normal pH 7.55 ⇒ marked alkalemia . PaCO₂ 33 is below 35 ⇒ respiratory arm is basic . HCO₃⁻ 28 is above 26 ⇒ metabolic arm is basic as well. Both arms are pushing the pH the same way ⇒ mixed (combined) alkalosis . In practice: acid lost from the stomach and CO₂ blown off — for example a ventilated post-operative patient on continuous NG suction. No compensating arm exists ⇒ compensation absent . Answer Mixed (combined) respiratory and metabol

pH 7.39 normal PaCO₂ 41 normal HCO₃⁻ 24 normal PaO₂ 66 LOW = hypoxemia pH 7.39 inside the range. PaCO₂ 41 inside 35–45 ⇒ respiratory arm normal. HCO₃⁻ 24 inside 22–26 ⇒ metabolic arm normal. Nothing is abnormal and nothing is compensating ⇒ the acid–base status is normal . There is nothing to compensate for, so no compensation label applies. But look at the fourth number: PaO₂ 66 is well below 80 ⇒ hypoxemia . This patient has a real, treatable problem that the acid–base analysis completely missed. Answer Normal ac

entries.h: 🗺️ All eleven gases on one plot
entries.t: 🧠 Diagonal = compensation. Same corner = mixed. If a point sits top-right or bottom-left, one system is helping the other. If it sits top-left or bottom-right, both systems are pushing the same way and nobody is helping.

entries.h: 📊 The three compensation states, side by side
entries.t: 🧠 "Full" does not mean "better." A fully compensated gas often means the disorder has been present for a long time. The patient is stable, not cured. 🩺

entries.h: SO WHAT? — WHAT THE GAS MEANS FOR THE PATIENT
entries.t: STEP 4 · ACT Naming the disorder is half the answer. The other half is which system to look at and how fast.

entries.h: 🫁🫘 Who fixes what, and how fast
entries.t: 🧠 Speed is a diagnostic clue. A fully compensated respiratory problem has been there for days. An uncompensated one started today.

entries.h: 🫁 Respiratory acidosis — what you actually do
entries.t: The problem is ventilation. CO₂ is not being blown off. 🛏️ Position upright; encourage deep breathing and effective coughing. 🫧 Look for the cause: airway obstruction, sedation/opioids, atelectasis, pneumonia, COPD exacerbation, chest-wall or neuromuscular weakness. 📈 Monitor level of consciousness — rising CO₂ makes patients drowsy and confused before they arrest. 🆘 Escalate for non-invasive or invasive ventilatory support when the pH keeps falling. ⚠️ In a chronic CO₂ retainer, oxygen is titrated carefully to the

entries.h: 🌬️ Respiratory alkalosis — what you actually do
entries.t: The problem is over-ventilation. CO₂ is being blown off faster than it is made. 🧘 Coach slow, controlled breathing; stay with the patient; reduce stimulation. 🔎 Rule out the dangerous causes before calling it anxiety: hypoxemia, pain, fever, sepsis, pulmonary embolism, salicylate toxicity , and over-set ventilator rates. 🖐️ Expect tingling around the mouth and in the fingers, light-headedness, carpopedal spasm. 🧠 Hyperventilation is a symptom. Ask what the body is trying to fix before you try to slow it down.

entries.h: 🧪 Metabolic acidosis — what you actually do
entries.t: Acid is being made or base is being lost. 🍬 Think DKA , lactic acidosis from shock or hypoxia, kidney failure, severe diarrhea (bicarbonate lost in stool), some poisonings. 💨 Kussmaul respirations — deep, rapid, sighing breaths — are compensation, not distress to be suppressed. 🧪 Check potassium: acidosis tends to shift potassium out of cells, so the serum value can look normal or high while total body potassium is low. 💧 Treat the cause — fluids, insulin, perfusion, dialysis as indicated.

entries.h: 🤮 Metabolic alkalosis — what you actually do
entries.t: Acid is being lost or base is being gained. 🤢 Think vomiting, prolonged NG suction , excessive diuretic use, potassium depletion, excessive alkali intake. 🧪 Watch potassium, chloride, magnesium and volume status — these usually need correcting for the alkalosis to resolve. 😖 Expect tingling, muscle twitching, tremor, tetany, and confusion in severe cases. 🫁 Compensation is limited: the patient cannot hypoventilate indefinitely.

entries.h: ✅ Getting the sample right — the part that ruins gases
entries.t: 🩸 Arterial sample, drawn per policy; apply firm pressure afterwards for the time your facility specifies, and longer if the patient is anticoagulated. 🫧 Expel air bubbles immediately — trapped air changes the PaO₂ and PaCO₂. ⏱️ Send it straight away ; delay allows continued cell metabolism and shifts the values. 📝 Document the oxygen delivery and flow rate at the moment of sampling — a PaO₂ means nothing without it. 🖐️ Check circulation to the hand before and after a radial puncture, per policy. ⚠️ A venous sample

entries.h: 🧍 What acidosis and alkalosis look like at the bedside
entries.t: 🧠 "Down and drowsy, up and twitchy." A falling pH depresses the nervous system; a rising pH makes it irritable. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🧠 ROME R espiratory O pposite · M etabolic E qual ⚖️ Normal pH? Compare to 7.40 . Below = acid winning. Above = base winning. 🕰️ Speed Lungs compensate in minutes. Kidneys take hours to days. 🔀 Same direction = MIXED Both arms acid, or both base ⇒ two problems, no compensator.

entries.h: 📋 The answer key for this set — cover it and rebuild it
entries.t: Gas pH / CO₂ / HCO₃⁻ Primary disorder Compensation 1 7.37 / 52 / 32 Respiratory acidosis Fully compensated 2 7.43 / 43 / 33 Metabolic alkalosis Fully compensated (pH normal; CO₂ only at the top of range) 3 7.26 / 62 / 27 Respiratory acidosis Partially compensated (+ hypoxemia) 4 7.53 / 30 / 24 Respiratory alkalosis Uncompensated 5 7.22 / 20 / 8 Metabolic acidosis Partially compensated 6 7.47 / 48 / 34 Metabolic alkalosis Partially compensated 7 7.42 / 30 / 19 Respiratory alkalosis Fully compensated 8 7.37 / 32 / 18

Q1: State ROME correctly and say what each half means. Show answer Respiratory Opposite, Metabolic Equal. In a respiratory disorder the pH and the PaCO₂ move in opposite directions. In a metabolic disorder the pH and the HCO₃⁻ move in the same direction. Q2: The pH is 7.38, PaCO₂ is 50 and HCO₃⁻ is 30. What is it? Show answer pH is normal but below 7.40, so acid is winning. The acid value is the PaCO₂, so the primary problem is respiratory acidosis, and because the pH is back in range it is fully compensated. Q3: W

entries.h: 🧠 Take these four lines into the exam
entries.t: ROME — Respiratory Opposite, Metabolic Equal. "7.40 breaks the tie." Normal pH? Look which side of 7.40 it sits on. "Same direction = mixed." Both values acid, or both base, means two problems. "Minutes vs days." Lungs compensate fast; kidneys compensate slowly — so full compensation means chronic. 🧠 Then finish the set: NG-092 (the method) · NG-138 (practice gases) · NG-173 (worked answers I) . PPIs · H2 Blockers · Antiemetics · GI Protectant · GI Stimulant · Statins · Miscellaneous Antilipidemics NG-203 PHARM · GI + LIPIDS Series: NCLEX Drug Review 5 of 8 ADHD-friendly visual edition Two systems, one page. The GI half is a tour of the stomach: turn acid off at the pump, turn it down at the receptor, coat what is already damaged, and move the contents along. The lipid half is about interrupting cholesterol in three different places — made in the liver, absorbed in the gut, or recycled through bile. Match

"-tidine" → H2 blocker. "-statin" → HMG-CoA reductase. "-setron" → 5-HT3 antiemetic. "-fibrate"/gemfibrozil → fibric acid.
