entries.h: 🍽️ The map — where every GI drug on this page acts
entries.t: 🧠 Off, down, coat, move. PPI turns acid off · H2 blocker turns it down · sucralfate coats the damage · metoclopramide moves the contents on. ⚙️
STEP 2 · MECHANISM Acid, nausea, mucosal repair, motility — then the three interruption points for cholesterol.

Action: block the final common step of gastric acid production — the H⁺/K⁺-ATPase proton pump on the parietal cell. Whatever the stimulus (histamine, gastrin, acetylcholine, food), the last door is shut. 🎯 Used for GERD, peptic and duodenal ulcers, as part of H. pylori regimens, and to protect a stressed stomach. ⏰ Most oral PPIs work best taken before a meal — commonly about 30 to 60 minutes before the first meal of the day. 💊 Delayed-release capsules and tablets are swallowed whole ; do not crush or chew. 🧠 "PRAZ

Action: competitively inhibit histamine at H2 receptor sites on the parietal cell ⇒ less acid secretion, especially the nocturnal and basal output. 📉 Weaker and shorter-acting than a PPI, but faster to start working. 🌙 Often dosed with or after meals and at bedtime. 🧓 Older adults with renal impairment can become confused on H2 blockers — dose is adjusted for kidney function. 🧠 Dimmer switch vs off switch. H2 blocker = dimmer. PPI = off switch.

entries.h: 🤢 Antiemetics — the nausea pathway and where each drug plugs in
entries.t: 🧠 "Setron stops serotonin; Phenergan parks dopamine." Different receptors is why they can be used together when one alone is not enough.

entries.h: 🩹 Sucralfate — a bandage, not an antacid
entries.t: ⚠️ Sucralfate needs an acid environment to form its paste and it binds other drugs . It is given on an empty stomach, typically about an hour before meals and at bedtime, and other oral medicines are separated from it — commonly by about two hours. Check the specific product and facility guidance.

Action: increases the resting tone of the lower esophageal sphincter and promotes gastric emptying and intestinal transit. It also blocks dopamine in the CTZ, so it works as an antiemetic. 🍽️ Used for diabetic gastroparesis , GERD and nausea when the stomach is not emptying. ⏰ Usually given before meals and at bedtime. ⚠️ Boxed warning: tardive dyskinesia. Risk rises with duration and cumulative dose, and the movements can be irreversible. Treatment is generally kept short — commonly no more than about 12 weeks.

entries.h: 💪 Statins — cutting cholesterol production at the top of the assembly line
entries.t: 🧠 "Statins stop the START." HMG-CoA reductase is an early step, so blocking it shuts the whole line down.

entries.h: 🧬 The other three lipid drugs — three different addresses
entries.t: 🧠 "Made, absorbed, recycled." Statins stop cholesterol being made ; ezetimibe stops it being absorbed ; cholestyramine stops bile acids being recycled ; fibrates target triglycerides .

entries.h: 📈 Which lipid drug moves which number
entries.t: 🧠 Statin for LDL, fibrate for triglycerides. That single sentence answers most lipid-drug selection questions.

entries.h: 🦠 Where acid drugs fit in H. pylori treatment
entries.t: Ulcer disease is frequently caused by Helicobacter pylori . Acid suppression alone will not cure it — the organism must be treated with antibiotics as well. 💊 Regimens combine a PPI with two or more antibiotics , sometimes with bismuth. The exact combination varies by guideline and local resistance. ⏳ Finish the entire course — stopping early is the main reason treatment fails. 🧪 Confirmation of eradication is done after therapy, per the prescriber's plan. 🧠 Acid drugs heal the crater; antibiotics remove the cause.

entries.h: 🧊 Antacids are not on this page — and that matters
entries.t: Antacids neutralize acid that already exists . The drugs on this page reduce or block acid production , or coat tissue. They are not interchangeable. ⚠️ Antacids also interfere with absorption of many drugs — including sucralfate, which is usually separated from an antacid by about 30 minutes. Check the specific instruction.

entries.h: 💉 IV pantoprazole in the acute setting
entries.t: 🩸 Used for upper GI bleeding and when the oral route is not available. 🎛️ Given per protocol as an intermittent infusion or continuous infusion, with a dedicated line or a documented compatibility check. 🧪 Monitor hemoglobin, hematocrit and hemodynamics — the drug does not replace resuscitation or endoscopy. 🧠 Protonix is the PPI you are most likely to hang as an infusion. 🚨
STEP 3 · ASSESS Three things on this page can seriously injure a patient: promethazine in a vein, metoclopramide over time, and a statin in a muscle.

entries.h: 🧍 Body map — where this page's adverse effects appear

entries.t: Promethazine is severely irritating to tissue. Extravasation or inadvertent intra-arterial injection can cause burning, blistering, tissue necrosis and gangrene , sometimes requiring amputation. 💉 Deep intramuscular injection into a large muscle is the preferred parenteral route. 🚫 Never give it subcutaneously or intra-arterially. 🩸 If IV is used, follow the facility's dilution and slow-administration protocol, use a large patent vein, and stop immediately if the patient reports burning or pain. 👶 It carries a boxe

Muscle breakdown releases myoglobin, which can injure the kidneys. 💪 Unexplained muscle pain, tenderness or weakness — especially if widespread. 🚽 Dark, tea- or cola-colored urine. 🧪 Creatine kinase rises; renal function is monitored. 📞 Teach patients to report muscle symptoms rather than wait for the next appointment. ⚠️ Risk increases with higher doses , with fibrates (gemfibrozil in particular), and with drugs that raise statin levels.

Because it blocks dopamine, metoclopramide can cause extrapyramidal symptoms — restlessness (akathisia), dystonic reactions, a Parkinson-like picture — and, with longer use, tardive dyskinesia . 👄 Look for lip smacking, tongue protrusion, grimacing, involuntary limb movements. ⏳ Risk rises with duration and cumulative dose; treatment is usually limited to about 12 weeks. 🧓 Older adults and women are described as higher-risk groups. 🧠 "Reglan moves the gut — and sometimes the face."

💓 Can prolong the QT interval — extra caution with electrolyte abnormalities, other QT-prolonging drugs, or known long-QT. 🤕 Headache and constipation are the common effects. 🧪 Correct low potassium and magnesium where they exist. 🧠 Zofran is the "clean" antiemetic — not sedating, not dopaminergic — which is exactly why it is chosen so often.

PPIs are safe and effective short-term. With prolonged use, watch for: 🧪 Low magnesium ; reduced absorption of vitamin B12 , iron and calcium. 🦴 Increased fracture risk described with long-term, high-dose use. 🦠 Increased risk of C. difficile and community-acquired pneumonia. 💊 Omeprazole can blunt clopidogrel activation — pantoprazole is often chosen instead. ⚠️ "Chronic reflux, been on omeprazole for years, now numb and tingling" — think B12. Do not dismiss long-term acid suppression as harmless.

entries.h: 🧲 The drugs that bind other drugs
entries.t: Sucralfate and cholestyramine both physically stick to things in the gut — including other medications. ⏰ Separate other oral drugs from them; a common instruction is about 2 hours apart, but the exact interval depends on the drug. 🥛 Cholestyramine also binds fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) . 💧 Cholestyramine powder is always mixed with fluid and never taken dry — the powder can cause esophageal irritation or obstruction. 🧠 "Sticky drugs need space." 📋

entries.h: TEACH — WHAT THE PATIENT MUST HEAR
entries.t: STEP 4 · EDUCATE Timing is the whole game on this page — before meals, after meals, at bedtime, or two hours away from everything else.

entries.h: ⏰ The timing table — memorize this block
entries.t: Drug When Why PPI (omeprazole, pantoprazole, esomeprazole) Before a meal — commonly 30–60 min before the first meal The pump is most active when a meal is coming H2 blocker (famotidine) With or after meals and/or at bedtime Covers meal-related and nocturnal acid Sucralfate Empty stomach — commonly about 1 hour before meals and at bedtime Needs acid to form its paste; food gets in the way Metoclopramide Before meals and at bedtime Works on the stomach that is about to fill Cholestyramine Mixed in fluid, with meals;

💪 Report any unexplained muscle pain, tenderness or weakness, and dark urine, straight away. 🧪 Liver enzymes are checked at baseline and as clinically indicated; report jaundice, dark urine with pale stools, or right-upper-quadrant pain. 🍊 Grapefruit raises levels of some statins — simvastatin and atorvastatin in particular. Rosuvastatin is much less affected. 🤰 Avoid in pregnancy. 🥗 The drug does not replace diet, exercise and smoking cessation — it is added to them. 🧠 "Muscles and liver." Two words cover almost a

💧 Always mix the powder in water, juice or another fluid; let it stand a moment, then drink. 🚫 Never swallow the dry powder — it can cause choking, esophageal irritation or obstruction. 💩 Expect constipation and bloating; increase fluid and fiber, and report severe constipation. 💊 Space other medications and fat-soluble vitamins away from the dose.

🚗 Promethazine causes marked drowsiness — no driving or hazardous activity. 👄 Dry mouth, blurred vision and constipation are the anticholinergic effects. 🍷 Alcohol and other CNS depressants stack with it. 🩺 Report any involuntary movements, muscle stiffness, or a "restless, can't-sit-still" feeling.

entries.h: 🍽️ Lifestyle teaching that goes with the GI half
entries.t: 🛏️ Elevate the head of the bed; avoid lying down for about 3 hours after eating. 🍫 Reduce known triggers — large fatty meals, chocolate, peppermint, caffeine, alcohol, citrus, tomato. 🚭 Smoking cessation matters: nicotine lowers esophageal sphincter tone and impairs ulcer healing. 💊 Review NSAID use — a major cause of ulcers that no acid suppressant fully undoes.

If the question mentions… Think Because Burning at the IV site during an antiemetic push Stop promethazine now Extravasation risk of severe tissue injury Lip smacking and tongue movements after weeks of a GI drug Metoclopramide Tardive dyskinesia Muscle aches + dark urine on a lipid drug Statin rhabdomyolysis Myoglobin release "Take it an hour before meals and don't take it with your other pills" Sucralfate Needs acid; binds other drugs Powder that must be mixed with fluid Cholestyramine Never taken dry Diabetic wi

entries.h: ⚠️ Statin + fibrate — the combination to question
entries.t: Adding a fibric acid derivative to a statin raises the risk of myopathy and rhabdomyolysis , and the risk is described as highest with gemfibrozil . 💪 Reinforce muscle-symptom teaching whenever both are on the list. 🧪 Renal function and creatine kinase are followed more closely. 📞 Any new muscle pain in a patient on both is reported, not observed. 🧠 Two lipid drugs = double the muscle homework.

Zetia works in the intestine, not the liver, so it is often added to a statin when LDL is still above target, or used alone when a statin is not tolerated. 🍽️ Can be taken with or without food. 🧲 If a bile acid sequestrant is also prescribed, ezetimibe is spaced away from it. 💪 Muscle symptoms are still reported, especially in combination therapy.

entries.h: 🚩 GI alarm symptoms that outrank any pill
entries.t: 🩸 Vomiting blood or coffee-ground material; black tarry stools. 🍽️ Trouble swallowing, food sticking, unintentional weight loss. 😖 Severe or sudden abdominal pain; a rigid, board-like abdomen. 😵 New anemia, dizziness or fainting. ⚠️ Never treat these as "reflux that needs a stronger antacid." They require assessment, not a dose change. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🔌 Off, down, coat, move PPI · H2 blocker · sucralfate · metoclopramide 💉 Phenergan burns Stop at the first report of pain at the site 🧲 Sticky drugs need space Sucralfate & cholestyramine bind other medicines 💪 Muscles & liver The two statin monitoring words

Q1: What exactly does a proton pump inhibitor block, and why is that stronger than an H2 blocker? Show answer It blocks the H⁺/K⁺-ATPase proton pump, the final step of acid production, so acid is shut off no matter which stimulus triggered it. An H2 blocker only blocks the histamine pathway. Q2: When is sucralfate given and why? Show answer On an empty stomach — commonly about an hour before meals and at bedtime — because it needs acid to form its protective paste, and food and other drugs interfere with it. Q3: A

entries.h: 🧠 The mnemonics to walk in with
entries.t: "Off, down, coat, move" — PPI, H2 blocker, sucralfate, metoclopramide. "Setron stops serotonin; Phenergan parks dopamine." "Made, absorbed, recycled" — statin, ezetimibe, cholestyramine (and fibrate for triglycerides). "Sticky drugs need space" — sucralfate and cholestyramine. 🧠 Rebuild the seven groups from those four lines before moving on to installment 6. Non-Steroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drugs NG-256 PHARMACOLOGY ADHD-friendly visual edition NSAIDs block the COX enzyme to stop prostaglandins from being made — that kills pain, fever, and inflammation . The catch: prostaglandins also protect the stomach, kidneys, and platelets , so blocking them broadly causes the three big NSAID dangers — GI bleed, renal injury, and cardiovascular risk . See also NG-100 Anti-inflammatory Agents (overview) and NG-232 Acetaminophen , the drug NSAIDs get swapped for when these risks are
STEP 1 · COX-1 vs COX-2 One enzyme, two jobs — protecting the body and causing the pain. NSAIDs can't fully tell the difference.

MECHANISM Nonselective NSAIDs block BOTH COX-1 and COX-2 — that's why they work fast but also cause GI/renal side effects. 🧠 "COX-1 keeps you safe, COX-2 makes you hurt." Nonselective NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen, ketorolac, aspirin) block both = pain relief AND stomach/kidney risk. COX-2 selective agents were built to spare COX-1 — but trade GI safety for cardiovascular risk.

Drug Notes Ibuprofen OTC, most common Naproxen Longer half-life Indomethacin Strong anti-inflammatory, gout Ketorolac (Toradol) Injectable, short-term only — high GI bleed risk Aspirin (salicylic/acetylsalicylic acid) Irreversibly inhibits platelets — antiplatelet effect 🧠 "-profen" and "-oxicam" style names, plus Toradol and aspirin by name — these are the ones the NCLEX expects you to recognize on sight.

🔥 Anti-inflammatory & antipyretic (fever reducer) 🦴 Rheumatoid arthritis & osteoarthritis — relieves joint pain/swelling 🦶 Gout — effective; a client stating "I can use ibuprofen or naproxen for gout pain" shows correct understanding 🩹 Mild-to-moderate pain, dysmenorrhea, headache 🧠 "AIF" — A nalgesic, I nflammation-fighter, F ever-reducer. Three jobs, one drug class. 🚨
STEP 2 · THE 3 BIG DANGERS GI, renal, cardiovascular — and the interaction that combines two of them into one kidney emergency.

entries.h: 🚨 The "Triple Whammy" — NSAID + ACE inhibitor/ARB + Diuretic
entries.t: The single most-tested NSAID interaction. Each drug reduces kidney blood flow/pressure by a different route — stack all three and the kidney can lose perfusion fast. 🧠 "Triple Whammy" = NSAID + ACE-I/ARB + Diuretic. Teach clients: "I will call my HCP before taking ibuprofen" if they're on a blood pressure pill and a water pill — that statement is a CORRECT understanding on an exam.

Loss of COX-1's protective mucus/bicarbonate layer → erosion, ulceration, bleeding. ✅ Take NSAIDs with food — do NOT take on an empty stomach ⚠️ Higher risk: elderly, prior PUD, combined with aspirin, corticosteroids, or anticoagulants 👀 Watch for: coffee-ground emesis, melena (black tarry stool), ↓ Hgb/Hct 🧠 A client on ranitidine (an H2 blocker acid reducer) plus an NSAID for their acid reflux is being managed correctly — the acid reducer protects the stomach while the NSAID is used.

Prostaglandins keep the afferent arteriole dilated — block them and kidney perfusion drops, especially with long-term use or in an already-volume-depleted client. 🧪 Rising creatinine above the normal range 🚽 Oliguria — urine output trending toward < 30 mL/hr , a classic oliguria threshold 📞 Client teaching gold standard: "I will call my HCP before taking ibuprofen" if they have kidney disease, heart failure, or are on ACE-I/ARB + diuretic 🧠 NSAIDs are "NOT good for the body" in one line: kidneys, heart failure, ast

entries.h: ❤️ Cardiovascular risk — worse with COX-2 selective agents
entries.t: 📈 Worsening HTN and CHF — NSAIDs cause fluid retention and blunt the effect of antihypertensives 🫀 COX-2 selective NSAIDs (e.g. celecoxib) carry the highest cardiovascular risk — increased MI/stroke risk 🩸 Thrombosis risk — "sticky blood," increased clot risk with COX-2 selective agents specifically (unlike aspirin, which is antiplatelet) ⚠️ Use caution or avoid in clients with known CHF or HTN 🧠 "Swelling heart, HTN worsening" — remember NSAIDs both raise blood pressure AND make the heart work against more fluid.

Trap What to know 🫁 Asthma worsening NSAID-exacerbated respiratory disease — some asthmatics react with bronchospasm 🧒 Avoid aspirin in children Risk of Reye's syndrome if given during a viral illness (flu, chickenpox) — use acetaminophen instead 👂 Early sign of salicylate (aspirin) toxicity Tinnitus — ringing in the ears; report to HCP 🩸 Increased bleed risk Aspirin's antiplatelet effect is irreversible for the life of the platelet (~7–10 days) 🧠 "A-A-A" — A void kids' A spirin = A void Reye's. And if the ears sta
STEP 3 · SAFE USE Correct client statements the NCLEX rewards — and the ones that should trigger more teaching.

entries.h: ✅ Client statements that show correct understanding
entries.t: 1 🍽️ "I don't take ibuprofen on an empty stomach." — take with food 2 📞 "I will call my HCP before taking ibuprofen" — if on ACE-I/ARB + diuretic, or has kidney/heart disease 3 🦴 "I can use ibuprofen or naproxen for gout pain." — NSAIDs are appropriate for gout flares 4 🩹 "I take occasional ibuprofen for my knees." — appropriate PRN use for mild joint pain 🧠 These four statements are the ones an NCLEX question rewards as "the teaching was effective" — memorize the pattern, not just the words.

🚫 Empty stomach always take with food 🧒 Aspirin in kids Reye's syndrome 💊 NSAID + ACE-I + diuretic triple whammy 🩸 With anticoagulants bleed risk stacks 🧠 Every item on this list either strips the stomach's protection or stacks a bleed/kidney risk .

🧪 Creatinine — rising above baseline = renal injury 🚽 Urine output — trending down toward oliguria 🩸 Hgb/Hct — dropping = possible GI bleed 👂 Tinnitus — early clinical sign of aspirin/salicylate toxicity, report immediately 🧠 "Cr up, urine down, Hgb down, ears ringing" — four red flags, four different organ systems, one drug class.

entries.h: 🔀 When NSAIDs get swapped for acetaminophen
entries.t: Acetaminophen has minimal effect on platelets and no significant GI erosion risk, so it is preferred over NSAIDs in: 🩸 Clients with hemophilia or other bleeding disorders 🫙 Clients with peptic ulcer disease 🧒 Children with viral illness (flu) — avoids Reye's risk from aspirin Tylenol and NSAIDs can be used interchangeably to reduce fever — when one reaches its max daily dose, the other can be alternated in. See NG-232 Acetaminophen for the liver-toxicity side of that trade-off. 🧠 "Bleeder or ulcer? Reach for Tyleno

SAY IT OUT LOUD ⚖️ COX-1 protects, COX-2 inflames Nonselective NSAIDs block both 🩸 GI bleed #1 risk — always take with food 💧 Renal risk Watch Cr & urine output, esp. long-term use 🚨 Triple whammy NSAID + ACE-I/ARB + diuretic = AKI risk

Q1: Why do NSAIDs cause both pain relief and stomach/kidney damage? Show answer Nonselective NSAIDs block both COX-1 (protective — stomach lining, renal blood flow, platelets) and COX-2 (inflammatory) — the same mechanism causes the benefit and the harm. Q2: What three drug classes together create the "triple whammy" nephrotoxic combo? Show answer NSAID + ACE inhibitor (or ARB) + diuretic — each reduces renal perfusion by a different mechanism. Q3: A child has the flu. Which OTC pain/fever reducer should be avoided

Mu-Receptor Agonists for Severe Pain NG-257 Pharmacology ADHD-friendly visual edition Opioids bind mu (μ) receptors in the brain, spinal cord, and gut to block pain signals — used for severe pain , not inflammation or fever. The whole topic is one trade: great pain relief for a predictable list of side effects, and respiratory depression is always the #1 priority . 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🚨 RR < 12 Hold the dose, stay with the patient, notify the HCP. 💉 Naloxone (Narcan) The antidote — a mu-rec
STEP 1 · THE MECHANISM One receptor family explains the drug class, the effects, AND the antidote.

entries.h: 🔑 Opioids are the KEY, mu (μ) receptors are the LOCK
entries.t: 🧠 "Same lock, whole-body effects." Because mu receptors sit in the brain (pain + sedation), the brainstem (breathing), and the gut (motility), one drug class explains almost every side effect on this page.

Opioids treat severe acute or chronic pain — post-op, trauma, cancer, MI. They are not anti-inflammatory and not antipyretic (that's NSAIDs/acetaminophen's job). 🧠 If the stem says "reduces fever" or "anti-inflammatory," it is NOT an opioid — cross it off.

mOrphine sulfate hydrOmOrphOne Dilaudid OxycOdOne Roxicodone OxyCOntin ER oxycodone cOdeine weaker, often combo Fentanyl synthetic, very potent Hydrocodone often combo product Methadone long half-life 🧠 "Full of O's, full of opioid." mOrphine → hydrOmOrphOne → OxycOdOne → OxyCOntin. Spot 2+ O's in a drug name on a med list = think opioid.

CLASS: Opioid / narcotic analgesic, Schedule II controlled substance (most agents). ACTION: Agonist at mu (and kappa/delta) opioid receptors → blocks pain transmission & perception. 🧠 Robo's map: Class → Action → Watch. If you can say what family a drug is in and what it changes, you can predict everything it watches for. 🚨
STEP 2 · LOW & SLOW Every adverse effect is a body system slowing down — memorize them as "low and slow."
🧠 "LOW & SLOW" — Low RR, Low BP, Low brain (sedation) + Slow gut (constipation), Slow everything else. If you can name the mu-receptor locations, you already know this list.
🧠 Assess RR BEFORE every dose — count for a full 60 seconds in a sedated patient. Depth matters too: shallow, irregular breathing is a red flag even above 12 .

entries.h: 😴 CNS sedation — the earliest warning sign
entries.t: Easily falls asleep mid-conversation — earlier & more sensitive than RR alone Unarousable = medical emergency, do not give another dose Use a validated sedation scale (e.g., POSS) — sedation always precedes respiratory arrest 🧠 Sedation is the smoke detector; apnea is the fire. Catch a rising sedation score before RR ever drops.

Opioids cause vasodilation → drop in BP on standing Dizzy / lightheaded on standing → assist to a seated position immediately Never let the patient get up unassisted 🧠 "Rise slow, or you'll fall low." Change positions slowly; dangle legs before standing.

N/V: opioids stimulate the chemoreceptor trigger zone — give antiemetic PRN, especially with first doses. Pruritus: caused by histamine release from mast cells — not necessarily a true allergy. Treat with antihistamine; document carefully so "allergy" isn't charted incorrectly. 🧠 Itching after morphine ≠ automatic allergy label — assess for hives, swelling, or anaphylaxis before charting "allergic."

entries.h: ⚠️ Who is at highest risk of respiratory arrest?
entries.t: 👵 Advanced age 70 and older 🫁 COPD / asthma underlying lung disease 🩹 First 24h post-op peak risk window 💊 Opioid-naive no built tolerance 🌙 CNS depressant combo benzos, alcohol, sleep meds 😴 Sleep apnea OSA 🧠 "Old, obstructed, opioid-naive, first day, and drugged twice." Any one of these on the chart = escalate your monitoring frequency. 🩺
STEP 3 · NALOXONE + PREVENTION One antidote reverses the emergency; one bowel plan prevents the everyday problem.

Mechanism: competitive mu-receptor antagonist — knocks the opioid off the receptor and reverses sedation, respiratory depression, and pupil changes. Naloxone's effect lasts roughly 30–90 minutes — usually shorter than the opioid it is reversing. The patient can re-sedate ("renarcotize") once it wears off, so frequent reassessment and repeat dosing must continue well past the first response. 🧠 "Narcan naps first." Naloxone falls asleep before the opioid does — never assume one dose is the end of monitoring.

1 🅰️ Assess ABCs — airway, breathing, circulation first 2 💨 Oxygen — support ventilation/oxygenation 3 💉 Give naloxone per order/protocol, titrate to breathing — not full alertness 4 📞 Notify HCP and prepare for a repeat dose if sedation/RR drop again 🧠 "ABC before Narcan." Airway/breathing/oxygen come first — naloxone doesn't help a completely obstructed airway.

Can precipitate acute withdrawal in opioid-dependent patients: agitation, pain surge, hypertension, GI cramping Give in small, titrated amounts when the goal is adequate breathing , not full pain return Reassess sedation & RR frequently — do not leave the room after one good reading Available IV, IM, subcutaneous, and intranasal (community/OD-reversal kits) 🧠 Reversing too fast = a wide-awake patient in severe pain and withdrawal. Titrate to breathing, not to a smile.

Start PRN/scheduled stool softener + stimulant laxative on day one of opioid therapy — do not wait for symptoms. Unlike sedation or nausea, constipation does not build tolerance and will persist for the entire course of therapy. 🧠 KEY TERM: CONSTIPATION. If a care plan lists opioid teaching and stool softeners aren't on it, the plan is incomplete.

❌ No driving or operating machinery until effects are known ❌ Avoid alcohol and other CNS depressants (sedative-additive, respiratory arrest risk) ⚠️ Fall risk — call for help before getting up, especially first 24–48h 📋 Take a proactive bowel regimen for the entire duration of therapy 📞 Report new confusion, RR change, or extreme drowsiness right away 🧠 "Slow down, don't drive, don't drink, don't stand alone." Four rules cover almost every opioid safety NCLEX stem. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🚨 RR < 12 Hold dose · stay · notify HCP 💉 Naloxone Mu-antagonist antidote — wears off before most opioids 💩 Constipation Doesn't build tolerance — prevent from day 1 😴 Sedation first Falling asleep mid-sentence beats RR drop as the earliest sign

Q1: What is the #1 priority adverse effect of opioids, and the hold parameter? Show answer Respiratory depression — hold the dose if RR is below 12/min, stay with the patient, and notify the HCP. Q2: What is the antidote for opioid overdose, and why can't you walk away after one dose? Show answer Naloxone (Narcan), a mu-receptor antagonist. Its effect (~30–90 min) is usually shorter than the opioid's, so the patient can renarcotize — reassess frequently and be ready to repeat the dose. Q3: Which opioid side effect

entries.h: PCA Pump vs Fentanyl · NG-259 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🅰️ PCA pump 🅱️ Fentanyl 🔀 Tell them apart ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Pharmacology · Pain Management

Two related but different exam traps NG-259 Pharmacology ADHD-friendly visual edition A PCA pump is a delivery device — a safety system built around one unbreakable rule: only the patient presses the button. Fentanyl is a specific opioid drug that can be delivered several ways, each with its own risk profile — the IV form is fast and short-acting; the patch is slow, long-acting, and dangerous around heat. Builds directly on the Opioids page (NG-257): same mu-receptor mechanism, same naloxone antidote, same bowel pl
SIDE A · PATIENT-CONTROLLED ANALGESIA A device, not a drug — the safety story is all about WHO is allowed to press the button.

Patient-Controlled Analgesia (PCA) pump: an IV infusion pump that lets the patient self-administer small preset doses of opioid on demand, for pain control after surgery or for long-term/chronic pain management. The pump is programmed with a demand dose , a lockout interval , and often a 4-hour dose limit — all safety ceilings set by the prescriber. 🧠 PCA = the patient IS the nurse's partner in dosing — but only within limits the pump enforces automatically.

entries.h: 🚫 The #1 PCA safety rule: only the patient presses the button
entries.t: If the patient is too sedated to press the button , that is the built-in safety brake — a sedated patient physically can't self-dose again. Someone else pressing it removes that brake entirely. 🧠 "PCA by proxy" is a named patient-safety hazard — the moment you see a family member's hand near the button on an NCLEX stem, the answer is to educate/stop them, every time.
🧠 The lockout interval means extra button presses cost nothing — the pump simply won't deliver a dose again until the timer clears.

entries.h: 🚨 NCLEX trap: pain despite the PCA
entries.t: If the patient reports ongoing pain even though they've been getting doses, the first action is NOT to assume the pump is broken or to page for more medication . First action = reassess the patient's pain — location, quality, severity, and confirm the pump is functioning and connected correctly before anything else. 🧠 AIR: A ssessment before intervention → I ntervention → R eassessment. Assessment always comes first, every single time.

entries.h: 🩺 Nursing care around a PCA pump
entries.t: Baseline sedation level & RR before starting, then reassess on a schedule (many facilities: sedation score with every vital sign check) Confirm the correct concentration, demand dose, lockout interval, and 4-hour limit are programmed against the order — an independent double-check by two nurses is standard for high-alert opioid infusions Educate the patient AND visible family/visitors at the bedside about the "patient only" rule on admission to the pump, not just once Keep naloxone available at the bedside per faci
SIDE B · A SPECIFIC, VERY POTENT OPIOID Same mu-receptor drug class as morphine — but the potency and delivery routes change the whole safety picture.

entries.h: ⚡ Potency: fentanyl is dramatically stronger than morphine
entries.t: Fentanyl is commonly taught as roughly 100 times more potent than morphine — a tiny microgram-range dose can equal a much larger morphine dose. This is why fentanyl dosing errors are especially dangerous. 🧠 "Small dose, big punch." Whenever a fentanyl number looks tiny compared to a morphine number, that's expected — it's a much more potent drug per microgram.

Rapid onset — effects within minutes Short duration — wears off relatively quickly compared to morphine Used for acute pain, procedural sedation, and as an anesthesia adjunct 🧠 IV fentanyl = fast on, fast off. Great for a quick procedure; not the drug you'd pick for round-the-clock chronic pain by itself.

entries.h: 🩹 Transdermal patch profile: persistent (chronic) pain ONLY
entries.t: For opioid-tolerant patients with chronic, persistent pain NOT for acute, post-op, or intermittent pain NOT for opioid-naive patients Onset is delayed — initial analgesic effect takes many hours to build; clarify with the HCP if fast relief is needed, the patch is the wrong tool Patch is typically changed on a scheduled interval (commonly every 72 hours / 3 days) per the prescriber's order 🧠 "P" is for Patch AND Persistent. If the stem says "new post-op patient" + "fentanyl patch," that's a red flag — question the

entries.h: 🌡️ Heat + fentanyl patch = a hidden overdose risk
entries.t: Direct heat over or near a fentanyl patch increases how fast the drug is absorbed, which can push a stable dose into overdose territory. Teach patients to avoid heating pads, hot tubs, saunas, electric blankets, and heated waterbeds directly over the patch site, and to notify the HCP if they develop a high fever. 🧠 "Hot patch, hot mess." Anything that warms the skin over a fentanyl patch turns a safe steady dose into a fast, dangerous one.

Remove the OLD patch before applying the new one — never double up Apply to clean, dry, non-irritated, mostly hairless skin; rotate sites Never cut a patch to adjust the dose Dispose of used patches per facility/DEA guidance (e.g., fold sticky sides together) — a used patch still contains active drug 🧠 "Old off, new on, never torn." One patch at a time, never cut, never left where a child or pet could find it.

entries.h: 🧪 Tolerance ≠ addiction — and the codeine-allergy clue
entries.t: Tolerance: needing an increased dose over time to get the same pain relief — an expected physiologic change, not addiction. Because fentanyl is synthetic , it is often the opioid selected when a patient reports a true codeine/morphine allergy — a common NCLEX-style teaching point. 🧠 Tolerance = the body adapting. Addiction = compulsive use despite harm. Don't let a rising dose requirement alone get mislabeled as addiction. 🔀
SIDE-BY-SIDE A PCA pump is HOW a drug is delivered; fentanyl is WHICH drug. They overlap — fentanyl can be run through a PCA — but they answer different exam questions.

entries.h: 📋 PCA pump vs. fentanyl — quick contrast
entries.t: Feature PCA Pump Fentanyl What it is A delivery device — any opioid can be programmed into it A specific drug — synthetic mu-agonist opioid Core safety rule Only the patient presses the button Match the route to the pain type — IV for acute, patch for chronic only Built-in ceiling Lockout interval + 4-hour dose limit N/A — potency itself is the risk (small dose, big effect) Best for Frequent, patient-driven acute or chronic pain dosing IV: fast acute relief. Patch: steady chronic/persistent pain in opioid-tolerant

entries.h: ✅ Everything both share with the Opioids page
entries.t: Mu-receptor mechanism → same adverse effect list (respiratory depression #1 priority) Naloxone is still the antidote if either delivery method oversedates the patient Opioid-induced constipation prevention still applies for the entire course 🧠 This page never replaces the Opioids fundamentals — it layers two extra safety rules on top: button ownership (PCA) and heat/potency (fentanyl).

PCA: the patient, and only the patient, presses the button. Fentanyl: tiny doses are powerful, and heat over a patch is dangerous. 🧠 Say both lines out loud before any pain-management exam — they cover the majority of NCLEX traps on this topic. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🚫 Button = patient only Never family, visitor, or nurse ⏱️ Lockout interval Blocks extra doses automatically 💉 Fentanyl ~100× morphine Small dose, big potency 🌡️ Heat + patch = danger Avoid heating pads, hot tubs, fever near the site

Q1: The patient's spouse offers to press the PCA button because the patient is asleep. What do you do? Show answer Stop and educate: only the patient may press the PCA button. This is "PCA by proxy" and is a known overdose hazard — a sedated patient can't self-dose, which is the pump's built-in safety brake. Q2: A PCA patient still reports 8/10 pain. What's the first nursing action? Show answer Reassess the patient's pain (location, quality, severity) and confirm the pump is functioning per the order — assessment b

entries.h: Peripherally Acting Antiadrenergics · NG-260 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 💊 What it does ⚠️ Watch for 🗣️ Teach ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Pharmacology · Antihypertensive Drug Classes

Reserpine & guanethidine-class agents — the older "empty the tank" antihypertensives NG-260 PHARM ADHD-friendly visual edition These drugs act at the peripheral nerve ending itself — inhibiting the release of norepinephrine before it can ever reach a receptor. That's a different target than the alpha-1 receptor blockers (NG-141) and a different location than clonidine's central brainstem action (NG-110/NG-243). Older, less commonly prescribed today, but still a testable class. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in D
STEP 1 · THE MECHANISM This is a different mechanism than an alpha-1 receptor blocker — it stops norepinephrine from ever being released, instead of blocking the receptor it would land on.

entries.h: 🧵 Presynaptic NE release blockade vs postsynaptic receptor blockade
entries.t: EXAM TIP Peripherally acting antiadrenergics inhibit the release of norepinephrine from adrenergic nerve endings in the peripheral nervous system — the signal never gets sent. That's different from an alpha-1 blocker, which lets NE release normally but occupies the receptor so it can't bind. 🧠 "Peripherally acting antiadrenergics" is an umbrella term for TWO different tricks — cut off the supply (presynaptic) or block the door (postsynaptic). Both happen outside the brain (peripheral), both end in vasodilation, but

Reserpine (Serpasil) — depletes norepinephrine from storage vesicles in the nerve ending; classic older antihypertensive Guanethidine — blocks the release of stored norepinephrine from the nerve terminal; rarely used today Doxazosin (Cardura) & Prazosin (Minipress) — appear in this drug class in some textbooks, but mechanistically they're postsynaptic alpha-1 receptor blockers (see NG-141) — a useful NCLEX distinction to make out loud Doxazosin: HTN 1–8 mg /day, BPH 1–16 mg /day PO. Prazosin: HTN 1–20 mg /day PO in

Hypertension BPH (for the alpha-1-blocker members of this group — see NG-160) 🧠 "Empty the tank, drop the pressure." Whether the tank is emptied at the source (reserpine) or the door is blocked at the destination (prazosin), norepinephrine's vasoconstricting effect never reaches the vessel — pressure falls either way. ⚠️
STEP 2 · THE DANGER LIST Generalized CNS effects plus the classic peripheral hypotension picture — and one very specific reserpine contraindication.

Generalized/CNS: dry mouth, drowsiness, sedation, anorexia, rash, malaise, weakness. Peripheral (specific to this class): hypotension, weakness, lightheadedness, bradycardia . 🧠 "Slow, dry, and dizzy." The generalized CNS depression plus the hemodynamic drop together explain almost every symptom on this list.

Active peptic ulcer disease Ulcerative colitis Mental depression Reserpine depletes catecholamines and can also deplete CNS serotonin/dopamine stores — this is why it's linked to worsening depression, and it increases vagal/GI acid activity, which is why it's avoided in active ulcer disease and ulcerative colitis. 🧠 "Reserpine empties more than the norepinephrine tank." Depleting catecholamines centrally too is exactly why it can unmask or worsen depression — a classic exam trap for an "old" drug.

Interacting drug Effect Other adrenergic drugs Increased risk of hypertension (opposing/rebound effects) Levodopa Decreased effect of levodopa; hypotension Anesthetic agents Increased effect of the anesthetic Beta-blockers Increased risk of hypertension — this pairing is documented in nursing pharmacology references; verify against a current drug guide before clinical application, as the direction of a hemodynamic interaction can vary by specific agent and clinical context Lithium Increased risk of lithium toxicity
STEP 3 · WHAT THE CLIENT NEEDS TO HEAR Orthostatic hypotension precautions are the heart of the teaching plan — plus the never-stop-abruptly rule shared with beta-blockers and clonidine.

Provide assistance getting out of bed or a chair if symptoms are severe. Instruct the client to avoid standing in one place for prolonged periods, and to avoid hot showers or baths , which add extra vasodilation on top of the drug's own effect. 🧠 "1 minute sitting, 1 minute standing, THEN walk." Two full pauses give the cardiovascular system time to catch up before the client moves.

Never stop the drug abruptly — taper only under provider guidance Report signs of heart failure — weight gain, difficulty breathing, extremity edema Don't take OTC cold/flu remedies or nasal decongestants without checking first — many contain adrenergic stimulants that fight the drug's purpose Inform dentists and other providers you're on this therapy Keep all follow-up appointments — close monitoring matters Caution with driving/hazardous tasks — drowsiness, dizziness, lightheadedness are possible 🧠 "Stopping sudd

entries.h: 🆚 Central vs peripheral — don't mix them up
entries.t: Site Example Central Clonidine — brainstem alpha-2 agonist (NG-110/NG-243) Peripheral — presynaptic Reserpine, guanethidine — block NE release (this page) Peripheral — postsynaptic Doxazosin, prazosin, tamsulosin — block the alpha-1 receptor (NG-141) 🧠 "Three drugs, three addresses, one goal: less sympathetic tone." Same destination (lower BP), three completely different roads to get there. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🧵 Presynaptic block Reserpine/guanethidine stop NE from ever being released ❌ Never stop abruptly Taper gradually to avoid precipitating adverse effects 🪑 Sit-1-min, stand-1-min Orthostatic hypotension precaution before ambulating 🚫 Reserpine + depression/PUD = contraindicated — catecholamine/serotonin depletion

Q1: How do peripherally acting antiadrenergics like reserpine lower blood pressure? Show answer They inhibit the release of norepinephrine from peripheral adrenergic nerve endings — a presynaptic mechanism, different from a receptor blocker. Q2: Why is reserpine contraindicated in a client with a history of depression? Show answer It depletes catecholamine (and CNS monoamine) stores, which can unmask or worsen depression. What the Body Does to the Drug NG-262 Pharmacology ADHD-friendly visual edition Pharmacokinetics = the journey a drug takes through the body : in, around, changed, and out. Four steps — Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism, Excretion (ADME) — explain why a pill takes longer to work than a shot, why liver failure changes your dosing, and why some drugs need blood levels drawn. Every other pharmacology page on this site leans on these concepts. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🚶 ADME Absorption → Distribu
STEP 1 · IN, AROUND, OUT Every drug you'll ever give follows the same 4-stop route through the body.

entries.h: 🚶 ADME — the drug's route through the body
entries.t: 🧠 "A Dizzy Man Excretes" — A bsorption, D istribution, M etabolism, E xcretion. Say it in order every time you think about a drug's journey.

entries.h: ① Absorption — getting into the blood
entries.t: Moves the drug from the site of administration into body fluids via active transport, passive transport, or pinocytosis. IV/IM = fastest absorption; IV = 100% bioavailability , no absorption step at all Oral = slowest — depends on GI motility, pH, food, and solubility Affected by: route, solubility, condition of body tissues 🧠 "Straight to vein, straight to work." IV skips absorption entirely — that's why it's the fastest route in an emergency.

entries.h: ② Distribution — only free drug works
entries.t: The systemic circulation carries the drug to body tissues. Depends on protein binding, blood flow, and solubility . Drug binds albumin or stays free — only free circulating drug is active Low albumin (liver disease, malnutrition, elderly) → more free drug → higher effect/toxicity risk Fat-soluble drugs cross the blood-brain barrier more easily 🧠 "Bound and gagged does nothing." A drug stuck to albumin is inactive until it's released.

entries.h: ③ Metabolism — the liver changes it
entries.t: Also called biotransformation — the body changes the drug to be more or less active, and more excretable. Mostly the liver (cytochrome P450 enzymes); also kidneys, lungs, plasma, intestinal mucosa Liver disease → drugs metabolize slower → higher risk of toxic accumulation 🧠 "Liver = the drug's chemistry lab." It rebuilds the molecule before the kidneys can flush it.

After the liver renders it inactive, it's excreted mainly by the kidneys via urine . Other routes: bile/feces, lungs (volatile drugs), sweat, breast milk Renal failure = drug accumulation risk — dose adjustments needed 🧠 "Bad kidneys, bad exit — the drug gets stuck inside." Always check renal function before dosing in older or renally-impaired clients. 🔄
STEP 2 · WHY ROUTE CHANGES THE DOSE Same drug, same dose, different route — the amount that actually reaches circulation can be wildly different.

entries.h: 🔄 First-pass effect — oral drugs get "taxed" by the liver first
entries.t: First-pass effect : the concentration of an oral drug is greatly reduced before it ever reaches systemic circulation , because it's absorbed through the intestine, travels via the portal vein , and passes through the liver first. Sublingual, rectal, and IV routes bypass some or all of this. 🧠 "Oral pays a liver toll before it can spend itself in the body." That's why oral doses of some drugs are much higher than IV doses of the exact same drug.

The drug must dissolve before it can be absorbed. Liquids and IV meds are already dissolved → absorb fastest. CAUTION A tablet/capsule must pass through the GI tract to dissolve. Enteric-coated / time-released capsules are built to dissolve only in the alkaline environment of the small intestine. 🧠 Never crush an enteric-coated or extended-release tablet — it destroys the coating meant to protect the stomach or delay release.

This phase is ADME itself — how the drug is transported and distributed through absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion. 🧠 Pharmaceutic → Pharmacokinetic → Pharmacodynamic. Dissolve it, move it, then let it act.

entries.h: 🎯 Pharmacodynamic phase — what the drug does
entries.t: Deals with the drug's action and effect on the body — two mechanisms: alteration in cellular function or alteration in cellular environment . Primary effect = the desired therapeutic effect Secondary effect = any other effect — e.g. sildenafil was developed for hypertension, its secondary effect treats erectile dysfunction 🧠 A secondary effect isn't a mistake — sometimes it becomes the drug's most famous use. ⏳
STEP 3 · TIMING THE DOSE This is the math behind why dosing schedules exist — and why some drugs need blood levels drawn.

entries.h: ⏳ Half-life decay curve — 50% gone every interval
entries.t: Half-life (t½) = the time it takes for the body to eliminate 50% of the drug. A short half-life needs frequent dosing; a long half-life needs infrequent dosing — but takes longer to reach a stable ("steady state") level. 🧠 "Half, half, half again." Each half-life cuts what's left in half — it never technically hits zero, but after ~4–5 half-lives it's clinically gone.

Onset of action = time to reach a therapeutic effect after administration Peak concentration = when the absorption rate equals the elimination rate (the highest point) Duration = how long the drug keeps producing a therapeutic effect 🧠 "Onset starts it, peak is the top, duration is how long it lasts."

entries.h: 🎯 Therapeutic index — narrow vs. wide window
entries.t: 🧠 Narrow window = tight rope, no net. Too little = no effect; too much = toxicity — with barely any room in between.

The therapeutic index is the range between the minimum effective concentration and the minimum toxic concentration . Narrow-index drugs (digoxin, warfarin, lithium, phenytoin, theophylline, aminoglycosides) require routine blood levels and careful dose titration — this connects directly to peak/trough monitoring and toxic ranges & antidotes. 🧠 "Wide window, wing it a little; narrow window, watch it like a hawk." ⚠️
STEP 4 · WHEN THE MATH GOES WRONG Different words for different kinds of "this didn't go as planned" — the vocabulary examiners love to mix up.

entries.h: 🚨 Adverse, allergic, anaphylactic, angiedema — severity ladder
entries.t: Term What it means Adverse drug reaction Undesirable effect — mild, severe, or life-threatening; can occur at first dose or after repeated doses Allergic reaction Immune-mediated hypersensitivity — the body treats the drug as a foreign invader; can be immediate or delayed Anaphylactic shock 🚨 Extremely serious, usually immediate — requires emergency treatment to support BP & breathing; can be fatal Angiedema Fluid collects in subcutaneous tissue — most commonly eyes, lips, mouth, throat → airway risk 🧠 "Adverse is

Toxic reaction — levels build up because the body can't excrete the drug Cumulative effect — seen in liver/kidney disease; one dose isn't cleared before the next is given Idiosyncrasy — an unusual, unpredictable reaction, often genetic Drug tolerance — decreased response over time, requiring a higher dose (e.g., opioids) 🧠 "Toxic builds up, tolerance wears off." Opposite problems, both from repeated dosing.

entries.h: 🔗 Drug interactions — additive vs. synergistic vs. antagonistic
entries.t: Type Effect Additive Combined effect equals the sum of each drug given alone Synergistic Combined effect is greater than expected — e.g. hypnotics + alcohol → increased CNS depression Antagonistic One drug blocks another — e.g. naloxone reverses opioids 🧠 Synergy stacks the danger, antagonism cancels it out.

Food interaction — some foods increase or decrease drug metabolism (e.g. grapefruit juice + many CYP3A4 drugs) Teratogen — any substance causing abnormal fetal development Pharmacogenomics — genetic makeup alters how a person responds to a drug 🧠 EXAM TIP influence on metabolism also includes age, weight, disease state, and route — not just genetics or food.

entries.h: 🧭 Sympathomimetic vs. sympatholytic vs. parasympathomimetic vs. parasympatholytic
entries.t: Term Effect Sympathomimetic Mimics the sympathetic nervous system ("fight or flight") Sympatholytic Blocks/inhibits sympathetic nervous system transmission Parasympathomimetic (cholinergic) Stimulates the parasympathetic nervous system via acetylcholine (ACh) Parasympatholytic (anticholinergic) Reduces parasympathetic nervous system activity 🧠 "Mimetic mimics, lytic blocks." Pair that with sympathetic (fight/flight) vs. parasympathetic (rest/digest) and you can predict the effect of almost any autonomic drug. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🚶 ADME Absorption → Distribution → Metabolism → Excretion 🔄 First-pass Oral drugs lose potency through the liver first ⏳ Half-life Time to eliminate 50% — sets dosing frequency 🎯 Narrow index Digoxin/warfarin/lithium need blood levels

Q1: What do the letters ADME stand for? Show answer Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism, Excretion — the four pharmacokinetic phases a drug moves through. Q2: What is the first-pass effect, and which routes avoid it? Show answer Oral drugs travel via the portal vein through the liver before reaching systemic circulation, reducing the amount that's active. IV bypasses it completely; sublingual and rectal routes bypass some of it. Q3: Define half-life. Show answer The time it takes for the body to eliminate 50% of t

entries.h: Withdrawal Meds · NG-277 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🍺 Alcohol 💉 Opioid 🩺 Safety ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Pharmacology · Substance Withdrawal Management

Alcohol vs. opioid withdrawal — different drugs, different priorities, one nurse watching vitals NG-277 PHARM ADHD-friendly visual edition Withdrawal management is not one protocol — it's two very different physiologic pictures. Alcohol withdrawal can kill via seizures and delirium tremens , so benzodiazepines are the safety net. Opioid withdrawal is miserable but rarely lethal on its own, so care focuses on symptom control and medication-assisted treatment (MAT) . 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🍺 Alc
STEP 1 · THE ONE THAT CAN KILL Untreated alcohol withdrawal can progress to seizures and delirium tremens — benzodiazepines are the life-saving drug class here.

EXAM TIP Benzodiazepines (e.g., chlordiazepoxide, diazepam, lorazepam) are first-line for alcohol withdrawal because they cross-tolerate with alcohol at the GABA receptor — they prevent the two most dangerous complications: withdrawal seizures and delirium tremens (DTs) . 🧠 "No benzo, no brake." Benzodiazepines are the only class on this page that directly prevents a withdrawal death — everything else is symptom comfort or long-term relapse prevention.

Many units dose benzodiazepines using the CIWA-Ar (Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol, revised) — a structured symptom score (tremor, sweating, anxiety, hallucinations, orientation, etc.). A higher score → more medication ; exact cutoffs vary by facility protocol. 🧠 "Score drives the dose." CIWA-Ar lets the nurse titrate benzodiazepines to the client's actual symptom burden instead of a fixed schedule.

Disulfiram deters drinking by causing a severe reaction (flushing, nausea/vomiting, palpitations, hypotension) if alcohol is consumed. Teach patients to avoid all alcohol sources — not just drinks. 🧠 "ARTS & CRAFTS caution." Rubbing alcohol, mouthwash, cooking wine, and alcohol-based hobby/craft products (glues, paints, hand sanitizer) can all trigger a reaction — teach clients to check labels broadly, not just beverages. 💉
STEP 2 · SYMPTOM CONTROL + MAT Rarely life-threatening on its own, but three very different tools are used together: full agonist, partial agonist, and non-opioid symptom control.
🧠 Full details on clonidine's withdrawal role are on NG-243 · Clonidine — this page places it alongside methadone/buprenorphine so you can see the whole picture at once.

🌡️ Long half-life — can accumulate; effects may lag behind dosing 🤢 Early signs of toxicity: nausea/vomiting, lethargy, frequent emesis 📉 Monitor: prolonged QT interval on ECG 😴 Client "falls asleep easily" — a red flag for over-sedation/toxicity, not just fatigue 🧠 "Sleepy and sick = stop and check." A methadone client who is unusually drowsy and vomiting needs an urgent reassessment, not just reassurance.
🧠 <90% on a methadone client is not "borderline" — treat it as an early sign of opioid over-sedation until proven otherwise.

As a partial agonist , buprenorphine has a ceiling effect on respiratory depression — a safety advantage over full agonists like methadone at typical doses. It's frequently combined with naloxone (an opioid antagonist) to deter misuse, since naloxone has little effect orally/sublingually but blocks euphoria if the product is misused by injection. 🧠 "Partial credit, full safety net." Buprenorphine won't fully activate the receptor the way methadone does, which is exactly why its overdose ceiling is safer. 🩺
STEP 3 · CROSS-CUTTING PRIORITIES Different drugs, same nursing job underneath: watch vitals, watch sedation level, and never assume "just withdrawal" explains a symptom.

1 🩺 Vital signs frequently — HR, BP, RR, temp, SpO₂ 2 😴 Sedation/LOC checks — especially with methadone or clonidine on board 3 📉 ECG for QT if on methadone 4 🧮 Symptom scoring (e.g., CIWA-Ar) to guide alcohol withdrawal dosing 5 🗣️ Full medication reconciliation — disulfiram + hidden alcohol sources, other CNS depressants 🧠 The tools differ by substance, but the underlying nursing job is the same: catch deterioration early, before it becomes a code.

entries.h: 🆚 Alcohol vs. opioid withdrawal — tell them apart
entries.t: Feature Alcohol Opioid Can it kill untreated? Yes — seizures, DTs Rarely, on its own Primary safety drug Benzodiazepines None required to prevent death; MAT for cravings Scoring tool CIWA-Ar Facility-specific opioid withdrawal scales exist, less universally standardized Long-term relapse prevention Disulfiram (deterrent), naltrexone (varies by protocol) Methadone / buprenorphine (MAT) 🧠 "Alcohol can kill you leaving it; opioids rarely do." That single fact is why the safety-drug priority is so different between the

⚡ New seizure alcohol withdrawal emergency 🌀 Confusion/hallucinations possible DTs — escalate 😴 Excess sedation methadone/clonidine toxicity 💓 Prolonged QT methadone — ECG changes 🧠 See NG-243 · Clonidine for that drug's specific withdrawal role and safety profile in more depth. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🍺 Benzos = alcohol safety net prevent seizures & DTs, dosed by CIWA-Ar 💉 MAT = methadone/buprenorphine full vs. partial opioid agonist for cravings 🩹 Clonidine = symptom control not MAT — see NG-243 🚫 Disulfiram = any alcohol source even rubbing alcohol/hobby products can react

Q1: Why are benzodiazepines the priority drug class in alcohol withdrawal? Show answer They cross-tolerate with alcohol at the GABA receptor and prevent the two most dangerous complications — withdrawal seizures and delirium tremens (DTs). Q2: What's the key difference between methadone and buprenorphine? Show answer Methadone is a full opioid agonist; buprenorphine is a partial agonist with a ceiling effect on respiratory depression, giving it a wider safety margin. Both are used for MAT in opioid use disorder. Q3
Painless bright bleeding or a rigid painful uterus. The pair that appears on nearly every maternity exam, and the exam you must never perform.

entries.h: ⚖️ The comparison that answers the question
entries.t: Where the placenta sits is the whole difference. Over the cervix, the blood has a clear way out and nothing hurts. Torn off the wall, the blood is trapped and the uterus goes board-hard. Swipe it sideways if it is cut off, or tap to open it full size. Two causes of third-trimester bleeding, and they are opposites in almost every respect. Painless + bright red = previa. Painful + board-like uterus = abruption. PLACENTA PREVIA ABRUPTIO PLACENTAE What it is Placenta implanted over the cervix Placenta separates early f

🩸 Previa Painless bright red bleeding, often first noticed on waking Uterus soft and non-tender Fetal position often abnormal — the placenta blocks engagement Bleeding may stop and recur 🚨 Abruption Sudden constant pain , often described as tearing Rigid, board-like uterus that does not relax Bleeding may be concealed behind the placenta — so the visible loss underestimates the real loss Signs of shock out of proportion to what you can see

In abruption, blood can be trapped behind the placenta. A rising fundal height, worsening pain and shock with little visible bleeding is a concealed abruption. Trust the vital signs, not the pad count.

1 Assess maternal vitals and fetal heart rate 2 Left side-lying position 3 Oxygen; two large-bore IVs 4 Type and crossmatch; CBC, coagulation studies 5 Continuous monitoring; prepare for C-section Nothing by mouth — surgery may be imminent Weigh pads to quantify blood loss (1 g ≈ 1 mL) Strict input and output; indwelling catheter RhoGAM if the mother is Rh negative — any bleeding event can sensitize her Steroids to mature fetal lungs if preterm delivery is likely

DIC is a real risk in abruption — the damaged placenta releases thromboplastin, which consumes clotting factors. Watch for bleeding from IV sites, gums and the nose , petechiae, and oozing that will not stop. Labs: low platelets, low fibrinogen, prolonged PT/aPTT, raised D-dimer.

No vaginal exam with suspected previa — ultrasound only Painless bright = previa. Painful rigid = abruption. Concealed abruption: shock out of proportion to visible bleeding Hypertension and cocaine are the classic abruption risks Two large-bore IVs, left side, oxygen — for both Sources. Written from NICHD , CDC Reproductive Health , MedlinePlus and OpenStax A&P 2e (CC BY 4.0).
A whole-body vascular disease, not a blood pressure number. The three symptoms that mean a seizure is coming, and how magnesium is monitored.

Vessels constrict and leak. Every organ gets less blood, and fluid moves out of the circulation into tissue. That single mechanism explains everything: the hypertension, the protein in urine, the facial edema, the headache, the liver pain and the seizures. Gestational hypertension Preeclampsia Severe features Blood pressure ≥140/90 after 20 weeks ≥140/90 ≥160/110 Proteinuria None Present Present Other — Edema of face and hands Headache, visual changes, RUQ pain , low platelets, raised creatinine Before 20 weeks it

These three mean a seizure may be imminent. Report immediately. 1 Severe headache not relieved by acetaminophen 2 Visual changes — blurring, spots, flashing lights 3 Epigastric / RUQ pain — the liver capsule stretching Epigastric pain in preeclampsia is not indigestion. It is a late, ominous sign and the patient may seize within hours.

Stay with her ; call for help Turn on her side ; protect from injury; do not restrain Nothing in the mouth Oxygen by mask once the seizure ends; suction as needed Note the time and duration ; assess fetal heart rate after Prepare for delivery once she is stable

H aemolysis · E levated L iver enzymes · L ow P latelets. A severe variant — and dangerous because it can occur with only mildly raised blood pressure . Presents with malaise, nausea and RUQ pain . Do not rule out severe disease because the blood pressure looks acceptable. Check the platelets and liver enzymes.

Magnesium prevents seizures. It is not an antihypertensive. That distinction is worth marks on its own — blood pressure is treated separately, usually with labetalol or hydralazine. Therapeutic range 4–7 mEq/L Serum magnesium — what is lost, in order mEq/L 4–7 therapeutic >8 reflexes lost >12 respiratory arrest

entries.h: 🚨 Monitoring, in the order things disappear
entries.t: Check Hold and report if Deep tendon reflexes Absent — the FIRST warning sign Respiratory rate <12/min Urine output <30 mL/hr — magnesium is cleared renally, so it accumulates Level of consciousness Lethargy, slurred speech Antidote: calcium gluconate — kept at the bedside, always. Reflexes go first. If you check one thing, check the reflexes.

Quiet, dim room ; minimal stimulation — light and noise can trigger a seizure Seizure precautions : padded rails, suction and oxygen at the bedside Left lateral position to maximize placental perfusion Daily weights; strict input and output; deep tendon reflexes each shift or more often Continuous fetal monitoring

Magnesium prevents seizures , it does not lower blood pressure Reflexes are the first thing lost in toxicity Calcium gluconate is the antidote Facial and hand edema is abnormal; dependent ankle edema is normal HELLP can occur with near-normal blood pressure The only cure is delivery 📌
