entries.h: Cast Care · NG-063 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🦴 Fracture & Trauma Care series: 1 · Fracture 2 · Buck's Traction & Post-Op 3 · Fat Embolism & Osteomyelitis 4 · Cast Care 🚨 Complications 🖐️ Assess 🩹 Teach ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Musculoskeletal · Fracture & Trauma Care Series · Page 4 of 4

Living With a Cast — Watching For Compartment Syndrome NG-063 Musculoskeletal ADHD-friendly visual edition A cast protects a healing bone — but a cast can also become the injury if swelling inside it cuts off blood flow. This page teaches the patient (and you) how to live with a cast day to day, and how to run the same neurovascular check as the 6 P's from the Fracture page (NG-056) every single time — because the earliest sign of compartment syndrome is pain that elevation and pain medicine don't touch . 📄 Simple
STEP 1 · WHAT CAN GO WRONG A cast can hide swelling from view — which is exactly why the assessment matters more than what you can see.

entries.h: 🚨 Compartment syndrome — the emergency this whole page is built around
entries.t: Compartment syndrome is an extremely painful condition that happens when pressure within the muscle compartments builds to dangerous levels — cutting off blood flow and oxygen and, left untreated, resulting in permanent tissue death. 🧠 "A cast doesn't stretch — but swelling doesn't stop." Once compartment pressure exceeds vessel pressure, the limb can lose blood flow and oxygen even though pulses may still be felt early on — don't wait for pulselessness.

😖 Unrelieved with opioids — even morphine doesn't touch it 📈 Not resolving with medication or elevation 🖐️ Extreme pain with passive movement — pain when someone else stretches the fingers/toes SAUNDERS Client reports severe, deep, unrelenting pain and pain as the nurse assesses finger movement. What condition? Answer: compartment syndrome — pain out of proportion to injury, worse with passive stretch.

⚡ Tingling, burning, numbness 🖐️ Trouble moving or extending fingers/toes — described as "great difficulty" KAPLAN A nurse is assessing a client with a short leg cast for compartment syndrome. Which finding matches? Answer: pain that increases with passive movement.

Watch for a "hot spot" on the cast — a localized area that feels hot , plus a foul odor coming from the cast. Both point to infection underneath, not just normal healing warmth. KAPLAN Three hours after arriving on the orthopedic unit, a client reports a hot feeling under the cast. First action? Answer: assess circulation in the casted extremity and change the client's position. 🧠 "Hot + foul smell = infection; cold + pale = compartment syndrome." Two different temperature clues point to two different emergencies —
STEP 2 · PMSC NEURO CHECK This is the 6 P's from NG-056, re-packaged as the bedside "PMSC" check you run on every casted limb.

🧠 PMSC is the cast-specific shorthand for the 6 P's (see NG-056 for the full definitions of pain, pallor, pulselessness, paresthesia, paralysis, poikilothermia). Any abnormal finding — even just one — gets reported.

💓 Pulses present , not pulseless 🖐️ Can move/grip fingers or wiggle toes ⚡ No tingling or numbness ⏱️ Capillary refill under 3 seconds 🎨 Skin color normal, not pale 🌡️ Extremity warm, not cold or cool 🧠 "NOT" is the operative word for every line above — the nurse is ruling OUT compromise, every single check.

entries.h: 🚨 When any of these appear — notify HCP immediately
entries.t: ❌ Pulselessness ❌ Numbness, tingling ❌ Cold, pale foot/hand ❌ Swelling that keeps increasing ❌ Pain unrelieved by elevation or analgesia SAUNDERS A plaster cast is placed on the lower extremity. Which instructions should be given to the client? Answer: notify the HCP immediately for numbness, swelling, or if the foot becomes cold and pale; assess capillary refill, temperature, color, and amount of pain. 🩹
STEP 3 · LIVING WITH THE CAST Keep it dry, keep it up, keep it empty of objects — and report pain that won't back down.

1 Clean & dry — NEVER wet. Cover the cast with a plastic bag for bathing/showers. 2 Elevate above the heart for the first 48 hours to limit swelling; continue elevating and icing as needed after. 3 Itch under the cast? Use a hair dryer on a cool setting — never insert an object. 4 Take it easy — no bearing weight on a plaster cast, no resting it on hard surfaces or letting fingers indent it while it's still setting. 🧠 "Bag it, prop it, blow it (cool), never poke it." Four rules, one cast — bathing, elevation, itchi

entries.h: ❌ Never do this to a cast
entries.t: 🪥 NO objects inserted coat hangers, pencils 💧 NO getting it wet plaster especially 🏋️ NO weight-bearing on a plaster cast 🪵 NO hard surfaces while setting 👉 NO finger indentations while damp 🧠 An itch feels urgent — an infected scratch wound under a cast is worse. Cool hair dryer only.
🧠 Handle a fresh plaster cast with open palms, not fingertips — fingertip pressure while it's still setting leaves indentations that can press on skin once hard.

entries.h: ⚔️ Normal cast pain vs compartment syndrome — tell them apart
entries.t: Expected post-fracture/cast pain 🚨 Compartment syndrome Improves with elevation, ice, and scheduled analgesia Not relieved by elevation or analgesia — even opioids Worse with active movement of the limb Worse with passive stretch — someone else moving the fingers/toes Gradually improves over days Pain that keeps climbing Sensation, pulses, color all normal Tingling/numbness, cold or pale skin may accompany it 🧠 The single red-flag phrase to remember: pain unrelieved by elevation and analgesia is not "a bad day" — i

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🚨 Pain unrelieved by elevation/analgesia = compartment syndrome red flag 🖐️ PMSC Pulses · Movement · Sensation · Color/temp — the cast's 6 P's check 💧 Keep it dry bag it for bathing; never insert objects for itching ⬆️ Elevate 48 hrs above the heart to control swelling

Q1: What is the earliest, most reliable red flag for compartment syndrome? Show answer Pain that is unrelieved by elevation and analgesia, especially pain with passive stretch of the fingers/toes. Q2: What does PMSC stand for, and why is it done on a casted limb? Show answer Pulses, Movement, Sensation, Color/temperature — the bedside version of the 6 P's used to catch neurovascular compromise early. Q3: How should a patient shower with a plaster cast? Show answer Cover the cast completely with a plastic bag — plas

entries.h: Crutch, Cane & Walker Training · NG-064 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🩼 Fit & Types 🚶 Gait Patterns 🪜 Stairs & Safety 🚶 Walkers ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Musculoskeletal · Med-Surg Mobility

Fitting, Gait Patterns, Stairs & Walker Safety NG-064 Musculoskeletal ADHD-friendly visual edition The device is only as safe as the technique. Crutches and canes both restore mobility while protecting a healing limb — but wrong fit or wrong gait turns an assistive device into an injury risk . This page goes deep on the mechanics: how to fit each device, the 4 crutch gait patterns, and exactly how weight moves on stairs. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🖐️ Weight on HANDS Never the armpits — axillary pr
STEP 1 · MEASURE IT RIGHT This builds on NG-167 (Ambulation) — that page covers the general body-mechanics/gait-belt overview. This page goes deep specifically on crutches, canes and walkers.

entries.h: 📏 Correct crutch fit — the numbers that get tested
entries.t: Weight bears on the hands/palms through the handgrips — the axillary pad is a balance point only, never a weight-bearing point. 🧠 "Pads for balance, palms for pounds." If a client is caught resting body weight on the crutch tops between steps, that's an immediate correction — nerve damage builds silently over minutes to hours of pressure.

entries.h: 🚨 The classic NCLEX trap: axillary nerve damage
entries.t: Crutch top pressing into the axilla compresses the brachial plexus . Presents as numbness/tingling in the hand , weak grip, and can progress to permanent nerve palsy ("crutch palsy") with prolonged pressure. Never let the client "hang" on the crutches between steps. 🧠 Armpit ≠ anchor. Any test question describing tingling hands or a client leaning heavily under the arms on crutches is pointing straight at brachial plexus compression.

Standard (single-tip) cane — mild balance/weakness on one side. Quad cane (4-point base) — more stability, e.g. hemiparesis. Held in the hand on the client's strong/unaffected side. Cane tip stays ~ 4–6 in. to the side of the foot; elbow flexed ~ 15–30° when the tip touches the floor. 🧠 "The cane babysits the bad leg from across the room." It's held opposite the weak leg so it can support that side's step.

Abbrev. Meaning NWB N on- W eight- B earing — no weight at all on the affected limb. TDWB / TTWB T oe- T ouch/ D own W eight- B earing — toes may touch the floor for balance only, no true weight. PWB P artial W eight- B earing — a set fraction of body weight allowed (e.g. 30–50%), per provider order. WBAT W eight- B earing A s T olerated — client self-limits based on pain. FWB F ull W eight- B earing — no restriction. 🧠 The weight-bearing order determines which gait pattern is used — that's why Section 2 pairs each
STEP 2 · MATCH THE GAIT TO THE ORDER Four crutch gaits exist because clients have four different weight-bearing statuses — pick the gait, don't guess it.

Gait Weight-bearing status 4-point Partial/full weight-bearing bilaterally; slowest, most stable — most closely resembles normal walking . 3-point One leg NWB or PWB, the other leg fully weight-bearing — the most common post-injury gait. 2-point Partial weight-bearing bilaterally; faster version of 4-point. Swing-to / swing-through Bilateral lower-extremity weakness or paralysis (e.g. paraplegia); swing-through is faster and covers more ground. 🧠 "3-point = 3 points of contact bearing weight." Two crutch tips + the

1 Advance both crutches forward together with the affected (bad) leg . 2 Shift weight onto the hands/crutches. 3 Swing the unaffected (good) leg through, past the crutches. 🧠 Bad leg travels with the crutches, good leg travels alone. That's the whole pattern.

entries.h: ⭐ Fitting & gait check — before the client walks away
entries.t: Client demonstrates weight on hands , not axillae. Elbows flex 15–30° at the handgrip. Gait matches the ordered weight-bearing status. Never use someone else's crutches — fit is individualized. 🧠 Re-teach on the spot if the client leans into the pads even once — bad habits under fatigue are how nerve injuries happen at home. 🪜
STEP 3 · UP GOOD, DOWN BAD One rule drives both crutches and canes on stairs — lead with the strong side going up, lead with the support going down.

entries.h: 🪜 Stairs with crutches — the tested sequence
entries.t: Up with the good leg, down with the bad leg — the crutches always travel with the affected leg. 🧠 "Good goes up to heaven, bad goes down to the basement." Whichever direction, the crutches stay glued to the affected leg's step.

entries.h: 🚨 Top-missed NCLEX pattern: cane on stairs
entries.t: Going up : lead with the strong leg, cane follows, weak leg last. Going down : cane descends first, weak leg next, strong leg last. 🧠 Same "good up / bad-side-support down" logic as crutches — the device (cane or crutches) always moves with the weaker side.
1 Cane + weak leg advance together . 2 Strong leg steps through, past the cane. 🧠 "The cane babysits the bad leg." They move on the same beat.

NG-167 covers the general assistive-device overview, gait belts, and body mechanics/fall-risk assessment that apply to every mobility aid. This page (NG-064) is the deep dive specifically on crutch and cane fitting and gait mechanics — read both together. ➡️ See NG-167 — Ambulation for gait-belt technique, walker use, and the broader fall-prevention checklist before any first ambulation. 🚶

STEP 4 · THE MOST-USED AID, THE LEAST-TAUGHT ONE A walker gives more support than a cane and needs less skill than crutches, which is why it is the aid most of your clients will actually go home with. The questions are about fit, sequence and the two things that cause falls .

All four legs of a standard walker are on the floor before any step is taken. Never "walk" a standard walker by shuffling two legs forward at a time — that is the single commonest error, and it is what tips a client over sideways. The walker stays about one step length ahead . Pushed out too far, the client leans forward to reach it, the center of gravity goes outside the base of support, and the walker becomes the thing that causes the fall. 🧠 "Walker, weak, well." Same logic as crutches and canes — the aid and th

Client stands inside the walker, arms relaxed at the sides. Handgrips sit level with the greater trochanter — the hip bone — or the crease of the wrist. Elbows flex about 15 to 30 degrees when gripping. Same angle as crutches. Too high and the shoulders shrug and tire; too low and the client stoops, which is both unsafe and exhausting.

Type Who it suits Standard (no wheels) Most stable. Must be lifted every step, so it needs upper-body strength. Used for non-weight-bearing and partial weight-bearing. Two-wheeled (front wheels) For a client who cannot lift a standard walker. Rear legs have glides or tennis balls so it slides, not catches. Four-wheeled (rollator, seat, brakes) For endurance problems rather than weight-bearing limits. Not for someone who needs to lean on it for weight — it rolls away.

entries.h: 🚨 The two things that cause walker falls
entries.t: The error What to teach instead Pulling up on the walker to stand. It is not anchored — it tips toward the client. Push up from the chair armrests , get steady, then reach for the walker one hand at a time. Backing into a chair blind and sitting down while still holding the walker. Back up until the legs touch the seat , reach back for one armrest, then the other, then lower. Lock a rollator's brakes first. 🚨 A walker is never used on stairs. If the question puts a walker on a staircase, the answer is about a diffe

Remove throw rugs and trailing cords — the classic exam answer. Rubber tips intact on every leg; replace them when worn smooth. Non-skid shoes that fit. No backless slippers. Clear a turning path; turn in a wide arc with small steps , never a pivot. Lighting on the routes to the bathroom and kitchen.

entries.h: 🆚 Cane vs walker vs crutches — one line each
entries.t: Aid The deciding fact Cane Mild one-sided weakness. Held on the strong side, advances with the weak leg . Walker Greater instability or bilateral weakness. Advance it, then weak, then strong. Crutches Weight kept off one limb entirely. Weight rides on the hands , never the axillae. 🧠 "Strong holds the cane, weak leans on the walker." ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🖐️ Hands, not armpits Weight on the handgrips — axillary pressure risks nerve palsy. 🩹 3-point gait Both crutches + bad leg together, then good leg. 🦯 Cane = strong side Cane + weak leg together, then strong leg. 🪜 Up good, down bad Unaffected leg leads up; device + affected leg lead down.

Q1: Where should crutch weight be borne, and what happens if it isn't? Show answer On the hands/palms through the handgrips. Resting weight on the axillary pads compresses the brachial plexus — numbness, tingling, weak grip, potentially permanent "crutch palsy." Q2: A client is non-weight-bearing on the left leg. Which crutch gait, and what's the sequence? Show answer 3-point gait — both crutches and the affected (left) leg advance together, then the unaffected (right) leg swings through past the crutches. Q3: A cl

entries.h: Calcium & Alendronate · NG-108 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics ⏱️ The Clash 🧪 Know Your Forms 📅 The Schedule ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Musculoskeletal · Pharmacology Course

Why They Can't Be Taken Together — Timing, Forms & Vitamin D NG-108 Musculoskeletal ADHD-friendly visual edition Calcium supplements and alendronate (a bisphosphonate) are both prescribed for osteoporosis — but they cannot be taken at the same time . Calcium physically blocks alendronate absorption in the gut. This page is entirely about the administration teaching that keeps both drugs working. For the full alendronate mechanism, empty-stomach protocol, and rare adverse effects (osteonecrosis of the jaw, atypical
STEP 1 · WHY THEY FIGHT Same goal — stronger bones — but taken at the same time, one cancels the other out.

entries.h: 🚫 Calcium physically blocks alendronate from being absorbed
entries.t: Alendronate absorption is already extremely poor ( <1% even under ideal conditions). Calcium, iron, magnesium, and aluminum-containing antacids all bind to it in the gut and drop that absorption even closer to zero. Separate calcium supplements from alendronate by several hours . 🧠 "Calcium is a magnet, alendronate is metal." Any mineral supplement taken with alendronate grabs onto it before the gut ever gets a chance to absorb it.

entries.h: 📋 The alendronate side of the schedule (recap)
entries.t: Full protocol lives on NG-238 Bisphosphonates — the short version needed here: Take first thing in the morning , on a completely empty stomach , with a full glass of plain water Stay upright — sitting or standing — for 30–60 minutes after Wait that same 30–60 minutes before eating, drinking anything else, or taking any other medication — including calcium

entries.h: ⚠️ Not just calcium — other blockers too
entries.t: 🧂 Iron supplements 🥛 Magnesium 🧴 Aluminum- or magnesium-containing antacids 💊 Multivitamins that contain minerals Any of these taken too close to alendronate can blunt its absorption the same way calcium does. 🧪
STEP 2 · NOT ALL CALCIUM IS THE SAME Two common calcium salts absorb differently — the difference decides whether the client needs to take it with food.

Feature Calcium carbonate Calcium citrate Elemental calcium per tablet ~40% — more calcium per pill ~21% — less per pill Needs stomach acid to absorb? Yes — take with food No — absorbs with or without food Best for Most healthy adults Older adults, PPI/H2-blocker users, low-stomach-acid clients Cost Cheaper, widely available (also an antacid) More expensive Common side effect Constipation, gas — more likely Somewhat gentler on the GI tract 🧠 "CARBonate needs CARBs (food)." Calcium carbonate needs stomach acid to di

entries.h: 🚫 Divided doses — >500mg at once is wasted
entries.t: Teach the client to split the total daily calcium requirement into doses under 500mg elemental calcium each, spread across the day — not one large dose.

Constipation is a common, expected side effect of calcium supplementation — not a reason to stop the drug. Increase fluids Increase ambulation/activity Add fiber as tolerated 🧠 "High CAL = Hard bowel. Low CAL = Loose bowel." Since calcium makes bones hard, think of it making bowels hard too — that's the trade-off, and it's expected, not dangerous.

entries.h: 🧪 No routine labs needed for alendronate itself
entries.t: Alendronate does not require frequent blood tests or routine lab monitoring on its own. Providers may still periodically check baseline calcium, vitamin D, and renal function as part of overall osteoporosis management — but this is not the same as required routine bloodwork for the bisphosphonate. 📅
STEP 3 · PUTTING IT ON A CLOCK Vitamin D is the piece that makes the calcium usable at all — then it's just a matter of timing everything around alendronate.

entries.h: ☀️ Vitamin D: the key that unlocks calcium absorption
entries.t: Without adequate vitamin D , the intestine cannot absorb dietary or supplemental calcium efficiently — vitamin D is converted to its active form ( calcitriol ) which works with parathyroid hormone to move calcium from the gut into the bloodstream and ultimately into bone. Sources: sunlight exposure, fortified foods (milk, cereal), fatty fish, and supplements Many calcium supplements are combined with vitamin D in the same tablet for this reason Low vitamin D = calcium supplementation underperforms no matter the dos

entries.h: 📅 A sample day — keeping alendronate & calcium apart
entries.t: This is one example schedule , not a fixed rule — the non-negotiable is keeping calcium/other minerals separated from alendronate by several hours , with alendronate always taken on an empty stomach first thing in the morning. 🧠 "Bone pill at dawn, calcium at noon and night." Alendronate opens the day alone; calcium shows up later, split, with food if it's the carbonate form. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD ⏰ Separate by hours calcium blocks alendronate absorption 🍽️ Carbonate + food citrate absorbs without food ☀️ Vitamin D required no D = poor calcium absorption 🚫 >500mg wasted split doses under 500mg each

Q1: Why can't a client take their calcium supplement at the same time as alendronate? Show answer Calcium (like iron, magnesium, and aluminum antacids) binds to alendronate in the gut and blocks its already-poor absorption. They must be separated by several hours. Q2: A client on a PPI for years is prescribed a calcium supplement. Which form absorbs best for her, and why? Show answer Calcium citrate — it doesn't require stomach acid to be absorbed, unlike calcium carbonate, which needs an acidic environment and sho

Disease-Modifying Antirheumatic Drugs NG-114 Musculoskeletal · Group D ADHD-friendly visual edition The drug class that actually SLOWS the disease — not just the pain. Used mainly for rheumatoid arthritis (RA) , DMARDs work by suppressing the immune system so it stops attacking the joints. Prototype = methotrexate , dosed ONCE WEEKLY — never daily. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🦠 Immunosuppressants DMARDs turn the immune system DOWN — that's how they help RA and how they cause infection risk. 🚨 WEEKL
STEP 1 · HOW IT WORKS DMARDs don't just numb pain — they turn down the immune attack that is destroying the joint.

entries.h: 🎯 Why DMARDs get added — pain relievers alone aren't enough
entries.t: When RA pain and immobility can no longer be controlled by NSAIDs and other anti-inflammatories alone, DMARDs are added. They have immunosuppressive properties that decrease the body's immune response — the immune attack on the synovium is exactly what's destroying the joint, so dialing it down protects the joint from further damage. 🧠 "DMARDs Modify the Disease." NSAIDs and steroids only treat the symptom (pain/swelling) — DMARDs are the only class that actually slows joint destruction.

Blocks an enzyme in the folate pathway, which shuts down rapidly dividing cells — including the overactive immune cells attacking the joint. At the low weekly RA dose it's immunosuppressive/anti-inflammatory (very different from the high daily doses used in chemotherapy). 🧠 Methotrexate = "Mother of DMARDs." It's the first-line, most-prescribed DMARD and the one every other drug on this page gets compared to.

Generic (trade) Dose Adalimumab (Humira) 40 mg subQ every other week Etanercept (Enbrel) 25 mg subQ twice weekly or 50 mg subQ weekly Both are TNF-alpha inhibitors — they block a specific inflammatory messenger instead of suppressing the whole immune system broadly. 🧠 -mab = m onoclonal a nti b ody. -cept = re cept or fusion protein (etanercept). Both end in a decoy that soaks up TNF-alpha before it can inflame the joint.

Hydroxychloroquine (Plaquenil) — antimalarial repurposed for RA, typically ~400–600 mg/day orally to start with lower maintenance dosing (weight-based limits apply); requires baseline & periodic eye exams (retinal toxicity). Sulfasalazine — a sulfa-based DMARD used for both RA and inflammatory bowel disease ; see the Sulfasalazine page (GI batch, NG-175) for full dosing/monitoring — same drug, two different disease uses. Anakinra (Kineret) — an IL-1 blocker; do NOT combine with etanercept, adalimumab, or infliximab
STEP 2 · SAFETY Immunosuppression is the whole point — and the whole danger. Labs, contraindications, and the drug interaction that raises toxicity.

entries.h: 🚨 Biggest NCLEX trap: WEEKLY, not daily
entries.t: Methotrexate for RA is prescribed once weekly , on the same day every week . Accidental daily dosing is a real, dangerous, and sometimes fatal medication error — it causes severe bone marrow suppression, GI ulceration, and liver injury. 🧠 "Methotrexate Monday." Pick one day, say it out loud, put it on the calendar — one dose, seven days apart, every time.

CBC — bone marrow suppression → pancytopenia (low WBC, RBC, platelets) LFTs (AST/ALT) — hepatotoxicity; avoid alcohol Renal function — methotrexate is renally cleared; reduced clearance = higher toxicity 🧠 "CLR" — C BC, L iver, R enal — the 3 labs that make methotrexate safe or dangerous.

Renal insufficiency, liver disease, alcohol abuse, pancytopenia, or folate deficiency → avoid methotrexate Congestive heart failure or neurologic demyelinating disease → avoid etanercept, adalimumab, infliximab Pregnancy — methotrexate is teratogenic; effective contraception required during therapy and for a prescriber-specified period after the last dose (references vary — commonly at least one ovulatory cycle up to 6 months for females and 3 months for males) 🧠 Methotrexate is absolutely contraindicated in pregna

Sulfa antibiotics + methotrexate = increased risk of methotrexate toxicity . Both compete for renal clearance and both affect folate metabolism — the combination compounds bone marrow suppression. 🧠 "Sulfa stacks the toxicity." Always ask about antibiotic allergies/current prescriptions before a methotrexate dose.

Nausea, stomatitis (mouth sores) Alopecia (hair loss) Sulfasalazine: GI upset, rash/photosensitivity, mild pancytopenia (retinal/ocular toxicity belongs to hydroxychloroquine , not sulfasalazine) 🧠 A sore mouth on methotrexate isn't "just an ulcer" — it's an early toxicity sign. Report it.

entries.h: 🩻 Before starting a biologic: screen first
entries.t: 1️⃣ TB screening — PPD skin test or quantiferon-gold, plus chest X-ray ▼ 2️⃣ Hepatitis B screening ▼ 3️⃣ Only if negative → start the biologic DMARD Biologics suppress the immune system's ability to keep latent TB contained — starting one in an undiagnosed latent-TB patient can reactivate active disease. Live vaccines are avoided while on any DMARD that suppresses immunity. 🧠 "No jab, no mab." Screen for TB and hep B before the first biologic dose — and hold live vaccines the whole time the patient is on it. 🗣️
STEP 3 · PATIENT EDUCATION What she needs to hear before she leaves the room — dosing, folic acid, injections, and when to call.

entries.h: 🍊 Folic acid supplementation — why it's given WITH methotrexate
entries.t: 🧠 "Folic acid protects the bystanders, not the target." It rescues normal fast-growing cells (gut lining, hair, marrow) from methotrexate's side effects without rescuing the overactive immune cells causing RA.

Teach proper injection technique and site rotation Have the patient demonstrate the technique before it becomes self-administered Report redness, pain, or swelling at the injection site Teach safe disposal (sharps container) 🧠 Return demonstration before discharge — never assume verbal teaching alone is enough for a subQ self-injection.

👄 Mouth sores 💧 Diarrhea 🌡️ Fever 🗣️ Sore throat 🩸 Easy bruising 🌸 Rash / itching 🤢 N/V Any of these can signal bone marrow suppression, infection, or hepatotoxicity — never "wait and see" on methotrexate. 🧠 "No problem is too minor." Even a cold or an open sore can become life-threatening on an immunosuppressant — that instruction line is on the exam.

🍊 Take folic acid as ordered 📅 Same day, once weekly 🚫 No alcohol 💊 Ask HCP before ANY OTC drug/supplement 🤰 Effective contraception during + after (per prescriber) 🩺 Report infection s/s immediately 💉 Rotate injection sites 🏃 Continue diet, exercise, PT as prescribed Treatment for RA is never "just the drug" — explain that management includes drug therapy plus diet, exercise, activity modification, and periodic physical therapy. 🧠 "DMARDs don't work alone." The drug slows the disease; diet, exercise, and PT protec

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🦠 DMARDs suppress immunity = they slow the disease, not just the pain 🚨 Weekly, never daily methotrexate dosing error = life-threatening 🍊 Folic acid reduces side effects, keeps the RA benefit 🩻 TB + hep B screen before any biologic (-mab/-cept) drug

Q1: How often is methotrexate dosed for RA? Show answer Once weekly, same day every week — NOT daily. Daily dosing is a dangerous medication error. Q2: Why is folic acid given with methotrexate? Show answer To reduce GI, mouth, and liver side effects from folate depletion — it doesn't block methotrexate's immunosuppressive/anti-RA effect. Q3: What must be screened before starting a biologic DMARD (e.g., adalimumab, etanercept)? Show answer TB (PPD/quantiferon + chest X-ray) and hepatitis B — biologics can reactivat

"Porous bone" — the silent thief of bone density NG-125 Musculoskeletal ADHD-friendly visual edition Bone resorption outruns bone formation — osteoclasts (the demolition crew) break down bone faster than osteoblasts (the construction crew) can rebuild it, leaving bones fragile, porous, and fracture-prone. It's called the silent disease because it has no symptoms until a bone breaks. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🏗️ Resorption > Formation Osteoclasts (break down) outpace osteoblasts (build up) → net b

STEP 1 · THE REMODELING IMBALANCE Bone is living tissue that's constantly being torn down and rebuilt — osteoporosis is what happens when demolition wins. From your lecture. Their mnemonic is ACCESS : Alcohol, Corticosteroids, Calcium low, Early menopause, Smoking, Sedentary. Diagnosed on a DEXA scan.

MECHANISM Bone remodels constantly: osteoclasts resorb (dissolve) old bone, then osteoblasts lay down new bone in its place. Normally these stay balanced. In osteoporosis, osteoclast activity outpaces osteoblast activity — bone is resorbed faster than it's replaced, so total bone mass and density drop over time. 🧠 "PORus bones = OsteoPORosis." The word itself tells you the pathophysiology — the bone becomes full of pores (holes) because breakdown has outpaced building.

Term What it means Osteopenia Lower-than-normal bone mass — the step before osteoporosis Osteoporosis Porous, fragile bone from low bone density — resorption > formation Osteomalacia Softening of bone from severe vitamin D deficiency — a mineralization problem, not a density problem 🧠 Osteo-mal-ACIA = mal (bad) + ACID-ish D. Malacia is about soft bone from missing vitamin D — different mechanism than porosis.

entries.h: ⚠️ Risk factors — who loses the seesaw
entries.t: 👩 Female , especially postmenopausal — estrogen normally restrains osteoclasts; losing it removes the brake 🎂 Older age , small/thin body frame 🌍 Caucasian or Asian ethnicity 👪 Family history of osteoporosis or fracture 🥛 Low calcium / vitamin D intake, low physical activity 🧠 "Thin white/Asian grandma" is the classic exam stem body type — low estrogen + low body mass + genetics all strip the bone's protection at once.

entries.h: 💊🏥 NCLEX TRAP — secondary causes: diseases & drugs that cause osteoporosis
entries.t: Diseases Hyperparathyroidism — too much PTH pulls calcium out of bone Cushing syndrome — chronic excess cortisol Diabetes mellitus Hyperthyroidism Medications 🚨 Corticosteroids (" -sone ") — e.g. prednisone — the #1 tested drug-induced cause Anticonvulsants (long-term use) Long-term heparin Long-term proton pump inhibitors (" -prazole ") 🧠 "Predni-SONE thins the bone." If a stem asks which medication increases risk for osteoporosis, glucocorticoids like prednisone are almost always the answer. 🔎
STEP 2 · SPOT IT There are almost no early clues — the disease hides until a bone gives out or a scan catches it.

🚨 Often asymptomatic — no pain, no warning, until a fracture happens 📉 Loss of height over time (vertebral compression) 🐫 Kyphosis — exaggerated rounded upper back ("dowager's hump"), common in elderly clients 🦴 Fragility fractures — break from a low-impact fall or even normal activity (classic sites: hip, vertebrae, wrist/Colles' fracture ) 😖 Back pain, most often from a new vertebral compression fracture 🧠 "The hip that broke the fall, not the fall that broke the hip." In an osteoporotic client, ask which came fi

entries.h: 🧍 Kyphosis & height loss — what it looks like
entries.t: 🧠 Dowager's hump = the rounded thoracic curve from multiple silent vertebral compression fractures stacking up over the years.

entries.h: 🧪 DEXA scan & T-score — the diagnostic clue
entries.t: DEXA (Dual-energy X-ray Absorptiometry) measures bone mineral density and reports it as a T-score — how many standard deviations the client's bone density is from a healthy young adult's peak bone mass. Standard WHO diagnostic categories — used to guide when to start treatment and to track response. 🧠 "Two-point-five and falling = disease." Remember one number: -2.5 is the osteoporosis cutoff on DEXA.

entries.h: ⭐ High-yield exam Q&A pulled straight from the source deck
entries.t: Kaplan-style: "Which medication increases risk for osteoporosis?" → Prednisone (a corticosteroid). HESI-style: "Which population has increased risk of osteoporosis?" → 60-year-old postmenopausal woman. HESI-style (SATA): Risk factors include steroid use, high caffeine intake, being white or Asian, postmenopausal state, and anticonvulsant therapy. Kaplan-style: Best prevention teaching for an at-risk client → walk (weight-bearing exercise) about 30 minutes, 4 times per week. 🩺
STEP 3 · BUILD & PROTECT THE BONE Prevention leans on exercise, nutrition, and fall-proofing the environment — drug therapy is only briefly mentioned here.

1 🚶 Weight-bearing & resistance exercise — e.g. walking 30 minutes, 4x /week. Loading the bone stimulates osteoblasts. 2 🥛 Adequate calcium & vitamin D intake — through diet, sunlight, and/or supplements (see NG-108 for the calcium teaching detail) 3 ☀️ Sun exposure — supports the skin's natural vitamin D synthesis 4 🚭 Stop smoking , decrease caffeine and alcohol — all accelerate bone loss 5 🚶‍♀️ Frequent ambulation to maintain bone stimulus and muscle strength 🧠 "Move it, feed it, sun it, quit it." Four verbs cove

entries.h: 🚨 Fall precautions — the #1 nursing priority once diagnosed
entries.t: 🧼 Rubber mats in the shower/tub 💡 Well-lit hallways ❌ No throw rugs 👟 Non-skid footwear, clear walkways 🦯 Assistive devices as needed 🧠 A fragile bone means every fall is a potential fracture. Fall precautions are as much a treatment for osteoporosis as any medication.

entries.h: 📈 Fracture risk timeline — how the disease usually presents
entries.t: 🤫 Years of silent bone loss (no symptoms) ▼ 📉 Gradual height loss, mild back pain from micro-fractures ▼ 🚨 Fragility fracture — hip, spine, or wrist — often the first diagnosis clue 🧠 Screening exists to catch step 1 — a DEXA scan is how you diagnose osteoporosis before the fracture, not after.

entries.h: 💊 Drug therapy — brief overview only (full detail lives on two other pages)
entries.t: Osteoporosis treatment centers on slowing bone resorption and supplying the raw materials for new bone. The two drug classes most tested with this topic are covered in depth elsewhere so this page can stay focused on the disease itself: 📍 Bisphosphonates (alendronate, risedronate) — mechanism, dosing, and the critical morning-administration teaching → see NG-238 Bisphosphonates. 📍 Calcium supplementation paired with alendronate — carbonate vs. citrate, vitamin D's role, and why the two must NOT be taken together →

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🏗️ Osteoclasts > osteoblasts = net bone loss = osteoporosis 🤫 Silent disease = often no symptoms until fracture 🧪 T-score ≤ -2.5 = diagnostic cutoff on DEXA 💊 Prednisone = classic drug-induced cause

Q1: In osteoporosis, which cell activity outpaces the other? Show answer Osteoclast (bone resorption/breakdown) activity outpaces osteoblast (bone formation) activity, causing net bone loss. Q2: What T-score on DEXA diagnoses osteoporosis? Show answer A T-score of -2.5 or lower. -1.0 to -2.5 is osteopenia; ≥ -1.0 is normal. Q3: A client asks which of her medications raised her fracture risk. She takes prednisone for asthma — what do you tell her? Show answer Corticosteroids like prednisone are a well-known drug-ind

Skeletal Muscle Relaxants — Class Overview NG-155 MUSCULOSKELETAL · PHARM ADHD-friendly visual edition This page is the systematic overview — how the whole drug class works, who it's for, and the class-wide safety rule (sedation = fall risk, always). Pairs with NG-156 (Muscle Relaxers Top Tips) — individual drug snapshots & NCLEX memory tricks for dantrolene, cyclobenzaprine, baclofen & carisoprodol live there, not repeated here. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🎯 Two jobs, two mechanisms Acute spasm/pa
STEP 1 · MECHANISM Two very different mechanisms share one drug class name — knowing which one tells you the whole safety profile.

entries.h: 🧠🦵 Centrally-acting vs peripherally-acting — where the drug actually works
entries.t: EXAM TIP Most skeletal muscle relaxants do not directly relax the muscle fiber itself — their benefit comes from a sedative effect on the CNS that blunts the perception of spasm and pain. Only one major drug works differently: dantrolene acts directly on the muscle . 🧠 "Central = calm the brain, Peripheral = plug the calcium." If a question says a drug works directly on the muscle , it's describing dantrolene — everything else in this class is working upstream, in the CNS.

🏋️ Muscle strain 🔙 Acute back pain 🩹 Other acute painful musculoskeletal conditions Drugs used here are almost always centrally-acting and meant for short-term use. 🧠 Spasm = short trip. Acute spasm drugs are a short course, not a lifestyle.

🧩 Multiple sclerosis (MS) 🧠 Cerebral palsy 🦴 Spinal cord injury These clients often need longer-term therapy — baclofen and dantrolene are the classic choices here. 🧠 Spasticity = a standing order. Neurologic spasticity is chronic — that's why abrupt stop of these drugs (baclofen especially) is so dangerous.

entries.h: 🌀 Why relaxants help either way — the spasm-pain-guarding cycle
entries.t: 💥 Injury or CNS lesion → muscle spasm ▼ 😣 Spasm → pain ▼ 🛡️ Pain → guarding / more tension ▼ 🔁 More tension → more spasm (cycle repeats) A muscle relaxant (central sedation or dantrolene's direct action) breaks the cycle at the spasm step, so pain and guarding can settle too. 🧠 Break one link, break the loop. You don't have to fix all three (spasm/pain/guarding) — interrupting spasm collapses the whole cycle. ⚠️
STEP 2 · SAFETY One adverse effect towers over the rest — sedation — plus the interactions and contraindications that show up on exams.

entries.h: 🚨 #1 universal risk: CNS depression → fall risk
entries.t: Every drug in this class can cause drowsiness and sedation . This is the single highest-yield safety point for the whole class — before you memorize one individual drug, know this. 🧠 "Sleepy stacks." Any CNS depressant on board — alcohol, opioids, antihistamines, sedatives/hypnotics — stacks with a muscle relaxant. Fall precautions and caution with driving/hazardous tasks apply to every drug in this class.

😴 Drowsiness, sedation, lethargy 🚽 Constipation or diarrhea 💓 Bradycardia or tachycardia 🌡️ Rash 🧠 GI & cardiac effects can go either direction (constipation or diarrhea; brady or tachycardia) — don't assume only one.

CNS depressants (alcohol, antihistamines, opioids, sedatives) → increased CNS depression MAOIs → risk of high fever & convulsions Haloperidol → increased psychosis Antihypertensives → increased risk of hypotension 🧠 "MAOI = fire & seizure." A muscle relaxant plus an MAOI (or within 14 days of one) is a red-flag combination — think hyperpyrexia + convulsions.

Drug Contraindicated in… Baclofen Muscle spasm caused by rheumatic disorders (not a spasticity/neurologic cause) Carisoprodol Known hypersensitivity to meprobamate (its active metabolite) Cyclobenzaprine Recent MI , cardiac conduction disorders , hyperthyroidism ; within 14 days of an MAOI Oral dantrolene Lactation ; active hepatic disease ; muscle spasm from rheumatic disorders 🧠 "Rheumatic disorders" keeps showing up — both baclofen and oral dantrolene are contraindicated when the spasm is from a rheumatic cause,
STEP 3 · PATIENT EDUCATION Four teaching points cover almost every question this class generates.

1 😴 May cause drowsiness — expect it 2 🚗 Do not drive or do hazardous tasks if drowsy 3 🍷 Avoid alcohol / other CNS depressants 🧠 "Limit" is always a trap. If an answer choice says to limit alcohol to a few drinks while on a muscle relaxant, it's wrong — the teaching is avoid , not limit.
🧠 "2–3 and done." For acute spasm, if a client is still on the same relaxant past 2–3 weeks with no reassessment, flag it.

entries.h: 🛑 Never abruptly stop — the class-wide taper rule
entries.t: This applies to any muscle relaxant taken regularly, but it is the single highest-yield point for baclofen : stopping suddenly can trigger rebound spasticity , hallucinations, or seizures . Always taper under provider guidance. ✅ Taper the dose gradually, per provider order ❌ Never stop cold — even if the client "feels fine" 🧠 Orthostatic dizziness on position change is expected , not a reason to hold the dose or stop 🧠 "Never abruptly stop (any muscle relaxant)." The full withdrawal picture for baclofen — and the

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🧠 Central vs 🦵 peripheral Most sedate the CNS; only dantrolene works directly on muscle (blocks Ca²⁺ release). 😴 Sedation = universal risk Fall precautions + avoid driving/hazardous tasks with every agent. 🍷 Avoid, don't limit No alcohol or other CNS depressants — ever, not "in moderation." 🛑 Never stop abruptly Taper — risk of rebound spasticity/seizures, especially with baclofen.

Q1: How do most centrally-acting muscle relaxants relieve spasm? Show answer Mostly through a sedative effect on the CNS that blunts perception of spasm/pain — they usually don't act directly on the muscle fiber. Dantrolene is the exception; it acts directly on skeletal muscle. Q2: What is the #1 safety concern shared by every drug in this class? Show answer CNS depression → drowsiness/sedation → fall risk. Caution with driving/hazardous tasks and avoid other CNS depressants (alcohol, opioids, antihistamines, sedat

Top Tips — Drug-by-Drug NCLEX Quick Reference NG-156 MUSCULOSKELETAL · PHARM ADHD-friendly visual edition This page is the quick-reference companion — one snapshot card per named drug with its own memory trick, plus the traps NCLEX loves. For class-wide mechanism (central vs peripheral), general contraindications, interactions & the sedation/fall-risk safety rule, see NG-155 (Muscle Relaxants) — not repeated here. → Open NG-155: Muscle Relaxants (class overview + mechanism) 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Driv
STEP 1 · MEET THE DRUGS Four named drugs, four separate personalities — one memory hook each.

Used for: 🌡️ Malignant hyperthermia — acute IV treatment 🧩 Chronic spasticity: spinal cord injury , cerebral palsy , multiple sclerosis Watch for: 😴 Sedation / drowsiness 🧪 Hepatotoxicity — monitor liver function ❌ Contraindicated: active hepatic disease , lactation , spasm from rheumatic disorders 🧠 "Calcium CONTRACTS, dantrolene BLOCKS." Less calcium release = less contraction. And: Dantrolene = treats the FIRE (malignant hyperthermia) but can BURN the liver — check LFTs.

Used for: acute muscle spasm — short-term only (max 2–3 weeks ). Watch for: 😴 Sedation, anticholinergic effects (structurally similar to tricyclic antidepressants ) ❌ Contraindicated: recent MI , cardiac conduction disorders , hyperthyroidism ❌ Within 14 days of an MAOI — risk of high fever & convulsions 🧠 "CycloBACKzzaprine" — relaxes the back, but makes you zzz's. And: it's a cousin of TCAs — so it inherits the classic anticholinergic list ("can't see, can't spit, can't pee, can't poop") plus the cardiac cautions

entries.h: 🚫 Baclofen — GABA-B agonist, never stop abruptly
entries.t: MOA: enhances GABA (an inhibitory neurotransmitter) at GABA-B receptors — "makes everything low & slow." Used for: decreased flexor/extensor spasticity — spinal cord injury, MS, cerebral palsy. Watch for: 😵 Orthostatic hypotension , dizziness on position change — expected , not a hold parameter 🤢 Nausea 🚨 Never abruptly stop — rhabdomyolysis, multi-organ failure, seizures, rebound spasticity ❌ Contraindicated: spasm from rheumatic disorders 🧠 "Baclofen — back off slowly." This is the single highest-yield safety poi

Used for: acute muscle spasm — e.g., after surgery on open fractures . Watch for: 🔒 Controlled substance — risk of dependence and abuse 😴 Drowsiness & sedation 🛑 Taper off — do not stop abruptly ❌ Contraindicated: hypersensitivity to meprobamate 🧠 "Carisoprodol → meprobamate." The metabolite is itself a controlled sedative-hypnotic — that's exactly why carisoprodol carries abuse potential and is a controlled substance. 🎯
STEP 2 · TOP MISSED QUESTIONS The traps test-writers reuse across this class — spot the pattern, not just the answer.

A classic SATA stem: "When providing education to a patient newly prescribed cyclobenzaprine, which instructions should be included?" Options mix real teaching with disguised distractors. Practice spotting the pattern rather than memorizing this exact stem: ✅ Likely correct: Report excessive/unusual drowsiness, especially before driving or hazardous tasks. Do not stop the medication abruptly after regular use. Avoid alcohol entirely. ❌ Classic distractor: "Limit wine to 3–4 glasses per day" — any answer that quanti

Test writers love testing whether you know dantrolene has two separate uses : emergency IV treatment of malignant hyperthermia AND oral use for chronic spasticity . Don't assume a dantrolene question is automatically about MH — read the scenario. 🧠 One drug, two hats: 🔥 MH = acute IV rescue · 🧩 spasticity = chronic oral therapy.

A client reports dizziness with position changes on baclofen. This is NOT a reason to withhold the dose or call it a contraindication — orthostatic dizziness is an expected side effect. Teach slow position changes instead. 🧠 Expected ≠ emergency. Save your "hold the dose" instinct for abrupt discontinuation, not routine orthostatic dizziness. 🗣️
STEP 3 · ONE-LINERS TO SAY OUT LOUD One teaching sentence per drug — grab-and-go for clinical or a quick quiz review.

Drug Say this Highest-yield trap Dantrolene "We'll be checking your liver function while you're on this." Hepatotoxicity monitoring Cyclobenzaprine "This is short-term — 2 to 3 weeks — and don't mix it with alcohol." TCA-like anticholinergic effects Baclofen "Never stop this suddenly, even if you feel better — we'll taper it." Rebound spasticity/seizures Carisoprodol "This is a controlled medication — take exactly as prescribed." Meprobamate metabolite, abuse potential 🧠 Class-wide add-on for all four: "Expect drow

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🔥 Dantrolene MH + spasticity · direct muscle action · watch the liver. 😵 Cyclobenzaprine TCA cousin · anticholinergic · short-term only. 🚫 Baclofen GABA-B agonist · never stop abruptly. 🔒 Carisoprodol → meprobamate · controlled substance.

Q1: Which two conditions does dantrolene treat, and how do the routes differ? Show answer Malignant hyperthermia (acute IV treatment) and chronic spasticity from spinal cord injury/MS/cerebral palsy (oral). Watch liver function — hepatotoxicity risk. Q2: Why does cyclobenzaprine carry anticholinergic side effects? Show answer It's structurally related to tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs), so it inherits dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention, and tachycardia — plus TCA-style cardiac cautions. RA — Chronic Autoimmune Joint Disease NG-163 Musculoskeletal · Group D ADHD-friendly visual edition RA is an autoimmune disorder — the body attacks its OWN joints, causing major inflammation & deformity . Mainly the small hand joints, but it's systemic — it can hit the skin, eyes, and lungs too. Bilateral. Symmetric. Body-wide. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🧬 Autoimmune, not wear-and-tear The immune system attacks the synovium — that's what separates RA from osteoarthritis (OA). 🖐️ Symmetric & small
STEP 1 · THE IMMUNE ATTACK The body mistakes its own joint lining for a threat — and the attack doesn't stay in the joint.

RA is thought to be an autoimmune disorder — the immune system targets the synovium (joint lining), causing chronic inflammation. Over time inflamed synovial tissue thickens into pannus , which erodes cartilage and bone — this is what produces the classic hand deformities. 🧠 "Pannus eats the joint." Pannus = the overgrown, angry synovial tissue that literally chews through cartilage and bone — that's why RA damage is often irreversible if untreated.

Because RA is an autoimmune, body-wide disease, it can cause collateral damage in: 🖐️ Joints — mainly small hand joints 🩹 Skin — rheumatoid nodules 👁️ Eyes — dryness, scleritis 🫁 Lungs — pulmonary nodules/fibrosis 🧠 RA is systemic; OA is not — this is the single highest-yield line examiners quote directly.

👩 Female sex — much higher incidence 🧬 Genetic susceptibility (family history) 🚬 Smoking 🎂 Peak onset ages 30–60 🧠 RA doesn't "wear out" a joint — it attacks one. Wear-and-tear thinking belongs to osteoarthritis, not RA. 🔎
STEP 2 · SPOT THE PATTERN Symmetric small-joint pain, systemic symptoms, stiffness that lingers, and the labs that confirm it.

entries.h: 🖐️ Signature pattern: symmetric, small joints, systemic
entries.t: Early signs What they mean Fatigue, anorexia, weight loss Systemic inflammatory symptoms — the whole body is involved Symmetrical pain & swelling, small joints of the hands Classic RA distribution — both hands, same joints Morning joint stiffness Lasts >30–60 min — inflammatory, not mechanical Low-grade fever Systemic inflammation marker 🧠 "RA is a mirror." Whatever happens to one hand happens to the other — symmetry is the tell.

entries.h: ⏱️ RA vs OA morning stiffness — do NOT mix these up
entries.t: Rheumatoid Arthritis Osteoarthritis (see NG-168) Autoimmune — systemic Wear-and-tear — local Stiffness >30–60 min Stiffness <30 min Symmetric, small joints (hands) Asymmetric, weight-bearing joints (knees, hips) Fatigue, low-grade fever, nodules No systemic symptoms 🧠 "Long stiff = autoimmune gift; short stiff = joints that just got stiff from use." If the question says stiffness lasting over an hour, think RA — not OA.
🧠 "Swan reaches UP, buttonhole caves IN." A swan's neck curves up and out; a boutonniere (buttonhole) sinks the middle joint in.

entries.h: 🧪 Labs — all trend UP in active RA
entries.t: 🧠 "RF and anti-CCP point AT RA; ESR and CRP just say something's inflamed." Anti-CCP is the more RA-specific antibody test.

Synovial fluid aspiration — analyzes joint fluid for inflammation Arthroscopy — direct visualization when X-ray/MRI are inconclusive Blood tests: RF (rheumatoid factor), ESR, CRP — plus anti-CCP for higher specificity 🧠 Confirming RA takes labs + imaging + fluid analysis together — no single test rules it in or out alone. 🩺
STEP 3 · PROTECT THE JOINT Heat and cold, low-impact movement, a medication ladder that ends in DMARDs, and one classic "never."

entries.h: 💊 Medication ladder — symptom control → disease control
entries.t: 1 NSAIDs — pain/inflammation relief, does not slow disease 2 Steroids — the "-sone" drugs, e.g. prednisone , for flares/bridge therapy 3 DMARDs — methotrexate first-line; see the DMARDs page (NG-114) for full dosing & safety 🧠 "NSAIDs and steroids calm the fire; DMARDs put it out." Only DMARDs actually modify/slow the disease course.

Alternate applying heat and cold to affected joints Low-impact exercise — swimming is ideal (non-weight-bearing) Warm shower or bath before bed to ease morning stiffness 🧠 "Heat loosens, cold calms." Heat before activity to loosen stiff joints; cold after activity to calm an inflamed one.

entries.h: 🚨 Classic never: don't prop the knees
entries.t: Do NOT elevate the knees with pillows at night — it feels comfortable in the moment but encourages flexion contractures , permanently limiting extension over time. 🧠 Comfortable now ≠ safe long-term — a flexed knee that never extends fully is a permanent mobility loss.

Assess and treat pain levels regularly Pain relief WITH activity , but MORE pain at rest — expect this pattern in RA, unlike OA where activity worsens pain Watch for joint contractures from prolonged immobility Coordinate PT/OT for joint protection and adaptive devices 🧠 "Rusty hinge rule." RA joints hurt more at rest and loosen with gentle motion — like a rusty hinge that eases once it starts moving. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🧬 Autoimmune & systemic RA attacks the synovium and can hit skin, eyes, lungs 🖐️ Symmetric small joints plus stiffness lasting >30–60 min 🧪 RF, anti-CCP, ESR, CRP all elevated in active disease 🚫 No pillow under the knees = prevents flexion contracture

Q1: What is the key difference between RA and osteoarthritis? Show answer RA is a systemic autoimmune disease; osteoarthritis is a local wear-and-tear disease. RA morning stiffness lasts >30–60 min vs OA's <30 min. Q2: What labs confirm rheumatoid arthritis? Show answer RF (rheumatoid factor) and anti-CCP (more RA-specific), plus ESR and CRP for general inflammation — alongside synovial fluid aspiration and arthroscopy. Q3: Why should you never put a pillow under an RA patient's knees at night? Show answer It promo

Degenerative Joint Disease & Total Knee Replacement NG-168 Musculoskeletal ADHD-friendly visual edition Osteoarthritis is "wear and tear," not autoimmune — cartilage wears down until it's bone-on-bone, and pain gets worse with activity, better with rest . When conservative care fails, a total knee arthroplasty (TKR/TKA) replaces the joint — and post-op nursing care is a heavily tested skill of its own. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🦴 OA = bone-on-bone Cartilage degenerates from wear; pain worsens wit

STEP 1 · WEAR & TEAR One mechanism explains every OA finding: the cartilage cushion wears away until bone grinds on bone. From your lecture. Not a systemic disease and non-inflammatory — a wear-and-tear disorder that is slow and irreversible. Risk: older age, female, genetics, obesity, prior joint injury, repetitive movement.

Progressive degeneration of the protective cartilage cushion results in bone-on-bone rubbing and massive pain. 🧠 "OA-Ouch pain." The cushion wore out — think of a worn-out shoe sole slapping the pavement.

Age — cumulative wear over decades. Obesity — extra load on weight-bearing joints. Repetitive stress/overuse on the joints (occupational, athletic). Prior joint trauma or injury. 🧠 Load + time = OA. Any factor that adds mechanical stress or years of use raises risk.

Crepitus — a "crunch" sound/feel with joint movement. Pain worse with activity, relieved by rest . Usually affects one joint at a time — typically a large, weight-bearing joint (knee, hip) — asymmetric . Heberden's nodes (DIP joints) and Bouchard's nodes (PIP joints) — bony hand nodules. 🧠 "Heberden's is Higher up the finger." Heberden's = distal (DIP, closer to nail); Bouchard's = proximal (PIP, closer to hand) — say them in that finger order to keep them straight.
🧠 Use the fingertip, not the alphabet. Heberden's is closest to the nail (H = high, at the tip = DIP); Bouchard's sits at the middle knuckle (PIP). 🔎
STEP 2 · TELL THEM APART These two get confused on every exam — one table settles it. See the Rheumatoid Arthritis page (NG-163) for RA's full autoimmune picture.

Osteoarthritis (OA) Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA) Degenerative — mechanical wear, NOT autoimmune Autoimmune — systemic inflammatory disease Morning stiffness <30 minutes Morning stiffness >30–60 minutes Pain worse with activity , better with rest Pain/stiffness worse with rest , improves with movement Asymmetric — one joint, usually large/weight-bearing (knee, hip) Symmetric — small joints of hands/wrists on both sides No systemic symptoms; local joint disease only Systemic — fatigue, low-grade fever, malaise, weight l

✔️ Joint pain that diminishes after rest ✔️ Joint pain that intensifies with activity ✔️ Node formation (Heberden's/Bouchard's) ✔️ Affects one joint , usually large 🧠 Select-all-that-apply questions test whether you know the OA pattern is activity-triggered , not inflammatory-triggered.

NSAIDs — first-line for pain/inflammation, but GI bleed risk. Corticosteroids ("-sone," e.g. prednisone) — can worsen cartilage breakdown and mask infection with long-term use. Glucosamine — supplement some clients use for joint support; evidence is mixed, but it's a commonly tested item. 🧠 "NSAIDS, glucosamine, prednisone" = the most-tested trio for OA symptom management. 🔪
STEP 3 · PROTECT THE NEW JOINT A total knee arthroplasty replaces the joint surface — nursing care afterward focuses on clots, motion, and neurovascular status.

A surgical procedure to replace the knee joint when conservative management of severe OA (or RA) fails. Also a common surgical intervention for RA-damaged joints. 🧠 The joint surfaces are replaced with metal/plastic components — the whole leg isn't hollowed out, just the worn cartilage/bone ends.

P ain (out of proportion) P allor P ulselessness P aresthesia P aralysis P oikilothermia (coolness) 🧠 Same 6 P's used for any extremity at risk of compromised circulation — see the Fracture (NG-056) page, where these first appear for compartment syndrome screening.

1 Flex the foot every hour while awake — ankle pumps to prevent DVT. 2 Early weight-bearing/ambulation as ordered, PT-directed. 3 CPM machine (continuous passive motion) to gradually increase knee flexion. 4 Ice, elevation of the whole leg (not just under the knee), and pain control to enable participation in PT. 🧠 "Flex it hourly, move it early." Motion is medicine after a TKR — both for the joint and for clot prevention.

entries.h: ❌ Never place a pillow under the operative knee
entries.t: Never place a support pillow directly under the new operative knee — it holds the joint in flexion for prolonged periods, which promotes a flexion contracture and blocks the surgical goal of full extension/flexion range. 🧠 Straight leg, straight recovery. A pillow under the knee feels comfortable but locks the joint in the wrong position — keep the leg extended when resting, per care team positioning orders.

entries.h: 🩸 Clot prevention: heparin bridges to warfarin
entries.t: Heparin and warfarin are often started at the same time in the hospital, because heparin works fast (immediate anticoagulation) while warfarin has a slow onset — it takes several days to reach a therapeutic effect. The two overlap until warfarin catches up, then heparin is stopped. 🧠 "Heparin sprints, warfarin walks." Start together, bridge the gap, then drop the sprinter once the walker (warfarin/INR) reaches target. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🦴 OA = wear & tear Pain worse with activity, better with rest; one joint at a time. ⏱️ <30 min stiffness OA's morning stiffness is brief — RA's lasts >30–60 min. 🦵 No pillow under the knee Prevents flexion contracture after TKR. 🩸 Heparin + warfarin Started together — fast bridge to slow, long-term anticoagulation.

Q1: How does OA pain differ from RA pain in timing? Show answer OA pain worsens with activity and improves with rest, with morning stiffness under 30 minutes. RA is the opposite — worse with rest/morning, improves with movement, and morning stiffness lasts over 30–60 minutes. Q2: A nurse is teaching a client after TKR. What foot/ankle instruction should be included? Show answer Flex the foot every hour while awake (ankle pumps) to promote circulation and reduce DVT risk. Q3: Why should a pillow never be placed dire

Below- & Above-Knee Limb Loss — Perioperative & Residual Limb Care NG-174 Musculoskeletal ADHD-friendly visual edition Amputation = surgical removal of a limb , most often for peripheral arterial disease & diabetic gangrene that no longer has enough blood flow to heal. The nurse's job splits into three windows: before (vascular status, prep), right after (bleeding, pain as a red flag, positioning), and rehab/home (residual limb shaping, phantom pain, contracture prevention). Positioning is the single most tested pi
STEP 1 · WHY & WHERE Amputation is almost always a circulation problem first — knowing the "why" explains every choice that follows.

entries.h: 🦵 The two levels — and why the exam always picks BKA
entries.t: KAPLAN LOGIC A client with type 1 diabetes gets a right BKA for gangrenous toes and asks why it's "so extensive." The answer: a below-the-knee amputation results in better circulation and healing than trying to save more distal, poorly-perfused tissue. 🧠 "B for Better, B for Below." BKA keeps the knee AND gets better blood flow to the cut edge — it's the level surgeons reach for whenever the vasculature allows it.

entries.h: ⚠️ Who ends up here — causes & risk factors
entries.t: 🩸 Peripheral arterial disease (PAD) — poor blood flow to the limb 🍬 Diabetes mellitus — the classic exam scenario: sugary blood → poor healing → infection → gangrene 🦠 Severe/uncontrolled infection that won't clear with antibiotics or debridement 💥 Trauma — crush injury, severe burns, frostbite 🎗️ Malignant bone tumor (e.g., osteosarcoma) 🧠 "Sugar can't heal what it can't feed." Diabetes damages small vessels first — that's why toes go before the whole foot, and the whole foot before the whole leg.

entries.h: 🖐️ Pre-op vascular assessment — the same 6 P's
entries.t: Before surgery, the nurse documents baseline circulation, motion & sensation distal to the planned incision using the same neurovascular check covered on the Fracture page in this series. Check What it tells you Pain, Pallor, Pulselessness Circulation to the limb Paresthesia, Paralysis Nerve function Poikilothermia (temp change) Perfusion / skin viability 🧠 See NG-056 Fracture for the full 6 P's breakdown — it's one skill reused across every orthopedic page.

entries.h: 💬 Psychosocial prep — grieving a body part before it's gone
entries.t: Limb loss triggers a real grief response — anticipate anger, denial, depression before & after surgery. Assess body image, involve the client in decisions, and set the expectation early that phantom limb sensations are normal so the client isn't blindsided by them later. 🩸
STEP 2 · THE FIRST 24–48 HOURS Immediately post-op, the nurse is hunting for bleeding and watching how pain behaves — not just treating pain.

entries.h: 🚨 Priority concern: pain that persists or climbs at the operative site
entries.t: KAPLAN LOGIC Immediately following a right BKA, the nurse is most concerned when the client reports persistent pain at the operative site — not routine surgical soreness that responds to analgesia. Persistent or worsening pain is the earliest clue to hemorrhage, hematoma, or impaired circulation to the residual limb. 🩹 Assess the dressing frequently — note any increase in drainage, and mark & time the outline of new bleeding 🔧 Keep a large clamp or tourniquet at the bedside for the first 24 hours in case of sudden

entries.h: ⏫ Positioning, part 1: elevate for 24 hours only
entries.t: Elevating the residual limb on a pillow for the first 24 hours reduces post-op edema. This is time-limited on purpose — continue to the next card.

Rigid or soft compression dressing shapes the residual limb & controls edema Monitor a surgical drain (if present) for amount & character of output A dressing that hasn't been changed/dated appropriately (e.g., dated two days prior with no reassessment) is a finding the nurse should intervene on , not ignore 🧠 An old, unassessed dressing hides new bleeding — always know when it was last checked. 🩹
STEP 3 · SHAPE, PROTECT, TEACH Once bleeding risk passes, the whole game shifts to preventing contractures, shaping the limb for a prosthesis, and validating phantom pain.

entries.h: ❌ NEVER: prolonged elevation or keeping the limb flexed
entries.t: Do not elevate the residual limb past the first 24 hours and do not let it rest flexed against pillows . Both habits shorten the hip or knee flexors, and the client ends up with a permanent hip or knee flexion contracture that can make an eventual prosthesis impossible to use. 🧠 "Lie on your belly, keep your hip healthy." Prone (stomach-lying) for 30 minutes, 3 times a day actively stretches the hip flexors — teach the client to push the residual limb down into the mattress while prone for extra stretch.

1 🧼 Wash daily with soap & water; dry thoroughly 2 🌬️ Expose to air part of the day rather than always covered 3 🪞 Inspect skin daily with a mirror — look for redness, breakdown, blisters 4 🛏️ After the first 24h, keep the limb flat and fully extended (not propped up on pillows, not left hanging down) to prevent contracture 🧠 "Clean, dry, exposed to air." Trapped moisture under a wrap all day breaks down skin before it ever gets to try a prosthesis.

entries.h: 🩹 Wrapping/shrinker technique — shaping for a prosthesis
entries.t: An elastic bandage or shrinker sock applied in a figure-8 pattern with even, decreasing distal-to-proximal pressure shapes the residual limb into a cone for a future prosthesis. Circular wrapping is never used — it constricts like a tourniquet and cuts off circulation.

entries.h: 👻 Phantom limb pain — real, neurological, not psychological
entries.t: Phantom limb sensation/pain is a genuine neurological event — cut peripheral nerves keep firing, and the brain's cortical map for that limb hasn't updated yet. It is not a psychological complaint and should never be dismissed as "not real." 💊 Managed with gabapentin/pregabalin , sometimes low-dose antidepressants or opioids for breakthrough pain 🪞 Mirror therapy — client watches the reflection of the intact limb moving to "retrain" the brain ⚡ TENS unit , massage, and early prosthetic use can reduce frequency 🗣️ Va

entries.h: 📊 BKA vs AKA at a glance
entries.t: Feature Below-Knee (BKA) Above-Knee (AKA) Circulation to the cut edge Better — most tested choice Used when BKA vasculature won't support it Knee joint Preserved Removed Energy to walk w/ prosthesis Lower Higher — more energy expenditure Contracture risk to prevent Knee flexion Hip flexion ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🦵 BKA = better circulation most tested rationale for level choice 🚨 Escalating op-site pain = priority — think hemorrhage, not routine soreness ⏫ Elevate 24h, then STOP prone 30 min x3/day to prevent flexion contracture 👻 Phantom pain is real never dismiss it as psychological

Q1: Why is a below-knee amputation preferred over above-knee whenever possible? Show answer It results in better circulation and healing to the residual limb, and it preserves the knee joint, which lowers the energy cost of walking with a prosthesis. Q2: A client is 12 hours post-op right BKA and reports persistent, worsening pain at the operative site. What is the nurse most concerned about? Show answer Hemorrhage or impaired circulation to the residual limb — this is not expected post-op soreness and should be re

Crystal Arthropathy — Uric Acid, Not Autoimmune NG-200 Musculoskeletal ADHD-friendly visual edition Gout is a crystal arthropathy — uric acid accumulates and crystallizes inside a joint, triggering intense pain and inflammation. This is NOT an autoimmune disease — nothing is attacking "self" tissue like in rheumatoid arthritis (see NG-163); it's a metabolic/chemistry problem where a waste product builds up until it precipitates out as sharp crystals. Classic first attack: the big toe . 📄 Simple Nursing original — o
STEP 1 · THE CRYSTAL, NOT THE IMMUNE SYSTEM Uric acid is a normal waste product — gout happens when there's too much of it to stay dissolved.

entries.h: 🧬 Pathophysiology — uric acid crystallizes inside the joint
entries.t: Uric acid accumulation causes pain & inflammation in the joints , which leads to destruction and — over time — arthritis (bone-on-bone pain from loss of cartilage). Uric acid is the breakdown product of purines (found in many foods and normal cell turnover). When more uric acid is made than the kidneys can clear — or the kidneys simply can't clear enough — it builds up in the blood ( hyperuricemia ) and precipitates into sharp, needle-shaped monosodium urate crystals inside a joint space. 🧠 "Sharp crystals, not sol

High- purine foods and alcohol raise uric acid production or block its excretion: 🍗 Meats chicken, steak, liver 🦐 Seafood crab, lobster, shrimp 🍷 Alcohol wine, beer, liquor ⚖️ Obesity higher uric acid load 🩸 Diuretics ↓ uric acid excretion 🧬 Family history genetic tendency 🧠 "MSA" — M eats · S eafood · A lcohol — the three trigger categories the source graphic leads with. Say it fast: "gout hates MSA."

entries.h: ⚔️ Gout vs Rheumatoid Arthritis — mechanism matters
entries.t: Gout Rheumatoid Arthritis (NG-163) Crystal arthropathy — not autoimmune Autoimmune attack on the synovium Usually one joint at first — big toe Symmetric , multiple small joints Diet/metabolism-driven Immune-driven, systemic (skin, eyes, lungs) 🧠 If the stem says "one red hot toe" → think gout. If it says "both hands, same joints, stiff over an hour" → think RA. 🔎
STEP 2 · SPOT THE ATTACK One joint, sudden and severe, with a lab test that confirms what's already obvious at the bedside.

KAPLAN A client experiences an acute bout of gouty arthritis. The nurse expects the client's affected foot to have which appearance? Answer: red — the joint is red, hot, swollen, and exquisitely tender.
HESI Pain and swelling of the right great toe — which test will the nurse expect the provider to order? Answer: serum uric acid levels.
🧠 Tophi are visible, palpable proof that uric acid has been too high for too long — untreated chronic gout, not just "another flare." 🩺
STEP 3 · TREAT THE FLARE, PREVENT THE NEXT ONE Two completely different jobs: calm today's attack, and lower uric acid so there isn't a next one.

entries.h: ⚔️ Big key difference — treat vs prevent
entries.t: Colchicine / NSAIDs Allopurinol (see NG-188) Treats the acute attack happening right now Prevents future attacks — long-term urate-lowering Anti-inflammatory action, fast relief Xanthine oxidase inhibitor — lowers uric acid production Not for daily long-term prevention Never start during an active flare — can prolong it 🧠 "Colchicine puts out today's fire; allopurinol stops tomorrow's." For the full allopurinol dosing, the Stevens-Johnson rash warning, and drug interactions, see the Uric Acid Inhibitors page (NG-18

💊 NSAIDs or colchicine for pain/inflammation 🧊 Rest and immobilize the joint; ice may help ⬆️ Elevate the affected limb 🚱 Avoid alcohol and high-purine foods during the flare 🧠 A red-hot, exquisitely tender toe is not the time to "walk it off" — rest and immobilize first.

⚖️ Lose weight — achieve/maintain a healthy weight 🚫 Avoid high-purine foods — meats, alcohol, seafood 💧 Increase fluid intake 📋 Monitor fluid I&O HESI Which interventions should the nurse implement for a patient with gout? (Select all that apply) Answer: increase fluid intake; document intake & output; observe for medication side effects.

entries.h: 🚨 Fluids matter for a specific reason
entries.t: Increasing fluid intake and monitoring I&O isn't just general good advice — as uric acid levels drop (whether from diet change or starting urate-lowering therapy), diluting the urine helps prevent uric acid from crystallizing into kidney stones while levels are shifting. 🧠 "Flush while you lower." Any time uric acid is actively being reduced, hydration protects the kidneys from a second crystal problem — this time in the urinary tract instead of the joint. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🔬 Crystal, not autoimmune uric acid crystals deposit in the joint — unlike RA's immune attack 🦶 Podagra red, hot, swollen first MTP joint — classic first attack 🧪 Serum uric acid the confirming lab, elevated in gout ⚔️ Colchicine now, allopurinol later treat the flare vs prevent the next one

Q1: Is gout an autoimmune disease? Show answer No — gout is a crystal arthropathy caused by uric acid crystal deposition. RA (NG-163) is the autoimmune joint disease, driven by the immune system attacking the synovium. Q2: What is podagra and what does it look like? Show answer Gout affecting the first metatarsophalangeal (big toe) joint — the classic first attack. The foot appears red, hot, swollen, and exquisitely tender. Q3: What lab confirms gout, and what foods should be avoided? Show answer Serum uric acid le

Lateral Spinal Curvature · Screening · Bracing vs. Spinal Fusion NG-211 Musculoskeletal ADHD-friendly visual edition Scoliosis is a lateral (sideways) curvature of the spine that bends it into an "S" or "C" shape instead of straight. Most often caught during adolescent growth spurts , it's screened with the Adam's forward bend test and staged by the Cobb angle on X-ray. Treatment tracks severity : watch it, brace it, or fuse it. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🌀 "S"-shaped spine Lateral curvature — say
STEP 1 · A SPINE THAT CURVES SIDEWAYS Most cases have no single known cause — but growth spurts and a handful of underlying conditions raise the risk.

Scoliosis — say the word: S for lateral curvature, an "S"-shaped spine instead of straight. Curves can also be single "C" shapes depending on where along the spine they occur. 🧠 "S is for Scoliosis, S is for S-shaped spine." The name tells you the shape.

Most idiopathic cases have no single identified cause ; one theory points to a possible defect of the intervertebral discs — the shock absorbers between vertebrae Strongly associated with periods of rapid growth , especially the adolescent growth spurt Most common in females, ages 10–12 Also seen with cerebral palsy , muscular dystrophy , and Marfan syndrome (neuromuscular or connective-tissue causes) 🧠 "Growth spurt, spine curves out." The faster the bones grow, the more likely an already-vulnerable spine curves b

entries.h: 🩺 What the curve does to the body
entries.t: Mild to severe back pain Stiffened spine that limits movement Severe, untreated cases can cause a deformity of the chest cavity , which can affect breathing & cardiac function 🧠 A curve isn't just cosmetic — severe curves can compress the chest and crowd the heart & lungs. 🔎
STEP 2 · SCREEN IT, MEASURE IT One bedside test screens for it; one X-ray measurement stages it and drives every treatment decision.

entries.h: 🙇 Adam's forward bend test — the screening tool
entries.t: Client bends forward at the waist, arms hanging, feet together. The examiner looks from behind for asymmetry — one side of the rib cage or back rising higher than the other (a "rib hump"). A positive test is followed by X-ray.
Lines are drawn along the most-tilted vertebrae at the top & bottom of the curve on X-ray; the angle between them is the Cobb angle — the number that stages the curve.

General treatment ranges — exact cutoffs vary by provider & growth status. Cobb angle Typical approach <10° Normal variant / not scoliosis 10–25° Mild — observation, repeat X-rays 25–40° Moderate — bracing, esp. if still growing >40–50° Severe — surgical candidate (spinal fusion) 🩺
STEP 3 · MATCH TREATMENT TO SEVERITY Watch mild curves, brace moderate ones during growth, and fuse severe curves — then protect the spine after surgery.
Periodic X-ray & Cobb angle rechecks to track progression No brace or surgery needed if the curve stays small

Used for moderate curves, especially while the client is still growing. Wear a cotton shirt underneath the brace at all times to protect the skin from irritation/breakdown. Bracing doesn't reverse the curve — it aims to prevent progression .

Reserved for severe curves (generally >40–50° ) or curves that keep progressing despite bracing. Rods & instrumentation are placed to straighten & permanently fuse the affected vertebrae. Post-fusion nursing priorities: 🪵 Log-roll to turn — keep the spine in one straight aligned line, use a draw sheet with adequate staff 🖐️ Regular neurovascular checks of the lower extremities (pulses, movement, sensation) — same skill as the 6 P's on the Fracture page in this series 💊 Aggressive pain control to support early mobil

Encourage continued social interaction — visiting friends, normal activities — bracing shouldn't isolate an adolescent Avoid participating in contact sports while braced or during post-fusion recovery, per provider guidance Body image support — a back brace during adolescence can be emotionally difficult; validate and involve the client in care ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🌀 Lateral curve "S"-shaped spine, screened by Adam's forward bend test 👧 Ages 10–12 rapid growth, most often females 📐 Cobb angle severity drives observe vs. brace vs. fuse 🪵 Post-fusion log-roll + neurovascular checks

Q1: What test screens for scoliosis, and what does a positive result look like? Show answer Adam's forward bend test — the client bends forward at the waist and the examiner looks for asymmetry, such as a rib hump on one side. Q2: What measurement on X-ray determines the severity and treatment path? Show answer The Cobb angle — the angle between the most-tilted vertebrae at the top and bottom of the curve. Q3: What is essential teaching for a client wearing a Boston brace? Show answer Wear a cotton shirt underneath
