entries.h: Pediatric Fluids & Dehydration · NG-411 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🧩 Peds 🏠 Hub 💧 Maintenance 👀 Assessing 🥤 Rehydrating ⚠️ Safety NG-411 · NUR 235

A child holds a far larger share of their body weight as water and turns it over far faster, so they dehydrate in hours rather than days. Weight is the measurement that matters — not what the parents think they drank.
The calculation this course asks for by name. Divide the daily total by 24 for the hourly rate. 1620 ÷ 24 = 67.5 mL/hr.
A child weighs 26 kg . First 10 kg → 1000 mL Next 10 kg → 10 × 50 = 500 mL Remaining 6 kg → 6 × 20 = 120 mL Total 1620 mL/day , which is 67.5 mL/hr
Infant — 1–3 mL/kg/hr Child — 0.5 mL/kg/hr Adolescent / adult — 40–80 mL/hr Output below this is the earliest hard number you get that a child is dry.
Weight is the truth. Everything else is a clue.

entries.h: ⭐ Percent lost = percent of body weight lost
entries.t: A child who was 10 kg last week and is 9.5 kg now has lost 500 g , which is 5% — and in a child, 1 kg lost is 1 liter of fluid . Mild · about 5% Thirsty Alert, moist-ish mouth, normal or slightly raised heart rate, urine still passing. Moderate · about 10% Dry & tachycardic Dry mucous membranes, sunken fontanelle, reduced skin turgor, fewer wet diapers, irritable. Severe · 15% or more Shock Lethargy, marked tachycardia, cool mottled skin, no tears, minimal urine. Blood pressure falls last.

entries.h: 🚨 The findings that matter most in an infant
entries.t: Sunken fontanelle — and remember bulging means the opposite problem, raised ICP Fewer wet diapers — ask how many today versus a normal day No tears when crying A change in behavior is a vital sign. Irritable, then lethargic, is the direction of travel.

entries.h: ✅ Oral rehydration first, when they can take it
entries.t: An oral rehydration solution — not water, not juice, not soda Small amounts, often : a teaspoon every few minutes beats a cup they will vomit Keep going through the vomiting — slow and small, do not stop Resume a normal diet as soon as they will take it; the old “rest the gut” advice is out

entries.h: 🚨 When it has to be IV
entries.t: Severe dehydration, shock, or a child who cannot keep anything down Only normal saline or lactated Ringer's Bolus by weight, then reassess — heart rate, mental state, urine output Strict intake and output, and daily weights on the same scale

entries.h: 💡 What tells you it is working
entries.t: In order: heart rate settles , then the child brightens up , then urine output rises , then weight climbs. If the heart rate has not come down, nothing else you see is reassurance.

entries.h: 🚨 A child can be given too much just as easily
entries.t: Crackles , rising heart rate and rising blood pressure Puffy eyelids, new peripheral edema, a sudden weight gain Always on a pump , never by gravity, and never a free-flowing bag Fluid is a drug in pediatrics. It is calculated, checked by two nurses, and pumped. Where this came from. Built from your NUR 235 module pages — the high-yield cards, exam traps and briefs for modules 1 to 4. The numbers here are the numbers your course teaches. 🧩 Peds

entries.h: The Hospitalized Child · NG-412 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🧩 Peds 🏠 Hub 💬 Preparing 💕 Separation 🧩 Play 📝 Consent NG-412 · NUR 235
Preparation, play and consent, matched to the age. What frightens a child changes completely between three and thirteen , and the exam answer follows the fear, not the procedure.

How long before, and in what words. Age How far ahead What actually helps Infant Just before Keep the parent present; comfort and swaddle after Toddler Minutes before Very short words. Two choices , never an open question Preschool An hour or so before Simple honest words; let them handle the equipment; say it is not a punishment School age Days before Explain how it works, give them a job, respect modesty Adolescent As early as possible Full explanation, privacy , and a say in decisions

entries.h: 🚨 The words that get you marked wrong
entries.t: Never promise it will not hurt. Say how long it will last and what they can do. Never call medicine candy or a treat. Do not use words that sound like something else to a literal thinker — a preschooler hears “dye” , “put you to sleep” and “take your vitals” exactly as they sound. Procedures happen in the treatment room . The bed stays a safe place.

entries.h: 💕 Separation, and what it looks like
😕 The three stages of separation anxiety
entries.t: 1 · Protest — crying, clinging, refusing the nurse. Loud, and the healthiest of the three. 2 · Despair — quiet, withdrawn, stops crying. Looks like settling. 3 · Detachment — cheerful with anyone, indifferent to the parent. The most worrying, and the easiest to mistake for adjustment. A quiet child is not necessarily a settled child. Despair is often mistaken for improvement — that is the trap.

Rooming in , and encouraging the parents to stay Keep home routines — bedtime, the same comfort object, the same words Consistent staff, so it is not a new face each time Say when you will be back, and come back when you said
A toilet-trained toddler who wets again, a school-age child who wants a bottle — this is normal under stress . Normalize it to the parents and do not treat it. It resolves at home.

Infant — solitary. Mobiles, rattles, faces. Toddler — parallel. Beside another child, not with them. Preschool — associative. Together but loosely organized. School age — cooperative. Rules, teams, collecting. Adolescent — the peer group itself.

Let a preschooler give the injection to a doll, handle the stethoscope, put the mask on the teddy first. It gives back control , which is exactly what the hospital takes away. For a school-age child, a job does the same work: hold the tape, count to ten, pick which arm.

The provider obtains consent — explains the procedure, risks and alternatives The parent or guardian signs it The nurse witnesses the signature and verifies understanding by teach-back If the parent cannot explain it back, the nurse stops and calls the provider. Witnessing a signature is not the same as obtaining consent. An adolescent should be asked for assent even where they cannot legally consent — and adolescents get confidentiality and a conversation without the parent in the room. Where this came from. Built

Opioid Analgesics · Anticonvulsants · Benzodiazepines · Antidepressants & Anxiolytics NG-043 PHARM Series: NCLEX Drug Review 1 of 5 ADHD-friendly visual edition Four CNS drug families, one study map: class (what family?) → action (what does it change?) → watch (safety & teaching). These are the drugs that show up over and over on NCLEX — learn the brand/generic pairs cold , then hang one mechanism and one trap on each. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 💊 Opioids ↑ pain threshold by altering perception —
STEP 1 · WHAT'S IN THIS SET Robo's 3-part study map for every drug on this page: CLASS → ACTION → WATCH .

💊 Opioid Analgesics ⚡ Anticonvulsants 😴 Benzodiazepines 🧠 SSRIs 🔁 SNRI 🌀 Tricyclic (TCA) 🕊️ Anxiolytic (Buspar) 🧠 "CABSSTA" — Class families in order: C NS opioids · A nticonvulsants · B enzos · S SRI · S NRI · T CA · A nxiolytic. Say it once out loud before you start.

Class Brand Name(s) Generic Name Opioid Analgesic Demerol Meperidine HCl Dilaudid Hydromorphone Duragesic, Sublimaze Fentanyl Morphine Sulfate Morphine Sulfate Vicodin, Norco Hydrocodone Anti- convulsant Dilantin Phenytoin Neurontin Gabapentin Tegretol Carbamazepine Depakote Valproic Acid Benzo- diazepine Xanax Alprazolam Valium Diazepam Ativan Lorazepam Versed Midazolam SSRI Celexa Citalopram Lexapro Escitalopram Oxalate Paxil Paroxetine Prozac Fluoxetine Zoloft Sertraline SNRI Effexor Venlafaxine TCA Elavil Amitr
STEP 2 · CLASS → MECHANISM → TRAP One card per class: what it is, how it works, the one nursing point that matters most, and the trap NCLEX loves to hide.

entries.h: 💊 Opioid Analgesics Demerol · Dilaudid · Duragesic/Sublimaze · Morphine · Vicodin/Norco
entries.t: Mechanism: ↑ pain threshold by altering pain perception in the CNS (bind mu-opioid receptors). ⭐ Key nursing point: Assess respiratory rate and sedation level before every dose — hold and notify the provider for significant respiratory depression or oversedation. Pair with a scheduled bowel regimen (opioids slow peristalsis → constipation is universal, not occasional). Trap 1: Meperidine (Demerol) builds up a toxic metabolite, normeperidine , especially with repeated dosing or renal impairment — can cause CNS excit

Mechanism: ↑ the interval between seizures / raise the seizure threshold so neurons fire less easily. ⭐ Key nursing point: Monitor blood levels for phenytoin (Dilantin), carbamazepine (Tegretol), and valproic acid (Depakote) — narrow therapeutic windows. Gabapentin (Neurontin) is also frequently prescribed off-label for chronic neuropathic pain. 🚨 NCLEX trap: Phenytoin causes gingival hyperplasia (teach meticulous oral hygiene); Tegretol can suppress bone marrow (watch CBC for infection/bleeding signs); Depakote is

Mechanism: enhance/facilitate GABA, the brain's main inhibitory neurotransmitter — opens the chloride channel more often, calming neuron firing. ⭐ Key nursing point: monitor sedation, respiratory status, and fall risk. Versed (midazolam) is commonly used for short procedural sedation. Never discontinue abruptly after regular use — withdrawal can include seizures. 🚨 NCLEX trap: Antidote = flumazenil . Benzo + opioid together is a black-box respiratory-depression combo — extra vigilance, not routine co-administration

entries.h: 🧠 SSRIs Celexa · Lexapro · Paxil · Prozac · Zoloft
entries.t: Mechanism: inhibit serotonin reuptake in the CNS, leaving more serotonin available at the synapse. ⭐ Key nursing point: full antidepressant effect takes about 2–4 weeks — teach patients not to expect immediate relief and not to stop early because "it isn't working yet." Watch closely for worsening mood or suicidal ideation early in treatment, especially in adolescents/young adults. 🚨 NCLEX trap: Combining an SSRI with another serotonergic drug (MAOI, tramadol, triptans, St. John's Wort) risks serotonin syndrome — a

Mechanism: Effexor (SNRI) blocks reuptake of both norepinephrine and serotonin at nerve endings. Elavil (TCA, older class) works similarly but also blocks histamine/cholinergic/alpha receptors, giving it more side effects. ⭐ Key nursing point: TCAs are cardiotoxic in overdose (widened QRS, dysrhythmias) — narrow therapeutic index, teach strict adherence and safe storage, especially with a depressed or at-risk patient. 🚨 NCLEX trap: Elavil's anticholinergic effects — dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention, con

Mechanism: exact mechanism not fully defined; thought to act by changing serotonin activity in certain brain regions. ⭐ Key nursing point: Buspar is not a PRN anxiety drug — it takes about 2–4 weeks of scheduled dosing to reach full effect, has minimal sedation, and carries no significant abuse/dependence potential, unlike the benzodiazepines above. 🚨 NCLEX trap: A student may confuse Buspar with a benzodiazepine because both treat anxiety — but Buspar will not help an acute panic attack right now, and it is not cr
STEP 3 · SAFETY & PATIENT TEACHING What to say at the bedside, and the one table that keeps benzos and SSRIs from blurring together.

💧 Start a bowel regimen with any scheduled opioid — do not wait for constipation to happen 🚗 No driving/operating machinery until effects on alertness are known 🍷 Avoid alcohol — additive CNS/respiratory depression 🩸 Anticonvulsants: report rash, sore throat, unusual bruising (possible marrow suppression) and keep lab-draw appointments for drug levels

🚫 Never stop a benzodiazepine or an SSRI/SNRI/TCA abruptly — taper under provider guidance ⏳ Antidepressants need 2–4 weeks for full effect — keep taking it even if symptoms haven't shifted yet 🍷 Avoid alcohol with any of these classes 🆘 Report worsening mood, agitation, or suicidal thoughts immediately, especially in the first weeks

entries.h: 📊 Don't mix them up: Benzodiazepine vs. SSRI
entries.t: Benzodiazepine SSRI Onset: fast — can relieve acute anxiety same-day Onset: slow — 2–4 weeks for full effect Mechanism: enhances GABA (inhibitory) Mechanism: blocks serotonin reuptake Dependence/abuse potential: higher , taper to stop Dependence/abuse potential: low, but taper to avoid discontinuation syndrome Antidote available: flumazenil No specific antidote — treat serotonin syndrome supportively 🧠 "Benzo = right now, SSRI = weeks from now." If the NCLEX question needs relief today, it's not describing an SSRI.

SAY IT OUT LOUD 💊 Opioids Check RR & sedation first — naloxone reverses ⚡ Anticonvulsants Dilantin/Tegretol/Depakote → drug levels 😴 Benzos "-pam/-lam" · GABA · flumazenil reverses 🧠 SSRI/SNRI/TCA Never combine with an MAOI — serotonin syndrome

Q1: Before giving a scheduled opioid, what must the nurse assess first? Show answer Respiratory rate and level of sedation — hold and notify the provider if depression/oversedation is present. Q2: Which three anticonvulsants need periodic blood level monitoring? Show answer Phenytoin (Dilantin), carbamazepine (Tegretol), and valproic acid (Depakote). Q3: What is the antidote for a benzodiazepine overdose? Show answer Flumazenil (Romazicon). Q4: Why is combining an SSRI with an MAOI dangerous? Show answer Risk of se

entries.h: Perfect Drug Card & Safe Medication Admin · NG-087 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🗂️ Template 📖 Vocabulary 🛡️ Safe Admin ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Pharmacology · Foundations Course

& Safe Medication Administration NG-087 Pharmacology ADHD-friendly visual edition Drug cards feel like an overwhelming wall of facts. They aren't — every drug you'll ever study fits into the same 5-field template . Learn the template once, then plug in any drug for the rest of the program. This is the study method every other drug page assumes you already know. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🗂️ The Fab 5 Name · Class · Mechanism → Indication · Side effects · Contraindications. ⚠️ Adverse ≠ side effect
STEP 1 · THE FAB 5 Every drug card, no matter the class, answers the same 5 questions in the same order.

entries.h: 🧾 The Fab 5 — filled in for a real drug (Lisinopril)
entries.t: 🧠 "Name it, Class it, Explain it, Watch it, Skip it." Every drug card on Earth is this same 5-box chain — only the words inside the boxes change.

entries.h: ①② Name & Class — the ID tags
entries.t: Every drug has 1 generic name but can have multiple brand/trade names EXAM TIP NCLEX tests generic names only, never brand names Class = the drug family — often told by its suffix (see the Drug Suffixes reference page) Generic Brand Warfarin Coumadin Ibuprofen Advil, Motrin Acetaminophen Tylenol 🧠 1 drug, 1 generic, many nicknames. Learn the generic first — that's the one that shows up on the exam.

entries.h: ③ Mechanism → Indication — the "why it works"
entries.t: Mechanism of action = how the drug works at the cellular/chemical level. Indication = what it's used for — the two are always connected by a chain of logic. Penicillin breaks down the bacterial cell wall → kills bacteria → treats infection Heparin/Warfarin block clotting factors → prevents clots → treats DVT/PE/AFib Labetalol blocks alpha & beta receptors → vessels relax, heart slows → treats hypertension 🧠 "Mechanism is the verb, indication is the reason." If you can explain the mechanism in one sentence, the indi

entries.h: ④⑤ Side Effects & Contraindications — the "watch for"
entries.t: Side effects = expected, usually tolerable. Contraindications = reasons to never give this drug to this client. Antibiotics for ear/GI/skin infections often cause nausea & vomiting (side effect) Acetaminophen + liver disease = contraindication (hepatotoxicity risk) 🧠 A side effect you monitor; a contraindication you don't even start. 📖
STEP 2 · EFFECT VOCABULARY These 4 words get mixed up constantly on exams — the difference is severity and predictability.

entries.h: 📊 Therapeutic → Side → Adverse → Toxic: one severity ladder
entries.t: 🧠 "Therapeutic is the goal, side is a shrug, adverse is an alarm, toxic is a buildup." Toxic effect specifically means the drug is accumulating — think renal failure or elderly clients who can't clear it.

entries.h: 🔗 Synergistic vs. ❌ Antagonistic vs. ➕ Additive interactions
entries.t: Interaction What happens Additive Combined effect = same as the sum of each drug alone Synergistic Combined effect is greater than expected — e.g. opioids + alcohol → dangerous CNS depression Antagonistic One drug blocks another — e.g. naloxone reverses opioids 🧠 Synergy stacks, antagonism blocks. Naloxone is the antagonist superhero of every opioid overdose question.

entries.h: 🤰 Pregnancy categories — safest to most dangerous
entries.t: A safest B C D X never A = well-controlled studies show no risk . X = studies show proven fetal harm — never given in pregnancy . 🧠 "A is Awesome, X marks eXit." Alphabetical order = risk order.

entries.h: 🚫 Contraindication vs. ⚠️ Caution — know which one stops you cold
entries.t: Contraindication = a reason never to give the drug to this client at all — e.g. acetaminophen in severe liver disease , pain medication + active alcohol use , caffeine-containing stimulants + Adderall . These aren't side effects to monitor — they're reasons to hold the drug and call the prescriber before it's ever given. 🧠 A side effect is something you watch . A contraindication is something you stop . 🛡️
STEP 3 · APPLY THE TEMPLATE SAFELY Knowing the card means nothing if the med doesn't reach the right client safely — this is where the 5 Rights page picks up.

entries.h: ✅ From card to bedside — the full loop
entries.t: 🗂️ Study the Fab 5 for this drug (name · class · mechanism → indication · side fx · contraindications) ▼ 🧾 Verify the order against the MAR — 3 checks: med room, order, bedside ▼ ✅ Confirm the 5 Rights — patient · drug · dose · route · time ▼ 📝 Document immediately & evaluate the response 🧠 Knowledge (the card) + Process (the rights) = safety. One without the other still causes errors.

entries.h: 🧪 Toxic effect — a Fab-5 red flag to watch
entries.t: Accumulation happens fastest when the client can't eliminate the drug — think renal failure , hepatic impairment , or the elderly with reduced clearance. 🧠 If a drug card doesn't mention how it's cleared, ask — renal vs. hepatic clearance changes your monitoring plan.

entries.h: 🎓 Client education is part of the card
entries.t: A complete drug card always ends with: what should the client watch for and report? That single question turns memorized facts into real teaching. 🧠 "If you can't teach it back, you don't know the card yet." ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🗂️ Fab 5 Name · Class · Mechanism → Indication · Side effects · Contraindications 📊 Severity ladder Therapeutic → Side → Adverse → Toxic 🧪 Generic names NCLEX tests generic, not brand 🤰 A→X Pregnancy category order = risk order

Q1: What are the 5 fields of a complete drug card? Show answer Name (generic + brand), class, mechanism of action leading to indication, side effects, and contraindications. Q2: What's the difference between a side effect and an adverse effect? Show answer Side effect = expected, usually mild. Adverse effect = unexpected and severe, like an allergic reaction with hives or respiratory distress. Q3: Naloxone reversing an opioid overdose is what kind of drug interaction? Show answer Antagonistic — one drug blocks the

entries.h: Adrenergic Blockers · NG-095 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 💊 What it does ⚠️ Watch for 🗣️ Teach ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Pharmacology · Adrenergic Drug Classes

Adrenergic Antagonists — the umbrella term for alpha- & beta-blockers NG-095 PHARM ADHD-friendly visual edition "Adrenergic antagonist" just means a drug that blocks a receptor the sympathetic nervous system uses. There are two families — alpha-blockers and beta-blockers — and some drugs (carvedilol, labetalol) block both at once . This page is the overview and the alpha side; beta-blockers get their own deep dive. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🚫 Antagonist = blocker Sits on the receptor and stops no
STEP 1 · THE MECHANISM Norepinephrine and epinephrine turn receptors ON — an adrenergic blocker's whole job is to sit on that same receptor and turn it back OFF.

entries.h: 🔒 Agonist turns it on · Antagonist blocks it
entries.t: EXAM TIP Block alpha receptors → vasodilation by relaxing the smooth muscle of blood vessels. In ophthalmic preps, alpha blockade also relaxes the iris dilator muscle, which is why alpha-blocker use is linked to intraoperative floppy iris syndrome during cataract surgery. 🧠 "Antagonist = anti-agonist." The blocker doesn't do anything itself — it just squats on the parking spot so norepinephrine can't park there. No signal in, no effect out.

Alpha-1 — blood vessels, bladder neck/prostate smooth muscle, iris dilator Alpha-2 — mostly presynaptic (brakes on further NE release); clonidine stimulates this one centrally — see NG-243 Clonidine Beta-1 — heart (rate & contractility) Beta-2 — bronchioles & vessels (bronchodilation, vasodilation) 🧠 "1 is the one right next to it." Beta- 1 = heart, right in your chest. Beta- 2 = the other two letters away — lungs.

Alpha-blockers Beta-blockers Block vascular & prostate/bladder-neck smooth muscle receptors Block cardiac (β1) ± bronchial/vascular (β2) receptors Main effect: vasodilation → BP drops Main effect: HR & contractility drop #1 safety issue: orthostatic hypotension #1 safety issue: bradycardia / never stop abruptly Deep dive: NG-141 Alpha Blockers Deep dive: NG-176 Beta Blockers (Cardio batch) 🧠 "Alpha drops the pipes, Beta drops the pump." Alpha-blockers relax the pipes (vessels); beta-blockers slow the pump (heart).

entries.h: 💊 The dual blockers — carvedilol & labetalol block BOTH
entries.t: A few drugs don't pick a side — they block alpha-1 AND beta receptors at the same time, giving both vasodilation and a slower heart rate in one pill. Generic Trade Use Dose / route Carvedilol Coreg, Coreg CR Essential HTN; HF — reduces disease progression 6.25 mg PO twice daily (starting dose) Labetalol Trandate HTN — usually an add-on to a diuretic 100 mg PO twice daily; also IV Wean, don't crash: in uncompensated HF needing IV inotropes, those must be tapered off before starting carvedilol — starting a beta-block
STEP 2 · THE DANGER LIST One drug class, a body-wide adverse effect list — group it by system instead of memorizing a wall of words.

System What to watch CNS 🧠 Dizziness, fatigue, weakness, anxiety, depression, drowsiness, insomnia, memory loss, mental status changes, nervousness, nightmares EENT 👁️ Blurred vision, dry eyes, intraoperative floppy iris syndrome , nasal stuffiness Resp 🫁 Bronchospasm, wheezing CV ❤️ Bradycardia , heart failure, pulmonary edema GI 🍽️ Diarrhea, constipation, nausea GU 🚻 Erectile dysfunction, decreased libido Derm 🩹 Stevens-Johnson syndrome , toxic epidermal necrolysis, itching, rashes, urticaria Endo 🍬 Hyperglycemia

History of serious hypersensitivity reaction Pulmonary edema or cardiogenic shock Bradycardia , heart block, or sick sinus syndrome Uncompensated HF needing IV inotropes — wean first Severe hepatic impairment Asthma or other bronchospastic disorders 🧠 "Slow heart, tight lungs, sick liver — say no."

Antidepressants → tremors Cimetidine → increased adrenergic-blocker effect Clonidine → increases clonidine's effect (two BP-lowering drugs stacking) Digoxin → digoxin toxicity risk 🧠 "Cimetidine slows the liver, so the blocker builds up." Same logic shows up with lots of H2-blocker drug interactions.

entries.h: 🚨 Hypotensive crisis on IV therapy — why epinephrine is the wrong answer
entries.t: Monitor BP, pulse, and ECG every 2 minutes until stable during IV administration. If a hypotensive crisis occurs, epinephrine is contraindicated — because alpha is blocked, epi's unopposed beta-2 effect can push BP down further ("epinephrine reversal"). Norepinephrine may be used instead — it's a much weaker beta-2 agonist, so its alpha-mediated vasoconstriction still wins. Instruct the client to change positions slowly to minimize orthostatic hypotension, and to notify the HCP if chest pain occurs during the IV in
STEP 3 · WHAT THE CLIENT NEEDS TO HEAR If it's an adrenergic blocker of any kind, orthostatic precautions and "never stop cold turkey" apply.

entries.h: ✅ Universal teaching for any adrenergic blocker
entries.t: 1 🪑 Rise slowly — sit, pause, then stand 2 🩺 Check BP/pulse before dosing per parameters 3 ❌ Never stop abruptly — taper under provider guidance 4 📞 Report chest pain, fainting, or new SOB right away 🧠 "Blocked receptors, gradual changes." Whatever adrenergic receptor is blocked, the body needs time to adapt — both starting the drug (slow position changes) and stopping it (taper).

NG-141 Adrenergic Alpha Blockers — tamsulosin, doxazosin, prazosin; first-dose orthostatic hypotension NG-160 Prostate – BPH — alpha blockers as first-line BPH therapy NG-260 Peripherally Acting Antiadrenergics — reserpine/guanethidine-class, an older mechanism NG-176 Beta Blockers (Cardio batch) — full cardioselective vs nonselective deep dive NG-243 Clonidine — a central alpha-2 agonist , not a blocker; easy to mix up on exams 🧠 "Antagonist blocks, agonist activates." Adrenergic blockers ≠ clonidine. Say it every

Adrenergic antagonist (this page) Adrenergic agonist Blocks the receptor — turns the signal off Stimulates the receptor — turns the signal on Alpha-blockers, beta-blockers, carvedilol, labetalol Epinephrine, norepinephrine, albuterol (β2 agonist), clonidine (central α2 agonist) Net effect on BP: usually lowers it Net effect on BP: usually raises it (except clonidine, which lowers it centrally) 🧠 "-onist just means 'acts on it' — the prefix tells you the direction." Ant agonist = ant i, against, blocks. Ag onist = g

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🚫 Antagonist = blocks the receptor, stops NE/epi from acting there 🩸 Alpha blocked = vessels relax = orthostatic hypotension risk 🫀 Beta blocked = HR/contractility drop — full detail on NG-176 🚨 Crisis? No epi Give norepinephrine — epi can drop BP further

Q1: What does "adrenergic antagonist" mean? Show answer A drug that blocks an adrenergic (alpha or beta) receptor, preventing norepinephrine/epinephrine from acting there — the opposite of an agonist. Q2: Why is epinephrine contraindicated during an alpha-blocker hypotensive crisis? Show answer With alpha blocked, epinephrine's unopposed beta-2 vasodilation can drop BP even further ("epinephrine reversal"). Norepinephrine is used instead because it has minimal beta-2 effect. Q3: Name two drugs that block BOTH alpha

entries.h: Anti-inflammatory Agents · NG-100 · Nursing Field Notes

The Overview Page — NSAIDs · Acetaminophen · Corticosteroids · DMARDs NG-100 PHARMACOLOGY ADHD-friendly visual edition Every anti-inflammatory drug interrupts the same fire — the body's inflammatory cascade — just at a different spot and a different speed . This page is the map for the whole pain & anti-inflammatory unit: compare the 4 big families here, then go deep on NSAIDs (NG-256) , Acetaminophen (NG-232) , and the DMARD Sulfasalazine (NG-175) on their own pages. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🗂️
STEP 1 · MEET THE FIRE One inflammatory cascade, four different places to jump in and shut it down.

entries.h: 🔥 The inflammation cascade — where each family blocks it
entries.t: BIG PICTURE Tissue injury releases arachidonic acid from cell membranes. The enzyme COX (cyclooxygenase) turns it into prostaglandins — the chemicals that cause pain, fever, and swelling . Every drug on this page interrupts that chain somewhere. 🧠 "Steroids block early, NSAIDs block the middle, Tylenol quiets the brain, DMARDs slow the whole loop." One sentence, four families.

GROUP MAP The single most-tested contrast: which one hurts the stomach/kidneys, which one hurts the liver, which one hurts the immune system. Class Example drugs Mechanism Best for Key risk NSAIDs 🔥 Ibuprofen, Naproxen, Ketorolac (Toradol), Indomethacin, Aspirin Block COX-1 & COX-2 → ↓prostaglandins Pain, fever, inflammation, gout, RA/OA GI bleed · renal injury · CV risk Acetaminophen 🧠 Tylenol Central COX inhibition — antipyretic/analgesic, weak peripheral anti-inflammatory Fever/pain when NSAIDs are risky (PUD, b

-sone / -lone = corticosteroid (methylprednisolone, fluticasone, beclomethasone) -profen / -oxicam / -fenac = NSAID (ibuprofen, meloxicam, diclofenac) -lukast = leukotriene inhibitor (montelukast, zafirlukast) Acetaminophen has no shared suffix — it's chemically its own thing (a para-aminophenol derivative), which is exactly why it doesn't act like an NSAID. 🧠 If the drug name ends in -sone/-lone , assume slow, broad, sugar-raising before you even read the question stem. 💊
STEP 2 · THE BROAD BLOCKER Powerful and slow — a maintenance drug that gets mistaken for a rescue drug on exams.

Drug Route Use Beclomethasone Inhaled Asthma maintenance / prevention Fluticasone Inhaled (also nasal) Asthma maintenance, allergic rhinitis Methylprednisolone (brand: Solu-Medrol) IV / PO — systemic Acute flares, after the rescue inhaler in an attack Slow onset — corticosteroids work over hours to days, not minutes. They calm swelling and inflammation broadly, but they are NOT the first drug given for the first sign of an acute attack . 🧠 "AIM" for an acute asthma attack, in order: A lbuterol 1st → I pratropium 2n

🍬 Hyperglycemia — monitor blood glucose, especially in diabetics 🦠 Oral thrush (Candida) — inhaled route; mouth sores/white patches 🧬 Immunosuppression / infection risk — systemic, long-term use 🦴 Osteoporosis — long-term systemic use ⛔ Never stop abruptly after long-term systemic use — adrenal insufficiency/crisis risk; taper down 🧠 Blood sugar UP, immune system DOWN. Picture a "-sone" pill sitting on a sugar cube while an immune cell falls asleep.

🔄 Use a spacer to improve delivery and cut mouth deposition 🚿 Rinse mouth after each use — spit, don't swallow the water ⏱️ Take on a scheduled, daily basis — not PRN ❌ Never use for the first sign of an acute attack — reach for the rescue inhaler (albuterol) instead 🧠 Rinse & spit, never for the fit. "Fit" = acute attack. Steroids don't touch an attack already happening. 🫁
STEP 3 · PREVENT, DON'T RESCUE Two more anti-inflammatory classes that only work if taken before the trigger — never during.
Montelukast , Zafirlukast (brand: Singulair) . 🧠 "Luke likes to SING (airway open)." Monte lukast keeps the airway singing — but only if taken every day, not as a rescue drug during an attack .

Blocks mast cell degranulation → prevents the release of histamine and inflammatory mediators before they start. 🧠 Cromolyn = the sunscreen of asthma drugs. Sunscreen only works if applied before sun exposure — cromolyn only works if taken before exercise.

🚑 Rescue — during an attack 🛡️ Preventer — before it starts Albuterol — fast-acting bronchodilator, first drug given Inhaled corticosteroids, leukotriene inhibitors, mast cell stabilizers — daily or pre-exposure only Works in minutes Works over hours to weeks — will not stop an attack already happening 🧠 If the NCLEX stem says "first sign of an acute attack" — the answer is always the rescue drug, never a "-sone," "-lukast," or Cromolyn. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🗂️ 4 families NSAIDs · Acetaminophen · Corticosteroids · DMARDs — each blocks the fire at a different point 💊 "-sone/-lone" = corticosteroid = slow, broad, sugar-raising, NOT a rescue drug 🛡️ Preventers only work BEFORE Leukotriene inhibitors + mast cell stabilizers — never during an attack 🚨 Deep dives next NSAIDs, Acetaminophen & Sulfasalazine each get their own page in this unit

Q1: Which anti-inflammatory family has the slowest onset and works "upstream" in the inflammatory cascade? Show answer Corticosteroids ("-sone/-lone") — they block inflammation broadly and take hours-to-days to work; never the first drug for an acute attack. Q2: A client is having their first sign of an acute asthma attack. What order do drugs get given? Show answer AIM — Albuterol 1st, Ipratropium 2nd, Methylprednisolone (Solu-Medrol) last. PDE5 Inhibitors — sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil NG-115 PHARM ADHD-friendly visual edition Phosphodiesterase type 5 (PDE5) inhibitors are oral drugs that block the enzyme (PDE5) that normally breaks down cGMP in the penis. More cGMP hanging around means more smooth muscle relaxation, more blood flow in, and an erection — but only with sexual stimulation . One interaction on this page is ABSOLUTE and can kill : nitrates. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🔗 Related page: the nitrate contraindication on
STEP 1 · THE MECHANISM One enzyme, one pathway — PDE5 inhibitors don't create arousal, they just let the body's own erection signal last longer.

EXAM TIP Sexual stimulation releases nitric oxide (NO) in the penis, which raises cGMP and relaxes smooth muscle, letting blood flow in. The enzyme PDE5 normally breaks cGMP back down, ending the erection. PDE5 inhibitors block that breakdown — cGMP lasts longer, so the erection lasts longer. 🧠 "No stimulation, no show." Sildenafil has no effect without sexual stimulation — it doesn't create arousal, it just lets an existing erection signal last. That's a key teaching point: the drug is not a substitute for arousal

Phosphodiesterase type 5 (PDE5) inhibitors Oral drugs, taken before planned sexual activity Sildenafil (as Revatio) is also used for pulmonary arterial hypertension Tadalafil, low daily dose, is also used for BPH 🧠 "5 for 5." PDE- 5 inhibitor. If you see -afil at the end of a drug name, think PDE5 inhibitor.

Allows blood flow into the penis, resulting in an erection — used for erectile dysfunction . Determine that ED is present before starting therapy. 🧠 The drug enables the physical mechanism; it does not create desire or arousal on its own.

Generic Trade Use Typical dose & timing Sildenafil Viagra (Revatio for PAH) Erectile dysfunction 25–100 mg PO, 30–60 min before sexual activity; not more than once/day Tadalafil Cialis ED, BPH 5–20 mg PO; daily low-dose for BPH, or as needed — effective up to 36 hr before activity Vardenafil Levitra, Staxyn Erectile dysfunction 5–20 mg PO, ~60 min before activity; window ≈ 4 hr ⚠️
STEP 2 · THE DANGER LIST One contraindication is absolute, one complication is a urologic emergency, and two symptoms mean stop and call.

PDE5 inhibitors and nitrates both raise cGMP / nitric oxide-driven vasodilation . Given together, the two vasodilating effects stack — the result can be severe, life-threatening hypotension and cardiovascular collapse . Always ask about ED medication use before giving a nitrate, and never give a PDE5 inhibitor to a patient on nitrate therapy. 🧠 "Blue pill, red flag." Any ED drug question that also mentions chest pain / nitroglycerin use is testing this exact interaction. See NG-216 · Nitrates for the nitrate side o

Do not take concurrently with alpha-adrenergic blockers (e.g., drugs for BPH) unless the patient is on a stable dose — both classes drop BP, and together they raise the risk of symptomatic hypotension . 🧠 Two vasodilators, two chances to fall — orthostatic teaching applies here too.
🧠 "4 is the floor." Any erection lasting longer than 4 hours is a urologic emergency, not something to "wait out."

👁️ Sudden vision loss one or both eyes 👂 Sudden hearing loss or decrease 🔔 Ringing in the ears tinnitus 💫 Dizziness with any of the above Also expect and teach: headache, flushing, GI upset, nausea, nasal congestion/runny nose as common (non-emergency) adverse reactions. 🧠 "Eyes, ears, and erections — all reported." Vision loss, hearing loss/ringing, priapism, and chest pain during sexual activity are the four "call now" symptoms for this drug class. 🗣️
STEP 3 · WHAT THE CLIENT NEEDS TO HEAR Timing, honesty with every provider about ED med use, and what this drug does not protect against.

1 ⏱️ Take as directed — timing before activity varies by drug 2 ❌ Not more than once per day for sildenafil 3 💬 Tell every provider and dentist you take an ED drug — before any nitrate is ever prescribed 4 🚨 Chest pain during sex → seek immediate medical attention , do not take a nitrate first 5 🛡️ No STI protection — this drug offers none; discuss protection separately 🧠 "If chest pain hits, don't reach for nitro." A patient on sildenafil who develops chest pain during intercourse must get emergency care — nitrogl

Antiretrovirals (e.g., protease inhibitors) — increase PDE5-inhibitor blood levels/effectiveness → higher side-effect risk Antihypertensives — increase the antihypertensive's effect → additive hypotension Nitrates — absolute contraindication , see above Alpha blockers — caution unless on a stable dose 🧠 Always screen the full med list, OTC drugs, and herbal products before giving these agents — several categories stack with the same vasodilation.

entries.h: 🆚 Not for women, not a cure, not stimulation
entries.t: Myth Reality "It creates arousal" No — it only sustains an erection once sexual stimulation has already started. No stimulation, no effect. "Women can take it too" Not indicated for use in women. "It's fine with my nitro spray" Absolute contraindication — risk of severe hypotension. "It protects against STIs" It does not — counsel on protection separately. 🧠 "Wingman, not magic." The drug supports a signal that's already there — it doesn't create desire, doesn't replace protection, and doesn't mix with nitrates. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD ⛽ Blocks PDE5 cGMP stays up, erection sustained — only with stimulation 🚫 Nitrates = ABSOLUTE no severe/fatal hypotension risk — see NG-216 ⏱️ Sildenafil/vardenafil ≈4h Tadalafil up to 36h — "weekend pill" 🚨 >4hr erection priapism — emergency

Q1: How do PDE5 inhibitors work? Show answer They block the enzyme PDE5, which normally breaks down cGMP — cGMP stays elevated, smooth muscle stays relaxed, and blood flow into the penis is sustained. They require sexual stimulation to have any effect. Q2: What is the one absolute contraindication, and why? Show answer Nitrates — both drug classes vasodilate through the same nitric-oxide/cGMP pathway, and combined they can cause severe, life-threatening hypotension and cardiovascular collapse. Sedative-Hypnotics · Antiplatelets · Anticoagulants · Loop, Thiazide & Potassium-Sparing Diuretics NG-124 PHARM Series: NCLEX Drug Review 2 of 5 ADHD-friendly visual edition This set is fluid, blood & clot management in one page. The diuretics are the trickiest — three classes, three different nephron addresses, and two of them pull potassium OUT while one holds it IN . Nail that one distinction and half this page is free points. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 💤 Z-drugs Ambien & Lunesta — short-term i
STEP 1 · WHAT'S IN THIS SET Robo's 3-part study map for every drug on this page: CLASS → ACTION → WATCH .

💤 Sedative-Hypnotics 🩸 Antiplatelets 🧂 K-Sparing Diuretics 🌊 Loop Diuretics 💧 Thiazide Diuretics 🧵 Anticoagulants 🧠 "Sleep, Stick, Squeeze, Save." Sedatives put you to Sleep · antiplatelets keep cells from St icking · diuretics Squeeze water out three different ways · anticoagulants Save you from a clot forming in the first place.

Class Brand Name(s) Generic Name Sedative- Hypnotic Ambien Zolpidem Tartrate Lunesta Eszopiclone Antiplatelet ASA (aspirin) Acetylsalicylic Acid Plavix Clopidogrel Potassium- Sparing Diuretic Aldactone Spironolactone Dyrenium Triamterene Loop Diuretic Bumex Bumetanide Demadex Torsemide Lasix Furosemide Thiazide Diuretic Diuril Chlorothiazide Sodium Hydrodiuril, HCTZ Hydrochlorothiazide Zaroxolyn Metolazone Anticoagulant Coumadin Warfarin Lovenox Enoxaparin — Heparin Sodium (from beef/pork) 🧠 Diuretic name clues: Lo
STEP 2 · CLASS → MECHANISM → TRAP One card per class — including the nephron map that finally makes the three diuretic classes make sense.

Mechanism: "Z-drugs" that act on GABA receptors to promote sleep onset — chemically different from benzodiazepines but produce a similar calming effect. ⭐ Key nursing point: for short-term insomnia management; give only when the patient can commit to a full night (about 7–8 hours) of sleep. Raise the side rails and instruct the patient to call for help before getting up — significant fall risk. 🚨 NCLEX trap: Being woken early after a dose can cause grogginess, confusion, or unsafe ambulation — treat it like a fall-

Mechanism: interferes with the first step of the clotting process — platelet aggregation (platelets clumping together at an injury site). ⭐ Key nursing point: monitor for bruising/bleeding, hold per provider order before surgery, and use with caution alongside other bleeding-risk drugs (anticoagulants, NSAIDs). 🚨 NCLEX trap: Pepto-Bismol contains aspirin (a salicylate) — easy to overlook as an OTC "hidden" source of aspirin in a patient with a true aspirin allergy or one already on antiplatelet/anticoagulant therap

entries.h: 💧 Diuretics — one nephron, three addresses Loop · Thiazide · K-Sparing
entries.t: 🧠 "Loop = biggest leak, Thiazide = medium leak, K-Sparing = patches the K⁺ hole." All three push sodium and water out — only the K-sparing class protects potassium while doing it.

Mechanism: inhibit reabsorption of Na⁺, Cl⁻, K⁺ & H₂O in the loop of Henle (also acts in the proximal & distal tubules) — the most potent diuretic class. ⭐ Key nursing point: monitor for hypokalemia , daily weight, I&O, and BP; ototoxicity risk with rapid IV administration or with other ototoxic drugs (e.g., aminoglycosides). 🚨 NCLEX trap: Hypokalemia from a loop diuretic can trigger digoxin toxicity in a patient also on digoxin — always correlate the K⁺ level with digoxin symptoms.

Mechanism: ↑ excretion of Na⁺, Cl⁻, K⁺ & H₂O in the distal tubule and ascending loop of Henle — gentler than loop diuretics, commonly first-line for hypertension. ⭐ Key nursing point: also causes hypokalemia — monitor potassium; can raise blood glucose and uric acid (caution in diabetes/gout). 🚨 NCLEX trap: Metolazone (Zaroxolyn) still works even with reduced kidney function and is often paired with a loop diuretic for a synergistic effect in resistant fluid overload.

Mechanism: block aldosterone at receptor sites in the distal tubule — excrete Na⁺, Cl⁻ & H₂O, but not K⁺. ⭐ Key nursing point: monitor for hyperkalemia (the opposite risk from loop/thiazide) — teach patients to avoid potassium supplements and salt substitutes (often KCl-based) unless directed. 🚨 NCLEX trap: Spironolactone can cause gynecomastia and menstrual irregularities from its anti-androgen activity — a teaching point students often forget belongs to this drug.

Mechanism: interferes with the blood clotting process (the cascade that forms fibrin) — used to prevent thrombus and embolus formation, not to break up an existing clot. ⭐ Key nursing point: heparin sodium is derived from beef or pork sources — assess for animal-product allergies before administration . Monitor aPTT for IV heparin and INR for warfarin; enoxaparin (Lovenox), a low-molecular-weight heparin, is given subcutaneously and generally does not require routine coagulation monitoring. 🚨 NCLEX trap: Antidotes
STEP 3 · SAFETY & PATIENT TEACHING Where each electrolyte lands, plus the bedside teaching that keeps these six classes from blurring together.

entries.h: 🧪 Potassium risk by diuretic class — low ↔ high scale
entries.t: Normal serum K⁺ (standard adult reference range): 3.5–5.0 mEq/L Bottom line: any patient on a loop or thiazide diuretic needs potassium monitoring for a LOW level; any patient on a potassium-sparing diuretic (or one combined with an ACE inhibitor/ARB) needs monitoring for a HIGH level.

🕗 Take in the morning to avoid nighttime urination/sleep disruption ⚖️ Daily weight — same time, scale, clothing; report a gain of about 2–3 lb in a day or 5 lb in a week 🩹 Rise slowly — orthostatic hypotension risk 🍌 Loop/thiazide: eat potassium-rich foods unless told otherwise; K-sparing: avoid extra potassium/salt substitutes

🪥 Soft-bristle toothbrush, electric razor 🆘 Report unusual bruising, black/tarry stools, pink-tinged urine, prolonged bleeding 💊 Avoid NSAIDs/extra aspirin unless approved 🥬 Warfarin: keep vitamin K intake (leafy greens) consistent , not eliminated — big swings change the INR 🧠 "Consistent, not zero." The #1 warfarin-diet myth is avoiding greens entirely — the real rule is a steady amount week to week.

entries.h: 📊 Antiplatelet vs. Anticoagulant — don't mix them up
entries.t: Antiplatelet (ASA, Plavix) Anticoagulant (Coumadin, Lovenox, Heparin) Blocks platelet aggregation — step 1 of clotting Blocks the clotting cascade — later steps forming fibrin Typical use: prevent arterial clots (MI, stroke) Typical use: prevent venous clots (DVT/PE), AFib stroke prevention No specific reversal agent routinely used Reversal: protamine (heparin), vitamin K (warfarin) ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 💤 Z-drugs Short-term only · fall risk after dosing 🩸 Antiplatelet Blocks platelet aggregation (step 1) 💧 Loop & thiazide Waste K⁺ — watch for hypokalemia 🧂 K-sparing Holds K⁺ in — watch for hyperkalemia

Q1: Which diuretic class is the most potent and acts at the loop of Henle? Show answer Loop diuretics (Bumex, Demadex, Lasix) — inhibit Na⁺/Cl⁻/K⁺/H₂O reabsorption in the loop of Henle. Q2: Which diuretic class is the exception — it does NOT cause potassium loss? Show answer Potassium-sparing diuretics (Aldactone/spironolactone, Dyrenium/triamterene) — they block aldosterone and spare K⁺, risking hyperkalemia instead. Q3: What OTC product contains hidden aspirin? Show answer Pepto-Bismol — it contains a salicylate

The Rights of Safe Medication Administration NG-131 Pharmacology ADHD-friendly visual edition Every single medication pass, every time , boils down to 5 checks before the syringe or pill touches the client : right patient , right drug , right dose , right route , right time . Miss one and it's a medication error — this is the page every other drug page on this site quietly assumes you already know. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → ✅ The core 5 are non-negotiable Patient · Drug · Dose · Route · Time — ch
FOUNDATION · MEMORIZE THESE "Please Do Da Right Thing" — every safe medication pass runs through the same 5 checkpoints, in this order, every time.

entries.h: 🧾 The checklist every nurse silently runs
entries.t: 🧠 "Please Do Da Right Thing" — P atient · D rug · D ose · R oute · T ime. Say it before every single pass until it's automatic.

Compare name + DOB (or MRN) on the ID band to the MAR Never use room number as an identifier Red/allergy band = stop and confirm before giving 🧠 "2 to confirm, 0 to assume." Ask the client to state their own name & DOB when they're able — don't just read the band and move on.

entries.h: 💊 Right Drug — read the label 3 times
entries.t: Compare drug name on the MAR to the label at pick-up, pour, and bedside EXAM TIP NCLEX tests generic names , not brand/trade names Watch look-alike/sound-alike pairs — e.g. hydr ALAZ ine vs hydr OXYZ ine 🧠 "3 looks before it goes in the mouth." Read the label when you grab it, when you pour it, and again at the bedside before it's given.

Confirm dose against the MAR and the prescriber's order Never round or estimate a calculated dose High-alert drugs (insulin, heparin, opioids) → independent double-check with a 2nd nurse 🧠 "When in doubt, recalculate — don't just double it, double-check it."

entries.h: 🚪 Right Route — as ordered, not as easiest
entries.t: IV/IM = fastest absorption ; oral is slowest and depends on GI transit. 🧠 If the order says PO and the client can't swallow — hold and call the HCP , don't just switch routes yourself.

entries.h: ⏱️ Right Time — on schedule, on purpose
entries.t: Give within the facility's window, typically ±30–60 min of scheduled time Time-critical meds (antibiotics, insulin, anticoagulants) → tighter window Late antibiotic doses let blood levels dip below the therapeutic range 🧠 See the Timing section below — peak & trough exist because of this exact right. 🧭
STEP 2 · BEYOND THE BIG 5 Practice varies — some programs teach 6 rights, some teach 9 or 10. These are the extra checkpoints you'll see added most often.

Chart time, route, site, and client response — immediately after giving, never before. 🧠 Never chart in advance — if you get pulled away, an undocumented-but-charted dose looks like a double-dose risk for the next nurse.

Know why this client is getting this drug — does the order make clinical sense for their diagnosis? 🧠 If a med doesn't match the diagnosis on the chart, question it before giving it — that's your last safety net.
Reassess afterward — did the drug do what it was supposed to? Pain down? BP down? Blood glucose corrected? 🧠 Giving the drug isn't the end of the task — evaluating the response closes the loop.

A cognitively intact client can refuse any medication . Educate on the risk of refusing, then document & notify the HCP — you cannot force it. 🧠 Autonomy beats compliance. Coercing a competent adult into taking a med is a rights violation, not good nursing.

It is your job as the nurse to teach — clear up confusion about why a drug is given, what to expect, and what to report . An informed client catches errors too. 🧠 "Un-teach the fear, teach the fact." A client who understands their meds is a second set of eyes on your safety checks. ⏱️
STEP 3 · WHY TIME MATTERS Right Time isn't just punctuality — it keeps drug levels inside the window where the drug actually works.

entries.h: 📈 Peak & trough — why "on time" is a safety right, not a courtesy
entries.t: Peak = the highest blood concentration after a dose (checks for toxicity ). Trough = the lowest level, drawn right before the next dose (checks the drug hasn't dropped too low to work ). Antibiotics like vancomycin and gentamicin are commonly monitored this way. 🧠 "Peak pokes up, trough is tough (the lowest point it can go)." A late antibiotic dose lets the trough drop too far — the infection gets a window to regrow before the next dose arrives.

Abbrev. Meaning QD / daily Once a day BID Twice a day TID 3 times a day QID 4 times a day Q4H / Q6H / Q8H Every 4 / 6 / 8 hours PRN As needed STAT Immediately, one time 🧠 B ID = b reakfast & bed (roughly) · T ID = t hree squares a day · Q ID = q uarter the day, 4 times.

Before giving digoxin , count the apical heart rate for 1 full minute . Hold the dose and notify the HCP if the apical pulse is below the facility's cutoff (commonly <60 bpm in adults) — a classic timing-and-assessment safety check tied to this right. 🧠 "Count a full 60 before the 60-second drug." No shortcuts on the apical count for digoxin.

entries.h: ✅ The 3 checks — med room, order, bedside
entries.t: 1 🏥 Med room / Pyxis — pull the drug, check label vs. MAR 2 📋 Order — recheck the MAR against the prescriber's order before pouring 3 🛏️ Bedside — final label check + 2 patient identifiers, right before giving 🧠 3 checks, 3 places — never skip the last one even if you're rushed. The bedside check is the one that catches wrong-room, wrong-patient errors. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD ✅ Please Do Da Right Thing Patient · Drug · Dose · Route · Time 🪪 2 identifiers Name + DOB, never room number 📈 Peak/Trough Highest / lowest blood level — give on time 🙅 Right to refuse Educate, document, notify — don't force

Q1: What are the "core 5" rights of medication administration? Show answer Right patient, right drug, right dose, right route, right time. Q2: What two identifiers confirm right patient? Show answer Name and date of birth (or medical record number) — never room number. Q3: What's the difference between peak and trough? Show answer Peak is the highest drug concentration after a dose; trough is the lowest, drawn right before the next dose. Q4: A cognitively intact client refuses their medication — what do you do? Sho
