Alpha-1 antagonists — tamsulosin, doxazosin, prazosin & phentolamine NG-141 PHARM ADHD-friendly visual edition Alpha-1 blockers relax smooth muscle in blood vessels, the prostate, and the bladder neck by blocking norepinephrine's vasoconstricting signal. That relaxation is the whole benefit for BPH — and the whole danger for BP. First-dose orthostatic hypotension is the single most-tested safety point in this class. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🩸 Alpha-1 blocked = vessels relax Smooth muscle in vess
STEP 1 · THE MECHANISM Block alpha-1 receptors → smooth muscle relaxes wherever that receptor sits. Where it sits determines what you use the drug for.

EXAM TIP All alpha-1 blockers relax smooth muscle by blocking norepinephrine — but tamsulosin is "uroselective" , meaning it prefers the alpha-1A receptor subtype concentrated in the prostate and bladder neck, with much less action on vascular alpha-1 receptors. Doxazosin and prazosin hit vascular alpha-1 receptors too, so they drop BP more. 🧠 "Uro-SELECT-ive SELECTS the urinary tract." Tamsulosin's job is the bladder neck, not the vessels — that's why it's FDA-approved only for BPH, not hypertension, while doxazos

Generic Trade Use Dose Tamsulosin Flomax BPH only 0.4 mg PO daily Doxazosin Cardura HTN, BPH HTN: 1–8 mg /day · BPH: 1–16 mg /day PO Prazosin Minipress HTN 1–20 mg /day PO, divided doses 🧠 "-osin" family. Tams u losin, dox a zosin, pra zosin — the "-zosin/-losin" ending is your alpha-1-blocker clue, the same way "-olol" flags a beta-blocker.

Phentolamine (Regitine, Oraverse) blocks alpha receptors broadly and is used very differently from the daily oral drugs above: HTN from pheochromocytoma (a catecholamine-secreting adrenal tumor) Pre-op BP control before pheochromocytoma surgery Antidote for tissue damage from IV dopamine or norepinephrine extravasation Dose: 5 mg given 1–2 hr pre-op, repeated PRN; can infuse at 0.5–1 mg/min during surgery. Route: IM, IV, or local injection. 🧠 "Phen-TOLL-amine tolls the alarm on a leaking IV." If a dopamine or norep
STEP 2 · THE DANGER LIST Every red flag in this class traces back to one thing: relaxed vessels drop blood pressure.

entries.h: 🚨 First-dose phenomenon — the #1 safety teaching point
entries.t: The first dose of any alpha-1 blocker causes the sharpest fall in standing BP — syncope and falls are the real risk , especially in older adults already on other antihypertensives. Give the first dose at bedtime , have the client already lying down, and warn them not to get up quickly overnight. 🧠 "First hit hardest." Every subsequent dose is tolerated better as the body adapts — but the very first one can drop someone to the floor.

Orthostatic hypotension , dizziness, syncope Weakness, fatigue Nasal stuffiness (vasodilation of nasal mucosa) Reflex tachycardia, palpitations Weight gain (fluid retention) 🧠 "Loosen the pipes, and gravity wins." Every symptom on this list is downstream of vessels relaxing more than the body can immediately compensate for.

Cerebrovascular spasm , dizziness, weakness Hypotension, MI, angina, arrhythmias, tachycardia Abdominal pain, diarrhea, nausea/vomiting — can aggravate peptic ulcer disease Flushing; local injection-site pain Contraindicated in coronary artery disease. 🧠 "A dilated vessel can also steal blood from where it's needed" — that's the angina/MI risk behind a drug that vasodilates hard and fast.

Interacting drug Effect PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil) Additive vasodilation → increased hypotension risk — this combo comes up constantly on exams Beta-blockers Increased hypotension Epinephrine or methoxamine (with phentolamine) Severe hypotension Ephedrine or phenylephrine (with phentolamine) Decreased pressor response — the alpha blockade cancels the vasopressor's job 🧠 "If it makes you hyper or shaky, check the drug book before combining it with an alpha blocker." Stacking any vasoactive drug on top o
STEP 3 · WHAT THE CLIENT NEEDS TO HEAR Position changes, timing of the first dose, and knowing which symptoms mean "call the office."

1 🛏️ First dose at bedtime , already lying down 2 🪑 Sit up, pause ~1 minute before standing 3 🚶 Stand still ~1 minute before walking 4 📞 Call light within reach — ask for help getting up 🧠 "Sit-a-minute, stand-a-minute." The two 1-minute pauses give the vasculature time to catch up before gravity takes over.

Change positions slowly — sit → stand, lying → sit Avoid hot showers/baths — heat adds more vasodilation on top of the drug Report chest pain during any IV infusion Don't drive or operate machinery until you know how the first dose affects you 🧠 "Hot water is a second vasodilator." Heat + alpha blockade stack the same way alcohol does.

entries.h: 🆚 Uroselective vs non-selective — tell them apart
entries.t: Feature Tamsulosin (uroselective) Doxazosin / Prazosin (non-selective) Target Alpha-1A — prostate/bladder neck mostly Alpha-1 broadly — vessels + prostate/bladder neck FDA-approved for BPH only HTN and BPH BP drop Minimal Significant — first-dose phenomenon more pronounced 🧠 "Select the target, spare the pressure — unless it doesn't select at all." Same logic as cardioselective vs nonselective beta-blockers (NG-176), just for the alpha-1 subtype instead. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🩸 Alpha-1 blocked = relaxed smooth muscle in vessels + prostate/bladder neck 🚨 First dose worst Give at bedtime — biggest orthostatic drop is dose #1 🎯 Uroselective = tamsulosin, targets prostate, minimal BP change 🧊 Phentolamine = antidote for dopamine/norepi IV extravasation

Q1: What is the #1 safety teaching point for a client starting an alpha-1 blocker? Show answer First-dose orthostatic hypotension — give the first dose at bedtime, teach slow position changes, and use fall precautions. Q2: Why is tamsulosin used for BPH but not typically for hypertension? Show answer It's uroselective for the alpha-1A receptor concentrated in the prostate/bladder neck, with minimal effect on vascular alpha-1 receptors, so it doesn't lower BP much. Q3: What is phentolamine used to treat when an IV i
🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🧠 What it does 🚨 Watch for 🩺 Teach ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Psych-Mental Health Pharmacology · Antidepressant Ladder — Rung 4 of 3 (last line)

Monoamine Oxidase Inhibitor — the powerful, last-resort antidepressant NG-154 PSYCH PHARM ADHD-friendly visual edition Very powerful antidepressants used for depression, panic disorder & social phobia — especially depression that is resistant to other meds . They sit at the top of the antidepressant ladder : last-line, because two things make them uniquely dangerous — tyramine food restrictions and a strict 2-week washout around other serotonergic drugs. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🥋 Last-line, mos
STEP 1 · THE MECHANISM One enzyme, shut down completely — three neurotransmitters flood the brain instead of just one.

entries.h: 🔬 Block the enzyme that breaks neurotransmitters down
entries.t: MOA Monoamine oxidase (MAO) is the enzyme that normally breaks down norepinephrine, serotonin, and dopamine once they've done their job. MAOIs irreversibly block that enzyme — instead of blocking reabsorption like an SSRI, they stop the neurotransmitters from being destroyed at all, so all three build up in the brain. 🧠 "MAOI blocks the trash collector." No breakdown crew for NE, serotonin, or dopamine — everything piles up. That's why it's the most powerful class, and also why the interactions are the most dangero

Phenelzine — brand: Nardil Selegiline Isocarboxazid Tranylcypromine 🧠 "MAOI's names don't rhyme like SSRIs do" — learn these four as a standalone set, since none of them share the familiar -ine/-am suffixes.
😔 Depression — especially treatment-resistant 😱 Panic disorder 😳 Social phobia 🧠 Powerful, but last resort — tried after SSRIs, SNRIs, and TCAs haven't worked. 🚨
STEP 2 · THE TWO BIG DANGERS This whole drug class is tested on two rules — food, and timing. Miss either one and the outcome is a crisis.

entries.h: 🧀 Danger #1 — Tyramine food restriction → hypertensive crisis
entries.t: MAO normally breaks down tyramine too. With the enzyme blocked, dietary tyramine builds up, displaces stored norepinephrine, and triggers a massive release of norepinephrine → hypertensive crisis . 🧀 Aged cheese no wine tasting 🍷 Wine 🍺 Beer no beer fest 🥓 Cured meats sausage, salami 🍫 Chocolate 🧂 OTC cold/diet meds decongestants 🧠 "No wine tasting, no beer fest." Aged cheese & wine, beer & sausage/salami, chocolate — anything aged, fermented, cured, or tap . This is the single highest-yield MAOI fact on NCLEX.

Never combine an MAOI with another serotonergic antidepressant — SSRIs, SNRIs, or TCAs — without a 2-week washout before starting the MAOI and after stopping it (fluoxetine needs even longer due to its long half-life, per most references). 🧠 "MAOI = Anti-depressant, STOP — count to 2 (weeks)." This washout rule appears on the SSRI page and the SNRI/TCA page too — it's the single rule that connects all four antidepressant classes.

entries.h: 🚨 Serotonin syndrome — same 5 signs as every other antidepressant class
entries.t: If the washout rule is broken, or an MAOI is combined with another serotonergic drug, serotonin syndrome can occur: 🧠 "A HOT DAT" — Agitation · HOT (hyperthermia) · Diaphoresis · Agitation-driven Tremor + clonus. Also watch for headache and increased agitation as early warning NCLEX key terms when starting or increasing an MAOI dose.

Like all antidepressants, if a patient states "this med isn't working after 2 weeks," assess first for further expressions of hopelessness, despair, suicidal thoughts, or self-harm before addressing onset timing. 🧠 Increased suicide risk is a shared antidepressant-class concern, not unique to MAOIs — but it's still a top MAOI safety priority. 🩺
STEP 3 · PATIENT EDUCATION Two rules to teach on day one — the diet list, and the drug-switching timeline.

1 🧀 Avoid tyramine-rich foods — aged cheese, cured/fermented meats, wine, beer, chocolate 2 💊 Check every OTC drug before taking it — including cold remedies & diet aids 3 ⏱️ Never start or stop another antidepressant without a 2-week washout 4 💬 Report severe headache, palpitations, or stiff neck — possible early hypertensive crisis 🧠 "Cheese, wine, and two weeks." If a nursing exam question mentions MAOI, the answer usually involves one of those three things.

entries.h: 🪜 Where MAOIs sit on the antidepressant ladder
entries.t: 🥋 This page = the top rung · see NG-205 (SSRI) and NG-187 (SNRI/TCA)

Headache + increased agitation when starting or increasing dose Massive HTN crisis risk = the word "tyramine" nearby 2-week washout = the phrase "switching antidepressants" 🧠 See NG-205 (SSRI) and NG-187 (SNRI vs. TCA) — all three antidepressant pages share the same serotonin syndrome symptom list and the same washout rule. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🧪 Block MAO = NE, serotonin, dopamine all build up 🧀 Tyramine = aged cheese, cured meats, wine, beer → HTN crisis ⏱️ 2-week washout = before AND after switching to/from any serotonergic antidepressant 🚨 Serotonin syndrome = agitation, hyperthermia, clonus/hyperreflexia, diaphoresis, tremor

Q1: Why do MAOIs require a tyramine-restricted diet? Show answer MAO normally breaks down dietary tyramine too. With it blocked, tyramine displaces stored norepinephrine, causing a massive NE release and hypertensive crisis. Q2: Name three tyramine-rich foods/drinks to avoid. Show answer Aged cheese, wine, beer, cured/fermented meats (sausage, salami), and chocolate. Q3: A patient wants to switch from an SSRI to an MAOI. What must happen first? Show answer A 2-week washout period, to prevent serotonin syndrome. Q4:

entries.h: Prostate – BPH · NG-160 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🌰 BPH basics 💊 The drugs 🗣️ Teach ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Pharmacology · Genitourinary Drugs

Two drug classes, two totaly different mechanisms — relax it fast, or shrink it slow NG-160 PHARM ADHD-friendly visual edition BPH = Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia — a non-cancerous growth of the walnut-sized gland wrapped around the urethra. Two drug families treat it, and they don't work the same way: alpha-1 blockers relax the muscle around the urethra in days , while 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors shrink the gland itself over months . This page is the pharmacology angle — for the full symptom/labs/TURP picture, see
STEP 1 · WHY THE PIPE PINCHES A quick anatomy refresher so the two drug mechanisms actually make sense — full pathophysiology, labs, and nursing assessment live on NG-052/NG-240.

entries.h: 🌰 The prostate wraps the urethra like a donut
entries.t: Symptoms in brief — hesitancy, weak stream, straining, nocturia, frequency, dribbling, incomplete emptying . For full symptom clusters, PSA/labs, catheterization, and TURP/CBI care, see NG-052 and NG-240 . 🧠 "A donut that swells shrinks the hole." The prostate doesn't grow into the urethra — it grows around it and squeezes it narrower.

entries.h: ⭐ Two ways to un-pinch the pipe
entries.t: Relax the smooth muscle around the pinch → alpha-1 blockers Shrink the gland doing the pinching → 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors (androgen hormone inhibitors) 🧠 "Loosen it or shrink it — those are the only two knobs." Every BPH drug on this page does one or the other. 💊
STEP 2 · TWO MECHANISMS, TWO TIMELINES Alpha blockers are the fast-acting first-line option; 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors are the slow gland-shrinkers, often added for larger prostates.

These two mechanisms are independent — that's exactly why they're sometimes combined (alpha blocker for fast relief + 5-ARI for long-term gland shrinkage in larger prostates). 🧠 "Finasteride starves the growth signal; alpha blockers open the door regardless of size." One drug removes the fuel (DHT), the other just opens the exit no matter how big the gland is.

Generic Trade Dose Tamsulosin Flomax 0.4 mg PO daily Doxazosin Cardura 1–16 mg /day PO for BPH Peripherally-acting alpha-1A blockers acting on prostate and bladder-neck smooth muscle. Uroselective agents like tamsulosin have minimal action on the vascular system. Full mechanism, first-dose orthostatic hypotension teaching, and the complete drug list live on NG-141 Adrenergic Alpha Blockers . 🧠 "Relax now, results in days." Alpha blockers are typically first-line for symptom relief because they act on existing muscl

Generic Trade Use / Dose Finasteride Proscar, Propecia Male-pattern baldness, BPH — 1–5 mg/day PO Androgen hormone inhibitor — prevents conversion of testosterone to DHT (5-alpha-dihydrotestosterone) , the hormone prostate growth depends on. Lowering DHT shrinks the gland and reduces symptoms — but takes 3–6 months to show benefit. 🧠 "Fina-STERoid shrinks the STER-oid-driven growth." Same drug (finasteride) treats male-pattern baldness for the identical DHT reason.

Used to relieve BPH symptoms — urinary frequency, decreased flow, nocturia Believed to reduce inflammation and lower DHT (same target as finasteride, herbal route) Does not cause impotence — but can aggravate GI disorders like peptic ulcer disease Typical use: 160 mg twice daily; symptom reduction reported in 1–3 months Not recommended as a tea — active constituents are not water soluble Usually taken for 6 months , then re-evaluated by the provider 🧠 "Saw palmetto = the herbal finasteride." Same DHT-lowering idea,
STEP 3 · WHAT THE CLIENT NEEDS TO HEAR Set expectations on timeline, flag the interaction that trips people up, and know the never-give list.

entries.h: 📈 Onset of action — set the expectation up front
entries.t: Tell the client not to expect finasteride to work like the alpha blocker — many stop it early thinking it "isn't working," when 3–6 months is normal before gland shrinkage shows up. 🧠 "Days vs. Dozens of weeks." Alpha blocker = this week. Finasteride = count in months, not days.

PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil/Viagra, tadalafil/Cialis) + alpha blockers = additive hypotension . Ask about erectile dysfunction medication use before starting or renewing an alpha blocker prescription. 🧠 "Two vasodilators, one blood pressure." Both drug classes drop peripheral resistance — stacking them stacks the drop.

Uncontrolled angle-closure glaucoma Intestinal obstruction or atony Hepatic impairment — use with caution On a beta-blocker too? Watch for additive hypotension 🧠 "Smooth muscle relaxers relax smooth muscle everywhere" — including the GI tract and the iris, not just the bladder neck.

Pregnant partners/handlers should not touch crushed/broken tablets — DHT-lowering drugs are linked to abnormal genital development in a male fetus Sexual side effects: impotence, decreased libido, decreased ejaculate volume Breast changes: tenderness, gynecomastia, nipple discharge — report to provider Finasteride can lower PSA values — tell the lab/provider the client is on it so results are interpreted correctly 🧠 "DHT built the prostate AND the baldness AND normal male genital development." One hormone, three re

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🌰 BPH = benign, age-related prostate growth pinching the urethra ⚡ Alpha blockers relax the muscle — fast, days 🐢 5-ARI (finasteride) blocks DHT, shrinks the gland — slow, months ⚠️ PDE5 + alpha blocker = additive hypotension — always ask

Q1: How do alpha-1 blockers help BPH? Show answer They block alpha-1 receptors on the smooth muscle of the prostate and bladder neck, relaxing that muscle so urine can flow — effect within days. Q2: How does finasteride work, and how long does it take? Show answer It blocks 5-alpha-reductase from converting testosterone to DHT, lowering DHT and shrinking the prostate gland over time — takes 3–6 months for benefit. Q3: What interaction should always be checked before starting an alpha blocker for BPH? Show answer PD

entries.h: Toxic Ranges & Antidotes 2 · NG-166 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🔑 Antidote match 🧪 Therapeutic ranges 🩺 Priorities ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Pharmacology · Toxicology Reference

Look-up card: narrow-window drugs, their antidotes, and their numbers NG-166 Pharmacology ADHD-friendly visual edition Some drugs have a tiny gap between "working" and "toxic" — a narrow therapeutic index . This card pairs the highest-yield drugs with their antidotes and their reference ranges . Ranges are standard adult values for study purposes only — always confirm against your facility's lab and current orders before making a clinical decision. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 💉 Opioids → Naloxone M
STEP 1 · LOCK & KEY Each overdose has one classic reversal agent — memorize the pairs, not just the list.
🧠 "Naloxone, flumazeNIL, acetylcysteiNE." Say the drug + antidote pair together, out loud, ten times — this is the fastest way to lock it in.

Drug / class Antidote Notes 💊 Opioid analgesics Naloxone Mu-receptor antagonist — see NG-257 😴 Benzodiazepines Flumazenil Can precipitate seizures, especially with chronic use or mixed overdose 🧊 Acetaminophen (Tylenol) Acetylcysteine (N-acetylcysteine, NAC) Protects the liver — most effective started early 🩸 Heparin Protamine sulfate Give slowly — risk of hypotension/anaphylactoid reaction 🌿 Warfarin (Coumadin) Vitamin K Reversal takes hours; FFP/PCC used when faster reversal is needed ❤️ Digoxin Digoxin immune Fa

entries.h: 🔗 Ties to another card in this set
entries.t: The Acetaminophen (Tylenol) page covers the overdose mechanism (hepatotoxicity) and the full acetylcysteine protocol in depth — this page is the quick-lookup version. 🧠 If a question mentions elevated LFTs after a Tylenol overdose , the answer is almost always acetylcysteine, started as early as possible.

Flumazenil can trigger seizures in patients physically dependent on benzodiazepines Protamine sulfate given too fast can cause severe hypotension Naloxone can precipitate acute opioid withdrawal 🧠 Every antidote is still a drug. Reversing one problem can create another — monitor closely after any antidote is given. 🧪
STEP 2 · NARROW WINDOWS Standard adult reference ranges for drugs where "a little too much" becomes toxic fast — confirm against your facility's lab before acting clinically.
🧠 Narrow window drugs need blood levels drawn — you cannot judge safety by symptoms alone until toxicity has already started.

Drug Therapeutic range Class / use ❤️ Digoxin 0.5–2.0 ng/mL Cardiac glycoside — HF, atrial fibrillation 🧠 Lithium ~0.6–1.2 mEq/L Mood stabilizer — bipolar disorder (exact range varies by text/lab & indication — always confirm locally) ⚡ Phenytoin (Dilantin) 10–20 mcg/mL Anticonvulsant 🫁 Theophylline 10–20 mcg/mL Bronchodilator — asthma/COPD ⚡ Carbamazepine 4–12 mcg/mL Anticonvulsant / mood stabilizer 😴 Phenobarbital 15–40 mcg/mL Barbiturate anticonvulsant ⚡ Valproic acid 50–100 mcg/mL Anticonvulsant / mood stabiliz

entries.h: 🩸 Peak vs. trough — draw it right
entries.t: 🧠 "Peak after, trough before." Draw the peak shortly after the dose infuses in; draw the trough right before the very next dose is due.

entries.h: 🚨 What raises toxicity risk for ALL of these
entries.t: Renal impairment — most of these drugs (or active metabolites) are cleared by the kidney Hepatic impairment — slows metabolism of many agents Dehydration and drug interactions that change clearance Missed or mistimed lab draws — a level drawn at the wrong time is misleading 🧠 Before trusting any level, ask: was it drawn at the right time, in a patient with normal kidney/liver function? 🩺
STEP 3 · CATCH TOXICITY EARLY Know the toxicity signs for the two highest-yield agents — digoxin and lithium — cold.

entries.h: ❤️ Digoxin toxicity — assess BEFORE you give it
entries.t: Always check the apical pulse for one full minute before giving digoxin — hold the dose and notify the HCP per facility parameters if it is too low (commonly taught: <60 bpm in adults). 🧠 "Slow heart, weird vision, sick stomach." Any one of the three should make you check a digoxin level before the next dose.

Early: GI upset, fine hand tremor Worsening: ataxia, slurred speech, confusion Severe: seizures, decreased LOC — medical emergency Adequate sodium and fluid intake matters — dehydration or a low-sodium diet can raise lithium levels toward toxicity. 🧠 Lithium follows salt. Low sodium/dehydration → the body reabsorbs more lithium → level climbs → toxicity risk rises.

1 🧪 Confirm the level was drawn at the correct time (peak/trough) 2 📋 Compare the result to the current facility reference range 3 🩺 Correlate with symptoms , not the number alone 4 📞 Hold the dose & notify the HCP if toxic or symptomatic 🧠 Number + symptoms, not number alone. A level can look "in range" and the patient can still be symptomatic if renal/hepatic function changed quickly.

entries.h: ⭐ How this page connects to the rest of pharmacology
entries.t: This is a reference/lookup card , not a stand-alone lesson — pair it with the drug-specific pages in this set (Opioids, Acetaminophen) for the full mechanism and nursing care behind each antidote. 🧠 When you see a toxic level or overdose symptom on an exam, run the same three questions: which drug → which antidote → what's the priority nursing action right now? ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 💉 Opioids → Naloxone 😴 Benzos → Flumazenil 🧊 Tylenol → Acetylcysteine 🩸 Heparin → Protamine · 🌿 Warfarin → Vitamin K ❤️ Digoxin 0.5–2.0 ng/mL Check apical pulse before every dose 🧪 Peak after, trough before Draw timing changes what the number means

Q1: A patient is found unresponsive with pinpoint pupils and slow, shallow breathing after taking an unknown medication. What antidote do you anticipate? Show answer Naloxone — the classic opioid overdose presentation (respiratory depression + miosis). Q2: What is the antidote for warfarin (Coumadin) toxicity/overdose? Show answer Vitamin K. It takes hours to work, so FFP or prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) may be used when faster reversal is needed. Q3: Before giving digoxin, what must the nurse assess, and w
🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🎯 What It Does 🚨 Watch For ✅ Teach ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Pharmacology · Pain & Anti-Inflammatory Unit — DMARD

Anti-inflammatory DMARD for RA and Inflammatory Bowel Disease NG-175 PHARMACOLOGY ADHD-friendly visual edition Sulfasalazine is a two-for-one drug — half sulfa antibiotic, half salicylate anti-inflammatory — used for rheumatoid arthritis and inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's disease & ulcerative colitis) . It works by decreasing colon inflammation through blocking prostaglandins . The single biggest safety gate before this drug is ever started: ask about a sulfa allergy first. See also NG-100 Anti-inflammatory Ag
STEP 1 · ONE DRUG, TWO HALVES A DMARD built from two active parts — that split is exactly why it works, and exactly why the sulfa allergy question matters.

entries.h: 🧬 Sulfapyridine + 5-ASA — split apart in the colon
entries.t: MECHANISM Sulfasalazine travels to the colon largely unabsorbed, where gut bacteria split it into two active pieces: sulfapyridine (the sulfa/antibiotic-related carrier) and 5-aminosalicylic acid (5-ASA / mesalamine) — the anti-inflammatory piece that decreases colon inflammation by inhibiting prostaglandin synthesis , the same chemicals that drive swelling and pain. 🧠 "SULFA-salazine = SULFA + salicylate." The name itself tells you both the allergy risk (sulfa) and the mechanism family (salicylate = anti-prostagla

🦴 Rheumatoid arthritis — DMARD, slows joint damage over time 🌀 Crohn's disease 🌀 Ulcerative colitis Both are forms of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) — this is the drug that bridges the rheumatology unit and the GI unit. 🧠 One drug, two units. If you see sulfasalazine on a GI exam, it's for Crohn's/UC. If you see it on a musculoskeletal exam, it's for RA. Same drug either way.

Like other DMARDs, sulfasalazine does not relieve symptoms immediately — it works over weeks by modifying the underlying inflammatory process, not just masking pain. 🧠 Never confuse a DMARD with a rescue drug. A client who stops taking it because "it's not working yet" after a few days needs more teaching, not a med change. 🚨
STEP 2 · THE SULFA GATE One contraindication screens out the drug entirely — the rest are manageable with teaching.

entries.h: 🚨 Contraindicated in sulfa allergy — screen before the first dose
entries.t: Sulfasalazine is contraindicated in a client with a known sulfa allergy. Because the drug is metabolized into sulfapyridine , an allergic client can react the same way they would to a sulfonamide antibiotic (e.g. sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim). 🧠 Sulfa allergy = automatic stop sign. This is the single highest-yield fact on this whole page — ask it before the first dose, every time.

🌞 Increased risk of sunburn with sun exposure 🧴 Wear sunblock , avoid direct sun exposure 🧠 "Sun-dried!" — picture the medication drying the skin out under the sun like a raisin. Sunblock + avoid direct exposure.

💎 Urine crystals — risk of kidney stones 🚽 Low urine output with elevated urine specific gravity (normal roughly 1.003–1.030 ) = dehydration, "high & dry" 🧠 "S-U-L-F" — S tones (crystals) · U rine output low · L ow fluid = high specific gravity · F luids fix it. Drink up.

Add-on Why 💧 8 glasses of water/day Prevents crystalluria/kidney stones and dehydration 🟢 Folic acid, 1 mg/day Sulfasalazine can interfere with folate absorption/metabolism — supplementation prevents deficiency 🧠 "Fluid & Folic acid" — the two F's that go with every sulfasalazine prescription. ✅
STEP 3 · WHAT'S NORMAL, WHAT'S NOT One harmless color change and one non-negotiable rule about stopping the drug.

entries.h: ✅ Expected — no need to call the HCP
entries.t: 1 🟠 Yellow-orange discoloration of the skin and urine — expected, harmless, no follow-up needed 2 🚫 Do NOT stop the medication for the color change alone 🧠 "Orange is OK." That's the one color change on this whole unit that is completely expected and needs zero intervention.

entries.h: ⛔ The one hard rule: don't stop early
entries.t: 🐢 As a DMARD, sulfasalazine needs continuous use to keep controlling inflammation 🚫 Continue the medication even after symptoms subside — stopping early risks a disease flare 🧠 Feeling better is not permission to stop. Same rule as antibiotics finishing the course — except here it's ongoing, not a fixed course.

🚨 Report any signs of an allergic reaction (rash, hives, difficulty breathing) immediately ☀️ Wear sunblock , avoid prolonged direct sun 💧 Drink 8 glasses of water/day 🟢 Take folic acid 1 mg/day as prescribed 🔁 Do not stop the medication without talking to the HCP 🧠 "Sun + fluids + folic acid + don't stop." Four teaching points, one sentence. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🧬 RA + IBD One DMARD, two indications — decreases inflammation by blocking prostaglandins 🚨 Sulfa allergy = contraindicated Screen before the first dose, always ☀️💧 Sun + fluids Photosensitivity + crystalluria — sunblock, 8 glasses water/day, folic acid 1mg/day 🟠 Orange is OK, stopping isn't Discoloration is harmless; never stop the med on your own

Q1: What must be screened for before starting sulfasalazine, and why? Show answer A sulfa allergy — sulfasalazine is metabolized into sulfapyridine, which is chemically related to sulfonamide antibiotics and can trigger the same allergic reaction. Q2: A client on sulfasalazine notices their urine and skin have turned yellow-orange. What should the nurse teach? Show answer This is an expected, harmless side effect — no follow-up is needed and the medication should be continued. Q3: What two supportive measures are r

entries.h: SNRI vs. TCA · NG-187 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🟣 SNRI 🔵 TCA ⚖️ Tell them apart ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Psych-Mental Health Pharmacology · Antidepressant Ladder — Rungs 2 & 3 of 3

Two older or dual-acting antidepressant classes — one modern & broad, one older & risky NG-187 PSYCH PHARM ADHD-friendly visual edition SNRIs block reuptake of two neurotransmitters — serotonin AND norepinephrine — and double as neuropathic pain drugs. TCAs are an older class that also boosts serotonin & norepinephrine, but drags a heavy anticholinergic side-effect profile and a genuinely dangerous overdose behind it. Same neurotransmitter targets, very different safety margins — that's the whole point of this comp
STEP 1 · DUAL & MODERN Rung 2 of the ladder — same serotonin trick as an SSRI, plus norepinephrine, plus a second job treating chronic pain.

entries.h: 🔬 Blocks TWO reuptake pumps at once
entries.t: MOA Like an SSRI, an SNRI blocks the serotonin reuptake pump — but it also blocks the norepinephrine reuptake pump , so both neurotransmitters build up in the synapse. That second target is what gives SNRIs their extra job: treating neuropathic pain , not just mood. 🧠 “SNRI = double duty.” One drug, two pumps blocked, two jobs done: mood and pain.

Duloxetine — think "DUAL-oxetine" : dual mechanism, dual purpose. 😔 Depression 🔥 Neuropathic pain — diabetic peripheral neuropathy 🦴 Fibromyalgia pain 🧠 "If a fibromyalgia patient on duloxetine says they're not depressed, they need education" — it's still the right drug. It's treating their pain , not (only) their mood.

Duloxetine helps with chronic pain and improves sleep quality in fibromyalgia patients — a two-for-one benefit worth pointing out in patient teaching. 🧠 SNRIs are often reached for second , after an SSRI trial, or first when chronic pain is part of the picture. 🔵
STEP 2 · OLDER & RISKIER Rung 3 of the ladder — an older class that hits more receptors than it needs to, and that's exactly the problem.

TCAs don't just block serotonin/norepinephrine reuptake — they also block acetylcholine receptors, causing a predictable dry-everything picture. 🧠 "Amy trips on things" — Amitriptyline causes orthostatic hypotension : teach slow position changes to avoid a dizzy fall. Imipramine — "Inhibit my PEEing" = urinary retention is its stand-out anticholinergic effect.

Amitriptyline — orthostatic hypotension Imipramine — urinary retention Indications: depression, anxiety, and neuropathic pain (diabetics & fibromyalgia) — TCAs treat pain too, like SNRIs, just with a rougher side-effect trade-off. 🧠 Two drugs, two classic teaching points: Ami triptyline = slow rise . Imi pramine = slow stream .

entries.h: 💀 Cardiotoxicity — the reason TCAs fell out of favor
entries.t: Narrow safety margin — in overdose, TCAs cause QT prolongation and life-threatening cardiac arrhythmias . Unlike SSRIs/SNRIs, a TCA overdose is a genuine cardiac emergency. 🧠 "TCAs can stop a heart before they stop a headache." A small dose miscalculation or an overdose attempt with a narrow-margin drug like this is a true cardiac emergency — assess for arrhythmia, monitor ECG. ⚖️
STEP 3 · SIDE BY SIDE Same neurotransmitter targets, very different risk profile — this is the table the "vs." title is asking for.

entries.h: ⚖️ SNRI vs. TCA — head to head
entries.t: 🟣 SNRI 🔵 TCA Mechanism: blocks serotonin + norepinephrine reuptake, selectively Mechanism: blocks serotonin + norepinephrine reuptake, PLUS acetylcholine & histamine receptors Drug: Duloxetine Drugs: Amitriptyline, Imipramine Signature side effects: nausea, dry mouth (mild), ↑BP at high doses Signature side effects: full anticholinergic tetrad — can't see, pee, spit, poop Overdose risk: relatively wide safety margin Overdose risk: narrow margin — cardiotoxic, QT prolongation, arrhythmia Shared use: neuropathic pain

entries.h: 🚨 Both interact with MAOIs the same dangerous way
entries.t: Never combine an SNRI or a TCA with an MAOI — risk of serotonin syndrome . A 2-week washout period is required when switching to or from an MAOI. 🧠 "MAOI = Anti... depressant STOP." Whichever antidepressant a patient is switching away from or onto an MAOI, count two weeks first. See NG-154 for the full MAOI washout rule.

entries.h: 🪜 Where these two sit on the antidepressant ladder
entries.t: 🪜 This page = Rungs 2 & 3 · see NG-205 (SSRI) and NG-154 (MAOI) for the rest of the ladder ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🎯 SNRI = dual reuptake block + treats pain (duloxetine) 💀 TCA = anticholinergic tetrad + cardiotoxic overdose 🚫 Never with an MAOI = 2-week washout, both classes 🚨 Serotonin syndrome = agitation, hyperthermia, clonus/hyperreflexia, diaphoresis, tremor

Q1: A fibromyalgia patient on duloxetine says they aren't depressed and asks why they're on an antidepressant. What do you teach? Show answer Duloxetine is an SNRI that also treats neuropathic and fibromyalgia pain — it's the right drug for their pain, not only for mood. Q2: What four things can't a patient do on a TCA? Show answer Can't see (blurred vision), can't pee (urinary retention), can't spit (dry mouth), can't poop (constipation) — the anticholinergic tetrad. Q3: Why is a TCA overdose more dangerous than a

Spot the Pattern — Suffix → Class → Mechanism NG-199 Pharmacology ADHD-friendly visual edition Drug names look random until you notice they aren't — the last few letters give away the whole drug class . This is the page you'll come back to constantly: bookmark it, don't memorize it once and forget it. Suffix first, then class, then mechanism — every time you see an unfamiliar drug name on an exam. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → ❤️ -olol / -pril / -sartan Beta blocker · ACE inhibitor · ARB — all treat
TABLE 1 Every one of these ends in blood-pressure-down or clot-prevention — the suffix tells you which lever it pulls.

entries.h: ❤️ Where each suffix acts in the cardiovascular system
entries.t: 🧠 "Heart, Vessel, Kidney, Blood — pick your target, pick your suffix." Almost every cardio drug name tells you exactly where it works.

Suffix Drug class Mechanism Examples -olol Beta blocker Blocks beta-adrenergic receptors → ↓HR, ↓contractility, ↓BP Metoprolol, Atenolol, Propranolol -dipine Calcium channel blocker (dihydropyridine) Blocks calcium into vascular smooth muscle → vasodilation Amlodipine, Nifedipine -pril ACE inhibitor Blocks angiotensin-converting enzyme → less angiotensin II, less aldosterone Lisinopril, Enalapril -sartan ARB (angiotensin receptor blocker) Blocks angiotensin II receptors directly Losartan, Valsartan -zosin Alpha-1 b

Suffix Class Example -tidine H2 blocker Cimetidine, Famotidine -prazole Proton pump inhibitor Omeprazole, Pantoprazole -setron 5-HT3 blocker (antiemetic) Ondansetron 🧠 "-TIDINE tames acid, -PRAZOLE plugs the pump, -SETRON stops the sick."

entries.h: 🔤 Anatomy of a drug name — find the suffix first
entries.t: 🧠 Cover the front of any drug name, read only the ending — that's the class-guessing trick this whole page is built on.

entries.h: 🎯 Practice drill — name the class from the suffix
entries.t: Drug Suffix Class (cover & guess) Atenolol -olol Beta blocker Valsartan -sartan ARB Diazepam -pam Benzodiazepine Ciprofloxacin -floxacin Fluoroquinolone Fluconazole -conazole Antifungal Vincristine vin- Vinca alkaloid (microtubule inhibitor) 🧠 Fold a paper over the "Class" column and quiz yourself from the suffix alone — that's the whole skill this page teaches. ⚡

Q1: A drug ends in "-pril" — what class is it and what does it do? Show answer ACE inhibitor — blocks angiotensin-converting enzyme, lowering blood pressure and reducing aldosterone. Q2: What's the difference between -mab and -tinib drugs? Show answer -mab = monoclonal antibody; -tinib = tyrosine kinase inhibitor. Both are targeted cancer therapies, but they work through completely different mechanisms. Q3: -cillin and -floxacin both treat bacterial infections — what's the mechanism difference? Show answer -cillin
🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🧠 What it does 🔎 Watch for 🩺 Teach ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Psych-Mental Health Pharmacology · Antidepressant Ladder — Rung 1 of 3

Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitor — the first-line antidepressant NG-205 PSYCH PHARM ADHD-friendly visual edition Blocks the pump that vacuums serotonin back out of the synapse , so more serotonin stays available to bind receptors. Selectively — unlike older classes, it leaves norepinephrine & dopamine reuptake mostly alone, which is exactly why SSRIs are gentler and sit at the bottom of the antidepressant ladder — tried first, before SNRIs, TCAs, or MAOIs. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🥇 First-
STEP 1 · THE MECHANISM One pump, blocked selectively — serotonin floods the synapse instead of getting vacuumed back up.

entries.h: 🔬 Block the reuptake pump → serotonin stays in the gap
entries.t: MOA Normally, a reuptake pump (transporter) on the presynaptic neuron sucks leftover serotonin back inside after it fires, ending the signal. SSRIs selectively block that pump — serotonin can't be reabsorbed, so it lingers in the synaptic cleft and keeps stimulating postsynaptic receptors. 🧠 “SSRI = the pump gets a boot.” No reuptake in → serotonin stays out in the synapse, longer & stronger. Selective because norepinephrine and dopamine pumps are left alone — that selectivity is what makes SSRIs gentler than TCAs

entries.h: 🔤 Say the name — it's the mechanism
entries.t: Selective = targets serotonin, mostly leaves NE/dopamine alone Serotonin = the neurotransmitter affected Reuptake = the neuron sucking the chemical back in Inhibitor = blocks that process 🧠 Inhibits the RE-uptake → keeps MORE serotonin around → serotonin levels are increased in the synapse.
Sertraline Escitalopram & Citalopram Paroxetine Fluoxetine 🧠 Most end in -ine or -(cit)alopram — build a personal flash list, since suffix alone isn't 100% reliable across classes.

😔 Depression — first-line 😰 Anxiety disorders 🎗️ PTSD 🌀 OCD & panic disorder (common off-label/expanded use) 🧠 “SSRI = Start Simple, Relatively safe, Indication-flexible.” One class, four psych diagnoses. 🔎
STEP 2 · SAFETY Three things this class is tested on hardest: serotonin syndrome, the black box warning, and never stopping cold-turkey.

entries.h: 🚨 Serotonin syndrome — the shared danger across every antidepressant class
entries.t: Happens when serotonin activity gets too high — usually from combining two serotonergic drugs (SSRI + MAOI, SSRI + triptan, SSRI + tramadol, SSRI + St. John's wort). Same 5 symptoms every time — memorize this list once, it repeats on SNRI/TCA and MAOI pages too: 🧠 “A HOT DAT.” A gitation · HOT = hyperthermia · D iaphoresis · A gitation-driven T remor + clonus. A patient who looks hot, shaky, and sweaty with jumpy reflexes after adding a second serotonergic drug = serotonin syndrome until proven otherwise.

Increased risk of suicidal thinking and behavior in children, adolescents, and young adults up to age 24–25 — highest risk is the first few weeks of therapy or right after a dose change . 🚨 ASSESS FIRST if the patient says "this medication isn't working after 2 weeks" — check for worsening hopelessness, despair, suicidal thoughts, or self-harm before anything else. 🧠 Young + new + increasing dose = watch closest. The warning isn't "SSRIs cause suicide" — it's a monitoring mandate in the vulnerable window before the

entries.h: 💊 Common side effects — NCLEX traps live here
entries.t: Effect Trap to avoid 🛌 Insomnia NOT sedation — don't get tricked into expecting drowsiness 💔 Sexual dysfunction Common reason patients self-stop — ask about it, don't assume they'll volunteer it ⚖️ Weight gain Can appear over months, not days 🤢 GI upset / nausea Usually improves after the first 1–2 weeks 🧠 “SSRIs keep you UP, not down.” Insomnia is the classic wrong-answer trap — students assume any psych med = sedating.

entries.h: 🪜 Where SSRIs sit on the antidepressant ladder
entries.t: Same ladder appears on the SNRI/TCA and MAOI pages — side-effect burden and safety-margin risk climb as you go up. 🥇 This page = Rung 1 · see NG-187 (SNRI vs TCA) and NG-154 (MAOI) for the rest of the ladder 🩺
STEP 3 · PATIENT EDUCATION Slow to start, slow to stop — the two teaching points that prevent the most calls back to the clinic.

1 ⏱️ Full effect takes 4–6 weeks — don't judge it a failure early 2 🚫 Never stop abruptly — taper under provider guidance 3 💬 Report worsening mood, hopelessness, or self-harm thoughts right away 4 💔 Sexual side effects — tell your provider, don't just quit the med 🧠 “Slow onset, slow taper.” Everything about this class moves on a weeks-long timeline in both directions — starting and stopping.

Stopping abruptly can cause dizziness, flu-like symptoms, irritability, "brain zaps," and rebound anxiety within days. 🧠 Never stop cold turkey. Always taper — the prescriber writes the schedule down.

Insomnia is expected — not sedation "Not working" at 2 weeks is expected , not a failed trial — but still assess for suicidality SSRI ≠ SNRI ≠ TCA ≠ MAOI — know which page's side effects belong to which class 🧠 See NG-187 (SNRI vs. TCA) and NG-154 (MAOI) to keep the four antidepressant classes from blurring together. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🧠 Block the pump = more serotonin stays in the synapse 🚨 Serotonin syndrome = agitation, hyperthermia, clonus/hyperreflexia, diaphoresis, tremor ⏱️ 4–6 weeks = true onset, never judge it early 🚫 Never stop abruptly = taper, always

Q1: What does SSRI block, and what does that do to serotonin levels? Show answer Blocks the presynaptic serotonin reuptake pump — serotonin stays in the synapse longer, so levels of available serotonin increase. Q2: A patient on sertraline says "this isn't working, it's been 2 weeks." What do you assess first? Show answer Assess for worsening hopelessness, despair, suicidal thoughts, or self-harm — the black box warning window — before reassuring them about onset time. Group them by theme, not just by name , and this page gets much easier. 📄 Simple Nursing or

💊 Cephalosporins 🧫 Antiprotozoal (Flagyl) 💧 Stool Softeners 🩹 Corticosteroids 👂 Aminoglycosides 🫁 Bronchodilators 🧠 "Cephs, Flagyl, softeners, steroids, mino's, and lungs." Six classes, six different jobs — but only two big safety themes to remember: allergy cross-reactivity, and don't-stop-abruptly.

STEP 2 · CLASS → MECHANISM → TRAP One card per class, plus two diagrams: the beta-lactam cell wall and the corticosteroid HPA-axis shutdown.

Mechanism: beta-lactam antibiotics — bind penicillin-binding proteins and disrupt bacterial cell wall synthesis, causing the cell to rupture. ⭐ Key nursing point: beta-lactam antibiotics include penicillins, cephalosporins, monobactams, and carbapenems — assess for an allergy to any beta-lactam before giving a cephalosporin, since cross-reactivity is possible. 🚨 NCLEX trap: A documented penicillin allergy doesn't automatically forbid a cephalosporin (cross-reactivity is real but not universal) — but it does mean th

Mechanism: disrupts DNA synthesis in anaerobic bacteria and certain protozoa. ⭐ Key nursing point: no alcohol products of any kind — including mouthwash, aftershave, deodorant, or bath splashes — for the duration of therapy and for a period afterward. 🚨 NCLEX trap: Patients forget mouthwash and cough syrup can contain alcohol — teach them to check labels, not just skip the wine.

Mechanism: ↓ the surface tension of the interfacing liquid in the bowel, allowing additional liquid to penetrate the stool — producing a softer mass, not increased peristalsis. ⭐ Key nursing point: this is prevention/comfort (e.g., avoiding straining after surgery or with hemorrhoids), not treatment for an already-impacted or acutely constipated patient — it is not a stimulant laxative. 🚨 NCLEX trap: A student may expect a bowel movement "soon" after Colace — it softens future stool, it does not force an immediate

entries.h: 🩹 Corticosteroids Celestone · Decadron · Deltasone · Solu-Cortef · Solu-Medrol
entries.t: Mechanism: ↓ inflammation, produce intentional immunosuppression, and are used to treat adrenocortical insufficiency (replace cortisol the body isn't making). ⭐ Key nursing point: monitor blood glucose (steroids raise it) and watch closely for masked signs of infection — steroids blunt the normal fever/WBC response, so infection can be present without the usual warning signs. 🚨 NCLEX trap: Never stop a corticosteroid abruptly after more than short-term use — the adrenal glands have downshifted their own production

Mechanism: bind bacterial ribosomes and block protein synthesis — bactericidal, typically reserved for serious gram-negative infections. ⭐ Key nursing point: nephrotoxic and ototoxic — monitor renal function (BUN/creatinine, urine output) and hearing (tinnitus, dizziness, hearing loss); peak and trough drug levels guide safe dosing. 🚨 NCLEX trap: Combining an aminoglycoside with another nephrotoxic or ototoxic drug (e.g., a loop diuretic) compounds the risk — report new tinnitus or a drop in urine output right away

entries.h: 🫁 Bronchodilators & Respiratory Meds Albuterol · Formoterol · Levalbuterol · Tiotropium · Advair · Brovana
entries.t: Mechanism: relax bronchial smooth muscle to open the airway (beta-agonists like albuterol, formoterol, levalbuterol, arformoterol; Spiriva/tiotropium works differently, as an anticholinergic bronchodilator). Advair combines a corticosteroid (fluticasone, anti-inflammatory) with a long-acting bronchodilator (salmeterol). 🚨 NCLEX trap: Albuterol (Proventil/Ventolin) is a fast-acting rescue inhaler; Advair and inhaled steroids are long-term control drugs — a controller inhaler will not stop an acute attack in progress
STEP 3 · SAFETY & PATIENT TEACHING Rescue vs. controller, and the taper rule that applies to more than just steroids.

entries.h: 📊 Rescue vs. Controller — inhaled respiratory drugs
entries.t: Rescue (fast-acting bronchodilator) Controller (long-term / anti-inflammatory) Albuterol (Proventil, Ventolin), levalbuterol (Xopenex) Advair (fluticasone/salmeterol), Brovana, tiotropium (Spiriva) Use: acute shortness of breath / attack, right now Use: scheduled, daily — prevents attacks over time Onset: minutes Onset: hours to days for full effect 🧠 "Blue for rescue, right now — orange/other for routine, over time." If the question describes a patient actively struggling to breathe, the answer is the rescue inhal

🚫 Never stop abruptly after regular use — must taper 🍽️ Take with food — GI upset/ulcer risk 🩸 Monitor blood glucose, especially in diabetic patients 🦠 Report any signs of infection promptly — fever may be blunted 🦴 Long-term use: bone density loss, weight gain, mood changes

❓ Always ask about penicillin/cephalosporin/any beta-lactam allergy history first 🩺 Aminoglycosides: report ringing in the ears, dizziness, or decreased urine output 🧪 Keep scheduled peak/trough lab draws — don't let them get missed 💧 Stay well hydrated unless fluid-restricted, to support kidney clearance ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 💊 Cephalosporins Beta-lactam family — cross-reactivity risk 🍷 Flagyl Zero alcohol, including mouthwash 🩹 Steroids Never stop abruptly — taper 👂 Aminoglycosides Nephrotoxic + ototoxic — trend levels

Q1: What four antibiotic groups belong to the beta-lactam family? Show answer Penicillins, cephalosporins, monobactams, and carbapenems. Q2: Why can't a patient on Flagyl use mouthwash with alcohol in it? Show answer Metronidazole blocks normal alcohol breakdown, causing a disulfiram-type reaction — flushing, nausea/vomiting, palpitations — even from small/topical amounts. Q3: Why must a corticosteroid be tapered instead of stopped abruptly? Show answer Exogenous steroids suppress the body's own adrenal cortisol pr

Six classes, four different attack sites on the bacteria — learn the mechanism map once and every drug in this set slots into one of four buckets. Then layer on the three antibiotics with their own unique black-box safety issue: sulfa, vancomycin, and the "-oxacin" fluoroquinolones. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive →
STEP 1 · WHAT'S IN THIS SET Robo's 3-part study map for every drug on this page: CLASS → ACTION → WATCH .

💊 Penicillins ⚠️ Sulfonamides 🔴 Vancomycin ☀️ Tetracyclines 🦵 Fluoroquinolones 🛡️ Carbapenems 🧠 "PVC-STF" won't spell anything nice, so use: P enicillins hit the wall · V anco hits the wall too, watch the ears/kidneys/skin · C arbapenems are the broad-spectrum big guns · S ulfa blocks folic acid · T etracyclines block ribosomes · F luoroquinolones ("-oxacin") block DNA gyrase.

STEP 2 · CLASS → MECHANISM → TRAP One mechanism map, then one card per class with its own safety trap.

entries.h: 🎯 Where each class attacks the bacteria
entries.t: 🧠 "Wall, ribosome, DNA, folate" — four targets, four families. If you can name the target, you can guess the class.

entries.h: 💊 Penicillins Amoxil · Omnipen · Unipen · Pipracil · Zosyn
entries.t: Mechanism: beta-lactam — disrupts bacterial cell wall synthesis, same family as cephalosporins and carbapenems. ⭐ Key nursing point: assess for a penicillin allergy history before every dose; watch for hives, wheeze, or anaphylaxis, especially with the first dose. 🚨 NCLEX trap: A penicillin allergy raises the same cross-reactivity question with cephalosporins and (less so) carbapenems — verify before substituting.

entries.h: ⚠️ Sulfonamides Bactrim · Bactrim DS · Septra · SMZ-TMP
entries.t: Mechanism: trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole blocks two sequential steps of bacterial folic acid synthesis, so bacteria can't make DNA. ⭐ Key nursing point: the source study sheet lists these as needing caution if sulfa-allergic : erythromycin-sulfisoxazole, sulfasalazine, dapsone, other sulfonamides, and — as commonly taught cross-sensitivity cautions — celecoxib (Celebrex), sumatriptan (Imitrex), furosemide (Lasix), and hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ). Clinical opinion on how strong this cross-reactivity really is varies

Mechanism: inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis at a different site than the beta-lactams — often reserved for resistant gram-positive infections (e.g., MRSA). ⭐ Key nursing point: watch for nephrotoxicity , ototoxicity , and Red Man Syndrome (flushing, itching, hypotension from histamine release with rapid infusion). Draw a peak about 30 minutes to 1 hour after the infusion ends, and a trough about 30 minutes before the next scheduled dose. 🚨 NCLEX trap: Red Man Syndrome is usually rate-related, not a true drug

Mechanism: bind bacterial ribosomes and block protein synthesis. ⭐ Key nursing point: increases photosensitivity — teach sunscreen/protective clothing. Do not take with dairy products, antacids, or iron supplements — calcium, magnesium, aluminum, and iron bind (chelate) the drug and reduce absorption. 🚨 NCLEX trap: Contraindicated in pregnancy and in children under 8 — can permanently discolor developing teeth and affect bone growth.

Mechanism: inhibit bacterial DNA gyrase, preventing bacterial DNA replication — name clue: the suffix -oxacin . ⭐ Key nursing point: black-box warning for tendon rupture (especially Achilles tendon) — teach patients to report tendon pain/swelling and to stop activity immediately if it occurs; adjust dosage for patients with renal impairment. 🚨 NCLEX trap: Tendon rupture risk is higher in older adults and those also taking corticosteroids — a combination worth flagging on a medication reconciliation.

Mechanism: beta-lactams with a very broad spectrum of activity — often reserved for serious or multi-drug-resistant infections when other antibiotics have failed. ⭐ Key nursing point: assess for beta-lactam allergy history, same as with penicillins/cephalosporins. Imipenem (Primaxin) is paired with cilastatin, which blocks a kidney enzyme that would otherwise break the drug down too quickly. 🚨 NCLEX trap: Because these are often "last resort" drugs, unnecessary or overly broad use contributes to antibiotic resistan
STEP 3 · SAFETY & PATIENT TEACHING General antibiotic teaching, plus the three special-case safety rules that stand out on this page.

entries.h: ✅ General antibiotic teaching — all six classes
entries.t: 💊 Finish the entire course even if feeling better 🕐 Take at evenly spaced intervals to keep blood levels steady 🦠 Report diarrhea that is watery or bloody — possible C. difficile superinfection ❓ Always confirm allergy history before the first dose

entries.h: 📊 Three special safety rules on this page — don't mix them up
entries.t: Drug Unique safety issue Vancomycin Infuse slowly to avoid Red Man Syndrome; monitor peak/trough, renal function, hearing Fluoroquinolones ("-oxacin") Black-box tendon rupture warning, especially Achilles tendon Sulfonamides Photosensitivity, adequate hydration, and caution with the broader sulfa cross-sensitivity list 🧠 "Vanco = ears & rate, Oxacin = tendons, Sulfa = sun." Three antibiotics, three completely different bodies-of-concern. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 💊 Penicillins Beta-lactam — ask about allergy first ⚠️ Sulfa Photosensitivity, hydration, cross-sensitivity caution 🔴 Vancomycin Infuse slow — Red Man Syndrome 🦵 "-oxacin" Tendon rupture black-box warning

Show answer About 30 minutes to 1 hour after the infusion ends. The trough is drawn about 30 minutes before the next dose. Insulins: Rapid · Short · Intermediate · Long-Acting · Premixed & Concentrated NG-224 PHARM Series: NCLEX Drug Review 5 of 5 ADHD-friendly visual edition One drug, six timing profiles. Every insulin does the same job — moves glucose into cells, converts it to glycogen, and shuts off the liver's own glucose release — the entire test is about WHEN each type kicks in, peaks, and wears off , and which one you can push into a vein. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 💉 IV = Regular ONLY The only insulin that ca

STEP 1 · WHAT'S IN THIS SET Robo's 3-part study map: TYPE → TIMING → WATCH . Timing values below are standard rounded teaching ranges — always verify against your current drug reference/facility policy, since exact figures vary slightly by source.

⚡ Rapid-Acting 🩹 Short-Acting (Regular) 🌫️ Intermediate (NPH) 🕰️ Long-Acting 🧪 Premixed 🔬 Concentrated (U-500) 🧠 "The faster it kicks in, the sooner it fades." Rapid & short-acting insulins act fast and leave fast; intermediate & long-acting act slow and stay all day. Match the insulin's timing to when the patient actually eats.
