STEP 2 · TYPE → TIMING → TRAP The same mechanism, six different clocks — plus the one insulin that can go straight into the vein.

entries.h: 🔬 What every insulin does at the cell
entries.t: Bottom line: insulin lowers blood glucose three ways — moves it into cells, converts it to storage (glycogen), and tells the liver to stop releasing more. Every category below just changes when this happens.

entries.h: ⏱️ Onset → Peak → Duration, side by side
entries.t: 🧠 "Rapid with meals, long for baseline." Rapid/short-acting insulin covers the food someone is about to eat; intermediate/long-acting insulin is the steady background dose, unrelated to a specific meal.

Action: moves glucose into cells, promotes glucose → glycogen conversion, and suppresses the liver's own glucose release — same as every insulin, just on a fast clock. ⭐ Key nursing point: give within about 15 minutes of a meal — food must be available and eaten close to administration or hypoglycemia can follow quickly. 🚨 NCLEX trap: Never give a rapid-acting insulin and then have the patient skip or delay the meal — verify the tray is present before injecting.

entries.h: 🩹 Short-Acting — Regular Humulin R · Novolin R · U-500
entries.t: Action: same glucose-lowering mechanism; clear in appearance. ⭐ Key nursing point: Regular insulin is the only insulin that can be given IV (commonly used in DKA/insulin drips). Insulin U-500 is a highly concentrated form — extra caution with dosing to avoid a 5x overdose error. 🚨 NCLEX trap: Confusing units and mLs with concentrated U-500 is a classic high-alert medication error — always double-check with another nurse per facility policy.

entries.h: 🌫️ Intermediate-Acting — NPH Humulin N · Novolin N
entries.t: Action: same mechanism, delayed onset and a broad mid-day peak; appearance is cloudy . ⭐ Key nursing point: gently roll (do not shake) the vial to resuspend before drawing up — must be given SQ only, never IV or IV drip . Time meals/snacks to cover the expected peak, when hypoglycemia risk is highest. 🚨 NCLEX trap: A cloudy insulin going into an IV line is a medication error — only a clear insulin (Regular) is IV-safe.

Action: same mechanism, delivered as a steady, flat basal dose across the day. ⭐ Key nursing point: glargine has no pronounced peak and is typically dosed once daily; detemir may be dosed once or twice daily depending on control needed. 🚨 NCLEX trap: Never mix glargine (or detemir) with any other insulin in the same syringe — its acidic formulation can cause precipitation and unpredictable dosing.

Action: a fixed-ratio combination of an intermediate component (cloudy, for background coverage) and a rapid/short component (for meal coverage) in one syringe or pen. ⭐ Key nursing point: convenient — fewer injections — but less flexible than dosing each component separately; timing must still match a meal for the fast-acting portion to work correctly. Given SQ only. 🚨 NCLEX trap: Because the ratio is fixed, a premixed insulin can't be fine-tuned the way separate rapid + long-acting doses can — not the right choic
STEP 3 · SAFETY & PATIENT TEACHING Mixing technique, and the emergency that matters more than any timing chart.

entries.h: 🌫️ Mixing Regular + NPH in one syringe — "clear before cloudy"
entries.t: 🧠 "Clear before cloudy, fast before slow." Contaminating the Regular vial with NPH would slow down your fast-acting insulin — always draw clean/clear first.

entries.h: 🍬 Hypoglycemia — the most deadly acute risk
entries.t: Standard adult reference: hypoglycemia is generally defined as blood glucose <70 mg/dL . 😓 Shaky, sweaty, confused, rapid heartbeat, hunger, irritability 🍬 Rule of 15: give 15g fast-acting carbohydrate, recheck glucose in 15 min , repeat if still low 🆘 If unconscious/unable to swallow: IM/IV glucagon or IV dextrose per protocol — do not give oral carbs 🧠 "Cold and clammy, need some candy; hot and dry, sugar's high." Classic contrast rhyme for hypo vs. hyperglycemia symptoms.

Hypoglycemia (low) Hyperglycemia (high) Onset: fast, minutes Onset: slower, hours to days Skin: cool, clammy, sweaty Skin: warm, dry Shaky, confused, irritable, hungry Thirsty, frequent urination, fruity breath (DKA) Treat: Rule of 15 / glucagon Treat: insulin per order, fluids, monitor for DKA/HHS ⚡
SAY IT OUT LOUD 💉 IV insulin Regular ONLY, never a cloudy insulin 📈 Glargine No peak, once daily, never mix 🌫️ Mixing Clear (Regular) before cloudy (NPH) 🍬 Rule of 15 15g carb → recheck in 15 min

Q1: Which insulin can be given intravenously? Show answer Regular insulin — it is the only clear, short-acting insulin approved for IV use. Q2: Which insulin has no pronounced peak, and what does that mean for dosing? Show answer Insulin glargine (Lantus) — it gives steady, flat basal coverage, typically dosed once daily, and must never be mixed with another insulin in the same syringe. Q3: When mixing Regular and NPH in one syringe, which do you draw up first? Show answer Regular (clear) first, then NPH (cloudy) —

entries.h: Herbal Supplements · NG-230 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🌿 Know them ⚠️ Interactions 🗣️ Always ask ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Pharmacology · Complementary & Alternative Agents

Not "just vitamins" — they interact like drugs because many act like drugs NG-230 PHARM ADHD-friendly visual edition Herbal & dietary supplements are NOT regulated by the FDA the same way prescription drugs are — no proof of efficacy is required before sale. Patients often don't think of them as "medications" and don't report them unless specifically asked. Yet several of the most common ones cause serious, well-tested bleeding and serotonin interactions. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🗣️ ALWAYS ask "
STEP 1 · WHAT EACH ONE IS FOR A quick field guide — what it's used for, matched to what it's tested on.

Herb Used for Nursing watch-point Saw Palmetto (SP) Swollen prostate — BPH (Benign Prostatic Hypertrophy) Mild GI upset; may add to effect of other hormone/BPH therapies Black Cohosh Menopause — hot flashes Possible hepatotoxicity reports; avoid with liver disease Hawthorn extract Heart / mild HF support Drug-drug interaction PRIORITY — can potentiate cardiac glycosides & antihypertensives Glucosamine Joint / arthritic pain ⚠️ Watch for hypoglycemia when combined with anti-diabetic medications Evening Primrose Oil

These raise bleeding risk, especially combined with anticoagulants/antiplatelets (warfarin, DOACs, aspirin, clopidogrel): 🌳 Ginkgo Biloba 🧄 Garlic 🫚 Ginger 🧴 Vitamin E 🐟 Omega-3 🌱 Ginseng 🧠 "The G's (mostly) bleed." Ginkgo, Garlic, Ginger, ginseng — plus Vitamin E and omega-3 — round out the bleed-risk crew.

Supplements are regulated as food-category products , not drugs — manufacturers don't have to prove safety or efficacy before selling them. Potency and purity can vary between brands and even between bottles. 🧠 "Not tested like a drug ≠ not acting like a drug." Just because it's sold OTC in the supplement aisle doesn't mean it's inert. ⚠️
STEP 2 · THE HIGH-YIELD DANGERS St. John's Wort is the single most heavily tested herb — it both weakens drugs and can trigger serotonin syndrome.

EXAM TIP St. John's Wort speeds up the liver's CYP450 enzymes , which clears many drugs faster than normal — so blood levels drop and the drug becomes less effective . 🧠 "St. John's Wort works against your other drugs." It doesn't just fail to help — it actively lowers the level of many drugs it's combined with, including birth control and warfarin. Reduced INR on a client taking both = St. John's Wort is the classic culprit.

entries.h: 🚨 St. John's Wort + antidepressants — serotonin syndrome
entries.t: St. John's Wort has serotonergic activity of its own. Combined with SSRIs, MAOIs, or TCAs , serotonin can build to dangerous levels. Never mix St. John's Wort with SSRIs, MAOIs, or TCAs — screen for it every time an antidepressant is on the med list. 🧠 "Sunshine herb, serotonin storm." St. John's Wort feels harmless because it's "natural" — but stacked serotonin from any source (herb + antidepressant) can kill.

Because so many supplements affect bleeding, sedation, or drug metabolism, the general teaching point is: stop most herbal supplements 2–3 weeks before a scheduled surgery , and always disclose supplement use during pre-op screening. Hawthorn is specifically flagged as a priority drug-drug interaction to review before any procedure. 🧠 "2 to 3, before they cut on me." Two to three weeks is the standard teaching window for stopping most herbal supplements pre-op. 🗣️
STEP 3 · THE NURSING PRIORITY If you don't ask, they usually won't tell you — this is the single highest-yield nursing action on this whole page.

1 🗣️ Ask specifically — "any vitamins, herbs, or supplements?" Don't assume they'll volunteer it 2 🩸 Screen for bleed-risk herbs if the patient is on any anticoagulant/antiplatelet 3 ☀️ Screen for St. John's Wort if the patient is on an antidepressant, OCP, or warfarin-type drug 4 🔪 Ask about supplements at every pre-op assessment — plan to stop 2–3 weeks out 5 🍬 Watch glucose if glucosamine + anti-diabetic medications are both on the list 🧠 "Ask like it's a drug — because it acts like one." This is the single test

Client is on… Ask about… Warfarin / DOAC / aspirin Ginkgo, garlic, ginger, vitamin E, omega-3, ginseng SSRI / MAOI / TCA St. John's Wort — serotonin syndrome risk Oral contraceptives St. John's Wort — reduced efficacy Anti-diabetic medication Glucosamine — hypoglycemia risk Cardiac / antihypertensive meds Hawthorn — priority drug-drug interaction

"BLEED & BLOCK": BLEED — ginkgo, garlic, ginger, vitamin E, omega-3, ginseng BLOCK — St. John's Wort blocks other drugs from working by speeding their clearance 🧠 One family raises bleeding risk, the other lowers everything else's effectiveness — know which is which. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🗣️ Not FDA-regulated patients don't report it — always ask 🩸 Ginkgo/garlic/ginger/vit E ↑ bleeding with anticoagulants ☀️ St. John's Wort induces CYP450 → ↓ OCP & warfarin efficacy; + serotonin syndrome risk 🔪 Stop 2–3 weeks pre-op disclose at every pre-op screen

Q1: A client on warfarin also takes ginkgo biloba and garlic supplements. What's the concern? Show answer Increased bleeding risk — ginkgo, garlic, ginger, vitamin E, omega-3, and ginseng all add to anticoagulant/antiplatelet bleeding risk. Q2: How does St. John's Wort reduce the effectiveness of oral contraceptives and warfarin? Show answer It induces liver CYP450 enzymes, which metabolizes those drugs faster — blood levels drop and efficacy is reduced (e.g., breakthrough bleeding on OCPs, falling INR on warfarin)
🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🎯 What It Does 🚨 Watch For ✅ Teach ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Pharmacology · Pain & Anti-Inflammatory Unit

Brand: Tylenol NG-232 PHARMACOLOGY ADHD-friendly visual edition Acetaminophen relieves fever and pain without the bleeding, ulcer, or major cardiovascular risks of NSAIDs — which is exactly why it's chosen for the client with a peptic ulcer, a bleeding disorder, or a kid with the flu. The trade-off: the single highest-yield fact on this whole drug is liver toxicity if the max daily dose is exceeded. See also NG-256 NSAIDs and the group's Toxic Ranges & Antidotes page. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🧠
STEP 1 · THE NSAID ALTERNATIVE Same fever/pain relief as an NSAID, almost none of the GI/renal/clotting risk — different mechanism entirely.

entries.h: 🧠 Central mechanism vs NSAIDs' peripheral mechanism
entries.t: MECHANISM Acetaminophen inhibits COX/prostaglandin production mainly in the central nervous system — that's why it lowers fever and blunts pain perception, but has only a weak effect on peripheral inflammation (swelling, redness) compared to NSAIDs. 🧠 "NSAID fights the fire at the scene. Tylenol turns down the alarm in the brain." Different location, different risk organ.
🌡️ Fever 🩹 Mild-to-moderate pain — headache, mild joint pain 🦴 Mild joint pain when NSAIDs are contraindicated 🧠 Fever + mild pain, minus the bleeding risk — that's Tylenol's whole job description.

entries.h: 🔀 Why it's chosen over an NSAID
entries.t: 🩸 Client has hemophilia or another bleeding disorder 🫙 Client has peptic ulcer disease 🧒 Child with the flu — avoids the Reye's syndrome risk tied to aspirin ➕ Tylenol & NSAIDs can be used interchangeably for fever — alternate to the other once one reaches its max dose 🧠 "No bleed, no ulcer risk" — acetaminophen is the safe swap whenever an NSAID's GI/platelet effect is the problem. 🚨
STEP 2 · LIVER TOXICITY The single highest-yield fact in this whole drug: exceeding the max dose is a liver problem, not a stomach problem.

entries.h: 🚨 Hepatotoxicity — how acetaminophen overdose destroys the liver
entries.t: Most acetaminophen is metabolized safely (glucuronidation/sulfation). A small fraction goes through CYP2E1 to a toxic metabolite, NAPQI , which is normally neutralized by glutathione . Overdose (or chronic alcohol use, which depletes glutathione and induces CYP2E1) overwhelms that buffer — NAPQI builds up and directly damages liver cells. 🧠 "A = Alcohol history = liver toxic." HESI's classic high-risk client: a client with an alcohol abuse history taking acetaminophen — depleted glutathione + induced CYP2E1 = fast

Acetylcysteine works by replenishing glutathione stores so the body can neutralize NAPQI before it destroys more liver cells. 🧠 "Acetylcysteine blocks Acetaminophen" — both start with "Acetyl," and both end up in the same sentence on the exam.

🧪 ALT and AST — the ATI-tested pair; rising liver enzymes signal hepatocellular injury 🧪 Bilirubin, PT/INR — worsening liver synthetic function in severe toxicity 🧪 Acetaminophen level — timed level used to guide antidote decisions (facility/toxicology protocol) 🧠 ATI question: "During an overdose, monitor for which labs?" → ALT and AST.

entries.h: 📈 Timeline — the danger of a "silent" overdose
entries.t: Hours 0–24: often few or no symptoms — nausea, malaise possible. Easy to underestimate. ▼ Day 2–3: labs start rising even as the client may feel briefly better — liver injury is silently progressing ▼ Day 3–4: peak hepatotoxicity — RUQ pain, jaundice, worsening labs; this is why any suspected overdose needs immediate evaluation, not "wait and see" 🧠 "Feels fine at hour 1 ≠ safe." The scariest part of acetaminophen overdose is that early symptoms are mild or absent — the danger builds silently before it's obvious. ✅
STEP 3 · STAY UNDER THE MAX Nearly every accidental overdose comes from combo products — not from someone deliberately taking too many Tylenol pills.

1 📏 Follow product/facility max daily dose — commonly cited around 3–4 g/day for healthy adults; the exact ceiling can vary by product, age, and liver function, so always check the label and facility policy rather than assuming a single fixed number 2 🔎 Check every combo product — many cold/flu remedies and prescription opioid combinations (e.g. opioid + acetaminophen tablets) already contain acetaminophen; doses stack fast without the client realizing it 3 🚫 Avoid alcohol while taking acetaminophen, especially wit

🤧 Cold/flu meds many contain it 💊 Opioid combo tabs e.g. oxycodone/APAP 🌙 Nighttime pain relievers check the label 🍺 + Alcohol compounds liver risk 🧠 Teach clients to read every label — "acetaminophen," "APAP," and "acetaminophen" are the same drug under different names.

"54-year-old male who abuses alcohol" — the classic high-risk acetaminophen client on HESI-style questions. 🍺 Chronic alcohol use → depleted glutathione, induced CYP2E1 🧓 Older age, malnutrition, or existing liver disease compound the risk 🧠 If the stem mentions alcohol history anywhere near acetaminophen, the answer is almost always about liver toxicity risk . ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🧠 Central action Fever + pain relief, minimal GI/renal/platelet effect 🍺 Alcohol = danger Chronic use depletes glutathione → liver toxicity risk 💊 Antidote Acetylcysteine — replenishes glutathione 🚨 Stay under the max Watch for hidden acetaminophen in combo products

Q1: Why is acetaminophen chosen over an NSAID for a client with a bleeding disorder or peptic ulcer disease? Show answer Acetaminophen has minimal effect on platelets and no significant GI erosion risk, unlike NSAIDs which block protective COX-1. Q2: What is the classic HESI "high-risk client" for acetaminophen toxicity? Show answer A client with a chronic alcohol abuse history — alcohol depletes glutathione and induces the CYP2E1 enzyme that makes the toxic metabolite NAPQI. Q3: What is the antidote for acetaminop

entries.h: Carbamazepine vs. Valproic Acid · NG-241 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🟣 Carbamazepine 🔵 Valproic Acid ⚖️ Tell them apart ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Psych-Mental Health Pharmacology · Mood Stabilizers & Anticonvulsants

Two mood-stabilizer / anticonvulsant drugs — two very different organ toxicities to watch for NG-241 PSYCH PHARM ADHD-friendly visual edition Both treat bipolar disorder & seizures , and both have a narrow therapeutic range requiring blood level monitoring — but their danger organs are opposite. Carbamazepine attacks the bone marrow & skin ; valproic acid attacks the liver, pancreas, and platelets — and is one of the most teratogenic drugs in psychiatry. This is a separate comparison from the antidepressant classes
STEP 1 · BONE MARROW & SKIN Sodium-channel blocker with two signature dangers: it can wipe out blood cell lines, and it can trigger a life-threatening skin reaction.

MOA Blocks voltage-gated sodium channels , stabilizing overexcited neurons — this is what makes it useful for both seizures and nerve pain. 🎭 Bipolar disorder — mood stabilization ⚡ Seizures 😖 Trigeminal neuralgia — neuropathic facial pain 🧠 "Carba-MAZE-pine calms a maze of overfiring neurons." Sodium channel blockade = fewer runaway electrical signals, whether that's a seizure or a nerve-pain flare.

Leukopenia (low WBC) → increased risk for a big infection . In severe cases, carbamazepine can cause aplastic anemia or agranulocytosis — the bone marrow stops making enough blood cells across one or more cell lines. 🧠 Report fever or sore throat immediately — with a suppressed WBC count, a simple sore throat can be the first sign of a serious infection.

Carbamazepine carries a known risk of triggering SJS — a severe, potentially life-threatening skin/mucous membrane reaction. Teach patients to report any new rash, blistering, or skin peeling immediately. 🧠 "Carba-MAZE-pine can maze up your skin." Any new rash on this drug is never "just a rash" — call the provider.

Carbamazepine induces liver enzymes that break down hormonal contraceptives, making oral contraceptives less effective . Patients need alternative birth control methods to prevent an accidental pregnancy. 🧠 "Carbamazepine cancels the pill." This is a distinct reproductive risk from valproic acid's teratogenicity — know both, don't mix them up. 🔵
STEP 2 · LIVER, PANCREAS & PLATELETS Remember it by the letter L — liver toxicity, low platelets, and one of the most teratogenic drugs a nursing student will learn.

MOA Increases availability of GABA , the brain's main inhibitory neurotransmitter, calming excessive neuronal firing. 🎭 Bipolar disorder — mood stabilization ⚡ Seizures 🤕 Also used for migraine prophylaxis in some practice settings 🧠 "vaLLLproic acid" — stretch out the L's: L iver toxic, L ow platelets. The whole side-effect profile lives in that one letter.

🫁 Liver toxicity 🩸 Low platelets Hepatotoxicity — watch for jaundice and rising ALT/AST liver labs Thrombocytopenia — big bleed risk , watch for bruising, bleeding gums, petechiae 🧠 "L for Liver, L for bLeeding." Both letters in valproic acid's name (the two L's) map straight onto its two lab-monitoring priorities.

Valproic acid can also cause pancreatitis . Teach patients to report sudden, severe abdominal pain, nausea, or vomiting. 🧠 Three organs to remember for valproic acid: liver , platelets , pancreas — the "3 P's and an L" isn't perfect, but liver + pancreas + platelets covers the monitoring priorities.

Valproic acid is strongly associated with neural tube defects when taken during pregnancy — this is one of the most important reproductive-safety facts in psych pharmacology. Counsel every reproductive-age patient before starting therapy. 🧠 "vaLLLproic — L for Life-changing risk in pregnancy." This is the single highest-stakes teaching point on this whole page for a reproductive-age patient.

Teach the client not to discontinue abruptly — stopping either carbamazepine or valproic acid suddenly can trigger rebound seizures . 🧠 Applies to both drugs on this page — always taper anticonvulsants under provider guidance. ⚖️
STEP 3 · SIDE BY SIDE Same job — mood stabilization and seizure control — completely different organs to monitor.

entries.h: ⚖️ Carbamazepine vs. Valproic Acid — head to head
entries.t: 🟣 Carbamazepine 🔵 Valproic Acid Mechanism: sodium channel blocker Mechanism: increases GABA availability Indications: bipolar disorder, seizures, trigeminal neuralgia Indications: bipolar disorder, seizures Danger organs: bone marrow (leukopenia, aplastic anemia, agranulocytosis) & skin (SJS) Danger organs: liver (hepatotoxicity), platelets (thrombocytopenia), pancreas (pancreatitis) Key symptom to report: fever, sore throat, new rash Key symptom to report: jaundice, easy bruising, severe abdominal pain Reproductiv

entries.h: 🧪 Narrow therapeutic range — why monitoring matters
entries.t: Both drugs have a narrow therapeutic range : too low a level and seizures/mood symptoms aren't controlled; too high a level and toxicity risk climbs fast. This is the same concept covered in more numeric detail on the Toxic Ranges & Antidotes page — this page intentionally does not restate specific lab-value numbers, to avoid conflicting with that dedicated reference. 🔗 See the Toxic Ranges & Antidotes page for exact numeric reference ranges ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🟣 Carbamazepine = bone marrow suppression + SJS, report fever/sore throat/rash 🔵 Valproic acid = liver, platelets, pancreas — and teratogenic 🫃 Reproductive risks differ Carbamazepine cancels the pill; valproic acid causes neural tube defects 🚫 Never stop abruptly = rebound seizure risk, both drugs

Q1: A patient on carbamazepine calls with a sore throat and fever. What's your concern? Show answer Bone marrow suppression (leukopenia/agranulocytosis/aplastic anemia) — a simple sore throat can signal a serious infection. Report and follow up with labs immediately. Q2: What does the "L" in valproic acid's memory trick stand for? Show answer Liver toxicity and Low platelets (thrombocytopenia) — plus watch for pancreatitis. Q3: Why is valproic acid a major concern for a reproductive-age patient? Show answer It's te

entries.h: Clonidine (Withdrawal & Off-Label) · NG-243 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🩹 Withdrawal use 🧒 ADHD use 🩺 Safety ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Pharmacology · Off-Label & Withdrawal Support

Off-label angle: withdrawal symptom control & ADHD — not the antihypertensive story NG-243 PHARM ADHD-friendly visual edition Clonidine is a central alpha-2 agonist that turns down sympathetic outflow from the brainstem. Its core antihypertensive mechanism, dosing, patch teaching, and rebound-crisis warning are already covered in depth elsewhere — this page focuses on the other jobs it does : taking the edge off opioid and alcohol withdrawal and treating ADHD . 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🔗 Core ph
STEP 1 · WHY IT HELPS DURING DETOX Withdrawal from opioids and alcohol both involve a norepinephrine storm — clonidine turns that storm down at the source.

entries.h: 🧠 Same brainstem brake, applied to withdrawal
entries.t: EXAM TIP When a client stops opioids (or, to a lesser extent, alcohol), the brainstem's own noradrenergic neurons — no longer suppressed by the substance — fire excessively , driving the classic autonomic withdrawal symptoms. Clonidine stimulates the same alpha-2 receptors that the missing substance used to keep in check , quieting that surge. 🧠 "Clonidine turns down the alarm, it doesn't remove the fire." It controls the autonomic symptoms of withdrawal — it does not treat cravings or provide the receptor-level su

Clonidine is a well-established adjunct for opioid withdrawal — it reduces sweating, tachycardia, anxiety, and GI cramping. It has no opioid receptor activity , so it does not treat the craving/reward component the way MAT drugs do. 🧠 See NG-277 · Withdrawal Meds for how clonidine fits alongside methadone and buprenorphine (medication-assisted treatment) in the full opioid-withdrawal picture.

entries.h: 🍺 Alcohol withdrawal — adjunct, not the primary drug
entries.t: Clonidine can help control the autonomic symptoms of alcohol withdrawal (tachycardia, hypertension, anxiety), but it does not prevent seizures or delirium tremens (DTs). Benzodiazepines remain the primary agent for seizure/DT prevention in alcohol withdrawal. 🧠 "Clonidine calms the shakes, benzos prevent the storm." Never rely on clonidine alone for alcohol withdrawal safety. 🧒
STEP 2 · THE OTHER OFF-LABEL ROLE A different formulation, a different population — same alpha-2 mechanism, applied to attention/impulse regulation.

🧠 "Kapvay ≠ Catapres, even though both are clonidine." The extended-release ADHD product is a distinct formulation and dosing schedule — mixing it up with the antihypertensive IR tablet or patch is a classic med-error trap.

Whether clonidine is being used for hypertension, withdrawal, or ADHD, abrupt discontinuation risks a rebound sympathetic surge — full mechanism covered on NG-110. In a child on Kapvay, this can look like rebound agitation or a BP spike. 🧠 The rebound-crisis warning travels with the drug across every indication — it's not unique to the antihypertensive use.

entries.h: ⭐ Why it crosses so many indications
entries.t: Because clonidine turns down brainstem sympathetic outflow broadly, it shows up anywhere a "too much fight-or-flight" state needs quieting — high BP, a withdrawal-driven catecholamine surge, or impulsivity/hyperarousal in ADHD. 🧠 One receptor, one brake, many use-cases — that's the throughline across all of clonidine's jobs. 🩺
STEP 3 · WHAT'S DIFFERENT IN THE DETOX SETTING Same core risks as NG-110 — but in withdrawal management, they're often stacked with other sedating or rate-lowering drugs.

entries.h: 🚨 Additive risk during detox — watch the stack
entries.t: Clients being treated for withdrawal are frequently also receiving benzodiazepines (alcohol withdrawal) or opioid agonist/partial-agonist therapy (methadone/buprenorphine). Clonidine's own sedation, hypotension, and bradycardia stack with all of these. 😴 Sedation + benzos/opioids = additive CNS depression 🩸 Hypotension monitor BP closely during taper 🫀 Bradycardia monitor HR, esp. with methadone's QT effects 🩺 Withhold & notify if BP drops significantly — hold dose, call provider 🧠 "Detox stacks sedatives." Every a

If blood pressure drops significantly after a dose (a general guideline: systolic drop of ≥ 20 mm Hg or systolic < 90 mm Hg ), withhold the next dose and notify the provider immediately rather than giving the next scheduled dose. 🧠 This threshold applies to centrally- and peripherally-acting antiadrenergics broadly — always confirm your facility's specific parameters.

entries.h: ❌ Key cautions specific to this context
entries.t: MAOIs — contraindicated in combination with clonidine Active hepatic disease — caution/contraindication Do not confuse withdrawal-management dosing with standard antihypertensive dosing without provider direction 🧠 Always cross-check the full medication list — withdrawal management often means several sedating or cardiac-active drugs are running at once.

entries.h: 🆚 Clonidine's job vs. MAT drugs — don't confuse the two
entries.t: Feature Clonidine Methadone / Buprenorphine (MAT) Receptor target Central alpha-2 (brainstem) Opioid mu receptor (full/partial agonist) What it treats Autonomic symptoms — sweating, tachycardia, anxiety, GI cramping Cravings + prevents withdrawal at the receptor level Is it MAT? No — symptom control only Yes — medication-assisted treatment Abrupt stop risk Rebound hypertensive crisis Return of withdrawal symptoms; overdose risk if combined with other opioids 🧠 "Clonidine quiets the alarm bell; MAT treats the fire."

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🩹 Withdrawal = symptom control blunts the norepinephrine surge — not MAT 🚫 No opioid receptor activity doesn't treat cravings the way methadone/buprenorphine do 🧒 Kapvay = ADHD form extended-release, distinct from IR/patch 🩺 Watch for stacking sedation/hypotension add up with benzos & opioids in detox

Q1: What symptoms of opioid withdrawal does clonidine actually treat? Show answer The autonomic symptoms driven by a norepinephrine surge — sweating, tachycardia, anxiety, GI cramping, piloerection, rhinorrhea, yawning. It does not treat cravings and has no opioid receptor activity. Q2: Is clonidine considered medication-assisted treatment (MAT) for opioid use disorder? Show answer No — MAT drugs (methadone, buprenorphine) act at the opioid receptor. Clonidine is an adjunct for autonomic symptom control only. Q3: W

Your BIO 262 course, written out as study material instead of a file list. Each week opens with the one idea that makes the rest make sense , then the mechanism, then a comparison table and the traps. Open only the week you are revising. ⭐ How to use this page. Everything is collapsed on purpose. Open one week, read the Big idea card, and stop there if that is all you have in you today. The tables and diagrams underneath are for when you have more room.

entries.h: Week 1 🩸 T cells & blood vessels Where lymphocytes are trained, and how vessel walls are built

entries.t: A T cell is a lymphocyte that got an education. It is born in bone marrow like every other blood cell, but it does not become useful until it passes through the thymus — which is what the T stands for. Vessels follow one rule too: the thicker the muscle layer, the closer to the heart's pressure .

1 · Born Bone marrow makes a naive lymphocyte 2 · Travels Moves to the thymus 3 · Positive test Can it recognize self MHC? If no → dies 4 · Negative test Does it attack self? If yes → dies 5 · Released Survivors leave as CD4 or CD8 Roughly 98% of them fail and are destroyed. That brutal filter is what stops your immune system attacking you.
When negative selection fails, self-attacking T cells escape — that is the root of autoimmune disease (type 1 diabetes, MS, rheumatoid arthritis). DiGeorge syndrome = no thymus = no working T cells.

entries.h: 🩸 The two T cells you must not swap
entries.t: CD4 — Helper CD8 — Cytotoxic Job Directs everyone else; releases cytokines Kills infected cells directly Binds MHC class II MHC class I Memory hook 4 = 2 × 2 (class II) 8 = 1 × 8 (class I) Lost in HIV Yes — this is the cell HIV destroys Preserved early on
A normal CD4 count is roughly 500–1500 . AIDS is defined at CD4 < 200 , which is when opportunistic infections take hold. That single number shows up constantly.

Layer What it is Why you care Tunica intima Endothelium, one cell thick Damage here starts atherosclerosis and clots Tunica media Smooth muscle + elastic fibers Constricts and dilates → controls blood pressure Tunica externa Collagen, anchors the vessel Holds shape, carries its own blood supply

entries.h: 📊 Artery vs vein, decided by the media
entries.t: Arteries have a thick tunica media because they take the ventricle's pressure head-on. They stay round when empty. Veins have a thin media, a wide lumen, and valves . They collapse when empty and hold about 65% of your total blood volume at any moment — they are the reservoir. Capillaries are endothelium only . One cell thick is the whole point: that is the only place exchange happens.

“Arteries carry oxygenated blood” is false . The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs; the pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood back. Arteries carry blood away from the heart. That is the actual definition.

entries.h: Week 3 🧪 Tissues & skin The four tissue types, and the organ made of all of them

entries.t: There are only four tissue types in the entire body. Every organ is a combination of them. Learn the four and you can reason about any organ you meet. Tissue One-line job Where Repairs? Epithelial Covers, lines, secretes Skin surface, gut lining, glands Excellent — divides fast Connective Binds and supports Bone, blood, fat, tendon, cartilage Varies — cartilage barely heals Muscle Contracts Skeletal, cardiac, smooth Poor — scars instead Nervous Conducts signals Brain, cord, nerves Almost none in CNS
Tissue that touches the outside world regenerates. Tissue that does the thinking does not. That is why a skin graze vanishes in a week and a spinal cord injury is permanent.

entries.h: 🧠 Connective tissue is the odd one
entries.t: It is the only type defined by its matrix rather than its cells — the non-living material the cells sit in. Change the matrix and you change the tissue completely: Liquid matrix → blood Gel matrix → cartilage Mineralised matrix → bone Loose fiber matrix → fat and areolar tissue

Layer Made of Key point Epidermis Stratified squamous epithelium No blood supply. Fed by diffusion from below Dermis Connective tissue Vessels, nerves, follicles, glands — where pain is felt Hypodermis Fat (subcutaneous) Insulation, cushioning, where SubQ injections go

entries.h: 🔥 Burn depth follows the layers exactly
entries.t: Superficial — epidermis only. Red, dry, painful. Heals itself. Partial thickness — into dermis. Blisters, and the most painful , because dermal nerve endings are exposed but alive. Full thickness destroys the nerves — so it is painless. Painless is worse, not better.

entries.h: ✅ The exam question this sets up
entries.t: Asked which burn hurts most, the answer is partial thickness , not full thickness. Students lose this mark constantly by assuming deeper always means more pain.

entries.h: Week 4 🦴 Bones Living tissue that doubles as the calcium bank

entries.t: Bone is not scaffolding. It is an organ that is rebuilt continuously — and it is where your body stores about 99% of its calcium . When blood calcium falls, the skeleton is spent to fix it. Bone strength is always the lower priority.

Cell Does Memory hook Osteo b last Builds new bone matrix B = Build Osteo c last Chews bone, releasing calcium to blood C = Crush Osteocyte Mature cell; senses strain, directs the other two The retired supervisor

Two hormones pull in opposite directions, and they are constantly confused on exams: PTH (parathyroid) Calcitonin (thyroid) Released when Blood calcium is LOW Blood calcium is HIGH Acts on bone Activates osteoclasts → breaks bone down Inhibits osteoclasts Kidney Reabsorbs calcium, activates vitamin D Excretes calcium Net effect Blood calcium ↑ Blood calcium ↓ Serum calcium 8.5 – 10.5 mg/dL < 8.5 hypo — tetany, Trousseau, Chvostek 8.5 – 10.5 normal > 10.5 hyper — stones, bones, groans

entries.h: ⭐ The mnemonic that carries the whole topic
entries.t: “Stones, bones, abdominal groans, and psychiatric moans.” That is hyper­calcemia: kidney stones, bone pain, constipation and ileus, confusion and depression. Flip every sign for hypocalcemia — instead of sluggish, everything becomes twitchy : tetany, spasm, tingling, positive Chvostek and Trousseau signs.

Estrogen restrains osteoclasts. When estrogen drops, that brake is released, resorption outpaces building, and bone density falls. Same logic explains steroid-induced osteoporosis: corticosteroids suppress osteoblasts , so building slows while chewing continues.

entries.h: Week 5 💪 Muscles & nerves How an electrical signal becomes a physical movement

entries.t: Muscle contraction is a calcium story. Every step exists to get calcium into the muscle cell, and relaxation is simply pumping it back out again.

1 · Signal Action potential reaches the axon terminal 2 · ACh Acetylcholine crosses the synaptic cleft 3 · Depolarize Muscle membrane fires 4 · Ca²⁺ Released from sarcoplasmic reticulum 5 · Slide Myosin pulls actin → contraction

The filaments never shorten. Actin and myosin slide past each other, so the sarcomere shortens while the proteins stay the same length. Calcium's actual job: it moves troponin and tropomyosin off the actin binding sites. Those sites are blocked at rest — calcium unlocks the door, it does not push .
ATP powers contraction — but it is also required to release myosin from actin. No ATP means the bridges cannot let go. That is rigor mortis.

Phase Ion moving Membrane Resting Na⁺/K⁺ pump holds the gradient −70 mV inside negative Depolarization Na⁺ rushes IN Shoots toward +30 mV Repolarization K⁺ flows OUT Falls back toward rest Refractory Pump resets gradients Cannot fire again yet

entries.h: ⭐ Why potassium is the dangerous electrolyte
entries.t: Resting potential is the potassium gradient. Change serum K⁺ and you change whether every nerve and muscle in the body — including the heart — can fire correctly. That is why potassium is the electrolyte that kills fastest , and why it is never given IV push.

Myelin insulates the axon so the signal jumps node to node (saltatory conduction) instead of crawling. Strip the myelin — as in multiple sclerosis — and conduction slows or fails. That is the whole disease in one sentence.

entries.h: Week 7 👀 Eyes & ears Two organs that turn physical energy into nerve signals

entries.t: Both organs are transducers. The eye converts light into electricity; the ear converts vibration into electricity. Everything else is plumbing that protects and focuses.

1 Cornea — does most of the bending 2 Pupil — iris sets how much enters 3 Lens — fine focus, changes shape 4 Retina — rods and cones fire 5 Optic nerve — to the brain Rods Cones Detect Dim light, movement Color, sharp detail Where Peripheral retina Concentrated at the fovea Memory hook Rods = niGHt Cones = Color

entries.h: 🚨 Glaucoma, and why it steals sight silently
entries.t: Aqueous humor cannot drain → pressure rises → the optic nerve is compressed. Because rods sit in the periphery , peripheral vision goes first and central vision stays normal for years — so it is painless and unnoticed until late. Acute angle-closure glaucoma is the exception: sudden severe eye pain, halos, a fixed pupil. That is an emergency.
1 Pinna funnels sound in 2 Tympanic membrane vibrates 3 Ossicles amplify (malleus, incus, stapes) 4 Cochlea — fluid waves bend hair cells 5 Vestibulocochlear nerve fires
The semicircular canals sit next to the cochlea and sense head rotation. That shared address is why ear infections and Ménière's disease cause vertigo — not just hearing loss.

Conductive — sound cannot get in . Wax, fluid, a perforated drum, otosclerosis. Often fixable. Sensorineural — the hair cells or nerve are damaged. Noise, ageing, ototoxic drugs. Usually permanent. Ototoxic offenders worth knowing: aminoglycosides (gentamicin), loop diuretics , high-dose aspirin, cisplatin.

entries.h: Week 8 🧬 Receptors & hormones Chemical messaging, and the feedback loop that governs it

entries.t: A hormone only affects a cell that has its receptor. The bloodstream carries it everywhere; the receptor decides who listens. That single fact explains why one hormone can do several unrelated things in different tissues.

The output shuts off its own trigger, like a thermostat: Hypothalamus → pituitary → gland → hormone → signals back to switch the hypothalamus off. Understand this loop and you can predict every lab pattern in endocrinology instead of memorizing them.

entries.h: ⭐ The lab trick that always works
entries.t: Compare the gland hormone with its stimulating hormone : Low T4 + HIGH TSH → the thyroid is failing. The pituitary is shouting. Primary hypothyroidism. Low T4 + LOW TSH → the pituitary is failing. Nobody is shouting. Secondary . Both hormones moving the same direction = the problem is upstream, in the pituitary.

entries.h: 🧥 Two ways a hormone gives its order
entries.t: Steroid (lipid-soluble) Peptide (water-soluble) Examples Cortisol, aldosterone, estrogen, testosterone Insulin, ADH, growth hormone Receptor sits Inside the cell On the cell surface Acts by Switching genes on → makes new protein Second messengers → activates existing protein Speed Slow (hours) but long-lasting Fast (seconds) but brief

entries.h: 🚨 Why steroids cannot be stopped abruptly
entries.t: Long-term steroid dosing convinces the hypothalamus there is plenty of cortisol, so it stops signaling and the adrenal glands atrophy . Stop suddenly and there is no cortisol from anywhere — adrenal crisis. Steroids are always tapered.

entries.h: 💧 The two water hormones students mix up
entries.t: ADH (vasopressin) Aldosterone From Posterior pituitary Adrenal cortex Retains Water only Sodium (water follows) Effect on Na⁺ Dilutes it — sodium falls Raises sodium Too much SIADH — concentrated urine, low serum Na⁺ Conn's — hypertension, low K⁺ Too little Diabetes insipidus — liters of dilute urine Addison's — low Na⁺, high K⁺

entries.h: ✅ Say it once and it sticks
entries.t: “SIADH soaks. DI drains.” SIADH holds water in and dilutes the blood. Diabetes insipidus pours it out and concentrates the blood.

entries.h: Week 9 🩸 Blood, vessels & clotting What blood carries, and how a leak gets sealed

entries.t: Clotting is a controlled emergency. The body must plug a hole fast enough to stop blood loss, but not so eagerly that it blocks a healthy vessel. Nearly every bleeding or clotting disorder is that balance tipping one way.
Component Share Job Plasma ~55% Water, albumin, clotting factors, electrolytes RBCs ~45% Carry O₂ on hemoglobin. No nucleus , live ~120 days WBCs + platelets <1% Defense and clotting

Ditching the nucleus frees space for more hemoglobin and lets the cell bend through capillaries narrower than itself. The cost: it cannot repair itself or divide , which is why it only lasts 120 days.

1 · Spasm Vessel constricts, cutting flow 2 · Platelet plug Platelets stick and pile up 3 · Cascade Factors activate in sequence 4 · Fibrin Mesh locks the plug in place 5 · Lysis Plasmin dissolves it once healed

entries.h: ⭐ The two pathways, and the two lab tests
entries.t: You do not need every factor. You need which test watches which pathway, because that is what drug monitoring depends on: Intrinsic Extrinsic Triggered by Damage inside the vessel Tissue injury outside the vessel Measured by aPTT PT / INR Drug monitored Heparin Warfarin Antidote Protamine sulfate Vitamin K

“PT / WEPT” — P T goes with W arfarin, E xtrinsic. Everything left over — aPTT — goes with heparin and intrinsic. Warfarin blocks vitamin-K-dependent factors, which is exactly why vitamin K reverses it . The antidote is the mechanism run backwards.

entries.h: 🚨 Virchow's triad — why clots form where they should not
entries.t: Three conditions, and a DVT usually needs more than one: Stasis — immobility, long flights, bed rest Endothelial injury — surgery, trauma, IV lines Hypercoagulability — pregnancy, cancer, estrogen, dehydration A post-op patient on bed rest has all three at once.

entries.h: Week 10 ❤️ The heart Cardiac output, and the three dials that change it

entries.t: One equation runs all of cardiology: CO = HR × SV Cardiac output is heart rate times stroke volume. Every cardiac drug and every cardiac disease works by changing one of those two numbers.

entries.h: 🎚️ The three dials on stroke volume
entries.t: Dial Plain English Raised by Lowered by Preload How full the ventricle is before it squeezes IV fluids, heart failure Diuretics, bleeding, nitrates Afterload The resistance it must squeeze against Hypertension, vasoconstriction ACE inhibitors, vasodilators Contractility How hard the muscle squeezes Digoxin, dobutamine, epinephrine Beta blockers, ischemia, acidosis

Stretch a healthy ventricle more and it squeezes harder — like a rubber band. More preload gives more stroke volume. But only up to a point. Overstretch it and force falls off , because the actin and myosin filaments no longer overlap properly. That drop-off is decompensated heart failure. It is why fluid overload makes a failing heart worse, not better.

entries.h: ⭐ Ejection fraction, and what the number means
entries.t: EF is the percentage of ventricular volume ejected per beat. Normal is 55–70% . A healthy heart never empties completely. EF < 40% → systolic failure — the pump is weak (HFrEF) EF normal but symptoms present → diastolic failure — the ventricle is stiff and will not fill (HFpEF)
SA node Pacemaker — 60–100/min AV node Delays, so atria finish emptying Bundle of His Into the septum Purkinje Ventricles contract bottom-up

entries.h: ✅ Two details that answer exam questions
entries.t: The AV delay is deliberate. Without it the atria and ventricles would contract together and nothing would move forward. Ventricles contract from the apex up , squeezing blood toward the outflow valves — like squeezing a tube of toothpaste from the bottom. If the SA node fails, the AV node takes over at ~40–60, and the Purkinje system at ~20–40. The further down the back-up, the slower and less reliable it is.

entries.h: Week 11 🛡️ Immunity Two defense systems, and how they hand over

entries.t: You have a fast, dumb system and a slow, clever one. Innate immunity responds in minutes to anything foreign. Adaptive immunity takes days but remembers forever. Innate Adaptive Speed Minutes to hours Days on first exposure Specific? No — same response to everything Yes — targeted to one antigen Memory? None Yes — the basis of vaccination Players Skin, mucus, neutrophils, macrophages, fever, complement B cells (antibodies), T cells

The four classic signs are all one process: vessels dilate and leak on purpose . Redness & heat — more blood arriving Swelling — fluid and cells leaving the capillary Pain — mediators and pressure on nerve endings It is not the infection. It is your response to it.

Active — you make the antibodies. Slow to build, long-lasting . Infection, or a vaccine. Passive — antibodies are given to you. Instant, but temporary . Placental transfer, breast milk, immunoglobulin injections. Instant protection is always temporary. Lasting protection always takes time to build.

entries.h: 🚨 Fever is a feature, not a fault
entries.t: The hypothalamic set point is deliberately raised — most pathogens replicate poorly at higher temperatures and immune enzymes work faster. Which is why shivering comes first : your body is generating heat to reach the new set point. Chills mean the fever is still climbing.

entries.h: Week 12 🦦 Respiratory Moving air, exchanging gas, and holding pH steady

entries.t: Breathing is two separate jobs. Ventilation moves air in and out. Respiration is the gas actually crossing into blood. A patient can ventilate beautifully and still not oxygenate.

Only pressure gradients. The diaphragm contracts and flattens → the chest volume rises → pressure inside drops below atmospheric → air is pushed in. Quiet exhalation is passive — the lung's own elastic recoil. It costs no energy.

entries.h: 🚨 Surfactant, and why premature babies struggle
entries.t: Surfactant reduces surface tension so alveoli do not collapse on themselves at the end of each breath. It is not produced in adequate amounts until roughly week 34–36 of gestation — which is precisely why preterm infants develop respiratory distress syndrome , and why mothers in preterm labor are given steroids to accelerate its production.

entries.h: 🧤 The oxyhemoglobin curve, without the math
entries.t: Shift Means Caused by RIGHT Hemoglobin releases O₂ more easily — tissues get more Acid, ↑CO₂, fever, exercise LEFT Hemoglobin holds O₂ tightly — tissues get less Alkalosis, ↓CO₂, hypothermia

entries.h: ✅ The memory hook that actually works
entries.t: “Right = Release.” Both start with R. And it makes physiological sense: a hot, acidic, hard-working muscle needs oxygen — so those exact conditions make hemoglobin let go of it.

entries.h: ⭐ ABGs — the method, not the memorization
entries.t: Take them in this order and you cannot get lost: pH 7.35–7.45 — below is acidosis, above is alkalosis CO₂ 35–45 — the lung number. Moves opposite to pH when respiratory HCO₃⁻ 22–26 — the kidney number. Moves with pH when metabolic Whichever value matches the pH direction is the culprit. Arterial pH 7.35 – 7.45 < 7.35 ACIDOSIS 7.35 – 7.45 > 7.45 ALKALOSIS

In chronic CO₂ retention the kidneys compensate by holding bicarbonate, so pH sits near normal with a high CO₂ and a high HCO₃⁻ . That is compensated respiratory acidosis, not a normal gas. A "normal" pH with two abnormal values is compensation, never health. 📝 Weeks 13 and 14 are not written yet. entries.h: 🧩 Which of the two to use
entries.t: Downloaded files is the reliable one. Download that module’s recordings from the podcasts and lectures page into one folder, put the .m3u in the same folder, and open it with VLC. It plays offline, which is what you want in the car anyway. Stream from Drive opens the files straight from Google Drive without downloading. These lectures run from 90 MB to 580 MB, and Drive shows a scan warning instead of the video for anything that big — which is what used to break every one of these. The links now go through the down

On your phone, use the orange 🎬 Open in VLC button. It hands the playlist straight to VLC by name. Tapping the plain link instead downloads the file, and Android gives it to Chrome's media viewer, which cannot read a playlist — that is the broken-image icon and the 0:00 . The orange button only appears on a phone, and only on the Drive playlists, because those are the ones that work over a link. Windows / Mac: double-click the .m3u , or drag it onto VLC. Downloaded files playlists list bare filenames on purpose. Pu

entries.h: Renal Failure - Acute & Chronic · NG-047 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🫘 Two failures 🧨 Causes 🔢 Numbers ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Renal + Fluid · Pathophysiology Course

Acute Kidney Injury vs. Chronic Kidney Disease → End Stage Renal Disease NG-047 Renal + Fluid ADHD-friendly visual edition THE MASTER PAGE. Everything in one place: what the kidney does, what acute vs chronic failure actually means, every cause, and every number. Three sister pages go deeper — NG-264 = the phases & stages (how each one moves through time), NG-265 = the labs & symptoms side by side, NG-266 = the nursing care, diet & drugs . Start here, then pick the one you need. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in
STEP 1 · KNOW WHICH ONE Same organ, two completely different stories — one is a sudden emergency you can reverse, one is a slow demolition you can only slow down.

entries.h: 🏭 First — what the kidney actually DOES (all 6 jobs fail together)
entries.t: Every symptom on every one of these pages is one of these six jobs going offline . Learn the six and you can predict the symptom list instead of memorizing it. 🧠 “A WET BED” — A cid-base · W ater balance · E lectrolytes · T oxins & waste removed · B P (renin) · E rythropoietin · D vitamin activation. Kidneys quit → the patient is A WET BED: soaked in fluid, waste and acid.

Sudden, short-term loss of kidney function. Hours to days. Sudden loss of kidney function from loss of circulation to the renal system, or from glomerular / tubular damage. ⏱️ Onset measured in hours–days 🔄 REVERSIBLE — if you find and fix the cause ⚠️ If not stopped & reversed it can lead to Chronic Renal Failure 🧠 Acute = “A cute little emergency.” Small window, fixable — find the cause today .

Long-term chronic damage to the kidneys — over years & years of destruction — resulting in permanent damage . 📆 Onset measured in months–years 🚫 IRREVERSIBLE — you can only slow it 🏁 Endpoint = Stage 5 = End Stage Renal Disease (ESRD) = needs treatment to live 🧠 Chronic = CHRONO = clock. Years on the clock, and the clock does not run backwards.

entries.h: 📈 Watch the two shapes — this is the whole difference in one picture
entries.t: 🧠 Acute is a POTHOLE 🕳️ — chronic is a LANDSLIDE 🏔️. You can drive out of a pothole. Nobody drives back up a landslide.

entries.h: ⚖️ Acute vs. Chronic — the side-by-side you will be tested on
entries.t: Feature ⚡ ACUTE (AKI / ARF) 🐌 CHRONIC (CKD / CRF) Onset Sudden — hours to days Gradual — months to years Reversible? YES — if the cause is fixed NO — permanent damage Course 4 phases → recovery (see NG-264) 5 stages → ESRD (see NG-264) Urine output Usually drops hard — oliguria <400 mL/24 hr , then a big diuresis May stay normal for years, then falls late Kidney size on imaging Normal size Small, shrunken, scarred Anemia Usually not early Expected — no erythropoietin Bones Normal Renal osteodystrophy — high phos, l
STEP 2 · WHERE IS THE PROBLEM Acute failure is a plumbing question: is the problem BEFORE the kidney, INSIDE it, or AFTER it? Chronic failure has its own top-tested list.

entries.h: 🚰 The plumbing map — PRE · INTRA · POST
entries.t: Blood comes in → the kidney filters → urine drains out . Break any of the three and the kidney fails. Name the zone first, then the cause follows automatically. 🧠 Say it as a road trip: PRE = can't get there (no perfusion) · INTRA = the place is trashed (toxins) · POST = can't get home (blocked drain). Ask "which zone?" before you ever ask "which cause?"

Answer first: the kidney is fine — it's just starving for blood . 🧱 Obstruction — blocks blood flow & oxygen (emboli, clots, tumors) 📉 Low blood pressure = low perfusion (shock, hypovolemia, dehydration from blood or volume loss) ; low MAP <65 💀 Shock = severely low BP 🫀 Low cardiac output — heart failure: the heart fails to pump EXAM TIP Prerenal is the most common cause of AKI and the most fixable — restore volume/pressure fast and the kidney recovers. 🧠 PRE = PERFUSION. Both start with P . No pressure → no filte

Answer first: the kidney tissue itself is damaged or poisoned . 🧫 Nephrotoxins — the #1 tested group 💊 Antibiotics: Vancomycin · Gentamicin ☢️ CT contrast dye — Contrast kills the kidney! 🦠 Acute kidney infection / inflammation Result: creatinine over 1.3 = bad kidney. 🧠 “Vanc, Gent & Dye — kidneys die.” Three words, three killers. Before contrast: check the creatinine , hydrate, and ask about metformin .

Answer first: urine is being made — it just can't get out . 🪨 Kidney stones 🎗️ Tumor 🧔 Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) — big swollen prostate Classic picture: bladder distention , urgency, dribbling, then sudden anuria . Relieve the blockage (catheter, stent) and output returns. 🧠 POST = the mail can't be delivered 📮. Letters are written (urine is made), the mailbox is jammed. Unjam it and the kidney is fine.

entries.h: 🐌 Causes of CHRONIC kidney disease — Top Tested Causes
entries.t: 🍬 Uncontrolled DIABETES uncontrolled high sugar · #1 🩸 Long-term HYPERTENSION uncontrolled high BP · #2 🪢 Nephrosclerosis scarring of the kidneys 🫧 Polycystic kidney disease PKD — inherited cysts 🛡️ Unchecked autoimmune disease body attacks the kidney 👴 Older age at risk for ESRD Diabetes and hypertension are the two MOST commonly tested — together they cause most dialysis in the U.S. Both damage the tiny glomerular vessels: sugar caramelizes them, pressure blows them out . 🧠 “Sugar & Squeeze” 🍬 + 🩸 — the two thing
STEP 3 · GFR & THE LABS GFR sets the stage. Creatinine, BUN, urine output and pH tell you how bad today is.

entries.h: 📉 GFR — Glomerular Filtration Rate · Over 90 mL/min = normal
entries.t: GFR = how many mL of blood the kidneys clean every minute. It is the single number that defines the 5 stages of CKD as the kidney gradually loses function. 🧠 Count DOWN by the same shape: 90 · 60 · 30 · 15. Halve it, halve it, halve it. 90 normal → 60 mild → 30 moderate → 15 severe → below 15 you need a machine.

entries.h: 🧪 KEY NUMBERS — memorize these four cold
entries.t: Value Normal (adult) Renal failure says… Creatinine 🧪 0.6–1.2 mg/dL Over 1.3 = bad kidney — the most specific kidney lab BUN 🧪 10–20 mg/dL Over 20 — but BUN also rises from dehydration, GI bleed & high protein Urine output 🚽 30 mL/hr minimum · 1–2 L/day 30 mL/hr or LESS = kidneys in distress pH 🫁 7.35–7.45 Metabolic ACIDosis — pH below 7.35 (kidney can't dump H⁺) GFR 📉 >90 mL/min Falls stage by stage; <15 = ESRD Best indicator of GOOD renal function: 1500 mL of urine in 24 hours — if the option list has a urine vol

entries.h: 🫙 The creatinine clearance test — the 24-hour jug
entries.t: Answer first: creatinine clearance estimates GFR , so it is more accurate than a single blood draw — but only if not one drop is missed . 🕛 24 hours — collect all urine in a container ❌ Discard the FIRST urine specimen (it was made before the clock started) ✅ Save the LAST specimen at the 24-hour mark ❄️ Keep the container refrigerated / on ice unless your facility says otherwise 🚫 One missed void invalidates the whole test — start over 🧠 “Dump the first, keep the last.” Picture flushing the first cup down the drai

entries.h: 🧫 Urine studies that go with it
entries.t: 🫙 Sterile container for a routine specimen / culture 🔬 Urinalysis (UA) — protein, blood, casts, specific gravity 💧 Specific gravity : high (concentrated) in prerenal · fixed ~ 1.010 when tubules are damaged 🥚 Protein / albumin in urine = early sign of diabetic kidney damage 🧠 Thirsty kidney = concentrated urine. A prerenal kidney is still working, so it hoards water. A damaged kidney can't concentrate at all — the urine goes flat.

Answer first: a ratio over 20:1 points PRERENAL (dehydration/low perfusion). A ratio near 10:1–15:1 points to damage inside the kidney. Why: when the kidney is just dry, it reabsorbs urea back into the blood — so BUN climbs faster than creatinine. 🧠 Big ratio = big thirst. BUN way out ahead of creatinine means give fluid , not blame the kidney . 🩺
STEP 4 · WHAT WE DO A 30-second overview — the full management, diet and drug detail lives on NG-266.

entries.h: ✅ The universal renal priorities — in order
entries.t: 1 🫀 Potassium & the heart first. K⁺ over 5.0 with ECG changes is the thing that kills today — see NG-265 . 2 💧 Fluid balance. Strict I&O + daily weight — 1 kg = 1 L of fluid. 3 🔎 Find & fix the cause. Fluid for prerenal · stop the nephrotoxin for intrarenal · unblock for postrenal. 4 🚫 Stop hurting it. No NSAIDs, no contrast dye, no magnesium antacids, renally dose everything. 5 🍽️ Renal diet. Low sodium · low potassium · low phosphorus · protein per stage. 6 🩸 Dialysis when the numbers or the symptoms demand it. 🧠

A — A cidosis that won't correct (pH <7.35 , low bicarb) E — E lectrolytes: refractory hyperkalemia I — I ntoxications / dialyzable poisons O — fluid O verload not responding to diuretics (pulmonary edema) U — U remia: pericarditis, encephalopathy, asterixis, uremic frost 🧠 Vowels dialyze: A-E-I-O-U. Any one vowel showing up = the machine, not another dose.

entries.h: 🗺️ Where to go next — your 4-page map
entries.t: 🫘 NG-047 you are here · the whole picture ⏱️ NG-264 4 phases & 5 stages 🧪 NG-265 labs & symptoms 🩺 NG-266 care, diet & drugs Related decks: NG-248 hemodialysis · NG-261 peritoneal dialysis · NG-263 renal anatomy. 🧠 One topic, four lenses: WHAT it is (047) → WHEN it happens (264) → HOW it shows up (265) → WHAT you do (266). ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🚰 PRE · INTRA · POST Can't get there · place is trashed · can't get out 🍬🩸 Diabetes + HTN = the two most tested causes of CKD 🫙 Discard the FIRST 24-hr creatinine clearance — save every drop after 📉 90 · 60 · 30 · 15 The 5 CKD stages. Under 15 = ESRD.

Q1: Define acute vs. chronic renal failure in one sentence each. Show answer ACUTE = sudden, short-term loss of kidney function; reversible if stopped, but if not stopped & reversed it leads to chronic. CHRONIC = long-term damage over years & years of destruction resulting in permanent damage, ending in ESRD. Q2: A client is hypotensive and dehydrated after a GI bleed and the creatinine rises. Which category of AKI? Show answer PRERENAL — decreased tissue "PRE-fusion." Volume loss → low BP → low perfusion (MAP <65)
