Fluid & Electrolyte Basics — tonicity, osmosis & what happens to a cell NG-213 RENAL + FLUID ADHD-friendly visual edition This page is the CONCEPT, not the bag. One law of physics — water chases salt across a membrane — explains every fluid shift you will ever be tested on. Learn it on a single red blood cell and the rest of fluid & electrolytes falls into place. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 💦 Water chases salt Water moves toward the saltier side of a membrane. That's osmosis. That's the whole page.
STEP 1 · OSMOSIS One sentence, one picture — and then every fluid question is just this sentence again.

entries.h: ⭐ Osmosis = water moves through a semipermeable membrane toward the higher concentration of solute
entries.t: Solute = the stuff dissolved (sodium, glucose, protein). Solvent = the water it's dissolved in. The cell membrane lets water through freely but holds most solute where it is — so the water is the only thing that can move, and it always moves toward the salt. Tonicity is simply the answer to: compared to the inside of the cell, is the outside saltier, weaker, or the same? 🧠 “Salt sucks. Water follows.” Wherever the particles pile up, the water comes running. Say it every time you see the word tonicity.

entries.h: 💦 Osmosis in one picture — the membrane experiment
entries.t: 🧠 “The salty side wins the water.” Notice what actually happened: the concentrated side got bigger . That is exactly why hypertonic IV fluid grows the vascular space and shrinks the cell.

entries.h: 🧠 Osmosis vs the other three movements
entries.t: Process What moves Osmosis 💦 Water , toward the higher solute — no energy used Diffusion 🌫️ Solute , high ➜ low concentration — no energy used Filtration 🚿 Water + solute pushed by pressure (this is how the glomerulus works) Active transport ⚡ Solute pushed uphill using ATP (the Na⁺/K⁺ pump) 🧠 “Osmosis = wOter.” Spell it wrong on purpose: osm-O-sis moves the O in H₂ O . Everything else moves particles.

Serum osmolality 275–295 mOsm/kg — the reference band (adult) Sodium 135–145 mEq/L — the biggest driver of osmolality Estimate: 2(Na) + glucose/18 + BUN/2.8 Urine specific gravity 1.005–1.030 — concentrated urine = dry patient Osmolality ↑ = concentrated blood = dehydration . Osmolality ↓ = dilute blood = overload / water excess . 🧠 “Sodium and water are best friends who can't stand each other's absence.” Where sodium goes, water follows — so a sodium result is really a water report.

entries.h: 🧲 Two pressures that decide where water sits
entries.t: Osmotic (osmolar) pressure — the pull created by solutes , mostly sodium. This is what IV tonicity manipulates. Oncotic (colloid) pressure — the pull created by proteins , mostly albumin (3.5–5.0 g/dL) , holding water inside the vessel. Hydrostatic pressure — the push of blood against the vessel wall, driving water out into the tissue. ⭐ Low albumin (liver failure, malnutrition, nephrotic syndrome, burns) = nothing left to hold water in the vessel → it leaks into tissue = edema and third spacing . The patient can b
STEP 2 · DRAW IT EVERY TIME Put one red blood cell in each solution and watch what happens — this single picture answers most tonicity questions.

entries.h: 🔴 One red blood cell, three solutions
entries.t: 🧠 Draw this on your scratch paper before you answer. Three circles: fat, normal, spiky . Label which side has more dots. The dots tell you which way the arrows point — and the arrows give you the answer.

Perfect balance (equilibrium) of solutes both inside & outside the cell, so no fluid shifts are made . Human blood is isotonic , so very little osmosis occurs — isotonic solutions have the same osmolality as body fluids . 🔴 The cell: unchanged — the normal biconcave disc keeps its shape and its ~7–8 µm size. 🧠 “I'm so perfect — I don't move.” Equal in concentration = equilibrium = no fluid shift.

LOWer osmolarity & LOWer concentration of solutes than body fluids. They cause the movement of water into cells by osmosis , swelling the cells like a BIG fat hippo — so they must be given SLOWLY to prevent cellular edema . 🔴 The cell: swells → becomes a sphere → membrane fails → hemolysis (it bursts and spills hemoglobin). 🧠 HYPO-tonic = HIPPO-tonic. A hippo sitting in a bathtub, getting fatter. Cells swell with fluid.

HIGHer osmolarity & HIGHer concentration of solutes than body fluids. Very thick salty solutions with more solutes & less water , causing water to be moved outside the cells , making the cells skinny like a hyper person . 🔴 The cell: shrivels into a spiky ball — crenation — and stops working properly. 🧠 HYPER-tonic = HYPER person. The friend who never sits still and never eats: very skinny cells.

entries.h: ⭐ The vocabulary that shows up in the answer choices
entries.t: Word Means Which solution caused it Hemolysis 💥 The RBC swelled until it burst , releasing hemoglobin Hypotonic (e.g. sterile water, D5W after the sugar is burned) Crenation 🌵 The RBC shrivelled with a spiky border Hypertonic (e.g. 3% NS) Cellular edema 🦛 Any cell swollen with water — in the brain this is cerebral edema Hypotonic Cellular dehydration 🌵 Cells emptied of water while the vessel fills Hypertonic Equilibrium ⚖️ Equal concentration on both sides — no net movement Isotonic 🧠 “Hemolysis = Hippo exploded. C
STEP 3 · WHOLE-PATIENT VIEW Now scale the one cell up to 42 liters of human — the compartments, the brain, and the blood pressure.

entries.h: 🫗 Where the water actually lives — the three compartments
entries.t: 🧠 “⅔ in, ⅓ out — and only 3 L is blood.” That tiny 3 L plasma box is why 1 L of isotonic fluid can spike a blood pressure, and why over-filling it so quickly becomes crackles and a BP over 180 .

entries.h: 🚨 The brain is the cell that can't afford to swell
entries.t: Same physics, opposite patient. ❌ Never give hypotonic fluid to a client with a head injury, stroke, or increased ICP. ✅ Hypertonic saline is therapy for that same brain. 🧠 “A swollen brain in a hard hat.” The skull will not stretch, so the first symptom of a swelling cell is always neuro : headache first, LOC changes next.

entries.h: 🚨 Cell SWELLING — what the patient looks like
entries.t: 🤕 Headache — the first and earliest complaint 🌀 New confusion, restless, agitated — “altered level of consciousness” ⚡ Seizures & coma if it keeps going 🧂 Often paired with hyponatremia — Na <135 mEq/L 🤢 Nausea/vomiting, blurred vision, widening pulse pressure with ↑ICP ✅ Do: stop or slow the infusion, protect the airway, seizure precautions, neuro checks, notify the provider, check the sodium. 🧠 “Water on the brain talks first.” Any new neuro change during an infusion is a fluid-shift alarm until proven otherwise.

entries.h: 🚨 Cell SHRINKING — what the patient looks like
entries.t: 🥵 Thirst , dry sticky mucous membranes, furrowed tongue 🌀 Restlessness, weakness, confusion (dehydrated brain cells) 🧂 Hypernatremia — Na >145 mEq/L 💧 Low urine output, high urine specific gravity >1.030 📈 Rising serum osmolality >295 mOsm/kg , ↑hematocrit ✅ Do: slow the infusion, recheck sodium, monitor I&O and daily weight, watch the BP — hypertonic fluid can overload the vessel while the cells dry out. 🧠 “Dry cells shout for water.” Thirst plus a rising sodium is the body begging you to stop pulling water out.

entries.h: 🚨 Too much of ANY tonicity → FVO → the same dangerous ending
entries.t: 💧 Infusion too fast / too much volume ▼ 🫗 Fluid volume overload (FVO) — crackles, JVD, bounding pulse, edema, weight gain 1 kg = 1 L ▼ 🩺 MONITOR: BLOOD PRESSURE — BP over 180 systolic = HTN crisis! ▼ 🧠 Risk for CVA / stroke 🧠 “Different bag, same ending.” Isotonic over-fills the vessel, hypertonic drags more in behind it — both roads end at BP >180 and a stroke risk. Rate is a nursing decision. Own it. 🎯
STEP 4 · EXAM TRAPS Where students lose points — read these twice.

🦛 HYPOTONIC ⚖️ ISOTONIC 🏃 HYPERTONIC Compared to the cell Fewer solutes outside Equal — equilibrium More solutes outside Osmolarity <275 mOsm/L 275–295 >295 Water goes INTO the cell Nowhere OUT of the cell The cell Swells 🦛 → hemolysis Unchanged 🙂 Shrinks 🏃 → crenation Compartment filled Intracellular Extracellular / vascular Intravascular Memory trick Hippo-tonic “I'm so perfect” Hyper person Watch for Headache → ↓LOC → seizures FVO, crackles, ↑BP FVO + cellular dehydration, Na >145 Absolutely not for ↑ICP · head

Isotonic in the bag (252 mOsm/L) · hypotonic in the body . Cells burn the dextrose within minutes and leave behind free water that swells them. If the question asks “what is in the bag?” → isotonic . If it asks “what happens to the client?” → hypotonic . 🧠 “D5W = a hippo in a tuxedo.” Dressed as isotonic, behaves like hypotonic.

entries.h: ⭐ Trap #2 — the percent sign is your compass
entries.t: Below 0.9% saline → hypotonic Exactly 0.9% saline → isotonic Above 0.9% saline ( 3%, 5% ) → hypertonic Bolt D5 onto an isotonic fluid → it becomes hypertonic in the bag 🧠 “Point-nine is the line.” Under it, over it, on it — that one number sorts every saline bag you'll ever see.

entries.h: ⭐ Trap #3 — “a lot of numbers” vs “very little numbers”
entries.t: The source's own trick, and it works: hypotonic labels look busy ( 0.225 · 0.33 · 0.45 ) = a lot of fluid IN the cell . Hypertonic labels look tiny ( 3% · 5% ) = very little fluid in the cell . 🧠 “Long label, fat cell. Short label, skinny cell.” Counter-intuitive on purpose — which is exactly why it sticks.

entries.h: ⭐ Trap #4 — swelling vs shrinking, sodium version
entries.t: Hyponatremia <135 = dilute blood → water moves into cells → brain swells → seizures Hypernatremia >145 = concentrated blood → water pulled out of cells → thirst, dry, confused Both are corrected slowly — a fast fix causes its own brain injury 🧠 “Low sodium = swollen brain. High sodium = shrunken brain.” Same two pictures from the cell panel, just drawn at patient size.

entries.h: ✅ What the nurse actually does with all of this
entries.t: 1 Know the tonicity before you spike the bag — read the label, not the habit. 2 Pump + slow rate for anything that is not isotonic; never “catch up” a behind-schedule infusion by opening it up. 3 Baseline then serial assessment: neuro status, lung sounds, edema, BP, weight, I&O. 4 Trend the labs: sodium, potassium, serum osmolality, BUN/creatinine, hematocrit. 5 Stop and report early — new headache, new confusion, new crackles. Those are the first words the cell can say. 🧠 “The bag is the order. The rate is the nur

SAY IT OUT LOUD 💦 Water chases salt Osmosis = water crosses the membrane toward the higher solute. 🦛 Hypo → SWELL Cell bloats → hemolysis · brain edema · headache first. 🏃 Hyper → SHRINK Cell shrivels → crenation · thirst, Na >145 . ⚖️ Iso → NO SHIFT Equilibrium at 275–295 · stays in the vessel.

Q1: Define osmosis in one sentence. Show answer Water moves across a semipermeable membrane from the area of LOWER solute concentration toward the area of HIGHER solute concentration. Water chases salt. Q2: An RBC is placed in a hypotonic solution. Draw what happens. Show answer Water rushes IN, the cell swells from a biconcave disc into a sphere, and it can burst — hemolysis. Q3: An RBC is placed in a hypertonic solution. Draw what happens. Show answer Water is pulled OUT, the cell shrivels with a spiky border — c

entries.h: Vitamins & Electrolytes · NG-227 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🩸 Blood builders ⚡ Potassium 🧲 Mag sulfate ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Renal + Fluid · Pharmacology

Iron · Folic acid · B12 · Potassium · Magnesium sulfate NG-227 RENAL + FLUID ADHD-friendly visual edition Five replacements, three jobs. Iron, folic acid and B12 BUILD the blood 🩸 · Potassium PUMPS the heart ⚡ · Magnesium MELLOWS the muscles 🧲. Every one of them is tested the same way: what does it do, what will hurt the client, and what do you teach? 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → ⬛ Black stools = NORMAL Ferrous sulfate turns stool dark/black. Expected — NOT a GI bleed. 🚨 NEVER push potassium = DEATH
STEP 1 · WHAT THEY DO Three building blocks make a red blood cell — iron, folic acid, B12 . Miss one and the client is anemic.

entries.h: 🧱 The three building blocks of a red blood cell
entries.t: 🧠 “I Feed Blood” — I ron · F olic acid · B 12. Three ingredients, one red blood cell. Any missing ingredient = anemia.

WHAT IT DOES Treats anemia related to iron deficiency. Iron is the part of hemoglobin that actually grabs the oxygen. WATCH FOR ⬛ Dark or black stools = NORMAL & EXPECTED — NOT a GI bleed HESI Do not stop the drug and do not report it as bleeding. 🚽 Constipation — increase fiber and fluids; a stool softener may be ordered 🤢 Nausea, epigastric pain, metallic taste 😬 Liquid iron stains teeth — dilute it and drink through a straw , then rinse the mouth 💉 Iron dextran IM — Z-track technique in a large muscle, do not ma

WHAT IT DOES Treats anemia (low blood cell count) and prevents neural tube defects in pregnancy. WATCH FOR 💊 SULFA drugs decrease folic acid absorption — sulfasalazine especially. A client on sulfa drugs needs a folic acid supplement . CAUTION 🧠 Folic acid corrects the anemia of B12 deficiency but does NOT fix the neurologic damage — a classic trap 💊 Also depleted by methotrexate, phenytoin and alcohol TEACH 🤰 Start BEFORE pregnancy — the neural tube closes in the first weeks, often before a person knows they are p

WHAT IT DOES Treats pernicious anemia — the body lacks INTRINSIC FACTOR, so it cannot absorb B12. WATCH FOR 🧠 Neurologic signs are the giveaway: numbness & tingling of hands/feet, unsteady gait, memory loss, confusion 👅 Beefy red, sore, smooth tongue (glossitis) and pallor 🩺 Other causes: gastrectomy / gastric bypass , ileal resection, Crohn's, strict vegan diet, long-term metformin or PPIs TEACH 💉 Without intrinsic factor, ORAL B12 will not be absorbed — replacement is lifelong IM (or intranasal) B12, usually mont

entries.h: 🔬 Why pernicious anemia needs an injection — follow the intrinsic factor
entries.t: 🧠 “Pernicious = permanent shots.” The stomach lost the key, so the gut route is closed forever — the needle is the only door left. ⚡
STEP 2 · WATCH FOR — THE DEADLIEST REPLACEMENT Potassium PUMPS the heart. Every question about it is really a question about the infusion rules.
NORMAL 3.5 – 5.0 mEq/L CRITICAL ≤2.5 or ≥6.5 🧠 “3.5 to 5 keeps you alive.” Below 3.5 you replace it. Above 5.0 you remove it. Never both at once.

🫁 Shallow respirations — the most deadly sign 🔨 Decreased DTR, muscle cramps, flaccid paralysis , fatigue 🚽 Constipation, hypoactive bowel sounds, paralytic ileus 🫀 Flat T waves · ST depression · U waves , PVCs 💊 Increases digoxin toxicity risk Top causes: K⁺-wasting diuretics , vomiting/diarrhea, NG suction, poor intake, DKA/insulin, hyperaldosteronism. 🧠 “Low K = everything sags” — sagging T waves, sagging gut, sagging limbs. Only the U wave pops up.

🫀 PEAKED T waves → widened QRS → V-fib & cardiac arrest ; bradycardia & hypotension 💪 Tingling/paresthesia → paralysis & muscle heaviness 🚽 Diarrhea , hyperactive bowel sounds Top causes: renal failure , K⁺-sparing drugs (spironolactone, -prils , -sartans ), cell death (crush/burns/tumor lysis), acidosis, salt substitutes. Never give a potassium supplement to a client whose K⁺ is already at or above 5.0. 🧠 “Tents on the monitor = too much K⁺.” Tall, tented T waves are the visual alarm.

entries.h: 💊 Which drugs WASTE potassium and which drugs SPARE it
entries.t: K⁺ WASTING diuretics end in -ide : furosemide , hydrochlorothiazide → the client loses potassium and often needs a supplement. K⁺ SPARING drugs : S pironolactone · S artans (losartan) · P rils (lisinopril) → the client keeps potassium. No potassium supplements and no salt substitutes with these. 🧠 “-IDE = it DIES (potassium leaves) · SSP = it STAYS Put.” Two letters and two initials sort every diuretic question you will ever see.

entries.h: 🚨 POTASSIUM IV — the four rules, in order
entries.t: 1 FIRST ACTION = put the client on a HEART MONITOR. 2 NEVER IV push potassium = DEATH. Never IM, never SubQ, never undiluted. 3 ONLY 10–20 mEq/hr — on an IV pump , always diluted. 4 Client reports burning/discomfort and the line is patent → SLOW the infusion rate. “Stop the infusion” is the most commonly chosen distractor — about 48% of test takers pick it. Also: confirm urine output ≥ 30 mL/hr before giving potassium · give oral KCl with food and a full glass of water · do not crush extended-release tablets · rech

📉 HYPOkalemia — replace safely 1 Cardiac monitor + assess respirations and bowel sounds. 2 Check urine output ≥ 30 mL/hr — no pee, no K⁺. 3 Oral KCl with food + potassium-rich foods (banana, avocado, potato, spinach, orange). 4 IV KCl — diluted, pump, 10–20 mEq/hr , monitored. 5 Replace the magnesium too , or the potassium will not stay up. 📈 HYPERkalemia — stabilize, shift, remove 1 IV CALCIUM GLUCONATE — protects the heart; does not lower the level. 2 Regular INSULIN + dextrose (D50) shifts K⁺ into cells; recheck
STEP 3 · MELLOWS THE MUSCLES · TEACH & MONITOR One drug, four indications — and one set of numbers that tells you when to stop it.
NORMAL 1.3 – 2.1 mEq/L CRITICAL <1.0 or >4.0 🧠 “Small number, big drug.” Magnesium lives in the low ones — anything ≥ 3 is heading for toxicity.

1️⃣ Replace low magnesium — the source card uses below 1.5 KAPLAN 2️⃣ Treatment for TORSADES DE POINTES NCLEX TIP — the twisting ventricular rhythm 3️⃣ Preterm labor — “wild contractions.” Magnesium mellows the uterine muscle (tocolytic) 4️⃣ Anticonvulsant — preeclampsia/eclampsia : it prevents and stops seizures M = MELLOWS the muscles. Uterus, skeletal muscle, airway, heart — magnesium calms them all. 🧠 “Mag mellows the mother and the monitor.” It quiets contractions, quiets seizures and quiets Torsades.

🔨 HYPERreflexia (increased DTR), tremors, twitching, tetany , seizures 🚽 Diarrhea , hyperactive bowel sounds 🫀 TORSADES DE POINTES and V-fib, prolonged QT Causes: alcoholism, malnourishment, Crohn's & celiac (malabsorption), chronic diarrhea, diuretics, long-term PPIs. 🧠 “No mag = no brakes.” Reflexes, bowels and the heart all rev up.

🔨 Decreased/absent DTRs — the earliest warning 🫁 RESPIRATORY DEPRESSION , paralysis & weak muscles 🚽 Hypoactive bowel sounds, constipation 🫀 Heart block , bradycardia, hypotension → arrest 🥵 Flushing, warmth, lethargy, slurred speech Causes: renal failure , magnesium antacids/laxatives, and too much magnesium sulfate infusion . 🧠 “Too mellow to move, too mellow to breathe.” Reflexes go, then the respirations, then the heart.

entries.h: 🚨 WHEN DO YOU STOP THE MAGNESIUM INFUSION?
entries.t: 🚨 ANTIDOTE = IV CALCIUM GLUCONATE Keep it at the bedside for every magnesium sulfate infusion. Sequence: STOP the magnesium → give IV calcium gluconate → support airway & breathing → notify the provider. Assess every hour on a mag drip: LOC → DTRs → respiratory rate → urine output → BP & cardiac rhythm → magnesium level. 👶 Possible findings in the NEWBORN of a client who received magnesium sulfate ATI 🍼 Flaccid muscle tone (floppy, poor suck) 🫁 Respiratory depression ➕ Lethargy, hypotension, decreased reflexes — ha

📉 HYPOmagnesemia / Torsades 1 Cardiac monitor + seizure precautions. 2 Torsades de Pointes → IV MAGNESIUM SULFATE. NCLEX TIP 3 Replace magnesium — IV on a pump for severe; oral for mild (expect diarrhea). 4 Check K⁺ and Ca²⁺ — they will not correct until the Mg does. 5 Re-assess DTRs & RR while infusing — you can overshoot into toxicity. 📈 HYPERmagnesemia / mag toxicity 1 🛑 STOP the magnesium — infusion, antacids, laxatives. 2 💉 IV CALCIUM GLUCONATE — the antidote , with cardiac monitoring. 3 Airway & breathing sup

SAY IT OUT LOUD ⚡ Potassium IV 1 monitor · 2 never push · 3 10–20 mEq/hr on a pump · 4 burning → slow it . 🛑 Mag stop signs RR < 12 · DTRs decreased · urine < 30 mL/hr → STOP + calcium gluconate . 🧲 Iron rules Black stool = normal · empty stomach 1 hr before meds · vit C helps, calcium blocks . 💉 B12 = lifelong shot No intrinsic factor = no oral absorption. Sulfa drugs steal folic acid → supplement.

Drug Indication Watch for Teach Ferrous sulfate (oral) Iron dextran (IV/IM) Anemia r/t iron deficiency Black stools = expected , constipation, GI upset; Z-track & anaphylaxis risk with IM iron Empty stomach 1 hr before meds · vitamin C / OJ boosts · calcium blocks · straw for liquid · “fresh fruits & whole grain bread” Folic acid Anemia · prevents neural tube defects Sulfa drugs (sulfasalazine) block absorption ; masks B12 anemia without fixing the neuro damage Start before pregnancy · leafy greens & fortified grai

Q1: A client taking ferrous sulfate reports black stools. What do you do? Show answer Nothing — reassure them. Dark or black stools are normal and expected with iron and are NOT a GI bleed. Q2: What increases iron absorption and what blocks it? Show answer Vitamin C / orange juice increases it. Calcium, dairy, antacids, coffee and tea block it. Take iron on an empty stomach 1 hour before other medications. Q3: Which statement shows iron teaching was effective? Show answer "I will eat more fresh fruits and whole gra

entries.h: Bladder Cancer & Cystoscopy · NG-239 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🚭 Cause 🔎 Clues 🧰 Before 🔦 During ✅ After ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Renal + Fluid · Med-Surg Course

& Cystoscopy — the scope that looks inside the bladder NG-239 Renal ADHD-friendly visual edition Two facts carry this whole page. The most common finding of bladder cancer is PAINLESS HEMATURIA — blood with no burning, no pain, no warning. And cystoscopy is a scope inserted through the urethra to view the bladder — the exam tests what you teach before it and what you report after it. 🔦 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🩸 PAINLESS hematuria THE most tested sign of bladder cancer. No pain ≠ no problem. 🚬 T
STEP 1 · WHAT STARTS IT Whatever the body filters out ends up sitting in the bladder — and the bladder lining soaks in it.

entries.h: 🚬 The three causes from the source — and why they work
entries.t: 🚬 Tobacco use the #1 risk factor 🧪 Chemical exposure dyes · rubber · paint 👪 Family history genetics Mechanism — say it in one sentence: carcinogens are filtered out of the blood into the urine, then SIT in the bladder and bathe the lining. The longer the urine sits, the longer the contact. 🧠 “The bladder is a holding tank.” 🪣 Anything the kidney throws away parks there. Smoke → blood → kidney → tank. That's why tobacco — an inhaled poison — causes a urinary cancer.

🚬 Tobacco use — smoking is the biggest single risk factor 🏭 Occupational chemicals — aromatic amines and dyes: painters, hairdressers, and rubber, leather, textile & chemical workers 👪 Family history 👴 Age over ~55 ; more common in men 🔁 Chronic bladder irritation — recurrent UTIs, long-term indwelling catheters, stones 💊 Prior pelvic radiation or certain chemo agents (e.g. cyclophosphamide) 🧠 "Smoke, stain, and strain." Smoke = tobacco · Stain = dyes/chemicals · Strain = chronic irritation.

entries.h: 🧱 Where the tumor sits — the bladder wall in layers
entries.t: 🧠 How deep = how big the surgery. Surface tumor = scope & scrape. Into the muscle = the bladder may have to come out. 🔎
STEP 2 · THE ONE SIGN If you remember nothing else on this page, remember two words: painless hematuria.

entries.h: 🩸 PAINLESS HEMATURIA — the most common finding MOST TESTED
entries.t: Answer first: asked “What is the most common finding of bladder cancer?” → painless hematuria. The blood may be bright red, tea-colored, or only visible on the dipstick, and it often comes and goes — which is exactly why people ignore it. 🧠 “No pain, still a problem.” Everyone assumes blood + no pain = "it's nothing." That assumption is exactly what the question is testing. Painless = look inside.

Cystoscopy = a scope inserted through the urethra to view the bladder. It's the definitive test because the provider can see the tumor AND biopsy it in the same visit . Urine cytology — looks for cancer cells in the urine CT urogram / ultrasound — staging & upper tract Biopsy / TURBT — the tissue diagnosis 🧠 “Cysto = bladder, scopy = look.” Same root as cystitis (bladder inflammation).

entries.h: 🩸 Three causes of hematuria — tell them apart
entries.t: Bladder cancer 🎗️ UTI / cystitis 🦠 Kidney stone 🪨 Pain? NONE — painless Burning, dysuria, suprapubic ache Severe flank pain in waves → groin Fever? No Often, especially if it reaches the kidney Only if infected — that's an emergency Pattern Comes & goes; may be gross or microscopic With the infection; clears with antibiotics With the stone; clears when it passes Other clues Tobacco/chemical history; later frequency & urgency Urgency, cloudy foul urine, WBCs & nitrites Restless, writhing, vomiting; crystals on UA Ne

❌ "Painful hematuria" → that's a UTI or a stone , not cancer. ❌ "Hematuria only with exercise" → not the classic sign. ❌ "Wait and see if it clears" → never . Gross hematuria in an adult gets worked up. ✅ "Painless hematuria" → the answer, every time. 🧠 Cover the word painless with your thumb and the question falls apart. That one word IS the answer. 🧰
STEP 3 · PREP & TEACH Consent, an empty bladder, and one exact sentence the exam wants you to say.

entries.h: 💬 Cystoscopy teaching: “You will feel PRESSURE during insertion of the scope.” HESI
entries.t: Not "you won't feel anything" (false reassurance) and not "it will be very painful" (fear). Pressure is honest and accurate — and it's the option to pick. 1 📝 Verify informed consent is signed and on the chart. 2 🍽️ NPO status per order — usually only if general or spinal anesthesia is planned. A simple office cystoscopy is often done with local anesthetic gel and no NPO. 3 🚽 Have the client empty the bladder right before the procedure (unless a urine specimen is being collected then). 4 🧪 Check labs & meds — coagu

entries.h: 🚻 Why the urethra matters — male vs female
entries.t: 🧠 Long road, more pressure. That's why the male client feels more of the "pressure" you warned him about — and why retention after the procedure is watched more closely.

Vital signs — especially temperature , so you can tell a new fever from a baseline one Last void & usual voiding pattern Allergies (including latex & anesthetics) Current urine appearance — so post-procedure change is obvious Anticoagulant & antiplatelet use 🧠 You can't call it "new" if you never wrote down the old.

"Will I be asleep?" → depends on the type; many are done awake with local gel . "How long?" → the look itself is brief ; longer if a biopsy or tumor resection is done. "Will it hurt to pee after?" → burning and pink urine for a day or two are expected . "Can I drive home?" → not if sedated — arrange a ride. 🧠 Prepared clients report symptoms sooner. Teaching before is what makes the "call us if…" list stick. 🔦
STEP 4 · WHAT ACTUALLY HAPPENS Sterile, through the natural opening, bladder filled with fluid so the walls can be seen.

entries.h: 🔦 A scope inserted through the urethra to view the bladder
entries.t: 🧠 Picture a flashlight going up a garden hose into a water balloon. 🔦 The balloon has to be filled to see its walls — that's why the client feels pressure and a strong urge to void .

entries.h: 🔪 TURBT — when the scope also treats
entries.t: Transurethral resection of bladder tumor. Same route as a cystoscopy, but the tumor is shaved off the bladder wall and sent to pathology. It both stages and treats non-muscle-invasive disease. Expect a catheter afterward, sometimes with continuous bladder irrigation (CBI) More bleeding than a plain look — watch for clots 🧠 Look = cystoscopy. Look + shave = TURBT.

entries.h: 💉 Intravesical BCG — chemo/immunotherapy INTO the bladder
entries.t: For non-muscle-invasive tumors, medication is instilled through a catheter into the bladder rather than given IV. ⏳ The client holds it in the bladder for the ordered dwell (commonly about 2 hours ) and changes position so it touches all the walls 🚽 Sit to void afterward to avoid splashing 🧴 Disinfect the toilet after each void per protocol (bleach, commonly for the first 6 hours ) 💧 Limit fluids before the instillation, then increase fluids after the dwell 🧠 “Hold it, roll it, then bleach it.” The drug has to bath

entries.h: 🩹 If the bladder must come out — cystectomy & urinary diversion
entries.t: For muscle-invasive disease, the bladder may be removed and the ureters diverted — most commonly an ileal conduit draining to a stoma and an external pouch. 🧠 Beefy red = alive. Dusky purple = dying. And mucus is expected — you routed urine through a piece of intestine, and intestine makes mucus. ✅
STEP 5 · THE TESTED LIST "The nurse teaches the client to report which findings after a cystoscopy?" — know this list cold.

entries.h: 🚨 AFTER PROCEDURE — NOTIFY HCP COMMON NCLEX QUESTION
entries.t: 🧠 “CLOT · CAN'T · °C · CRAMP.” Four C's to call about: C lots & bright red blood · C an't urinate ( >100 mL retained) · temperature over 38 °C / 100.4 °F · C ramping pain that analgesics won't touch.

entries.h: ⭐ The priority question — frequency, urgency & dysuria after cystoscopy KAPLAN
entries.t: Scenario: a client has frequency, urgency and dysuria after cystoscopy . Those are all expected — so what is the highest nursing priority ? ✅ OBTAIN VITAL SIGNS — monitor for FEVER ▼ Because those same symptoms are also the early signs of a UTI — and the scope just entered a sterile space. ▼ A temperature over 100.4°F (38°C) turns "expected" into "report." Then: push fluids, offer a warm sitz bath, give the ordered analgesic, and document the urine's appearance. 🧠 Assess before you comfort. The symptoms are expecte

1 💧 Increase fluids — dilutes the urine, eases the burning, flushes out small clots (unless fluids are restricted). 2 🛁 Warm sitz bath or moist heat to the lower abdomen for spasms. 3 💊 Mild analgesics as ordered ; antispasmodics if prescribed. Note that some bladder analgesics turn the urine orange — expected, not bleeding. 4 📏 Measure output & check for retention — bladder scan if the client can't void; report retained volume over 100 mL per protocol. 5 🚫 Activity limits — avoid heavy lifting, strenuous exercise

Answer first: urine left in the bladder after voiding is post-void residual . A residual of more than about 100 mL signals retention — from swelling, clots or spasm after the scope. Retention ➜ pressure back up the ureters and a perfect medium for infection Assess with a bladder scan — noninvasive, do it before you catheterize Report per protocol; expect an order for catheterization if the client can't void 🧠 Full bladder, empty answer. If they "can't go," scan first — don't just keep waiting.

🚭 Smoking cessation — the single biggest thing the client can change 💧 Fluids & frequent voiding — less carcinogen contact time 🔁 Surveillance — repeat cystoscopies on schedule; recurrence is common 🩸 Any new painless hematuria gets reported , forever 💬 Body-image & sexuality support after cystectomy/urostomy; refer to ostomy resources 🧠 The sign that found it is the sign that finds it again. Painless blood — call, every single time. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🩸 Painless hematuria Most common finding of bladder cancer — the answer. 🚬 Tobacco · 🧪 chemicals · 👪 family Carcinogens filter into urine and soak the bladder lining. 💬 “You'll feel PRESSURE” The cystoscopy teaching line. Not "no pain," not "severe pain." 🌡️ Priority = VITAL SIGNS Frequency/urgency/dysuria after cystoscopy ➜ check for fever first . 🚨 Report after cystoscopy Clots & bright red blood · can't urinate ( >100 mL ) · temp >100.4°F (38°C) · pain analgesics won't relieve. ✅ Expected after P

Q1: What is the most common finding of bladder cancer? Show answer Painless hematuria. Blood in the urine with no burning, no fever and no flank pain — and it often comes and goes. Q2: Name the three causes the source highlights. Show answer Tobacco use, chemical exposure and family history. Carcinogens are filtered into the urine and sit in the bladder, bathing the lining. Q3: What exactly is a cystoscopy, and what do you teach beforehand? Show answer A scope inserted through the urethra to view the bladder. Teach

entries.h: BPH II · NG-240 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🧨 Cause 🔎 Clues & labs 🩺 Care 🔪 TURP & CBI ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Renal + Fluid · Med-Surg II

Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia · PSA · TURP & continuous bladder irrigation NG-240 Renal + Fluid ADHD-friendly visual edition Part 2 is the surgical half. A prostate that keeps growing eventually stops responding to pills — then it's TURP 🔪, a 3-way Foley 🚿, and a set of rules about urine color and irrigation that the NCLEX asks over and over: output must always be MORE than input. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🌰 BPH = benign Too many normal cells — not cancer — squeezing the urethra. 🧪 PSA before DRE
STEP 1 · THE GLAND THAT GREW Age plus hormones make a walnut into a lemon — and the urethra is running straight through the middle of it.

entries.h: 🌰 Where the prostate sits — and why size matters so much
entries.t: The prostate is a walnut-sized gland that sits directly below the bladder and completely encircles the urethra . Its normal job is making fluid for semen. Starting around age 40–50 , hormone changes (mainly DHT ) make the cells multiply — hyperplasia . Because the gland is a ring around the pipe, growth goes INWARD and closes the pipe. That single fact explains every symptom, every drug and every surgery on this page. 🧠 “Walnut 🌰 → lemon 🍋 → grapefruit 🍊.” The gland grows through fruit sizes while the hole in the m

entries.h: ⭐ Who gets it — the risk picture
entries.t: 👴 Age is the risk factor — starts around 40–50 ; roughly half of men by 60 and most men by their 80s have some BPH 🧬 Hormonal shift: aging changes the testosterone-to- DHT balance 👪 Family history · obesity · sedentary life · diabetes 🚫 BPH does NOT cause prostate cancer — but a man can have both, so screening still matters 🧠 Benign ≠ harmless. “Benign” only means not cancer . This benign gland can still shut down a kidney.

entries.h: ⚠️ What makes BPH suddenly become an emergency
entries.t: 💊 Anticholinergics & antihistamines — stop the squeeze 🫗 Decongestants (pseudoephedrine) — tighten the bladder neck 🍺 Alcohol binge · large fluid load at once 🥶 Cold weather · immobility · surgery & anesthesia 💩 Constipation / fecal impaction pressing on the urethra ⏳ Holding urine too long Acute urinary retention is a urologic emergency — it needs immediate catheterization. 🧠 “Cold pill + cold night + held it too long.” That sentence is the classic ED admission for acute retention in a man with BPH. 🔎
STEP 2 · FIND IT Two symptom families, one finger exam, and one lab everybody mis-times.

⏳ Hesitancy — can't get started 💨 Weak, intermittent stream · straining 💧 Post-void dribbling 🫗 Feeling of incomplete emptying 🚨 Complete inability to void = acute retention 🧠 Obstructive = the pipe. Everything in this list is about how the urine leaves .

🌙 Nocturia — up multiple times a night; usually the reason they finally come in 🔔 Urgency · frequency 💧 Small voided volumes · overflow incontinence 🔥 Dysuria if a UTI has set in 🧠 Irritative = the tank. The overworked, thickened bladder is twitchy — it complains constantly even though little comes out.

entries.h: 👆 The DRE — digital rectal exam tells BPH from cancer
entries.t: Smooth & rubbery = benign. Hard & nodular = report it. 🧠 “Rubber ball = benign 🎾. Rock = report 🪨.” Two textures, two totaly different conversations with the provider.

PSA is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. It is prostate specific, not cancer specific — BPH itself raises it. 💊 Finasteride lowers PSA by roughly half — the provider mentally doubles the result while the client is on it. 🧠 “Blood before finger.” P SA comes before the P oke. If a question has the nurse doing a DRE and then drawing the PSA, that's the error.

📟 Bladder scan / PVR — how much is left behind 🧪 Urinalysis & culture — rule out UTI/hematuria 🧪 BUN & creatinine — is the obstruction hurting the kidneys? 📊 IPSS / AUA symptom score — grades severity and tracks response 💨 Uroflowmetry — measures stream strength 📷 TRUS (transrectal ultrasound) + biopsy if cancer is suspected 🔭 Cystoscopy — direct look at the urethra & bladder 🧠 Scan · dip · draw · score. Four cheap tests before anybody talks about surgery. 🩺
STEP 3 · PILLS BEFORE SCALPELS Watchful waiting, then relax it, then shrink it — surgery is what happens when all of that fails.

entries.h: 💊 Alpha blockers vs 5-alpha reductase inhibitors — the exam's favorite comparison
entries.t: 🚪 ALPHA-1 BLOCKERS 🌰 5-ALPHA REDUCTASE INHIBITORS Drugs Terazosin · Tamsulosin · doxazosin · alfuzosin ( -osin ) Finasteride · dutasteride ( -steride ) What it does RELAXES smooth muscle in the bladder neck & prostate SHRINKS the gland by blocking testosterone → DHT Gland size Unchanged Actually smaller Onset Days ⚡ 3–6 months 🐢 Signature side effect Orthostatic hypotension , dizziness, retrograde ejaculation ↓ libido, ED, gynecomastia Lab effect None on PSA Lowers PSA ~50% Big teaching First dose at bedtime ; chan

💧 Fluids 2–3 L/day , but limit in the evening for nocturia ☕ Cut caffeine & alcohol — bladder irritants and diuretics ⏰ Timed voiding q 2–3 hr · double voiding 🚫 Avoid anticholinergics, antihistamines, decongestants 🚶 Exercise; treat constipation 👀 Watchful waiting is legitimate care for mild symptoms 🧠 Front-load the fluids. Same total volume, drunk earlier in the day = same hydration, far less nocturia.

entries.h: 🔪 When do the pills stop being enough?
entries.t: 🚨 Recurrent acute urinary retention 🦠 Recurrent UTIs · 🪨 bladder stones 🩸 Persistent gross hematuria from the prostate 🧪 Rising creatinine / hydronephrosis 😩 Symptoms intolerable despite maximum medical therapy 📗 HESI: “BPH refractory to treatment with other medications?” ✅ Anticipate a TURP. 🧠 “Refractory = resect.” The word refractory in a BPH stem is the exam telling you surgery is next. 🔪
STEP 4 · THE SURGICAL HALF Two surgeries, one catheter with three lumens, and a short list of things you must never do.

entries.h: 🔪 TURP vs prostatectomy — through the pipe or through the belly
entries.t: After EITHER procedure a 3-way Foley catheter is used for continuous bladder irrigation (CBI). It does two jobs: puts pressure on bleeding tissue and allows urine drainage without clots plugging the catheter. 🧠 “TURP goes THROUGH, prostatectomy CUTS.” T = T hrough the urethra, no scar. Prostate ectomy = -ectomy means cut it out.
🧠 “More out than in, or something's plugged in.” Every CBI question reduces to that rhyme. And the irrigant is not urine — subtract it before you chart output.

entries.h: 🩸 Urine color timeline — the numbers to memorize
entries.t: 📘 Kaplan: “24 hours after TURP the nurse notices bright red urine. First action?” ✅ Contact the health care provider immediately — bright red is arterial-looking bleeding, not the expected pink. 📗 HESI: “ 5 days after prostatectomy the client reports small blood clots. First action?” ✅ Advise the client to follow up with the HCP immediately — clots days later are not expected. 🧠 “Red → rosé → clear.” Like wine getting weaker: 0 hr red 🍷 · 24 hr rosé 🌸 · then clear 💧 . Going backwards in that sequence is always a ca

entries.h: 🚨 SEVERE PAIN during continuous bladder irrigation — the classic question
entries.t: “A client reports SEVERE PAIN with continuous bladder irrigation after a TURP. First nursing action?” 1 🔎 ASSESS the amount & character of urine output — light pink color = BEST ▼ 2 🧮 Compare output to input — output must be MORE than input, not “equal to” or “less than” ▼ 3 🔗 Check the tubing for kinks, clots and dependent loops; check the bladder for distention ▼ 4 🚿 Obstructed? Manually irrigate per order / increase the CBI rate as ordered, then notify the HCP Why pain matters: severe pain usually means the cath

entries.h: ❌ The NEVER list after prostate surgery
entries.t: ❌ Never let output be less than (or equal to) input — that is an obstruction until proven otherwise. ❌ Never chart the irrigant as urine output — subtract it first, or you will report a wildly false output. ❌ Never stop the irrigation because the urine looks bloody — bleeding needs MORE flow (per order), not less, or clots will form. ❌ Never take a rectal temperature, give an enema, or insert a rectal suppository — the prostate bed sits right against the rectum and can be made to bleed. ❌ Never release or adjust ca

entries.h: ✅ Post-op teaching — what they go home knowing
entries.t: 💧 Fluid intake 2–3 L/day — flushes the bladder and prevents clots (HESI answer) 🦠 Observe for signs of UTI — fever, chills, burning, cloudy foul urine (HESI answer) 💪 Kegel exercises for control after the catheter is removed 💩 Stool softeners; high-fiber diet; no straining 🚫 No heavy lifting, driving or sexual activity until cleared (often 4–6 weeks ) ☕ Avoid alcohol & caffeine early — they irritate the bladder 📞 Report bright red bleeding, clots, fever, or inability to void 🧠 “Drink, don't strain, watch for burn.”

entries.h: ⭐ Two things that are EXPECTED — don't panic
entries.t: 📘 Kaplan: “Third day post-op TURP, the catheter is removed and the client has uncontrolled dribbling after urinating.” ✅ Temporary incontinence is EXPECTED following urinary catheter removal — reassure and teach Kegels. Retrograde ejaculation is also common after TURP: semen goes backward into the bladder, so the urine looks cloudy after sex. It is harmless but affects fertility — tell them before discharge . 🧠 Expected vs emergency. Dribbling and cloudy urine after sex = expected. Bright red urine and no output =

entries.h: 🚨 TUR syndrome — the classic complication to recognize
entries.t: If a large volume of hypotonic irrigating fluid is absorbed through the open prostate vessels, the client becomes fluid-overloaded and dilutionally hyponatremic . Modern practice uses isotonic saline with bipolar equipment, which has made this much less common — but it is still classic test content. 🧠 Neuro first Confusion, restlessness, agitation, headache, visual changes , seizures 💓 Vitals Bradycardia + hypertension , nausea/vomiting, respiratory distress from overload 🧪 Serum sodium — normal adult 135–145 mEq/L

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🌰 Ring around the pipe Prostate grows inward → obstruction → residual → AKI 👆 Smooth = benign Hard & nodular = report. Draw PSA before DRE . 🚿 Output > input Always. Subtract irrigant to chart true urine output. 🩸 Red → pink → clear 0 hr bloody · 24 hr light pink · 36 hr small clots max 😖 Pain on CBI = assess output & patency FIRST — it's a clot, not just pain ❌ Nothing rectal No rectal temps, enemas or suppositories after prostate surgery 💧 2–3 L /day + watch for UTI = the discharge SATA answers 💧

Q1: BPH refractory to medication — what do you anticipate? Show answer A TURP — transurethral resection of the prostate. Q2: What is the expected assessment finding immediately after a TURP? Show answer Bloody urinary drainage. It should lighten to light red/pink by about 24 hours. Q3: 24 hours after TURP the urine is bright red. First action? Show answer Contact the health care provider immediately. Q4: Severe pain during continuous bladder irrigation — first nursing action? Show answer Assess the amount and color

entries.h: Glomerulonephritis vs. Nephrosis · NG-246 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🦠 Side A · Glomerulonephritis 🥩 Side B · Nephrosis ⚖️ Tell them apart ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Renal + Fluid · Compare & contrast

Two ways the glomerulus breaks — one leaks BLOOD, one leaks PROTEIN NG-246 RENAL + FLUID ADHD-friendly visual edition Both are inflammation & scarring of the glomerulus , and both can end in renal failure . The deciding clue is what is leaking out: Glomerulonephritis leaks BLOOD after a strep infection 🦠 · Nephrosis leaks MASSIVE PROTEIN from an autoimmune attack 🥩. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🦠 GN = after STREP Inflammation + scarring → blood in urine, high BP . Deadly: renal failure & HTN crisis.
THE STREP ONE An infection somewhere else sends the immune system to attack the kidney by mistake — and the filter starts bleeding.

Glomerulo = the glomerulus · nephr = kidney · itis = inflammation . So: inflammation & scarring of the kidney's filter. KEY ASSESSMENT Ask about a recent strep infection. The client will often say “I had a sore throat a couple of weeks ago but it went away.” That sentence is the diagnosis. 🧠 “The strep leaves, the antibodies stay.” The bug is gone — the immune complexes it left behind are what clog the filter. That's why the client feels fine, then suddenly doesn't.

entries.h: 🔬 What is happening inside the glomerulus
entries.t: 🧠 “Nephr-ITIS = the filter is on FIRE.” A burnt screen has holes in it — big enough for red cells to squeeze through, but the screen is still mostly there, so only some protein escapes.

🤕 Headache & mental status changes — the brain sign of a hypertensive crisis. 🤢 Nausea & vomiting 💧 Oliguria — no or low urine output (<30 mL/hr / <400 mL/day) ⚖️ New, sudden, rapid weight gain 🥩 Increased protein in the urine NCLEX TIP 🌡️ Fever + a recent strep infection Also expect: periorbital/facial edema (worst in the morning), tea- or cola-colored urine , and hypertension . 🧠 “HONeW” — H eadache & mental changes · O liguria · N ausea/vomiting · W eight gain. Say it like “ho-new” — everything on this list is N

Lab In glomerulonephritis WBC (blood) HIGH — there was an infection UA protein Raised, but LOWER than nephrotic UA blood / RBC casts PRESENT — the signature finding ASO titer Elevated = proof of recent strep BUN & creatinine Rising — the filter is failing Blood pressure HIGH 🚨 🧠 ASO = “A Strep Occurred.” The titer is the receipt for an infection the client already got over.

entries.h: 🚨 DEADLY COMPLICATION: Renal failure & hypertensive crisis
entries.t: 🔥 Glomeruli inflamed & scarred ▼ 💧 Can't filter → oliguria → fluid stays in ▼ ⚖️ Sudden weight gain + edema + rising BUN/creatinine ▼ 🩸 HYPERTENSIVE CRISIS → headache, vision changes, altered mental status, seizure Never chart a new headache with confusion in a glomerulonephritis client and move on — that is the crisis announcing itself. Take a BP and call the provider. 🧠 Water can't leave → pressure can't drop. Every symptom of GN is one sentence: the fluid has nowhere to go. 🥩
THE PROTEIN ONE Nephrotic syndrome = N asty protein loss. Same inflammation and scarring — but the holes are so big that albumin pours out.

entries.h: ⭐ The key difference: HIGH, massive amounts of protein dumped into the urine
entries.t: 🧠 “Nephrotic = Nasty protein loss.” Albumin is the sponge in the bloodstream. Lose the sponge and the water walks out into the tissues — that's why nephrotic edema is everywhere , not just the face.

entries.h: 🧨 CAUSE: autoimmune — the body attacks itself
entries.t: Classically LUPUS (systemic lupus erythematosus) and other autoimmune disease, where the immune system attacks its own glomerulus. Also: diabetes, long-standing hypertension, and some infections and drugs can damage the glomerulus the same way. 🧠 Lupus = “the wolf that bites its own kidney.” No outside germ to blame — the attack is coming from inside the house.

entries.h: 🧠 TRIGGERS: the 4 S's that set off an immune response
entries.t: 😖 STRESS emotional or physical 🦠 SICKNESS or sepsis / infection 🚬 SMOKING ☀️ SUN and hot temperatures Teach it: avoid the sun and wear sunscreen, stop smoking, manage stress, and report any infection early — a flare is what damages the kidney further. 🧠 “Stress · Sick · Smoke · Sun” — four S's, one flare. Picture a lupus butterfly rash lighting up on a hot sunny day.

entries.h: 🧪 Labs that name it — and why edema follows
entries.t: Also expect: hyperlipidemia (the liver over-produces when albumin drops), clotting risk (anticlotting proteins are lost in the urine too — watch for DVT), and infection risk (immunoglobulins are lost as well). 🧠 “Low albumin, high everything else.” Protein down in the blood, protein up in the urine, cholesterol up, clots up, infections up. One leak, five problems. ⚖️
THE DECIDING CLUE If you only remember one line: GN bleeds after strep · Nephrosis dumps protein from autoimmune.

entries.h: 👀 The 3-second visual: look at the cup, look at the swelling
entries.t: 🧠 Brown cup vs bubble cup. Hold the two specimens up side by side: iced tea = glomerulonephritis, beer foam = nephrotic. That single picture answers most compare questions.

entries.h: ⚖️ Side-by-side — every line that separates them
entries.t: Feature 🦠 GLOMERULONEPHRITIS 🥩 NEPHROSIS (nephrotic) Cause INFECTION — typically strep, usually gone in 14 days AUTOIMMUNE — lupus; triggered by the 4 S's What leaks BLOOD 🩸 + some protein MASSIVE PROTEIN 🥩 Protein loss LESS — lower proteinuria on UA MORE — high proteinuria on UA Urine looks like Tea / cola colored, RBC casts Frothy, foamy Key blood lab WBC HIGH , ASO titer elevated ALBUMIN LOW — hypoalbuminemia Edema Periorbital / facial, moderate Generalized — anasarca, ascites Blood pressure HIGH 🚨 — HTN crisis

entries.h: 💊 TREATMENT A — Glomerulonephritis: kill the cause, drop the pressure
entries.t: 1 🎯 Treat the cause & remove the trigger — the cause here is INFECTION 2 💊 Educate: finish ALL the antibiotics — even after they feel better 3 🥩 LIMIT protein NCLEX TIP — less protein in = less waste for a broken filter 4 🧂 Restrict sodium & fluid , strict I&O, daily weights 5 🩸 Antihypertensives — the ABCD 🧠 “ABCD drops the BP; the D drops the K⁺ too.” Both of these -ide diuretics waste potassium (careful — not every drug ending in -ide does; the K⁺-sparing amiloride is the exception) — so a client on furosemide o

entries.h: 💊 TREATMENT B — Nephrosis: calm the immune system
entries.t: 1 💊 STEROIDS — “-sone”: PREDNISONE — shuts down the autoimmune attack on the glomerulus 2 🎯 Remove the trigger — the 4 S's : stress, sickness, smoking, sun 3 🧂 LOW SODIUM diet + fluid limits to control the massive edema 4 ⚖️ Daily weight & abdominal girth — the fastest way to track anasarca (1 kg = 1 L) 5 🩸 ACE inhibitors / ARBs are also used here — they reduce how much protein spills out ⚠️ Steroid teaching: take with food, never stop a steroid abruptly (taper), expect higher blood glucose , watch for masked infec

⚖️ Daily weight , same time/scale/clothes — best fluid measure. 💧 Strict I&O ; report output <30 mL/hr . 🩸 Blood pressure every shift; report new headache or confusion. 👀 Assess periorbital edema first thing in the morning. 🦠 Protect from infection — both are immune-compromised states. 🧪 Track BUN, creatinine, albumin, potassium and the UA. 🧠 Scale, cuff, cup. Weight, blood pressure, urine output — three assessments catch almost every deterioration in either disease.

❌ “Give more protein — they're losing it!” In glomerulonephritis you LIMIT protein , because the broken filter cannot clear the waste it makes. ❌ “Antibiotics fix nephrotic syndrome.” No — that's the autoimmune one. Steroids. ❌ “The strep infection is still there.” Usually it is already gone — that's why the client feels blindsided. ❌ Ignoring a leg that is swollen on one side in nephrotic syndrome — think DVT , they lose clotting inhibitors in the urine. 🧠 Losing protein does NOT mean eating protein. That single r

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🦠 GN = strep → 2 weeks later blood in urine · high BP · limit protein 🥩 Nephrotic = Nasty protein loss low albumin · full-body edema · steroids 🩸 ABCD for BP ACE/ARB · Beta · CCB · Diuretic “-ide” (K⁺ wasters) 🚨 Report headache + confusion · oliguria · sudden weight gain

Q1: A client had strep throat 2 weeks ago and now has cola-colored urine and a BP of 178/104. Which disease? Show answer Glomerulonephritis. Post-strep, blood in the urine, hypertension — and the infection itself is usually already gone. Q2: What is the one key difference in nephrotic syndrome? Show answer HIGH, massive amounts of protein dumped into the urine — far more than glomerulonephritis. Blood albumin falls (hypoalbuminemia). Q3: Name the 4 S triggers of an autoimmune flare. Show answer Stress · Sickness or

The machine version of the kidney · AV fistula care · DDS NG-248 Renal ADHD-friendly visual edition Hemodialysis is a machine version of the kidney. Blood leaves the body, runs past a filter, and comes back clean — it removes waste, excess fluid & electrolytes the failed kidney can no longer clear. Almost every test question is about the access arm 🖐️ or pulling fluid off too fast 🧠. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🧼 “DIAL” = the soap Any word with DIAL — think Dial soap . It cleans the blood . 🖐️ Thri
STEP 1 · THE CIRCUIT Blood out, through a filter, back in — and the whole thing runs through one precious arm.

entries.h: 🩸 The hemodialysis circuit — follow one drop of blood
entries.t: Blood out ➜ pump ➜ dialyzer ➜ air trap ➜ blood back. The dialyzer is the artificial kidney. It does not "make urine" — it lets waste diffuse out of the blood into a fluid called dialysate running the other direction. Dirty blood out Clean blood back Dialysate Waste removed 🧠 “DIAL the soap.” Any time you see the word DIAL — dialysis, dialyzer, dialysate — picture a bar of Dial soap scrubbing the blood clean . Soap in, dirt out.

Diffusion — solutes move from high to low : urea, creatinine, K⁺ leave the blood. Ultrafiltration — pressure pulls water off. That's how fluid comes off. 🧠 Diffusion cleans, ultrafiltration dries. One takes the trash , the other takes the water .

entries.h: 🚪 Three ways in — pick the right access
entries.t: Access What it is Ready to use AV fistula ⭐ best / longest life Surgeon sews the client's own artery to vein Needs weeks to mature — commonly 6 wk–4 mo (varies) AV graft Synthetic tube bridges artery → vein Sooner than a fistula, but clots & infects more Central venous catheter Large tunneled/temporary line in a central vein Immediate — but highest infection risk ; short-term 🧠 “Fistula First.” Own vessels > plastic graft > catheter. The catheter is the fastest and the most dangerous .

entries.h: 🖐️ The AV fistula — feel the THRILL, hear the BRUIT
entries.t: No thrill + no bruit = the fistula has clotted. That is not "wait and see" — report it immediately. 🧠 “Thrill you Touch, Bruit you Blisten.” (Say it wrong on purpose — B ruit = listen with the B ell.) T hrill = T ouch. Teach her to check it several times a day at home.

🎾 Squeeze or grip a “rubber ball” or sponge — exercise enlarges the vein. 💧 Keep the arm warm , keep the client hydrated and not hypotensive — low BP clots a new fistula. 👀 Look at the site daily for redness, warmth, drainage. 🧠 Ball in the hand, blood in the vein. Squeezing is the fistula's workout. 🩺
STEP 2 · SET THE BASELINE Weight, vitals, fistula, and the meds you must NOT give — this is where the exam lives.

1 ⚖️ Weigh the client — current AND previous weight. Weight is the #1 measure of fluid status. 1 kg = 1 L of fluid. 2 🌡️ Full vital signs — especially BP (baseline for the hypotension that follows) and temp (infection screen). 3 🖐️ Assess the fistula — FEEL a thrill , HEAR a bruit , inspect for infection & bleeding. 4 💧 Assess fluid status — lungs, edema, JVD, breath sounds, I&O. 5 💊 HOLD the meds that will be washed out or drop the BP. 🧠 “W-V-F-F-M” → W eigh · V itals · F istula · F luid · M eds. Say it as “We Ver

entries.h: 💊 HOLD antihypertensives — dialysis already drops the BP
entries.t: Dialysis pulls volume off. Give a BP pill on top of that and you get hypotension during the run — the most common complication of hemodialysis. 🧠 “A-B-C-D-D” — A CE/ARB · B eta blocker · C alcium channel blocker · D iuretic · D ilator. Five letters, five held bottles.

entries.h: 🧪 “Washed out” meds — the dialyzer eats them NCLEX TIP
entries.t: Small, water-soluble molecules cross the membrane and get thrown away with the dialysate. Giving them before the run wastes the dose — give them AFTER dialysis. Washed out Examples Antibiotics 💉 Penicillins , cephalosporins Digoxin ❤️ Narrow therapeutic range — and a low K⁺ after dialysis makes dig toxicity worse Water-soluble vitamins 🍊 B vitamins, C , folic acid — replaced daily in dialysis clients 🧠 “A-D-V goes down the drain” — A ntibiotics · D igoxin · V itamins (water-soluble). Picture them swirling down the

entries.h: 🧪 Labs that drive the treatment STANDARD ADULT RANGES
entries.t: Lab Normal In renal failure BUN 10–20 mg/dL 📈 HIGH Creatinine 0.6–1.2 mg/dL 📈 HIGH (best kidney marker) Potassium 3.5–5.0 mEq/L 📈 HIGH ⚠️ peaked T waves Phosphorus 3.0–4.5 mg/dL 📈 HIGH Calcium 8.6–10.2 mg/dL 📉 LOW (mirror of phosphorus) Hgb / Hct 12–18 g/dL 📉 LOW (no erythropoietin) 🧠 Phosphorus and calcium are on a see-saw ⚖️ — one up, the other down. Every time.

Phosphate binders (calcium acetate, sevelamer) — give WITH meals , not between. They bind the phosphorus in the food. Epoetin alfa — replaces the erythropoietin the kidney no longer makes; treats the anemia. Monitor BP and Hgb . Active vitamin D (calcitriol) — the failed kidney can't activate vitamin D, so calcium can't be absorbed. 🧠 Binders eat with you. If the client swallows it away from food, there's no phosphorus there to bind — wasted dose. ⚙️
STEP 3 · WATCH THE BRAIN & THE BP Everything that goes wrong during the run goes wrong because something was pulled off too fast.

Definition: solutes are removed too quickly from the blood. Urea stays high inside the brain cells, so water rushes into the brain — the cells swell, and ICP rises . Untreated it goes to seizures, coma & death . 🔎 KEY SIGNS 😵 Restless & disoriented (first change = LOC) 🤢 Vomiting 🤕 Headache ➕ later: twitching, seizures, ↓LOC 🚑 PRIORITY ACTION NCLEX TIP 1️⃣ STOP or SLOW the dialysis — fix the cause first. 2️⃣ Report to the provider. 3️⃣ Seizure precautions · protect the airway · reorient. 🧠 “Fast dialysis = swollen

Why: volume is coming off faster than the vessels can refill. 😵‍💫 Dizzy, nauseated, pale, diaphoretic, cramping ✅ Slow/stop ultrafiltration , lay flat & raise the legs (Trendelenburg per policy) ✅ Give normal saline bolus per order · recheck BP 🧠 Water out too fast = pressure down. Same fix as DDS: slow the machine.

Signs: sudden dyspnea, chest pain, cyanosis, ↓LOC 1️⃣ Clamp the line · stop the pump 2️⃣ Place left side-lying, head down (traps air in the right atrium) 3️⃣ 100% oxygen · call for help 🧠 “Clamp · Left · Low · O₂.” Air floats — so put the air where it can't reach the lungs.

The circuit is heparinized to stop clotting, so during and just after a run the client bleeds easily . Watch: gums, GI bleed, bruising, the needle sites Hold pressure longer after any stick Antidote to heparin: protamine sulfate 🧠 Heparin in the tubing = thin blood in the client.

From rapid fluid and sodium shifts, usually late in the run. ✅ Slow the ultrafiltration rate ✅ Normal saline per order 📉 Often a sign the client gained too much between treatments 🧠 Big gain = rough run. Cramping is the body's receipt for skipping the fluid restriction. ✅
STEP 4 · PROTECT THE ARM Weigh, watch the BP, guard the access — and the four NO-NOs she has to know by heart.

entries.h: ⚖️ Post-dialysis assessment — weight tells the story
entries.t: 🧠 The scale is the kidney's report card. 1 kg = 1 L = 2.2 lb . A client who gains 2 kg between runs drank 2 L more than they should have.

entries.h: 🚫 The fistula arm NO-NOs — never on that arm
entries.t: 🩺 NO blood pressure use the other arm 💉 NO IVs or lab draws no venipuncture ⌚ NO tight clothing or watches / jewelry 😴 NO sleeping on it compression clots it 🧴 NO creams or lotions skin breakdown + infection 👜 NO lifting >5 lb no purse on that arm Every one of these does the same thing: it squeezes the fistula shut or lets bacteria in . A clotted fistula means surgery. 🧠 “No BP, no needles, no bling, no bag, no bed, no balm.” Six NOs — say them in one breath while pointing at your own arm.

entries.h: 🚨 Report to the HCP — the 5 P's distal to the shunt NCLEX TIP
entries.t: P allor — pale skin below the fistula P aresthesia — numbness or tingling P ulses diminished P oor cap refill (over 3 seconds ) P ain distal to the shunt These mean the fistula is stealing blood from the hand . ✅ Mild pitting edema of that arm is NORMAL. 🧠 5 P's = “Please Protect Pale Poor Painful hands.” Edema = fine. Cold, white, numb = call.

🔥 Infection — warm, red, tender, or drainage at the shunt site 🩸 Bleeding — hold firm pressure, do NOT occlude the flow 🔇 No thrill / no bruit = clotted = report NOW 🧠 Hot & red = infected. Silent = clotted. Both get a phone call.

entries.h: 🍽️ Diet & fluid teaching for the dialysis client
entries.t: Restrict Why · examples Potassium 🍌 The kidney can't excrete it → fatal dysrhythmias . Limit bananas, oranges, potatoes, tomatoes, avocado, salt substitutes. Sodium 🧂 Sodium holds water → weight gain, edema, high BP between runs. Phosphorus 🥛 Dairy, dark colas, nuts, processed foods. Take binders with meals . Fluid 💧 Usually restricted; goal is a small gain between treatments. Exact limit is individualized — follow the order. Protein 🍗 Different rule: pre-dialysis CKD restricts protein, but on hemodialysis protein

🤚 Check the thrill several times a day — teach the client and the family. ⚖️ Weigh daily at the same time, same clothes; report rapid gains. 💉 Never skip a treatment — missed runs = hyperkalemia + fluid overload. 🆘 Carry ID that says "dialysis access — no BP/no sticks this arm." 🧠 Touch it, weigh it, show up. Three habits that keep a dialysis client alive. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🧼 DIAL = clean blood Machine kidney: removes waste, fluid & electrolytes . 🖐️ Thrill + bruit Feel the buzz, hear the whoosh — before every run. 🧠 DDS = brain swells Restless · vomiting · headache ➜ SLOW/STOP + report . 💊 Hold BP meds + antibiotics, digoxin & water-soluble vitamins get washed out . 🚫 That arm No BP · no sticks · no watch · no lotion · no >5 lb purse · no sleeping on it. 🖐️ 5 P's Pallor · Paresthesia · Pulses ↓ · Poor refill · Pain = report . Pitting edema = OK. ⚖️ 1 kg = 1 L Weigh be

Q1: You assess the fistula and feel nothing and hear nothing. Now what? Show answer No thrill + no bruit = the fistula has clotted. Report to the provider immediately — do not use the access. Q2: Two hours into dialysis the client is restless, disoriented, vomiting and has a headache. Priority? Show answer Dialysis disequilibrium syndrome — solutes removed too fast, brain cells swell, ICP rises. STOP or SLOW the treatment first, then report to the provider. Seizure precautions. Q3: Which meds are held before dialys
