entries.h: Kidney Stones · NG-249 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🪨 The stone 🔎 Clues 🧰 Before ⚡ During ✅ After ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Renal + Fluid · Med-Surg Course

Renal calculi · urolithiasis · lithotripsy & nephrostomy NG-249 Renal ADHD-friendly visual edition Renal calculi = a hard, calcified stone in the renal system — usually made of calcium . The pain is famous: “like a knife in the back,” equivalent to childbirth . Three nursing moves carry the whole topic: relieve the pain 💉, strain ALL the urine 🧺, and flood them with fluid 💧. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🪨 “LITH” = stone Uro lith iasis · Nephro lith iasis · Lith otripsy — all the same rock. 🔪 Knife-i
STEP 1 · WHAT & WHERE Name the stone by where it sits, then learn the four kinds — because the diet changes with the kind.

entries.h: 🔤 Say the word — it tells you the location
entries.t: Word Means Where Renal calculi Hard stone calcified in the renal system Kidney Renal lithiasis Lith = stone Stone in the renal (kidney) Uro lith iasis Stone in the urinary system Anywhere in the tract Uretero lith iasis Stone in the ureter The tubes connecting the kidney & bladder — where the worst pain comes from Nephro lith otomy Nephro = kidney · tomy = cut Surgery to remove the stone 🧠 Any word with “LITH” = a stone. Think monolith — a giant rock. Lith otripsy = "stone crushing." Learn one root, decode five wor

entries.h: 📍 Where stones get stuck — the 3 narrow points of the ureter
entries.t: A stone floating in the kidney can be silent. Pain starts when it enters the ureter and jams at one of three natural narrowings. Where it sticks decides where it hurts. 🧠 “Three toll booths on the ureter.” 🚧 Top (UPJ) = flank . Middle (iliac crossing) = lower belly . Bottom (UVJ) = groin + gotta go . The lower the stone, the lower the pain.

entries.h: 🔬 The FOUR stone types — the type picks the diet
entries.t: The trap: people assume a calcium stone means "stop eating calcium." Do NOT slash dietary calcium — low calcium in the gut lets more oxalate get absorbed and can make stones worse . Restrict oxalate and animal protein , keep calcium normal, unless the provider orders otherwise. 🧠 “CUSC” — C alcium · U ric acid · S truvite · C ystine. Say it "cusk." And pH: Uric acid loves ACID; Struvite loves ALKALINE. (U-A and S-A… Uric = Under 5.5, Struvite = Super alkaline. )

entries.h: ⚠️ Who gets stones — the risk list
entries.t: 💧 Dehydration — the #1 modifiable cause. Concentrated urine crystallizes. 🥩 High animal protein & high sodium diet 🦠 Recurrent UTIs (struvite) 🦶 Gout / high purine (uric acid) 🦴 Hyperparathyroidism & prolonged immobility — both dump calcium into the blood and urine 👨‍👩‍👧 Family history · previous stone (recurrence is common) 🌡️ Hot climates & heavy sweating 🧠 Immobility makes stones. Bones dissolve into the blood when nobody's weight-bearing — that calcium ends up in the urine. It's also why we walk stone clients.

💧 Low urine volume / high solute load ▼ 🧂 Salts supersaturate and crystallize ▼ 🪨 Crystals clump into a stone ▼ 🚧 Stone enters the ureter ➜ obstruction + spasm = COLIC 🧠 Think sweet tea. Too much sugar, not enough water = crystals at the bottom of the glass. Kidneys work the same way. 🔎
STEP 2 · SPOT IT Extreme wave-like pain plus blood in the urine — and a fever that changes everything.

entries.h: 🔪 EXTREME PAIN — “like a knife in the back,” equivalent to childbirth
entries.t: 🧠 “Colic = a stone rolling in a spasming tube.” The waves come from the ureter squeezing around the rock. Restless + writhing = renal colic. Still as a statue = peritonitis. That single contrast answers a lot of questions.

Answer first: the sharp stone scrapes the ureter lining ➜ blood in the urine . It may be visible (gross) or only on the dipstick/micro. 🩸 RBCs — the classic finding 💎 Crystals — can name the stone type 📊 pH — <5.5 acidic hints uric acid ; >7 alkaline hints struvite or calcium phosphate 🦠 WBCs / bacteria / nitrites = infection on top of the stone 🧠 Sharp rock, scraped pipe, bloody urine.

🤢 Nausea & vomiting , diaphoresis, pallor — the pain is that severe 🚽 Urgency, frequency, dysuria when the stone is low (near the bladder) 📉 Oliguria or anuria = obstruction — report immediately 🫃 Abdominal distention , decreased bowel sounds (reflex ileus) 🌡️ Fever & chills = INFECTION — emergency 🧠 A stone with a fever is a surgical emergency — an obstructed, infected kidney can go to urosepsis fast.

Test What it does Non-contrast CT of the abdomen/pelvis ⭐ The gold standard — sees essentially all stones, including uric acid stones that x-ray misses. No contrast needed. KUB x-ray Kidney-Ureter-Bladder film. Shows radiopaque (calcium, struvite) stones; misses uric acid stones. Renal ultrasound No radiation — preferred in pregnancy and children; shows hydronephrosis. Urinalysis + urine culture Hematuria, crystals, pH, and any infection. Stone analysis 🧺 The strained stone is sent to the lab — that result decides
STEP 3 · PAIN · FLUIDS · STRAIN Most small stones pass on their own. Your job before any procedure is six numbered actions.

entries.h: ✅ Priority intervention for urinary calculi with flank pain = RELIEVING PAIN CAUTION
entries.t: 1 💉 Administer analgesics. Pain is the priority. Opioids and/or NSAIDs (e.g. ketorolac) per order — NSAIDs also reduce the ureteral swelling. Give antiemetics for the vomiting. Give it on a schedule, not "as the pain returns." 2 💧 Fluid intake 3 L/day (oral and/or IV as ordered) — flushes the stone down and dilutes the urine so new ones can't form. 3 🧺 STRAIN ALL URINE for stones. Every void, every time, into the strainer — the stone goes to the lab. 4 🚶 AMBULATION — “walk & move.” Gravity and movement help the sto

entries.h: 🧺 How to strain urine — teach it exactly NCLEX TIP
entries.t: 🧠 “No stone, no answer.” If the stone goes down the toilet, nobody ever learns what kind it was — and she can't be taught the right diet.

Alpha blockers — e.g. tamsulosin — relax the smooth muscle of the distal ureter so the stone slips through. Teach: orthostatic hypotension , change positions slowly. NSAIDs — e.g. ketorolac — pain + swelling. Caution with impaired kidney function. Opioids — for severe colic per order. Antiemetics — the vomiting is part of the picture. Allopurinol — lowers uric acid for uric-acid stone formers. 🧠 “-osin loosens.” Tamsul osin relaxes the ureter — and it drops the blood pressure on standing.

📝 Informed consent signed & on the chart 🍽️ NPO per order if sedation/anesthesia is planned 🩸 Labs: CBC, coagulation studies, BUN/creatinine ; hold anticoagulants per order 🦠 Treat UTI first — procedures on an infected tract can trigger sepsis 🤰 Pregnancy status; allergy check (contrast, shellfish/iodine as applicable) 💬 Teach what to expect afterward — this is where the exam questions live 🧠 Consent · NPO · Labs · No infection. The universal pre-procedure four. ⚡
STEP 4 · BREAK IT · GRAB IT · SUCK IT OUT Three ways to get a stone out, ranked from least to most invasive.

entries.h: ⚡ Shockwave lithotripsy (ESWL) — shock waves break LARGE stones into smaller stones that can be easily passed
entries.t: Expected finding after lithotripsy? Stone fragments in the urine. That is the goal, not a complication. 🧠 “Litho-TRIP-sy = TRIP the stone and break it.” Big rock in ➜ gravel out. If the stone doesn't break the first time, the procedure can be repeated.

entries.h: 🪛 Percutaneous nephrolithotomy / nephrolithotripsy (PCNL) — the needle & scope
entries.t: What it is: Also called nephrolithotomy — the HCP sticks a needle & scope into the kidney through the back (flank) to suck out the stones. Used for large or staghorn stones that shock waves can't clear. 🧠 “Percutaneous = punch through the skin.” And the one-line teaching point: teach the client with a new nephrostomy tube to report BACK PAIN to the provider — back pain means urine has nowhere to go. 🔒

A thin scope goes up through the urethra and bladder into the ureter . The stone is grabbed with a basket or lasered into fragments — no incision at all. A ureteral stent is often left to hold the ureter open Expect flank discomfort, urgency, frequency and pink urine while the stent is in Teach the client to keep the stent removal appointment 🧠 Scope up, basket out. The stent is a temporary drinking straw holding the ureter open.

entries.h: 🪜 Which procedure, in order of invasiveness
entries.t: 💧 Pass it — fluids, pain control, tamsulosin, strain ▼ ⚡ ESWL — shock waves from outside, no incision ▼ 🎣 Ureteroscopy — scope up the natural path, basket/laser ▼ 🪛 PCNL — flank incision into the kidney, for big/staghorn stones 🧠 Least cutting first. Size and location choose the procedure — big stone, bigger approach. ✅
STEP 5 · NORMAL vs NOT NORMAL This is the single most tested block: what she should expect, and what earns a phone call.

entries.h: 🚦 After lithotripsy — NORMAL vs NOT NORMAL ATI
entries.t: 🧠 “Bruise & blood = fine. Fever & no flow = phone.” Bruising and a day of pink urine are the receipt for the shock waves. A fever or no urine is never expected.

entries.h: 🔧 Nephrostomy tube care — PRIORITY: maintain tube patency CAUTION
entries.t: 1 💧 Irrigate ONLY with an order , using STERILE normal saline , small volume, gently. Never force against resistance. 2 🔒 NEVER clamp a nephrostomy tube — the kidney has no other way out. 3 🎒 Keep the bag BELOW the level of the kidney ; secure the tube so it can't be pulled. 4 👀 Expect SEDIMENT in the bottom of the bag — those are the loose fragments draining out. 5 📞 Teach the client to REPORT BACK PAIN — new back/flank pain means the tube is clogged and urine is backing up. Also report no drainage, fever, or leak

entries.h: 🍽️ Diet — restrict animal protein, limit purines
entries.t: Rule Details Restrict protein 🥩 “Animal meats.” Animal protein makes the urine acidic and raises calcium & uric acid excretion. Key urolithiasis teaching = restriction of animal protein . Limit purines 🍺 Red meats, organ meats, beer — plus sardines, anchovies, gravy. Purines break down into uric acid . Limit sodium 🧂 High sodium pushes more calcium into the urine. Limit oxalate 🥬 Spinach, rhubarb, beets, nuts, chocolate, strong tea, sweet potatoes — for calcium oxalate formers. Keep calcium NORMAL 🥛 Do not slash di

💧 3 L of fluid a day , mostly water, spread across the day 🧺 Keep straining until told to stop — fragments pass for days 🚶 Stay active ; no bed rest 💊 Finish antibiotics; take pain meds before the pain peaks 🌡️ Call for fever/chills, no urine output, uncontrolled pain, heavy bleeding 🔁 Stones recur — keep follow-up appointments and get the stone analyzed 🧠 Water is the cheapest prescription in this whole chapter.

Obstruction ➜ hydronephrosis — urine backs up and swells the kidney; can permanently damage it Infection ➜ urosepsis — fever, chills, hypotension, confusion. Emergency. Hemorrhage — especially after PCNL; watch VS, Hgb, flank swelling Recurrence — very common without a diet & fluid change 🧠 Blocked + infected = the kidney is on a clock. That combination goes to the OR, not to the med list. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🪨 LITH = stone Renal calculi = hard calcified stone, usually calcium . 🔪 Priority = PAIN Flank pain in waves ➜ relieve the pain first . Restless & writhing. 🧺 Strain · 💧3 L · 🚶Walk No bed rest. No massage. 🩸 Hematuria Blood in urine up to 24 h after lithotripsy = normal. Fever = not. ⚡ Lithotripsy Shock waves break BIG stones into small ones. Expect fragments in urine. 🔧 Nephrostomy PRIORITY = patency . Sterile NS if ordered. Never clamp. Report back pain . 🥩 Diet Restrict animal protein , limit pur

Q1: A client arrives with severe right flank pain from urinary calculi. What is the priority intervention? Show answer Relieving the pain — administer the ordered analgesics (opioid and/or NSAID) plus an antiemetic. Then fluids 3 L/day, strain all urine, and ambulate. Q2: What is the expected finding in the urine after lithotripsy? Show answer Stone fragments. Also expected: bruising and pain over the flank, and blood in the urine for up to 24 hours. NOT expected: fever or chills, inability to urinate, uncontrolled

entries.h: Peritoneal Dialysis · NG-261 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🫙 How it works 🌡️ Before 🔁 During ✅ After ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Renal + Fluid · Med-Surg Course

Fill · Dwell · Drain — your own belly lining is the filter NG-261 Renal ADHD-friendly visual edition The peritoneal cavity is filled with a hypertonic solution to PULL solutes out. No machine filter, no blood outside the body — the peritoneal membrane is the dialyzer. Three test magnets live here: sterile technique 🧤, cloudy drainage ☁️, and sudden trouble breathing 🫁. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🧲 Hypertonic PULLS Sugary dialysate drags water & waste across the peritoneum. ☁️ Cloudy = peritonitis
STEP 1 · THE BELLY IS THE FILTER One catheter, one membrane, one sugar gradient — that's the entire machine.

entries.h: 🩹 The set-up — catheter, cavity, two bags
entries.t: The peritoneal cavity is filled up with hypertonic solution to PULL solutes out. A permanent peritoneal catheter tunnels through the abdominal wall into the peritoneal space. Fluid runs in by gravity from a bag hung ABOVE and drains out by gravity into a bag BELOW . Fresh dialysate in Peritoneal membrane Effluent out Sterile exit site 🧠 “Bag up, belly full, bag down.” Picture a hot-water bottle in the belly ♨️ — it goes in warm, sits and soaks up the trash, then drains into a bag on the floor.

entries.h: 🧲 Why a SUGARY solution pulls fluid
entries.t: Answer first: the dialysate is hypertonic (high dextrose). Hypertonic = more particles than the blood , so water is pulled OUT of the capillaries into the belly by osmosis . Waste follows by diffusion . Stronger dextrose = more fluid removed. Concentrations commonly run from about 1.5% up to 4.25% — the provider picks it based on how much fluid must come off. 🧠 “Sugar is a sponge.” The sweeter the bag, the more water it sucks out.

Peritoneal 🫙 Hemo 🩸 Filter The client's own peritoneum A machine dialyzer Where At home , often nightly Center, ~3×/week Speed Slow & gentle — steadier BP Fast — hypotension & DDS risk #1 danger Peritonitis ☁️ Access clotting / bleeding Diet More liberal; protein loss is higher Tighter K⁺ & fluid limits 🧠 PD is the slow cooker 🍲, HD is the pressure cooker ♨️. Slow & steady vs fast & risky.

Outflow should be equal to or MORE than inflow — that extra volume is the fluid you pulled off the client. Less out than in = a problem to solve (see DURING). 🧠 “Fill · Chill · Spill.” Three beats, always in that order. Chill = the dwell, where the actual dialysis happens. 🌡️
STEP 2 · WEIGH · WARM · STERILE "Proper preparation for peritoneal dialysis" — the exam wants two actions and one technique.

1 ⚖️ Take the weight. Empty bladder first, same scale, same clothes. This is the baseline for how much fluid you removed. 1 kg = 1 L . 2 🌡️ WARM the solution. The FIRST action before infusing is to warm the dialysate. 3 🧤 Sterile technique — PRIORITY. Mask, hand hygiene, sterile field, scrub the connection. The catheter is a straight road to the peritoneum. 4 📏 Baseline assessment. Vital signs, abdominal girth, lung sounds, exit-site inspection, last bowel movement. 5 🚽 Have the client empty the bladder before the

entries.h: 🌡️ Why warming is the FIRST action KAPLAN
entries.t: 🧠 “Cold cramps, warm welcomes.” If a question asks the first action before an exchange, the answer is warm the dialysate — not "check the drain," not "position the client."

entries.h: 🧤 Sterile technique is the PRIORITY — this is how peritonitis starts CAUTION
entries.t: Every touch of that catheter is a possible direct inoculation of the peritoneum . Contamination almost always happens at the connection or the exit site . 😷 Mask on the nurse and the client for connect/disconnect. 🧼 Hand hygiene → sterile gloves → scrub the connection port. 🩹 Exit-site care daily with the ordered solution; keep it dry ; report redness, warmth or drainage. 🚿 Teach: showers, not tub baths or swimming pools (varies by policy). 🔍 Inspect every bag: expiration, clarity, leaks, correct dextrose concentra

entries.h: 🧪 What the numbers should show STANDARD ADULT RANGES
entries.t: Lab Normal PD watch-out BUN 10–20 mg/dL Should trend DOWN with good exchanges Creatinine 0.6–1.2 mg/dL Trend, not one value Potassium 3.5–5.0 mEq/L Can go LOW with frequent exchanges Glucose 70–110 mg/dL fasting 📈 Rises — dextrose is absorbed. Watch diabetics. Albumin 3.5–5.0 g/dL 📉 Falls — protein is lost in the effluent 🧠 Sugar UP, protein DOWN. The two labs peritoneal dialysis changes that hemodialysis doesn't.

Answer first: peritoneal dialysis loses protein into the drained fluid every single exchange, so the client needs MORE dietary protein , not less. 🥚 High-quality protein — eggs, fish, poultry, lean meat 🍬 Watch carbohydrate/calories — the dextrose counts as sugar 🥦 Fiber & fluid — constipation blocks outflow (see DURING) 🧠 Protein leaks out the drain. Refill it with the plate. 🔁
STEP 3 · TROUBLE & FIRST ACTIONS Three scenarios come up over and over: can't breathe, won't drain, and the belly turns hot.

entries.h: 🚨 Sudden respiratory distress ➜ FIRST ACTION: raise the HOB KAPLAN
entries.t: Why it happens: too much fluid, infused too fast — the full abdomen pushes the diaphragm UP and the lungs can't expand. 🔎 KEY SIGNS 🫁 Crackles in the lung bases 💨 Rapid respirations 😮‍💨 Dyspnea — sudden onset during or after a fill 🚑 PRIORITY INTERVENTION 1️⃣ Raise the HOB — first action. 2️⃣ Slow or stop the inflow ; drain the fluid per order. 3️⃣ Reassess lung sounds, SpO₂, respiratory rate; notify the HCP. 🧠 “Breathing beats circulation.” A client on peritoneal dialysis who suddenly starts breathing faster — the

entries.h: 🚱 Insufficient outflow — assess in this order KAPLAN SCENARIO
entries.t: Answer first: Patient ➜ Device ➜ Intervention. Assess the client before you touch the tubing, and touch the tubing before you reposition. 1 🧍 Assess the PATIENT — abdominal distention and CONSTIPATION . A full bowel is the most common reason fluid won't drain. ▼ 2 🔌 Assess the DEVICE — catheter kinks , closed clamps, obstruction , fibrin clots, the bag not low enough, tubing trapped under the client. ▼ 3 🔄 INTERVENE — reposition the client to a side-lying position ; turn side to side; get them up and walking if all

entries.h: 🩸 Other things you may see in the drain
entries.t: Finding What it means ☁️ Cloudy PERITONITIS — report 🚨 🩸 Blood-tinged Can be expected in the first few exchanges after catheter placement, and in menstruating clients. New or bright bleeding = report. 🧵 Fibrin strands Stringy white bits — can clog the catheter; report per protocol 💛 Clear, pale yellow ✅ Expected 🧠 Pale yellow = pass. Cloudy = call.

🍬 Hyperglycemia — dextrose is absorbed; check glucose, especially in diabetics. 📉 Hypotension / hypovolemia — too much fluid pulled off with strong dextrose. 💧 Leakage at the exit site — report; increases infection risk. 🫃 Hernia & back pain — from the constant intra-abdominal volume. 🍽️ Anorexia / fullness — the belly is literally full; offer small frequent meals during a drain. 🧠 A belly full of sugar water explains all five: high sugar, low pressure, leaks, bulges, no appetite. ✅
STEP 4 · THE ONE YOU MUST NOT MISS Drain, measure, weigh — and stare at the color of that bag.

entries.h: 🚨 PERITONITIS — key signs to REPORT to the HCP
entries.t: What to do: notify the HCP · send the effluent for cell count, Gram stain & culture before antibiotics if ordered · expect antibiotics , often added to the dialysate (intraperitoneal) or IV per order · continue to monitor temp, HR, pain and the appearance of every bag. 🧠 “No one likes cloudy dayyyys — and nobody likes cloudy drainnnnage.” ☁️ Sing it. Cloudy fluid is white blood cells in the belly — that is infection, not sediment.

entries.h: ✅ After every exchange — the documentation habit
entries.t: 1 📏 Measure inflow and outflow and record both. Outflow should be ≥ inflow. 2 ➖ Calculate the difference. Outflow − inflow = fluid removed. A negative number means the client kept fluid — report it. 3 👀 Describe the effluent — color and clarity, every single bag. 4 ⚖️ Weigh the client after the drain, plus vital signs, lung sounds & edema check. 5 🩹 Exit-site check and dressing per policy. 🧠 “In, out, difference, describe, weigh.” If you can't say how much came back, you don't know what the treatment did.

entries.h: 🏠 Home teaching — what she tells the client
entries.t: 😷 Mask + handwashing every connection — no shortcuts, no exceptions. ☁️ Call for cloudy fluid, fever, or belly pain — do not wait for the next clinic visit. ⚖️ Weigh daily , log every exchange, log in/out volumes. 💩 Prevent constipation — it stops the drain. Fiber, fluids, ordered stool softener. 🩹 Keep the exit site clean, dry, and secured so the catheter isn't tugged. 🧊 Store bags clean & dry; check expiration and clarity before use. 🧠 Mask · Measure · Move the bowels. Three habits that prevent the three biggest

entries.h: ⭐ Priority order when several things happen at once
entries.t: 🫁 Breathing problem — dyspnea/crackles ➜ raise HOB FIRST ▼ 🚨 Signs of peritonitis — fever, cloudy drain ➜ report to HCP ▼ 🚱 Poor outflow ➜ patient, then device, then reposition ▼ 📋 Comfort & documentation 🧠 ABC still wins. Airway/Breathing outranks infection; infection outranks a slow drain. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🫙 Fill · Dwell · Drain Hypertonic solution PULLS solutes & water across the peritoneum. 🌡️ Warm it FIRST Before: 1. weight · 2. warm the solution. Never a microwave. ☁️ Cloudy drainage + fever + tachycardia = PERITONITIS ➜ report to HCP. 🫁 Sudden dyspnea FIRST: raise HOB. Breathing over circulation. 🧤 Sterile = PRIORITY Every connection is a door straight into the peritoneum. 🚱 Won't drain? P atient (distention · constipation) ➜ D evice (kinks) ➜ I ntervene (side-lying). 🍗 Protein UP Protein is lost

Q1: What is the first action in proper preparation for peritoneal dialysis? Show answer Warm the dialysate. (Take the weight, warm the solution — cold fluid causes cramping, chills and vasoconstriction, which means a poor exchange.) Never use a microwave. Q2: A client on peritoneal dialysis suddenly begins to breathe more rapidly. First action? Show answer Raise the head of the bed. The full abdomen is pushing the diaphragm up — breathing over circulation. Then slow/stop the inflow and drain per order, and notify t

entries.h: Renal Anatomy & Physiology · NG-263 · Nursing Field Notes
entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🧱 Parts ⚙️ Jobs 🧪 Numbers ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Renal + Fluid · Anatomy & Physiology

Renal Anatomy & Physiology — the nephron, top to bottom NG-263 RENAL + FLUID ADHD-friendly visual edition The kidneys work like 2 washing machines 🌀 — they wash the blood of waste by filtration , regulate fluid volume by reabsorption , and stimulate red blood cell production by making erythropoietin . Every renal disease on your exam is one of those three jobs breaking. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🌀 2 washing machines Filter waste · balance fluid · build blood. Three jobs, one organ. 🧠 “FRE the PEE
STEP 1 · THE PARTS You cannot reason about renal failure until you can point to the piece that broke — so learn the map first.

entries.h: 🫘 The kidney, sliced in half — every part labeled
entries.t: Blood comes in through the renal artery , gets scrubbed in the cortex , the waste water drains down the pyramids into the calyces and renal pelvis , and leaves as urine down the ureter . Cortex filters · medulla concentrates · pelvis collects. 🧠 “Cortex Cleans, Medulla Milks, Pelvis Pours.” Outside filters, the middle squeezes water back, the inside pours what's left into the ureter. Waste always travels outside → in → down.

entries.h: 🔬 The nephron is the functional unit
entries.t: About 1 million nephrons per kidney . Inside each one sits the glomerulus — a network of small blood vessels that filters the blood of waste. Kidneys take about 20–25% of cardiac output — roughly 1,200 mL of blood every minute. They make about 180 L of filtrate a day and give back ~99% of it — only 1–2 L leaves as urine. 🧠 180 in, 1.5 out. The kidney filters a bathtub and hands you back a soda bottle . That's how aggressive reabsorption is.

entries.h: 🩸 Follow the blood — artery to vein
entries.t: Renal artery (dirty blood in) ▼ Afferent arteriole — Arrives, wide ▼ 🫧 GLOMERULUS — filtration happens here ▼ Efferent arteriole — Exits, narrow ▼ Peritubular capillaries & vasa recta ▼ Renal vein (clean blood out) 🧠 A = Afferent = Arrives. E = Efferent = Exits. The exit hose is narrower than the entrance hose — that back-pressure is exactly what squeezes filtrate out.

entries.h: ⭐ The nephron — every segment and the one job it does
entries.t: HIGH YIELD Learn this and you get diuretics, electrolytes and renal failure for free. Each segment moves a different thing, so each one has its own drug and its own lab. 🧠 “Pee Down Any Damp Corridor.” P roximal → D escending → A scending → D istal → C ollecting duct. Then hang the drugs on it: Loop on the Ascending, Thiazide on the Distal, Spironolactone on the Collecting duct.

entries.h: 🚰 Where the urine goes once it leaves
entries.t: 🧠 “Kidney, Ureter, Bladder, Urethra” = KUB — the same three letters as the abdominal X-ray that looks for stones. One acronym, whole plumbing. ⚙️
STEP 2 · THE JOBS Three phases make urine — and seven jobs make you alive. Say them out loud.

entries.h: ⭐ Three phases of urine formation HESI
entries.t: Q: What are the three phases of urine formation? A: Filtration, reabsorption, and secretion. 🧠 “Filter it, Fetch it back, Flush the rest.” Three F's, in order. Secretion is the kidney's trash chute — it's how potassium, acid and most drugs actually leave you.

entries.h: 🧠 “FRE the PEE” — the source mnemonic, unpacked
entries.t: F — F iltration of medications & waste R — R eabsorption, run by ADH (Anti-Diuretic Hormone) E — E rythropoietin (stimulates RBC production in bone marrow) And the three things filtration is supposed to dump: H — H ydrogen ions (too much = high acidity = metabolic acidosis) U — U rea → the BUN (Blood Urea Nitrogen) C — C reatinine (over 1.3 = bad kidney) 🧠 “FRE the PEE — but HUC it out.” F ilter, R eabsorb, E rythropoietin. What gets hucked out: H ydrogen, U rea, C reatinine. If they stay in, the labs climb.

entries.h: ⭐ All 7 kidney jobs: A WET BED
entries.t: A — A cid–base balance (dumps H⁺, keeps HCO₃⁻) W — W ater balance E — E lectrolytes (Na⁺, K⁺, Ca²⁺, PO₄³⁻, Mg²⁺) T — T oxin & drug removal B — B lood pressure control (renin → RAAS) E — E rythropoietin → red blood cells D — vitamin D activation → calcium absorption 🧠 Kidneys fail = “A WET BED.” Acidosis, water overload, high K⁺, drug toxicity, hypertension, anemia, low calcium/bone disease. Every complication of renal failure is one letter of this.

entries.h: 💧 ADH — “ A dd D a H ₂O”
entries.t: ADH is made in the hypothalamus, stored in the posterior pituitary , and works on the collecting duct . More ADH = more water pulled back into the blood = less urine, darker and more concentrated. 🧠 “Add Da H₂O.” ADH adds water to the blood , so it subtracts water from the urine . High ADH = small dark pee; no ADH (DI) = a firehose of clear pee.

entries.h: 🩸 Erythropoietin — why kidney patients are anemic
entries.t: 🧠 EPO = “Every Person's Oxygen.” Dead kidneys make no EPO → no new red cells → chronic anemia, fatigue and pallor even though nothing is bleeding.

⬇️ Low BP / low renal blood flow ▼ RENIN released from the kidney ▼ Angiotensin I → (lungs, ACE) → Angiotensin II ▼ Vasoconstriction + ALDOSTERONE ▼ 💧 Na⁺ & water held · K⁺ dumped · BP ↑ Why it matters: a failing kidney thinks it is dry even when the body is drowning, so it keeps firing RAAS — that's why renal patients are hypertensive and fluid-overloaded at the same time. 🧠 “Aldosterone = Save Salt, Sack K⁺.” Sodium in, potassium out. Every ACE inhibitor, ARB and spironolactone question is just this chain being b

entries.h: 🦴 Vitamin D & calcium — the quiet job
entries.t: The proximal tubule converts vitamin D to its active form (calcitriol). Active vitamin D lets the gut absorb calcium . Failing kidney → no activation → low calcium → parathyroid pulls calcium out of bone . Failing kidney also can't dump phosphate → high phosphate , which drives calcium down further. 🧠 Calcium and phosphate are on a seesaw ⚖️ — one up, the other down. Renal failure sits on the phosphate end, so calcium flies up out of the bones. That's renal bone disease. 🧪
STEP 3 · WHAT THE LABS MEAN Four numbers tell you how a kidney is doing. Learn the bars, not the paragraphs.

entries.h: 🧪 The four kidney numbers — low · normal · high
entries.t: 🧠 “BUN is a Big Unreliable Number; Creatinine is the Cold hard truth.” If both are up → kidney. If only BUN is up → think dehydration or GI bleed first.

entries.h: 🧪 What each lab is actually telling you
entries.t: Lab Normal (adult) If it's HIGH, think… GFR >90 mL/min LOW is the bad direction — <60 for 3 months = CKD Creatinine 0.6–1.2 mg/dL Kidney damage — >1.3 = bad kidney BUN 10–20 mg/dL Dehydration, GI bleed, high protein, kidney BUN : Creatinine 10:1 – 20:1 >20:1 = pre-renal (dry) 💧 Potassium 3.5–5.0 mEq/L Kidney can't excrete K⁺ → cardiac arrest risk 🚨 Urine output ≥30 mL/hr LOW is bad — oliguria = kidneys in distress 🧠 Potassium is the killer. Of every renal lab, K⁺ is the one that stops a heart. When a renal question

entries.h: ⏳ Half-life — and why renal patients overdose
entries.t: Half-life = the time it takes for half of the medication to be eliminated from the body. Bad kidney = long half-life = drug stacks up. That is why renally-cleared drugs get dose reductions in CKD. 🧠 “Half gone, half stays.” It takes roughly 4–5 half-lives to clear a drug — or to reach steady state on a new one.

entries.h: 🚨 Nephrotoxic — protect the kidney you have
entries.t: 💉 Aminoglycosides gentamicin 🧴 Vancomycin check trough 🩻 IV contrast dye hydrate first 💊 NSAIDs ibuprofen, naproxen 🧪 ACE / ARBs watch creatinine + K⁺ 🍄 Amphotericin B “ampho-terrible” Never give an NSAID to a client in acute kidney injury — it constricts the afferent arteriole and drops the GFR further. ✅ Do instead: hydrate before and after contrast, check creatinine & GFR before nephrotoxic drugs, monitor strict I&O and daily weights (1 kg = 1 L) . 🧠 “A VaNilla Ice cream cone” — A minoglycosides · V ancomycin ·

entries.h: ✅ Daily weight is the best fluid monitor
entries.t: Same time , same scale , same clothes , after voiding. 1 kg = 1 L = 2.2 lb of fluid. New, sudden, rapid weight gain = fluid retention , not fat. Report >1 kg (2.2 lb) gain in a day, or >2 kg in a week. 🧠 Weight beats I&O. Charts lie, scales don't — a client can drink from the sink, but they can't hide a kilogram. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🌀 3 phases Filtration → Reabsorption → Secretion 🔬 Nephron = functional unit · glomerulus = the filter 🧪 GFR >90 · Cr >1.3 normal filter · bad kidney 🛏️ A WET BED Acid · Water · Electrolytes · Toxins · BP · EPO · vit D

Q1: Name the three phases of urine formation. Show answer Filtration, reabsorption, and secretion. Q2: What is the functional unit of the kidney, and what filters inside it? Show answer The nephron — about 1 million per kidney. Inside it the glomerulus, a network of small blood vessels, filters waste out of the blood. Q3: A normal GFR is what number? Show answer Over 90 mL/min. Under 60 for 3 months = chronic kidney disease; under 15 = end stage. Q4: BUN is 32 and creatinine is 1.0. Kidney failure or dehydration? S

Chronic failure grinds through 5 STAGES over years. This page is only about where the patient is on the clock and what changes at each step. entries.h: THE 4 PHASES OF ACUTE RENAL FAILURE
entries.t: STEP 1 · WEEKS One insult, four acts. The urine output tells you which act you're in — and each act has its own way of killing the patient.

entries.h: 📈 Watch the urine output — it draws the whole story
entries.t: 🧠 “Off · Low · Flow · Grow.” Off set (onset) → Low (oliguric) → Flow (diuresis) → Grow (recovery). Four beats, in that order, every single time.

Answer first: from the moment of the insult until symptoms appear — hours to days . 🩸 The insult happens: shock, contrast dye, gentamicin, blocked ureter 🧪 Labs may still look near-normal; urine output starts sliding ⭐ This is the ONLY phase where you can still fully reverse it Nursing: restore perfusion, stop the nephrotoxin, relieve the obstruction, watch hourly output. 🧠 Onset = the golden hour of the kidney. Nobody looks sick yet — that's exactly why the exam puts the right answer here.

entries.h: 2️⃣ Oliguric phase 🚱 — less than 400 mL in 24 hours
entries.t: Answer first: LOW output = thick, sticky urine. Everything the kidney should be dumping now stays in the body. ⏳ Usually lasts 1–2 weeks — the longer it lasts, the worse the prognosis 🔺 K⁺ ↑ · phosphorus ↑ · BUN ↑ · creatinine ↑ 💧 Fluid volume OVERLOAD — edema, crackles, JVD, hypertension, weight gain 🫁 Metabolic acidosis , pH <7.35 🚨 Hyperkalemia in this phase is the #1 cause of death Nursing: fluid restriction, daily weights, cardiac monitor, hold potassium, prep for dialysis. 🧠 OLIG = “Oh, Little Is Going out.”

Answer first: Diuresis = Drain urine — 3–6 L per day ! The kidney can filter again but cannot concentrate yet, so water pours out. ⏳ Lasts about 1–3 weeks 🔻 Now the danger flips: hypovolemia, hypotension, hypokalemia, hyponatremia 🧪 BUN & creatinine start falling near the end of this phase ⚠️ The trap: huge urine output looks like the patient is better — they can go into shock while everyone celebrates Nursing: replace fluid & electrolytes, strict I&O, orthostatic BP, watch for dehydration. 🧠 Diuresis = the dam BRE

entries.h: 4️⃣ Recovery phase 🌱 — SLOW, up to 1 year
entries.t: Answer first: function returns gradually — up to 12 months for full recovery. 📈 Urine output normalizes toward 1–2 L/day ; ability to concentrate returns last 🧪 BUN & creatinine drift back down over weeks ⚠️ Many patients are left with some permanent loss — a scar on the GFR 🐌 If it doesn't recover → it becomes CHRONIC kidney disease Nursing: keep avoiding nephrotoxins, follow-up labs, teach that the kidney is still fragile for a year. 🧠 “A year to heal.” Broken bone = 6 weeks. Broken kidney = up to 1 year . That n

entries.h: 🔁 The danger FLIPS between phase 2 and phase 3 — this is the most-missed idea on the page
entries.t: EXAM TIP Same patient, same disease, opposite nursing action two weeks apart . The question always tells you the urine output — that is how you know which action is right. 🧠 “Full then Flush.” Phase 2 you take fluid away ; phase 3 you give it back . Read the output before you pick an answer. 🪜
STEP 2 · YEARS There are 5 stages of CKD as the kidney gradually loses function — and GFR is the only number that decides which one.

entries.h: 🪜 GFR — Glomerular Filtration Rate · Over 90 mL/min = normal
entries.t: 🧠 “90 · 60 · 30 · 15 · dead-stop.” Each stage is roughly half the last. Say the four numbers, then add “under 15 = the machine.”

entries.h: 🪜 What actually happens at each stage
entries.t: Stage GFR Kidney & patient Stage 1 90+ Kidney damage · normal function. Found only on labs — protein in urine, abnormal imaging. Patient feels fine. Control the sugar & BP here. Stage 2 89–60 Kidney damage · mild loss of function. Still mostly silent; BP creeping up. Stage 3 59–30 Moderate to severe loss. Symptoms begin: fatigue, anemia , phosphorus ↑ / calcium ↓ , edema, nocturia. Nephrology referral. Stage 4 29–15 Severe loss. Uremic symptoms, acidosis, hyperkalemia. Place dialysis access & discuss transplant now
🧠 A-N-O-P: A nuria 100 · O liguria 400 · N ormal 1500 · P olyuria 3000+ . Small number, small letter.

entries.h: ⭐ Best indicator of GOOD renal function
entries.t: 1500 mL of urine in 24 hours If the answer choices list urine volumes, the healthy kidney is the one making about 1–2 L a day . Hourly, that's the familiar 30 mL/hr floor. Do the math with her: 30 mL/hr × 24 = 720 mL — that's the bare minimum , not the goal. The goal is double that. 🧠 “Fifteen hundred = fine.” Both start with F. Under 400 = failing, over 3000 = flooding. 🔀
STEP 3 · WHICH CLOCK Phases or stages? Reversible or forever? Here's how the two timelines connect — and where they merge.

entries.h: 🔀 The fork in the road — every AKI ends in one of two places
entries.t: 🧠 Acute is a door, chronic is a hallway. The door can swing back — once you're in the hallway you only walk one way.

entries.h: ⏱️ Phases vs. Stages — don't mix the vocabularies
entries.t: ⚡ ACUTE = 4 PHASES 🐌 CHRONIC = 5 STAGES Unit of time Hours → weeks → up to 1 year Years → decades Named by Urine output pattern GFR number The steps 1 Onset · 2 Oliguric · 3 Diuresis · 4 Recovery 1 ( 90+ ) · 2 ( 89–60 ) · 3 ( 59–30 ) · 4 ( 29–15 ) · 5 ( <15 ) Direction Can go back up Down only Worst moment Oliguric phase — hyperkalemia & fluid overload Stage 5 / ESRD — uremia, needs dialysis to live Nurse's job Find the cause, survive the phases Slow the slide, prepare for replacement therapy 🧠 “Phases flow, stages

Answer first: a CKD patient who gets dehydrated, septic, or gets contrast dye can drop acutely on top of their chronic baseline. Clue: a known CKD patient whose creatinine jumps fast from their usual number. Treat the acute insult — some of it is recoverable. 🧠 A pothole in the middle of the landslide. Fix the pothole; the landslide keeps going.

In the oliguric phase, potassium is the killer. A patient who is anuric cannot excrete K⁺ at all. ❌ Never give IV potassium to a patient who is not making urine ❌ No potassium-sparing diuretics, no salt substitutes ✅ Cardiac monitor + K⁺ level before every replacement decision 🧠 “No pee, no K.” The shortest rule in renal nursing — and one of the most-tested. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🔤 Off · Low · Flow · Grow Onset → Oliguric → Diuresis → Recovery 🚱 Under 400 mL /24 hr = oliguric = K⁺ up, fluid up, acid up 🌊 3–6 L /day = diuresis = replace fluid, watch for hypokalemia 🪜 90·60·30·15 5 CKD stages · under 15 = ESRD

Q1: Name the 4 phases of acute renal failure in order. Show answer 1. Onset of injury (initiation) · 2. Oliguric phase · 3. Diuresis ("polyuric") phase · 4. Recovery phase. Q2: Define the oliguric phase by number, and name its two biggest dangers. Show answer Less than 400 mL in 24 hours — LOW output, thick sticky urine. Dangers: HYPERKALEMIA (cardiac arrest) and FLUID VOLUME OVERLOAD (pulmonary edema). Also metabolic acidosis and rising BUN/creatinine. Q3: A client in AKI suddenly puts out 4.5 L in 24 hours. What

Every number lined up beside the sign it produces, plus the top 2 missed NCLEX questions — both about potassium . Sisters: NG-047 = master overview & causes · NG-264 = the 4 phases & 5 stages · NG-266 = nursing care, diet & drugs. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🫀 K⁺ over 5.0 = PRIORITY Potassium Pumps the heart. It kills first, so you treat it first.
STEP 1 · THE NUMBERS A failing kidney is a broken washing machine — nothing gets rinsed out, so everything piles up in the blood.

entries.h: 🧺 Excess waste & electrolytes in the blood — the broken washing machine
entries.t: 🧠 “SPUKA in the wash” — S odium · P hosphorus · U rea · K ⁺ · A cid. Five things that should have gone down the drain and didn't. Every renal symptom is one of these five backing up.

entries.h: 🧪 The renal lab panel — normals on the left, renal failure on the right
entries.t: Lab Normal (adult, typical) Renal failure Potassium K⁺ 🫀 3.5–5.0 mEq/L HIGH — over 5.0 . Treat first. Sodium Na⁺ 🧂 135–145 mEq/L Retained (source: HIGH). Note: because water is held too, the serum value often reads normal or even low — total body sodium is still high. Phosphorus 🦴 3.0–4.5 mg/dL HIGH Calcium 🦴 ≈8.6–10.2 mg/dL (varies by lab) LOW — phosphorus rises, calcium falls; no activated vitamin D Magnesium 💊 1.3–2.1 mEq/L HIGH — that's why magnesium antacids are banned BUN 💩 10–20 mg/dL Over 20 Creatinine 🧪 0.

entries.h: 📊 See the directions at a glance
entries.t: 🧠 Picture a seesaw: phosphorus UP forces calcium DOWN. They are always opposite — if the exam says phos is high, calcium is low, and the patient itches. 🔎
STEP 2 · WHAT YOU SEE Head to toe, every symptom traces back to one lab on the page above.
🧠 “Frosty, itchy, tired, wet.” Four words = the classic chronic renal patient: uremic frost , itching , anemic fatigue , and fluid- wet lungs.

MEMORY TRICK — 3 P's: P otassium is a P riority since it P umps the HEART muscles. High potassium changes how the heart's muscle cells fire — “HIGH PUMPS in the heart” — producing peaked T waves & ST elevation , then wide QRS, then arrest. EXAM TIP The ECG picture tells you how urgent it is. Peaked T = get moving. Wide QRS = move NOW. 🧠 “Tall Tents, Steep Steps, Wide Waves.” 6–7 tall tented T · 7–8 ST steps up · over 8 the QRS goes wide. Higher K⁺ = uglier, wider, deader.

Kaplan question: “Patient with chronic kidney disease?” → Oliguria is EXPECTED . Don't pick oliguria as the "unexpected/report immediately" answer in a known CKD patient — it's the disease doing exactly what the disease does. Report the new or life-threatening finding instead. 🧠 Expected ≠ emergency. In CKD, low urine is the baseline. The emergency is what the retained potassium and fluid are doing to the heart and lungs .

Answer first: the kidneys release erythropoietin , the hormone that stimulates bone marrow to produce red blood cells . No kidney → no EPO → no red cells. 😮‍💨 Fatigue, pallor, dyspnea on exertion, tachycardia 💊 Treated with epoetin alfa / darbepoetin + iron 🩸 Bleeding risk is up too — uremia makes platelets sluggish 🧠 EPO = “Every Person's Oxygen.” Kidneys don't just make urine — they order the red cells that carry oxygen.

🫁 CRACKLES wet, fluid-filled lungs 🦢 JVD jugular vein distention 💥 BOUNDING pulses from that fluid excess ⚖️ Weight UP 1 kg = 1 L retained 🦵 Pitting edema legs, sacrum 🩸 BP UP hypertension 😮‍💨 Dyspnea · orthopnea can't lie flat 🫀 S3 gallop overloaded heart Priority action: raise the head of the bed, oxygen, assess lung sounds, hold fluids, notify the provider — loop diuretic if the kidneys still make urine, dialysis if they don't. 🧠 “Wet lungs, fat neck, big pulse.” Three findings in a row = FVO. Contrast with FVD

entries.h: 🚨 Critical complication: Hypertensive crisis — Priority key signs!
entries.t: 1 🤕 Headache — often the very first complaint 2 🤢 Nausea & vomiting 3 🧠 Change in mental status — confusion, blurred vision, restlessness Why it happens: retained sodium and water expand the volume, and damaged kidneys keep pumping out renin — pressure climbs until vessels in the brain, eyes and heart are at risk. Act on it: that triad in a renal patient is a report-now finding, not a "recheck in an hour" finding. 🧠 “Head, Hurl, Haze.” Headache → hurling → hazy thinking. Three H's climbing the BP ladder = hypertens
STEP 3 · WHAT FIRST These are the top 2 missed NCLEX questions — and both are decided by one thing: is the HEART already changing?

entries.h: ⚡ The hyperkalemia order — and the rule that decides #1
entries.t: Answer first: ECG changes present → IV calcium gluconate FIRST (it protects the heart muscle). No ECG changes → shift the potassium with IV insulin + dextrose. 1 💉 IV Calcium Gluconate — for dysrhythmias . Stabilizes the heart membrane in minutes. Does NOT lower the K⁺ level — it just buys time. ▼ 2 💉 IV 50% Dextrose + Regular insulin — pushes K⁺ out of the blood and into the cells. Works in ~15–30 min. Only regular insulin goes IV. Watch for hypoglycemia. ▼ 3 💊 Kayexalate (sodium polystyrene sulfonate) — removes K

entries.h: ⭐ Top 2 missed NCLEX questions — worked through
entries.t: Q · End stage renal disease Q · Missed 3 dialysis sessions K⁺ 7.2 , BUN 35 , creatinine 3.8 , urine output 300 mL in 24 hr . Which order is PRIORITY? K⁺ 8.1 , WIDE QRS complexes, HR 58 , lethargy. Which order does the nurse implement FIRST? Choices: IV 50% dextrose & regular insulin · sodium polystyrene sulfonate · hemodialysis · IV calcium gluconate Same menu of choices — but the heart is already changing. ✅ IV 50% Dextrose & regular insulin — no dysrhythmia is described, so shift the potassium fastest. ✅ IV calci

entries.h: 🧠 The trick question: chronic renal failure order list
entries.t: Source's list for chronic renal failure: 1. IV regular insulin & 50% dextrose · 2. IV loop diuretic · 3. Dialysis · 4. “Put in for vacation time?” The joke is the teaching point: the fourth option is a distractor. Renal questions always hide one obviously wrong choice — eliminate it first , then rank the three real ones by who protects the heart soonest . 🧠 Loop diuretics only work if there's a working nephron. In ESRD with no urine, a loop diuretic is nearly useless — that's when the answer becomes dialysis .

entries.h: ✅ What you do at the bedside, right now
entries.t: 🫀 Cardiac monitor on any K⁺ over 5.0 🧪 Recheck the K⁺ — and ask if the sample was hemolyzed (falsely high) 🚫 Stop all potassium: IV fluids with K, salt substitutes, K-sparing diuretics 📋 Review meds for ACE inhibitors / ARBs / NSAIDs that raise K⁺ 📞 Notify the provider with the level AND the rhythm — both drive the order 🧠 Level + Rhythm = the whole report. Never call with just a number; the ECG is what picks the drug. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 3️⃣ The 3 P's Potassium · Priority · Pumps the heart 💉 Squiggle = Gluconate ECG changes → calcium gluconate FIRST 🧺 SPUKA backs up Sodium · Phosphorus · Urea · K⁺ · Acid 🤕 Head · Hurl · Haze = hypertensive crisis · report now

Q1: Why is potassium the priority electrolyte in renal failure? Show answer The 3 P's — Potassium is a Priority since it Pumps the HEART muscles. High K⁺ (over 5.0) causes peaked T waves, ST elevation, wide QRS and cardiac arrest. Q2: Match the K⁺ level to the ECG change. Show answer Peaked T waves: 6–7 mEq/L · ST elevation: 7–8 mEq/L · Wide QRS complex: over 8 mEq/L. Normal K⁺ is 3.5–5.0. Q3: K⁺ 8.5 mEq/L in a client with kidney disease who is weak, lethargic and bradycardic. First order? Show answer IV calcium gl

Nursing interventions, the renal diet food-by-food, and every drug you give vs every drug you avoid . This is where the HESI and Kaplan food questions live. Sisters: NG-047 = master overview & causes · NG-264 = 4 phases & 5 stages · NG-265 = labs & symptoms. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → ⚖️ 1 kg = 1 L Daily weights are the #1 fluid assessment. 1 kg gained = 1 L retained. 🚫
STEP 1 · MONITOR & PROTECT Two jobs, all day long: measure the fluid, and stop anything that would hurt the kidney further.

entries.h: ⚖️ Daily weights — 1 kg = 1 liter of fluid retained
entries.t: Answer first: the scale is a more reliable fluid measure than I&O, because nobody forgets to record a weight the way they forget a urinal. 🧠 “A kilo is a carton of milk 🥛.” One kilogram, one liter, one carton. If she gained two cartons overnight, that fluid is sitting in her lungs — assess breath sounds first .

1 ⚖️ Daily weights — same time, same scale, same clothing. 1 kg = 1 L . 2 💧 Strict I&O — every mL in and out, including ice chips, IV flushes and med volumes. 3 🚰 Fluid restriction — commonly the previous day's urine output plus about 500–600 mL . Amounts vary by facility & provider — follow the order. 4 🫁 Assess lungs, edema, JVD & BP every shift — this is how overload announces itself. 5 🫀 Cardiac monitor whenever K⁺ is over 5.0 . 6 🧪 Track the labs — K⁺, Na⁺, phosphorus, calcium, BUN, creatinine, H&H, pH. 7 🦠 In

entries.h: 🩸 Hemodialysis — the machine version of the kidney
entries.t: Source definition: the machine version of the kidney, used to wash the blood. It is only used for a number of years until a kidney transplant is available. 🖐️ Assess the access every shift: feel the thrill , hear the bruit . No thrill/bruit = clotted = report immediately . 🚫 Never take BP, draw blood, or start an IV in the fistula arm ⚖️ Weigh before and after every treatment — that difference is the fluid removed. 💊 Some meds (especially antihypertensives ) are held before dialysis to prevent hypotension — follow
STEP 2 · FOUR LOWS Low sodium · low potassium · low phosphorus · protein adjusted to the stage. Every food question on the exam comes from these four lists.

NCLEX TIP Renal diets are individualized to the patient's labs and stage by a renal dietitian — the lists above are the ones these exams test. 🧠 “An apple a day keeps the potassium away 🍏.” When a food question involves a high potassium level, look for the apple — it's the answer more often than any other food on the NCLEX.

entries.h: 🧂 NO SODIUM — and NEVER a salt substitute
entries.t: 🥫 No canned / packaged foods 🌭 No processed meats — deli meat, bacon, hot dogs, sausage 🧂 No salt shaker ; season with herbs, lemon, garlic, vinegar 🚫 NO salt substitutes — they are potassium chloride Why: sodium drags water with it → more edema, more hypertension, more work for the heart. HESI Statement that shows a need for further education : “I should reduce my sodium intake by using a salt substitute.” ❌ 🧠 “Salt substitute = Secret Potassium.” The label says salt-free; the bottle is full of K⁺. In renal failur

🥬 Leafy veggies spinach 🥑 Avocados 🥕 Carrots 🍅 Tomatoes sauce & juice too 🍓 Strawberries 🍊 Oranges & orange juice 🍌 Bananas the classic 🍏 APPLES BEST choice ✅ HESI Q: Best food choice for a potassium of 6.5 ? A: Apple slices or apple juice — low K⁺. 🧠 “Bananas, Oranges, Potatoes, Spinach — BOPS your potassium up.” Anything that BOPS — skip it. Reach for the apple.

🥛 No milk · 🍮 no pudding · 🥣 no yogurt NCLEX TIP 🧀 Cheese, ice cream — same problem 🥤 Dark colas, nuts, seeds, whole grains, dried beans Why: phosphorus rises → calcium falls → itching, muscle cramps and brittle bones (renal osteodystrophy) . 🧠 “Phosphorus and calcium ride a seesaw 🎢.” Phos up = calcium down. Cut the dairy, take the binder, save the bones.

KAPLAN Rationale for a low-protein diet? → to preserve renal function . Protein breakdown makes urea — less protein in, less waste for a dying kidney to filter. KAPLAN Teaching is effective when the client says: “I will eat red bell peppers and avoid red meats .” ✅ ⚠️ The exception: once a client is on dialysis , protein needs go UP — dialysis pulls protein out with the waste. Pre-dialysis = restrict; on dialysis = replace. Exact grams are set by the renal dietitian and vary. 🧠 “Before the machine, keep protein lea

entries.h: 🍽️ The four lows on one plate
entries.t: Restrict Say NO to Because Sodium 🧂 Canned/packaged food, processed meats, salt shaker, salt substitutes Water follows salt → edema, HTN, heart failure Potassium 🍌 Bananas, oranges, strawberries, tomatoes, avocado, carrots, spinach, potatoes, salt substitutes K⁺ >5.0 stops the heart Phosphorus 🥛 Milk, yogurt, pudding, cheese, dark colas, nuts Phos up → calcium down → itching & brittle bones Protein 🥩 Red meats (pre-dialysis) Less urea to filter — preserves renal function Fluid 💧 Free water beyond the order — ice ch
STEP 3 · AVOID & GIVE First the five drugs that finish off a kidney — then the ones that replace what the kidney stopped making.

entries.h: 🚫 AVOID: the top drugs that can cause kidney failure
entries.t: 🧠 “No More Very Good Dye” — N SAIDs · M ilk of Magnesia · V ancomycin · G entamicin · D ye. Five words, five ways to finish a kidney.

entries.h: ☢️ Before contrast dye — what the nurse does
entries.t: 🧪 Check the creatinine / GFR first 💧 Hydrate before and after per order — IV fluids protect the kidney 🩸 Ask about metformin and any nephrotoxic meds 🐚 Ask about iodine / shellfish / prior dye reactions 📈 Recheck creatinine after — contrast injury shows up in 24–72 hours 🧠 “Cement in the washer.” Picture pouring wet concrete into a washing machine — that's contrast dye in a fragile kidney. Flush it out with fluids or it sets.

💊 Magnesium- or aluminum-containing antacids — the kidney can't clear them 🧂 Potassium-sparing diuretics & K⁺ supplements — no pee, no K ❤️ ACE inhibitors / ARBs — protective in chronic proteinuric CKD, but they raise K⁺ and are usually held in acute injury . Monitor K⁺ and creatinine. 💓 Digoxin and many others are cleared by the kidney → doses must be reduced ; watch for toxicity 🧠 “Renal dose everything.” A normal dose in a failing kidney becomes an overdose by tomorrow.

entries.h: 💊 GIVE: replacing what the kidney stopped doing
entries.t: Problem Drug Nursing pearl Anemia 🩸 Epoetin alfa / darbepoetin + iron Replaces missing erythropoietin. Monitor BP — it can rise. Hgb is titrated to a target, not maxed out. High phosphorus 🦴 Phosphate binders — calcium acetate, sevelamer Give WITH meals — they bind the phosphorus in the food. Given between meals they do nothing. Low calcium / vit D ☀️ Calcitriol (activated vitamin D) The kidney normally activates vitamin D; now it can't. High potassium 🫀 Sodium polystyrene sulfonate (Kayexalate); insulin + D50; cal

entries.h: 🍽️ Phosphate binder timing — see it once, never miss it
entries.t: 🧠 Binder = a net 🥅. You only catch fish while the fish are swimming by. No meal = no fish = no point.

entries.h: 📚 Teaching she can hand the patient
entries.t: ⚖️ Weigh yourself every morning , same scale, same clothes — call for a gain of 2–3 lb in a day or 5 lb in a week ( threshold varies — use your provider's number ) 🧂 Read every label for sodium, potassium, phosphorus 🚫 No OTC ibuprofen/naproxen — ask before any new medicine or supplement 🩹 Protect the fistula arm — no BP cuffs, no blood draws, no tight sleeves or jewelry 💉 Keep vaccinations current; report fever early 🗓️ Never skip dialysis — missed sessions are how potassium reaches 8.0+ 🧠 “Scale, Label, No-Ibupro

SAY IT OUT LOUD ⚖️ 1 kg = 1 L Daily weight, same time, same scale, same clothes 🚫 “No More Very Good Dye” NSAIDs · MOM · Vancomycin · Gentamicin · Dye 🍏 Apple = the answer Low potassium — apple slices or apple juice 💊 Binders WITH meals No food = no phosphorus to bind = no point

Assess breath sounds and respiratory status first — that fluid goes to the lungs. Then edema, JVD, BP. Q2: Name the top drugs to avoid because they can cause kidney failure. Show answer NSAIDs · Milk of Magnesia (magnesium antacid) · antibiotics vancomycin and gentamicin · CT contrast dye ("thick cement in the washer — contrast kills the kidney!"). entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🫘 Transplant 🔪 Biopsy ⚖️ Before & after ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Renal + Fluid · Procedures

Kidney Transplant & Renal Biopsy — prep, priority, and what goes wrong NG-267 RENAL + FLUID ADHD-friendly visual edition One procedure gives a kidney 🫘, the other takes a piece of one 🔪. That difference sets everything else: the transplant's enemy is REJECTION & INFECTION , the biopsy's enemy is BLEEDING . Learn the prep, the position, and the one thing you assess first afterward. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 💊 Transplant BEFORE Immunosuppressants — started before surgery to prevent organ rejection.
GIVING A KIDNEY A donor kidney is placed low in the abdomen — the old kidneys usually stay right where they are.

entries.h: 🫘 Where the new kidney actually goes
entries.t: 🧠 “New kidney rides shotgun.” The graft sits low and in front, not up under the ribs — that's why the nurse can feel the transplant and why site pain is such a useful assessment.

Started before the transplant to help prevent organ rejection — and continued for life . Calcineurin inhibitors — tacrolimus, cyclosporine Antiproliferative — mycophenolate Corticosteroids — prednisone (“-sone”) Never stop an immunosuppressant because the client “feels fine” — feeling fine is the drug working. Stopping it is how a graft is lost. 🧠 Immunosuppressants = the price of the kidney. They buy acceptance of the organ and they sell you infection risk. Every teaching point after transplant is one of those two

entries.h: 💧 AFTER: watch the urine output like a hawk
entries.t: 🧠 “30 is the floor.” Under 30 mL/hr is the single number that turns a routine post-op check into a phone call.

entries.h: ⭐ Rejection vs Infection — the two things you're watching for
entries.t: EXAM TIP Rejection and infection overlap — both give fever and malaise. The tie-breakers: rejection adds HIGH BP and PAIN OVER THE GRAFT; infection leads with a LOW-GRADE FEVER. 🧠 “Rejection Rises, Infection Simmers.” Rejection rises — BP up, creatinine up, weight up. Infection simmers — a low-grade temp and nothing else obvious. Report either one.

Q: Teaching for a client with end-stage kidney disease awaiting a kidney transplant ? A: “Hemodialysis is sometimes needed after the surgery.” The new kidney does not always wake up right away — that's called delayed graft function, and dialysis bridges the gap until it works. 💊 Lifelong immunosuppressants , taken at the same time every day, never skipped. 🦠 Infection precautions: hand hygiene, avoid crowds & sick contacts, no live vaccines . 🌡️ Report any fever , even a low one, plus site pain or a drop in urine o
TAKING A PIECE A tissue sample is taken from the kidney to determine specific diseases — and the kidney is one of the bloodiest organs you can stick a needle into.

entries.h: 🔬 What it is and how it's done
entries.t: A tissue sample is taken from the kidney to determine specific diseases — it's how glomerulonephritis, nephrotic syndrome, lupus nephritis and transplant rejection get confirmed instead of guessed at. 🧠 Prone with a pillow = “push the kidney to the surface.” Face down, belly propped, breath held — three things that stop the needle from missing.

entries.h: 🚨 BEFORE: discontinue blood thinners at least 7 DAYS before
entries.t: Never assume “nothing” means nothing — ask specifically about herbals, vitamins and fish oil . Clients do not think of supplements as medicine, and every one of these thins the blood. 🧠 “Check your EGOS at the door.” E -vitamin E · G -Ginkgo, Ginseng, Garlic · O -Omega-3 · S -St John's Wort. Leave the EGOS outside for 7 days before a biopsy.

entries.h: ⭐ AFTER — the PRIORITY is vital signs every 15 minutes for the 1st hour
entries.t: Then: bed rest per protocol (often 24 hours ), push fluids to flush the tract, and teach no heavy lifting or strenuous activity for about 2 weeks . 🧠 “15-15-15-15.” Four sets of vitals in the first hour, then lie on it. The whole point of the position is to squash the hole you just made in a very vascular organ. ⚖️
THE DECIDING CLUE Same organ, opposite worries: the transplant fears the immune system, the biopsy fears the blood.

entries.h: ⚖️ Side-by-side — the whole comparison in one table
entries.t: 🫘 KIDNEY TRANSPLANT 🔪 RENAL BIOPSY Purpose Replace a failed kidney in end-stage kidney disease Take a tissue sample to determine specific diseases Key BEFORE Immunosuppressants to prevent organ rejection Stop blood thinners ≥ 7 days — including supplements Position Post-op semi-Fowler's; graft sits in the lower abdomen DURING: prone, pillow under abdomen · AFTER: on their back, on the affected side Priority AFTER Hourly urine output — ≤30 mL/hr = kidneys in distress Vital signs every 15 min for the 1st hour Top com

entries.h: 🚨 Bonus emergency: hyperkalemia in end-stage kidney disease
entries.t: Kidneys that don't work can't dump potassium — and a high K⁺ is what stops the heart. Which orders would you anticipate? Also seen: IV calcium gluconate to protect the heart muscle while the other measures work, and sodium polystyrene sulfonate to pull potassium out through the gut. 🧠 “Shift it, Spill it, Suck it out.” Shift with insulin+D50 · Spill it with a loop diuretic · Suck it out with dialysis. Only the last one is a cure.

💧 Strict I&O and hourly output early on. 🩺 Vital signs on a schedule — trends beat single readings. 🩸 Watch H&H , BUN , creatinine and potassium . 👀 Look at the urine every time — color is free data. 🌡️ Report fever , site pain, or a change in output. 📝 Confirm informed consent is signed before either procedure. 🧠 Vitals, output, urine color. Three things you can check in ninety seconds that catch both hemorrhage and rejection.

❌ Waiting for a high fever after transplant — a low-grade temp is the #1 infection sign. ❌ Thinking supplements are harmless — EGOS thin the blood just like warfarin. ❌ Getting a post-biopsy client up to walk — bed rest , lying on the affected side. ❌ Charting output of 25 mL/hr after transplant without calling — that's distress . ❌ Giving an NSAID for post-procedure pain — bleeding risk and nephrotoxic. 🧠 Small numbers, big deal. A temp of 99.8°F and an output of 25 mL/hr both look boring on a flowsheet and both a

SAY IT OUT LOUD 💊 Immunosuppressants BEFORE transplant — prevent organ rejection, taken for life 💧 30 mL/hr or LESS = kidneys in distress after transplant 🌡️ Low-grade fever = #1 infection sign · rejection = HTN + pain at site 🩸 Biopsy: 7 days off thinners then VS q15 min × 1 hr, on the affected side

Q1: Post kidney transplant, output has been 26 mL/hr for two hours. What does that mean? Show answer 30 mL/hr or less = kidneys in distress. Report it — think rejection, obstruction or a vascular problem with the graft. Q2: What is the #1 sign of infection in a transplant client? Show answer A LOW-GRADE fever. Immunosuppressants blunt the immune response, so there may be no high fever, no redness and no pus. Q3: Two signs of organ rejection? Show answer Hypertension and pain/tenderness at the graft site. Also decre

UA — Urine Analysis · read every line on the strip NG-269 RENAL + FLUID ADHD-friendly visual edition A UA is a picture of the kidney taken through the toilet 🚽. Each pad on the strip answers one question: how hydrated? · is there infection? · is there bleeding? · is protein or sugar leaking? Learn the normal band for each line and abnormal jumps off the page. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 💡 Light = hydrated Dark = dehydrated — unless on diuretics, SIADH or DI. 💧 Spec. gravity 1.003–1.030 1.003 = liqu
STEP 1 · A DIRTY SAMPLE IS A WRONG ANSWER Half of UA test questions are not about the result at all — they are about how you got the specimen.

Never collect a specimen from the urine drainage bag — that urine is old, warm and not sterile. It will grow bacteria that were never in the client. 🧠 “Clean, Skip, Catch, Ship.” Clean the area · skip the first squirt · catch the middle · ship it to the lab in an hour. First morning void is the most concentrated and the best sample when you get a choice.

entries.h: ⭐ Sterile specimen from a Foley — the exact 4 steps KAPLAN
entries.t: 🧠 “Clamp · Chill · Cleanse · Collect.” Four C's in order. Forget the clamp and there is nothing at the port to draw; forget to unclamp and you just gave the client urinary retention.

Discard the first void and write down the time — that's the start. Save every drop for the next 24 hours. At the end time, have the client void one last time and add it in . Keep the container on ice or refrigerated . One missed void = start over . ❌ 🧠 “Toss the first, keep the last.” The one you throw away is the urine made before the clock started — it doesn't belong to your 24 hours.

entries.h: 🔬 What a full UA actually reports
entries.t: Physical: color · clarity · odor · specific gravity Chemical (the dipstick): pH · protein · glucose · ketones · blood · nitrites · leukocyte esterase · bilirubin Microscopic: RBCs · WBCs · bacteria · casts · crystals · epithelial cells 🧠 Look · Dip · Scope. Three layers, in that order — and the exam question almost always lives in the dip layer. 🔎
STEP 2 · LOW · NORMAL · HIGH Every line gets a bar. Find where the client's number lands, and the diagnosis walks up to you.

entries.h: 🎨 COLOR — the fastest hydration read in nursing
entries.t: 🧠 Think lemonade → iced tea. Lemonade urine = well watered. Iced-tea urine = dry as a bone. Cola-colored is a whole different alarm — that's blood or myoglobin.

entries.h: ⭐ Every UA component on a low–normal–high bar
entries.t: HIGH YIELD Green band = normal. Anything outside it has a name. 🧠 “Nothing should be in pee but pee.” Protein, glucose, ketones, blood, nitrites and leukocytes should all read negative . The moment one turns positive, it names its own disease.

entries.h: 🩸 RBC in urine = hematuria — the big three causes
entries.t: 🪨 Kidney stones — the stone scrapes the tract on the way down. 🎗️ Bladder cancer — classic clue is painless hematuria. 🔪 Post-operative TURP — some pink drainage is expected ; bright red with clots is not . Also on the list: trauma, glomerulonephritis, anticoagulants, and a menstruating client (recollect). 🧠 “Stones, Suspicious growth, Surgery.” Three S's that put blood in the bowl (the growth is bladder carcinoma ). Painful hematuria = stone. Painless hematuria = cancer until proven otherwise.

Finding What it means WBC / leukocyte esterase Inflammation or infection — usually a UTI Nitrites Gram-negative bacteria present → think pyeloNephritis Cloudy + foul odor Pus and bacteria in the specimen WBC casts Infection is up in the kidney , not just the bladder 🧠 Bladder burns, kidney BLOWS UP. Cystitis = burning + frequency. Pyelonephritis adds fever, chills, and CVA/flank tenderness — that's the one you escalate.

entries.h: 🔬 Under the microscope — casts tell you WHERE the damage is
entries.t: 🧠 Casts are molds of the tubule. Whatever was sitting in the tubule got shaped like a tube and washed out — so a cast proves the problem is inside the kidney, not the bladder.

entries.h: 🧫 Urine Culture & Sensitivity — two different answers
entries.t: ⏱️ Order of operations: Draw the culture BEFORE the first dose of antibiotic. Then start the broad-spectrum drug; narrow it when sensitivities return. 🧠 “Culture = WHO. Sensitivity = WHAT KILLS IT.” Culture the criminal, sentence it with the sensitivity. 🩺
STEP 3 · MATCH THE PATTERN Test questions never give you one value — they give you a panel and dare you to pick the one that matters.

entries.h: ⭐ NCLEX exhibit — read the whole UA, then answer
entries.t: Client with a history of diabetes . The UA reads: Component Result Normal? Specific gravity 1.030 🚩 top of range — concentrated / dry Protein None ✅ normal — rules OUT nephrotic syndrome Glucose High 🚩 abnormal — diabetes / hyperglycemia Red blood cells None ✅ normal — rules OUT stones & bladder CA Leukocytes Medium 🚩 abnormal — infection What does the nurse suspect? Dehydration from low fluid intake, plus a possible UTI. The high specific gravity says dry ; the leukocytes say infection ; the glucose just confirms

entries.h: 🧪 Common NCLEX blood panel — which value is the kidney red flag?
entries.t: 🧠 Creatinine is the kidney's own handwriting. BUN can be raised by dehydration, steroids, a GI bleed or a steak dinner — creatinine only climbs when the filter is broken.

entries.h: 🚨 UA findings you escalate, not chart
entries.t: 🩸 Gross hematuria with clots — especially after TURP or biopsy. 🌡️ Nitrites + fever + flank pain → pyelonephritis, needs antibiotics now. 🥩 New heavy proteinuria + edema → nephrotic syndrome workup. 💧 Urine output under 30 mL/hr → kidneys in distress. 🟤 Cola / tea-colored urine after crush injury or a statin → rhabdomyolysis. 🧠 Color + fever + output. Three things you can assess without a lab — and any two of them together buy a phone call to the provider.

💧 Fluids 2–3 L/day unless fluid-restricted for renal or cardiac disease. 🚽 Void every 2–4 hours and always after intercourse . 🧻 Wipe front to back , cotton underwear, no bubble baths or douches. 💊 Finish the entire antibiotic course even after the burning stops. ⚠️ Tell them phenazopyridine turns urine bright orange — it's harmless and it stains clothing. 🧠 “Flush, wipe, finish.” Water flushes bacteria out, wiping keeps them from getting in, and finishing the antibiotic keeps them from coming back stronger. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 💧 1.003 vs 1.030 liquidy body vs dry body 🩸 RBC in urine = stones · bladder cancer · post-op TURP 🦠 WBC = UTI · N = pyeloNephritis nitrites climb to the kidney 🥩 Protein high = Nephrotic 🍬 Glucose high = Diabetes

Q1: Specific gravity is 1.003. Wet or dry? Show answer Wet — a liquidy body. Dilute urine from over-hydration, diuretics or diabetes insipidus. 1.030 is the dry, concentrated end. Q2: Nitrites are positive. What are you thinking? Show answer Look for the “N” — Nitrites means pyeloNephritis, a kidney infection. Bacteria convert nitrates to nitrites. Q3: List the exact steps to get a sterile specimen from a Foley. Show answer 1) Clamp the drainage tube below the port. 2) Wait 15–30 minutes. 3) Scrub the port with an
