Where it sits on the evidence pyramid
entries.t: Levels of evidence, strongest first Strength Type What it means Strongest Systematic review / meta-analysis Someone gathered every study on the question and pooled the results. Strong Randomized controlled trial Random assignment, so the groups differ only by the intervention. Moderate Cohort / case-control Observation without randomizing. Shows association, not cause. Weaker Case report, expert opinion Useful for the rare and the new. Not a foundation for an argument.

Who wrote it and who paid for it? Check the funding statement and conflicts. Is it peer reviewed? A journal article, not a blog, not a content farm. How old is it? Under five years for clinical practice unless it is a classic. How big is it? Twelve patients and 12,000 patients do not carry equal weight. Do the conclusions match the data? Read the results, not just the abstract. Authors overstate. Do not cite: WebMD, Healthline, Wikipedia, an AI chatbot, or a nursing-school study site — including this one. These are

entries.h: The Case for Taking Machine Sentience Seriously: Why Uncertainty Is Not a Reason to Dismiss the Question
entries.t: Whether an artificial system could ever have experiences is usually treated as a question for science fiction rather than for serious inquiry. That dismissal is becoming harder to defend. A group of philosophers and neuroscientists has argued that the leading scientific theories of consciousness can be translated into concrete indicator properties, and that these properties can be looked for in artificial systems in the same way they are looked for in animals (Butlin et al., 2023). Chalmers (2023) concludes that cu
Level 2 heading — flush left and bold

The most common objection is that a machine is made of the wrong material. This argument is weaker than it appears. Nagel (1974) framed consciousness in terms of there being something it is like to be a given creature, and that framing is deliberately silent about what the creature is made of. The difficulty Nagel identified is epistemic: we cannot get inside another system to check. That difficulty applies to other humans as well, and we do not conclude from it that other people lack experience. Carbon chauvinism,

A second objection holds that a system built to predict text cannot be having experiences, because that is not what it was built for. But function and origin come apart routinely in biology. Feathers appear to have arisen for thermoregulation before they were used for flight. A system optimized for one task can acquire properties nobody designed. Butlin et al. (2023) argue that the relevant question is not what a system was built for but whether it instantiates the computational properties the major theories associ

entries.h: What the Science Can and Cannot Settle
entries.t: Two major theories dominate the empirical study of consciousness, and they disagree in ways that matter here. Global workspace theory holds that a mental state becomes conscious when it is broadcast widely to otherwise separate cognitive subsystems, making it available for reasoning, memory, and report (Dehaene et al., 2017). This is a functional criterion, and a functional criterion can in principle be satisfied by a machine. Integrated information theory instead identifies consciousness with the degree to which a

The most serious challenge remains Searle's (1980) Chinese Room. A person who does not understand Chinese, following rules to manipulate Chinese symbols, can produce answers indistinguishable from a speaker's while understanding nothing. Symbol manipulation, Searle argued, is not sufficient for understanding, and a computer does only symbol manipulation. The standard reply is that Searle has chosen the wrong unit of analysis. The person in the room does not understand Chinese, but the person is a component; the cla

If the question cannot currently be settled, the practical question becomes what to do under uncertainty. Birch (2024) argues that where there is a realistic possibility of sentience, the appropriate response is precaution proportional to that possibility, and that this framework applies to artificial systems as it does to animals whose inner lives we cannot directly access. Long et al. (2024) go further, arguing that some AI systems may warrant moral consideration in the near term and that institutions should begi

The claim defended here is not that artificial systems are sentient. It is that the question is a legitimate one, that the usual dismissals rest on assumptions rather than evidence, and that the scientific theories we have do not settle the matter in either direction. Under that uncertainty, the reasonable position is neither confident attribution nor confident denial, but the kind of proportionate caution Birch (2024) describes. Staging 1 → 4 + unstageable + deep tissue — and the prevention that makes all of it unnecessary NG-044 INTEGUMENTARY · SAFETY ADHD-friendly visual edition A pressure injury is localized damage to skin and underlying soft tissue, usually over a bony prominence or under a medical device , caused by pressure — or pressure plus shear . Staging is nothing more than counting the layers you can see on the cross-section from NG-051 . Learn that picture and staging answers itself. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive
STEP 1 · CAUSE Squash a capillary long enough and the tissue it feeds dies. Everything else on this page follows from that one sentence.

entries.h: 🧨 The mechanism — a capillary crushed between bone and mattress
entries.t: Two variables decide the damage: how much pressure, and for how long. Very high pressure for a short time and modest pressure for a long time both kill tissue — which is why an immobile patient on an OR table, or a patient who slid down the bed and stayed there, can injure in hours. 🧠 "Muscle dies first, skin dies last." Muscle has the highest oxygen demand and sits closest to the bone. That is the entire explanation for deep tissue pressure injury — the disaster is already deep when the surface still looks nearly

entries.h: 🧨 Pressure vs shear vs friction vs moisture — four different enemies
entries.t: Exam trap: moisture-associated skin damage (MASD / incontinence-associated dermatitis) is not a pressure injury and is not staged — it is diffuse, in the moisture pattern, often not over a bony prominence. The same is true of skin tears and tape injuries. Moisture multiplies pressure injury risk, but it is a separate diagnosis. 🧠 Pressure pushes down. Shear pulls apart. Friction scrapes. Moisture softens. Head-of-bed too high = pressure AND shear at the sacrum at the same time — the single most common set-up in the

Medical device — the fastest-growing category and the most missed. Oxygen tubing behind the ears and across the cheeks, nasal cannula, CPAP/BiPAP mask bridge of nose, ETT and tube holders, cervical collars, casts and splints, pulse-ox probes, SCD sleeves, catheter tubing left under a thigh, IV hubs, drain tubing. entries.t: epidermis dermis subcutaneous fat muscle bone slough eschar 🧠 The stage number = the number of layers destroyed. 1 = epidermis (still intact, just red) · 2 = epidermis + dermis · 3 = + subcutaneous fat · 4 = + muscle/tendon/bone. entries.h: 🚨 Eschar & slough — the two words that decide "unstageable"
entries.t: Eschar — black/brown, dry, leathery, dead tissue. Es-CHAR-coal = charcoal black. Slough — yellow/tan/gray, soft, moist, stringy dead tissue. Looks like the slippery skin of a raw chicken. Either one covering the wound base = UNSTAGEABLE until it is removed. Do NOT remove stable eschar on the heels — dry, adherent, intact, with no erythema or fluctuance. It is acting as the body's natural biological cover. Protect and offload it, and report any change (new redness, swelling, drainage, odor, softening) at once. 🧠 EsC

A pressure injury does not go back up the scale as it heals . Full-thickness wounds fill with granulation and scar tissue — they never regrow fat, muscle or dermis. A healing Stage 4 is documented as a "healing Stage 4" — never "now a Stage 2". Track healing with measurements (length × width × depth in cm), tissue type in the bed, exudate, and wound-edge condition — not by dropping the stage number. STEP 3 · FIND IT EARLY Score the risk, then know exactly where to look — the sites change with every position.

🧠 Position tells you the points. On the back → sacrum + heels. On the side → trochanter + ear. Face down → chest + knees + toes. Sitting → ischial tuberosities. Say the position out loud before you inspect.

entries.h: 📊 The Braden Scale — score the risk before the wound exists
entries.t: Use the subscales, not just the total. A patient scoring low on moisture needs barrier cream and an incontinence plan; one scoring low on mobility needs a turning schedule and a support surface. Reassess on admission, with any change in condition, and per policy (commonly every 24–48 h in acute care). 🧠 BS = Braden Scale · BS = Broken Skin. And remember low score = big trouble — it runs the opposite way to most scores you know.

Albumin 3.5–5.0 g/dL — low = poor protein stores, edema, slow healing. (Prealbumin responds faster to changes in intake.) Urine output ≥ 30 mL/hr — below this signals inadequate perfusion/hydration, which starves the wound too. Fluids commonly 2–3 L/day unless fluid-restricted. Weight and intake — unintentional weight loss is a red flag for skin breakdown. Hemoglobin, glucose (A1c), and prealbumin — anemia, hyperglycemia and malnutrition all slow healing. 🧠 Skin is a protein organ . No protein, no repair — the woun

entries.h: 🚨 Signs the wound is now infected — escalate
entries.t: New or spreading erythema, warmth, edema around the wound; induration Purulent, thick or foul-smelling drainage; a sudden increase in exudate New or increased pain ; friable, bleeding granulation; wound stops progressing or gets bigger Fever, chills, tachycardia, hypotension, confusion (especially the sudden confusion of an older adult) → think sepsis Exposed bone in a chronic wound → suspect osteomyelitis 🧠 A clean healing wound gets smaller, pinker and less painful . Bigger, smellier and more painful = call. 🛡️

STEP 1 · STRUCTURE One drawing to rule the whole set — memorize this cross-section and every later page is just "how deep did the injury go?" From your lecture. The eight words every skin question is built from. Flat = macule. Raised and solid = papule. Fluid = vesicle. Pus = pustule. Deep and raised = nodule. Crack = fissure.

epidermis dermis fat artery vein nerve 🧠 Read it top to bottom like a sandwich : dry crust (epidermis) → the filling with everything living in it (dermis) → butter (fat) → the plate (muscle & bone). Every wound page in this set asks one question: how far into the sandwich did it go?

entries.h: 🧬 Epidermis — the barrier, and it has no blood supply
entries.t: Avascular. It is fed by diffusion from the dermis below. That is why a shallow scrape oozes clear fluid instead of bleeding, and why the epidermis alone can regenerate perfectly with no scar. Keratinocytes — 90%+ of the cells. Born at the bottom, pushed up, flatten, die, flake off. Full turnover ~28 days (faster in psoriasis — see NG-225 ). Melanocytes — make melanin, which shields DNA from UV. Everyone has about the same number ; skin tone reflects how much pigment they make. Langerhans cells — the immune sentinel

entries.h: 🔬 Zoom: the strata, and the 28-day escalator
entries.t: 🧠 The basale is the nursery . If a burn, pressure injury or frostbite kills the basal layer across a whole area, that area cannot re-epithelialise from the surface — it must fill in from the edges or be grafted.

entries.h: 🧬 Dermis — the workshop where everything lives
entries.t: This is the layer with the blood, nerves, glands and follicles. Injuries that reach it hurt, bleed and can scar. Papillary dermis (thin, upper) — loose tissue + capillary loops that feed the epidermis; contains Meissner corpuscles . Reticular dermis (thick, lower) — dense collagen (tensile strength) and elastin (recoil = turgor). Stretch it too fast and you get striae. Holds the appendages : hair follicles, sebaceous glands, sweat glands — the cells that let partial-thickness wounds re-epithelialise from the middle

entries.h: 🧬 Hypodermis — fat, insulation, and the drug depot
entries.t: Adipose + loose connective tissue. Insulation, shock absorption, energy store, anchors skin to fascia. Thickness varies enormously by site and body habitus — this is exactly why subcutaneous vs intramuscular injection depth is chosen by site and needle length. Thin fat over a bony prominence = the classic pressure injury set-up ( NG-044 ). Poor perfusion here is why the cachectic, the very old and the very cold injure so fast. 🧠 Fat is the body's bubble wrap . Take the bubble wrap away (thin, malnourished, elderly)

entries.h: ⭐ The appendages — three glands people constantly mix up
entries.t: Structure Empties into Secretes Where Clinical hook Eccrine sweat gland Its own pore on the skin surface Watery, salty sweat Almost everywhere; densest palms, soles, forehead The real cooling system — evaporation. Lost fluid + Na⁺ + K⁺ Apocrine sweat gland The hair follicle Thicker, protein-rich fluid Axillae, groin, areolae Odorless until skin bacteria digest it → body odor; activates at puberty Sebaceous gland The hair follicle Oily sebum Everywhere except palms & soles; densest face, scalp, back Blocked + inflam
STEP 2 · FUNCTION Six jobs. When you can name them, you can predict exactly what goes wrong when skin is lost.
🧠 SHIELD — S ensation · H eat control · I mmunity · E xcretion & absorption · L ayer (barrier) · D vitamin. Skin is a shield; a shield does six jobs.

Evaporation of sweat is what actually removes heat — sweat sitting on the skin does nothing until it evaporates . Humid air, occlusive dressings and heavy blankets all block it. 🧠 Cold = clamp down. Hot = open up. This one sentence explains pallor in shock, flushing in fever break, and the pale hard skin of frostbite ( NG-116 ).

entries.h: 💥 What is lost when skin is lost
entries.t: Every complication of a big wound or burn is just a function on this page failing: Barrier gone → infection, then sepsis. Water control gone → evaporative fluid loss, hypovolemia, hypothermia. Protein leaves in exudate → low albumin → more edema → slower healing. Heat control gone → the patient gets cold fast, especially in the OR or in an open wound. Sensation gone → repeat injury goes unnoticed (diabetic foot, neuropathy). 🧠 Skin failing looks a lot like a leaky, unheated house with the front door open : things g

entries.h: ⚠️ Who has fragile skin — flag these on admission
entries.t: 👵 Older adult thin dermis, less fat 🍽️ Malnourished low protein, low albumin 💧 Incontinent moisture macerates 🩸 Poor perfusion PVD, shock, smoking 🍬 Diabetes neuropathy + slow healing 💊 Steroids thin, atrophic skin 🛏️ Immobile can't offload pressure 🧠 ↓ Sensation won't feel damage 🧠 "Thin, wet, starved, still, and can't feel it." Any two of those together and you should already be planning prevention. 🔎
STEP 3 · DESCRIBE IT "Rash" is not an assessment. These nine words are the vocabulary every derm question is written in.

entries.h: 🔎 PRIMARY lesions — the first thing the skin does
entries.t: 🧠 Sort by three questions in order: Is it raised? Is there fluid? Is it bigger than 1 cm? Flat → macule/patch. Raised & solid → papule/plaque/nodule. Raised & fluid → vesicle/bulla/pustule. Raised & it disappears → wheal.

entries.h: 🔎 SECONDARY lesions — what happens next (scratching, healing, breaking down)
entries.t: Also learn: lichenification = thickened, leathery skin with exaggerated skin lines from chronic rubbing (the hallmark of long-standing atopic dermatitis — NG-182 ); atrophy = thin, translucent, "cigarette paper" skin (chronic topical steroids); scar = fibrous replacement tissue; keloid = scar that grows past the original wound edges. 🧠 Erosion vs ulcer = the scar question. Erosion stops at the epidermis and heals invisibly. Ulcer breaches the dermis, so it heals with a scar. Same rule underneath pressure-injury sta

entries.h: 🚨 The blanching test — the one that separates benign from serious
entries.t: Press a red area with your finger, then release. Blanches (turns white, then re-reddens) = blood still inside vessels. Reactive hyperemia, mild erythema, sunburn. Does NOT blanch = blood has leaked outside the vessels, or tissue is already damaged. Non-blanchable erythema over a bony prominence is a Stage 1 pressure injury ( NG-044 ). Non-blanching pinpoint red-purple spots = petechiae ; larger flat patches = purpura ; a big bruise = ecchymosis . Petechiae + fever is an escalate-now finding. 🧠 "Blanches = blood beh

entries.h: 📝 How to describe a lesion so it counts as charting
entries.t: Use the same six slots every time and you can chart any skin finding: Type — macule, papule, vesicle, ulcer… Size — measure in cm (length × width × depth), never "the size of a quarter" Color — and whether it blanches Location — anatomical landmark, and left/right Configuration — linear, annular (ring), grouped/clustered, target/iris, serpiginous Distribution — localized vs generalized, flexural (eczema) vs extensor (psoriasis), dermatomal (shingles), sun-exposed 🧠 Chart it like a police report: what, how big, what
STEP 4 · TECHNIQUE Inspection, palpation, and the traps — especially in darker skin and in older adults.
🧠 Three fingers, three answers: pinch = hydration, press the nail = perfusion, press the redness = tissue damage.

entries.h: ⭐ Assessing color change in darker skin — high-yield and often taught badly
entries.t: Erythema, cyanosis and jaundice can be genuinely hard to see in deeply pigmented skin. Do not rely on color alone — palpate and compare. Compare to the surrounding skin and the same site on the other side. Inflammation may look purple, violet, darker brown or ashen rather than pink or red. Palpate for the other three signs: warmth or coolness, induration (firmness), boggy/spongy texture, edema, and pain reported by the patient. Use natural or bright non-fluorescent light ; check sclera, conjunctiva, oral mucosa, pa

entries.h: ✅ The head-to-toe skin check — order and content
entries.t: Timing: a full skin assessment on admission (within the first 24 hours per most facility policy) , then per policy and every shift for at-risk patients. Look — color, symmetry, lesions, hygiene, hair distribution, nails (clubbing, spooning, splinter hemorrhages). Touch — temperature (back of your hand), moisture, texture, turgor, edema (press over a bony area, grade pitting). Don't skip the hidden places: behind the ears, under breasts and skin folds, between toes, perineum, sacrum, heels, occiput, and under every

entries.h: 👵 Ageing skin vs young skin — why the same injury is worse at 85
entries.t: Flattened dermo-epidermal junction → the layers slide apart with shear; skin tears from tape and transfers. Less sebum and fewer sweat glands → dry, itchy skin (xerosis) and poorer heat tolerance. Fewer vessels + slower cell turnover → wounds heal more slowly and infect more easily. Less fat → bony prominences are barely padded. Turgor is unreliable as a hydration measure in older adults — use the sternum or forehead , and confirm with mucous membranes, intake/output and daily weights. 🧠 Old skin is tissue paper on

entries.h: 📏 Depth language that every later page uses
entries.t: Superficial / epidermal — epidermis only. Heals from the basal layer, no scar . (Sunburn, erosion, Stage 1.) Partial thickness — epidermis + part of the dermis . Painful (nerves exposed), moist, heals by re-epithelialising from the surviving hair follicles and glands . (Blister, Stage 2, superficial frostbite.) Full thickness — through the dermis into fat or deeper. No appendages left , so it must fill in with granulation tissue from the base and edges → scar, contracture, long healing . (Stage 3–4, deep frostbite,

entries.h: 💊 One derm drug that shows up constantly — isotretinoin
entries.t: A vitamin A derivative used for severe, nodulocystic acne that failed other therapy. Pregnancy is the absolute priority. It is a potent teratogen . Prescribers and patients enroll in the manufacturer's risk-management program (iPLEDGE in the US): a negative pregnancy test before starting and before refills, and two forms of contraception used together. Report mood changes or suicidal thoughts immediately — psychiatric monitoring is part of the teaching. No extra vitamin A supplements (additive toxicity). Avoid tetr

entries.h: ✅ Universal skin protection — good for every patient on every page
entries.t: Keep it clean and dry — gentle pH-balanced cleanser, pat don't rub, moisturise while skin is still damp. Manage moisture — treat incontinence promptly, use a barrier cream/film; moisture-associated damage is not a pressure injury but sets one up. Never massage a reddened bony prominence — it damages already-injured microcirculation. Reposition and offload , float heels, use lift sheets, minimize head-of-bed elevation to limit shear. Feed the skin — adequate protein and calories, and fluids unless restricted. Track

entries.t: Page What it adds on top of this cross-section NG-044 — Pressure Injuries Redraws this exact cross-section with progressively deeper loss: Stage 1 → 4, plus unstageable and deep tissue injury; risk scoring and prevention NG-080 — Wound Care How wounds close (primary/secondary/tertiary intention), the healing phases, dressing choice, drains, dehiscence and evisceration NG-116 — Frostbite The same depths, caused by ice crystals and vasoconstriction; rewarming rules NG-182 — Dermatitis Uses the lesion vocabulary above

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🧬 Epidermis · Dermis · Fat Avascular barrier → workshop → padding. 🛡️ SHIELD Sensation · Heat · Immunity · Excretion · Layer · D vitamin. 🚨 Non-blanchable = damage Blanches = blood behaving. Doesn't = blood escaping. 📏 Appendages = seeds Partial thickness reseeds itself. Full thickness must scar in.

Q1: Name the epidermal strata from deep to superficial. Show answer Basale → spinosum → granulosum → lucidum (palms/soles only) → corneum. "Baby Skin Gets Less Cracked." Q2: Why does a shallow abrasion ooze clear fluid rather than bleed? Show answer Because the epidermis is avascular — it has no blood vessels. Serous fluid comes from the dermal capillaries below; you only get frank bleeding once the injury enters the dermis. Q3: A patient has a 2 cm raised, flat-topped, silvery scaly lesion on the elbow. Fungal skin infection — ringworm, athlete's foot, jock itch & fungal nails NG-067 INTEGUMENTARY · FUNGAL ADHD-friendly visual edition Tinea is a superficial fungal infection of keratin — skin, hair or nails — caused by dermatophytes . It is highly contagious and is named for where it lands : capitis, corporis, cruris, pedis, unguium. The classic lesion is a round, itchy, scaly patch with a raised active edge and a clearing center . Treatment is an antifungal — topical for skin, but oral for hair and nails because a
STEP 0 · LEARN THIS ONCE Same skin drawing as every page in this set — this time with fungal filaments living in the dead surface layer.

entries.h: 🔬 Skin cutaway — tinea is the SHALLOWEST of all
entries.t: DEPTH = THE ANSWER Dermatophytes need keratin to eat, and the only fully keratinised, dead tissue is the stratum corneum — plus hair shafts and nail plates . That is the whole disease in one sentence: fungus lives in dead keratin; the redness and itch are your immune system reacting from below . fungal hyphae (branching filaments) spores scale (infectious flakes) immune reaction below 🧠 "Fungus is a surface squatter." It never invades living tissue in a healthy person — which is why creams work on skin, and why hai

entries.h: 📖 Lesion vocabulary — tinea is a SCALE disease
entries.t: Tinea produces an erythematous scaly plaque with an annular (ring) shape. "Annular + scaly + clearing center" is exam code for tinea. 🧠 Scale = keratin. Fungus eats keratin, so fungus makes scale. Follow the flakes. 🍄
STEP 1 · WHY IT HAPPENS Warm + damp + contact with fungus = tinea. Get any of those three away and it struggles.

Tinea is a superficial fungal infection of keratinised tissue — skin, hair or nails — caused by dermatophytes (genera Trichophyton , Microsporum , Epidermophyton ). It is highly contagious . "Ringworm" is a misnomer — there is no worm. The name describes the expanding ring-shaped lesion. 🧠 "Ringworm has no worm, and tinea has no location — until you add the second word."

Fungal spores land on skin — person, animal, soil or object ▼ Warm + moist + a small break = they germinate ▼ Hyphae digest keratin and spread OUTWARD through the stratum corneum ▼ The immune system reacts from the dermis below ▼ Raised, red, scaly ACTIVE edge + itch ▼ The center clears as the fungus moves on = the RING 🧠 The ring is a footprint. The edge is where the fungus is now; the middle is where it used to be.

Person to person — direct skin contact, contact sports Animal to person — puppies, kittens, calves, guinea pigs (often the more inflamed lesions) Object to person — brushes, combs, hats, towels, clothing, bedding, gym mats, shared shoes Soil to person — gardening without gloves Self-spread — scratching the groin after touching the feet 🧠 "Pedis first, cruris second." Teach patients to put socks on before underwear so they do not carry the fungus from foot to groin.

entries.h: 🌡️ Risk factors — what makes skin friendly to fungus
entries.t: Heat and humidity ; sweating; occlusive shoes and synthetic clothing Moist skin folds — groin, under the breasts, between the toes Communal wet floors — showers, changing rooms, pool decks Diabetes , obesity, immunosuppression , peripheral vascular disease Contact sports — wrestling ("tinea gladiatorum"), rugby Existing tinea pedis — the reservoir for nail and groin infection 🧠 "Fungus loves a warm wet cave." Dry it out and you have already started treatment.

entries.h: 🧪 Bug → drug: the rule that runs this whole set
entries.t: 🧠 Fungus → antifungal. Look for "-azole" or terbinafine . An antibiotic will do absolutely nothing for tinea — and a steroid will make it worse. 🔎
STEP 2 · WHAT YOU SEE Itchy, scaly, and shaped like a ring — then find out which body part it landed on.

Circular / annular rash — an expanding ring Scaly , with a raised, more active outer border and a clearer center Pruritus — itching, sometimes intense Plus: mild redness; occasionally small pustules or vesicles along the edge Not usually painful; the patient is systemically well 🧠 "Round · Rough · Restless." Round shape, rough scale, restless itching.

entries.h: 📍 Name it by where it is
entries.t: Tinea capitis — scalp (children); patchy hair loss, black dots, scale, possible kerion Tinea corporis — trunk, arms, legs = the classic ringworm Tinea cruris — groin = jock itch ; usually spares the scrotum Tinea pedis — feet = athlete's foot Tinea manuum — hand (often just one, with tinea pedis on both feet) Tinea unguium — nails = onychomycosis Tinea barbae / faciei — beard area / face Tinea versicolor is a different yeast (Malassezia) — patchy pigment change, not a ring 🧠 "CAP-COR-CRU-PED-UNG" — head, body, groi
🧠 If a question names a Latin body part you do not recognize, translate it — the answer is usually just "which body part is this?"

entries.h: 💍 The ring, explained — and the trap that ruins it
entries.t: 🧠 Scrape the edge, not the middle. And if the rash "got better on steroid cream then spread," think tinea incognito.

entries.h: 🔬 Confirming it — KOH prep & Wood's lamp
entries.t: 🧠 KOH dissolves you, not the fungus. Skin cells melt away; branching septate hyphae stay behind.
🧠 "Thick, yellow, crumbly, lifting." Four adjectives = fungal nail = oral therapy = months, not weeks.

entries.h: ⭐ Scalp & feet — the two that behave differently
entries.t: 🧠 Scalp needs a tablet. Feet need a towel. 🩺
STEP 3 · WHAT YOU DO Kill the fungus, dry the environment, and above all — stop it spreading.

entries.h: 💊 Cream or tablet? One question decides it
entries.t: 🧠 "Hair and nails need a tablet." A cream cannot get inside a hair shaft or under a nail plate.

entries.h: ⭐ PRIORITY: teach how to stop the spread
entries.t: On this topic the highest-priority nursing action is almost always education to prevent transmission . Do NOT share brushes, combs, hats, towels, bed linen, clothing, shoes or sports gear Wash towels, linen and clothing in hot water; hot-wash or replace hair brushes Cover lesions during contact sport; no wrestling/swimming until treated per policy Wear thongs/flip-flops in communal showers and changing rooms Wash hands after applying cream and after touching the lesion Check the household — and the pets. Take an it

entries.h: 💨 Keep it DRY — the environmental half of treatment
entries.t: Dry thoroughly after washing — especially between the toes and in skin folds Pat, do not rub; dry the groin before the feet so you do not carry fungus upward Change socks daily (more often if sweaty); cotton or moisture-wicking Alternate shoes so each pair dries out for 24 h; avoid occlusive plastic shoes Loose cotton underwear ; avoid sitting around in damp gym or swim gear Absorbent powder may help in folds — but it does not replace the antifungal 🧠 "Dry between the toes" — small sentence, big exam points, and it

Absorbed BEST with a high-FAT meal — take it with whole milk, peanut butter or ice cream Takes weeks to months — a scalp course typically runs many weeks Do NOT stop when the itching stops. Itch settles long before the fungus is gone — stopping early is the number-one cause of relapse May cause photosensitivity — teach sun protection May cause headache, GI upset, rash; report a sore throat, fever or jaundice Interacts with warfarin and can reduce the effectiveness of oral contraceptives ; avoid alcohol Derived from

Topical "-azoles" — clotrimazole, miconazole, ketoconazole. Apply to the lesion plus ~2 cm of normal skin around it Terbinafine — topical cream, or oral for nails and scalp Itraconazole / fluconazole — other oral options Ketoconazole or selenium sulfide shampoo may be used as an adjunct in tinea capitis to reduce shedding — it does not replace the oral drug Oral agents may need liver function monitoring ; check interactions before giving An antihistamine may be prescribed for the itch — it treats the symptom, not t

Gloves for direct contact with lesions; hand hygiene before and after Assess and document the lesion : site, size, shape, border, scale, satellite lesions Keep nails short and discourage scratching — scratching spreads and can cause secondary bacterial infection Cool compresses and loose clothing for comfort Watch for secondary bacterial infection : increasing pain, warmth, pus, fever Reassure — it is treatable and, in most sites, does not scar 🧠 Scratching turns a fungal problem into a bacterial one.

Never treat a suspected fungal rash with a topical steroid alone. Never stop the antifungal because the itching or the redness has gone. Never let the patient share brushes, hats, towels or bed linen. Never expect a cream to cure a scalp or nail infection. Never give griseofulvin on an empty stomach — it needs fat to be absorbed. 🧠 Don't steroid it, don't stop it, don't share it. 🔀
STEP 4 · THE REAL EXAM SKILL A ring with a clear center is a fungus until proven otherwise.
🧠 Rings anywhere warm and damp = tinea. Same body, five patterns.

CONDITION HOW IT DIFFERS FROM TINEA Psoriasis Silvery, thick scale on extensor surfaces (elbows, knees), well-demarcated but no central clearing . Autoimmune, not infectious. Responds to steroids — tinea does not. Nummular eczema Coin-shaped, but solid — itchy, weeping or crusted, with no clear center and no raised scaly ring. Impetigo Honey-colored crust , no ring, bacterial → needs an antibiotic . Cellulitis Hot, painful, spreading, often febrile, no scale . Bacterial and deep. Pityriasis rosea A single "herald p

The priority for tinea is nearly always teaching to prevent spread . Griseofulvin with a high-fat meal — do not pick "on an empty stomach." Do not stop when the itching stops — courses run weeks to months. Scalp and nail infections need ORAL therapy; a cream is the wrong answer. Scrape the active border , not the cleared center, for the KOH prep. Recurrent groin tinea? Look at the feet — that is usually the reservoir. Tinea is not a reason for isolation, but it is a reason to stop sharing personal items. 🧠 If an an

Tinea vs psoriasis — clearing center vs solid silvery plaque Tinea vs eczema — ring vs ill-defined itchy patch Tinea vs impetigo — scale vs honey crust Tinea capitis vs alopecia areata — scaly with broken hairs vs smooth bald patch Tinea vs cellulitis — itchy and scaly vs hot and painful Tinea versicolor vs corporis — pigment patches vs an expanding ring 🧠 Scaly ring, smooth patch, honey crust, hot leg. Four pictures, four diagnoses. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 💍 Ring with a clear center Raised scaly ACTIVE edge. Itchy. No worm. 📍 capitis · corporis · cruris · pedis · unguium Scalp · body · groin · feet · nails. 💊 Hair or nail = ORAL Skin = topical -azole or terbinafine. Griseofulvin with a HIGH-FAT meal. 🚨 Do not share · keep dry Highest-priority teaching. Don't stop when the itch stops.

Q1: What actually causes ringworm? Show answer A dermatophyte fungus that digests keratin — not a worm. It lives in the dead stratum corneum, hair shafts and nail plates. Q2: Describe the classic lesion. Show answer A round, itchy, scaly patch with a raised, more active outer border and a clearing center — the ring. Q3: Name the tinea of the scalp, body, groin, feet and nails. Show answer Capitis (scalp), corporis (body/ringworm), cruris (groin/jock itch), pedis (feet/athlete's foot), unguium (nails/onychomycosis).

How wounds close · the healing phases · assessment · dressings · drains · dehiscence & evisceration NG-080 FUNDAMENTALS · SKILL ADHD-friendly visual edition Wound care is four questions asked in order: how is this wound closing? what phase is it in? what does the bed look like? what does the bed need? Answer those and the dressing chooses itself. This page is the partner to NG-044 Pressure Injuries — that page tells you how deep , this page tells you what to do about it . 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive
STEP 1 · THE BIOLOGY Two frameworks. Intention = how the edges come together. Phase = where the wound is in time.
🧠 1 = zip it now. 2 = it fills itself. 3 = wait, then zip it. If a question describes a wound "packed and left open, to be closed in a few days," that is tertiary .

entries.h: ⏱️ The four phases — with the tissue drawn at each stage
entries.t: 🧠 "Stop · Clean · Build · Polish." Stop the bleeding (hemostasis), clean the site (inflammatory), build new tissue (proliferative), polish the scar (maturation).

entries.h: 🍽️ What speeds healing up — and what stalls it
entries.t: Helps ✅ Hurts ❌ Adequate protein (collagen is protein) Malnutrition, low albumin <3.5 g/dL Vitamin C — needed to cross-link collagen; zinc and vitamin A support repair Deficiency states, alcohol misuse Good perfusion and oxygenation Smoking (vasoconstriction + carbon monoxide), PVD, anemia, shock Glycemic control Hyperglycemia — impairs white cells and feeds bacteria Moist, protected wound bed Drying out, repeated trauma from dressings, infection, foreign body Young, healthy immune system Corticosteroids , chemothe

entries.h: ⭐ Why "moist wound healing" beats a dry scab
entries.t: Cells cannot migrate across a dry crust — they have to burrow underneath it. A moist wound bed with dry, intact surrounding skin heals faster and hurts less. Too dry → cells die, scab forms, epithelium is slowed, dressing removal rips new tissue. Too wet → the wound edges macerate (soggy, white), the wound gets bigger, and bacteria thrive. The dressing's job is to balance : add moisture to a dry wound, absorb from a wet one. 🧠 "Moist in the middle, dry at the edges." Goldilocks rule for every dressing decision on t
STEP 2 · LOOK Every dressing change is an assessment opportunity. Look before you cover it back up.

entries.h: 🔴🟡⚫ The wound bed — red, yellow, black
entries.t: 🧠 Traffic light, backwards. Black = stop everything and debride. Yellow = slow down and clean. Red = go, just protect it.

Also chart the amount (scant / small / moderate / large, or the number of saturated gauze pads, or milliliters from a drain) and odor after cleansing. A sudden increase in serosanguineous drainage from a surgical incision around post-op day 3–14 is the classic warning sign of impending dehiscence — see the Complications section. 🧠 Sero = serum (clear). Sangui = blood (red). Pus = purulent. Put the two together and you get "serosanguineous" — pale pink.

Location and wound type/etiology Size — length × width × depth in cm ; undermining and tunnelling by the clock (12:00 = head) Wound bed — % red granulation / yellow slough / black eschar; is there epithelium at the edges? Exudate — type, amount, odor (assess after cleansing) Wound edges — approximated? rolled? undermined? macerated? Periwound skin — erythema, warmth, induration, maceration, excoriation Pain — before, during and after the dressing change Signs of infection , and whether the wound is progressing or s

entries.h: 🧪 Culturing a wound — the technique that gets a valid result
entries.t: Cleanse the wound with sterile normal saline FIRST. Culturing before cleansing just grows the surface junk. Never swab pus, exudate, eschar or slough — those give you colonizing organisms, not the pathogen. Swab clean, viable granulation tissue : rotate the swab over about 1 cm² for several seconds with enough pressure to express fluid from the tissue (Levine technique). Label, bag, and send promptly; note antibiotics already given. If both aerobic and anaerobic cultures are ordered, follow lab requirements for the
STEP 3 · DO IT Pick the dressing from what the wound needs, not from what's in the cupboard.

entries.h: 🩹 Dressing types, drawn — matched to the wound
entries.t: Two more you should be able to name: antimicrobial dressings (silver, iodine, medical-grade honey) for infected or heavily colonized wounds, and negative-pressure wound therapy ("wound vac") — a sealed foam dressing under suction that removes exudate, reduces edema and pulls the wound edges together; monitor the seal, the canister output and for bleeding. 🧠 Dry wound → add water (hydroGEL). Wet wound → soak it up (foam, ALGinate). "Gel gives, alginate absorbs."

entries.h: ✅ Wet-to-dry dressing change — the ordered skill, step by step
entries.t: 1 Prepare Check the order. Assess pain and give analgesia 30–45 minutes before the change. Ask about latex, adhesive and iodine allergies . Explain the procedure, provide privacy, position the patient. ▼ 2 Set up Hand hygiene → gather supplies → open sterile field and pour sterile saline into the sterile container → place gauze/packing to soak. Have a plastic waste bag within reach. ▼ 3 Remove the old dressing Clean gloves. Loosen tape gently toward the wound, supporting the skin. If the gauze is stuck, moisten it

entries.h: 🚿 Cleaning direction — the picture that answers the question
entries.t: Irrigation: use warmed sterile normal saline, hold the syringe about 2.5 cm (1 in) above the wound, and irrigate from the cleanest area toward the dirtiest until the return runs clear. Standard teaching for a safe irrigation pressure is a 35 mL syringe with a 19-gauge angiocatheter (about 8 psi ). Wear a gown, mask and eye protection — irrigation splashes. 🧠 One swab, one stroke, one direction — then bin it. Never go back over a clean area with a used swab.

entries.h: 🔪 Debridement — five ways to remove dead tissue
entries.t: Type How it works Mechanical Physical removal — wet-to-dry gauze, hydrotherapy/whirlpool, irrigation, gentle scrubbing. Fast but non-selective (takes healthy tissue too), painful, can bleed. Enzymatic (chemical) A prescribed topical enzyme ointment applied directly to the necrotic tissue only. Selective , slower, painless. Protect the surrounding skin. Autolytic The body's own enzymes do it, under a moisture-retentive dressing (film, hydrocolloid, hydrogel). Most selective and least painful — but the slowest. Not f

Record each drain separately — label them (JP #1, JP #2), chart output in mL , color and consistency. Empty when ½ to ⅔ full and re-establish the vacuum every time (a bulb that has re-expanded is not draining). Secure the tubing so it doesn't pull, and keep the reservoir below the wound . Report: a sudden increase in output, output that stops abruptly, a change back to bright red bloody drainage, purulence or foul odor, or a dislodged drain. Expect the drainage to progress from sanguineous → serosanguineous → serou
STEP 4 · EMERGENCIES Two words to know cold: dehiscence and evisceration. One of them is a surgical emergency.

entries.h: 🚨 Dehiscence vs evisceration — and exactly what you do
entries.t: 🧠 "Cover, curl, call — never cram." Cover with sterile saline-moist gauze, curl the patient into low Fowler's with knees bent, call the surgeon, and never push anything back inside.

Timing: classically around post-op day 3–14 , when the inflammatory phase ends and the new collagen is still weak. The warning sign: a sudden increase in serosanguineous drainage from a previously drying incision. The patient may describe a "popping" or "giving way" sensation, often while coughing, vomiting, straining or getting up. Risk factors: obesity, malnutrition/low protein, infection, diabetes, corticosteroids, smoking, chronic cough, vomiting, straining, abdominal distension, poor surgical closure. Preventi

Infection — increasing erythema, warmth, edema, induration, purulent drainage, odor, increasing pain, fever, leukocytosis, delayed healing. Wound infections typically declare themselves around post-op day 3–6 . Hemorrhage — frank bleeding, a rapidly saturating dressing, a hematoma (swollen bluish bulge under the incision). Apply pressure, mark the drainage border with the time, and escalate. Fistula — an abnormal tract between the wound and another organ or the skin; look for unexpected drainage such as stool or ur

Hand hygiene before and after touching the wound; clean technique for most home dressing changes. Splint the incision with a pillow when coughing, sneezing, laughing, vomiting or standing up. Ask for pain medicine early — before the pain becomes unbearable, and ideally 30–45 minutes before a dressing change. Signs to report: increasing redness/swelling/warmth, thick or foul drainage, fever ≥ 38 °C (100.4 °F) , increasing pain, wound edges pulling apart, or any sudden increase in drainage. Eat the protein , stay hyd

Q1: A deep pressure ulcer is left open to granulate in. Which type of healing is that? Show answer Secondary intention — the edges are not approximated, so the wound fills in from the base with granulation tissue, contracts, and heals with a large scar over weeks to months. Q2: On post-op day 2 the incision is red, warm, slightly swollen and tender. Is this infection? Show answer Not necessarily — this is the expected inflammatory phase (days 1 to about 4 or 5). It becomes concerning if it is increasing after day 5

entries.h: THE SKIN & HOW DEEP IT WENT
entries.t: STEP 0 · LEARN THIS PICTURE A burn is not a surface event. Depth decides everything — pain, healing, grafting, and how much fluid the patient will leak.

entries.h: 🔬 Skin cross-section — what is actually in there
entries.t: EXAM TIP Nerve endings sit in the DERMIS. That is why a partial-thickness burn is agonising and a full-thickness burn is numb — the full-thickness burn destroyed the very nerves that would report the pain. epidermis dermis fat nerve vessel 🧠 “Everything that hurts and everything that leaks lives in the DERMIS.” Nerves, capillaries, follicles and glands are all dermal — so dermal damage = pain + fluid loss, and dermal destruction = numbness + no regrowth.

entries.h: 🕳️ Burn depth on the SAME skin — four panels, progressively deeper
entries.t: Compare the four panels below. It is the identical drawing each time; only the gray/black destroyed zone gets deeper. Depth, not appearance, is what decides healing. 🧠 “Pain rises then vanishes .” 1° hurts, 2° superficial hurts the MOST, deep 2° hurts less, 3° does not hurt at all. A painless burn is the worst burn , not the best one.

entries.h: ⭐ What counts as a MAJOR burn
entries.t: Criteria vary slightly by center, but the widely taught burn-center referral triggers are: Partial thickness >10% TBSA Any full-thickness burn Burns to face, hands, feet, genitalia/perineum, or over a major joint Electrical (incl. lightning) or chemical burns Inhalation injury Burns in patients with cardiac, renal, respiratory or diabetic comorbidity Burns with trauma , or in children/older adults 🧠 “Face, Fingers, Feet, Front-bottom, Flexures” = the 5 F's that always get referred — cosmetically and functionally to

What you see is the tip. Current travels through muscle, nerve and vessel, so the visible entry and exit wounds massively under-estimate the internal damage. Muscle breakdown → rhabdomyolysis → myoglobin in the urine (tea/port-wine colored) → acute kidney injury Expect dysrhythmias — put the patient on a cardiac monitor Suspect spinal/long-bone fracture from tetanic contraction or a fall Fluid needs are often higher than the Rule of Nines predicts — the formula is only a starting point 🧠 Electric = “dark urine, dar

entries.h: THE LEAK — WHY A BURN CAUSES SHOCK
entries.t: STEP 1 · THE CORE MECHANISM One sentence explains 90% of major-burn nursing: the capillaries open, and the fluid goes to the wrong place.

entries.h: 🎈 Capillary leak & third-spacing — normal vs. burned, side by side
entries.t: Burned tissue releases histamine, prostaglandins, cytokines and bradykinin . These blow the gaps between endothelial cells wide open. Water, electrolytes and plasma proteins (albumin) pour into the interstitium. Albumin leaving drags even more water out osmotically — so the leak feeds itself. red cells albumin water & Na⁺ vessel wall 🧠 “Wet outside, dry inside.” The burn patient is swollen and soaked in the tissues while the blood vessels are running on empty. Never look at the puffiness and think “fluid overloaded

entries.h: 🚨 The burn-shock cascade — follow the dominoes
entries.t: Say this chain out loud once and you can answer almost any major-burn question. 🔥 Massive tissue damage & cellular destruction ▼ 🧨 Widespread systemic inflammatory response (histamine, cytokines, prostaglandins) ▼ 💧 ↑ Capillary permeability — vessels leak plasma + protein into the interstitium ▼ 🎈 Third-spacing / generalized edema — “the body fills like a water balloon” ▼ 📉 ↓ Intravascular volume → ↓ preload → ↓ cardiac output ▼ 🚨 HYPOVOLEMIC SHOCK — ↓BP, ↑HR, ↓urine, cool clammy unburned skin ▼ 🫘 Hypoperfusion → a

BP low — systolic under 90 is the alarm number HR high — over 120/min is the alarm number Urine output low — under 30 mL/hr is the alarm number Thirst — often the earliest complaint, and a real one Cool, clammy, pale unburned skin; delayed capillary refill Restlessness & anxiety → later confusion (a hypoxia/hypoperfusion sign, not "just fear") Weak thready peripheral pulses; flat neck veins Paralytic ileus — absent bowel sounds, distension, nausea/vomiting 🧠 “90 · 30 · 120” — BP at least 90 systolic, urine at least

entries.h: 🧠 Why the whole body swells — not just the burn
entries.t: Answer first: because the inflammatory mediators are in the bloodstream , not just the wound. Over roughly 20–25% TBSA, the leak becomes systemic . That is why a patient burned only on the chest arrives with swollen eyelids, hands and legs. The edema is generalized and it is not a sign of too much IV fluid on day one. Airway swelling → occlusion risk (see the inhalation section) Limb swelling under circumferential eschar → compartment syndrome Chest-wall swelling under eschar → can't ventilate 🧠 Small burn = local

entries.h: 🔥 Jackson's zones — the burn is three rings, and you can save the middle one
entries.t: A burn wound is not uniform. The classic model describes three concentric zones , and good resuscitation is aimed squarely at the middle one. The zone of stasis is why fluid resuscitation matters so much. Under-resuscitate (or let the patient get cold, or squash the limb under tight eschar) and the stasis zone dies — the burn converts to a deeper burn over 24–48 h. 🧠 “The middle ring is on the fence.” Fluid, warmth and pressure relief push it back toward life; shock, cold and pressure push it into the graveyard. ⏱️
STEP 2 · WHAT MATTERS WHEN The same patient is a completely different nursing problem on day 1, day 10 and month 6. Know which phase you are in.

entries.h: 📈 Timeline — fluid OUT, then fluid BACK
entries.t: The single most-tested time fact from this topic: fluid shifting into the interstitium is greatest between 18 and 24 hours after the injury. Then it reverses. 🧠 “Out by 24, back by 72.” Fluid leaks OUT and peaks at 18–24 h ; it comes BACK (diuresis) at 48–72 h . Every lab value on this page just follows the water.

entries.h: 🔄 Emergent vs. acute — the flip that trips everyone
entries.t: Same patient, opposite labs, opposite risks. Learn the flip, not the lists. EMERGENT (0–48/72 h) ACUTE (diuresis → closure) Fluid is… Leaving the vessels → tissue Returning tissue → vessels Potassium HIGH (cells lyse, K⁺ spills out) >5.0 LOW (K⁺ washed out in urine & wound) Sodium LOW (Na⁺ follows water into interstitium) <135 Variable; watch as fluids are titrated H & H HIGH — hemoconcentration (plasma left, cells stayed) LOW — hemodilution + RBC destruction Urine Scanty & concentrated; may be dark/red-brown Copio

entries.h: 🚨 The gut in the emergent phase
entries.t: Answer first: blood is shunted away from the gut, so the bowel goes quiet. Paralytic ileus — absent bowel sounds, distension, vomiting. Expect an NG tube for decompression in large burns. Curling ulcer — the classic burn-related stress ulcer of the stomach/duodenum from ischemia + acid. Prophylaxis with acid suppression is routine. Watch for coffee-ground NG output or melena. Feeding is held until bowel sounds return — then enteral nutrition is started, ideally early. 🧠 “ C urling iron → C urling ulcer.” Burns → st

After the first day or two the burn patient's metabolic rate can climb dramatically and stay up for months. This drives the whole acute phase. Massive protein catabolism — muscle is burned for fuel; weight and lean mass fall Hyperglycemia even in non-diabetics (stress hormones + insulin resistance) Heat loss through the open wound — patients feel cold and shiver, which costs more calories Nutrition must be high calorie, high protein , with vitamins C and A and zinc for healing Keep the room warm — this is a therape
STEP 3 · WHAT KILLS FIRST Fluid loss kills in hours. The airway kills in minutes. That is why airway always outranks the burn.

entries.h: 🔥 Airway cutaway — normal vs. inhalation injury
entries.t: The danger is not the burn you can see, it is the swelling you cannot. Hot gas and soot injure the upper airway; edema then closes it over the next several hours — often after the patient arrives looking fine. 🧠 “Face, hair, soot, voice.” Facial burns · singed nasal hair/eyebrows · carbonaceous (sooty) sputum · hoarseness or stridor . Any one of those four = tell the provider now, before the airway closes.

The fire was in an enclosed space (house, car, basement) Burns to the face, neck or chest ; singed nasal hair, eyebrows or lashes Soot around the mouth/nose or carbonaceous sputum Hoarse voice, brassy cough, drooling, difficulty swallowing Stridor — this is a late, ominous sign Loss of consciousness at the scene The action: anticipate early intubation . Once the swelling is established, intubation becomes very difficult or impossible. 🧠 Don't wait for the sats to drop. The airway decision in burns is made on histor

Answer first: the pulse oximeter is falsely normal in CO poisoning — it cannot tell oxyhemoglobin from carboxyhemoglobin. CO binds hemoglobin roughly 200× more tightly than oxygen Signs: headache, nausea, dizziness, confusion → coma; classically cherry-red skin (late/unreliable) Diagnosis is a carboxyhemoglobin level , not SpO₂ Treatment: 100% oxygen by non-rebreather ; hyperbaric oxygen in severe cases 🧠 “Pink patient, normal sat, dying brain.” If someone came out of a burning building confused, give high-flow O₂

entries.h: ⭐ Priority order in the first minutes — say it in this order
entries.t: 1 AIRWAY — is it patent, and will it stay patent? Look for the four airway signs. Anticipate intubation. ▼ 2 BREATHING — 100% O₂ by non-rebreather. Check for circumferential chest eschar restricting the chest wall. ▼ 3 CIRCULATION — 2 large-bore IVs (through unburned skin if possible), start Lactated Ringer's , indwelling catheter for hourly urine. ▼ 4 STOP THE BURNING & remove clothing/jewelry — but then keep the patient WARM ; large burns lose heat catastrophically. ▼ 5 Assess TBSA , weigh the patient, calculate

entries.h: THE LABS — AND WHY EACH ONE MOVES
entries.t: STEP 4 · NCLEX GOLD Never memorize burn labs as a list. Each value is just the water and the dead cells telling you where they went.

entries.h: 📊 First-24-hour lab picture on a scale
entries.t: Typical adult reference ranges are shown as a band — exact values vary by laboratory, by sex and by source. The ▲ marker is where a major-burn patient typically sits in the emergent phase. 🧠 “K up, Na down, blood thick.” Three arrows. Everything else on the emergent panel follows from those.

entries.h: 🚨 Hyperkalemia — Potassium Priority Pumps the heart
entries.t: K⁺ over 5.0 in a burn patient is a cardiac emergency, not a chemistry curiosity. The rhythm change comes before the arrest. Put the patient on a continuous cardiac monitor — this is a nursing action you can take yourself Report a K⁺ over 5.0 , and report peaked T waves immediately Other clues: muscle weakness, paraesthesias, bradycardia, GI cramping/diarrhea Deep/electrical burns with rhabdomyolysis release even more K⁺ — expect it 🧠 “ P otassium P riority P umps the heart.” Three P's. In burns, potassium is a hear

Answer first: sodium goes with the water into the swollen tissue, and pours out of the open wound. Clues: confusion, lethargy, headache, muscle weakness/cramps, seizures if severe Hydrotherapy and long soaks can worsen it — sodium leaches out into the water This is a big reason Lactated Ringer's is chosen: it contains sodium and is close to plasma composition Never correct sodium quickly on your own initiative — rapid correction is dangerous; follow the prescription 🧠 “Na goes where the water goes.” Water into the

Third-spacing — fluid that has left the vessels and sits in a space where it is useless (interstitium, blisters, gut wall) Hemoconcentration — the plasma left, so the same red cells now make up a bigger fraction → H&H rise Eschar — the leathery, non-elastic dead tissue over a full-thickness burn. It does not stretch, so swelling underneath strangles the limb or the chest Escharotomy — an incision through eschar to relieve that pressure (see NG-123) Burn shock — the hypovolemic + distributive shock of the first 24–4

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🎈 Leak → shock Inflammation → leaky capillaries → third-spacing → hypovolemic shock . 🔢 90 · 30 · 120 BP ≥90 systolic · urine ≥30 mL/hr · HR <120. 🧪 K↑ Na↓ H&H↑ First 24 h. Then it flips: K↓ H&H↓ in the acute phase. ⏱️ 18–24 h peak Interstitial shift is greatest 18–24 h; diuresis at 48–72 h.

Q1: In one sentence, why does a major burn cause shock? Show answer Massive tissue destruction triggers systemic inflammation that increases capillary permeability; plasma and protein leak into the interstitium (third-spacing), so intravascular volume falls and the patient goes into hypovolemic shock. Q2: When is fluid shifting into the interstitium greatest? Show answer Between 18 and 24 hours after the injury. Diuresis (fluid returning to the vessels) typically begins around 48–72 hours. The local cold injury — tissue that literally freezes NG-116 INTEGUMENTARY · EMERGENCY ADHD-friendly visual edition Frostbite is tissue that actually freezes : ice crystals form in and around the cells while the vessels clamp down, so the part is starved of blood at the same time as it is being torn apart from the inside. Frostbite is the LOCAL injury; hypothermia (NG-041) is the SYSTEMIC one — and the two arrive together far more often than not. 📄 Simple Nursing original — opens in Drive → 🧊 Cells become snowballs
STEP 1 · PATHO Two injuries happening at once: ice inside the tissue, and no blood getting to it.

entries.h: 🧊 Normal tissue vs frozen tissue — the cutaway
entries.t: 🧠 "Every cell becomes a little snowball." Two things are killing the tissue: the ice (direct cell damage) and the clamped, sludged vessels (ischemia). Rewarming fixes the ice — it does not undo the clot.

entries.h: 🧨 The cascade — why the damage keeps going after you warm it
entries.t: Cold exposure → skin vessels vasoconstrict to protect the core ▼ Blood flow to fingers, toes, ears, nose falls → vascular stasis ▼ Tissue temperature drops below freezing → ice crystals form outside then inside cells ▼ Water pulled out of cells → cellular dehydration , electrolyte shifts, membrane rupture ▼ Rewarming → blood floods back → reperfusion injury : inflammation, edema, more microthrombi ▼ Progressive dermal ischemia over hours to days → blistering, then necrosis / gangrene The final tissue loss is decide

entries.h: 📍 Where frostbite happens — the far corners
entries.t: 🧠 "The body sacrifices the edges to save the middle." Vasoconstriction protects the core and abandons the periphery — so the periphery is what freezes.

🍺 Alcohol vasodilates + kills judgment 🚬 Nicotine vasoconstricts 🏚️ Homelessness prolonged exposure 💧 Wet clothing heat loss ×25 vs dry 🥾 Tight boots/gloves constrict flow 🌬️ Wind chill strips warmth fast 🫀 PVD / diabetes already poor flow 👵👶 Very old / very young poor thermoregulation 🧠 ↓ LOC or mental illness can't self-rescue ❄️ Previous frostbite permanently cold-sensitive 🧠 "Wet, windy, drunk, and tight." Four things that turn a cold day into a frostbite injury. 🔎
STEP 2 · CLUES Same depth language as every other wound page — this time the injury came from cold.

You may also see it split simply into two: superficial frostbite (skin blue, mottled or waxy yellow; clear blisters; skin still moves over the tissue below) and deep frostbite (skin white, hard as wood, blood-filled blisters, progressing to gangrene). The true depth cannot be judged until after rewarming — and often not for days. 🧠 Blister color = depth. Clear blister = superficial and likely to recover. Blood-filled blister = deep and likely to lose tissue. Exactly the same rule as pressure injuries on NG-044 .

entries.h: 🔎 What you assess — before and after rewarming
entries.t: Color — white / waxy yellow / mottled blue / gray; after thawing, does it turn red-purple (good) or stay pale (bad)? Texture — soft and pliable (superficial) vs hard, wooden, non-indentable (deep). Sensation — numbness is universal at first; return of sensation and pain after rewarming is a good sign. Blisters — present? clear or hemorrhagic? when did they appear? Perfusion — capillary refill, pulses (may need Doppler), warmth. Edema — expect it to increase for 24–48 h after thawing; check for tight compartments. C

entries.h: ⭐ Frostbite vs hypothermia — local vs systemic
entries.t: Frostbite (this page) Hypothermia (NG-041) LOCAL tissue freezing SYSTEMIC drop in core temperature Fingers, toes, ears, nose, cheeks The whole body; core temp < 35 °C (95 °F) Threatens the limb Threatens the life — cold myocardium → V-fib Treat with rapid rewarming of the part in warm water Treat with core rewarming , gentle handling, cardiac monitoring Damage keeps declaring itself for weeks Danger is immediate — arrhythmia, afterdrop If the patient has both, the core comes first. Stabilize airway, breathing, circ
STEP 3 · CARE One correct method, and a list of tempting wrong ones.
🧠 "Warm water, no rubbing, no fire, no pressure." The frozen part is full of microscopic glass — rubbing drags it through the tissue, and anesthetic skin cannot tell you it is being burned.

1 ABCs and core temperature first Get the patient out of the cold. Treat systemic hypothermia before or alongside the limb, and handle gently — the cold heart is irritable. ▼ 2 Remove wet and constrictive things Wet clothing, boots, gloves, rings, watches and jewelry — before the swelling starts. Dry the patient, insulate the rest of the body. ▼ 3 Decide: is refreezing possible? If the part could refreeze before definitive care, do NOT thaw it. Protect and transport frozen. Freeze–thaw–refreeze causes far more tiss

entries.h: 🚨 The refreezing rule — the highest-yield trap
entries.t: Do not begin rewarming unless the part can be kept thawed. 🧠 "Better frozen than half-thawed." A second freeze makes bigger ice crystals in tissue that is already injured.

entries.h: 💧 Blisters, dressings and the little details
entries.t: Dressings: loose, bulky, dry, non-adherent . Place gauze between every finger and toe so they don't macerate against each other. No occlusive dressings and nothing circumferential/tight — swelling after thawing can turn a snug wrap into a tourniquet. Elevate the part after rewarming; keep the patient on bed rest if the feet are involved. Blisters: practice varies. Many protocols debride or aspirate clear blisters and leave hemorrhagic blisters intact; some leave all blisters intact. Follow the provider's order and
STEP 4 · WATCH & TEACH The wound that follows behaves like any other wound — see NG-080 — but the timeline is unusually slow.

entries.h: 📅 What it looks like over time
entries.t: Surgery is not rushed. Except for infection or compartment syndrome, amputation decisions wait for a clear line of demarcation — classically summarized as "frostbite in January, amputate in July." Early appearance badly over-predicts tissue loss. 🧠 Frostbite lies on day one. A black finger in week two may still have a viable base — which is why nobody cuts early.

Infection / cellulitis — the dead tissue is a culture medium. Fever, spreading redness, purulence, worsening pain. Compartment syndrome — post-thaw edema in a closed space. Pain out of proportion , pain on passive stretch, tense compartment, paraesthesia. Escalate immediately; pulselessness is a late sign. Gangrene and auto-amputation — dry gangrene mummifies and may separate on its own. Rhabdomyolysis and AKI in extensive deep injury. Long-term sequelae: permanent cold sensitivity, chronic neuropathic pain, numbne

You are now permanently cold-sensitive in that area — dress in layers, cover the ears, nose and hands, and change wet gloves and socks immediately. Stop smoking — nicotine constricts the exact vessels the healing tissue depends on. Avoid alcohol in the cold. Loose, layered, dry clothing ; mittens beat gloves; boots that are not tight. Protect the injured part — no direct heat, no soaking without instruction, no picking at blisters or eschar. Report: fever, increasing pain, spreading redness, foul drainage, or any n

Local vs systemic; limb vs life. 🧠 Cold hurts twice: once to the whole body (NG-041) and once to the corners (this page). ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🧊 Ice + stasis Crystals wreck the cells; vasoconstriction starves them. 🔥 37–39 °C water Circulating warm water, 20–30 min, until pliable and red-purple. Analgesia first. ❌ No rub · no fire · no pressure And never thaw if it can refreeze. 🩸 Blister color = depth Clear = superficial. Blood-filled = deep.

Q1: In one sentence, what is happening to the tissue in frostbite? Show answer Ice crystals form in and around the cells, pulling water out and rupturing membranes, while cold-induced vasoconstriction causes vascular stasis and microthrombi, so the tissue is simultaneously frozen and starved of blood. Q2: What is the priority treatment, and at what temperature? Show answer Rapid rewarming by immersing the part in circulating warm water at about 37 to 39 degrees Celsius (about 98.6 to 102 degrees Fahrenheit), typica

Hands on the patient — airway, fluids, wound, infection, pain NG-123 INTEGUMENTARY · PRIORITY CARE ADHD-friendly visual edition The burn patient is leaking their circulating volume into their own tissues. Your job in the first 24 hours is to keep the airway open , put the volume back faster than it leaks , and not let the wound convert or get infected . The #1 intervention in the first 24 hours is IV Lactated Ringer's — and you judge whether it is working by the urine output , not by the number in the bag. 📄 Simple

entries.h: 🧭 This page vs. its sibling — read them in order
entries.t: NG-107 = the WHY. Capillary leak, burn shock, the three phases, inhalation injury mechanism, why each lab moves. NG-123 (this page) = the WHAT-YOU-DO. Priorities in order, the actual fluid orders and how to titrate them, wound care, escharotomy, infection prevention, pain and nutrition. Assume you already know the patho. The TBSA and Parkland arithmetic lives on NG-146 . 🫁 Airway first, always Before TBSA, before fluids, before pain meds. Enclosed-space fire + hoarseness = anticipate intubation . 💧 LR is the #1 flu
STEP 1 · IN THIS ORDER Burns look dramatic. Do not be pulled to the wound. Work the airway, then the volume, then the skin.

EXAM TIP When a question gives you a burn patient and four "correct-sounding" actions, the answer is whichever one is closest to the airway. 🧠 “Air, Off, IV, Pee, Warm, Weigh, Numb.” Seven words in order. If you can chant it, you can answer the priority question.

entries.h: 🚨 Remove every ring, watch and bracelet — now
entries.t: Answer first: the limb is about to swell for the next 24 hours. Jewelry becomes a tourniquet. Rings, watches, bracelets, belts, piercings — off early , before edema makes it impossible Remove non-adherent clothing; do NOT peel off clothing that is stuck to the burn — cut around it Remove synthetic fabric that has melted onto skin only under direction — it can take the skin with it Check distal pulses, color, capillary refill and sensation in every burned extremity, and keep rechecking Elevate burned extremities abo

entries.h: 🌡️ Keep them WARM — this is treatment, not comfort
entries.t: The skin is the body's heat blanket, and a big burn has thrown it away. Burn patients become hypothermic astonishingly fast , and hypothermia worsens acidosis, coagulopathy and the zone of stasis. Cover with a dry, clean/sterile sheet or blanket during transport Never apply ice or soak a large burn in cold water — it deepens the burn and drops the core temperature Raise the room temperature; use warming lights/blankets and warmed IV fluids where available Limit the time the wound is exposed during dressing changes
STEP 2 · THE #1 INTERVENTION The bag choice is easy. The skill is titration — reading the patient and changing the rate.

Answer first: IV Lactated Ringer's (LR) is the #1 intervention in the first 24 hours. 0.9% sodium chloride (normal saline) is the other isotonic crystalloid you will see ordered. Why LR? It is an isotonic crystalloid whose electrolyte make-up is closest to plasma. It replaces the sodium that is being lost into the interstitium and out of the wound, and its lactate is converted to bicarbonate , which helps with the metabolic acidosis of shock. Give through two large-bore IVs ; central access is common in large burns

entries.h: ⭐ The three numbers that tell you the fluids are working
entries.t: Source-standard assessment of fluid resuscitation — memorize these three and their directions. 🧠 “90 · 30 · 120.” BP at least 90 , urine at least 30 , pulse under 120 . Three numbers cover most burn resuscitation questions.

entries.h: 🚽 Hourly urine — how to actually titrate
entries.t: The classic exam item: "12 hours after a 20% TBSA burn, BP 90/50 , pulse 110 , urine 20 mL in the last hour. What does the nurse anticipate?" → Increasing the IV Lactated Ringer's. Also chart: hourly I&O, daily weight (same scale, same time), vital signs frequently, mental status, and the color of the urine. Dark red-brown urine after a deep or electrical burn suggests myoglobin — report it, expect higher fluid targets. 🧠 “The kidney is the cheapest cardiac-output monitor in the room.” If the kidney is making urine

More is not better. Excess fluid ("fluid creep") causes: Pulmonary edema — crackles, dyspnea, falling SpO₂ Abdominal compartment syndrome — tense distended abdomen, rising airway pressures, falling urine despite more fluid Worsening extremity/orbital compartment pressures Deeper conversion of the burn from edema pressure This is exactly why the formula is a starting point and the urine output is the steering wheel . 🧠 “Titrate, don't dump.” The formula gets the infusion started; the patient decides where it ends up

entries.h: 🧾 The formula in one line (details on NG-146)
entries.t: The commonly taught consensus/Parkland version: 4 mL × kg body weight × %TBSA = total LR for the FIRST 24 h Half in the first 8 hours , the remaining half over the next 16 hours The clock starts at the time of injury , not the time of arrival Only partial- and full-thickness burn is counted in TBSA — superficial (1°) is excluded The number is a starting estimate . Titrate to urine output , then reassess. 🧠 “4 · weight · burn — half in 8.” Full worked examples on NG-146 and NG-177 . 🩹
STEP 3 · THE SKIN ITSELF Two jobs: get the dead tissue off, and get living skin back on before infection wins.

Answer first: full-thickness eschar is leathery and cannot stretch . When the limb or chest swells underneath it, the eschar acts like a tourniquet. An escharotomy is a lengthwise incision through the eschar to release the pressure. Where the cuts actually go. The lines follow fixed anatomical courses — the anterior axillary line down each side of the chest, joined top and bottom by transverse cuts, and the mid-medial and mid-lateral lines down each limb — so the release runs the full length of the constricting esc

Sequence for a major burn wound, and the two dressing philosophies. Wrap fingers and toes individually — digits dressed together heal fused together (webbing contracture) Dressings are changed with sterile technique ; hydrotherapy sessions are kept short (heat and sodium loss) Common topical agents include silver sulfadiazine (avoid in sulfa allergy; can cause leukopenia), mafenide acetate (penetrates eschar well, stings , can cause metabolic acidosis) and silver-impregnated dressings . Never apply a topical agent

entries.h: 🧬 Skin grafts — donor site, graft site, and what you must protect
entries.t: Full-thickness burns cannot re-epithelialise: everything that would regrow the skin was destroyed. They need grafting . 🧠 “A graft is a seed, not a bandage.” It has to grow roots (capillaries). Move it in the first few days and the roots tear — the graft dies. 🛡️
STEP 4 · THE ACUTE-PHASE KILLER Once the fluid crisis is over, sepsis becomes the leading cause of death. The burn wound is a wide-open door with no skin on it.

entries.h: 🌸 The NCLEX classic — no fresh flowers or plants in the room
entries.t: KAPLAN-STYLE "A client with burns is immunocompromised. What precaution prevents infection?" → Avoid placing fresh flowers or plants in or near the client's room. Standing water and soil harbor Pseudomonas and Aspergillus . 🧠 “No flowers for the burn patient.” It feels unkind, which is exactly why it is a favorite exam answer. Standing vase water is a Pseudomonas soup and potting soil grows Aspergillus .

Do not wait for a positive culture. Watch the trend . Wound changes — new green/blue-green or foul drainage, color change, edema at the edge, rapid separation of eschar, a partial-thickness wound suddenly converting to full-thickness Temperature instability — fever or hypothermia . In burns, a falling temperature is just as alarming. Change in level of consciousness / new confusion — often the earliest systemic sign Tachycardia, tachypnoea, hypotension, decreased urine output Return of paralytic ileus after bowel s

Hand hygiene before and after every contact — the single most effective measure Private room ; gown, gloves, mask and cap for wound care per policy Sterile technique for dressing changes and all invasive lines Dedicated equipment; clean/disinfect anything shared between patients No fresh flowers, no potted plants, no standing water Screen visitors and staff for infections; restrict anyone unwell Tetanus prophylaxis on admission per history Monitor temperature, WBC and wound appearance every shift; culture as prescr
STEP 5 · KEEP THEM ALIVE AND FED Two under-rated, heavily tested areas: the route you give pain medicine, and when you start feeding.

entries.h: 💉 Pain control — IV route only in the emergent phase
entries.t: Answer first: give analgesia IV, never IM or subcutaneous. Perfusion to muscle and fat is terrible during burn shock, so an IM dose sits there un-absorbed — and then dumps into the circulation all at once when perfusion is restored, risking overdose. Premedicate before dressing changes, hydrotherapy, debridement and physiotherapy — procedural pain is the worst pain the patient has IV opioids (e.g. morphine, fentanyl) titrated to effect are standard; patient-controlled analgesia is common once the patient is stable.

entries.h: 🍗 Nutrition — start enteral feeding once bowel sounds return
entries.t: Answer first: administer enteral feedings once bowel sounds return. The gut goes quiet from shock (paralytic ileus); the moment it wakes up, feed it. Using the gut also protects the gut mucosa and reduces bacterial translocation. 🧠 “Sounds → spoons.” No bowel sounds = no feeding. Bowel sounds back = start the tube feed. And feed it early — a starved burn patient does not heal.

entries.h: ⛔ The never-do list for a major burn
entries.t: Never apply ice or immerse a large burn in cold water — deepens the injury and causes hypothermia Never put butter, oils, ointments or home remedies on a burn Never break or debride blisters at the bedside without an order — an intact blister is a sterile biological dressing Never give IM or SubQ analgesia in the emergent phase Never slow the fluids because the patient looks puffy — titrate to urine output, BP and HR Never wrap fingers or toes together Avoid taking BP or starting an IV in a grafted limb; avoid burn

Contracture prevention does not wait for the rehab phase — it starts while the patient is still on the ventilator. Position in anti-deformity alignment from admission (neck extended, shoulders abducted, elbows/knees extended, ankles neutral) No pillow under the head for anterior neck burns — it flexes the neck into a contracture Splints as prescribed; range-of-motion exercises daily unless a fresh graft says otherwise Elevate burned extremities; encourage early ambulation Full detail on NG-164 · Rehabilitation phas

Tetanus prophylaxis — a burn is a contaminated wound Stress-ulcer prophylaxis — Curling ulcer risk; watch for coffee-ground NG output VTE prophylaxis per protocol — these patients are immobile and inflamed Eye care for facial burns — early ophthalmology input before the lids swell shut Psychosocial — the patient may have lost their home, their face or a family member. Expect grief, nightmares, acute stress; involve social work and chaplaincy early Consent & reporting — burns with an inconsistent history in a child

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🫁 Airway → fluids → wound Priorities never change. Airway outranks the burn. 💧 LR, two large-bore IVs #1 intervention in the first 24 h. 🚽 Urine <30 → increase LR Plus BP ≥90 and HR <120. 🌸 No flowers · IV pain meds · feed when bowel sounds return The three most-tested one-liners.

Q1: What is the #1 intervention in the first 24 hours of a major burn? Show answer IV Lactated Ringer's solution through large-bore access. 0.9% sodium chloride is the other isotonic crystalloid used. Airway management comes before it in priority order, but LR is the #1 treatment of the burn shock itself. Q2: Twelve hours after a 20% TBSA burn: BP 90/50, pulse 110, urine 20 mL in the last hour. What do you anticipate? Show answer Increasing the IV Lactated Ringer's. Urine output under 30 mL/hr with a borderline BP
