Burns III · TBSA estimation & the Parkland fluid calculation — the math page NG-146 INTEGUMENTARY · CALCULATION ADHD-friendly visual edition The Rule of 9's is a fast way to estimate the percentage of the body burned — the Total Body Surface Area (TBSA) . You need that number for one reason: it is the input to the fluid-resuscitation formula. Once you have TBSA, the Parkland formula tells you how many milliliters of Lactated Ringer's to give in the first 24 hours — and the urine output tells you whether that number

entries.h: 🧭 This page vs. its sibling — they are NOT the same page
entries.t: NG-146 (this page) = the NUMBERS. Rule of 9's, the palm rule, Lund–Browder, pediatric proportions, the Parkland formula, the 8-hour/16-hour split, and worked practice problems. NG-164 = the REHABILITATION PHASE. What happens after the wounds close: contracture prevention, positioning and splinting, pressure garments, water-based lotion, daily exercise, scar maturation, itch, sun protection, nutrition and psychosocial recovery. Both come from the same source infographic, so they share a title — but do not study them
STEP 1 · GET THE PERCENTAGE Divide the adult body into chunks of 9% (plus one 1% chunk). Front and back are counted separately.

entries.h: 🧍 Adult Rule of 9's — anterior & posterior, fully labeled
entries.t: EXAM TIP Every region is split front/back. A whole arm is 9% — but only the front of that arm is 4.5% . That single habit fixes most Rule-of-Nines errors. head & neck upper trunk lower trunk arms legs perineum 1% 🧠 “NINE ones: 9 head, 9+9 arms, 18+18 trunk, 18+18 legs, +1 for the perineum.” Add them: 9 + 18 + 36 + 36 + 1 = 100 . If your total is not 100, you dropped a piece.

entries.h: ⭐ The three habits that stop Rule-of-Nines mistakes
entries.t: ↔️ FRONT ≠ BACK always ask which side 1️⃣ ADD THE 1% perineum is easy to forget 🚫 SKIP 1° BURNS superficial is not counted 🧍 WHOLE LIMB? arm 9 · leg 18 ➗ HALF IT one surface = half the region ✅ SUM CHECK can't exceed 100 Only partial-thickness (2°) and full-thickness (3°/4°) burns are included in TBSA. A superficial (1°) sunburn is NOT counted — it does not leak the way deeper burns do, so counting it would over-estimate the fluid. 🧠 “First degree doesn't count.” If the stem says “reddened, painful, no blisters, bl

entries.h: 👶 Children are NOT small adults — the proportions change
entries.t: Answer first: a child's head is proportionally much bigger and the legs proportionally smaller . Using the adult chart on an infant badly under-estimates the burn. The most accurate method in children is the Lund–Browder chart , which assigns a different percentage to the head and legs for each age band. The pediatric Rule of Nines above is the quick bedside version. 🧠 “Babies are all head.” Head 18 , each leg 13½ in the infant. As the child grows, the head loses ~1% per year and the legs gain it back. 🖐️
STEP 2 · WHEN 9's WON'T WORK Rule of 9's is fast but blunt. Use the palm rule for scattered burns and Lund–Browder when accuracy matters.

Answer first: the patient's own palm including the fingers is roughly 1% of their TBSA. Use it for patchy, scattered or irregular burns that don't fill a whole 9% region. 🧠 “One hand, one percent.” Count palms for splash and spatter burns; count nines for whole-region burns.

A printed chart that assigns a percentage to each small body segment and adjusts the head/thigh/leg values by exact age band . Most accurate method, and the standard in burn centers Essential in children , where Rule of 9's is crudest Slower — you shade a diagram and add up small numbers Rule of 9's is the rapid field/ED estimate ; Lund–Browder is the definitive one done later 🧠 “Nines for now, Lund–Browder for later.” Fast first, accurate second.

Counting a whole leg (18%) when only the front was burned ( 9% ) Counting the 1° sunburn region into TBSA Forgetting the perineum's 1% when the stem specifically mentions it Using adult percentages on a toddler Adding to more than 100% Using the nurse's palm instead of the patient's 🧠 Read the stem twice: “anterior”, “posterior”, “entire”, “circumferential”. Those four words change the answer. 🧮
STEP 3 · TURN % INTO mL Three numbers multiplied together. The hard part is not the multiplication — it is knowing what each number means.

The commonly taught version of the consensus (Parkland) formula for the first 24 hours after a major burn, given as Lactated Ringer's . 4 mL × body weight (kg) × %TBSA = total LR in the first 24 h → ½ over the first 8 h · ½ over the next 16 h 🧠 “ 4 for the 4 -alarm fire · half in 8 .” Four milliliters, weight, burn percent — then cut it in half and put the first half in the first eight hours.

entries.h: ⏳ The clock starts at the TIME OF INJURY — not arrival
entries.t: This is the highest-yield trap in the whole topic. If a patient is burned at 08:00 and reaches you at 10:00, you have 6 hours left to deliver the first half — so the rate has to be higher, not the same. 🧠 “The burn started the stopwatch, not the ambulance.” Always ask what time did this happen?

entries.h: ➗ Turning the total into an hourly rate
entries.t: Exam questions often want the mL/hr , not just the total. Two divisions: first 8 h rate = (total ÷ 2) ÷ 8 next 16 h rate = (total ÷ 2) ÷ 16 The first-8-hour rate is always double the next-16-hour rate If hours have already been lost, divide by the hours remaining in that block Weight in pounds? ÷ 2.2 to get kilograms first 🧠 “Front-load it.” The leak is worst early, so the fluid goes in fastest early.

The capillary leak begins to seal, so the plan changes. Crystalloid volume is reduced and titrated down as urine output allows Colloid (e.g. albumin) is often added in the second 24 hours in many protocols, once capillaries are less leaky, to hold fluid in the vessels Maintenance fluid (often with dextrose) replaces evaporative loss Electrolytes flip: potassium falls , H&H falls with hemodilution — see NG-107 Watch hard for the swing to fluid overload during diuresis: crackles, JVD, dyspnea, sudden weight gain 🧠 “D
STEP 4 · DO THE MATH Cover the answer, work it on paper, then check. Three of these are lifted straight from the classic question banks.

entries.h: 🎓 Example 1 — full-thickness burns to ALL posterior surfaces
entries.t: A client has full-thickness burns to all posterior body surfaces . Using the Rule of 9's, calculate the % TBSA affected. back of head & neck …… 4.5% entire back (upper 9 + lower 9) …… 18% back of both arms (4.5 × 2) …… 9% back of both legs (9 × 2) …… 18% 4.5 + 18 + 9 + 18 = 49.5% TBSA Why students miss it: they use whole-limb values (9% per arm, 18% per leg) instead of halving for the posterior surface only. 🧠 “All the back = just under half the body.” 49.5% — remember it as “about 50%.”

A client has partial-thickness burns to the anterior legs and the perineum . Calculate the % TBSA. front of right leg …… 9% front of left leg …… 9% perineum …… 1% 9 + 9 + 1 = 19% TBSA Why students miss it: they forget the perineum's 1% and answer 18%, or they count whole legs and answer 37%. 🧠 “18 + the little 1.” When the stem says perineum , it is because that 1% is the point of the question.

entries.h: 🎓 Example 3 — now turn it into milliliters
entries.t: The client above weighs 100 kg with 19% TBSA . Calculate the Lactated Ringer's fluid resuscitation needed. 4 mL × 100 kg × 19 %TBSA = 7,600 mL in the first 24 hours ½ = 3,800 mL in the first 8 hours → 475 mL/hr ½ = 3,800 mL over the next 16 hours → 237.5 mL/hr 🧠 “Same halves, different speeds.” Equal volumes, but the first one has to go in twice as fast.

entries.h: Practice A · 70 kg adult, burns to the entire front of the trunk and the whole right arm
entries.t: TBSA? Show answer Anterior trunk 18% + whole right arm 9% = 27% TBSA . Parkland total and first-8-hour rate? Show answer 4 × 70 × 27 = 7,560 mL in 24 h. Half = 3,780 mL in the first 8 h → 472.5 mL/hr ; then 3,780 mL over 16 h → 236.25 mL/hr .

entries.h: Practice B · 80 kg adult, burns to the head and neck (all round), anterior trunk, and both anterior legs
entries.t: TBSA? Show answer Head and neck all round 9% + anterior trunk 18% + anterior legs 9 + 9 = 45% TBSA . Parkland total? Show answer 4 × 80 × 45 = 14,400 mL in 24 h. First 8 h: 7,200 mL → 900 mL/hr . Next 16 h: 7,200 mL → 450 mL/hr . (A burn this size also needs an airway assessment first — head and neck burns.)

entries.h: Practice C · 154 lb adult, posterior trunk and the back of both legs, burned 3 hours before arrival
entries.t: Weight in kg and TBSA? Show answer 154 ÷ 2.2 = 70 kg . Posterior trunk 18% + posterior legs 9 + 9 = 36% TBSA . Total, and the rate for the remainder of the first 8-hour block? Show answer 4 × 70 × 36 = 10,080 mL total. Half = 5,040 mL must be in by 8 hours after the injury . Three hours are already gone, so it has to run over the remaining 5 hours → 5,040 ÷ 5 = 1,008 mL/hr . Then 5,040 mL over the next 16 h → 315 mL/hr . Titrate to urine output throughout. 🧠 Do these on paper, out loud, three days in a row. Burn ma

SAY IT OUT LOUD 9 · 9 · 18 · 18 · 18 · 1 Head · each arm · front trunk · back trunk · each leg · perineum = 100% . 🖐️ 1 palm = 1% Patient's palm + fingers. Use it for scattered burns. 🧮 4 × kg × % Parkland total of LR for 24 h. Half in 8 h, half in 16 h, clock from injury . 🚽 Urine rules the rate ≥30 mL/hr, BP ≥90, HR <120. The formula only starts the infusion.

Q1: What percentage is the anterior trunk in an adult? Show answer 18% — chest 9% plus abdomen 9%. The posterior trunk is another 18%. Q2: A whole arm, all the way round? A whole leg? Show answer Arm = 9% (4.5% front + 4.5% back). Leg = 18% (9% front + 9% back). Q3: Is a first-degree sunburn counted in TBSA? Show answer No. Only partial-thickness and full-thickness burns are counted. Including superficial burns would overestimate the fluid requirement. Q4: What are the infant modifications? Deep bacterial skin infection — spot it, mark it, escalate it NG-147 INTEGUMENTARY · INFECTION ADHD-friendly visual edition Cellulitis is an acute bacterial infection of the deep dermis and subcutaneous tissue , usually Staph aureus or Group A Strep , that gets in through a break in the skin — most often on a lower leg . Because it is deep, the redness has no crisp border ; it spreads. The exam answer is almost always the same three moves: mark and date the margin, elevate the limb, give the antibiotic on time — an
STEP 0 · LEARN THIS ONCE Every page in this set uses this exact drawing. Learn the layers once and each disease becomes "the same picture, with something different happening in it."

entries.h: 🔬 Skin cutaway — where cellulitis actually lives
entries.t: DEPTH = THE ANSWER Impetigo sits in the top of the epidermis . Tinea sits in the dead keratin . Cellulitis is the deep one: deep dermis and subcutaneous fat — and because the infection is deep, the redness you see on the surface has no crisp edge . bacterial inflammation cocci (staph clusters / strep chains) edema fluid neutrophils 🧠 "Deep = diffuse." The deeper the infection, the blurrier the border. Superficial infections draw sharp lines; deep infections smudge.

entries.h: 📖 Lesion vocabulary — you need this for all five pages
entries.t: Exam questions describe lesions instead of naming them. Learn the eight words and the description tells you the disease. 🧠 "Flat, Firm, Fluid, Foul, Flake." Macule is flat · papule/plaque are firm · vesicle/bulla are fluid · pustule is foul (pus) · crust and scale are the flakes left behind. 🦠
STEP 1 · WHY IT HAPPENS A break in the barrier + bacteria on the skin + a host who cannot fight back = cellulitis.

Cellulitis is an acute bacterial infection of the deep dermis and subcutaneous tissue , most often caused by Staphylococcus aureus or Group A Streptococcus , classically in a lower limb (over the shin/tibia). 🧠 "CELLulitis = the CELLar." It lives in the basement of the skin — the deep layers — not the attic.

Break in the skin barrier ▼ Staph / Strep get into the deep dermis ▼ Bacterial enzymes + toxins spread through tissue planes ▼ Inflammation: vessels dilate & leak ▼ Redness · warmth · swelling · pain — spreading outward ▼ Untreated → abscess · lymphangitis · bacteremia 🧠 Strep makes enzymes that dissolve tissue planes, which is exactly why the redness spreads instead of staying in a neat circle.

entries.h: 🚪 Portals of entry — always look for the front door
entries.t: 🧠 "No door, no cellulitis." If you cannot find a break, look harder — between the toes, under a dressing, in a skin fold, at an old IV site.

Trauma / any wound — the doorway Diabetes — poor perfusion, neuropathy, impaired white cells Tinea pedis (athlete's foot) — cracks between the toes Lymphedema — stagnant lymph cannot clear bacteria Venous insufficiency — sluggish flow, fragile skin Obesity — moist skin folds, poorer perfusion Previous cellulitis — damaged lymphatics recur Immunosuppression — steroids, chemo, HIV 🧠 "Damp, damaged, diabetic." Wet skin, broken skin, and bad sugar control — the three setups.

Each episode scars the lymphatics . Damaged lymphatics → more swelling → less clearance of bacteria → the next episode is easier to get . Breaking that cycle is nursing work: treat the athlete's foot , moisturise dry cracked skin, manage edema (compression once infection is controlled and arterial flow is adequate), and control blood glucose. 🧠 Vicious circle: swelling → infection → scarring → more swelling.

entries.h: 🧪 Bug → drug: the rule that runs this whole set
entries.t: 🧠 Name the organism and the drug class names itself. Bacteria → antibiotic. Fungus → "-azole"/terbinafine. Virus → "-cyclovir". Autoimmune → calm the immune system down. 🔎
STEP 2 · WHAT YOU SEE Think infection: the four cardinal signs plus a body that is starting to react systemically.

Erythema — red, with a poorly-defined spreading border Warmth — compare with the other limb using the back of your hand Edema — tight, shiny, sometimes peau d'orange dimpling Pain / tenderness — and it hurts more than it looks like it should Fever , malaise, sometimes chills 🧠 "RHOP" — R ed, H ot, O edematous, P ainful. If all four are on ONE limb, think cellulitis.

Red streaks running up the limb ( lymphangitis ) + tender nodes Fever > 38 °C / 100.4 °F , rigors, tachycardia, hypotension, confusion Fluctuance — a soft, boggy pocket = abscess , needs drainage Pain out of proportion , dusky/purple skin, bullae, crepitus , rapid progression Redness clearly past the marked line despite 48 h of antibiotics Never assume "it just needs more time" when the redness is racing past the line and the patient is febrile. 🧠 "Streaks + spikes = speak up." Red streaks or a fever spike means es

entries.h: 📈 How bad is this? The escalation ladder
entries.t: 🧠 Pain out of proportion is the necrotising fasciitis flag. The skin can look almost normal while the patient is in agony — that mismatch is the whole point.

entries.h: ⭐ Deep vs superficial — cellulitis vs erysipelas
entries.t: 🧠 "Erysipelas = Edge you can feel." Both start with E. Cellulitis fades; erysipelas has a step you can run your finger over.

WBC ↑ with a left shift (normal adult 4.5–11.0 × 10⁹/L ) CRP / ESR ↑ — inflammation markers, useful for trending Blood cultures if febrile/systemically unwell — before the first antibiotic dose Wound or abscess culture if there is drainable pus Blood glucose / HbA1c — undiagnosed diabetes shows up this way Imaging (ultrasound) if abscess or DVT is suspected 🧠 Cultures before antibiotics — once the drug is in, the culture may grow nothing and you lose the answer.

Measure the erythema (cm) and compare with the marked outline Limb circumference at a marked point — same spot, same tape, every time Temperature , pulse, BP, respiratory rate, mental status Pain score — a rising score with a shrinking rash is a red flag Distal pulses, capillary refill, sensation — is perfusion intact? Photograph per facility policy (with consent) alongside the marked line 🧠 Same spot, same tape, same time. Trends only mean something if you measure the same way twice. 🩺
STEP 3 · WHAT YOU DO Kill the bacteria, drain the pus if there is any, drop the swelling, and prove it is getting better.

entries.h: 🖊️ THE nursing intervention: mark and date the margin
entries.t: 🧠 "Draw it, date it, watch it." If the exam offers "outline the border of the erythema with a skin marker and note the date/time," that is almost always the answer.

Choice is prescriber-driven and depends on severity and local resistance patterns, but the families you should recognize: Penicillins — e.g. dicloxacillin, amoxicillin-clavulanate Cephalosporins — e.g. cephalexin (oral), cefazolin (IV) Clindamycin — an option in penicillin allergy If MRSA is suspected or there is purulence: doxycycline, TMP-SMX, or IV vancomycin Nursing: ask about allergies first, give doses on time to keep blood levels steady, and teach finish the whole course . 🧠 Purulent = think MRSA. Non-purule

entries.h: ⬆️ Elevate the limb — free and effective
entries.t: Raise the affected limb above the level of the heart whenever the patient is resting. Gravity drains the edema, which lowers pressure, improves perfusion and speeds antibiotic delivery to the tissue. Pair it with a bed cradle or pillows so the linen is not pressing on tender skin. 🧠 "Toes above the nose" is the memorable version — heart level is the real target.

Analgesia before dressing changes and repositioning Cool compresses for comfort — never ice directly on the skin Hydration and antipyretics for fever Skin care: moisturise the surrounding skin, treat any tinea pedis Glucose control in diabetes — hyperglycemia stalls healing Mobility when able, plus VTE prevention for the swollen immobile limb Hand hygiene and standard precautions; contact precautions if there is draining pus per facility policy 🧠 ELEVATE: E levate · L abs · E rythema marked · V itals · A ntibiotics

Never massage or vigorously rub a cellulitic limb — you push bacteria along tissue planes. Never apply a hot pack to numb, neuropathic or poorly-perfused skin — burns are silent. Never squeeze or "pop" an abscess at the bedside — drainage is a provider procedure. Never stop antibiotics because the redness improved — relapse and resistance follow. Never apply tight compression before infection and arterial flow have been assessed. 🧠 Don't rub, don't pop, don't stop.

entries.h: 🗣️ Patient teaching — what they take home
entries.t: Finish every dose , even after it looks better Elevate the limb at home; keep moving to prevent clots Come back for: fever, red streaks, spreading past the line, new pus, worsening pain, vomiting the antibiotic Wash and cover every cut; keep skin moisturised so it does not crack Dry between the toes and treat athlete's foot — that is the recurrence prevention step Diabetes: check your feet daily , including between the toes and with a mirror 🧠 "Finish · Elevate · Return." Three sentences the patient can repeat back
STEP 4 · THE REAL EXAM SKILL Five skin conditions, five patterns. Distribution and appearance narrow it before you read a single lab value.
🧠 One leg = cellulitis. One band = shingles. Around the mouth = impetigo. Rings = tinea. Elbows & knees with silver = psoriasis.

entries.h: 📊 Red leg differential — the three that get confused
entries.t: CELLULITIS STASIS DERMATITIS DVT Sides One leg Usually both One leg Onset Days Months–years Hours–days Skin Hot, red, tender, spreading Brown staining, scaly, itchy Swollen, may be pale or dusky Fever Common No No (usually) Itch vs pain Pain Itch Ache / tightness Treatment Antibiotics Emollients, compression, topical steroid Anticoagulation 🧠 "Both legs itch = it is not an infection." Bilateral, itchy, chronic → stasis dermatitis, and it gets misdiagnosed as cellulitis constantly.

Cellulitis vs erysipelas — fuzzy border vs sharp raised border Cellulitis vs abscess — diffuse firmness vs a fluctuant pocket (needs drainage) Cellulitis vs necrotising fasciitis — pain that fits vs pain out of all proportion Cellulitis vs contact dermatitis — painful + febrile vs itchy with a shape that matches an exposure Cellulitis vs gout — spreading limb redness vs an exquisitely tender single joint (classically the great toe) 🧠 Pain says infection. Itch says inflammation or allergy. That single question sorts

The rash spread past the line → notify the provider , do not simply re-mark it and wait. Blood cultures come before the first antibiotic dose, not after. "Cellulitis of both lower legs" in an afebrile, itchy patient → question the diagnosis. Elevation is the answer more often than students expect. Recurrent cellulitis → the missed intervention is usually treating tinea pedis . Cellulitis itself is not spread person-to-person like impetigo — but draining pus is infectious material. 🧠 If an option says "mark and date

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🦠 Deep dermis + fat Staph or Strep. Deep = fuzzy border. 🔥 Red · Hot · Swollen · Tender Usually ONE lower leg, often febrile. 🖊️ Mark + date the margin Then elevate above the heart. 🚨 Red streaks = escalate Streaking, fever, fluctuance, pain out of proportion.

Q1: Which skin layers does cellulitis involve, and why does that matter for what you see? Show answer The deep dermis and subcutaneous tissue. Because it is deep, the erythema has a poorly-defined, fading border rather than a sharp edge. Q2: Name the two usual organisms. Show answer Staphylococcus aureus and Group A Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes). Q3: What is the classic bedside nursing intervention for tracking progress? Show answer Outline the border of the erythema with a skin marker and write the date a

After the wounds close — contractures, scars, garments, and getting a life back NG-164 INTEGUMENTARY · RECOVERY ADHD-friendly visual edition The rehabilitation phase begins once the wounds have fully healed and typically runs for ~12 months or more depending on the severity of the burn. The emergency is over — infection is no longer the big risk — and the enemy changes completely. Now it is scar tissue that shrinks , joints that freeze , skin that no longer moisturises or sweats itself , and a person who has to fac

entries.h: 🧭 This page vs. its sibling — they are NOT the same page
entries.t: NG-164 (this page) = the REHABILITATION PHASE. Contracture prevention, positioning and splinting, pressure garments, water-based lotion, daily range-of-motion exercise, scar maturation, itch, sun protection, nutrition for healing, and psychosocial recovery. NG-146 = the NUMBERS. Rule of 9's, the palm rule, Lund–Browder, pediatric proportions, the Parkland formula and worked fluid calculations. Both share a source title. Study this one for recovery , that one for arithmetic . 🅦🅦🅔 W ater-based lotion · W ear pressure
STEP 1 · WHERE YOU ARE Third phase, longest phase, least dramatic phase — and the one that decides what the patient's life looks like.

entries.h: 🗓️ Where rehab sits in the three phases
entries.t: EXAM TIP Questions are usually solvable just by identifying the phase . Emergent = fluid · Acute = infection · Rehab = function. 🧠 “Fluid · Infection · Function.” Three phases, three one-word priorities. Say the phase first and the answer usually appears.

Starts when the burn wounds are fully healed / covered Lasts around 12 months , longer for severe burns — some scar remodeling continues for 18–24 months Goal: return to the highest possible level of function and independence , physically, socially and psychologically Team: nurse, physiotherapist, occupational therapist, dietitian, psychologist/social worker, plastic surgeon — reconstructive surgery is usually delayed until the scar has matured Patient's job: the daily unglamorous work — lotion, garment, exercise,

Contractures — shortened scar tissue locking a joint. The number-one preventable disability. Hypertrophic scarring & keloids — raised, red, itchy, thickened scar Loss of range of motion and muscle wasting from immobility Chronic pruritus (itch) and dry, fragile skin Heat intolerance — grafted areas cannot sweat Neuropathic pain and altered sensation Depression, anxiety, PTSD, body-image disturbance, social withdrawal Heterotopic ossification — bone forming in soft tissue around a joint (uncommon but classically lis
STEP 2 · POSITION AGAINST COMFORT Healing scar tissue physically shrinks. If you let a joint rest bent, the scar sets it there permanently.

entries.h: 🔬 What a contracture actually is — normal vs. contracted joint
entries.t: Healed burn scar is collagen laid down in dense whorls instead of neat parallel bundles. It is less elastic and it actively shortens as it matures. Across a joint, that shortening drags the joint closed. 🧠 “Scar is a rope that keeps getting shorter.” Stretch the rope every single day or the joint gets tied shut.

entries.h: 🧍 Anti-deformity positioning — the whole body, joint by joint
entries.t: The position of comfort is the position of contracture. Burn patients naturally curl up — flexed, adducted, pillow under the head. Every one of those is exactly wrong. 🧠 “Stretched, straight, spread and square.” Neck stretched (no pillow) · elbows/knees straight · shoulders spread to 90° · ankles square at 90°.

Answer first: no pillow for an anterior neck burn. A pillow flexes the neck, and a neck flexion contracture can permanently fix the chin to the chest — it interferes with eating, airway management and appearance. Position the neck in slight hyperextension — a small rolled towel under the shoulders , not the head Same principle for an axillary burn — arms abducted so the armpit does not seal shut Hand burns: splint in the functional position, and wrap digits individually Anterior chest/abdomen burn: avoid a curled-u

Range-of-motion exercises daily , ideally several times a day — active whenever the patient can, passive when they can't Best time to exercise is when the patient is premedicated and after a dressing change or warm shower, when tissue is most pliable Splints are usually worn at night / during rest , and removed for exercise, unless prescribed otherwise Inspect skin under every splint and garment for pressure areas Ambulate early ; use pressure wraps on legs before standing to reduce pooling and pain Do not exercise
STEP 3 · WHAT YOU TELL THE PATIENT Three discharge instructions carry most of the exam weight. Learn them as one word: WWE .

entries.h: ⭐ W · W · E — the whole rehab teaching plan
entries.t: 🧠 “W-W-E: like the wrestling — you have to Wrestle the scar every day.” W ater-based lotion · W ear the garment · E xercise.

Why: the burn destroyed the sebaceous (oil) glands and sweat glands . Healed skin cannot lubricate itself, so it is dry, tight, fragile and intensely itchy . Apply a water-based, non-perfumed moisturiser several times a day , especially after bathing Avoid perfumed, alcohol-based or oil/petroleum-heavy products unless prescribed — they irritate or trap heat Massage it in gently along the scar — the massage itself helps soften the scar Bathe in lukewarm water with mild soap; pat dry, don't rub For itch: cool compres

Why: constant, even pressure over a healing scar keeps collagen laying down flat and organized instead of piling up into a raised hypertrophic scar. Custom fitted; worn as prescribed — commonly up to 23 hours a day , removed only for bathing and skin care Worn for many months (often 12–24) until the scar has matured — pale, flat and soft Must be snug but not painful ; check for numbness, tingling, color change or reduced pulses Inspect the skin underneath at every removal; report blisters or open areas Two sets so
STEP 4 · WHAT THE SKIN CAN'T DO ANY MORE Healed burn skin is not replacement skin. Knowing what it lost explains every teaching point.

entries.h: 🔬 Normal skin vs. healed burn scar — what is missing
entries.t: Scar tissue has no hair follicles, no sebaceous glands, no sweat glands and less melanin. That single sentence explains dryness, itching, heat intolerance, sun sensitivity and color change. 🧠 “No hair, no oil, no sweat, no tan.” Four things the new skin cannot do — and four teaching points fall straight out of them.

entries.h: 📈 Scar maturation — it gets worse before it gets better
entries.t: Warn the patient in advance: for the first months the scar becomes redder, thicker and itchier . That is normal maturation, not a complication. It then slowly fades, flattens and softens over 12–24 months . 🧠 “Angry at six months, quiet at eighteen.” Tell the patient this on day one so they don't panic — or give up on the garment — at month three.

entries.h: ☀️ Sun protection — for at least a year
entries.t: Answer first: healed burn skin has less melanin and burns fast . Sun exposure also causes permanent, blotchy hyperpigmentation of the scar. Avoid direct sun to healed areas — commonly taught as for at least 1 year / until the scar matures Use a high-SPF broad-spectrum sunscreen on exposed healed skin, reapplied often Better still: cover up — long sleeves, wide-brim hat, shade at midday No tanning beds, ever 🧠 “New skin has no sunglasses.” The melanin that used to protect it burned off with the dermis.

Grafted and scarred skin cannot sweat and has poor blood-flow control, so temperature regulation is impaired. Overheats quickly in hot weather or during exercise → heat exhaustion risk Teach: exercise in the cool part of the day, drink fluids, take cool breaks, avoid saunas/hot tubs Also feels the cold more — the insulating fat and vasomotor control are gone Sensation may be reduced → check water temperature with an unburned area or a thermometer to avoid scalding 🧠 “No sweat, no thermostat.” Every hot-weather acti
STEP 5 · THE PERSON Healing needs calories, and living needs a plan. Both are examinable.

entries.h: 🍗 Nutrition keeps working long after discharge
entries.t: The hypermetabolic state can persist for months . A burn survivor who stops eating for healing loses the graft take, the strength and the weight they fought for. 🧠 “You cannot build a wall without bricks.” Protein is the brick, calories are the labor, vitamin C is the mortar.

entries.h: 🧠 The psychosocial work — do not skip this in an exam answer
entries.t: A visible burn changes how the patient is seen and how they see themselves. Expect, normalize and screen for: Body-image disturbance — avoidance of mirrors, refusing visitors, covering up even indoors Depression & anxiety ; PTSD with nightmares, flashbacks and avoidance of anything fire-related Grief — for appearance, function, a home, or people lost in the same event Social withdrawal , fear of staring/questions, reluctance to return to work or school Sexuality and intimacy concerns — raise them; the patient often

🧴 LOTION water-based, several ×/day 👕 GARMENT as prescribed, ~23 h/day 🤸 EXERCISE ROM every day ☀️ SUN cover up · SPF · 1 year+ 🥩 PROTEIN high cal, high protein 🌡️ HEAT can't sweat — pace yourself 🚫 NO SCRATCH cool, cotton, short nails 📞 REPORT open areas, fever, ↓ROM 💚 SUPPORT groups & counseling Tell the patient to call if: a healed area breaks down or opens; drainage, increasing redness, swelling or fever; a joint is losing movement; the garment causes numbness, tingling or color change; pain or itch becomes unm

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🅦🅦🅔 W ater-based lotion · W ear pressure garments · E xercise (ROM) daily. 🦴 Position against comfort No pillow for neck burns · shoulders 90° · elbows & knees straight · ankles 90°. ✨ Scar peaks then fades Worst at 3–6 months, mature by 12–24. Garments until mature. 🛡️ Infection is NOT the risk here Rehab-phase priority is function , not sepsis.

Q1: When does the rehabilitation phase begin and how long does it last? Show answer It begins once the wounds have fully healed, and typically lasts around 12 months or more depending on the severity of the burn. Scar remodeling can continue for 18–24 months. Q2: Give the three patient-education points as a mnemonic. Show answer W-W-E. Water-based lotion helps · Wear pressure garments · Exercise daily (range of motion). Q3: Is infection the main risk in the rehabilitation phase? Show answer No. The wounds are close

Work through NG-107 (patho) , NG-123 (treatment) , NG-146 (Rule of 9's & Parkland) and NG-164 (rehab phase) first. Then come here and try to beat the questions before reading the answers. Cover the options with your hand. Answer out loud. Then uncover. ↔️ Front or back? The #1 calculation error. A posterior arm is 4.5% , not 9%. Halve every limb when only one surface is burned. 🚽 Low urine = MORE fluid Never a diuretic, never "slow the rate." Under-perfusion is fixed with Lactated Ringer's . ⏱️ 18–24 h Interstitial

entries.h: HOW TO ATTACK A BURN QUESTION
entries.t: STEP 0 · THE SYSTEM Four questions, asked in the same order every time. They eliminate most distractors before you even read them.
🧠 “Phase · Airway · Number · Urine.” Four words. Run them in order on every burn stem before you look at the options.

entries.h: 🧾 The numbers you must have memorized cold
entries.t: Head/neck 9% · each arm 9% · anterior trunk 18% · posterior trunk 18% · each leg 18% · perineum 1% Patient's palm plus fingers ≈ 1% (the palm alone is often taught as ≈0.5%) Parkland: 4 mL × kg × %TBSA , half in 8 h , half in 16 h , clock from injury Targets: urine ≥30 mL/hr · systolic ≥90 · HR <120 Peak interstitial shift 18–24 h · diuresis 48–72 h Emergent labs: K⁺ >5.0 · Na⁺ <135 · Hgb and Hct both elevated (typical adult reference bands ≈ Hgb 12–18 g/dL, Hct 36–54% — ranges vary by lab and by sex) 🧠 If a number

entries.h: ⭐ Read the stem for these five words
entries.t: ANTERIOR / POSTERIOR → halve the limb values ENTIRE / CIRCUMFERENTIAL → use the whole-region value (and think escharotomy) PERINEUM → they want the extra 1% HOURS AFTER THE INJURY → the resuscitation clock, and which phase you are in FULL-THICKNESS / PARTIAL-THICKNESS → both count in TBSA; a superficial (1°) area does not 🧠 Physically underline those words. On a real exam, mouth them. The stem is telling you the answer. ①
RULE OF NINES Two classic items. Both are missed for the same reason: whole-limb values used for a single surface.

entries.h: 🎓 Question 1 — full-thickness burns to ALL posterior body surfaces
entries.t: A client has full-thickness burns to all posterior body surfaces . Using the Rule of Nines, calculate the percentage of total body surface area affected. ❌ 36% — This counts only the back of the trunk (18%) plus the back of both legs (18%) and forgets the head and the arms entirely. ❌ 45% — A tempting "round number." It drops the posterior head and neck (4.5%). ✅ 49.5% — Correct. Back of head & neck 4.5 + entire back 18 + posterior arms 4.5 × 2 = 9 + posterior legs 9 × 2 = 18. ❌ 76.5% — The classic error: whole arm

A client has partial-thickness burns to the anterior legs and the perineum . Using the Rule of Nines, calculate the percentage of total body surface area affected. ❌ 9% — Only one leg was counted. The stem says legs , plural. ❌ 18% — The two anterior legs are right, but the perineum's 1% was dropped. If the stem names the perineum, the 1% is the point of the question. ✅ 19% — Correct. Anterior right leg 9 + anterior left leg 9 + perineum 1 = 19% TBSA. ❌ 37% — Whole legs (18% each) were used instead of the anterior
4 × kg × %TBSA The multiplication is easy. The marks are lost on the split, the units and the clock.

The client above weighs 100 kg with 19% TBSA . Calculate the Lactated Ringer's fluid resuscitation needed in the first 24 hours . ❌ 1,900 mL — Someone used 1 mL instead of 4 mL. The constant is 4 . ❌ 3,800 mL — That is only half the total, i.e. the volume for the first 8 hours. The question asked for the whole 24 hours. ✅ 7,600 mL — Correct. 4 mL × 100 kg × 19 = 7,600 mL of LR in the first 24 hours. ❌ 15,200 mL — The total was doubled instead of halved. Halving applies to the timing , not to the total. 4 mL × 100 k

A 70 kg client sustained burns to 36% TBSA at 06:00 and arrives in the emergency department at 09:00. The Parkland formula is prescribed. How much LR should be infused by 14:00 ? ❌ 10,080 mL — That is the entire 24-hour total, not the first-8-hour portion. ✅ 5,040 mL — Correct. Total = 4 × 70 × 36 = 10,080 mL. Half = 5,040 mL must be in by 8 hours after the injury , i.e. by 14:00. ❌ 5,040 mL by 17:00 — This restarted the clock at arrival. The 8 hours run from 06:00, so the deadline is 14:00, not 17:00. ❌ 2,520 mL —
JUDGMENT ITEMS These three are the most-missed non-calculation burn questions in the bank.

entries.h: 🎓 Question 5 — the client is not responding to the fluids
entries.t: A client is undergoing fluid replacement after being burned on 20% of her body 12 hours ago . Assessment: BP 90/50 , pulse 110 , urine output 20 mL over the past hour . The nurse anticipates which prescription? ✅ Increasing the IV Lactated Ringer's — Correct. Urine under 30 mL/hr with a borderline BP and a rising pulse means the patient is under-resuscitated . The fix for hypovolemia is more isotonic fluid. ❌ Administering a diuretic (e.g. furosemide) — The most attractive wrong answer. It "treats" the low urine nu

entries.h: 🎓 Question 6 — when is the third-spacing worst?
entries.t: A client has an extensive burn injury involving 45% of total body surface area . When planning for fluid resuscitation, the nurse should consider that fluid shifting to the interstitial spaces is greatest during which time period? ❌ During the first 2 hours after the injury — Leaking has started, but it has not peaked. Most of the shift is still ahead of you. ❌ Between 6 and 12 hours after the injury — Still climbing. Tempting because this is when the first (faster) half of the fluid is running. ✅ Between 18 and 24

entries.h: 🎓 Question 7 — which lab would you expect?
entries.t: A client has a severe burn injury covering 35% of the total body surface area . The nurse is most likely to note which finding on the laboratory report? ✅ Hematocrit 60% (0.60) — Correct. Plasma has leaked out of the vessels while red cells stayed behind, so the Hct is falsely elevated — hemoconcentration . A typical adult reference band is about 36–54% (varies by lab and sex). ❌ Hematocrit 28% — A low Hct fits the acute phase (hemodilution once fluid returns, plus red-cell destruction) — not the first 24 hours. ❌
TEACHING & SAFETY These feel like "common sense" questions, which is exactly why they are missed.

A client with burns is immunocompromised . What precaution should be taken to prevent infection? ✅ Avoid placing fresh flowers or plants in or near the client's room — Correct. Standing vase water harbors Pseudomonas and potting soil harbors Aspergillus and other fungi. Both are dangerous to a patient with no skin barrier and a suppressed immune system. ❌ Place the client in a semi-private room — The opposite. A private room with protective isolation is indicated; a roommate is an infection source. ❌ Restrict all f

A client is entering the rehabilitation phase after a major burn. Which statement indicates that teaching has been effective ? ✅ "I'll use a water-based lotion several times a day, wear my pressure garment as prescribed, and do my exercises every day." — Correct. That is the whole W-W-E teaching plan: W ater-based lotion · W ear pressure garments · E xercise daily (range of motion). ❌ "I'll take the pressure garment off whenever it feels tight or hot." — Wrong. It is supposed to be snug; it is commonly worn up to 2

A client is brought to the emergency department after being rescued from a house fire . There are burns to the face and neck , the voice is hoarse , and there is soot around the nose and mouth . Which action does the nurse take FIRST ? ✅ Assess the airway and apply 100% oxygen by non-rebreather, anticipating early intubation — Correct. Enclosed-space fire + facial/neck burns + hoarseness + soot = inhalation injury . Airway swelling worsens over hours; intubate before it closes. Airway always outranks the burn. ❌ Ca

SAY IT OUT LOUD 49.5% & 19% All posterior surfaces = 49.5% . Anterior legs + perineum = 19% . 7,600 mL 4 × 100 kg × 19% → 3,800 in 8 h , 3,800 in the next 16 h. ↑ the LR Urine 20 mL/hr, BP 90/50, P 110 → increase Lactated Ringer's . Never a diuretic. 18–24 h · Hct 60% · no flowers Three one-line answers worth memorizing verbatim.

entries.h: 🎯 Final speed round — 10 answers, no options
entries.t: 1. All posterior surfaces = ? Show answer 49.5% TBSA (4.5 + 18 + 9 + 18). 2. Anterior legs + perineum = ? Show answer 19% TBSA (9 + 9 + 1). 3. 100 kg, 19% TBSA — total LR in 24 h? Show answer 7,600 mL. Half (3,800 mL) in the first 8 hours, half over the next 16 hours. 4. When does the resuscitation clock start? Show answer At the time of injury — not at arrival, not when the IV is started. 5. Urine 20 mL/hr at 12 hours — what do you anticipate? Show answer Increasing the IV Lactated Ringer's. Never a diuretic, neve

entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🧬 Atopic 🧪 Contact ⚖️ Tell them apart 🩺 Care & teach ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Skin & Wound · Dermatitis · Pathophysiology Course 🩹 SKIN & WOUND SET NG-051 Skin (foundation) NG-044 Pressure Injuries NG-080 Wound Care NG-116 Frostbite NG-182 Dermatitis NG-225 Psoriasis NG-204 Skin Cancer

Atopic vs Contact Dermatitis — two itchy rashes with completely different stories NG-182 INTEGUMENTARY · IMMUNE ADHD-friendly visual edition Both look like an angry, itchy rash. The difference is where it came from . Atopic dermatitis is inside-out : an inherited leaky skin barrier plus an over-reactive immune system, flaring for years in the bends of the joints . Contact dermatitis is outside-in : something touched the skin, and the rash is shaped exactly like whatever touched it . 📄 Simple Nursing original — open
SIDE A · INSIDE-OUT A chronic, relapsing, inherited condition — the skin's brick wall is leaky and the immune system is trigger-happy.

entries.h: 🧬 Why atopic skin flares — the barrier cutaway
entries.t: 🧠 Atopic skin is a wall with crumbling mortar. Water leaks out (dry, itchy) and irritants get in (inflamed). That is why moisturiser is not "extra" — it is the treatment.

entries.h: 🤝 The atopic triad — always ask about all three
entries.t: 🌿 Atopic dermatitis the skin 🫁 Asthma the lungs 🤧 Allergic rhinitis the nose These three travel together and often appear in that order through childhood — the "atopic march." A family history of any of them raises the odds of the others. Serum IgE is often elevated and eosinophils may be raised, but the diagnosis is clinical. 🧠 "Skin, sneeze, wheeze." If a child has bad eczema, ask about night cough, wheeze and a permanently runny nose — you may be the first person to connect them.

entries.h: ⚠️ Cardinal feature: the itch comes first
entries.t: Atopic dermatitis is "the itch that rashes," not the rash that itches. Pruritus is the defining symptom — it is often worst at night and wrecks sleep for the child and the parents. Acute flare: erythematous papules and vesicles, weeping serous exudate , crusting. Subacute: drier, scaly, red plaques. Chronic: lichenification (thick, leathery skin with exaggerated skin lines), excoriations, pigment change, fissures. Always: dry skin (xerosis) between flares. The skin is never truly "normal." 🧠 Wet → dry → leather. Ac

entries.h: 🔬 Acute → subacute → chronic — the same eczema, three faces
entries.t: 🧠 Wet → flaky → leathery. Acute needs drying and calming, subacute needs greasing, chronic needs the scratching stopped.

entries.h: 🗺️ Where it shows up — and it MOVES with age
entries.t: This single contrast answers the classic exam confusion. Eczema hides in the creases ; psoriasis sits on the points . Full detail on the psoriasis side: NG-225 — Psoriasis . 🧠 "Eczema bends, psoriasis extends." Infants are the exception — babies get it on the cheeks and the outsides of the limbs, and the rash migrates into the creases as they grow.

🧼 Harsh soap strips the lipid mortar 🧴 Fragrance perfumed products 🧥 Wool & synthetics scratchy fabric 🥵 Heat & sweat overheating, hot showers 🏜️ Dry air winter, indoor heating 🐈 Aeroallergens dust mites, dander, pollen 😰 Stress a real, documented trigger 🦠 Infection often S. aureus Food allergy triggers eczema in a minority of infants and young children — do not restrict a child's diet on your own ; that needs an allergy evaluation. 🧠 Hot, dry, scratchy, stressed. Four words that cover most flares — and all four a

entries.h: 🚨 Complications — the two you must recognize
entries.t: Secondary bacterial infection (usually Staphylococcus aureus ): honey-colored crusting , pustules, worsening redness and pain, fever. Broken, scratched, weeping skin is an open door. Eczema herpeticum — herpes simplex spreading across eczematous skin. Clusters of monomorphic "punched-out" vesicles and erosions, rapidly spreading, with fever and a sick-looking child. This is a dermatological emergency — escalate urgently for antiviral treatment. Sleep deprivation and its knock-on effects on school, work, mood and fa
SIDE B · OUTSIDE-IN Something touched the skin. The rash is a photograph of whatever it was .

entries.h: 🧪 Irritant vs allergic — two different mechanisms
entries.t: 🧠 Irritant = a burn. Allergic = a grudge. An irritant damages anybody's skin the first time; an allergen only reacts in someone the immune system has already met it in — and it takes a day or three to show up.

entries.h: 🔎 The rash is shaped like the culprit
entries.t: Common culprits to know: irritants — soaps, detergents, solvents, bleach, alcohol gel, frequent hand-washing, saliva (lip-lickers), urine and stool. Allergens — urushiol (poison ivy/oak/sumac), nickel (jewelry, snaps, watch backs, belt buckles), fragrance, preservatives, neomycin , hair dye (PPD) and rubber accelerators in gloves. 🧠 "If the rash has a straight edge, a human-made object made it." Ask: what touches your skin at work, at home, in your hobby, and what is new in the last 3 days?

entries.h: 🌿 Poison ivy — the myths you have to correct
entries.t: Blister fluid does NOT spread the rash. New patches appear later because thinner skin reacts later, or because there was more urushiol there. The rash is not contagious person-to-person. But urushiol on clothing, boots, tools, gloves and pet fur absolutely re-exposes you — wash all of it. Wash the skin with soap and cool water as soon as possible after exposure — ideally within minutes. Once it is bound, washing no longer prevents the reaction. The rash appears hours to a few days after exposure and typically lasts

entries.h: ⚠️ Latex — know which reaction you are being asked about
entries.t: Irritant contact dermatitis — dry, cracked hands from glove occlusion, powder and hand-washing. Not an allergy at all. Type IV allergic contact dermatitis — delayed, itchy, eczematous, usually to rubber accelerator chemicals ; appears 24–72 h after wearing gloves. Type I latex allergy — IgE-mediated, immediate : urticaria, angiedema, wheeze, anaphylaxis . This is the life-threatening one. Cross-reactive foods ("latex–fruit syndrome"): banana, avocado, kiwi, chestnut. Ask about them. High-risk groups: healthcare wor
STEP 3 · COMPARE The table the exam question is written from.

entries.h: ⭐ Atopic vs Irritant contact vs Allergic contact
entries.t: Feature Atopic dermatitis Irritant contact Allergic contact Cause Inside-out : inherited barrier defect + over-reactive immune response Outside-in : direct chemical/physical damage to the barrier Outside-in : Type IV delayed hypersensitivity (T-cell mediated) Immune memory? Yes — chronic immune dysregulation, ↑ IgE No — anyone gets it with enough exposure Yes — needs prior sensitization First exposure? N/A — lifelong tendency Reacts on the first exposure No reaction the first time; reacts on re-exposure Timing Chro

entries.h: ⚖️ Eczema vs psoriasis — the other classic mix-up
entries.t: Eczema (atopic dermatitis) Psoriasis FLEXURAL — inside the elbows and behind the knees EXTENSOR — outside of elbows, front of knees, scalp, lower back Itch is severe and the dominant symptom Itch is variable; may burn or sting instead Ill-defined edges; weeping and crusting in flares Sharply demarcated , thick plaques with silvery-white scale Lichenification, excoriations, dry skin between flares Scraping the scale can cause pinpoint bleeding (Auspitz sign); Koebner phenomenon — new plaques at sites of injury Usual

entries.h: 🔁 The itch–scratch cycle — why it never just settles
entries.t: 🧠 Scratching feels like treatment and behaves like fuel. Every intervention on the next section exists to break this loop. 🩺
STEP 4 · MANAGE Most of this is teaching — and most of the teaching is about moisturiser.

entries.h: ✅ Atopic dermatitis — the daily routine that actually works
entries.t: 1 Bathe smart Short (5–10 min), lukewarm bath or shower once daily. Fragrance-free, non-soap cleanser — no bubble bath, no scrubbing, no washcloths on inflamed skin. Pat dry, don't rub. ▼ 2 "Soak and seal" Apply emollient within about 3 minutes of getting out, while the skin is still damp. Thick ointments and creams beat lotions. Apply liberally, at least twice a day and every time after washing hands — even when the skin looks fine. ▼ 3 Treat the inflammation Topical corticosteroids to active areas, at the lowest

entries.h: 💊 Topical steroid potency by body region — thin skin needs weak steroid
entries.t: 🧠 "Weak where the skin is thin." Face, eyelids, armpits and groin get the gentlest preparation; palms and soles can take the strongest.

entries.h: ✅ Contact dermatitis — the treatment is detective work
entries.t: Identify and remove the agent. Nothing else works if the exposure continues. Take a full history: occupation, hobbies, new products, jewelry, cosmetics, topical medicines, plants, gloves. Wash the area with mild soap and cool water as soon as possible after exposure; wash contaminated clothing, tools and pets. Cool compresses and colloidal oatmeal baths for weeping, itchy skin; calamine for symptom relief. Topical corticosteroids for localized disease; systemic corticosteroids for severe or widespread reactions (cl

entries.h: 👨‍👩‍👧 Teach the family — the sentences that land
entries.t: "This is not contagious and it is not your fault." Say it out loud, especially to parents and to school-age children. "Moisturiser is medicine." Every day, forever — not only when it flares. "Use the steroid properly and you'll use less of it." Under-treating a flare from steroid fear leads to longer, worse flares. Use as prescribed, on the areas prescribed. "Short nails, cotton clothes, cool room." Call for: honey-colored crusting, pus, fever, rapidly spreading painful blisters/punched-out sores (possible eczema h

entries.h: 🗺️ Where this page sits in the set
entries.t: NG-051 — Skin : the barrier, Langerhans cells and the lesion words (vesicle, plaque, lichenification, excoriation) used all over this page. NG-225 — Psoriasis : the extensor-surface, silvery-scale counterpart. Learn the two together or you will mix them up. NG-080 — Wound Care : for excoriated, weeping or secondarily infected skin. 🧠 Creases + itch + asthma = eczema. Points + silver scale + nails = psoriasis. Straight edges = contact. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🧬 Eczema bends Flexural creases · chronic · intensely itchy · atopic triad. 🧪 Contact copies the object Sharp, geometric borders in the shape of what touched it. ⏱️ Irritant fast · allergic slow Irritant = same day, burns. Allergic = 12–72 h later, itches (Type IV). 🚨 Punched-out vesicles + fever Eczema herpeticum — escalate now.

Q1: Name the atopic triad. Show answer Atopic dermatitis (eczema), asthma, and allergic rhinitis. They often appear in that order through childhood — the "atopic march." Q2: Where is atopic dermatitis found in an infant, and where in an older child? Show answer Infants: cheeks, scalp, trunk and the extensor surfaces of the limbs, typically sparing the diaper area. Older children and adults: the flexural creases — antecubital and popliteal fossae — plus neck, wrists and ankles. Q3: A rash appeared 2 days after garde

Herpes simplex & herpes zoster — the viruses that live in your nerves NG-202 INTEGUMENTARY · VIRAL ADHD-friendly visual edition Shingles is reactivation of the varicella-zoster virus — chickenpox that has been asleep in a nerve ganglion for decades. When immunity dips it travels back down the nerve and blisters the skin that nerve supplies: one dermatome, one side, stopping at the midline , with burning pain 2–3 days before the rash. Herpes simplex does the same trick on the lip or genitals. All of them are treated
STEP 0 · LEARN THIS ONCE Same skin drawing as every page in this set — this time the disease arrives down the nerve instead of through the surface.

entries.h: 🔬 Skin cutaway — the only one that comes from the INSIDE
entries.t: DEPTH = THE ANSWER Bacteria and fungi come in from outside. This virus lives in a sensory nerve ganglion and travels down the axon into the epidermis it supplies. That is why the rash is banded, one-sided and painful before it is visible . virus particles inflamed sensory nerve intra-epidermal vesicle erythematous base 🧠 "Grouped vesicles on a red base" is the sentence that means herpes family — cold sore, genital herpes or shingles.

entries.h: 📖 Lesion vocabulary — this is a vesicle disease
entries.t: Vesicle → pustule → crust, all in a band. Highlighted below. 🧠 Scattered = chickenpox. Clustered in a band = shingles. Clustered on the lip = cold sore. 🦠
STEP 1 · WHY IT HAPPENS An old virus, a tired immune system, and a nerve that remembers exactly where it goes.

Shingles (herpes zoster) is reactivation of the varicella-zoster virus — the virus that caused chickenpox — from a sensory nerve ganglion, producing a painful blistering rash in the dermatome that nerve supplies. Herpes simplex (HSV-1 / HSV-2) behaves the same way: it hides in ganglia and reactivates as grouped vesicles in the same spot each time. 🧠 "Chickenpox once, shingles later." No chickenpox (or vaccine virus) = no shingles.

Chickenpox in childhood ▼ Virus travels UP sensory nerves and goes dormant in the dorsal root ganglia ▼ Years later, cell-mediated immunity drops ▼ Virus reactivates and travels DOWN the axon ▼ Nerve inflammation = burning pain FIRST ▼ Grouped vesicles appear in that ONE dermatome 🧠 It is an "opportunistic" reactivation — the virus waits until your defenses are down before it attacks.

entries.h: 🧬 Where it comes from — chickenpox that never left
entries.t: 🧠 The ganglion is the hotel. The virus checks in after chickenpox and checks out when your immune system stops watching the door.

Age — risk rises sharply after 50 , as VZV-specific immunity wanes Immunosuppressive drugs — corticosteroids, chemotherapy, transplant drugs, biologics Cancer , especially hematological; HIV ; other immunodeficiency Another active infection (e.g. pneumonia) occupying the immune system Major physical or emotional stress , fatigue, poor nutrition Surgery, trauma, radiation 🧠 "Old, ill, stressed, suppressed." Four words, all the risk factors.

entries.h: 🧪 Bug → drug: the rule that runs this whole set
entries.t: 🧠 Virus → "-cyclovir". Antivirals suppress , they do not cure — the virus stays in the ganglion for life. 🔎
STEP 2 · WHAT YOU SEE Pain first, then a one-sided band of grouped blisters that refuses to cross the midline.

Prodrome: burning, tingling, itching, numbness or stabbing pain in one strip of skin, 2–3 days before the rash Rash: red papules → grouped vesicles on an erythematous base → pustules → crusts Unilateral , following one dermatome , most often the trunk (thoracic) — it stops at the midline Paraesthesia — burning, numbness, tingling, hypersensitivity to touch Low-grade fever < 38 °C / 100.4 °F , headache, malaise, fatigue Itching as it crusts 🧠 "Pain, then band, then blisters." In that order, every time.

Clinical — the dermatomal pattern plus grouped vesicles is usually enough PCR / viral swab of vesicle fluid if the picture is unclear or the patient is immunocompromised A direct fluorescent antibody test may be used where available Consider testing for immunosuppression (including HIV) in a young patient with shingles Ophthalmology review without delay if the eye or nose tip is involved 🧠 Shingles in a young adult is a question, not just a diagnosis — why are their defenses down?

entries.h: 🗺️ Dermatomes — why the rash stops at the midline
entries.t: 🧠 T4 nipple, T10 umbilicus. Two landmarks that show up in exams over and over.

entries.h: ⏱️ The timeline — and the two clocks you are watching
entries.t: 🧠 Clock 1 = 72 hours for the drug. Clock 2 = crusted over for the contagion.

entries.h: 🚨 Shingles on the face — the two emergencies
entries.t: 🧠 "Nose tip = eye trip." Lesions on the tip of the nose (Hutchinson's sign) mean the eye is at high risk — urgent ophthalmology.
🧠 The rash is temporary; the nerve damage may not be. Treat the pain aggressively and early — that is the prevention. 🩺
STEP 3 · WHAT YOU DO Antiviral early, pain controlled properly, and everyone around the patient protected.

entries.h: 🦠 Who can catch what — the rule everyone gets wrong
entries.t: 🧠 Shingles gives chickenpox, not shingles. Say that sentence out loud until it sticks.

Acyclovir · valacyclovir · famciclovir Start as early as possible , ideally within 72 h of the rash appearing They shorten the illness and reduce the risk of postherpetic neuralgia — they do not eradicate the virus Encourage fluids — adequate hydration matters, especially with IV acyclovir, which can affect the kidneys Give doses on time ; monitor renal function as prescribed For HSV, the same drugs are used episodically or as daily suppression 🧠 "-cyclovir = virus." And early beats perfect — a dose today is worth

Localized shingles in an immunocompetent patient: standard + contact precautions ; cover the lesions with a dressing Disseminated zoster , or zoster in an immunocompromised patient: airborne + contact precautions — negative-pressure room until lesions are crusted Chickenpox (varicella) : always airborne + contact Staff and visitors must be immune — non-immune, pregnant or immunocompromised people should not care for or visit the patient Keep away from newborns , pregnant people without immunity , and the immunosupp

entries.h: 😖 Pain — treat it like nerve pain, not a scrape
entries.t: Assess it properly and regularly — this pain is frequently under-treated Neuropathic agents : gabapentin or pregabalin, tricyclic antidepressants Topical : lidocaine patch or gel; capsaicin (only on intact, healed skin) Analgesics as prescribed; opioids may be needed short-term for severe acute pain Cool compresses , calamine, colloidal oatmeal baths for comfort Loose cotton clothing — even fabric can hurt (allodynia); a bed cradle keeps sheets off the skin 🧠 Plain acetaminophen/NSAIDs alone rarely touch nerve pain

Keep lesions clean, dry and COVERED with a non-adherent dressing Do not rupture the blisters — the fluid is infectious and the skin is a barrier Keep nails short ; discourage scratching (secondary bacterial infection risk) Watch for secondary infection : increasing pain, spreading redness, pus, fever Hand hygiene before and after all contact; gloves for lesion care Support rest, nutrition and fluids — the immune system needs them Acknowledge the emotional load : the pain is exhausting and often invisible to others

Recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix) — 2 doses, recommended for adults 50 years and older , and for immunocompromised adults 19+ per current guidance It is recommended even if the person has already had shingles or does not remember having chickenpox It is not a live vaccine; expect a sore arm, tiredness or aches for a day or two — that is a normal response Varicella (chickenpox) vaccine in childhood prevents the primary infection in the first place Vaccination is the most reliable way to lower the risk of shingle

Never let a non-immune, pregnant or immunocompromised person care for or visit the patient. Never break the blisters — the fluid is loaded with live virus. Never treat facial shingles as routine; ask about the eye every time. Never delay the antiviral waiting for a test result. Never tell a patient shingles is "caught" from someone else's shingles — it comes from their own dormant virus. 🧠 Don't pop it, don't delay it, don't expose the vulnerable. 🔀
STEP 4 · THE REAL EXAM SKILL One band that stops at the midline is shingles. Everything else is something else.
🧠 One band, one side, stops at the midline. No other rash on this page does that.

HSV-1 HSV-2 VZV (shingles) Classic site Lip border, mouth Genital area One dermatome, often trunk Pattern Small recurring cluster Painful grouped ulcers Unilateral band, stops at midline Latent in Trigeminal ganglion Sacral ganglia Dorsal root ganglia Recurs? Often, same spot Often, decreasing over time Usually once, can recur Treatment All three: the "-cyclovir" family — acyclovir, valacyclovir, famciclovir 🧠 Same family, same drugs, different postcode.

SHINGLES CHICKENPOX Which event Reactivation First infection Spread One dermatome, one side All over the body Age Usually older adults Usually children Pain Severe, comes first Itch > pain Precautions Contact (airborne if disseminated / immunocompromised) Airborne + contact 🧠 Same virus, two chapters.

A contact does not "get shingles" — a non-immune contact gets chickenpox . The patient is contagious until every lesion is crusted , not until the pain stops. Antiviral within 72 h of rash onset — do not pick "wait for the culture." Localized, covered shingles in a well patient = contact precautions; disseminated or immunocompromised = airborne . Pain before a rash in one strip of skin is shingles until proven otherwise. Lesions on the nose tip → the eye is at risk → urgent referral. Shingles pain is neuropathic —

Shingles vs cellulitis — blistered band with burning nerve pain vs diffuse hot red swelling Shingles vs contact dermatitis — dermatomal vs shaped like whatever touched the skin Shingles vs impetigo — clustered vesicles on a red base vs honey crust Shingles vs tinea — painful band vs itchy ring HSV vs impetigo — recurs in the same spot after tingling vs new golden crusts anywhere 🧠 Burning band = virus. Hot swelling = bacteria. Itchy ring = fungus. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD ⚡ One dermatome, one side Stops at the midline. Grouped vesicles on a red base. 😣 Pain 2–3 days first Burning/tingling before any rash. Treat as NEUROPATHIC pain. ⏱️ "-cyclovir" within 72 h Shortens it and lowers postherpetic neuralgia risk. 🦠 Contagious till crusted A non-immune contact gets CHICKENPOX. Cover the lesions.

Q1: What causes shingles? Show answer Reactivation of varicella-zoster virus — the chickenpox virus — from a sensory nerve ganglion where it has been dormant since the childhood infection. Q2: Describe the rash in one sentence. Show answer Grouped vesicles on an erythematous base, unilateral, following a single dermatome, and stopping at the midline. Q3: What comes before the rash, and why does it matter? Show answer Burning, tingling, itching or stabbing pain in that strip of skin, 2–3 days earlier, because the ne

entries.t: 🏠 Study Hub 🖼️ Infographics 🧨 Cause & risk 🔬 The 3 types 🔤 ABCDE ☀️ Prevent & teach ⚡ Quick recall Nursing Field Notes / Skin & Wound · Skin Cancer · Pathophysiology Course 🩹 SKIN & WOUND SET NG-051 Skin (foundation) NG-044 Pressure Injuries NG-080 Wound Care NG-116 Frostbite NG-182 Dermatitis NG-225 Psoriasis NG-204 Skin Cancer

Basal cell · Squamous cell · Melanoma — and the ABCDE that catches the deadly one NG-204 INTEGUMENTARY · ONCOLOGY ADHD-friendly visual edition Skin cancer is uncontrolled growth of skin cells after their DNA has been damaged — nearly always by ultraviolet light . Which cell mutates decides which cancer you get: the basal layer → basal cell carcinoma, the keratinocytes above it → squamous cell carcinoma, the melanocytes → melanoma. The layers are drawn on NG-051 ; this page shows what happens when each one goes wron

STEP 1 · CAUSE Ultraviolet light breaks DNA. Enough breaks in the wrong genes and the cell stops obeying the "stop dividing" signal. From your lecture. Basal cell is common and rarely spreads. Squamous cell may spread to nodes and organs. Melanoma is the dangerous one — and it is the one ABCDE is for.

entries.h: ☀️ UVA vs UVB — how deep the damage goes
entries.t: UVB is mostly absorbed in the epidermis — it causes sunburn and directly damages keratinocyte and melanocyte DNA. UVA penetrates into the dermis , driving photo-ageing and also contributing to cancer. Tanning beds emit high-intensity UVA and are a recognized carcinogen — a tan is DNA damage made visible. 🧠 UV B = B urn (surface). UV A = A ging (deep). "Broad-spectrum" on the bottle means it covers both.

☀️ UV exposure frequent sunburns 🛏️ Tanning beds never safe 👷 Outdoor occupation cumulative dose 🧑‍🦰 Fair skin light skin, blond/red hair, freckles 👪 Family history parent with melanoma 🔵 Many moles >50 nevi or atypical nevi 💊 Immunosuppressants transplant & HIV meds 🩹 Prior skin cancer or chronic wound/scar 👴 Older age lifetime UV adds up ☢️ Radiation / arsenic occupational Darker skin does not mean immunity. Skin cancer is less common in deeply pigmented skin but is more often found late — and it favors the palms

entries.h: 📖 Key terms you get tested on
entries.t: Nevus / nevi = mole(s). Melanocytic = made of pigment cells. Neoplasm = tumor = a new abnormal growth. Benign = stays put, well-defined, grows slowly, doesn't invade. Malignant = invades locally and can metastasise. Actinic (solar) keratosis = premalignant rough, dry, "sandpaper" scaly patch on sun-damaged skin — a precursor to squamous cell carcinoma. Treat it. Dysplastic / atypical nevus = irregular mole; a marker of increased melanoma risk. Metastasis = spread to distant sites via lymph or blood. Breslow depth =
STEP 2 · WHICH CELL? Find the cell of origin on the cross-section and everything else about the cancer follows.

entries.h: 🔬 Three cells, three cancers — the origin cutaway
entries.t: 🧠 Bottom, middle, pigment. B asal cell starts at the b ottom of the epidermis. S quamous starts in the s quamous cells above it. Melanoma starts in the melanocytes — and it is the one that digs downward .

entries.h: 👁️ What they look like on the skin
entries.t: 🧠 Pearly = basal. Scaly & crusty = squamous. Multicolored & changing = melanoma. Three words, three cancers.

Feature Basal cell (BCC) Squamous cell (SCC) Melanoma Cell of origin Basal layer keratinocytes Keratinocytes above the basal layer Melanocytes How common Most common skin cancer Second most common Least common of the three How dangerous Locally destructive; rarely metastasises Can metastasise — higher risk on the lip, ear, and in immunosuppressed patients Most deadly ; metastasises early and widely Classic look Pearly/waxy papule, rolled translucent border, telangiectasias, central ulcer that bleeds and re-scabs Fi

entries.h: 🧪 Diagnosis — nothing is decided by looking
entries.t: Full-body skin examination in good light, including scalp, between toes, soles, nails, genital area — and the "ugly duckling" check: the mole that doesn't look like the patient's other moles. Dermoscopy to magnify surface patterns. Tissue biopsy is required for definitive diagnosis — but only for lesions that are genuinely suspicious (irregular, uneven, changing). Normal moles are not biopsied. For suspected melanoma, a full-thickness (excisional) biopsy is preferred so the pathologist can measure Breslow depth ; s

entries.h: 🚨 Melanoma in darker skin — the pattern that gets missed
entries.t: People with darker skin get melanoma less often but die of it more often , largely because it is found late. Look at the palms, soles, between the toes, nail beds, mucous membranes and the eyes — not just sun-exposed areas. A new, widening, irregular dark band in a nail , especially with pigment spilling onto the surrounding skin ( Hutchinson sign ), needs referral — not "wait and see." Teach sun protection to everyone. Pigment reduces risk; it does not remove it. 🧠 "Check the soles and the nails." The single most
STEP 3 · SCREEN Five letters. Benign on the left, suspicious on the right, every time.

entries.h: 🔤 The ABCDE plate — benign vs suspicious, side by side
entries.t: E is the most important letter. A lesion that is abrupt, sudden or rapidly changing in color, size or shape gets referred even if the other letters look reassuring. Add the "ugly duckling" sign : the mole that looks different from all of that person's other moles. 🧠 A symmetry · B order · C olour · D iameter · E volving. Chant it in that order, and remember "Irregular is BAD, and change is worse."

A sore that will not heal , or heals and reopens repeatedly. A lesion that bleeds, oozes, crusts or itches without an obvious cause. New pain, tenderness or numbness in a mole. Redness or swelling extending beyond the border of a mole. Spread of pigment from a mole into the surrounding skin. A new pigmented lesion in an adult — most moles appear before about age 30. Any lesion in a chronic wound, burn scar or old radiation site (Marjolin ulcer → SCC). 🧠 "Won't heal, won't stop bleeding, won't stay the same." Any on

entries.h: ✅ How to teach a monthly self-skin exam
entries.t: Once a month, in good light , after a bath or shower. Use a full-length mirror plus a hand mirror ; ask a partner or family member for the back and scalp. Work in a fixed order: face → ears → neck → chest → abdomen → arms and hands ( including palms, between fingers and nail beds ) → back and buttocks → legs → soles and between the toes → scalp (part the hair) → genital area. Take photos or draw a body map so change is obvious next month. Report anything meeting ABCDE, anything that doesn't heal, or any "ugly duckl
STEP 4 · TEACH This is where nursing actually changes the outcome — and it is heavily tested.
🧠 "30, 15, 2." SPF 30+ , applied 15 minutes before, reapplied every 2 hours (and after water). Three numbers, most of the teaching questions.

entries.h: 👨‍👩‍👧 Everything else the patient needs to hear
entries.t: Shade and clothing beat sunscreen. Sunscreen is the last line, not the first. Infants under 6 months should be kept out of direct sun and covered with clothing/shade; use sunscreen on babies only as advised by their provider. Some medicines cause photosensitivity — you burn much faster. Common examples include tetracyclines, sulfonamides, some diuretics, amiodarone, some psychiatric medicines, and isotretinoin (see NG-051 ). Ask, and teach strict sun protection. Radiation-therapy skin and old burn scars stay sun-se

Before: confirm consent and site marking, review anticoagulants and allergies, explain what a biopsy or Mohs day actually involves (long day, staged excisions, repeated waiting). After a surgical excision: keep the dressing clean and dry per order, watch for bleeding, infection and dehiscence, teach wound care and suture-removal timing — see NG-080 . Topical chemotherapy (for superficial lesions/actinic keratoses): warn that the treated area is meant to become red, crusted and sore before it heals; apply with glove

entries.t: NG-051 — Skin : the basal layer, keratinocytes and melanocytes that become these three cancers; plus the lesion vocabulary and assessment technique. NG-080 — Wound Care : post-excision wound care, and the chronic wound that can turn into an SCC. NG-182 — Dermatitis and NG-225 — Psoriasis : benign inflammatory rashes you must not mistake for cancer — and vice versa. A "patch of eczema" that never clears in one fixed spot deserves a second look. 🧠 One stubborn spot that behaves differently from everything around it i

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🔤 A·B·C·D·E Asymmetry · Border · Color · Diameter >6 mm · Evolving (the big one). 🔬 Pearly · Scaly · Multicolored Basal cell · squamous cell · melanoma. 🚨 Melanoma travels Least common, most deadly. Depth decides prognosis. Biopsy is definitive. ☀️ 30 · 15 · 2 SPF 30+, 15 min before, reapply q2h. Avoid 10–4. Never tanning beds.

Q1: What do the letters ABCDE stand for? Show answer Asymmetry (halves don't match), Border irregularity (notched, scalloped, blurred), Color variation (mixed brown, tan, black, red, white or blue), Diameter greater than 6 mm (bigger than a pencil eraser), and Evolving — any change in size, shape, color, or new itching or bleeding. Q2: Which skin cancer is most common, and which is most deadly? Show answer Basal cell carcinoma is the most common. Melanoma is the least common of the three but the most deadly because
