The honey-crusted rash — highly contagious, mostly in children NG-209 INTEGUMENTARY · PEDS INFECTION ADHD-friendly visual edition Impetigo is a very common, highly contagious superficial bacterial skin infection of infants and children, caused by Staph aureus and/or Group A Strep . Itchy red sores around the nose and mouth burst and dry into the unmistakable honey-colored crust — and that crusting stage is when it spreads fastest, by hands, towels, linen and toys. Nursing care is half skin care and half stopping th
STEP 0 · LEARN THIS ONCE Same skin drawing as every page in this set — this time with a shallow blister forming right under the surface.

entries.h: 🔬 Skin cutaway — impetigo is the SHALLOW one
entries.t: DEPTH = THE ANSWER The blister forms under the stratum corneum , so its roof is paper-thin. It ruptures almost immediately, and the fluid dries into the honey-colored crust . Because it never reaches the dermis, ordinary impetigo does not scar . blister fluid / pus honey crust staph & strep cocci neutrophils 🧠 "Impetigo is a roof problem." The infection is in the roof of the skin, so it peels and crusts instead of swelling and spreading like cellulitis.

entries.h: 📖 Lesion vocabulary — impetigo uses four of these words
entries.t: Impetigo is a vesicle → pustule → crust story, and the bullous form adds the bulla . Highlighted below. 🧠 Vesicle is small, bulla is big. "B" for BIG bulla. 🦠
STEP 1 · WHY IT HAPPENS Common bacteria + a child's skin + a scratch = the most contagious rash on the ward.

Impetigo is a very common, highly contagious superficial bacterial skin infection caused by Staphylococcus aureus and/or Group A Streptococcus , affecting mostly infants and young children . It lives in the top of the epidermis — that is why it crusts rather than swells, and why it usually heals without a scar. 🧠 "Impetigo — infant-igo." The name itself tells you the age group.

Bacteria colonize the nose & skin surface ▼ A tiny break — scratch, bite, eczema, cut ▼ Bacteria multiply just under the stratum corneum ▼ A thin-walled vesicle fills with pus ▼ It ruptures → oozes → dries into HONEY-COLORED CRUST ▼ The child scratches → new lesions + other children 🧠 Itch is the engine. Scratching is what seeds the next lesion and the next child — which is why short nails is a real intervention, not a nicety.

entries.h: ⭐ Who gets it & what makes it worse
entries.t: Age 2–5 years is the classic peak; can occur at any age Crowding — daycare, school, siblings, sports teams Warm, humid weather and summer months Broken skin — eczema, insect bites, chickenpox, scabies, minor trauma Poor hygiene or limited access to washing facilities Skin-to-skin contact sports — wrestling, rugby 🧠 "Hot, crowded, scratched." Those three words cover nearly every risk factor.

entries.h: 🚨 How it travels — and the five places you break the chain
entries.t: 🧠 Fomite = an object that carries the bug. Towel, toy, doorknob, wrestling mat. Impetigo spreads by contact , not by air.

entries.h: 🧪 Bug → drug: the rule that runs this whole set
entries.t: 🧠 Bacteria → antibiotic. The only extra decision in impetigo is topical or oral — and that is decided by how much skin is involved. 🔎
STEP 2 · WHAT YOU SEE A child, itchy sores around the nose and mouth, and a crust the color of dried honey.
🧠 "Golden crust on a small face." If the stem says honey-colored or golden-yellow crust in a child, the answer is impetigo — every time.

Itchy red sores , classically around the nose and mouth ; also hands, feet, arms and legs Sores burst and dry into a stuck-on, honey/golden crust Lesions at different stages at the same time — new ones keep appearing Regional lymph nodes may be swollen and tender Usually little or no fever and the child is otherwise well Itch, not pain — pain suggests the deeper form (ecthyma) or cellulitis 🧠 Itchy + crusty + a well child = impetigo. Painful + hot + an unwell child = think cellulitis.

Mostly clinical — the appearance is the diagnosis Swab for culture & sensitivity if it is widespread, recurrent, not responding, or MRSA is suspected Consider checking for an underlying cause: eczema, scabies, head lice, chickenpox If PSGN is suspected later: urinalysis (blood + protein), BP , and renal function 🧠 Swab before starting the antibiotic if a swab is being taken at all.

entries.h: 📈 How one sore evolves — and its most contagious moment
entries.t: 🧠 The crust is not the "healed" stage. Students lose marks here: a crusted lesion is still shedding bacteria.

entries.h: 🔬 Three forms — non-bullous vs bullous vs ecthyma
entries.t: NON-BULLOUS BULLOUS ECTHYMA Depth Superficial epidermis Superficial epidermis Into the dermis Lesion Small vesicles → honey crust Large flaccid bullae > 1 cm Punched-out ulcer, thick crust Where Face, around nose/mouth Trunk, arms, diaper area Legs, buttocks Pain Itchy Itchy, may be tender Painful Scars? No No Yes Treatment Topical, or oral if extensive Usually oral antibiotic Oral antibiotic 🧠 "Ecthyma etches." Only the deep one leaves a mark.
🧠 "Throat → heart. Skin → kidney." Strep throat can lead to rheumatic fever; strep skin infection is the one linked to glomerulonephritis. 🩺
STEP 3 · WHAT YOU DO Treat the skin, and stop it reaching the rest of the class.

entries.h: ✅ Stop the spread — the five teaching points
entries.t: 🧠 "School · Soap · Separate · Short nails · Soak." Five S's, in the order you would teach them.

entries.h: 💊 Topical or oral? The decision rule
entries.t: TOPICAL — for a few localized lesions : mupirocin ointment applied to the lesions after gently removing crust. (Retapamulin and ozenoxacin are alternatives where available.) ORAL — when it is widespread , bullous , ecthyma , involves multiple household members, or has failed topical therapy: a cephalosporin (cephalexin) or an anti-staph penicillin; clindamycin or TMP-SMX / doxycycline if MRSA is suspected. 🧠 "A few = cream. A lot = pill."

Gloves on. Standard + contact precautions for draining lesions Soak with warm soapy water or a saline compress to soften the crust Gently lift the softened crust — do not scrub or pick at dry crust Pat dry, then apply the ointment to clean skin — ointment on top of crust does not reach the bacteria Cover loosely with a non-adherent dressing to stop scratching and shedding Dispose of dressings as infectious waste; hand hygiene after removing gloves 🧠 Soften, lift, treat, cover. Ointment on crust is wasted ointment.

entries.h: 🗣️ Family teaching — say it exactly like this
entries.t: "It is very catching — mostly by touch and by shared things." "Keep them home from school/daycare until the treatment has been in for 24–48 h and the sores are drying up." " Wash your hands before and after touching the sores or putting on the cream." " Their own towel, their own bedding — washed separately in hot water." " Nails short and filed , and try to keep the sores covered ." " Finish the whole course , even when it looks better." "Come back if the sores spread , get painful , or the child develops fever ,

Never let the child share towels, bedding, washcloths or clothing. Never scrub or forcibly pick dry crusts — soften them first. Never send the child back to school just because the sores look drier. Never apply ointment on top of a thick crust and call it treated. Never skip hand hygiene between lesion care and any other patient contact. 🧠 Don't share, don't scrub, don't send back early.

24–48 h: no new lesions appearing; existing sores start drying 3–5 days: crusts loosening and falling away, redness fading 7–10 days: skin healed, usually with no scar (temporary pink or pale patches are normal) Not improving in 48 h? — reassess: wrong depth (ecthyma), resistant organism, poor adherence, or an untreated underlying condition such as scabies or eczema 🧠 "48 hours is the checkpoint." No improvement by then means something else is going on. 🔀
STEP 4 · THE REAL EXAM SKILL Crusty and around the mouth is impetigo. Learn what it is NOT.
🧠 Around the mouth + golden crust = impetigo. Same body, five patterns — distribution answers the question first.

CONDITION HOW IT DIFFERS FROM IMPETIGO Cold sore (HSV-1) A tight cluster of small vesicles on the lip border , preceded by tingling; recurs in the same spot. Impetigo is more scattered, oozier, and crusts golden. Cellulitis Painful , hot, swollen, spreading, often febrile , deep. Impetigo is itchy, superficial and crusty in a well child. Eczema (atopic dermatitis) Chronic, dry, itchy, flexural . Watch out: eczema is a common portal of entry , so a child can have both — a suddenly weeping, crusted eczema patch is us

The crusting stage is the MOST contagious , not the least. School exclusion is tied to treatment started + lesions drying , not to how the sores look alone. Teaching must include separate laundry in hot water — a frequently-chosen wrong-if-omitted option. The renal complication follows strep skin infection; rheumatic fever follows strep throat . Ointment goes on clean skin after the crust is soaked off. A painful, punched-out ulcer that scars is ecthyma — it needs an oral antibiotic. 🧠 If the option mentions hot wa

Impetigo vs cellulitis — crusty & itchy vs hot & painful Impetigo vs HSV — golden crust vs grouped vesicles that recur in one spot Impetigo vs tinea — crust vs ring with a clear center Non-bullous vs bullous — tiny vesicles vs big floppy blisters Impetigo vs ecthyma — heals clean vs punches into the dermis and scars 🧠 Crust, cluster, ring, ulcer. Four words, four diagnoses. ⚡

SAY IT OUT LOUD 🍯 Honey-colored crust Child · around nose & mouth · itchy. 🚨 Crusting = most contagious Contact + fomites: towels, linen, toys. 💊 Few = cream · Lots = pill Mupirocin topically; oral for widespread, bullous or ecthyma. 🏫 5 S's School out · Soap · Separate laundry · Short nails · Soak the crust.

Show answer Itchy red sores that burst and dry into a stuck-on, honey-colored (golden) crust, classically around the nose and mouth of a young child; also hands and feet. Q3: At which stage is impetigo most contagious? Show answer When the vesicles rupture and crust — the oozing/crusting stage. A crusted lesion is still sh

Autoimmune skin — silvery plaques, and the one word patients need to hear NG-225 INTEGUMENTARY · AUTOIMMUNE ADHD-friendly visual edition Psoriasis is a chronic autoimmune disease in which the body attacks its own skin, pushing keratinocyte turnover from about 30 days down to 3–5 days . Immature cells pile up as well-demarcated red plaques topped with thick silvery scale on extensor surfaces — elbows, knees, scalp, sacrum and nails. There is no organism , so it is not contagious — that sentence is the single most im
STEP 0 · LEARN THIS ONCE Same skin drawing as every page in this set — but look closely: there is no organism anywhere in it.

entries.h: 🔬 Skin cutaway — normal on the left, psoriatic plaque on the right
entries.t: NO ORGANISM Cellulitis, impetigo, tinea and shingles all have something living in the picture. Psoriasis does not. The immune system is the pathogen — which is why it is treated by calming immunity down, and why it can never be caught from another person. ① THICK SILVERY SCALE — keratinocytes shed before they mature (parakeratosis: they still carry their nuclei) ② NO granular layer — the maturation step is skipped entirely ③ DILATED, TORTUOUS CAPILLARIES — climbing high into long dermal papillae → the plaque is red

entries.h: 📖 Lesion vocabulary — psoriasis is the PLAQUE + SCALE disease
entries.t: A plaque is a raised, flat-topped lesion larger than 1 cm . Add silvery scale and you have psoriasis. 🧠 Plaque = a papule that grew up. Bigger than 1 cm and flat on top. 🔥
STEP 1 · WHY IT HAPPENS An immune system that attacks its own skin, plus a trigger that sets it off.

Psoriasis is a chronic autoimmune inflammatory disease in which immune cells attack healthy skin, causing massively accelerated division of epidermal cells . The immature cells pile up on the surface as thick, silvery, scaly plaques . It is lifelong , comes in flares and remissions , and is not curable — but it is very controllable. 🧠 "Psoriasis = skin in a hurry." Nothing is invading; the factory is just running far too fast.

Genetic predisposition + a trigger ▼ T lymphocytes are wrongly activated in the skin ▼ They release cytokines (TNF-α, IL-17, IL-23) ▼ Keratinocytes divide ~ 10× too fast — 3–5 days instead of ~30 ▼ Immature cells stack up + capillaries dilate and grow ▼ Raised red plaque with silvery scale 🧠 The cytokines in that box are exactly what the biologic drugs block — TNF, IL-17, IL-23.

entries.h: ⏩ The speed problem — 30 days vs 4 days
entries.t: 🧠 The scale IS the cells. Silvery flakes are keratinocytes that were rushed to the surface before they finished.

entries.h: 🎯 Triggers — and the one that is NOT a trigger
entries.t: 🧠 "S · S · S — Stress, Sickness, Sepsis." And the trap: SUN IS GOOD , not a trigger. Sunburn is bad because it is trauma .

entries.h: 🧪 Cause → treatment class: the rule that runs this whole set
entries.t: 🧠 No organism → no antibiotic, no antifungal, no antiviral. You calm the immune system instead. 🔎
STEP 2 · WHAT YOU SEE Sharp-edged red plaques with silvery scale, on the outside of joints, in a patient who feels well.

Well-demarcated plaques — you can trace the edge with a finger Raised and flat-topped , deep red or salmon-pink underneath Thick, loose, SILVERY-WHITE scale on the surface Symmetrical and on EXTENSOR surfaces — elbows, knees, scalp, sacrum Itching, burning or soreness ; plaques may crack and bleed Nail changes — pitting, oil-drop discoloration, lifting, thickening The patient is systemically well — no fever, no pus, no spreading redness 🧠 "Sharp · Silver · Symmetrical · Stretched-out (extensor)." Four S's.

Plaque (vulgaris) — by far the commonest; the classic silvery plaques Guttate — sudden crop of small "raindrop" spots on the trunk, often after strep throat , common in children and young adults Inverse (flexural) — smooth, shiny, red patches in the skin folds with little scale Pustular — sterile pustules; generalized pustular psoriasis is a medical emergency Erythrodermic — widespread redness and shedding; emergency (fluid loss, temperature instability, infection risk) Nail and scalp psoriasis often accompany any

entries.h: ⭐ Two signs with names — Auspitz & Koebner
entries.t: 🧠 Auspitz = A for After you lift the scale (bleeding). Koebner = K for Knock/injury makes new plaques.

entries.h: 🗺️ Extensor vs flexural — plus the nails
entries.t: 🧠 Psoriasis is on the OUTSIDE of the joint. Eczema is on the INSIDE. That one line sorts most stems.

entries.h: 🦴 Psoriatic arthritis — psoriasis is not only skin-deep
entries.t: 🧠 "Skin first, joints later." Ask about morning stiffness at every visit — early referral prevents permanent damage. 🩺
STEP 3 · WHAT YOU DO Moisturise relentlessly, calm the immune system as far as you need to, and treat the person, not just the plaque.
🧠 Every rung sits on emollient. If "apply moisturiser regularly" is an option, it is rarely wrong.

entries.h: 🧴 THE two NCLEX answers: moisturise & sunlight
entries.t: 1. Moisturise frequently. Apply a thick emollient immediately after bathing, onto damp skin , to trap water in. Use lukewarm (not hot) water, a mild non-soap cleanser, and pat dry — never rub. 2. Sunlight in moderation is GOOD. Controlled UV light slows the overactive skin cells. Do not tell a psoriasis patient to avoid the sun — but do teach them to avoid sunburn , which is trauma and can trigger Koebner. 🧠 Students answer "avoid sunlight" and lose the mark. Sun helps. Sunburn hurts.

Emollients — the foundation, used every day forever Topical corticosteroids — the mainstay for flares; use the lowest effective potency for the shortest time , and only mild preparations on the face and folds (skin thinning, striae) Vitamin D analogues (calcipotriene/calcipotriol) — often paired with a steroid Coal tar — effective; warn about staining and smell Salicylic acid — lifts thick scale so other treatments can get in Calcineurin inhibitors — steroid-sparing option for the face and folds Apply thin , rub in

Methotrexate is dosed WEEKLY, never daily. Daily dosing is a fatal medication error. Folic acid is usually prescribed alongside it Methotrexate is teratogenic — it must be stopped and effective contraception used; check pregnancy status. Monitor FBC, LFTs, renal function ; avoid alcohol Biologics (infliximab, adalimumab, etanercept; IL-17/IL-23 inhibitors) — screen for latent TB and hepatitis first ; hold for active infection; teach infection precautions and injection technique Live vaccines are generally avoided o

entries.h: 🗣️ Teaching — start with the sentence that matters most
entries.t: "You cannot give this to anyone. It is not an infection." Say it first, and say it to the family too Moisturise daily , especially after bathing; lukewarm water, gentle cleanser, pat dry Protect the skin — avoid scratching, picking scale, tight clothing and sunburn (Koebner) Use treatments as prescribed , even when the skin looks better; flares will come and go Stop smoking, moderate alcohol , manage weight, manage stress Report : joint pain or morning stiffness, widespread redness, pustules, fever, or signs of inf

Never imply psoriasis is contagious, or use isolation precautions for it. Never give methotrexate daily — it is a weekly dose. Never scrub, pick or forcibly remove the scale — that is trauma and Koebnerises. Never use potent topical steroids on the face or skin folds without a specific order. Never tell the patient to stay out of the sun. Never start a biologic without checking TB/hepatitis screening and for active infection. 🧠 Don't isolate, don't scrub, don't dose it daily, don't ban the sun.

Erythrodermic psoriasis — widespread redness and shedding over most of the body. The skin barrier fails: fluid and protein loss, hypothermia, high-output heart failure, sepsis risk Generalized pustular psoriasis — sheets of sterile pustules with fever and feeling very unwell Often triggered by abrupt withdrawal of systemic steroids , severe infection or drug reactions Nursing: monitor temperature, fluid balance and vital signs; warm environment; meticulous skin care; IV fluids as prescribed; urgent dermatology revi
STEP 4 · THE REAL EXAM SKILL Silvery scale on the outside of joints, in a well patient, with no organism.

entries.h: 🗺️ Where each one shows up — the whole set, plus eczema
entries.t: 🧠 Psoriasis = extensor. Eczema = flexural. The two most confused rashes, separated by one word.

PSORIASIS ECZEMA TINEA Cause Autoimmune Barrier defect + allergy/atopy Fungal infection Where Extensor: elbows, knees, scalp, sacrum Flexural: inner elbows, behind knees Warm, moist: trunk, groin, feet, scalp Edge Sharply demarcated Ill-defined, blends out Raised active ring with a clear center Scale Thick, SILVERY Fine, dry, may weep or crust Fine scale at the edge Symptom Itch, soreness, cracking Intense itch Itch Contagious? NO NO YES Steroid response Improves Improves Worsens (tinea incognito) 🧠 If a steroid ma

Sunlight is GOOD. The most-missed question on this topic. Psoriasis is NOT contagious — no isolation, no gloves-for-fear, and say so to the family. Methotrexate is WEEKLY. Check the frequency on every order. Moisturise after bathing on damp skin — not "avoid moisturiser because it is greasy." Do not pick or scrub the scale — Koebner makes new plaques. New small "raindrop" spots after a sore throat = guttate psoriasis. Widespread redness + shedding = erythrodermic = emergency, treat like a barrier failure. Joint pai

Psoriasis vs tinea — solid silvery plaque vs a ring with a clear center Psoriasis vs eczema — extensor & sharply edged vs flexural & ill-defined Psoriasis vs cellulitis — chronic, scaly, well patient vs acute, hot, febrile patient Psoriasis vs seborrhoeic dermatitis — thick silvery scale vs greasy yellowish scale on the scalp and nose folds Nail psoriasis vs fungal nail — pitting and oil-drop vs thick crumbly yellow-brown; test if unsure Psoriatic arthritis vs rheumatoid — DIP joints and sausage digits vs MCP/PIP a

SAY IT OUT LOUD ⚡ 30 days → 3–5 days Autoimmune acceleration of keratinocyte turnover. 🩹 Silvery plaques, EXTENSOR Sharp edges. Elbows, knees, scalp, sacrum, nails. 🚫 NOT contagious · ☀️ sun helps Moisturise daily. Avoid sunburn (Koebner). 🦴 Ask about joints Psoriatic arthritis hits the DIP joints. Methotrexate is WEEKLY.

Q1: What is happening in the skin in psoriasis? Show answer Autoimmune T-cell activation drives keratinocytes to divide far too fast — turnover falls from about 28–30 days to 3–5 days — so immature cells pile up as thick silvery scale on a red, thickened plaque. Q2: Describe the classic lesion and where it appears. Show answer Well-demarcated, raised, flat-topped red plaques with thick silvery-white scale, symmetrically on extensor surfaces — elbows, knees, scalp and hairline, lower back/sacrum — plus nail changes.
The arm on the operative side changes the rules for the rest of that patient’s life. Positioning, lymphedema and what to teach.

Taking the axillary nodes takes away the drainage route permanently. That is the whole reason the arm rules never expire. Swipe it sideways if it is cut off, or tap to open it full size. Procedure Removes Lumpectomy The tumor and a margin; breast preserved Simple mastectomy Whole breast; nodes left Modified radical Whole breast + axillary lymph nodes Sentinel node biopsy Only the first draining node — far less lymphedema risk The lymph nodes are the part that matters for nursing care. Removing axillary nodes remove
Semi-Fowler’s with the affected arm elevated on a pillow — above the level of the heart, to drain lymph by gravity Turn on the back or unaffected side , never the operative side

No blood pressure cuff on that arm No venipuncture, no injections, no IV lines, no finger sticks No tight jewelry, watches or sleeves No heavy lifting — typically nothing over 5–10 lb initially Protect from cuts, burns and sunburn; wear gloves for gardening and washing up Use an electric razor for the underarm Put a sign above the bed. Every clinician who walks in needs to know which arm.

Jackson-Pratt or Hemovac , usually for 1–3 weeks Teach the patient to empty, measure and record output Recompress the bulb to restore suction after emptying Drains usually come out when output falls below about 30 mL/day Report sudden increase, bright red bleeding, or foul odor

Start early: hand, wrist and elbow movement, ball squeezing — usually within 24 hours Wait for shoulder exercises until the surgeon clears them — typically after drains are out, to protect the suture line Then progress to wall climbing with the fingers , hair brushing, rope turning Full shoulder range too early disrupts the incision. Too late causes a frozen shoulder. Follow the surgeon's schedule.

Lymphedema is swelling of the arm because lymph has nowhere to drain. It can appear months or years later, and once established it is managed rather than cured. Report: heaviness, tightness, rings or sleeves getting tight, visible swelling, or any redness, warmth or fever — that is cellulitis and needs antibiotics urgently. Infection in a lymphedematous arm spreads fast because the immune drainage is gone. Never treat a red, warm arm as minor.

Keep the arm elevated when resting Skin care — moisturise, treat every scratch promptly Compression sleeve as prescribed, including for air travel Maintain a healthy weight; gentle regular exercise helps drainage

entries.h: 💐 The part that is not physical
entries.t: Body image, sexuality and fear of recurrence are central, not peripheral. Look for readiness cues — whether the patient looks at the incision is the classic indicator of beginning acceptance. Offer, but do not push, information about prostheses, reconstruction and support groups. Let the patient set the pace and the topic.

No BP, no needles, no constriction on the affected arm — for life Elevate the arm; turn to back or unaffected side Hand and elbow exercises early; shoulder exercises only when cleared Redness and warmth in that arm = infection , treat urgently Looking at the incision signals psychological readiness Sources. Written from MedlinePlus , National Cancer Institute , NINDS and OpenStax A&P 2e (CC BY 4.0).
Identified by what came before the rash, where it starts, and how it spreads — plus which isolation each one needs.

Nits are glued to the hair and will not slide; dandruff slides. Impetigo is the honey-crusted one. Swipe it sideways if it is cut off, or tap to open it full size. Illness Signature Precautions Measles (rubeola) Koplik spots in the mouth first, then rash face downward ; the 3 Cs — cough, coryza, conjunctivitis AIRBORNE Varicella (chickenpox) Lesions in all stages at once — macule, papule, vesicle, crust. Intensely itchy AIRBORNE + CONTACT Rubella Mild pink rash face downward; posterior cervical lymphadenopathy Drop
M easles · T uberculosis · V aricella — negative pressure room, door closed, N95 . Everything else on that table is droplet or contact.

Never give aspirin to a child with a viral illness - Reye syndrome. Acetaminophen or ibuprofen instead. Reye syndrome causes acute encephalopathy and liver failure, and it is associated with aspirin during varicella or influenza. This is why pediatric aspirin all but disappeared. Untreated strep throat can become rheumatic fever and permanently damage heart valves. The whole antibiotic course must be finished, even once the child feels well. Strep can also cause acute glomerulonephritis 1–3 weeks later — tea-colore

Keep fingernails short ; mittens for infants — scratching causes scarring and secondary infection Cool baths with oatmeal or baking soda; calamine lotion Antihistamines for itch; acetaminophen for fever Contagious from 1–2 days before the rash until all lesions have crusted

Treat for comfort , not for the number Light clothing, cool room, fluids No cold baths, no alcohol rubs - both cause shivering, which raises temperature Febrile seizures come from a rapid rise in temperature, not from how high it gets

entries.h: 💉 When to worry about a rash
entries.t: A purpuric or petechial rash with fever is meningococcal until proven otherwise. Emergency. A rash that does not blanch when pressed Rash with difficulty breathing, swelling of the face or tongue — anaphylaxis Rash with a stiff neck, severe headache or photophobia

Koplik spots = measles. All stages at once = varicella Roseola: fever breaks, THEN the rash My Tiny Vampire for airborne No aspirin — Reye syndrome Finish the strep antibiotics — rheumatic fever Non-blanching rash + fever = emergency Sources. The pilosebaceous unit · Three factors · Isotretinoin safety NG-393 Skin & Wound ADHD-friendly visual edition Acne is a chronic inflammatory condition of the pilosebaceous unit — the hair follicle and its oil gland. Three things have to line up: too much sebum , a follicle that plugs itself , and bacteria multiplying in the plugged space. Most of what people blame — chocolate, greasy food, poor hygiene — is not on the list. The unit Pilosebaceous — hair follicle plus oil gland Does NOT cause it Chocolate, greasy fo

From your lecture. Follow the cross-section left to right — healthy follicle, then plugged and closed (whitehead), plugged and open (blackhead), then inflamed (papule) and infected (pustule). The three factors, in order Increased sebum production — androgen-driven, which is why it starts at puberty and flares premenstrually. Abnormal keratinisation — the follicle lining sheds cells that stick together and plug the opening. Cutibacterium acnes (still written Propionibacterium acnes on many slides) multiplies in the

Naming the lesions Comedones — the plugged follicle. Open = blackhead (dark from oxidized keratin, not dirt). Closed = whitehead . Papule — small, raised, red, solid. Pustule — the same with visible pus. Nodules and cysts — deep, painful, and the ones that scar. Distribution follows the oil glands: face, neck, chest, upper back and shoulders. Water-based, non-comedogenic cosmetics; remove make-up before bed. Improvement takes 6 to 8 weeks . Stopping early because “it is not working” is the commonest failure. Benzoyl peroxide bleaches towels and clothing — warn her. The drugs, stepwise Benzoyl peroxide — antibacterial, first line, expect dryness. Topical retinoid

entries.h: ⭐ The whole plan in six lines
entries.t: One course a day , not three. Mon 258 · Tue 234 · Wed 235. Thursday is quiz day — all three courses mixed together. Friday goes to whatever you got wrong on Thursday. Saturday is the long block: patho, A&P, and next week's preview. Sunday off. Actually off. When an exam is within 7 days, the exam overlay replaces Friday and Saturday. The single most important rule on this page. Never try to catch up. If you miss three days, you do not do four days' work on Thursday. You rejoin the plan at today and let the missed d

Three switches a day is thirty minutes of your hour gone before you learn anything. One course a day means one switch. You get your whole hour. entries.h: ⏱️ What one hour actually looks like
entries.t: The hour has a fixed shape so you never spend any of it deciding. Same four blocks every single day. 0–10 Recall Yesterday's three cards. Say the answers out loud before you look. Getting it wrong here is the point — that is what makes it stick. 10–35 Learn Today's module in One bite . One bite, then Next. Do not scroll ahead to see how many are left. 35–50 Test That module's quiz. Answer first, then check. Read the rationale even when you got it right — it explains the wrong answers too. 50–60 Capture Write three

Do not stretch all four blocks. Repeat the middle: Recall, Learn, Test, Learn, Test, Capture. Two modules, or one module plus one ATI template. Recall and Capture stay at ten minutes no matter how long the session is.

entries.h: ✅ Why it starts with a test and ends with writing
entries.t: Starting with recall means the hour opens with your brain producing instead of consuming — that is the difference between recognizing a fact and being able to retrieve it under exam pressure. Ending with three lines gives the hour a finish line you can see. There is a card on the desk that was not there an hour ago.

With three courses you will almost always have an exam within seven days. So this is not the exception — it is most weeks. When it happens, Friday and Saturday switch over to the exam. Monday to Thursday do not change. Do not stop the other two courses to cram for one. That is how you win an exam this week and lose the next two. T−3 ⭐ Spotlight only Open every module page for that exam and hit Exam spotlight . Only the high-yield card. No reading anything else. That is 6–14 facts per module and it is the right amou

entries.h: ⚠️ Two exams in the same week
entries.t: It happens roughly four times this semester — see the map below. When it does: the earlier exam gets T−3 and T−2. The later one gets the day between them. Do not split each day in half; you will do neither properly.

Built from the exam groupings already on your three course pages. Exams usually land at the end of their week range , so treat this as the shape of the semester, not the dates — pencil in the real ones when your syllabus lands. Reading the map. A cell in your course color is one exam that week . A red cell marked ⚠️ is a collision — two exams in the same week. The pale gray rows are the weeks with nothing due. Week 🩺 NUR 258 🤰 NUR 234 🧒 NUR 235 What it means 1 Sensory Contraception Peds care Build the habit. Nothin

NUR 258 sits one week ahead of the other two, nearly all semester. Its exam lands the week before 234 and 235 collide. That gap is the plan's shock absorber. Weeks 5, 9 and 11 are your genuinely light weeks — use them to get ahead, not to rest twice.

Three finals and a unit exam in one week cannot be revised in that week. NUR 234's final is comprehensive over all fourteen weeks. So from week 11 , Saturday's second hour becomes final review — oldest material first, because week 1 is the part you have not seen since week 1.

entries.h: 📚 The review layer — content mastery & NCLEX
entries.t: Older material does not get its own study day — there isn't one to give. It gets attached to the new material instead. Three rules, and they cost almost no extra time.

entries.h: 💊 Rule 1 — drugs get learned the day they appear
entries.t: When a drug turns up in any course, open its card in the Drug Guide that same day. Two minutes. Pharmacology is heavily weighted on NCLEX and it is the subject that decays fastest when studied alone. Learned attached to a patient, it stays.

entries.h: 🧬 Rule 2 — patho and A&P are the fallback, not a subject
entries.t: You do not study pathophysiology on a schedule. You study it the moment something will not make sense . When a mechanism will not stick — why estrogen causes clots, why the right lower lobe aspirates, why insulin needs collapse after birth — that is Saturday hour 1. Go to Physiology or Pharmacology and fix that one thing. A mechanism you understand needs revising once. A fact you memorized needs revising five times.

entries.h: 🧠 Rule 3 — Thursday carries the old courses
entries.t: The Super Mega Quiz holds everything — NUR 125, 175, 198 and all three current courses. Shuffled, unfiltered. That is not a shortcut, it is the whole point: NCLEX does not tell you which course a question came from. Practicing retrieval without the label is the skill the exam actually tests. Once a month, make Thursday NUR 198 / 175 / 125 only . That is your content mastery insurance. What you want Where it lives When Drugs Drug Guide · Pharmacology The day the drug appears Mechanisms Physiology · patho pages Satur
It will go wrong. Fourteen weeks, three courses, a job and a life. A plan that only works on good days is not a plan.

Do Recall and Test only . Skip Learn entirely. Fifteen minutes of retrieval beats sixty minutes of reading, and it beats zero by more than you would think. Never skip a day because you cannot do the whole hour.

Rejoin at today. If today is Wednesday, you do Wednesday. The missed material comes back on Thursday in the quiz anyway — that is what the mixed quiz is for . It finds your gaps without you having to remember where they are. Do not build a catch-up backlog. Backlogs are what make people quit in week 6.

Open the module page, press One bite , and read one bite . Then you are allowed to stop. You almost certainly will not stop — but the deal has to be real, or it stops working. The hard part is starting, not continuing.

entries.h: 👀 You read it and nothing went in
entries.t: That is reading, not studying, and it is the commonest way to waste an hour. Close the page and try to say the last chunk out loud. If you cannot, that is your signal — go back and do that chunk as a quiz instead of a read. If you could, you did not need to re-read it anyway.

Let it be the one whose exam is furthest away — deliberately, and on purpose, not by accident. Then use the next light week (5, 9 or 11) to bring it back. Choosing what to drop is a plan. Dropping whatever you happen to run out of time for is not.

entries.h: ✅ Before week 1 — a short setup list
entries.t: You have about a week and a half. Do not study ahead. Do these instead — they are worth more than a head start on week 1 content. Get the three syllabi and write the real exam dates onto the map above. Pick your hour — the same hour every day. Which hour matters far less than it being the same one. Buy index cards. Physical ones. The Capture block needs something your hands do, away from a screen. Do one practice day now on any module, so week 1 is not also the week you learn the routine. Tell someone the plan. Out

Ctrl + P prints it flat on white with the colors removed, so it works on paper and does not drink your ink. Stick the default week and the collision map somewhere you will see them. Last thing. This plan asks for about ten hours a week and assumes you will miss some of them. It is built to survive being followed imperfectly — that is the only kind worth having.
